iewing with perfect hindsight,

sors who witnessed the Mongol invasions were not so
optimistic. The historian Ibn al-Athir prefaces his ac-
count of the Mongol conquest with the following words:
I have been avoiding mentioning this event for many years
because I consider it too horrible. I have been advancing
with one foot and retreating with the other. Who could easi-
ly write the obituary of Islam and the Muslims? For whom
could it be easy to mention it? Would that my mother had
not given birth to me; would that I had died before it hap-
pened and been a thing forgotten. However, a group of
friends urged me to record it since I knew it ﬁrst-hand. Then
I saw that to refrain from it would proﬁt nothing. Therefore,
we say: this deed encompasses mention of the greatest
event, the most awful catastrophe that has befallen time. It
engulfed all beings, particularly the Muslims. Anyone
would be right in saying that the world, from the time God
created humans until now, has not been stricken by its like.
Histories contain nothing that even approaches it.1
Cataclysm or preﬁguration of great things to come, the
Mongol conquest of the thirteenth century left Iran with
a new ruling dynasty. Eventually, like their cousins in
China, the Ilkhans of Iran began the process of assimi-
lating themselves to the civilizations of their subjects.
As a good Iranian monarch and patron of learning,
Ghazan Khan (r. 1295–1304) commissioned his vizier,
Rashiduddin Fazlullah, to compile an aggregate history
of all the peoples of the world. The ﬁrst tome of this
mammoth undertaking, which he entitled Jāmi‘u’t-
tawārīkh (Compendium of Chronicles), is the history of
1Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 12:358.
the Turco-Mongolian peoples, their rise to power, the
conquests of Genghis Khan, and the rule of his progeny.
The second tome contains the histories of all other na-
tions of the world, Persians, Arabs, Greeks, Chinese, In-
dians, and Franks.
Scarcely to be outdone in good works by his own
master, Rashiduddin founded outside of Tabriz an ab-
wābu’l-birr, a pious charitable foundation modeled on
Ghazan Khan’s complex at Shamb-i-Ghazan in Tabriz.
Rashiduddin named his foundation Rab‘-i-Rashīdī, and
it consisted of a tomb, a hostel for dervishes (khānaqāh),
a hospice for visitors (dāru’ḍ-ḍiyāfa), a hospital and
pharmacy, a theological school, a repository and scripto-
rium for Korans and books of hadith, a school for
orphans (baytu’t-ta‘līm), a chapel for continuous recita-
tion of the Koran (dāru’l-ḥuffāẓ), and a library (baytu’l-
kutub). Fortuitously, an original copy of the document of
incorporation in Rashiduddin’s own handwriting has
survived.2 In an addendum to the original articles of en-
dowment, Rashiduddin also added a scriptorium for
copying his own works to ensure that they would weath-
er the ages: 
I hereby stipulate that the superintendent of endowment
have copied every year complete copies of the following
books composed by me, as follows: Majmū‘a-i-Rashīdiyya,
which consists of four books, Tawḍīḥāt, Miftāḥu’t-tafāsīr,
Sulṭāniyya, and Laṭāyif [al-ḥaqāyiq]—two copies, one in
Arabic and one in Persian; Jāmi‘u’t-tawārīkh in however
many volumes the superintendent thinks proper, and such
that they will not readily suffer damage—two copies, one in
Arabic and one in Persian; Āthār u aḥyā—two copies, one
in Arabic and one in Persian; Bayānu’l-ḥaqāyiq—two
copies, one in Arabic and one in Persian; Taḥqīqu’l-
mabāḥith, which was written in several volumes—one copy
in Arabic and one in Persian; and As’ila wa-ajwiba wa-
ta‘līqāt, which was written in several volumes—one copy in
Arabic and one in Persian.
Of each of these, in accordance with the description giv-

Wages for copying, materials, and supplies are to be pro-

The rooms in which the copyists sit and do the copying

and the rest of the books composed by me, to be endowed to

during the superintendence of ___ to be an endowment to

By the terms of this endowment, multiple copies of
Jami‘u’t-tawarikh—at least two every year, one in Ara-
bic and one in Persian—were to be produced. Of these,
only four copies made during Rashiduddin’s lifetime
have survived. One is fragmentary and in Arabic; it con-
sists of two fragments of one manuscript, one in the
Khalili Collection and another in Edinburgh University
Library, undated but assignable to A.H. 714 (A.D. 1314).
Three other manuscripts are in Persian, and they are all

in Istanbul, Topkapı Sarayı Kütüphanesi: H.1653, dated
714 (1314); H.1654, dated 717 (1317); and R.1518, also

produced in multiple copies in two languages in perpetu-
ity, there are singularly few copies extant today. What
happened? 
For all Rashiduddin’s careful planning, he did not
reckon, as he should have, with the almost invariable
end met by Ilkhanid viziers. The vizierate under the
Ilkhans was not what could be described as a good long-
term career choice, although it was usually life-long.
The early sixteenth-century historian Khwandamir de-
scribes Rashiduddin’s fate as follows:
Khwaja Rashiduddin Fazlullah was as clever as Aristotle
and as wise as Plato. He knew the rational and traditional
sciences to perfection and wrote constantly. Among the ef-
fulgences of his jewel-scattering pen, his Jami‘u’t-tawarikh
is well known among historians. As has been reported previ-
ously, Khwaja Rashid attained the post of vizier during
Ghazan Khan’s time, and he enjoyed great good fortune
until the end of Ghazan Khan’s life. When Öljäitü Sultan
took over the reins of rule, he showed the vizier more favor
even than his brother had and raised his rank over that of
anyone, and the just vizier promoted justice and equity
among all the people, elite and common alike, and the
learned enjoyed his favor particularly as he established
schools and charitable institutions and placed in trust choice
plantations and real estate for their upkeep. No one ever
came away from the table of his generosity disappointed or
deprived, and to this day the remnants of his charity remain
in Iraq and Azerbaijan, and he is praised and extolled in
prose and poetry for his liberality and beneﬁcence. “The
traces we leave behind are indicative of ourselves: gaze
therefore upon our monuments.” 
Toward the end of his life Öljäitü Sultan became quite in-

timate with Khwaja Alishah Jilan and made certain deci-
sions without Khwaja Rashid’s knowledge. This hurt the
vizier, and he complained to the padishah, saying, “If your
humble servant has precedence over Alishah in the ofﬁce of
vizier, then my advice should be followed. Otherwise he
should be given autonomy in the administration and I should
be his superior in other matters. At present Khwaja Alishah
should have free reign in three areas, and I will concur: ﬁrst,
he should undertake to administer all divan affairs while I
tend to accounts of years past; second, affairs that pertain to
viziers should be relegated to me so that I may conduct them
with the sultan’s favor and assistance; third, the realm
should be divided into two parts, each of which should be
supervised by one of us.”
Öljäitü Sultan replied, “Khwaja Rashid and Khwaja Al-
ishah are both worthy servants. Rashid is an aged and wise
man, and Alishah is a young, competent man without equal.
It is in the best interests of the empire that both should ad-
minister in concord, the one exercising compassion and the
other reverence, and neither overstepping the bounds of har-
mony and agreement.” In accordance with this command the
two viziers agreed to a grudging truce and co-operated once
again in the administration. However, when Sultan Muham-
mad Khudabanda died [in 1316] and Sultan Abusa‘id came
to the throne, the two viziers fell to quarreling again. Al-
though Khwaja Alishah wanted to prove malfeasance
against Khwaja Rashid, he was unable to achieve success. 
Around this time a group of employees in the divan went
to Khwaja Rashid, as was their custom, and said, “If you
permit, we will provoke an inquiry to prove Khwaja Al-
ishah’s malfeasance in a certain amount.” Khwaja Rashid
was much too digniﬁed to participate in such a scheme and
said, “I will tell Khwaja Alishah to satisfy you himself.”
Thus despairing of Khwaja Rashid, these people began to
frequent Khwaja Alishah, with whom they schemed to put
the good Khwaja Rashid in a bad light. Khwaja Alishah
bribed Sultan Abusa‘id Khan’s deputies to turn the sultan
against Khwaja Rashid, and they accused him of many
faults before the padishah. Around the end of the month of
Rajab 717 [September 1317] they had him dismissed from
ofﬁce. Amir Sevinch, although unhappy about the khwaja’s
dismissal, fell gravely ill around that time. That winter,
when Sultan Abusa‘id Khan had gone to Baghdad, Amir
Sevinch died in the vicinity of Muhawwal on the 20th of
Dhu’l-Qa’da [January 24, 1318]. 
When the sun entered Aries the sultan returned to Sul-
taniyya, and Amir Chupan went to Azerbaijan to hunt.
While there he summoned Khwaja Rashid, who had been
living in Tabriz since his dismissal, and said, “Your pres-
ence at the padishah’s court is as necessary as salt in food.
Without your good inﬂuence the affairs of civilians and sol-
diers alike are in shambles. Of course you must accept to
serve again and administer the empire.” Khwaja Rashid
replied, “I have spent a lifetime in imperial service, and my
vii

youthfulness has turned to old age. The time of youth, which
is the season for acquiring success, has ended, and the
sapling of my youthful hopes and aspirations has been bent
over by the cold autumn wind of weakness and inﬁrmity.
As bent as a bow is my back because the arrow of dear
youth has ﬂown. / It is difﬁcult for me to stand, and fate
says, “Arise, for this house is no place to sit.”
What I attained in the vizierate has been attained by no other
vizier. Now thirteen of my sons have reached middle age,
and it would be better for them to serve instead of me. I
shall occupy myself with making up for things I have
missed, and let my masters forget me.”
No matter how much Khwaja Rashid insisted on remain-
ing in retirement, Amir Chupan insisted that he accept to re-
turn to ofﬁce, and in the end the khwaja acceded. When the
news reached Khwaja Alishah and those who had plotted
the vizier’s downfall, they grew worried and bribed
Abubakr Aqa, Amir Chupan’s closest companion, to turn
the amir against the vizier. Although Chupan Noyan liked
Khwaja Rashid, he was so malleable that anyone could twist
him however he wished. Finally Khwaja Rashid’s enemies
reported to Amir Chupan that Khwaja Rashid’s son Khwaja
Ibrahim, who had been Öljäitü Sultan’s sharbatdar, had poi-
soned the padishah at his father’s instigation and that was
why Sultan Muhammad had died. Amir Chupan repeated
this to Sultan Abusa‘id, and two other amirs who had taken
bribes testiﬁed to its veracity. Therefore an order for the viz-
ier’s execution was issued, and on the 17th of Jumada I 718
[July 17, 1318] in the vicinity of Uma in the village of
Khashgudar, the executioner ﬁrst cut off Khwaja Ibrahim’s
head in his father’s presence. Then he stepped before Khwa-
ja Rashid, who said to him, “Say to Alishah, ‘You have had
me killed for no crime. It will not be long before fate will re-
quite you of me, and the only difference between us will be
that my grave will be older than yours.’ ” Then the execu-
tioner cut the khwaja in two at the waist. The soldiers pil-
laged the Rab‘-i-Rashidi, which belonged to Khwaja
Rashid, and the amirs conﬁscated the khwaja’s and his sons’
property to the divan. 
Mawlana Jalaluddin Qaliqi composed the following verse
as a chronogram for Khwaja Rashid:
When the guide (rashīd) of the nation and religion departed
for the next life, / The secretary of history penned for him:
May he rest in peace.1
Ghazan Khan died in 1304, just about the time the
Jami‘u’t-tawarikh
was
being
completed.
Ghazan’s
brother and successor, Sultan Muhammad Khudabanda
Öljäitü, told Rashiduddin to continue Tome One in
Ghazan’s name. The last date mentioned in our text is
705 (1305–6); the entire work, including the appendices,
was completed in 710 (1310–11). The portion of the
1Khwandamir, Habibu’s-siyar 3:199–201.
Rab‘-i-Rashidi endowment document that deals with
copying was executed in Dhu’l-Hijja 713 (March
1314)2—presumably copying began fairly soon there-
after—and Rashiduddin was put to death in 1318. There
were thus only four years at most during which copies
could have been produced before the destruction of the
Rab‘-i-Rashidi and an end to Rashiduddin’s grand plans
for his books. Even if we allow for copies to have been
made before the provision in the document of endow-
ment, when we take into consideration the inevitable
ravages of time, it is little wonder that so few copies
from Rashiduddin’s lifetime have survived. Those that
remain bear eloquent witness to the care that was lav-
ished on production and illustration.
Rashiduddin does not list his sources as such, but he
refers to Ibn al-Athir’s history, al-Kāmil fī’t-tārīkh.
Even a cursory examination shows that he used Ibn al-
Athir extensively for the history of the Islamic world,
but he rearranged the material into running narratives in-
stead of the strict year-by-year chronology to which Ibn
al-Athir adhered. It is also obvious that Rashiduddin
used Ata-Malik Juwayni’s Tārīkh-i Jahāngushāy (Histo-
ry of the World Conqueror) for the Mongol conquest of
Central Asia and the initial incursions into Iran.
For Mongolian history, in addition to having access to
the knowledge and expertise of Bolad Chingsang, Qubi-
lai Qa’an’s Mongolian emissary at the Ilkhanid court, it
is clear that Rashiduddin had some written material on
Mongol history with which to work. He says more than
once that there were scattered, unorganized leaves of
Mongol history written “in Mongolian expression and
script” kept in the treasury. The Mongols, he says,
from age to age…have kept their true history in Mongolian
expression and script, unorganized and disarranged, chapter
by chapter, scattered in treasuries, hidden from the gaze of
strangers and specialists, and no one was allowed access to
learn of it. (text p. 34)
He also refers to the records of Mongol genealogy as the
Altan Daftar, the “Golden Register,” “which is always
kept in the khans’ treasury by great ofﬁcers” (text p.
186). Whatever those “leaves of history” were, they
were obviously closely related to the source or sources
of the Manghol-un niucha tobcha’an, the Secret History
of the Mongols, for the record of Mongol legend and
history found in the Secret History and that found in the
Jami‘u’t-tawarikh are too close to be coincidental, but
they are different enough that the one could not have
originated directly with the other. The Persian scribes
2Rashiduddin, Vaqfnama, 252.
viii

who copied the Jami‘u’t-tawarikh were working with a
text in a language they knew perfectly well but which
was full of unfamiliar and bizarre-looking Mongolian
names. They had little or no difﬁculty copying the Per-
sian correctly, but they stumbled badly on the Mongo-
lian names and terms. The same scribes who would nev-
er mistake a Muhammad (ﺪـﶊ) for a Mahmud (ﻮد ـﶊ) seem
to have been incapable of keeping a Butu (ﻮــﺗﻮــﺑ) separate
from a Buqu (ﺑﻮﻗﻮ).
The Secret History of the Mongols has an unusual his-
tory of transmission. The text as we now have it is in
Middle (medieval) Mongolian, and it is written not in
Mongolian script but in a phonetic transcription in Chi-
nese characters with a parallel translation into Chinese.
It is speculated that once a column of the Mongolian in
Mongolian script may have existed, but if it did it has
been lost.
Chinese scribes who copied the Mongolian
column of the Secret History were working with what
would have been to them total nonsense. Now, simply
because of the extra concentration involved, a skilled
copyist can usually reproduce complete gibberish more
faithfully than he can a meaningful text that has unfamil-
iar words in it, which is what the Persian scribes were
working with. On this basis, it is reasonable and safe to
assume that the text of the Secret History has been more
faithfully reproduced than Rashiduddin’s text. We have
therefore taken the Secret History of the Mongols as rep-
resenting a version of events—or at least of the people’s
names—that is “more correct” in that it is more trust-
worthily preserved than the Persian sources, and since
the variants that show up in Persian manuscripts of the
Jami‘u’t-tawarikh often point to reconstructions of
names that are either identical or very close to the names
as they appear in the Secret History, we have emended
the translation to make the names agree with the Secret
History to the extent possible given their reconstructed
spellings in Persian. This accounts for much of the bur-
den of the notes that accompany the translation.
Since so much of the difﬁculty of the Persian text lies
in the given names, it may not be out of place to devote
a short discussion to the types of names that occur. In
the ﬁrst parts of the history the names are Mongolian
and Turkic. In addition to all the names that mean “Hap-
py” (Öljäitü), “Lucky” (Qutlugh), “Serene” (Örüg), etc.,
those that have to do with strength and power, like
“Iron” (Temür); “Steel” (Bolad); “Bull” (Buqa), and a
host of names designed to ensure that the child would
survive, it was a Mongol custom, as it is and has been
among many peoples of the world, for new-borns to be
named after the ﬁrst thing the mother sees after giving
birth. We thus have Mongols and Turks named “Dog”
(Noqai), “Kettle” (Qazan, Ghazan), “Mirror” (Tolui),
“Three Old Women” (Üch Qurtqan), “Donkey Driver”
(Kharbanda), etc. Among the Christian tribes and na-
tions that joined Genghis Khan, there are Christian
names like Cyril (Quril), George (Görgüz), Cyriacus
(Qurjaquz), and Marcus (Marghuz). The Mongols also
named their children after recent conquests and battles;
that is how Tämüjin (later Genghis Khan) got his name
(see text p. 232). The various Qurumshis (for victories
over Khwarazm), the Oruses (for victories over the
Rus), the Majars (for victories over the Magyars), and
probably most of the Sartaghs and Sartaghtais (for victo-
ries over the Sarts = Persians) were so named. Later,
when the Mongols, particularly those in China, became
Tibetan Buddhists, they adopted Buddhist names from
Tibetan like Irinjin Dorji. In its Persian garbﲔ ــ ـﯾﻨﺠﺮـﻳا7دور
is a transcription of the Mongolian (which cannot toler-
ate an initial r), which came from the Tibetan renchin r-
dorje, which in turn was either a translation or an exact
equivalent of the Sanskrit rÆv¿ ratnavajra. The name
Qunchuqbal is also probably derived from the Tibetan
kun-tu-hjug-bral ‘freedom from sin,’ the Tibetan equiva-
lent of the Sanskrit inraex nirodh. In the east we en-
counter a very few Mongols with Chinese names, like
Qubilai Khan’s son Jimgim, which reﬂects an older pro-
nunciation (zhem gim) of the modern Chinese 真金zhen
jin ‘true gold.’
Unfortunately for us, just about the time the Ilkhans
converted to Islam and began having normal Muslim
names like Ahmad and Ali, with which copyists would
have had no difﬁculty, the text ends. Properly speaking,
all the “Qutluqs” in our text should be Qutlugh, and all
the “Tuqluqs” should be Tughlugh, but given the appar-
ent lack of distinction between postvocalic q and gh,
spelling in Ilkhanid times was somewhat chaotic in this
regard. Since it is not feasible to “correct” all the names
in the Jami‘u’t-tawarikh, it was felt better to leave them
as they are spelled in the text. I have tried, insofar as
possible, however, to “iron out” the discrepancies in
spelling in any one person’s name, so if a particular
“Tuqluq” appears later as “Tughluq,” I have changed it
to be consistent with the ﬁrst spelling.
Furthermore, in English we do not have the luxury of
leaving a proper name for which we do not know the
vowels as a series of vowelless consonants. When faced
in Persian with an unfamiliar name likeﺗـﺮﮐـﺮ(trkr), which
could be pronounced any number of ways, the Persian
ix

reader mentally registers the consonants and then goes
on without much ado. Since a normal English reader
would not know what to make of TRKR, we are obliged to
provide something more. In this case, a guess is better
than nothing, and there are many guesses in this transla-
tion, but they are signaled as such in the notes.
Turkish and Mongolian terms, generally military, in-
truded massively into Persian during the Mongol period.
There is, of course, nothing unusual in having a con-
queror’s vocabulary seep into a native language, as Nor-
man French entered English. A few of these words, like
the Norman element in English, became domesticated
over time and are still used in Persian today, like gho-
ruq > qoroq, an area of limited access. Mostly, howev-
er, the Turco-Mongolian vocabulary of Persian was tran-
sient, and terms that were once very frequently used,
like yasamishi (troop array), olja (booty), and huljamishi
(swearing allegiance) have long since disappeared from
Persian, not to mention those that were of less common
occurrence. As frequently used as such terms may have
been among the bureaucratic class in Rashiduddin’s day,
even then they were felt to be foreign—and were recog-
nizably so—and are not only strange but meaningless to
today’s Persian speaker. To maintain the ﬂavor of the
original in its own time, I have left these terms in the
text in Turkish or Mongolian and provided an English
equivalent in parentheses. All such terms are deﬁned in
notes at the ﬁrst instance and also in the glossary.
In the sections that deal with China, all Chinese words
have been transcribed according to the Pinyin system.
The vast majority of Western sources dealing with the
Chinese part of the Genghisid empire were written be-
fore the adoption of Pinyin for transcribing Chinese, and
they use the older Wade-Giles transcription system. For
those who are not specialists in Chinese, the Pinyin sys-
tem has several peculiarities that need to be explained:
both zh and j indicate the j sound of English (= Wade-
Giles ch), and both ch and q indicate the ch sound of
English (= Wade-Giles ch‘). The Pinyin z is pronounced
like dz (= Wade Giles ts and tz); and the c indicates a ts
sound (= Wades-Giles ts‘ and tz‘).
The Chinese t is generally transcribed into Persian as
ت(sometimesط, both pronounced t), as in
=ﻮ ـــﯾﻨﻔTayanfu
for 太原府Taiyuanfu, while the Chinese d is spelled
with eitherد(d) orت(t), as inﺪو ـﯾداDaidu for 大都Da(i)
Du andﺗـﻮﻧـﮏ

for 六盤Liupan). Although k (ک) could be distinguished
from g (گ) in Persian, it was common practice in manu-
script copying to disregard the distinction altogether,
and the distinction between j (ج) and ch (چ) was made
only intermittently and inconsistently. It is accepted

the translation that deal with China and Chinese names,
I have often given a transcription of the Persian with the
Chinese equivalent in square brackets, e.g., Gim Jiu
[Jinzhou]. Interestingly, in every instance in which
Rashiduddin and Marco Polo record the same names,
they both record the Persian version of the name, like
the Persian Tayanfu, which is Marco Polo’s “Taianfu,”
for Taiyuanfu; the Persian Khojanfu, Marco Polo’s “Ca-
cionfu,” for Hezhong fu; and the Persian Kenjanfu,
which is Marco Polo’s “Quengianfu,” for Jingzhaofu,
which is better known by its other name, Xi’an (Sian).
Had he so chosen, Rashiduddin could have availed
himself of Arabic vocabulary and been very precise in
the deﬁnition of groups of various sizes. Instead, he opt-
ed to use one word,ﻮم ـﻗqawm, for all groupings. He does
not, therefore, distinguish among nations, tribes, or
clans, although he occasionally uses the wordﻪ ـ ـ ـﺷﻌﺒshu‘-
ba ‘branch’ for a branch of a family tree. When the Eng-
lish terms ‘nation,’ ‘tribe,’ and ‘clan’ are used, they are
dictated by sense and by the necessity to introduce some
variety into the text. The Naiman, for instance, were a
large confederation, and they would certainly have qual-
iﬁed to be designated a nation. The Borjiqin, on the oth-
er hand, were a small family grouping who would not be
called anything more than a clan in English. The reader
x

should bear in mind that Rashiduddin does not distin-
guish these groupings in any way.
In a text that deals largely with the world conqueror
Tämüjin, a word must be said concerning his title,
“Genghis Khan,” and our use of the conventional Eng-
lish spelling instead of attempting to reconstruct a more
“correct” original. The most frequently defended specu-
lation for the origin of the “Genghis” part of the title is
that it was Chinggiz, which, it is thought, like the dAlA-I
dalai (the Mongolian for ocean) in the Dalai Lama’s ti-
tle, may ultimately have had some connection with the
Turkish tengiz ‘sea, ocean’ (which is the modern Repub-
lican Turkish deniz and shows up as the personal name
Tänggiz and Dänggiz in our text). True, an initial t-
could have been affricated in Mongolian to ch- before a
high front vowel (tengiz > chengiz > chingiz, chinggiz),
but, unfortunately, at the stage at which t became ch, a
ﬁnal z would have been an original r, i.e. chinggiz would
have been derived from tengir, not tengiz.1 On text p.
421 Rashiduddin gives his version of the etymology. He
states that ching in Mongolian means strong, which is
true, and that the plural of ching is chingiz, which is not
true. There is, for certain words, a Mongolian plural in -s
~ -z, but there is no -iz plural and never has been.
Rashiduddin thinks that the “plural” was used to make
the title more grandiose, i.e. he thinks chinggiz khan
means “khan of the strong,” and he draws a parallel with
the Persian shāhānshāh, which does mean “king of
kings.” As interesting as Rashiduddin’s specuation is,
since it is wrong, it probably indicates that even Mongo-
lians in Rashiduddin’s time did not know what “Genghis
Khan” meant. In sum it is far easier to use the recog-
nized and time-honored English “Genghis” than it is to
worry about what the original Mongolian may have
been, particularly when we have it only in Persian and
Chinese,2 both of which obscure so much of the name
that it is impossible to tell precisely what Rashiduddin
and his contemporaries may have said. It is clear only
that they usually wrote the name asﲒ ــ ـﭼﻨﮑ, and sometimes
asﭼﻨﮑﮑ
ـــ ـــ ـــ ـــ
ﲒ, and they probably pronounced Chingīz or
Chinggīz. Finally, one can do no better than to quote
Doerfer: 
Es hat im Mo[ngolischen] eine Tabuisierung von Herrscher-
namen nach deren Tode gegeben.… Wenn aber überhaupt
irgendwo Tabuisierung eines Names angebracht war, und
wenn sie überhaupt irgendwo die Chance hatte, sich
1See Gerhard Doerfer, Türkische und mongolische Elemente
im Neupersischen 1:315.
2The Chinese transcription of the name is 成吉思 Chénggísī.
deﬁnitiv durchzusetzen, dann doch wohl bei dem Names des
Ciŋgis, des größten Herrschers, den die Mo. überhaupt
hervorgebracht haben. Die Lösung ist also: Es gibt keine
Lösung, wir können den Namen überhaupt nicht kennen,
und daher auch nicht etymologisieren. Daher dürfte auch
heute noch (und wird vielleicht für immer) Banzarovs Wort
gelten: этимология его остается такой же загадкой, какой
она была сто лет тому назад ‘die Etymologie dieses
Names bleibt dasselbe Rätsel, das es vor hundert Jahren
war.’3
It should be obvious that the modern Persian pronuncia-
tion “Changīz” and the modern Turkish rendering as
“Cengiz” are not justiﬁable on any grounds except as
convention. The Persian pronunciation has probably
resulted from an association withﮓــﭼﻨchang ‘claw,’ and
the Turkish pronunciation from an association withﮓ ــﺟﻨ
ceng ‘battle.’
This translation is not meant to take the place of the
Persian texts available. There is only so much a transla-
tor can do in attempting to reconcile massive textual
variants. For philological study nothing can take the
place of the actual texts, and to facilitate comparison
with editions of the Persian text I have incorporated ref-
erences throughout the translation. The numbers given
in square brackets and bold face refer to the Rawshan–
Mūsavī edition (Jāmi‘ al-tawārīkh, edited by Muḥam-
mad Rawshan and Muṣṭafā Mūsavī in two volumes,
Tehran: Nashr-i Alburz, 1373—JTRM in the notes); this
edition has the advantage of presenting a superbly edited
text of the entirety of Tome One in two companion vol-
umes. The “M” numbers in square brackets in the ﬁrst
part refer to the 1965 Moscow edition (Джами’ ат-
таварих, volume 1, part 1, edited by A. A. Romaske-
vich, L. A. Khetagurov, and A. A. Ali-zade, Moscow:
Glavnaya Redaktsiya Vostochnoy Literatury, 1965; JTR-
KA in the notes). The “M” numbers in square brackets in
part two, chapter two, section four refer to the 1980
Moscow edition (Джами’ ат-таварих, volume 2, part 1,
edited by A. A. Ali-zade, Moscow: Glavnaya Redak-
tsiya Vostochnoy Literatury, 1980—JTAZ in the notes).
The “B” numbers from section ﬁve through section
eleven refer to Blochet’s edition (Djami el-tévarikh:
Histoire générale du monde, edited by Edgar Blochet,
Leyden: E. J. Brill, 1911—JTBl in the notes). The “A”
numbers from section twelve to the end refer to Ali-
zade’s 1957 Baku edition (Джами’ ат-таварих: Сбор-
ник Летописей, volume 3, edited by A. A. Ali-zade,
Baku: Azärbayjan SSR Elmlär Akademiyasï Näshriyy-
3Ibidem.
xi

atï, 1957—JTAZ in the notes).
There are two dating systems used simultaneously in
this text, Turco-Mongolian solar years and Islamic lunar
years. The solar years (Year of the Horse, Year of the
Monkey, e.g.) were taken from the Chinese, and they oc-
cur in twelve-year cycles. Chinese and Turco-Mongolian
years begin on the new moon nearest the ﬁfteenth degree
of Aquarius. The ﬁfteenth of Aquarius falls on the fourth
or ﬁfth of February; adjusting for the nearest new moon
would mean plus or minus ﬁfteen days, i.e. the year be-
gins in late January or early February. These years thus
correspond closely to Western years, with a slight over-
lap. A chart of the cyclical Sino-Turkic years and their
Christian equivalents for the period covered by this
work is given as an appendix. Islamic lunar dates, which
have no convenient correspondence with solar years,
have been converted to their Western equivalents. 
Illustrations were planned for various sections of the
book, and they are referred to in the text. There was to
be a portrait of every ruler on his throne surrounded by
his wives, sons, and commanders. Unfortunately, few of
the illustrations survive.
The modern division of the Jami‘u’t-tawarikh, which
was proposed by E. G. Browne and adopted by the Rus-
sians and others in subsequent editions, has been shown
in the table of contents. Otherwise I have left the divi-
sion
into
tomes,
parts,
chapters,
and
sections
as
Rashiduddin intended. The new division, while good
and rational on certain grounds and successful in equal-
izing the vast differences in length among the sections,
is too Iranocentric. Rashiduddin did not treat the
Ilkhanids—and they did not see themselves—as any-
thing other than what they were, successors to Genghis
Khan. The sections on them should not, therefore, be
presented as a departure from Part Two, which is
Genghis Khan and all his successors, but very much a
part thereof.
A ﬁnal note on the perennial bugaboo of transcription
and transliteration. Mongolian names are transcribed, as
noted above, as they appear in the Secret History of the
Mongols, with the occasional slight alteration because of
the Persian-script rendering of those names. The only
departure from the normal transcription of Mongolian is
the use of ä for e (i.e. Bärkä instead of Berke), a practice
not unknown to Mongolianists. Since in this work we
have so many names of so many different origins—all of
which are represented in the Perso-Arabic script—I saw
no proﬁt in representing similar Mongolian and Turkish
names and words with different systems of transcription,
particularly since it is often difﬁcult or impossible to tell
whether a given word is coming from Turkish or Mon-
golian or a combination of the two. In addition, I have a
personal aversion to representing with the vowel e any-
thing that is written in the Arabic script with an alif.
Thus, all words and names of Turkish or Mongolian ori-
gin are transcribed uniformly with the vowels i, u, ü, o,
ö, a, and ä. The e vowel I have reserved for the older
Persian vowel ē (the “majhūl y”) and for certain Turkic
names and words that are written in the Arabic script
with a y to represent ē. Persian and Arabic words and
names are transcribed as normally transliterated but
without the added confusion of dots and macrons. I am
conﬁdent that “Ali,” “Ahmad,” and “Mahmud” will be
recognizable for what they are without resorting to
marks that are unnecessary for those who know and
meaningless for those who don’t.
Since I am fairly helpless in the face of Chinese, and I
did not have another lifetime to learn enough simply to
check the accuracy of Rashiduddin’s informants in what
amounts to only a few pages in this work, I was very
fortunate to have the assistance of Drs. Kenneth Chase
and Jiger Janabel, both of whom have been extraordinar-
ily generous with their time and knowledge of the Chi-
nese language and Chinese history and helped me
through the relevant sections of the Yuan shi and Sheng-
wu qin-zheng lu. For graciously assisting in proofread-
ing, thanks go to Gulnora Aminova and Yonggyu Lee;
and for unstinting help in chores of every description, I
proffer my gratitude to my student and assistant Ali-
Reza Korangy.
I hope that, whatever its failings may be, this transla-
tion will succeed in presenting in a uniform version the
great work of Rashiduddin and his colleagues to an Eng-
lish-reading audience, and that it may be of use to histo-
rians and those interested in all the various parts of the
world that were inﬂuenced to one degree or another by
the Mongol conquest and its aftermath.

PREFACE
HE REASON for prefacing this in-
troduction and writing this fore-
word is that prior to now a
rough draft of this book, which
contained the history of the
world-conquering
monarch
Genghis Khan, his glorious fa-
thers and forebears, and his il-
lustrious offspring, was, as will
be explained in the dedication,
organized and arranged by com-
mand of Sultan Sa‘id Ghazan Khan from miscellaneous
folios and scrolls and various registers and notebooks.
Even during his reign, which was the object of jealousy
of the reigns of Dara, Ardavan, Afredun, and Anoshir-
van,1 clean copies were made of some of the rough
drafts, but before the copying was completed and the
penning of this section could be commenced, the falcon
of that just monarch’s pure spirit responded to the call,
[2] O thou soul which art at rest, return unto thy lord,
well pleased with thy reward, and well pleasing unto
God,2 and took ﬂight on the eleventh of Shawwal 703
[May 17, 1304] in the vicinity of Qazwin,3 the gate to
paradise, leaving behind the cage of its noble shell and
making its nest in the heights of paradise in the assembly
of truth, in the presence of a most potent king.4
Since his might was greater than that of the world,
highest paradise became his place. / May thousands of
blessings from God pour down every instant upon his
spirit.
Five or six years prior to his death, Ghazan Khan had
promulgated a pious, wise, and affectionate will, in
which he reafﬁrmed the heir designate. He had had it
written intelligently and eloquently and declaimed in the
presence of all the ladies, commanders, ministers, and
grandees of court; and he was most insistent in encour-
aging all to observe its ﬁne points. In accordance with

the register of the kingship of all realms of the inhabited
quarter of the earth, to do battle with whose unruly ene-
my Mars draws his dagger from the scabbard of re-
venge, with the radiance of whose world-adorning mind
the earth-illuminating sun beautiﬁes its light-ﬁlled coun-
tenance, in harmony with whose celebratory banquet
Venus tunes her harp, to arrange whose administration
Mercury unfailingly sees to every jot and tittle, and to
broadcast whose splendid characteristics to the ends of
the earth the moon girds its loins with its halo.
The kingdom was illuminated by him, religion became
strong through him, the throne was ennobled by him,
and fortune was rejuvenated.
After messengers arrived and heralds had delivered the
news, the imperial retinue set out under God’s protection
from Khurasan, where the victorious camps had been,
for Persia and Azerbaijan, the seat of the sultan’s throne
and the banners of the kingdom. [4]
Fortune before and luck behind, impeccability in his
heart and victory at his side.
In his perfect princely concern and abundant imperial
feeling, he constantly dispatched messengers to reassure
all his servants and retainers, and they gave out the good
news of his imminent arrival. Thus he placed the balm
of affection on hearts that had been wounded, and all,
thus encouraged and gladdened, raced out in droves to
greet him and attain the felicity of kissing the ground be-
fore him. On Monday, the second of Dhu’l-Hijja of the
year mentioned above [July 6, 1304], he arrived in the
City of Islam, Ujan, at the magniﬁcent ordu.1
Into the sphere of fortune came successfully and
triumphantly that princely asylum, that sun of princes.
All the princes and princesses entered into fealty to the
emperor, and the voice of fortune cried out from behind
the curtain of the unseen:
O time, good news! Once again from the celestial sphere
of kingship the sun of the east has risen above the
horizon of might and majesty. / The falseness of tyranny
and the envier of Islam is manifest; the proof of justice
and the world-conquering prince has arrived. / For the
world, religion, fortune, injustice, and sedition have
arrived support, refuge, a friend, extermination, and
annihilation. / The garden of fortune had withered, but it
was refreshed when the water of his justice arrived to
cause it to grow and ﬂourish.
[5] For several days serious matters were looked into,
1For ordu and all such Persian, Turkish, and Mongolian
words in the text, see the glossary.
the best policy for the state was investigated, conditions
for stability and organization were achieved, and the
qualiﬁcations for awareness and security were met. Af-
ter that, a large quriltai was held, and at the most auspi-
cious hour, at dawn, on Monday the ﬁfteenth of Dhu’l-
Hijja 703 [July 19, 1304]
Under favorable auspices and auspicious star, replete
with good luck and felicity, / Like Jamshed the shah sat
upon the throne, men and fairies loins girt before him. /
In his service were seated and standing in lines battle-
scarred commanders and princes of renown. / The
celestial spheres having entrusted to him their turning,
the world gave its labors to his command.
The truth is that from the creation of the world and the
beginning of Adam’s progeny, in no generation has the
throne of rule been graced by anyone possessed of such
auspiciousness, for former monarchs have subdued most
of the realms of the world by dint of blood-stained
sword and fortress-conquering mace, and even if some
have attained [the throne] through inheritance, it did not
happen without contest or dispute, particularly during
the days of the Mongols, when is it clear and patent to
all how much strife, unrest, and disorder have occurred
in every revolution, how much blood has been spilled by
glittering sword with the outbreak of the ﬁre of sedition,
how many heads have rolled, how brisk the market of
pillage and plunder have become while all sorts of goods
lie in a slump, [6] how many grand and noble families
have been exterminated and reduced to naught by mas-
sacre and rapine until after all that a royal enthronement
would take place. Even so, for a long, long time the ba-
sis of the throne would be shaky, and every day some-
thing would happen to cause distress and unrest, and no
stability could be achieved. When the turn of rule came
to his regal reign and the days of his ever-increasing for-
tune, the architect of eternal divine favor and the painter
of godly felicity designed the foundation of the ediﬁce
of his good fortune in such a way that, without the dust
of untoward events being stirred up by the steed of the
celestial spheres, and without a drop of blood being
spilled upon the ground from the cloud of the sword by
the wrathful hand of fate, the broad expanse of the realm
of security, cleansed of all fears and dangers and orga-
nized on perfect and polished law, came under the con-
trol of the deputies of His Majesty the Sultan, and the
pearl-shedding pen scribed these lines on the page of the
age:
O spreader of equity, during the days of your justice no
blade has stuck its head out from the scabbard. / During
2
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

your reign the world has become such that until
doomsday ‘blade’ is of no use as anything but as a
rhyming word in panegyrics of you.
For these reasons it is clear and obvious that the selec-
tion of His Majesty the Emperor for divine favor is of a
special sort, and the basis for this special favor is very
ﬁrm and stable. One of the learned men of the age, who
is the Sahban of the time in eloquence and the Hassan of
the era in his panegyrics of His Majesty, contemplated
the meaning of the letters of his blessed name in accor-
dance with the dictum “Titles are sent down from heav-
en” and versiﬁed it as follows: [7]
Last night I contemplated the name of Shah Kharbanda1
for a time, / Thinking perhaps there is a meaning in this
name of which the reader is unaware. / While I was thus
perplexed, a voice came to me, saying, “O well-wisher
of the happy king, / There is a meaning in the letters of
this word that is quite appropriate to the king. / Add up
one by one the values of the letters of ‘Shah Kharbanda’
/ So that you may know that the meaning is ‘the special
shadow of the Creator.’ / There are nine letters in one,
and ﬁfteen in the other, and they are equivalent in
numerical value.2 / You’d say that name is nine
marvelous oyster shells stuffed with pearls ﬁve and ten, /
Or else this royal name is a talisman cast upon the door
of God’s treasury.” / When I realized the mystery of this
name, my mind was put at ease. / I comprehended the
meaning and said, “Long live Shah Kharbanda! / May
the sun of his majesty and rule shine eternally from the
celestial sphere.”
After congratulations were offered, he had an investi-
gation made of his brother Sultan Sa‘id Ghazan Khan’s
yasaq and yosun, of his customs and habits, and a re-
view of his issuance of orders was made. In fraternal de-
votion and affection and in complete appreciativeness
and chivalry he saw that it was proper for all the com-
manders and ministers to remain in ofﬁce as they had
been, and he reafﬁrmed them all in their posts, with the
administration of the realm in the same manner and

When he acceded to the throne, since ‘donkey-driver’ was not
considered an appropriate name for a ruler, it was changed to
Khudābanda (‘slave of God,’ a Persian translation of the com-

ﺪﻩ ـــﯾﻨﻨﺮـﻓآ, ‘the special

fashion with no change or alteration. All were convinced
that [8]
With his organization the affairs of the realm are such
that only in beauties’ tresses can anyone discover
disorganization.
Therefore, when the various sections of this history,
rough draft and clean copy, were perused by the royal
personage, by virtue of his perfect intelligence, vast
knowledge, and imperial perspicacity he made major
corrections and reorganizations, and since the whole
thing went to clean copy during his felicitous reign, it
seemed proper that it be in his blessed name and that the
beginning of the book be adorned with his royal titles.
By virtue of his pleasing qualities and innate chivalry,
however, he did not allow it but said, “Let it be complet-
ed still in the name of Sultan Sa‘id Ghazan Khan, and let
the dedication be adorned by his titles.” In accordance
with the royal command, that is how it is being written.
Since the Padishah of Islam has a constant interest in
various sciences and the arts of history and storytelling
and spends most of his felicitous time acquiring various
accomplishments, after reading and correcting this histo-
ry he said, “Until now no one at any time has made a
history that contains the stories and histories of all in-
habitants of the climes of the world and the various
classes and groups of humans, there is no book in this
realm that informs about all countries and regions, and
no one has delved into the history of the ancient kings.
In these days, when, thank God, all corners of the earth
are under our control and that of Genghis Khan’s illus-
trious family, and philosophers, astronomers, scholars,
and historians of all religions and nations—Cathay,
Machin, India, Kashmir, Tibet, Uyghur, and other na-
tions of Turks, Arabs, and Franks [9]—are gathered in
droves at our glorious court, each and every one of them
possesses copies of the histories, stories, and beliefs of
their own people, and they are well informed of some of
them. It is our considered opinion that of those detailed
histories and stories a compendium that would be per-
fect should be made in our royal name, and it should be
written in two volumes along with an atlas and gazetteer
and appended to the history so that the aggregate of that
book would be peerless and include all sorts of histories.
Inasmuch as the opportunity is at hand, and the compo-
sition of such a memorial, the likes of which no kings
have ever possessed, is possible, it must be completed
without neglect or delay so that it may cause our name
and fame to endure.”
PREFACE
3

As ordered, all the learned and reliable people of the
nations mentioned above did research, made extracts
from the contents of their ancient books, and penned
another volume on the histories of all inhabitants of the
climes. Yet another volume of atlas and gazetteer was
added and appended to this blessed history. The totality
was entitled Compendium of Chronicles, and the details,
stories, and legends it contains, as well as how they are
arranged, are given in the table of contents, which will
follow immediately after this preface.
[On the nature of history]
It is absolutely certain that no historian has ever wit-
nessed with his own eyes the events and things of which
he writes and reports. Furthermore, those who deal with
events and incidents, which are the stuff of history, have
not heard of these things directly but write and speak of
them through the tradition of transmitters.
Now tradition is of two sorts. One is uninterrupted,
which leads to knowledge and of which there is no
doubt, just as we know, through uninterrupted tradition,
of the existence of the prophets, monarchs, [10] and fa-
mous people who lived in prior generations and of the
existence of distant cities like Mecca, Cairo, and other
far-away places. Although we have never seen them, we
know of them in a manner that admits of no hesitation.
All religions and faiths are based on this uninterrupted
sort of tradition. In some instances such uninterrupted
tradition has weight with the generality of people, and in
other instances only with a particular group.
The second sort of tradition is periodic. This is the
sort isolated individuals read. It may be true or false, and
it may be subject to variance or debate. Most stories and
accounts that people tell are of this periodic sort.
Through experience it is palpably certain that if a person
to whom an event happened yesterday recounts it today,
he will certainly not remember it as it was but will
change and alter his expression and words at every
gathering in which he retells it. It is for this reason that,
despite the fact that in religious matters the greatest of
precaution has been taken, there is much variance—so
much so that even some reports of the Prophet’s sayings
are considered dubious owing to differences among
narrators. Ancient scholars, having done much research,
selected some, which they call sihah (true), while the
rest are left in the realm of doubt, hesitation, and
abeyance. Most of the differences of opinion among
religious leaders on legal matters is due to this.
Furthermore, it is not right to reject disputed things, for
in religion a person who rejects may go astray. 
It is therefore certain that the histories of so many dif-
ferent peoples and long periods of time cannot be veri-
ﬁed absolutely, and the traditions that have been and still
are being handed down are neither equal nor in agree-
ment. As a matter of course, every one recounts a thing
as it has come to him through uninterrupted tradition or
as he has heard it, and it often happens that a transmitter
adds to or subtracts from his report according to whim.
[11] If he does not tell an absolute lie, he colors his ex-
pression in a way that leads to variance. Since the imple-
mentation of the divine way is as has been mentioned,
and human nature has been fashioned in this manner,
then anyone who thinks he can report otherwise is mud-
dle-headed and wrong-thinking. This being so, if a histo-
rian tries to write only what is veriﬁable and incontro-
vertible, then he can introduce absolutely no story
whatsoever, for anything he introduces will have been
narrated by some group or other of great men who wit-
nessed it, heard it related by others, or read it in old
books—in any case, as has been mentioned, it will be
subject to controversy. If for this reason they give up
writing and speaking, thinking, “God forbid, people
might object or disapprove,” then of course all tales, nar-
ratives, and incidents in the world will be forgotten, and
the generality of people will be deprived of the beneﬁt
they might derive therefrom. Therefore, it is the duty of
the historian to take the stories and narratives of every
nation and group, however those people have recorded
and reported them in their own books, and to relate and
rewrite them from the well-known and current books of
those nations based on accounts of the most reliable peo-
ple—and “the responsibility be upon the narrator.”
Now that it has been explained that every group and
class of people relate and hand down accounts of their
history according to their own beliefs, and that they will
naturally prefer their own beliefs to anyone else’s and
will exaggerate the truth thereof, it is not possible for all
people to be unanimous in all cases. This is obvious to
everyone. When a historian narrates from different peo-
ples, there will doubtlessly be a difference in his words,
and some people in some places [12] and stories will
differ, but the good and bad, or the fault and virtue, will
not rebound upon him, for he, as has been said, is re-
counting the history of others. As a matter of course a
real veriﬁcation is impossible to make, as has been said.
Inasmuch as all are agreed that uninterrupted tradition is
given weight and accepted—and although uninterrupted
Muslim tradition is the most reliable of all—nonethe-
4
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

less, the basis of the accounts of various peoples cannot
be laid on that. Therefore, perforce everything that is re-
lated by any group must be considered reliable, for we
have said over and over that it carries weight either with
the generality of people or with a particular group, and
that which is related periodically may possibly be true or
false. A historian’s duty, as we have said, must be to ex-
tract and write from what reliable people have said and
from reliable standard books. If he makes any change
therein according to his own imagination, it will become
positively worthless and incorrect. 
The reason I have said all this is that when this poor
one was ordered to compose this Compendium of
Chronicles, I copied out everything I found written in
the well-known books of every nation, everything that
was known to every tribe through uninterrupted tradi-
tion, everything that the wise and learned of every group
had reported according to their belief—all this I copied
out without change or alteration, and it is possible, due
to my own failure to comprehend or to my misunder-
standing of a narrator, that some things may have
slipped by. Nonetheless, I was desirous of making a
most concerted effort in my selection of stories, but it
was not possible to make much headway in that regard,
for everyone knows that great talent and expertise in all
branches of knowledge are necessary for such a labor,
and I did not see these things in myself. Given a long
period of time in one’s youthful years and with total
leisure, these things can be accomplished, [13] but I be-
gan this labor at the end of my years of maturity.
When this poor one was brought to the imperial court
as a deputy and ordered to deal with important adminis-
trative matters, although I did not have the capacity for
such a great labor, and the strength of my intellect and
mind was insufﬁcient, to comply with the order it was
imperative to occupy myself with it and to exert myself
to the utmost. Since my strength of mind was inadequate
to that, how could it have been adequate to gather histo-
ries, which is one of the greatest of all tasks? 
For the aforementioned reasons, and with the excuses
offered, I place my hope in the general kindness of the
great ones who will peruse this book, hoping that wher-
ever there is a mistake or slip, they will cover it with for-
giveness and disregard, correct it, add whatever they
consider appropriate, and excuse this poor one who
labors under an order.
Although the histories of some peoples who are inﬁ-
dels and idolaters are nothing but fabulous concoctions
and erroneous myths unacceptable to the rational mind,
they too have been included so that those of insight may
take heed and so that the people of Islam and faith may,
by reading it, become informed of the corrupt beliefs of
those in error and thereby avoid those things and give
thanks for the blessing of correct guidance and the light
of faith, which is the ultimate of all divine gifts and be-
stowals. God the Exalted is he from whom aid must be
sought, and upon Him is all reliance and trust.
When this servant of the state wrote these words on
his own shortcomings and a justiﬁcation of himself and
other historians, and included them in the introduction to
the Compendium of Chronicles, it was submitted to His
Majesty. When it came before the august gaze, he was
kind enough to deign to say, “That which has been re-
ported and written by miscellaneous persons prior to this
may have contained additions or deletions, but they are
to be excused [14] according to what you have men-
tioned, and you too will be similarly excused. The grand
deeds and branches of the family that have been record-
ed from Genghis Khan’s time down to the present—and
that was the major goal and what is the most useful to
us—are all correct and true, and no one can object to it.
No one has ever written or recorded the likes of this, and
those who are aware of these stories and of every por-
tion of those pages, are in full agreement and cannot
deny it. No one has ever written a history more carefully
researched or clearer than this.”
Since it so pleased the Padishah of Islam, I rendered
thanks to God Almighty. Although I know myself to be
deﬁcient in all regards, since it was acceptable to such a
majesty and was received with a gaze of acceptance and
pleasure, how can I express my gratitude? God willing,
its beneﬁt will reach all those who seek to proﬁt from
and look into it.
May God, in His kindness, keep this slave-rewarding
monarch forever on the throne and in everlasting august-
ness in the shadow of His mercy, through the Prophet
and his family. Finis. [15]
e
PREFACE
5

The contents of this book, which is the Compendium of Chronicles, in three tomes.
OME ONE was ordered completed in this time by the Shahanshah of Islam Öljäitü Sultan—may his king-
ship last forever—in the name of his brother Sultan Sa‘id Ghazan Khan.1 It consists of two parts.
Part One is an exposition of stories of the appearance of the Turkic nations and how they branched off
into various tribes and an explanation of the fathers and forefathers of every tribe in general, and it consists of
an introduction and four chapters.
The introduction contains the geography of some of the places inhabited by the Turks and a list of the
names and epithets of each division of that nation, insofar as has been ascertained.
Chapter One contains stories of the nations of Oghuz, the grandson of Abulja Khan, Japheth the son of the
Prophet Noah, and of the clans of his uncles who were with him. There is a mention of his lineage and
branches. [16]
Chapter Two is on the Turkic tribes that are now called Mongols but which in times past had other names
and epithets and each had a leader and commander.
Chapter Three is on the Turkic tribes who have also had separate monarchs and leaders but who do not
have a close relationship to the tribes mentioned in previous chapters.
Chapter Four is on the Turkic tribes that were anciently styled Mongol. This chapter contains two sections,
one on Dürlükin Mongols and the other on the Niru’un Mongols.
Part Two is on the rule of Mongol, Turkic, and other monarchs and contains two chapters.
Chapter One is on the fathers and forefathers of Genghis Khan. It consists of ten sections, (1) Dobun
Bayan, (2) Alan Qo’a and her three sons, (3) Alan Qo’a’s son Bodonchar, (4) Bodonchar’s son Dutum
Mänen, (5) Dutum Mänen’s son Qaidu Khan, (6) Qaidu Khan’s son Bai Singqor, (7) Bai Singqor’s son
Tumina Khan, (8) Tumina Khan’s son Qabul Khan, (9) Qabul Khan’s son Bartan Bahadur, and (10) Bartan
Bahadur’s son Yesügä Bahadur.
Chapter Two is on the history of Genghis Khan and his illustrious offspring, [17] some of whom became
qa’ans in every age, others of whom did not attain a speciﬁc rulership, along with a summary history of the
rulers of the world who were contemporary with them down to the present. There are sections (1–3) on
Yesügä Bahadur’s son Genghis Khan, who lived seventy-two years and ruled for twenty-three, (4) Genghis
Khan’s third son and heir Ögödäi Qa’an, who lived for ___ years and ruled for twelve, (5) Genghis Khan’s
eldest son Jochi Khan, who lived for forty years and ruled for ___, and his family, (6) Genghis Khan’s
second son Chaghatai Khan, who lived for ___ years and ruled for ___, and his family, (7) Genghis Khan’s
fourth son Tolui Khan, the heir to his yurts, who lived for ___ years and ruled for ___, (8) Ögödäi Qa’an’s
eldest son Güyük Khan, who became qa’an after his father and lived for ___ years and ruled for ___, (9)
Tolui Khan’s eldest son Mänggü Qa’an, who became qa’an after Güyük Khan and lived for ___ years and
ruled for eight years, (10) Tolui Khan’s son Qubilai Qa’an, who became qa’an after Mänggü Qa’an and
lived for eighty-two years and ruled for thirty-ﬁve years, and his brother Ariq Bökä, (11) Qubilai Qa’an’s
grandson Temür Qa’an, who is monarch at this time and whose age at present is ___ and has been on the

OME TWO was commissioned by the Shahanshah of Islam Öljäitü Sultan in his own regal name. It
consists of two parts.
Part One is the history of the Sultan of Islam from his birth until the present, when this book is being
bound.
Part Two consists of two chapters.
Chapter One consists of two sections.
Section One is a summary history of all the prophets, caliphs, and monarchs of all nations from the
time of Adam until the present, which is the ___th month of the year seven hundred ___ of the Hegira.2
Section Two is a detailed history of every nation of the inhabited quarter of the globe.3 [20] Although
some of this material has already been recorded in previous sections, it is mostly what has not been
included and cannot be found there. Another part is the history that had not been discovered by the
ancient rulers and historians of this realm and of which they were unaware. During this imperial era,
by royal command, the books of every nation were acquired, and the wise of every group were
summoned, and insofar as possible that which was ascertained was written down. That is the history
that has been recorded here.

in the month of ___ in the year 70_. Through the limitless years that will be his reign historians who are

It must be realized that the magnitude of the inﬁnite
divine essence is not such that it can be spoken of or
written about by a frail, weak servant. Although all
creatures and beings of the worlds above and below,
from the moon to the ﬁsh,1 from the throne of heaven to
the expanse of the earth, both those that speak and those
that are silent, both those that are animate and those that
are inanimate, ﬁrst and last, inwardly and outwardly,
express their laud and praise of their creator and

Every thing extols God in its own tongue, / animals with
their mute tongues, humans through rational speech. /
Know that the praise of plants is their increase. What is
the confession of inanimates? Their very being, / [22]
For in every thing is a sign of him that indicates that he
is one.
The condition of those who love the beautiful awe-
someness of the divine and that of those who yearn for
the limpid waters of intimate union, who are wayfarers
on the path of seeking and travelers in the desert of
quest, must be like a thirsty man who wishes for water
constantly, while awake and while asleep, and who can
never be given enough to drink to assuage his thirst.
What does such a thirsty person know of the sweetness
of the Euphrates or the Nile or the limpidity of Tasnim

This being so, confession of one’s inability and admis-

the truth because they lack the capacity while others
would not be able to accept it because of the differences
of opinion and beliefs among religions and nations and
disdain for following anybody else. They would then
fall into denial. That is why it is divinely ordained that
only tokens of those mysteries be revealed so that the
people of the world may witness them with their own
eyes and so that no one may deny them, and so by that
means they may recognize the necessary object of wor-
ship, know his power and other attributes, and believe.
Such persons adopt the characteristics of those who at-
tain everlasting life through acts of charity and faithful
sincerity. They are remembered for their goodness over
all the earth and throughout time, like Abraham, the
friend of God, who, alone among all his polytheistic
and idolatrous kith and kin, [24] became a monotheist
worshipper of God and took on divine characteristics
and godly attributes. As is well known in tales and oft
mentioned in histories, one of his noble characteristics
and qualities was a natural generosity, an innate virtue.
In accordance with the poetry that says,
If it is within your grasp, do not be timid, for you can
subdue what is within your grasp,
he always kept food on his table, and no traveler or
wayfarer was denied his bounty. On account of the sin-
cerity and affection he had for God, he was called
“Friend of God.”1 As is written in books, in order that
his sincere faith might be proven and conﬁrmed before
the people of the world God afﬂicted and tested him by
ordering him to sacriﬁce his beloved child, Ishmael.2
Abraham immediately submitted to God’s order and
quickly summoned Ishmael, to whom he said, O my
son, I saw in a dream that I should offer thee in sacri-
fice: consider therefore what thou art of opinion I should
do. In reply he said, O my father, do what thou art com-
manded: thou shalt find me, if God please, a patient per-
son.3 When Abraham saw Ishmael’s submissiveness, he
1Khalīlullāh, Abraham’s Arabic epithet, equivalent to the
Biblical ! ְאֺהַ ב of 2 Ch. 20:7.
2It is a commonplace—though by no means the only—Is-
lamic interpretation that the son Abraham was ordered to sac-
rifice was Ishmael, the progenitor of the Arabs, and not Isaac.
The son is not mentioned by name in the Koranic narrative.
3Kor. 37:102.
hastened in all sincerity and earnestness to bind his ten-
der hands and feet and lay him face down on the earth.
Then he calmly placed a gleaming knife across his
throat in order to carry out the sacriﬁce in accordance
with the rituals of his religion. As is recorded, every
time the knife touched his throat [25] it turned away
and refused to cut. When Abraham had complied with
all the necessary stipulations of obedience and God had
shown the people that his pure intention and sincere
trust were so great that he would not withhold from
God a child he had been granted after living eighty
years in childlessness, God sent Gabriel to Abraham
with a ram to redeem Ishmael and to prevent him from
killing his son. To him he said, O Abraham, now hast
thou verified the vision. Thus do we reward the
righteous.4
Commentators have interpreted in several ways why
God afﬂicted and tested Abraham and what the ultimate
intention of divine wisdom was in this case, but what is
the most in conformity with reality and reason is that,
regardless of how obvious to God Abraham’s generosi-
ty, friendship, and sincerity were, he wanted him to put
them into practice so that he would be worthy of re-
ward. Although the Prophet is reported to have said,
“Deeds are by intentions,” what he meant was that the
correctness of an action is dependent upon the inten-
tion; otherwise, so long as intentions are not coupled
with action, no deed is done, and an individual is not
worthy of reward since reward and punishment are
meaningless for uncommitted good and evil. A com-
mand without efﬁcient or effective cause is far from
justice and wisdom, and this is conﬁrmed by the Koran-
ic text that says, And that nothing shall be imputed to a
man for righteousness, except his own labour.5 It is
therefore incumbent that a person put his sincere inten-
tion into practice in order that the Creator, in his mercy,
compassion, and kindness, may give him a reward in
accordance with the text, God may recompense them ac-
cording to the utmost merit of what they shall have
wrought, and may add unto them of his abundance a more
excellent reward,6 and, He will double it unto him mani-
fold.7 [26] Therefore God wanted Abraham, who, alone
among all his peers, had become a believer and a
monotheist and had garbed himself with good qualities,

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

to put into practice his sincerity with regard to generosi-
ty so that as recompense in the best way, instead of one
child, so many tribes and branches of his progeny and
stock would appear, and in accordance with the text,
We formerly gave unto the family of Abraham a book
and wisdom; and we gave them a great kingdom,1 so
many thousands of prophets, saints, rulers, and kings
would come into existence from among his progeny.
Thereby the people of the world would realize that wor-
shipping God and taking on divine characteristics result
in incalculable reward. Therefore no hesitation or ap-
prehension would remain, and they would make every
effort to attain that felicity instead of practicing heed-
lessness, timidity, and sloth. Abraham the Friend of
God charged his children to keep an orderly record of
the genealogical tree of their sons and grandsons, gen-
eration after generation, and not to allow other nations
to intermarry with them so that their lineage would re-
main free of the very suspicion of admixture and so that
every one of his descendants would know his fathers
and forefathers in detail. 
Since they have maintained this practice until now, it
is clear and obvious to those of knowledge that, from
the time Abraham’s sons began to beget and multiply
until today, which has been nearly four thousand years,
all the prophets, kings, and elite of religions and nations
have been—and will continue to be until doomsday—of
his progeny. The most outstanding member of that fam-
ily, the sun of the celestial sphere of that dynasty, the ti-
tle page of the register of prophets, the greatest and best
of all existing things, the quintessence of all creatures,
seal of the prophets and best of apostles is Muhammad
Messenger of God—upon whom and upon whose house
be prayers and salutations. God sent him to all creatures
and promised him that all people in the world would
follow his religion. [27] It was the divine will from all
eternity that if in every era and epoch controversy befell
the people of Islam, or if they swerved a hair’s breadth
from the path of the ancient law, which is the straight
and narrow way, they would deserve chastisement that
would wake them from their sleep of heedlessness,
sober them up from the drunkenness of pride, and re-
new the ﬁrm foundations of Islam in such a way that it
would be an object of jealousy to all past generations in
bygone years. Divine favor ordained from all eternity
that the chastisement of the Islamic peoples would be at
1Kor. 4:54.
the hand of a nation that would be monotheistic and
God-fearing, not polytheistic or enemies of religion. In
the end the strengthening and ordering of the affairs of
the nation would be achieved through the might of
those terrifying peoples, and through the blessing of an
innate disposition to monotheism they would enter the
religion of Islam and command all people to comply
with its divine commandments and strictures. They too
would constrain themselves with the judgments of the
law and force themselves to comply with the duties it
imposes. Indeed, Islam would reach a point through
their might and power that no polytheist would dare to
criticize Islam. From east to west all would become
Muslim unhypocritically, and the inimitable message of
the Prophet would never be effaced regardless of the
passage of days, months, and years. Indeed, the longer
time passed, the ﬁrmer the foundation would become,
and the sounder the bases and principles would be.
Until the end of the world and the extinction of time,
the star of that state would be in constant ascendance
toward the zenith, and moment by moment the victories
achieved by that nation would be on the increase. An
incontrovertible proof of the truth of this assertion is
that after the pillars of Muslimism [28] were shaken by
cataclysms, and the structure of order was undermined
by catastrophes brought by time, so many great rulers
arose from among the sons and descendants of the Em-
peror of the World, Genghis Khan, the all-conquering,
irresistible monarch, the likes of whom the Creator had
never brought forth in any era or epoch, a star-blessed,
world-conquering emperor the likes of whom the celes-
tial sphere with all its thousands of eyes had never seen.
Each one subdued climes and brought so many cities
and towns without number under his command that the
vast expanse of the kingdoms of the world from east to
west and from north to south is in the grasp of their
might and power, and their command ﬂows like the
wind in every direction and to every part of sea and
land, over the souls and lives of humans and the djinn.
In this era, which is the year two and seven hundred of
the Hegira, in the realm of the land of Iran, which is the
quintessence of the inhabited quarter of the earth, the
monarchy and imperial throne belong to…Sultan Mah-
mud Ghazan Khan.2 Among Genghis Khan’s progeny,

who are the lords of the rulers of the earth and the age,
he has perfect knowledge and wisdom, abundant intel-
lect and native ability, great might and magnitude, re-
markable courage and perspicacity, justice and equity,
generosity and kindness, extreme competence in admin-
istration, and expertise in ruling. [29] He propagates the
Yosun and Yasaq and patronizes the arts, and he is the
envy of all princes. The necks of the unruly of the
world are held in check by obedience to him; all are
tamed to his orders; with his insightful intelligence, the
most minute point of knowledge or wisdom is not hid-
den behind a veil of doubt. With his perfect eloquence,
master philosophers and mystics have no opportunity to
raise questions or give answers. He is acquainted with
the arts of etiquette and various rare crafts of the age.
His comprehending psyche speaks with proof an
answer to each and every problem the intellect fails to
comprehend. If he wants, he can show the way by night
to the incapable if he raises the veil from before the
intelligent mind.
All of his regal attention is focused upon laying the
foundations of justice and refortifying the structures of
clemency and mercy for the generality of the subjects
and all classes of people. He spends all his hours ac-
quiring the paraphernalia of a good name and success.
Through the inﬂuence of the Muhammedan miracle,
through the purity of his enlightened breast, he chose
the religion of Islam and caused all his soldiers, some
of whom were Mongol monotheists and others of whom
were of idolatrous and polytheistic nations like the
Uyghur et al., to convert to Islam. Like Abraham the
Friend of God he sought to be free from the inﬁdels,
with his own hand he smashed all the idols, and he
totally blocked the way to inﬁdelity and polytheism. He

ordered heralded throughout all parts of the realm: Our
people, obey God’s preacher: and believe in him.1 [30]
Therefore they broke the idols and tore down the idol-
temples, building mosques and houses of worship in
their places. Everything that was abominable and
heretical he has eradicated, and moment by moment he
issues new orders to elevate the name of Islam and
make ﬁrm the religion and principles of the law. He
continues to magnify the peoples of Islam more and
more, as all people in the world can witness.
The market of religion became brisk when the king of
the world Ghazan Khan adopted the religion of the
prophet. / He laid a new foundation for the propagation
of the pure law; he completely abolished the customs of
polytheism, inﬁdelity, and heresy.
It follows upon these introductory remarks that the
reason God wanted to elevate the might and glory of
Genghis Khan, his forefathers and ancestors, and his
children and offspring and to raise the condition of that
family was to strengthen the religion of Islam and prop-
agate the law, since from one monotheistic generation
so many nations and tribes have branched off, whose
numbers
are beyond counting and cannot ﬁt into the strictures of
record or report.
The quintessence of those renowned tribes and great
clans was the World-Seizing Emperor Genghis Khan,
and the quintessence of his children and progeny—to
whom the sultans of the world and crowned heads
among humanity have placed rings of servitude in their
ears [31] and thrown the stole of thralldom over their
shoulders—is the king who gives asylum to the world,
Sultan Mahmud Ghazan (may his kingdom last forev-
er). It is therefore incumbent to explain how they came
to enjoy God’s favor and to express the history and con-
ditions of the branches of those tribes.2 [32]
A mention of the composition of this book, which is
entitled Ghazanid History.3
It is not concealed from the minds of the intelligent and
perspicacious or those possessed of vision and insight
that history consists of recording and arranging. For
every strange incident and marvelous unusual event that
happens and is recorded in registers and on folios, the
wise call the beginning of that event its date, and the
1Kor. 46:31.
2This section lacking in JTK; taken from JTRKA.
3I.e. Tome One of the Compendium of Chronicles.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

extent and quantity of time can be known thereby.
Therefore, the beginning of every nation and every state
has a ﬁxed date, and what event has ever been more
magniﬁcently appropriate for making it a date than the
beginning of Genghis Khan’s rule? In a short span of
time he conquered many of the kingdoms of the world
through his piercing insight, his never-failing strategy,
his perfect perspicacity, and his great policies, and he
wrathfully trampled and consigned to annihilation evil-
doers who were like Pharaoh in their natures and like
Zahhak in their deeds,1 each of whom, puffed with the
wind of pride, said, “I and none but me.” Having made
the world face one direction, having made all hearts of
one mind, and having swept the domination of over-
bearing tyrants and the injustice of aggressors from the
circle of kingdoms, he bequeathed it to his renowned
offspring and mighty descendants. To their eternal and
everlasting happiness and felicity the celestial spheres
took vows and promises.
It is the custom of wise men and scholars to record
the dates of the important events, [33] both good and
bad, of every time so that thereafter they may serve as
examples to their insightful descendants and followers,
so that in ages to come they may know the conditions
of the past, and so that the names of renowned mon-
archs and successful princes may thereby remain forev-
er on the face of the pages of time, for with the passage
of days and months and through long ages and years
untoward events may efface and erase them.
The course of time, long as it is, causes words to fall
from one’s hand.
An example of the truth of this assertion is that despite
the vast kingdom that Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna ac-
quired, with its effulgence of pomp and abundant
wealth, innumerable possessions, treasure troves be-
yond counting, paraphernalia of success and the good
things of this world, today his good name and renown
remain solely because of the poetry of Unsuri and Fir-
dawsi and the writings of Utbi.2
1Zahhak (Ḍaḥḥāk), the monstrous and tyrannical usurper of
Persian kingship.
2‘Unṣurī is the very well-known Ghaznavid court poet who
