thor of the Shāhnāma, which was commissioned by Sultan
Maḥmūd and completed in 1010; ‘Utbī is Abu-Naṣr Muḥam-
mad al-‘Utbī (d. ca. 1040), author of al-Yamini, which has
been described as “a turgid history” of the Ghaznavids Amir
Sabuktagin and Sultan Mahmud (see Storey, Persian Litera-
In this world the good relics of Mahmud of Ghazna’s
career have remained bound by rhyme.
Hence it can be known that poets and historians are the
best propagandists.
One nation has been called “Turks” since ancient
times, and they dwell in territories the length and breath
of which stretch from the Oxus and Jaxartes to the far-
thest reaches of the east and from one end of the
Qipchaq Steppe to the end of the territory of Manchuria
and Cathay. In those places they live in the mountains,
valleys, and plains, for they are not accustomed to re-
siding in villages and cities. Being far away from the
land of Iran, they are little mentioned in the histories of
the ancients. [34] Indeed, in only some books is the
merest mention of them introduced, and no people of
experience have been located to recount in detail their
history as it was. 
Although all the tribes and branches of the Turks and
Mongols resemble each other, and although they all
originally had one name, the Mongols were one type of
Turk, and there are great differences among them, as
will be explained for each one in the proper place.
Another result of this difference is that their stories and
history have not reached these parts in a veriﬁable
manner.
When the khanate and rule of the world came to
Genghis Khan and his glorious offspring, all the king-
doms of the inhabited quarter of the globe submitted to
him—Chin and Machin, Cathay, Hind and Sind, Tran-
soxiana and Turkistan, Syria, Anatolia, As, Rus, Circas-
sia, Qipchaq, Kilar, and Bashghurd, which more or less
represent from the east to the west and from the north to
the south. In past times some of the great men of the
age and erudite of the time have recorded the world
conquest and rule of Genghis Khan and his offspring at
variance with the way it happened and contrary to the
belief of the Mongol princes and commanders, but this
was due to a lack of knowledge of the history of that
time and of the magniﬁcence of those events.
However, from age to age, they have kept their true
history in Mongolian expression and script, unorga-
nized and disarranged, chapter by chapter, scattered in
treasuries, hidden from the gaze of strangers and spe-
cialists, and no one was allowed access to learn of it.
This continued until this era, when the imperial crown
and throne of Iran, which are coveted by all the rulers
ture 1:250).

of the world, were ennobled by the blessed being of the
Padishah of Islam, Sultan Mahmud Ghazan Khan—
may his kingship last forever. In his highmindedness
[35] he focused his blessed attention upon arranging
and organizing it and issued a royal decree for this ser-
vant of the Ilkhanid state, the compiler of this arrange-
ment, Fazlullah son of Abu’l-Khayr known as Rashid,
physician of Hamadan, to take the original histories and
genealogies of all the Turks who resemble the Mongols,
chapter by chapter, and arrange the tales and stories
about them that are preserved in the royal treasuries,
some of which were deposited with His Majesty’s com-
manders and courtiers. Until now no one has had access
to them altogether, and no one has had the felicity to
put them together in an arrangement, every historian
having related a bit of it without knowing the truth of
the situation, having taken it from the mouths of the
vulgar however he pleased or felt like, without any-
one’s having veriﬁed the truth. After ascertaining which
were true and sifting and poring over them, I should
organize and arrange them with polished phrases and
then publish these “precious virgin brides of history,”
which had remained veiled in obscurity until the
present. 
That of which there was only a summary, without a
detailed mention in that book, I should investigate with
the wise and learned of Cathay, India, Uyghur,
Qipchaq, and other nations since all classes and groups
of people are in attendance at His Majesty’s imperial
court. In particular [I was to consult] the grand amir,
magniﬁcent noyan, commander of Iran and Turan, ad-
ministrator
of
the
realms
of
the
world,
Bolad
Chingsang, who has no peer on the face of the inhabited
quarter of the globe in any of the various arts and crafts
or in his knowledge of the genealogy of the Turkic
tribes and their history, particularly of the Mongols.
[Then I was to compose] books of history, taking the
technical jargon and recomposing it in such a way that,
from beginning to end, it would be comprehensible and
understandable to elite and common alike, and so that
the unusual and great events and incidents that hap-
pened during the time of Mongol ascendance [36] not
be effaced or erased with the passage of time through
the months and years or remain hidden and veiled in
obscurity, for in this era no one is aware or informed of
those things, and with the passage of time youthful and
adolescent sons of lords grow unaware of the names
and titles of their fathers, grandfathers, and uncles and
of the events that occurred in times past. How can it be
proper for the offspring and descendants of the great of
every tribe not to be aware or informed of the currents
of events that enveloped their fathers or of their geneal-
ogy and names? This is particularly true of those for
whom God has decreed all sorts of favor, to whom he
has given great success in grand deeds, and in the hands
of whose will he has placed the reins of the unruly
world. He has brought under their command realms dis-
tant and near that the mightiest rulers and most power-
ful khans were never able to subdue in any era, whose
histories they had not heard, and of whose sciences they
knew nothing. Since Genghis Khan’s offspring have at-
tained this fortune and felicity, and the wise, the
learned, and historians are an integral part of His
Majesty’s court, and the realization of these things has
been possible, how can it be proper that its history re-
main neglected so that any- and everybody can speak
and write his own recounting, without knowledge or re-
search? In any case, the reviviﬁcation of the good name
of fathers and forebears and the renewal of the memory
of the words and deeds of ancestors can only be accom-
plished through chosen offspring and pleasing descen-
dants who are outstanding and selected by divine
assistance. 
By a child is a father’s name kept alive; through
children a father’s deeds remain.
When the royal command for the undertaking and
completion of this matter was issued, [37] this least of
all servants saw no option but to obey. My mind occu-
pied with learning the history of the Mongols and their
stories and legends, I exerted my utmost to comply, and
after study and research, I have organized and codiﬁed
the contents of those disarranged leaﬂets that were
found in the treasury. Everything I heard from wise
men of state who were in attendance at court and from
learned historians of every sort I adapted and veriﬁed
and then included. It will be written section by section
in clear wording so as to be easily comprehended by
different minds, and, God willing, it will be noticed by
the imperial gaze so as to cause felicity in both this
world and the next and so that this servant’s hopes and
wishes may be fulﬁlled. And God is the one who grants
success. ❧

10The Persian Chīn, essentially the same word as our
‘China,’ has several varying and distinct meanings.
When coupled with other large geographical areas of the
world, as here, it normally designates Chinese Turkistan,
Khotan &c. When Chīn is paired with Māchīn it means
the area south of the Yellow River, the realm of the
Southern Song, while Māchīn is south of the Yangtze,
the area also called Manzī. For China north of the Yel-
low River the term Khitāy is used in Persian, for which
we will employ the derivative Cathay. The term original-
ly designated the territory of the Khitai, or Khitan; but
since it continued to be used in Persian to designate the
area around Peking long after the disappearance of the
Khitai, we will use the Anglicized term, which has the
advantage of being similarly vague and impossible to
confuse with any modern nation state.
11Throughout Jami‘u’t-tawarikh, the term Rūm (de-
rived from ‘Ρώµη via the Syriac !"ܪܗܘ) indicates the
lands that were then, or had formerly been, part of the
Byzantine Empire (East Rome). Although it is more a
political designation than a geographical one, Rūm basi-
cally indicates Anatolia (Asia Minor)—exclusive of up-
per Mesopotamia, which is called Diyarbekir—and, for
Rashiduddin anyway, includes Constantinople. The au-
thor of Taqwīm al-buldān, Abu’l-Fida (1273–1331),
who was the prince of Hama and could be expected to
know exactly what was meant by the term bilād al-Rūm
in his own day, defines the “land of Rūm” as bounded
on the west by the Mediterranean and the Sea of Mar-
mara, on the south by Syria and Mesopotamia, on the
east by Armenia, and on the north by Georgia and the
Black Sea (Taqwim, 378). Thus, to the east Malatya and
Erzurum are included in Rūm, but the Amid (modern
Diyarbakır)–Raqqa–Mosul triangle is in Mesopotamia.
The term Rūm will be translated throughout as Anatolia
unless absolutely unavoidable.

Oghuz Khan’s uncles Or Khan, Kür Khan,
and Küz Khan, and his brothers and their sons
who did not join Oghuz divided into two
branches. One separated so long ago that its di-
visions are not known in detail. The other is
known in detail.
The nations whose origins are so ancient
that their divisions are not known in detail
[43] The first division consists of the nations
who are now called Mongols but whose name
was not originally Mongol since this word was
coined after their time. Every division of these
nations became numerous divisions, and each
has a characteristic name: Jalayir, Sönit, Tatar,
Märkit, Kürlü’üt, Töläs, Tumat, Bulaghachin,
Kärämüchin, Orasut, Tamghaliq, Targhut, Oyi-
rat, Barghut, Qori, Talangut, Kästimi, Urianqa,
Quriqat, and Saqayit.
The second division consists of nations, also
dwellers in the wilderness, that have become
like the above-mentioned nations but have only
recently been called Mongols. This group is
numerous and consists of innumerable tribes.
The names of some of the tribes and subdivi-
sions that have been found will be given in de-
tail later. They are the Kerayit, Naiman,
Öng’üt, Tangqut, Bäkrin, and Qirqiz.
The tribes of whom it is known that they
originated with two persons who went to
Ärgänä-qun and begat and multiplied are
known generically by the word Mongol, as are
others who resemble them. In short, the begin-
ning of the usage of this word was during their
time. The Mongols were one of the Turkic na-
tions, and since they were favored by divine
grace, numerous branches of them appeared
over a period of nearly four hundred years, and
they outnumbered all other nations. Because of
their prestige, others in the area became known
by their name, since most Turks are called
Mongols, [44] as happened before when the
Tatars were dominant and all were called Tatar.
Among the Arabs, Indians, and Cathaians they
are still known as Tatars. 
The original Mongols gradually divided into
two groups. As for the first branch, each of the
branches that appeared from the original Mon-
gols who were in Ärgänä-qun took a particular
name and epithet and emerged from Ärgänä-
qun. They were the Nüküz, Uriangqat, Qunqi-
rat,
Kilungghut,
Qirjin,
[H]ushin,
Suldus,
Ildürkin, Oriyat, Qongqotan, Arulat, Ikiräs,
Olqunu’ut,
Qorolas,
Eljigin,
Qongli’ut,
Baya’ut, and Kinggiyat.

that branched off from Dobun Bayan’s wife

Alan Qoa was of the Qorolas tribe. These
tribes consist of two divisions, as follows.

❦ CHAPTER ONE
THE HISTORY AND STORIES OF THE NATIONS OF OGHUZ AND THE TWENTY-
FOUR BRANCHES OF HIS SONS AND THEIR OFFSPRING AND OF SOME OF HIS
BROTHERS AND COUSINS WHO JOINED HIM
rom them came into existence the
nations of the Uyghur, the Qipchaq,
the Qanqli, the Qarluq, and the
Qalach. According to what is unan-
imously narrated by their own wise
men and in accordance with what is mentioned
in Islamic histories and recorded in the Torah
of the Israelites, where it is said that the
prophet Noah divided the earth into three divi-
sions from south to north, the first division he
gave to his son Ham, who became the father of
the blacks; the middle part he gave to Shem,
who was the father of the Arabs and the Per-
sians; and the third part he gave to Japheth,
who was the father of the Turks and was sent
to the east. The Mongols and Turks say the
same, but the Turks’ name for Japheth is Abul-
ja Khan, and they do not know for certain
whether Abulja Khan was a son or a grandson
of Noah, but they are agreed that he was of his
progeny and near to him in time. They are also
agreed that all the Mongols, various types of
Turks, and nomads are descended from him.
They explain this as follows: Abulja Khan was
a nomad, and his summer pastures were at Or
Tagh and Kür Tagh,1 [48] which are huge, high
mountains. In the vicinity is a city named
Ipanch.2 His winter quarters were also in that
1Or Taq and Kür Taq probably refer to the modern
Karatau mountains in Kazakhstan and the Talasskiy
Alatau mountains in Kyrgyzstan.
2Readingﺎﱋ ــﯾﭙ ا(Ipanch) with Togan (Oguz Destanı, 17)
for JTRM’sﺎﱋ ـ ـﯾﻨ ا. Spelledﺞ ـ ـ ـﯾﻔﻨ, it is defined by Kashghari
vicinity, in a place called Borsuq, Qaqiyan, and
Qarqorum (also called Qaraqorum).3 The cities
of Talas and Qari Sayram are also in the vicini-
ty.4 Qari Sayram is an ancient, large, and mag-
nificent city. Those who have seen it say that it
is a one-day journey from beginning to end and
that it has forty gates. At present it is inhabited
by Muslim Turks. It belongs to Qaidu and to
the ulus of Qonchi. The place where his sons
reside is nearby.
Abulja Khan had a son named Dib Baqui—
dib means throne-place and locus of high of-
fice, and baqui means the great chieftain of a
tribe.5 This child was even more splendid than
his father, and he had four sons named Qara
(Compendium 2:341) as a “city near Ila.” Togan (Oguz
Destanı, 81) places it near the modern Ayaguz in Kaza-
khstan, west of Lake Zaysan.
3Togan (Oguz Destanı, 81) identifies the Borsuq desert
in Kazakhstan. “Qaqiyan” is unidentified. “Qaraqorum”
is not, of course, the Qaraqorum in Mongolia that was
Ögödäi Qa’an’s capital but another place of the same
name. Qorum means a large rock or massive pile of
rocks, and qara qorum means a large black rock, a com-
mon topographical appellation.
4Qari Sayram (“Old Sayram”) is Sayram. For it and
for Talas, see notes 4 and 5 to text p. 40 above.
5Togan (Oguz Destanı, 82) speculates that the “Dib”
part of the name is derived from the Sanskrit dev deva.
The “Baqui” part of the name is almost certainly a gar-
bled version of yavquy or yabquy for yabghu, a title of
great antiquity (see Clauson, Etymological Dictionary,
873). I have left “Baqui” as is because it occurs in this
form in so many texts that to tamper with it would con-
stitute hypercorrection.

Khan, Or Khan, Kür Khan, and Küz Khan.1 All
of those nations were heathens. Qara Khan
succeeded his father, and he had a son who
would not take his mother’s breast to suckle
for three days and nights. This caused his
mother to weep and plead, and every night she
saw the child saying to her in a dream, “Moth-
er, if you become a worshipper and lover of
God, I will drink your milk.” Because her hus-
band and all of the tribes were heathens, the
woman feared that if she worshipped God
openly they would kill both her and her child.
Therefore she believed in God in secret and
loved God with all sincerity, and thereafter the
infant took his mother’s breast and suckled.
When a year had passed, the child was ex-
tremely pure and beautiful, and traces of reli-
gious guidance and favor shone from his brow.
When his father perceived these things in him,
he said, “No child from our nation has ever
been born with such a form and shape. [49]
This boy will stand out among his peers and
will achieve perfection.” He then consulted his
relatives concerning the child’s name, but the
one-year-old child spoke and said, “Name me
Oghuz.” Those present were astonished; and
on account of the words he spoke, which indi-
cated God’s guidance, they named him Oghuz.
When he reached maturity, his father, Qara
Khan, selected for him one of his cousins, a
daughter of Küz Khan and an extremely beau-
1Of these four, the names of Qara Khan and Or Khan
are certain. The other two, our “Kür Khan” and “Küz
Khan” for lack of anything more certain, are spelledﺮ ــــــﮐ
andﮐـﺰin JTK; Togan (Oguz Destanı, 17) also spells them
this way; the Russian translators (JTSL1/1:81) give Кара-
хан, Ор-хан, Коз-хан, and Гур-хан; in the Ottoman
translation (JTYZ), they are spelledﻮن ــﮐandﻮر ــﮐ, probably
to be read as Gün and Gür respectively. Gün Khan, one
of Oghuz’s sons, comes later; Gür Khan is probably the
result of a confusion with the Gür Khan title of the
Qarakhitai rulers.
tiful and chaste girl. In secret Oghuz said to the
girl, “If you become a worshipper of God and a
lover of the truth, I will love you and be close
to you.” She thought this extremely strange
and refused, saying, “I will tell your father to
destroy you.” Therefore Oghuz paid no atten-
tion to her. When his father saw that he did not
love her, he chose another of his brother Küz
Khan’s daughters for him. When she was taken
to Oghuz, he spoke the same words to her. She
too refused to believe in God. Oghuz did not
love her either and would not go to her. 
When Qara Khan saw that Oghuz was disin-
clined to this girl too, he married him to a
daughter of his other brother, Or Khan. She
had not yet been brought to his tent when one
day Oghuz was returning from the hunt and
saw Or Khan’s daughter beside a river watch-
ing her maids washing clothes. Oghuz ap-
proached her and said to her in secret, “You
know I have taken two of my cousins, but I do
not love them and have no converse with them.
I wanted them to believe in God and love Him,
but they refused to listen and disbelieve. [50]
Now I have been married to you. If you con-
fess the oneness of God and believe in and
love Him, I will take you and love you.”
“I do not know who or what God is,” the girl
replied, “but I will not disobey you.”
“That is all I desire,” said Oghuz, “and I
command that you believe in God and love
Him.”
“I accept your words,” she said, and she be-
lieved in God.
After that, Oghuz took her and loved her, al-
ways going to her and not to the others. Since
he believed in God, he did not want to mingle
with his father and uncles because they were
heathens. Therefore he continually remained
away from them and hunted separately from
them. He constantly had the name of God,
which is Allah in Arabic, on his lips, but no
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER ONE
23

one knew what the word meant. While he con-
stantly intoned beautifully the word Allah, the
tribe thought he was singing for pleasure and
that it had become a habit with him.
One day Qara Khan gave a banquet for his
daughters-in-law and asked them, “Since the
first two wives are nicer than the third, why is
it that my son loves her more and goes to her
and converses with her while he pays no atten-
tion to the others?”
Since the first two wives were unhappy with
their husband and extremely jealous, they
seized the opportunity to get back at their hus-
band by saying, “He has adopted another reli-
gion and believes in and loves the god of heav-
en and earth. He wanted us to join him, but we
refused and paid no attention to his words.
That is why he is on bad terms with us. This
latest wife has joined him in believing in God,
[51] and that is why he loves her and hates us.”
At that time Oghuz was out hunting with his
liege men and some of his friends. Qara Khan
gathered his brothers, nephews, relatives, and
commanders and said, “My son Oghuz seemed
greatly favored by fortune in his infancy, and I
was extremely fond of him. Now, however, he
has taken up wicked ways and turned his back
on our religion. He cannot be left alive.” All
present were pained by these words, but they
unanimously agreed that he should be put to
death. When Oghuz’s wife who supported her
husband learned of this, she immediately sent a
neighbor woman she trusted to warn him.
Oghuz got ready for battle by summoning all
his liege men and friends, and they gathered in
the hunting field. His father, uncles, and rela-
tives mounted to attack him, ranks were ar-
rayed on both sides, and battle broke out. Dur-
ing the fighting Qara Khan was struck with a
sword and died of his wounds. Because a large
contingent of his fellow tribesmen and uncles
had joined him, they fought with each other for
nearly seventy-five years and cast the nation
and army into strife and turmoil. Finally Oghuz
triumphed, seizing the land from Talas and
Sayram to Bukhara, and the realm submitted to
him. Some of his uncles and nephews who had
joined him made their habitation in the east,
and in their view it is established that the
entirety of the Mongols are descended from
them. At that time all were heathens, but with
the passage of time they and their families too
became monotheists. 
When Oghuz took over that realm and en-
joyed sovereignty, he pitched a golden tent and
gave a large banquet at which he honored his
relatives [52] and commanders and rewarded
all the soldiers. The group of his uncles and
clansmen who had joined him he named
Uyghur, the meaning of which in Turkish is to
unite and assist. All the tribes of the Uyghur
are descended from them. He named another
tribe
Qanqli.
The
Qipchaq,
Qalach,
and
Aghacheri tribes also spring from the group
who were with Oghuz and married into his
family. The reason for the naming of each will
now be given in detail.
The Uyghur.
When the dispute broke out between Oghuz
and his father and uncles over the worship of
God and they began fighting, some of Oghuz’s
relatives united with him, taking his part and
giving him assistance. Some others took sides
with the father, uncles, and brothers. Those
who joined and helped Oghuz he called
uyghur, a Turkic word meaning “having joined
and helped us.” This group was constantly with
Oghuz. When he set out to take other realms he
sent them back through the Darband area,
where they settled down to protect that land
until he should return. All the Uyghur tribes
are descended from this group.1
1See Clauson, “The Name Uygur,” JRAS (1963): 147.
24
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The Qanqli.
At the time Oghuz was fighting his father,
uncles, brothers, and cousins and raiding the
province, these were among the tribes that
joined him. While others were pillaging and
carrying their plunder on animals, these used
their minds to devise carts to carry their plun-
der. [53] Since a cart is called qanqli in Turk-
ish, they were given this name.1 All the Qan-
qlis spring from them.
The Qipchaq.
When Oghuz was defeated by the It-Baraq
tribe, with whom he did battle, and took up
residence on a spit of land between two rivers,
a pregnant woman whose husband had been
killed in battle went into a large hollow tree
and gave birth. When this was reported to
Oghuz, he had compassion on her and said,
“Since this woman has no husband, let the
child be my son.” And he became like Oghuz’s
own son. He called him Qipchaq, a name de-
rived from qobuq, which means a hollow tree
in Turkish. All the Qipchaqs descend from this
boy. Eighteen years later Oghuz raided the It-
Baraq tribe, came to the land of Iran, and sub-
dued that realm. After many years he returned
to his province. It was reported that the It-
Baraqis had rebelled again, so he dispatched
Qipchaq’s family to settle among the It-Baraq
and the Yayaq so that he would be secure from
their
rebelliousness.
From
that
time
the
Qipchaqs’ summer and winter pastures have
been there.
The Qarluq.
It is said that when Oghuz was returning
from the province of Ghor and Ghoristan to his
old territory, along the way he came to a large
mountain and it was snowing hard. On account
1Qanqli, qangli, and qanghli are all attested as variant
spellings of a word meaning cart.
of the snow several households lagged behind.
Since it had been ordered that no one should
lag behind, Oghuz was displeased and said,
“How can anyone lag behind because of
snow?” He called those households qarluq, that
is, those of the snow (qar). [54] All the Qarluq
tribes sprang from this group.
The Qalach.
It is said that when Oghuz had taken Isfahan
and was on his return journey, a woman gave
birth to a child along the way, but she was so
malnourished that she had no milk, and the
child was hungry. Her husband therefore re-
mained behind. A jackal had caught a par-
tridge, and the man threw a stick at it, took the
bird, and gave it to his wife to eat. Her breasts
then filled with milk, and she nursed the child
until it was full. Several days later the man
reached the army, and since it had been or-
dered that no one was to lag behind for any
reason, Oghuz was vexed and said, “Qal,
ach”—that is, “Stay, hungry one”—for which
reason his family was called Qalach.
The Aghacheri.
This name did not exist long ago. When the
Oghuz tribes came to this realm, a group of
them who held territory in forested areas be-
came known as aghach eri, that is, man of the
forest, just as some of the Mongol tribes whose
territory is near a forest are called hoyun irgän,
which means forest people.
∂
The Turcomans who were with Oghuz are
those that have been mentioned. Although at
first he named all the tribes that were allied
with him “Uyghur,” later several tribes were
distinguished by other names for reasons men-
tioned. The name Uyghur stuck with the oth-
ers, and that is how they became known. 
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER ONE
25

From Oghuz’s offspring there came into ex-
istence twenty-four branches, as recorded in
detail in the list, each with its own name and
epithet. All the Turcomans in the world are de-
scended from this nation [55] and are the off-
spring of Oghuz’s twenty-four offspring. 
The word Turcoman did not exist long ago,
for all the tribes who dwelt in the wilderness
and looked like Turks were called simply
Turks, each tribe having its own particular epi-
thet. When the Oghuz tribes left their own ter-
ritory and went into Transoxiana and Iran and
begat and multiplied, because of the climate
their features gradually changed into those of
Tajiks. Since they were not Tajiks, the Tajik
peoples called them turkmān, i.e. Turk-like
(turk-mānand). For this reason this name was
applied to all the branches of the Oghuz peo-
ples, and that is how they became known. Of
the twenty-four branches of Oghuz’s offspring,
half belong to the right wing of the army, and
the other half belong to the left wing. Today
each of these tribes knows with which people
its branch originated. 
Oghuz had six sons. Their names are Gün,
Ay, Yulduz, Gök, Taq, and Dengiz.1 In a later
appendix to this history I shall give the details
of them as it has come in their own histories.
Oghuz conquered the totality of the realms of
Iran, Turan, Syria, Egypt, Anatolia, and the
Franks, as well as other lands. After having
subdued them all, he turned back to his origi-
nal territory of Or Tagh and Kür Tagh. When
he arrived there he held a great assembly, at
which he had extremely fine golden tents
pitched, and made a huge banquet. It is related
that nine hundred mares and ninety thousand
[56] sheep were slaughtered for the banquet.
All the khans, commanders, and leaders of the
1Gün, ‘sun’; ay, ‘moon’; yulduz, ‘star’; gök, ‘sky’; taq
~ tagh ‘mountain’; dengiz, ‘sea.’
army were invited, and he rewarded them all
well. In particular he singled out for honor his
six sons, who had been with their father during
his
conquests
and
had
made
outstanding
showings.
Several days later his sons went hunting.
They found a golden bow and three golden ar-
rows, which they took to their father, asking
how they should be divided. He gave the bow
to the elder three sons and the three arrows to
the younger three, saying, “The nations who
spring from those who hold the bow shall be
known as Buzuq”—which means to break.2
This word became their epithet because it was
necessary to break the bow to divide it. The
right hand of the army would then belong to
these three and their families. He made the epi-
thet of the tribes that sprang from the sons to
whom he gave the arrows Üchoq—originally
üch oq, meaning three arrows—saying, “The
army of the left hand will belong to these three
sons
and
their
offspring.”
He
also
said,
“Henceforth their offspring shall be known by
these epithets, and let each one know to which
side of the army he belongs.” Since the right
wing was larger, he gave the bow, which is a
symbol of kingship, to them, while he gave the
arrows, which are symbols of subservience, to
those who were of the left hand. He also divid-
ed all the territories of the right and left hands
in this manner, saying, “The royal throne and
the succession to me belong to the Buzuq. Af-
ter me the rule will go to Gün, my eldest son, if
he is alive. If not, it will go to my second son,
Ay.” [57]
After Oghuz’s death, in accordance with his
will, Gün Khan ascended the throne and ruled
for seventy years. His father had had a viceroy
2Buzuq actually means ‘broken.’ Some modern inter-
pretations take the word to be buz-oq by analogy with
üch-oq, but the meaning given makes it certain that
buzuq is intended.
26

named Irqil Khoja of Yangikent,1 and he was
Gün Khan’s advisor and minister too. One day
he said to Gün Khan, “Oghuz was a great king.
He seized the realms of the earth and possessed
treasuries, property, and animals without num-
ber. He left it all to you, his sons, and each of
you has been divinely blessed with four sons.
May it not be that henceforth your sons fight
and squabble over property and land. It would
be best for each of them to have separate posts,
routes, names and epithets. Let each have a
sign and a device by which their decrees,
stores, herds and flocks may be distinguished
in order that none dispute with another. Let
each of your sons and their descendants have
his own name and epithet and his own way in
order to insure the permanence of their good
fortune and the continuance of their renown.”
Gün Khan approved of this suggestion, and
Igit Irqil Khwaja set about making arrange-
ments. After each of the six sons had adopted
the names Buzuq or Üchoq and had been as-
signed to the right or left wing of the army, he
1According to Togan (Oguz Destanı, p. 96, note 537a),
Irqil Khoja is a legendary sage among the Buryats and
Yakut-Sakas.
established anew the names, devices, and signs
of each of their sons. To each of the twenty-
four he assigned an animal to be their totem
(onqun). This word is derived from inaq,2
meaning “blessed” in Turkish, as they say inaq
bolsun, meaning “may it be blessed.” It is
customary for the totem of a tribe, since it is
used as a symbol of auspiciousness, not to be
hunted or harmed or for the flesh to be eaten.
Until now this is observed, [58] and each of the
tribes knows its own totem. He also stipulated,
when there was a banquet and food was being
distributed, which piece of meat should go to
which branch so that, no matter where they
were, at a banquet the portion of each was de-
cided and they would not fight with each other
over food.
The names of the twenty-four sons, by which
names the tribes and branches became known
and which became the proper names of the
tribes, will be given along with the device, the
totem, and the piece of meat assigned to each.

Inasmuch as the stories and histories of these
will be given separately in an appendix to this
royal history, there is no sense in going on at
length here. These tribes, as has been ex-
plained, were all monotheistic, [62] and God
had willed during the time of the prophethood
of the Lord of Apostles, our Prophet Muham-
mad the Chosen, that they be annexed to the
Muslims, and in the end it so happened. For
long eons and many years after Oghuz and his
sons there were many rulers from this nation,
and in every era there have mighty sovereigns
from
the
twenty-four
branches
mentioned
above in whose family the rule remained. For a
long time the rule was in the Salur branch;
thereafter it was in the Äymür branch, and then
other branches became mighty sovereigns, as
will be told in the history of the Oghuz in the
appendix to this history. Their domination
reached this land of Iran, and in this realm
there are many renowned sovereigns and great
commanders from the Oghuz family, but not
everyone knows that he is descended from
Oghuz. The Turcomans know precisely which
ruler and which commander is from which
branch of these tribes. The sultans of the
Seljuq dynasty and their forebears, who were
great and mighty sovereigns and ruled in the
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER ONE
29

realms of Turan and Iran for nearly four
hundred years, having brought from the far-
thest reaches of Egypt to the borders of Cathay
under their sway, were from the Qiniq branch.
A summary account of their history will also
be appended to the history of the Oghuz at the
end of this book.
Inasmuch as the Uyghurs are also Turks, and
their habitation is near the realm of the Mon-
gols, and they have been mentioned in this his-
tory as being cousins of Oghuz, they too merit
a history, some of which will be given in the
appendix. Likewise will be given the histories
of the nations of Khitai, Qarakhitai, Chin and
Machin (which the Mongols call Nankiyas and
the people of Cathay call Manzi),1 the Jurchids,

that did not reach this land in ancient times,
now that we have become aware of them, we
wanted to add them to this history, but since to

them and given them separately in an appendix

❦ CHAPTER TWO
THE TURKIC NATIONS THAT ARE NOW CALLED MONGOLS BUT IN TIMES PAST
WERE SEPARATE NATIONS, EACH WITH ITS OWN LANGUAGE AND NAME
ach of these nations had a leader
and a commander, and from each
of them branched off tribes and
clans, like the Jalayir, the Oyirat,
the Tatar, &c., as will be explained
in this chapter. Their yurts (grazing grounds)
and dwelling places were in designated areas,
and their features and language resembled
those of the Mongols, for at that time the Mon-
gol branch was one of the Turkic nations,
whereas now, because of their great fortune,
might, and magnificence, all the other nations
have been subsumed under the name Mongol.
The histories of these nations are as follows.
The Jalayir nation and their branches, along
with some of the history connected to this
nation that lies outside the history of
Genghis Khan and other histories.
In ancient times these tribes were many, and
each branch [66] had its own commander and
leader. During Genghis Khan’s time, and in
this time too, there have been and are many
commanders from among them in Turan and
Iran. Their dwelling place was the Onon, and it
is related that in olden times the army of
Cathay so massacred that place that few were
able to escape. When they took flight, they
killed Monolun, the wife of Dutum Mänen, as
will be told in her story.1 The other tribes of the
Jalayir held a trial and asked why they had
committed such a horrible deed. Some of them
were put to death, and others were imprisoned
1See below, text p. 229f.
and made slaves to Qaidu Khan, the son of Du-
tum Mänen, and his sons and relatives. By in-
heritance they came to Genghis Khan’s father,
and by that means these tribes were his ötägü
boghol,2 and many of them became important
and respected commanders during his and his
dynasty’s time, as will be explained.
The Jalayir nation consists of ten large divi-
sions, each of which has become a separate
and numerous tribe: (1) Jat, (2) Toqra’ut, (3)
Qongqa’ut, (4) Kümsä’üt, (5) Oyat, (6) Nilqan,
(7) Kürkin, (8) Tolangqit, (9) Büri, (10)
Sungqut.
The most famous and greatest of all the
Jalayir tribes in Genghis Khan’s time was
Muqali Guyang of the Jat tribe, who was in
charge of the entire left wing of Genghis
Khan’s army.3 His sons are also called by the
epithet Guyang, which means great khan in the
Cathaian language.4 When Genghis Khan sta-
2For the term ötägü boghol (‘hereditary slaves,’
thought to be a loan translation from the Chinese), see

Amir Burtas, a commander of a thousand, is

Another commander in Genghis Khan’s time

Among the commanders of a thousand of the

Muqali Guyang’s brother, Taisun by name,1

The Sönit Nation
The tribe called the Qabturghas2 are a sub-di-
vision of the Sönit. There have been few of the
Qabturghas in this realm, although there are a
few slaves the Mongols have brought from the
uluses of the Qa’an, Qaidu, and Toqtai.
There have been many officers from the
Sönit nation. During Genghis Khan’s time,
there was Chormaqan,3 his qorchi, and after
Genghis Khan’s death when Börkä, Jäbä, and
Sübätäi came to Iran and returned via the
Temür Qahalqa (Iron Gates), they went to
Ögödäi Qa’an’s presence and made obeisance.
He outfitted Chormaqan with four tümäns of
tamma troops and dispatched them here. (A
tamma troop is one singled out, detached from
units of a thousand and a hundred, and sent to
a region where they are stationed.) Several
great regiment and tümän commanders came
with him, but since they were of other lines of
descent, they will be mentioned under those
branches; however, since this officer’s story is
exceptional we will give it in detail where he is
mentioned.
A tümän commander of this army was Baiju
Noyan of the Besüt tribe, a relative of Jäbä’s.

When Chormaqan died, the Qa’an appointed
Baiju in his stead. When Hülägü Khan arrived
in this land, Baiju Noyan made valiant efforts
in the taking of Baghdad, for which he was
promoted to the rank of tümän commander. Af-
ter his death his son Adak was awarded his fa-
ther’s tümän, and when Adak died, Arghun
Khan awarded some of his tümän to Qayatai
Boralghi and some to Ghazan of the Jalayir
tribe, Eshik Tughli’s elder brother. After them,
Gaikhatu gave it to Inabeg, the brother of the
aforementioned Ghazan. When he colluded
with Sögä, the Padishah of Islam had him exe-
cuted and gave the army to Adak’s son
Sülämish. [74] When he rebelled he was exe-
cuted,1 and his regiment was transferred to
Toqachar and others.
Another
tümän
commander
was
Yäkä
Yisa’ur of the Qorolas tribe. During Genghis
Khan’s time he was a very important comman-
der and maintained naqachu’i with him.2 When
they came to this realm he retained his tümän
for a long time, and after him his son Khwaja
Noyan took his place. Khwaja Noyan’s sons
were Tona and Mulaghar, both of whom were
commanders of regiments; and Tona’s sons
were Turatu Gürägän, Barula, and Qurumshi.
They were executed because they rebelled with
the officers after Arghun Khan’s time.
Another tümän commander was Malikshah,
to whom was given a company made up of
Uyghurs, Qarluqs, Turcomans, Kashgharis, and
men from Kucha. When he died his position
was given to his son Hinduchaq. He killed the
malik of Qum without provocation, and for
that reason Amir Arghun had him executed at
the gates of Tus by order of Mänggü Qa’an,
1For the execution of Sülämish, see text p. 1289.

and his tents were divided among the urughs of

Beg, was assigned to his position. When Ket
Buqa was killed in battle in Egypt, Salar Beg

Of the regimental commanders who came

Another was Äskä Noyan, after whose death

was captured by the Egyptians during Tödö’än
and Tuqu’s battle and taken to Anatolia.
Another officer was the junior Chaghatai.
When [Genghis Khan’s son] Chaghatai was no
longer living, his name became taboo, and
thereafter [this one] was called Sönitäi because
he was of the Sönit nation. In the beginning he
was a regimental commander. When Tagha-
char’s father, Qutu Buqa, died, his position was
given to Sönitäi, whose sons were Emgächin
Bahadur and Taghai. Emgächin’s sons were
Boralghi and Tai Buqa. Boralghi’s sons were
Jibrail and Mikail. When Sönitäi died his post
was given to Hulqutu Qorchi of the Mangqut
tribe, the uncle of Qutlughshah Noyan. In

and the Padishah of Islam gave it to Aldu.
There were many other commanders from
the Sönit nation. For instance, during Genghis
Khan’s time there was an officer named Temür
who had a brother named El Temür who was a
ba’urchi in the ordu of Genghis Khan’s chief
wife, the mother of the four sons, Börtä Füjin.
He was commander of a company of a hundred
in her personal thousand. Also during his time
there was a commander of the right wing
named Ögäläi Chärbi and one of the left wing
named
Tämüdär
Noyan,
Genghis
Khan’s
qorchi. He had an extremely tall and graceful
son who, during Mänggü Qa’an’s time, was
called Mubarak Qorchi, and there was a bit of
weakness and languor in his nature for which
he was known. Emgächin and Buqadai Aqtachi
were relatives of Tämüdär Noyan’s. [76] The
Elügän Jasa’ul who was in Abaqa Khan’s time
was of the Sönit nation. This is all that is
presently known. 
The Tatar Nation
Their name has been famous throughout the
world since ancient times. Many lines of them
have branched out, and the total of this nation
was
seventy
thousand
households.
Their
dwelling place and yurts, separate tribe by tribe
and branch by branch, were well delineated
and near the territories of Cathay. The yurt for
which they were especially known was a place
called Bu’ir Na’ur.1 At most times they have
been in obedience and paid tribute to the rulers
of Cathay, although they have rebelled in every
age, and rulers of Cathay have mounted armies
against them to bring them back into submis-
sion. They have also disputed and quarrelled
with each other, and there was war among
these tribes for many long years. At the time
the Tatars were allied with the Dörbän, Salji’ut,
1For the Bu’ir Na’ur, see note to text p. 40.
and Qataqin, they all dwelt below certain rivers
that become the Angara when they join. The
Angara is an extremely large river, and a tribe
of Mongols called Usutu Mangqun live there.
That area presently belongs to them. The river
is near a city called Qataqas. Where this river
and the Käm2 river join is part of Qirqiz territo-
ry. It is reported that this river goes to a
province near which is a sea of silver. [77] The
name of that territory is Alaqchin Adutan
Mänggü Bala’urnan. All their horses are said to
be ala (dappled). Every horse has the body of a
four-year-old camel. All their implements and
vessels are of silver. There are many birds
there. Sorghaqtani Beki sent three commanders
there, Tongqaliq of the Güchügür clan, Bäkchü
of the Qara’ut, and Mungqur Jätä of the ___
clan, with a thousand men in a ship. They
brought much silver back to the shore, but they
couldn’t put it in the ship. Not more than three
hundred men of that troop returned: the rest
perished from the putrid air and excessive
dampness. All three commanders came back
safely and lived long.
They are especially known for wielding
knives, and at the slightest provocation they
stab each other and use their swords without
remorse, like the Kurds, Shul,3 and Franks. The
law that exists among the Mongols now did not
exist in their time, and vengeance, wrath, and
envy were dominant in their natures.
With their great numbers, if they had agreed
with one another and not fought, neither the
Cathaians nor any other creature could have
withstood them, and even though there was
constant enmity and rancor among them, in an-
cient times they were usually dominant over
2See note to text p. 143 below.
3The Shul are the inhabitants of Shulistan, a region al-
ways mentioned in conjunction with either Kurdistan or
Luristan. It is the present-day Mamasani in Iran. See text
pp. 507.

most nations of the region. Because of the glo-
ry, might, and respect they commanded, other
types of Turks, in all their variety and names,
made themselves known by their name, and all
were called Tatar. Indeed they considered it an
honor to call themselves Tatar, just as at
present,
because
of
the
great
fortune
of
Genghis Khan and his urugh, because they are
Mongols, other tribes of Turks like the Jalayir,
Tatar, Oyirat, [78] Öng’üt, Kerayit, Naiman,
Tangqut, &c., each of which has its own spe-
cial name and sobriquet, all are proud to call
themselves Mongol. Whereas before they used
to deride this name, now their sons imagine
that they have been known as Mongols from
long ago, although it is not so. In ancient times,
the Mongols were but one of all the tribes of
nomadic Turks, but divine favor shone upon
them, meaning that Genghis Khan and his
urugh were to be of the Mongol race and many
branches of them would come into existence.
Particularly from the time of Alan Qo’a on,
which has been three hundred years more or
less, many branches have appeared that are
called the Niru’un clans, and they have ac-
quired prominence and glory. They have all be-
come known as the Mongol nation. At that
time the other tribes were not called Mongol,
but since they were close to one another in
terms of shape, form, vocabulary, accent, cus-
toms and manners, regardless of the difference
in dialect and customs that had existed in an-
cient times, now it has come about that peoples
of Cathay, Jurcha, Nankiyas, Uyghur, Qipchaq,
Turcoman, Qarluq, Qalach, and all the prison-
ers and Tajik races that have been brought up
among the Mongols are also called Mongols.
All that assemblage takes pride in calling itself
Mongol. Prior to this, because of the strength
and glory of the Tatars, the same thing hap-
pened, and that is why all Turkic peoples are
still called “Tatar” in the realms of Cathay,
Hindustan, Chin and Machin, the lands of the
Qirqiz, Kilar-Bashghurd, the Qipchaq Steppe,
the territories of the north, the Arab peoples,
Syria, Egypt, and North Africa.
The tribes of the Tatar are well known and
famous there, and each separately had an army
and a ruler. [79]
They consist of six tribes, as follows: Tu-
tuqli’ut Tatar, Alchi Tatar, Chaghan Tatar,
Küyin Tatar, Ayira’ut Tatar, and Buruqui Tatar.1
The Tutuqli’ut tribe is the most important of
the Tatar tribes. It is customary for every male
of this tribe to be called Tutuqlitai, and for
every female to be called Tutuqlijin. Among
the Alchi Tatar they are called Alchitai and
Alchiyin. Among the Küyin they are called
Küyitäi and Küyijin. Among the Ayira’ut they
are called Ayiratai and Ayirajin.
Although these tribes had often fought with
each other and were constantly killing, plun-
dering, and pillaging one another, it so hap-
pened that war broke out between them and the
Mongol tribes. Then they united [because]
there was an old blood feud between the [two
groups]. The reason for it is as follows. During
Qabul Khan’s time, the khan of the cream of
the Mongols from whose family come most of
the Qiyat clans, and the Niru’un Mongol clans,
the Niru’un Mongols, his collaterals, and the
other branches of the Mongols, who prior to
him each had its own special name and epithet,
were all uncles and forebears of his. They all
united to help him in the name of kinship and

friendship during his difficulties. It happened
that Sayin Tegin, a brother of Qo’a Qulqu of
the Qunqirat clan, Qabul Khan’s wife, was ill,
and a shaman from the Tatar nation named
Jorqul Bödöi was summoned to treat him. He
came and treated him, but Sayin Tegin died.
The [Qungirat] made a pact with the shaman
and sent him home. After that, Sayin Tegin’s
elder and younger brothers went and killed the
shaman Jorqul. Therefore a feud arose between
the Tatar nation and them. By virtue of being
blood brothers and allies to Sayin Tegin, it was
necessary for Qabul Khan’s sons to assist his
clans. [80] That is why dispute and war broke
out between them. Many times battles were
fought, and every time any on either side had a
chance they killed and pillaged each other.
This feud lasted many years. Once, in the be-
ginning, the Tatar captured Hambaqai Khan,
one of the rulers and chiefs of the Tayichi’ut
clans, the families of which were collaterals
and therefore related to Qabul Khan, as was
stated in that section. They sent Hambaqai
Qa’an to the king of Cathay, the Altan Khan,
since they knew that he had been offended by
and harbored an old hatred of Qabul Khan be-
cause he had killed the Altan Khan’s emis-
saries and liege men, as will be told, and be-
cause of the attacks made by him and the
Mongols, who were relatives of his and united
with him, while the Tatars were obedient fol-
lowers [of the Altan Khan]. They also under-
took this audacious act because of the old ha-
tred and enmity they had for him. [When] the
king of Cathay ordered Hambaqai Khan to be
nailed to a wooden donkey with iron spikes, he
said, “Others captured me. It is not appropriate
or right for you, and it is unchivalrous, to com-
mit such a heinous act against me. The Mongol
tribes, all of which are related to me, will rise
up in revenge, and your kingdom will suffer
thereby.” The Altan Khan paid no attention and
had Hambaqai Khan nailed to the wooden don-
key and killed. He gave one of Hambaqai
Khan’s liege men named Bolghajai leave to go
and take the bad news to the Mongol nation.
After that, Qutula Khan took to war an army of
Mongols against the king of Cathay and plun-
dered the country. This story will be told in the
section on Qabul Khan.1 [81]
Another time the Tatars captured Ökin Bar-
qaq, Qabul Khan’s eldest son and ancestor of
the Qiyat clans, and sent him to the Altan
Khan, who had him killed too by being nailed
to a wooden donkey. Until the time of Genghis
Khan [these nations] were perpetually at war
with each other, and on both sides they at-
tacked, killed, and pillaged each other. Finally,
as will be told in the section on Genghis Khan
and his family, he fed all the Tatar tribes and
the kings of Cathay to the sword, rendered
them all low, took them captive, and brought
the entire territory under his command, as can
be seen today. 
Now some of the battles Mongol rulers
fought with the chieftains and rulers of the
Tatar will be mentioned.
One was as follows. There was a ruler of the
Tatar named Matur who did battle with Qabul
Khan’s son Qada’an Bahadur. In the initial
clash Qada’an Bahadur struck him and his
horse with his lance so hard that they were
both felled. Wounded as badly as he was, he
nonetheless did not die but was laid up for a
long time. When he recovered he went back
out to do battle, and this time Qada’an Bahadur
struck him in the back with his lance with such
force that it went right through his spine. He
died on the spot, and his soldiers were put to
plunder. This story will be given in the section
on Qabul Khan and his sons.2

Another was as follows. In Genghis Khan’s
time, although he had engaged in battles with
the Tatars before, he once had the opportunity
to overwhelm them, kill many of them, and pil-
lage the lot. This came about as follows. One
of the Tatar clans, whose leader and chief was
Mä’üjin Sä’ültü,1 had done rebellious battle
with the Altan Khan, the king of Cathay. The
king of Cathay mounted his army, [82] put a
great general named Chingsang at the head,
and sent them off to war. Since [the Tatars] did
not have the power to resist, they took fright
and withdrew in rout. Genghis Khan learned of
this, mounted immediately along with the sol-
diers who were around him, and attacked them,
killing many and plundering everything they
had. It is well known that among the trophies
taken in that battle were a silver cradle, a bro-
cade quilt, and other fine items. In those days
the Tatars were the wealthiest of the nomads.
After that, Mä’üjin Sä’ültü’s son Ulaq Udur
and his brother Qirqan Taishi joined forces
with every group of the Mongol tribes and oth-
ers and fought Genghis Khan, as will come in
the history of Genghis Khan.
When God made Genghis Khan strong and
vanquished every enemy he had—like the
Qataqin, Salji’ut, Tayichi’ut, and Dörbän clans,
Ong Khan the ruler of the Kerayit, Tayang
Khan, Güshlüg Khan the ruler of the Naiman,
Toqto’a Beki the ruler of the Märkit, and oth-
ers who were inimical to him—the main
Tatars, who had constantly assisted these
tribes, were powerless. Because they were
murderers and enemies of Genghis Khan and
his forefathers, he ordered that they be massa-
cred without a single one left alive. He even is-
sued a decree that women and children be
killed and pregnant women’s bellies slit open
so that they would be reduced to naught, being
1The Megüjin Se’ültü of the Secret History (§132–34).
as they were the cause of turmoil and strife. Of
the clans and tribes of Genghis Khan’s own
relatives many were killed, and no one dared to
protect them or hide them, and even the few
who remained did not dare to make themselves
known. [83]
Nonetheless, at the beginning of Genghis
Khan’s rule, and thereafter also, all the Mongol
and non-Mongol tribes intermarried with the
Tatars. Genghis Khan also took girls from
them. Of his wives, Yesülün and Yesügän were
Tatars. Genghis Khan’s elder brother, Jochi
Qasar, had also married from among them, as
had many of the commanders. Therefore, se-
cretly some children of the Tatar women were
hidden.
Genghis Khan turned over a thousand Tatars
for Jochi Qasar to kill. To please his wife, who
interceded on their behalf, he killed five
hundred of them and hid the other five
hundred. Later, when Genghis Khan found out
about this, he was angry with Jochi Qasar and
said, “This is one of Jochi Qasar’s offenses”—
he had already committed several offenses, as
will be told in his history.
In short, after Genghis Khan’s wrath at the
Tatar nation and his annihilation of them, only
a few remained in scattered corners for one
reason or another, and the children who had
been hidden were brought up in the camps and
tents of the commanders and their Tatar wives.
Children were also born of the few pregnant
women who had not been killed, and those
Tatars who are alive today are descended from
them. Of that group there have been, both in
Genghis Khan’s time and later, great and im-
portant
commanders
and
camp
stewards,
serving as ötägü boghols. From then on, down
to the present, there have been great comman-
ders in every ordu and every ulus, and once
again they intermarry with Genghis Khan’s
family. [84] In every ulus there are many of
40
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

that tribe who did not become commanders
and were attached to regiments. Each of them
knows to what branch of the Tatar he belongs.
One of the Tatar children who gained impor-
tance and became an officer in Genghis Khan’s
time and who was raised by him and his wives
was Qutuqu Noyan, who is also called Shigi
Qutuqu. His story is as follows. When the
Tatar nation was plundered, Genghis Khan as
yet had no children, and his chief wife, Börtä
Füjin, wanted a child. Once Genghis Khan saw
a child by the roadside. He picked it up and
sent it to Börtä Füjin with a message saying,
“Since you are always wishing for a child, take
this one and raise it.” The lady brought him up
with no less honor than had he been her own,
and when he was grown he was called Shigi
Qutuqu and Qutuqu Noyan. He used to call
Genghis Khan “echigä,” meaning father, and
Börtä Füjin “bärigän ekä.” They say that when
Börtä Füjin died he put his hand on her grave
and cried out, “O my sayin ekä (good moth-
er)!” and mourned for her in this manner. He
survived Genghis Khan. Ögödäi Qa’an called
him aqa (elder brother), and he used to sit
above Mänggü Qa’an with [Ögödäi’s] sons. He
was an attendant on Tolui Khan’s and Sorqagh-
tani’s sons.1 He died during Ariq Bökä’s re-
bellion. Among his sons are ___ in service to
the Qa’an, appointed as ___.
Qutuqu Noyan lived to the age of eighty-two.
He conducted very proper trials and treated the
accused fairly and sympathetically. He would
often tell people not to confess out of fear. “Do

Beki’s
name
is
spelled—and
mis-
spelled—in so many various ways throughout the text

that a standard has to be adopted. We opt for the spelling

not be afraid,” he used to say. “Just speak the
truth.” It is well known among inquisitors that
from that time until the present inquiries in the
province of Mongolia [85] and that area are
conducted upon the principles laid down by
him. There were many reasons for his great-
ness, and some have been committed to writ-
ing. Of two reports made by trustworthy narra-
tors, one is as follows. 
At the age of fifteen, when Genghis Khan’s
ordus were moving during the winter, and it
was very cold and there was a lot of snow,
Güchügür Noyan of the Besüt tribe had been
put in charge of the camps. Suddenly a herd of
antelope appeared beside the road, running
across the snow. Qutuqu said to Güchügür
Noyan, “I am going to chase these antelopes.
There is so much snow they won’t be able to
run, and I’ll catch them.”
“All right,” said Güchügür as Qutuqu chased
off after the antelopes.
That
night,
when
the
camps
stopped,
Genghis Khan was looking for Qutuqu, who
had not returned. When he asked Güchügür
about him, he said, “He went off after some
antelopes.” 
Genghis Khan got furious and said, “That
child will die in the snow and cold.” And he
struck Güchügür with a cart stick.
When Qutuqu arrived late that night Genghis
Khan asked, “What have you been doing?”
“Out of thirty antelopes,” he said, “not more
than three got away. I hit the rest and brought
them down in the snow.” 
Genghis Khan was amazed by the child’s
bravery and sent Güchügür Noyan and a troop
of horsemen to recover the antelopes. There-
after Qutuqu gained a favored place in his
heart.
The second story is as follows. Before the
last episode, one day when Qutuqu was twelve
years old, Genghis Khan was out riding and
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER TWO: TURKIC NATIONS NOW CALLED MONGOLS
41

there were no men in the tent. A rider from the
enemy Tayichi’ut was passing by. Genghis
Khan’s youngest son, Tolui, was five years old,
and he was running around playing outside the
tent. From his saddle the Tayichi’ut snatched
him up to carry him away with his head under
his arm. [86] Tolui’s mother came out and
grabbed the kidnapper by one arm. Qutuqu
came and grabbed the other arm, but the kid-
napper held the prince’s head so tightly they
could not get him out of the kidnapper’s grasp.
Beki Baraq, who was tending sheep, leapt up,
attacked the kidnapper, and got the prince out
of the man’s arms. Genghis Khan arrived, went
out in pursuit of the kidnapper, and killed him.
He was greatly pleased by Qutuqu’s coura-
geous struggle with the kidnapper.
Another [story is as follows]. There were two
children, brothers. One was named Quli and
the other Qara Mönggätü Uha, and they were
of the Tutuqli’ut Tatars. Since Genghis Khan’s
two wives he had married from the Tatar na-
tion, Yesülün and Yesügän, were of that
“bone,” they felt sorry for the two boys and
asked Genghis Khan if they could have them.
He gave them to them, and they were put to
work as cooks in Yesülün’s camp. Quli, the el-
der, gained importance even at that time be-
caused Genghis Khan trusted him, and he be-
came an officer. After that he was attached to
Tolui Khan’s camp and was highly respected.
After Tolui Khan died an officer was sought
who could be in charge of Tolui Khan’s son
Sübügätü’s camp and officers. Sorqaghtani
Beki and her sons and officers chose Quli Noy-
an. He said to Sorqaghtani Beki, “How can you
give me to such a person?”
“He is of Tolui Khan’s family,” she replied.
“I wanted to serve a son to whom you gave
birth,” he said. The point of this story is that he
enjoyed such status that he could speak this
boldly in front of Tolui Khan’s son Sübügätü,
to whom he had been given. 
Of his sons in this land were Dörbäi Noyan,
the commander-in-chief of Diyarbekir, [87] his
son Burachu, and Burachu’s son Dänggiz, a
regimental commander.
Qara Mönggätü Uha, on the other hand, did
not gain much repute during Genghis Khan’s
time, but he had a son named Sali, who be-
came an officer of importance during Mänggü
Qa’an’s time. The reason for this is as follows.
There were two fortresses in Tangqut territory.
One was called Tükji and the other Tuqina.
Mänggü Qa’an had besieged it himself and
was watching from afar to see how they
fought. He saw a person with a short helmet
take a lance in his hand and charge the ram-
part. From the other direction came a person
holding a sword, charging the first. The first
man did not retreat but got up on the wall,
struck the swordsman with his lance, and
knocked him down. When Mänggü Qa’an saw
such bravery, it pleased him, and he immedi-
ately ordered the man with the short helmet
summoned from the army and brought before
him. When he recognized him by his helmet
and asked him questions, the man related ex-
actly as he had witnessed, so he knew for cer-
tain that it was he. He therefore rewarded him
and gave him the rank of commander, and he
became an advisor of importance in his
service.
Before this happened, [Mänggü Qa’an] dis-
patched two tümäns of the army to Hindustan
and ordered them to remain in Qunduz,
Baghlan, and the Badakhshan area. One named
Mönggädü was made commander of this con-
tingent, and when he died, it was given to one
named Huqutu. He too died, and the above-
mentioned Sali Noyan was sent out to be com-
mander of the two tümäns in his stead. This
was just about the time that Hülägü Khan was
42
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

assigned to go to Iran. To Sali Noyan, Mänggü
Qa’an said, “The territory where you will be is
the frontier of Hindustan and Khurasan and ad-
jacent to the territory to which Hülägü Khan is
going. You will be like a branch of his army,
[88] that is, you and your men are subordinate
to him, and you must obey his command.”
Sali Noyan then asked, “How long will I be
there?”
“You will be there for ever,” he said.
Sali Noyan took his army to Hindustan and
Kashmir, conquered many territories, got much
plunder, and sent many Indian slaves to
Hülägü Khan. Most of the Indians who are
now in enchü villages are remnants of them.
After [Sali Noyan] died, his son Oldu Noyan
was put in command of that force. Oldu’s
brothers [were] Abushqa, who commands the
countries and military forces there, and Älkän,
who is a regimental commander. Oldu had two
sons, Begtut, the commander of the qara’una
troop that is in Khurasan, and Dältäk, who is
an attendant upon His Majesty.
In Genghis Khan’s time, Yesülün Khatun
said, “Quli Noyan and his brother Mönggätü
Uha have grown up, are in attendance upon
you, and enjoy your trust. If you so order, let
their relatives and clansmen be assembled from
wherever they may be.” It was so ordered, and
all the Tatars who were left were gathered. All
those who had no relatives were attached to
them. In this land are thirty households of
those few dispersed Tatar they assembled.
Oldu Noyan asked—and the Padishah of Is-
lam’s decree was issued—for the old regiment
to be reunited, and they are with him.
As has been mentioned, Yesülün Khatun and
Yesügän Khatun were both Genghis Khan’s
wives. They had a brother named Qutuqut. He
was a great officer and commanded a regiment
in the left wing of Genghis Khan’s army.1
Joma2 Gürägän, who was in this land, and
Nuqdan, Abaqa Khan’s first wife and the moth-
er of Gaikhatu, were Qutuqut’s cousins.
Genghis Khan had a concubine whose name
is not known, [89] but she was the mother of
his youngest son, Orchaghan, who died young.
Of the Chaghan Tatar tribe in this land are
Gäräi and his brother Doladai, Muhammad,
Jandan, and their sons. Gür Buqa Bahadur,
who leads the troop on the frontier of Khart-
birt3 and Malatya, is also of this tribe.
Of the Küyin Tatar is the Samaghar Noyan
who was Hülägü Khan’s aqtachi; during Abaqa
Khan’s time he was a grand and important offi-
cer.4 Toghan, Mulai, and Buqa Qorchi’s father
Küyitäi were of this tribe.
Of the Nira’ut Tatar tribe there is no one
known to be of consequence. However, in
Jochi Khan’s ulus there are many soldiers [of
this tribe], but since they are not well known or
of importance, no further research has been
made.
Of the Alchi Tatar there is no one in this land
known to be of enough consequence to write
about. However, in Jochi Khan’s ulus, the chief
wife of Jochi Khan’s son Batu, Boraqchin, was
of the Alchi Tatar. Törä Qutluq, the wife of
Tödä Mänggü, the ruler of that ulus, was also
of that tribe. 
Of Batu’s officers there was one named Et
Qara, a great commander who was of this tribe.

Among the officers of Mänggü Temür, the
ruler of that ulus, is Beg Temür, a great com-
mander who was also of that tribe. It has not
been ascertained from which clan these Tatar
commanders are descended. 
There was Yesün To’a Akhtachi, the com-
mander of the akhtachis. He commanded four
of Genghis Khan’s gäzigs and the elite compa-
ny of Genghis Khan’s regiment and was at-
tached to Börtä Füjin’s great ordu.1 He had a
son named Begdash, whom Qubilai Qa’an sent
as an emissary to Hülägü Khan.
[Now] will be written one by one stories
attributed to some of the officers and ladies
and grandees of the Tatar tribes, which have
been ascertained from everyone and gleaned
from every book. [90]
It is related that when Qoridai Bayir and
Kümüs Saijang2 of the Alchi Tatars both went
to war with Sariq Khan, the ruler of the Keray-
it, Qoridai Bayir rode forward. Kümüs Saijang
said to him, “You are riding forward, but actu-
ally in stationing the qaravul and the yasavul
and reconnoitering you will be committing a
fault. It would be better for me to go forward.”
Qoridai said, “Tänüktü[i]!3 Just because you
were the son and brother of the khalaf (favorite
son), you want to usurp the ways of past fa-
thers and forefathers. It would be better for you
to go alone, raid whatever you want, and return
with the army.” 
Kümüs Saijang replied, “I would not be able
to raid without you,” and moved his men off.
Sariq Khan had decamped and was coming.
Thrice they raided him. They stationed troop
after troop of soldiers to strike and were going
on his heels. Finally Kümüs Saijang was going
1For Yesün To’a see text p. 593 below.
2The reading of the name Saijang is uncertain. See

3Tänüktüi, Mongolian for “you are mistaken.” See

in pursuit with three hundred horsemen, and
Sariq Khan’s soldiers were thinking to them-
selves, “This enemy army is coming without
reinforcements or rear guard.” They therefore
attacked them valiantly, separated Kümüs Sai-
jang from the main body, and captured him.
Sariq Khan asked him, “Where were you
going?”
“I had heard,” he replied, “that in the Burqan
forest wooden branches had grown tall. I was
coming to cut wood for arrows.”
“It was very courageous [to come just] to cut
[arrows],” said Sariq Khan as he looked at him
askance.
“You cannot look at me askance,” said
Kümüs, “for your urugh were also unable to
look at me thus. Your origin was thus.”
Sariq Khan said, “Why do you let this ‘no-
ble’ warrior talk so much? Kill him!” [91]
“Your sword will not work on me,” he
replied, “without mine working on you.” But at
any rate they killed him, and Sariq Khan said,
“Among the Alchi Tatar, who hold seventy
sects, there was no man other than Kümüs Sai-
jang. Now it is time to drive them off.” Then
he ordered his tents pitched at the Orkhon Riv-
er, and he assembled his troops stealthily in the
moonlight. One of his soldiers fled and took
word to Qoridai Bayir.
Qoridai Bayir turned around and started
moving up the Orkhon River. Moving among
his [Sariq Khan’s] tents, he took the same route
they had taken and came upon them. Sariq
Khan’s soldiers looked upon them with con-
tempt, but suddenly he attacked Sariq Khan
and drove him away such that of the forty
tümäns of soldiers he had he escaped with only
forty men. All the rest were killed.
During the rout a woman, Tarbai Qayan, fled
with Sariq Khan and got out. At that time Chi-
la’un was a commander.
44
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The woman said, “We had conquered high-
land and lowland. If all grew few, why should
we not grow few, and if all fall to pieces, why
should we not fall to pieces?”
“This woman speaks the truth,” said Sariq
Khan. Therefore he set forth and came under
the protection of Säkitäi Ötügü, Buyuruq
Khan’s qorchi. Afterwards El Qutui was born
of that woman. Since he had entered the pro-
tection of that tribe, he gave his daughter to
Qurjaghush Buyuruq Khan. Her name was
Törä Qaimish, and she was the sister of Qajir
Khan.
After that, Qajir Khan and Sariq Khan
formed an army together and attacked the
Tatar. [Qajir Khan] conquered the Ulus Ki-
raichin for Sariq Khan and gave them to him.
At that time Ong Khan and his mother, Elma
Khatun, were captives of the Tatar. They also
rescued them. [92] A man named Eljitäi loved
Elma Khatun, and since he was a pernicious
person, they [i.e. Qajir Khan and Sariq Khan]
gave him to them [i.e. Elma Khatun and Ong
Khan] [as though he] stank.1
Törä Qaimish’s sons were Yulamaghus, Tai
Temür Taishi, and four others whose names are
not known.
After that, the Mongols went to Sariq Khan,
who said, “Of the hundred women that I pos-
sess there is not one I really like. One has un-
derstanding, but I do not command her hands
and feet. Another whose hands and feet are
nice, I do not command her understanding, and

there is no beauty who is servile, skilled, and

After that, Ötügü, Buyuruq Khan’s qorchi,

Sariq Khan said, “We have embraced these

Buyuruq Khan said, “I have breathed life

After that, Sariq Khan said, “That man was

road and turning back at a place called Tui
Taghachu. 
The Mongols said to each other, “Sariq Khan
has come hungry and weak.” As an örgäjüt
(auxiliary gift), they gave every one of his men
ten geldings and had them dismount as guests.
Sariq Khan said, “O my little Mongol broth-
ers, do not ever be allies to each other: be as
distant as someone on the other side of a
mountain. Come be anda so that you may be
brethren to each other.1 My little Mongol
brothers, do not seek privacy with a woman
who has a monarch, i.e. husband, and do not
enter crooked valleys.”
The Märkit Tribe
They are also called the Uduyut tribe.2 If
some of the Mongols call them Mäkrit, the two
words [Mäkrit and Märkit] mean the same
thing, just as the Bäkrin tribe is also called
Käbrin. Their branches and lineage will now
be given.
The Uduyut Märkit tribe consists of four
branches: Uhaz,3 Mudan, Tudaqlin, and Je’ün.
This tribe had many soldiers and was fero-
ciously warlike and powerful. They are a type
of Mongol. They fought battles with Genghis
Khan and Ong Khan, and stories of them will
come in the proper places. 
1Berezin (5:70) translates as: будьте далеки отъ

1/1:114) translates: О, мой младшие братья-монголы,
никогда не становитесь друг другу сватами и таким
же образом будьте далеки от всякого, кто связан с
той [чуждой вам] стороной, за исключением тех
случаев, когда станете [с другими] побратимами
[анда], чтобы быть вам родственниками друг друга.
The variants in the texts are so massive that it is difficult
to make much sense of this passage.
2They are the Uduyid clan of the Märkit in the Secret
History.
3The Uuas of the Secret History.
Once they gained victory over Genghis
Khan, who was in the full bloom of youth, and
took him captive. (At that time it was not
customary to kill captives outright; they just
took something from them and let them go.)
This came about as follows. 
One day Genghis Khan was on his way to do
something. When he came to a high hill he
went up on it. Without his horse’s saddle strap
coming loose [94] and without the breast band
coming open, his saddle, with him in it, came
off his horse’s back, and he fell. Astonished by
this, he said to himself, “Perhaps God does not
want me to go down this road and tend to my
affair.” He thought about turning back, but the
devil got the better of him and he went merrily
along his way. Without warning, a number of
Märkits loomed before him, carried him off,
and kept him prisoner. After a time something
was sent from Genghis Khan’s home, and they
got him back.
Another time, when mischief-makers had
caused trouble between Genghis Khan and
Ong Khan, the two of them parted from each
other—the Märkit people had often been at
odds with both Genghis Khan and Ong Khan
before that and fought battles with them, and
once Ong Khan had raided them, but when
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan were at daggers
drawn with each other, the Märkit were united
with and friendly to Ong Khan and his brother
Jagambu. As it happened, they were victorious
that time and raided Genghis Khan’s home and
camp and carried away his chief wife, Börtä
Füjin, whom they sent to Ong Khan. When
Genghis Khan learned of this, he sent a trusted
friend to ask Ong Khan for her to be sent back.
Ong Khan had respected her honor and sent
her back in the emissary’s company. Along the
46
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

way Jochi Khan was born, as has been said in
the section on the Jalayir.1
The ruler and chief of the Märkit in Genghis
Khan’s time was Toqto’a Beki. He had a broth-
er named Qudu. Genghis Khan took a daughter
of his, Qoruqchin by name,2 for Qubilai Qa’an
when he was thirteen years old. (Although she
was the first of his wives, since she had no
children her status was lower than that of the
other wives.) Once Ong Khan [95] raided Toq-
to’a Beki without warning. [Toqto’a Beki] had
many women, and they carried off two of
them, Qutuqtai and Qiliq by name. His brother
Qudu and his son Chila’un, who was born of
Ong Khan’s daughter, were taken captive, but
they later escaped.
Orkhan was also a brother of Toqto’a Beki’s.
Toqto’a Beki had six sons: Tögüz, Tusaqa,
Qudu,
Chila’un,
Chibuq,
and
Qultuqtai
Märgän.3 His brother was also named Qudu.
Chila’un’s mother was Ong Khan’s daughter.
His five older sons were killed. Tögüz was
killed by Ong Khan; Tusaqa and his men were
killed in an ambush by Genghis Khan; Chi-
la’un and Chibuq were killed in battle with
Genghis Khan; and Qudu went to the Qipchaq
when he fled from battle, and there he was
killed. 
They often did battle with Genghis Khan, as
will be explained in the history. In the final
battle
Qultuqtai
Märgän,
Toqto’a
Beki’s
youngest son who was an excellent archer, fled
to the Qipchaq. Jochi Khan dispatched a troop
in pursuit of him, and he was captured. Having
heard of his prowess at archery, he set up a tar-
get and ordered him to shoot. He shot and then

We have fought so many battles with them and
suffered untold trouble and difficulties on ac-

there is no place better than the grave.” There-

In the end Toqto’a Beki was killed in battle.
Another officer of the Märkit peoples was
Dayir Usun, the chief and leader of the Uhaz
clan of the Märkit. He once submitted and
gave
Genghis
Khan
his
daughter,
Qulan
Khatun, who gave birth to a boy named Köl-

Dayir Usun rebelled again, and he was cap-
tured and plundered by Genghis Khan’s sol-
diers, who carried off his wife Törägänä
Khatun. She was given to Ögödäi Qa’an, who
had four sons by her, the eldest and chief of
whom was Güyük Khan, as will be related
later.
Since the Märkit tribe consisted of evil, sedi-
tious men and they had fought many battles
with Genghis Khan, he issued a decree that not
one of them be left alive and that they should
all be killed. The few who remained were ei-
ther in their mothers’ wombs or hidden by
some of their relatives.
The ladies and officers descended from them
are as follows.
Oghul Qaimish was Güyük Khan’s first wife,
by whom he had two sons, Khwaja and Naqu.
Qulan Khatun was Genghis Khan’s wife, and
by her he had a son named Kölgän.

Jamal Khwaja, Qulan Khatun’s brother, com-
manded a company of a hundred in Genghis
Khan’s thousand.1
In Genghis Khan’s final battle with Tayang
Khan, the ruler of the Naiman, Toqto’a Beki
was with him and fought hard. When Tayang
Khan was killed and Toqto’a and one of his
sons took refuge with Buyuruq Khan of the
Naiman, [97] Genghis Khan attacked Toqto’a
Beki, and he was killed in battle. His brother
Qudu and his sons Chila’un, Chibuq, and Qul-
tuqtai wanted to take his body for burial, but
they did not have a chance to get it, so they
took his head and left. When they reached the
frontier of Uyghur territory they sent an emis-
sary named Bögän2 to the Idiqut, who killed
the emissary. They therefore did battle with
each other, and the Idiqut sent envoys to in-
form Genghis Khan of their whereabouts. 
When the leaders of the Jä’üriyät clan sub-
mitted to Genghis Khan and then rebelled and
fled, Taghai Dalu was among their chiefs. He
was attacked along the way and killed by a
Märkit commander named Qodun Orchang,3
who plundered their people. That is why the
Jä’üriyät are not a numerous people.
The Kürlü’üt Tribe
This tribe [lives] near and adjacent to the
Qunqirat, Eljigin, and Barghut tribes. Their
brands are the same, they claim to be related,
and they intermarry. These three or four tribes
never fought against Genghis Khan, and he
never divided them or gave them as slaves to
anyone. Because they had never opposed him,
he trusted them as guards. During his time they
1See below, text p. 593.
2The name Bögän is attested in the Secret History
§202.

were always allies and were in Jädäi Noyan’s
guard company. Even today they still serve in
the companies of his sons.
During Genghis Khan’s time there was an of-
ficer from the Kürlü’üt tribe [98] named
Äbügän Noyan. His son Borongtai Noyan was
also an important commander in Genghis
Khan’s time. His son Tortaqa Noyan4 was at-
tached to Ariq Bökä and went around with
him. Since he had not committed any great of-
fense, Qubilai Qa’an made him a great com-
mander and made him chief officer of the bu-
reau of the ministry, and no officer had higher
status. After that [Qubilai Qa’an] sent him
against Qaidu and put him in charge of that
campaign. Because he was slandered by cer-
tain people, Qubilai Qa’an summoned him to
court. He took fright and fled with a few of his
liege men, joining Ariq Bökä’s son Yobuqur
and Mänggü Qa’an’s grandson Ulus Buqa (the
son of Zhirägi), both of whom supported
Qaidu. He remained with them until Qubilai
Qa’an died, and then he picked up the two
above-mentioned princes and took them before
Temür Qa’an. He is there now.
During Hülägü Khan’s time, Qara Yurtchi,5
the father of Mazuq, was the chief of all the
yurtchis and was one of the commanders who
came [to Iran] with Hülägü. Mänggü Qa’an
spoke to them and gave them advice. During
Abaqa Khan’s time there was Ündür Buqa, the
son of Qaraki, Mazuq’s elder brother; he had
been a sükürchi for Hülägü Khan. When his fa-
ther died he became the chief of the yurtchis.
The Mazuq Noyan of the present is of his
family.
Every group of this tribe had and has a spe-
cial name, as follows: Jongqorqin, Oymaqut.

Shigügäi Noyan, who was a yarghuchi in
Hülägü Khan’s time, went with Gharaqai to
Khurasan. He was of the Kürlü’üt tribe. [99]
The Targhut Tribe
In this land there is a person who came from
the Qa’an named Tarqudai, who was of this
tribe. Nothing is known of other officers who
may have been; however, of the great ladies,
Bartan Bahadur’s chief wife, the mother of
four sons, was of this “bone,” and her name
was Sünigil Füjin.1
The Oyirat Tribe2
The yurt and dwelling place of these Oyirat
tribes were at the Sekiz Mörän (Eight Rivers).
The Tumat tribe anciently used to dwell at
these rivers. The rivers emerge from that place
and all join together to form a river called the
Käm. It then flows into the Anqara Mörän. The
names of these rivers are as follows: Kök
Müran, On Mörän, Qara Usun, Sambai Tun,
Aqri Mörän, Uq Mörän, Jürchä Mörän, and
Chaghan Mörän.3
This tribe has been numerous since ancient
times. It is divided into several branches, and
each has a separate name, as follows: Ügälät,
Baghatut, Qoit, Kirgüt.
