Although their language is Mongolian, it dif-
fers slightly from that of the other Mongol peo-
ples. For example, the others call a knife ki-
tuqa, but they call it madagha. There are many
such words.
They have always had a ruler and leader. In
Genghis Khan’s time, although they were [ini-
tially] opposed, they submitted in the best fash-
ion and were obedient, as will be narrated in
the history. Genghis Khan formed alliances

anda-quda relations with them. [100] At that

named Oghul Qoymish, whom Mänggü Qa’an
married. (Genghis Khan had previously enter-
tained the notion of marrying her himself, but

Gürägän. She had a daughter named Orghudaq,
who was married to Shadai, son of Su’unchaq
Aqa. Now Jibish and his sister Gunjishk, the
4Here her name is given as Mänglügän; on text p. 971
it is Mänggügän.
50
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

wife of the Padishah of Islam, are children of
that Orghudaq. She had another daughter
named Öljäi who was the wife of Mänggü
Temür, and by her he had two daughters, one
of whom was the above-mentioned Ara Qut-
luq. After Mänggü Temür, his son Anbarchi
married her and had by her a daughter, Qutuq-
tai, who was married to Arab son of Samaghar.
There have been and are many commanders
from the Oyirat clans in Iran and Turan, but it
is not known from which clan each of them
hails, [103] although amongst themselves they
know their origin and lineage. Among them is
Amir Arghun Aqa, although he was not origi-
nally given much importance. They say that
during Ögödäi Qa’an’s time, in a year of
famine and want [Amir Arghun’s] father sold
him for a flank of beef to a commander of the
Jalayir, Ilügä Qada’an by name. That officer
had served as Ögödäi Qa’an’s atabeg, and
when he enrolled his son as a käbtä’ül (night
watchman) in Ögödäi Qa’an’s guard, he sent
Arghun Agha along with him. Since he was a
talented and competent man, he gradually rose
to prominence until he attained the rank of
governor and basqaq of the land of Iran. His
sons, like Gäräi Malik, Tatarji, Nawroz, Lagzi,
Hajji, Yol Qutluq, Bulduq, and Oyiratai, and
his grandsons Küräk, & al. are numerous. He
also had many daughters, and some of them
were married to rulers and commanders. His
sons Nawroz and Lagzi married daughters of
the imperial family and became sons-in-law.1
El Sükürchi and his son Toghan are also of
the Oyirat tribe.
In the final battle when Toqto’a Beki was
killed, he did not do battle with Genghis
Khan’s troops but submitted. He led them
against Toqto’a Beki and raided him, during
which fray he was killed.
1See text pp. 972 and 1057.
The Barghut, Qori, and Töläs Tribes, and the
Tumat Tribe that has branched off from them
These tribes are near each other, and they are
called Barghut because their dwelling place is
the other side of the Selenga, the last places
and lands that the Mongols inhabit. It is called
Barghujin Tögüm. [104] Many other tribes,
like the Oyirat, Bulaghachin, and Kärämüchin,
used to dwell in that region. Another tribe
called the Hoyin Uriangqa, were also near that
area. Each one separately had a leader and
chief. Genghis Khan conquered them all, as
will be narrated in the history.
Of this Barghut tribe in this land was
Jochighan, Arghun Khan’s atabeg, and his wife
Bulughan and his sons Tartai and Boralghi
Kükältash. Boralghi’s son Satalmish was for-
merly an important commander in the time of
the Padishah of Islam. He married Mänggü
Temür’s daughter Kürdüchin, who was former-
ly married to the sultan of Kirman, Soyurghat-
mish. Tartai’s sons Qutluq Temür, Esän Temür,
Bulan, and Hulqun are regimental comman-
ders. Qutluq Temür’s son was Taghai, who at
present is married to Kürdüchin, the [former]
wife
of
Satalmish.
Esän
Temür’s
son
is
Muhammad.
Long ago the Barghut killed Jädäi Noyan’s
father because he supported Genghis Khan.
They wanted to kill Jädäi Noyan too, who was
a nursing infant. Relatives of his mother’s hid
him among their tribe, raised him, and entrust-
ed him [to] Genghis Khan. Until now they
claim to be relatives and friends and have all
sorts of established rights.
The Barghut tribe was and is friendly to the
Eljigin clan also. Although they are not related
by blood, they claim kinship and friendship
and therefore intermarry.
Ariq Bökä had a concubine who gave birth to
Naira’u Buqa. She was of the Töläs clan,
which is a branch of the Barghut. Bartan Baha-
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER TWO: TURKIC NATIONS NOW CALLED MONGOLS
51

dur’s chief wife, the mother of his children
named Sünigil Füjin, was also of the Barghut
tribe.1 [105]
The Tumat Tribe
This tribe’s dwelling place was near Barghu-
jin Tögüm. They too were related to and a
branch of the Barghut. They dwelt on the fron-
tier of Qirqiz territory, and they were a very
pugnacious
tribe
and
army.
Their
chief,
Taitu’ul Soqar,2 came to Genghis Khan and
submitted. When Genghis Khan was occupied
with the conquest of the land of Cathay, he re-
mained there for six years. When he returned
he heard that the Tumat had rebelled again. He
ordered Nayagha Noyan of the Ba’arin clan to
go. He was told that he was ill, so he sent
Boroghul Noyan, as will be related in the sec-
tion on the Hushin tribe concerning Boroghul
Noyan. In short, they fought fierce battles, and
he brought the Tumat into submission. Howev-
er, Boroghul Noyan was killed in battle.3 Since
they were a maleficent tribe, many of them
were killed. There is no one among the com-
manders of that tribe known to have achieved
renown.
The Bulaghachin and Kärämüchin Tribes
They dwell near each other in the vicinity of
Barghujin Tögüm, the end of Qirqiz territory.
In this land no one from them is known, and
there are no men of renown from these clans.
[106]
The Orasut, Talangut, and Kästimi Tribes
These tribes also resemble the Mongols. It is
well known that they know Mongol medicines
well and are good at treating the Mongols.
1Cf. p. 99 above, where she is said to be of the Tar-
ghut.
2He is the Daiduqul Soqor mentioned in the Secret
History §240.
3For Boroghul’s death, see text p. 458 below.
They are also said to be of the “forest” tribes
because they dwell in the forests along the
frontier of Qirqiz and Kämkämchi’üt territory.
There are many Mongols from “forest” people
since every tribe whose yurts are in a place that
is forested is called a “forest” tribe, like the
Tayichi’ut, who were called a “forest” tribe be-
cause their dwelling place was in Mongolia
and Qirqiz and Barghut territory.
These tribes’ territory was on the other side
of the Qirqiz, about a month’s journey away.
Some of Genghis Khan’s brothers and uncles
were styled as “forest” clans, as will be related
in this history.
In summary, the forest tribes are many. If
there were two brothers from one clan, [and if]
one’s yurt was near a forest and the other’s was
in the plains, the clans that branched off from
them got two different names. There is, howev-
er, a great difference between one forest clan
and another, since the distances between one
forest and another can range anywhere from
ten days to a one- or two-month journey.
These tribes mentioned rebelled when the
Qirqiz surrendered. Genghis Khan sent his son
Jochi Khan. He crossed the Selenga and the
other frozen rivers on the ice, seized the
Qirqiz, and seized that tribe too on his way
back. [107]
The “Forest” Uriangqat Tribe
This tribe has no connection to the other Uri-
angqat. They got this name because their yurts
were in the forests. They never possessed tents
of any sort, and their clothing was made from
animal skins. They had no cattle or sheep but
raised and caught instead mountain oxen,
mountain rams, and jür (antelope), which is
like a mountain sheep, which they milked and
drank. They really look down on people who
keep sheep—so much so that a father or moth-
er will curse a daughter by saying, “I’ll give
you to someone who will make you follow af-
52
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ter sheep.” The [daughters] get so upset that
they hang themselves in grief and sorrow.
When they migrate they load their belongings
on mountain oxen and never go out of the for-
est. When they reach the place where they
camp they build a small shelter or hut from the
bark of toz (birch) and other trees and make do
with that. When they score birch trees, some-
thing sweet like milk comes out, and they
drink that instead of water. They imagine that
no life could be better and no one could be bet-
ter off than they.
A bird that knows nothing of limpid water will
keep its beak in brackish water all year long.
They think that people who live in cities, cul-
tivated countryside, and plains are in painful
torment. Since there are many mountains and
forests in their territory and it snows prodi-
giously, in winter they catch much prey on the
snow [108] by making a board they call a
chana (sled). They stand on it and, having
made reins of leather, they take hold of a pole
and stick it into the ground, and, like someone
driving a ship through water, drive it across
plain and prairie, uphill and down, so that they
catch up with mountain oxen and other ani-
mals. They pull another chana alongside the
one on which they are seated, and they load on
it the prey they kill. Even if they put two or
three thousand maunds [of weight] on it, with
only a little effort it goes easily across the
snow. If anyone is ignorant or a novice, when
he makes it run he may lose his footing, espe-
cially going downhill and when going fast.
Anyone who has learned how to do it can
make it go easily, but no one would believe it
without seeing it.
A report of this reached the Padishah of Is-
lam. He ordered a group brought from that ter-
ritory to make [a sled]. It was demonstrated to
be as had been described, without mistake. He
has recently ordered them to make another one.
The chana is known throughout most of the
territory of Turkistan and Mongolia, and it is
particularly practised in the region of Barghu-
jin Tögüm [among] the Qori, Qirqiz, Orasut,
Talangut,1 and Tumat.
This group maintains its customs tenaciously,
and they are always in the forests. However, in
Genghis Khan’s time and that of his glorious
family, that area became the yurt of other Mon-
gol tribes, and they mingled with other Mon-
gols. The Suldus tribe’s yurt is in the vicinity
of those forests.
There is no one from that tribe who became
famous
in
this
land.
[109]
However,
in
Genghis Khan’s time there was a regimental
commander of the left wing named Udachi,
who was of this tribe. After that, he was select-
ed to keep watch with his regiment over the
great ghoruq (sanctuary) of Genghis Khan in
Burqan Qaldun. They never go out on cam-
paign. Tolui Khan and his urugh, aside from
Qubilai Qa’an and Mänggü Qa’an, and other
members of Genghis Khan’s family are buried
elsewhere.
The Quriqat Tribe
Prior to now, when Genghis Khan was at war
with the Tayichi’ut and gathering troops, this
tribe was united with Genghis Khan. This will
be mentioned in the history. However, it is not
known which officer, either then or now, was
of this tribe.
The Saqayit Tribe
When Genghis Khan was at odds with the
Tayichi’ut, this tribe was united with Genghis
Khan and added to his forces. They will be
mentioned in the history. However, neither at
that time nor at present is anyone known of
this tribe who became famous. [110]
1For the Talangut, see Louis Hambis, “Notes sur trois
tribus de l’Yénissei supérieur: les Us, Qapganas et Ta-
langut,” Journal Asiatique 245 (1957): 25–36.
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER TWO: TURKIC NATIONS NOW CALLED MONGOLS
53

❦ CHAPTER THREE
THE TURKIC TRIBES THAT HAVE ALSO HAD SEPARATE MONARCHS AND
LEADERS BUT DO NOT HAVE A CLOSE RELATIONSHIP TO THE TRIBES
MENTIONED IN THE PREVIOUS DIVISION OR TO THE MONGOLS YET ARE
CLOSE TO THEM IN PHYSIOGNOMY AND LANGUAGE
ach of these nations has had a
monarch or leader, their yurts and
dwelling places were delineated,
and each has branched off into
various subdivisions. These na-
tions are held in high esteem at this time by the
other Turks previously mentioned and by the
Mongol Turks because Genghis Khan’s family,
who are the monarchs of the Mongols, con-
quered
and
subdued
them
through
God’s
might. In ancient times these nations were of
more importance and mightier than any other
groups of Turks, and they had powerful mon-
archs. The stories of each of these nations will
be mentioned separately. [112]
The Kerayit Nation
Their tribes and subdivisions, and stories
connected to them, aside from those stories
that will come in the history of Genghis
Khan or elsewhere.1
Summer and winter pasturing territories of
the Kerayit tribes:
Summer pastures: belonging to Ong Khan:
Talan Daban, Güsä’ür Na’ur.
1The name of this nation occurs variously as Kerayit,
Kerait, Kereit, Kereyid, Gereyid, Qarayit, and Qara’it.
Rashiduddin spells itﺖ ـــﯾﺮا ـــﮐ, and we will transcribe it as
“Kerayit.” See Antoine Mostaert, “Ordosica,” Bulletin of
the Catholic University of Peking 9 (1934): 52 and D.
M. Dunlop, “The Keraits of Eastern Asia,” BSOAS 11
(1944): 276–89.
His army’s territories: Right Wing: Tulsutan,
Jalsutan.
Left
Wing:
Elät
Tarat,
Ubjiya,
Kötigär, Urut, Ükürüt, Yilit, Tartit.
Winter pastures: Ötigin Mörän, Uru’in, Tush
Bara’u, Kürkin, Shira, Qulusun, Ötigü Qolan,
Jala’ur Qolan.
They had powerful monarchs from within
their own tribes, and at that time they pos-
sessed more might and power than other na-
tions within those borders. Christian mission-
ary activity reached them, and they converted
to that religion.
They are a sort of Mongol. Their dwelling
place is along the Onon and Kerulen Rivers,
the land of Mongolia, which region is near the
frontier of Cathay. [113] They had many dis-
putes with many tribes, particularly with the
Naiman. During the time of Genghis Khan’s
father, Yesügäi Bahadur, their monarch was
Ong Khan, who was a friend to Yesügäi.
Genghis Khan repeatedly helped Ong Khan, as
will be related in the history, but in the end
they had a falling-out and fought battles with
each other. Ong Khan was taken prisoner and
became a slave of Genghis Khan’s, as will be
told in the history.
The leader of this Jirqin clan in Ong Khan’s
time was Güyük Bahadur, who ruled a gürä’än
of ten thousand and whose yurt was in Qara’un
Jidun and Chigär Chilghar. When Genghis
Khan defeated Ong Khan and routed his tribes,
Güyük Bahadur had four sons, Muinuq, Sar-

ta’u, Ilä’ügän, and Saiqan Kökchü. They took
fright at the rout and, deciding to fight for
Genghis Khan, joined him with a hundred
men. They were with him and fought bravely
when he battled the Tayichi’ut, Qataqin, and
Salji’ut. Their progeny became many, and at
present in the Qa’an’s service and in other
uluses are many clans descended from them.
Muinuq had a son named Möngkä. Dörbäi (son
of Toquz Buqa son of Möngkä son of Muinuq)
came with Güyüji of the Besüt to His Majesty
as emissaries from Mangqan Kä’ün son of Ma-
lik Temür.
The Kerayit consist of many tribes and
groups, all of which followed Ong Khan, as
follows:
The Kerayit
It is related that in ancient times there was a
monarch who had eight sons, [114] all of
whom were dark-skinned, for which reason
they were called Kerayit.1 After that, with the
passage of time, the separate offspring of each
of the sons took on a name and epithet. The di-
vision among whom the monarchy is held until
today is known simply as the Kerayit. The oth-
er sons became servants to the brother who
was monarch, and there was no monarch from
among them.
The Jirqin
They are a heroic and important tribe of Ong
Khan’s nation. Bakhudsar and Jirqudai, the
shahna of Shiraz, and his brothers Baqcha
Taghai and Qutluq Buqa Bitigchi and his sons
Besüd and Dörbäi were from among them.
Achiq Shirun,2 Ong Khan’s great commander
who was requested by Genghis Khan to be sent
1Folk etymology derives Kerayit from the Turkish
qara et, ‘black ﬂesh.’ See Khwandamir, Ḥabību’s-siyar
3:18.
2The Achiq Shirun of the Secret History §181.
as an envoy to him, was also from among
them.
The Tongqayit3
Yesil Noyan4 and his son Tughluq Qushchi
were of this branch. Taichu Bahadur, who
gained renown with Alinaq Bahadur, and
Taichu Bahadur’s son Ghazan, who rebelled
during Sögä’s time, were all from this branch.
The Saqiyat
They were also a clan.
The Toba’ut
Alinaq Bahadur, Elchi Totqa’ul and his son
Sati were of this tribe. At this time Äbügän Bi-
tigchi is of them. [115]
The Albat
Elängär Ba’urchi,5 who was an ev-oghlan of
Genghis Khan’s chief wife, Börtä Füjin, and
who led a troop of a hundred, was of this tribe. 
❈
Ong
Khan’s
grandfather
was
named
Marghuz,6 and he was called Marghuz Buyu-
ruq Khan. At that time the Tatar tribes were
enormously powerful and strong, but they sub-
mitted to the monarchs of Cathay and the Ju-
rchids. At that time the leader of the Tatar
monarchs was a person called Na’ur Buyuruq
Khan, and their yurt was in the vicinity of a
place called Bu’ir Na’ur. When they had a
chance, the king of the Kerayit captured
Marghuz Buyuruq Khan and sent him to the
king of the Jurchids, who had him killed by be-

TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER THREE
55

ing nailed to a wooden donkey. After a time
Marghuz’s wife, Qutuqtai Härigchi—härigchi
means glowing and liquescent, and she was
called härigchi because her face was “glowing
and billowing” with beauty—sent a message to
the Tatar tribe, whose yurt was nearby, saying,
“I want to hold a banquet for the king of the
Tatars, Na’ur Buyuruq Khan.” She offered him
a hundred sheep, ten mares, and a hundred
ündürs of kumiss—an ündür being a very large
bag made of sewn skins that is loaded on carts,
each bag holding a hundred maunds of kumiss.
Wishing to extract vengeance for her hus-
band’s death, she hid a hundred fully armed
warriors in the ündürs and had them loaded on
carts. When they arrived she turned the horses
and sheep over to the ba’urchis to cook and
said, “When it is time for the banquet I will
bring the kumiss on carts.” [116] When every-
one was seated for the banquet the hundred
carts with the ündürs were brought before the
tent and unloaded. The warriors leapt out and,
together with the lady’s other servants, seized
and killed the king of the Tatars. They also
killed most of the Tatar tribesmen who were
present. It is well known that this is how
Marghuz’s wife took revenge for her husband.
It has been found in another book in Mongo-
lian that Qurjaquz Buyuruq Khan dwelt in a
place called Orta Balqasun, and he had given
Gürkhan and Ong Khan a yurt in Yagh
Yabghan and Tai Temür Taishi and Yulam-
aghus one in Qaraghas Burughus, saying,
“When they are together, they cannot get
along. After my death they will not leave the
Kerayit nation alone from night till morning or
from morning till night.” Therefore he kept
them apart. His wife, Törä Qaimish, used to
practice magic, and every time he went hunt-
ing, she would immediately bring him down.
Since he was suffering at her hands, he ordered
two concubines of his to kill her, and so they
did. After that he was worried about his sons
and wanted to conceal from them what he had
done. Seizing upon some pretext, he killed the
two concubines.
After a time Buyuruq Khan also died. Ong
Khan said to Tai Temür Taishi and Yulam-
aghus, “When our father was alive we used to
shoot arrows and bet we wouldn’t miss. Why
should now Eljitäi be chief of the people?”
And he lured them from their places to him-
self. When he had the chance he attacked them
both, and they went to Toqto’a for protection.
Toqto’a said, “Why should we expose our-
selves to attack for their sakes?” He seized
them both and sent them to Ong Khan, who
killed the two of them on the spot.
After that Gürkhan said, “The water in my
elder brother’s eyes had not yet dried, [117]
and the skin on his back had not hardened. You
kill my elder brother and destroy the younger.
What will happen to the ulus?” Therefore he
chased Ong Khan away and plundered his
goods.
Ong Khan was fleeing with a hundred men
when Yesügäi Qa’an happened by and took
him up. After that he said, “We should be
friends with this man and become anda with
him.”
“Friendship with him is not advisable,” said
Qutula Qa’an, “for we know him. It would be
better to become anda with Gürkhan, for he is
a gentle man with a good disposition. This man
killed his own brothers and sullied his lance
with their blood. Now that he resembles a wild
ox struck by an arrow and a wild ass with a
heavy burden around its neck, he has come un-
der our protection.”
Yesügäi Bahadur refused this advice and be-
came friends and anda with him. He raided
Gürkhan, drove him away, and gave his ulus to
Ong Khan.
56
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Marghuz had two sons, Qurjaquz1 Buyuruq
and Gürkhan. (The gür khans who were kings
in Transoxiana and Turkistan were of the
Qarakhitai nation; this Gürkhan was the son of
Marghuz, the king of the Kerayit, and should
not be confused with the former.) One of Qur-
jaquz Buyuruq’s sons was named Toghril—he
is the one the kings of the <Qara>khitai named
Ong Khan,2 which means monarch of a
province. Qurjaquz Buyuruq’s other sons were
called Ärkä Qara, Tai Temür Taishi, Buqa
Temür, and Ilqa Sangun Ilqa—sangun means
prince.3 Earlier his name had been Jagambu
Kerayidai. When the Tangqut seized him and
found him to be a capable man, they called him
Ja’a Gambu, which means the commander of a
province
and
great
leader:
ja’a
means
province, and gambu means great.4
At any rate, after their father’s death, Ong
Khan, that is Toghril, [118] having been sent to
the frontier and made commander, the other
brothers, Tai Temür Taishi and Buqa Temür,
took their father’s place. Ong Khan came,
killed his brothers, and took his father’s posi-
tion. Ärkä Qara had fled and taken refuge with
the Naiman tribe, who helped him, retook the
province, and gave it to him, driving Ong Khan
out and taking his position. Again Genghis
Khan’s father helped Ong Khan, drove Ärkä

3Sangun ‘prince’ from the Chinese 相公xianggong
‘excellency’ (Doerfer, TMEN 3:234 §1221). In the Se-
cret History (passim) the title occurs as Senggüm, a

4For a discussion of possible etymologies, see Doerfer,
TMEN 3:1 §1017. In the Secret History the name occurs
as Jaqa Gambu.
Qara off, and gave his place to Ong Khan.
Once more, Ong Khan’s uncle, Gürkhan, came,
drove Ong Khan off and took his place.
Genghis Khan helped Ong Khan yet again,
drove Gürkhan off, and gave the position back
to Ong Khan. In the end, the rule stabilized
with him. Jagambu was always in agreement
with his brother Ong Khan.
There was an officer named Kögsä’ü Sabraq
who belonged to Buyuruq Khan, the king of
the Naiman, who was a brother to Güshlüg
Khan. He got together a troop and raided the
families of Ong Khan’s brothers, Ilqa Sangun
and Jagambu, as well as Ong Khan’s own
aghruq.5 After that, Ong Khan gave his son
Sangun an army and dispatched him after the
enemy. He asked Genghis Khan for assistance,
and he sent Bo’orchi Noyan, Boroghul Noyan,
Muqali Guyang, and Chila’uqan Bahadur. The
story will be given later in the history.6
Jagambu had four daughters. One was asked
for in marriage by Genghis Khan for himself,
and her name was Ibaqa Beki. Another he re-
quested for his eldest son, Jochi, and her name
was Begtutmish Füjin. Another he requested
for his youngest son, Tolui Khan, and her name
was Sorqaghtani Beki. She was the mother of
four sons, Mänggü Qa’an, Qubilai Khan,

Khan said to Tolun Chärbi, “What say you?

Perceiving Genghis Khan’s indirect order,
Tolun Chärbi said, “Although I too love her,

to Küi Temür. Genghis Khan then said to the
lady, “These officers have so many wives.

love you more than the others?”
“All women’s bodies are fairly much alike,”
she replied. “Since a man is powerful and
dominant and a woman is meant to be dom-
inated, she must seek to do what pleases her
husband and not to do what displeases him.
She must be at one with the desire of his mind
and keep his house in accordance with his
wishes. If this is so, no doubt his love will
increase.”

The Naiman Nation, consisting of several
branches
Prior to Genghis Khan’s time, the rulers of
the Naiman were Narqish Tayang and Anyat
Qa’an. When they attacked the Qirqiz, Anyat
Qa’an presented gifts nine times nine to his el-
der brother Narqish Tayang. Narqish sum-
moned him forward and took his head in his
embrace. When they parted he said, “It is as
though we have no one to make us presents, or
I do not want you.” Anyat Qa’an’s sons were
Buyuruq and Tayang. While Tayang Khan was
away, Buyuruq decamped and passed so close
by his tents that the tent tops loaded on camels
could be seen from Tayang Khan’s tents.
Tayang Khan said, “I too am a ruler. If Buyu-
ruq comes and descends here, the choice is his.
1Secret History §122: “A[l]tan Odcigin, the son of

If he doesn’t come, the choice is his.” Buyuruq
did not descend and left. Tayang said, “We had
made ready to receive him as a guest. Now that
he has gone, let us host ourselves.” During the
banquet [125] Qubadkin Qur said while play-
ing the lute, “When Anyat Qa’an and Narqish
Tayang were together, would you think they
hadn’t made every man of the Naiman a prince
and every woman a lady and that many chil-
dren had not been born? You two were like the
horn of a bull antelope and the horn of a cow, a
pair. Now that you two brothers do not agree,
the Naiman nation, which billowed like waves
in the sea, will be broken and dispersed.”
When Tayang Khan heard these words, his
cheeks ﬂushed and he said, “Say to Buyuruq
that we were wrong. Wait for us in an appro-
priate place until we come. Whether he comes
out to greet us or not, the choice is his.” In re-
ply Buyuruq said, “The proverb is well known:
oft times a people reaches greatness but does
not have understanding, and oft times they
reach goodness. After this, if we are in good
health we will come together.” So saying, he
decamped and departed in another direction.
Since they were brothers and could not agree,
God altered their condition.
Summer pastures: Talaq was the yurt of their
king, and Jajiya Na’ur was the place of his
army.
Winter pastures: Adri Abaqa, a mountain;
Baqras Ölüm; Achiriq Na’ur; Alaitaring, a
river.
This nation used to dwell in the wilderness.
[126] Some lived in the forbidding mountains,
and others on the plains. Among the places
they inhabited were the region of the Altai and
Qaraqorum (where Ögödäi Qa’an built a splen-
did palace in the wilderness), the mountains of
Al’ui Siras, and the Black Irtysh (where the
Qanqli also dwelt), the Irdish Mörän, which is
the Irtysh River, the mountains between the
river and the territory of the Qirqiz, and the ad-
jacent region as far as the land of Mongolia
(the territory in which Ong Khan dwelt, and
for that reason there were constant disputes be-
tween the Naiman and Ong Khan), up to the
territory of the Qirqiz and as far as the edge of
the deserts that are adjacent to Uyghuristan.
The rulers of the Naiman nation were mighty
and powerful, their armies numerous and well
maintained, and their customs like those of the
Mongols. In ancient times their rulers were
entitled Güshlüg Khan or Buyuruq Khan.
Güshlüg means strong and mighty monarch.1
They say another reason for calling him Güsh-
lüg was that there was a king of that nation
who ruled over humans and the djinn, and he
had such strength that he could milk the djinn
and make yoghurt, whey, and kumiss from it to
drink. After that, the officers said, “It is a sin,”
and abandoned him. This is just a story. The
[Naiman rulers] were called buyuruq because it
means commander.2 Of course, every ruler had
his own original name given him by his mother
and father.
Tayang Khan’s officers of the Naiman nation
were Qoru Sübächü and Titig Sa’al, who cap-
tured and killed Ong Khan in Näkün Usun
when he fled from Genghis Khan. They took
his head to Tayang Khan, who did not approve
[of their action]. He had the head encased in
silver and kept it over his throne for a long
time, as has already been explained in the sec-
tion on the Kerayit.3 [127]

The ruler of the Naiman before the conflict
with the Genghis Khan was called Inanch Bil-

lieve, and bilgä is a magnificent title. Bügü
Khan was a mighty ruler of the past who held a
place of great importance among the Uyghur
and many tribes. They say he was born of a
tree. At any rate, this Inanch Bilgä Bügü Khan

merable titles to people, and so also do they
now maintain the custom. Their titles are unbe-
lievably numerous, and the ranks for each na-
tion and every province are extremely appro-
priate. They give titles to people so that every
person knows his rank and how far he can go.
If, for instance, there are a hundred persons at
a gathering, by the titles they have been given

it is obvious how much rank each has and

Buyuruq Khan. After their father’s death, these

The original capital, however, was held by the

They disliked each other intensely. While still
alive, their father had discerned in their natures
this rivalry and obstinacy and said, “I know
that Buyuruq Khan will never agree that
Tayang Khan should take my place, even for a
few days. Buyuruq Khan is like a camel that
will not budge until a wolf has eaten half of its
leg.” In the end that is just how it was.
Tayang and Buyuruq fought many battles
with each other. During Genghis Khan’s battles
with Ong Khan they both participated valiantly
but separately, [130] refusing to co-operate or
assist each other, as will be described in the

how
many

with

and whose yurts were adjacent to theirs was
the Bätäkin tribe.1 Their ruler’s name was

The Öng’üt Nation
During and before Genghis Khan’s time,
[131] these tribes were attached militarily to
the rulers of Cathay, the Altan Khans. They
were a separate nation who resembled the
Mongols, and they consisted of four thousand
households. The rulers of Cathay who are
called Altan Khan built a wall to protect their
territory from the tribes of the Mongols, Ker-
ayit, Naiman, and nomads in the vicinity. In
Mongolian the wall is called öngü, and in
Turkish it is called yoqurqa.3 It stretches from

In the beginning the wall was entrusted to the
Öng’üt nation, who were made to promise and

extended along the crest of the Khinghan between the
Khitans and Khongirads, and the other along the outer
fringe of the southern Mongolian grasslands. This, run-
ning from the Khinghan to the borders of Hsi Hsia, was
known to the Chinese as the Wai-pao and to the nomads
as the Ongu. It was the charge of this rampart, falling
under the jurisdiction of the commander for the north-
west, that had given to its guardians their name of
Ongud. As military works, neither can have been intend-
ed to withstand more than raiding expeditions.”

The Tangqut Nation
This nation used to dwell principally in vil-
lages and towns, but they were highly mili-
taristic and warlike. They fought many battles
with Genghis Khan and his family. Their
leader and ruler was called Lung Shadurghu.
The Tangqut’s territory contains many cities,
towns, and fortresses.1 Many mountains sur-
round it on all sides, and the entire territory ex-
ists because of a huge mountain situated in
front called Alashan. It is surrounded by
Cathay, Nankiyas and Manzi. [135] Ching
Temür dwells near that territory. 
During Ögödäi Qa’an’s time there was an
army there. In Qubilai Khan’s time he had sent
___. 
Formerly the Mongols called it Qashin, but
when Ögödäi Qa’an’s son Qashi, Qaidu’s fa-
ther, died, the name Qashin became taboo.
From that time on they have also called the ter-
ritory Tangqut, and that is the name by which it
is known today.
In Genghis Khan’s and Ögödäi Qa’an’s times
they went to that territory several times and
dispatched armies. Since they were a pugna-
cious and powerful nation, they stirred up sedi-
tion and fought battles. They finally submitted
but then rebelled again. The first time, when
Genghis Khan had taken most of the Märkit
tribes, in the Year of the Ox, corresponding to
601 [1205], he went to fight that region. Inside
the frontier was a mighty fortress called Ligi
and a large city called Asa Kinglus.2 He took it,

became taboo to Mongols with the death of Prince

destroyed it, and plundered the province,
taking the many camels that were there. The
third year after that, the Year of the Rabbit,
which is called Taulai Yil [1207], Genghis
Khan went off during the autumn and winter
with a huge army and many soldiers to fight
and conquer the region. He subdued most of it.
The fourth year, Morin Yil, or Year of the
Horse [1210], Genghis Khan spent the summer
in his ordu and then mounted in the autumn,
headed for there. He took a large city called
Äriqay,3 and forced into submission every
place that held out and had a fortress, giving
order to the realm. He asked for the daughter
of the ruler, Lung Shadurghu,4 and stationed a
shahna there to guard the realm. 
When he began his campaign against the
Tajiks’ realm, he returned to his ordu in Taqiqu

been there for a while he heard that [136] the
ruler of Tangqut had rebelled again. This
stirred his zeal, but because he had grown old,
he knew that his time for departure was nigh.
Summoning his sons, commanders, and ret-
inue, he delivered his last testament and words
concerning ruling and commanding and advice
to his sons. In the autumn of that year he
launched an expedition against Qashin. The
ruler, Lung Shadurghu, apologized, saying, “I
was afraid and did wrong. If he gives me

oath and granted him respite for a fixed
amount of time. During that time Genghis
Khan fell ill and stipulated that when he was
dead they should not reveal his death or cry out
and wail so that the enemy, unaware, would

Sükürchi and his son Toghrilcha are from this

The story of Buda is as follows. When he
was thirteen years old he was taken captive
from Tangqut, and then he herded cows in the
ordu. One day while hawking Genghis Khan
saw him put his hat on the end of a stick, stand
before it, and offer it a cup. Genghis Khan
asked him, “What are you doing, and what is
this?” 
“I am a boy who was taken captive from the
Tangqut,” he replied. “I get bored from being
alone, so I put my hat on the end of a stick and
say, ‘Of us two one is bigger, and it is better
for me to serve the hat, [which is a sign] of
greatness.’ ” 
Genghis Khan liked this reply, and since he
saw in him signs of competence and maturity,
he took him to his great ordu and to Börtä
Füjin, where he was given work preparing food
in the kitchen. Since his ascendant was favor-
able, he gradually rose to the rank of comman-
der of a hundred, and thereafter he became an
officer
of
the

regiment.
During
Ögödäi Qa’an’s time, when all the realm of
Cathay had been subdued and rendered sub-
missive, that region and all the soldiers there
were turned over to him. [138]

The Uyghur Nation1
As has been mentioned in the preface to this
book, since Oghuz (son of Qara Khan, son of
Dib Baqui, son of Abulja Khan Japheth, son of
Noah) was a montheist, he fought with his un-
cles, brothers, and cousins. Some of them
helped him, and he vanquished the others. He
conquered many lands and assembled a huge
following. He rewarded his relatives, comman-
ders, and soldiers, and the group of relatives
who had joined him he named Uy-ghur, which
means “to join together and help” in Turkish.
This name then was applied to all that group
and their branches and offspring and their fam-
ilies. When some of those clans acquired par-
ticular names for some reason, like the Qarluq,
the Qalach, the Qipchaq, &c., the name
Uyghur stuck to the rest. According to this, all
the Uyghurs are descended from them, but it
has been so long that it is not known in detail
for what or how the divisions of their clans and
branches were named. They are therefore reck-
oned absolutely as a branch of the Turks, with-
out the interpolation of the foregoing, and for
this reason, even though mention of them was
made in the section on Oghuz, it has been nec-
essary to repeat in this chapter tribes that re-
semble the Turks according to what the
1In A.D. 744 an Uyghur confederation invaded the
Mongolian core lands of the Türk Khaghanate and set up
a ruling oligarchy of their own at Ordu Baliq (Qara Bal-
ghasun) that lasted until the confederation broke up in
A.D. 840. After that the Uyghur tribes dispersed, some
westwards toward the Qarluqs in Eastern Turkistan,
some southwards to Tibet, and others eastwards to East-

group was carried off by the Qirghiz to the north. The

low is the old Uyghuristan along the course of the Ork-
hon River, where Qaraqorum was built.
Uyghurs report. However, since their stories
and legends would take up a lot of room, we
have relegated to a separate history their events
and beliefs as mentioned and recorded in their
own books and appended it to this blessed his-
tory. Here only a summary of what is appropri-
ate to the branch will be introduced. [139]
It is said that in the territory of Uyghuristan
are two very large mountains. One is called
Buqratu Buzluq, and the other is Ishqunluq
Tängrim.2 Qaraqorum is situated between these
two mountains, and the city the Qa’an built is
called after that mountain. Next to those two
mountains is another mountain called Qut Taq.
Near those mountains there are ten rivers in
one place and nine in another. Long ago the
dwelling place of the Uyghur tribes was in
those two river [systems], mountains, and
plains. Those who were in the ten rivers were
called the On Uyghur, and those who were in
the nine rivers were called Toquz Uyghur. The
ten rivers are also called the On Orqon, and
their names are as follows: Ishlik, Ötingär,
Buqiz, Uzqundur, Tular, Tardar, Adar, Üch
Tabin, Qamlanchu, Ötigän.3
Nine tribes dwelt in the first three rivers, and
five tribes in the [next] four. Those who were
in Qamlanchu, which is the ninth, are called
the Ong people. Those who were in Ötigän, the

tenth, are called the Qumuq Atiküz people.1
Aside from the tribes that dwelt at these rivers,
there were one hundred twenty-two tribes in
the vicinity, but their names are not known.
Many years and generations passed without
these Uyghur tribes’ having a specific ruler or
leader. At any given time anyone from any
group would become commander of his tribe
through dominance. After that, the generality
of the tribes convened a council to regulate
their overall affairs, saying, “We must have a
ruler in absolute command whose order will be
effective among us all.” They all unanimously
and willingly elected one from the Ishlik tribe
named Mängütäi, who was the most intelligent
person of the tribes, and they entitled him
eltäbär.2 They also elected another known for
his competence [140] from the Uzqundur tribe
and entitled him kül erkin.3 They were both
made rulers over the collected tribes, and their
families ruled for a hundred years. 
Since unusual events that are related and
some of the beliefs they hold, as told by them,
have been relegated to a separate history of the
Uyghurs and appended to this felicitous histo-
ry, only a summary account will be given. 
Recently the idiomatic usage of the Uyghur
has been to call their ruler Idiqut, which means

Khan’s time the Idiqut was Barchuq. When the
Gür Khan conquered the realm of Transoxiana
and Turkistan, the Idiqut submitted to him.
[The Gür Khan] sent him a shahna named
Shaugäm. Once he got established he began to
act aggressively toward the Idiqut and his com-

ever, Altun Beki died. Some time later he affi-
anced Alajai Beki to him, but before she could
be turned over to him, the Idiqut died. His son
Käsmäs went before the Qa’an, became Idiqut,

Other things that happened to them during

The Bäkrin Nation
They are also called the Mäkrin. Their
dwelling place is in the rugged mountains of
the province of Uyghuristan. [142] They are
neither Mongols nor Uyghurs. Because they
dwell in inaccessible mountains they travel
well in mountainous terrain and are all moun-
tain climbers. They constitute one regiment.
They submitted to Genghis Khan, and their
commander and leader was with him. Since
their land is near Qaidu’s ulus, he seized them
and attached them to himself. At that time their
commander’s name was Jinanch.
During Genghis Khan’s time their chief
brought him a girl and offered her to him.
Genghis Khan approved of her and loved her
very much. Her name was Mögä Khatun, but
he had no children by her. It was Genghis
Khan’s command that the Mäkrin tribe display
their daughters so that he might take whichever
one he liked for himself or his sons. After
Genghis Khan’s death, this lady was taken by
Ögödäi Qa’an, and he loved her more than his
other wives—so much so that they were jeal-
ous of her. Chaghatai also loved this Mögä
Khatun, and before he learned that Ögödäi
Qa’an had taken her, he sent a message, say-
ing, “Of all my stepmothers and my father’s
bärigäns, give me Mögä Khatun.” Ögödäi
Qa’an replied, “I have taken her. Had your
message arrived earlier, I would have sent her
to you. If you desire another, [let me know so
that] I can give her to you.” Chaghatai said,
“She was what I wanted. If I can’t have her, I
don’t want another.” The Qa’an did not have
any children by her either. 
Qashin’s wife, the mother of Qaidu, was
from the Mäkrin tribe. Her name was Säbginä.1
There was a contingent from this tribe with
Hülägü Khan, and in this realm they are
renowned as mountaineers and climbers. [143]
The Qirqiz Nation2
Qirqiz and Kämkämchi’üt are two adjacent
regions, and the two form one realm. The
Kämkämji’üt is a large river.3 It borders the
province of Mongolia on one side, is adjacent
on another side to the Selenga River where the
Tayichi’ut tribes dwell, borders the large river
called Angqara Mörän [the Angara River] near
the province of Ibir-Sibir, and ends at the vil-
lages and mountains where the Naiman peo-

ples dwell. The tribes of the Qori, Barghut, Tu-

There are many towns and villages in this

rulers are called Inal even though they have
other names. The part of that province that is
important and known is called generically

Rabbit corresponding to 603 [1207], Genghis
Khan sent two emissaries named Altan and
Buqura to these two rulers, calling upon them

when one Tumat tribe that dwelt in Barghujin

fused and rebelled. Genghis Khan dispatched
his son Jochi Khan [144] with an army against
them, and their chief, Buqa, went out in the
vanguard, put the Qirqiz to flight, and returned
via the eighth river. When Jochi Khan arrived,
the Kämkämji’üt River was frozen. He crossed
on the ice, rendered them submissive, and
withdrew.
1See text p. 422 below.
The Qarluq Nation
Although this nation has been mentioned in
the section on Oghuz, since they went before
Genghis Khan in his time and their tale will be
told in the narrative, a summary account is giv-
en here also. During Genghis Khan’s time the
ruler of the Qarluq was named Arslan Khan.
When Genghis Khan sent Qubila Noyan of the
Barulas tribe to that area, Arslan Khan submit-
ted and went before Qubila. Genghis Khan
gave him a girl from his own urugh and com-
manded that he be called Arslan Sartaqtai
(meaning Tajik2), saying, “How can he be
called Arslan Khan?”
The Qipchaq Nation
The reason for mentioning the Qipchaqs
here, since they are mentioned in the section
on Oghuz, is the same as was said above for
the Qarluqs. The chief of the Qipchaqs in
Genghis Khan’s time was a commander of the
Qipchaq named Könchäk, the head of the
sükürchis. He had a son named Qumurbesh
Qonichi. Once he was sent on a mission to the
Padishah of Islam. They are descendants of the
rulers of the Qipchaqs. [145]
2The “Sart” part of names like Sartaqtai is the epithet

when the population was divided between non-military

manned the military, the dīvān-i sārt dealt with civilian

ome stories about them will come
in the history of Dobun Bayan and
Alan Qo’a. These Mongol tribes
form two divisions, the Dürlükin
Mongols and the Niru’un Mon-
gols. By Dürlükin Mongols is meant the Mon-
gols generally, while the Niru’un are those that
came into being from a single origin, i.e. from
the womb of Alan Qo’a, whose story is well
known to the Mongols.
The first section is on those who are called
Dürlükin
Mongols.
They
are
the
various
branches and clans that were born from the lin-
eage of the remainder of the Nüküz and Qiyan
Mongol tribe that had gone into Ärgänä-qun
and existed before the time of Dobun Bayan
and Alan Qo’a.
The second section is on those who are
called Niru’un Mongols. They are the tribes
descended from Alan Qo’a after the death of
her husband, Dobun Bayan. Alan Qo’a was of
the Qorolas tribe, [146] which is a branch of
the Dürlükin Mongols. According to the Mon-
gols, she became pregnant from light after the
death of her husband, and three sons were
born. Those who are descended from those
sons are called the Niru’un. The word niru’un
means pure loins and is a reference to the pure
line that came into existence from light. The
clans that stem from Alan Qo’a and her sons
comprise three divisions.
The first is the one descended from Alan
Qo’a down to the sixth descendant, Qabul
Khan. All these, their sons, grandsons, and
families, are called Niru’un without qualifica-
tion. Qabul Khan’s brothers and their families
are also called Niru’un.
The second, although they are Niru’un, are
called Qiyat, and they are the group descended
from Qabul Khan in the sixth generation of de-
scent from Alan Qo’a.
The third, although they are Niru’un and
Qiyat and descended from Alan Qo’a, and they
are also descended from her sixth descendant,
Qabul Khan, are called Qiyat Borjiqin. They
are all descended from Qabul Khan’s grandson
Yesügäi Bahadur, Genghis Khan’s father. [147]
SECTION ONE
THE TRIBES OF THE MONGOL TURKS CALLED DÜRLÜKIN
These are those branches and clans that are
descended from the Nüküz and Qiyan who
went into Ärgänä-qun. They existed before the
time of Dobun Bayan and Alan Qo’a.
As was explained in the preface to this
blessed history, the Mongol tribes are one class
of the Turkic tribes, and their physiognomy
and language closely resembled each other.
Those tribes are all descended from Japheth,

the son of the prophet Noah—upon whom be
peace. Japheth is called Abulja Khan by them,
and he is the ancestor of all groups of Turks.
However, when long ages pass, one forgets
one’s condition. The Turks had no books or
writing and were unable to record the history
of four or five thousand years. They thus have
no reliable ancient history, except for a few in-
cidents fairly close to the present, which they
often repeat and teach to their children.
These tribes had their yurts and lands adja-
cent one to another, and it was well defined
from where to where each one’s yurt was. All
of their yurts stretched from the borders of
Uyghur territory to the borders of Cathay and
Manchuria in the territory that is now called
Mongolia. These places and names have been
previously mentioned in detail. The tribe that
has been called Mongol since ancient times
[148] developed a dispute and rivalry with the
other Turkic tribes that turned into outright
hostility and war two thousand years ago, more
or less. It is related by trustworthy sources that
the other tribes overcame the Mongol tribes
and so slaughtered them that no more than two
men and two women survived. Fleeing from
their enemies, those two households went to a
harsh place surrounded by mountains and
forests, with only one narrow, rugged road
leading in on every side, which made access
very difficult. In the midst of those mountains
was a grassy plain called Ärgänä-qun. (Qun
means mountain flank, and ärgänä means wall,
so Ärgänä-qun means a wall-like cliff.) The
two men were named Nüküz and Qiyan.
For years they and their progeny remained
there, multiplying through intermarriage. Each
branch of them became known by a specific
name and epithet, and they became an omaq.
(The word omaq means to be of a specific
“bone”
and
lineage.)
Those
omaqs
also
branched out, and at this time the Mongol
tribes report that those who came into being
from these branches are more closely related to
each other, and they are the Dürlükin Mongols.
The word Mongol was originally mong ol,
which means “left behind” and “simpleton.” In
the Mongolian language qiyan is a strong tor-
rent that tumbles down from a mountain to the
ground and is swift, fast, and powerful. Since
Qiyan was a courageous warrior and very bold,
this word was made his name. Qiyat is the
plural of qiyan. Those who were nearer in de-
scent to him were called Qiyat in ancient
times.
When this group became numerous in those
mountains and forests, and the land was con-
straining them, they took counsel with each
other to figure out how to get out of that nar-
row prison. They found a place in the moun-
tains where there was an iron mine, where they
always used to smelt iron. They gathered to-
gether and brought loads of kindling and char-
coal from the forest. Then they killed seventy
horses and oxen, skinned them, and made iron-
smiths’ bellows from them. They placed the
huge amount of kindling and charcoal at the
base of the cliff and so arranged it that they
could cause the seventy large bellows to blow
at once, and thus the cliff was melted, produc-
ing
immeasurable
quantities
of
iron
and
opening a road, through which they moved out.
From that stricture they emerged into a spa-
cious plain. [149]
They say the original branch called after
Qiyan wielded the bellows, and thus the tribe
known as the Nüküz and the tribe of the Uri-
angqat, who are a branch thereof, also wielded
the bellows. Several other tribes also claim to
have participated, but the tribes mentioned
above do not consider their claim legitimate.
They report that the Qunqirat tribe, which con-
sists of several subdivisions as will be ex-
plained later, as well as the Nüküz and Qiyan,
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER FOUR, SECTION ONE: THE DÜRLÜKIN
73

who came into existence in Ärgänä-qun, left
before the others without consultation in such a
way that they trampled on the braziers and
fires of the other clans. Those tribes therefore
believe that the gout endemic among the Qun-
qirat results from their having departed before
the others without their agreement and from
having arrogantly trampled on their braziers
and fires. They therefore have a bone of con-
tention with the Qunqirat. The Mongols who
now live here and have seen Ärgänä-qun report
that it is a rugged place but not overly so. Their
purpose in melting the cliff was to open anoth-
er road for themselves.
Since Dobun Bayan, Alan Qo’a’s husband,
was descended from Qiyan, [150] and Alan
Qo’a was of the Qorolas tribe, [and] Genghis
Khan’s lineage goes back to them, as has been
reported, they therefore do not forget the melt-
ing of the iron or the ironsmithing. On the
night that begins the new year it is the custom
of Genghis Khan’s family to gather ironsmiths,
a forge, and charcoal, heat a bit of iron, place it
on an anvil, beat it with a mallet, stretch it out,
and give thanks.
Although in ancient times the tribes were
called Qiyat, as explained, when they multi-
plied and split into many branches and clans
after Dobun Bayan, every clan got its own par-
ticular name and epithet, and the epithet of
Qiyan fell into disuse. After that, Alan Qo’a’s
descendant in the sixth degree, Qabul Khan,
produced six sons. Since they were all warriors
of great importance and princes, the Qiyat epi-
thet was reapplied to them. From that time
some of [Qabul Khan’s] sons and progeny
have been called Qiyat. In particular, the sons
of one of his sons, Bartan Bahadur by name,
who was Genghis Khan’s grandfather, have
been called Qiyat. Bartan Bahadur’s eldest son
was named Möngätü Qiyan. (Möngätü means a
person who has many birthmarks.) He had a
large birthmark on his neck, and he was a great
warrior. Many of the Qiyat who are now in the
Qipchaq Steppe are descended from him, his
cousins, and his relatives. 
Although Genghis Khan and his forefathers
and brothers were of the Qiyat tribe, the sons
of Yesügäi Bahadur, Genghis Khan’s father,
were called Qiyat Borjiqin. Therefore they are
both Qiyat and Borjiqin. (In the Turkish lan-
guage borjiqin means someone with yellowish
gray eyes.) [151] They were extremely brave
and valiant warriors, so much so that they be-
came proverbial for manliness. When the other
tribes went to war with each other, they would
take refuge with them, give them presents and
gifts, and ask them for help with their might
and power; and with their help and assistance
they would triumph over powerful enemies.
What the Mongols know of their condition is
the bit that has been stated.
Many tribes came into being from them, as
will be detailed, and the reason for going on at
such length and in such detail is that those
tribes, the Niru’un tribes, and Genghis Khan’s
forefathers are they who are all of the one
branch descended from the two persons who
went into Ärgänä-qun and multiplied over a
long period of time. In the second and third
sections will be explained the branches and
clans that came into being from them, which
are called altogether the Dürlükin Mongols and
from whose progeny came many tribes, some
of which came into being from the lineage of
Dobun Bayan and Alan Qo’a and branched out
into many clans.
Before now, during the time of Genghis
Khan and his renowned urugh, there were offi-
cers from the Nüküz and Qiyan tribes. At
present in this land of Iran, Cha’urchi, a regi-
mental commander whose sons Qara and [his
son] Sübätäi are regimental commanders, was
of the Nüküz tribe. During Abaqa Khan’s time

There is a branch of the Niru’un who are also

China and Ölögchin China. They were sons of
Charaqa Lingqum, who took to wife his broth-
er’s widow, the mother of Tumina Khan, and

section on the Tayichi’ut.
Since the tribes of Nüküz and Qiyan split off
after the ancient Mongols were reduced to
naught, their story is the beginning of a sepa-
rate history and it is necessary to mention those
who preceded but who are not known in detail.
A detailed explanation of the lineage, branches,
and progeny that came into being from them
until the time that Alan Qo’a and her sons ap-
peared, who are called the Dürlükin Mongols,
each separately with a line or two of their his-
tory that is pertinent to a mention of the branch

The Uriangqat Tribe1
This tribe descends from Qiyan and Nüküz.
There is another group called the “Forest Uri-
angqat,” but they are separate and distinct. The
forest people live near each other on the bor-
ders of the region of Barghujin Tögüm, where
the Qori, Barghut, and Tumat tribes dwell.
1 Reference to the Uriangqat occurs in the Secret His-
tory as the attributives Uriangqadai (§12) and Uriangqa-
jin (§38).
Their clans and branches are not original Mon-
gols, as was stated in the last section.
These Uriangqat claim that they helped run
the seventy bellows in Ärgänä-qun. It is their
custom, when there is a lot of thunder and
lightning, to curse the sky and the thunder and
lightning and cry out against them. [153] If
lightning hits an animal and it dies, they do not
eat its flesh and avoid it. They claim that when
they do this storms dissipate. Other Mongols
do the opposite and do not come out of their
houses when there is a storm but sit trembling
inside.
There is said to be a lot of lightning in Mon-
golia, and the Mongols believe that lightning
storms come from an animal like a dragon, and
in that region they witness it coming down out
of the air onto the ground, striking its tail
against the earth, coiling around itself, and
pouring fire from its mouth. A poet has versi-
fied this as follows: “It resembles a crocodile
that yokes the celestial sphere when its dark,
angry body emerges from the sea. / It roars like
a dragon when it convulses against the world;
it rains down fire and smoke from its maw and
teeth.” In this regard trustworthy Mongols in-
sist that they have seen it many times. Since it
gets unusually cold in Mongolia, particularly
in the region called Barghujin Tögüm, there
are constant lightning storms. They also report
that if they pour wine, kumiss, or yoghurt on
the ground, it has a property to cause lightning
to strike animals, particularly horses. If wine is
poured, its effect is even greater, and the light-
ning will certainly strike their animals and
tents.
For
this
reason
they
take
extreme
measures to avoid it. If anyone takes his ugh
(felt stockings) off his feet and wants to dry
them in the sun, the same thing will happen.
Therefore, when they dry their stockings, they
cover the tops of their tents and dry them in-
side. [154] In their opinion these things have
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER FOUR, SECTION ONE: THE DÜRLÜKIN

been proven by experience and are peculiar to
that region. Since there are many lightning
storms in that area that are highly devastating
to them, they attribute the occurrence to some
cause or other.
They also say that for one reason or another
the djinn have appeared and spoken to them.
There are many such superstitions in those
countries. There are innumerable well-known
shamans with whom the djinn speak, especial-
ly in the region near the farthest reaches of civ-
ilization, which is called Barghu and Barghujin
Tögüm. There are many shamans there.
The Uriangqat tribe had many commanders
in Genghis Khan’s time, and there are still a lot

was one of the commanders of the left wing,

mand of a regiment, a commander of the right

be taken around in a cart. He had a reputation
for being soft, for which reason Ögödäi Qa’an

The Qunqirat Tribe4
This tribe is also descended from the two
persons who went into Ärgänä-qun. As has
been mentioned, it is related that the Qunqirat
tribe left that place without warning and with-
out consultation with the others, trampling
their braziers as they went. The Mongols be-
lieve that the gout so prevalent among the
Qunqirat is a result of that action and that the
crime infected their feet. In ancient times the
other Mongols developed a bone of contention
with the Qunqirat for having left first. This is
well known among them.
Many clans have branched off from the Qun-
qirat, each with a separate name and epithet.
Therefore in the list the name of each is given
separately. Since they were originally branches
of this tribe, they are mentioned also in this
original branch, as is reasonable, so as to be
more easily understood.

It is related that their lineage goes back to
three boys born of a golden pot.1 This is merely
an allusion that means that the person who
gave birth to the boys was an intelligent and
very learned individual of culture and educa-
tion who is likened to a “golden pot.” (This ex-
pression is particularly in use among the Mon-
gols, and they customarily say when they see
the king, “We have seen the king’s golden
countenance.” By “golden countenance” they
understand what is meant [158] since the same
expression is used among other tribes, gold be-
ing a noble, much sought-after, and highly pure
substance. Otherwise, to be born of a golden
pot is irrational and impossible.) At any rate,
the names of those three boys and the branches
that came into existence from them are as fol-
lows. The first boy was Churluq Märgän, an-
cestor of the clans that are now called Qunqi-
rat. The second boy was Qabai Shira, who had
two sons, Ikiräs and Olqunu’ut. The third boy
was Tosboda’u, who also had two sons,
Qaranut and Qongli’ut.
The first son, Churluq Märgän. When several
branches of the original Qunqirat tribe had
come into existence, each with its own particu-
lar name and epithet by which it was known
(as will be mentioned later), the name Qunqirat
was applied to some of the remainder. At this
time they are known by that name. This
Churluq Märgän was the ancestor of this
group. The word märgän means someone who
shoots arrows straight. He was on bad terms
with his brother Qabai Shira. One day he got
furious with him and wanted to shoot him.
Qabai Shira got afraid, bent over double on
horseback, lowered his head to the horse’s
side, and watched to see whether his brother
1The “golden pot” (bastū-yi zarrīn) is a translation of
the Mongolian name of the progenitor, Altan Quduqa.
See below, text p. 163.
was going to shoot or not. The brother saw his
face and had compassion. Calming his anger,
he said, [159] “How can I kill my brother?
Since, on the other hand, I have arrow to bow,
how can I not shoot and not teach him a les-
son?” Then he shot so that the arrow grazed his
ear and throat without hitting his face. There-
after his epithet became Märgän.
The Qunqirat dwell in the vicinity of the
öngü, which is like Alexander’s dam separat-
ing the realm of Cathay from the territory of
the Mongols. They call that place Abjiya, and
there they dwell.
There have been many officers and ladies of
Qunqirat lineage in every era. Those who are
known
will
be
reported.
During
Genghis
Khan’s time among his great officers was one
from the Qunqirat tribe, Tärgä Ämäl, chief of a
group of them. He submitted to Genghis Khan
and accompanied him. Genghis Khan gave him
a daughter of his named ___. As he was giving
her he said, “Your daughter is a frog and a tur-
tle. How can I take her?” Highly offended,
Genghis Khan had him executed.
There was another group of the Qunqirat.
Their leader and chief was Däi Noyan. He had
two sons, Elchi Noyan2 and Huqutu Noyan,
and a daughter named Börtä Füjin. Genghis
Khan asked for her as a very young man, but
her father objected strongly. Since Elchi Noyan
had a friendship with Genghis Khan, he endea-
vored to give him his sister, who was older
than he was. Däi Noyan had a brother, Daritai,
who had four sons, Qata, Buyur, Tägüdär, and
Junqur. Most of them and their offspring mar-
ried girls from Genghis Khan’s family and
were given positions such that they sat above
the sons and were all commanders of the left

The Ikiräs Clan
[Altun Quduqa’s] second son was Qabai Shi-
ra. He had two sons, Ikiräs and Olqunut. The
entire Ikiräs clan is descended from Ikiräs.
Mänggü Qa’an’s chief wife, Qutuqtai Khatun,

ludai Gürägän,1 [162] who was the son of Butu
Gürägän,2 who was married to Genghis Khan’s
eldest daughter, Füjin Beki. 
The Olqunu’ut Clan
The Olqunu’ut clan is all from the “bone” of
Olqunut. The Taichu Gürägän who married
Genghis Khan’s youngest daughter, Altan, was
of this clan. His story is long and will be given
separately. He had a son named Chochintai,3
who
married
Mänggü
Qa’an’s
daughter
Shirin.4 When she died he was given her sister,
Bichiqa.
Yesügäi Bahadur’s wife, Genghis Khan’s
mother, Ö’älün Füjin, was of this clan. Olar
Gürägän’s son Taichu Gürägän, who married
Genghis Khan’s youngest daughter Altaluqan,

The Qaranut and Qorolas Clans
The third son [of Altan Quduqa] was Tosbo-
dai. He had two sons, Qaranut and Qongli’ut.
Qongli’ut married one of his father’s wives
and had by her a son named Misär Ölüg, who
also married one of his father’s wives and had
by her a son named Qorolas, from whom the
Qorolas are descended. He married a Cathaian
woman and had a son by her named Eljigen,
from whose “bone” all the Eljigin clan de-
scend. Each of these in succession will be de-
tailed. The three branches that form three sepa-
rate clans from Tosbodai’s sons are as follows.
[163]
Qaranut was Tosbodai’s elder son, and all the
clan called Qaranut are descended from him.
Qongli’ut had a son named Misär Ölüg. (The
word ölüg means a person who fears nothing.
Carrion is also called by this term.) It was his
custom, once he slept, not to wake up for three
days. He was extremely strong. They say that a
tent pole in his hands was like a whip. They
also say that in the spring he used to gather
shells by the seashore and put them in a horse’s
nose bag to cook and eat. Once he was bring-
ing a bag full of shells and along the way went
to sleep under the bag and did not wake up for
three days. Since he had not moved, a bird
called a yirau, thinking him dead, had laid an
egg on his back.

This Misär Ölüg married his father’s wife
and had by her a son named Qorolas, from
whose lineage stems all the Qorolas clan. Al-
though the origin of the Qorolas stems from
the Altan Quduqa who was born of a golden
pot,1 and they and the Qunqirat and Ikiräs stem
from one origin and are therefore aqa-ini to
each other, they have always been at odds and
at war. When Genghis Khan was in Baljiuna,
Jamuqa drove away the Qorolas and Ikiräs,
whose chief was Bütüg Khan,2 and plundered
them. The Ikiräs fled from them and went to
Genghis Khan, uniting with him in Balji’una.
There were three thousand soldiers from the
Qorolas with Otchi Noyan. [164] Doratu
Gürägän was of this clan. 
Butu Gürägän was the brother of Genghis
Khan’s mother,3 and Genghis Khan gave him
his eldest daughter, Füjin Beki. By her he had a
son named Därgäi Gürägän. He gave another

Gürägän. Butu Gürägän’s father was Näkün.5
When Näkün was with the Tayichi’ut tribe, he

because Jochi Qasar had put them to flight by

The Eljigin Clan
Misär Ölüg married a Cathaian wife. Her sto-
ry is as follows. She mounted a donkey and set
out from Cathay, determined to find a husband.
Her name was Dauqai Yabudaq. (In the Catha-
ian language dauqai means ‘flower,’ and yabu-
daq means ‘riding a donkey.’6) [165] Misär
Ölüg had a son by her named Eljigen because
eljigen means donkey and that woman had
come on a donkey. The whole Eljigin clan de-
scends from that son, and there were many
well-known officers and great ladies during his
time. In this land Gharaqai Noyan and his sons
Jai Temür, Amir Ali, Tasu, and Abachi are from
them. Of Eljigen’s lineage are Tasu, Qoru
Qachar Bahadur,7 Sartaq Bahadur, and the Bu-
lughan Khatun who is the Padishah of Islam’s
wife [and] daughter of Amir Tasu. Amir Tasu
came on behalf of the Qa’an as nökär to
Arghun Aqa in order to command the territory
that belongs to the Qa’an. Tasu’s sons are
Kharbanda, Haritai, and Musalman Shüsünchi.
These several branches and clans that have
been mentioned came into being from that

“golden pot.” They are all branches of one
tribe and, as mentioned, all close cousins to
each other. However, each clan has become
separate, formed a military unit, and multiplied
thereafter. Qoru Qachar Bahadur and Sartaq
Bahadur, who have been mentioned, were
brothers during Genghis Khan’s time. When
the division was made, they went to Tolui
Khan in Jädäi Noyan’s regiment, became
anda-quda with the Mangqut tribe, and went at
Genghis
Khan’s
decree
and
brought
the
Targhut tribe in. The chief of the Targhut was
called Qada’an Daldurqan.1 At that time they
swore an oath and made a pact, saying, “We
are like brothers and family to one another.
Just as the Mongols do not marry each other’s
daughters, neither will we; and each of us who
marries a girl from another tribe will observe
the etiquette of daughter-in-law and son-in-
law.” At present they still live in this fashion.
Boralghi Kükältash and Tartai Bariyan were
descended from this Qada’an. [166]
The Oriyat Tribe
Three branches have appeared of the Oriyat,
the Qonqotan, the Arulat, and the Oriyat
Kilungghut. These names were originally the
names of three brothers, from each of whom a
line branched off, multiplying and becoming a
separate clan. Each clan then acquired a sepa-
rate name and epithet after the name of the per-
son with whom they originated.
The Qongqotan Clan
The first son was Qongqotan. The meaning
of this word is someone with a big nose, and
that is why he got this name. There were great
officers of his lineage. In Genghis Khan’s time
Münglig Echigä was descended from him.
When Ong Khan proved treacherous and sum-
1He is called Qada’an Daldurqan of the Targhud in the
Secret History (§124, 172)
moned Genghis Khan on the pretext of giving
his daughter to [Genghis Khan’s] son, whereas
he actually wanted to seize him, Genghis Khan
was on his way when he stopped at Münglig
Echigä’s home and consulted with him. Müng-
lig Echigä kept him from going.2 He was al-
ways with Genghis Khan, in good times and
bad. Genghis Khan gave him his mother,
Ö’älün Ekä, and he sat above all the officers
next to Genghis Khan and on his right. Müng-
lig Echigä had a son named Kököchü, whom
the Mongols used to call Täb Tängri.3 It was
his custom to inform of hidden things and pre-
dict the future. He used to say, “God speaks to
me and goes into heaven.” He always used to
come to Genghis Khan, and say, “God has
commanded that you be the ruler of the
world.” It was he who gave him the title
Genghis Khan (Chingiz Khan), saying, “By
God’s command your name must be thus.”
[167] In Mongolian ching means strong, and
chingiz is the plural. The reason for this name
was as follows. At that time the great rulers of
the Qarakhitai had the title Gür Khan. Gür also
means strong, and a ruler was not called gür
khan until he became extremely grand. In
Mongolian chingiz khan means the same, but
even more so because it is a plural. This word
is used very much as, for example, shahanshah
[‘king of kings’] is used in Persian. 
Täb Tängri was accustomed to go in winter
to a place called Utan Kävrän, which is the
coldest place in the territory, and sit naked in
the ice, which would melt from the heat of his
body and rise in steam. The common Mongols
and their ancestors say that he used to go up
into heaven on a gray horse. This is an exag-
geration and fabrication of the common peo-

ple. He did possess the power to lead and de-
ceive, and he spoke audaciously to Genghis
Khan, but since some [of what he said] was in
conformity with Genghis Khan’s nature, he
liked him. After that, when he spoke too much
and boldly meddled in everything, Genghis
Khan realized through his perfect intelligence
and perspicacity that he was a crazy, sick man.
One day he told his brother Jochi Qasar to kill
him when he entered the camp and started his
meddling. Jochi Qasar was such a powerful
warrior that he could grab a man in his two
hands and break his back like a twig. In short,
when Täb Tängri entered and began his med-
dling, [Jochi Qasar] kicked him two or three

him. His father, seated in his place, picked up
his hat, not imagining that they would kill him.
When he saw that he had been killed, he fell
silent, remaining grave and dignified. [168] He
was in charge of a regiment of the left wing.
[Münglig Echigä] had three other sons, all of
whom were great officers and in command of
regiments. One was named Tolun Chärbi; the
second was Sökätü Chärbi. These two were
both regimental commanders of the right wing.
The third son’s name was Sutu, and he was a
commander of the left wing. Descended from
him in this territory is Chekän Khatun’s hus-
band, Tumina, and Abishqa, who went as emis-
saries to the Qa’an. Tödächü Yarghuchi and his

and urugh, [as was] Bürküt Qorchi, who was in

There was an officer in Genghis Khan’s time
who was given to Ögödäi Qa’an along with a
troop. His name was Dayir, and he was an at-
tendant upon Chaghatai. There was another of-
ficer of Genghis Khan’s named Yisa’ur Qorchi.
After Genghis Khan and Tolui Khan died, he
became an attendant upon Tolui Khan’s sons
and Sorqaghtani Beki.
Among the other great officers of Genghis
Khan’s youth was one from this clan named
Charagha Äbügän. His story comes in the his-
tory. Among his sons in this land are El Temür,
the regimental commander Baiju, and his
brother Mas‘ud, who was the shahna of Shiraz.
The qorchi officers of this clan who were in
Abaqa Khan’s time were Etälgü and Bürküt
and their sons.
The Arulat Clan1
The second son was Arulat. This word means
someone who is his mother and father’s dar-
ling. The whole Arulat clan descends from this
son, and there have been great officers and
ladies of this line in every age. 
During Genghis Khan’s time [169] there was
Borghochin Noyan of this clan.2 In this land of
this clan are Beglämish and Ujan3 and [Ujan’s]
son Saru, who is alive now. Borghochin Noyan
was Genghis Khan’s companion from his
childhood and never rebelled against him. He
performed valiant feats and was in the right
wing, sitting above the officers. 
They say that when Genghis Khan was a
mere youth and went to do battle with some of
the Tayichi’ut, he received arrow wounds in
the mouth and neck and returned in a weak-
ened state. Borghochin Noyan and Boroghul
Noyan were with him. They helped him off his
horse in the midst of a blinding snowstorm.
Borghochin took hold of his horse and in that
state warmed a stone and poured water on it
until steam arose. Then he held [Genghis
Khan’s] mouth over the steam so that the dead

To
Boroghul he said, “Don’t worry and don’t be
upset. You be an arrow, and I’ll be the stew so
we’ll fill his thigh with flesh.” With this exalt-
ed thought, powerful resolve, and strength of
character,
once
again
Genghis
Khan
and
they—as will come in the history—rose to
prominence, and he rendered the world obedi-
ent and subdued. 
Borghochin Noyan, Boroghul Noyan, and
[Muqali Guyang1] of the Jalayir nation were
old nökärs of Genghis Khan’s who always ac-
companied him. When he gave a command to
all
the
officers,
he
did
not
give
it
to
Borghochin and Boroghul. They knelt and
said, “How is it that you do not command us?”
1The person named here must be Muqali Guyang, al-
though it is almost impossible to see how his name
could be turned into the text’s garbled اوﰏ ﻛﻮﺟﻮ.
“Your status is too great for me to give you a
specific command,” he replied.
In
Ögödäi
Qa’an’s
time,
[Borghochin’s]
nephew Boroltai was given command of his
tümän. During Mänggü Qa’an’s time Boroltai’s
son Balchiq commanded it. In Qubilai Qa’an’s
time Borghochin Noyan’s son was in command
of that tümän, and after him, also in Qubilai
Qa’an’s time, Boroltai’s son Jirqamish com-
manded it.
Boroltai had many sons who were also great
officers. One of them was Öz Temür Ba’urchi,
a great and fortunate commander who was
highly renowned.
In this land there are of Borghochin Noyan’s
progeny Beglämish and his son Ujan, who
have been mentioned, and Tüläk, who was ex-
ecuted for having rebelled with Sögä. There
was also Toqolqu Chärbi, a regimental com-
mander of the left wing. Beglämish was
Borghochin Noyan’s brother. Of their progeny
at this time is Tabayin2 Turqaqun, a great com-
mander in the Qa’an’s service. In the Cathaian
language tabayin means chief; Turqaqun is his
name.
Genghis Khan said of Borghochin Noyan,
“His rank is lower than that of a khan and
higher than that of officers and the qarachu
(commoners).” [171]
Borghochin
Noyan
said
in
Mongolian,
“When the crow misspeaks, I didn’t. When the
bird is perplexed by a mirror, I was not and did
not make a mistake. When the dust of the earth
went up to the sky and came down from the
sky to the earth, I did not mistake the way.
Therefore have I attained the rank that they call
me Borghochin.”
His initial contact with Genghis Khan was as
follows. When Genghis Khan was still a young
man and his followers and soldiers had desert-
2Most MSS have Z)ﻳﻦ here. A variant س also occurs.
84
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ed, he was in a weakened position. One day
some Mongol thieves came and stole his hors-
es. Learning of it immediately, he was not able
to gather his liege men but at once went out af-
ter the thieves by himself. Along the way he
spied a rider stopped. It was Borghochin.
When he came up to him he asked, “Who are
you, and why are you stopped?”
“I was waiting to talk to you,” he replied.
“I’ll be the manglai (forward), and you be
my gäjigä (rear),” said Genghis Khan.
Borghochin said, “The horses are yours.
What reliance do you have on me? I may run
away when you chase [the thieves] off. Let me
be in front and you bring up the rear. That way
I won’t be able to run away and will have to
fight.”
There was much discussion and a great deal
of insistence. Finally, with Genghis Khan
taking up the rear and Borghochin going in
front, they chased the thieves away and
recovered the horses. Genghis Khan liked this
very much and developed a total trust in him.
He became his attendant and gained impor-
tance.1 [172]
The Oriyat Kilungghut Clan
The third son was Oriyat Kilungghut. He got
this name because he was squint-eyed. All the
Kilungghut branches and clans descend from
him, and they are numerous. Badai and Qishliq
were of this clan, and they were called Kilung-
ghut Tarkhan.
Genghis
Khan
made
them
tarkhan. Although they are of the Kilungghut
clan, Tarkhan became the proper name of that
clan, and their descendants are many. Of
Badai’s sons were Tarkhan Khwarazmi and
Sadaq Tarkhan. Of Qishliq’s sons was Aqutai,
a captain of a thousand. Badai and Qishliq
were the head grooms of Yäkä Chärän, a great
officer of Ong Khan’s. The reason they were
1The episode occurs in the Secret History §§90–92.
made tarkhan will be explained in the history
of Genghis Khan.
The Qirjin clan is a branch of the Kilung-
ghut. Of all the cousins, the very fat Qongqatai
Qabcha Qabai who was in Khurasan was of
this clan.
The Hushin Tribe
One of the great commanders of this clan in
Genghis Khan’s time was Boroghul Noyan.2
He was initially a bökä’ül and ba’urchi in
Genghis Khan’s service. Later he became
greater, then he became a captain of the guard,
then a commander of a thousand. After that he
was an important commander in the right wing,
second to Borghochin Noyan. They performed
many valiant feats, and they were so important
and dear to Genghis Khan that he said, “Isn’t it
a shame that Borghochin will die? Isn’t it a
shame that Boroghul will die?” [173] The ser-
vices rendered by Boroghul will be chronicled
in the history of Genghis Khan. He was killed
in battle against the Tumat, a Mongol tribe, al-
though he defeated them.3 In Ögödäi Qa’an’s
time his son Jübükür Qubila took his place.
After that, in Qubilai Qa’an’s time, there was
Tuqchi Gürägän, also of [Boroghul’s] progeny.
He became gürägän by marrying Shirin, who
was Qutuqtu’s daughter and Hülägü Khan’s
niece. She was Kälmish Aqa’s sister and was
born of Qulan Khatun.
There was another great commander named
Hushidai Baiqu. Genghis Khan gave him and
his troop to Jochi, and he commanded Batu’s
right wing. At the end of his life he said, “I am
old and feeble. I can’t do this any longer.”

There was a man of the Jä’üriyät tribe named
Yäldäka,
whose
mother
he
had
married.
[Hushidai] brought [Yäldäkä] and made him
his

After
that
[Yäldäkä]
took
[Hushidai’s] place. At the present time great

In this land are Ghurbatai Gürägän and his
sons Beglämish and Bitigchi, who are alive

Boroghul Noyan, named Hushijin.1 He had a
son by her named Ayachi.
The Suldus Tribe2
Since there are numerous officers from this
tribe, we will take up first those who were
more famous and grandiose in Genghis Khan’s
service and whose histories are better known
and explain things first that are of greater
importance.
When Genghis Khan was young and the
Tayichi’ut tribe [174] was determined to op-
pose him, his soldiers and followers deserted
him and his rule had not yet gained strength.
One day he mounted and was on his way to do
something. He saw a rock rolling down the
road without anything pushing it. It was com-
ing toward him. To himself he thought, “This
is very strange. I should not be traveling along
this road.” He paused a moment and then,
putting it out of his mind, went merrily along
his way.
It chanced to happen that Targhutai Qiriltuq,
the ruler of the Tayichi’ut nation who was his
enemy, caught him, took him captive, and held
him in a dushakha.3 At that time it was custom-
1(H)ushijin, i.e. of the Hushin tribe, as below on text

2The Suldus are mentioned in the Secret History §120;
they were of some prominence during Timurid times,
