ary not to kill captives right away. There was
an old woman named Tayichu Egächi. (She
was called Tayichu because she was of the
[Tayichi’ut] nation. She had a husband from
the Märkit, but his name is not known. The
Qa’an’s emissary Ucha’urghai who came with
Angatai Elchi is descended from her.) At any
rate, the old woman used to comb Genghis
Khan’s hair and wait on him. Every time his
neck was irritated by the dushakha, she placed
a bit of felt on it and consoled him. After a
while, one day Genghis Khan got a chance to
escape with the dushakha. There was a large
lake in the vicinity. He went there and sank be-
neath the water with the dushakha so that only
his nose was above the surface. A group of the
Tayichi’ut came in pursuit, looking for him.
Among them was Sorghan Shira of the Suldus,
the father of Chila’ughan Bahadur, who was
the father of Sodon Noyan. His tent was near-
by. Suddenly he spied Genghis Khan’s nose,
and he realized that it was he. He made a
furtive motion for him to lower his head more
in the water and said to the group, “You go
look elsewhere. [175] I’ll keep watch here.” So
saying, he got them to go away.
When night fell, he got Genghis Khan out of
the water, removed the dushakha from his
neck, and took him home, where he hid him on
a cart under a lot of wool. When the posse
tracked him down to that place, they suspected
that he was in Sorghan Shira’s house. They
searched high and low, even sticking stakes
into the wool several times, but there was no
trace of him. (Since God had willed that he en-
joy fortune, at no time did he suffer pain or
wounds on his blessed body.) Not having
found him, they left. Sorghan Shira then gave

him a dark brown mare, a bit of meat, a roast-
ing skewer, a bow, arrows, and every tool and
implement necessary for traveling—though
some say no, he sent him on his way without
giving him a flint. No matter how much oblig-
ation they admit, they still blame him some-
what for not having given him some tools and
a flint. Let us here excuse him until the matter
is completely revealed: “perhaps he has an ex-
cuse for what you blame him.”
During that time Genghis Khan’s mother,
wives, and clan had given up hope of seeing
him again. His fourth son, Tolui Khan, was a
child. During the last few days he had been
constantly saying, “My father is coming, riding
a mare.” His mother kept rebuking him and
boxing his ears, saying, “What kind of non-
sense is this child saying? He constantly re-
minds us of him and causes us grief.” But the
child would not cease and kept on talking. 
Finally, on the day on which Genghis Khan
would arrive, Tolui Khan said, “My father is
coming riding on a brown mare with two larks
[176] hanging from his saddle ring.” 
“What has possessed this child?” the mother
asked, but he kept insisting that his father was
coming. After a while Genghis Khan arrived,
riding a brown mare, with two larks hanging
from his saddle ring. All rejoiced at his arrival,
though they were astonished at Tolui Khan’s
words, which they related to Genghis Khan
and in return for which they gave alms.
When Sorghan Shira realized that his having
hidden Genghis Khan was no longer secret, he
knew it was necessary to get out of the midst
of the Tayichi’ut. Decamping with his house-
hold and followers, he went to Genghis Khan,
who welcomed him and his sons and followers
and honored him greatly.
Chila’uqan Bahadur was Sorghan Shira’s
son, and he was very brave and manly. Once in
battle he fell from his horse unexpectedly, and
the enemy galloped at him to kill him. He leapt
up, charged the rider on foot with his lance,
and put him to flight, chasing him for a league.
Genghis Khan was astonished and said, “How
can a man who has fallen from his horse have
the strength to get up and do battle? Even if he
does get up, how can he charge a rider and de-
feat him?
Have you never seen a man on foot do battle or
bring the heads of the unruly under his claw?
I have never seen the likes of this champion.”
After Genghis Khan had repeatedly done bat-
tle with the Tayichi’ut, finally, in the last battle,
Chila’ughan Bahadur fought the Tayichi’ut
ruler, Targhutai Qiriltuq, [177] who was a
mighty warrior, tall and huge. Chila’ughan Ba-
hadur was short. He struck Qiriltuq in the pu-
bic region with his lance and wanted to shake
him loose from his horse, but he couldn’t. He
let go of the lance, stuck the end of the lance in
the ground, and jabbed so hard that it passed
through his pubic region and went into his bel-
ly. As he fell from his horse he said, “I thought
that if my gut was ripped to shreds by a sword
I wouldn’t die. That such a miserable, insignif-
icant person, the son of Sorghan Shira, like a
bunch of cardoon1 the shamans use as a small
whip, should strike me with a lance, not have
strength, and let go of it so that I would be
killed thus.”
Of Bezhan low was the plain with might: / craft
turns to flaw when the sun turns its back.
In the end Targhutai died of that wound and
entrusted his soul to Mâlik, [warden of Hell].
Chila’ughan Bahadur’s son was Sodon Noy-
an. In Genghis Khan’s time he was a comman-
der of the right wing and of great importance.
He was still alive during Ögödäi Qa’an’s time

The Ildürgin Clan
This clan is a branch of the Suldus tribe.
During Genghis Khan’s time when he was

The Baya’ut Tribe3
This tribe consists of several branches, but
only two are well known. One is called Jädäi-

The Jädäi is a river in Mongolia, and since they
dwelt there, they were called after the place
and it became their proper name. Those who
dwell in the plains are called the Kähärün
Baya’ut.
Their yurt is the Selenga River and the two
extremes of Qurban Kähät and Börä Ündür,
which is the great ghoruq. At the farthest ex-
tremity, where the river divides into three
branches, Sodon Noyan was given a yurt. At
present the Suldus clans dwell there, and it be-
longs
to

are

SECTION TWO OF CHAPTER FOUR
THE TRIBES OF [MONGOL] TURKS CALLED NIRU’UN
They are one of the Mongol tribes descended
from Alan Qo’a, who was a Qorolas by de-
scent, and the Qorolas are a branch of the Dür-
lükin Mongols. According to their claim and
report, Alan Qo’a became pregnant from a
light, without the benefit of a husband, and
gave birth to three sons. Those who are de-
scended
from
these
three
are
called
the
Niru’un, which means loins and is a reference
to the pure line that came into existence from
light. The clans descended from Alan Qo’a and
her three sons consist of three divisions.
The First Division
The first division are those descended from
Alan Qo’a down to the sixth generation, Qabul
Khan. They are called altogether the Niru’un.
Qabul Khan’s brothers and sons and their off-
spring are all called the Niru’un clans. Their
divisions follow.
The Qataqin Clan1
This clan belongs to the Niru’un, and they
branched off from Alan Qo’a’s eldest son,
Buqu Qataqi. They were hostile to Genghis
Khan, [184] and therefore they are numerous
in every ulus even though they are not so well
known or famous. Those who were of impor-
tance in Genghis Khan’s time were as follows.
A’uchu Bahadur was a great commander and
leader who was allied with Buyiruq Khan of
the Naiman. Other great commanders who
were in his time are ___.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The Salji’ut Clan1
This clan descends from Alan Qo’a’s middle
son, Bu’utu Salji. There are many commanders
of this lineage, but many of them were killed
because they were so often hostile to Genghis
Khan. At that time there was an officer from
this clan named Samuqa. Although he was not
a military leader, Genghis Khan gave him a
troop several times and sent him on important
missions. One of those was when one of Altan
Khan’s great commanders deserted Altan Khan
along with his troop and was inclined to
Genghis Khan. Samuqa was sent with a troop
to escort the commander and his troop to
Genghis Khan. After that, he besieged and took
the city of Jungdu, which is now called Daidu,2
with the Cathaian soldiers who had submitted.
He got hold of all the possessions, treasuries,
and officers of Altan Khan that were there.
Several other times he was sent on important
missions. 
[Samuqa] was the one who used to get angry
whenever the word goat was used. This was
because when he was a child he copulated with
a goat, and of course anyone who fornicates
with a goat will be called one by people. He
fought with Shigi Qutuqu Noyan over this, and
there was very bad blood between them. Later
they made up and [185] decided that hence-
forth the word ‘goat’ would not be said. Some-
one said to him, “If you say the word goat, I’ll
give you something.” He said it, and when
Qutuqu Noyan learned of it he said, “You quar-
reled with me over this, and then we promised
not to say the word goat any more. You say
1The Salji’ut are mentioned in the Secret History §42
(Salji’ud).
2Readingداى
دو(Daidu) for the text’sــــﻳدا
ﺮزو. “Jungdu”
(中都Zhongdu) is Peking. See text p. 901 below for the
new capital Daidu (大都Da(i) Du) built by Qubilai
Khan.
‘goat’ for the sake of some miserable thing and
you can tolerate it.” Qutuqu Noyan drew his
sword and ran after him to strike him, but [the
blow] landed in front of the saddle horn and
did not reach him. Then people intervened and
stopped them.
In the land of Iran there are Shaykh Sevinchi
and his brother Baltu Sevinchi of this clan.
When Genghis Khan was orphaned of his fa-
ther as a child and his relatives who had at-
tended his father, Yesügäi Bahadur, deserted
him, and after that several clans of the Dür-
lükin Mongols united with him and became
subject to him, he consulted with Jamuqa
Sächän and sent an emissary to the Qataqin
and Salji’ut clans. It was their custom at that
time to speak in cryptic and enigmatic rhyming
words, and the message they sent with the
emissary was of that type. They did not under-
stand it and were perplexed. A youth in their
midst said, “The meaning of these words is as
follows: ‘Many clans like the Qataqin, Tatar,
and Dürlükin, which are unrelated to us, have
all becomes friendly and united with us. Let us,
who are aqa-ini and blood relations to each
other, unite and be friends.’ ”
Rejecting this, they took some sokhtu (a kind
of sausage the Mongols cook from innards and
blood) from the kettle and threw it on the emis-
sary to drive him away with derision. Because
of that, great enmity and hostility arose, and
battle and sedition ensued between them.
Many times they took out their troops and did
battle. [186] In the end Genghis Khan won and
killed untold numbers of them. However nu-
merous they may have been, few of them sur-
vived. Since those who remained were rela-
tives, they submitted and became subservient,
and some of them became clients of other
Mongol tribes. 
This clan was not left with any status from
their relationship to Genghis Khan, except that
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER FOUR, SECTION ONE: THE DÜRLÜKIN
91

he ordered that their daughters not be sought or
given in marriage because they were related to
him, and in this way they were distinguished
from other Mongol tribes.
The Tayichi’ut Clan1
In some manuscripts of Mongol history it is
recorded that the Tayichi’ut clan stems from
the second son of Dutum Mänen, Nachin. In
the Altan Daftar, which is always kept in the
khans’ treasury by great officers, it has been
seen to be clearly recorded that the Tayichi’ut
originate with Charaqa Lingqum, the son of
Qaidu
Khan.
Nachin’s
lineage
is
found
nowhere else. There is only this much—that he
rescued his nephew Qaidu from the Jalayir,
and they left together and took up residence at
the Onon River. For this reason the [first] ver-
sion must be more correct.
When the Tayichi’ut clans became numerous,
perhaps Nachin’s sons mixed in with them and
adopted their name. It is most likely so. Other-
wise some mention of his sons would have
come somewhere.
The clans of the Tayichi’ut consist of numer-
ous branches. Their origin and lineage are as
follows. Qaidu Khan had three sons, and the
eldest was named Bai Singqor, from whom
stems the branch of Genghis Khan’s forefa-
thers. The third son was named Cha’ujin, [187]
and from him descend the two clans of the
[H]ärigän2 and Sanchi’ut. The middle son was
named
Charaqa
Lingqum,
and
all
the
Tayichi’ut clans are descended from him.
Charaqa Lingqum is a Cathaian name and
epithet. Lingqum means great commander, but
since the Mongols do not know what lingqum
means, they say linqum.3

When
Charaqa
Lingqum’s
brother
Bai
Singqor died, he married his brother’s widow,
the mother of Tumina Qa’an, and had by her
two sons, Kündü China and Ölögchin China. 
By the wife he had chosen himself he also
had sons, one of whom succeeded him and be-
came famous. He was Sorqadu China,4 and he
was the qu‘dūd of Tumina Khan. His son who
succeeded him was Hambaqai Qa’an, who was
the qu‘dūd of Qabul Khan. Hambaqai Qa’an’s
son and successor was Qada’an Taishi, who
was the qu‘dūd of Bartan Bahadur. At that time
all the aqa-inis were in accord with each other.
The Tatar nation was subservient to the ruler
of Cathay. They ambushed Hambaqai Qa’an
and sent him to the Altan Khan of Cathay to be
nailed to a wooden donkey and killed. Qutula
Qa’an, one of Qabul Khan’s sons, went out to
wage war against Cathay in revenge for that
act and killed many of them. After that, during
the time of Yesügäi Bahadur, the Tayichi’ut
clans had become numerous with sons, broth-
ers, and cousins; and in Genghis Khan’s time,
as will be related in the history, they began to
dispute and quarrel, but the sons of Kündü
China and Ölögchin China took Genghis
Khan’s part. During his time the grandsons of
Hambaqai Qa’an and Qada’an Taishi who were
famous and leaders and chieftains of their peo-
ple and who fought alongside Genghis Khan
[188] were as follows:
Tödä’ä, the son of Qada’an Taishi, had a son
named Jochi Khan (different from the Jochi
who was a son of Qutula Qa’an, was allied
with Genghis Khan, and was an elder brother

of Altan). The father of Sodon Noyan of the
Suldus and Jäbä of the Besüt were attached to
him, and their story has already been given in
the section on them.1 They fled from him and
went over to Genghis Khan.
Jäbä belonged to Tödä’ä. His name was
Jirqutai, but Genghis Khan named him Jäbä
because when he went to Genghis Khan he
asked him, “Who killed my white-muzzled
horse that Chila’uqun Bahadur was riding?”
“I did,” he replied. 
Genghis Khan said, “This man is worthy of
jäbälämishi (being clad in mail),”2 by which he
meant being a warrior. Therefore his name be-
came Jäbä.
They said that once during Yesügäi Baha-
dur’s time when they went out to do battle with
the Tayichi’ut, he had made a rendezvous with
the Qongqotan clans, but they got to the battle
early, and many of them were killed by the
Tayichi’ut. All of a sudden Yesügäi Bahadur
arrived and saved the Qongqotan from the
Tayichi’ut, who had killed so many of them
that seventy carts were loaded with their bones.
This became a well-known saying.
Adal
Khan,
a
descendant
of
Hambaqai
Qa’an, was in Yesügäi Bahadur’s time. He was
not contentious or rebellious. [189] His son
Tarqutai Qiriltuq was at the end of Genghis
Khan’s time. The word qiriltuq means stingy
and envious. Since he had these qualities he
was so nicknamed. He initiated seditiousness
against Yesügäi Bahadur and fought hostile
battles against Genghis Khan.
Until the end of Qada’an Taishi’s time the
Tayichi’ut clans had a ruler and chief of impor-
tance under whose command they obeyed will-
ingly. For that reason their elder, the Tödä’ä
who was in Genghis Khan’s time, and his rela-

and

me and my brethren.” Tarqutai said, “Baghachi
has taken my targhun emä (meaning wife and
children). I want to show him my manliness
and
strength.”
Because
of
this
dispute
Baghachi gave in, but later he regretted it and
turned away. Although Tödä’ä was not en-
throned as ruler, he was the son of a ruler and
of considerable influence. He had sons, the el-
dest of whom was the Toghril whom Genghis

In the end, when Genghis Khan overcame

Quril Bahadur was a cousin of Tarqutai Qiril-

Angqu Huquchu was also a cousin of theirs.
Their genealogical chart and names have

Dalu,

and

Yadaghana. Jamuqa was also united and then

again went back on their word.
Chula and Qachi’un Beki were commanders
of the Tayichi’ut. Ong Khan’s brother, Jagam-
bu was a friend and ally of his. When Ong
Khan was fighting Genghis Khan he was in

every ulus from this clan. In this land the sons
of Kältägä Udachi, Sarkis, Qabai, and Sam-
aghar, are of this clan.
The Härigän and Sanchi’ut Clans
They are two clans descended from Qaidu
Khan’s youngest son, Cha’ujin, the younger
brother of Bai Singqor and Charaqa Lingqum,
as has been stated in the section on the
Tayichi’ut. The details and branches of the two
will now be given.
1The To’oril De’ü of the Secret History §180.
The first branch, the Härigän. In Iran no one
of importance from this clan is known, but in
Mongolia people of this “bone” are numerous,
and there are many great men from this clan.
[192]
The second branch, the Sanchi’ut. Many
from this clan have attained greatness, but
there is no one of importance known in this
land. In Genghis Khan’s time when he was di-
viding the officers and army among the
princes, he gave Möngädü Noyan from this
clan to Jochi Khan. In Batu’s time he com-
manded the army. At present there is a great
commander named Charkas of this lineage
who is with Toqtai. 
The Chinas Clan
Although they too are of the Tayichi’ut clan,
during
Genghis
Khan’s
fight
with
the
Tayichi’ut they were allies of Genghis Khan.
This branch came into existence from two of
Charaqa Lingqum’s sons, as was explained in
the section on him, for he married his brother’s
widow and had by her two sons, Kündü China
and Ölögchin China. Chinas is the plural of
china, and the two names mean male wolf and
female wolf. Those descended from them are
called the Chinas. Some of this clan are also
called Nüküz. Another tribe of the Dürlükin
Mongols are also called Nüküz: they are a
branch of those who emerged from Ärgänä-
qun by melting the mountain with ironsmith’s
bellows, as was explained in previous sections.
Cha’urchi, a regimental commander in this
land was of this lineage, but no one of impor-
tance from the Chinas branch is known in this
land. [193]

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The Noyaqin, Uru’ut, and Mangqut Clans1
The eldest of Tumina’s nine sons was named
Jaqso. From his sons three lines arose. One is
called the Noyaqin clan, another is called the
Uru’ut, and the third is called the Mangqut
clan. In Genghis Khan’s time the Noyaqin and
Uru’ut were at one with the Tayichi’ut and
hostile to Genghis Khan. At present there is no
one from those clans. During Genghis Khan’s
reign the leaders of the Uru’ut, insofar as is
known, were Udut and Budut, who were op-
posed [to Genghis Khan]. 
According to one version it is related that the
clans that have been interralted for a long time
and spring from one origin are: the Qongqotan,
Sönit, Qirqiz, Barulas, Ba’arin Ilinggut, Eljit,
Kökömän, Uru’ut, Mangqut, Oruna’ut, Arulat,
and Besüt.
One of the important officers in Genghis
Khan’s service was Jädäi Noyan, and we will
give his history in this chapter [although] it is
not known if he was of the Noyaqin clan. 
The Mangqut clan, like the Uru’ut, also
mostly took the part of the Tayichi’ut, except
for Quyildar Sächän, who was in league with
Genghis Khan along with his followers and
allies and performed valiant feats, as will be
described separately. Genghis Khan called him
anda.
Also of the Mangqut clan at that time were
three
brothers
who
decided
to
join
the
Tayichi’ut. The youngest brother said to the
others, “What bad have we seen of Genghis
Khan that we would separate ourselves from
him and join his enemies?” The others flew
into a rage, and the elder brother hit him on the
waist with a mace. The middle brother and all

(Noyakin), as are the Uru’ut (Uru’ud) and the Mangqut
(Mangghud).
The
Mangqut
are
mentioned
in
the
Qinzheng lu, 3395 as the Mangwu (忙兀).
his liege men shot him with arrows and killed
him. [194] They also plundered his family,
children, herds, and flocks. He had a nursing
babe by a woman he had married from the
Barghut tribe, who were nearby. The woman’s
relatives carried the babe away on their horses.
The uncles tried to kill it, but they hid the child
in a stack of wool, and when the uncles came
searching they even poked the wool with
skewers, but since God was protecting it, it
suffered no harm. After a time [the uncles still]
suspected that the child was with them, and
once again they came to kill it, but this time
they hid it under a kettle. Since the child was
destined to live, they did not find it. Several
years later when God gave Genghis Khan
strength and weakened the Tayichi’ut and the
other clans that were obedient to them, the
Barghut took the child they had kept, which
was named Jädäi, and turned it over to Genghis
Khan. Genghis Khan rewarded them and treat-
ed the child sympathetically and consolingly.
When he grew up he became a great comman-
der and was known as Jädäi Noyan. When
Genghis
Khan
completely
defeated
the
Tayichi’ut, and the Uru’ut and Mangqut had no
choice but to submit, he killed most of them
and gave the rest as slaves to Jädäi Noyan. Al-
though they were his kin, they became his
slaves by decree, and until now the Uru’ut and
Mangqut troops are slaves to Jädäi Noyan’s
progeny. He was one of the great commanders
of the right wing and always accompanied
Genghis Khan. In Ögödäi Qa’an’s time he was
still alive and served Sorqaghtani Beki and
Tolui Khan’s sons. After that, in Qubilai
Qa’an’s time, his grandson Mangqudai took
over his command. [195]
Of Mangqudai’s progeny in this land was the
father of Qutlughshah Noyan, a regimental
commander of the Mangqut clan. His brother
Hulqutu Qorchi became an officer of the guard
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER FOUR, SECTION ONE: THE DÜRLÜKIN
95

and commander of the Qara’unas’ tümän.
Hulqutu’s sons were Chapi and his brother
Jalaluddin. Manqudai’s sons were Qutlughshah
Noyan, who was a great commander for the
Padishah of Islam, and Temür Buqa, who was
a regimental commander. They had two or
three other brothers who died. Märtäd is also a
cousin of theirs. In Hülägü Khan’s time
Qudusun Noyan of the Mangqut clan was a
great officer of the guard, but Hülägü Khan
dismissed him as officer of the guard and put
his relative Temür in his place. He was still
alive during Arghun Khan’s time. Hushidai, a
shahna of Baghdad, was also of this clan.
The story of Quyildar Sächän is as follows.
He was usually allied with Genghis Khan, per-
formed valiant service, and was called anda.
When he returned from battle with Ong Khan,
went to Baljiuna, and then left there, his army
consisted of 4,600 men who were traveling as
a bölük [unit]. Of them 2,300 men were of the
Uru’ut and Mangqut clans, and 2,300 were
Genghis Khan’s men and others. Of the Uru’ut
and Mangqut contingents all that were Uru’ut
were commanded by Kähätäi Noyan, and the
Mangquts were commanded by Quyildar. One
of the valiant feats he performed was as
follows. 
When Genghis Khan was fighting Ong Khan
in Qalajin Älät, his followers were few, while
Ong Khan’s were many. Genghis Khan asked
his commanders, “What shall we do?” Kähätäi
Noyan, the leader of the Uru’ut clan, hesitated,
rubbing his whip over his horse’s mane and
saying nothing. Quyildar Sächän said, “Let my
brother and my ally look [196] at that hill be-
hind the enemy. Its name is Köyidän. I’ll
gallop there. If God gives me a way to pass
through the enemy, I’ll plant my standard on
that hill. When the soldiers see it, let them
come in that direction, and we will smite the
enemy. If God does not grant me passage and I
die, let Genghis Khan take charge of protecting
my children.” So saying, he galloped off,
found a way, and smote the Kerayit army.
(This story will be given in detail in the
history.1)
After him, his son Möngkä Qalja took charge
of his command. The Mulqar Qalja who came
with Chormaqan Noyan was descended from
him. There are also many of his progeny in the
Qa’an’s service. In this land are his sons Khali-
fa and Mäkritäi. The Nüregäi Yarghuchi who
was an officer and courtier in Abaqa Khan’s
time and also after that during Gaikhatu
Khan’s reign was also of his progeny.
There was an officer of the Mangqut clan
who was allied with Ong Khan. His name was
Taghai Qulqai, and he was also called Taghai
Kähärin. (Kähärin means thief and liar, and
among the Mongols anyone who is so de-
scribed suffers. Since he became known by
such a bad name, he was always depressed.) 
During Genghis Khan’s time there was an
important
commander
of
the
Uru’ut
clan
named Kähätäi Noyan, and he had a brother
who was also a great commander named Bujir.
Kähätäi Noyan became extremely great and
was one of the commanders of the left wing.
One story about him is as follows. One night
he was commanding the guard in Genghis
Khan’s camp. Genghis Khan had a nightmare,
woke up, and asked for a light. In the camp
was a lady named Ibaqa Beki, the daughter of
Jagambu, and he said to her, “I have always
been good to you, and I have seen nothing bad
from you. I have just had a dream, and God
commanded me to give you away. You must
not be angry.” Then he called out, [197] “Who
is outside?” Kähätäi Noyan, who was on
guard, answered, “It’s me.” He summoned him
inside and said, “I give this lady to you. Take
1See text p. 385 below.
96
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

her.” Kähätäi Noyan was petrified, but Genghis
Khan consoled him and said, “Do not fear. I
am speaking right.” He said to the lady, “As
mementos, leave me one cook and the golden
goblet from which I drink kumiss,” and he
gave all the rest, everything in the camp, ev-
oghlans, horses, retainers, stores, herds and
flocks, to the lady and handed her over to
Kähätäi Noyan.
The Dörbän Clan1
This clan is Niru’un. They are close to the
Ba’arin clan and spring from the same origin.
During Genghis Khan’s time they were allied
with the Tayichi’ut and were very hostile to
Genghis Khan. One of their officers who is of
importance and well known is the Bolad Aqa
who is in Qubilai Qa’an’s service.2 He was
both a chingsang and a ba’urchi, and he came
to this land as an envoy. He is an influential of-
ficer and well known. His father Yürki was
Genghis Khan’s ba’urchi and was attached to
the camp of his chief wife, Börtä Füjin. He
commanded a company of a hundred in the
personal thousand. Amir Bolad’s sons are in
service to the Qa’an. Amir Saruq Qorchi, who
was chief of the qorchis, was also of this clan.
There have been great officers and ladies from
this clan in every age. Qubilai Qa’an had a
wife from this clan named Dörbäjin, the moth-
er of Hügächi. [198]
The Ba’arin Clan3
The Ba’arin clan is closely related to the
Dörbän, and they spring from one origin. The
Suqai’ut also spring from the Ba’arin. Their

origin is as follows. There were three brothers
from whom these two branches descend. 
Among the great and well-known officers
from the Ba’arin during Genghis Khan’s time
was an officer named Nayaqa Noyan, one of
the commanders of the left wing, one rank
lower
than
Muqali
Guyang.
He
was
a
sütüküsün, meaning that he was like an over-
seer shahna and second in command. In his
youth he was called Naya Jusur (jusur means
hypocritical and shameless), for it was the
Ba’arin clan’s custom to play rough games and
indulge in many pranks at which they had not
the slightest shame. Nayaqa Noyan lived to be
extremely old, over a hundred, and he was still
alive in Ögödäi Qa’an’s time. He said that
when Genghis Khan married his first wife, he
ate some of the food from the groom’s banquet
and remembered it.
Once, when Genghis Khan was fighting the
Tayichi’ut, [Nayaqa Noyan’s] father, Shir-
gü’ätü Äbügän, was with the Tayichi’ut and
biding his time until he captured two of their
leaders and princes, Huquchu and Targhutai
Qiriltuq, and took them to Genghis Khan. 
Genghis Khan made his sons, Naya and
Alaq, his companions, and they were always
with him. Alaq Noyan had a son named
Kökchü, who was executed in ___ on charges
of ___. He had a son named Bayan who served
as a bakhshi to Qubilai Qa’an. When Hülägü
Khan set out for Iran, he was with him. [199]
When Qubilai Qa’an sent Sodon’s son Sartaq
and Abdul-Rahman, as envoys to Hülägü
Khan, he summoned Bayan.4 When Sartaq re-
turned, Bayan went with him. Abdul-Rahman
remained behind here in order to complete an
audit of accounts. When Bayan came before
Qubilai Qa’an, he was rewarded and given a
command. Achuqan, Sübätäi Bahadur’s grand-
4See text p. 198f. above.
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER FOUR, SECTION ONE: THE DÜRLÜKIN
97

son, was made a liege man to him, and they
were sent with thirty tümäns of Mongol sol-
diers and eighty tümäns of Cathaian soldiers to
wage war on the Nankiyas. They went there
and within seven years took the entire realm of
the Nankiyas. Bayan’s son Noqai was in this
land. 
During Genghis Khan’s time there was also a
regimental commander of the right wing from
the Ba’arin named Mangqal Türkän. He had a
relative, also a regimental commander of the
right wing, named Qorchi Noyan.
The Suqai’ut Clan, a sub-branch [of the
Ba’arin]
They
came
about
as
follows.
Ba’arin’s
youngest brother—it has already been said that
there were three brothers—had a maid in his
house who caught his eye. When he had a
chance he laid hands upon her, and she became
pregnant. His wife found out about it and tor-
tured the maid, beating her to make her miscar-
ry, but it didn’t happen. When it was time for
her to give birth, she brought forth the child in
private and, in fear of the wife, she cut a bit of
sable from the husband’s fur coat, wrapped the
infant in it, and placed it in the midst of a
tamarisk forest. By happy chance, the father
was wandering through the tamarisk forest and
heard a baby crying. He picked it up, recog-
nized his fur coat, and realized that since it was
the maid’s time, [the child] must be hers. He
brought it back and gave it to the mother to
take care of and raise—the wife paid no
attention. 
The sons who were later born of that child,
although they are Ba’arin, are nonetheless
called by the name Suqai’ut because in Mon-
golian the name of tamarisk wood is suqai.
[200] They are now a separate clan, and there
have been and are many officers from their
“bone.” 
They say that Genghis Khan turned loose a
man of the Ba’arin clan as ongqun, just as they
make
horses
and
other
animals
ongqun,
meaning that no one should appropriate it and
that it is free and tarkhan (immune). That per-
son’s name was Beki, and he sat above every-
one in the camp. He entered, like the princes,
from the right side, and his horse was tethered
together with Genghis Khan’s. When he had
become very old, Genghis Khan said, “Let one
of the Suqai’ut clan get down on all fours so
that Beki can stand on his back to mount.” For
that reason the Suqai’ut clan are called “Beki’s
grooms.” They are also called dorechi aq-
tachi,1 although they get very angry and deny
it, attributing it to a joke.
In Genghis Khan’s time there were two
brothers from this clan, and both were com-
manders in the left wing. One was Ükär Qalja,
and the other was Qutus Qalja. Other comman-
ders of the Suqai’ut clan were the brothers
Tamuqa Noyan and Qara Noyan. Tamuqa had
three sons, first Jangqun, who was a totqavul
commander in Hülägü Khan’s time, second
Qutu Buqa Noyan, who was a great comman-
der of importance, and third Tangana Totqavul.
There were also Charaqatai and Jangqun Noy-
an’s son Boralghi. Qutu Buqa Noyan’s sons
were Taichu and Tachar Noyan. Taichu died
young, and so did Tachar’s son Mubarak.
Charuq survives. Tangana’s sons are Yagh-
laghu,
Musa,
Qarabagh,
Sulayman,
Esän
Temür, Abdal, and Charaghatai. Charaghatai’s
son is Äbügätäi. [201]
1The obscure expression may mean “stirrup-holding
groom.” See Doerfer, TMEN 1:330 §204.

The Barulas Clan1
The Qubilai Noyan of Genghis Khan’s time
was of this clan. His sons are presently in ser-
vice to the Qa’an. In this land was Saighan
Taraqai of his progeny. He was sent with Jäbä
and a large army against Tayang Khan in the
last battle. Two commanders of importance
from this clan came to this land with Tägüdär.
Their names were Kököchü Bahadur and ….
Kököchü Bahadur was renowned for his in-
telligence, competence, and eloquence.
The Hadargin Clan2
Their leader in Genghis Khan’s time was
Moqur Qauran. (Qauran means as rough-tem-
pered as a file; since he had this characteristic,
he got this name.) He commanded the regiment
of the Hadargin clan and was one of the com-
manders of the right wing. Recently most of
that troop were in the Qipchaq Steppe with No-
qai. Since they had contemplated rebellion
against Noqai and his sons, they raided them,
and now they are greatly dispersed throughout
that land. The Büküräi who was here was a
grandson of Moqur Qauran.
The Jä’üriyät Clan3
This clan is descended from Tumina Khan’s
seventh son, whose name was Udur Bayan,
and they are also called the Jäjirät. In Genghis
Khan’s time they were quite hostile and op-
1The Barulas clan of the Genghisid period later be-
came known as the Barlas. It was the clan from which
Amir Temür sprang. They are mentioned in the Secret
History §§46, 120.
2The name of this clan is spelled consistently through-

the Adargin of the Secret History (§46), and we will opt
for “Hadargin.” Khetagurov (JTSL 1/1:190) also reads

3The Jä’üriyät (~ Jä’üräyit) are mentioned in the Se-
cret History §44 (Je’üreyid).
posed to him. They submitted several times but
then rejoined the enemy. 
Among their well-known leaders [202] at
that time was Jamuqa Sächän. He was called
sächän because he was very intelligent and
crafty. Genghis Khan used to call him anda,
but he was always plotting against him and
wishing he could be ruler. Toqto’a Beki, the
ruler of the Märkit, raided Jamuqa Sächän and
carried off all his household. He wandered
around for a while with only thirty liege men.
After that, he had no choice but to send a mes-
sage saying, “I submit to obey my father Toq-
to’a Beki and will fight for him.” Toqto’a Beki
accepted and gave him amnesty. He came to
him and served him for a while. Since he was
very crafty and tricky, he was always worming
his way into Toqto’a Beki’s officers’ confi-
dence. 
One day he saw a quail that had hatched its
eggs in some grass. He marked the spot. The
next day he and a group of officers gathered
there, and he said, “Last year I was passing by
here, and a quail had made a nest at the bottom
of this grass. Let me see if the nest has re-
mained this year as it was and if the quail has
produced young or not.” He approached and
saw that the quail had flown from the grass,
leaving its nest and young there. [The officers]
believed him and said in amazement, “What an
intelligent and clever person who can remem-
ber a patch of grass from last year to this with-
out mistake!” 
With the likes of this trick he garnered status
for himself with Toqto’a Beki and his officers.
One day he thought up a stratagem. Early the
next morning, before Toqto’a Beki had risen
and without the guards’ being aware of him—it
was not customary for anyone to go before
[Toqto’a Beki] so early—he and thirty of his
liege men burst into Toqto’a Beki’s tent with-
out warning. There was no one with him. Toq-
TOME ONE, PART ONE, CHAPTER FOUR, SECTION ONE: THE DÜRLÜKIN
99

to’a was extremely frightened and thought that
he would do whatever he wanted. Jamuqa said,
“Your sentries are most [203] incompetent and
off-guard. Why don’t they protect you? I have
come in like this on purpose to see whether
they were aware and guarding you or not.”
Toqto’a Beki was quivering from fright as he
realized the truth of the situation, although [Ja-
muqa] represented himself as having acted out
of concern. In that state Toqto’a Beki was so
afraid that he swore an oath and poured kumiss
onto the ground from a golden goblet—as is
their custom—swearing, “Your a’ughruq and
your household I give to you. Henceforth I will
do you no ill on any pretext.” [He extracted
this oath from Toqto’a] lest he find some op-
portunity to kill him. Then Jamuqa apologized
for what he had done and served Toqto’a Beki
until he had given back all that he had taken
from him. Then he returned to his own home
and yurt.
Many times after that he fled from Genghis
Khan, rebelled, and went to Genghis Khan’s
enemies, Ong Khan and Tayang Khan. Once
many tribes of every stripe of Mongol gathered
and elevated him as ruler, awarding him the ti-
tle Gür Khan. When Genghis Khan set out to
do battle with them, he triumphed over them
every time he mounted an expedition. Seeing
that he was not the man to offer resistance to
Genghis Khan, Jamuqa raided his own liege
men who had elected him ruler and rejoined
Genghis Khan. Several other times he rebelled
and
stirred
up
enmity
and
war
between
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan. 
Finally he met his end as follows. He fled
and was captured by his own liege men, who
turned him over to Genghis Khan’s soldiers.
While thus taken prisoner, he said in the pres-
ence of the envoys who were taking him away,
“My anda makes a sign behind his head and
knows well how to order valiant deeds.”1
When they brought him as a captive before
Genghis Khan, he asked, “When Jamuqa was
captured, what did he say?” His words were re-
peated. Genghis Khan realized to what he was
alluding. [204] The words he uttered meant
that “If my own liege men, whose lord I was,
took me captive and proved faithless, to whom
will they be faithful?” Genghis Khan ordered
[of] that group, who were his relatives and
cousins, numbering sixty persons, [that] the
thirty liege men who had taken him captive be
separated and executed. The thirty others sur-
rendered. Their leader, Ölüg Bahadur, became
a great man of importance and performed
valiant feats. Since he called Jamuqa anda, he
did not want to kill him, so he gave him and
his liege men and household to his nephew
Elji’idäi Noyan, whom he loved. Several days
later Elji’idäi killed him. It is reported that
Elji’idäi ordered him cut limb from limb, and
[Jamuqa] said, “You are right. I was planning
to dismember you if I won. Now that you have
won, dismember me quickly.” He kept asking
them to hurry, showing them his joints as if to
say, “Cut here and don’t worry.”
Among the leaders of this clan in Genghis
Khan’s time were Qaliqudar, Ölüg Bahadur,
Maghui Yadaghana, and Taghai Dalu. Since
they were very hostile, Genghis Khan killed
many of them. Of the few who remained and
are now in Iran, one is Ara Temür Ba’urchi, a

regimental commander, and his brother Jäjirä-
tai Qo’an. 
In the initial stages of Genghis Khan’s quar-
rel with the Tayichi’ut, a relative of Jamuqa
Sächän’s, Taichar, went to raid the home of
Jochi Tarmala of the Jalayir. Jochi Tarmala
shot him with an arrow and killed him. For this
reason Jamuqa and the Jäjirät clan joined the
Tayichi’ut and other tribes [205] and started a
war with Genghis Khan, as is mentioned in the
history. 
Also during Genghis Khan’s time there was a
great
commander
from
this
clan
named
Qosha’ul, who had a brother named Jusuq.
When Genghis Khan took the territories of
Cathay and Jurcha, he wanted to station a troop
in that region to guard the province and sub-
jects. “These two are brave and courageous
men,” he said, so two men were detached from
every group of ten to form three units of a
thousand each, and they were given to them
and the territory entrusted to them. Before that
Qosha’ul’s name was something else, but be-
cause his contingent had been detached from
units of ten [in pairs], he was dubbed with this
name, which is derived from that meaning.1
When Genghis Khan was in Baljiuna and gath-
ering soldiers from wherever he could, Jochi
Qasar had gotten separated previously, and his
household and possessions were raided by Ong
Khan. He and a few escaped and rejoined
Genghis Khan only after having to eat carrion
along the way. Genghis Khan wanted to take
Ong Khan unawares, so he purposefully sent a
message, purporting to come from Jochi Qasar,
with Qali’udar of the Jä’üriyät and Cha’urgha
Ilaghan of the Uriangqat, who was also called
Chavur, which means ‘shaking the head,’
which he was constantly doing. [To Qali’udar
and Cha’urgha, Genghis Khan] said, “Say to
1In Turco-Mongolian qosh means ‘pair.’
him as though coming from Jochi Qasar, ‘I
have tried hard to follow my elder brother,
Genghis Khan, and rejoin him. I have found no
trace of him and have not been able to track
him down. Now my home is the forest, and my
pillow a clod of earth. If you will be so kind as
to give me back my wife, children, and house-
hold, I will submit and join you.’ ” When this
message was delivered to Ong Khan, he re-
joiced and believed it. He poured a bit of blood
into a bull’s horn to seal an oath and sent it off
by an envoy, Itürgän by name, with them.
[206] As soon as Genghis Khan had dispatched
the emissaries, he led his soldiers in their wake
and proceeded day and night. As the two emis-
saries were coming back with Itürgän, they
saw Genghis Khan’s banner from afar and
feared that Itürgän would realize what was
happening and take flight to relay the news.
One of the two got down from his horse and
said, “There is something caught in my horse’s
hoof.” He had Itürgän hold the horse’s leg so
that he could inspect the hoof and clean it out
with a pick. Thus he distracted Itürgän for a
moment [until] Genghis Khan arrived, seized
Itürgän, and sent him to Jochi Qasar, who had
remained in the a’ughruq. Then he sent the
two envoys to scout ahead, and they took Ong
Khan unawares and defeated his army.
The Buda’at Clan2
This clan branched off from Bat Gälgäi, Tu-
mina Khan’s fifth son. During Genghis Khan’s
time their leader was Oridai.3 When Genghis
Khan was fighting the Tayichi’ut, he was allied
with Genghis Khan and added his forces to his.
There have been and are many officers from
this clan, but at present none is known.
2The Buda’at are mentioned once in the Secret History
§46 (Buda’ad).
3This Oridai is elsewhere called Qoridai.

The Doqolat Clan1
They branched off from the eighth of Tumina
Khan’s sons, Bodonchar. When Genghis Khan
was battling the Tayichi’ut, [207] this clan was
with Genghis Khan and formed part of his
forces. However, neither at that time nor at the
present is anyone known who was of impor-
tance or famous. 
The Besüt Clan2
This branch came into existence with Tumina
Khan’s ninth son, Besütäi, the youngest of all
the brothers. There have been many officers
and grandees from among them. Initially they
opposed Genghis Khan, but later some of them
submitted and performed valiantly. It is a Mon-
gol custom for the youngest son to be called
otchigin because he remains at home and is the
center around which the family revolves.
When Genghis Khan’s urugh holds a yasal or a
yasamishi—yasal is an expression for reviving
their customs and practices—they summon
members of this clan, to whom this practice
pertains,
and
the
shamans
perform
the
yasamishi according to custom.
One of the famous people of this clan during
Genghis Khan’s time was Jäbä. His story is as
follows. When these clans were opposing
Genghis Khan, and he triumphed over them, he
took their households. Some became exiles,
and Jäbä was among that number. One day
Genghis Khan was hunting, and Jäbä stumbled

in the attributive (Dogholadai, §46). Although they do
not seem to have played a great role during Genghisid
times, they later became known as the Doghlat, or
Dughlat, and were of major significance in Chinese
Turkistan during the heyday of the Chaghatayid khans of
Moghulistan. Their fortunes until the middle of the six-
teenth century are chronicled by Mirza Haydar Dughlat
in his Tarikh-i-Rashidi.
2The Besüt (Besüd) are mentioned in the Secret Histo-
ry §§47, 120, e.g.
into the middle of the hunting circle. Genghis
Khan recognized him and wanted to do combat
with him. Borghochin Noyan said, “I will go
out to fight him.” He requested a horse from
Genghis Khan and was given a chaghan aman
qula, meaning a [dun] horse with a white muz-
zle. He mounted and went out to fight. He shot
an arrow at Jäbä and missed. Jäbä shot an ar-
row and hit the horse, which fell dead. Jäbä
fled, and after a time, since he had neither
strength nor aid, he came and submitted. Since
he was a good warrior, Genghis Khan gave
him the command of a unit of ten men. [208]
When he served well, he made him comman-
der of a hundred. When he performed valiantly,
he became commander of a thousand and then
ten thousand. He served for a long time and
participated valiantly in expeditions. After
Tayang Khan’s son Güshlüg Khan fought with
Genghis Khan and took flight, he went to the
Gür Khan, the ruler of the Qarakhitai in
Turkistan and Transoxiana. He married [the
Gür Khan’s] daughter and returned to Naiman
territory, where he assembled an army. Then he
mutinied against the Gür Khan and attacked
him, took him captive, killed him, and took his
place. Seven years later, as will be mentioned
in the history, Genghis Khan sent Jäbä and the
army, and they put Güshlüg to flight. He went
in defeat to the frontier of Badakhshan, where
he was killed. When the news reached Genghis
Khan, he sent advice to Jäbä not to get over-
confident from such a great victory, i.e. from
putting Güshlüg to flight, since, as he said, “It
was on account of their overconfidence that I
defeated Ong Khan, Tayang Khan, Güshlüg
Khan, and others.”
Since Jäbä had shot and killed the dun horse,
when he came to submit he knelt and said, “I
know that I am guilty of having killed the dun
horse. If Genghis Khan pardons me and is gen-
erous, I will bring many such horses to him.”
102
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

After that, when he returned from battle with
Güshlüg Khan, he brought a thousand dun
horses with white muzzles from that region
and presented them as gifts. When Genghis
Khan was in the vicinity of Balkh and Taligan,
he sent him along with Sübätäi and Börkä of
the Jalayir and the army to that region. Börkä
died along the way, and they came out and
took some of the cities of Arab and Persian
Iraq, pillaging and killing. He went to the re-
gions of Georgia and [209] Tiflis, where many
Georgians assembled and came out to do bat-
tle. Jäbä sent Sübätäi with the army against
them while he himself and five thousand
warriors hid themselves. Sübätäi took flight in-
tentionally, and the Georgians came out in
pursuit of him. Jäbä leapt from ambush and
outflanked them, killing them all. This was
their custom in most battles. From there they
withdrew, emerging through the Iron Gates,
and the people of Derbent brought forth tuzghu
(offering of food) and submitted. They passed
on from there and went to the territory of the
Rus, killing and pillaging everywhere they
went. They had promised Genghis Khan to fin-
ish the job within three years, but it was ac-
complished in two and a half.
Jäbä’s younger brother Mönggädü Sa’ur was
in Tolui Khan’s retinue. He had seven sons.
The youngest was named Orus, and he came
here in Hülägü Khan’s service in a guard com-
pany of quiver bearers. His brothers remained
there.
When
Abaqa
Khan
was
sent
to
Khurasan, he made Orus the commander of
four guard companies, and he performed
valiantly. When Abaqa Khan became ruler and
returned from Khurasan, he had Orus return
and sent him to guard the frontier of Herat and
Badghis, putting under his command the army
in that area, and there he remained. Two years
later he sent Taisun1 there, and he made many
good showings and killed the region and tribe
of Nägüdär. When he brought out Junjadar and
many captives, he killed them all along the
way at Abaqa Khan’s order. At that time Qutui
Khatun crossed the river. Orus performed ser-
vices in that regard and escorted her until she
reached Tus, performing good services. He
died after the battle with Baraq.
His sons during Abaqa Khan’s time were
Qara Täri and Abachi. Qara Täri’s son at this
time is a kharbanda (donkey-driver). [210]
Abachi’s son Zangi is commander of a regi-
ment and Hindu is a ba’urchi. 
Among Jäbä’s sons was Sunqusun, a regi-
mental commander. His son Qarayit is now
[among] the ev-oghlans of Öljäi Khatun, and
his brother Bahadur went to Egypt on a
mission.
Among Jäbä’s relatives at present are many
in service to the Qa’an. Qada’an, a great com-
mander and governor, Noqai, a great bitigchi,
and Baiju were relatives of Jäbä. Ögödäi Qa’an
sent him with Chormaqan and put him in
charge of a company of a thousand. After that
he was put in charge of a unit of ten thousand.
Baiju subdued Anatolia and prided himself and
boasted of it, saying, “I rendered Anatolia sub-
missive.” Hülägü Khan summoned him, found
him guilty, and had him executed. He took a
full half of his possessions. At Mänggü Qa’an’s
order his tümän was given to Chormaqan’s son
Shirämün. 
Baiju Noyan’s son was Adak, who was put in
charge
of
a
regiment.
His
son
was
the
Sülämish who was in Anatolia. The Padishah
of Islam rewarded him and gave him five thou-
sand horsemen. There he was made comman-
der of a tümän, revolted, and killed Bayanchar
1This name occurs here asﻦ ـ ـﻳﺴﻮـﺗ(JTK) andﲔ ـ ـﺑﺴﻮـﺗ(JTRKA

and Buchqur, for which crime he was execut-
ed. This will be explained in detail.
The last time Genghis Khan did battle with
Tayang Khan, he sent Qubilai of the Barulas
and Jäbä to the front. The second time he sent
Jäbä with the army to Cathay and Jurcha,
which they call Tungging.1 Without laying
siege he pulled back without warning and trav-
elled fifty leagues in ten days so that [the ene-
my]
felt
secure.
Then
he
stationed
his
a’ughruq, turned around, and galloped swiftly
and unencumbered until he reached the city
gate and took it by surprise through such a
ruse.
Also of this clan were two important officers,
Dägä and Güchügür. [211] Their story is as fol-
lows. When they were with the Tayichi’ut,
their father and older and younger brothers
were killed. Their mother, Baidu Khatun,
asked her sons, “Has it ever happened that he
treats helpless women and orphans well?” In
that hope she picked up the two of them and
brought them to Genghis Khan, with whom
they found favor. He gave Güchügür a regi-
ment and made Baidu Khatun tarkhan, saying,
“The way of orphans is to be tarkhan.” He
made Dägä an akhtachi of the sutan adun, i.e.
the royal horses. He ordered that Güchügür be
given the mares, and Baidu Khatun was put in
charge of the kumiss. Dägä’s son was Udui,
and he is now a tümän commander with Ching
Temür and has many sons. One of Güchügür’s
sons was Börtäjin Qorchi, Tolui Khan’s com-
mander of the watch guard. Another was Qubi-
la Qorchi, who was in charge of a regiment.
His son Char Buqa was attached to Qubilai
Khan, and his son Güyüji came here as an en-
1Tungging (for 東京Dongjing), the eastern capital of
the Jin empire, Liaoyangfu, the modern Liaoyang in
southern Manchuria (Jurcha). See below, text p. 443.
voy from Mingqan Kä’ün, the son of Malik
Temür.
The Sügän Clan
They are among the Niru’un clans. Initially,
when Genghis Khan was doing battle with the
Tayichi’ut tribes and gathering forces, this clan
allied themselves with him because they were
kin. The name of their leader is not known.
The Qingqiyat Clan
They too are of the Niru’un. Since they were
related they also joined Genghis Khan when he
was fighting the Tayichi’ut. [212] Their leader
was Daqai Bahadur. Other notices about them
will be given in the proper places. 
❈
It was necessary to mention in detail and to
recount the divisions of the branches of the
elite Mongols, other Mongol clans, those who
resemble the Mongols, and the tribes of
Cathay, Tangqut, Uyghur, &c. because their
history will come during Genghis Khan’s time,
for at the very beginning of his rule he brought
them under his command with God’s assis-
tance and turned them all into slaves and sol-
diers. That which has been ascertained through
diligent research has been reported in order for
it to be known how many clans and branches
they were, for what reason each one branched
off, what the nature and customs of each clan
were like, and where their dwelling places and
yurts were. Now that we have finished with
this, we will commence the history of the ruler
of the world, Genghis Khan, and his descen-
dants—in particular the Padishah of Islam,
Sultan Mahmud Ghazan Khan, which is the ul-
timate goal and purpose of composing this
blessed book—and we will give in detail and
with full explanation where, how, and why
Genghis Khan’s branch and that of each of his
cousins and relatives began. [213]

HISTORY OF THE RULERS OF THE MONGOL AND TURKIC PEOPLES AND

❦ CHAPTER ONE
THE HISTORY OF GENGHIS KHAN’S FOREBEARS AND ANCESTORS, TEN
STORIES IN ALL, PRECEDED BY AN INTRODUCTION ON HOW THEY APPEARED
Introduction, on Genghis Khan’s ancestors
and how, where, and when they attained
fortune.
t should be borne in mind that
the Turkic nations and various
Mongols that have been dealt
with never, as a whole, had a
mighty monarch to rule over all
peoples. Each nation had its own
monarch and leader, but most of
the time they were at war and at
odds with each other—like the
Arabs who dwell in this realm, each tribe of
whom has its own separate leader who refuses
to follow any other.
Since the people of Cathay were next to
these people and their territory and camping
grounds, in every epoch the Cathaians killed
many of the tribes who practiced nomadism in
Cathaian territory, while the tribes in turn raid-
ed and plundered the Cathaian realm. Because
the rulers of Cathay were constantly vexed by
Mongol nomads, they took every precaution
against them, like constructing a wall like
Alexander’s Dam between Cathay and the
tribes.1 [216] In Mongolian that wall is called
1Alexander’s Dam (sadd-i Iskandar) is a reference to
the Koranic legend of the enormous wall Alexander
constructed to keep the Gog and Magog at bay. See Kor.
18:92–97.
öngü, and in Turkish it is called yoqurqa.2 One
end of it is at the Qara Mörän (Yellow River),
an extremely large river impossible to cross,
and the other end is at a river on the frontier of
the territory of the Jurchids. The rulers of
Cathay recognized the Öng’üt tribe as devoted
military servants and turned the Öngü wall
over to them, and they have constantly guarded
it. In Genghis Khan’s time, their leader, Ala
Qush Tegin by name,3 joined Genghis Khan,
who assigned him to the wall, a bit of which
has already been stated in the section on the
Öng’üt. This will all be explained in detail lat-
er in its proper place, God willing.
The
above-mentioned
tribes
have
many
histories and stories, but they have not reached
this land, and the history of their forebears has
not been ascertained in detail. Each tribe
knows some of its own stories, but they had no
history by which to record former generations
and eons past.
More recently, from the time that God de-
creed that Genghis Khan’s ancestors should en-
joy fortune and kingship and that the descen-
dants of Dobun Bayan and Alan Qo’a, from
whom Genghis Khan was descended, should
be singled out for glory among all the branches
of the Mongols, although there are no estab-
2For yoqurqa see Doerfer, TMEN 1:557 §409.
3See note to text p. 131 above.

lished dates, it has been approximately four
hundred years, for from the contents of the
chapters of history contained in the treasury, as
well as from the reports of aged men with
worldly experience, it can be ascertained that it
was during the first part of the caliphate of the
House of Abbas and the time of the reign of the

have appeared in this family have become so
numerous that it is not possible to enumerate
them individually, nor would they fit within the
covers of a volume. [217] Although the lineage
and branches are not known in detail, what is
known and has been remembered will be con-

We will now begin the stories and histories
with a mention of the lineage of Genghis Khan
and his relatives from Dobun Bayan and Alan
Qo’a. We will explain each branch separately
and give a genealogical chart. [218]
(1) The story of Dobun Bayan and his wife,
Alan Qo’a, and the legends that pertain to
their history, exclusive of what can be found
everywhere; comprising two parts.
Part One: The beginning of their history.
Trustworthy historians of the Turks report that
all the Mongol tribes are descended from the
two persons who went into Ärgänä-qun. One
of those who emerged from there was an im-
portant commander, a leader and chief of
tribes, Börtä China (Blue Wolf) by name, from
whom Dobun Bayan, Alan Qo’a’s husband,
and several other clans were descended. He
had many wives and sons. By his chief wife,
Qo’ai Maral,2 he had a son, the most important
1The House of Abbas reigned as caliphs from A.D. 749;
the Samanids ruled in Khurasan and Transoxiana a.d.
819–1005.
2Qa’ai Maral means ‘White Doe.’ See Secret History
§1: “There was a bluish wolf which was born having his

Tamach, who had five sons, the eldest of

er, and entered other territories. They say that
the Dörbän tribe is descended from them be-

four branches. 
One day one of the offspring of the youngest
son, Qolun Saqal by name,7 had killed a moun-
tain ox, and someone from the Baya’ut tribe,
Ma’aliq by name,8 brought his son, and he sold

to Alan Qo’a, and most of the Baya’ut, who are
servants and urugh to Genghis Khan, are de-
scended from that boy.
Qorichar Märgän had a son who succeeded

doe.” The Secret History’s Mongolian original of this

(dull white doe) respectively (see Cleaves, Secret Histo-
ry, xxix; Manghol-un niuca tobca’an, 1). Here the ani-

substituted ‘man’ for ‘wolf’ and ‘woman’ for ‘doe,’ and

who succeeded him named Yäkä Nidün.1 He
had a son named Säm Sä’öchi who succeeded
to his father’s position. He had a son named
Qarchu,2 who succeeded his father. To him was
born Dobun Bayan. Their yurt was the area of
the Onon, Kerulen, and Tughula,3 three rivers
that arise from Burqan Qaldun mountain. [220]
Part Two: A description of Dobun Bayan
and his wife Alan Qo’a, and their
descendants.
Dobun Bayan had an extremely chaste wife,
Alan Qo’a by name, of the Qorolas tribe. By
her
he
had
two
sons,
Bälgünütäi
and
Bügünütäi.4 Two Mongol tribes are descended
from them. Some reckon them of the Niru’un
tribe because their mother was Alan Qo’a, but
others consider them Dürlükin because they
reckon the Niru’un only to be from the three
sons to whom Alan Qo’a gave birth after the
death of her husband. There is much dispute in
this regard, but the better known version—
which is also analogically closer to the truth—
is the latter. There is no one from the descen-
dants of these two in this realm—aside from
one person who is in a hazara. Even in Mon-
golia they are said to be few.
Dobun Bayan, Alan Qo’a’s husband, died
young. [221]
1Yeke Nidün in the Secret History §2.
2This is the Qarchu of the Secret History §3. Another

ther of Dobun Mergen.
3The Tughula, or Tu’ula, is now known as the Tula

The beginning of the story of Alan Qo’a and
her sons who were born after the death of
her husband.
In order for divine wisdom to make manifest
traces of its power, it necessarily brings into
being a strange and marvelous thing in every
age of the world of generation and corruption,
and the locus of that thing is a peerless, noble
person, favored by the divine gaze and protect-
ed by divine mercy so that this thing may
cause those of insight to learn a lesson and
those of the world to witness His perfect power
and so that by rendering thanks for God’s infi-
nite bounties they may continue forever and
that they may know for certain that the contin-
uum of the creation of beings, in general and in
particular, is tied to the will of the creator.
Whatever He willed He did, and whatever He
wills He does: “God doeth that which he
pleaseth and commands what he wills.”5
Proof of this claim is the marvelous story of
Alan Qo’a, from whose pure womb, according
to the Mongols—and the responsibility is his
who related it—were born three sons without
the intermediary of marriage or consort, and
their story is one of the strangest of the strange.
Their sons—in accordance with the dictum, “A
race descending the one from the other”6—
form innumerable branches and uncountable
clans, and until the end of the world and the
human race they will be well remembered on
account of the blessed existence of the quintes-
sence of that family, the monarch of Islam,
[222] succorer of God’s religion, Sultan Mah-
mud Ghazan Khan—may God extend his king-
ship forever, God willing.
Now begins the story of Alan Qo’a and her
three sons who were born after the death of her
5Kor. 14:27. 
6Kor. 3:34.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
107

husband, according to the reports of the Mon-
gols, in two parts.
Part One: A preface to the story of Alan
Qo’a and the offspring of her sons
It is related that Dobun Bayan, the husband
of Alan Qo’a, died young. It was divinely fore-
ordained that the rule of the all-conquering em-
peror appear in the world in order to bring all
nations of the world under his command and
tame the unruly into subservience by his per-
son, which would be so strong that he could be
the emperor of the world and leader of all na-
tions, and so that after him all the monarchs
and rulers of the face of the earth be of his lin-
eage. It is like an oyster shell in which a
matchless pearl is cultivated for years without
anyone’s knowing which shell it is. Divers
constantly search for it by plunging into the
sea, bringing forth many shells, and obtaining
many pearls. Each of those pearls has its use.
Merchants arrange them on strings and sell
them as befits each nation and person, and they
are used for barter. However, the ultimate goal
of all this is that one renowned unique pearl.
[223] With its perfect power, destiny made
Alan Qo’a’s pure womb the oyster shell for the
precious pearl of Genghis Khan’s existence
and created his true life spark therein from
pure light.
The many clans and tribes descended from
Alan Qo’a are so numerous that if the individu-
als were to be counted they would exceed a
million, yet each of them has a clear and unam-
biguous family tree, for it is a Mongolian cus-
tom to preserve one’s relationship to one’s fa-
thers and forefathers, and every child born is
taught and inculcated with his genealogy like
all others in that nation. There is not one
among them who does not know his tribe and
lineage. Nations other than the Mongols do not
have such a custom—except for the Arabs,
who also keep their genealogy. [These others]
are like ordinary pearls produced by the oyster
shells brought forth from the bottom of the sea
of creation by divers of divine wisdom for the
sake of that one priceless pearl. The quintes-
sence of them all is Genghis Khan, and in par-
ticular his renowned offspring, the king of
world asylum, helper of God’s religion, Sultan
Mahmud Ghazan Khan—may God extend his
kingship forever—who has strengthened the
religion of Islam and patronized Muslims. He
has revived every portion of the Islamic code
and custom that had fallen into lassitude with
the passage of time and suffered from the
hands of infidels and polytheists. He has totally
eliminated vain ways and re-established the
foundations of Islam.
How many a root has been extricated from
Chin and Khotan so that a mandrake like you
could be brought to Khurasan!
In accordance with the foregoing, once, after
Alan Qo’a’s husband died, she was asleep in
her house when a light entered through the
vent of the tent and went into her belly. [224]
She was astonished and too afraid to tell any-
one about it. After a time she discovered that
she was pregnant. When the time for giving
birth was near, her husband’s brothers and rela-
tives gathered and said, “How can a woman
without a husband find a mate in secret to be-
come pregnant?” 
“Since I have conceived without a husband,”
said Alan Qo’a in reply, “you of course think
that what you imagine and suspect is true.
However, there is no doubt that ‘some sus-
picions are sinful.’ How can I have committed
a disreputable act that would bring shame?
Yes, every night when I am asleep I see a lumi-
nous shape coming softly and gently to me,
and then it slowly withdraws. I see with my
eyes outside of this state. Whatever suspicion
you have of me is untrue. These children I
have conceived are of another species. When
108
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

they grow up and become monarchs and khans
over all people, you and all the common peo-
ple will realize how I was.”
When Alan Qo’a replied thus, and her chasti-
ty and purity were clear to them, they did not
chastise or bother her, for they realized that
what she said was true.
To Alan Qo’a were born three sons. The el-
dest was named Buqun Qataqi,1 from whose
line comes the entirety of the Qataqin clans.
The middle son’s name was Buqatu Salji,2 and
he was the ancestor of the Salji’ut clans. The
youngest son’s name was Bodonchar Qa’an.
He was the finest fruit of this tree, and many
clans, as will be later given in detail, trace their
descent from him. Genghis Khan’s lineage is
also from him. 
The relationship of Alan Qo’a and her three
sons is shown in the following diagram. [225]
The offspring of these three sons are called
Niru’un unqualifiedly, a reference to Alan
Qo’a’s pure womb, and these tribes enjoy great
pre-eminence.
Division the second: a report of the
offspring of Alan Qo’a’s three sons
Know that the many branches and clans that
descended from these three sons are known as
the Niru’un, meaning from pure loins, referring
to the pure loins and womb of Alan Qo’a.
1In the Secret History §17, Bughu Qatagi.
2In the Secret History §17, his name is given as
Bughatu (and Bughutu at §42) Salji.
These tribes enjoy pre-eminence, and among
all the other tribes they are like pearls in an
oyster shell or fruit on a tree. The Mongol
tribes that are not Niru’un, as has been stated
in the introduction, are all called Dürlükin. The
tribes descended from Bälgünütäi and Bügünü-
täi, even though they have the same ancestry,
are also called Dürlükin because their father
was Dobun Bayan.
The clan of Mongols who are now called
ötägü
boghol
received
this
name
during
Genghis Khan’s time.3 Ötägü boghol means
that they are hereditary slaves of Genghis
Khan’s fathers and forefathers. [226] Some of
them are those who performed pleasing ser-
vices during Genghis Khan’s time and estab-
lished their rights, and that is why they are
called ötägü boghol. Those who maintain their
status as ötägü boghol will be mentioned indi-
vidually in the proper places. At this point it
was necessary to mention this much simply in
order that the reader may know what these
words mean.
Although all the branches that are Niru’un
are related to Genghis Khan, and although
great officers and khans emerged from them,
nonetheless when Genghis Khan was ruler of
the earth, all Mongol tribes—both those that
were related to him and those that were unre-
lated—became his slaves. In particular, those
of his relatives, uncles, and cousins who united
with his enemies during his time of difficulties
and fought against him are inferior in rank to
his other relatives. There are also many who
became slaves of slaves, and in the proper
place it will be explained at what time and for
what reason they became slaves. [227]
3For ötägü boghol, see above, text p. 66.

(2) The story of Bodonchar Khan, his wives
and sons, and their offspring, in two parts
Part One: An introduction to his sons
Bodonchar was Alan Qo’a’s third son. In his
own time he was the leader and monarch of
many Mongol tribes, and he was an extremely
brave warrior. He had two sons. The elder’s
name was Buqa, and the younger’s name was
Buqatai.1 Genghis Khan’s lineage and that of
many other Niru’un tribes go back to Buqa,
who was his father’s designated heir. After his
father’s death he succeeded to his father’s posi-
tion and post. He had a son named Dutum Mä-
nen. Buqatai also had a son, whose name was
Nachin. This Nachin requested in marriage a
girl from the Mongol tribes and used to fre-
quent their place as a son-in-law. They say that
some of the Tayichi’ut tribes are descended
from him, but this claim has no basis in fact
since in the books of history kept in the imper-
ial treasury, which the great officers have pre-
served and which is called the Altan Daftar
(The Golden Record), it says that the Tayi-
chi’ut tribes are descended from Charaqa
Lingqum, one of the sons of Qaidu Khan and
grandson of Dutum Mänen. The only mention
of Nachin is that he helped his nephew Qaidu
Khan escape from the Jalayir and protected
him. He came away with him, and they settled
near each other in the Onon and Kerulen area.
It is possible, since the Tayichi’ut tribes were
numerous, that Nachin’s sons united with
them, mingled with them, and took their name,
particularly inasmuch as they were cousins.
1According to Secret History §43, Bodonchar’s sons
were Barim Shi’iratu Qabichi Ba’atur and Je’üredei. The
Buqa of the Jami‘u’t-tawarikh takes Qabichi Ba’atur’s
place as Dutum Mänen’s father. Barim Shi’iratu Qabichi
appears in the Jami‘u’t-tawarikh several generations lat-
er as the second son of Tumina Khan (text p. 245
below).
That is how this mistake must have happened,
for otherwise his progeny would have had a
separate mention. His progeny is also Niru’un,
but it has not been ascertained which of the
Niru’un tribes that have been mentioned are
descended from him.
Part Two: A description of Bodonchar and
his son’s offspring
As has been mentioned, Bodonchar had two
sons, Buqa and Buqatai. Buqa’s son was Du-
tum Mänen, the progenitor of Genghis Khan’s
line. His story will be given shortly. Buqatai’s
son was Nachin, whose branch is not known
for certain. Their relationship is as follows:
[229]
Another version says that Dutum Mänen was
the son of Bodonchar, but they are correct who
make him a son of Buqa, for that is what the
ancient manuscript says.
(3) The story of Dutum Mänen son of Buqa
son of Bodonchar Khan, his wife Monolun,
and his sons, in two parts.
Part One: Preface and Introduction.
Dutum Mänen was Genghis Khan’s ancestor
in the seventh degree, which the Mongols call
dutaqun. He had nine sons. When he died, his
wife, Monolun by name and mother of those
sons, was left behind. Her sons each took a
bride from a different tribe in a different direc-
tion and went there as sons-in-law. Monolun
was rich and well provided for, and her resi-
dence and yurt were in a place called [A]nosh
110
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Ärgi1 and Black Mountain. Every few days she
would order the herds gathered. The horses and
sheep were too many to be counted, but when
enough animals stood to cover the ground with
their hooves from the top of the mountain,
where she dwelt, down to the bottom, where a
large river flowed, she would say, “All have
been gathered.” Otherwise she would order
people to go out in search of the herds and
flocks.
At that time there were several tribes of the
Mongols called Jalayir and of the Dürlükin (an
explanation of whom has already been given)
[230] that dwelt in the vicinity of the Kerulen.
They were seventy gürä’äns (gürä’än means a
circle of tents pitched in the wilderness). At
that time a gürä’än was what they called a
thousand of these tents so dwelt in. By this
reckoning that tribe consisted of seventy thou-
sand households. The Kerulen being near the
territory of Cathay, they and other Mongol
tribes as well were perpetually at war with the
Cathaians. At that time a large army from
Cathay came to raid and plunder them. When
the Jalayir saw the army, knowing that the
Kerulen River lay between them and there was
no crossing nearby, and relying on the Catha-
ians’ being unable to cross, they waved their
hats and sleeves in derision and called out to
them, taunting them, saying, “Come over and
plunder our animals!” Since the Cathaian army
was
numerous,
they
gathered
sticks
and
branches, built a bridge during the night,
crossed the river, massacred the Jalayir down
to
toddling
infants,
and
plundered
their
animals.
There was one separate clan of the Jalayir off
to one side the enemy did not reach. Seventy
householders of them fled with their women
and children and came to the territory of
1Reading ارﮔﯽ (ärgi ‘escarpment’) for the text’s اوﰽ.
Monolun, Dutum Mänen’s wife. Since they
were suffering from hunger, they pulled from
the ground and ate the root of a plant called
südüsün, which is eaten in that region. By that
act the place where Monolun’s sons raced their
horses became pitted and rough. Monolun
asked, [231] “Why do you create such rough-
ness and ruin my sons’ racing ground?” They
therefore seized Monolun and killed her.
Since each of Monolun’s sons had joined a
different tribe, and their relatives had become
many, they refused to tolerate this from [the
Jalayir], so they blocked their way and killed
eight of their sons.
[Monolun’s] youngest son, Qaidu by name,
had married into the Känbä’üt tribe, and his
uncle, Nachin, had also gone to that tribe as a
son-in-law, as previously mentioned. When
[Nachin] heard of the affair of the Jalayir and
his brother’s sons, he hid Qaidu under a large
vat-like jar in which the Mongols put kumiss.
When that clan of the Jalayir committed this
act, the other remaining Jalayir clans made an
enquiry of the seventy men, saying, “With
what elder and younger brothers did you con-
sult to commit such an outrageous act?” In re-
venge and vengeance they killed them all, and
their women and children became slaves to
Monolun’s son Qaidu, although several of their
small children were kept and made slaves to
[the Jalayirs’] families. From that date until
now that clan of the Jalayir have been heredi-
tary slaves and were inherited by Genghis
Khan and his offspring. Great officers have
arisen from them, as will be mentioned under
their respective branches.
Nachin and Qaidu decamped and left that
place. Qaidu took up residence in Borqujin
Tögüm (Barghujin Hollow), one of the Mon-
gols’ frontiers. For irrigation and crossing he
constructed a crossing over the river and called
