it Qaidu-jin Olum [Qaidu’s Ford].1 Nachin
took up residence downstream on the Onon
River, and his offspring formed a separate
branch, [232] of which nothing is known, as
was stated in the previous story.
Part Two: The relationship of Dutum
Mänen, his wife Monolun, and the branch of
their sons
Dutum Mänen had nine sons, as was report-
ed. Eight of them were killed, and their names
are not known. The one who survived was
Qaidu Khan, from whom Genghis Khan’s il-
lustrious lineage descends. The relationship of
this branch is as follows: 
The mother of these nine sons was Monolun
Khatun, who is also called Monolun Targhun
(“Monolun the Fat”). When, for the reasons
mentioned in the history, the Jalayir clans
killed her and her eight sons, Qaidu Khan, the
youngest, escaped because his father’s cousin
Nachin hid him under a kumiss vat. Some of
the Jalayir tribes then became their slaves be-
cause of that crime. [233]
(4) Beginning of the story of Qaidu Khan
Many people have had great hopes that did
not come to fruition and were dashed, and
many are the hopeless raised by God to exalted
positions. Some initially experience various af-
flictions, and after suffering difficulties and
losing hope they are granted relief—“relief af-
ter
constraint,
and
with
difficulty
comes
ease”—and in a little while they become chiefs
1Olum is a good Mongolian word for ford or crossing.
See Doerfer, TMEN 1:178 §55.
and leaders and attain high position. Now
God’s purpose in both states must be for the
people of the world to know of His omnipo-
tence and learn a lesson—“despair not of the
mercy of God”2—lest they lose hope of His
merciful court. Proof of this contention is the
history of Qaidu Khan, for after so many diffi-
culties God rewarded him with all sorts of
bounty. “God strengthens with his help whom
he pleaseth. Surely herein is an example unto
men of understanding.”3 [234]
The story of Qaidu Khan son of Dutum
Mänen, and of his sons, in two parts.
Part One: Introduction to him and his sons.
Qaidu Khan was Genghis Khan’s ancestor in
the sixth degree, which is called borqai in the
Mongolian language.
When Qaidu Khan’s brothers were killed by
the Jalayir, as was mentioned in the previous
story, he left that territory with his cousin and
settled in Mongolia in the place mentioned. It
was God’s will that the pearl of Genghis
Khan’s existence be nourished with the pas-
sage of time in the shell of the loins of [Qaidu
Khan’s] offspring, so He bestowed fortune
upon Qaidu Khan, from whom Genghis Khan’s
lineage comes, so that he had wives, followers,
flocks, and herds beyond number. Three sons
upon whom fortune smiled were also born to
him. 
The first was named Bai Singqor, and he was
Genghis Khan’s ancestor. The middle son was
Charaqa Lingqum. The youngest was named
Cha’ujin, and from him descend the two clans
Örtägin and Sanchi’ut.4 In Chinese lingqum
2Kor. 12:87.
3Kor. 3:13.
4The Charaqai Lingqu and Cha’ujin Örtegei of the Se-
cret History §47. In the Secret History, however, the
clans that descend from Cha’ujin are Oronar, Qong-
qotan, Arulad, Sönid, Qabturghas, and Geniges.
112
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

means great commander,1 and since they were
near the territory of Cathay, Cathaian idioms
and titles gained currency among them. [235]
Because the ordinary Mongols did not know
what lingqum meant, they called him Charaqa
Lingqu. According to the version in the Altan
Daftar, he is the ancestor of all the Tayichi’ut
clans, and that version is nearer to the truth
than any other.
The Tayichi’ut are a numerous and powerful
tribe, and mighty monarchs have emerged
from among them. They have gone on numer-
ous campaigns and expeditions. Each clan had
its own separate commanders and leader, but
they were all in accord. In every age and epoch
they elevated a monarch or a khan from
amongst themselves and followed him. When
as a boy Genghis Khan was bereft of his father,
most of his father’s followers and warriors
went over to the Tayichi’ut, and that is why he
and the Tayichi’ut fought many battles and
skirmishes, as will be explained in the course
of his history. Although Genghis Khan was
only a child and had few warriors, since des-
tiny’s ultimate purpose in creating all these
tribes and clans was to elevate Genghis Khan’s
might, how could a thousand powerful men
stand against one so chosen for fortune? Had
the Tayichi’ut clans understood the wisdom in
this, they would have chosen to serve him
while he was yet a youth; however, since the
mind of man cannot fathom the depths of di-
vine wisdom, they can be excused. They strove
and fought as hard as they could, but the way
of right guidance was blocked to them, and so
they wrongheadedly chose to fight and resist
Genghis Khan until the root of the tree of
Genghis Khan’s fortune reached the water of
perfection, spread its shade, and bore fruit.
Then all the Tayichi’ut and their rulers, as well
1See note to text p. 187 above.
as the other tribes who were united with them,
were overcome and conquered by God’s might.
They all chose to submit and become Genghis
Khan’s slaves, [236] soldiers, and subjects
against their will and by force, as will be
narrated.
The branches of Charaqa Lingqum and
Cha’ujin will be reported in this story, and as
much of their history as needs be will be ex-
plained so that it will not be necessary to treat
each separately. Their genealogical chart will
also be given in this story.
Lingqum’s branch is as follows. He had sev-
eral sons, and his eldest son succeeded him.
His name was Sorqadu China2, the qu‘dud of
Tumina Khan.3 He had a son named Hambaqai
Qa’an, who ruled for a time and was the
qu‘dud of Qabul Khan. His history is quite
well known. Once the Tatar nation seized him
without warning and sent him to Altan Khan of
Cathay, who, out of the unbridled enmity and
hatred he harbored for them, nailed him to a
wooden donkey with iron spikes. Hambaqai
Qa’an’s son was Qada’an Taishi, the qu‘dud of
Bartan Bahadur. His son was the Tödä’ä who
lived during Genghis Khan’s time and was one
of the leaders of the Tayichi’ut. However, their
monarch in Genghis Khan’s time was Tarqutai
Qiriltuq, son of Adal Khan. Those of his
cousins who were chiefs of the Tayichi’ut were
Quril Bahadur,4 A[’u]chu, and Angqu Huqu-
chu.
Charaqa Lingqum had other sons. When his
elder brother, Bai Singqor, died, he took [Bai
Singqor’s] wife as a yengä and had two sons
by her. One was named Kündü China, and the

4Quril is the Mongolian for Cyril.

other was Ölögchin China.1 Two other tribes
are descended from him through these two
sons, and they are called the Chinas tribe

means male wolf, and ölöchgin china means
[237] female wolf. They were united with
Genghis Khan. The Chinas clan is also called

Nüküz, with whom they have nothing in com-
mon other than the name. By the time of
Yesügäi Bahadur the Tayichi’ut clans had be-

part.
Cha’ujin, Qaidu Khan’s third son, had sons,
and he was the ancestor of many branches. The
Örtägin and Sanchi’ut are descended from him.
These clans were with Genghis Khan during
the dispute with the Tayichi’ut. As much of
their history as is known will be mentioned un-
der the branches of that tribe. 
All these tribes are Niru’un. [238]
Part Two: The relationship of Qaidu Khan,
his wife, and their sons.
As previously reported, Qaidu Khan had
three sons, Bai Singqor, Charaqa Lingqum, and
Cha’ujin. Since Genghis Khan’s lineage goes
back to Bai Singqor, a separate story will be
devoted to him next. The relationship of Qaidu
Khan and his wife and the chart of the branch-
es of their three sons and their offspring—ex-
clusive of the offspring of Bai Singqor, which
will be given separately—is as follows: 
1This is at total variance with the Secret History §47.

In some manuscripts Bai Singqor’s name and

The Örtägin and Sanchi’ut clans are descend-
ed from Cha’ujin Hörtägäi. [239] The Qong-
qotan also stem from this origin. One of his
sons was named Yesütü, and another was
named Oronar. When these two boys ran, a

they and their sons were named Qongqotan.
Details have already been given in the part on
the Qongqotan. There are many branches of
the Qongqotan, and most of them were sup-
porters of Genghis Khan and his sons.
As for Charaqa Lingqum, it is stated in some
manuscripts that he was a son of Nachin, but it
is more correct to say that he was a son of
Qaidu Khan because in the family tree it is said
that Charaqa married his bärigän (elder broth-
er’s wife), i.e. Bai Singqor’s wife, and by her
had two sons, Kündü China and Ölögchin Chi-

na. Consequently he must have been slightly
junior to Bai Singqor because if he had been
Nachin’s son, he would have been his [Bai
Singqor’s] cousin and Bai Singqor’s wife

by Mongolian custom it would have been inap-

them
and
were
called Tayichi’ut. All
of
Cha’ujin Hörtägäi’s clans and sons, as well as
his relatives and dependents, who were with
the Tayichi’ut, since they were chiefs and
rulers of that tribe, were called Tayichi’ut, just
as now every tribe that has mingled with the
Mongols and taken on their nature and united
with them, even though they are not Mongols,
is called Mongol nonetheless. [240]
Of the sons and grandsons of Qaidu Khan’s
son Charaqa Lingqum and the Tayichi’ut clans
there have been many commanders, some prior
to Genghis Khan’s time and others during his
time. They have always failed to get along, and
their names appear in every register and every
tale, just as they appear everywhere in the his-
tory we have written. However, since it is
known for certain whose son each of them is, it
has been possible to create a separate branch
for each of them. Their names will now be
written so that the leaders and chiefs of the
Tayichi’ut be known: Jochi and his troops were
united with Genghis Khan; Quril Bahadur was
in Genghis Khan’s time; Qachi’un Beki was
with Ong Khan and opposed to Genghis Khan;
Udur Bayan was in Genghis Khan’s time;
Baghachi was in Genghis Khan’s time; Adal
Khan was before Genghis Khan’s time; he had
a son during Genghis Khan’s time named Tar-
qutai Qiriltuq, who was opposed to [Genghis
Khan] and rebelled; he was a bad man (qiriltuq
means jealous), and he fought much with his
own relatives; Angqu Huquchu was in Genghis
Khan’s time.
Hambaqai Qa’an had two sons, Qada’an
Taishi and Tödä’ä. Qada’an Taishi succeeded
to Hambaqai Qa’an’s place. When the Tatar
tribes seized Qada’an Taishi, they sent him to
the king of Cathay to be killed. The rule then
should have gone to his brother, Tödä’ä, [241]
but because his cousins would not agree with
him he could not become ruler. Because of
their inability to agree the Tayichi’ut never had
a ruler or leader, and therefore they were over-
thrown. [242]
(5) The story of Qaidu Khan’s son Bai
Singqor and the branches of his sons, in two
parts.
Part One: An introduction to him and his
sons.
Bai Singqor was Genghis Khan’s ancestor in
the fifth degree, which is called bodakür in
Mongolian. His son was Tumina Khan, and al-
though he certainly must have had other sons,
no mention of them has come down. The only
one of his sons known is Tumina Khan.
Part Two: The relationship of Bai Singqor
and his wife and the branch of his son
Tumina Khan.
Bai Singqor may have had other sons, but
since Genghis Khan’s line branches off with
Tumina Khan, the others have not been men-
tioned. Tumina Khan was Genghis Khan’s bu-
datu, i.e. his ancestor in the fourth degree.
[243]
(6) Beginning of the story of Tumina Khan.
When divine grace favors a person, a little on
his part will yield a lot, and he will surpass
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
115

others as assistance comes to him moment by
moment and his affairs blossom and multiply.
It is like a mulberry seed and a poppy seed. Al-
though in size, weight, and form they are equal
and similar, when the poppy seed sprouts it
produces a weak stalk and does not last more
than a season, while the mulberry seed is the
germ of a tree that grows, produces a hundred
thousand stalks, bears fruit, and is beautiful. Its
root is strong, firm, and stable, and its branches
are high and unshakeable. It lasts for many
long years, and from it is produced choice
fruit. From its leaves comes silk, which is the
finest raiment. It is unlike other trees, which,
although they too have numerous branches, do
not bear fruit and serve little purpose. So also
when God selects a servant for his favor, he
causes traces thereof to appear in that person’s
career and grants him fortunate and worthy
sons. When such favor is extreme, that per-
son’s sons are capable of being leaders and
worthy of greatness: among their contempo-
raries they become chiefs of tribes, [244] and
by virtue of his renowned predecessors his and
his innumerable offspring’s names remain for-
ever. This is like Tumina Khan, from whom
came into being a splendid line of mighty
khans and forbidding emperors, each of whom
was a sun in the firmament of success. Their
memory will last through the ages, God will-
ing, because of the blessed existence of the
Padishah of Islam, Sultan Mahmud Ghazan
Khan, who is the sun in the firmament of that
family.
(7) The story of Bai Singqor’s son Tumina
Khan, in two parts.
Part One: An introduction to him and his
sons, and a mention of their lines.
Tumina Khan was Genghis Khan’s ancestor
in the fourth degree, which is called bodatu in
Mongolian. He had nine intelligent and compe-
tent sons, from each of whom a clan branched
off to become important and well known. Now
each of those clans numbers twenty to thirty
thousand households and the number of men
and women may reach a hundred thousand in-
dividuals. This must not be attributed to exag-
geration, for it has been the Mongols’ custom
from ancient times on to keep their origin and
genealogy, and since they have no religious
community or religion in which to instruct as
others do, fathers and mothers inculcate into
every child that is born their tribe and genealo-
gy. They have maintained this as a constant
rule, and even now the rule is of great impor-
tance for them. The Arabs also do this. [245] It
is well established what name and epithet each
of the nine branches has acquired, and now
their sons and grandsons are called by that
name. Of the nine sons, the five elder ones
were of one mother, and the other four were by
another. Their names and those of the grand-
sons of each branch are as follows.
(1) Those who are the elder and born of one
mother.
The first son was Jaqso,1 from whom the
Noyaqin, Uru’ut, and Mangqut clans descend.
He had sons, the eldest of whom, and the one
who succeeded him, was Budun, and his eldest
son was Jochiya, and his eldest son was Märk-
itäi, and his son was Sügä Beki, the qu‘dud of
Genghis Khan’s sons.
The
second
son
was
Barim
Shi’iratu
Qabuchu, from whom the ___ clan descends.
He had a son named Urum, and he had a son
named Cha’urdai Baichu. Ja’urdai Baichu’s el-
dest son was Shibai, who was the qu‘dud of
Genghis Khan’s sons.
1A Noyakin named Jungso is mentioned in the Secret
History §120. The “Jaqso” here may reflect the same
name.

The third son was Qachula, from whom the
Barulas clan is descended. His eldest son was
Erdämtü1 Barula, and his eldest son was
Tödö’än. His eldest son was Jochiya, and his
eldest son was Buluqan Qilich, who was the
qu‘dud of Genghis Khan’s sons.
The fourth son was Säm Qachi’un, from
whom the Hadargin clan is descended. His son
was Adar Kidäi, and his eldest son was
Na’uqun. Na’uqun’s son was Huqu, and his el-
dest son was the Borchu who was the qu‘dud
of Genghis Khan’s sons. [246]
The fifth son was Bat Gälgäi, from whom the
Buda’at clan is descended. His eldest son was
Kölgän Märgän, and his eldest son was Tar-
qutai. Tarqutai’s eldest son was Qoridai, [and
his son was] Jirqidai, who was the qu‘dud of
Genghis Khan’s sons.
(2) Those who were younger and by a
different mother.
The sixth son was Qabul Khan, from whom
Genghis Khan was descended. Several other
lines descended from him, and since they will
all be mentioned, we will not go on at length
here.
The seventh son was Udur Bayan, from
whom the Juri’at clan is descended.
The eighth son was Bodonchar Doqolan,
from whom the Doqolat are descended.
The ninth son was Besütäi, who was also
called Jochi Naghu, from whom the Besüt are
descended. He was the otchigin. The word
1This is the Erdämchi Barula who figures in Amir

otchigin means the youngest son, who stays in
the home and yurt, i.e. “master of the fire.”
All of the above-mentioned brothers and
their sons became numerous and many clans.
They were all champions and of importance;
however, only the names of those who were el-
der and succeeded [their fathers as leaders]
have been written. Of the others nothing is
known.
The names of Tumina Khan’s grandsons who
succeeded to their fathers’ positions have been
written so that it may be known which of them

and grandsons, down to the fifth generation,
which is that of Genghis Khan’s sons. To be
easily understandable, [247] their names are
written in a chart, as follows.
All these branches and clans served Genghis
Khan, and they still continue to do so now.
Some of them performed valiant feats; others
united with enemies, but in the end they re-
ceived their just deserts, most being killed, and
those who remained became slaves, as will be

Some of their history has been mentioned in

Part Two: On Tumina Khan, his wife, and
the branches of his sons.
As was said in the previous part, Tumina
Khan had nine sons. The branches of them and
their sons at present are other than the sons of
Qabul Khan. Since the latter are ancestors of
Genghis Khan, their history will be given sepa-

[248]
(8) The Story of Qabul Khan son of Tumina
Khan, in two parts.
Part One: Introduction to him and his sons.
Qabul Khan was Genghis Khan’s great-
grandfather. The Mongols call the great-grand-
father elänchik. Many lines branched out from
him, and his sons and grandsons are called the
Qiyat. 
His eldest son was Ökin Barqaq.1 Ökin
means girl, and he was so called because he
was so extremely beautiful and handsome that
all who gazed upon the beauty of his coun-
tenance were inflamed and dazzled. He had a
large, broad, and very round face and a full
double chin. He was called “Ökin” Barqaq,
and he died young. He had a son named Sorqa-
du Yürki, and his grandson was Sacha Beki.
1The
Secret
History’s
Ökin
Barqagh
and
Ökin
Baraqagh (§§48, 139).
All the Yürkin Qiyat descend from him. The
story of their opposition to Genghis Khan will
come in the proper place.
The Tatar tribes were subservient to the ruler
of Cathay, the Altan Khan, who was an im-
placable enemy to Qabul Khan because Qabul
Khan had killed his emissaries. Furthermore,
Qabul Khan’s sons were at odds with the Tatar
tribes for a reason that will be mentioned. The
Tatars were therefore constantly lying in am-
bush. [249] Once they succeeded in capturing
Ökin Barqaq and sent him to the Altan Khan,
who ordered him killed by being nailed to a
wooden donkey with iron spikes. 
The
second
son
was
Bartan
Bahadur,
Genghis Khan’s grandfather. The branches of
his sons will be mentioned separately later.
The third son was Qutuqtu Münggür, from
whom are descended many clans. He had a son
named Taichu, from whom some of the Qiyat
are descended.

The fourth son was Qada’an Bahadur, from
whom many clans and officers are descended.
There are many stories about them.
The fifth son was Qutula Khan.1 Despite the
existence of his brothers, he ruled after his fa-
ther. His history would take too long to tell, but
although he was initially united with Genghis
Khan, he later allied himself with Ong Khan.
The story will be told in the proper place in the
history of Genghis Khan. His elder son, who
succeeded him, was Jochi Khan. He and his
hazara were allied with Genghis Khan and
formed part of his army. Qutula Khan had
another son named Altan. He was initially
allied with Genghis Khan, but later he got of-
fended and went over to Ong Khan because
when Genghis Khan was fighting the Tatars, it
had been established that there would be no
looting. [Altan] broke his word, and Genghis
Khan confiscated his share of the booty. In the
end he was killed by Genghis Khan’s soldiers.
The sixth son was Tödö’än Otchigin.
The genealogical chart of Qabul Khan and
his wife [250] and sons is as follows:
1Qutula Khan’s name varies in spelling in the
Jami‘u’t-tawarikh as Qutula ~ Qutila. We will opt for
Qutula throughout, as in the Secret History §§53, 57.
[251]
Part Two: The history of Qabul Khan and
his sons; the battles and engagements they
fought, insofar as has been ascertained.
There are many stories about Qabul Khan,
and he is held in the highest regard by the
Mongol peoples, for he was the ruler and
leader of his tribes and followers. Since he and
his sons were all champion warriors and very
brave and courageous, their repute spread to
the realm of Cathay to the Altan Khan and his
commanders. Since [Qabul Khan] was consid-
ered to be of importance by the Altan Khan,
who wanted to gain access to him and create a
bond of friendship, he dispatched emissaries to
invite him [to enter into negotiations]. When
[Qabul Khan] went there, the Altan Khan re-
ceived him with great honor and had delicious
foodstuffs and unlimited wine brought. Since
the people of Cathay were known for their
trickery and treachery and for doing away with
powerful adversaries by secret deceit, and
since they had a reputation for giving poison,
Qabul Khan suspected they would put poison
in his food. On the constant pretext of going
outside to relieve himself, he kept going and
coming, and since the weather was warm he
kept going into the water, claiming that it was
to cool off. He had also wagered that he could
stay under water for the length of time it took
them to eat a sheep. As he was accustomed to
do, he stayed under water and regurgitated
everything before returning to the Altan Khan
[252] and continuing to eat and drink prodi-
giously. The Cathaians were amazed, for he
kept saying that God had made him so strong
and powerful that he had the strength not to get
full or weak and not to vomit no matter how
much he ate or drank. 
Later he went before the Altan Khan one day
dead drunk, clapping his hands and dancing,
and pulled the Altan Khan’s beard in derision.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
119

When the commanders and guards saw such
audacity and hilarity, they said, “What levity is
this he does with our king?” and started to at-
tack him, but when he saw the Altan Khan
laughing and happy, he stepped forward and
said, “I have been bold and audacious. If the
Altan Khan accuses me of an offense and lets
me live, it is up to him. I am defenseless, and
what I did I did.” Since the Altan Khan was a
tolerant and intelligent ruler, he realized that
Qabul Khan possessed clans and followers. If
he had him killed for this slight, his relatives
would rise up in enmity to avenge him, and
there would be long drawn-out hostilities.
Therefore, attributing [Qabul Khan’s actions]
to levity and playfulness, he assuaged his
wrath and spared his life. He ordered much
gold, jewels, and textiles brought from the
treasury and stacked to Qabul Khan’s height.
All this he gave him and then let him return
home in great honor.
In private the officers said to the Altan Khan,
“It is not wise to permit him to depart and ig-
nore his action.” Immediately an envoy was
sent on his heels to bring him back. Qabul
Khan said, “We have completed the discourse
and negotiations between us and them, and we
parted with permission. What does this sum-
mons mean?” He spoke roughly, and the en-
voys turned back. 
The next time the Altan Khan sent an envoy
to summon him, Qabul Khan was away from
his tent, [253] and his wives said to the envoys,
“He has gone to bring his sons and daughters-
in-law.” The envoys turned back. Along the
way they saw Qabul Khan and several com-
panions coming in haste. They recognized him,
seized him, and took him away. Along the way
they came to the tent of his anda, Salji’utai.
When he informed Salji’utai of what was go-
ing on, he said, “He has not summoned you for
good. He intends to kill you.” [Salji’utai] had a
fast grey stallion. He gave it to him and said,
“When you have a chance, whip it and make it
run. They will not be able to catch up with
you.” By night the envoys tied his legs with a
stirrup, but one day he got a chance to turn his
reins, spur his horse, and get away. They were
unable to catch up with him before he got
home. The envoys came in pursuit. A daughter-
in-law he had requested from the Qorolas
named Matai had a new, decorated tent. He had
it fixed for the envoys and invited them in. Af-
ter that, because his sons were not there, he
said to his daughters-in-law and the servants,
“I have taken you and keep so many servants
and retinue so that at a time like this, when
there is mortal danger, you can act in conso-
nance with me to kill these envoys. If you
don’t, I’ll kill you. If the Cathaians attack me, I
won’t survive, but I’ll get to you first. As they
say, ‘Death in a group is pleasant.’ ” All united
with him to attack the envoys and kill them,
and thereby he escaped with his life. Some
time later Qabul Khan fell ill and died. [254]
Stories about his sons.
They were all champion warriors and so
courageous that not one of them ever turned
away from a fierce army, and no enemy ever
had the chance or strength to equal them.
There are many tales of their prowess.
One story is as follows. Since they were ex-
tremely brave, in the midst of a battle, they
would separate themselves from their liege
men and stand on the sidelines. Then they
would break the ranks of those who were at-
tacking their liege men, plunder them thor-
oughly, and take their plunder home. Usually,
by the time they arrived home, their wives
would have cried their eyes dry because they
feared they had fallen prey to danger on ac-
count of their great bravery and foolhardiness,
but they remained nonetheless. Before Toqa of
the Qorolas tribe they remained at the door. Af-
120
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ter that, Qada’an Bahadur and Qutula Qa’an
went separately to Qorolas territory to their
own yurts. Lürüg Multang and Burtaq Bahadur
had learned that the Bayat were constantly dri-
ving the Qorolas away, and they were amazed.
Suddenly they arrived and began to stir up
trouble. Qada’an Bahadur mounted a mare and
drove them away, and he unhorsed one of them
and took his horse. When they saw this, they
said, “Who are these people who perform such
deeds? They aren’t from the Bayat Qorolas, are
they? Their women run out abreast with their
soldiers, and their herdsmen come into battle
fearlessly.” An order was given for them to
wait until the army was assembled, and they
asked one of the women who had run out be-
fore the soldiers [255] who they were. “We are
of the Ögölät,” she said. They wondered who
the Ögölät were.
After that, Qutula Qa’an and Qada’an Baha-
dur, together with the twenty liege men they
had, raised their spears and charged. The sol-
diers said, “What people are these that come so
bravely? This is no game to them.” Some said,
“These are the same ones, one of whom
charged us, unhorsed a man, and took his
horse. There he is!” Lürüg Multang and Burtaq
Bahadur said, “Someone from among these
thousand brave and courageous men should
charge them.” So saying, they turned their
reins and went into battle. Qutula Qa’an struck
Lürüg Multang with his spear that it went
through his breastplate and sank into the flesh
of his arm, and piercing his breastplate and his
shoulder, it sank into his thigh. From the
severity of the wound he pulled so hard on the
reins in making an effort not to fall that the bit
cut the horse’s tongue off. Immediately there-
after Qada’an Bahadur unhorsed Burtaq.
When their youngsters and qafādārs were
brave,
both
left
the
midst
of
the
army
unharmed. Türüg Multang apologized, saying,
“I used to look upon Qutula Qa’an in amaze-
ment. Suddenly I fell under the hooves of his
white horse.” His horse was called Khaqan-
chin.
Another story.
Qada’an Taishi sent emissaries to Tödö’ür
Sälkächigin of the Märkit tribe with a message,
saying, “Let us be at peace with each other and
put the broad high hills under our hooves. Let
us traverse the highways together and be in
agreement with one another.” When the emis-
saries delivered the message, he kept on sharp-
ening his knife without giving an answer. [256]
The emissaries asked, “O Anda Noyan, what
do you mean by sharpening your knife and not
giving us a reply?” 
Tödö’ür said, “I am sharpening my knife in
order to pluck Qada’an Anda’s one eye out.”
When they returned and repeated his words
to Qada’an Bahadur, he said, “His words are
really very seditious. We have not desired bat-
tle until now. They have started it.” Then he
said, “If I exempt you from paying silver, what
sort of man am I?” And he cut off his horse’s
mane and threw it away. From the right wing
he sent someone to his elder brother Qutula
Qa’an, and from the left wing he sent a mes-
sage to his quda (ally), Arigh China. On the
third day he assembled his army and mounted.
He captured Tödö’ür Sälkachigin alive. His
son Toqtai1 received nine wounds during that
battle, but he managed to escape with the left
wing.
Qada’an Taishi said to Tödö’ür, “O anda,
two days ago you would have bitten my eye
out. Today I will pluck yours out with my
hand.” And so saying, he plucked out his eye
1This “Toqtai” seems to be the person generally
known as Toqto’a Beki, the ruler of the Märkit. The fa-
ther’s name (Tödö’ür Sälkächigin?) occurs so garbled
that it is difficult to ascertain what the reading should be.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
121

and killed him. The left wing of his army was
captured and unhorsed.
Three years later, when Toqtai’s wounds had
healed, he arrayed his army and sent an emis-
sary to Qada’an, saying, “The Mongols used to
designate the site and the day of battle before
they fought. Let us too now maintain this cus-
tom of battle.”
When the emissaries arrived, Qada’an Taishi
assembled all his officers and had much ku-
miss brought. At the quriltai he said, “O offi-
cers, think long and hard and advise me what
to reply to the emissaries.” No one could give
an answer. Qada’an said, “I knowingly let my
colts go and, having completely milked their
mothers, I brought them to you. So reply to the
emissaries.” They did not say anything. Then
he spoke in another expression [257] and said,
“The emissaries of a nation have come. Do not
give a specific answer, for that is why I have
made this gathering for consultation.” They
gave no reply then either. When Qada’an
Taishi saw how things were, he said to the
emissaries, “I have made such a gathering and
assembled the officers of the ….1 Since they do
not give a reply, you must return.”
At that point his elder brother Adal Khan
said, “O Qada’an Taishi, why don’t you give
an answer? Why do you leave it to others?”
After that he said to Baradai Sächän, who was
an Urghutai man, “You are as cunning as a
jackal. Use some of your cunning sweet talk.
When you were thirteen years old did you not
do battle with the Tatars, whose chieftains
were Kütün Baraqa and Jali Buqa? Now is like
then. Do you send to your elder brothers and
chieftains in order to discover your own manli-
ness? .Don’t you see that the crane, as large as
it is, eats weeds and mud, while the falcon, for
all its smallness, eats meat and fat? What is the
1An unknown word, دﻻی.
point of useless words? One must speak of
killing, striking, and seizing.”
When Qada’an heard this, he said to the
emissaries, “Tell Toqtai that two rams butt
heads and will not let go of each other until
one of them is wounded or defeated. If they
come back, they will butt heads again until one
of them is wounded. You are just like that.
Wanting to take revenge for your father, what
injury will you not do to your own head? On
my right hand I have an elder brother named
Qutula Qa’an. He springs from the earth of
Ghorqonas Jubur, the abode of demons, and in
comparison to his voice the rumbling of tall
mountains is weak. His grip is so strong that he
can break the grip of a three-year-old bear.
From the might of his attack the water of three
rivers would move, and from his wounds he
can inflict the sons of three mothers would fall
to weeping.
“On my left I have an ally named Arigh Chi-
na. When he hunts in thick forests [258] he
catches blue wolves and throws them to the
ground. He gnaws off the heads and legs of
leopards, and he can break the necks of lions.
He originates from the land of Adar Jubur,
which is also an abode of demons.
“And in the center of the army is one named
Qada’an Taishi. If he attacks a mountain or a
cliff, his hands and feet do not miss. When the
three of us are together, we will throw you out
of your land and deprive you of family, retinue,
and retainers. Now, although this speech is
long, you my children who are emissaries have
been sent because you are the most under-
standing and best of your tribe. You must not
forget these words. Say, ‘Now this is what we
will do, and we will do battle.’ ”
After that, when the emissaries had been put
on their horses and sent off, Qada’an Taishi
said, “O officers, must have I relied on your
great numbers in speaking so boldly. Tell me
122
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

whether the reply I made was correct or not.”
Once again Urghutai said to Bardai Sächän,
“Just as a person can find his way through a
trackless plain and can cross a large, deep riv-
er,
you
have
spoken
without
error
and
correctly.”
Then Qada’an Taishi said, “Before the ene-
my arrives and stands at the doors of our tents,
we must go and stand at the doors of our ene-
my’s
tents.”
In
reply
to
this
the
young
ba’urchis and cupbearers said, “When they
come from Qara Selenga, which is their territo-
ry, to Qara Onan, which is our territory, we
will beat them on the head and kill them.”
Qada’an Taishi said, “Do you think they are
weaklings? It has been said that one should not
boast about doing battle and one should not go
beyond one’s ability. You are speaking big
words. It is possible to kill a snake, which re-
sembles a belt and has neither hands nor feet,
[259] but how is an enemy who has both hands
and feet going to allow you strike him one the
head? You say that you will do battle when
they come here. A pampered man with a full
belly cannot strike hard enough for his fist to
go through paper; a fat horse can walk around
a hill, but it can’t run up to the top. It would be
best for us to make our horses run in hopes of
getting their fresh grass and to make our
youths run in hopes of eating their portions of
meat, for if they come here to do battle,
thoughts of your families, wives, and children
will run through your minds and distract you.
You all know that my father, Hambaqai Qa’an,
appointed me as your chief and ruler. When I
mount and set out for there, you must not lag
behind or make any opposition. If you oppose
me it will be clear what loss I, Qada’an Taishi,
will suffer: it will be a loss that the entire
Taichi’ut nation will suffer.” And that very day
he mounted his troops on all sides and set
forth.
And
when
Toqtai’s
emissaries
delivered
Qada’an Taishi’s message, he, as was his cus-
tom, greased the tuq, got his army mounted,
and went out to face them in all readiness.
When they began the battle Toqtai Beki re-
ceived seven wounds and went with his right
wing above the Selenga River, and Qada’an
Taishi set out in pursuit. Unable to catch up
with him, he turned back, captured Toqtai’s left
wing and center, and dismounted.
All six sons were of one mother, and her
name was Qo’a Qulqu. (Qo’a means pure, and
Qulqu is a name.) This lady was from the Qun-
qirat. She had a younger brother named Sayin
Tegin, and it was on his account that Qada’an
Bahadur fought many battles with the Tatar.
[260] It came about as follows.
Once Sayin Tegin fell ill, and a shaman from
the Tatar nation named Jorqul Bödöi was sum-
moned to treat him. He worked his shamanism,
but he died. They gave the shaman something
and sent him back home. After that, Sayin Te-
gin’s brothers went and killed the shaman, and
because Qabul Khan’s sons were blood-brother
allies to Sayin Tegin, it was necessary for them
to fight the Tatar tribes. They drew up ranks at
a place called Naran Sangdan. Qada’an Baha-
dur and Matur Bahadur, the first warrior of the
Tatar, stood opposite each other at a distance to
which a qodali (blunt arrow) would reach,
cried out, and invited to battle. Qada’an Baha-
dur picked up a lance, charged Matur, and
struck the lance on his saddle horn with such
force that it split the saddle horn and went into
Matur’s and his horse’s bodies. Man and horse
were both wounded and felled. Matur suffered
from that wound for a year, but when he
recovered he went back out to a place called
Bula Ilgit. There the two of them did combat
again, and Qada’an Bahadur struck Matur in
the back so hard that the lance went through
his stomach, killing him. It was in that battle
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
123

that the horse of Husun Äbügän’s father, Qayin
Mänen, who was on Qada’an Bahadur’s side,
was shot in the neck with an arrow and killed.
Therefore he was coming on foot, and ten
horsemen with spears were coming. He turned
toward them, put them all to flight with blows
of his sword, and emerged triumphant and vic-
torious. After that, Qabul Khan’s sons did
many battles with the Tatar, and mention of
these stories and other feats they performed
will be made later.
Among Qabul Khan’s six sons, Qutula Qa’an
became the ruler, and he served as khan for a
time.
Although
his
brothers
were
all
champions, [261] he was greater than they
were in strength and bravery. Mongol poets
have composed much poetry in praise of him
and described his bravery and courage. They
say that his voice was so loud that it could
reach the other side of a hill and resembled an
echo reverberating from a mountain or cliff.
His hands resembled a bear’s claws. He could
take the burliest and strongest man and bend
him and break his back as effortlessly as if he
were an arrow shaft. It has been related that on
winter nights he would place logs on the fire
and sleep naked next to it. As the fire burned,
embers would fall on his body and burn it; he
paid no attention, and when he woke up he
would think he had been bitten by lice. He
would just scratch himself and go back to
sleep. His food at every meal was a large por-
tion of sheep and an arghut (leather skin) of
kumiss, and he was still not satisfied. Because
the Tatar tribes had captured and sent to the Al-
tan Khan his brother Ökin Barqaq and his fa-
ther’s cousin Hambaqai Qa’an, the grandson of
Charaqa Lingqum, and the Altan Khan had
killed them by nailing them to wooden don-
keys, he gathered his army and set out for
Cathay, where he did battle with the Altan
Khan’s peoples and armies and pillaged some
of his territories. 
When Genghis Khan set out for Cathay and
mounted to wage war on the Altan Khan, he
besought the deity, saying, “Inasmuch as the
rulers of Cathay unjustly killed Hambaqai
Qa’an, Ökin Barqaq, and Qada’an Bahadur,
who were my elder brothers, let me go to
avenge them, and I ask Thee, O great God, for
assistance and strength.” Thereupon he mount-
ed and set forth. [262]
Qutula Qa’an goes to war with the Altan
Khan, the ruler of Cathay, to avenge the blood
of Hambaqai Qa’an; the armies of Cathay are
defeated, and much plunder is taken; he falls
captive to the Dörbän tribe on his return jour-
ney, but he escapes and reaches home just as
they are about to mourn his loss.
Hambaqai Qa’an, the grandson of Charaqa
Lingqum, the son of Sorqadu China, who was
then the ruler of the Tayichi’ut tribe, went to
the Tatar tribes in order to choose one of their
daughters for himself. They were offended,
saying, “How can he ask for our daughters like
this?” and seized him and several of his liege
men. Since they were followers of and obedi-
ent to the Altan Khan, they sent him there, and
the Altan Khan ordered, as was their custom,
that he be nailed to a wooden donkey until he
died. As they were conducting him to the place
of execution, he sent one of his liege men
named Bolghajai to the Altan Khan with a
message, saying, “You did not take me with
manliness and virtue or with your own troops.
Others captured me and brought me to you. If
you kill me in such a vile and mean way, you
will make enemies of Qada’an Taishi, Qutula
Qa’an, Tödä’ä, and Yesügäi Bahadur’s sons,
who are kinfolk to our clans and the Mongol
nation, and you will stir up a vendetta, for they
will certainly rise up to requite my blood. It is
unwise of you to do this.” [263]
124
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The Altan Khan took this lightly and said
mockingly, “You who have brought this mes-
sage, go and inform that group.” And when he
had killed Hambaqai Qa’an, he gave the
above-mentioned Bolghajai a pack horse and
sent him off to take the news to his people.
Along the way he came across the Dörbän tribe
and asked them for a horse. They refused. “If
upon the morrow I do not bring our troops here
like a heavy mountain and flowing water, what
sort of man am I?” he said to them. “Beware
lest you have regret and say, ‘Why did we not
grant Bolghajai’s request?’ ” They paid no at-
tention, and he made the Cathaians’ pack horse
continue. Since the horses had grown tired, he
left them along the way and went on foot to
take the news of how Hambaqai Qa’an had
been killed to his son Qada’an Taishi, his son
Tödä’ä, Qutula Qa’an, the leader of the tribe,
and Yesügäi Bahadur, who was a cousin to
Hambaqai Qa’an’s father. 
(The lineages of those who have been men-
tioned are as follows. Hambaqai Qa’an was the
son of Sorqadu China, the son of Charaqa
Lingqum, the son of Qaidu Khan. Qada’an
Taishi was the son of Hambaqai Qa’an. Tödä’ä
was the son of Qada’an Taishi, the son of
Hambaqai Qa’an. Qutula Qa’an was the son of
Qabul Khan, the son of Tumina Khan, the
[grand]son of Qaidu Khan. Yesügäi Bahadur
was the son of Bartan Bahadur, the son of Qab-
ul
Khan,
the
son
of Tumina
Khan,
the
[grand]son of Qaidu Khan.)
When the bad news arrived, Qada’an Taishi,
Tödä’ä, and Yesügäi Bahadur took counsel
with many Mongol clans and tribes to avenge
the blood of Hambaqai Qa’an. Qutula Qa’an
was appointed khan, and all the troops inclined
to him as they set out in the direction of
Cathay. When they arrived there, they fought
and defeated the Altan Khan’s army, killing
many Cathaians. They pillaged [264] and loot-
ed beyond measure, distributed the loot among
the soldiers, and withdrew. Qutula Qa’an was
journeying unescorted with a pair of horses.
When the Dörbän tribe saw him unescorted,
they took advantage of the opportunity, gath-
ered their forces, and attacked him on the road.
His soldiers and liege men scattered, and he es-
caped to reach a place where there was a large
morass. He drove his horse into it, but the
horse fell and got stuck in the mud. He put one
foot on the saddle and nimbly jumped onto the
bank. The enemy, coming from behind, ap-
proached his direction and called out, “What
can a Mongol separated from his horse do?
Come back with your mind at ease!” He paid
no attention, shot a few arrows at them, and
drove them away. Then he went back to the
water’s edge, grabbed his horse by its mane,
pulled it from the mud without difficulty, and
cast it onto the ground. Then he mounted and
set out, leaving the enemy on the other side of
the water. 
Qutula Qa’an’s soldiers and liege men who
had been routed arrived before he reached
home. Since he had not followed them, it ap-
peared certain that he had been killed. Yesügäi
Bahadur had a meal prepared and took it to
Hambaqai Qa’an’s people, Qada’an Taishi,
Tödä’ä, and Qutula Qa’an’s wife to inform
them of the death and offer a toast. When he
informed them, Qada’an Taishi and Tödä’ä
cried and wept aloud. Qutula Qa’an’s wife
said, “Since the band of younger brothers came
together and went out together and were dis-
persed, I find it strange to think that anything
could have happened to them. Now that I hear
this news I don’t believe it. [265] ‘I believe not
these words from anyone; perhaps I am asleep
and dreaming.’ Qutula Khan is he of whom
they have said that his voice is like an echo
against the sky and his hand is like a three-
year-old bear’s claw. He is not one whose fate
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
125

is in the hands of the Dörbän. God willing, he
is occupied with some task and will show up
without warning.”
When Qutula Khan pulled his horse from the
mud and set forth, he said to himself, “How
can those men do such a thing to me and I not
take anything from them to return home emp-
ty-handed?” He turned around, and in the area
in which their herds were grazing he caught a
fine stallion, rustled a herd of mares, and set
out at a gallop. Since it was springtime, there
were a lot of duck eggs in the plains, but he
didn’t have anything to put them in. He took
his felt stockings off and filled them with duck
eggs, hung them from his saddle ring, mounted
the stallion bareback, and, leading his own
horse, drove the mares until he reached home.
Yesügäi Bahadur had taken the food and they
were busy with the mourning, and when their
gaze fell upon him they all rejoiced. His wife
said, “Didn’t I say he wasn’t a man who could
be captured?”
A world champion was Dastan of Sam: not in
jest does he put his head in the noose. [266]
The Tayichi’ut clans hold a council after
Hambaqai Qa’an.
As has been described, the Tatar tribes cap-
tured Hambaqai Qa’an and took him to the Al-
tan Khan, who killed him. After a while his rel-
atives, sons, and the commanders of the
Tayichi’ut gathered to elect someone as ruler
in his stead. They deliberated for a time, un-
able to decide on any one. Qada’an Taishi set-
tled in the plain of Köy Kähär and went to the
Gürkhan, the uncle of Ong Khan, the ruler of
the Kerayit. Gürkhan was in Kükäbäs Qo-
qanas. They stayed there for ten days. When it
was
time
to
return,
Gürkhan’s
ba’urchis
brought a goblet of rice wine for them to make
a toast. Qada’an Taishi ordered his liege men
to take a draught, and then he finished it all off.
Since the liege man all vomited, it had no ef-
fect on them, but Qada’an Taishi did not vomit
and said, “They have given me spring poison.”
He fell ill and died during the spring. When it
was autumn, they assembled one day and said
to Nurdu Bilgäshi, one of their cousins and a
great tribal leader, “What say you in this re-
gard? Whom do you consider worthy?” 
“Let Targhutai Qiriltuq say,” he replied. 
Targhutai Qiriltuq, also one of the cousins
and the son of Adal Khan, said, “What can I
say? Let Mätügän Sächän say.”  [267]
“What can I say?” said Mätügän Sächän.
“Should I leap like a sparrow into a snare so
that my foot may get caught in a trap? The
black swallow went on top of a qaraghana
tree1 and did not fall into a snare. What qualifi-
cations have I, a common slave, to speak? You
lords speak wise and good words so that we
commoners can be kept amused like a colt that
drinks the milk of two mares and gets full and
fat. If you agree in council on one person,
everything and all the people will be as you
wish. If you do not agree, all sorts of dis-
sention and strife will befall your nation.” In
this regard he spoke many rhymed words,
proverbs, and homilies and left the gathering,
weeping. At that session no one was elected
ruler.
After that, despite research, it is not known
upon what individual the choice fell, but it
comes in the history that when Yesügäi Baha-
dur died young and the Tayichi’ut tribes op-
posed Genghis Khan, Adal Khan’s son Tarqutai
Qiriltuq was more in opposition than anyone,
and Tödä’ä, Quril Bahadur, A’uchu, Huquchu,
and several other commanders—as will be
mentioned—gave Tarqutai Qiriltuq the leader-
ship and rule, as has been mentioned previous-
ly. It is certain that after Qutula Khan’s death,
his nephew, Yesügäi Bahadur, the son of Bar-
1The Siberian peashrub, Caragana arborescens.
126
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

tan Bahadur and father of Genghis Khan,
ruled. Although there are many stories about
Qabul Khan’s sons other than Bartan Bahadur,
in this history we will content ourselves with
this much, and the stories of Bartan Bahadur
and his sons will be written in a separate sec-
tion. [268]
(9) The story of Bartan Bahadur, son of
Qabul Khan, in two parts.
Part One: Introduction to him and his sons
and those who branched off from them.
Bartan Bahadur was Genghis Khan’s grand-
father, which is called äbügä in Mongolian. He
had a chief wife named Sünigil Füjin of the
Targhut tribe. By her he had four sons.
The first was Mönggädü Qiyan,1 who had
many sons, but his heir was Chingshi’ut,2 who
commanded Mönggädü Qiyan’s soldiers, clan,
and followers in Genghis Khan’s time, and he
attended Genghis Khan with the Tayichi’ut and
his own soldiers. After them were their sons
Köki Noyan and Mögätü Bahadur. Mögätü Ba-
hadur was a hazara commander and leader of
the Mönggädü Qiyan clan. Due to their having
multiplied at that time, they now constitute
more than a tümän of Mongols. Most of that
clan are in the Qipchaq Steppe with Toqta, and
their officers are numerous and important.
There are also some in service to the Qa’an.
The Qiyat clans are many, but these are sepa-
rate Qiyat. Of the branches of the Qiyat some
who are known are ___. Some stories connect-
1His name appears variously in the Secret History as
Mönggetü Kiyan (§213), Münggetü Kiyan (§120), and
Menggetü Kiyan (§50).
2There is a Jüngshöi in the Secret History §202 whose
name may be the same as the text’s “Chingshi’ut.” On
text p. 330 below, it is “Chingshut.” Berezin (13:47)
reads Джинкшутъ, and Smirnova (JTSL 1/2:46) reads
Чаншиут.
ed to them will come throughout the history,
whence information can be had. [269]
The second son was Näkün Taishi, from
whom is descended the Hoyin clan, and they
are called the hoyin irgän. The reason is that
they rebelled during Genghis Khan’s time and
deserted him, going to the Tayichi’ut tribe and
into the forest. Their epithet therefore became
the “forest clan” in belittlement. The Tayichi’ut
and several other tribes are also known by this
name because every tribe whose yurt is near a
forest is known as a “forest tribe.”
Since
the
forests
are
in
territories
far
removed from one another, their tribes, clans,
and divisions had no contact with each other.
Although they call them all “forest tribes,” ac-
cording to the location of the forest it is clear
to them which tribe is meant.
Näkün Taishi had many sons. The eldest,
who succeeded him, was Quchar. He could
shoot arrows extremely far and accurately and
gained renown for that. He could shoot so far
that the Mongols praised him for it, saying ex-
aggeratedly, “Quchar’s arrow flies so far that it
disappears.” When Genghis Khan was bereft
of his father as a child and his clans inclined to
the Tayichi’ut, Quchar allied himself and his
soldiers with Genghis Khan, served him for a
long time, and performed valiant feats. When
Genghis Khan was doing battle with the Tatars
and had stipulated, saying, “Let us fight to-
gether and not take booty. After that, what we
find we will divide equally so that the battle-
field not be osal (sloppy).” Qabul Khan’s son
Altan, Qutula Khan’s son, this Quchar, and
Genghis Khan’s uncle Daritai Otchigin broke
their promise and took booty. Genghis Khan
ordered their booty taken from them. They
therefore rebelled. [270] When Genghis Khan
was in dispute with Ong Khan, they took Ong
Khan’s side, helped and aided the enemy, and
stirred up strife and war. When Ong Khan was
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
127

defeated, they fled and went to the Naiman.
They fought Genghis Khan once again, and in
the end God gave him victory and killed
Quchar and Altan. For this reason those of his
sons and family who remain have neither im-
portance nor renown. Relative to Genghis
Khan’s other relatives they are also few.
Näkün Taishi had a grandson named Bügün
Cha’uqat. Genghis Khan favored him and went
around with him. His sons and their clans are
with Chaghatai’s offspring, but they do not
have much importance.
The third son was Yesügäi Bahadur, the fa-
ther of Genghis Khan. The Qiyat and Borjiqin
Qiyat are descended from him. Borjiqin means
having gray eyes, and as it happens the sons
who were born to Yesügäi Bahadur and to his
sons and offspring down to the present mostly
have gray eyes and are of a yellowish color.
This is attributed to the fact that when Alan
Qo’a was pregnant she said, “A light like a per-
son comes before my eyes at night and then
goes away. It is of a yellow color in form and
has gray eyes.” When this trait re-emerged in
the eighth generation, which was Yesügäi Ba-
hadur, they said it was the sign Alan Qo’a had
spoken of, that her sons would be rulers, and it
indicated the truth of her words and that it was
imminent.
Since stories connected to Yesügäi Bahadur’s
branch will come separately, we will not go on
at length here. [271]
The fourth son was Daritai Otchigin. Be-
cause he opposed Genghis Khan mightily, in
the end his family became slaves. Even though
at first, when Genghis Khan’s clans and sol-
diers went over to the Tayichi’ut, he and his
soldiers were allied with him, after a time he
allied himself with the Tayichi’ut. He came
back to Genghis Khan, but he rebelled again
over the matter of taking booty, as has been re-
lated, and went to Ong Khan. He then went to
the Naiman, and then he allied himself with the
Dörbän tribe and fought Genghis Khan many
times. Finally he came back to him, but he, Al-
tan Khan, and Quchar were killed, and many of
his clan and family were put to death. He had a
son who was his heir and successor, Tanyal
Bey. At Genghis Khan’s order he and two
hundred of his men were given to Genghis
Khan’s nephew Elji’idäi Noyan, and they were
ranked as his slaves. His family is still with
Elji’idäi Noyan’s family now. 
Of that clan and family is Burqan, who came
[to Iran] with Hülägü Khan. Although he did
not have the rank to sit in the row of sons,
Hülägü Khan ordered that since there were few
princes to sit in the row, Burqan should be al-
lowed to sit in the row of sons. Of his sons was
Kürüh,1 commander of a division of a thou-
sand, to whom Burqan’s post was transferred.
Of his relatives was Boralghi Qiyatai, Arghun
Khan’s sükürchi (parasol bearer) and inaq (ad-
visor). He was one of the officers who plotted
treachery against Arghun Khan. [272]
Part Two: On Bartan Bahadur and his wife,
and a genealogical chart of their sons.
As has been written in detail, Bartan Bahadur
had four sons. A genealogical tree of him and
his wife Sünigil Füjin, and of his sons and
grandsons, aside from Yesügäi Bahadur’s sons,
which will be given separately, is as follows.
[273]
1In all manuscripts the name isــــﮐ
ﺮوﻩ(Kürüh?). Berezin
(13:51) reads it as Куругъ; Smirnova (JTSL 1/2:48) reads
it as Курух.
128
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Beginning of the history of Yesügäi Bahadur
When the divine will decreed from all eterni-
ty that a fortunate, mighty, and powerful one
who would be a cavalier in the field of world
conquest and raiser of the edifice of rule
should be garbed in the raiment of existence
and seated on the throne of mastery in the
world of generation and corruption at a specif-
ic time, the hand of divine power gradually
nourished the pearl of his being in the shells of
his ancestors’ and ancestresses’ loins and
wombs until, level by level and stage by stage,
he was brought near the level of perfection.
When it came time for the appearance of signs
of
that
fortune,
first
the
dawning
lights
gleamed from the veil of the horizon of cre-
ation. An example is the career of Yesügäi Ba-
hadur, whose peerless person was a shell in the
sea of world rule and the rising of the stars of
his fortune was a preface to the arrive of the
retinue of Genghis Khan’s rule, and from their
renowned and mighty sons, offspring, and
progeny, particularly the Emperor of Mankind,
the Padishah of Islam, Succorer of God’s Reli-
gion, Sultan Mahmud Ghazan—may the ropes
of the tents of his rule be reinforced and held
tight by the pegs of eternity, and may the those
who
support
him
be
infinite
in
number,
through the Unlettered Prophet and his noble
family, upon him and upon them be prayers
and peace. [274]
(10) The Story of Yesügäi Bahadur son of
Bartan Bahadur, in two parts.
Part One: Introduction to him, details of his
sons, and some stories about them.
Yesügäi Bahadur was Genghis Khan’s father,
and the Mongols call the father echigä. He was
the ruler of many Mongol clans, and his aqa-
ini, i.e. his uncles and his uncles’ sons, were all
obedient to him and followers of his, and they
unanimously
elected
him
ruler.
He
was
renowned for his bravery and courage, and he
fought many battles with other Mongol tribes,
especially with the Tatars and the commanders
and soldiers of Cathay. His fame and renown
spread abroad, and he was respected and feared
by all. He had many wives from every clan, the
chief of whom and mother of his important
children and sons was Ö’älün Füjin. She was
also called Ö’älün Ekä, and she was from the
Olqunu’ut clan. In the Cathaian language füjin
means lady,1 and their terminology was used
because their territory was nearby. Taichu
Gürägän, to whom Genghis Khan gave his
youngest daughter, Altalun, was Ö’älün Ekä’s
brother. By this great lady he had four sons and
no daughters. Another son, the youngest of all,
was by a different lady, and his name was Bäl-
gütäi Noyan, but he did not achieve the impor-
tance of the other four.
Yesügäi Bahadur’s first son, Tämüjin
The first, [275] eldest, and best son was
Tämüjin, who was named Genghis Khan when
he became ruler at the age of fifty-one and
killed the ruler of the Naiman. Stories about
him are too numerous to be related, but some
of them will come in the history.
Yesügäi Bahadur’s second son, Jochi Qasar
The second son was Jochi Qasar. Jochi is a
name, and qasar means ‘wild beast.’ He was
given this name because he was huge, power-
ful, and mighty. They say his shoulders and
chest were so broad and his waist so narrow
that when he lay down on his side a dog could
go under him. He was so strong that he could
grab a man in his two hands, bend him, and
break him in two like a wooden arrow shaft.
Most of the time he was allied and cooperative
with his brother Genghis Khan, although dur-
1The Mongolian füjin is borrowed from the Chinese
夫人 furen.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
129

ing the battle with Ong Khan he was separated
from him. Several other times incidents took
place for which he was charged with insubor-
dination. However, in Genghis Khan’s big bat-
tle with Tayang Khan, the ruler of the Naiman,
he ordered Qasar to command the center of the
army. He performed valiant feats in that battle,
and therefore Genghis Khan rewarded him and
gave him and his sons fraternal and princely
rank and status over all the brothers and
nephews. Until the present it is customary that,
of all the uncles and cousins of Genghis
Khan’s family, only Jochi Qasar’s offspring are
seated in the row of princes. The others sit in
the row of commanders. Some stories about
Jochi Qasar and his sons will come in the
course of the history of Genghis Khan.
He had many children. It is related that he
had nearly forty sons, but only three are well
known, Yegü, Tuqu, and Yesünggü.1 However,
in Genghis Khan’s decree the names of Yegü
and Yesünggü appear, [276] but Tuqu’s does
not. Yegü was short, and Tuqu was even short-
er, while Yesünggü was tall and red of face and
kept his countenance and beard drawn. When
Jochi Qasar died, his most respected son, Yegü,
took his place. When Yegü died, his son Har-
qasun took over his post. After him, his uncle
Yesünggü succeeded. During Mänggü Qa’an’s
and Qubilai Qa’an’s time Jochi Qasar’s succes-
sor was Yesünggü, and his name and repute are
well known. He participated in weighty mat-
ters and consultations of affairs of state, and
they respected him greatly. In accordance with
the rule for all the army and his father’s clan,
he was in charge of the aqa-inis. When dispute
broke out between Qubilai Qa’an and Ariq
Bökä, Yesünggü was with Qubilai Qa’an and
served in his army, as will be related in the his-
tory of Qubilai Qa’an. They say that when he
1Yesünggü ~ Yesünggä. See text pp. 872–77.
attended a quriltai with Qubilai Qa’an at the
age of seventy-five, not one strand of his hair
had turned white. When Genghis Khan was di-
viding the army among his sons, he gave one
thousand to the sons of Jochi Qasar who were
grown, like Yegü, Tuqu, and Yesünggü, and he
gave a hundred men from the miscellaneous
corps. After that, everyone of his progeny who
commanded his place took command of those
troops, and now, due to their having multiplied,
they are many. In Mänggü Qa’an’s time several
of Jochi Qasar’s great wives were still alive,
and he held them in great respect and honor.
Yesünggü’s and Jochi Qasar’s offspring’s yurt
and dwelling place are inside Mongolia, on the
northeastern side, in the vicinity of the Argun,
Kökä Na’ur Lake, and the Qailar, near the lo-
cation of the yurts of Jibu, Otchi Noyan’s son,
and his grandson Taghachar. [277] Yegü’s
son’s name was Yantaq, and he had another son
named Harqasun, who commanded a company
of a hundred. Tuqu’s son Äbügän also com-
manded a company of a hundred. In Qubilai
Qa’an’s time Yesünggü’s son Ämägän com-
manded in Jochi Qasar’s place and his ulus.
Ämägän’s son Siktür, who was also in Qubilai
Qa’an’s time, succeeded to his father’s posi-
tion. In the end he conspired with the grand-
sons of Taghachar, the offspring of Otchi Noy-
an, and plotted against Qubilai Qa’an, but
Qubilai Qa’an had them executed and dis-
persed their troops. 
One branch of Jochi Qasar’s offspring came
to this land. They were here during Abaqa
Khan’s time, and some of them are still here
now.
Jochi Qasar had another son named Maqul-
dar. He was known for a slight weakness in his
constitution. His mother was Altan Khatun of
the Qorolas clan. Maquldar had two sons. One
was Jirqidai, and he had five sons, (1) Qipchaq
was born of a concubine, and he had two sons,
130
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Taichu and Hulqutu; (2) Suqu was born of a
khatun, and he had no sons; (3) Kökä was born
of a khatun, and he had no sons; (4) Tödägän
was born of ___ Khatun; and (5) Tärgil1 was
born of a khatun, and he had three sons, Baba,
Boralghi, and Bolad.
Maquldar’s other son died in childhood, and
his name is unknown.
Jochi Qasar had another son named Qar-
alchu. His history is as follows. Jochi Qasar
had a slave named Toqtai who had a good-
looking wife named Kökchin. Jochi Qasar saw
her once in the fields [278] and was taken by
her good looks. He slept with her and then,
worried that since he had been with her, she
might have become pregnant, he ordered her
kept by herself. After nine months she gave
birth to a son he named Qaralchu and gave to
his wife, Altan Khatun, saying, “You have one
son. Let this one be a son to you also.” Altan
Khatun brought the child up. Qaralchu had
seven sons, whose names and those of the
grandchildren they produced are as follows: (1)
Temür, who had no sons; (2) Sali, who had no
sons; (3) Mügädü, who had two sons, Bügrätäi
and Qurumshi; (4) Qutuqu, who had a son
named Arslan who came with Hülägü Khan,
rebelled, and died; (5) Sali Buqa, who had two
sons, Qurjan and Jamuji; (6) Muidar, who had
one son named Örüg Temür; and (7) Qurtqa,
who had no sons.
They say that when Ögödäi Qa’an was ruler
and Chaghatai was living apart from him
among his nation, [Chaghatai] sent a message
to Ögödäi Qa’an, saying, “Those with whom
we are intimate and with whom we eat and
drink are few. If the Qa’an would be so kind as
to send a few people from this clan, he is the
ruler.” Ögödäi Qa’an appointed several people
1For the text’sﮏـﮐﺮـﺗ, readﺮﰻ ـﺗ. See Hambis, Yuan Che,
p. 28.
of Jochi Qasar’s offspring, among them Qar-
alchu. Altan Khatun, who had reared him, said,
“How can we let him go alone?” So she ac-
companied
him,
bringing
her
grandson
Jirqidai, who was still an infant, and came to
Chaghatai. When Baraq, Chaghatai’s grandson,
went to battle against Abaqa Khan, [279] Qar-
alchu’s sons and Jirqidai, as has been men-
tioned, accompanied him and fought. When
Baraq took flight and his troops were dis-
persed, the next year they held council and
said, “Before this, the Qa’an sent us. Now let
us go to Abaqa Khan and fight for him.” They
all came, appeared before Abaqa Khan at Sug-
hurluq, and presented gifts, for which they
were rewarded. He ordered Kökä to accompa-
ny Arghun. After that, he ordered Suqu to ac-
company him. He made Tödä’än an idächi. He
went around with Gäräi2 and Hindu. Tärgil was
also made an idächi, but since he was incom-
petent he was dismissed and attached to the
retinue. [In his place] he appointed Toqtai.
Temür, Sali, Mügädü, and Qutuqu were in a
tamma (garrison) in Shirämün Noyan’s tümän.
Sali Buqa, Muidar, and Qurtqa accompanied
Abaqa Khan as princes.
Yesügäi Bahadur’s third son, Qachi’un
The third son was Qachi’un. He had many
wives
and
sons,
but
his
successor
was
Elji’idäi,3
who
was
of
great
importance.
Ögödäi Qa’an, Mänggü Qa’an, and Qubilai
Qa’an all respected and honored him greatly
and consulted with him on weighty matters.
His ulus and yurt were directly to the east in-
side Mongolia near the wall the Cathaians built
2Berezin (JTB 13:94) transcribes this name as Кирей
(13:59). I take this to be the name that much later in the

131

from the Qara Mörän (Yellow River) to the Ju-
rcha River. It is near the territory of the Ju-
rchids, and the places that are nearby are the
ancient yurt of the Ikiräs clan, the place called
Qalajin Älät and the vicinity of the Alghui Riv-
er. Until now his sons and troops serve the
Qa’an. In this land there is no one of their off-
spring. When Genghis Khan was dividing the
troops among his sons, [280] he gave Elji’idäi
Noyan three thousand men whose leader was
Aqsa’udai Ujqash Guyang (Aqsa’udai is the
name of a clan, Ujqash is a personal name, and
Guyang is a title). He was of the Naiman tribe.
Other commanders were of the Uriangqut and
Tatar tribes, and most of the three thousand
soldiers were Naiman, Uriangqut, and Tatar.
By this time they have multiplied and become
numerous.
Elji’idäi had many sons, and his successor
was Chaqula. He too had many sons, and his
successor was Oqlaqur. He also had many
sons, and he was succeeded by Qada’an. He
too had many sons, and his successor was
Shinglaqar.1 Qubilai Qa’an ordered Elji’idäi’s
branch counted as a test, and they turned out to
be six hundred individuals. This son was the
last who conspired with Otchi Noyan’s off-
spring and other princes against Qubilai Qa’an,
who had them all executed and dispersed their
troops.
Yesügäi Bahadur’s fourth son, Tämügä
Otchigin
The
fourth
son
was
Tämügä
Otchigin.
Tämügä was his name, and otchigin means
master of the fire and yurt. The youngest son is
always called Otchigin. He became known as
Otchi Noyan. He had a great lady wife named
Sandaqchin of the Olqunu’ut clan. She was a
relative of Genghis Khan’s mother, and there-
1In Hambis, Yuan Che, the name occurs as both
Shinglaqar (3111) and Shingnaqar (3211).
fore she was greatly revered and respected. Of
all the Mongols, Otchi Noyan loved building,
and everywhere he went he built palaces,
pavilions, and gardens. Genghis Khan loved
him more than any of his brothers and seated
him above his own elder brothers. Until now
his sons still sit above the sons of the other two
brothers. When Genghis Khan was distributing
the troops among his sons, he gave him five
thousand men, [281] two thousand of whom
were of the Oronar clan of the Kilungghut
clans, one thousand of whom were of the Besüt
clan, and two thousand of whom had been as-
sembled from various clans.
He had many sons. His successor was
Taghachar Noyan. He also had a large ulus and
many troops, and through multiplying and gen-
eration the five thousand men became a large
and consequential army. His territory and yurt
were in the northeast, the farthest reaches of
Mongolia, so far in that direction that there
were no other Mongol tribes. He was always at
quriltais and councils on weighty matters with
Qubilai Qa’an, and he was respected and
revered. When Ariq Bökä rebelled against
Qubilai Qa’an, Qubilai Qa’an made him leader
of the army and sent him to do battle. He de-
feated Ariq Bökä’s troops. After that, he was
continually sent on campaigns by Qubilai
Qa’an’s order.
Otchi Noyan lived an exemplary life and
reached a fine old age. He had many sons, and
his successor was Jibu, who also had many
sons. His successor was Taghachar, and he too
had many sons and served Qubilai Qa’an with
the many troops that were under his command.
He had many sons, and his successor was
Achul. He too had many sons, and Nayan was
his successor. Qubilai Qa’an ordered them
counted. Otchi Noyan’s offspring were seven
hundred individuals. Nayan was at the end of
Qubilai Qa’an’s time. He conspired with the
132
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

princes who were his cousins like Siktür of
Jochi Qasar’s offspring, Shinglaqar of Elji’idäi
Noyan’s offspring, Äbügän of Kölgän’s off-
spring, the offspring of Ögödäi Qa’an’s son
Kötän, and other princes who were with Qubi-
lai Qa’an. They all conspired [282] to join
Qaidu and rebel against the Qa’an. When the
conspiracy was unmasked, the Qa’an led his
army, seized them, executed some of them, and
disbanded their troops. Now there is no one
left of their ulus. 
Yesügäi Bahadur’s fifth son, Bälgütäi Noyan
The fifth son was Bälgütäi Noyan. He was
born of a different mother and was not includ-
ed among the other brothers. He was always in
Genghis Khan’s service. When Genghis Khan
was hosting a banquet with the Yürkin Qiyat
clan, the chiefs of which were Sacha Beki and
Taichu, a dispute broke out. During the dispute
Bälgütäi Noyan, who was guarding the kiriyäs
[dismounting place], received a sword cut on
the shoulder. This story will be told during
Genghis Khan’s history.1
He had many sons. One of them was Ja’utu,
who was his successor. He was called Ja’utu
because he had a hundred wives and a hundred
sons.2 He grew so old that he couldn’t recog-
nize his wives or sons. When Qubilai Qa’an
sent his son Nomoghan and other princes to do
battle with Qaidu, those princes held council
and decided to attack Nomoghan and take him
captive. Ja’utu was present at that council and
agreed with them. When he returned, there was
a commander, Tachar Noyan, of Elji’idäi Noy-
an’s offspring. He sent a message to the Qa’an,
saying, “Ja’utu has taken such-and-such a step.
Shall I execute him or not?” The Qa’an said, “I
owe him a debt of gratitude. I will not kill
1See text p. 282f.
2I.e., the name Ja’utu is thought to be derived from
jaghun ~ ja’un ‘hundred.’
him.” The debt was that during the battle with
the Qa’an Ja’utu had helped the Qa’an, and for
that reason he did not kill him. He sent him to
the shores of Chin, setting a guard over him.
[283] Ja’utu at that time wore rough Cathaian
boots, and he used to go out and collect kin-
dling himself to cook food. The guards said,
“We will bring it.” He said, “It is appropriate
for me to do it since I initially served well but
in the end I suffered loss and committed a
crime, but he spared my life.” Thus was his
end, and thus did he live.
Qubilai Qa’an had his offspring counted, and
they
numbered
eight
hundred
individuals.
“How is it,” he asked, “that from the offspring
of Jochi Qasar’s sons, who were forty persons,
eight hundred have been born, while from the
sons of Bälgütäi and Ja’utu, who were a
hundred, only eight hundred individuals and no
more have been born?” The reply was given
that Jochi Qasar’s offspring were wealthy and
rich, while Bälgütäi Noyan’s were poor. There-
fore they had multiplied less. At present his
offspring serve the Qa’an
The details of the branch of Yesügäi Baha-
dur’s sons, except for Genghis Khan, are as has
been mentioned. [284]
The battles and encounters Yesügäi
Bahadur fought.
Most of Yesügäi Bahadur’s battles and en-
counters were with the Tatar tribes, who were
the most famous of the Turkic tribes at that
time and had the largest armies. From the time
that
hostilities
broke
out
between
Qabul
Khan’s sons and the Tatar tribes over the death
of Sayin Tegin, Qabul Khan’s wife’s brother,
and their murder of Jorqul, the Tatar shaman
(as has been mentioned in the history of Qabul
Khan3), there was constant strife on both sides
and they fought battles with each other. In the
3See text p. 259f.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER ONE: GENGHIS KHAN’S ANCESTORS
133

end Yesügäi Bahadur defeated them. After that,
Genghis Khan brought the entire tribe, and
many others as well, into servitude and captivi-
ty, as can be seen today that all the Turkic
tribes are servants and soldiers of Genghis
Khan’s offspring. 
Just at the time of Genghis Khan’s blessed
birth, Yesügäi Bahadur was off on a military
expedition against the Tatar. He killed Tämüjin
Ögä and Qori Buqa, the rulers of the Tatars,
and plundered their goods and possessions.
When he returned home, Genghis Khan had
been born. He took this as a good omen and
named him Tämüjin. This will be mentioned in
the history of Genghis Khan, God willing.
[285]
Part Two: Genealogical Chart of Yesügäi
Bahadur and his wife and sons.
As was mentioned in the previous section,
Yesügäi Bahadur had five sons, and they had
large families and many sons. Aside from
Genghis Khan, those who are the most famous
and of the most importance have been written
about. In this section we will give a genealogi-
cal chart of him and his wife and the names of
their sons and grandsons. 
[The section on] the Lord of the World,
Genghis Khan, will follow as a separate histo-
ry. His name was Tämüjin. He was thirteen
years old when his father died, and most of his
relatives and followers abandoned him. For
twenty-eight years he was in distress, but
thereafter his fortune waxed. When he defeated
Ong Khan, the ruler of the Kerayit, he was
named Chingri, meaning magnificent emperor.
[286] After that, when he killed Tayang Khan,
the ruler of the Naiman, and the rule was con-
firmed on him, a nine-legged white banner was
erected and he was named Chinggiz (Genghis)
Khan. The one who so named him was Müng-
lig Echigä’s son Täb Tänggri (whose name was
Kököchü, and whose epithet was Täb Tänggri).

THE HISTORY OF GENGHIS KHAN AND HIS ILLUSTRIOUS OFFSPRING, SOME OF WHOM HAVE BECOME
RULERS IN EVERY ERA, OTHERS OF WHOM HAVE NOT BEEN RULERS OF A SPECIFIC ULUS, ALONG WITH A
SUMMARY ACCOUNT OF THE RULERS OF THE WORLD CONTEMPORARY WITH THEM DOWN TO THE YEAR
705 OF THE HEGIRA [A.D. 1305–6]
THE BEGINNING OF THE STORY OF GENGHIS KHAN
ay it not remain concealed
from those of thought and con-
templation that every destruc-
tion of a country or dispersal
of a people that occurs through
changeability and mutability in the world of
generation and corruption is caused by divine
grace and justice and contains within its folds
great and magnificent godly wisdom. The car-
rying out of God’s fiat in creating infinite be-
ings necessitates that, since with the passage of
eons all things must fall into lassitude, and
with the turning of days and nights nations and
realms must fall into ruin, in every epoch a
great and mighty lord of fortune be singled out
by heavenly assistance and garbed in a raiment
of power in order to do away with that lassi-
tude and degeneration and to endeavor mighti-
ly with his glittering sword to lay anew the
foundation and base, to cleanse the field of
realms, which has become a snare of destruc-
tion, of the defilement of all types and sorts of
evil and self-serving men, and to cause the dust
of sedition and corruption to settle.
The gist of the foregoing is that before his
time, since in all parts of the world different
views had appeared as well as all sorts of ob-
stinate people, and the bonds of orderly world
rule had been damaged by strife and discord,
as necessitated by divine will and eternal wis-
dom, the lord of the world Genghis Khan, the
great warrior in the battle of world conquest,
placed the foot of might in the stirrup of for-
tune and unleashed the hand of domination
over the proud. Like the wind, sparks from the
ﬂame of his glittering lance raised the dust
from the realms of the evil of the day, and
blows from his citadel-cracking mace and his
blood-shedding sword felled all opponents.
Since his personal determination was in con-
formity with destiny, everything to which he
turned his face fell subject to him, and every-
one to whom he motioned became obedient to
his command. Those who resisted forfeited not
only their own lives but also those of their
families. After subjugating many of the realms
of the world in a short time, he had the cus-
toms and laws of the imperial yasaq [or-
dinance] and yosun [custom] arranged and cod-
ified, and he put into practice customs of
spreading justice and nurturing subjects. He
commanded that the bases and foundations of
the realm be reaffirmed by the words of the
leaders of every community and the gates of
beneficence and reward be opened to all class-
es of people.
Inasmuch as during the completion of his
task of world conquest [289] his hosts encoun-

tered Islamic urban areas, divine wisdom or-
dained that, as a balm to that wound, the peo-
ples who had inﬂicted those very wounds
would become Muslim in order that the perfec-
tion of divine power be clear and obvious to all
people in the world. This conversion took
place through the magnificent being of the
Padishah of Islam, Emperor of Mankind, Shad-
ow of God, Supporter of God’s Religion Sultan
Mahmud Ghazan Khan—may God make his
rule eternal—the pearl of the ocean of Genghis
Khan’s offspring and sun of the sky of the im-
perial dynasty for all to see, in the mirror of
whose blessed radiant conscience, which with-
out exaggeration is a goblet that reveals the
world of reality, was reﬂected the reality of
faith through divine guidance, and on the tablet
of whose tranquil breast, which is truly a locus
of the emanation of divine lights, the rule of
the power of Islam took root. He brought all
the Uyghur, Mongol, and fire-worshipping
peoples into the circle of the religion of Islam,
totally overthrew their illicit idol houses and
temples, cleansed the face of the earth of poly-
theists and opponents of religion, propagated
the ordinances of the Muhammadan law, re-
pulsed the darkness of the unjust, and eliminat-
ed the people of hostility and tyranny in such a
way that in no era or time after the epoch of
prophecy has Islam been so adorned or the
people so at peace as in this age. How can
those of us who have attained the felicity of
living in this imperial era and happy time give
thanks for this great gift and mercy? The bur-
geoning of the bazaar of Islam and the end to
misery and anxiety our fathers hoped for and
sought have been given to us, and the gates of
safety and security [290] have been opened to
us through great imperial kindness. “That is
God’s grace. He bestoweth it upon whom He
willeth.” And praise be to God for that! 
May God the exalted keep and preserve the
Padishah of Islam, the monarch who provides
refuge to the world, protector of God’s reli-
gion, Sultan Mahmud Ghazan Khan, forever,
and may he make the days of his reign last for
all time and eternity. May God pray for our
Prophet Muhammad and his noble family!
[291]
