JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

SECTION ONE
ON THE PROGENY OF GENGHIS KHAN, HIS WIVES, SONS, DAUGHTERS, AND SONS-IN-LAW, AND A
GENEALOGICAL CHART OF HIM AND HIS OFFSPRING
Although the history of his forebears back to
Alan Qo’a has been given in a separate section,
his genealogical tree will be given clearly and
in detail in this section for the reader’s quick
reference before going on to other matters. We
will also mention by what names the Mongols
refer to their fathers and forefathers.
Genghis Khan’s descent is as follows: his fa-
ther (in Mongolian, echigä) was Yesügäi Baha-
dur; his grandfather (in Mongolian, äbügä)
was Bartan Bahadur; his great-grandfather
(elänchik) was Qabul Khan; his great-great-
grandfather (bodatu) was Tumina Qa’an; his
ancestor in the fifth degree (bodakür) was Bai
Singqor; [293] his ancestor in the sixth degree
(borqai) was Qaidu Khan; his ancestor in the
seventh degree (dutaqun) was Dutum Mänen;
and his ancestor in the eighth degree was
Bodonchar. There is no term for ancestors
above the seventh degree: they are called echi-
gin-äbügä in the aggregate. The ancestress of
them all was Alan Qo’a. 
(According to one report Alan Qo’a was his
ancestress in the tenth degree because Bodon-
char is said to have had two sons, Buqa and
Nachin, and Buqa’s son was Dutum Mänen.
Inasmuch as this differs from the preceding re-
port it has been given here as a variant lest
anything be omitted.) 
It has been established through ancient tales
and legends that Genghis Khan was the quin-
tessence of all the Niru’un tribes descended
from Alan Qo’a. After his emergence the peo-
ple of the world witnessed how he had been
singled out for divine assistance to subjugate
with his mighty power and strength and en-
slave all the tribes of the Turks and Mongols
and others as well. Like one matchless pearl in
the midst of others, he rose to a superior posi-
tion from among all those tribes by virtue of
the nobility of his person and refinement of his
characteristics. He brought the realms of all
climes of the world under his control and rule,
and his glorious sons and renowned offspring
became possessors of crowns and thrones in all
directions throughout the seven climes. In the
end, the religion of Islam, through the strength-
ening of the lord of the world, succorer of
God’s
religion,
Sultan
Mahmud
Ghazan
Khan—may God extend his reign forever—
[294] who was the ultimate reason for the exis-
tence of all those tribes and clans, became so
firm and strong that all, from far and near, Turk
and Tajik, bear witness to the wish that, God
willing, the fortune of this imperial era in-
crease daily forever.
Inasmuch as stories concerning Genghis
Khan will be given in detail in their proper
places in the second section of the history,
here, as an introduction, a short summary will
be given in order that the reader be aware in a
general way, and in order that Genghis Khan’s
wives and the branches of his sons that will
come be more understandable. We say, there-
fore—and
success
is
through
God—that
Genghis Khan was orphaned of his father in
childhood at the age of thirteen. When the
many tribes that had previously gathered obe-
diently around his father, Yesügäi Bahadur,
saw Genghis Khan as a mere child, they aban-
doned him. Since his mother, Ö’älün Ekä, was
extremely competent and intelligent, she pre-
served and protected him and the followers and
soldiers left by Yesügäi Bahadur. Many times
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION ONE: GENGHIS KHAN
137

Genghis Khan experienced setbacks, and sev-
eral times the Tayichi’ut clans seized the op-
portunity to take him prisoner, but God deliv-
ered him from the brink of death. Inasmuch as
it had been God’s will from all eternity that he
become ruler of the world, he gradually grew
in strength until, by virtue of painful labors and
having forbearance in the face of great obsta-
cles, he was able to bear difficult tasks with pa-
tience so that when he attained rule and ease he
was able to appreciate such a great good thing
and be grateful, and also so that when he
reached lofty heights he was capable of keep-
ing every person in the world in his proper
place. [295]
Despite his setbacks and the multiplicity of
difficulties, he was magnificently brave and
courageous as well as extremely intelligent,
skilled, farsighted, and cultured. His name and
reputation
for
generosity
and
beneficence
spread in all directions, affection for him ap-
peared in all natures, and nations inclined to
him so that he grew strong and mighty and ren-
dered his friends victorious and prosperous and
his enemies vanquished and despised. He often
quarreled with and suffered various torments
from his and his father’s relatives and cousins
because they were envious of him, particularly
the tribes of the Tayichi’ut, who were neigh-
bors and whose yurts were nearby. It was more
important to deal militarily with them than
with those who were unrelated and separated
by greater distances. Finally he conquered that
nation and brought those who remained under
the yoke of subjugation, as will be described.
After that, a tribe of his relatives united with
Ong Khan, the ruler of the Kerayit with whom
Genghis Khan had a long-standing friendship
and father-son relationship, and planned to as-
sassinate him. Since their dwelling place and
yurts were near and contiguous with his, it was
necessary to launch a campaign against them.
Many battles were fought until Genghis Khan
finally conquered and annihilated them.
After that, he campaigned against Mongol
tribes that lived in the vicinity of his yurts,
most of whom were inimical and envious.
[296] Genghis Khan having done battle with
them before, enmity and rivalry existed, and
rancor was fixed in their breasts. The environs
of the territory near Genghis Khan had been
cleared of opposition as far as the borders of
the Naiman, and some of Genghis Khan’s ene-
mies, both his relatives and Mongol tribes, had
gone to [the Naiman], where they initiated ag-
gression against him. For these reasons it be-
came necessary to wage war with them until
they were vanquished and subjugated. After
that, the emperor of Cathay, the Altan Khan, an
extremely great ruler to whom most of the
Mongol and Turkish tribes submitted because
they were in the vicinity of the territory of
Cathay, expected that Genghis Khan too would
submit in the same way. As has been said in
the preceding section, the emperors of Cathay
had killed several of Genghis Khan’s ances-
tors, for which reason enmity and hostility ex-
isted between them. When God gave Genghis
Khan strength and power, and many soldiers
gathered around him, he considered it neces-
sary to take revenge for the ancient wrong. He
set out with a large army against the Altan
Khan, subjugated most of the realm of Cathay,
and vanquished their rulers and those who op-
posed him, and those who survived became
obedient and submissive by the sword. After
that, he stationed his army in that area for five
years and withdrew of his own volition.
After that, he conquered the realm of Tibet
and Tangqut, which was in his territory. [297]
It was in his mind to go against Cathay to con-
quer that realm once and for all and also to
subdue the province of Qarajang, which is next
to Cathay and near Mongolia. The Hindus and
138
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

people of Qarajang call it Kandar, and the
Tajiks call it Qandahar.1 He therefore deter-
mined to wage a campaign, but Güshlüg
Khan,2 the son of the Naiman ruler, had ﬂed to
Turkistan when his father was killed, and he
and some Mongol tribes that were hostile to
Genghis Khan had taken over the province of
Turkistan, which was held by the Gür Khan of
the Qarakhitai. When the Gür Khan died and a
report of the situation reached Genghis Khan,
he cancelled his plans to go to Cathay and that
region and undertook to deal with Güshlüg’s
sedition. He dispatched Jäbä with the army and
vanquished
him
too.
Güshlüg
had
taken
Turkistan, a realm of great length and breadth,
from the Gür Khan upon the advice of Sultan
Khwarazmshah, and Güshlüg took over part of
it and the Khwarazmshah took over the other
part. When Genghis Khan’s army removed
Güshlüg, Sultan Khwarazmshah seized all of
the realm of Turkistan along with Otrar, the
frontier. Not only was this an affront to
Genghis Khan’s dignity, but also a group of
Muslim merchants Genghis Khan had sent to
the sultan as a show of unity and friendship
were capriciously killed in Otrar by the sul-
tan’s uncle Inalchuq, who was called Ghayir
Khan. Genghis Khan was so overcome by fury
and rage that he forgot about Cathay, Chin, and
Qarajang and set out immediately for Turkistan
and Iran. Together with his sons and with the
help of his officers he subjugated both realms.
[298]
1Qarajang/Kandar/Qandahar, Marco Polo’s Carajan, is
Yunnan in southwestern China.
2Güshlüg Khan’s name, usually so spelled in the
Jami‘u’t-tawarikh, appears variously as Güchülüg in the

er Persian sources. The name comes from the Turkic
güchlüg ‘powerful’ (cf. modern Turkish güçlü). We will
write Güshlüg, as in the Persian.
After [Genghis Khan’s death], Ögödäi Qa’an,
together with his brother Tolui, took the entire
realm of Cathay. With their nephews they took
the realm of Kiral-Bashghurd,3 Bular, the
Qipchaq Steppe, Rus, Circassia, and As to the
farthest reaches of the north, and to the south
as far as Abyssinia. They likewise took the
realm of Solanggha [Korea].
During Mänggü Qa’an’s reign his brother
Qubilai Qa’an took what remained of Cathay,
and in one fell swoop their brother Hülägü
Khan took Baghdad, the territory and fortress-
es of the Heretics (Ismailis), Syria, and the
realm of the land of Iran all the way to the far-
thest reaches of Anatolia.
While Qubilai Qa’an was emperor, he took
Chin, Qarajang, and part of Hindustan. 
So too it continues until now: year by year,
and day by day, Genghis Khan’s progeny and
offspring are still conquering territories in their
vicinities, and such magnificent things have
been and continue to be done through the for-
tune of Genghis Khan and his family. Each and
every one of these things will be reported in
detail in the proper place. This has been just a
summary account as an introduction. Now we
will begin with the details of Genghis Khan’s
wives and a mention of how many children he
had by each wife. [299]
Genghis Khan’s Wives and Sons
Genghis Khan had nearly five hundred wives
and concubines, and each was taken from a
different tribe. Some he requested after the
Mongolian fashion of marriage, but most he
took as booty when he conquered a territory or
tribe. However, those who were great ladies
and attained great prominence were five, as
follows.

ans. See note to text p. 40 above.

The First Wife, Börtä Füjin, daughter of Däi
Noyan, chief and ruler of the Qunqirat
nation
She was the most important and grandest of
all the wives, and she was the mother of the
four elder sons who were of importance and of
five daughters.
The eldest son was Jochi,1 from whom are
descended all the rulers and princes in the
Qipchaq
Steppe.
It
is
related
that
when
Genghis Khan fought the Märkit nation and
they were victorious, Börtä Füjin was pregnant
with Jochi. The Märkits carried her off as
booty, and since at that time there was peace
between the Märkit and Ong Khan, they sent
her to Ong Khan, who held her in honor and
respect. Because of the old friendship he had
with Genghis Khan’s father and because he
called Genghis Khan “son,” he kept her like a
daughter-in-law. [300]
“Why don’t you take her for yourself?” the
officers asked. 
“She is my daughter-in-law,” he replied. “It
would be unchivalrous to look upon her with a
view to treachery.” 
When Genghis Khan was informed of this,
he sent Säbä, the grandfather of Sartaq Noyan
of the Jalayir tribe, to Ong Khan to request the
return of the lady. Ong Khan complied and
turned her over to him. Jochi was born while
they were on the road back to Genghis Khan,

The second son was Chaghatai,2 to whom

Details of the branch of his sons will come in

The third son was Ögödäi Qa’an,5 who be-

Their stories will be related in the proper

Noyan.6
Genghis Khan called him nökär, and most of

him on his campaigns. In the Mongolian lan-
guage tolui means mirror.1 From the time he
died until now this word for mirror has been
taboo. The word for mirror in Turkish is küzgü,
[301] and now the Mongols also call a mirror

Temür Qa’an and the Padishah of Islam Ghaz-

es of his progeny have become qa’ans and
padishahs in every clime, and the story of each
will come separately.
These four sons of Genghis Khan were all in-
telligent, competent, courageous, and valiant,
and they were loved by their father, the army,
and the subjects. They were like four pillars to
Genghis Khan’s realm, and he envisioned each
of them as a ruler and called them the “four
külügs”2—külüg being a word applied to a man
or horse that is superior to or faster than others.
Aside from those [sections] we will write for
each, there are many stories connected to these
four sons that will come in the course of the
narrative about Genghis Khan. From these will
be learned the commanders and armies that
were formed and given to each son. There also

The word külüg (KiloEt, хөлөг) is still used in modern
Mongolian for a strong, swift horse.
The names of the five daughters by this lady,
and the names of those to whom they were giv-
en in marriage are as follows.
The eldest daughter was Füjin Beki. She was
first requested for Sangun’s son and Ong
Khan’s grandson Tusaqa, but the union did not
take place, and that occasioned displeasure. Af-

The second daughter was Chächäyigän.4 She

The third daughter was Alaqai Beki. She was
given to Chigüi,5 son of the ruler of the
Öng’üt.6 [302]
The fourth daughter was Tümälün. She was
given to the son of the ruler of the Qunqirat
whose name was Gürägän. Although gürägän
means son-in-law, his name was actually
Gürägän.
The fifth daughter was Altalun, also called

Khan] called him Cha’ur Sächän. Taichu
Gürägän was Genghis Khan’s mother’s broth-
er, and Genghis Khan loved this one more than

There are many stories about these five
daughters and their husbands. Since the lineage

This has been a brief mention of the children
born of the chief wife, Börtä Füjin.1
The Second Wife, Qulan Khatun
She was the daughter of Dayir Usun, chief of
the Uhaz clan of the Märkit, who submitted
and, as ordered, brought his daughter to
Genghis Khan. By her he had a son named
Kölgän, but he did not attain the status of the
four sons already mentioned.
The history of Kölgän and the line of his
sons is as follows. He had four sons. The eldest
was named Qucha. When his father died he
was given six thousand men and awarded his
father’s position. Qucha had a son named
Uru’udai. He too inherited his father’s position
and army and became a retainer of Qubilai
Qa’an’s. [303] He had a son named Äbügän,
and he inherited his father’s place and army;
however, when Taghachar Noyan’s offspring,
Naya’a and other princes, rebelled against
Qubilai Qa’an and decided to join Qaidu, when
Qubilai found out about it he had him and the
others executed.
The Third Wife, Yesügän2
She was of the Tatar nation. By her Genghis
Khan had a son named Cha’ur, who died in
infancy.
1The Secret History (§238) says that there was a
daughter called Al Altun, who was given to the “idu’ud
of the Ui’ud,” i.e. the Idiqut of the Uyghur. 
2In the Secret History §155f. she is named Yesügen
Qadun, daughter of Yeke Cheren of the Tatar.
The Fourth Wife, Gungju Khatun3
She was the daughter of the Altan Khan, the
emperor of Cathay. It is well known that she
was not beautiful, but because her father was
an extremely great emperor she was given
great importance and respect. Genghis Khan
had no children by her. She lived until Ariq
Bökä’s time and died thereafter. In this lady’s
ordu was an Örmüg girl who was a ba’urchi
(cook), Huqutai by name, and she acquired
great inﬂuence and renown.
The Fifth Wife, Yesülün4
She was a sister to the above-mentioned
Yesügän and was also of the Tatar nation.

SECTION TWO
THE HISTORY OF GENGHIS KHAN FROM HIS BIRTH UNTIL THE TIME HE BECAME KHAN AND RULER, AN IL-
LUSTRATION OF HIS THRONE, WIVES, PRINCES, AND OFFICERS DURING HIS ENTHRONEMENT AS KHAN,
THE LINEAGE OF THE OFFICERS, MENTION OF THE BATTLES HE FOUGHT AT EVERY TIME AND THE VICTO-
RIES HE ACHIEVED, THE LENGTH OF HIS RULE UNTIL THE END OF HIS TIME, AND A MENTION OF HIS
DEATH
Since this book is organized so that we record
first the lineage of the offspring of every tribe
and ruler, and then we begin with the history
itself, the number of Genghis Khan’s wives
and details of his sons and daughters have al-
ready been mentioned in the first section of
this chapter. Now, beginning with stories of
Genghis Khan from the time of his birth, a
summary account of several years will be giv-
en because for the first part of his career stories
about him are not known in detail year by year.
Thereafter, according to what has come in the
records and histories of the Mongols, stories
will be given in detail year by year. Although
compilers and writers of ancient histories have
produced books of every sort, [since] they have
reproduced stories of various times without or-
der, readers have been unable to make full use
of them. In the year-by-year history that the
late Ibn al-Athir produced,1 although he put
much effort into it, the stories of each [307]
1The reference is to Izzuddin Ibn al-Athir (1160–
1233), author of al-Kāmil ﬁ’t-tārīkh, a universal history
to A.H. 628 (A.D. 1230–31). As Rashiduddin observes,
Ibn al-Athir arranged his material by events as they hap-
pened year by year; there is therefore no continuity to
the narrative. Almost all the periodic summaries of
dynasties and rulers of the Islamic world in the Jami‘u’t-
tawarikh appear to have been extracted from Ibn al-
Athir.
ruler are not ordered, and although they follow
more or less in sequence, the order is not
known. This much is certainly apparent to
those who read the book. Therefore, it seemed
appropriate to the author of this book to record
in sequence, for every few years of Genghis
Khan’s history that is written, the histories of
other rulers of various parts who were contem-
porary with him so that the affairs of rulers
contemporary with each other might thereby be
known in general.
Since the ultimate goal of composing this
book and gathering these stories together is to
compile the blessed history of Ghazan Khan,
and this principle of organization was not
adopted in previous histories of long ago, and
also since it would be too long, according to
the above-mentioned principle, from Genghis
Khan’s birth until the end of his life, and after
him until the present time, every few years
deemed appropriate the history of Genghis
Khan and his sons and things that became
customary during their times will be written
about, and the history of other rulers at that
time, as much as is known and verifiable and
fits the context, will be appended thereto,
down to this regal era and blessed time so that
the reader may learn about the conditions of
all. The principle of organization is then as has
been stated. [308]
The History of Genghis Khan from the time of his birth, from the beginning of Qaqai Yil,
the Year of the Pig, which corresponds to the year 549 of the Hegira and began in the
month of Dhu’l-Qa‘da [January 1155], until the next Qaqai Yil, also the Year of the Pig,

which corresponds to the year 562 of the Hegira and began in the month of Rabi‘ II
[February 1167]. During this period his father, Yesügäi Bahadur, was alive. During the last
year, the thirteenth, Yesügäi Bahadur died, and the thirteen-year-old Genghis Khan was
bereft of him.
Since in Genghis Khan’s and his father’s
time astrologers did not record times by astro-
nomical observation and historians did not
record the day or month, the hour and day of
his birth are not known with exactitude. How-
ever, it is very well known to many Mongolian
princes, commanders, and grandees that he
lived for seventy-two years and died in his sev-
enty-third year. Reliable astronomers have
recorded the date of his death since he was so
extremely great and such a perfect ruler. They
have reported that he died in Qaqai Yil, the
Year of the Pig, in the middle autumn month
fifteen days from the end of the month. Since
that was the seventy-third year from his birth,
his birth must then have occurred in the middle
of the year, [310] reckoning the length of his
life as seventy-two whole years.
Since he spent his life until the age of forty-
one partially in childhood and partially in de-
privation, and historians did not record it year
by year, the history of these forty-one years
will be written as a whole. Thereafter until the
end of his life has been detailed year by year,
and we too will follow that system.
Having thus established the principle of
organization, let us record the thirteen-year
history of Genghis Khan from his birth to the
death of his father.
While his father, Yesügäi Bahadur, was at the
zenith of might and fortune and ruled and led
all the tribes that were attached to his fathers
and uncles, they made him their leader and
chief and followed him obediently. Others
tribes, like the Tatar and others, as has already
been said in the section on the Tatar, were in-
imical to him, and many battles were fought
between them. In the above-mentioned Qaqai
Yil, when Yesügäi Bahadur mounted to do bat-
tle with the Tatar, his wife, Ö’älün Ekä, was
pregnant with Genghis Khan. The rulers of the
Tatar were Tämüjin Ögä and Qori Buqa.
Yesügäi Bahadur did battle with them and,
having defeated and crushed them, he returned
triumphant and victorious. He also plundered
their families, ﬂocks, and herds and camped in
a placed called Deli’ün Boldaq. There, after
some time, during the above-mentioned Qaqai
Yil, under a favorable ascendant Genghis Khan
was born, holding a blood clot the size of a
knuckle bone [311] like a piece of congealed
liver. The signs of world domination were ob-
vious upon his brow, and the luminescence of
luck and success shone from his countenance.
Since Yesügäi Bahadur’s victory over his ene-
my, the Tatar and their ruler, Tämüjin Ögä, had
recently occurred, he took it as a good omen
and named his son Tämüjin after the Tatar
king.
During his lifetime Yesügäi Bahadur was the
chief and leader of the Niru’un and of his aqa-
ini, but enmity existed between him and the
rulers and commanders of other tribes, particu-
larly the Tatar tribes. Now, because they have
mingled with the Mongols and resemble them
in form and epithet, they are all called Mongol,
but in ancient times each had its own name and
epithet, and they were not classified as Mon-
gol. Yesügäi Bahadur did battle with most of
those tribes and brought some of them under
his sway. Most of them, both friends and ene-
mies, were obedient to him out of fear of his
power and dominion and in order to preserve
their lives, and his condition was highly regu-
146
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

lated and splendid. Aside from Genghis Khan
he had several other sons, as was stated in his
history. During this period of thirteen years he
was firmly entrenched as ruler of his tribes,
and every few months he would mount for a
campaign to repel his enemies among the Tur-
kic tribes that surrounded his ulus. In most bat-
tles victory was his, but certain of his relatives
were jealous of him, as the proverb says, al-
aqārib ka’l-‘aqārib [relatives are like scor-
pions]. Because of the rancor and enmity they
harbored in their breasts, and since they had no
strength or power to resist, they planted the
seed of revenge and enmity inwardly until the
end of his life. When Yesügäi Bahadur died as
a young man, [312] the Tayichi’ut tribes—who
were collateral relatives of Genghis Khan’s on
his father’s side, as was stated in the section on
his ancestors—were stronger and had larger
fighting contingents, and their leaders were
rulers of consequence. Although they had been
friendly and obedient during Yesügäi Baha-
dur’s time, after he died they manifested their
enmity and hostility.
Genghis Khan was thirteen when his father
died, and his brothers were also children. His
mother, Ö’älün Ekä of the Olqunu’ut tribe, was
highly intelligent and competent, but because
of Yesügäi Bahadur’s death they fell on hard
times. The details of that period are not known.
Inasmuch as the history of Genghis Khan has
been written in summary from his birth, which
occurred in Qaqai Yil, which corresponds to
the year 549 and began in the month of Dhu’l-
Qa‘da [January 1155], until he was thirteen
years old, let us now write the history of the
sultans and other rulers of climes who were
contemporaries of Genghis Khan during those
thirteen years. After that, we will return to
Genghis Khan’s history after those thirteen
years. [313]
The history that is known of Genghis Khan’s contemporaries, the monarchs and khaqans
of Cathay, Chin, the Kerayit, the Naiman, the Mongols, the Uyghur, Turkistan, Kiral-
Bashghurd, Qipchaq, Orus, Circassia, As, Transoxiana, and the caliphs and sultans of Iran,
Anatolia, Syria, Egypt, &c. who ruled from the beginning of the Qaqai Yil that began in
Dhu’l-Qa‘da of 549 of the Hegira [January 1155] through the next Qaqai Yil, which began
in Rabi‘ ii 562 of the Hegira [February 1167], a period of thirteen whole years, as well as
unusual events that happened during that period.
A history of the rulers of the Khitai and
Qarakhitai during this period
Those who ruled that territory during this pe-
riod were not of the lineage of the ancient
monarchs of that realm. In the 280’s of the He-
gira [A.D. 893–902] the ruler of the Khitai, the
Qarakhitai, the Jurchids, Manzi (which is also
called Chin), Machin, and Nankiyas, was a
person of the ancient lineage of kings named
Liang Tai Zu.1 During his reign a nomadic
commander named Chuolizhi Abaozhi rebelled
and seized part of the kingdom of the Khitai,
Qarakhitai, and Jurcha.2

Nine generations after that, the ruler of the
Jurcha rebelled, [314] took that realm from the
<Qara>khitai,1 and overthrew them in the
510’s [1116–25].2 In the year 522 [1128] the
ruler of the Jurcha seized dominion over all the
kingdom of Cathay. Gao Zong,3 the rightful
ruler of Cathay, took refuge from him in
Machin, with which he and his sons contented
themselves and where they remained until the
end of their time.
The ruler who took over the realm of the
<Qara>khitai and the Jurcha called himself Dai
Liao,4 meaning monarch of the world. When
Genghis Khan seized realms, the people of
Cathay named him by this term Dai Wan,5
meaning great ruler, because his command en-
compassed the world.

history of Ghazan Khan the history of the

The history of the rulers of Turkistan and
Transoxiana during this period.
When the ruler of the Jurchids rebelled
against the ruler of the <Qara>khitai and, as
previously explained, annihilated him, a high-
ranking officer [316] of the Qarakhitai named
Tushi Taifu fled from there and emerged in
Qirqiz and Uyghur territory and Turkistan.2 He
was an intelligent and extremely competent
man who with good strategy gathered around
himself a group from that region and seized the
entire area of Turkistan. His epithet became
Gür Khan, which means exalted monarch. This
took place in 522 and 523 [1128–29]. When
this Gür Khan died, he left an eight- or nine-
year-old son who was installed in his father’s
place, and he too was called Gür Khan. He
lived a long time, ninety-two Turkish years, or
ninety-five lunar years. He died around the
year 610 [1213].3 In the year in which Genghis
Khan was born this Gür Khan was thirty-four
years old and had reigned for nearly twenty-

who were Genghis Khan’s contemporaries

At the time of Genghis Khan’s birth Muqtafi
of the Abbasid House was caliph in Baghdad.
He was alive until 556 [1161], in which year
he died and his son Mustanjid was installed as
caliph.4
In the year Genghis Khan was born the
caliph of the Ismailis in Egypt was Zafir.5 He
was killed in Muharram of that year, and his
son Fayiz was installed as caliph. He died in
the year of Muqtafi’s death, 556,6 and his
cousin, Adid, was installed as caliph.7
In Khurasan, the Seljuqid Sultan Sanjar b.
Malikshah was ruling.8 Two years prior to
Genghis Khan’s birth the Oghuz tribes took
him to a hunting preserve and imprisoned him
there. [318] In Ramadan of the year of Genghis
Khan’s birth he escaped and ﬂed to Termez.9
Ali Beg, the chief of the Qarluq clans, a mortal
enemy of the sultan’s, died, and the Qarluqs
pledged obedience to the sultan. Thereafter he
was afﬂicted with colic and dysentery and died

in Rabi‘ I 552 [April 1157].1 The Oghuz moved

In Persia, the Seljuqid Sultan Muhammad b.

Around that time he gathered an army and laid

As he lay dying, he ordered his commanders

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1155–116
151

The history of unusual events that occurred
during this period in all parts of the world
In the year 553,1 the city of Baghdad was so
inundated that most city quarters were de-
stroyed, like Qarah Zafar, Mukhtara, Muq-
tadiyya, Darb al-Qabbar, Rayan, Khirbat Ibn
Jurada, Qarah al-Qadi, part of Qati‘a, part of
Bab al-Azaj, some of Ma’muniyya, Qarah
Abu-Shahm, Qarah Ibn Zarin, part of Za-
fariyya, and the ramparts. On the southern side
Imam Ahmad Ibn Hanbal’s grave and others
were so ﬂooded that dead bodies ﬂoated on the
water.2
1According to Ibn al-Athir (Kamil 11:248, the inunda-
tion took place on 8 Rabi‘ II 554 (April 29, 1159), not
553. See account in next note.
2Ibn al-Athir’s account is as follows (Kamil 11:248):
“In this year [554], on the eighth of Rabi‘ II [April 29,
1159], the Tigris began to ﬂood, and al-Qawraj upstream
from Baghdad was inundated. Then the crest approached
Baghdad, and the fields and the city trench were filled.
The water damaged the walls and breached them on Sat-
urday the nineteenth of the month [May 10]. Some of
the walls collapsed and dammed the water. Then the wa-
ter created another breach, but it was neglected in hopes
that it would recede without the walls collapsing; how-
ever, the water was overwhelming, and it was impossi-
ble to stop it. Qarah Zafar, al-Ajama, al-Mukhtara, al-
Muqtadiyya, Darb al-Qabbar, Kharabat Ibn Jurada, al-
Rayyan, Qarah al-Qadi, some of al-Qati‘a, some of Bab
al-Azaj, some of al-Ma’muniyya, Qarah Abi al-Shahm,
some of Qarah Ibn Zarin, and some of al-Zafariyya were
inundated.
The water seeped underground into some buildings,
and they collapsed. As people began to cross over to the
western side, the price for crossing escalated to many di-
nars, which was more than most people could pay. Then
the waters began to subside, bringing down the walls.
The water that was inside the walls remained, seeping
into the quarters that had not been ﬂooded. Much de-
struction was wrought, and quarters could not be recog-
nized except by mounds of rubble. People had to esti-
mate the boundaries of their property.
In Sha‘ban 557 [July–August 1162] thirty
thousand Georgians came to the city of Dwin,3
a dependency of Azerbaijan, and killed more
than ten thousand persons. They also took
many captives and burned the city mosque.
When Atabeg Shamsuddin Eldigüz of Tabriz
heard about it, he assembled a large army and
set out to wreak vengeance on them with the
help of Shah-i-Arz, Sökmän Qutbi’s son the
governor of Akhlat, Aq Sonqur’s son the gov-
ernor of Maragha, and more than fifty thou-
sand horsemen. They arrived in Georgia in Sa-
far 558 [January 1163] and did battle for an
entire month. In the end, the army of Islam was
victorious, killing many and taking much plun-
der.4 
Also in Safar of that year sectarian violence
broke out among the cadis of Isfahan. The
fighting lasted seven days, and people were
killed and houses were destroyed on both
sides. [323] The Heretics besieged Qazwin.
Now that the history of rulers contemporary
with Genghis Khan from the Qaqai Yil that be-
gan in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 549 [January 1155] to the
next Qaqai Yil, which began in Rabi‘ II 562
[February 1167], a period of thirteen years, and
the unusual events that happened during this
period have been written, we will next begin
the history of Genghis Khan after this thirteen-
year period and proceed according to the same
principle. [324–25] 
On the western side, the cemetery of Ahmad Ibn Han-
bal and other cemeteries were inundated, the mausolea
sank, and dead bodies rose to the surface of the water. It
also happened in al-Mashhad and al-Harbiyya. It was a
dreadful thing.”
3Dwin was the old capital of Armenia. Its ruins are lo-
cated about twenty kilometers south-southeast of mod-
ern Erevan.
4Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 11:286f.
152
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The history of Genghis Khan after the age of thirteen, when he was orphaned of his father,
from the beginning of Quluqana Yil, the Year of the Rat that began in Rabi‘ I 563
[December 1167], until Bars Yil, the Year of the Tiger that began in Safar 590 [January–
February 1194], a period of twenty-seven years. In the last year Genghis Khan was forty
years old.
Since his condition during this period is not
known year by year, it will be written general-
ly. During this time he fought battles with the
Tayichi’ut clans, and several times they took
him captive and held him in chains. However,
with God’s help, he escaped in destitution. Fi-
nally, after these twenty-eight years, God gave
him strength and assistance, and things picked
up for him. When Genghis Khan lost his father
in childhood, the Tayichi’ut clans, the leaders
of which were relatives and envious, revealed
the old hatred they had kept hidden during his
father’s
lifetime.
Targhutai
Qiriltuq,
Adal
Khan’s son and Qabul Khan’s grandson, and
his cousin Quril Bahadur, both of whom were
kings and rulers of Tayichi’ut clans, began to
disobey and act arrogantly out of the envy they
had harbored during Yesügäi Bahadur’s time.
[326] Because the Tayichi’ut were the greatest
of the branches, gradually it came about that
the other relatives and soldiers who followed
Yesügäi Bahadur turned away from his sons
and joined the Tayichi’ut so that they became
mighty and strong. Some of them became
known as the hoi-yin irgän, or people of the
forest, because their yurt was in the forest.
At that time Yesügäi Bahadur’s and his sons’
yurt was in the Onon and Kerulen vicinity.
When most of Yesügäi Bahadur’s followers de-
camped and joined the Tayichi’ut, Tödö’än
Qahurchi, the aqa of all, also began to decamp.
Genghis Khan, who was then called Tämüjin,
went to him himself and humbly asked him not
to go. Refusing to listen and quoting a proverb
in Mongolian that means “I have made my de-
cision to go, I am no longer free to act, and it is
impossible to remain,” he mounted and rode
away. Genghis Khan’s mother, Ö’älün Ekä, got
herself to horse, raised her tugh (insignia), had
her soldiers mount, and went in pursuit of
those who had ﬂed in order to turn them back.
When they clashed, ranks were drawn and they
did battle. In the end she managed to make
some of her clans and ulus return. During the
battle Charaqa Äbügän, who was an old man
and one of the great amirs, was hit in the back
by an arrow. When he returned from the battle
Genghis Khan went to inquire after him.
Charaqa said, “After your late father’s death
the clans and soldiers turned away from you in
rebellion. I wanted to prevent them from doing
it, but heavenly fate was lying in ambush for
me and wounded me without warning.” [327]
When Genghis Khan perceived that his wound
was serious and he wouldn’t recover, he wept.
No sooner had he come away than Charaqa
died. (The amirs El Temür, Bürküt, and Etälgü
in Hülägü Khan’s and Abaqa Khan’s time were
descended from him.) 
The beginning of Jamuqa Sächän’s
rebellion; he joins the Tayichi’ut; the
Tayichi’ut, the Ikiräs, and others plan to
attack; [Genghis Khan] learns of their plan
and organizes thirteen gürä’äns of soldiers
and defeats his enemy.
Also during that time, Jamuqa Sächän, who
was from a branch of the Niru’un and the chief
and commander of the Jäjirät clan, had a rela-
tive named Taichar. He and a few horsemen
went to a place called Ölägäi Bulaq in the
vicinity of Sa’ari Kähär, Genghis Khan’s yurt,
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1167–1194
153

to steal animals from the house of Jochi Tar-
mala of the Jalayir tribe because some Jalayirs
had killed Dutum Mänen’s wife Monolun and
her sons and taken Genghis Khan’s ancestors
prisoner. (From [Jochi Tarmala] are descended
many amirs in that area, like Elgäi Noyan.)
Getting wind of this, Jochi Tarmala sent his
household away and hid himself among the
horses and herds. When Taichar arrived, Jochi
Tarmala shot him with an arrow and killed
him. For this reason Jamuqa Sächän laid the
foundation of hostility toward Genghis Khan,
began to stir up sedition, and joined the
Tayichi’ut clans with his own clan and sol-
diers. Aside from him, other tribes and clans
also joined the Tayichi’ut, among them one
from the Ikiräs, which is a branch [328] of the
Qunqirat, and one from the Qorolas clan, who
are Dürlükin Mongols. There were also the
Uru’ut clan and the Noyaqin, who are Niru’un.
Agreeing to help one another, this group set
out to attack Genghis Khan. For a long time
they fought with him. Genghis Khan was un-
able to overcome them, and finally things got
so bad that all his followers left him. Once
Genghis
Khan
fell
captive
to
them,
and
Sorghan Shira of the Suldus tribe rescued him,
as has been mentioned.1
Over a period of several years all sorts of
things happened until once again God came to
Genghis Khan’s aid and made him strong.
Once
his
tribes
were
reassembled,
the
Tayichi’ut and others who had conspired with
them finally set out with thirty thousand horse-
men to attack Genghis Khan while he was un-
aware of their treachery and deceit. Fortunately
someone from the Ikiräs, Näkün by name, who
was with the Tayichi’ut, was sympathetic to
Genghis Khan because his son Butu was
Genghis Khan’s attendant. The tribes were in a
1See text pp. 174ff. above.
place called Güräl’ü (which later became one
of Genghis Khan’s yurts). To expose the
treachery and deception, Näkün sent Genghis
Khan a message with two men from the Baru-
las clan, Mütka and Totaq, who had gone there
on a mission and were on their way back.
Genghis Khan was in Dalan Balji’us. These
two came in secret via a road between two hills
called A’ula’ut [and] Turqa’ut2 and warned
Genghis Khan of the setting forth of the ene-
my. [329] Thus forewarned, Genghis Khan im-
mediately arrayed his soldiers and informed
the tribes and clans that were friendly to and
supportive of him. When they assembled, they
were assigned to units of ten thousands, thou-
sands, hundreds, and tens—thirteen gürä’äns
in all. (A gürä’än means a ring, and in olden
times when a tribe encamped in a place in a
circle with the chief in the middle, they called
it a gürä’än. It is also used when an enemy ap-
proaches and they camp in this fashion so that
strangers and enemies cannot get in.) The dis-
positions of the thirteen gürä’äns are as
follows:
(1) Genghis Khan’s mother, Ö’älün Ekä, and
her clans and followers, relatives, ev-oghlans
of the ordu, servants, and persons who were at-
tached to her.
(2) Genghis Khan and his sons, liege men,
and persons like amirs, amirs’ sons, and guards
who were attached to him.
(3) Boltachu Noyan, a descendant of Qabul
Khan’s elder brother Säm Qachi’un; [some] of
the ___ clan, which is a branch of the Kerayit,
along with the Hadargin tribe, the leader of
which was Moqur Qauran of the Niru’un (the
Büküräi who was in Khurasan was descended
from him); and the Qorolas clan of the Dür-
lükin, whose chief was Cha’urqa.
2A’ula’ut and Turqa’ut are the Secret History (§129)’s
Mounts Ala’u’ud and Turgha’ud.
154
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

(4) The sons of Sorqadu Yürki and his broth-
er Qoridai (they are of the Niru’un and Qiyat
clan), along with the Buda’at clan, who are
also Niru’un. 
(5 and 6) The sons of Sorqoqtu Yürki and
Sacha Beki and his cousins Taichu and the
Jalayir clans. (Sorqoqtu means having a birth-
mark on the body.) The Yürkin Qiyat are de-
scended from him, and Amir Nurin is of his
urugh.1
(7) Utuchu’s sons , Qudu and Ardangi2 of the
Qiyat and Gäräidäi clans. They had several
other brothers, but [330] they took the place of
those who were attached to them. [?]
(8) Mönggädü Qiyan’s sons, Chingshi’ut and
his
brothers,
who
were
Genghis
Khan’s
cousins; and the Baya’ut clan of the Dürlükin,
whose chief was Önggür.
(9) Genghis Khan’s uncle Daritai Otchigin;
and his cousin Quchar, the son of Näkün
Taishi; Dalu, a relative of theirs; the Doqolat
clan of the Niru’un; and the Nüküz, Quriqan,
Saqayit Onjin clans of the Dürlükin.
(10) Genghis Khan’s cousin Jochi Khan, son
of Qutila Khan, and his followers.
(11) Altan, who was also a son of Qutula
Khan.
(12) Daqai Bahadur of the Qinqiyat, who are
Niru’un, and the Sügän, also Niru’un.
(13) Kündü China and Ölögchin China, sons
of Charaqa Lingqum. They are called Nüküz,
but they are not the original Nüküz because
they are Niru’un, as detailed in the section on
the Tayichi’ut.
These thirteen gürä’äns of soldiers camped
in circles according to the arrangement detailed
above.
In
this
same
fashion
the
thirteen
1This must be the Amir Nurin Aqa who figures promi-
nently in the history of Ghazan Khan and was executed
in 1297 (see text p. 1310).
2Berezin (text 13:153; trs. 13:95) reads differently and
translates as дѣти Отоджуху-Дорданги.
gürä’äns of soldiers on Genghis Khan’s side
assembled. The Tayichi’ut forces decamped,
passed beyond A’ula’ut [and] Turqa’ut hills,
camped in Dalan Balji’us,3 and stood facing
Genghis Khan. The two sides did battle, and
God helped Genghis Khan, who defeated thirty
thousand horsemen with his thirteen gürä’äns.
By the heat of the sun of Genghis Khan’s for-
tune the enemy were swept away like dust
motes in the air. The Uru’ut and Buiru’ut clans,
whose chiefs were Uru’ut and Buiru’ut, joined
and submitted. At that place there was a large
forest on the river bank. [331] Genghis Khan
camped there and commanded seventy caul-
drons set over fire and the seditious enemies
who had been captured boiled in them. Fright-
ened by that, the Jä’üriyät submitted and
joined,
bringing
their
tents
near
Genghis
Khan’s yurt.
Once again some of them rebelled, and in
that battle the Tayichi’ut tribes, which were ex-
tremely numerous, powerful, and mighty, were
dispersed, and every one fell away in a differ-
ent direction.
Ölüg Bahadur and Taghai Dalu submit to
Genghis Khan along with the Jä’üriyät
clans attached to them, but they break their
word and become enemies again.
This came about as follows. They [i.e. the
Jä’üriyäts] were near Genghis Khan’s yurt.
One day they mounted together to go hunting
and formed a hunting circle on the hill called
Uchal Jalaman, which is located in the middle
of a vast plain. They completely encircled
Genghis Khan’s utu (meaning the center of the
hunting ground) and closed the circle, having a
very good hunt. To Genghis Khan they said,
“Let us sleep together there.” They were four
[hundred] persons altogether. Since they had
3This is the Dalan Baljud of the Secret History §129.
See note to text p. 40 above.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1167–1194
155

neither kettle nor fodder, two hundred went
with their tents, and two hundred persons slept
there together with Genghis Khan, who or-
dered them given what kettles and fodder they
needed. The next day they hunted, and they
were given more than their share of the kill and
shown much sympathetic kindness.
As they were parting from each other and
setting off for their homes, they were profusely
grateful
to
Genghis
Khan,
saying,
“The
Tayichi’ut tribe left us and dispersed, paying
no attention to us. [332] Genghis Khan, with-
out prior cause, showed us such favor and
goodness. He is a ruler who takes care of his
subjects and knows how to command.” All
along the way they expressed their thanks to
Genghis Khan, and they spread the word to all
the clans.1 When they reached their homes one
of the chiefs, Ölüg Bahadur, took counsel with
Maghui Yadaqaya as a consequence of their
thanks, saying, “Let us do valiant deeds for
Genghis
Khan
and
obey
his
command.”
Maghui Yadaqaya did not agree, saying, “What
bad have the Tayichi’ut done us? They are also
aqa and ini. How can we turn away from them
without cause and go to Genghis Khan?”
When he refused to agree, Ölüg Bahadur went
to Genghis Khan with Taghai Dalu and the
Jä’üriyät tribe, which was attached to them,
and said, “We have come like a woman with-
out a husband, a herd without a master, a ﬂock
without a shepherd. The sons who are of the
chief wife will kill us. We together will wield
our swords in friendship to you and kill your
enemies.”
In reply to Ölüg Bahadur, Genghis Khan
said, “I was like a person asleep whose fore-
lock you have pulled and awakened. I was sit-
ting, and you pulled me up by the chin. I will
do whatever is possible to earn your trust.”
1Emend text’s ﭼﺎو to ﺟﺎر (jar) ‘herald, announcement.’
And he treated them kindly and ingratiated
himself with them. 
Some time later, when they had gained in-
ﬂuence and power, the Jä’üriyät amirs went
back on their word and roamed through the ter-
ritory until finally a Märkit named Qodun Or-
chang defeated Taghai Dalu. Then the Jä’üriyät
tribe were left powerless and dispersed. After
that, the chief of the Jä’üriyät tribe, Jamuqa
Sächän, who was known for his intelligence,
competence, and judiciousness, but who was
also very tricky—and Genghis Khan [333]
called him anda—however much he kept to
the terms of fraternity and outwardly claimed
friendship and dedication, inwardly he was in-
imical and harbored thoughts of opposition and
gaining power for himself. During the time of
the strength of the Jä’üriyät tribe and after their
dispersal, he was always jealous of Genghis
Khan and, although outwardly he claimed to be
a friend, inwardly he was an enemy. Many
times he united with his opponents and ene-
mies, and those stories will come in their prop-
er places.
After a while, the above-mentioned tribes
united,
saying,
“The
commanders
of
the
Tayichi’ut harass us and are aggressive toward
us for no reason. This prince Tämüjin would
give the shirt off his back and the steed on
which he rides. The person who can maintain
the territory, keep the army, and guard the ulus
is he.” After much thought and consultation
they went to Genghis Khan and willingly sub-
mitted to rest in the shadow of his fortune.
Chila’uqan Bahadur, the son of Sorghan
Shira of the Sulduz tribe, and Jäbä of the
Besüt come to Genghis Khan before the
Tayichi’ut clans do.
Before the Tayichi’ut clans came, Chila’uqan
Bahadur, the son of Sorghan Shira of the Sul-
duz tribe, and Jäbä of the Besüt (a branch of
the Niru’un) came to Genghis Khan. Both were
156
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

attached to Tödä’ä and of his elite. (This
Tödä’ä was the son of the Qada’an Taishi who
was chief of a branch of the Tayichi’ut.) They
both deserted him and came to Genghis Khan.
The reason for Chila’uqan Bahadur’s desertion
[334] of the Tayichi’ut was that when Genghis
Khan was at enmity with the Tayichi’ut, once
without warning they found an opportunity to
seize Genghis Khan. With good tactics Chi-
la’uqan Bahadur rescued him, as has been
mentioned in the section on the Sulduz.1
The reason Jäbä left the Tayichi’ut and came
was that the Tayichi’ut had grown weak, and
Jäbä was wandering alone in the mountains
and forests. When he saw that there was no
benefit in that, he turned in helplessness to
Genghis Khan and submitted. This story has
been given in the section on the Besüt, by read-
ing which the details may be learned.2
Shirgü’ätü Äbügän of the Ba’arin and his
sons Naya’a and Alaq come to Genghis
Khan.
When most of the Tayichi’ut clans turned to-
ward Genghis Khan, a great amir of the
Ba’arin clan, Shirgü’ätü Äbügän by name—
from whom is descended the Bayan who was
sent from there to Qubilai Qa’an—picked up
his two sons, Naya’a and Alaq, and came.
Naya’a was alive through Genghis Khan’s time
and, after him, during the times of Ögödäi
Qa’an and Mängü Qa’an. He lived a hundred
twenty years. During Mängü Qa’an’s reign he
said, “When Genghis Khan was born, I ate of
the meat at his banquet.” This story has already
been given in the section on the Ba’arin.3 Any-
way, Shirgü’ätü Äbügän, who had brought his
two sons, captured Huquchu Bahadur of the
___ tribe, and Targhutai Qiriltuq, the chief of
1See text p. 174.
2See text p. 207.
3See text p. 198 (Naya’a ~ Nayaqa).
the Tayichi’ut, brought them to a place called
Qutuqul Nu’ud and held them there for a time.
[335] When he released them and let them go,
they took ﬂight. It was during that time that
Jochi Cha’urqa, the leader of the Dolangqayit
clan, a branch of the Jalayir, submitted to
Genghis Khan at a place called Turaqun
Singut.
Genghis Khan gives a banquet [attended by]
his mother, Ö’älün Ekä, and Ökin Barqaq’s
sons and family, and Genghis Khan’s
cousins Sacha Beki and Taichu, the chief of
the Yürkin Qiyat, and their mothers; a
dispute breaks out among them at the
banquet, Genghis Khan overwhelms them,
and therefore hostility ensues.
One day Genghis Khan’s mother, Ö’älün
Ekä, Genghis Khan, and his brothers Jochi
Qasar and Otchigin Noyan gathered in the for-
est with Sacha Beki and Taichu, the chief of
the Yürkin of the Qiyat, at the Onon River.
Having arranged for mares and ündürs of ku-
miss, they held a banquet. 
The ba’urchis placed one large wooden bot-
tle of kumiss for Genghis Khan’s mother,
Ö’älün Ekä, Sacha Beki, and Sacha Beki’s “big
mother” (meaning his father’s wife who was
elder to his own mother) Quhurchin Khatun,
and they filled a bottle of kumiss to the brim
and placed it before Sacha Beki’s “little moth-
er” (meaning the youngest of his father’s
wives), Emü’äi. When Quhurchin Khatun saw
that they had filled a second bottle of kumiss
and placed it before Emü’äi while she had to
share one with the others, she was mortally of-
fended, ﬂew into a fit, and struck Shiki’ür
Ba’urchi,4 Genghis Khan’s head ba’urchi. Shi-
ki’ür cried out in a loud voice, [336] saying,
“Only because Näkün Taishi and Yesügäi Ba-
hadur are not alive has she struck me so!”
4See Secret History (§130).
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1167–1194
157

Genghis Khan and his mother took this toler-
antly and said nothing. 
During the banquet, the kiriyäs1 of Genghis
Khan, Sacha Beki, and their mothers was being
manned by Genghis Khan’s brother Belgütäi
Bahadur, and he was holding the reins of
Genghis Khan’s horse. A man of the Qataqin
clan, Qataqitai by name, stole a tether, and he
was a liege man of Büri’s, a commander of the
Tayichi’ut. Büri was allied with Sacha Beki, so
he protected Qataqitai. For that reason he and
Belgütäi Noyan had words, and things went so
far that Büri struck Belgütäi on the shoulder
with his sword so that the ﬂesh was cut.
Genghis Khan’s liege men were creating a
ruckus
when
Belgütäi
Noyan
said,
“This
wound is nothing to me. There is no necessity
for haste in requiting it, for it is not fitting for
them to be on bad terms on account of me.”
With great insistence he forbade any show of
hostility. However, when they saw that they
had
wounded
him
and
struck
Shiki’ür
Ba’urchi, they clashed and struck each other
with branches of trees. Genghis Khan’s liege
men came out on top, and Quhurchin Khatun
and Qorijin Khatun were both seized and held.
Therefore Sacha Beki and all the Yürkin clan,
who were his followers, parted from Genghis
Khan. 
Afterwards, in order to make peace, they sent
the two ladies back, and emissaries on behalf
of both sides had come together to discuss a
truce when news arrived that a great amir
named Chingsang was coming with an army
from the Altan Khan of Cathay to attack
Mä’üjin Sä’ültü, [337] one of the commanders
of the Tatar, and his clans. Genghis Khan
mounted to help him fight the Tatar clans.
1The word occurs in the Secret History (p. 61, note 5):
“This word [kirü’ese] is glossed: ‘[place where] one
lights off a horse.’ ” See also Doerfer, TMEN 1:464–66
§330.
Genghis Khan learns that Mä’üjin Sä’ültü
of the Tatar and his followers have ﬂed with
their women and children in retreat from
Chingsang; Genghis Khan mounts to attack
and seize them; Chingsang honors Genghis
Khan.
Genghis Khan was informed that because the
Tatar tribe did not obey the Altan Khan’s or-
ders and also because they did not have the
strength to offer resistance, they had been
forced to take their women, children, ﬂocks,
and herds and decamp, and they were headed
his way. The Tatar were strong and well sup-
plied, and from ancient times on, Genghis
Khan’s forefathers and uncles had done battle
with them, as will mentioned in the proper
places.
When Genghis Khan saw such an opportuni-
ty, he immediately assembled the soldiers who
were nearby and set out from the Onon to at-
tack them, sending a message for the Yürkin
clan to mount also, but after waiting for six
days they did not show up. Genghis Khan then
set out with the few soldiers who constituted
his gürä’än. He blocked Mä’üjin Sä’ültü’s way
at a placed called Ulja[r], attacked his troops,
seized him, and killed him. He also took all
their ﬂocks and herds and possessions. 
It was during that raid that they found a sil-
ver cradle and gold-brocaded quilt, and be-
cause at that time such luxury items were rare
among the Mongols, [338] they were consid-
ered grand and gained renown. 
Since this suited the Altan Khan and his
amirs, Chingsang was pleased and praised
Genghis Khan highly, giving him the title of
ja’ut quri2—which means magnificent com-
2Although it is clear that it meant something like Ward
of the Marches, no satisfactory explanation of this title
has been given. For a review of possibilities, see Doer-
fer, TMEN 1:282 §152.
158
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

mander in Cathaian—before returning to the
Altan Khan. It was also at that time that
Chingsang gave the title of Ong Khan, which
means ruler of a kingdom, to Toghril, the ruler
of the Kerayit.
Genghis Khan decides to award a portion of
the spoils taken from the Tatar to the
Yürkin clan, who deserted him during the
battle with the Tatar; some of them rebel
nonetheless, and he attacks them and kills
most of them.
When Genghis Khan defeated the Tatar and
his soldiers and followers were enriched, he
wanted to placate the Yürkin clan and give
them something of what had been plundered.
He decided to go to them, but along the way
some of the Yürkin clan united with a group of
rebels, killed two of Genghis Khan’s soldiers,
took the horses from fifty men, and stripped
them of their clothing. 
When this was reported to Genghis Khan, he
said, “They struck my brother Belgütäi Noyan
on the shoulder with their sword, and when I
say, ‘Let us make peace,’ they don’t. Now they
have united with rebels, and I am forced to
deal with them.” 
He mounted in anger and [339] went to at-
tack them through the desert, striking at
Dolo’an Boldaq and killing and plundering
many of them. Sacha Beki and Taichi both
took ﬂight with their wives, children, and a few
others and escaped.
Ong Khan’s brother Jagambu deserts Ong
Khan, and around him gathers a clan of the
Kerayit called the Tongqayit; Genghis Khan
does battle with that clan and subdues them.
After dealing with the Yürkin, Genghis Khan
mounted, determined to do battle with Jagam-
bu, the brother of Ong Khan, the ruler of the
Kerayit, Jagambu having deserted his brother,
and Genghis Khan struck and defeated him.
The Tongqayit clan was a branch of the Keray-
it that were always servants and soldiers of the
Kerayit ruler. (The Amir Ayachi Totqavul who
was in this land and his sons are of this “bone,”
as are many other amirs, as has been men-
tioned in the section on the Kerayit.) The
Tongqayit were dispersed for a while, but then
they all came to Genghis Khan. Since Genghis
Khan was on friendly terms with Ong Khan, he
sent Jagambu and the Tongqayit clan back to
him. After that, Jagambu was united with Ong
Khan for a while, until once again they re-
belled and went over to Tayang Khan, the ruler
of the Naiman, as will be explained.
Now that the history of Genghis Khan during
these twenty-seven years has been given in
summary, we will commence the history of the
rulers of Cathay, Qarakhitai, [340] Chin and
Machin, and the caliphs, sultans, and maliks of
Iran who were contemporary with Genghis
Khan during this period. The details having
been given, we shall return to the history of
Genghis Khan, God willing. [341]
History of the rulers of Cathay, Qarakhitai, Chin, and Turkistan, and the caliphs, sultans,
and kings of Iran who were Genghis Khan’s contemporaries from the beginning of
Quluqana Yil, the Year of the Rat that began in Rabi‘ I 563 [December 1167], until the end
of Bars Yil, the Year of Tiger that began in Safar 590 [January 1194], a period of twenty-
seven years, in the last year of which Genghis Khan was forty years old; and the unusual
events that happened during the period.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1167–1194

The history of the rulers of Cathay,
Qarakhitai, and the Jurchids who were in
this period.
Liang Tai Zu1 [ruled a total of] twelve years,
of which eight were before, and four were dur-
ing, this period.
Shi Zong [ruled for] twenty-nine years.2
The history of the rulers of Machin who
were in this period.
Nan-Song Gao Zong3 ruled a total of forty
years, of which thirty-eight were before this
period and two were during it.
Xiao Zong ruled a total of twenty-two years,
all of which were during the period.4
Guang Zong reigned a total of four years, of
which three years were during the period.5
[342]
The history of the rulers of Turkistan and
Transoxiana who were in this period.
The same Gür Khan who was mentioned be-
fore was in Turkistan.
The history of the caliphs, sultans, kings, and
atabegs of Iran, Anatolia, Syria, Egypt, &c.
who were in this period.
History of the caliphs in Baghdad.
During the first part of the above-mentioned
period, the caliph was al-Mustanjid-bi’llah. He
died in the year 566 [1170],6 and Mustadi’ suc-

see note to text p. 314 above.

(ruled from 1127 and abdicated in 1162).
4Xiao Zong (孝宗) of the Southern Song, r. 1162–
