ceeded to the caliphate. He died in the year 575
[1180],7 and al-Nasir-li-dini’llah succeeded.
In Egypt, Adid was the caliph of the Ismailis.
He died on ashura, the 10th of Muharram, in
the year 565 [October 4, 1169], and Salahuddin
Yusuf, the nephew of Asaduddin Sherkoh, had
become ruler in Egypt in his uncle’s place, as
will be explained. On the first Friday after
Adid’s death, the khutba was read in the name
of the caliph of the House of Abbas in Bagh-
dad, and the caliphate of the Ismailis in Egypt
came to an end. The total of those caliphs in
North Africa and Egypt was fourteen individu-
als, and the length of their caliphate was two
hundred seventy-two years.8
History of the sultans.
In Khwarazm, El Arslan, the son of Atsiz, oc-
cupied the sultan’s throne. He died on the 19th
of Rajab 567 [March 17, 1172] after having
ruled for nearly seventeen years. His youngest
son, Sultanshah, [343] the designated heir, suc-
ceeded him with his mother, Malika Tärkän, as
regent. The elder brother, Täkish, was in Jand.
An envoy was sent summoning him, but he re-
fused to go. Then they sent an army to attack
him. Täkish found out about it and went to the
Gür
Khan
of
the
Qarakhitai,
whom
he
promised the wealth and treasures of Khwa-
razm and agreed to sent a stipulated amount as
annual tribute. The Gür Khan dispatched his
son-in-law Fu-ma9 and a huge army to go with
Täkish. When they arrived near Khwarazm,
Sultanshah and his mother took refuge with
Malik Mu’ayyad, the ruler of Khurasan.
7al-Mustadi’ died on 2 Dhu’l-Qa‘da 575 (March 30,
1180) according to Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 11:459.
8He dates Fatimid rule from 293/905 (the usual date is
297/909) to 565/1169 (the usual date is 567/ 1171),
giving 272 lunar years.
9Fuma (駙馬), the Chinese title for imperial son-in-
law.
160
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Täkish mounted the throne in Khwarazm on
Monday the 22nd of Rabi‘ II 568 [December
11, 1172] and sent Fu-ma back with all honors
in discharging his indebtedness. 
Sultanshah’s mother sent Malik Mu’ayyad
gifts of precious jewels and treasures and of-
fered him the kingdom of Khwarazm. Desirous
of it, he assembled an army and set out for
Khwarazm to help Sultanshah and his mother.
When they reached the town of Subarlay,1
which is under water at this time, Täkish had
already camped there. Their troops poured out
of the desert in droves and were able to get
there. Malik Mu’ayyad [Ay]-Aba was in the
vanguard. Täkish attacked that troop, killing
most of them, and Malik Mu’ayyad [Ay]-Aba
was brought before him as a captive. He or-
dered him cut in half at the gate to the court on
Arafa day of ___.2 Sultanshah and his mother
ﬂed to Dihistan. Täkish went out in pursuit,
seized that area, killed Malika Tärkän, and re-
turned.
In
his
ﬂight
Sultanshah
went
to
Shadyakh to Toghanshah, Malik Mu’ayyad’s
son who had taken his father’s place, and there
he remained for a time. He then joined the sul-
tans of Ghor, [344] who showed him great
honor.
Sultan Täkish consolidated his position in
Khwarazm, but he ordered killed one of the
Gür Khan’s representatives who constantly
came and, not satisfied with the agreed-upon
tribute, made exorbitant demands and did not
observe the niceties of etiquette. Therefore en-
mity broke out between him and the Gür Khan.
Recognizing this as his golden opportunity,
Sultanshah set out against the Gür Khan, am-
1According to Ibn al-Athir (Kamil 11:377), the place
was called Subarnay, a hamlet twenty leagues from
Khwarazm.
2The date 556 is spelled out in Arabic in the text, but it
is obviously wrong. Ibn al-Athir (Kamil 11:377) places
this under the rubric of the year 568.
ply provisioned by Ghiyasuddin of Ghor.
When he reached the Gür Khan, he sent Fu-ma
back out with a troop. Sultan Täkish [opened
the dykes and] ﬂooded the Oxus in their way
and got busy readying himself for battle in the
city. When Fu-ma saw that the people of
Khwarazm were not inclined to Sultanshah, he
pulled back. Sultanshah took a troop from him
and without warning attacked Malik Dinar, an
Oghuz amir, in Sarakhs. Malik Dinar threw
himself in the moat, but they pulled him back
into the fortress by his hair. Sultanshah went to
Merv and took up residence there, sending the
Qarakhitai commanders back. He kept attack-
ing Sarakhs until most of the Oghuz were dis-
persed. Malik Dinar remained immovable in
the citadel. He sent an envoy to Toghanshah,
the chief of the Oghuz, and requested Bistam
in place of Sarakhs. Toghanshah sent Amir
Umar Firozkohi for Malik Dinar to turn the
Sarakhs fortress over to before he went to Bis-
tam. When Sultan Täkish reached Jajarm on
his way to Persia, Malik Dinar joined Toghan-
shah, who sent Qara Qush, one of his father’s
slaves, to Sarakhs and recalled Amir Umar.
Sultanshah attacked Sarakhs with three thou-
sand cavalry, and Toghanshah also set out from
Nishapur with ten thousand horsemen, headed
for there. Battle was fought in Dhu’l-Hijja 576
[April 1181], [345] and Sultanshah won, taking
innumerable articles of booty. He then seized
power over Sarakhs, Tus, and that part of
Khurasan and constantly attacked Toghanshah
until Toghanshah’s troops were exhausted and
his commanders joined Sultanshah. He was too
weak to do anything but take refuge with Sul-
tan Täkish and the sultan of Ghor and ask for
help. Once he went himself with a troop of a
thousand, but it profited him little. He contin-
ued with such lack of success until he died on
Sunday night the 12th of Muharram 581 [April
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1167–1194
161

15, 1185].1 His son Sanjarshah was enthroned,
and his tutor Mängli Beg gained power. He be-
gan exactions and extortions, and on account
of his cruelty most of Toghanshah’s officers
joined Sultanshah. 
In fear of Sultanshah, Malik Dinar went to
Kirman, and the Oghuz Turks who had been
lurking everywhere joined him. At the begin-
ning of 582 [March 1186] Sultan Täkish went
from Khwarazm to Khurasan. Sultanshah went
to Khwarazm, but they did not allow him in,
and Täkish camped at the gates of Merv. Sul-
tanshah retreated. Then he came from Amuya
with fifty warriors, attacked Täkish’s camp by
night, and went into the city. Täkish retreated,
and in Rabi‘
I 582 [May–June 1186] he
camped outside the city of Shadyakh and be-
sieged Sanjarshah and Mängli Beg for two
months before retiring under a truce. The great
chamberlain Shihabuddin, Sayfuddin Mardan-
sher the majordomo, and Baha’uddin Muham-
mad Baghdadi the secretary were sent to con-
clude the treaty and arrange terms of tribute
with Mängli. With the sultan’s retinue no
longer around, Mängli Beg seized them and
sent them to Sultanshah, where they remained
in prison until an agreement was reached be-
tween the brothers. [346] Sultanshah went to
Shadyakh a second time and laid siege, but
since the citizens overcame him, he set out for
Sabzavar and installed a catapult. The people
of Sabzavar cursed him, and in revenge he
made every endeavor to take the city. In fear,
the people of the city took refuge with Shaykh
Ahmad Badili, a saint greatly respected by Sul-
tanshah. Through his intercession their offens-
es were forgiven, and he went inside Sabzavar
as promised and dwelt there for a time before
going to Merv. 
1According to Ibn al-Athir (Kamil 11:379), Toghan-
shah died in Muharram 582 (March–April 1186).
On Friday the 14th of Muharram 583 [March
26, 1187], Sultan Täkish camped on the out-
skirts of Shadyakh and set up catapults. Mängli
Beg grew fearful and had the sayyids and
imams intercede. The sultan gave him amnesty
and swore an oath to that effect. Mängli Beg
went out, and the sultan entered the city on
Tuesday the 7th of Rabi‘ I [May 17, 1187] to
“spread the carpet of justice.” He put a warden
in charge of Mängli Beg until he gave back
everything he had taken illegally. In expiation
for the blood of Qazi Burhanuddin and in ac-
cordance with a writ issued by the imams, he
was ordered executed. 
Nishapur was turned over to the Khwarazm-
shah, and his eldest son, Nasiruddin Malik-
shah, was stationed there as his representative.
In Rajab of that year [September 1187], he re-
turned to Khwarazm. Sultanshah went back to
the gates of Nishapur and laid siege. Both sides
fought hard, and most of the walls were de-
stroyed. Malikshah constantly sent messengers
to his father to inform him of the situation. Sul-
tan Täkish came with a large army and ordered
an underling from Nasa to inform Sultanshah
of the sultan’s arrival. He burned the catapults
and retreated. Sultan Täkish went to Nishapur
and rebuilt what had been destroyed. [347]
That winter he was in Mazanderan, and all the
officers of Khurasan joined him to be received
warmly and be given rewards. In the spring a
truce was made between him and his brother
Sultanshah in the meadows of Radkan. The
sultan gave the area of Jam, Bakharz, and Zer-
i-Pul to Sultanshah, and he honored the minis-
ters who had captured and sent Mängli Beg
and then withdrew. 
On Tuesday the 18th of Jumada I 585 [July 4,
1189], Sultan Täkish mounted the throne in
Radkan, and his name was broadcast in all di-
rections, and all were singled out for rewards
and gifts. That fall he returned to Khwarazm. 
162
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The sultans of Ghor had fallen out with Sul-
tanshah, who had done battle with his brother
Täkish several other times. They did battle
again in Marv Rud, and Sultanshah was defeat-
ed. On both sides the wisdom of a truce was
acknowledged, and on the surface a cease-fire
was arranged, although because Sultanshah
dominated his brother and had taken several
actions that would justify breaking a pact, the
sultan moved against him from Khwarazm in
586 [1190] and took by force and destroyed the
fortress of Sarakhs, which was in the hands of
Sultanshah’s men. That summer he went to
Radkan,
where
once
again
the
grandees
arranged a truce between the brothers and out-
wardly an agreement was concluded. 
In 588 [1192], Qutayba Khatun, the mother
of Qutlugh Inanch, the son of the Atabeg Ja-
han-Pahlavan Muhammad b. Eldigüz, was go-
ing to poison Sultan Toghril b. Arslan Shah b.
Toghril b. Muhammad b. Malikshah the Sel-
juqid, but a servant girl warned him. “Don’t
drink it!” the sultan said, but she drank it and
died. [348] The sultan imprisoned Qutlugh
Inanch. After he was released he sent envoys to
Täkish, offering to turn over the realm of Per-
sia to him and requesting assistance so that
they could attack Sultan Toghril. The sultan set
out at once for Persia. Qutlugh Inanch regret-
ted what he had done and holed up in a
fortress. The sultan arrived and took the
fortress of Tabarak in one or two days, and his
soldiers got plenty of booty. That summer he
was in the vicinity of Rayy, but the air was so
putrid that many of his soldiers died. When
Sultan Toghril learned of the quarrel between
Sultan Täkish and Inanch, he sent presents and
gifts, and the hostile air between them was
cleared. Sultan Täkish stationed Amir Tam-
ghach, one of his Turkish offices, with a troop
in Rayy and withdrew. Along the way heralds
arrived to say that Sultanshah had laid siege to
Khwarazm.
In
all
haste
he
set
out
for
Khwarazm, and when he reached Dihistan,
heralds arrived to say that Sultanshah had
pulled back. The sultan went to Khwarazm and
spent that winter frolicking. In the spring he set
out for Khurasan to attack his brother. When
he reached Abivard, the grandees requested
that a truce be made between them, but it could
not be arranged. Just then the castellan of the
Sarakhs fortress, Chighir by name, threw the
keepers of the fortress into chains and dis-
patched a messenger to Abivard to summon the
sultan. The sultan went hastily, and the castel-
lan turned over the treasury and stores. In grief
Sultanshah died two days later on Tuesday
night the last of Ramadan 589 [September 29,
1193].1 The sultan gained control of Sultan-
shah’s realms and treasuries, and at his son
Qutbuddin Muhammad’s request he sent a
messenger to Khwarazm. He gave him Nisha-
pur, [349] and to his younger son, Nasiruddin
Malikshah, who had formerly been the gover-
nor of Nishapur, he gave Merv. Both sons be-
came puissant in their respective realms. 
During those days news arrived that Sultan
Toghril had broken his pact. Tamghach had
been harassed by him, and he had taken back
the fortress at Tabarak. The sultan set out to
take revenge, and at the beginning of 590 [De-
cember 1193], he headed for Persia. Qutlugh
Inanch and the commanders of Persia came out
as far as Simnan to greet him, and the sultan
sent him back in the vanguard of the Persia
army. Toghril, who had made a large camp
three leagues from Rayy, raised his banners in
opposition, and when Inanch approached he
mounted, took hold of a heavy mace with
which he had performed valiant deeds, and
drove his army before him like a madman, rec-
iting these lines from the Shahnama:
1Date confirmed by Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 11:384.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1167–1194
163

When, from that massive army, the warrior
arose, the faces of our renowned fighters
turned pale. / I picked up my mace and sta-
tioned the army right there. / I gave such a yell
from the saddle that the earth ground them
down like a gristmill.
Like a lion-man, he felled several riders with
his ox-headed mace, but he was so intoxicated
that the mace hit his horse’s knee and he was
thrown. Just then Qutlugh Inanch came upon
him and, not recognizing him, was about to de-
liver a blow. In order to make himself known,
the sultan raised the ﬂap of his helmet, and
Inanch said, “You are what I was looking for!”
With one blow he killed him and then he
loaded his body on a camel [350] and took it to
Sultan Täkish. 
Täkish prostrated himself in thanks and sent
to Baghdad the head of this man who had vied
with the Caliph Nasir for the caliphate. On
Thursday the 29th of Rabi‘ I 590 [March 24,
1194] his body was raised on a gibbet in the
marketplace. One of Sultan Toghril’s compan-
ions was taken before Nizamulmulk Mas‘ud
the vizier, who said to him, “All this commo-
tion about little Toghril amounted to nothing
more than the fact that he didn’t have the pow-
er to stand against the Padishah of Islam’s
vanguard.”
The
companion
immediately
replied,
“ ‘Human was more powerful than Bezhan.
Craft becomes a defect when the sun turns its
back.’ ”
Sultan Täkish set out from Rayy for Bagh-
dad, taking most of the fortresses of Persia.
The Caliph Nasir expected that the sultan
would turn over some of Persia to the caliphal
administration. When the sultan did not re-
spond, the caliph sent his vizier, Mu’ayyidud-
din Ibn al-Qassab, to the sultan with a patent of
investiture, robes of honor, and other diplomat-
ic gestures.
When he reached Asadabad, more than ten
thousand Kurds and Arabs gathered around
him. Stupidly he sent a message to the sultan,
saying, “Your patent of investiture has been is-
sued by the caliphal chancery, and the minister
of the realm has come this far to discharge de-
liverance of same. It would be an appropriate
show of gratitude for you to come with a few
men and much humility and walk on foot hold-
ing the minister’s reins.” The sultan, imagining
that these words concealed treachery and a
plot, sent his soldiers out to meet the vizier and
attack him and his men. The vizier ﬂed, and
the honor of the caliphate was lost. The sol-
diers pursued them as far as Dinawar.
The sultan went to Hamadan and sent out tax
collectors to gather the taxes of Persia. [351]
He gave Isfahan to Qutlugh Inanch and made
him commander-in-chief of Persia. Giving
Rayy to his son Yunus Khan, and setting May-
achuq over the army as his atabeg, he returned
triumphantly to Khurasan. Along the way he
heard that his son Malikshah was ill due to the
putrid air in Merv. He summoned him, but by
the time he reached Tus he had regained his
health, so his father gave him the emirate of
Nishapur again. He assigned to Sultan Muham-
mad estates in Khurasan and made him a mem-
ber of his retinue.
In Persia were Sultan Arslan b. Toghril b.
Muhammad b. Malikshah the Seljuqid and the
Atabeg Eldigüz. When Sultan Arslan died, his
son Sultan Toghril mounted the throne with El-
digüz’s son Jahan-Pahlavan as his atabeg.
When Jahan-Pahlavan died Qizil Arslan want-
ed to become atabeg, but it was not possible.
The end of the sultan has already been given in
the preceding section on Sultan Täkish the
Khwarazmshah.
In Anatolia, Sultan Izzuddin Qilich Arslan b.
Mas‘ud b. Qilich Arslan had taken over the
rule of Konya, Sivas, and Aqsara. Hostilities
164
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

broke out between him and Zu’n-Nun b. Dan-
ishmand, the lord of Malatya, and Qilich Ar-
slan took over his territory. Zu’n-Nun ﬂed to
Atabeg Nuruddin of Aleppo, who led his army
out and took Sivas, the fortress at Mar‘ash, and
many of his possessions. Qilich sent envoys to
intervene, but Nuruddin would not listen.
Without warning news arrived that the Franks
had rebelled. Nuruddin accepted a truce and
stationed a troop with Zu’n-Nun, and Sivas re-
mained under his control until his death. After
that, Qilich Arslan took it back.
In Kirman the ruler was Toghrilshah b.
Muhammad Abi’l-Fawaris. [352] He died at
the beginning of 563 [October 1167], leaving
four sons, Arslanshah, Tärkänshah, Turanshah,
and Bahramshah. Due to the entrance of the
Oghuz into the area and their meddling in the
affairs of Kirman, Bahramshah grew fearful
and went out to kill, rape, and pillage until Ma-
lik Dinar, the Oghuz commander who was the
son-in-law of Toghanshah b. Mu’ayyad [Ay]-
Aba the governor of Nishapur, came to Kir-
man. In Rajab of 583 [September 1187] the
city of Bardasir, the seat of Kirman, was turned
over to him, and he put the affairs of the region
in order. 
In Ghor and Ghazna were Sultan Ghiyasud-
din and Sultan Shihabuddin. In 590 [1194] bat-
tle was fought between Sultan Shihabuddin of
Ghor and the ruler of India. The Indians were
defeated, and their ruler was killed. It is related
that the ruler had seven hundred war elephants
and a million men. [353]
History of the maliks and atabegs
In Mazanderan was Shah Ala’uddin Hasan b.
Rustam b. Ali b. Shahryar.
In Persia and Azerbaijan was Atabeg El-
digüz. In 563 [1167–68] Aq Sonqur, the lord of
Maragha, made a request of Baghdad that the
khutba be in the name of his ward, the son of
Sultan Muhammadshah b. Mahmud the Sel-
juqid. This news reached Atabeg Eldigüz in
Hamadan, whose wife’s son, Arslan Toghril b.
Muhammad
b.
Malikshah,
was
supreme
throughout his realm. Eldigüz was offended by
this and sent his son Jahan-Pahlavan Muham-
mad with an army to do battle with Aq Sonqur.
Aq Sonqur went in defeat to the fortress of
Royindiz on the frontier of Maragha. Jahan-
Pahlavan laid siege, but in the end a truce was
arranged and Jahan-Pahlavan returned to his
father in Hamadan. This took place in 563
[1167–68].
In 567 [1171–72] Atabeg Eldigüz died in
Hamadan,
and
his
son
Jahan-Pahlavan
Muhammad became atabeg with such power
and might that when Sultan Toghril b. Arslan
became sultan, he was ruler in name only in
the khutba and coinage while the absolute ruler
was Atabeg Jahan-Pahlavan. 
When Aq Sonqur died in Maragha, his son
Falakuddin took his place. Because they had
taken control of Tabriz, [354] he led his army
against Jahan-Pahlavan, but he laid siege to
Falakuddin in Royindiz and sent his brother
Qizil Arslan to lay siege to Tabriz. The army of
Maragha captured two of his men and took
them into the city. Qazi Sadruddin had them
clad in robes of honor and sent to Jahan-Pahla-
van. He was delighted and made a truce at the
cadi’s suggestion, under the terms of which
they were given Tabriz, and Maragha was giv-
en to Falakuddin.
Jahan-Pahlavan stationed Qizil Arslan in
Tabriz and withdrew to Persia. When Jahan-
Pahlavan died Qizil Arslan went to Persia, hop-
ing to become absolute atabeg like his brother,
but Sultan Toghril had grown up and become
independent and paid him little attention. Bat-
tle was fought, Qizil Arslan was defeated, and
most of his men went over to the sultan. Qizil
Arslan was in dire straits for a while, but later
he regained power, assembled an army, seized
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1167–1194
165

the sultan, and threw him into chains. He had
drums sounded at his gate five times a day and
claimed the sultanate. 
One night in Sha‘ban 587 [August–Septem-
ber 1191] while he was asleep in his house,
someone killed him. It was never known who
did it. People have attributed it to the fact that
not long before, out of religious fanaticism, he
had had a large number of proponents of the
great Shafiite imam al-Muttalibi hanged in the
marketplace in Isfahan.
In Mosul and Diyarbekir was Atabeg Qut-
buddin Mawdud b. Zangi b. Aq Sonqur, the
governor of Diyarbekir and brother of Atabeg
Nuruddin Mahmud of Syria. He died in 565
[1169–70], and his youngest son, Sayfuddin
Ghazi, took his place. In 571 [1175–76] battle
was fought between him and Salahuddin the
ruler of Egypt, and Sayfuddin ﬂed. [355] He
died in Safar 576 [July 1180], and his brother
Izzuddin Mas‘ud took his place. He died at the
end of Sha‘ban 589 [August 31, 1193]. 
Mujiruddin Qara-Arslan b. Daud b. Saqman
b. Artuq was the lord of Hisn Keyfa and most
of Diyarbekir. When he died his son Nuruddin
Muhammad took his place. He died in 581
[1185–86], and his son Qutbuddin Saqman was
installed in his stead.
In Anatolia was Atabeg Nuruddin. He inau-
gurated a courier pigeon service in Syria along
the Baghdad road in 567 [1171–72], and it is
still functioning.1 In Shawwal 568 [May 1173],
when Salahuddin of Egypt did not come to
fight the Franks, he set out for Egypt, but he
fell ill and died on the 11th of the month [May
26, 1173]. His eleven-year-old son Isma‘il was
installed in his place and named Malik Salih.
When he died his cousin Sayfuddin Qazi, the
son of Qutbuddin Mawdud the lord of Mosul,
seized the realms he had possessed.
1Agrees with Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 11:375.
In Egypt was Asaduddin Sherkoh, the son of
Shadi b. Marwan the Kurd, who was first a tax
gatherer in Tikrit and then became lord and
ruler. When Adid, the caliph of the Ismailis,
had grown weak, his vizier, Shawar, had
sought to gain dominance over him, but Adid
sent to Atabeg Nuruddin of Syria requesting
assistance to deal with his vizier. Nuruddin
sent Sherkoh with two thousand men. Fright-
ened, the vizier took took over the kingdom
and asked the Franks for help. Sherkoh crossed
the Nile and camped in the west. Battle was
fought, and the combined armies of Egypt and
the Franks were routed [356] and took refuge
on the shore. Sherkoh seized Alexandria and
stationed his nephew Salahuddin Yusuf there
while he went and took Upper Egypt. The
Franks gained control of Egypt and Cairo.
Kamil Shuja‘, son of the vizier Shawar, sent a
message to Atabeg Nuruddin, inviting him to
an entente cordiale, undertaking to send a year-
ly tribute to him. Nuruddin agreed to this, and
in 564 [1168] Sherkoh took Egypt and killed
the vizier Shawar. Sherkoh ruled for two
months and five days, and on the 22nd of Ju-
mada II [March 23, 1169] the above-mentioned
ruler died and Salahuddin Yusuf became ruler
of Egypt in his uncle’s place. He sent his
younger brother Shamsuddin Turanshah to Nu-
bia, which he took with much plunder, and
then he sent him to take the Yemen.
On the second Friday in Muharram 565 [Oc-
tober 4, 1169], when Adid died, the khutba was
read in the name of the caliphs of Baghdad.
Also during that year a quarrel erupted be-
tween [Salahuddin] and Nuruddin over the
kingship of Egypt. Battle was fought between
Salahuddin and Sayfuddin Ghazi, the lord of
Mosul and parts of Diyarbekir, in 571 [1175–
76]. Sayfuddin took ﬂight, and Salahuddin
seized the territories that had been held by Ma-
lik Salih, the son of Nuruddin, like Manbij and
166
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

that area. He laid siege to the fortress at Alep-
po, where Malik Salih was, but since it was not
possible to take it by force he withdrew under
a truce.
In 581 [1185–86] he took Mayyafariqin and
attacked Mosul. Conquest was impossible, and
thereafter until the end of his life he performed
great deeds. He took many territories from the
Franks and of Diyarbekir and other areas. Each
of his sons, brothers, and relatives became a
ruler in a region of the realm on his behalf.
[357]
In 589 [1193] he died in Damascus, having
made his youngest son, Nuruddin Ali, his suc-
cessor. He was installed in his father’s place in
Damascus and ruled as Malik Afdal, although
some of his relatives who governed parts of
Syria did not recognize him and followed
another brother, Usman, whom they called Ma-
lik Aziz. He had been in Egypt and sought au-
tonomy. In 590 [1194] he laid siege to Damas-
cus. Malik Afdal sought help from his uncle
Malik Adil, who, along with Malik Zahir
Ghazi the lord of Aleppo, Nasiruddin Muham-
mad the son of Taqiuddin the lord of Hama,
Asaduddin Sherkoh the grandson of the elder
Sherkoh and lord of Hisn [Keyfa], set out from
Mosul and Diyarbekir with a huge army to as-
sist Malik Afdal. When Malik Aziz saw how
strong Malik Afdal was, he agreed to a truce on
terms that Jerusalem and the dependencies of
Palestine would be annexed to Egypt and be-
long to Malik Aziz, while Damascus, Tiberias,
and the dependencies of the Jordan Valley
would be Afdal’s. Jabla, Latakiya, and the
shore would be Malik Zahir’s, and the fiefs
that Malik Adil had originally possessed in
Egypt would remain as they were. Then each
of the rulers returned to his own territory.
In North Africa was Yusuf b. Abdul-Mu’min.
He took the territory of Qafsa,1 one of the de-
pendencies of Ifriqiya (North Africa).
In Fars was Atabeg Tägäla, but he died in the
year ___,2 and Atabeg Muzaffar b. Sa‘d b. Zan-
gi took his place. He was a very courageous
and brave man.
Unusual events that occurred during this
period
In the year 565 [1170] an enormous earth-
quake occurred in Syria, Diyarbekir, [358] and
the lands of the Franks. It was so severe that
most of the cities in those regions were
destroyed.3
Now that the events of this period have been
given, we will return to the history of Genghis
Khan. [359] 
1Qafsa (see Abu’l-Fida, Taqwim, 142), the modern
Gafsa in Tunisia.
2The Salghurid Tägälä (or Dägälä) ruled from 1175 to
1194. His death date is lacking in the text.
3Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 11:354: “In this year a terrifying
and sustained major earthquake also occurred on 12
Shawwal 565 (June 29, 1170). No one had ever seen
anything like it. It occurred generally throughout most of
Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, Mosul, Iraq, and other
places, but the worst was in Syria. It wrought devasta-
tion in most of Damascus, Baalbek, Homs, Hama,
Shayzar, Baarin, Aleppo, and other places. Walls and
fortresses were destroyed, houses collapsed upon their
inhabitants, and untold numbers were killed.”
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1167–1194
167

The history of Genghis Khan from the beginning of Taulai Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that
began in Rabi‘ I 591 [February 1195], until the beginning of Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig
that began in Jumada II 599 [February 1203], a period of nine years.
In the last year of this period Genghis Khan
was forty-nine years old. During this nine-year
period he and Ong Khan were friends, and he
fought battles with Toqto’a Beki, the ruler of
the Märkit; with Buyuruq Khan, the brother of
the ruler of the Naiman; with the Tayichi’ut,
Qorolas, Ikiräs, Dörbän, and Tatar tribes; and
with the Qataqin and Salji’ut clans, all of
whom he vanquished. He annihilated the Ker-
ayit ruler Ong Khan and the Naiman ruler
Tayang Khan, and the title Genghis Khan was
given to him.
The beginning of the friendship between
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan.
This came about as follows. Because they
were neighbors, there was a long-standing
friendship
and
alliance
between
Genghis
Khan’s father, Yesügäi Bahadur, and Ong
Khan. During hard times Yesügäi Bahadur
helped Ong Khan and rescued him from the
brink of disaster. They called each other anda.
As the proverb says, “Love is inherited,” [360]
so Genghis Khan continued in the path of af-
fection and called [Ong Khan] “father.” Ong
Khan was the ruler of the Kerayit and Tonqayit
nation and of other tribes who were in the Ker-
ayit [confederation]. They constituted a large
people and a numerous army, and their ancient
rulers were renowned. They bore a resem-
blance to the Mongol clans, and their manners
and customs, as well as dialect and language,
were close to each other’s. 
Ong Khan was originally called Toghril. In
the Turkish and Kerayit language toghril is
tongrul,1 and it means a bird whose name is
1See Doerfer, TMEN 3:346f. §1345.
well known among the people, although no one
has ever seen it, like the phoenix of the west.
They report that it is a bird shaped like a hawk,
and its beak and claws are as hard as steel. In
one attack it can fell and kill two or three
hundred birds. They say, “We give it credence
even though we haven’t seen it because
hunters and dwellers in the wilderness have of-
ten witnessed anywhere from one to three
hundred birds of different sorts, their heads
severed from their bodies and their wings and
legs broken, falling from the sky in one place.
Logically the thing that is killing them must be
a mighty bird with sharp, powerful talons.”
They have named it dongrul. It is also well
known among the Mongols, who have named
it ___. This is the meaning of Toghril, which
was his original name. Later, as has been ex-
plained,2 the Altan Khan’s minister, Chingsang,
gave him the title Ong Khan, meaning the ruler
of a region.
[Ong
Khan’s]
grandfather’s
name
was
Marghuz, and Marghuz had two sons. The el-
der was called Qurjaquz Buyuruq Khan, and
the meaning of buyuruq is to command. (The
ruler of the Naiman, Tayang Khan, also had a
brother called Buyuruq Khan; he will be men-
tioned later in the history of the Naiman. He
has been mentioned here lest the two be con-
fused in the mind.) [361] Marghuz’s other son
was
named
Gürkhan.
(The
ruler
of
the
Qarakhitai in Turkistan and Transoxiana was
also called Gür Khan, meaning mighty and
magnificent khan.) 
Qurjaquz Buyuruq Khan had several sons.
One was the Toghril, whose title was Ong
2See above, text p. 338.
168
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Khan; the second was Ärkä Qara; and the third
was Jagambu, whose name was originally Ker-
ayidai. They had several other brothers, but the
successor to the father was Toghril. Kira’i had
been taken captive as a child by the Tangqut
people, and he had remained among them for a
time, growing powerful and respected. Since
he was intelligent and competent, they named
him Jagambu. Ja means province, and gambu
means
magnificent
commander,
[together]
meaning mighty commander of provinces. Al-
though he was originally allied with his brother
Ong Khan, in the end he deserted him once or
twice, as will be mentioned in the proper place.
Ärkä Qara had a yen to lead and rule and
vied with Ong Khan. Ong Khan first killed the
brothers who were allied with Ärkä Qara and
then attacked him, as will be mentioned. When
Ong Khan became friendly and allied with
Genghis Khan, Jagambu was anda to Genghis
Khan. Genghis Khan asked for one of Jagam-
bu’s daughters, Ibaqa Beki, for himself, but he
gave her to Kähätäi Noyan. Another, Begtut-
mish Füjin, he requested for his eldest son,
Jochi, and another, Sorqaghtani Beki, he re-
quested for Tolui Khan. [Jagambu] had another
daughter who was given to the son of the ruler
of the Tangqut. She was extremely beautiful
and chaste, and when Genghis Khan took
Tangqut and killed the ruler, he looked for her
everywhere but could not find her. [362]
Ong Khan had two sons. The elder was San-
gun, which means prince in the Cathaian lan-
guage; and the younger was Abaqu,1 whose
daughter
was
the
Toquz
Khatun
whom
Genghis Khan requested for Tolui Khan. After
Tolui Khan’s death Hülägü Khan took her by
inheritance.
The reason Ong Khan and Yesügäi Bahadur
were friends and became anda to each other is
1See above, text p. 119.
as follows. After the death of his father, Buyu-
ruq Khan, Ong Khan killed several of his own
brothers and nephews because of his dispute
with Qurjaquz over who was to rule. (Brothers:
Tai Temür Taishi;2 nephews: Buqa Temür.) Be-
cause of that, his uncle Gürkhan went to war
with him. Ong Khan was defeated and depart-
ed, wandering around for a time. Then he took
refuge with Yesügäi Bahadur, who helped him,
mounting an expedition, attacking Gürkhan,
and driving him to Qashin. Taking the king-
dom from him, he gave it to Ong Khan. With
such a debt of obligation, they became anda.
After that, when Ong Khan’s younger brother
Ärkä Qara saw that Ong Khan had killed his
brothers and taken over, he retreated and ﬂed
to Naiman territory to Inanch Khan. Inanch
Khan was kind to him, and after a while he
helped him by sending an army to recapture
the Kerayit nation and army from Ong Khan
and drive him away. Around that time Yesügäi
Bahadur died. Ong Khan passed through three
provinces and took refuge with the ruler of
Turkistan, the Gür Khan of the Qarakhitai. In
that province too, in the cities of the Uyghur
and Tangqut there was bulqaq (unrest), and he
was left wandering and weak. He was finally
reduced to a state in which he had only five
goats, with whose milk he had to make do, and
two or three camels with which he made a
meagre living. [363] After spending a time in
such a miserable state, he heard of the emer-
gence of the mighty Genghis Khan. 
Based on the friendship he had enjoyed with
Genghis Khan’s father, Yesügäi Bahadur, in
Luy Yil, the Year of the Dragon corresponding
to 592 [1196], he came to a place called
Güsägü[r] Na’ur,3 near Genghis Khan’s yurt, a
2See above, text p. 116, and Secret History §177,
where he is called Tai Temür Taisi.
3The Güse’ür Na’ur of the Secret History §151.

169

place he had been with Yesügäi Bahadur. He
dispatched two envoys, Taghai and Sü’ägäi, up
the Kerulen River to Genghis Khan to inform
him of his arrival. Genghis Khan mounted and
set out to greet him. When they met, Ong Khan
said, “I have become lean and hungry.”
Genghis Khan pitied him, took a qubchur
(levy) from the Mongols, and settled him in the
midst of his own gürä’än and ordus. That au-
tumn, when the two of them camped together
at the Selenga River in the valley called
Qara’un Qabchal, which means black forest,
because he and Yesügäi Bahadur had been
anda, he and Genghis Khan became like father
and son and banqueted each other. After con-
sultation they became allies and mounted in
the spring to attack the rest of the Yürkin clan,
which Genghis Khan had raided and plundered
before. A few of them were left, and they were
camped in a place called Tälädü-in Amasar.1
There they attacked them, hunting down and
seizing both Sacha Beki and Taichu. [364]
Genghis Khan launches an attack on
Toqto’a, the leader of the Märkit people,
and gives all the booty to Ong Khan.
In Moghai Yil, the Year of the Serpent corre-
sponding
to
593
[1197],
Genghis
Khan
launched an attack on Toqto’a, the commander
of the Märkit nation. Although the Märkit were
separate from the Mongols, they were power-
ful and strong. Battle was fought at Qaras
Müräs, on the Kerulen River near the Selenga
in a place called Mürüchä Sä’ül.2 He struck the
Uru’ut, a branch of the Märkit, killing and
plundering, and everything he took in that bat-
tle he gave to Ong Khan and his liege men. 
After that, in Yunt Yil, the Year of the Horse
corresponding to 594 [1198], when Ong Khan
1The Teletü (or Telegetü) Amasar of the Secret History
§136.
2The Mürüche Se’ül of the Secret History §177.
had regained his strength and army, he mount-
ed another expedition against the Märkit, this
time without consulting Genghis Khan. He
struck them at Buqara Kähärä,3 killing Toq-
to’a’s son Tögüz Beki and carrying off his two
daughters, Qutuqtai and Cha’arun, and round-
ing up Toqto’a’s brothers Qudu and Chila’un
along with their herds and folk. Of all that, he
gave nothing to Genghis Khan. Toqto’a Beki
ﬂed to a place called Barqujin. That place is
below the Selenga River, in the east of Mongo-
lia, and the tribe of Mongols who are called the
Barqut were so called because they lived in
Barqujin—they are known by this name even
today. [365]
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan mount
together and go to make war on Buyuruq
Khan, the brother of Tayang Khan, the
ruler of the Naiman.4
In Qonin Yil, the Year of the Sheep corre-
sponding to 595 [1199], Genghis Khan and
Ong Khan mounted to attack Buyuruq Khan of
the Naiman. Although at that time the ruler of
the Naiman was Tayang Khan, who was Buyu-
ruq Khan’s elder brother, Buyuruq Khan did
not obey him and had a separate army and
province. They were on very bad terms with
each other. 
Most of the Naiman rulers were called either
Güshlüg Khan or Buyuruq Khan. Güshlüg
means powerful, mighty, and commanding. 
The Naiman believe that Güshlüg had such
power over demons and fairies that he could
milk them and make kumiss out of it, and that
he had similar power over other animals and
wild beasts. After that, the Naiman comman-
ders said, “This is a sin,” and they forbade it;
therefore he stopped milking them.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Tayang Khan’s name was originally Tai
Buqa, but the rulers of Cathay gave him the ti-
tle Tai Wang, meaning son of a khan.1 In their
parlance khan is a title of middling rank. Since
the Mongols did not understand the language
of Cathay and had a different dialect, with us-
age they said Tayang, and that is how he came
to be known. Their father’s name was Inanch
Bilgä Bügü Khan. Inanch means to believe,
bilgä is a great name, and Bügü Khan was the
name of a mighty ruler in whom the Uyghurs
put great stock.
Tayang Khan’s son who was his successor
was Güshlüg Khan, whose story will be given
later. [366]
In short, Genghis Khan and Ong Khan set
out to make war on Buyuruq Khan. One of his
clans was in Qizil Bash near the Altai. They
seized and plundered those people. Buyuruq
Khan
had
retreated
to
the
province
of
Kämkämchi’üt, a tributary of Qirqiz territory.
One of his amirs, Yedi Tuqluq,2 came out to re-
connoiter. (In Turkish the name Yedi Tuqluq
means
someone
who
commands
seven
standards.) When Genghis Khan’s scouts saw
him, they put them to ﬂight, and they retreated,
headed into the hills. When they reached the
slope, Yedi Tuqluq’s saddle strap broke, and he
and the saddle fell. He was captured and taken
before Genghis Khan.
That winter one of Buyuruq Khan’s com-
manders was camped in that area. His name
was Kögsä’ü Sabraq. (Kögsä’ü means some-
one whose voice is hoarse from bronchial
coughing; Sabraq is a place name, after which
he was called.) Genghis Khan and Ong Khan
did battle once with that commander in a place
in Naiman territory called Bai Taraq Belchir.
(It is called Bai Taraq Belchir because in an-
1See note at text p. 129 above.
2He is the Yedi Tublugh of the Secret History §158.
cient times a request was made on behalf of a
Naiman ruler for the Öng’üt ruler’s daughter
named Bai Taraq. They met at that spot and
held the bridal banquet there. Belchir means a
grassy plain. They put the two together and
made the place name. Since the Mongols do
not understand the name, they call Bai Taraq
“Badtaraq.”3 [367]
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan launch an
attack on Kögsä’ü Sabraq, Buyuruq Khan’s
commander-in-chief; Ong Khan takes ﬂight
by night, and Kögsä’ü Sabraq reaches Ong
Khan’s brothers and plunders all their
herds and ﬂocks.
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan had come to-
gether in the place mentioned above in order to
do battle with Kögsä’ü Sabraq. Since they had
already done battle once, the next time both
sides arrayed their ranks before clashing. They
bivouacked by night, thinking to do battle the
next morning, and the soldiers slept in järgäs
(circles). Ong Khan had fires lit around his
camp, and by night he slipped away to a moun-
tain called Shinggir.4 When day broke Jamuqa
Sächän, a great commander from the Jajirat
clan of the Niru’un who had come with
Genghis Khan and was always known for his
disagreeableness and contentiousness, recog-
nized Ong Khan’s standard, galloped to him,
and said, “Khan! Khan! You have seen that my
aqa-ini resemble sparrows headed from sum-
mer pasture to winter pasture.” By this he
meant, “My relative Genghis Khan is decided
upon ﬂight, and I have always said, ‘I am your
sparrow.’ ” In this manner did he treacherously

called
it
