171

slander him. When Ubchiritai Gürin Bahadur
heard these words, he said, “It is not appropri-
ate to speak so disloyally among friends and
aqa-ini.” (Ubchiritai Gürin Bahadur was a
great commander of Ong Khan’s. Ubchiri is a
red fruit that grows in that region; women rub
it on their faces instead of rouge. Since Gürin
Bahadur’s face was red, they called him after
the fruit. They say it was [368] Genghis
Khan’s custom to make an oily wax from that
fruit and rub it on his mustache.)
When Ong Khan separated himself with that
stratagem and went home, the Märkit ruler
Toqto’a’s brother Qudu and Toqto’a’s son Chi-
la’un (of both of whom it has been previously
said that Ong Khan brought them into submis-
sion) both rebelled again with Ong Khan’s dis-
appearance and rejoined their own army. When
Genghis Khan witnessed this low action on the
part of Ong Khan, he said, “Ong Khan wanted
to cast me into the midst of calamity and fire
while he withdrew.” For that reason Genghis
Khan also pulled back to a place called Sa’ari
Kähär. Ong Khan reached a place called Tatal
Tuqula. His brothers Nilqa Sangun and Jagam-
bu followed in his wake with their riders and
retinues until they came to a place called Edär-
ü Altai, where there is a river and a thick for-
est. Kögsä’ü Sabraq came in pursuit with his
men, ambushing them in that place and pillag-
ing all their possessions, herds, and ﬂocks.
From there he went to the borders of Ong
Khan’s ulus and drove back all the folk, horse-
men, retinue, and animals he had [assembled]
in the vicinity of Tälädü Amasar. Nilqa Sangun
and Jagambu, both having managed to escape
with their lives, went to Ong Khan, who imme-
diately gave a contingent to his son Sangun
and sent them in pursuit of the enemy while
dispatching a messenger to Genghis Khan to
inform him of the situation and to ask for help.
[369]
Ong Khan requests assistance from Genghis
Khan to deal with the Naiman troops that
had driven his goods and herds off, and
Genghis Khan sends his four great
commanders to recapture Ong Khan’s
possessions and return them to him.
When Ong Khan was again in desperate
straits, he sent a messenger to Genghis Khan,
saying, “The Naiman have plundered my army
and people. I ask my son to assist me with the
Four Stalwarts (meaning Genghis Khan’s four
champion warriors). Maybe they can get my
army, possessions, and kingdom back.”
Genghis Khan dispatched the four, Bo’orchi
Noyan, Muqali Guyang, Boroghul Noyan, and
Chila’un Bahadur, with troops to help Ong
Khan. By the time they arrived, the Naiman
army had defeated Sangun, killed two of Ong
Khan’s great commanders, Tigit Quri and
Itürgän Buqu, and wounded Sangun’s horse in
the thigh so badly that he nearly fell and was
taken captive. The four commanders arrived
just as they were going down in defeat. 
When he set out, Bo’orchi Noyan had said,
“I do not have a jäbälägü (armored) horse.” He
requested one of Genghis Khan’s renowned
horses, one whose name was Chigi and de-
scriptions of which occur in several places.
Genghis Khan gave him the horse, saying,
“When you want it to run well, stroke its mane
with your whip, but don’t whip it.”
When Bo’orchi saw that Sangun’s horse was
wounded and on the verge of being captured,
he galloped in to save him and gave his own
horse to Sangun. When he mounted Chigi, no
matter how hard he whipped it, it wouldn’t go.
Sangun left him where he was and departed.
[370]
Suddenly
he
remembered
Genghis
Khan’s words and stroked the horse’s mane
with the whip. It shot off like a streak of light-
ning, enabling him to catch up with Sangun
and the army. Together they stationed their
172
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

liege men back and deployed the army before
attacking the enemy and putting them to ﬂight.
They took back Ong Khan’s soldiers, folk,
goods, and animals, gave them back to him,
and returned to Genghis Khan, safe and sound
and triumphant and victorious.
Ong Khan was very glad and highly grateful
for the assistance. “Once last year,” he said,
“having been defeated by my enemy, I went
hungry and naked to my ‘son’ Genghis Khan.
He kept me, filled my belly, and clothed my
naked men. How can I repay such debts, and
how can I express my thanks to you, my good
son?”
They say that later Ong Khan summoned
Bo’orchi Noyan one day to give him a reward.
He was on guard duty, having tied Genghis
Khan’s sable [insignium] around himself. “Ong
Khan has summoned me,” he said.
“Go,” said [Genghis Khan]. He untied the
sable, gave it to someone else, and departed.
Ong Khan gave him a suit of clothing and ten
golden munqurs. (The word munqur, originally
one of their technical terms, is what they call a
very large goblet, larger than a chelpä. These
days, however, since we do not understand the
term, we use it to designate a small goblet.)
Bo’orchi took the goblets, returned to Genghis
Khan, knelt, and showed them to him, saying,
“I have done wrong.”
“How so?” he asked.
“Because,” he said, “I left your sable and
went to Ong Khan for the sake of these goods.
If anything had gone wrong while it was my
turn as guard, or if anyone had tried to attack
you, I would have been at fault.”
Genghis Khan was pleased by these words
and [371] rewarded him, saying, “Take the
goblets. They are yours.”
After that, during the same winter, a report
arrived that Toqto’a, the ruler of the Märkit
who had ﬂed to Barqujin, had re-emerged.
Genghis Khan took counsel with Jochi Qasar,
realized that there was no truth to the rumor,
and paid no attention to the report.
Genghis Khan’s great quriltai with Ong
Khan at Sa’ari Kähär, and they ride against
the Tayichi’ut.
In the spring of Bichin Yil, the Year of the
Monkey corresponding to 596 [1199–1200], in
the vicinity of the place called Sa’ari Kähär,
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan met, formed an
assembly, and held a great quriltai. 
It is related that at the time they assembled
for the quriltai Ong Khan intended to seize
Genghis Khan. Usun Noyan of the Ba’arin car-
ried a bow into the banquet, and he had secret-
ed a knife in his boot. He was sitting between
Ong Khan and Genghis Khan and was eating
meat, looking back while he was speaking.
Ong Khan realized that his treachery had been
discovered, so he was not able to capture him.
For that reason Genghis Khan … the Ba’arin
tümän….
After the quriltai they mounted to ride to-
gether against the Tayichi’ut people. At that
time the chiefs and leaders of the Tayichi’ut
were Angqu Huquchu, Quril, Qudu’udar,1 and
other commanders who were their brothers and
relatives but of lower rank, such as Targhutai
Qiriltuq and the likes of him. [372] (Targhutai
is a name, and qiriltuq means envious.) Toq-
to’a Beki was the ruler of the Märkit nation,
and he had ﬂed to Barqujin. At that time he
sent his brothers Qudu and Orchang to the
Tayichi’ut to ask for assistance. The entire host
assembled in Onon, which is a plain in Mongo-
lia. Genghis Khan and Ong Khan attacked
them and did battle. The Tayichi’ut tribes were
defeated and ﬂed in rout. Genghis Khan’s
troops charged off in pursuit of Targhutai Qiril-
1For the text’sﻗـ
ﻮدردار, readـﻗ
ﻮدودارfor the Qudu’udar of
the Secret History §148.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1195–1203
173

tuq and Qudu’udar as far as the place called
Alangut Tudas. There they killed them both.
Angqu Huquchu and Toqto’a Beki’s brothers
Qudu and Orchang escaped together to Barqu-
jin. Quril went among the Naiman. Angqu
Huquchu means “of great wrath.” They say he
initiated the hostilities between Genghis Khan
and the Tayichi’ut.
The Qataqin and Salji’ut clans become
allies on oath, do battle with Genghis Khan
and Ong Khan, are defeated, and take ﬂight.
The Qataqin and Salji’ut clans had previous-
ly initiated hostilities with Genghis Khan, and
several years prior to this Genghis Khan and
Jamuqa Sächän had jointly sent an emissary to
them to make an alliance. It was a Mongol cus-
tom in olden days for most messages to be sent
in rhetorically ornate rhyming words and cryp-
tic expressions. The envoy’s message was
styled in that manner, and when he delivered it
they did not understand it. [373] The envoy
was a clever young man with presence of
mind, so, comprehending that they had not un-
derstood, he said, “The meaning of the words
is simple. Genghis Khan sends a message say-
ing that Mongol peoples who are strangers to
us have all become our friends and allies. It is
therefore fitting that we too, who are kin,
should be friends and allies and have a
jirghamishi (celebration).” Too envious and
mean to accept, and in disregard of the inviola-
bility of the envoy, they took from the kettle
sheep tripe (into which they mix blood and
cook into something like sausage) and threw it
in his face, cursing him and sending him back
in disgrace. For that reason hostilities broke
out.
Several times before that, they had done bat-
tle and allied themselves with the Tayichi’ut,
especially with the sons of Qada’an Taishi,
who were a branch of the Tayichi’ut, Tödä’ä,
Quril, and Targhutai Qiriltuq. They were fanat-
ically devoted to them and fought Genghis
Khan with enmity and hatred.
At that time, since most of the Tayichi’ut
tribes had gathered, and the Dörbän, Tatar, and
Qunqirat tribes had also joined them, they
swore an oath together. Among the Mongols
there is no greater oath, and it is made as fol-
lows. With a sword they strike down together a
stallion, a bull, a ram, and a dog and say, “O
God! O Heaven! O Earth! Hear that we swear
such an oath. Here are the males of these ani-
mals. If we do not keep our oath and break our
word, let us be as these animals are.” In this
manner they swore an oath that they would do
battle with Genghis Khan and Ong Khan.
As they were setting forth, Däi Sächän of the
Qunqirat, [374] the father of Alchu [Elchi Noy-
an], sent a message secretly to Genghis Khan,
saying, “Your enemies have sworn such an
oath and are headed out in your direction.”
When Genghis Khan learned of this, he mount-
ed with Ong Khan at Qutun Na’ur, which is
near the Onon, to repel those tribes. They met
at the place called Bu’ir Na’ur, stood opposite
each other, arrayed their ranks, and fought a
fierce battle. In the end Genghis Khan was tri-
umphant, and his enemies were crushed.
Jagambu has a falling-out with his brother
Ong Khan, takes counsel with some
commanders, and goes to the ruler of the
Naiman.
During the winter of that year Ong Khan de-
camped early from the Kerulen and went in
formation to Quba Qaya. Others also de-
camped and followed him. His brother, Jagam-
bu, spoke with his amirs Altun Ashuq, El
Qutur, El Qongqur, and Qulbari, and sent a
message, saying, “This elder brother of mine is
of a desultory temperament. He can’t stay in
one place. Out of meanness he has ruined all
his elder and younger brothers and forced them
to go into Qarakhitai territory. With such a
174
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

manner and disposition, he cannot let the peo-
ple rest in peace. What are we to do with
him?”
Altun Ashuq kept these words secret and
then divulged them to Ong Khan. Ong Khan
ordered El Qutur and El Qongqur to be seized
and chained. He had them brought in chains
into his tent, [375] where he loosed their bonds
and said to El Qutur, “When we were going to
Tangqut territory, what did we say? There you
spoke and made a promise that could not be
broken. How could I think as you do?” And he
spat in his face. The amirs who were present
also spat in his face. In that state Altun Ashuq
said, “I came into this council, but I cannot al-
low an attack on my ruler. I do not consider it
chivalrous to abandon him.”
After that, Ong Khan’s four great comman-
ders, El Qutur, El Qongqur, Narin Toghril, and
Alin Taishi, switched their allegiance to the
Naiman ruler, Ong Khan’s enemy, and left.
Jagambu sent a messenger to the Naiman ruler,
saying, “Altun Ashuq has squealed on me to
my brother Ong Khan and made me like a
piece of putrid liver or carrion in his eyes. I
have therefore detached my heart from him
and am coming to you.” Then they all went to-
gether to Tayang Khan, the ruler of the
Naiman.
Left without them, Ong Khan spent the win-
ter in Quba Qaya, and Genghis Khan spent the
winter on the borders of Cathaian territory in a
place called Chägächär.
Genghis Khan mounts to do battle with the
Märkit commander Ulaq Udur and some
Tayichi’ut and Tatar commanders who were
with him, and they are defeated.
After that, Genghis Khan assembled his
troops in one place and mounted to do battle
with some Märkit, Tayichi’ut, and Tatar com-
manders named Ulaq Udur of the Märkit,
Qirqan Taishi [376] of the Tayichi’ut, and
Chaqur and Kälbäkär of the Tatar, all of whom
were leaders and chiefs of consequence at the
time. Ulaq Udur was then the chief of his peers
and one of those who entertained notions of
ruling. 
An intelligent and wise old man of the
Baya’ut tribe who was around then said,
“Sacha Beki of the Yürkin Qiyat desires to
rule, but he is not up to it. It will likewise not
be possible for Jamuqa Sächän, who constantly
causes confusion among the people and en-
gages in trickery and disloyalty to further his
aims.
Jochi
Bara
(meaning
Jochi
Qasar,
Genghis Khan’s brother) also has this desire,
and he is renowned for his strength, skill, and
archery, but he will not attain rule either. Ulaq
Udur of the Märkit people, who is also ob-
sessed with ruling and has shown great power
and magnificence, will not attain the rule ei-
ther. This Tämüjin (meaning Genghis Khan)
possesses the form, manner, and talent to be
leader and monarch. He will attain the rule.”
He spoke these words in a Mongolian ayalghu
[song] with rhymes and rhetorical artifice. In
the end it turned out exactly as he said:
Genghis Khan became monarch and killed all
the others, aside from his brother, as will be
explained in the proper place for each one.
This digression has been introduced here only
because Ulaq Udur was mentioned. Let us re-
turn to the narrative.
When Genghis Khan set out to do battle with
this group, they met and fought in a place
called Talan Nämürgäs.1 Genghis Khan defeat-
ed and plundered them, but some managed to
escape and regroup. At that time Jochi Qasar
was separated from Genghis Khan, and Jäbä
was with him. [377] The Qunqirat tribe was in-
clined to join Genghis Khan and submit to
him, but Jäbä encouraged Jochi Qasar to drive
1The Dalan Nemürges of the Secret History §153.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1195–1203
175

the Qunqirat away, for which they changed
their minds and mistrusted him. For this reason
Genghis Khan was angry with Jochi Qasar and
took him to task.
The Qunqirat go to Jamuqa Sächän of the
Jajirat; together with the Ikiräs, Qataqin,
and others, they elect him Gür Khan; he
sets out to do battle with Genghis Khan,
who is warned of their approach and defeats
them.
After that, in Tavuq Yil, the Year of the
Rooster that began in Jumada I 597 [February
1201], after the Qunqirat had been attacked
and made homeless, they went to Jamuqa
Sächän. They held council with the Ikiräs,
Qorolas, Dörbän, Tatar, Qataqin, and Salji’ut,
assembled at the Käm River,1 and raised Ja-
muqa as Gür Khan. (The term gür khan means
emperor of rulers and kings.)
When he became the Gür Khan, they enter-
tained notions of launching a campaign against
Genghis Khan. Their council and decision
were overheard by a man named Qoridai. He
then went to the tent of one of his brothers-in-
law, Märkitäi of the Qorolas clan by name, on
some personal business and related the news to
him. Märkitäi said to Qoridai, “You must go
tell Genghis Khan.” He gave him a gray horse
of his own, which had a wart on its ear, to
mount and go.
“If you’re going to send me,” Qoridai said,
“at least give me a reliable steed.” He did not
him give one. Qoridai got on the nag and set
out. [378] Along the way he came across a
gürä’än (meaning a troop encamped in a cir-
cle), the chief of which was Qo[ri]lan2 Bahadur
of the Hoyin clan (meaning the “forest peo-
1This “Käm” River is the Kän, or Gän, an afﬂuent of
the Argun River in western Manchuria. See Hambis,
“Notes sur Käm,” p. 285.
2On text p. 164 the name occurs as Qorilan.
ple”) of the Tayichi’ut tribes. It was night when
he arrived, and a man named Qara Märkitäi of
the Qorolas clan and his liege men were on
guard duty in the gürä’än. They seized him
and recognized him. Since Qara Märkitäi was
sympathetic
to
Genghis
Khan,
he
helped
Qoridai, gave him a qali’un (brown with black
mane and tail) stallion, and set him on his way,
saying, “If you want to escape the foe, you can
get away on this horse and nobody can catch
you. If anybody gets away from you, you can
catch up with him. Trust implicitly in this
horse, mount, and go!”
Qoridai set out, and along the way he was
met by a group that was taking a white tent to
Jamuqa. They attacked him, trying to capture
him, but he galloped away so fast that he dis-
appeared from view. When he reached Genghis
Khan and related the news, Genghis Khan im-
mediately mounted to do battle. He did battle
with Jamuqa and defeated him in a place called
Yedi Qurqan. The Qunqirat tribe also surren-
dered there. 
After that, in the spring of Noqai Yil, the
Year of the Dog beginning in Jumada I 598
[January 1202], Genghis Khan set out from the
banks of the river known as Ulqui Shilügäljit
to do battle with the Anchi Tatar and the
Chaghan Tatar. He ordered that no one should
take booty and that after the battle and foe had
been dispensed with, booty could be taken and
divided equally. All agreed to this, but Näkün
Taishi’s son Quchar, Qutula Qa’an’s son Altan,
and Genghis Khan’s uncle Daritai Otchigin
[379] broke their word and started taking booty
before the battle was over. This displeased
Genghis Khan, so he dispatched Qubilai and
Jäbä to take the booty from them. This angered
them, and they lost their affection and began
covertly to take Ong Khan’s part. In the end
they too were instrumental in creating a rift be-
176
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

tween Genghis Khan and Ong Khan, fought
Genghis Khan, and were finally all killed.
An alliance is made among the Naiman
ruler’s brother Buyuruq Khan, the Märkit
ruler Toqto’a Beki, and the Tatar, Qataqin,
and other tribes; they launch an attack on
Genghis Khan and are destroyed in a
snowstorm.
After that, in the autumn of the above-men-
tioned Year of the Dog, an alliance was made
among the brother of the Naiman ruler, Buyu-
ruq Khan, the Märkit ruler Toqto’a Beki, and
the Dörbän, Tatar, Qataqin, and Salji’ut tribes
under the leadership of Aquchu Bahadur1 and
Qutuqa Beki, the ruler of the Oyirat. These
were they who had repeatedly done battle with
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan and then ﬂed to
take refuge with the above-mentioned Buyuruq
Khan. Together they mounted a huge army and
headed off to do battle with Genghis Khan and
Ong Khan. 
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan had stationed
their scouts at a place called Chägächär Moun-
tain and Chi’urqai.2 One of the scouts returned
from there, saying that the Naiman army was
approaching. [380] Genghis Khan and Ong
Khan decamped from Ulqui Shilügäljit and
were headed for the Öngü, which was the yurt
of Na’achar Aqa in the vicinity of Qara’un
Jidun. The Öngü is like Alexander’s Wall con-
structed along the frontier of the realm of
Cathay. Ong Khan’s son Sangun was in the tip.
He came to the hill on the other side of which
one reached Öngü. Scarcely had he reached it
when Buyuruq Khan said, “They are Mongol
people. Let us scatter them all at once.” He had
1This is the A’uchu Ba’atur of the Secret History §141,
also named A’uchu on text p. 184 above.
2These are the Chegcher and Chiqurqu of the Secret
History §142, which are mentioned several times
together.
sent out as vanguard a group composed of his
own soldiers and of the Mongol tribes who
were with him [under the command of]
Aquchu Bahadur of the Qataqin clan and Toq-
to’a Beki’s brother Qudu of the Märkit. The
vanguard met Sangun and began to fight, but
before battle was enjoined they pulled back.
Sangun also set out and entered Öngü.
They had done jadalmishi so that a snow-
storm would come. (Jadalmishi is as follows:
they recite a charm and put different kinds of
stones in water, and it creates a great rainfall.)
The snowstorm turned back on them, and they
wanted to withdraw and get out across the
hills. They dismounted in a place called Köy-
itän.3 It is well known that at that place Buyu-
ruq Khan of the Naiman and the Mongol tribes
that were allied with him lost the use of their
hands and legs on account of the extreme cold,
and the wind and darkness were so intense that
many men and animals fell off the cliffs and
mountainsides to their destruction.
Genghis Khan and Ong Khan camped on the
edge of an aral [island]. At that time Jamuqa
and the group that had elevated him to be Gür
Khan had joined Buyuruq Khan. Despite this
situation he was inclined once more toward
Genghis Khan, so he raided the tents of the
people that had elected him ruler and went
over to Genghis Khan. [381] Genghis Khan
and Ong Khan left Öngü and spent the winter
at a wintering site known as Abji’a Kötägär.4
That site was the Qunqirat’s winter pasture,
and when battle was done between Qubilai
Qa’an and Ariq Bökä they fought at that place.
The ground there is waterless chöl [desert], and
the inhabitants make do with snow.
3The Battle of Köyiten is well known (Secret History
§143).
4Abji’a Ködeger is mentioned twice in the Secret His-
tory §§187, 191.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1195–1203
177

That winter Genghis Khan requested San-
gun’s sister, Cha’ur Beki, for his eldest son,
Jochi Khan. Ong Khan requested Genghis
Khan’s daughter Füjin Beki for Sangun’s son
Tusaqa,1 but [neither match] took place, which
occasioned rancor between them. 
Jamuqa goes to Ong Khan’s son Sangun
and causes him to break with Genghis
Khan; they and other tribes ally, and
Genghis Khan does battle with them in
Qalajin Älät.
Since Jamuqa Sächän was basically jealous
of and malevolent toward Genghis Khan, as
well as being treacherous and evil, he now
went to Sangun and said, “My elder brother
Genghis Khan is in cahoots with Tayang Khan,
who is your enemy. He is constantly sending
envoys to him.” He insinuated this thought into
Sangun’s mind, and he was so gullible he
thought it was true and made a pact with Ja-
muqa, saying, “When Genghis Khan mounts,
our soldiers will come in from the ﬂanks and
attack him.
As
has
been
mentioned,
since
Genghis
Khan’s uncle Daritai Otchigin and his cousins
Qutula Qa’an’s son Altan and Näkün Taishi’s
son Quchar had been angered by Genghis
Khan over the matter of the booty he had taken
from them when they broke their word during
the battle with the Tatar, [382] they too joined
the conspiracy. Taghai Qulatai2 of the Mangqut
and Moqur Qauran, the leader of the Hadargin
clan of the Niru’un, also conspired with this
group to attack Genghis Khan.
Sangun had then decamped and was headed,
separately from his father, to a place called
Älät. He sent one of his commanders, Sayiqan
Tödä’än by name, as a messenger to his father
to make it so that Genghis Khan and his sol-
1In the Secret History §165 he is Tusaqa.
2On text p. 196 above, Taghai Qulqai.
diers would mingle with Sangun and his men
when they camped, thus giving him a chance
to attack. He took counsel with Jamuqa, who
called Sangun anda and was anda to Genghis
Khan. Through the above-mentioned messen-
ger he sent a message saying, “This man who
claims to be your friend and supporter, the son
of Ö’älün Ekä (meaning Genghis Khan), has
contemplated such treachery. We are consider-
ing making a preemptive strike and attacking
him.”
Ong Khan, thinking these words extremely
unlikely and highly displeasing, said, “Jamuqa
is a blatherer, of no consequence, and untrust-
worthy. His words should not be listened to.”
Several days then passed, and Genghis Khan
became separated from them and camped far-
ther away until the next spring of the Year of
the Pig, corresponding to 599 [1203], when
Sangun sent a messenger to his father, saying
with all petulance, “Intelligent men who are
far-sighted are saying such things. How can
you not listen?”
When Ong Khan heard this insistence, he
said, “It was through him that we became
somebody. He has helped us many times, risk-
ing his possessions and his head. [383] How
can one think of attacking him? What can I
say? The more I tell you no, the more you
refuse to listen. In my old age I say let my
bones rest in one place. Now that you hear, if
you can do this thing, God willing you will
prove capable.” This he said and became very
sad.
After that, they sneaked into the meadow
where Genghis Khan was camped and burned
it in such a way that he did not know it was
they who had done it. Then they plotted, say-
ing, “Once before, he asked for our daughter
Cha’ur Beki for his son Jochi, but we did not
give her. Now let us send word and say, ‘We
will give our daughter. Come for the banquet.’
178
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Let them give a buljar (ceremonial engage-
ment meal) for us to eat. When he comes we
will seize him.” To this end they dispatched
Bundai Qijat. (In the Naiman language and that
of some other Mongols a bökä’ül is called
qisat, which the Mongols call qijat.) 
When the message was delivered, Genghis
Khan set out with two liege men. Along the
way he stopped to sleep at the tent of Münglig
Echigä of the Qongqotan, the father of Täb
Tängri. The next morning he took counsel with
Münglig Echigä, who said, “Our animals are
lean. Let’s fatten them up. Let’s send one per-
son for the banquet but not to partake of the
buljar.” 
Genghis Khan sent the messenger back and
went home. 
After that, Ong Khan and Sangun planned to
mount an attack on Genghis Khan while he
was off guard. One of Ong Khan’s great com-
manders, Yäkä Chärän by name, went home
and said to his wife, Alaq Yidun, “If somebody
goes to inform Genghis Khan of what has tak-
en place, he will reward him handsomely.”
“I hope nobody hears the nonsense you say
or gives it credence,” his wife said.
One of Yäkä Chärän’s herdsmen, Qishliq by
name, had come to bring milk. [384] Standing
outside, he heard this exchange and said to his
servant Badai, “Did you hear what they are
saying?”
Chärän’s son Narin Köhän was standing out-
side, filing arrows. He heard the conversation
between his father and mother and said, “May
your tongues be cut out! What is this you are
saying? What secrets are you divulging?”
Badai comprehended and said to Qishliq,
“Now we know what’s up.” Immediately they
went to inform Genghis Khan. (The group of
tarkhans who are now known, Khwarazmi
Tarkhan, Aqutai Tarkhan, and Sadaq Tarkhan,
are all descended from Qishliq and Badai.
From that time until now, they and their clans
have been tarkhans and great amirs for this
reason.)
After that, when Genghis Khan understood
perfectly what the words meant, he stopped in
the place called Aral and ordered his tents to
move toward the Silji’üljüt hills. He sent Jälmä
as scout to Mau Ündür behind the mountain.
Ong Khan was headed for the front side of
Mount Mau Ündür, to a place where red wil-
low trees were growing, which the Mongols
call Hula’an Buruqat. Two of Alchidai Noyan’s
liege men, Taichu and Chigitäi Yadir, had taken
the horses out in herds. They saw the enemy
and immediately galloped to inform Genghis
Khan, who was off guard in Qalajin. At once
Genghis Khan mounted, and when the sun had
risen the length of a lance, the armies of both
sides drew up their ranks opposite each other.
Since Genghis Khan’s forces were few, while
Ong Khan’s were numerous, he took counsel
with his commanders. “What are we to do?” he
asked. One of the commanders who was there
was Kähätäi Noyan of the Uru’ut, [385] and
another was Quyildar Sächän of the Mangqut,
who were related to each other. (When the
Uru’ut and Mangqut clans had gotten angry
and left Genghis Khan to join the Tayichi’ut,
these two had not rebelled and continued to
perform
valiantly
in
his
service.)
When
Genghis Khan took counsel, Kähätäi Noyan
stroked his horse’s mane with his whip and sat
pensive and hesitant, not giving a ready an-
swer. Quyildar Sächän was Genghis Khan’s
anda, and he said, “Khan anda of mine, let me
go and plant my standard behind the enemy on
the hill called Köyitän and thus show my valor.
If I die, I have two or three sons. Genghis
Khan will take charge of caring for them and
bringing them up.”
___ of Mangqut lineage also said, “All this is
obscuring [our real purpose]. Let us charge
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1195–1203
179

them, trusting in God, and see what lot God
has in store for us.”
In short, Quyildar galloped as he had said,
and God helped him and made a way for him
to pass through the foe and plant his standard
on Köyitän Hill. Genghis Khan and the other
commanders attacked in concert, throwing into
rout the Jirqin clan of the Kerayit, Ong Khan’s
best
troop. After
that,
they
defeated
the
Tongqayit, also of the Kerayit, and then Qori
Silemün Taishi, one of Ong Khan’s great com-
manders. They were about to kill Ong Khan’s
sentries and guards when Sangun charged and
was struck in the cheek by an arrow. With that,
the Kerayit’s dominance was diminished and
they stopped, for otherwise there would have
been fear of total disaster.
This battle is well known and quite famous
among the Mongols, and they still tell of it as
the Battle of Qalajin Älät. [386] The ground is
on the frontier of Cathaian territory, and be-
cause of their multitudes [Genghis Khan] was
unable to stay there. When he withdrew, most
of the army deserted him. He went to Baljiu-
na,1 a place where there were a few small
springs, insufficient for them and their animals
too. Therefore they squeezed water from the
mud to drink. After that they emerged from
there and went to places that will be men-
tioned.
The group that was with Genghis Khan at
that time in Baljiuna were few, and they are
known as the Baljunatu, meaning that they
were there with him and did not desert him.
Their rights were therefore firm, and they held
precedence
over
the
others.
When
they
emerged from there, some of the soldiers and
tribes regrouped around him, as will be told.
1Lake Baljiuna, the Baljuna of the Secret History, still
exists. It is, according to Poppe (“Geographical Names,”
p. 40), what is now called Озеро Балезино at 51° N,
113° 35′ E in the Chita region of the Russian Federation.
Genghis Khan sends a message to Tärgä
Amäl, the commander of the Qunqirat, and
he submits with all his followers.2
After that, when Genghis Khan was returning
from the Battle of Qalajin Älät, [his men] as-
sembled in a place at a river called the Or Nu’u
Mörän in the vicinity of Kältägäi Qada,3 which
is a river and large cliff—it is the place where
Taghachar’s tribe is. A count of the soldiers
was held. They numbered four thousand six
hundred. Decamping from there, they went to-
ward the Qalqa River in two divisions, two
thousand three hundred with Genghis Khan on
one side of the river, and two thousand three
hundred with the Uru’ut-Manqut clans on the
other side.
As they were headed downhill they reached
the vicinity of the tents of Tärgä Amäl,4 who
was one of the commanders and chiefs of the
Qunqirat. [387] They sent an envoy to him to
say, “Prior to now we were anda-quda, and
you have maintained a proper avuncular rela-
tionship.5 If you submit, we too will be peace-
able and friendly. If you are hostile, we too
will be hostile.” When they returned a friendly
answer
and
surrendered,
on
this
march
Genghis Khan camped near a lake and stream
called Tünggä Na’ur and Quruqa Qoroqan in
order to rest and recuperate.
2This section corresponds to §176 of the Secret
History.
3This place is described as Qalqa-yin Or Nu’u-yin
Keltegei Qada (‘Keltegei Qada of [Mount] Or Nu’u of
the Qalqa [River]’) in the Secret History §175.
4In the Secret History §176, Terge and Amel are two
persons, but here they have been conﬂated into one.
5The Persian word used here,ﻮﰃ ـﻟﺎـﺧkhālū’ī, is the rela-
tionship of a maternal uncle. It is the exact equivalent of
the Mongolian naqachu plus the Persian abstraction ī on
text p. 74 above. Since Genghis Khan’s mother was
from the Olqunu’ut of the Qunqirat, the Qunqirat are re-
ferred to as maternal uncles.
180
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Genghis Khan sends an emissary to Ong
Khan, reminding him of the obligations he
owed him.
After that, Genghis Khan assigned a man
named [H]arqai Je’ün of the Ildürgin to go to
Ong Khan as emissary and deliver a message
saying, “At this time I have camped in Tünggä
Na’ur and Quruqa Qoroqan. The grass here is
fine, and the geldings have grown fat. Now, O
khan my father, aforetime your uncle Gürkhan
said to you, ‘You did not allow me the place of
my elder brother, Buyuruq Khan, and you an-
nihilated my two brothers Tai Temür Taishi and
Buqa Temür.’ Therefore he chased you away,
sent you into the narrows called Qara’un
Qabchal, and surrounded you there. From there
you emerged with several men. Who got you
out if not my father who rode on military expe-
ditions with you? A man of the Tayichi’ut
named Udur Qunan and another named Buqaji
went with you along with a few men, and from
there [my father] went, passing through a place
and a plain called Qara Buqa [388] and cross-
ing Qulatan Tülängütäi, headed up the qabchal
(defile). Gürkhan was at a place called Qurban
Täläsüt. He drove [Gürkhan] out of there and
put him to rout. It is not known whether he
went forth with twenty men or thirty. When he
went into Qashin territory he never came out
again and was seen no more. My late father
took the kingship from Gürkhan and gave it to
you, and therefore you became anda with my
father. I call you ‘khan-father’ for the same
reason. Of all the favors for which you are in
my debt, this is the first. 
“Another time, O khan father of mine, when
you had become covered and hidden beneath
the clouds, and where the sun sets you were
nowhere to be found, in the midst of Cha’uqut
territory I called out in a loud voice to Jagam-
bu Anda. I motioned by taking off my hat, and
I did dalaimishi, i.e. I waved my hands. There-
by I brought Jagambu Anda, and when I
brought him he sat in ambush in repayment of
my enmity. Another time a troop1 of the Märkit
tribe put Jagambu Anda to ﬂight. In chivalry
and manliness I rescued him. Why would
someone who brings Jagambu Anda from
Cha’uqut territory (meaning the territory of
Cathay) and saves him from the hands of the
Märkit want to kill him? For your sake I killed
my elder brother and destroyed my younger
brother. If anyone asks who they are, they are
Sacha Beki, who was my elder brother, and
Taichu Qori, who was my younger brother.
This is another favor you owe me.
“Another time, O khan father of mine, you
came to me like the sun emerging from behind
a cloud, like a fire slowly coming out. [389] I
did not leave you hungry until midday but fed
you all. I did not leave you naked for a month
but clothed you all. If anyone asks, ‘What does
he mean?’ then say, ‘In the place of the hill of
Qadiqliq, that is the place where there was ar-
row wood, behind the place called Mürüchä
Sä’ül,2 I did battle and raided the Märkit peo-
ple, seizing all their herds, ﬂocks, tents, camps,
and fine clothing and giving them to you.’ As I
have said, I did not let noon go by before alle-
viating your hunger, and I did not let a month
pass before clothing your nakedness—these
deeds constitute the third obligation I hold over
you.
“Another time, after that, when the Märkit
people were in the plain of Buqara Kähärä, we
sent an emissary to Toqto’a Beki to spy and
gather information. When there was an oppor-
tunity you did not stop and wait for me. You
galloped away before me and took captive
Toqto’a Beki’s and his brother’s wives and
Qutuqtai Khatun and Cha’arun Khatun. You
1Reading ﺳـﭙﻪ (sipah) for the text’s ﺷـﺒﻪ.
2The Mürüche Se’ül of the Secret History §177.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1195–1203
181

gave me nothing. After that, when we rode
against the Naiman and drew up our battle
lines opposite them at Baidaraq Belchir, you
captured both Qudu and Chila’un. They sur-
rendered to you and then escaped with their
soldiers and folk. Then Kögsä’ü Sabraq made a
taplamishi (encounter), staged a raid with the
Naiman army, and plundered your folk. At that
time I sent Bo’orchi, Muqali, Boroghul, and
Chila’un, all four, and when I had recovered
your ulus I gave it back to you. This is the
fourth favor your owe me.
“Another time, from there we came together
at the Qara River, there where Hula’an Nu’ut
is,1 near the mountain named Jorqal Qun, [390]
and there we made a pact that if a snake with
fangs and teeth brought its fangs and teeth be-
tween us, we would not part from one another
until we had spoken with tongues, mouth, and
teeth, that is, if anyone were to speak words of
selfish interest or otherwise between us, we
would not give it credence, get angry, or part
ways until we had come together and investi-
gated it.2 Now we have not come together to
investigate and verify the words spoken to cre-
ate discord between us, yet you have parted be-
lieving them and relying on them.
“Another, O khan father of mine. After that, I
ﬂew like a falcon to Mount Jurqu. I left Bu’ir
Na’ur and caught cranes whose feet are bound
and which are gray in color. If you ask which
they were, they were the Dörbän and Tatar
folk. Another time I became a gray falcon,
passed through Kökä Na’ur, caught blue cranes
with blue feet for you, and gave them to you. If
you ask which they are, they are the Qataqin,
1The Hula’anu’ud Bolda’ud of the Secret History
§177.
2Cf. Secret History §177: “If, by a serpent with teeth, /
We are provoked [into dissension], / Let us not yield
ourselves unto his provocations. / Let us believe [only
when] verifying by teeth and by mouth.”
Salji’ut, and Qunqirat people, the very ones
with whose help you now threaten me. This is
another of the favors for which you are indebt-
ed to me.
“Another thing, O khan father of mine. What
have you done that I should be obliged to you?
What profit has accrued to me from you? I
hold all these obligations over you, and you
have profited greatly from me. O khan father
of mine, why do you threaten me? Why do you
not rest in ease and comfort? Why do you not
let your daughters-in-law and sons sleep in
peace? I, your son, have never said that my
portion is small and I want more, or that it is
bad and I want better. When one of a cart’s two
wheels breaks it cannot travel. If an ox gets
hurt, and the driver is alone and sets out having
put his load on the ox, a robber will steal [the
cart]. If he doesn’t take the ox and leaves it
with the cart, [391] it will sicken and die. If
one of a cart’s two wheels is broken and the ox
tries to pull it, it cannot. If it exerts itself to
pull it uphill, the ox’s neck will be chafed, and
it will get restless, jump around, and exhaust it-
self. Like a cart with two wheels, I was one
wheel of your cart.” This was the message
Genghis Khan sent to Ong Khan. 
The message Genghis Khan sent separately
to Altan and Qucha[r] was as follows:
“You two thought you would kill me, cast me
on the black earth, and leave me or else hide
me beneath the ground. Before now, the first
time we said even to Bartan Bahadur’s sons
and to Sacha and Taichu, ‘How can our place,
the Onon Mörän, be without a lord?’ I strove
much, and I said, ‘You become monarch and
khan.’ You did not accept. I had no choice but
to say to you, Quchar, ‘You are the son of
Näkün Taishi. Among us, you become khan.’
You were not willing. To you, Altan, I said,
‘You are the son of Qutula Qa’an. He reigned.
Now you too be the ruler.’ You were not will-
182
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ing either. When you insisted, saying to me,
‘You become khan,’ I became khan on your ad-
vice, and I said, ‘I will not allow the dwelling
place of our forefathers and ancestors to be ef-
faced, and I will not let their customs be lost or
fall into abeyance.’ I thought that since I was
ruler and leader of the army into many territo-
ries, it was necessary to bind to me by promise
those attached to me. I took many herds,
ﬂocks, and tents and people’s wives and chil-
dren, and I gave them to you. I encircled prey
in the plains for you, and I drove prey from the
mountains toward you. You two, Altan and
Quchar, do not allow anyone to camp at the
head of the Three Rivers.”1
Then Genghis Khan said, “Say to Toghril,
‘My little brother [392] Toghril, you are the
slave of my forefathers’ and ancestors’ gate. I
call you “little brother” because the bo’ol
(slave) Nögtä,2 who was your father’s grandfa-
ther, was brought in captivity by both Charaqa
Lingqum and Tumina Khan. The son of Nögtä
Bo’ol was Sübägäi Bo’ol. The son of Sübägäi
Bo’ol was Kököchü Qirsa’u, and the son of
Kököchü Qirsa’u was Yägäi Qongtaqar, and
his son is you, Toghril. Whose people do you
want to seize? If you seize even my people, Al-
tan and Quchar will not give them to you and
will not allow it. If the father the khan does not
1Cf. Secret History §179: “Suffer ye not to be pitched
by any one at the head of the Three Rivers” (explained
in note as “the Kelüren, the Tule, and the Onon which
issue from Mount Burqan Qaldun”).
2JTK hasﻪ ــﮐﺘﻮـﻧ(Nögtä); Secret History §180 has Oghda.
The discrepancy can be explained by assuming a writ-
ten, Uyghur-script Mongolian source common to both
the Secret History and the Jami‘u’t-tawarikh. The JT’s
Nögtä would derive from noikde-- in Uyghur script; the Se-
cret History’s Oghda would derive from FoGde--. In the
Uyghur script initial no and o are written the same ex-
cept for a dot. A confusion between g and gh was not
uncommon in Uyghur script during the Mongol period.
JTRM’s ﺋﻮﮔﺘﻪ should be disregarded.
drink from that blue3 goblet, you, my little
brother Toghril, how much can you drink?4
Now, Altan and Quchar, you both did liege ser-
vice in accompanying my good father. You do
not let it be said that before now anything that
was done was through Ja’ut Quri,5 but make it
such that you remember me when something
goes wrong. The Qa’an my father tires easily
and is inconstant. He has grown tired of one
like me. He will grow tired of you too. Now
that you are in his retinue you must enjoy life
this year. You may not be alive by next
winter.’ ”
After that, Genghis Khan said, “O khan fa-
ther of mine, send messengers, and when you
send them, it would be better if you sent both
Altan Ashuq and Qulbari. Otherwise, send one
of the two. On the day of battle Muqali Baha-
dur’s black gelding remained behind with sad-
dle and silver bridle. Send those with them
also. If Sangun Anda does not send both Bilgä
Beki and Tödö’än, let him send one of them.
Let Jamuqa Anda also send two messengers,
and let both Chula and Qachi’un also send
messengers, and let Achiq and Shirün both
send messengers. Otherwise let Buqa and Tayir
also send messengers. Let Altan and Quchar
both send messengers. When the messengers
come, if I take the low road, let them seek me
at Bu’ir Na’ur above the river. If I go by the
back road, [393] I will go out via Qabqar Qal-
tuqan and go down via the Three Rivers. Let
them come and seek me in those places.”

note.  JTRM omits the word.

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1195–1203
183

When the messengers arrived and repeated
these words to Ong Khan, he said, “He is right.
He has been dealt with unjustly, but my son
Sangun knows how to reply.”
Sangun replies to Genghis Khan’s
messengers, saying, “We will do battle, and
whichever of us emerges will be khan.”
Sangun said, “When was he wont to call me
anda? He was wont to call me tohto’a bö’ä.1
When was he wont to say ‘khan father’? He
was wont to say kidu’achi äbügän.2 When
were we wont to send messengers? We shall do
battle. If he is victorious, our people will be
his. If we are victorious, his people will be
ours.”
Having said this, he ordered his two great
commanders, Bilgä Beki and Tödö’än, saying,
“We mount with the army. Raise the standards,
sound the drums, bring in the steeds for us to
mount, and let us set forth against Genghis
Khan!” 
The chieftain of the Qunqirat who drank
the water at Baljiuna surrenders and joins
Genghis Khan, and other tribal leaders
submit to him.
When Genghis Khan sent an envoy to Ong
Khan, he forced into submission all those who
were the greatest of the Qunqirat tribe and
went to Baljiuna. The Ikiräs clan chased out
Butu of the Ikiräs clan, and he was coming
from them in defeat. At that time he joined
Genghis Khan, and they stayed there together
and drank the water of Baljiuna. [394]
1The Mongolian words of the Secret History §181,
“tohto’a bo’e” (‘the sorcerer Toghto’a’). Senggüm’s
words were, “Was he not wont to say, ‘The sorcerer
Toghto’a walketh, having joined [unto himself] the tail
of a Sartaghchin sheep’?”
2The words of the Secret History §181, kidu’aci ebu-
gen (‘old man killer’).
At that time Jochi Qasar was separated from
Genghis Khan, and his wife and child were
raided by Ong Khan’s soldiers at Qara’un
Jidun, and he took ﬂight and was coming. He
was so destitute that he had to boil carrion and
boots and drink it. To eat he had only a ram’s
neck. He reached Genghis Khan at Baljiuna.
After the previous battle he had fought with
Genghis Khan at Qalajin Älät, Ong Khan went
to Qit Qulqat Älät.
Genghis Khan’s uncle Daritai Otchigin and
Altan Je’ün, the son of Genghis Khan’s fa-
ther’s uncle Qutula Qa’an, and Quchar Beki
the son of Genghis Khan’s uncle Näkün Taishi,
and Jamuqa of the Jajirat, and the Ba’arin clan,
and Sü’ägäi, and Toghril of the offspring of
Nögtä Bo’ol, and Taghai Qulaqai, who was
called Taghai Kähärin of the Mangqut tribe,
and Qutuqut of the Tatar nation—all these unit-
ed and held a council, saying, “Let’s launch a
surprise attack on Ong Khan and become
rulers ourselves. Let us not join either Ong
Khan or Genghis Khan, and let us not pay any
attention to them.” [News of] this council of
theirs reached Ong Khan, who mounted to at-
tack and raid them. For that reason Daritai
Otchigin and the ___ clan of the Ba’arin, the
Saqayit clan, [some] of the Kerayit, and the
Qujin clan surrendered, became obedient to
Genghis Khan, and joined him. Altan Je’ün,
Quchar Beki, and Qutu Temür of the Tatar
went to Tayang Khan of the Naiman. [395]
Genghis Khan mounts at the Onon River to
do battle with Ong Khan, who is defeated
and then killed in Naiman territory by Qori
Sübächi, one of Tayang Khan’s
commanders; Sangun is also killed by Qilich
Qara, a commander of the Qalach clans;
Genghis Khan mounts the throne.
In the summer of the Year of the Pig, corre-
sponding to 599 [1203], Genghis Khan was
drinking the water of Baljiuna. In the autumn
184
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

of that year he left there and assembled his fol-
lowers at the Onon River. Setting out to fight
Ong Khan, he dispatched Qali’udar of the
Jä’üriyät and Cha’urqan of the Uriangqat, both
of whom were known to be attached as liege
men to Jochi Qasar, as emissaries to Ong Khan
to speak on Jochi Qasar’s behalf. They were
coached to say, “We were sent by Jochi Qasar,
and he says, ‘I have had enough of my elder
brother. Who can stand to see his retinue? As
much as I have wanted to find a way out, I
haven’t been able to find one to join him. I
have heard that my wife and son are with the
khan my father. For a long time my home has
been made of twigs and grass, and my pillow
has been of mud clods and stone. I sleep alone,
without friend or intimate. I place my reliance
on the khan my father and am sending these
messengers in secret to him to ask for my clan,
soldiers, wife, and child. When I reach my
family I will surrender and be obedient and en-
ter with correct heart.’ ”
Since the messengers were known to belong
to Jochi Qasar, and Ong Khan knew them of
old, he did not suspect either that Genghis
Khan had sent them as a trick or that he had
coached them. [396] Since Genghis Khan was
in dire straits at that time, and Jochi Qasar was
wandering around aimlessly, he imagined for
certain that the words contained nothing but
truth and sincerity. He approved of the contents
and treated the messengers with honor before
sending them back. He sent one of his liege
men, Itürgän by name, along with them. By
way of oath, he put a bit of blood in some bark
[of the tree from which] they derive glue and
sent it with them, for such is the custom of the
Mongols to swear oaths to each other on blood.
The three set out together and were traveling
along the road, and Genghis Khan was coming
from the other direction with his army to attack
Ong Khan. Suddenly Qali’udar’s eyes fell
upon Genghis Khan’s standard. He thought, “I
hope Itürgän doesn’t see it too and run away,”
for his horse was very fine. Immediately he got
off his horse, picked up his horse’s leg on the
pretext that a stone had gotten caught in its
hoof and was making it lame. He had Itürgän
dismount and said to him, “Hold my horse so I
can clean its hoof out.” Itürgän took the horse’s
leg while Qali’udar was cleaning the horse’s
hoof with a pick in order to keep Itürgän
distracted. 
Suddenly Genghis Khan arrived with his sol-
diers. He spoke to Itürgän and sent him to
Jochi Qasar since in that battle too, his belong-
ings having been pillaged, he was still without
a mount. Genghis Khan sent the two messen-
gers forward to reconnoiter. That night he did
not dismount but kept riding until he caught up
with Ong Khan at a place called Jäje’er Ündür. 
There they did battle, and Ong Khan was de-
feated. [Genghis Khan] seized the entirety of
the Kerayit kingdom and army. Ong Khan and
his son Sangun, in rout, got away with a few
men, and Ong Khan was saying along the way,
[397] “I have been separated from one from
whom it was fitting that I be separated; I have
been parted from the person who was de-
serving of separation. I suffer all this distance,
calamity, sorrow, torment, homelessness, and
helplessness from a person with a swollen
face”—by this he meant his son Sangun,
whose face and cheeks were of that descrip-
tion. He was so angry that he spoke of him in
this manner without mentioning his name. 
Driven out in ﬂight, Ong Khan went to
Naiman territory. Two of the Naiman ruler
Tayang Khan’s commanders, one named Qori
Sübächü and the other named Titig Sa’al,1 who
were scouts in that area, caught him there,
1See note to text p. 120 above.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1195–1203
185

killed him, and took his head to their ruler,
Tayang Khan. 
Tayang Khan was displeased by that action
and said, “Why did you kill such a great and
elderly ruler? He should have been brought in
alive.” He ordered Ong Khan’s head plated in
silver, and for a long time he kept it over his
throne as a mark of respect (as has been men-
tioned in the sections on the Kerayit and the
Naiman1).
Ong Khan’s son Sangun took ﬂight when his
father was captured and killed, and he escaped
to a village called Isiq Malghasun, on the edge
of the desert, on the frontier of Mongolia. Pass-
ing through there, he entered the territory of
Buritabet,2 i.e. the province of Tibet. After pil-
laging parts of that area and living there for a
while engaging in destruction, the tribes and
people of Tibet got together and surrounded
him in a place to take him captive. He escaped
and ﬂed from them pell-mell. On the frontier
of the province of Khotan and Kashgar he
came to a place called Kushan Sarkashma. A
commander [398] of the Qalach tribe there
named Qilich Qara, who was the commander
and governor of that place, seized him and
killed him. They say that later the commander
sent Sangun’s wife and child he had captured
1See above, text pp. 120 and 126.
2This name for Tibet is attested by Carpini: Cùm autê
exercitus ille Mongalorum rediret, venit ad terram Bu-
rithabeth, cuius habitatores pagani sunt, & hos Tartari
bello vicerunt (p. 84, lines 15–17) “And in traueiling
homewardes, the sayd armie of the Mongals came vnto
the lande of Burithabeth (the inhabitants whereof are Pa-
gans) and conquered the people in battell” (p. 118).
to Genghis Khan and submitted to him. This
was the end of the rulers of the Kerayit nation
and the extinction of their state. God knows
best.
Genghis Khan mounts the throne of the
khanate after vanquishing Ong Khan, who
was a redoubtable monarch.
When Genghis Khan attacked Ong Khan’s
troops and defeated him and his son, and [Ong
Khan] left in rout, the Kerayit tribes became
subject to [Genghis Khan], and he brought the
realm and people under his control. 
During the winter of that year, Tonquz Yil,
corresponding to 599 [1203], he hunted in a
place
called Tämä’än
Kä’är.
Coming
tri-
umphant and victorious from battle, he re-
turned happy and cheerful to his tents and
camp. When he achieved such a great victory,
and when he had been selected as ruler, tribes
came from all directions to submit. He made a
huge assembly at which he announced good
and harsh ordinances in thanks for that great
blessing and mounted the throne of the khanate
under good auspices.
Now that a detailed history of Genghis Khan
has been written from the beginning of Taulai
Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that began in Rabi‘ I
591 [February 1195], [399] until the end of
Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig that began in
Jumada II 599 [February 1203], a period of
nine years, let us write a summary history of
the khans, caliphs, sultans, maliks, and atabegs
who were Genghis Khan’s contemporaries dur-
ing this period. Thereafter we will pick up
Genghis Khan’s history at that point. [400] 
A brief history of the khaqans of Cathay, Machin, Jurcha, the Qarakhitai, Turkistan, and
Transoxiana, and the caliphs, sultans, maliks, and atabegs of Iran, Syria, Egypt, North
Africa, Anatolia, &c. who were contemporary with Genghis Khan during the seven-year
period from the beginning of Taulai Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that began in Rabi‘ I 591
[February 1195], until the end of Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig that began in Jumada II

599 [February 1203], a period of nine years, and unusual events that took place during this
period.
Dates of the rulers of Cathay during this
period.
Shi Zong [ruled a total of] twenty-nine years,
[of which] twenty-three were before, and six
were during, this period.1
Xian Zong [ruled] a total of one year.2
Zhang Zong [ruled a total of] nineteen years,
[of which] two [were during the period].3
Dates of the rulers of Machin during this
period.
Guang Zong [reigned a total of] four years,
three years before and one year [during the
period].4
Ning Zong [reigned a total of] thirty-two
years, eight years [of which were during the
period].5 [401]
History of the caliphs, sultans, maliks, and
atabegs of Iran, Syria, Egypt, and Anatolia
during the period.
History of the caliphs in Baghdad.

period was al-Nasir-li-dini’llah,6 who sent his
vizier Mu’ayyiduddin Ibn al-Qassab after the
conquest of Khuzistan to take Persia. When he
arrived in Hulwan,7 Jahan Pahlavan’s son Qut-

Ibn al-Qassab took over the land of Khuzistan. When he
took it over, he left it for Maysan, a dependency of
Khuzistan. Then Qutlugh Inanch, son of Pahlavan, the
ruler of the country (the Khwarazmshah’s takeover of
which has been previously mentioned), came to him ac-
companied by a group of amirs, and the caliph’s vizier
received him warmly. The reason he had come was that
battles had been fought between him and the Khwa-
razmshah’s army under the command of Mayachuq in
Zanjan, and Qutlugh Inanch and his army had been de-
feated. He then headed for the caliph’s army to take
refuge with the vizier Mu’ayyiduddin, who gave him
horses, tents, and other things he needed and awarded
him and the amirs with him with robes of honor, and
then decamped to Kirmanshah. From there he went to
Hamadan, where the Khwarazmshah’s son and May-
achuq were with their army. As the caliph’s army ap-
proached, the Khwarazmians vacated the town and
headed
for
Rayy.
The
vizier
took
possession
of
Hamadan in Shawwal of this year [A.H. 591, i.e. Septem-
ber 1195]. Then he and Qutlugh Inanch went out after
the Khwarazmians, taking over every town through
which they passed, like Kharraqan, Mazdaghan, Sava,
and Ava, and they proceeded to Rayy. The Khwarazmi-
ans left the city for Khwar-i-Rayy, and the vizier sent
soldiers out in pursuit of them. The Khwarazmians aban-
doned Rayy for Damghan, Bistam, and Jurjan, and the
caliph’s army returned to Rayy, where they camped.
Qutlugh Inanch and the officers who were with him
agreed to rebel against the vizier and the caliph’s army
because
they
saw
that
there
were
none
of
the
Khwarazmshah’s soldiers in the area and they had de-
signs on it. They entered Rayy, and the caliph’s vizier
laid siege. Qutlugh Inanch departed, and the vizier took
over the city, which the soldiers pillaged until the vizier
had it heralded that plunder was to cease. Qutlugh
Inanch and those with him went to Ava, where the vizier
had a shahna who forbade them to enter. They thus de-
parted. The vizier went in pursuit of them toward

army had assembled around Qutlugh Inanch and that he
was headed toward the city of Karaj and was camped in
a pass near there. The vizier went out after them, and
when they were near each other a fierce battle broke out.
Qutlugh Inanch was defeated but managed to escape
with his life. The vizier left the battlefield for Hamadan,
outside of which he camped. He remained there for
History of the sultans.
In Khwarazm and some of Persia and
Khurasan, Sultan Täkish Khwarazmshah was
ruling.1 At the beginning of this period he
launched a campaign against Ghayir Bügü
Khan the Uyghur. When battle was done, Sul-
tan Täkish was defeated and returned to
Khwarazm. In Rabi‘ II 593 [February 1197] his
son and heir apparent Malik Shah died.2 After
much grief, Täkish summoned [Malik Shah’s]
elder son, Hindu Khan, to Khwarazm and
made Qutbuddin Muhammad the designated
heir in his stead. There was such intense enmi-
ty between the two that when Qutbuddin be-
came sultan Hindu Khan ﬂed and took refuge
with enemies.3
In short, Qutbuddin ruled Khurasan compe-
tently. In 594 [1197–98], Täkish sent him to
wage war against Ghayir Bügü Khan. When
battle broke out, Bügü Khan ﬂed, and Qutbud-
din Muhammad took him and his commanders
captive and brought them to his father. The
around three months. Then the Khwarazmshah Täkish’s
messenger came to him to forbid him to take the territo-
ry from his army, to summon him back, and to offer
terms of truce. The vizier did not respond, so the
Khwarazmshah
proceeded
in
all
seriousness
to
Hamadan. The vizier Mu’ayyiduddin Ibn al-Qassab had
died in the beginning of Sha‘ban [June 1196], and a bat-
tle was fought between [the Khwarazmshah] and the
caliph’s army on the 15th of Sha‘ban 592 [July 14,
1196], and many soldiers were killed. The caliph’s army
was defeated, and the Khwarazmians took much booty
from them. The Khwarazmshah took over Hamadan,
disinterred the vizier, cut off his head, and sent it to
Khwarazm to make it appear that he had killed him in
the battle. Then news came to the Khwarazmshah from
Khurasan that necessitated his return, so he pulled out
and returned to Khurasan.”

Khwarazmshah spared his life and appointed
him to the rank of amir.
In Rabi‘ I of the same year1 he heard that
Mayachuq, who was in Persia on his behalf,
was contemplating a rebellion because of the
vast distance between them. He set out for
Rayy to attack him. When Mayachuq heard of
this, he took ﬂight, with the sultan’s army in
pursuit, to Mazanderan,2 where he took refuge
in a fortress. They laid siege, and in the end
they captured him and took him to the
Khwarazmshah. Through the intercession of a
group of nobles the sultan spared his life and
ordered that in expiation for his rebellion he
should spend the rest of his life in one of the
frontier areas. 
The sultan took Isfahan and gave it to his son
Tajuddin Alishah. From there he went to be-
siege
the
fortress
of
Alamut.
Sadruddin
Muhammad Wazzan, the head of the Shafiites
of Rayy, was killed in that fortress, and the viz-
ier Nizamuddin [403] Mas‘ud b. Ali was
stabbed. 
In Jumada II 596 [March 1200], Täkish or-
dered Qutbuddin Muhammad to attack Quhis-
tan. He went and besieged the fortress of Tur-
shez for four months.3 The sultan went from
Khwarazm against the heretics. When he
reached
the
station
of
Chah-i-Arab
near
Shahristana, he died of diphtheria on the 19th
of Ramadan 596 [July 3, 1200]. Heralds were
immediately dispatched to take the tidings to
his son Qutbuddin Muhammad, who hastened
as fast as he could to Shahristana. After the
rites of mourning he was elevated to the rule
and given the title Ala’uddin and the name
1According to Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 12:152, this took
place in the year 595—that would be January 1199.
2Correcting the text’s Mardin to Mazanderan in accor-
dance with Ibn al-Athir (Kamil 12:152). Mardin would
have been a long way to ﬂee from Rayy.
3Turshēz is the modern town of Kāshmar in Khurasan.
Sanjar.4 Three years of his history will be in-
cluded in the next section on the sultans of
Ghor.
In Ghor, Ghazna, parts of Khurasan, and
Hindustan, Sultan Ghiyasuddin and Sultan Shi-
habuddin were on the throne. When Sultan
Ghiyasuddin heard that the Khwarazmshah had
died, he ordered three days during which the
nawbat was not sounded and mourning was
observed. Hindu Khan b. Malik Shah b.
Khwarazmshah, afraid of his uncle Sultan
Ala’uddin
Muhammad,
resorted
to
Sultan
Ghiyasuddin and asked him for assistance.
Ghiyasuddin promised to help him. 
Sultan Ala’uddin had sent Chighir the Turk
to be the amir of Merv. Sultan Ghiyasuddin
sent Muhammad b. Chärig, the governor of
Taligan, to Chighir with a message containing
promises and threats saying, “You must have
the khutba and coinage in my name.” 
In reply he said, “Get me amnesty from
Ghiyasuddin so that I may enter fealty to him.”
Because Ghiyasuddin knew that the Khwa-
razmshah had no power or strength left, he
coveted the realm of Khurasan. [404] He sum-
moned Shihabuddin from India so that together
they might take Khurasan. By the time he
arrived Ghiyasuddin had already entered Panj
Deh and Marv Rud, and in Jumada I 597 [Feb-
ruary 1201] the two brothers set out with the
army to take Khurasan. Chighir kept his
promise and turned over the city of Merv to
them. They gave it to Malik Shah’s son Hindu
Khan and proceeded from there to Sarakhs,
which they took peacefully and turned over to
Amir Zangi, their cousin. They also gave him
Nasa and Bavard as fiefs. They took Tus and
sent a message to Alishah b. Khwarazmshah in
Nishapur, saying, “Leave the province.” Al-
ishah and the Khwarazm army there agreed to
4Ala’uddin Muhammad ruled 1200–1220.

189

put up a defense, fortified the walls, and got
ready for battle. Sultan Ghiyasuddin pointed to
the wall, and several towers and the walls col-
lapsed. The Ghorids attributed this to a miracle
and shouted Allahu akbar. The Khwarazmians
grew fearful and took refuge in the congrega-
tional mosque. The Nishapuris drove them out
of the city, and the Ghorids looted it and took
Alishah captive and brought him to Ghiyasud-
din. His maternal aunt was there, and she said
to
Ghiyasuddin,
“Do
they
act
thus
with
princes?” Ghiyasuddin said, “No, but they do
act like this,” as he took Alishah by the hand
and seated him next to himself on the throne.
He turned over Nishapur to his cousin and son-
in-law Ziya’uddin Muhammad b. Ali, and he
turned over Alishah to his brother Shihabud-
din. He himself then went to Herat. Shihabud-
din attacked Quhistan, where he massacred and
pillaged. The governor of Quhistan sent a mes-
sage to Ghiyasuddin saying, “Since there is a
binding pact and covenant between us, why is
your nephew committing such atrocities in our
area?” [405] Sultan Ghiyasuddin sent a mes-
sage to his nephew saying, “Why are you ha-
rassing the realm of my friends? Get out of
there.” Shihabuddin refused.
“Shall I carry out Ghiyasuddin’s order?”
asked the envoy.
“Let it be done,” replied Shihabuddin. The
envoy drew his sword and cut the tent rope.
With that, he decamped unwillingly, and, too
angry to stop in Ghazna, he proceeded toward
India.
In 598 [1201–2] Sultan Ala’uddin Muham-
mad Khwarazmshah came and retook the areas
of Khurasan that the Ghor sultans had taken
from his men. This came about because after
Sultan Shihabuddin went to India, Sultan
Ala’uddin sent Sultan Ghiyasuddin an ultima-
tum saying, “It was my hope that you would
succeed my father and help me to get the
Qarakhitai out of my province and to take it
back from them. Since you didn’t do it, I ex-
pect that at least you will not harass my
province and that you will leave. Otherwise,
name where and when we will do battle.” 
The upshot of all this was that after much
running around, the Khwarazmshah retook part
of Khurasan and laid siege to Herat. When Sul-
tan Shihabuddin heard of the siege, he went to
Khurasan to attack Khwarazm, and Sultan
Muhammad went to Khwarazm before him and
ﬂooded the roads. After eliminating the waters,
Shihabuddin went to Khwarazm, and they
fought a fierce battle. In the end Shihabuddin
was victorious and defeated the Khwarazmi-
ans.
At the same time, in Jumada I 599 [January
1203],1
Sultan
Ghiyasuddin
Abu’l-Fath
Muhammad b. Sam Ghori died leaving a son
named Mahmud. The news reached his brother
Shihabuddin in Tus, and he went to Herat and
held mourning. [406] Sultan Khwarazmshah
took refuge with and sought assistance from
the Qarakhitai, who were dominant in Tran-
soxiana, and many soldiers led by Tayangu of
Taraz came from them to attack the Ghorids.
Sultan Usman of the seed of Afrasiab, the ruler
of Samarkand, was also with them. When Sul-
tan Shihabuddin realized that there was noth-
ing to be gained from war, he lit fires by night
and withdrew. Sultan Muhammad went out in
pursuit, and when he reached the border of
Hazarasp, the Ghorids turned around and gave
battle, although they were defeated in the end.
Shihabuddin and a few men leapt forth, and he
killed four elephants with his own hands, and
the Ghorids took [two elephants] from him.2
1Date confirmed by Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 12:180.

lent passage in Ibn al-Athir (Kamil 12:187), which

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

When the Ghorids reached Andkhud, the
Qarakhitai army caught up with them, and they
did battle. Many were killed on both sides. The
sultan holed up with a few men in the Andkhud
citadel. The Qarakhitai army breached the
wall, and finally a truce was made on terms
that they be given another elephant, and they
left. Shihabuddin escaped the brink of destruc-
tion and got to Taligan with nine men. The
governor there, Husayn Kharmil, sent tents and
supplies, and he set out for Ghazna, taking
Husayn Kharmil along.
When the news of the Ghorid defeat was
broadcast, Tajuddin Yulduz, Shihabuddin’s old
slave, intended to take the fortress of Ghazna,
but the castellan would not allow him in, and
on account of the blatherings of the Qalach
tribes and other trouble-makers, they did much
mischief. When Sultan Shihabuddin reached
Ghazna, he ordered Yulduz killed. The amirs
interceded for his life to be spared. 
Aybak went to Multan and killed the sultan’s
representative and took over the area, saying
that the sultan had been killed and from that
time on he was the sultan. [407] At this point
Sultan Shihabuddin went to India and seized
him along with all his liege men and put them
to death before returning to his seat. 
In Anatolia was Sultan Sulayman b. Qilich
Arslan.1 In Ramadan 597 [June 1201], he took
the city of Malatya from his brother Mu‘izzud-
din Qaysarshah after a few days of siege. After
that he went to Erzurum, and the son of
Muhammad b. Saltuq, one of the old kings,
came out to greet him and make peace. The
had become fatigued (a‘yat), and the infidels [the
Qarakhitai] took two elephants from him. Shihabuddin
entered Andkhuy [Andkhud] along with those who were
with him; the infidels surrounded him, but then they
sued for a truce on condition that he would give them
another elephant. He did so and was saved.”
1Ruknuddin Sulayman II, ruled 1196–1204.
sultan had him seized and imprisoned. He took
Erzurum by dint of the sword, and the dynasty
there came to an end.2
History of the maliks and atabegs in
Mazanderan and Persia.
At the beginning of this period, Jahan-Pahla-
van’s son Qutlugh Inanch was a malik and
commander-in-chief of the army. When he
died, Jahan-Pahlavan’s amirs and slaves gath-
ered and made Gökchä their leader. They took
Rayy and environs and headed for Isfahan.
When they received news that the caliph’s
army was approaching, they sent a messenger
to Sayfuddin Toghril, the commander, to ac-
knowledge their loyalty to the caliph. When
Toghril reached Hamadan, Gökchä went out to
greet him and accompany him to Isfahan,
which he put under his control and sent a mes-
senger to Baghdad requesting the governorship
of Rayy, Isfahan, Qum, Kashan, Ava, and Sava
up to Mazdaqan on condition that those territo-
ries actually belong to the caliphal administra-
tion, but he would govern and keep order. His
request was granted, and an investiture was
forwarded. [408] Within a short time he had
become powerful and his army numerous.
In Azerbaijan and Diyarbekir was Malik
Adil, the brother of Salahuddin Yusuf. He
came from Karak to Damascus to his nephew
Malik Afdal and was assigned to protect Di-
yarbekir. The remainder of his history and that
of the other rulers of Diyarbekir will come im-
mediately below under the rubric of the history
of Syria and Egypt because they are so inter-
twined that if they were treated separately not
only would there be much repetition but it
would also be hard to understand.
In Syria and Egypt, as was reported previ-
ously, a truce had been established among
Salahuddin Yusuf’s sons, by the terms of
2Agrees with Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 12:169.

which Jerusalem and the Syrian dependencies
of Palestine, along with Egypt, would be Malik
Aziz Usman’s; Damascus, Tiberias, and the de-
pendencies of the Jordan Valley and Gaza
would be Malik Afdal’s; Jabla, Latakiya, and
the shore would be Malik Zahir’s.1 The Egypt-
ian fiefs of Malik Adil, their uncle, would re-
main as they were. 
After a while Malik Aziz broke the pact by
leading his army from Egypt to Syria in order
to take Damascus from his brother and to leave
Egypt to Adil. On this basis they went to Egypt
[409] with an army of Kurds. In secret Adil
sent a message to Aziz, telling him to gather
his army and remain firm. He advised Afdal
that it was unwise to be hasty in taking Egypt
since “the foe,” i.e. the Franks, were on his
heels. Thus he put his plan into abeyance, and
peace was made between them on terms that
Jerusalem and all of Palestine, Tiberias, and
the Jordan would be annexed to what Afdal al-
ready possessed, and Adil would reside in
Egypt with Aziz, his fiefs intact. Afdal went to
Damascus, and Adil accompanied Aziz to
Egypt.
In Rajab 593 [May 1197], Malik Adil and
Malik Aziz, along with their army, went from
Egypt to Syria and laid siege to Damascus. Af-
dal’s amirs misled him, and the kingdom
slipped from his hands. They sent him to the
fortress of Sarkhad, and Egypt became Aziz’s
and Damascus Adil’s. Afdal sent an Ethiopian
named Ali to the Caliph Nasir in Baghdad,
with the following two lines of poetry to re-
quest assistance:
My lord, if Abubakr and his friend Uthman
usurped Ali’s right by means of the sword, /
Then look at the writing of this name, how his-
tory repeated itself.
1Correcting the text’s Afzal to Zahir. See above, text p.

Aziz Usman, the king of Egypt, died on the
20th of Muharram 595 [November 22, 1198].
The amirs gathered and summoned Afdal. On
the 5th of Rabi‘ I [January 5, 1199] he reached
Egypt.
His
brothers,
the
amirs,
and
the
grandees of Egypt went out to greet him. Both
his brother Malik al-Mu’ayyad Mas‘ud and
Fakhruddin Charkas2 had arranged banquets,
but he chose to go to his brother’s quarters.
Fakhruddin Charkas was a great amir, [410]
but he grew suspicious and ﬂed to Jerusalem,
which he seized. There were servants of [the
caliph] Nasir with Afdal who gathered around
him, such as Qaracha Zardkash, Sara-Sonqur,
and Maymun Qaysari, the lord of Bilbays.
They found themselves in total agreement with
one another and send a message to Malik Adil
saying, “Come. We will help you take Egypt.”
He was occupied with the siege of Mardin,
hopeful of taking it and not letting Egypt get
away. Afdal entered the city of Cairo on the 7th
of Rabi‘ I [January 7, 1199] and heard that the
Charkas had ﬂed. A group of Nasir’s amirs
were in league with him. He seized some of the
Nasirites who were in Egypt, like Shuqayr, Ay-
bak Aftas, and Elbegi, all of whom were brave
and courageous, and imprisoned them. Afdal
was ensconced in Egypt. The minister was
Sayfuddin Barkaj. The rulers of Syria sent a
message to Afdal inviting him to take Damas-
cus. Afdal despised this and refused to cooper-
ate. The news reached Adil, who stationed his
son Kamil in Mardin and went in haste to
Damascus, summoning the Nasirites from
Jerusalem. They set out, and his son Malik
Kamil also arrived, thus furnishing Adil mas-
sive support. When Afdal saw that things were
not going to be easy, he went to Egypt, while

his brother Zahir went to Aleppo and Sherkoh,

In 596 [1199–1200] Malik Adil amassed his
troops to attack Egypt, and Afdal came out
with a small force. Battle was fought, and Af-
dal went in defeat to the fortress at Sarkhad,
taking control of Mayyafariqin, Hani,1 and Ja-
bal Jur.2 Malik Adil then became ensconced in
Egypt with the khutba and coinage in both Ma-
lik Mansur’s name and his own. 
Afdal came back to take Damascus [411]

would be Afdal’s.3

Also in that year Malik Zahir took the Najm

In the Maghreb, Ya‘qub b. Yusuf b. Abdul-
Mu’min was king. Many fierce battles were

bruary 17, 1199], and his son Mahmud suc-

volted against his father, submitted to him, and
he consolidated his kingdom.7 [412]
In Fars…
In Kirman was Malik Dinar, one of the
Oghuz amirs. He died of delirium in Dhu’l-
Qa‘da 591 [October 1195], the first year of this
period, and his son Ala’uddin Farrukhshah,

died in Rajab 592 [June 1196], and the Oghuz
wrought much havoc. After that, the shahna of
