JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The History of Genghis Khan from the beginning of Quluqana Yil, the Year of the Rat that
began in Jumada II 600 [February 1204], through Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that be-
gan in Sha‘ban 606 [January 1210], a period of seven years; during the last year Genghis
Khan was fifty-six years old
During this period he did battle with Tayang
Khan and killed him. He set up a nine-footed
standard and was given the title Genghis Khan.
Several times he went to battle in Tangqut and
also fought Toqto’a, the ruler of the Märkit,
and Tayang Khan’s son Güshlüg. He also
called upon the ruler of the Uyghur to submit.
The ruler of the Öng’üt informs Genghis
Khan of Tayang Khan’s intention.
In the spring of Quluqana Yil, the Year of the
Rat that began in Jumada II 600 of the Hegira
[February 1204], Tayang Khan, the ruler of the
Naiman, sent an emissary, Joqanan by name,1
to the ruler of the Öng’üt people, Ala Qush Te-
gin Quri, saying, “They say that in this area
there has recently appeared a monarch (by
which he meant Genghis Khan). I know for
certain that in the sky the sun and the moon are
two, but on the earth how can there be two
monarchs in one kingdom? You be my right
hand [415] and support me with troops so that
we can take his sable” (by which he meant his
insignium).
Ala Qush sent one of his elite men, Torbi
Dash[i] by name, to Genghis Khan and in-
formed him of this, and by that, the best of all
possible ways, he submitted to him. This story
will come in the proper place, God willing.
Tayang Khan launches an attack on
Genghis Khan but he is defeated.
Although Genghis Khan already knew of
Tayang Khan’s hostility, when he was made
aware of the situation by Torbi Dashi’s words,
1Joqanan (from the Syriac !"#$% Yōḥannān, for John)
is Yoqunan in the Secret History §190.
he held a quriltai in the spring of the Year of
the
Rat
in Tämä’än
Kähär
[and] Tülkin
Chä’üt.2 The amirs said of one accord, “Our
horses are lean. Let us fatten them up, and we
will ride with you.” 
“Liege men,” said Otchigin Noyan, Genghis
Khan’s uncle, “why make our horses’ leanness
an excuse? Now that we have heard such
words, let us ride on campaign. What is fitting?
Either let Tayang Khan take us, or let us take
him, and then let them say, ‘They took Tayang
in this place.’ God knows whether we will take
him or he will take us. In any case let us
mount.”
After that, Genghis Khan’s brother Belgütäi
said, “O Genghis Khan, if the Naiman people
take your sable, let our bones not stick together
in one place. They have dominance because
they are a large nation and have many herds
and flocks. What can he do with a large nation
and many herds and flocks if we make a pre-
emptive strike? How difficult can it be to take
his sable?” [416]
Genghis Khan was pleased by their words,
and on the fifteenth of the month3 he set out to
do battle with Tayang Khan at Kältägäi Qada
at the Qalqa River. After they had been on that
campaign for a long time and battle had not
taken place, in that same Year of the Rat, in au-
tumn, all were assembled once again, and
Qubilai and Jäbä were sent forward to strike.
Tayang Khan was at the Altai River in the
2Teme’en Ke’er and Tülkin Che’üd in the Secret His-
tory §190.
3The Secret History §193 has: “the sixteenth day of
the first moon of summer.”
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1204–1210
195

vicinity of Qangqai.1 The forward detachment
returned, and Toqto’a, the ruler of the Märkit,
and Alin Taishi of the Kerayit amirs, who had
taken flight, had gone there. The Oyirat, whose
leader was Qutuqa Beki, and Jamuqa of the Ja-
jirat, and the Dörbän, Tatar, Qataqin, and
Salji’ut clans all assembled with Tayang Khan.
It so happened that a horse with a saddle
strapped to its belly belonging to Genghis
Khan’s army ran away and went among the
Naiman soldiers. When they saw how skinny
the horse was, Tayang Khan took counsel with
his commanders, saying, “The Mongols’ hors-
es are lean. We will do dogfights and slowly
fall back until they come after us. Their horses
will become even weaker and ours will be-
come baraq [shaggy]. Then we will stand and
fight.”
Qori Sübächü, one of Tayang Khan’s great
commanders, said in reply, “Your father Inanch
Qa’an never showed his back or his horse’s
rump to anyone. You have taken fright in an
hour. Since it is so, Gürbäsü Khatun should be
brought.” (By Gürbäsü he meant the lady
Tayang Khan loved.) The commander spoke
these words and left in wrath and anger.
Tayang Khan then had no choice but to stand
and fight. [417]
Genghis Khan said to Jochi Qasar, “You
command the qol,” meaning the center of the
army, and Genghis Khan assigned each one.
When Jamuqa Sächän saw Genghis Khan’s de-
ployment from afar, he turned to his liege men
and said, “The method and deployment of the
anda (meaning Genghis Khan) are different.
The Naiman will not leave the skin of a calf or
goat for anyone.” Turning around, he departed
and left the battlefield. On that day they fought
a pitched battle. Near sundown Tayang Khan’s
army, broken and routed, turned their faces
1The Qangghai of the Secret History §194.
from the battle. Tayang Khan suffered so many
serious wounds that his body was deeply cut in
several places. He took refuge on a steep cliff.
Qori Sübächü and several other commanders
were with him, but no matter how hard they
tried to make him get up and stand again to
battle, he was too badly wounded to move. Af-
ter that, Qori Sübächü and other commanders
and liege men said, “You all be patient until I
say words I know will rouse his zeal and make
him get up.”
“Tayang Khan,” he said, “have we become
mountain goats to scale cliffs? Get up and let’s
fight!”
Hearing these words, he was not provoked
into getting up.
“Tayang Khan,” he said again, “your wives,
especially your beloved Gürbäsü, have all
adorned themselves and made the camps ready
in expectation of you. Get up, and let’s go!”
He heard these words too, but he still
couldn’t make a move.
“If
he
had
the
slightest
ability,”
Qori
Sübächü said to the other commanders, “he
would have moved or given a reply. Now, be-
fore we see his death, let’s go and fight oppo-
site him so that he can see our deaths.” [418]
Coming down from the cliff, they fought hard
until they were killed.
Although Genghis Khan wanted to take them
alive, they absolutely would not allow it and
preferred to be killed. Genghis Khan marveled
at this and approved of such great fidelity and
devotion. “How can anyone who has such men
have anything to worry about?” he said.
When it was night Tayang Khan’s army was
defeated. Genghis Khan’s army went out in
pursuit of them, and the defeated men were so
afraid and terrified that they stumbled into
harsh mountain terrain. By night many of the
Naiman soldiers slipped and tumbled to their
deaths down the steep mountain cliffs called
196
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Naqu Qun. This story is very well known
among the Mongols. In that battle the Dörbän,
Tatar, Qataqin, and Salji’ut tribes all surren-
dered and went before Genghis Khan. The
Märkit did not submit and ran away instead.
Tayang Khan’s son Güshlüg escaped to his fa-
ther’s brother Buyuruq Khan.
Genghis Khan rides to do battle with the
Märkit nation, who are defeated.
After that, in the winter of the same Year of
the Rat corresponding to 600 of the Hegira
[1203–4], Genghis Khan launched a campaign
against Toqto’a Beki, the ruler of the Märkit,
and the many tribes that had been allied with
Tayang Khan but took flight after his defeat.
Along the way, they first encountered the
Märkit clan called the Uhaz. Their chief and
elder, Dayir Usun, had camped at the head of a
river called Ta’ur Mörän. [419] “We have no
wish for battle,” they said. Dayir Usun picked
up his daughter Qulan Khatun and took her as
a gift to Genghis Khan.
“They have no horse or quadruped to ride in
Genghis
Khan’s
retinue,”
they
reported.
Genghis Khan then ordered them dispersed
among the companies of a hundred, set a shah-
na over them, and stationed them in the
aghruqs. The group that was in the aghruq as-
sembled and fought, but everything they had
pillaged was taken away from them. That
group ran away. Genghis Khan surrounded the
Uru’ut Märkit clan in a fortress called Daiqal
Qorghan.1 After seizing the clan called the Mu-
dan, another clan called the Todaqlin, and
another clan called the Je’ün, he withdrew.
Toqto’a and his sons fled to Buyuruq Khan,
1Daiqal is the taiqal of the Secret History, which is
glossed in Chinese as ‘mountain-top’ but rendered as a
proper name in the continuous Chinese translation. See
Secret History, p. 132, note 1. Qorghan is the Turkish
for ‘fortress.’
Tayang Khan’s brother who controlled a sepa-
rate kingdom and army. The Uhaz Märkit,
whose leader was Dayir Usun, became re-
bellious again and took up a position in the
vicinity of the Selenga River in the Quru
Qabchal fortress.
Genghis Khan put Boroghul Noyan and
Chimbai, Chila’uqan Bahadur’s brother, in
charge of the army of the right wing and sent
them to deal [with the rebels]. They went there
and captured the entire clan that had taken
refuge in the fortress. [420]
Genghis Khan rides against the territory of
Qashin, which is called Tangqut, and
subdues their fortresses and towns.
When Hükär Yil, the Year of the Buffalo that
began in Jumada II 601 [January 1205], com-
menced auspiciously, Genghis Khan arrayed
his army and set out on a campaign against
Qashin, the territory that is also called Tangqut.
When they went there they came first to a
fortress called Ligi,2 an extremely impregnable
place. They laid siege to it, and in a short while
they took it and destroyed all its ramparts and
foundations. From there they went to a city
called Keng Losi,3 a really magnificent city.
That too they took and plundered. They took
and raided some other parts of Tangqut and
drove away all the animals they found there.
They returned to Genghis Khan with much
booty and many camels and animals.
Genghis Khan’s great quriltai at which he
set up a nine-footed white standard and was
given the epithet Genghis Khan; he sets out

197

to do battle with Buyuruq Khan, the ruler
of half the Naiman people, and he captures
him.
When Bars Yil, the Year of Tiger that began
in Rajab 602 [February 1206], commenced
auspiciously,
at
the
beginning
of
spring
Genghis Khan ordered a nine-footed white

rulers meaning “strong and mighty monarch.”
When the assembly of the quriltai was over,
they set out to attack Buyuruq Khan, who was
hunting with falcons in the area of Ulugh Taq
at a place called Suja’u. Genghis Khan and the
army fell upon him like fate and destroyed
him, taking his land, home, wives and children,
and herds and flocks. When his nephew Güsh-
lüg Khan’s father Tayang Khan had been
killed, Güshlüg Khan had escaped and gone to
his uncle Buyuruq Khan. Toqto’a Beki, the
ruler of the Märkit, was also with him, as has

a
place
called
Ärdish
(Irtysh)
along
the

The conquest of the province of Tangqut,
which the Mongols used to call Qashin.
In the autumn of the Year of the Rabbit cor-
responding to Rajab 603 [February 1207],
since the province of Tangqut had rebelled and
1The “nine-footed” white standard is explained in the

refused to pay tribute or heed orders, Genghis
Khan rode out once again to do battle. That
time he conquered the entire province, [422]
returning victorious and triumphant.
The commanders of the Qirqiz submit.
Also in the Year of the Rabbit, Genghis Khan
sent two emissaries, one named Altan and the
other Bu’ura, to the commanders and rulers of
the Qirqiz.2 First they reached an area called
___, the commander of which was ___. After
that, they arrived in another area called Yeti
Oron, the commander of which was called
Orus Inal. These two commanders showed re-
spect for the two emissaries and sent back with
them two of their own envoys, one named Elig
Temür and the other Atqiraq, along with a
white falcon, and thus they submitted to
Genghis Khan.
Toqto’a Beki, the ruler of the Märkit who
had repeatedly fought battles and stirred up
strife, is seized and killed.
In the Year of the Dragon beginning in Rajab
604 [January 1208], when Genghis Khan re-
turned from conquering the Tangqut towns and
the Qirqiz, and after the commanders of those
areas had surrendered, he dismounted at his
own tents and spent the entire summer there.
That winter he mounted under good auspices
to deal with Toqto’a Beki and Güshlüg, both of
whom had fled from the battle with Buyuruq
and gone into the territory of Ärdish. Along the
way the scouts and advance men unexpectedly
encountered a clan of the Oyirat whose leader
was Qutuqa Beki. Since this clan was not capa-
ble of offering resistance [423] they surren-
dered and joined. They guided Genghis Khan’s
army. They made a surprise attack on Toqto’a
Beki and Tayang Khan’s son Güshlüg Khan.
Both were brought down, and their possessions
2See text p. 143 above.
198
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

and herds and flocks were all taken in plunder.
Toqto’a was killed in battle, but Güshlüg got
out with a few men, taking refuge in the Gür
Khan Qarakhitai’s territory, where he remained
for a time. The Gür Khan won him over and
called him “son.” After a time he gave him his
daughter. His end will be given later in the
proper place, God willing.
The Uyghur people submit, and Genghis
Khan rewards the Idiqut, their ruler.
In the spring of Moghai Yil, the Year of
Snake beginning in Sha‘ban 605 [February
1209], when the Idiqut, the ruler of the
Uyghur, heard of Genghis Khan’s might,
majesty, and generosity—at that time the
Uyghur paid tribute to the Gür Khan, one of
whose great commanders, Shaugäm by name,
sat over them as a commandant—the Idiqut fa-
vored Genghis Khan. He killed Shaugäm the
commandant and decided to send envoys to
Genghis Khan. Rumors of this had reached
Genghis Khan, and he had sent two envoys to
the Idiqut. One was named Alp Ülüg,1 and the
other was Darbai.2 When they arrived, the
Idiqut rejoiced greatly over their arrival and
honored them. In their company he sent two of
his
own
ambassadors, Alghish3

Ish-
Ayghuchi and Temür Tutuq, to Genghis Khan
[424] to say on his behalf, “From all comers
and goers I have heard reports of the might and
majesty of the world-conquering monarch. I
have rebelled against the Gür Khan of the
Qarakhitai. I wanted to send emissaries and re-
port on the Gür Khan’s situation and every-
1Reading اوﻟﻮگ (Ülüg) for the text’s اوﻧﻮک.
2In the Secret History §238, the Idiqut’s ambassadors

thing else I know in general and in detail, and I
wanted to do valiant service willingly. I was in
the midst of such thoughts when Genghis
Khan’s envoys arrived. It was, it seemed to me,
as though the sky had been cleared of clouds
and the bright sun had come out from behind
them and broken up the ice that had frozen on

I rejoiced greatly in my heart. Henceforth I of-
fer all the territory of the Uyghur and am
Genghis Khan’s slave.” In such words was the
message couched.
Prior to this, when Toqto’a Beki was felled
during battle by an arrow wound and killed, his
brother Qudu and all four of his sons, Chila’un,
Majar, and Qul[t]uqan Märgän (märgän means
a good archer, and since he was he was so
called), got out of the battle alive. They wanted
to take Toqto’a’s body away, but there was no
opportunity, so they picked up his head in
haste and fled from Ärdish to Uyghur territory,
where they sent a messenger named Äbügän to
the Idiqut. The Idiqut killed their messenger,
and therefore they did battle at the river called
Jäm Mörän, where they were defeated. The
four, along with Güshlüg, departed from there
and went to other regions, as will be men-
tioned.
Since the Idiqut realized that they were
Genghis Khan’s enemies, not only did he not
allow them to stay but he also gave battle and
drove them away. When the situation was
made known, he sent four of his liege men, Ar-
slan Ögä, [425] Charuq Ögä, Bolad Tegin, and
Inal Qaya Süngächi,6 to Genghis Khan, who
was pleased by this action.

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1204–1210
199

Based on the foregoing, when the two en-
voys mentioned above arrived with Genghis
Khan’s envoys and gave their report, Genghis
Khan showed them favor and made a decree
saying, “If the Idiqut truly has it in his heart to
perform deeds of valor, let him pick up what
he has in his treasury and bring it here.” On
this mission he dispatched Alp Ülüg and Dar-
bai once more. When they arrived there, the
Idiqut opened the door of his treasury, picked
up what coins and goods were suitable and ap-
propriate, and headed out to Genghis Khan’s
presence. 
When Genghis Khan was sending the envoys
to the Idiqut the second time, in the summer of
Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse corresponding
to 606 [1210]—and that summer he stayed in
his ordu—the Idiqut was preparing his arms
and had not yet arrived. When autumn came
and Genghis Khan had mounted to do battle
with the Tangqut, which they used to call
Qashin, he came to a city called Erighaya. He
put the realm of Tangqut under marshall rule,
the ruler of the Tangqut gave him his daughter,
and he returned victorious and triumphant.
When he came back under good auspices, the
Idiqut had arrived, and the ruler of the Qarluq,
Arslan Khan, also submitted. 
That was in the spring of Qonin Yil, the Year
of the Sheep corresponding to 607 [1211]. The
whole story of the Idiqut, including that of Ar-
slan Khan, will come later, God willing.
Now that a detailed history of Genghis Khan
has been written from the beginning of Qu-
luqana Yil, the Year of the Rat that began in Ju-
mada II 600 [February 1204], until the end of
Morin Yil, [426] the year of the horse that be-
gan in Sha‘ban 606 [January 1210], a period of
seven years, during the last year of which
Genghis Khan was fifty-six years old, we can
begin a brief history of the khaqans, caliphs,
sultans, maliks, and atabegs who were contem-
porary with Genghis Khan during this seven-
year period in various realms east and west.
After that we will return to the history of
Genghis Khan after this period. [427] 
A brief history of the khaqans of Cathay, Machin, Jurcha, the Qarakhitai, Turkistan, and
Transoxiana, the caliphs, sultans, maliks, and atabegs of Iran, Syria, Egypt, North Africa,
Anatolia, &c. who were contemporary with Genghis Khan during the seven-year period
from the beginning of Quluqana Yil, the Year of the Rat that began in Jumada II 600 [Feb-
ruary 1204], until the end of Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that began in Sha‘ban 606
[January 1210], and unusual events that took place during this period.

period.
Zhangzong [ruled a total of] nineteen years,
of which two were before, and ten were after,
the seven years.1

period.

of which eight were before, and seventeen
were after, the seven years.2 [428]

History of the caliphs and sultans during
this period.
In Baghdad was the caliph of the Abbasid
Dynasty al-Nasir-li-dini’llah.1
In Khwarazm and parts of Khurasan and Per-
sia
was
Sultan Ala’uddin
Muhammad
b.
Khwarazmshah. Because of the death of his fa-

Khan, the sultans of Ghor, as was said in the
previous section, attacked him and took back
most of the towns of Khurasan from his son
and representatives. Battles raged between
them, and he was somewhat weakened. During
these years, as the fortune of the sultans of
Ghor was waning, and Sultan Shihabuddin
died, as will be mentioned, Sultan Muham-
mad’s fortune waxed. He became strong and
set out to take Khurasan. Izzuddin Husayn
Kharmil, the governor of Herat, offered his al-
legiance before any of the other amirs and sent
a message telling him to come to Herat first.
[429] Fearful least the Qarakhitai make a pre-
emptive strike and get hold of Balkh and that
area, the sultan set out for that area. When he
reached Herat, Izzuddin Husayn Kharmil went
out to greet him and turn over the city. The
amirs of Ghiyasuddin Mahmud, Ghiyasuddin
Ghor’s son, were opposed, but the sultan’s sol-
diers drove them away and scattered them. 
When the sultan reached Balkh, the gover-
nors of the fortifications surrendered the keys
of the fortresses and supply stores to him, and
once again Khurasan was in his hands. During
this period he conquered Mazanderan and Kir-
man. Returning victorious from Persia in 606
1The Caliph al-Nasir ruled from 1180 to 1225.
[1209–10], all of Transoxiana was his. He gave

In Anatolia was Sultan Ruknuddin Sulayman
[son of] Qilich Arslan.2 His nephew, the gover-

and no matter how long Sultan Ruknuddin laid
siege to him, he was not successful. Finally he

brothers and sons. In retribution for this
shameful act of treachery and breach of
promise, Ruknuddin was stricken five days lat-
er with colic and died on the seventh day.3 His
son Qilich Arslan was installed in his place.

a

and Multan to collect two years’ worth of taxes
to enable him to mount a campaign against

sons are on the road and committing brig-
andage. Because of them, it is absolutely im-
possible to send money from Lahore and Mul-

Aybak, the leader of the army of Hindustan, to
them with promises and threats. They gave no
reply. Complaints of them were coming in
from all over Sind and India. The sultan put off
his Cathay campaign, and mounted against
them on the 5th of Rabi‘ I 602 [October 20,
1205]. Hearing that they were between Jhelum
and Sodhra with a large force, he drove for-
ward with all speed and arrived there on the
5th of Rabi‘ II [November 19]. A pitched battle
was fought, lasting from dawn to noon. With-
out warning, Qutbuddin Aybak arrived with his
army, attacked them, and put them into a seri-
ous rout during which many were killed. The
Indians went near a large mountain and lit
many fires. When the Muslims drew near
them, they threw themselves into the fires and
were all burned. [432] “The loss both of this
world, and of the life to come: this is manifest
perdition.”3 The army of Islam took so much
booty that five Indian slaves were sold for one
dinar.
Kokar’s son fled when his brothers and fami-
ly immolated themselves. Rai Bal’s son the
lord of Judi took refuge with Qutbuddin and
begged and pleaded. Qutbuddin responded
positively and asked the sultan to spare his life.
The sultan was in Lahore until the 15th of Ra-
jab [February 25, 1206]. Thereafter he went to
Ghazna and dispatched Baha’uddin Sam, the
lord of the Bamian, to outfit the army for a
campaign against Samarkand. On the first of
Sha‘ban [March 13], he crossed at the Jhelum

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

crossing, and on the banks of the Indus at a
place called Damyak he set up a court tent in
such a fashion that half the tent was over the
water. Since he had overthrown the Kokarites
and killed and imprisoned many of them, two
or three Hindus came to assassinate him. One
day without warning they emerged from the
water at the time of afternoon nap. He was in
the tent. They stabbed him nearly twenty
times. After a while when his men went in,
they found him lying dead, prostrate on his
prayer mat.1 Realizing that Indian assassins
had done it, the amirs and ministers assembled
around the vizier Mu’ayyidulmulk and took an
oath to maintain the treasury and kingdom
until a successor could be found. They stitched
up his wounds and took him and two thousand
loads from the treasury to Ghazna in a litter,
claiming that he was ill. When his death was
made public, disagreement broke out among
the amirs. Some expressed their preference for
Shihabuddin Sam Malik, while others were for
Ghiyasuddin Mahmud, Sultan Ghiyasuddin’s
son.
A group of corrupt clerics from Ghazna said
to the slaves, “Mawlana Fakhruddin Razi
hatched a plot with the Khwarazmshah. On his
advice the sultan sent people who killed Shi-
habuddin.”
[433]
They
attacked
Mawlana
Fakhruddin, who took refuge with the vizier
Mu’ayyidulmulk, who managed to save him
from them and send him to a distant place
where he would be safe from them. 
Baha’uddin Sam was the governor of Bami-
an. His father was Shamsuddin Muhammad b.
Mas‘ud, a cousin of Sultan Shihabuddin and
Ghiyasuddin. They gave him their sister in
marriage and Bamian as a fief, and his fortunes
rose thanks to them. He had a son by that wife

the

At the time that Shihabuddin arrived, he be-

Jalaluddin and said, “Go to Ghazna. Let

make peace with Ghiyasuddin Mahmud on

When Shihabuddin died in India, Shihabud-
din’s amirs assembled. He had an intelligent
slave who was Aybak’s successor. They put
him on the throne, and he became known
throughout the world as Sultan Shamsuddin of
Hindustan. [434] Qabacha took over Sind, La-
hore, and Multan, while Zabulistan and Ghaz-
na were seized by Tajuddin Yulduz after much
strife and unrest. 
In Herat and Firozkoh, Sultan Ghiyasuddin’s
son Amir Mahmud took over. Izzuddin Husayn
Kharmil, the governor of Herat, was inclined
to follow Sultan Muhammad Khwarazmshah,
as has been said before. These differences oc-
casioned the downfall and extinction of the
sultans of Ghor and the rise of the Khwarazm-
shah sultan.2
History of the maliks and atabegs in

named Aytoghmish. He assembled soldiers and

In Constantinople, which is in Rûm, the

a time, the Byzantine emperor’s brother, who

The Greeks grew weak. Since Constantinople
is a very large city, there were nearly thirty
thousand Franks residing there. They plotted
with the Franks outside and set fire to the city,
a quarter of which was burned. Then they
opened the gates, and the army of the Franks

Unusual events that took place during the
period.
In the year 600 [1203–4] there was such a
great earthquake in Syria, Egypt, Anatolia,
Sicily, and Cyprus that it reached Mosul and
Persia. Much damage was done in Syria. 
Also during these years the Georgians went
to Azerbaijan, killing and looting. From there
they went to Akhlat and reached Malazgird.
Not a single creature stood in their way as they
pillaged, murdered, and took captives. In the
end the lord of Akhlat assembled an army and
went to Qilich Arslan’s son the lord of Erzu-
rum. He sent his army together with the lord of
Akhlat’s, and when they reached the Georgians
a pitched battle took place. The Georgian com-
mander and many of his soldiers were killed
during the battle, [439] and those who re-
mained alive fled in rout. The Muslims re-
turned home victorious and triumphant, bear-
ing much booty and many captives.6
Now that a summary history of the khaqans,
caliphs, sultans, maliks, and atabegs of the var-
ious regions from east to west who were con-
temporary with Genghis Khan during this peri-
od has been written, let us turn once more to
the history of Genghis Khan and record in de-
tail what transpired after this seven-year peri-
od, God willing. [440]

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The History of Genghis Khan from the beginning of Qonin Yil, the Year of the Sheep that
began in Sha‘ban 607 [January 1211], the year in which he launched a campaign against
Cathay and did battle with Altan Khan, the ruler of Cathay, through Bars Yil, the Year of
the Tiger that began in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 614 [January 1218], a period of eight years
In the last year of this period Genghis Khan
was sixty-four years old, and during this period
he first took care of Cathay and then returned
to deal with Güshlüg and the Märkit ruler
Qudu. Those who rebelled after submitting,
like the Qirqiz, Tumat, etc., were all seized and
killed.
The ruler of the Qarluq and the Idiqut
submit.
In the spring of the Year of the Sheep corre-
sponding to 607 [1211], Arslan Khan, the khan
of the Qarluq, came to Genghis Khan and sur-
rendered. He presented gifts at the Kerulen,
and in that same place, after him, the Idiqut,
the ruler of the Uyghurs, arrived and presented
gifts, saying, “If Genghis Khan is so kind and
ennobles his slave, let me receive a red cloak1
and a golden belt ring for having heard from
afar and having drawn nigh. [441] Let me be a
fifth to Genghis Khan’s four sons, and let me
perform more valiant service.” Genghis Khan
realized that he was asking for one of his
daughters, so he said, “Let me give him a
daughter, and let him be a fifth son.”2
The beginning of Genghis Khan’s expedition
to Cathay, Qarakhitai, and Jurcha, and the

kingdom the Mongols call Cha’uqut.
In the spring of the Year of the Sheep that be-
gan in Sha‘ban 607 [January 1211], when
Genghis Khan set out for the towns of Cathay,
he first dispatched Toquchar of the Qunqirat—
who
was
also
called
Dalan
Turqaqtu
Toquchar3—with two thousand men to guard
the lowlands so that when he went to Cathay,
his rear and the ordu also would be safe from
the Mongols, Kerayit, and Naiman tribes, most
of whom he had brought into submission, lest
some scattered tribes reunite and rebel. After
this precaution had been taken and the army
had been arranged, in autumn of that year he
mounted on campaign under good auspices and
set out to conquer the territories of Cathay,
Qarakhitai, and Jurcha, which the Mongols call
Cha’uqut. 
In the idiom of the people of Cathay, Cathay
is called Khan-zi.4 That territory’s border with
Machin [stretches] along the Qara Mörän (Yel-
low River) to the sea.5 Machin is called Manzi
by the Cathaians.6 Another border is with Jur-
cha, which is a Mongolian term: in the Catha-
ian language it is called Nuji.7 Another frontier

which one may refer.1 The ruler who fought
Genghis Khan and his army was of the tribe
and territory of Jurcha, of the sons of Da Jin
Wang Aquda.2 Aquda was his name; the rest
are titles. The Mongols call Aquda “Haqutai.”
Those of his offspring who were rulers were all
called Altan Khan by the Mongols.3 The name
of the last Altan Khan, the one who fought
against Genghis Khan and Ögödäi Qa’an, was
Sä’üsä in the Cathaian language.4 The story of
his end will be given in detail. Here he has just
been mentioned as an introduction before we
return to the narrative.
When Genghis Khan divided the army into
two divisions, he held it arrayed for battle in
expectation of the arrival of the foe. [445] Al-
tan Khan’s army was quite magnificent and led
by the Jiujin mentioned above. Having sum-
moned another commander named Ming'an,5
he said to him, “You have been among the
Mongols before, and you know Genghis Khan.
Go and say to him, ‘What have we done to you
to provoke you to come mounted for a cam-
paign?’ If he replies harshly, curse him.”
Ming’an went to Genghis Khan as Jiujin had
told him to do and delivered the message.
Genghis Khan ordered him seized and held
until after the battle, when he could question
him.

Then the armies stood opposite each other,
and battle broke out. The Mongol army, despite
their few numbers, quickly defeated the army
of Cathay, <Qara>khitai, and Jurcha, and so
many of them were killed that the entire plain
stank of putrification.6 They went in pursuit of
those who had fled until, in a place called Hui-
ho pao,7 they came across a contingent that
was their rear guard, led by Hu-sha. They
crushed them too and put them to flight. The
battle was of such a large scale and so
renowned that the battle Genghis Khan did at
Hünägän Daba’an is [still] very well known
among the Mongols. Renowned warriors of
Cathay and Jurcha were annihilated in that bat-
tle, and Genghis Khan returned from there tri-
umphant and victorious. 
Then he inquired into the message of the
commander Ming’an, who had been seized and
held. “What did I do to you,” he asked, “that
you spoke ill of me in front of everyone?”
“I had thought before of coming to you and
surrendering,” replied Ming’an. “I feared they
would be suspicious and not let me. When Jiu-
jin wanted to send someone to deliver the mes-
sage to you, I volunteered and used it as an ex-
cuse to come to you. Otherwise how could I
have come?” [446] Genghis Khan was pleased
by his words and set him free. 
After that, they took the city of Xuandefu,8
which was one of the great cities, and de-
stroyed it. From there they went to the city of

Genghis Khan himself, along with Tolui
Khan, who was called Yäkä Noyan, took the
middle way with the center. He harassed the
two great cities of P‘ing-yang fu and Taiyuanfu
without stopping.1 He took and destroyed
every village, city, and town he came to, and
then he turned back.2 
Earlier he had had Muqali Guyang turn back
and sent him to the great city called Mizhou.3
He took that city and then waited for the
arrival of Genghis Khan’s imperial retinue in
the vicinity of the city of Zhongdu, which the
Mongols used to call Khanbaligh.4 (At present
the Qa’an has caused that city to flourish and
named it Daidu.5) One of the Altan Khan’s
folgten der Meeresküste und zogen nach Osten. Sie er-

people hesitated, sometimes inclined in one di-

of the regions and provinces were devoid [of

ruler of every realm.

Toquchar Bahadur of the Qunqirat to join
Sübädäi Bahadur. He had stationed Toquchar
Bahadur at his rear with two thousand scouts to
protect the aghruqs and ordus when he was un-
dertaking the Cathay campaign, and he had sat
for a time without riding with the army. When
all was ready they left together and did battle
with Qudu at the Jäm Mörän, which is in Mon-
golia. They defeated the Märkits and killed
them all so thoroughly that no one remained
except for one of the younger sons named Qul-
tuqan Märkän. He was a really expert archer.
They picked him up and took him to Jochi
Khan. On account of his expertise at archery,
Jochi Khan sent a messenger to Genghis Khan
asking that his life be spared. Because he had
suffered so much from the Märkits, Genghis
Khan thought he should not be allowed to initi-
ate sedition again and sent a reply to Jochi
Khan saying, “I have stored up so many realms
for you. What good will he do you?” Therefore
he too was killed, and of that clan no trace re-
mained. [458]
Genghis Khan sends Boroghul Noyan to
fight the Tumat tribe, whose leader was
Taitu’ul Soqar; the Tumat are defeated, but
Boroghul is killed in the battle.
During
the
same Year
of
the
Buffalo,
Genghis Khan learned that Taitu’ul Soqar,1 the
chief of the Tumat who had previously submit-
ted, had rebelled again during his absence in
Cathay. That tribe constituted a separate army,
and they were a warlike and seditious people.
He assigned Nayaqa Noyan of the Ba’arin and
Dörbän Noyan to mount a campaign against
him. Nayaqa Noyan pleaded illness, and when
he was apprised of this, Genghis Khan thought

When Boroghul Noyan heard this, he asked
the amirs, “Did you mention me to the emper-
or, or did he think of it himself?”
“He said it himself,” they replied.
“I will go under Genghis Khan’s good for-
tune,” he said, “but I am going instead of
another’s blood.” Entrusting his wife and chil-
dren to the emperor, he went on campaign and
conquered the Tumat, reducing them to naught.
However, he was killed in battle. When
Genghis Khan heard what Boroghul Noyan
had said, he remembered how indebted he was
to him and was very saddened by his death.
Showing compassion to his sons, he said, “I
am like the liver and innards to those he left
behind. They must not grieve, for I will keep
them well.” After that, he maintained Boroghul
Noyan’s sons in respect and honor and reward-
ed them variously. [459]
Genghis Khan awards Muqali the title
Guyang and sends him with the army to
conquer the land of Cathay.
In Bars Yil, the Year of the Tiger beginning
in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 614 [January 1218], Genghis
Khan gave Muqali the title Guyang.2 Previous-

Guyang, meaning ruler of a region. When he

him a division of ten thousand Öng’üt soldiers,
a thousand qoshiquls, four thousand of the

Uru’ut tribe,1 two thousand of the Ikiräs led by

The Altan Khan was in the city of Nanjing
and was still holding some of the kingdom of
Cathay. He also had a large army around him.
