The story of his end will come in the section
on Ögödäi, for it was during his reign that the
entirety of the kingdom of Cathay and the Al-
tan Khan was subjugated. [460]
When Genghis Khan turned over that area to
Muqali Guyang, since he intended himself to
lead the entire armies of the right and left to
Turkistan and Iran, he considered it prudent to
deal first with Güshlüg the Naiman and the
other tribes that were rebellious in every corner
and then undertake the campaign.
Güshlüg takes refuge with the Gür Khan of
the Qarakhitai; Güshlüg proves treacherous
to the Gür Khan; Güshlüg is killed, and the
fortune of the Naiman rulers is ended by the
Mongols.
Also during the year mentioned above,
Genghis Khan’s soldiers led by Jäbä Noyan
seized and killed Güshlüg Khan in Sarigh Qol
in the vicinity of the mountains of Badakhshan.
When his father Tayang Khan was killed, he
fled and went to his uncle Buyuruq Khan.
When Buyuruq Khan was killed, he fled to-
gether with the ruler of the Märkit, Toqto’a.
When Genghis Khan himself attacked them a
second time and Toqto’a was killed, Güshlüg
took flight again and went via Beshbaliq to the
frontier of Kucha. All this has been mentioned
previously. After that, in the Year of the Drag-
on beginning in Rajab 604 [January 1208], he
went from there to the Gür Khan, the ruler of
the Qarakhitai. From the Year of the Dragon
until he was killed in Badakhshan it was eleven
years. From the Year of the Rat corresponding
to 600 [1204], when Genghis Khan did battle
with and killed Güshlüg Khan’s father Tayang
Khan [461] and Güshlüg fled, until he entered
Kucha was four years, making a total of fifteen
years. 
It is related that when Güshlüg reached the
Gür Khan’s camp, he named those close to him
with his own name, made himself a kötälchi
222
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

(equerry), and sat at the gate. When they went
before the Gür Khan, Gürbäsü came out, saw
Güshlüg, and said, “Why have you not taken
him in?” They took him in, and his officers
grew angry. 
Gürbäsü was the Gür Khan’s chief wife, and
she had a daughter named Qonqu. That girl im-
mediately fell in love with Güshlüg, and three
days later she was given to him. Since she was
imperious, she would not allow them to put a
boghtaq on her but insisted that they put a
niksa (?) on her in the Cathaian fashion in-
stead. She made Güshlüg renounce Christianity
and adopt idolatry.
In short, Güshlüg took refuge with the Gür
Khan, who was a great monarch and ruler over
all the towns of the region of Turkistan and
Transoxiana, supported by a large army and a
numerous cavalry and retinue. Sultan Muham-
mad Khwarazmshah’s forefathers had accepted
to pay an imposed annual tribute in the amount
of thirty thousand dinars in gold and advised
their sons to continue to keep the pact and nev-
er to quarrel with the Gür Khan, for he was,
they said, a “mighty dam behind which looms
powerful opponents”—i.e. the Mongols, Nai-
mans, and other Turks who merited concern.
The Gür Khan welcomed [Güshlüg] warmly
and honorably, and after a while he gave him
his daughter and made him a member of his
retinue. After a time, when Sultan Muhammad
Khwarazmshah’s affairs were on the rise after
he had taken Ghor, Ghazna, Khurasan, and
Persia—as well as some of Turkistan—and ac-
quired great might and magnificence, [462] he
began to chafe under the burden of paying trib-
ute to infidels and the amount imposed by the
Gür Khan. He assembled soldiers from all di-
rections and led his troops to Bukhara to take
the towns of Transoxiana. He also sent friendly
messages to the rulers of surrounding territo-
ries and gained their support through promises
of good things, particularly Sultan Usman, the
ruler of Samarkand and a descendant of
Afrasiab. Since that group had grown weary of
the Gür Khan over such a long period of time,
they accepted Sultan Muhammad’s invitation
and joined him. In secret he also sent a mes-
sage to Güshlüg and lured him over.
Inasmuch as Güshlüg could see the shakiness
of the Gür Khan’s situation and realized that
the Gür Khan’s great officers in the east were
rebellious and using stories of the world-con-
quering Genghis Khan as pretexts, since many
of the Gür Khan’s officers agreed with him,
and since he had also heard that his father
Tayang Khan’s amirs and their old servants
were still around in various spots, a half-baked
notion kept nagging at him and he thought that
if he assembled his father’s remaining soldiers
he would be able to wield authority as before.
With the help of that army and the Gür Khan’s
soldiers who were in league with him, he
would seize the Gür Khan’s kingdom, grow
powerful,
and
perform
outstanding
feats.
Yielding to the temptation of this wicked
thought, he turned against the poor Gür Khan
and said to him, “I have been away from my
people and tribe for a long time, and Genghis
Khan is busy waging war on Cathay and that
area. I have heard that many of my tribesmen
and clansmen are wandering around aimlessly
in the vicinity of the Imil, Qayaliq,1 and Besh-
baliq, and when they hear my cry, they are ha-
rassed by enemies no matter where they as-
semble. [463] If I might obtain leave from the
Gür Khan, I will go, gather them together, and
render support to the Gür Khan in case of unto-
ward events. As long as I am alive I will be
your sincere servant and obey any order you
give.”
1Qayaligh, on the lower Ili River, southeast of Lake
Balkhash near the modern Kapal.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1211–1218
223

The Gür Khan was such a simpleton that he
believed these words and gave him leave to de-
part. Güshlüg left and followed his whims.
When news of his appearance was broadcast in
Turkistan, those remaining of his father’s
clansmen and soldiers, who had fled from the
onslaught of the swords of Genghis Khan’s
army, assembled around him. He then raided in
every direction and garnered booty until his
band had become large and he was well sup-
plied with men and material. Then he set out in
the Gür Khan’s direction, striking and taking
the towns and regions of his kingdom.
The Gür Khan had grown too old and weak
to deal with him. Learning of Sultan Muham-
mad’s advance upon the Gür Khan, Güshlüg
Khan grew even dizzier as envoys arrived from
both directions. It was decided that the sultan
would head toward the Gür Khan from the
west while Güshlüg came from the east, and
together they would catch the Gür Khan in the
middle and eliminate him. If the sultan got
there first, the Gür Khan’s realm as far as Al-
malyk, Khotan, and Kashgar would be his. If
Güshlüg got there first, the kingdom would be
his up to the [Jaxartes] River at Fanakat.1
These stakes having been set, Güshlüg arrived
first, and the Gür Khan’s soldiers were away.
He drove forward in haste, and at Balasaqun he
attacked the Gür Khan, who did battle with as
many soldiers as were nearby. Güshlüg suf-
fered defeat and withdrew in rout to regroup.
[464] Sultan Muhammad Khwarazmshah, to-
gether with Sultan Usman of Samarkand, also
advanced on the Gür Khan. When he reached
the province of Taraz, Tayangu, the Gür
1Fanakat, known variously as Banakat and Binakath,
was on the Jaxartes downstream from Khujand, approxi-
mately at the confluence with the Angren. Just north of
Fanakat was the fortress of Shash (~ Chach, Old
Tashkent), which was renamed Shahrukhiyya when it
was rebuilt at the end of the fourteenth century.
Khan’s commander-in-chief, was there with an
army. The two sides did battle, and Tayangu
was felled by Sultan Muhammad, and his
troops were routed. When Güshlüg learned of
the Gür Khan’s weakness, he made himself
battle-ready and, even though his soldiers were
scattered, he set out in all haste, attacked him,
and took him down. Left with no alternative,
the Gür Khan wanted to humble himself before
Güshlüg, but he would not allow it, for he
looked upon him as a father and outwardly
maintained respect, even though he had treach-
erously usurped not only the entire realm of
Turkistan he had held but his position as ruler
as well. Two years later the Gür Khan died of
grief, and the treasury, possessions, and army
that had been built up over a period of thrice
thirty and five years of good fortune and suc-
cess all fell into Güshlüg’s hands. 
Güshlüg maintained his position for a few
years. In the beginning he had married a girl of
the Qarakhitai tribe, most of whom were idol-
aters, and she had converted him to idolatry.2
When his authority in the Qarakhitai realm had
grown strong, he stretched forth the arm of ag-
gression against the subjects and began to
practice unwarranted tyranny. Every year he
sent his soldiers into Muslim homelands in that
area to devour and burn the grain. When the
crops had been thus lost for several years, the
people, sorely pressed for grain, were forced to
submit to his orders. It went so far that soldiers
entered the cities, and a soldier was quartered
in every householder’s dwelling. Corruption
2According to Juvaini (Juvaini/Boyle, p. 64), and fol-
lowing him Mirza Haydar Dughlat (Tarikh-i-Rashidi, fol
137b, trs. p. 185), Güshlüg’s wife was the Gür Khan’s
stepdaughter and probably a Buddhist Qarakhitai. The
Naiman were Christian. The early sixteenth-century his-
torian Khwandamir (Habibu’s-siyar 3:26) turns them
around: “The wretch was an idolator, and his wife fol-
lowed the Christian religion.” See above, text p. 461.
224
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

and vice became rampant among the Muslims,
and idol-worshipping polytheists did anything
they wanted, with no one to stop them. [465]
From there he went to Khotan and took it. He
alienated the people there by forcing them to
give up their Muhammadan religion and giving
them the choice of adopting either Christianity
and the Trinity or idolatry after the manner of
the people of Cathay. Wanting to establish his
absolute authority by forcing the leaders of Is-
lam to yield through rational argumentation, he
had it heralded throughout the city that all who
wore the garments of learning and piety should
present themselves in a certain meadow. As or-
dered, the religious authorities of Khotan all
came out of the city together, and the leader of
the community, Imam Ala’uddin Muhammad
Khutani, stood up and went before Güshlüg,
his tongue sharpened by speaking the truth,
and the two of them began a religious debate.
When voices were raised, truth triumphed over
falsehood, and the learned overwhelmed the
ignorant. Imam Ala’uddin bested Güshlüg,
who was overcome with astonishment. En-
raged, he hurled an unworthy insult against the
Prophet. Imam Ala’uddin Muhammad said,
“Filth in your mouth, enemy of God’s reli-
gion!” 
Güshlüg ordered him seized and tortured
with all sort of painful torments, but he en-
dured patiently. After various exactions they
nailed him spread-eagle to the door of his own
college. With his demise the Muslims were at
once shattered, and the infidels’ tyranny over
the Muslims began in earnest. As the people
raised their hands in supplication, suddenly the
arrow of their prayer hit the target, and the
tyrannical infidel was dealt a set-back by the
world-conquering
emperor,
Genghis
Khan.
This came about as follows.
As has already been said, when Genghis
Khan had finished fighting in Cathay, he as-
signed Muqali Guyang and many soldiers to
guard Cathay and the eastern direction while
Genghis Khan himself set out for the west. He
sent Jäbä Noyan ahead with a huge army to
deal with Güshlüg, who was then in Kashgar.
[466] The Mongol army had scarcely begun to
fight when Güshlüg took flight. Jäbä Noyan
and his men had it heralded in the city that
everyone could practice his own religion as his
forefathers and ancestors had done. Güshlüg’s
soldiers who were living in the city in Muslim
homes were all annihilated, and the Mongol
army went out in pursuit of Güshlüg. Every-
where he stopped they harassed him until final-
ly he took a wrong road in the mountains of
Badakhshan, and he was caught and killed in a
valley called Sarigh Qol.1 The people of
Badakhshan got untold booty in cash and
jewels.
It is clear that every creature who brings
harm to the Muhammadan religion is soon
overcome,
and
he
who
propagates
and
strengthens the Islamic code, even if he be not
a follower, will succeed and enjoy greater for-
tune day by day.
(Güshlüg had a sister named Esin, and she
had sons. One was Yoshmut, and another was
Öljäi Äbügän Abachi. Abachi has two thou-
sand men. She also had a brother named Buchu
Äbügän, who died. He had a son named
Ja’uqu, who is with Tügmä the son of Khwaja
(Hoqu), and his mother was of the Naiman
tribe. Arimjanus Shal, Taru Shal, Bayan Shal,
and Tonka Shal are four brothers and relatives
of Güshlüg Khan. “Shal” means prince. The
Naimans who were gürä’än were called Yedi
Temür. Qausuzmish and Küstüzmish were the
sons of one of the four brothers.) [467]
1Sarigh Qol (Yellow Valley) is the area from which the
modern Sarykolskiy Mountains, southwest of Kashgar
on the border between Tajikistan and China, take their
name.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1211–1218
225

Now that the history of Genghis Khan has
been written in detail from the beginning of
Qonin Yil, the Year of the Sheep that began in
Sha‘ban 607 [January 1211], through Bars Yil,
the Year of the Tiger that began in Dhu’l-Qa‘da
614 [January 1218], a period of eight years,
during the last year of which Genghis Khan
was sixty-four years old, we will now begin a
summary
history
of
the
caliphs,
sultans,
khaqans, maliks, and atabegs who were his
contemporaries in this period. After that we
will return to his history, God willing. [468] 
A summary history of the emperors of Cathay and Machin, the rulers of the Qarakhitai,
Turkistan, and Transoxiana, the caliphs, sultans, maliks, and atabegs of Iran, Syria, Egypt,
North Africa, etc. who were Genghis Khan’s contemporaries from the beginning of Qonin
Yil, the Year of the Sheep that began in Sha‘ban 607 [January 1211], through Bars Yil, the
Year of the Tiger that began in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 614 [January 1218], a period of eight years,
and unusual events that took place.
Dates of the rulers of Cathay during this
period.
Zhangzong [reigned a total of] nineteen
years, [of which] nine were before and two
were after this eight-year period.1
Dates of the rulers of Machin during this
period.
Ningzong [reigned a total of] thirty-two
years, [of which] fifteen were before, and nine
were after, this eight-year period.2 [469]
History of the rulers of the Qarakhitai,
Turkistan, and Transoxiana during this
period.
The same Gür Khan was ruling as before.
During these years, as has been mentioned,
Tayang Khan’s son Güshlüg of the Naiman,
who had married [the Gür Khan’s] daughter,
proved treacherous and usurped the kingdom.
The Gür Khan sickened of grief and died.
Güshlüg was also killed during this period, and
those realms were turned over to Genghis
Khan. 
1Zhangzong (章宗) of the Jin, ruled 1190–1209 (by
Rashiduddin’s calculation, 1200–1219).
2Ningzong (寧宗) of the Southern Song, ruled 1195–
1225.
History of the caliphs, sultans, maliks, and
atabegs during this period.
History of the caliphs. In Baghdad was the
Caliph al-Nasir-li-dini’llah. During these years
he took away the sales tax that had been im-
posed on the people, like the tamgha of these
times. It had produced much revenue. The rea-
son was that the daughter of a wine-seller died,
and a cow was brought to be given as alms.
When the account was made there was men-
tion of the sales tax. The caliph said, “Hence-
forth let no sales tax be taken from any crea-
ture.” He built many hospices in Baghdad and
ordered it heralded on both sides of Baghdad
that the poor should break their fast in the hos-
pices. Mutton, bread, qatuq, and taffy were
given away there.
History of the sultans.
In Khwarazm, Persia, Khurasan, and Ghazna
was Sultan Muhammad Khwarazmshah. Be-
cause all the rulers of those realms [470] had
been exterminated, and he had become an au-
tonomous ruler, his fortunes waxed greatly. He
had also brought parts of Turkistan and Tran-
soxiana under his sway. His history consists of
several stories.
226
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The story of his launching a campaign
against the caliph in Baghdad. In the year 614
[1217–18] the sultan led his army on a cam-
paign to Baghdad. Because insults had previ-
ously been exchanged between him and the
Caliph Nasir, and he harbored hopes of aveng-
ing the insults, the sultan had acquired a legal
writ from the jurists of his realms, in particular
Mawlana Fakhruddin Razi, saying that the
House of Abbas had no right to rule as caliphs
and that the legal right to the caliphate lay with
the sayyids of Husaynid descent. In order to
right this wrong it was incumbent upon every-
one with sufficient power to raise to the
caliphate any Husaynid sayyid who was wor-
thy, especially since the House of Abbas had
retired from undertaking holy war against the
infidels. [The sultan] nominated Sayyid Ala’ul-
mulk of Termez, one of the great sayyids, to be
raised to the caliphate and then set out. 
When he reached Damghan, he heard that
Atabeg Sa‘d of Fars had gone to Rayy intent
upon taking Persia. The sultan galloped with a
mounted entourage and met Atabeg Sa‘d at
Khayl-i-Buzurg. No sooner were ranks drawn
than the army of Fars was defeated. Atabeg
Sa‘d was captured, and the sultan wanted to
kill him, but the atabeg had the malik of Zozan
intercede on his behalf, and the sultan spared
his life. He promised to cede the fortresses of
Istakhr and Ashkanavan1 along with two thirds
of the income of Fars [471] and left his eldest
son, Zangi, as a hostage. He requested permis-
sion to withdraw, and the sultan’s retinue set
out for Hamadan. Atabeg Özbeg, who had
come from Azerbaijan to Hamadan in hopes of
taking Persia, was routed. The soldiers wanted
to pursue him, but the sultan said, “To take two
great rulers in one year is not a good omen. Let
him go.” The sultan continued on to Baghdad.
1For Ashkanavan, see Juvaini/Boyle 2:366, note 16.
At the beginning of autumn, between Gariwa
[and] Asadabad a heavy snowstorm occurred
by night. It was so bad that many of the men
and most of the animals perished. This was the
first blow to the sultan. As a consequence he
cancelled his campaign and stopped in Persia
for a few days to arrange affairs there.
The story of the Khwarazmshah’s
thoughtless killing of merchants and envoys,
an act that results in strife.
When the sultan returned from Persia, a mes-
senger arrived from Ghayir Khan, the amir of
Otrar, to announce merchants attached to
Genghis Khan. Before thinking or planning,
and on the mere opinion of jurists, the sultan
immediately ordered that those Muslims, who
had taken refuge in the sanctuary of his realm,
be killed and their possessions taken as booty.
When your fate turns dark, everything you do
goes wrong.
This came about as follows.
At the end of the Khwarazmshah’s reign the
people enjoyed untold security and welfare.
The fires of unrest [472] had been quenched,
and the roads were so cleared of bandits and
thieves that merchants poured in from all di-
rections in hopes of profit. Since the Mongols
were nomads and far from cities, articles of
clothing and furnishing were of particular val-
ue among them, and the profits to be had by
dealing with them were fabled. Therefore,
three merchants from Bukhara set out for that
region, laden with all sorts of commodities,
gold-spun suits of clothing, zandaniji,2 muslin,
and other goods they thought suitable for those
people. 
At that time Genghis Khan had cleared most
of Cathay and Turkistan of rebels and oppo-
nents and stationed patrols on the roads to let
2Zandanījī, a coarse cloth made in Bukhara; the Arabi-
cized attributive to Zandani(g), a village near Bukhara.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1211–1218
227

merchants pass in safety and send their goods,
as they thought suitable, to Genghis Khan.
They sent these three merchants there. When
they arrived, one of them displayed his cloth,
stating a price of two or three ingots for what
was worth ten or twenty dinars. Genghis Khan
was enraged by this unjust talk and said, “This
person thinks we have never seen clothing be-
fore!” Then he ordered all sorts of expensive
clothing that was in the treasury shown to him.
After that his wares were inventoried and taken
as booty, and he was arrested. 
Then Genghis Khan ordered the merchant’s
companions and their wares brought in. No
matter how much he insisted, they refused to
give a price for their clothing, saying, “We
have brought these goods in the emperor’s
name.” Genghis Khan was pleased by their
speech and ordered a gold ingot given them for
each large suit and a silver ingot for every two
[pieces] of zandaniji muslin. Then he sum-
moned their other comrade and gave him the
same price for all the clothing that had been
plundered from him. [473] He showed them all
sorts of favor, for at that time Muslims were
kept in honor and respect and housed in clean
white tents as a mark of auspiciousness and
respect. 
When they were about to depart he ordered
the ladies, princes, and amirs to send along
with them two or three of their retainers with
gold and silver ingots to go to the sultan’s
realm to trade and acquire rarities to be
brought back. In obedience to the command,
each one of them appointed one or two of his
people,
and
four
hundred
fifty
Muslims
assembled. 
Genghis
Khan
assigned
Mahmud
of
Khwarazm, Ali Khwaja of Bukhara, and Yusuf
Kanka of Otrar to accompany the merchants as
ambassadors to the Khwarazmshah and deliver
a message saying, “The merchants of that re-
gion have come before us, and as you will
hear, we are also sending a group of merchants
thither in their company to bring back rarities
from those lands and to acquire valuable items
from there. The greatness of your family and
the nobility of your dynasty are not unknown,
and the expanse of your kingdom and range of
your authority are well known to all in most
climes of the earth. You are a dear son to me,
and so also are all Muslims. Since the frontiers
near us have been cleared of enemies and all
are under subjugation, on both sides neighbor-
liness is firm. It is demanded by intelligence
and chivalry that on both sides the path of co-
operation be followed, and in case of untoward
events we should aid and assist each other and
keep the roads safe from danger so that mer-
chants, through whose coming and going the
world flourishes, may come and go without
anxiety. Henceforth let all causes for fear and
concern be erased through our agreement,
[474] and let all those who would cause cor-
ruption and strife be eliminated.”
When
the
ambassadors
and
merchants
arrived in Otrar, the amir there, Inalchuq by
name and a relative of the sultan’s mother,
Tärkän Khatun, had taken the title Ghayir
Khan. One of the group was an Indian who,
having been acquainted with him in former
days, called him Inalchuq as he had been ac-
customed to do. Also, out of pride in the great-
ness of his khan, he did not attach much impor-
tance to him. Ghayir Khan was enraged by this
and had him arrested—to be sure, he also
coveted the merchants’ goods. To announce
this he sent an envoy to the sultan in Persia.
Without listening to Genghis Khan’s advice
and without thinking, the Khwarazmshah is-
sued a decree allowing their blood to be spilled
and their goods seized. Little did he realize that
by making their blood and goods licit his own
life would be forfeited.
228
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Everyone who possesses wisdom will look to
the consequences of his actions. / No matter
what you wish to enter in upon, it is necessary
to look for a way out.
With this decree in hand, Ghayir Khan not only
deprived them of life but in so doing also de-
stroyed the world. Before the decree arrived,
one of them managed to trick his way out of
prison and hide in a hole. When he learned of
his companions’ deaths, he took off in haste to
inform Genghis Khan of what had happened.
This report so affected Genghis Khan that he
lost all control. In a conflagration of ire and
wrath he went alone to a hill, put his belt
around his neck, uncovered his head, and put
his forehead to the ground. For three days and
nights he humbled himself and pleaded with
the deity, saying, [475] “O great God! O cre-
ator of Tajik and Turk! I cannot contain myself
in the face of this outrage. With your assistance
give me strength to wreak vengeance.” After
perceiving an answer to this prayer within him-
self, he came down refreshed and glowing, de-
termined to make arrangements for battle. 
Since the Güshlüg affair lay ahead, he began
by dealing with him. An army was dispatched
and, as has been explained, he was eliminated
and envoys were sent to the sultan to remind
him of the treachery that had issued from him
without justification and instructing him to pre-
pare himself for battle with the army that was
moving in his direction. Since the Khwarazm-
shah was too proud and conceited to have
thought of the consequences of his action, he
was trapped in a web of calamity and catastro-
phe. “Having a view to consequences makes
one safe from disasters.”
The story of how Sultan Muhammad
Khwarazmshah learns that Genghis Khan’s
army is headed in his direction, of his
insistence on doing battle with a troop on
the border, and of his return in
stupification.
When news of Genghis Khan’s army reached
Sultan Muhammad Khwarazmshah, he gave
Persia to his son Ruknuddin and set out from
Hamadan for Khurasan. After stopping in
Nishapur for a month, he headed for Bukhara,
where he engaged in sport and frivolity before
going to Samarkand. From there he proceeded
to Jand with a large army, and from there he
went to the borders of Turkistan and his own
realm. 
At that time Genghis Khan’s armies had been
sent to deal with the Qirqiz and Tumat tribes
and to capture Güshlüg and Qudu, the son of
the Märkit ruler who had raised an army after
being defeated and put to flight, and they were
then [476] in the region of the Turkistan fron-
tier in pursuit of tribesmen who had escaped.
The Khwarazmshah’s patrol sent word that the
Mongol army was nearby. The sultan set out
after them, and some Mongol storytellers say it
was the very troop in charge of which Genghis
Khan had put Sübädäi Bahadur and Toquchar
of the Qunqirat and sent them to fight Qudu.
When they had done battle with Qudu at the
above-mentioned place and killed him and
many of his men, the news reached Sultan
Muhammad, and he mounted to attack them.
He found a wounded man in the midst of those
slain in the battle and, having obtained infor-
mation from him, he set out in pursuit of the
Mongol troop. The next day between the two
rivers ___ and ___,1 as dawn was breaking, he
caught up with them and arrayed his men. The
Mongol soldiers withdrew from fighting and
said, “We have no authority from Genghis
1In JTK the names areﲆ ــﻗﻴandﺞ ــﻗﻴ; JTRM reads, with Ju-
vaini/Boyle 2:370, asﲆ ـ ـﻗﻴ(Qaili?) andﺞـﻤـ ـ ـﻗﻴ(Qaimich?),
for which Boyle notes (ibidem, note 30) that Minorsky
suggested an emendation toﻗﻨﻘ
ــ ــ ــ
ﲆ(Qanqli) andﻗﺒﺠ
ــ ــ ــ
ﺦ
(Qipchakh) and a possible identification as the Irghiz
and the Turghai rivers.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1211–1218
229

Khan to fight the Khwarazmshah. We have
come on another mission.” Since the sultan
would not listen to them and would not turn his
reins from battle, the Mongols also headed into
the field, and the two right wings faced each
other. Some of the Mongols charged the center,
and there was fear that the sultan would be
captured. However, the sultan’s son, Sultan
Jalaluddin, came forth, repelled those charges,
which even a mountain would not have been
able to withstand, and got his father out of
harm’s way.
Gird your loins in your father’s presence as
one finer even than a raging lion.
Sultan Jalaluddin fought throughout the day
until evening. After sunset both armies went to
their camps and settled down. The Mongols lit
fires, decamped, and withdrew. When they
came to Genghis Khan they reported the valor
and bravery they had witnessed from Sultan
Jalaluddin. [477] Since Genghis Khan realized
that there was no buffer between them, and all
the rulers who kept them apart had been elim-
inated, he mustered his forces and got ready to
attack
Sultan
Muhammad’s
realm.
Even
though the sultan had initiated the strife, for
the reasons just given Genghis Khan did not
want to attack him and sought in every way
possible to tread the path of amity and neigh-
borliness. In fact, he did not move to do battle
with the sultan until he had taken several in-
sulting and hurtful actions that called for re-
venge. The first was that he thoughtlessly and
unforesightedly killed the group of merchants
and ambassadors he had sent to seek friendship
and peace with friendly messages, paying ab-
solutely no attention to what they had to say.
Second was that he fought with his soldiers un-
willingly. Third was that the sultan usurped
entirely all the lands in Turkistan that had been
held by Güshlüg after he was killed by
Genghis Khan’s soldiers. Altogether these
things caused a vengefulness and enmity and
created a desire for redress and expiation. 
In short, after the battle the sultan returned to
Samarkand, where a perplexity and hesitation
began to gnaw at him and an inner unrest upset
him externally. Since he had witnessed the
might and power of his opponent and he well
knew what causes had motivated this strife had
taken place, moment by moment anxiety and
torment began to overwhelm him and traces of
regret began to be apparent in his words and
deeds. So overwhelmed was he by fear that the
doors of clear thought were closed to him, and
sleep and rest departed. Giving in to his des-
tiny, he submitted to what God had ordained.
The astrologers were also saying that his as-
cendant had moved into dark degrees and ill
portents were observable. [478] As a precau-
tion until the ill portents had passed, he should
undertake no action against an enemy. The as-
trologers’ words also became appended to the
causes for his downfall. 
He pulled his reins in and stationed most of
his soldiers, approximately four hundred thou-
sand in all, in Turkistan and Transoxiana.
Twenty thousand were positioned in Otrar with
Ghayir Khan, ten thousand in Fanakat with
Qutlugh Khan, and thirty thousand in Bukhara
with Amir Ikhtiyaruddin Küshli, the master of
his stables, Ali Hajib entitled Inanch Khan,
Khamid-Bur Tayangu and other amirs. In
Samarkand he stationed his uncle Toghanchaq
and the amirs of Ghor, Kharmil and Kharzur,
the son of Izzuddin Kart, Husamuddin Mas‘ud
and another troop with Hindu. Fakhruddin
Habash (known as Ayyar Nasawi) and the
army of Sijistan he stationed in Termez, and
Mahmud Khan was assigned to Sarakhs. His
cousin Ay Muhammad was put in Balkh, Utruk
Pahlavan in Jand, Daghalchuq Malik in Khut-
talan, Alpar Taisi in Qunduz, and Askütä Khan
in Yarkand. 
230
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

He ordered the ramparts of Samarkand re-
paired, and he rode around the ditch and said,
“If each of the soldiers that are going to attack
us throws his whip into this ditch, it will fill up
right away.” With these words the citizens and
soldiers lost heart. 
The sultan set out via Nakhshab, and every
place he came to he said, “Do what you must
to save yourselves, for resistance to the Mon-
gol army is futile.” He sent someone to take his
wife
and
mother,
Tärkän
Khatun,
from
Khwarazm to Mazanderan. 
As he consulted with every advisor to try to
find a way to deal with the coming disaster,
terrifying news poured in moment by moment
and things fell further to pieces. [479] Those of
experience, especially his son Jalaludin, said,
“It is too late to do anything about Transoxi-
ana. We must strive not to lose Khurasan and
Persia. We should recall the troops we have
stationed in every city, spend whatever is nec-
essary and make the Jaxartes a moat; otherwise
we will have to take refuge in Hindustan.”
Sultan Muhammad approved of this rather
feeble plan and pulled back to Balkh. Just then
Imadulmulk of Sawa arrived, having been sent
by [the sultan’s] son Ruknuddin from Persia
with gifts and presents. The sultan received
him warmly, and he invited the sultan to Per-
sia, saying, “There we will assemble the
armies of Persia and launch our operation
strategically and from a position of strength.” 
Sultan Jalaluddin rejected this proposal, say-
ing, “The best thing to do would be to gather
as many of our soldiers as possible and go out
again at their fore. If the sultan’s heart is feint,
let him go to Persia unencumbered and give
the army to me to lead to the frontier and strike
so that by doing what is within our power we
will not be ashamed before the creator or his
creatures. If we fail, we will not be the target
of arrows of censure, tongues will not be
loosed in blame, and people will not say that
before now they have taken tribute from us or
that now they find us negligent or unoccu-
pied.” Several times he repeated these words
with all insistence. He knew it was necessary
to wait for his father’s permission, but Sultan
Muhammad was so stunned and perplexed that
he could not respond. Considering his son’s
wise proposal a child’s plaything, he clung to
the notion that his lucky star was merely in
eclipse.
The rest of his story, which takes place after
this period, will come after the history of
Genghis Khan, God willing. [480]
In Anatolia was Sultan Ghiyasuddin Kay-
khusraw. During these years he took the city of
Antioch
from
the
Greeks,
giving
them
amnesty. He had laid siege and destroyed sev-
eral towers on the ramparts, and he had almost
taken the town when the inhabitants requested
assistance from the Franks who were on
Cyprus, which is opposite Antioch. An army
came, and Ghiyasuddin withdrew. The Franks
entered the city, and Ghiyasuddin stationed
some of his soldiers in the mountains between
Antioch and his territory to keep anything from
being taken there from his territory. After a
time [famine] broke out in the city, and the in-
habitants told the Franks, “Go deal with the
Muslims, for we are suffering.” Hostilities
broke out between the inhabitants and the
Franks, and the Antiochans called the Muslims
in to help. They did battle with the Franks,
who took refuge in the citadel. The Muslims
sent someone to Konya to summon Ghiyasud-
din. He hastened there with his army, and the
day after he arrived they turned the city over to
him. The citadel was besieged and taken, and
the Franks were captured.
History of the maliks and atabegs.
In Mazanderan was Shah Husamuddin. He
died during these years, leaving three sons.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1211–1218
231

The eldest succeeded and exiled the middle
son from his territory. He went to Alishah, the
Khwarazmshah’s brother, and asked him for
assistance. On the Khwarazmshah’s order Al-
ishah led an army to Mazanderan, but when
they were past Gurgan, the eldest son, who had
become the ruler, died and the youngest son
took over in his stead. Alishah raided Mazan-
deran, and the son who had become ruler went
to the fortress of Kura. [481] No matter how
hard they tried besieging him, they could not
score a victory. Nonetheless, the territory came
under their domination, and the middle son be-
came governor on their behalf with the khutba
and coinage in the Khwarazmshah’s name.
In Persia, Jahan Pahlavan’s slaves Aytogh-
mish and Mängli were governing. Aytoghmish
went to Baghdad and was in [the caliph’s] ret-
inue there for a time. The caliph honored him
by making him the governor of Isfahan and
Hamadan. He got as far as Barjam’s territory,
and there he was waiting for the arrival of
troops from Baghdad when the caliph dis-
missed Sulayman b. Barjam as amir of the Tur-
comans and put his younger brother in his
place. Sulayman informed Mängli, who dis-
patched a troop in haste to assist Sulayman.
Without warning they seized Aytoghmish and
sent his head to Mängli.1 With that, Mängli’s
fortune waxed, troops gathered around him,
and he seized the entire province of Persia.2
Since there was great rancor between him and
Jahan Pahlavan’s son Atabeg Özbeg, the gov-
ernor of Azerbaijan, the caliph sent a message
to Atabeg Özbeg encouraging him to make war
on Mängli and promising him assistance. He
ordered Jalaluddin Muhammad, the lord of the
Ismailis’ fortresses,
to
reinforce
him
and
1According to Ibn al-Athir (Kamil 12:301), Aytogh-
mish was killed in Muharram 610 (May–June 1213).
2To here the summary agrees with Ibn al-Athir (Kamil
12:301).
promised him that when they got rid of
Mängli, part of the territory would be the
atabeg’s, part the caliph’s, and part Jalaluddin
Muhammad’s. The caliph dispatched Muzaf-
faruddin Kök-Böri, the lord of Arbela and
Shahrazor with an army. They went to attack
Mängli in Hamadan. He took refuge in a
mount near Karaj, and the armies surrounded
the mountain. Mängli fled by night, and his
soldiers dispersed. The caliph’s army took the
territory,
which
was
divided
as
he
had
promised. [482] Atabeg Özbeg gave his por-
tion to his brother’s slave Oghulmish since he
had performed valiantly during battle. The sol-
diers returned home, and Mängli went in defeat
to Sava, the shahna of which was his friend.
He asked for permission to enter the city, and
the shahna let him in, quartered him in his own
house, took his weapons, and wanted to put
him in chains and send him to Oghulmish.
Mängli requested that [the shahna] himself kill
him and not send him to Oghulmish. The shah-
na took Mängli’s head and sent it to Atabeg
Özbeg, who forwarded it to Baghdad.3
You may know that when the chips are down,
no one will help you at all.
In Azerbaijan was the Atabeg Özbeg who has
just been mentioned.
In Diyarbekir, the lord of Mosul, Izzuddin
Mas‘ud b. Nuruddin Arslanshah b. Izzuddin
Mas‘ud b. Qutbuddin Mawdud b. Imaduddin
Zangi b. Aqsunqur died during these years.
Having made his son Arslanshah, who was
only ten years old, the heir, and also having ap-
pointed Badruddin Lu’lu’ to manage the king-
dom as he had done for him and his father, Nu-
ruddin, he died during the night. That very
night Badruddin sent messengers to the maliks
to renew their pledge of fealty and to the caliph
for the issue of a writ of succession. The next
3Agrees with Ibn al-Athir, Kamil 12:306f.
232
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

morning, all these things having been done, he
sat in mourning. The messengers quickly re-
turned, their missions accomplished. From
Baghdad edicts and patents confirming Nurud-
din’s succession and Badruddin’s regency were
sent. 
Nuruddin spent most of his time sulking. His
uncle [483] Imaduddin Zangi, who held the
fortresses of Shush and [Tall A]‘far, had de-
signs on ruling Mosul. Together with Muzaf-
faruddin of Arbela he took the fortresses of
Hakkari and Zawzan,1 and time and again
Badruddin sent his messages of advice, but he
refused to listen. Badruddin sought assistance
from Malik Ashraf, the son of Malik Adil. He
agreed and sent a troop to reinforce him.
Badruddin went to war with Imaduddin, and
Muzaffaruddin of Arbela sent troops to rein-
force Imaduddin. Battle was fought. Badruddin
defeated Imaduddin’s men. From Baghdad en-
voys arrived and made a truce between them.
Arslanshah died after Nuruddin’s truce, and his
younger brother Nasiruddin Mahmud, who was
only three years old, was made ruler. Because
he was an infant, Imaduddin’s desire for the
kingdom grew even greater. He set out for
Mosul. Just then Badruddin sent his son with a
troop to help Malik Ashraf, and together they
went to Egypt to assist [Malik Ashraf’s] broth-
er, Kamil. The troop that had been sent by Ma-
lik Ashraf to help Badruddin was led by Izzud-
din Aybak and was in Nisibis. Badruddin
summoned them, and they crossed the Tigris
and met three leagues from Mosul. Izzuddin
Aybak attacked the left wing, where Imaduddin
Zangi was, and defeated him. Muzaffaruddin,
who was in the center, attacked Badruddin’s
left wing and defeated him. Badruddin went to
Mosul, and Muzaffaruddin went to Arbela. En-
1Hakkari is the modern Hakkâri on the Great Zab Riv-
er in the extreme southeast of Turkey.
voys were sent, and a truce was made. Malik
Ashraf took Sinjar and went to Mosul to help
Badruddin. Nasiruddin Muhammad, the lord of
Amid, was with him, and they attacked Arbela.
[484] The caliph’s envoys arrived, a truce was
made, and everyone returned home. The lord
of Mayyafariqin was Malik Awhad Najmuddin
Ayyub b. al-Adil.2 He took the city of Mush
and set out against Akhlat, with the lord of
which he did battle and was defeated, returning
to Mayyafariqin with only a few men. His fa-
ther sent help, and he did battle with Balban,
the lord of Akhlat. Defeated, Balban withdrew
into Akhlat and requested assistance from
Mughisuddin, the lord of Erzurum. He went
himself, took advantage of the opportunity, and
killed Balban. He wanted to seize Akhlat, but
the people of Akhlat sent someone to summon
Najmuddin. When he arrived they turned the
rule over to him, and he took control of most
of the territory in that area. Once again they re-
belled against him, and once more he took the
city by force after a massacre and much
plunder.
In Syria and Egypt was Malik Adil,3 and
each of his sons was governing in a portion of
the kingdom. In the year 614 [1217–18] Adil
dispatched his son Malik Mu‘azzam Isa, the
governor of Damascus, with a large army to
Nablus to repel the Franks who, having re-
quested reinforcements from all directions and
having
gathered
in
Acre,
plundered
and
wrought havoc from Beisan to Banyas, and to
keep them out of Jerusalem. The Franks went
from the Acre plain to lay siege to the fortress
at Tur [Mount Tabor], which they besieged for
seventeen days. Their commander was hit by
an arrow and died, and they fled. Adil de-
2al-Malik al-Awhad of Akhlat, d. 1210.
3The Ayyubid al-Malik al-‘Adil I Sayfuddin, ruled
1200–1218.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1211–1218
233

stroyed the fortress since it was near Acre and
difficult to maintain. The Franks departed from
Acre and went to sea, disembarking at Damiet-
ta in Egypt [485] where the Nile separated
them from Damietta proper where the river
spills into the sea. They camped there and dug
a deep trench around themselves, and there
they constructed engines of war. Adil’s son
Malik Kamil, who was the governor of Egypt,
camped opposite them in Adiliyya, and the
Franks fought for a time until [the site] was
taken by force. [The Egyptians] broke the
chains [that had been put in place] so that their
engines could not come or go.1 In place of the
chains Malik Kamil had a very strong boom
(chambar) made to prevent the Franks from
coming or going.2 They fought a fierce battle,
and Kamil seized several ships and scuttled
them on the rocks. In short, they fought for
several days. Since the Nile was in between,
the Damiettans had no fear of the Franks and
opened their gates and engaged in commerce.
In Fars was Atabeg Muzaffaruddin Sa‘d b.
Zangi, a bit about whom has already been stat-
1“There was on the Nile at that time a highly fortified
tower of great strength and powers of resistance. It had
steel
chains,
immensely
robust
and
thick,
which
stretched across the Nile to prevent ships arriving by the
high seas from entering into Egypt” (Maqrizi/Broad-
hurst, p. 166).
2“To prevent the Franks from passing up the Nile, al-
Kámil had laid a great boom (jisr) to take the place of
the chains” (Maqrizi/Broadhurst, p. 172).
ed in the section on the Khwarazmshah. When
he went to Fars after plotting with the sultan,
and his son Atabeg Abubakr heard of this, he
went out to do battle in disagreement. He lay in
ambush at the gate of Tang-i-Faruq and at-
tacked his father. In that attack he fell from his
horse and was taken captive. His father had
him imprisoned and sent him to the Qal‘a-i-
Sapedar and then kept his agreement with the
sultan. 
In Kirman, Atabeg Sa‘d’s nephew was rul-
ing. When he rebelled against him, after a
while the malik of Zozan became the governor
of that area on behalf of the Khwarazmshah
and became very strong and powerful. [486]
❈
Now that the history of the khaqans, caliphs,
maliks, and atabegs of the various territories
who were contemporaries of Genghis Khan
from the beginning of Qonin Yil, the Year of
the Sheep that began in Sha‘ban 607 [January
1211], through the end of Bars Yil, the Year of
the Tiger that began in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 614 [Janu-
ary 1218], a period of eight years, has been
summarily written, we will commence the his-
tory of the next period. [487]
 
234
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The History of Genghis Khan from the beginning of Taulai Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that
began in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 615 [January 1219], through Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig that
began in Safar 624 [January 1227], a period of nine years
At the beginning of this period he set out for
Turkistan and the realms of the land of Iran.
Within six years he had completed his dealings
with those lands, and in the seventh, the Year
of the Rooster that began in Safar 622 [Febru-
ary 1225], he returned to his ordus. Upon hear-
ing that the province of Tangqut had rebelled
again, he mounted on an expedition for there
and reconquered it. In the Year of the Pig men-
tioned above, fifteen days after the midpoint of
autumn, which corresponds to Ramadan [of
that year], he died. Although he died in his sev-
enty-third year, since it was an incomplete
year, he lived seventy-two years, as all Mon-
gols are agreed. 
Genghis Khan’s world-seizing, world-
conquering banners head in the direction of
Sultan Muhammad’s realm after successive
conquests there.
At the beginning the Year of the Rabbit,
which commenced in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 615 but
most of which corresponds to the year 616,1
[488] the dust of Güshlüg’s sedition had settled
and the roads had been cleared of opponents
and rebels. Genghis named his sons and com-
manders
of
ten
thousand,
thousands,
and
hundreds, organized them, and had them as-
semble for a quriltai. He laid down new regula-
tions and mounted for a campaign against the
Khwarazmshah’s realm.
In the Year of the Dragon he summered along
the Irtysh River and sent emissaries to the sul-
tan to announce his intended campaign and to
warn of the revenge for the murders of the
1Dhu’l-Qa‘da 615 began in January 1219. The year
616 began in March 1219.
merchants and other things the sultan had done
the year before. He advanced in the autumn,
taking the entire territory that lay on his way.
When he reached the vicinity of Qayaliq, the
chief of that area, Arslan Khan, came to sub-
mit, was rewarded, and set out as an auxiliary
to the Mongol army. From Beshbaliq came the
Idiqut of the Uyghur with his horde, and from
Almalyk came Suqnaq Tegin with his army.
Genghis Khan reaches Otrar, and it is taken
by the Mongol army.
At the end of autumn in the Year of the Drag-
on, Genghis Khan and his mighty army
reached the city of Otrar, and his court tent was
pitched opposite the fortress. The sultan had
given a huge army to Ghayir Khan, and
Qaracha the chamberlain had been sent to rein-
force him with ten thousand horsemen. They
had repaired and reinforced the fortifications
and ramparts and assembled engines of war.
Genghis Khan ordered [489] Chaghatai and
Ögödäi to lay siege with several divisions, and
Tolui Khan was assigned soldiers to go to Jand
and Barchinlighkent. A group of officers was
sent to Khujand and Fanakat, and units were
dispatched in all directions, while Genghis
Khan himself headed for Bukhara. (The story
of how Bukhara and Samarkand were taken
will come in good time.) 
Battles were fought in Otrar for five months,
and in the end the people of Otrar were
reduced to dire straits and Qaracha gave his
consent to surrender and turn over the city.
Since Ghayir Khan knew that he was the cause
for all this trouble, he did not imagine in any
way that he would be allowed to live. Qaracha
did not insist very much, and by night he de-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
235

parted through the gate with his soldiers. Mon-
gol soldiers captured him and took him to the
princes, who said, “You, with all you have
been through together, have not kept faith with
your master. We cannot expect you to keep
faith with us.” So saying, they had him and all
his men killed. The city was taken, all the peo-
ple were driven out like a ﬂock of sheep, and
everything was pillaged. Ghayir Khan and
twenty men went to the citadel gate, and peo-
ple came out in groups of fifty and were killed.
Battle lasted for one month, and most were
slain. Ghayir Khan was left with two men, but
they continued fighting courageously. The
Mongol soldiers surrounded him in the citadel,
but he went out on the roof and refused to sur-
render until those two liege men had also been
killed. When there were no weapons left, he
threw bricks and kept fighting. The Mongols
took everything around him and reduced the
ramparts and walls level with the ground. Of
the peasants and craftsmen who had escaped
the sword, some were sent as levy to Bukhara,
Samarkand, and those areas.1 [490] Ghayir
Khan was killed in the Kök Saray, and the sol-
diers departed.
1The “levy” (ḥashr) consisted of civilians corvéed and
driven before the Mongol army as what would later be
called “human cannon fodder.”
Prince Jochi sets out for Jand and
Barchinligh, which he takes.2
By order of Genghis Khan, Prince Jochi set
out in the year mentioned above with Ulus Idi
for Jand.3 First he came to the entrepôt of Sigh-
naq,4 which is on the banks of the Oxus. In the
vanguard he dispatched as an emissary Husayn
Hajji, who had long been a merchant in
Genghis Khan’s service and was a respected
member of the retinue, to deliver a message to
the people of the area and advise them as an
act of kindness to surrender in order that their
lives and possessions might be safe. However,
before he could deliver his message and ad-
vice, maleficents and common rabble created
an uproar and, shouting Allahu akbar, killed
him, thinking it an act of great merit. When
Jochi learned of this, he arrayed his army to
fight from sunup to sundown. They battled in
successive waves until they conquered the
town, and, closing the gates of forgiveness and
compassion, they killed all in one instant in re-
venge. The governorship of the area was given
to the slain Husayn Hajji’s son. 
2The taking of Barchin during Ögödäi Qa’an’s time is
mentioned by Carpini: Quedam autem ciuitas, nomine
Barchin, diu restitit eis. Ciues enim in circuitu ciuitatis
foueas multas fecerant, propter quas non poterant à Tar-
taris capi, donec illas repleuissent (p. 87, lines 20–23),
“But a certeine citie called Barchin resisted them a long
time. For the citizens had cast vp many ditches and
trenches about their citie, in regard whereof the Tartars
could not take it, till they had filled the said ditches” (p.
121).
3The “Ulus Idi” throughout this passage is actually
one of Jochi’s posthumous titles, but it has been mistak-
en through this passage for the name of another indi-
vidual. See Juvaini/Boyle 1:86, note 1.
4Sighnaq, or Sughnaq, lies in ruins six or seven miles
north of Tyumen-Aryk in Kazakhstan. See Barthold,
Turkestan, 179.
236
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Leaving there, they proceeded to take Öz-
gand and Barchinlighkent.1 Then they set out
for Ashnas,2 where there was a throng of rabble
and common soldiers. They were unrelenting
in fighting, but most were killed. [491] The
news reached Jand, and Qutlugh Khan, the
commander-in-chief stationed there by the sul-
tan, crossed the Oxus by night and took the
desert road to Khwarazm. When news of his
abandonment of Jand was received, he sent
Chin Temür3 on a mission to Jand, won them
over, and thus avoided hostilities. Since there
was no leader or governor in Jand, and every-
one was speaking however he wanted and
thinking in his own best interests, the common
people rose up and attacked Chin Temür, but
with kindness and sympathy he informed them
of the fate of Sighnaq and the murder of Hajji
Husayn and thus quieted them down and con-
cluded an agreement with them, saying, “I will
not allow any foreign army to form an attach-
ment with this place.” They were content with
that undertaking and did not harm him. Chin
Temür suddenly left them and went to Jochi
and Ulus Idi to inform them of the situations
he had witnessed. They set out for there, and
on the 4th of Safar 616 [April 21, 1219], they
camped outside the city, and the soldiers got
busy digging a trench and preparing defenses.
The people of Jand closed the gates and began
to fight from the ramparts. Since they had nev-
er before experienced war, they were aston-
ished how the Mongols could scale the walls of
the fortress by placing ladders against the walls
and swarming over the ramparts from all direc-
1Location of Özgand unknown. Perhaps in the Kara-
Tau mountains. See Barthold, Turkestan, 179.
2The ruins of Ashnas lie on the left bank of the
Jaxartes, seventeen miles from the river and twenty
miles from the post station of Ber-Kazan. See Barthold,
Turkestan, 179, note 4.
3See Juvaini/ Boyle 1:88, note 7.
tions. The Mongols opened the city gates and
drove all the citizens out, but they treated them
mercifully—except for a few leaders who had
spoken harshly with Chin Temür. Those they
killed. For nine days and nights they kept the
citizens standing in the plain while the city was
given over to general plunder. Thereafter Ali
Khwaja, a native of Bukhara [492] who had
joined Genghis Khan’s service before his
emergence, was appointed governor. Then they
headed for the city of Yangikent,4 which they
took and left in the care of a shahna. From
there Ulus Idi headed for Qaraqorum.5 Of the
nomads and Turcomans who were in that
vicinity, two thousand men were appointed to
go to the Khwarazm expeditionary force.
Tainal was in charge of them. After going sev-
eral stages their own bad luck forced them to
rebel and kill the Mongol whom Tainal had
stationed at their head as deputy. Tainal was in
the vanguard, and when he heard the news he
turned back and killed most of that tribe. Some
managed to escape in ﬂight. Another tribe went
in the direction of the Oxus and amassed there,
as will be told in the proper place.
Fanakat and Khujand are taken, and what
happened to Temür Malik.
When Genghis Khan arrived in Otrar and
dispatched his sons and amirs in all directions,
he sent to Fanakat the three, Alaq Noyan, Sik-
tür, and Taghai, with five thousand men from
various parts who had allied themselves with
them. They went there and fought a three-day
battle with Elätgü Malik,6 who was there with
4Yangikent now lies in ruins known as Jankent, “to the
south of the Syr-Darya, about three miles from the for-
mer Khivan fortress of Jan Qal‘a, fifteen miles from
Kazalinsk” (Barthold, Turkestan, 415f.).
5Thus in the text, but it may be Qara Qum. See Juvai-
ni/Boyle 1:89, note 9.
6See Juvaini/Boyle 1:91 and Khwandamir, Habibu’s-
siyar 3:30.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
237

a troop of Qanqlis. On the fourth day amnesty
was sought and the people surrendered. The
soldiers, lords, and common people were sepa-
rated. Some of the soldiers were killed with
swords and others with a barrage of arrows.
The women and children were divided among
units of a thousand and a hundred, and the
young men were sent out to the levy and
moved toward Khujand.1 [493] When they
arrived there, the citizens took refuge in the
fortress. 
One of Temür Malik’s liege men, a valiant,
brave, and courageous man, had reinforced a
high fortress in the middle of the Jaxartes at
the point where the river splits and taken a
thousand renowned warriors inside. When the
army arrived, the fortress could not be taken
because neither arrows nor catapult stones
could reach it. The young Khujandis were dri-
ven there in the levy, and reinforcements were
brought in from Otrar and the towns and vil-
lages that had been taken. Finally fifty thou-
sand men from the levies and twenty thousand
Mongols were assembled. All were divided
into units of tens and hundreds, and a Mongol
was appointed to command each unit of ten
Tajiks. On foot, they transported rocks from
the mountains a league away and threw them
into the Jaxartes.
Temür Malik had constructed twelve war-
ships, roofed over and sealed with felt polished
with clay and vinegar, and provided with small
ports. Every day at dawn he sent off six of
these in all directions to fight. Fire, arrows, and
naphtha had no effect on them, and when
stones were thrown into the water he had the
ﬂoodgates opened so that by night they were
able to make surprise attacks. The army was at
its wit’s end over what to do with him. After
1Khujand is the modern Khodzhent on the Jaxartes in
Tajikistan.
that, the Mongols arranged many projectiles
and mangonels and fought hard. When Temür
Malik was hard pressed, he brought by night
seventy boats he had outfitted for the day of
his escape. Loading his household and baggage
in them, he put his warriors in them too while
he himself and a group of his fighting men got
in the warships, lit torches, and set out across
the water like lightning. When the Mongol sol-
diers found out about this, [494] they raced to
the bank of the river, but everywhere Temür
Malik saw a group of them, he drove his skiffs
and warships there and chased them away with
arrows that never failed to hit their targets.
Then he raced his ships over the water like the
wind until he reached Fanakat. With one blow
he broke the chain that had been stretched
across the water to prevent ships from passing
and continued on his way without a care. The
soldiers kept fighting him from both banks
until he reached the vicinity of Jand and
Barjligh. 
When Jochi found out about him he stationed
soldiers in several places on both sides of the
Oxus, had a bridge built of boats, and set in
motion carts and crossbows. Learning of the
ambush, Temür Malik got out of the water next
to the Kent gulf and continued on horseback.
The Mongols continued in pursuit of him, but
he would come forward with his ships and
stand to fight while his household got farther
away, and then he would retreat. Several days
passed in such struggle. Most of his men were
killed, and the Mongols were increasing in
number every moment. Finally his household
was seized, and he and a few men were left,
but they continued fighting bravely, refusing to
give up. When those men too were killed, he
had no weapons left save three arrow shafts.2
2Omitted from the narrative is that Temür Malik was
being pursued by three Mongols. See Juvaini/ Boyle
238
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

When he shot one arrow without a point, it
blinded a Mongol. To the others he said, “Two
shafts remain, just your number, and I be-
grudge you my arrows. It would be better for
you to withdraw and save yourselves.” The
Mongols withdrew, and he reached Khwarazm,
where once again he took up the struggle. Then
he and a group of men went to Yangikent.
There was a shahna there. He killed him and
returned. Not considering it wise to remain in
Khwarazm, he set out on the sultan’s heels for
Shahristana, where he joined him. [495] For
the period in which the sultan was being
chased around he performed valiant service for
him. After that he went to Syria in the guise of
a Sufi, and when the fires of sedition had died
down he was drawn back home by patriotism.
He set out and lived a few years in the town of
Osh1 in Fergana, with no knowledge of his
family or sons. Once he went to Khujand on
business, and there he saw his son, who had
found favor with the Qa’an and regained his
father’s properties and possessions. He went to
his son and said, “If you saw your father again,
would you recognize him?”
“I was a nursing infant when my father left,”
he replied. “How could I recognize him? How-
ever, I have an Indian slave who did see him.”
The slave was summoned, and he told of the
marks on Temür Malik’s body by which he
could be recognized. When he saw them he
confirmed Temür Malik’s veracity. The news
spread abroad that he was still alive, although
one group of people refused to acknowledge
him because they were holding things that be-
longed to him. He therefore thought of going
to the Qa’an, and along the way he chanced
upon Qadaqan Oghul, who ordered him bound
1:93.
1Emend the text’sاوروسtoاوش(Osh). It is the modern
Osh in Kyrgyzstan at the extreme eastern end of the Fer-
gana Valley.
and held for an investigation into his past resis-
tance to the Mongols. He spoke boldly in this
manner:
Sea and mountain beheld me in battle with a
group of renowned warriors from Turan. /
What can I say? The stars are my witnesses. In
manliness the world lies beneath my feet.
He also recognized the Mongol who had been
hit by his broken arrow. When the prince had
asked him many questions and he had not
maintained proper etiquette or respect in his re-
sponses, in anger the prince shot an arrow at
him and hit him. [496]
He writhed and then gave one sigh, no longer
worrying about good or evil.
And that was his end. 
Genghis Khan arrives in Bukhara, and the
details of its liberation.
We have already mentioned that at the end of
autumn in the Year of the Dragon the spring of
which corresponded with Dhu’l-Hijja of 616
[February 1220], when Genghis Khan arrived
in Otrar, he dispatched Chaghatai and Ögödäi
to conquer Otrar and Jochi and the amirs with
everyone’s troops to somewhere else. Until the
second month of spring in the Year of the
Snake, the beginning of which corresponded
with Dhu’l-Hijja 617 [January 1221], which
was more or less five months, the princes and
amirs were occupied with the conquest of the
towns to which they had been assigned. All
that happened as has been described. 
Now we will list in order the towns that fell
to Genghis Khan during this winter from the
time he set forth from Otrar until all the
princes and amirs rejoined him and he sent
Jochi, Chaghatai, and Ögödäi out again to con-
quer Khwarazm while he himself and Tolui
Khan crossed the Oxus at Termez and headed
toward Iran.
This came about as follows. When Genghis
Khan assigned the princes and commanders to

conquer those territories, he himself set out
from Otrar along the Zarnuq1 road to Bukhara,
accompanied by his youngest son, Tolui Khan,

warning at dawn. The people of the area ﬂed
into the fortress in fear of this huge army.
Genghis Khan sent Danishmand the chamber-
lain in to them to inform them of the arrival of
his retinue and to advise them. A group of sedi-
tious people wanted to molest him, but he
shouted out, saying, “I am Danishmand the
chamberlain, a Muslim and a Muslim born. I
have come as an emissary at Genghis Khan’s
command to save you from a maelstrom.
Genghis Khan has arrived here with a mighty
army of brave warriors. If you imagine you can
oppose him, he will turn the plain into an Oxus
of blood in an instant. If you listen to advice
and submit to him, your lives and property will
remain safe.”
When they heard these reasonable words,
they saw it was in their best interests to obey.
The leaders came forth and sent out a delega-
tion with a variety of food offerings. When
they were presented, he asked about the leaders
of Zarnuq. Angered by their complaisance, he
sent an envoy to summon them. They immedi-
ately went before him and were shown various
favors and granted amnesty of their lives. An
order was given for the men of Zarnuq to be
driven into the plain. The young men were as-
signed to the levy for Bukhara, and the others
were given permission to return home. Zarnuq
was then renamed Qutlugh Baliq. 
A Turcoman guide from that area who knew
the roads very well led the army along a track-
less route to the border of Nur.2 From that time
on, that road has been called the Khan’s Road.
1Zarnuq, also read as Zurnuq.
2Nur is the modern Nurata in Uzbekistan.
Dayir Bahadur, who was in the vanguard, sent
a messenger to inform them of Genghis Khan’s
arrival and to deliver promises and threats. Af-
ter emissaries were exchanged, the people of
Nur went before Genghis Khan bearing gifts of
food and surrendered. [498] After accepting
the tribute he said, “Sübädäi will come to you
in the vanguard. Turn the city over to him.”
When Sübädäi arrived they obeyed the order.
Sixty chosen men were sent to Dabus in the
company of the son of the amir of Nur, El
Khwaja by name, as reinforcements. When
Genghis Khan arrived they went out to greet
him and presented suitable fodder and offer-
ings of food. Genghis Khan received them with
regal warmth and asked, “What is the normal
amount of taxes due the sultan from Nur?”
“Fifteen hundred dinars,” they replied.
“Pay this amount in cash,” he said, “and you
will not be subject to further harassment.”
They paid and were saved from being killed
and pillaged.
From there they proceeded to Bukhara, arriv-
ing in the outskirts of the city around the be-
ginning of Muharram 617 [March 1220] and
dismounting at the citadel gate. Then the sol-
diers arrived and encircled the city. The army
of Bukhara numbered twenty thousand, and
they were led by Kök Khan and the other
amirs, Khamid Bur Tayangu, Sevinch Khan,
and Küshli Khan.3 They emerged from the
fortress by night with their people, but when
they reached the banks of the Oxus, [the Mon-
gols] fell upon them. At dawn the next
morning the gates were opened, and a throng
of leaders and dignitaries went before the em-
peror. Genghis Khan mounted to have a look at
the city and fortifications. Then he entered the
city, rode to the congregational mosque, and
3He was Ikhtiyaruddin, the Khwarazmshah’s grand
equerry. See Juvaini/Boyle 1:103, note 19.

stopped in front of the maqsura. Tolui Khan
dismounted, went up on the pulpit, and asked,
“Is this place the sultan’s palace?”
“It is the house of God,” they replied.
“The plain is empty of fodder,” he said. “Fill
our horses’ bellies!” The doors to the city
storehouses were opened, [499] and grain was
brought out. The chests that held Korans were
turned into mangers for the horses, and harps
and wine were tossed into the mosque. The
singers of the city were brought to sing and
dance, and the Mongols also sang in their own
manner.
Sayyids,
erudite
learned
men,
shaykhs, and beasts of burden were lined up
together to carry out the orders of these people.
After that, Genghis Khan left the city and sum-
moned the common people. He mounted the
pulpit in the festival prayer space, and after
enumerating the sultan’s acts of opposition and
treachery in great detail, he said, “O people,
know that you are great sinners, and your lead-
ers are at the head of the pack in sin. You ask
me why I say this. I say it because I am the
scourge of God. If great sins had not been
committed by you, the great God would not
have sent you one like me as a torment.”
Then he asked, “In whom do you trust and
rely?” Each named a representative from
among his own people. Then he appointed a
Mongol or a Turk as a basqaq for each one to
keep the soldiers from harassing anyone. When
he had finished with that, he concluded his
speech by summoning the rich and wealthy
and ordering them to give over their buried
wealth. Two hundred seventy persons were as-
signed, one hundred ninety citizens and the rest
foreigners. In accordance with his order they
exacted property from the trustees, taking
everything they gave and demanding more be-
sides. Then he ordered fire set in the city quar-
ters, and most of the city was burned in a few
days, all except the congregational mosque and
some palaces made of brick. 
Then the people of Bukhara were sent to do
battle with the citadel. On both sides catapults
were put in place; bows were strung; stones
and arrows were sent ﬂying. From inside, vials
of naphtha were hurled. [500] For days the on-
slaught was resisted. Finally the people in the
citadel were reduced to dire straits, and the
citadel moat was filled level with the ground
with various things animate and inanimate.
The men of the Bukhara levy took the citadel
and set fire to it. The lords and nobles of the
age, who were so refined that their feet had
never touched the ground, were ignobly taken
prisoner and “drowned in a sea of annihila-
tion.” Of the Qanqlis, no one taller than a whip
was spared. More than thirty thousand men
were put to death, and the women and children
were taken away as slaves. When the city had
been cleared of rebels and the walls had been
leveled to the ground, all the people of the city
were driven into the festival prayer area, and
the young men were taken off in the levy to
Dabusiyya. From there Genghis Khan set out
for Samarkand, intending to take it.
Genghis Khan heads for Samarkand and
takes it with his world-conquering army.
At the end of spring in the Moghai Yil men-
tioned above, which began in Dhu’l-Hijja 617
[January 1221] but most of which was in 618,1
Genghis Khan set out for Samarkand. Sultan
Muhammad
Khwarazmshah
had
entrusted
Samarkand to 110,000 men, 60,000 of whom
were Turks, with sixty demon-shaped ele-
phants. There was such a huge throng of com-
mon people and elite alike that they could not
be numbered. In addition he had fortified the
walls of the fortress and constructed several
1Dhu’l-Hijja 617 began on January 27, 1221; the year
618 began on February 25, 1221.

241

outer walls around the perimeter [501] and
connected the moat to water. 
When Genghis Khan arrived in Otrar he
heard reports of the enormity of the army in
Samarkand and the strength of its fortress and
citadel, and all were agreed that it would take
years to reduce the city itself to capitulation,
not to mention the citadel. As a precaution he
thought it best to clear the surrounding areas
first, and to that end he set out for Bukhara,
took it, and then drove an enormous levy to
Samarkand. At every place he reached along
the way, those who surrendered were un-
harmed, but at those places that resisted, like
Sar-i-Pul and Dabusiyya, he stationed a contin-
gent to lay siege.
When he reached Samarkand, the princes and
officers who had been sent to Otrar and other
territories had completed their conquests. They
and the levies that had been sent there came,
Kök Saray was chosen as a place for the court,
and as the various contingents arrived they
camped encircling the city.
Genghis Khan himself rode around the ram-
parts and outer walls for a day or two, contem-
plating tactics for taking them. During that
time news arrived that the Khwarazmshah was
in his summer place. Jäbä Bahadur and Sübätäi
Bahadur, both great generals, were dispatched
with thirty thousand men, and Alaq Noyan and
Yisa’u[r] were sent to Wakhsh and Taligan. 
After that, at dawn of the third day, more
Mongol soldiers and levies than could be num-
bered encircled the city walls. The next day
Alpär Khan, Shaykh Khan, Balan Khan, and a
host of khans did battle outside, and many
were killed on both sides. That night all re-
turned to their bases. The next day Genghis
Khan himself mounted, [502] stationed all the
soldiers around the perimeter of the city, and
with arrow and blade forced the city fighters
into the plain and battlefield. The citizens,
scared by the battle that day, divided into
factions.
The next day the Mongols, itching to fight,
and the citizens, hesitant, began the battle
again. Suddenly the cadi and the shaykhu’l-is-
lam came to Genghis Khan with a group of
people and then went back into the city, having
been given promises. The next morning at
prayer time they opened the gates to let the sol-
diers in. That day the Mongols got to work de-
stroying the ramparts and outer fortifications,
leveling them to the ground. The men and
women were driven out into the plain by the
hundreds, accompanied by Mongols, but the
cadi and shaykhu’l-islam and their dependents
were exempted from the exodus. Nearly fifty
thousand men remained safe under their pro-
tection. It was heralded that anyone who hid
would be killed, and as the Mongols were busy
looting they killed many they found hidden in
nooks and crannies. The elephant drivers took
their elephants before Genghis Khan and asked
for fodder for them. He ordered them turned
loose in the plains to forage for themselves.
The elephants were turned loose, but they per-
ished of hunger.
That night the Mongols came out of the city,
and the defenders of the fortress were in great
fear. Alpär Khan and a thousand warriors ready
to die attacked the army, emerged from the
fortress, and took ﬂight. The next morning the
soldiers again stood encircling the citadel, and
arrows and stones were sent ﬂying from both
sides. The ramparts and outer works of the
fortress were destroyed, and the water canal
was also ruined. By evening they had taken the
gates and gotten inside. A thousand warriors
and champions took refuge in the mosque,
from inside which they fought hard with ar-
rows and naphtha. The Mongols also hurled
naphtha, took the mosque and everyone in it,
[503] and burned the lot. They drove the peo-
242

ple of the citadel out into the plain, separating
the Turks from the Tajiks, and dividing them
into groups of hundreds and tens. For the Turks
they made nughula1 (side locks) and forelocks,
and they put the rest to death—all Qanqlis,
more than thirty thousand under the command
of Barishmas Khan, Taghayi Khan, Sarsigh
Khan, Ulagh Khan, and some twenty-odd of
the sultan’s other commanders whose names
Genghis Khan wrote in detail to Ruknuddin
Kurt.
When the city and fortress alike lay in ruins,
and many officers and soldiers had been exe-
cuted, the next day those who were left were
counted. Of the total, thirty thousand registered
as craftsmen were distributed among the offi-
cers, commanders, and ladies. An equal num-
ber was assigned to the levy. The remainder
were given permission to depart, and as a to-
ken of appreciation for their safety they were
levied an amount of 200,000 dinars, which
Siqatulmulk and Amir Amid Buzurg, two high-
office-holding dignitaries of Samarkand, were
ordered to collect. He assigned a shahna and
took

of

levy
with
himself
to
