Khwarazm. Several other times after that they
requested levies, and few persons escaped
from those levies because that region was
totally devastated.
Genghis Khan spent that summer and au-
tumn in the vicinity of Samarkand. [504]
The end of Sultan Muhammad
Khwarazmshah and how he met his death.
When Genghis took Samarkand in the sum-
mer of the Year of the Snake that began in
Dhu’l-Hijja 617 [January 1221] but most of
which fell in 618, which was the third year of
his campaign, he constantly received reports of
Sultan Muhammad and how strong or weak his
army was, for whenever Genghis Khan’s
scouts captured the sultan’s officers or depen-
dents—or whenever they surrendered of their
own accord—they reported that the sultan was
afraid, perplexed, and hesitant, a man without
rest. His son Jalaluddin had told him, “We
should assemble the soldiers we have left scat-
tered all over the place and strike the foe to-
gether.” However, since the sultan’s luck was
on the downturn, he refused to listen.
Knowing the sultan’s situation and having
learned during the siege of Samarkand that the
sultan was in his summer camp, Genghis Khan
had sent Jäbä of the Besüt clan with one tümän
as a gäjigä after the sultan and Toquchar Baha-
dur of the Qunqirat with another tümän on
Jäbä’s heels, saying, “Go in pursuit of Sultan
Muhammad Khwarazmshah, and wherever you
find him, if he comes out with an army and
you do not have the strength to contend, stop
where you are and inform me. If he is weak,
fight. Since constant reports tell of his weak-
ness and fear, he will probably not have the
strength to stand against you. With the strength
of the great God, do not return until you have
captured him. [505] If he cannot withstand you
and takes refuge with a few men on some steep
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
243

cliff, or in a cave, or in some narrows, or if he
hides himself from the sight of men like a
fairy, you must be like the breeze and come out
of his territory. Win over all who surrender,
give them written assurance, and leave behind
a shahna. Take by force any who contemplate
resistance. As I charge you, you should com-
plete this task within three years, return via the
Qipchaq Steppe, and rejoin us in Mongolia,
our ancient yurt. By approximation it is plain
that by that time we should have done with
Iran and returned home triumphant and victori-
ous. I am shortly going to dispatch Tolui Khan
after you to take the cities of Khurasan, Merv,
Herat, Nishapur, Sarakhs, and those territories;
and I will send Jochi, Chaghatai, and Ögödäi
with armies to conquer Khwarazm, which is
the greatest of all the cities and capital of Sul-
tan Muhammad Khwarazmshah. Through the
strength of the great God, it should take us this
same amount of time to accomplish these sev-
eral tasks and reach home.”
So saying, he dispatched them and later his
sons to conquer Khwarazm. He himself rested
for a while from the rigors of travel with Tolui
Khan in the vicinity of Samarkand. Jäbä,
Sübädäi,
Toquchar,
and
thirty
thousand
warriors crossed at the Panjab ford and set out
in pursuit of Sultan Muhammad Khwarazm-
shah. Prior to that, the sultan had been on the
river bank at Termez, but when he heard of the
fall of Bukhara and then of the capture of
Samarkand, he bade farewell to kingship and
lit out. With him he had a group of his moth-
er’s Turkish relatives, who were called Uranis.
[506] They wanted to kill him, but one of them
informed the sultan, who changed his sleeping
place during the night and left his tent. At
dawn the felt of the tent looked like a sieve be-
cause it had been pierced by so many arrows.
With this, the sultan’s apprehension increased,
and he proceeded in haste to Nishapur. Every
place he came to, he advised the people to rein-
force their citadels and fortresses, and this
resulted in the people’s fear increasing a thou-
sandfold. When he reached Nishapur, he in-
dulged in wine and song in order to stave off
his grief over his fate.
Jäbä and Sübädäi first reached Balkh. The
grandees of the city sent out a delegation bear-
ing food offerings. A shahna was appointed,
and they passed on. Picking up a guide there,
they sent Taisu Bahadur. When they had gone a
way they requested fodder, but the people did
not give it and shut the gates. Because the
Mongols were in a hurry they proceeded with-
out stopping. The people of the city beat drums
and hurled curses at them. Perceiving this in-
sult, they turned back and put ladders against
the fortress. On the third day they got onto the
ramparts and killed everyone they found. Since
they did not have time to make a camp, they
burned and smashed all their heavy baggage.
When news of their approach reached Nisha-
pur, the sultan set out for Isfarayin, claiming to
be going hunting, but he headed for Persia.
When it was reported that a foreign army was
nearby, he cancelled his trip to Persia and
headed for the fortress at Farzin. That very day
he sent his wives, children, and mother to
Tajuddin Toghan in the Qarun fortress and took
counsel with the commanders of Persia on how
to deal with the foe. It was considered best for
them to take refuge in Ushturan Koh. The sul-
tan went to inspect the mountain and said,
“This place cannot serve us as a refuge.” 
Then he sent a messenger to summon the
malik of Hazarasf Lur, a great ancient king
[507] and a man of strategic and tactical
knowledge. When Malik Nusratuddin Hazarasf
arrived, he went into court still covered with
the dust of the road and kissed the ground in
seven places. The sultan consulted with him,
and the malik said, “It would be best for us to
244
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

decamp immediately. There is an impregnable
and highly fortifiable mountain between Lur
and Fars called Tang-i-Balu.1 It is a region
filled with good things, and we can make it our
asylum and get help from the Lur and the
Shul—in one night we can gather a hundred
thousand foot soldiers. When the Mongols
arrive we can face them with stout hearts and
fight like men.”
“His purpose is to show open enmity to
Atabeg Sa‘d of Fars,” the sultan thought. Re-
jecting his plan as a fancy, he said, “It was our
thought to take up residence here among these
soldiers and send out in all directions to assem-
ble armies.” 
He was still thinking about that when Jäbä
and Sübädäi reached Nishapur. They sent
emissaries to the dignitaries there, Mujirul-
mulk, Ziya’uddin Zuzani, and Fariduddin, the
vizier and comptrollers of Khurasan, calling
upon them to surrender and follow Genghis
Khan and requesting provisions and fodder.
They sent out three persons bearing offerings
of food and accepted surrender. Jäbä advised
them, saying, “Avoid struggling against ‘fire
and water’ and go out immediately when the
Mongol army arrives. Do not place any re-
liance on the strength of your walls or the
abundance of your provisions if you want your
homes to remain safe.” As a token they gave
them a seal in the Uyghur script and a draft of
an edict from Genghis Khan, the contents of
which were as follows: “Let commanders, dig-
nitaries, and subjects know that the entire sur-
face of the earth, from where the sun rises to
where it sets, has been given to us by God.
[508] Mercy will be shown all who submit and
to their children and dependents, but those who
do not submit and resist will be destroyed
1Readingﻮ ــﺑﻠﮓ ـ ـﺗﻨ(Tang-i-Balu) for the text’sﻮ ـ ـﺗﮑﮓ ـ ـﺗﻨ.
See Juvaini/Boyle 2:383, note 68.
along with their children and relatives.” Giving
them a writ to this effect, they went on their
way.
Jäbä went via Jawhara, and Sübädäi via Jam,
to Tus. They allowed every place that surren-
dered to remain, but they annihilated everyone
who resisted. The villages to the east of Tus,
such as Tufan and that area, surrendered and
were given amnesty of their lives, but the peo-
ple of Tus itself were stubborn, and therefore
the territory was massacred and looted. 
From there they went to the meadows of
Radkan.2 Sübädäi liked that plain and did not
harass the inhabitants but stationed a shahna
and went on to Khabushan,3 where he engaged
in a lot of killing because of their lack of
deference. 
In short, everywhere they went, they ob-
tained necessary food and clothing without
stopping and passed on through. As was pru-
dent, they marched or halted by day or night on
the heels of information concerning Sultan
Muhammad Shah, the Khwarazmshah. In in-
habited areas that lay on their path they round-
ed up whatever fine horses and good pack ani-
mals they found. In Khurasan there were many
walled villages and fortified towns, but they
paid them no attention because they had a
greater task to perform. Sübädäi went from
there to Isfarayin, and Jäbä took the Juwayn
road to Mazanderan, where he killed many
people, particularly in Darulmulk and the city
of Sarabad. Sübädäi went to Damghan, where
the people sought refuge in the mountains, but
the common folk and soldiers remained in the
city, refusing to come out to surrender. As a
result, many of them were killed. Coming to
2The Rādkān meadows figure prominently in the liter-
ature of the Ilkhanid and Timurid periods. Rādkān is sit-
uated around forty-five miles northwest of present-day

3Khabushan is the modern Quchan in Khurasan.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
245

Simnan, he killed a host of people, and also in
Khwar-i-Rayy. 
At that point, the sultan arrived from Rayy to
consult with Atabeg Nusratuddin Hazarasf of
Lur [509] concerning the sultan’s vanguard and
to inform him of the arrival of the Mongols.
After his attack of clouded vision, the sultan
realized that things had to be done at the right
time. Fearing an attack on Hazarasf, he set out
for the Lur, and all the other maliks and leaders
ﬂed into nooks and crannies. Sultan Muham-
mad Khwarazmshah and his sons took the road
to the Qarun fortress. Along the way they came
across a contingent of Mongols coming in
droves. One troop, recognizing the sultan,
reached for their arrows, shot, and hit the sul-
tan’s ventilator in several places. The sultan
ran pell-mell for shelter to save himself from
the maelstrom, and when he reached Qarun he
stayed there for a day. Then, taking a guide and
several horses from his officers, he set out for
Baghdad. Just then the Mongols arrived and,
thinking the sultan was in the fortress, began a
fierce battle. Once they realized that the sultan
had left the fortress, they pulled back.
The sultan withdrew and turned his reins to-
ward the fortress of Sarjahan and from there to
Gilan. Su‘luk, one of the Gel’s amirs,1 came
out to greet him and, encouraging him to stay,
gave him various undertakings. The sultan left
after seven days and went to the province of
Spandar.2 He had nothing left and was ab-
solutely destitute. From there he went to one of
the regional dependencies of Amul and took
counsel with the amirs of Mazanderan he felt
he could trust. The wisdom of taking refuge for
a few days on one of the islands was seen. 
1Gel is the title of the ruler of Gilan.
2Spandār is what is generally called Rustamdār in later
sources. It is the middle region along the Caspian littoral
in modern Iran, with Gilan to the west and Mazanderan
to the east.
The sultan went to an island and stayed there
for a while. When news of this became known
on the island, as a precaution he moved to
another island, his transfer simultaneous with
the arrival of a group of Mongols [510] Jäbä
Noyan had sent from Rayy to pursue the sul-
tan. When they failed to find him, they turned
back and laid siege to the fortresses in which
were the sultan’s wife and treasures. They took
them and carried everything off to Genghis
Khan in Samarkand. 
When this dreadful news reached the sultan
and he realized that his wife had been violated,
his sons had been put to the sword, and his
womenfolk were captive in the hands of
strangers, he was so dumbfounded and stunned
that the world turned dark before his eyes. He
writhed in worry and anxiety and bemoaned
that catastrophic and horrible event until he
gave up the ghost. “We are God’s, and to Him
are we going to return.”3
O world, how faithless and mean you are: you
raise your prey and then hunt it down.
He was buried on the island, although several
years later his son Sultan Jalaluddin ordered
his bones moved and reinterred in the fortress
at Ardahin.
Sultan Khwarazmshah had previously nom-
inated his son Uzlaq to be his successor, but he
demoted him while on the island in the
Caspian
and
nominated
Sultan
Jalaluddin
instead.
After his father’s death, Sultan Jalaluddin
heard that the Mongol army was no longer in
Khurasan and Persia since, by Genghis Khan’s
orders, they did not stop anywhere but kept
moving in haste. Feeling safe, he went to
Mangyshlak, [511] took as pack animals some
horses he found in that region, and sent heralds
to Khwarazm. Uzlaq Sultan, the former heir

apparent, was in Khwarazm with Aq Sultan
and the elite commanders Buji Pahlavan,
Uzlaq Sultan’s maternal uncle, Küch-Ay Tegin,
Oghul Hajib, and Temür Malik, with ninety
thousand Qanqli horsemen. The Mongol army
had not yet arrived. When Sultan Jalaluddin
arrived the climate was changing, and every
faction was inclined to a different one of the
brothers. In trepidation over Sultan Jalalud-
din’s audacity, in secret the amirs hatched a
treacherous plot to kill him. One of them in-
formed the sultan, and he took advantage of
the opportunity to take the Nasa road to
Shadyakh. He got away from the amirs in the
vicinity of Ustuva at Shayaqan Hill, but he en-
countered a contingent of Mongols with whom
he did battle for a while. He killed several men
and got out of their midst to safety.
The very moment the sultan left Khwarazm
news came of the arrival of the Mongol army.
Uzlaq Sultan and Aq Sultan saw little sense in
remaining in Khwarazm, so they took ﬂight on
the heels of their brother. The next day they too
encountered the same troop that had done bat-
tle with Sultan Jalaluddin. Not recognizing
them as princes, the Mongols killed them and
all who were with them. 
The sultan reached Shadyakh. For three days
he occupied himself with preparations for the
road, and in the middle of the night he put his
trust in God and set out for the western region
to which his father had assigned him. There
was only a moment between his departure and
the arrival of the Mongol army. When the sul-
tan reached the gate, he stationed Malik El-
diräk there to hold back for a moment any sol-
diers [512] who might come. Of his own
accord Eldiräk took a road different from the
one the sultan had taken. When the Mongols
arrived they set out in pursuit of Malik Eldiräk,
and Sultan Jalaluddin travelled forty leagues
that day on the other road, coming within one
station of Ghaznin. When news of his appear-
ance was broadcast people came to him from
all directions. 
During the period in which these things took
place, Genghis Khan was still in Samarkand,
and he assigned his three elder sons to
Khwarazm. Now we will report on this and
then return to the history of Genghis Khan,
God willing.
Genghis Khan dispatches his sons Jochi,
Chaghatai, and Ögödäi to Khwarazm, and
it is taken by them.
As previously reported, when Genghis Khan
had completed his conquest of Samarkand, he
sent
Jäbä,
Sübädäi,
and
Toquchar
into
Khurasan and Persia after Sultan Muhammad
Khwarazmshah while he himself spent that
summer in that area resting and fattening up
the horses, intending to go himself later after
the sultan. When Transoxiana had been com-
pletely conquered and other regions had been
secured, Khwarazm—its original name was
Gurganch but the Mongols call it Urung-
gächi1—[513] was left standing in the middle
like a tent with a broken rope. Wanting to take
it too, Genghis Khan then assigned his eldest
son Jochi along with Chaghatai and Ögödäi to
Khwarazm with an army as numerous as the
sands of the desert. In the autumn of that year
they set out with the commanders of the right
wing, and they sent out an enormous troop in
the vanguard, which they call yäzäk.
As has been said before, after the death of his
father,
Sultan
Jalaluddin
had
gone
to
Khwarazm but withdrawn because of attacks
by some of the amirs. His brothers and the old
sultan’s grand commanders who were there an-
1Gurganch, Arabicized as Kurkanj but usually called
Jurjāniyya (Abu’l-Fida, Taqwim, 478), was the seat of
Khwarazm and lay on the west bank of the Jaxartes. It is
the modern Kunya-Urgench in northern Turkmenistan.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
247

nounced the arrival of the princes and set out
for Khurasan, but along the way they were
killed by Mongol soldiers. The throne of
Khwarazm then sat empty. Among the sultan’s
chief military officers were a Turk named
Khumär, who was a relative of his mother,
Tärkän Khatun; Moghul Hajib; Buqa Pahla-
van; Sipahsalar Ali Marghini; and another
group, and the city was crowded and congested
beyond description. Inasmuch as there was no
leader in the cosmopolitan area for them to
consult when adversity struck, they named
Khumär sultan by virtue of his kinship [to
Jalaluddin’s mother].
One day a few horsemen from the Mongol
army rode up to the gate and drove their ani-
mals on past. A group of shortsighted individu-
als, thinking those few were the entire Mongol
army, went after them on horseback and on
foot. The Mongols, ﬂeeing from them like
prey, got as far as the edge of the Khurram
Garden, one league from the city. The Mongols
then unleased from behind the wall an ambush
of fighters who surrounded the citizens [514]
and killed nearly a hundred thousand of them.
On the heels of those ﬂeeing in rout, the Mon-
gols hurled themselves into the city through
the Qaplan Gate and went as far as the place
known as Tannura. As the sun was setting, the
foreign army turned back and went into the
plain. The next day they went back to the city,
but this time Faredun Ghori, commander of the
sultan’s army, was waiting at the gate to resist
with five hundred horsemen. Just then Princes
Jochi, Chaghatai, and Ögödäi arrived with the
army and rode around the city to have a look at
it. After that they dismounted, the soldiers
camped encircling the city, and they sent in
emissaries to invite the people of the city to
surrender. Since there were no rocks in the
vicinity of Khwarazm, they cut large mulberry
trees and used them in the catapults instead of
stones. As was their custom, day after day they
addressed the people of the city with orders,
threats, and promises while the two sides ex-
changed arrows until suddenly the levies
arrived and were put to work. First they or-
dered a trench dug, and they spent two entire
days on it. They then worked in concert to di-
vert the water of the Oxus, which the levies
had cut off from the city. Three thousand men
from the Mongol army were put to work on
that project. The citizens, however, ambushed
the levy and surrounded them, and on account
of that victory the citizens grew bolder in battle
and more daring in their resistance. 
Due to differences in temperament a quarrel
broke out among Jochi and Chaghatai, who
could not get along together; and because of
their disagreement and obstinacy, their atten-
tion to battle ﬂagged and necessary direction
was
neglected.
[515]
That
is
why
the
Khwarazmians were able to kill so many Mon-
gol soldiers that to this day there are said to be
mounds of bones collected around the old city
of Khwarazm. 
This lasted seven months, and still the city
had not been taken. During all this time, when
the princes had set out together, gone to
Khwarazm, and laid siege to it, Genghis Khan
came to Nakhshab, where he camped for a
while. Then, crossing the Oxus at Termez, he
went to Balkh and conquered the city and re-
gion. From there he went to besiege the
fortress at Taligan. 
During the very time he was beginning the
siege of the fortress there, a messenger came
from his sons in Khwarazm, saying that
Khwarazm could not be taken, that many sol-
diers had perished, and that one of the causes
was the lack of cooperation among Jochi,
Chaghatai, and Ögödäi. When Genghis Khan
heard this, he grew angry and ordered Tolui,
the youngest brother, to go. He was known for
248
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

his competence. When the messenger arrived
and delivered the order, Tolui set out as or-
dered. Skillfully and cleverly he went to a dif-
ferent brother each day and treated them with
kindness and ﬂattery, and thus, thanks to his in-
genuity, he created a truce among them. He
also worthily undertook to direct military af-
fairs and put the Yasa on a firm footing. After
that, the soldiers fought in concert, and that
very day they raised their standard on the
ramparts.
They entered the city and set fire to the quar-
ters with vials of naphtha. [516] The inhabi-
tants took refuge in the back quarters and
fought in the lanes. The Mongols fought hard
and took the city quarter by quarter and house
by house, burning and pulling down as they
went. Finally, within seven days, they had tak-
en the entire city. They drove the people at
once into the plains, where they separated a
hundred thousand craftsmen and tradesmen
they sent to the east. The women and children
were taken prisoner, and the rest were divided
up among the soldiers to be killed. It is report-
ed that each individual soldier got twenty-four
Muslims, and the number of Mongol soldiers
was in excess of fifty thousand. In short, the
soldiers killed them all and then got busy loot-
ing and pillaging, destroying what was left of
the buildings and city quarters. 
Since Genghis Khan had heard of Shaykh
Najmuddin’s reputation,1 he sent someone to
him to say, “I shall annihilate Khwarazm. That
great one must get out and join us.” 
“I
have
lived
among
these
people
in
Khwarazm for seventy years with both the bit-
ter and the sweet that fate has bestowed,” the
shaykh replied. “If, now that a catastrophe is
about to descend, I were to ﬂee, it would not be
1Shaykh Najmuddin Kubra (1145–1221), eponymous
founder of the Kubrawiyya Order. 
chivalrous.” His body was [never] discovered
among the slain, no matter how hard they
searched.
Now that the story of the commanders who
were appointed to go in pursuit of the sultan
and the story of the princes who went to
Khwarazm have been completed, [517] let us
return to the story of Genghis Khan and tell in
what
he
was
engaged
after
liberating
Samarkand and in which direction he went,
God willing.
Genghis Khan and his youngest son Tolui
Khan, who was called Yäkä Noyan and
Ulugh Noyan; troops are sent in pursuit of
Sultan Muhammad Khwarazmshah; the
conquest of the lands that lay on the way,
such as Nakhshab and Badakhshan; he
crosses the Oxus at Termez and conquers
Balkh, Taligan, and that area and dispatches
Yäkä Noyan to conquer Khurasan.
As has been said in several places, in Moghai
Yil, the Year of the Snake that began in Dhu’l-
Hijja 617 [January 1221] but most of which
corresponds to the year 618, Genghis Khan
was besieging Samarkand. At the beginning of
that summer, he sent Jäbä Noyan, Sübätäi Noy-
an,
and
Toquchar
in
pursuit
of
the
Khwarazmshah. He took Samarkand that same
summer, and after the conquest he sent his stal-
warts to Khwarazm. 
At the beginning of autumn he and Tolui
Khan decamped from Samarkand and went to
the meadows of Nakhshab and from there to
Termez along the road the Mongols call Temür
Qahalqa (Iron Gates), which includes the ter-
ritories of Kish, Nakhshab, and Termez. From
there he sent Tolui Khan forward with a large
army to conquer Khurasan, [518] assigning
him one out of every ten men. Genghis Khan
himself headed for Termez, and when he
arrived there he sent emissaries to call upon the
people to surrender. Trusting in the invincibili-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
249

ty of their fortifications and overproud of their
own manliness, the inhabitants refused. After
eleven days of battle the city was taken, and in
revenge the people were driven out and all
killed.
An old woman pleaded, saying, “Don’t kill
me, and I’ll give you a large pearl.” They
asked her to show it. “I’ve swallowed it,” she
said. They slit open her belly and took out the
pearl. Because of that, they also slit open the
bellies of all the dead.
From there Genghis Khan went to the region
of Kangurt and Shuman and took them. He
cleared the area through massacre and sent his
army to take the Badakhshan area, partially
with persuasion and partially with violence.
When no trace of opposition was left there, and
all regions on that side of the river had been
conquered, he set out to cross the Oxus. 
By that time the winter of that year was over,
and at the beginning of Moghai Yil, the Year of
the Snake that began in Dhu’l-Hijja 617 [Janu-
ary 1221] and extended into 618, he crossed
the Oxus at Termez and set out for Balkh, the
greatest of the metropolitan areas of Khurasan.
At that time it had been ___ since Jäbä and
Sübädäi had crossed in pursuit of the sultan.
[519]
Genghis Khan camped outside of Balkh. The
leaders of the city came forward and offered
their submission and obedience, and they pre-
sented various gifts and tribute. After that, on
the pretext of making a count, all the inhabi-
tants of Balkh were taken out into the country-
side, divided up among the soldiers as usual,
and killed. The walls and ramparts of the city
were destroyed, fire was set to the houses and
city quarters, and it was completely destroyed.
From there, Genghis Khan went to the
fortress at Taligan, laid siege, and took it. From
there he proceeded to Taligan itself. The moun-
tain called Nusrat Koh was very strong and
filled with brave men and supplies. No matter
how many emissaries were sent to propose that
they surrender, they refused. The siege lasted
seven months, and the fortress was so strong
that it could not be taken.
During the spring that Genghis Khan was be-
sieging Taligan, the princes Jochi, Chaghatai,
and Ögödäi were in the midst of taking
Khwarazm. Tolui went out via the Iron Gates,
stationed his right and left wings, and went
himself in the center. Via Maruchuq and
Baghshur he took the entire realm as well as
Merv. From there to Nishapur he took att the
outlying towns and cities like Abivard, Nasa,
Yazar, Tus, Jajarm, Juvayn, Baihaq, Khwaf,
Sangan, Sarakhs, and Zurabad, each of which
was as large as a city. He also took the city of
Nishapur. By the end of the spring of that year
he had taken all those towns.
From Taligan, Genghis Khan had sent an
emissary to tell his son Tolui Khan to return
before the weather turned hot. He returned as
ordered, and along the way he attacked the
province of Quhistan. He crossed the Fakhran
River [520] and took Herat and the surround-
ing
countryside.
From
there
he
rejoined
Genghis Khan. By the time he arrived Genghis
Khan
had
already
conquered
the
Taligan
fortress after many battles, and they were in
the process of destroying it. Tolui Khan arrived
and paid homage.
A short while later Chaghatai and Ögödäi
arrived from Khwarazm to pay homage. Jochi
went directly from Khwarazm to his aghruqs.
During the battle of Taligan a cross-bow arrow
hit
Chaghatai’s
son
Mö’ätügän,
Genghis
Khan’s favorite grandson whom Chaghatai had
made his successor. He dies of that wound. For
that reason Genghis Khan hastened the libera-
tion of Taligan, and when it was taken he or-
dered as a punishment that every living thing,
human, animal, beast, and bird, to be killed,
250
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

and no prisoners or plunder was to be taken.
The site was to be turned into a desert, it was
not to be rebuilt, and no creature was to live
there. It was named Ma’uquruqan, and until
now not a creature lives there. He also ordered
that no one should inform Chaghatai of this
event, and when he arrived and asked for him,
he was told that he had gone somewhere.
Later, one day, all the sons were present, and
Genghis Khan made known his will. In anger
he turned to Chaghatai and said, “You do not
listen to my words or my orders!” Chaghatai
was afraid, but he bent his knee and said, “If I
do not obey your orders, may I die!” Then
Genghis Khan said, “Your son Mö’ätügän has
been killed in battle. I order you not to weep,
and this time you will not disobey me!” Dumb-
founded by the news, Chaghatai could scarcely
contain himself, but he was also unable to dis-
obey Genghis Khan’s order, so he hid his pain
and did not cry but kept on eating and drink-
ing. [521] After a time, on the pretext of re-
lieving himself, he went out into the fields and
wept silently for a moment. Pulling himself to-
gether and drying his tears, he returned.
Then Genghis Khan and his sons and armies
rested during the summer in the hills of Tali-
gan. At that time Sultan Jalaluddin was in
Ghaznin. Khan Malik, the ruler of Merv, joined
him with a cavalry forty thousand strong, and
the sultan married his daughter. Sayfuddin
Ughraq, a Turcoman chieftain, also joined the
sultan with forty thousand men, and the amirs
of Ghor joined him likewise.
The story of Khan Malik
When Genghis Khan dispatched Jäbä and
Sübädäi in pursuit of Sultan Muhammad and
then sent Toquchar Bahadur on their heels,
Khan Malik did not think it politic to remain in
Merv with the sultan’s affairs in such disarray
and so he had gone with his army and follow-
ers to the borders of Ghor and Gharcha, where
he
broached
the
subject
of
submission.
Genghis Khan gave him time and said that
when Jäbä and Sübädäi reached his land with
their troops they would pass through without
harassment. Toquchar, who was sent out after
the others, disobeyed orders by harassing the
area like other areas, and while he was fighting
with a group of mountain-dwellers he was
killed.
Khan Malik sent an emissary to Genghis
Khan, saying, [522] “I advised the sultan of
Khwarazm, but he refused to listen. His lack of
fortune led him to oppose you, and therefore
that which happened to him happened. I have
previously sent a servant to make my submis-
sion known, and I have said that I will strive
with correct heart, and I have opposed the sul-
tan. Now Jäbä Noyan has come and passed
through without opposition. After him came
Sübädäi Noyan, and he too passed through
without harm. After them came Toquchar, and
although the mountain-dwellers claimed that
they were in submission, he refused to listen,
drove away tariqchis and many of my subjects,
and fought with the people until he was killed.
What has happened to Genghis Khan’s good
men that such ignoramuses have been sent on
important affairs?” With the emissary he sent
several suits of clothing as a gift and also be-
cause he was in trepidation over what had hap-
pened to Toquchar. Around that time he heard
that Sultan Jalaluddin had gone, after his fa-
ther’s death, to Ghaznin, to which he (Khan
Malik) had previously been assigned. After
soldiers gathered around him from all direc-
tions he secretly sent a message to Sultan
Jalaluddin saying that he would come to him. 
Genghis Khan dispatched Shigi Qutuqu with
several
other
commanders
like
Tögächäk,
Mulqur, Ükär Qalja, and Mulqar Qalja, with
thirty thousand men to that area to stand guard
and protect the roads in Ghaznin, Gharjistan,
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
251

Zabul, and Kabul and to conquer as much of
the territory as they could. They were also sup-
posed to serve as scouts so that Genghis Khan
himself and his son Tolui Khan could conquer
Khurasan at their leisure. Khan Malik was near
the area where Shigi Qutuqu and his troops
were, and they thought he was in submission,
but in secret he sent a message to Sultan
Jalaluddin telling him to stay in Parwan until
he arrived. He also sent a similar message to a
group of Qanqlis who were in the area, and
then, summoning them according to a previous
arrangement, he set forth. [523] Shigi Qutuqu’s
reconnoiterers reported that Khan Malik and
his followers and confederates were heading
for Sultan Jalaluddin. Shigi Qutuqu immediate-
ly set out after him with his troops, catching up
with him at night, when there was [no] chance
to attack him. As a precautionary measure they
dismounted and waited until dawn, but Khan
Malik had ridden all through the night, and by
the next morning he had reached Parwan, his
place of rendezvous with the sultan. The Qan-
qlis and other troops were there in full force,
and there was a host of soldiers. Several days
prior to that, Tögächäk and Mulqur, who had
been with Shigi Qutuqu, had laid siege to the
fort at Walian, and they were close to taking it.
Sultan Jalaluddin deposited his baggage in Par-
wan and took a troop to attack them, killing
around a thousand scouts of the Mongol army.
Since the Mongol army was then reduced in
size, they crossed the river and camped on the
other side. From both sides the troops engaged
in exchange of fire. The Mongols decamped by
night and went to Qutuqu Noyan, and once
again they set out in pursuit of Khan Malik. 
When Khan Malik joined the sultan, he said,
“The Mongol army is on its way.” The sultan
mounted and rode forward about a league to
meet the Mongols, and when the lines were ar-
rayed, the sultan entrusted the right wing to
Khan Malik, the left wing to Sayfuddin Malik,
with himself and his aghruq in the center. then
he ordered all the soldiers to dismount with
their horses’ halters bound to their waists, and
they fought a valiant fight.
The next day the Mongols ordered every
horseman to make an image of a man from felt
and other things and to mount them on their
horses and secure them behind themselves. All
this was done by night, and the next day they
arrayed their ranks. When the sultan’s soldiers
saw such a mass of troops, they thought the
Mongols had been reinforced [524] and started
fleeing. The sultan shouted, “We have many
troops! Let us hold our ranks and encircle them
from the right and left.” As the soldiers made a
tight formation, the sultan had the battle drums
sounded, and all at once they attacked. The sul-
tan’s troops were more numerous, and they
moved to encircle the Mongols, but Qutuqu
Noyan had said, “When we are fighting, if you
pull back, keep my standard in your view.” Just
then, when they were almost surrounded, they
lost heart and withdrew. The reason for this is
that in that area are many pits and rills, and the
Mongols kept falling from their horses. Since
the sultan’s men had very fine mounts, they
caught the Mongols and killed them. Many of
the Mongol troops perished in this battle.
When the news reached Genghis Khan, al-
though he was extremely angry, he said,
“Qutuqu is accustomed to return victorious and
triumphant. Never had he experienced any set-
back from fortune. Now that he has seen diffi-
culty, he will have been warned, and it will be
be a good experience for him to know of dif-
ferent conditions.” Immediately Genghis Khan
got his troops in order and set out after Shigi
Qutuqu, and the commanders who had been
with Shigi Qutuqu and the troops that re-
mained and had become scattered converged.
After the battle Sultan Jalaluddin had with-
252
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

drawn and returned to his tents. His troops had
taken much booty from the Mongols. During
the distribution of spoils an argument broke
out
between
Khan
Malik
and
Sayfuddin
Ughraq over an Arabian steed. Khan Malik
struck Ughraq with his whip, and the sultan did
not order an investigation because he had no
confidence in the Qanqlis. Sayfuddin grew an-
gry, and although he stayed there that day, that
night he departed in anger and went to the
mountains of Kirman and Sayqaran. This was a
great blow to the sultan’s force, and when he
heard that Genghis Khan was coming with
many troops, [525] in his consternation he was
unable to think straight. Unable to come up
with a remedy, he set out for Ghaznin, intend-
ing to cross the Indus. When Qutuqu Noyan re-
joined Genghis Khan he reported every per-
son’s feats and failures. Among his com-
manders were Ükär Qalja and Muqur Qalja1 of
the Ba’arin clan, and he complained of a short-
coming on their part arising from the levity and
silliness that was part of their nature, saying,
“Persons who are expert at jokes, ridicule, and
buffoonery think they possess an art, but dur-
ing tests of manhood such persons are of no
use whatsoever. They are nothing more than
women.” In Mongolian buffoons are called
qalja.
Genghis Khan goes in pursuit of Sultan
Jalaluddin, who is defeated on the banks of
the River Indus and crosses over.
When Shigi Qutuqu came before Genghis
Khan and gave his report, Genghis Khan had
completed the conquest of the fortress at Tali-
gan, the princes had returned from Khwarazm,
and Tolui Khan had returned triumphant from
Khurasan. Together with the army they sum-
mered in the hills of Taligan and rested. 
1This should be the Qutus Qalja mentioned on text p.
200.
Immediately upon receiving a report, he or-
dered all to mount, and an enormous army set
forth from Taligan in the Year of the Horse in
pursuit of Sultan Jalaluddin, travelling so fast
that there was no time to cook food. When he
arrived in that place, he asked Shigi Qutuqu,
“How did you stand, [526] and how stood the
sultan?” He answered. Scoffing at Shigi’s and
the sultan’s tactics, he said, “You didn’t know
the place of battle, and you were both at fault.”
When he reached Ghaznin, he heard that the
sultan had passed through there fifteen days
previously, heading to cross the Indus River.
Genghis Khan stationed Baba Yalavach as
shahna and set out in all haste after the sultan,
who had prepared boats on the river bank prior
to crossing. Urkhan, who was in in the rear as
auxiliary, resisted the Mongol scouts and de-
feated them.
When Genghis Khan learned this, he rode by
night and had the sultan blocked at dawn. The
Mongol soldiers stood in several circles one
behind the other like a bow with the Indus Riv-
er like the string. When the sun rose, the sultan
found
himself
“between
fire
and
water.”
Genghis Khan had ordered that the sultan be
not shot but taken captive. He had also dis-
patched Ükär Qalja and Qutus Qalja to drive
the edge of sultan’s troops from the river bank.
Those two strove hard and surrounded the
edges of the sultan’s troops. After that, the
Mongols attacked, striking the right wing com-
manded by Khan Malik and killing most of
them. Khan Malik ﬂed in rout toward Pursavur
(Peshawar), but the Mongols blocked his way
and killed him.
They also removed the left wing, but the sul-
tan in the center and seven hundred men held
their ground, fighting from dawn until noon.
Despairing of his life, he sent troops out right
and left. Since there was a prohibition against
shooting him with an arrow, they closed the
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
253

circle around him. [527] When he realized that
it was beyond his competence to fight “with a
mountain,” he mounted a rested horse and at-
tacked the Mongol troops, driving them back.
Still galloping, he turned around, put his shield
to his back, grabbed his parasol and standard,
whipped his horse, and crossed the river like
lightning. When he gained the far bank he
cleaned his sword with water. 
Genghis Khan was amazed by this feat and,
pointing him out to his sons, said, “Such a son
should come from a father!
In all the world no one has either seen or
heard of such a man among the renowned
ancients.
After saving himself on the shore from such a
battle, he will perform many valiant feats.”
When the soldiers saw the sultan hurling
himself into the river, they wanted to go in
pursuit, but Genghis Khan forbade them. 
In a reliable history it has been stated that
when the sultan realized that resistance was fu-
tile, he had his wife, child, and the women of
the harem drowned in the water lest they fall
into the infamy of captivity. He also threw his
treasuries into the water. Only then did he
charge into the river and cross.
The sultan’s soldiers were all killed. In
another version, all his male children, even
nursing infants, were killed, and the women of
his harem were taken prisoner. Since most of
the sultan’s treasury was gold in cash and jew-
els, he had ordered it all thrown into the Indus
that day. After that, Genghis Khan ordered
divers to go down and bring out what they
could. When the spoils had been divided they
camped as was their custom. [528]
Genghis Khan sends Bala Noyan to India in
pursuit of Sultan Jalaluddin.
After that, Genghis Khan sent Bala Noyan of
the Jalayir and Dörbäi1 Noyan with a large
army into India in pursuit of Sultan Jalaluddin.
They went into the midst of Hindustan but
found no trace of him. Turning back, they took
the fortress of Nandana2 in Hindustan, which
had been held by Qamaruddin Karmani but
had been taken by one of the sultan’s amirs.
After killing many there, they set out for Mul-
tan.3 As there were no stones in Multan, they
made rafts, filled them with catapult stones,
put them onto the river, and took them to Mul-
tan. When they arrived they set up mangonels
and almost took the place, but inclement
weather intervened. They massacred and plun-
dered the territories of Multan, Lahore, Pe-
shawar, and Malikfur,4 crossed the Indus, and
rejoined Genghis Khan.
Genghis Khan withdraws from the banks of
the Indus, camps in Parwan, and massacres
and plunders west of there.
When Sultan Jalaluddin crossed the river,
and Bala Noyan and Dörbäi Noyan were sent
in pursuit, Genghis Khan withdrew up the In-
dus River in the spring of Qonin Yil, which be-
gan in Muharram 620 [February 1223]. Ögödäi
was sent down river to conquer that area and
massacre and pillage to the west. Artisans and
craftsmen were sent to the east, others were
massacred, and the city was destroyed. [529]
Then he sent a messenger to Genghis Khan,
1The Dörbetei Dörbei Doghshin of the Secret History
§261.
2For the text’sﻪ ــ ــﺑﻴ, readﻪــﻧﺪ ــ ــﻧﻨ(Nandana, in the Jhelum
District, Punjab). See Juvaini/Boyle 1:141, note 2.
3The modern Multan in Pakistan.
4Malikfur (~Malikpur) was in the Rawalpindi district.
See Juvaini/Boyle 2:413, note 6.
254
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

saying, “If so ordered, I will go lay siege to
Seistan.”
Genghis Khan replied, “The weather has
turned hot. You come back, and I’ll send other
troops to lay siege.”
Ögödäi returned via Garmser, and Genghis
Khan camped that summer in the plains the
Mongols call Parwan,1 waiting for Bala Noyan.
He took and pillaged the territories that were in
that area. When Bala Noyan and Dörbäi Noyan
arrived, he decamped.
When he reached the fortress at Gunavand
Qorqan, Ögödäi rejoined him, and that winter
was spent in the vicinity of Buya Katur.2 The
governor there, Salar Ahmad, surrendered and
made arrangements for as much fodder and
other necessities as he could. Most of the sol-
diers fell ill on account of the foul air, and
Genghis Khan gave an order for four hundred
maunds of cleaned rice to be given per indi-
vidual in every household. The order was
obeyed. 
After that, Genghis Khan put the affair of
Sultan Muhammad and his son aside and sent
Jäbä and Sübädäi to conquer the sultan’s ter-
ritories in Arran, Azerbaijan, Persia, and Shir-
van. His mind at rest on that score, he stationed
shahnas in all the cities he had conquered.
When the soldiers had recovered he thought of
pulling back via Hindustan to Tanqut territory,
but when he had gone one stage news arrived
that Tangqut had rebelled again. Difficult
mountains and dense forests also lay along the
way, the air was foul, and the water poisonous.
He turned back and went to Peshawar. [530]
Then, together with all his sons, he turned back
along the very way he had come.
1Readingــــﭘ
ﺮوان(Parwan, located between Bamian and
Ghazna in Afghanistan) for the text’s ﯨﱰوان.
2JTK hasﻮر ــﮐﺘﻪـﺳﻮـﻟ; JTBl hasﻮر ــﮐﺘﻪـﯾﻮـﺑ, which Boyle reads
as Buya Katur. It is unidentified in any case.
After conquering the lands of the Tajiks,
Genghis Khan heads for home; and events
that transpired along the way.
After conquering the lands of the Tajiks,
Genghis Khan left Peshawar and headed back
for his original dwelling place and old yurt in
Bechin Yil, the Year of the Monkey that began
in Muharram 621 [January 1224]. The reason
for his haste was a report of rebellion by the
Tangqut people, who had gone against him be-
cause he had been absent so long. Taking a
route through the mountains, he ordered the
aghruq he had stationed in the Baghlan vicinity
to decamp. He crossed the Oxus and spent that
winter in the vicinity of Samarkand. Setting
out from there, he ordered Tärkän Khatun, the
mother of Sultan Muhammad, and the sultan’s
wives to go out in front and bewail the sultan’s
kingdom in loud voices until all the soldiers
had passed by. 
When he reached the river at Fanakat, all his
sons except Jochi joined him, and a large quril-
tai was held. After that, decamping from there,
they proceeded stage by stage at a slow and
easy pace until they reached their old home,
where they had lived for so many years in hap-
piness and prosperity.
Now that the story of Genghis Khan has
reached this point, we shall begin the rest of
the story of Jäbä Noyan and Sübädäi. 
After Sultan Muhammad died on an island in
Mazanderan, [531] Sultan Jalaluddin went to
Khwarazm, but he withdrew because of the un-
cooperativeness of the amirs and his brothers.
Along the way he encountered the Mongol
army coming troop by troop after Jäbä Noyan.
They clashed and fought, and the sultan went
to Nishapur and then to Ghaznin. His brothers,
Uzlaq Sultan and Aq Sultan, and their amirs set
out after him in trepidation over news of the
arrival of the Mongol army into Khwarazm,
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
255

but they were killed by the same soldiers with
whom the sultan had clashed. 
Now what did the two commanders, Jäbä and
Sübädäi, do and what territories did they take
before they returned home to Genghis Khan
via the Qipchaq Steppe?
Jäbä and Sübädäi go to Persia.
When Sultan Jalaluddin took ﬂight from
Nishapur and headed for Ghaznin, Jäbä and
Sübädäi sent a messenger to Genghis Khan to
say, “Sultan Muhammad has died and his son
Jalaluddin has ﬂed in that direction. We are no
longer worried about him, and in accordance
with your command we will spend a year or
two conquering as many lands that lie before
us as we can and then return via the Qipchaq
Gates to the rendezvous point commanded in
Mongolia, God willing and through Genghis
Khan’s fortune.” Thereafter he dispatched en-
voys for the purpose of taking care of neces-
sary business, and since he had not yet settled
down, no fewer than three or four hundred en-
voys went. [532]
In short, when they began the conquest of
Persia, they first took Khwar and Simnan.
From there they went to Rayy, where they
killed and plundered. Then they went to Qum,
the inhabitants of which they totally wiped out
and the children of which they took captive.
Sayyid Majduddin Ala’uddawla surrendered,
sending tribute in steeds and textiles and ac-
cepting to have a shahna. 
Since they had heard that there was a large
number of the sultan’s soldiers assembled in
Sanjas under the leadership of Beg-Tegin1
Silahi and Küch Buqa Khan, they headed for
them and wiped them out.
From there they went to Zanjan, where they
massacred many times the number they had
done in other cities. Leaving nothing there,
1See Juvaini/Boyle 1:147.
they went back to Qazwin. They held a pitched
battle with the Qazwinis and took the city by
force. The Qazwinis, as was their wont, fought
inside the city with knives until nearly fifty
thousand men had been killed on both sides.
They massacred and plundered most of the
towns of Persia. When winter set in, they were
in a big battle in the vicinity of Rayy. At that
time Genghis Khan was in the Nakhshab and
Termez area. The cold that year was extreme.
They headed for Azerbaijan, killing and loot-
ing everywhere along the way. When they
reached Tabriz, the governor, Atabeg Özbeg,
son of Jahan Pahlavan, hid himself and sent
someone to ask for a truce. He also sent much
tribute and many animals. They turned back
under a truce to spend the winter there. Their
way lay toward Georgia, and ten thousand
Georgians faced them and did battle. The
Georgians were defeated, and most were
killed. Since most of the roads in Georgia were
narrow and there were difficult hills, they
turned back and headed for Maragha. [533]
When they returned to Tabriz, the governor,
Shamsuddin Tughra’i, sent out enough tribute
to satisfy them, and they passed on. They laid
siege to Maragha, and because the ruler was a
woman who sat in Royin[diz], there was no
one in the city who could offer resistance or
think up a strategy. They started fighting, but
the Mongols had put the Muslim prisoners out
in front to attack the walls, and they killed
everyone who turned back. They fought in this
fashion for several days. In the end, they seized
the city by force and put high and low alike to
death. Everything that could be easily carried
they took away, and the rest they burned and
smashed. Then they set out for Diyarbekir and
Arbela, but when they heard of Muzaffaruddin
Kök-Böri’s numerous troops, they turned back.
256
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Inasmuch as Jamaluddin Ayba,1 one of the
Khwarazmshah’s slaves, had stirred up strife
again with a group of people, killed the shahna
of Hamadan, seized Ala’uddawla for having
capitulated, and imprisoned him in the fortress
at Girit, a dependency of Lur, they went again
toward Hamadan. Although Jamaluddin ___
came forth to surrender, it was to no avail, and
he and his liege men were martyred. They laid
siege to the city and carried out a general
massacre. 
In Rajab 618 [August–September 1221], af-
ter devastating Hamadan, they set out for
Nakhichevan, where they massacred and loot-
ed. Finally they forced Atabeg Khwamosh to
surrender. From there they went to Arran. First
they took Saraw2 and massacred and looted.
Then came Ardabil likewise. From there they
went to the city of Baylaqan, which they took
by storm, killing old and young alike. After
that, they attacked Ganja, the greatest of the
cities of Arran. They took it and destroyed it
too. [534] From there they headed for Georgia,
where the people had assembled an army and
were ready for battle. When they were about to
face each other, Jäbä hid himself and several
thousand soldiers, and Sübädäi went forward
with the army. At the very beginning of the
battle the Mongols retreated with the Geor-
gians in pursuit. Along the way they took the
city of Shemakha by siege, massacring and
taking many captives. Since they could not get
through Derbent, Jäbä sprang from ambush
and caught [the Georgians] in a trap. In an in-
stant thirty thousand Georgians were killed.
From there they set out for Derbent and Shir-
van. They sent a message to the Shirvanshah
1In JTK the name is given asﻪ ـ ـﯾﻨ ا, which could conceiv-
ably be the name Inä. Smirnova (JTSL 1/2:228) tentative-
ly reads the name as Абиз.
2Sarāw is the modern Sarāb between Ardabil and
Tabriz.
telling him to send representatives for truce
talks. He dispatched ten of his nobles. The
Mongols killed one of them and seized the oth-
ers, saying, “If you show us the way through
Derbent, we’ll spare your lives; otherwise
we’ll kill you too,” They guided them through
out of fear for their lives. When they reached
that territory, there were many people there.
Together with the Qipchaqs they sent a mes-
sage, saying, “We and you are one group and
of one sort. The Alans are aliens to us. We have
made a pact with you not to harm one another.
We will give you whatever gold and clothing
you want. Leave them with us.” So saying,
they sent a lot of goods. The Qipchaqs turned
back, and the Mongols achieved victory over
the Alans, massacring and looting as much as
they could. The Qipchaqs, in hopes of peace,
scattered in safety in their own territory, but
without warning the Mongols attacked them
and killed everyone they found, taking many
times over what they had been given before
turning back. Some of the Qipchaqs who re-
mained ﬂed to the lands of the Rus. The Mon-
gols wintered in that area, which was all pas-
ture lands. [535]
From there they went to the city of Sudaq on
the coast of the sea that is attached to the Gulf
of Constantinople.3 They took that city, and the
people scattered. After that, they attacked the
towns of the Rus and the Qipchaqs who had
gone there. They got ready by assembling large
forces, and when the Mongols saw how many
they were they retreated. The Qipchaqs and
Rus thought they were retreating out of fear
and pursued them a ten-day’s distance. Then,
without warning, the Mongols turned around
3Sudaq was in the Crimea, and “the sea…attached
&c.” is the Black Sea. William of Rubruck calls Sudaq
“Soldaia”: “In medio vero quasi in cuspide ad meridiem
habet ciuitatem quae dicitur Soldaia, que ex transuerso
respicit Synopolim [the modern Sinop]” (p. 145).
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
257

and attacked them, and before they could as-
semble themselves many were killed. They
fought for a week, and in the end the Qipchaqs
and Rus were routed. The Mongols went in
pursuit and so destroyed their towns that most
were empty of human beings. From there they
traveled until they rejoined Genghis Khan,
who had returned from [Tajik] territory.
Genghis Khan reaches his original home
yurt from the land of the Tajiks and
descends there in his ordus.
Genghis Khan returned from the land of the
Tajiks, and in Bechin Yil, the Year of the Mon-
key corresponding to the summer and winter of
621 [1224], when he reached his camp sites,
Qubilai Qa’an, who was eleven years old, and
Hülägü Qa’an, who was nine years old, went
out to greet him. By chance he had felled a
hare and an antelope on the frontier of Naiman
territory near Imil-Qojin1 on the other side of
the Ili River, near Uyghur territory. [536] The
Mongol custom is the first time boys hunt,
their thumbs are greased (yaghlamishi),2 that is
they are rubbed with fatty meat. Genghis Khan
greased their thumbs himself. Qubilai grabbed
his thumb softly, but Hülägü grabbed it hard.
Genghis Khan said, “This rascal has done my
thumb in!”
When he set out from there, he ordered a
great camp made, a golden throne set up, and a
large banquet held. Since the ground in that
place was soft, dust rose up. He ordered every-
one to lay stones in his campsite and tent. All
laid stones except Genghis Khan’s brother
Otchi Noyan, who laid wooden planks instead
of stones. He was therefore accused of a dis-
obedience. During those few days Genghis
Khan had gone hunting, and Otchi Noyan did
1Reading اﳝﻞ (Imil) for the text’s ﻣﺎﲤﻞ.
2For the Turco-Mongolian custom of yaghlamishi, see
Doerfer, TMEN 4:98f. §1800.
not go to the right-hand circle but remained a
bit behind. For seven days he was stationed in
the ordu for that offense. When he said that
henceforth he would not commit any offenses,
he was excused and granted access.
In the spring of Tavuq Yil, the Year of the
Rooster that began in Safar 622 [February
1225], he camped in his ordus, and that sum-
mer he was at home and pronounced strict reg-
ulations. When he heard that the Tangqut had
rebelled again, he ordered the army mustered
and set out in that direction.
Genghis Khan goes to attack the territory of
Tangqut the last time, and his battle with
the monarch of that place.
In the autumn of Tavuq Yil, the Year of the
Rooster corresponding to 622 [1225], [537]
Genghis Khan mounted an expedition to the
territory of Qashin, which they call Tangqut.
He ordered Chaghatai to be behind the ordus in
command of a wing. Jochi had died, and
Ögödäi was with his father. Because Sorghaq-
tani Beki was pregnant, Tolui Khan remained
behind for several days and then joined
Genghis Khan.
During those days, Ögödäi’s sons Güyük and
Kötän were being sent back. They asked if he
would give something as an honor and reward
or not. He said, “I have nothing. Everything
that belongs to Tolui, who is the lord of home
and the great yurt, he commands.” Tolui gave
them clothing and all sorts of things. Genghis
Khan gave the grandfather of Qubuchaq, the
shahna of Herat, to Güyük, saying, “You have
an illness. He will prepare food for you.”
When he reached the Tangqut territory, he
took
most
of
the
cities,
like
Ganzhou,3

modern Zhangye in Gansu) and clearly recognizable in

Suzhou,1 and Hezhou.2 He besieged the city of
Dörmägäi3 and hurled fire into it, and as it was
burning, the ruler of that land, Shadurghu by
name, who was called [I]lu[qu Burq]an in the
Tangqut language,4 and the great city that was
his residence was called Äriqai in the Tangqut
language but Eriqaya in the Mongolian lan-
guage,5 came out with five hundred thousand
men to do battle against the Mongols. Genghis
Khan went out against him in battle. In that re-
gion are many na’urs (lakes) formed from the
Qara Mörän (Yellow River), and they were all
frozen over. Genghis Khan stood on the ice
and ordered the soldiers to cross. Many were
killed during the crossing. They say that three
dead men were stood on their heads, for it is an
established custom among the Mongols to
stand one dead man on his head for every
hundred thousand killed.

After that, Shadurghu [538] was routed and
went back into the city. Genghis Khan said,
“Since he has been defeated like this, hence-
forth he will not have any power.” So saying,
he paid no further attention to him and passed
on by his city, taking other cities and territories
while proceeding in the direction of Cathay.
At the beginning of spring of Noqai Yil, the
Year of the Dog corresponding to 623 [1126],
he came to Olqun Talan Qodun.6 While there,
he suddenly began to think of his own condi-
tion, for he had a dream that indicated that his
death was proximate. Of all the princes, Jochi
Qasar’s son Yesuqa [Yesünggü] Aqa was
present. Of him he asked, “Are my sons
Ögödäi and Tolui near or far?” (They were in
their own military circles.) He told the amirs
and those present that they were two or three
days away. Immediately someone was sent to
summon them.
At dawn the next day, while they were eat-
ing, he said to the amirs and those present, “I
have a confidential secret and advice for my
sons. I want to be alone for a time so that we
can tell our secrets to one another and have a
consultation in that regard.” 
Genghis Khan meets in private with his sons
who were present and makes his last will.
When the amirs and men were far away,
Genghis Khan sat in private with his sons. Af-
ter giving them much advice, he said, “My
sons, know that the time for my last journey
and my passing is nigh. Through divine
strength and heavenly assistance, I have con-
quered for you, my sons, a vast and far-ﬂung
empire that overshadows a year’s distance in
every direction. [539] Now I charge you in re-
pelling enemies and elevating friends to be of
6Below, text p. 578, the name of this place is written
Onqulun Talan Qidun.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
259

one mind and one face so that you may pass
your days in comfort and enjoy kingship.” 
He made Ögödäi Qa’an the heir, and after
completing his charge and last will, he gave
advice, saying, “You go to your realms and
peoples, for your realms are being neglected. I
do not want my death to be in a tent or for me
to go for the sake of name and repute. After
me, you must not change my Yasaq. Chaghatai
is not here, but when I have passed away let
him not dispute my words in his kingdom.
Now you must go.”
After that, he bade them both farewell and
sent them back to their realms and people as he
himself set off for the Nankiyas.
Genghis Khan heads for the Nankiyas; the
onset of his illness; the ruler of the Tangqut
comes to submit and asks for respite in
turning over the city.
After completing his last will and dismissing
his sons, Genghis Khan set out for the
Nankiyas. The rulers of those cities came one
after another to submit. When they reached the
frontier of the Jurchid realm, the king of the
Jurchids, having heard that Genghis Khan was
approaching, sent out emissaries bearing gifts,
among them a tray of regal round pearls, to say
that they surrendered. Genghis Khan said,
“Give pearls to all who have pierced ears.”
Those present who did not have pierced ears
immediately pierced them [540] and were giv-
en pearls. Still there were many left. “It is a
day for giving,” he said. “Scatter them all and
let the people pick them up.” Knowing that the
day of his death was nigh, he attached little
value to them, and many of the pearls were lost
in the dust. For a long time people searched for
them in that place and got them out of the
ground.
Thereafter, Shadurghu, the king of Tangqut,
thought to himself, “I have rebelled against the
emperor several times, and every time he has
come to kill and loot my territory. Henceforth
it would be wise not to contend with him. One
must surrender to Genghis Khan.” He sent
emissaries and sought a truce and pact bound
by oaths, saying, “I was afraid. Accept me as a
son.” Genghis Khan granted his wish. The
ruler asked for a month’s respite in order to
arrange his offering of tribute and get the peo-
ple out of the city. The respite was granted. He
wanted to do kichämishi with him. Genghis
Khan said, “I am indisposed. Have patience
until I am better.” To Tolun Chärbi he said,
“Serve him and be his shigha’ul” (meaning
host). He went as commanded and served, but
Genghis Khan’s illness grew worse by the day.
The death of Genghis Khan, and the sudden
death of the ruler of the Tangqut and people
of that city; the commanders return with his
coffin in secret, and the revelation of his
death and his burial.
Realizing that he was surely going to die
from his illness, Genghis Khan charged his
commanders, saying, “Do not reveal my death,
and absolutely do not wail or moan lest the foe
realize what has happened. When the people of
Tangqut [541] come out on the promised day,
annihilate them all!”
When fifteen days had passed of the middle
month of autumn in the Year of the Pig, which
corresponded to Ramadan 624 [August–Sep-
tember, 1227], he departed this mortal world,
leaving throne and kingdom to his renowned
offspring. The commanders, as ordered, con-
cealed the event until the people came out and
they slew them all. Picking up his coffin, they
set out upon the return, slaying every creature
they encountered along the way until they
reached the ordus. All the princes, ladies, and
commanders who were nearby assembled and
held mourning. 
In Mongolia there is a great mountain called
Burqan Qaldun. From one side of this moun-
260

the north, the Chikö;4 on the northwest, the

from the mid-southwest, the Burachitu; from

One day Genghis Khan was out hunting, and
he spied a lone tree growing by itself. He liked
the shape of the tree very much. Dismounting
in its shade for a while, [542] he experienced
an inner joy. “This place,” he said, “is suitable
for my burial site. Mark it well.” During the
mourning those who had heard this recounted
it. The princes and commanders chose that site
in accordance with his order, and they say the
very year he was buried there innumerable
trees and grass grew in that plain, and now
there is such a thick forest that it is impossible
to get through. The first tree and the site of his
burial can no longer be recognized. Even those
who have long served as guardians of the
reservation can no longer find their way there.
Of his offspring, his youngest son and his
sons and their progeny who remained in that
territory are buried there. The other sons and
their progeny are buried elsewhere. The gho-
ruqchis (guardians) of that great ghoruq have
never told the commanders or their peoples
[where it is].
Mourning was held each day in a different
camp. When the news reached nearby places
and distant sites, every several days ladies and
princes arrived from every direction to hold
mourning. Some groups were so far that it took
three months for them to arrive and conduct
mourning ceremonies. “Everything will perish
except His face. His is the command, and unto
Him shall you be returned.”7 Praise to His
friend, and prayers and greetings upon His
prophet and his pure family.
May God cause the shadow of protection of
the Padishah of Islam, Emperor of the Earth
6Neither the Russian translator nor Poppe offers an
identification for “Burachitu”; Dulä is identified as the
Tola (Tuul).
7Kor. 28:88.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
261

and Time, Lord of the rulers of Iran and Turan,
locus of the Merciful’s grace and benefi-
cence…, [543] heir to Genghis Khan’s throne,
shadow of God, helper of God’s religion, to
continue over the heads of all peoples until the
end of the world. “God has mercy on a servant
who says amen.”
The history of Genghis Khan has now been
given from the beginning of Taulai Yil, the
Year of the Rabbit that began in Dhu’l-Qa’da
615 [January 1219], through Tonquz Yil, the
Year of the Pig that began in Safar 624 [Janu-
ary 1227]. At the beginning of this nine-year
period he set out for Turkistan and Iran and ac-
complished that mission in six years, returning
to his camp in the spring of the seventh year,
the Year of the Rooster that began in Safar 622
[February 1225]. Then he launched a campaign
against the Tangqut, who had rebelled. During
the third year of this campaign he died during
the middle of the autumn in the Year of the Pig.
Now we will give the history of his contempo-
raries during these nine years. [544]
A summary history of the khaqans of Cathay and Machin, the caliphs, sultans, maliks, and
atabegs of Iran, Syria, Egypt, etc. who were Genghis Khan’s contemporaries during his last
nine years, from the beginning of Taulai Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that began in Dhu’l-
Qa’da 615 [January 1219], through the end of Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig that began in
Safar 624 [January 1227], and unusual events that took place.
History of the rulers of Cathay during this
period.
Zhang Zong.1 Hsing-sheng.2 Shou-hsü.3

of his caliphate and rule were orderly and up-

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

din, until he crossed the Indus in the fourth
year of the period, have likewise already been
reported in the course of the history.
As for what transpired after that time, it was
as follows. When Sultan Jalaluddin crossed the
river and escaped Genghis Khan’s clutches, he
spent a day or two in a forest until nearly fifty
men whose lives had not been ended in the wa-
ter joined him and learned that a group of rene-
gades, both mounted and on foot, were still
robbing
and
wreaking
havoc
within
two
leagues of the sultan’s camp. The sultan or-
dered his comrades each to take a staff and am-
bush them. They killed most of them and took
their animals and weapons. Then groups from
all around joined them, some on horses and
others on oxen. News arrived that there were
four military men from Sind in the area. The
sultan attacked them with one hundred twenty
men, put most of them to the sword, and reout-
fitted his men with the plunder. When word of
the sultan’s defeat and end of his rule reached
Hindustan, six thousand horsemen gathered
[546] from the mountains of Balala and
Bankala and attacked them.1 The sultan and the
five hundred horsemen he had went out against
them, gave battle, and annihilated most of
them. Some came over to him, and his army
grew to nearly three thousand. Then he set out
for Delhi.
When he reached the frontier, he dispatched
a messenger to Sultan Shamsuddin, who had
formerly been a friendly neighbor, to say that it
would be chivalrous if they helped each other
in adversity and to request a place where he
could stay for a while. Since the sultan’s great
audacity was well known in the world, Sultan
Shamsuddin contemplated his response for a
day or so, and finally he realized that he was
1Balala and Bankala (also read as Nikala) were in the
Lahore vicinity. See Juvaini/Boyle 2:412, note 4.
fearful of the sultan’s domination, so in the end
he killed the messenger and sent a grandee out
with suitable offerings of food and gifts, apolo-
gizing that there was [no] place with a friendly
climate that would suit the sultan’s constitution
in the environs of Delhi which he could turn
over to him to save himself from the foe.
When the sultan heard this, he withdrew
back to the vicinity of Balala and Bankala.
There a troop of soldiers joined him, and his
horde of horsemen reached nearly ten thousand
in number. From there he sent Tajuddin Malik
Khalaj with a troop to the Judi mountains to
raid and pillage, and they returned with much
booty. Then he sent a messenger to the Rai of
the Khokar to request his daughter in marriage.
The Rai granted his request and also sent his
son with a troop to the sultan, who granted the
son the title Qutlugh Khan. The governor of
the province of Sind was an amir named
Qubacha. He claimed to be sultan and had an
implacable enmity with the Rai of the Khokar,
Sangin. He camped one league from Uchh, on
the banks of the Indus, [547] with twenty thou-
sand men. The sultan sent a man named Özbeg
with a detachment to attack him. Özbeg and
seven thousand men launched a surprise attack.
Qubacha’s forces were routed in the first
charge. Qubacha got in a boat, and set sail for
the fortress of Akkar-u-Bakkar,2 which was on
an island. Özbeg fell upon Qubacha’s camp,
dismounted, and sent the good news for the
sultan to come. Qubacha went in defeat from
Akkar-u-Bakkar to Multan. 
Since it was hot, the sultan set out to summer
in the Judi hills [in] Balala and Bankala. Along
the way he besieged the fortress of Parasravar,3
2“Akkar-u-Bakkar” seems to be Bhakkar, the island
fortress at the modern Sukkur in Pakistan. See Juvaini/
Boyle 2:414, note 11.
3For the text’sــﻳ
ﴪام, readــﭘ
ﺮﴎور(Parasravar, or Paras-
rur, the modern Pasrur in Sialkot).
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
263

and during that battle he was hit in the arm by
an arrow. When the fortress was taken and
everyone was killed, he pulled back and passed
through the outskirts of Multan. He sent an
emissary to Qubacha inviting him to battle.
Qubacha came out, and after a time the sultan
retreated to Uchh in defeat. The people there
came out to do battle; the sultan pitched fire
into the city and left in the direction of
Sadusan.1
Fakhruddin Salari, the governor on behalf of
Qubacha, and Lachin Khitai, the head of the
army, were with Orkhan, the sultan’s vanguard.
[Lachin] came out to do battle and was killed,
and Orkhan besieged the city. Fakhruddin
Salari came before the sultan in fear with his
sword and burial shroud. The sultan went into
the city and stayed there for a month, reward-
ing Fakhruddin and giving him the governor-
ship of Hindustan before setting out for Debul
and Damrila.2 Chatisar,3 the governor of that
area, ﬂed to an island. The sultan descended in
that area and sent Khass Khan with a troop to
raid Nahrwala4 and bring many camels from
there, and the sultan had a congregational
mosque constructed on the site of the fortress.
During all this, news arrived from Persia that
his brother [548] Sultan Ghiyasuddin was en-
sconced in Persia, although most of the sol-
diers of the garrisons were loyal to Sultan
Jalaluddin. Baraq Hajib laid siege to Guvashir
in Kirman.5 The sultan went from there to
1The location of Sadusan has not been established, but
it was near the modern Sehwan.
2Readingدﻣـﺮﯾـ¢
(Damrila) for the text’sدﻣـﺮﺑـ¢
. See Juvai-
ni/Boyle 2:416, note 18.
3Readingﴪ ـ ـ ـﭼﺘﻴ(Chatisar) for the text’sﴪـﺟ. Chatisar
was a local Rajput ruler.
4Nahrwala was the capital of Gujarat; it is the modern

5Guvāshīr is the seat of Kirman; it is also known in its
