Makran, but on account of the putrid air many
of his men were lost along the way.
When news of the sultan’s arrival reached
Baraq Hajib, he sent offerings of food and
asked for news. When he arrived he asked for
one of his daughters in marriage. The sultan
had him married. The castellan of the fortress
of Narmashir came and handed over the keys
to the fortress to the sultan.
In the year 620 [1223–24], the sultan went
into the fortress and held a marriage ceremony.
Two days later he mounted to go hunting and
to graze his horses. Baraq Hajib remained be-
hind on the pretext of suffering from the gout.
Along the way the sultan was informed of his
pretended illness and realized that he had re-
mained behind in order to rebel. Therefore he
sent one of his elite to Baraq Hajib to say,
“Since we will soon be setting out for Persia,
let Baraq Hajib come to the hunting ground.
Since he is a man of experience, particularly
with regard to Persia, we will consult with him
and act as he sees fit.”
In reply the chamberlain said, “I have stayed
behind because of a sore foot. It would be best
for the sultan to carry out his decision to leave
as soon as possible, for Narmashir is [not] a
suitable place for a ruler’s throne, and this area
cannot support his retinue and followers. This
fortress must have a castellan, and no one can
be more loyal than I, an old servant whose hair
has turned white in your court, but I have taken
this land by the sword, and it will not be possi-
ble for the sultan to return to the fortress.” He
sent the messenger back, ejected the remainder
of the sultan’s retinue from the fortress, and or-
dered the gates closed.
Since the sultan did not have the power to re-
sist or take revenge, [549] he set out for Shiraz
and sent a messenger to Atabeg Sa‘d to an-
Fida, Taqwim, 336.
264
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

nounce his arrival. The atabeg sent his son Sal-
ghurshah with five hundred horsemen to greet
him and apologize for not coming himself. “I
could not come myself,” he said, “because I
have taken a vow, which can in no way be bro-
ken, not to go out to greet any living creature.”
The sultan accepted this apology and showed
Salghurshah great honor and respect. When he
reached the city of Fasa on the borders of Shi-
raz, the atabeg sent all sorts of food worthy of
such a guest and gifts and presents suitable for
a sultan’s table, such as gold, jewels, utensils,
clothing, a court tent, implements for wine
storage, and a kitchen, with Tajik, Turkish,
Abyssinian, and Indian slave boys to take
charge of every task. He also expressed his de-
sire to see him in person and gave the sultan a
“pearl nourished in the oyster shell of the
atabegian family” in marriage, and by creating
this son-in-law relationship the bonds of mutu-
al trust were strengthened on both sides. He
spend a few days there and then took the road
to Isfahan.
In a place called Takht-i-Surkh near the bor-
der of Isfahan was Atabeg Ala’uddawla b.
Atabeg Sam, the grandson of Ala’uddawla
Garshasp b. Ali b. Farmarz b. Ala’uddawla the
Elder of the Buyid House, who was resident in
the protected town of Maybud. He went out to
present the sultan with offerings of food and
other regal gifts, and because he was an old
man, the sultan called him “father,” sat him
next to himself, and entitled him Ata Khan. He
had a thousand Turkish slaves in his service,
all excellent horsemen and champion warriors.
After that he usually was in the sultan’s retinue
with five hundred of his horsemen, and the sul-
tan named him governor and amir of the city of
Isfahan. [550] He became firmly ensconced at
court, and his form of address from the
supreme divan was “most mighty imperial fa-
ther most dear.” The atabegs of Yazd were his
father’s brothers and nephews, and the renown
and importance they possessed were due to
him. His seat was the city of Maybud, where
he was for sixty-three years, although he was
also atabeg in Yazd for a time. He lived for
eighty-four years. In the year 624 [1227] he
was martyred in Isfahan.
In short, the sultan arrived and learned that
his brother Ghiyasuddin was in Rayy with the
ministers and army commanders. Unencum-
bered and with only a few horsemen, the sultan
raised
his
white
banners
when,
without
warning, Ghiyasuddin attacked, and some of
the heads of the army scattered in fear. The sul-
tan compassionately sent word to his mother,
saying, “Now, when sedition is rife and the foe
on all fronts overwhelming, is no time for con-
tention.” Ghiyasuddin promised to help him
and came to his brother with his elite. The sul-
tan rewarded him and assigned all of the amirs
to high rank. Tax gatherers were sent out, and
all were given written orders and decrees.
Through his presence the kingdom regained a
modicum of order. The head of his chancery
and chief executive officer was Nuruddin
Munshi, who composed an ode in praise of the
sultan, the first line of which is as follows: “
Come, soul, for the world is again happy and
joyous through the splendor of the great prince
Sultan Jalaluddin.”
At the beginning of 621 [1224] he set out to
winter in Tustar, sending in the vanguard Elchi
Pahlavan with ten thousand men. Along the
way Sulaymanshah joined him and gave the
sultan his sister. [551]
He stayed no more than one month in the an-
cient and splendid city of Shapur, and the
amirs and atabegs of the Lur came to him.
When the horses were fat he set out for Bagh-
dad, thinking that the Caliph Nasir-li-dini’llah
would help him against his enemies. He sent
an emissary to announce his arrival, but [the
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
265

caliph] sent a pigeon to Arbela so that Muzaf-
faruddin Kök-Böri would take his army and
get rid of the sultan. Before the Arbela army
arrived, however, Qoshiq Temür had grown
overconfident in his own strength, and when
the sultan drew near he sent a message to
Qoshiq Temür, saying, “We have come here to
take refuge with the caliph, for powerful ene-
mies have raised their heads, and no army has
the power to resist them. If I am helped by the
caliph, it will be my job to repel those who
have taken over.” Qoshiq Temür paid no atten-
tion to these words and drew up his battle
ranks. The sultan was forced to fight. He
placed a contingent of his army in ambush and
attacked [Qoshiq Temür’s men] with five
hundred of his cavalry and then turned around.
Imagining that they were in rout, Qoshiq
Temür set out in pursuit, but when he reached
the ambush spot, the sultan’s men emerged
from their hiding places and took down Qoshiq
Temür’s men from the rear. Qoshiq Temür was
killed, and his army went in defeat to Baghdad.
The sultan rode down the Daquq road, [552]
pillaging until he was past Tikrit.
Spies arrived to report that Muzaffaruddin
Kök-Böri was coming with the Arbela army to
ambush the sultan. The sultan and a few horse-
men attacked Muzaffaruddin and took him
captive. The sultan pardoned him, and Muzaf-
faruddin went forth with great embarrassment
and expressed regret, saying, “Until today we
had [not] known of the sultan’s fine moral
character.”
The
sultan
spoke
regally
and
praised him for having kept the roads clear of
bandits. Then he clad him in honor and gave
him permission to withdraw. Muzaffaruddin
went to the city and gave further favor by
many pleasing actions.
From there the sultan went to Azerbaijan. At
that time Atabeg Özbeg, Jahan-Pahlavan’s son,
was governing Tabriz. He left his wife, Sultan
Toghril the Seljuqid’s daughter Malika Khatun,
in the city and ﬂed to the fortress of Alinja. In
622 [1225] the sultan camped in the outskirts
of Tabriz. One day Sultan Toghril’s daughter
came out on the ramparts, saw the sultan, and
fell in love with him. She claimed that her hus-
band had divorced her, but Qazi Qawamuddin
Haddadi would not listen to her. Qazi Izzuddin
Qazwini, however, said, “If you appoint me to
the chief justiceship, I will allow you to be
married.” He was made cadi and gave the
queen in marriage to the sultan, and the city
was turned over to him. When the sultan en-
tered the city, the people of Tabriz welcomed
him. [553] When this news reached Atabeg
Özbeg, he was overcome with grief at the loss
of his position.
Soldiers ﬂocked to the sultan from all direc-
tions, and he set out with thirty thousand men
for the lands of the Georgians to take revenge
for their having several times raided parts of
those territories. One morning at dawn he at-
tacked the Georgians, who were still drowsy
from sleep, and led away their commanders,
Shalva and Ivane and others, in chains and fet-
ters. Shalva had an enormous body. When he
was brought before the sultan, the sultan asked,
“Where is your splendor and championship?”
“This is what the sultan’s fortune has done,”
he replied. At once he embraced Islam.
The sultan went in triumph to Tabriz. Shalva
[and Ivane] were honored so that they would
assist in the conquest of Georgia; and Marand,
Salmas, Urmia, and Ushnuviya were given to
them.
Shalva and Ivane accepted to undertake vari-
ous things, and with their promises they
seduced the sultan, who sent them off to con-
quer Georgia. In secret, however, they had
summoned their armies and stationed them in
ambush, but someone informed the sultan, and
after ascertaining the truth, he killed them and
266
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

attacked their troops, killing most of them, al-
though a few managed to escape. After that af-
fair, the sultan took Tiﬂis and all Georgian ter-
ritories and destroyed some of their churches,
building mosques in their stead. [554]
Messengers brought news that the Mongol
army had crossed the Oxus and was in
Khurasan. The sultan set out for Persia. When
he reached Isfahan, more than a hundred thou-
sand horsemen and foot soldiers went out from
Isfahan to repel the foe. Arraying his troops, he
put the right wing under the command of his
faithless brother Ghiyasuddin, and he himself
took charge of the center. From the other side
came Baju Noyan, Yaqu Noyan, Esän Toghan,
Taimas, and Tainal with the Mongol army, and
they did battle at the gate of Sin, a dependency
of Isfahan. Ghiyasuddin, to spite his brother,
turned his reins away with Elchi Pahlavan and
took ﬂight to Luristan. 
When the armies clashed, the Mongol right
wing took out the sultan’s left wing and drove
them to Luristan. The sultan’s right wing took
out the Mongol left wing and drove them to
Khwar-i-Rayy. The armies clashed, and the
sultan was left in the center, surrounded on
both sides. 
Atabeg Ruknuddin Abu’l-Fath Ala’uddawla
of Maybud, who was known as Ata Khan, was
killed in the battle. The sultan was severely
overwhelmed until he managed to get out of
the midst. He rushed off in the direction of
Luristan. They stopped to rest in a gorge. There
the scattered soldiers rejoined him. The people
of Isfahan believed that the sultan had been un-
horsed and looked for him among the dead.
Some thought he had been taken captive. Sud-
denly messengers arrived saying that the sultan
was coming. The people of the city went out to
greet him. When he dismounted, because he
was angry with most of his retinue he ordered
that those who had failed in battle should be
dressed in women’s headgear and paraded
around the city. Those who were not numbered
among the officers but had performed bravely
[555] were all rewarded with lands and admit-
ted to court. This event took place in Ramadan
624 [August 1227].1 After that, the sultan went
to Tabriz and made preparations for a cam-
paign in Georgia.
The history of Sultan Ghiyasuddin.
Sultan
Ghiyasuddin,
Sultan
Muhammad
Khwarazmshah’s second son, emerged from
the Qarun fortress, which he had frequented,
after the death of his father and the defeat of
his brother and headed for Kirman, to which
his father had assigned him. The castellan of
Narmashir paid no attention to him, so he went
to Persia while his brother was in India. In Per-
sia he assembled a large force, and Baraq Ha-
jib and Oghul Malik also joined him to attack
Atabeg Sa‘d and wreak havoc in the province
of Fars. Atabeg Sa’d had gone to the Safed
fortress to go hunting, and they rounded up all
the animals they could find and withdrew.
Conversations were held between Baraq Hajib
and the vizier Tajuddin Karimushsharq. Baraq
Hajib grew angry and set out with his soldiers
for India. Along the way he took Kirman and
stayed there. The next year Ghiyasuddin set
out for Fars. The atabeg abandoned the city
and left. Ghiyasuddin’s soldiers pillaged and
then went to Khuzistan, where a truce was
made with the governor Muzaffaruddin, and
they withdrew. After that, he was busying him-
self assembling forces in Rayy when Sultan
Jalaluddin arrived without warning. [556]
1According to Nasawi, the Battle of Isfahan took place
on 22 Ramadan 625 (August 25, 1228); see Boyle, “His-
tory,” 330, and Juvaini/Boyle 2:437, note 45.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
267

The story of Sultan Ruknuddin, son of the
Khwarazmshah.
When his father pulled out of Persia, he left
him there in his stead. The officers of Persia
rebelled, and the father send in reinforcements.
He seized them all, and after attaining power
he gave them posts. Imadulmulk of Sawa was
his vizier, and when the sultan returned from
Transoxiana, he sent him to bring the sultan to
Persia. Ruknuddin went out to greet him.
When that did not take place, the sultan went
to an island in the Caspian, and Ruknuddin and
a few men went to Kirman. A number of sol-
diers belonging to the malik of Zozan gathered
around him, and he went into the city and gave
away the treasures of the malik of Zozan. Then
he set out for Persia. When he reached Isfahan,
Qazi Ruknuddin took fright and hanged him-
self. The sultan did not consider it prudent to
take up residence in the city. They went into
the city, and the citizens, with the permission
of the cadi, rioted, and nearly a thousand per-
sons were killed. Therefore the sultan went to
Rayy. When the Mongol army arrived, he went
o the fortress of Firozkoh. After six months of
siege they got him out, but no matter how
much they insisted that he bend his knee, he re-
fused. In the end they martyred him and his
dependents. 
In Rum was Sultan Izzuddin Kaykavus b.
Kaykhusraw b. Qilich Arslan. During these
years he died of consumption, and his brother
Ala’uddin Kayqubad, [557] who had been im-
prisoned, was taken out and elevated to the
rule since his son was an infant. His uncle and
the lord of Erzurum were opposed, but Malik
Ashraf, the lord of Akhlat, made a truce be-
tween them.
In Mosul was the important ruler Sultan
Badruddin Lu’lu’. During these years he laid
siege to the fortress of Shush.1 From the
fortress of Aqr went Imaduddin Zangi b. Ar-
slanshah to Daru’l-Mulk Tabriz to Atabeg
Özbeg. The atabeg made him a member of his
retinue. The siege lasted a long time without
results. Badruddin left his army there and went
to Mosul. When the defenders of the fortress
were reduced to dire straits they surrendered.
History of the maliks and atabegs.
In Tabriz was Atabeg Özbeg. His story has
already been given during Sultan Jalaluddin’s
history.
In Diyarbekir was Muzaffaruddin Kök-Böri,
and his story too has already been given. [558]
In Sinjar was Qutbuddin Muhammad b. Ima-
duddin Zangi b. Qutbuddin Mawdud b. Aq
Sonqur. He died, and his son Shahanshah was
installed in his place.
In other cities were the sons of Malik Adil. In
Syria was Malik Mu‘azzam, one of Malik
Adil’s sons. 
In Egypt was Malik Kamil.
In Shiraz was Atabeg Muzaffaruddin Sa‘d b.
Zangi, whose history has already been given.
In Kirman was Malik Shuja‘uddin. As Baraq
was going to India he passed by there. The Kir-
manis attacked him in hopes of taking Chinese
slaves from his harem and retinue. Although he
kept saying, “I entertain no hostility toward
you,” they would not listen. He and his men
fought bravely, killing many of the Kirmanis
and Malik Shuja‘uddin as well. They then took
the city and laid siege to the citadel until Sul-
tan Jalaluddin arrived. However, as has been
reported, Baraq tricked him and became the
absolute ruler. [559] 
In Seistan…
History of rare and unusual events that took
1Shush, a fortress twelve leagues from Mosul (Ibn al-
Athir, Kamil 12:411).
268
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

place during the nine-year period.
Left blank: what may be discovered will be
written.
Now that the history of Genghis Khan that
was recorded in books, scrolls, and chronolo-
gies has been written, partially in general and
partially in detail, we wanted to add to what
has been described a summary account of what
occurred throughout his life as a chronology so
that those who so desire can learn of those
events in a summary fashion and know with
what he was occupied during each year and not
have to look back and reread. [560]
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN, 1219–1227
269

❦ A SHORT CHRONOLOGY OF GENGHIS KHAN BY THE YEARS OF HIS LIFE
It is well established among the Mongols that
Genghis
Khan
lived
seventy-two
Turkish
years. He was born in a Tonquz Yil, a Year of
the Pig, and he also died in a Tonquz Yil, in
Tangqut territory. His coffin was taken to his
ordus in that year, corresponding to the 14th of
Ramadan 624 [August 28, 1227], and his death
was revealed. 
By calculating backwards astronomically it
has been ascertained that the Tonquz Yil that
was the year of his birth fell in Dhu’l-Qa‘da
549 [January 1155], i.e. he died in the seventy-
fifth lunar year of his life. The reason for the
difference is that Turkish years are solar, and
approximately every thirty years there is one
lunar year more. Although he died in his sev-
enty-third Turkish year, he died in the middle
of the year; and since both the year of his birth
and the year of his death were incomplete
years, it follows, as previously established, that
the length of his life was seventy-five lunar
years, or seventy-three Turkish solar years, [of
which two were] incomplete, so in terms of
years of solar months this would be seventy-
two years. [561] 
Section: A summary year-by-year history during that period. Some of this period comprises
the time during which his father was alive and he was a child, and some includes the time
during which he suffered setbacks—a total of forty years.
Subsection: During which his father Yesügäi
Bahadur was alive and he was a child,
thirteen years
This thirteen-year period began in Tonquz
Yil with the birth of Genghis Khan, which fell
in the month of Dhu’l-Qa‘da 549 [January
1155], and ended also in a Tonquz Yil, the Year
of the Pig that fell in Rabi‘ II 562 [February
1167]. During this period his father, Yesügäi
Bahadur, was alive and a mighty and prosper-
ous ruler of his people. Most of the Qiyat and
Niru’un clans, to which they belonged, as well
as other Mongols, were his followers. Since
Genghis Khan was a child during that time and
never away from his father, his story has been
related in an over-all general fashion and not
repeated here.
Subsection: After the death of his father, a
time of setback and trouble, twenty-seven
years.
This period of twenty-seven years [562] be-
gan in Quluqana Yil, the Year of the Rat that
fell in Rabi‘ II 563 [January 1168], and ended
in Bars Yil, the Year of the Leopard that fell in
Safar 590 [January 1194]. At the beginning of
this period, since Yesügäi Bahadur had died,
the child Genghis Khan was bereft of his fa-
ther, and the commanders and many clans of
the Mongols and his father’s relatives mutinied
and left him for reasons that have been de-
scribed. He was thus dealt a severe setback and
suffered difficulties from everyone. After that
God had mercy on him by regulating his af-
fairs, and he attained the rulership. Since his
condition during this period was unhappy, it

has not been given year by year but only in
general as follows.
His father, Yesügäi Bahadur, was the ruler of
the Mongol tribes and had followers among his
aqa-inis and those who had branched off from
their forefathers. When he died, most of those
tribes inclined to the Tayichi’ut and deserted
Genghis Khan. His mother, Ö’älün Ekä of the
[Olqunu’ut] clan, made heroic efforts and kept
some of them [from leaving]. During those
years Genghis Khan suffered many trials from
the Tayichi’ut and other collateral tribes, like
the Jä’üriyät, Märkit, Tatar, etc. Many times he
was seized by each of those tribes, but he es-
caped their clutches with various tactics, and
since felicity and fortune were slated for him,
he gradually attained success. Earlier on, he
fought with the Tayichi’ut and raided them. Af-
ter many hostilities he annihilated most of that
tribe, and some submitted. [563] He overcame
the other Niru’uns, Tatars, Märkits, and other
united opponents, and his army grew in num-
bers until he became strong and powerful at the
end
of
the
above-mentioned
twenty-seven
years. This is a summary account of this peri-
od. Thereafter, when he had become strong, his
history is known year by year.
A detailed year-by-year account.
This consists of two sections, one for the
years before he was given the title Genghis
Khan, and the other for the years after that, a
total of thirty-three years.
The period before he was given the title of
Genghis Khan, eleven years.
The beginning of this period of eleven years
was Taulai Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that fell
in Rabi‘ I 591 [February 1195], and it ended in
the Year of the Ox that fell in Jumada II 601
[1205].
Taulai Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that began
in Rabi‘ I 591 [1195].
Genghis Khan was in his forty-first year,
[564] and in this year he returned from battle
with Jagambu, the brother of Ong Khan, the
ruler of the Kerayit and the Tongqayit branch
of the Kerayit that had united against him and
stirred up sedition. Upon his return to his ordus
he reveled and rested.
Luy Yil, the Year of the Dragon that fell in
Rabi‘ I 592 [1196].
In this year Genghis Khan had grown so
greatly in strength that Ong Khan, the ruler of
the Kerayit and a mighty and important ruler,
came to him in helplessness and asked for as-
sistance. Ong Khan, in a struggle over the
rulership of his people, had killed most of his
brothers and uncles, but one brother named
Ärkä Qara had escaped and ﬂed to the king of
the Naiman, Inanch Khan, who sent a troop,
drove Ong Khan away, and took the kingdom.
Ong Khan went to the Gür Khan of the
Qarakhitai, but when he did not find security
there either, he returned, went into Uyghur ter-
ritory and got a few head of sheep, on whose
milk he sustained himself. In that state of desti-
tution he took refuge with Genghis Khan. In
the spring of this Year of the Dragon, he joined
him in a place called Güsägür Na’ur. Genghis
Khan felt sorry for him, gave him money and
soldiers, and restored him to the rulership.
Prior to this, once before, Ong Khan’s uncle
had taken the kingdom from him by force, and
Ong Khan [565] had taken refuge with Yesügäi
Bahadur, who took the kingdom from the uncle
and gave it to him. They called each other
anda.
Moqai Yil, the Year of the Serpent
corresponding to Rabi‘ I 593 [1197].
In the autumn of this year Genghis Khan did
battle with the king of the Märkit people, Toq-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN’S CAREER
271

to’a Beki, and defeated him. All that was taken
in booty he gave to Ong Khan to enrich him.
Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that fell in
Rabi‘ II 594 [1198].
Genghis Khan remained in his place during
this period. Ong Khan, having grown strong,
left without consultation, attacked the Märkit
people, and carried away the wife of Toqto’a
Beki, the chief of that tribe, as booty. His
brother made one of Toqto’a’s sons surrender
and brought him and his followers in.
Qonin Yil, the Year of the Sheep that fell in
Rabi‘ II 595 [1199].
During this year Genghis Khan and Ong
Khan did battle with Sariq Khan, the brother of
Tayang Khan, the ruler of the Naiman. They
struck his tribe at a place called Qizil Bash. He
ﬂed in defeat to the territory of Kämkämji’üt.
Yedi Tuqluq, his scout, had ﬂed from Genghis
Khan’s scouts [566] and gone up on a moun-
tain. His horse’s girth strap came loose, he and
the saddle fell off, and he was captured.
During that winter he did battle with Kögsä’ü
Sabraq, the commander of Buyuruq’s army.
Once again Kögsä’ü Sabraq came, the armies
were arrayed on both sides, and it was agreed
that battle would be fought the next morning.
That night Ong Khan had fires lit in his camp
and took ﬂight. When Genghis Khan rejoined
him after being separated, Kögsä’ü Sabraq
came in pursuit with Buyuruq Khan’s army
and raided the tents of Ong Khan’s brother and
some of his soldiers. Ong Khan asked Genghis
Khan for help again, requesting his four com-
manders. Genghis Khan sent them with troops
to strike Buyuruq Khan’s forces, and they took
back and restored everything that had been tak-
en from Ong Khan and his brother and their
people.
Bichin Yil, the Year of the Monkey that fell
in Rabi‘ II 596 [1200].
In the spring of this year Genghis Khan held
consultations with Ong Khan in Sa’ari Kähär,
and together they mounted to wage war against
the Tayichi’ut and other tribes allied with
them. They struck, and many of the comman-
ders and soldiers submitted and joined them.
After that, the Qataqin, Salji’ut, Dörbän, Tatar,
and other tribes united to attack Genghis Khan
and Ong Khan. Forewarned by spies, they set
out together, attacked, and defeated them.
Some of Ong Khan’s commanders grew suspi-
cious of him, and they were reprimanded.
[567] That winter Genghis Khan parted from
Ong Khan and did battle at Talan Nämürgäs
with some of the Tayichi’ut, Tatars, and others
who had reunited. He defeated them and pil-
laged their baggage and possessions.
Tavuq Yil, the Year of the Rooster that fell
in Jumada I 597 [1201].
During this year Genghis Khan learned that
the Ikiräs, Qorolas, Dörbän, Tatar, Qataqin,
and Salji’ut tribes had assembled at the Käm
River and elevated Jamuqa Sächän of the
Jäjirät as gür khan. Jamuqa was defeated at
Yedi Qurqan, and at that same place the Qunqi-
rat clan submitted.
Noqai Yil, the Year of the Dog that began in
Jumada II 598 [1202].
In this year Genghis Khan mounted a cam-
paign against the Anchi Tatar and the Chaghan
Tatar. He had stipulated that no booty or plun-
der was to be taken until the battle was over,
but his uncle Otchi, Qutula Qa’an’s son Altan,
and Näkün Taishi’s son Quchar disobeyed and
took booty. Genghis Khan ordered everything
to be taken from them, so they went over to
Ong Khan in anger and started stirring up trou-
ble, as will be related later.
272
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

In the autumn of this year Genghis Khan and
Ong Khan learned that the Naiman ruler’s
brother Buyuruq and other clans allied with
him were launching a campaign against them
with a massive force. [568] They did battle
with them, and they went to the border of
Öngü and Cathay, which is a mighty wall built
to separate Cathay from Mongolia. It was at
that time that Genghis Khan requested the
daughter of Sangun, Ong Khan’s son, for mar-
riage to his son Jochi. Sangun requested
Jochi’s daughter for his son. Because the mar-
riages were not concluded there were bad feel-
ings on both sides. Ong Khan’s son contem-
plated attacking Genghis Khan, but Ong Khan
kept him from doing it.
Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig that began in
Jumada II 599 [1203].
In the spring of this year Genghis Khan was
in his ordus. Ong Khan and Sangun summoned
him on the pretext of asking for a daughter in
marriage, but while he was on his way there
Echigä prevented him from going. After that,
Ong Khan and Sangun conspired to lead their
army and ambush Genghis Khan. A spy
learned of this in time to warn him. Battle was
fought, and Genghis Khan went in defeat to
Baljiuna, a small spring, where he spent sever-
al days drinking water squeezed from the mud.
After that, he set out for another place, and
from there he sent a messenger to Ong Khan
and Sangun and their commanders to remind
them of the rights and obligations of every de-
scription they owed him. They refused to make
a truce. It so happened that some of Ong
Khan’s officers became alienated from him,
plotted treachery, and deserted him. Some of
them joined Genghis Khan. Genghis Khan’s
brother Jochi Qasar [569] was separated from
him at that time, and Ong Khan’s soldiers raid-
ed and pillaged his tent and baggage. He
reached Genghis Khan hungry and naked.
Genghis Khan sent a message in Jochi Qasar’s
name to Ong Khan saying, “I have tried hard to
rejoin my brother, but I can find no trace of
him. If my khan-father will give me back my
tent, I will submit.” By this ruse Ong Khan
was taken unaware.
During that winter, he wintered in a place
called Tämä’än Kähär and camped in his tents.
Before
this
victory
he
had
brought
the
Tayichi’ut and other Mongol tribes under his
command and subdued and become the ruler of
the Mongol commanders from among his aqa-
inis and others who had joined Ong Khan.
When he killed Ong Khan, who was a ruler of
puissance of an ancient family, the throne, pos-
sessions, and realm became his. 
During this year the title Genghis Khan was
bestowed upon him. “Genghis Khan” means
the same as “Gür Khan,” i.e. mighty and pow-
erful ruler. It was always customary in that
land for great rulers to be called Gür Khan, and
when the Mongols clans of the Niru’un and
some of the Dürlükin banded together and
gave Jamuqa Sächän the title of Gür Khan, that
is why they gave him that name, although it
did not prove to be lucky. The same name, but
in Mongolian, was given to Genghis Khan,
who up until this point had been called
Tämüjin, the name his father had given him.
Astronomers and some historians date the
beginning of his rule from this year, and thus
they report that he was born in a Year of the
Pig, his father died in a Year of the Pig, he be-
came ruler in a Year of the Pig, and he died in a
Year of the Pig.
In Mongolian histories the beginning of his
rule is dated from this year, when he killed the
Naiman Tayang Khan [570] and received the
title Genghis Khan.1
Quluqana Yil, the Year of the Rat beginning
1This paragraph is not in the Turkish translation JTAJ.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN’S CAREER
273

in Jumada II 600 [1204].
In the spring of this year, when Ala Qush Te-
gin of the Öng’üt sent a message saying that
Tayang Khan, the Naiman ruler, had asked him
for assistance to make war on Genghis Khan,
Genghis Khan gathered his aqa-ini and held a
great quriltai. In the autumn of this year he
launched a campaign against Tayang Khan,
striking him along with the Märkit ruler
Qutuqu and the Qataqin, Salji’ut, and other
tribes that had allied themselves with him. Last
of all he killed Tayang Khan.
Hükär Yil, the Year of the Buffalo beginning
in Jumada II 601 [1205].
In this year Genghis Khan launched a cam-
paign against Qashin territory, which is called
Tangqut, took the fortress of Li-chi and the city
of K‘eng Lo-szu1 and pillaged the realm of
Tangqut, taking many captives.
SECTION. AFTER RECEIVING THE TITLE
OF GENGHIS KHAN, A PERIOD OF
TWENTY-ONE YEARS AND A PARTIAL
YEAR, MAKING TWENTY-TWO YEARS.
This period began in Bars Yil, the Year of the
Leopard that began in Rajab 602 [1206], and
ended in Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig that
began in Rajab 624 [1227], the year he died.
[571]
Bars Yil, the Year of the Leopard that began
in Rajab 602 [1206].
In this year Genghis Khan was fifty-two
years old. Having recently defeated and killed
the Naiman ruler Tayang Khan and a group of
other rulers who had joined him, he returned to
the area of the Onon, his original yurt, having
attained great power and status. He ordered a
white, nine-footed standard raised and a great
gathering held. Kököchü Täb Tängri, the son
1Readingﻮﳻ ـﻟﮓ ـــﮐﻴﻨKeng Luosi. See note to text p. 420
above.
of Münglig Echigä, a noble man who claimed
miraculous powers, had said, “God has given
the rulership of the face of the earth to you.”
That day he came forward and made manifest
his claim to miraculous powers, saying, “Now
that the rulers of this clime, each of which was
called Gür Khan, have been conquered by you
and their realms taken by you, you too shall
have the title chingiz, which means the same,
i.e. king of kings. God has commanded that
your title be Genghis Khan, for chingiz is the
plural of ching, and chingiz is the intensive
form of ching. Therefore, the meaning of chin-
giz khan is emperor and king of kings.” The
amirs approved of this and confirmed him in
that title. He had acquired extremely great
power and strength and was known as the lord
of the world. After that he launched a cam-
paign against Buyuruq, whom he ambushed in
his winter grounds, killed, and seized his
realm. [572]
Taulai Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that fell in
Rajab 603 [1207].
In this year Genghis Khan launched a cam-
paign because the Qashin territory had rebelled
again, and he subdued that realm. Also in this
year he sent emissaries to the Qirqiz. They
submitted and sent their own emissaries with a
white falcon as a gift in the company of
Genghis Khan’s emissaries.
Luy Yil, the Year of the Dragon that fell in
Rajab 604 [1208].
In this year Genghis Khan spent the summer
at home. In the winter he set out to make war
on the ruler of the Märkit, Toqto’a Beki, and
Güshlüg, Tayang Khan’s son, who had con-
spired together and stirred up trouble. Toqto’a
Beki was killed in battle, and his brothers and
people ﬂed to Uyghur territory. Güshlüg also
took ﬂight and went to the Gür Khan of the
Qarakhitai, the ruler of Turkistan.
274
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Moghai Yil, the Year of the Serpent that fell
in Sha‘ban 605 [1209].
In this year Genghis Khan summoned the
Idiqut, the ruler of the Uyghur, who had al-
ready dispatched his emissaries to submit. He
sent messengers to give information on Toq-
to’a’s brother and sons. [573]
Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that fell in
Sha‘ban 606 [1210].
During the summer of this year Genghis
Khan was at home. In the autumn he set out
once more to make war on Tangqut territory to
chastize
them.
The
ruler
of
that
realm,
Shidurghu, gave him his daughter.
Qonin Yil, the Year of the Sheep that fell in
Sha‘ban 607 [1211].
In the spring of this year Genghis Khan was
at the Kerulen. Arslan Khan, the ruler of the
Qarluq, and the Idiqut, the ruler of the Uyghur,
came to him there and was received favorably.
Toquchar Noyan of the Qunqirat and two thou-
sand horsemen were assigned to act as scouts
at the rear, and in the autumn the army set out
for Cathay, where they took many cities. 
Bechin Yil, the Year of the Monkey that fell
in Ramadan 608 [1212].
In this year Genghis gave each of [his sons] a
troop, assigning each of them to lay siege and
take a particular city in Cathay. Many cities
were taken.
Tavuq Yil, the Year of the Rooster that fell
in Ramadan 608 [1213].
In this year Genghis Khan went to the vicini-
ty of the city of Chung-tu, the capital of
Cathay. The Altan Khan took counsel with his
officers whether to do battle or not. Having de-
cided that it was in their best interests to make
peace, they sent emissaries to submit. [574]
[The Altan Khan’s] daughter Gungju Khatun
was given to Genghis Khan, who then pulled
back. The Altan Khan went to the city of
Namging in the east of Cathay on the banks of
the Qara Mörän (Yellow River). Genghis
Khan’s troops took Jungdu and removed the
Altan Khan’s treasures that were there. Many
provincial governors surrendered.
Noqai Yil, the Year of the Dog that fell in
Shawwal 610 [1214].
In this year Genghis Khan was still in
Cathay, and he, his sons, his commanders, his
retinue and followers, and his supporters were
all occupied with seizing lands and provinces.
Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig that fell in
Shawwal 611 [1215].
In this year Genghis Khan was still in
Cathay. He dispatched Samuqa Bahadur with
an army to take some territories there. He dis-
patched Tolun Chärbi toward Chaghan, and he
took many regions.
Quluqana Yil, the Year of the Rat that fell in
Shawwal 612 [1216].
In this year Genghis Khan dispatched Muqali
Guyang to retake the areas that had been taken
before but had fallen into rebellion. He retook
them all. [575]
Hükär Yil, the Year of the Buffalo that fell
in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 613 [1217].
In this year Genghis Khan set out from
Cathay for his original territory. He sent
Sübädäi Bahadur to wage war on the Märkit
nation, and for that campaign he had carts rein-
forced with iron so they would not break in the
difficult mountains; and with him he sent the
two thousand he had left behind previously
with Toquchar Bahadur. They went and swept
away Qudu, Toqto’a Beki’s brother, and what
was left of the Märkit army. He sent Boroghul
Noyan and Dörbän Noyan to annihilate the Tu-
mat tribe, which had previously surrendered
but then rebelled. Boroghul Noyan was killed
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN’S CAREER
275

during battle, and Genghis Khan showed ex-
ceptional favor to those he left behind.
Bars Yil, the Year of the Leopard that fell in
Dhu’l-Qa‘da 614 [1218].
In this year Genghis Khan turned over to
Muqali Guyang and the entire army of the left
wing, along with some of the army of Cathay
that had submitted, the territory of Cathay he
had conquered and confirmed on him the title
of Guyang, which means a king’s realm in
Cathaian. He sent Jochi to retake the Qirqiz
territory that had rebelled.
Taulai Yil, the Year of the Rabbit that fell in
Dhu’l-Qa‘da 615 [1219].
In this year Genghis Khan gathered his ordus
and [576] held a great quriltai at which the
armies were arrayed, and he mounted for a
campaign against the Tajiks.
Luy Yil, the Year of the Dragon that fell in
Dhu’l-Hijja 616 [1220].
In this year Genghis Khan was on the road in
his own territory and spent the summer at the
Irtysh River. When the horses had been fat-
tened, in the autumn he made a circle and took
the territory that lay on his way. When he
reached Otrar, he stationed Jochi, Chaghatai,
and Ögödäi to take that place and other cities
in that part of Turkistan while he himself went
with Tolui Khan to Bukhara.
Moghai Yil, the Year of the Serpent that fell
in Dhu’l-Hijja 617 [1221].
In
this
year
Genghis
Khan
camped
in
Bukhara. Also in this year he took Samarkand
and other cities in that vicinity. The princes
came to him. Jochi took Yangikent, Barchin-
lighkent, and that area and came back. He sent
Jäbä Noyan and Sübädäi Noyan in pursuit of
Sultan Muhammad to Khurasan, Persia, and
Azerbaijan. He dispatched Jochi, Chaghatai,
and Ögödäi to lay siege to Khwarazm while he
himself went to Nakhshab and Termez in order
to cross the Oxus. In the vanguard he sent
Tolui Khan with an army to conquer the cities
of Khurasan. He took most of the fortresses
and crossed the Oxus, took Balkh, and went to
Taligan, which he besieged. [577]
Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that fell in
Muharram 619 [1222].
During this solar year two lunar years began.
In the spring of this year Genghis Khan laid
siege to Taligan. Tolui Khan took all the cities
and outlying areas of Khurasan. Genghis Khan
sent an emissary to him to tell him to return be-
cause the weather was warm. He returned, and
along the way he plundered the province of
Quhistan, took the city of Herat, where he mas-
sacred and pillaged, and rejoined Genghis
Khan as he was destroying the fortress at Tali-
gan. Chaghatai and Ögödäi also arrived there.
Jochi had gone to rejoin his aghruq and ulus.
Also in this year news arrived that Sultan
Jalaluddin had gone to the banks of the Indus,
where he fought with Qutuqu Noyan and was
defeated. In this year Genghis Khan set out in
pursuit of Sultan Jalaluddin, whom he put to
ﬂight across the Indus. He sent Bala Noyan in
pursuit as he turned back.
Qonin Yil, the Year of the Sheep that fell in
Muharram 620 [1223].
In the spring of this year Genghis Khan
turned back from the banks of the Indus. He
sent Ögödäi Qa’an to conquer the western
parts of that region. He massacred and pil-
laged, but when the weather turned hot he was
recalled. He rejoined his father on the Bor-
aghul plain, and there they summered until
Bala Noyan returned from India, [578] having
taken the cities there and stationed a shahna.
276
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Bechin Yil, the Year of the Monkey that fell
in Safar 622 [1224].
In the summer of this year Genghis Khan
turned back and spent the summer on the road.
Then he set out for home, proceeding at a
leisurely pace.
Tavuq Yil, the Year of the Rooster that fell
in 623 [1225].
In this year Genghis Khan dismounted in his
own ordus. It was the seventh year since he
had ridden out on the Tajik campaign. He spent
the entire summer there, and in the autumn he
set out for Tangqut territory, which he had
pacified several times but which had rebelled
again. That winter he besieged Dörmägäi and
set fire to it.1 The ruler of that realm,
Shidurghu by name, came out of the city of
Eriqaya, the greatest of the cities of that realm,
with five hundred thousand soldiers and gave
battle. Three hundred thousand men were
killed.
Noqai Yil, the Year of the Dog that fell in
Safar 623 [1226].
In the spring of this year in Onqulun Talan
Qidun,2 Genghis Khan suddenly felt ill. Sum-
moning his sons Ögödäi and Tolui, who were
there, he withdrew and spoke to them in pri-
vate. [579] He made Ögödäi Qa’an his heir and
gave them permission to withdraw to their
realms and homes. He himself set out for
Nankiyas. When he reached a place on the
frontier of Tangqut and Jurchid territory, the
Jurcha sent emissaries with trays of pearls,
which Genghis Khan gave away. The Tangqut
1For the name Dörmägäi, see text p. 537 above.
2On text p. 538 above, the name of this place is writ-
ten Ulqun Talan Qodun. In JTAJ 68, it is Onqun Talan
Qoduq. In JTRM it is “Arbāqā.”
ruler saw it was in his best interests to surren-
der, but he requested a month’s respite in order
to prepare his tribute and have his men come
out. Genghis Khan was stricken by symptoms
of an illness.
Tonquz Yil, the Year of the Pig that fell in
Safar 624 [1227].
During this year, the seventy-third from the
year of his birth, Genghis Khan completed his
seventy-second year and died of the illness he
had in Tangqut territory. Prior to that, when he
was giving his last will to his sons and sending
them back, he stipulated that when his death
occurred it was to be kept secret. They were
not to mourn or wail lest it become manifest.
The commanders and soldiers were to wait pa-
tiently until the Tangqut ruler and people came
out. They were then to kill them all and not let
the news of his death reach the territory earlier
lest the people rise up. In accordance with his
will, they kept the death hidden, and when the
people of Tangqut came out they put them all
to the sword. They picked up Genghis Khan’s
coffin and set forth, killing every creature they
saw along the way lest the news be spread
abroad. In this Year of the Pig, corresponding
to the 14th [of Ramadan] 624 [August 28,
1227], they delivered his body to his ordus and
announced the death. [580] Mourning was held
in the four great camps, and he was buried in
the place he had designated for his burial.
“Everything will perish except His face. His is
the command, and unto Him shall you be
returned.”3
Now that we are finished with the year-by-
year history of Genghis Khan, we will com-
plete the third section. [581] ❧
3Kor. 28:88.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWO: GENGHIS KHAN’S CAREER
277

❦ SECTION THREE OF THE STORY OF GENGHIS KHAN
ON HIS GOOD CHARACTER AND NOBLE CUSTOMS, ON THE GOOD DECREES, WORDS OF WISDOM, AND
ORDERS HE SPOKE AT VARIOUS TIMES, ON THE TIMES OF EVENTS THAT TOOK PLACE DURING HIS RULE
THAT WERE NOT INCLUDED IN THE PREVIOUS TWO SECTIONS; BECAUSE THEY HAVE BEEN LEARNED FROM
MISCELLANEOUS PERSONS AND BOOKS, THEY ARE BEING WRITTEN SEPARATELY.
Genghis Khan said,1 “If there are people whose
sons do not listen to the wisdom of their fa-
thers, whose younger brothers do not heed the
words of their elder brothers, whose husbands
do not trust their wives, whose wives do not
obey their husbands, whose mothers-in-law do
not like their daughters-in-law, whose daugh-
ters-in-law do not respect their mothers-in-law,
whose adults do not support their children,
whose young persons do not accept the advice
of their elders, whose masters do not seek the
affection of their slaves, and who do not com-
prehend their yosun and yasaq with intelli-
gence and competence—among such people
thieves, brigands, and robbers spring up and
drive them from their homes—that is, they pil-
lage and plunder them. Their herds and ﬂocks
can find no rest, [582] and they do not rest the
horses they have ridden to the front. Conse-
quently those horses become exhausted, die,
and rot away to nothingness. Such people are
incompetent and worthless. When Genghis
1Much of the Persian in this section is very obscure,
particularly in syntax. It all has the feel of having been
rendered into Persian from Mongolian, which, of course,
it probably was. Fortunately we have the Chaghatay
Turkish translation made by the anonymous Jalayirid at
the end of the sixteenth century (JTAJ). Since in many re-
gards his text seems to have been better, or at any rate he
seems to have understood better what was meant, I am
including the Turkish translation in the footnotes with
each passage in this section. The few phrases included in
the Turkish but missing from the Persian are signaled by
<…>.
Khan attained fortune and all came under his
command, and his strict yasaq gave them or-
der, those who were learned and brave he made
commanders of the army; to those who were
nimble and quick he entrusted the aghruq and
made
them
herdsmen;
the
unlearned
he
whipped lightly and sent them off to be shep-
herds. Thereby his fortune waxed day by day
like the moon, and through God’s power divine
assistance came down from heaven, and good
fortune grew from the earth to help him. His
summer pasture lands became places of revelry
and celebration, and his winter quarters were
commodious and comfortable. Since by the
grace of the great God I have comprehended
these things, and I have deduced these articles
of wisdom myself, therefore our ease, prosperi-
ty, and revelry have reached such a degree.
Henceforth, for however many years—five
hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand—that my
offspring will come into existence and rule as
khans, my progeny, no matter how grand they
may become, will safeguard themselves with
the Genghisid yosun and yasaq and will not re-
place it. They will enjoy favor from heaven,
and they will always have pleasure and enjoy-
ment. God will grant the entire world to them,
and the people will pray for them. They will
live long and enjoy the good things of this
world. [The proverb] ‘He who punishes well
rules long’ is an allusion to this.’ ”2

He also said, “Among my offspring, many
emperors will come into existence after this. If
the grandees and warriors who will serve them
do not maintain the yasaq strictly, the empire
will become shaky and end. They will wish
they had Genghis Khan, but they will not have
him.”1
❈
He also said, “Commanders of ten thousand
and a thousand who come at the beginning and
end [583] of the year and listen to words of
wisdom and then return home can most likely
lead troops, but those who sit at home and do
not listen to words of wisdom are like a rock
that falls on a large body of water, or an arrow
that is shot into a reed bed and disappears.
Such persons are not worthy of being leaders.
<Whoever can keep his own house in order
can also keep territory in order; anyone who
can keep ten men under his command is wor-
thy of being given the command of a thousand
or ten thousand men.>”2

He also said, “Everyone who is capable of
cleaning out his own insides is capable of
cleansing a kingdom of banditry.”1
❈
He also said, “Let any officer who cannot
keep order in his own squad be branded a
criminal along with his wife and children, and
let another be chosen as officer from his
squad—and companies of a hundred, a thou-
sand, and ten thousand likewise.”2
❈
He also said, “Every word upon which three
learned men are agreed can be repeated every-
where; otherwise it cannot be trusted. Measure
your own words, and those of others, against
the words of the learned: if they are in confor-
mity they can be spoken; otherwise they
should not be spoken.”3
❈
He also said, “No one who goes to an elder
should speak until the elder asks him a ques-
tion. Then let him give an appropriate answer
to the question. If he speaks more than this and
they listen, well and good; otherwise, it is like
beating cold iron.”4
❈

“When a man gets drunk on wine and
darasun [rice wine], he is just like a blind man

and skill in a wine-drinker nor are there morals
or good conduct. He does bad things: he fights
and kills. It keeps a person from doing the
things he knows how to do and from practising
the skills he possesses, and when one loses
these two, [it is like bringing food from the fire
and throwing it into the water]. If a ruler is
avid for wine and tarasun, he cannot perform

who is avid for drinking wine will suffer great
catastrophe; common people who like to drink
will lose their ﬂocks and herds and everything

❈
When Genghis Khan set out on his expedi-
tion to Cathay against the Altan Khan, as was
his custom he went up alone on a hill, unloosed
his belt and threw it over his neck, opened the
ties of his tunic, knelt, and said, “O God, you
know all from long ago. You know that the Al-
tan Khan initiated hostilities and began our en-
mity. Ökin Barqaq and Hambaqai Qa’an were
abducted by the Tatars and sent before the Al-
tan Khan, who killed them, my elders and an-
cestors, though they were innocent of any
crime. [If you consider me right in what I
think,] I ask for vengeance and retaliation for
their blood. I want you to let men, fairies, and
demons help and assist me.” He prayed thus in
all humility, and afterwards he arose and de-
parted. Through his sincerity of intent, he
gained victory over the Altan Khan, who was
such a mighty and splendid emperor with vast
lands and impregnable fortresses without num-
ber, and those realms came under his and his
sons’ control.2

my sole purpose to make their mouths as sweet
as sugar by favor, to bedeck them in garments
spun with gold, to mount them upon ﬂeet-foot-
ed steeds, to have them drink sweet, clear wa-
ter, to provide their animals with grassy mead-
ows, and to have all harmful brambles and
thorns cleared from the roads and paths upon
which they travel, and not to allow weeds and
thorns to grow in their pastures.”1

One day Möngkä Qalja, who was one of the
commanders of consequence, asked, “They
call you the lord of might and a champion.
What signs of victory and conquest have you?”
In reply he said, “Before I mounted the
throne of kingship I was once riding alone
along a road. Six men were waiting to ambush
and kill me. When I got near them I drew my
sword and attacked. They started shooting ar-
rows at me, but they all missed me and not one
hit me. [590] I killed them all with my sword
and went on my way safe and sound. As I was
returning I passed by the bodies of those six.
Their horses were wandering around owner-
less. I rounded all six up and brought them
home.”2

and put forth feathers during the winter, of rid-
ing a fine horse he has fattened, and hunting
blue-headed birds in springtime greenery—and
of wearing fine clothes and garments.”
Genghis Khan said to Boroghul, “You say.” 
Boroghul replied, “A man’s greatest pleasure
consists of flying birds like falcons against
grey herons until they bring them down with
their talons and catch them.”
Then he asked Doladai Qubilai, and he said,
“A man’s greatest pleasure is hunting and fly-
ing falcons.”
Then Genghis Khan said, “You have all spo-
ken well, but a man’s greatest pleasure is to de-
feat his enemies, to uproot them, to take what
they have, to make their women weep so that
tears run down their noses, to mount their fair-
gaited, fat-thighed stallions, and to clothe the
bellies and navels of beautiful ladies with thin
nightclothes and to look at and kiss their
rouged cheeks, and to suck their sweet, ruby-
colored lips.” [592] ❧

COMMANDERS OF DIVISIONS OF A THOUSAND AND COMPANIES OF A
HUNDRED IN GENGHIS KHAN’S ARMY
Those that were attached to the center and
right and left wings and, after his death,
were inherited by his fourth son, Tolui
Khan, known as Yäkä Noyan, and those he
gave to his brother, nephews, and mother in
accordance with what was contained in the
Altan Daftar, with the exception of many
who were too distant to be known: 129,000
individuals.
Division One: Those attached to the qol,
bara’un qar, and je’ün qar,1 that is the
center and wings, and were then inherited
by Yäkä Noyan: 101,000 individuals.
The Center: Genghis Khan’s own personal
regiment, all ev-oghlans and persons who
were attached to the ordus: 1,000
individuals.
At that time it was customary for the person-
al regiment not to be more than one thousand
even though it was the greatest of all the
regiments.

Khan’s array (38,000 vs. 62,000), is called in Mongolian

The commander of Genghis Khan’s regiment
was a person named Chaghan of the Tangqut
nation. [593] He was raised from childhood by
Genghis Khan, who used to call him his fifth
son. He used to send out pack horses, provi-
sions, ropes, etc. from this regiment, and
Genghis Khan’s portion was demanded from
him without concern. [When he was eleven
years old, Chaghan used to go out and watch
over the cows. Once Genghis Khan saw him in
the field watching over a herd of cows and
with stalks of grass stuck on his head. “Why
have you made such a device on your head?”
he asked. “I am watching the cows,” he
replied, “and the cows are my subjects. That
which is on my head is a sign for the cows.”
Genghis Khan liked this response and provided
for him. Later he said, “Be my fifth son.”
Chaghan used to distribute horses and provi-
sions from Persia to the camps and to this regi-
ment in just this manner.]2 After Genghis
Khan’s death, at Ögödäi Qa’an’s order he went
to Cathay as head of the princes and comman-
ders. When he was sent to Cathay, Buda, who
was also of the Tangqut nation and had been

taken captive, was appointed commander of
the personal hundred and regiment in his stead.
Buda was from Börtä Füjin’s ordu.
The companies of one hundred and one thou-
sand were composed as follows.
(1) Genghis Khan’s great hundred was first
commanded by the great Chaghan Noyan;
when he went to Cathay it was commanded by
Buda Noyan.
(2) El Temür Ba’urchi’s hundred. He was of
the Sönit tribe, the younger brother of Temür;
he was from Börtä Füjin’s ordu.
(3) Yürki Ba’urchi’s hundred. He was of the
Dörbän clan, the grandfather of the Bolad Aqa
who was a great amir here, also of Börtä
Füjin’s ordu.
(4) Olda’ur Qorchi’s hundred. He was of the
Jalayir tribe and was shahna of the four ordus.
(5) Elängär Ba’urchi’s hundred.1 He was
from the Albat branch of the Kerayit nation,
and of Börtä Füjin’s ordu.
(6) Jamal Khwaja’s hundred. He was of the
Märkit nation and a brother of Qulan Khatun’s.
(7) The elder Qongqiyadai’s hundred. He
was of Yesülün Khatun’s ordu.
(8) Yesün To’a’s hundred. He was of the
Tatar and an akhtachi amir attached to Börtä
Füjin’s ordu. The Begtash the Qa’an [594] sent
on an embassy to Hülägü Khan was his son.
The eight companies of a hundred that are
known have now been listed. Others will be
written in as they are learned.

Those attached to the right and left wings:
100,000 individuals.
The commanders of the right wing were
Bo’orchi [Borghochin] Noyan and his
sütüküsün (lieutenant commander)
Boroghul Noyan: 38,000 individuals.
The elite regiment of Bo’orchi Noyan of the
Arulat tribe, the greatest of Genghis Khan’s of-
ficers. In the beginning he was an officer of the
guard; later he became a commander of ten
thousand, and then he commanded the right
wing. When he died during Ögödäi Qa’an’s
reign, his place was taken by Boroldai. During
Mänggü Khan’s time, it was Balchiq. During
Qubilai Qa’an’s time Bo’orchi Noyan’s son El
Temür
took
command,
and
after
him,
Boroldai’s
son
Jirqamish
took
command.
[Bo’orchi] had many other sons, all great com-
manders. One was Öz Temür, chief of the
ba’urchis; he was a well-known inaq. Well
known
in
this
land
were
his
offspring
Beglämish and his son Ujan,2 and the Tüläk
who was executed for having conspired with
Sögä. [595]
The elite regiment of Boroghul Noyan, the
sütüküsün of Bo’orchi Noyan’s regiment and
one of Genghis Khan’s great officers and com-
panions. He was of the Hushin tribe and sur-
passed Bo’orchi Noyan’s rank, for in the right
wing there was no one greater than he. In the
beginning he was a bökä’ül and a ba’urchi, and
then he became a guard. Later he became a
commander of a tümän. In Ögödäi Qa’an’s
time his son Jübükür Qubilai took his place. In
Qubilai Qa’an’s time was Tuqchi Gürägän, to
whom was given Kälmish Aqa’s sister and
Hülägü Khan’s niece, Shirin.

The regiment of Jädäi Noyan of the Mangqut
nation. In Qubilai Qa’an’s time his grandson
Mangqutai took over his command. The histo-
ry of Jädäi Noyan and his relatives has already
been given in detail in the section on the
Mangqut.1 Amir Qutlughshah is descended
from him.
The regiment of Kingqiyadai Noyan of the
Olqunu’ut clan. During Qubilai Qa’an’s time
his grandson Buqa took over his command.
The great Turatu Gürägän and Yisa’ur are de-
scended from him.
The
regiment
of
Tolun
Chärbi
of
the

was called Kököchü Täb Tängri.
The regiment of Sökätü Chärbi of the
Qongqotan clan, a brother of the Tolun Chärbi
mentioned above. In this land the husband of

scended from him.
The regiment of Bala Noyan of the Jalayir
nation. In Qubilai Qa’an’s time he was suc-
ceeded by a man named Maqui. The emissary

The regiment of Arghai Qasar Noyan of the
Jalayir nation, an elder brother to Bala Noyan.
The regiment of Toghril of the Suldus tribe
and a relative of Sodon. The great amir Chärän
Ba’urchi who was in Mängü Qa’an’s service
was a kinsman of his. Qubilai Qa’an had him
executed for having led Ariq Bökä astray.
The regiment of Sodon Noyan of the Suldus,
who was very famous. He was still alive dur-

Ba’aritai Qorchi Noyan’s regiment of the

The regiment of the Öng’üt tribe. They num-

The regiment of Muqali Guyang of the
Jalayir nation. Since he was an important com-
mander and performed valiant feats, Genghis
Khan put all the clans of the Jalayir army un-
der his command. The regiments assigned to

return, was one of his sons. Cha’uqur and
Omoq are descended from him.
The regiment of Yesü Buqa Taishi of the Uri-
angqat, the son of Jälmä Uha, who was one of
Genghis Khan’s trusted officers. At that time
the great commanders who were of importance
were Borghochin Noyan, Boroghul Noyan,
Jälmä Uha, and Sodon Noyan. Qara’una Chu-
pan, a commander of a thousand, was a
nephew of Yesü Buqa Taishi’s. In the Cathaian
language taishi means a great teacher and mas-
ter,1 and Ögödäi Qa’an gave him the name
taishi as a pleasantry. He had to be brought to
court in a cart because he always suffered from
the gout.2 
Kähätäi Noyan’s and Bujir Noyan’s regi-
ment.3 These two were brothers from the
Uru’ut clan, a branch of the Niru’un tribe. Be-
cause they were great commanders and volun-
tarily performed valiant feats, [600] Genghis
Khan put all the soldiers from their tribe under
them, and their regiment amirs were those they
appointed, although their names have not been
learned in detail. In all they were four thou-
sand. One night Genghis Khan had a dream, as
a result of which he gave his wife Ibaqa Beki,
the daughter of Jagambu of the Kerayit, to
Kähätäi Noyan, as has been stated in the
history.4
The regiment of Butu Gürägän of the Ikiräs
clan, a branch of the Dürlükin close to the
Qunqirat clan. He married one of Genghis
Khan’s daughters, as has been described. He
was of importance and performed valiant feats
stoutheartedly, so Genghis Khan put him in
charge of all the soldiers from the Ikiräs clan.

He appointed his own regimental commanders.
In all they were three thousand, but their
names are not known in detail.
The regiment of Yäkä Qutuqut Noyan of the
Tatar nation, a great and inﬂuential comman-
der. His cousin was Joma Gürägän. He had two
full sisters, Yesülün and Yesügän. Genghis
Khan married both of them, and they were
among his four chief wives. Their story and
that of their tribes and the Tatar nation have
been given in detail.
The regiment of Elchi Noyan. Huqutu Noy-
an, Qata, Buyur, [Tägüdär],5 and Junqur—
these five commanders were of the Qunqirat
clan. Elchi and Huqutu were brothers, and their
father was Däi Noyan, the ruler of the Qunqi-
rat. Genghis Khan’s chief wife, Börtä Füjin,
was their sister. The other four commanders
were their cousins, the sons of Däi Noyan’s
brother Daritai. [601] There were—and still
are—many imperial sons-in-law from them
during Ögödäi Qa’an, Mänggü Qa’an, and
Qubilai Qa’an’s times, and they sat above the
emperors’ sons. Salji’utai Gürägän, the hus-
band of Kälmish Aqa, was one of them, and so
was the Äbügän Gürägän who came as an
emissary from there. The entire Qunqirat divi-
sion they commanded numbered five thousand
individuals.
The regiment of Quyildar Sächän of the
Mangqut clan of the Niru’un. His regiment was
also of that clan, and he was Genghis Khan’s
anda and of great importance. He performed
very great feats and sat in rank below Muqali
Guyang. He was never absent from service. In
this realm Khalifa and Mäkritäi are descended
from him. Other amirs who are in service, like
Nüregäi Noyan,6 are also descended from him.

The regiment of Naya’a Noyan of the
Ba’arin clan, from which clan all his soldiers
came. Since he was a great officer who had
submitted voluntarily and performed valiant
feats, Genghis Khan put the Ba’arin troops un-
der him, and he appointed the regimental com-
manders as he wished. In total they numbered
three thousand individuals. He was the sütü-
küsün
(second
in
command)
of
Muqali
Guyang, the commander-in-chief of the troops
of the left wing.
The regiment of Sutu Noyan of the Qong-
qotan clan, a son of Münglig Echigä. Their
histories have been given in the preceding por-
tion of this book.1
The regiment of Jalayirtai Yisa’ur of the
Jalayir. He is not the Yisa’ur who came here.
Kürüt,2 who was sent as emissary to the Qa’an,
[602] and who was Arghun Khan’s son Yesü
Temür’s amir-ordu, is descended from this
Jalayirtai Yisa’ur.
The regiment of Önggür Noyan of the
Baya’ut, a branch of the Dürlükin. Genghis
Khan’s
chief
bökä’ül
and
ba’urchi
was
Güchügür Noyan of the Besüt clan. Among the
Naiman his nickname, Qisat,3 means a bökä’ül
[taster], i.e. he verifies [food].) When he grew

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THREE: ARMY COMMANDERS
295

Olqunu’ut clans, Genghis Khan gave her these
three thousand, but their names are not known.
When he was giving the commanders men-
tioned above and their troops to his sons and
the others, he said, [612] “I give you these
commanders, but you, my sons, are still chil-
dren while they are experienced. If they ever
commit an offense, do not kill them of your
own accord, but consult me. After I am gone,
consult one another and then carry out what is
required by the Yasa.” He gave this advice so
that such great commanders would serve them
willingly and so that, if they committed an of-
fense, [the sons] would consult together and
make the offense clear so that they would not
think of doing it again and so that they would
confess and admit their mistakes and know that
their punishment was due to their offense, not
out of wrath or whim.
Aside from the troops Genghis Khan as-
signed, all the soldiers of the great comman-
ders attached to the right and left wings and to
the center whose names have been listed, and
other commanders whose names have not been
ascertained, all served in his retinue. After his
death, by rule, they served in the retinue of the
great lady Sorqaghtani Beki and her sons
Mänggü Qa’an, Qubilai Qa’an, Hülägü Khan,
and Ariq Bökä.
When Ögödäi Qa’an became khan, of his
own accord and without consulting the princes
and commanders, he gave to his son [Kötän the
troops of] Amir Toladai Ba’urchi, the brother
of Anga Noyan and an amir of the Sönit tribe,
along with one thousand Sönit troops and two
thousand Sulduz that had been attached to
Yäkä Noyan’s sons. Genghis Khan’s great
commander Shigi Qutuqu of the Tatar, whom
Genghis Khan called his fifth son, Sodon Noy-
an of the Sulduz, [613] Jädäi Noyan of the
Mangqut, Mönggäsar Qorchi of the Jalayir,
Botijin Qorchi of the Besüt, Qubilai Qorchi of
the Baya’ut, Yisa’ur Qorchi of the Qonqotan,
and other tümän commanders were in the ser-
vice of Sorqaghtani Beki and Mänggü Qa’an
and his brothers. They said, “Ögödäi Qa’an has
given his son Kötän the Suldus and Sönit
troops that belong to us. Since Genghis Khan
gave them to [Tolui Khan’s] ordu in the divi-
sion, how can we allow this infraction of his
orders? Let us state this in Ögödäi Qa’an’s
presence. What say you?” 
In reply Sorqaghtani Beki said, “What you
say is right, but of the things [Genghis Khan]
garnered, of what have we received so little
that we would have cause for complaint? We
too belong to the Qa’an, and he is the ruler. Let
him command as he sees fit.” Since she spoke
with intelligence and competence, the com-
manders all fell silent. However, on this ac-
count ill feeling arose between Kötän and Tolui
Khan’s sons. When the families of Ögödäi
Qa’an and Mänggü Qa’an differed, Kötän be-
came alienated [from his own family]. As a
consequence, when Mänggü Qa’an also divid-
ed their troops, he left Kötän’s as they were, as
has been explained. After that, Qubilai Qa’an
also left his sons as they were, and they always
served him stoutheartedly. At present all his
offspring are with Öljäitü Qa’an and command
their troops as usual, and they are in every way
at one with the offspring of Yäkä Noyan.
All the troops that were attached to Yäkä
Noyan, and which were more recently with
Qubilai Qa’an, serve Temür Qa’an. All the
troops that Genghis Khan gave [614] to his
brothers, nephews, his fifth son Kölgän, and
his mother Ö’älün Ekä, and by now they have
multiplied and become many times the number
they were originally.
During the years that Qubilai Qa’an was con-
quering the realms of Cathay, Nankiyas, Qara-
jang, Jürcha, Tangqut, and Tibet, he stationed
some of those innumerable troops as guards on
296
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

the borders of Cathay and Jürcha and in the
yurts of Mongolia that are adjacent to these ar-
eas and placed them in summer and winter pas-
tures. The totality of Yäkä Noyan’s troops
mentioned above was inherited by his sons
Mänggü Qa’an, Qubilai Qa’an, Hülägü Khan,
and Ariq Bökä, and it is their custom for all
who are descended from them to take over
their fathers’ commands.
When Mänggü Qa’an took over his father’s
territory and after that, when the khanate was
established on him and he wanted to conquer
the realms of Iran completely, although com-
manders, both during Genghis Khan’s time and
during Ögödäi Qa’an’s time, were sent numer-
ous times [615] with troops, and in the end
Chormaqan was sent with troops. Nonetheless,
not all [of the lands in the west] had been com-
pletely conquered or subdued, for the caliph in
Baghdad, the overlord of the padishahs, was
still a foe, as were the sultans of Rum who
were renowned, the atabegs of Shiraz, the ma-
liks of Syria and Egypt, and the Heretics; and
even the lands that had been taken were shaky
and could be lost at a moment’s notice. After
consultation, [Qubilai] assigned the task [of
subduing these realms] to his brother Hülägü
Khan, in whom, of all the brothers and princes
of the Genghisid family, could be seen traces
of daring, wisdom, power, and fortune, and he
was sent with troops to complete the task of
taking Iran. Those who went with Sali Noyan
to Kashmir, Badakhshan, and Balkh were all
under Hülägü Khan. Of all the other troops, of
those held by Yäkä Noyan’s offspring and the
other princes, two of every ten individuals
were taken out of the count in such a way that
nothing of the base count would be lessened,
and all were given as enchü [appanage] to
Hülägü Khan to come to this land and reside
ensconced. When he conquered it, that territory
and its troops became his and his sons’. There-
fore, they assigned two of every ten of their
brothers and sons who were not in the number,
along with their slaves and servants, and they
assigned their great amirs, brothers, and sons
who were worthy of being tümän commanders,
and sent them all to Iran with Hülägü Khan.
Those amirs’ sons all became commanders of
units of ten thousand, one thousand, and one
hundred. Just as some of the sons of the great
commanders from Genghis Khan’s time and
their offspring were in Hülägü Khan’s service,
and each one held a commission and post of
his own. [616] Down to this time most of their
offspring and descendants still hold their fa-
thers’ posts, and every son of a great comman-
der who is here has relatives in service to
Temür Qa’an and to other important princes
and commanders there—except for a few
wretches who alienated themselves due to vain
thoughts and fancies, were branded as crimi-
nals, and fell from the rank of commander but
who are still alive.
As has been mentioned, all the military per-
sonel who dwell today from the banks of the
Oxus River to the borders of Egypt and Syria
have been attached personally to Hülägü Khan
and his successors on the throne. At present
they all belong to the Padishah of Islam, with a
separate troop and the personal troops of his
father, Arghun Khan, for during Abaqa Khan’s
time the amirs all voluntarily gave their sons
and brothers, together with their liege men, as
enchü to Arghun. All the following separately
are the personal enchü of the Padishah of Is-
lam: those Abaqa Khan gave as enchü, those
Abaqa

❦ SECTION FOUR
THE HISTORY OF ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN, SON OF GENGHIS KHAN, IN THREE PARTS
Here will be given stories that pertain to him,
of his acts, deeds, and words with regard to
ruling, justice, and generosity, aside from what
has already been mentioned in the history of
his father, brothers, and relatives, so that the
reader may know immediately. His story has
been placed first, before the stories of his
brothers Jochi and Chaghatai, who were elder,
because he was Genghis Khan’s heir and the
qa’an of the time, and his rule came immedi-
ately after Genghis Khan’s.
Part One is on his lineage, a detailed account
of his wives, his sons and their progeny down
to the present; a genealogical chart of him and
his offspring.
Part Two is on the history of his reign, a pic-
ture of his throne, his wives, princes, and offi-
cers at his coronation, and a mention of the
battles he fought and the victories he attained.
Part Three is on his good character, his pro-
nouncements, decrees and orders, and events
that occurred during his reign not included in
the above two parts but learned [618] from
miscellaneous books and persons. 
Part One. On his lineage, a detailed account
of his wives and his sons and grandsons
down to the present; a genealogical chart of
him and his offspring.
Ögödäi Qa’an was the third son of Genghis
Khan and his wife Börtä Füjin of the Qunqirat
tribe, Däi Noyan’s daughter who was the moth-
er of the four major sons and five daughters.
His brothers and sisters have been mentioned
in the section on Genghis Khan.
Ögödäi’s name was originally ___, but he did
not like it, so later his name was changed to
Ögödäi, which means “ascending upwards.”1
He was known for his intelligence, compe-
tence, knowledge of tactics and strategy, gravi-
ty and self-possession, courage, and justice, al-
though he was also pleasure-loving and a
drinker, for which Genghis Khan sometimes
took him to task and gave him advice. 
After Genghis Khan had tested his sons and
discovered for what each of them was suited,
he had some hesitation over the throne and of-
fice of qa’an. Sometimes he thought of Ögödäi
Qa’an, and other times he considered his
youngest son, Tolui Khan. Although the Mon-
gol custom had always been, from ancient
times on, for the father’s yurt, home, and tent
to be taken over by the youngest son, he said,
“The throne and rule are difficult jobs. Let
Ögödäi take them, and let Tolui rule the choic-
est part of the yurt, home, ﬂocks, treasures, and
armies I have built up.” Every time he held
council with his sons in this regard, since they
saw that this was their father’s view, they con-
curred and supported him. [619]
In the end, when he was stricken with an ill-
ness in Tangqut territory, as has been said, he
went off in private and made Ögödäi his heir,
settling the throne and office of qa’an on him.
He also assigned each son a separate path, say-
1A folk etymology. See Doerfer, TMEN 1:167–69 §49
and text p. 300, note 5 above. In Chinese dynastic lists
he is given retrospectively the title 太宗Tai Zong, the
Chinese title for the first successor to the founder of a
dynasty. 

ing, “Let anyone who is desirous of hunting
join Jochi.1 Let any who desire to know cus-
toms and wisdom well go to Chaghatai. Let all
who are inclined to manliness and generosity
and desire good things and possessions join
Ögödäi. Let all who are desirous of courage
and renown, the fray of battle, territorial ex-
pansion, and world rule serve Tolui.” He also
assigned to his sons commanders and troops,
and, as was said in his history, to each of them
he appointed a separate portion of the empire.
[620]
His wives and concubines.
Ögödäi Qa’an had many wives and sixty
concubines. Those of his wives who were of
importance and well known are the following
four: 
(1) The first wife was Boraqchin of the ___
clan, the daughter of ___. She was the greatest
of all.
(2) The second wife was Törägänä of the
Uhat Märkit.2 In some versions it is related that
she had been the wife of Dayir Usun, the chief
of the Märkit, and when her husband was
killed she was brought in as booty and taken
by Ögödäi. Prior to that, Dayir Usun had given
his daughter Qulan Khatun to Genghis Khan.
Another version is that she was of that nation
but not the wife of Dayir Usun. It is related

that when they seized the brothers Qudu,

but Chaghatai did not approve of this. Ögödäi,
however, went haughtily and took Törägänä
Khatun by force. Genghis Khan approved and
gave the other two ladies to others. This lady
did not possess great beauty, but she was total-
ly domineering by nature. As will be related in
the story of Güyük Khan, she ruled for a long
time, but because she paid no attention to
Genghis Khan’s will [621] and did not heed the
advice of her aqa-ini, she created strife among
the aqa-ini and family of Genghis Khan. This
will be related in the history of Güyük Khan.
(3) The third was Mögä Khatun, daughter of
Jinanch of the Bäkrin tribe.
(4) The fourth was Jajin. [622]
Ögödäi Qa’an’s sons.
Ögödäi Qa’an had seven sons. The mother of
the five elder sons was Törägänä Khatun. The
other two were each by a different concubine.
The names of the seven sons and their off-
spring, insofar as has been ascertained, are as
follows. 
The first son, Güyük.3
His yurt was in the land of the Qobaq4 in the
places called Bari Mingraq, Imil, and Yursa’ur.
Although Ögödäi Qa’an’s designated heir was

The third son, Köchü.
This son turned out to be extremely intelli-

had it in mind to make him his heir, but Köchü

(1) Shirämün, whose mother was Qataqash

(2) Boladchi, born of ___ of the ___ tribe; he

(3) Sösä, whose mother was ___ of the ___

When Köchü died, Möngkä Qa’an brought

the friendship he had had with Shirämün’s fa-

successor, but in the end Shirämün plotted

this crime. When Möngkä Qa’an sent his
brother Qubilai Qa’an to Cathay, Qubilai re-
quested Shirämün from his brother and took
him along on account of their friendship. [625]

The fifth son, Qashi.
Since Genghis Khan had just conquered the

of

he

in

from

overindulgence in wine. Since he died during

called Tangqut.
He had a son named Qaidu, born of Sanga
Khatun of the Bäkrin tribe.3 He lived to be ex-
tremely old and was alive until the year 705
[A.D.1305]. 
Qaidu was raised in Genghis Khan’s camp,
and after Ögödäi Qa’an he served in Möngkä
Qa’an’s retinue. After him, he was with Ariq
Bökä, conspiring and making efforts to elevate
him to the khanate. When Ariq Bökä went be-
fore Qubilai Qa’an and submitted to him,
Qaidu was wary of Qubilai Qa’an because it
was the law that no creature should change the
Qa’an’s command or decree, and any who did
would be branded as criminals. He had trans-
gressed the law and rebelled, and from that
time until the present, on account of his re-
bellion, many Mongols and Tajiks [626] have
been annihilated, and ﬂourishing land has been
devastated. 
At first Qaidu did not have many troops or
followers since when Ögödäi Qa’an’s offspring
plotted against Möngkä Qa’an, their troops
were taken away and dispersed (except Kötän’s
sons). Qaidu, however, was extremely intelli-
gent and competent as well as crafty, and he
accomplished everything through deceit and
trickery. He strategically gathered two or three
thousand soldiers from all nooks and crannies.
Then, when Qubilai Qa’an was far away in
Cathay for the conquest of Machin, he re-
belled. When he and his family were sum-
moned for quriltais, the first, second, and third
years they made excuses and did not go. Little
by little he assembled troops from all direc-
tions and, cultivating a friendship with Jochi’s

In the year 701 [1301–2],3 Qaidu and Baraq’s

Sarban crossed the Oxus with a troop and is
in the vicinity of Badakhshan and the Panj Ab,1
attacking Khurasan at every opportunity. The
Padishah of Islam’s troops have repeatedly de-
feated him. In the autumn of 702 [1302] Prince
Kharbanda led a troop to Sarakhs, where he
heard that Sarban’s troops were in the vicinity
of Maruchaq. He attacked them, killing many
and pillaging. It had been Sarban’s intention to
go to Khurasan that winter with a large force.
With him were Görgüz’s son Qutlugh Buqa’s
son Uighurtai and Nawroz’s brother Oyiratai,
[629] and they encouraged him to wreak hav-
oc, and with that desire they went to the Tus
vicinity.
Prince
Kharbanda
retreated
from
Sarakhs along the Bavard road, where he as-
sembled the army at Elji’idäi’s Spring and then
attacked them without warning in the Tus area.
When ranks were arrayed, they pulled back at
nightfall. During the night they ﬂed, with
troops in pursuit as far as Ribat-i-Sangbast.
They wanted to stand in battle, but they
couldn’t and had to ﬂee in rout. The snow and
cold got to them, and many men and animals

The

Qaidu
had
a
daughter
named
Qutulun
Chaghan. He loved her the most of all his chil-

with her. Several times when Qaidu’s emis-

This is the fourth year Qaidu has fought
Kammala [630] in a place called Täkälkü, a
hill near the Chapqa River.2 First they did bat-

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

tle in Qoba Taq, and then they made a ren-
dezvous to do battle at Mount Qaraltu. Buqu
Masar [?] arrived on the third of the month, the
middle month of autumn, and the qa’an’s
troops reached Qaidu on the second. Dua was
straggling behind. They did battle with Qaidu,
and suddenly Qaidu was wounded and with-
drew with his troops. He died a month later at
