his ordu ten days after that.
He was between fifty and sixty years old.
They say he had in his beard only nine scat-
tered hairs, which were turning white. He was
of an average height and stood straight. He did
not drink wine or kumiss and did not eat salt.
may eliminate the threat of Temür Qa’an’s army.’ Dua
Khan used various pretexts not to send Qaidu Khan any
assistance, and Qaidu perforce was obliged to move
slowly toward Qaraqorum with his few troops to meet
Temür Qa’an’s hundred battalions. Although Qaidu’s
army was less than a hundredth the size of Temür
Qa’an’s, he was intent upon battle and fought ceaseless-
ly for three days and nights. On the fourth night, since
he was wounded and almost captured, he ordered all his
warriors to light fires in several places. When Temür
Qa’an’s men saw the ﬂames of so many fires, they
thought that assistance had reached Qaidu from some
source. That very night Qaidu’s men decamped and
withdrew, but the Cathaian commanders, imagining that
Qaidu was trying to trick them into drawing closer, fell
into the trap and did not pursue him. At the same time,
Dua Khan and the warriors of Chaghatai Khan’s nation
joined Qaidu, and the two princes, after making plans,
banded together and headed for Temür Qa’an’s army.
The two sides clashed on the banks of the Irtysh, and
both sides fought so valiantly that the bloodshed was in-
credible. Dua was twice wounded in the leg, and several
of his kinsmen were felled. In the end Qaidu was victori-
ous. The Cathaians, routed, set fire to the meadows be-
hind them so that no one could pursue them. After this
victory Qaidu Khan fell ill with dyspepsia, and some of
the ignorant Cathaians who called themselves physicians
gave him twenty-five pills, and the illness turned into
dysentery. Qaidu Khan died in the month of Rajab in the
year 702 [February 1303].”
His offspring and that of some of the princes
who died with him dwell at a very high moun-
tain called Sinqorliq, in an area between the Ili
and Chu Rivers where there are many villages,
the two largest of which are Tarsakent and
Qarnaliq. From there to Samarkand is a two-
week journey. Qaidu’s daughter Qutulun lives
there. Her husband, Aitqun, is a lively, tall,
good-looking man. She chose him herself for
her husband, and by him she has had two sons.
She dwells there contentedly and tends the
qoruq of her father. 
Qaidu had another daughter, younger than
the former, named Qutuchin Chagha. She was
married to Tübsin son of Tarai Gürägän of the
Olqunu’ut. (Tarai Gürägän was married to the
daughter of Hülägü’s brother Süb[üg]ädäi, who
was born of a concubine.) This Tübsin loved a
maid and planned to run away with her to the
Qa’an’s court, but he divulged his secret to an
equery who informed on him. [631] Qaidu had
him killed for this. 
He had other daughters.
After Qaidu died, since Qutulun Chaghan
was desirous of leading the military and run-
ning affairs, she wanted her brother Orus to
take her father’s place. Dua and Chapar yelled
at her, saying, “You should mind your scissors
and needles. What have you to do with king-
ship and chieftainship?” She was insulted and
avoided them, inclining instead to Orus, stir-
ring up sedition and strife.
This has been a summary mention down to
the present of one of Ögödäi Qa’an’s grand-
sons, Qaidu by name, who has in recent years
taken hold of some of Ögödäi Qa’an’s ulus by
force and invasion. Now let us continue with
the branch of the Qa’an’s sons, God willing. 
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
305

The sixth son, Qada’an Oghul.
His mother was a concubine named Ärgänä,1
and he was brought up in Chaghatai’s ordu.
During Ariq Bökä’s rebellion he was in Qubilai
Qa’an’s retinue, and the second time the Qa’an
sent troops to fight Ariq Bökä, he made him
the leader of the army, and he killed Ariq
Bökä’s general Alamdar. After that he re-
mained in Qubilai Qa’an’s retinue as before.
He had seven sons as follows:2
(1) Dorji, and he had two sons, Sösä and
Asugiba.3
(2) Qipchaq, the one who was with Qaidu
and made peace between him and Baraq. He
was sent to Iran to help Baraq, but he turned
back in anger as a ruse. He has a son named
Quril.
(3) Qada’an Öbük. He had two sons, Lahauri
and Mubarakshah. [632]
(4) Yäbä, who was also in Qaidu’s retinue.
He had two sons, Örüg Temür and Esän Temür.
(5) Yisa’ur, whose sons are unknown.
(6) Qurumshi,4 whose sons are not known.
(7) Ajiqi, who had a son named Örüg Temür.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Part Two of the history of Ögödäi Qa’an. The history of his reign, a picture of his throne,
wives, princes, and amirs at his enthronement, and the battles he fought and victories he
attained.
His early reign, and a depiction of his
enthronement.
When, in the Year of the Pig corresponding
to 624 [1227], Genghis Khan died—as all peo-
ple must—having reached the Tangqut frontier
on his way to Nankiyas territory, his coffin was
taken to Kerulen, his home yurt, and there
mourning was observed. The princes and amirs
held council together concerning the kingship
and then went to their own places of residence.
For nearly two years the throne remained un-
occupied. Then they thought that if anything
happened and there was no leader or ruler, or-
derly kingship might suffer. It behooved them
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
307

therefore to make haste to install someone as
qa’an. On this sensitive mission they sent
emissaries to each other and made preparations
for a quriltai. When the severity of winter had
been broken and the beginnings of spring were
apparent, [635] all the princes and amirs came
from all directions to the ancient yurt and great
ordu. From the Qipchaq Steppe came Jochi’s
sons Orda, Batu, Shiban, Tangqut, Bärkä,
Bärkächär, and Toqa Temür; from Qayaligh
came Chaghatai Khan with all his sons and
grandsons; from the Imil and Qobaq1 came
Ögödäi Qa’an with his sons and family; and
from the east came their uncles Otchigin [and]
Belgütäi
Noyan
and
their
cousins,
and
Qachi’un’s son Elji’idäi Noyan. From all direc-
tions came commanders and dignitaries of the
army, and they all gathered at Kerulen. Tolui
Khan, who was called Yäkä Noyan and Ulugh
Noyan and was the lord of his father’s hearth
and home yurt, was there too.
Those assembled spent three days and nights
in revelry and enjoyment, and after that they
discussed kingship and the kingdom until, in
accordance with Genghis Khan’s will, they set-
tled the office of qa’an on Ögödäi.
“In accordance with Genghis Khan’s will, we
must install you as emperor with God’s help,”
the sons and princes said first to Ögödäi, “so
that refractory leaders may gird their loins in
service, and so that all, far and near, Turk and
Tajik, may be obedient to your command.”
“Although such was Genghis Khan’s de-
cree,” replied Ögödäi, “I have elder brothers
and uncles. My younger brother Tolui Khan in
particular is more worthy than I to undertake
this job, for it is the Mongolian custom for the
younger son to take his father’s place in the
home and run the paternal yurt. Ulugh Noyan
is the youngest son of the great ordu, and he
1Readingـــــﻗ
ﻮ5ق(Qobaq, the modern Kobuk) for JTK’s
ﻗﻮ5ن and JTAZ’s ﻗﻮ^ق.
was in attendance upon our father at all times,
day and night. He has seen, heard, and learned
the yosun (custom) and yasa (ordinance). How
can I be enthroned as qa’an when he is here?”
Of
one
accord
the
princes
said,
[636]
“Among all his sons and brothers, Genghis
Khan entrusted this great labor to you and gave
you the power to bind and loosen. How can we
change his decree?”
After much insistence, Ögödäi Qa’an real-
ized that he must carry out his father’s order
and his uncles’ and brothers’ wish, so he con-
sented. All removed their hats, put their belts
over their shoulders, and, in Hükär Yil, the
Year of the Ox corresponding to 626 [1229],
Chaghatai took his right arm, Tolui Khan took
his left arm, and Otchigin took his belt, and to-
gether they sat him on the emperor’s throne,
while all those present, one by one, both inside
and outside of the court tent, bent their knees
as they congratulated him on his accession and
named him qa’an.
The Qa’an then ordered the possessions and
treasures brought forth, and he commanded
that
those
innumerable
things
be
divided
among his relatives and the tribes and clans.
When the banquet and bestowal ceremonies
were over, he ordered, in accordance with their
ancient law and custom, that food be given for
three days for the repose of Genghis Khan’s
soul, and forty beautiful girls from the families
of the commanders who were in attendance
were chosen and dispatched to his soul, clad in
costly raiments and bedecked with gems and
jewels, with select horses.
Now that the story of the Qa’an’s enthrone-
ment is over, let us begin with his history in the
same fashion as we wrote for Genghis Khan,
i.e. after the completion of every several years,
we will give the history of the rulers of sur-
rounding and neighboring kingdoms and of
those of his lineage who ruled autonomously
308
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

over various areas. Then we will return to his
history. And so on, until his story is completed.
[637] \
The history of Ögödäi Qa’an from the
beginning of Hükär Yil, the Year of the Ox
that began in Rabi‘ I 626 [January 1229],
the year of his accession, until Morin Yil, the
Year of the Horse that began in Jumada I
631 [February 1234], a period of six years.
During this period, after consolidating the
kingdom and army, he mounted a campaign to
subdue Cathay and the territories that had not
yet been taken. Having annihilated the Altan
Khan, he returned victorious to his capital.
The Qa’an begins to give orders, and he
issues ordinances and orders administrative
affairs.
When the Qa’an was established on the
throne of empire, the first ordinance he issued
was as follows. “All commands previously
given by Genghis Khan should be kept in ef-
fect and immune to any change or alteration.
Any crime or offense committed by anyone up
to the day of our accession is herewith par-
doned by us, but henceforth, if anyone dares
undertake an act not in conformity with old or
new ordinances, he will suffer chastisement
and retribution in keeping with the offense.”
[638]
Before the Qa’an was enthroned, actually
during the very year Genghis Khan died, the
princes and amirs who had remained in
Genghis Khan’s camp had held council and
sent Genghis Khan’s nephew Elji’idäi Noyan
and the Qa’an’s son Güyük Khan to the fron-
tier of ___1 territory in order for them to take
it. They had pillaged and conquered that terri-
1In JTAZ this name is given asﺎن ـ ـﻧﻘﻮـﻗ(Qunqan?); a vari-
ant in JTAZ’s MS H hasﺎن ـ ـﯾﻘﻮر ـﻗ(Quriqan?). In JTK&Bl and
JTRM it isﺎن ــﺗﻘﻮر ـﻗ. It may refer to the Quriqat mentioned on
text p. 43.
tory and left a Tangqut officer named Bahadur
there with a troop as a tamma (garrison) to
guard the area. Everyone had something to say
about this action, but when the Qa’an acceded
to the throne he silenced all those who were
speaking against the action with the ordinance
mentioned above. Then he assigned troops to
all the frontiers of the empire to guard and
maintain the borders.
In the direction of Iran strife and sedition
were still rife. Sultan Jalaluddin was still vying
for supremacy, so [the Qa’an] dispatched
Chormaqan Noyan and a group of officers with
thirty thousand horsemen to deal with him. He
sent Köktäi and Sübädäi Bahadur with an
equal number of soldiers in the direction of the
Qipchaq Steppe, Saqsin, and Bulghar. To
Cathay, Tibet, Korea, Jürcha, and those areas
he sent a group of great generals ahead while
he and his younger brother[’s son] Möngkä
Qa’an set out behind them for the parts of
Cathay that had not yet submitted and in which
the emperor of Cathay still held sway
The Qa’an and his brother Tolui Khan move
toward Cathay and conquer what is still in
rebellion.
In Bars Yil, the Year of the Leopard that be-
gan in Rabi‘ I 627 [January 1230], [639] the
Qa’an and his brother Ulugh Noyan set out for
Cathay, for during Genghis Khan’s reign, as
has been explained, the Altan Khan, the emper-
or of Cathay whose name was Sä’üsä,2 aban-
doned the city of Zhongdu (Peking), one of his
capitals, along with many of its dependencies,
and went to Nanjing and that area, where many
troops gathered around him.
Until that time Sä’üsä was still acting as em-
peror, and the Qa’an wanted not only to drive
him from the territories that Genghis Khan and
2Sä’üsä, the nickname Ögödäi gave the Chinese em-
peror. See note at text p. 544.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
309

his army had taken and which were under
Mongol control but also to conquer the entirety
of that realm. To this end he took with himself
Tolui Khan and Kölgän and some of his other
nephews and sons and a huge army, dispatch-
ing Tolui Khan with twenty thousand soldiers
to Tibet, while he himself went to the right into
the Cathaian territory the inhabitants of which
are called hula’an tägäläns, i.e. people who
wear red jackets. Since the Qa’an’s road was
long, Tolui Khan made excursions along his
way, and by the next year, which was the Year
of the Rabbit corresponding to 628 [1231],
there were no provisions or supplies left and
the soldiers had grown extremely lean and
hungry. Things got so bad that they were
forced to eat human ﬂesh, any- and everything
animal, and dry grass. They went onto moun-
tains and plains in hunting circles until they
came to the first city, the name of which was
Khojanfu Balghasun,1 on the banks of the Yel-
low River. They laid siege, and after forty days
the inhabitants sought amnesty and turned over
the city. Nearly ten thousand soldiers got away
in boats, but their women and children were
taken captive, and the area was laid waste be-
fore they proceeded. [640]
Tolui Khan reaches a place called Tungqan
Qahalqa, where the Altan Khan’s troops
had constructed a chapar, and that place,
which is like a pass, is taken.
As Tolui Khan approached Tungqan Qa-
halqa,2 he thought that since the place was a
difficult rocky stretch lying between mountains
and with an unassailable pass, the foe would
certainly have taken it, intending to defend it
1Khojanfu Balghasun is Hezhongfu (河中府), Marco
Polo’s “Cacionfu” and the modern Puchow in Shansi.
2This Tungqan is the Tunggon of the Secret History
§251, the Chinese Tongguan (湩關, the modern Tong-
guan in Shaanxi).
and keep him from passing. And so it was.
When he arrived he saw that a hundred thou-
sand of the Altan Khan’s soldiers under the
command of Qoda Sangum,3 Qobägädür,4 and
several others had constructed a chapar (barri-
cade) on the plain and at the foot of the moun-
tain and were standing there, troops arrayed,
ready for battle and overconfident of their own
superior strength relative to the Mongols’ small
number. When Tolui Khan saw how many they
were, he summoned Shigi Qutuqu Noyan in
private and took counsel with him.
“Since the foe has taken up and fortified such
a position and is standing battle-ready,” he
said, “it is difficult to do battle with them. The
best thing would be for you to take some three
hundred horsemen and make a sortie near them
to see whether or not they will leave their posi-
tions.” As ordered, Qutuqu Noyan sallied forth,
but the enemy absolutely would not budge
from his position lest the chapar be spoiled
and their order lost. Overconfident in their own
vast numbers relative to the few Mongols, they
looked upon the Mongols with contempt and
made great boasts, saying, “Let us encircle
these Mongols and their ruler and seize them,
and then we will do thus and so to their
women.” So saying, they said such vile things
and made such hideous wishes that God disap-
proved of their pride and overbearing confi-
dence and overturned them in the end. [641]
When they paid no attention to Qutuqu Noy-
an’s sally and refused to give up their position,
Tolui Khan said, “As long as they do not move
from their position it is impossible to do battle
with them. If I pull back, our ranks will be bro-
ken, and they will grow even bolder. It would
be best for us to head for the areas held by
3Qoda Sangum is the Wanyen Heda, the duke of
Ruiguo, of the Qinzheng lu.
4Qobägüdür, the Höbegedür of the Secret History
§251.
310
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

their emperor. If possible, we will join Ögödäi
Qa’an and the great army.” He then assigned as
scout with a thousand cavalrymen Toqolqu
Chärbi, the younger brother of Borghochin
Noyan of the Arulat clan, to take up the rear
while the main body set out to the right. When
the Cathaian army saw that the Mongols had
turned away from battle and were headed in
another direction, they called out, saying, “We
are standing here. Come on, let’s do battle.”
The Mongols paid no attention and kept go-
ing. There was nothing the Cathaians could do
but move out, abandoning their position, and
go in pursuit. For three days the Mongol army
proceeded with the Cathaians on their heels,
and the Mongols went in fear and trepidation
because the Cathaians were so numerous.
Then, without warning, the Cathaians struck
Toqolqu Chärbi, who was leading the rear
guard. Ahead was a canal and mud. Forty
Mongols were thrown into the mud and killed.
Toqolqu Chärbi joined his troop and sent a re-
port.
Tolui
Khan
ordered
them
to
work
jadamishi. (Jadamishi is a tactic as follows.
There are several stones of various types that
have the property, when they are taken out and
washed in water, of producing immediately—
even in the heart of summer—wind, cold,
snow, rain, and hail.) Among them was a man
from the Qanqli tribe who knew well how to
work the stones. As ordered, he began to cast
the spell, and the soldiers all put on their rain
gear. [642] For three days and nights they did
not get off their horses, and the Mongols made
it to villages in the midst of Cathaian territory
from which the villagers had ﬂed, abandoning
their animals. There they took shelter while the
Qanqli worked the jada stones in such a way
that the rain came behind the Mongols. On the
last day it turned to snow and hail, and to it
was added a chill wind. The Cathaians were
dumbfounded by a cold in summer more se-
vere than anything they had ever experienced
in winter.
Tolui Khan ordered each unit of ten thousand
to go to a different village and take their horses
inside and keep them covered, for it was so
cold that it was impossible for the Cathaians to
camp in the open with such snow and hail. For
three days it was absolutely impossible to
move. On the fourth day it was still snowing.
When Tolui Khan saw that his troops were
rested and well fed, and that they and their ani-
mals were unharmed by the cold, while the
Cathaians were so cold they were standing
head to tail like a ﬂock of sheep, their clothing
light and their weapons frozen, he ordered the
kettle drums sounded. All his soldiers donned
their felt cloaks and mounted. “It is time for
battle,” he said, “time for a good name. One
must be manly.” Like lions pouncing on a herd
of antelope, the Mongols attacked the Catha-
ians and killed most of them, although some
escaped into the mountains, where they per-
ished. Both of the generals mentioned above
got away with five thousand men by throwing
themselves into the river, from which few
emerged alive. For the derisive boasts they had
made and the heinous thoughts they had
voiced, some Cathaian captives were sodom-
ized. [643]
With such a victory in hand, Tolui Khan sent
messengers to bear the good news to the Qa’an
as he set out in triumph. The Qara Mörän (Yel-
low River), which comes from the mountains
of Kashmir and Tibet and provides a border be-
tween Cathay and Nankiyas, cannot be crossed
at any time, but it was necessary for him to
cross, so he sent Chaghan Buqa of the Uru’ut
clan to look for a way across. As it happened,
there had been massive ﬂooding that year, and
a great deal of rock and gravel had been
washed down, collecting at various places
along the river and causing it to overﬂow onto
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
311

the plains in branches a league in width and
breadth.
Chaghan Buqa located the qa’an. When Tolui
Khan had become separated, the qa’an had
heard that the enemy had overcome Tolui, who
was far away from the main contingent of the
army, and this caused the qa’an much concern.
When he received the news of Tolui’s victory
and safety, he rejoiced. Since such an unex-
pected great victory had been achieved, he sta-
tioned Toqolqu Chärbi and some other com-
manders there with a troop to deal once and for
all with the Altan Khan and conquer all Catha-
ian territory. They returned successful under
good auspices, and Tolui requested permission
to go forward, but he died unexpectedly along
the way.
It is reported that the qa’an had fallen ill sev-
eral days prior to that and was at death’s door.
Tolui Khan went to his sick bed, where the
shamans, as was their custom, were reciting in-
cantations and washing his sores with water
from a wooden bowl. Out of the great love he
had for his brother Tolui took the bowl and
said in supplication, [644] “O eternal God, you
know that if there is sin, I have sinned more,
for I have deprived so many people of life and
taken their women and children captive and
caused them to weep. If you are taking the
Qa’an away on account of beauty and skill, I
am better looking and more skilled. Leave him
and take me instead.” Having said this in sup-
plication, he drank the water with which they
had been washing his sores. Ögödäi Qa’an re-
gained his health, and Tolui requested permis-
sion to depart. Several days later he fell ill and
passed away. The story is well known. Tolui
Khan’s wife Sorqaghtani Beki used to say,
“The person who was my beloved and my dar-
ling sacrificed himself for Ögödäi Qa’an.”
The Qa’an summered in Cathay in Altankada
and then, decamping, he returned victorious
and triumphant to his capital in [Moghai Yil,
the Year of the Serpent]. [645]
Doqolqu Chärbi does battle with the
Cathaian forces and is defeated; the Qa’an
sends reinforcements; the Nankiyas come to
his assistance, and he annihilates the Altan
Khan and achieves total victory over
Cathay.
After a time the Cathaian forces gathered and
did battle with Doqolqu Chärbi. He was defeat-
ed and, pulling far back in rout, he sent a mes-
sage to the qa’an asking for assistance. The
qa’an said, “From the time of Genghis Khan
on, battle has been done so many times with
the armies of Cathay, and we have continually
defeated them and taken most of their territory.
Now that they have struck our troops, it is a
sign of their impending doom, like a lamp that
ﬂickers and burns brightest just before going
out.” He ordered auxiliary troops sent to Do-
qolqu Chärbi.
Since there was an ancient enmity between
the rulers of Machin (which the Mongols call
Nankiyas) and the rulers of Cathay, who were
of the Jürchid race, the Qa’an ordered the
Nankiyas also to go to assist from one direc-
tion while the Mongols went from the other in
order to lay siege together to the city of Nan-
ching. As commanded, they took a large army
to Nan-ching, the perimeter of which is said to
be forty leagues. It had three rampart walls,
and two sides were on the Yellow River. [646]
The Mongols and Nankiyas together laid siege,
many catapults and ladders were placed against
the walls, and miners got busy boring into the
foundations of the ramparts. 
It was abundantly clear to the commanders of
Cathay that the city would be taken, and they
fretted, saying, “Our ruler is weak of heart. If
we tell him the truth, he will die of fright, and
we will be totally undone. It is best to keep it
secret.”
312
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

As usual, the ruler and his wives and concu-
bines besported themselves in his palaces and
pleasure pavilions. When the wives and concu-
bines realized that the city was going to be tak-
en, they began to weep. The Altan Khan asked
the reason, and he was told of the state of the
city. Refusing to believe it, he went out onto a
rampart wall and saw for himself. Convinced,
he thought of ﬂight. Getting into a boat with
his wives, he departed the city via a large irri-
gation canal diverted from the Yellow River
and went to another province.
When the Mongols and Nankiyas discovered
this, they sent soldiers out after him, and they
besieged the other city, from which he also es-
caped by boat and gone to yet another. Similar-
ly they pursued him and laid siege. Since his
route of escape was far and blocked, the Mon-
gols and Nankiyas hurled fire into the city. The
Altan Khan realized that they would take it, so
he said to his generals and wives, “After such a
long time of honorable rule, I don’t want to fall
captive to the Mongols and die with a bad
name.” He dressed one of his quiver bearers in
his clothes, sat him on the throne, went out,
and hanged himself. He was buried.
In some accounts it is stated that he put on a
patched cloak in the guise of a wandering
dervish and disappeared, and in the history of
Cathay it is said that when fire was pitched
into the city [647] he was burned up, but nei-
ther of these is correct, for it has been ascer-
tained that he hanged himself and died.
Two days later the Mongols took the city and
killed the one who had been seated in the Altan
Khan’s place. The Nankiyas troops entered the
city, and when the Mongols learned that the
one they had killed was not the Altan Khan,
they demanded him. First it was reported that
he had been burned, but the Mongols did not
believe it and demanded his head. When the
Nankiyas troops realized what had happened,
although they were enemies of the Altan Khan,
they joined in preventing his body from being
exhumed and his head turned over, and togeth-
er with the Cathaians they offered the excuse
that he had been burned. The Mongols de-
manded his head as proof, but the Cathaians
figured that if they gave them a different head,
the Mongols would never know the difference.
In the end they gave them a man’s arm. The
Mongols were angry at the Nankiyas over this
affair, but they did not want to quarrel with
them at that juncture.
In short, Toqolqu Chärbi and the army con-
quered the entirety of the realm of Cathay in
the manner described. This victory occurred in
Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that began in
Jumada I 631 [February 1234]. Also during
that same year he took innumerable turqaqs
(day guards) and gäzigtäns (bodyguards) out of
Solanggha (Korea) and sent them to the Qa’an
with Ong Su[n] at their head.1
Now that a detailed six-year history of the
Qa’an has been written from the beginning of
Hükär Yil, the Year of the Buffalo that began in
Rabi‘ I 626 [January 1229], through the end of
Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that began in
Jumada I 631 [February 1234], [648] we will
begin a summary history of the khaqans,
caliphs, maliks, sultans, and atabegs of king-
doms east and west, and of those who gov-
erned autonomously in some territories on be-
half of the Qa’an. Afterwards we shall return to
the history of the Qa’an, God willing. [649]

&c., and amirs who governed some

Shouxu.1 This Shouxu was the last of the em-

History
of
the

during this period.
History of the caliphs.
The caliph of the House of Abbas in power in
Baghdad was al-Nasir-li-dini’llah. He died at
the beginning of 627 [began November 20,
1229] and was succeeded by his son, Zahir. He
died in 628, and al-Mustansir-bi’llah was
raised to the caliphate.
History of the sultans.
Sultan Jalaluddin was in power in Persia and
Azerbaijan. At the beginning of 625 [1227] he
withdrew from Isfahan and went to Tabriz,
whence he set out for Georgia. Afraid that he
would take over by force, the sultan of Anato-
1Shouxu (守緒) = Ai Zong (哀宗) of the Jin, ruled
1224–34. See note to text p. 544 above.
2Li Zong (理宗) of the Southern Song, ruled 1224–64.
lia and the maliks of Syria, Armenia, and that
area all rose up to repel him. They all gathered
in one place with their Georgian, Armenian,
Alan, Sarir, Lagzi, Qipchaq, Svan, Abkhaz,
and Chanet soldiers. Distressed by the multi-
tude of the foe’s horsemen, the sultan camped
near them in Mindor and took counsel with
Yulduzchi the vizier and the grandees of the
realm.
“It would be best,” said Yulduzchi, “since the
number of our men is not a hundredth of theirs,
for us to pass through Mindor and deprive
them of water and firewood [651] until they
are weakened by hunger and thirst and their
horses are lean. Then we can enter the battle-
field with good tactics.”
The sultan was infuriated by this and threw
an ink pot at the vizier’s head, saying, “They
are a ﬂock of sheep. Does a lion complain that
there are too many sheep in a ﬂock?” For his
insidious suggestion Yulduzchi was fined over
fifty thousand dinars. “No matter how difficult
it may be,” said the sultan, “we must fight
trusting in God.” 
The next day they arrayed their ranks. In the
midst of his soldiers, the sultan looked to the
enemy hosts like a mountain amidst a plain. In
order to study them the sultan went up on a hill
and saw Qipchaq banners with twenty thou-
sand men. He sent Qoshqar with a loaf of
bread and a bit of salt to remind the Qipchaqs
of the past debts they owed him. The Qipchaqs
immediately turned their reins and retired to a
corner of the field. 
Then the Georgian soldiers came forward. To
them he sent a message, saying, “You arrived
today. You must be tired. For the present let the
warriors of both side skirmish, and we will
watch from the sidelines.” The Georgians were
pleased, and that day both sides parried and
feigned until evening. Finally one of the gal-
314
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

lant aznavurs1 [knights] came forward, and the
sultan
Charged forth from the army like a lion and
came valiantly before Hujir.
With a throng of onlookers on all sides, the
sultan, galloping,
Threw at his belt a lance that broke open his
caftan and breastplate.
The Georgian had three sons, each of whom
came forward on foot, one after the other. The
sultan annihilated each of them with a single
charge. Another aznavur, exceedingly terrify-
ing in form, [652] charged into the arena, and
since the sultan’s horse was exhausted, the az-
navur almost overcame him, but in an instant
the sultan leapt down from his horse and un-
saddled him with a blow from his lance that
killed him. Seeing the sultan like this, the sol-
diers attacked and put the entire foe to ﬂight.
The sultan came to Akhlat. The inhabitants
closed the gates and refused to listen to reason.
The sultan kept the town under siege for two
months, by which time the inhabitants were
nearly dead from hunger. The sultan ordered a
massive attack from all sides, and entry into
the city was gained. The sultan took up lodg-
ings in Malik Ashraf’s palace, and Ashraf’s
brother Mujiruddin and his slave Izzuddin Ay-
bak withdrew into the citadel without provi-
sions. Mujiruddin came out first, and the sultan
received him with all honor. Then Aybak also
came out, and the sultan’s treasury was filled
again with Malik Ashraf’s possessions. Be-
cause he had vanquished the Georgians and
taken Akhlat, his fame and renown spread
abroad, and the kings of Egypt and Syria fol-
lowed the caliph of Baghdad in sending emis-
saries with gifts and presents to his court. Once
again his prospects were on the rise.
1Aznavur (ազնաւուր) appears to be of Armenian origin,
but it is used only of Georgians.
From there he went to Khartbirt, where he
fell ill. While he was in that state, the sultan of
Erzurum was showered with all sorts of favors
because he had assisted the sultan’s soldiers
with provisions and fodder during the siege of
Akhlat. “Ala’uddin of Anatolia has made peace
again with the kings of Aleppo and Damas-
cus,” he said, “and they are going to attack the
sultan in unison. They are busy gathering sol-
diers, and they constantly threaten me, telling
me that if I hadn’t assisted the sultan at the
gates of Akhlat with provisions, he wouldn’t
have been able to remain there.” As soon as the
sultan heard this, he mounted, his illness
notwithstanding. When he reached the plains
of Mush, he came across six thousand men
who were going to help the allies, and he
wiped them out in one fell swoop. [653] Sever-
al days later the armies were near each other,
and the sultan of Anatolia, Malik Ashraf, and
the other rulers joined forces. With implements
and provisions beyond reckoning, they drew
up their ranks on top of a hill with the naphtha-
throwers and crossbowmen standing in front
with ox-hide shields, and the cavalry and in-
fantry behind. 
When it was time for battle, the sultan want-
ed to get out of his litter and mount a horse, but
he was too ill to hold the reins, and his horse
turned around and went to the rear. His atten-
dants said he should be allowed to rest for a
while, and therefore his personal banner was
carried back. Believing this signaled a retreat,
the left and right wings took ﬂight, while the
foe, thinking the sultan was pulling a ruse to
draw them out onto the plain, sent heralds
through the troops telling them not to budge.
Sultan Ala’uddin of Anatolia was so over-
whelmed by fear that he was unable to control
his mount, and Malik Ashraf had to have hob-
bles placed on his animal’s legs. When the sul-
tan’s soldiers scattered in rout in all directions,
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
315

the sultan was forced to go to Akhlat, where he
summoned those he had stationed to guard the
town, and then departed for Khoy. Malik
Ashraf’s brother Mujiruddin was sent back
with all honors. Taqiuddin was given permis-
sion to depart to intercede on his behalf with
the Caliph al-Mustansir-bi’llah. Husamuddin
Qaymari ﬂed, and his wife, Malik Ashraf’s
daughter, was sent back in purdah with every
show of respect. Izzuddin Aybak was impris-
oned in the Dizmar fortress, and there he died.
While all this was happening, news arrived
that Chormaqan Noyan had crossed the Oxus
with a large force and was headed for the sul-
tan. The sultan assigned the vizier Shamsuddin
Yulduzchi to guard the fortress of Kiran1 [654]
and turned his wife over to him while he him-
self went to Tabriz. Although he was not on
good terms with the caliph or the maliks and
sultans of Anatolia and Syria, he sent a repre-
sentative to each of them to inform them of the
advent of the Mongols. The message was as
follows: “The Tatar are extremely numerous,
more than ever before. The soldiers of this area
are in fear and trembling of them. If you do not
assist me with numbers and matériel, then I,
who am like a bulwark, will leave, and it will
be impossible for you to stand against them,
and the consequences will be upon yourselves,
your children, and all Muslims. Each of you
assist me with a troop and a banner so that
when the news of our unity reaches them, they
will be somewhat discomfited, and our soldiers
will take heart. If you do not take this serious-
ly, then you shall see what you shall see.”
Let each of you think of a way to preserve his
life, and exert your wisdom in this endeavor to
the utmost.
However, the mighty fortune of Genghis Khan
and his offspring cast disunity into their midst,
1The modern Kilan, north of the Araxes.
and the sultan’s hopes were dashed. Without
warning news arrived that the Mongol army
had reached Saraw.2 The sultan set out for
Bishkin.3 One night the roof of the house in
which he was staying caved in. He did not con-
sider this an ill omen but bore it sturdily. The
next day he set out for Mughan. After he had
camped there five days, the Mongol army ap-
proached. The sultan abandoned his para-
phernalia and went into the mountains of Qa-
ban. When the Mongols found the sultan’s
camp empty, they turned their reins and left.
The sultan stayed in Urmia and Ushnuviya
during the winter of 628 [1230–31]. The vizier
Sharafulmulk was falsely accused of having
coveted the sultan’s wife and treasury during
his absence when communications had been
cut. [655] Because of this, when the sultan
reached that area, the vizier was too afraid to
come out of the fortress and asked for a safe-
conduct. At his request the sultan sent Buqu
Khan4 to escort him out. “I raised Yulduzchi
from the depths of abasement to the zenith of
glory,” the sultan said, “and this is how he re-
pays me!” He handed him over to the castellan
and ordered his goods plundered. The vizier
died
in
that
prison. The
sultan
went
to
Diyarbekir.
When the Mongol army came to Chormaqan,
he chastised them, saying, “Why did you turn
back and not pursue the sultan in all earnest-
ness? When a foe like this is weak, how can he
be given a respite?” In pursuit he dispatched
Amir Naimas and a group of amirs with a huge
contingent of soldiers.
2The modern Sarab, between Tabriz and Ardebil.
3The modern Mishkin near Ahar.

The sultan had sent Buqu Khan back as a
yäzäk (forward detachment) to reconnoiter the
Mongols. When he reached Tabriz, he was in-
formed that news had come from Persia saying
that they had dispersed and there was no trace
of them there. Without verifying the report,
Buqu Khan returned and gave the sultan the
news that the Mongols had pulled out. With the
receipt of this good news, the sultan and all his
officers and soldiers rejoiced and celebrated,
spending two or three days indulging in pride-
ful self-congratulations. At midnight the Mon-
gols attacked them, and the sultan was asleep,
drunk as could be. Informed of their arrival,
Orkhan went to the sultan’s bed, but no matter
how much he called to him, he wouldn’t wake
up, so he threw cold water on him until he
came to and saw what was happening. As he
started to ﬂee, he told Orkhan not to move his
standard and to fight long enough to allow him
to get a head start. Orkhan sat patiently for a
moment, and then he too took ﬂight. The Mon-
gols, thinking he was the sultan, lit out after
him, but when they realized their mistake,
[656] they returned and killed everyone they
saw.
The sultan was traveling alone and in all
haste. There is a disagreement over how he
met his end. Some say he was hiding under a
tree in the mountains one night when a band of
Kurds came upon him and slit his belly open in
order to get his horse and clothing. They
donned his garments and weapons and went
into a town, where some of the sultan’s elite,
recognizing the clothing and weapons, seized
the Kurds. When the lord of Amid was ap-
prised of this, he put them to death. The sul-
tan’s body was brought to Amid and buried
there, and a dome was raised over his grave.
Others report that of his own volition he gave
them his weapons and garments and, taking
their rough clothing, set out to wander in the
guise of a Sufi. In either case, his rule came to
an end. [657]
As for Sultan Ghiyasuddin, in 624 [1227],
when the Mongols were being battled at the
gates of Isfahan, he abandoned the right wing
with which his brother had entrusted him and
set out for Khuzistan via Luristan. The Caliph
Nasir sent him a writ of governance, so he
turned back from there. When Sultan Jalalud-
din was with the Armenians and Georgians, he
went to Alamut. Ala’uddin welcomed him with
all honors, and after a time he departed for
Khuzistan again. To announce his state, he sent
an emissary to Baraq Hajib in Kirman, and
once again they made an alliance, and it was
decided that Baraq would come out as far as
the Abarquh desert to meet him. The sultan set
out with his mother for Kirman, and Baraq
went out to the above-mentioned place to greet
him with nearly forty thousand horsemen. 
Baraq was polite as usual for two or three
days, but since the sultan had no more than
five hundred horsemen, Baraq took it into his
head to ask for the sultan’s mother. He came
one day and, sitting down on the same carpet
as the sultan, began to address him as “son”
and assign places of high-ranking dignitaries to
all his amirs. A message was sent offering mar-
riage to the sultan’s mother. Since the sultan
realized that he was in no position to do any-
thing about it, he complied. [658] The sultan’s
mother first objected and refused, but in the
end she gave in and allowed herself to be affi-
anced. After much insistence she took a group
of servants wearing chain mail under their tu-
nics and let the marriage be consummated.
A few days after they reached the city of Gu-
vashir, the seat of Kirman, two of Baraq’s rela-
tives came to the sultan and said, “You
shouldn’t trust Baraq, for he is treacherous and
deceptive. We have found a way. If we get rid
of him, you be sultan and we’ll be your slaves.

It would be best.” The sultan’s pure nature did
not allow him to contemplate breaking an oath,
but since that family’s fortune was on the
wane, one of his relatives secretly carried a re-
port of these words to Baraq, who immediately
had an investigation of his relatives and Ghiya-
suddin carried out. The report was confirmed,
and in the prince’s very presence he ordered
his relatives hacked limb from limb, and the
prince was held in the fortress. After that, he
sent orders for him to be throttled with a bow
string. The prince cried out, “Didn’t we swear
we wouldn’t kill each other? Why is he
breaking his oath for no reason?” When his
mother heard his voice she cried out, but both
were strangled. His soldiers were also all killed
in this manner.
Baraq sent Sultan Ghiyasuddin’s head to the
Qa’an with a message, saying, “You have two
enemies, Jalaluddin and Ghiyasuddin. I am
sending you the head of one of them.” Thus
was the history of the Khwarazmshahs.
In Anatolia was Sultan Ala’uddin, whose his-
tory during this period was included in that of
Jalaluddin.
In Mosul was Sultan Badruddin Lu’lu’. [659]

In Mazanderan was ___.
In Diyarbekir was Malik Muzaffaruddin, the
lord of Arbela and other cities, except for
Mosul and vicinity.
In Syria were the sons of Malik Adil b.
Ayyub, Malik Mu‘azzam and Malik Ashraf.
Something of Malik Ashraf’s history has al-

In Egypt, Malik Kamil b. Malik Adil Sayfud-

In Fars was Atabeg Muzaffaruddin Sa‘d b.
Zangi, who died in the year ___ in Bayza.
Khwaja Ghiyasuddin Yazdi, his vizier and ad-
ministrator, kept his death secret and sent his
ring to the Qal‘a-i-Saped to have Sa‘d’s son
Atabeg Abubakr released from prison and sent
to him. Then, ﬂinging open the door of the
pavilion, he said to the amirs and soldiers,
“The Atabeg commands that his successor be
Abubakr.” The amirs threw their belts over
their necks, and he became atabeg.
In Kirman, Baraq Hajib was supreme. His
history has already been given in the course of
the history of Sultan Ghiyasuddin. [660]
In Seistan was Malik Shamsuddin.
History of the Mongol amirs who were
governors of provinces
In Khurasan, Chin Temür of the Qarakhitai
had been appointed to the governorship of that
land and also of Mazanderan. This came about
as follows. When Khwarazm was conquered,
Jochi Khan stationed him as a shahna in
Khwarazm, and during the Qa’an’s reign, when
Chormaqan was sent to Iran, the Qa’an ordered
the leaders and basqaqs of provinces to go on
campaigns themselves and assist Chormaqan.
Chin Temür set out from Khwarazm as ordered
via Shahristana. From every direction came an
amir on behalf of a prince, and Chormaqan as-
signed an amir on behalf of every prince to
Chin Temür, as follows: on behalf of the Qa’an
was Külbolad, Nosal on behalf of Batu, Qizil
Buqa on behalf of Chaghatai, and Yegä on be-
half of Sorqaghtani Beki and the princes.
Since Chormaqan had neglected to take care
of Khurasan, rebels and riffraff were causing
trouble in the provinces at every instant.
Qaracha and Yaghan Sonqur, two of Sultan
Jalaluddin’s
amirs,
were
making
raids
in
Nishapur and that area, killing the shahnas
Chormaqan had stationed over the provinces
and seizing those who dared speak of submis-
sion to the Mongols. When Chormaqan dis-
patched Külbolad and Chin Temür to deal with
Qaracha in the Nishapur and Tus area, Külbo-
lad returned after defeating Qaracha. When the
318
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

news of trouble in Khurasan had reached the
Qa’an, he had ordered Tayir Bahadur to take a
troop from Badghis to repel Qaracha and ﬂood
their homes and dwellings. He had set out as
ordered, but along the way he heard that
Qaracha had been defeated by Külbolad and
taken refuge in the citadel of Seistan. [661]
Tayir Bahadur laid siege and spent two years
drilling mines until he took it. Then he sent an
emissary from Seistan to Chin Temür, saying,
“The administration of Khurasan has been as-
signed to me. Withdraw your control.”
“The report of rebellion by the people of
Khurasan was false,” replied Chin Temür.
“Why should so much territory and so many
subjects be destroyed on account of Qaracha’s
crime? I am sending an emissary to the Qa’an’s
court to report the situation. I will proceed
however I am ordered.”
Tayir Bahadur pulled out, infuriated. Chor-
maqan also sent an envoy to get Chin Temür
and the amirs to return and to turn over the ad-
ministration of Khurasan and Mazanderan to
Tayir Bahadur. 
Chin Temür now assigned Külbolad, one of
the Qa’an’s elite, and the amirs of Khurasan
and Mazanderan to go to the Qa’an’s court.
Around the same time, Malik Baha’uddin of
Su‘luk came out of his fortress on condition
that he be sent to the Qa’an, and Chin Temür
pulled out of Mazanderan. Most of the wardens
of fortresses in Khurasan surrendered when
they heard about Malik Baha’uddin. When he
came before Chin Temür he was received with
all honor. From Mazanderan, Ispahbad Nus-
ratuddin of Kabudjama was selected, and to-
gether the two of them, escorted by Külbolad,
set out for court in the year 630 [1232–33].
Since no amir from that area had gone to court
before, the Qa’an was overjoyed by their
arrival and ordered banquets given at which
they were amply rewarded. Chin Temür and
Külbolad were also shown great favor, and the
Qa’an said, “In all this time during which
Chormaqan has been gone and conquered such
vast territories, he hasn’t sent one lord to us.
Now Chin Temür, despite the paucity of his
numbers and lack of assistance, has performed
such a service, and we appreciate it.” [662] So
saying, he assigned to Chin Temür the gover-
norship of Khurasan and Mazanderan and or-
dered that Chormaqan and the other amirs not
interfere. Külbolad was made a partner to Chin
Temür, and the Ispahbad was given lands from
the border of Kabudjama to Astarabad. Malik
Baha’uddin was made malik over Khurasan,
Isfarayin, Juvayn, Bayhaq, Jajarm, Jurbadh,
and Arghiyan. Each of them was given a gold
paiza and two decrees sealed with the red seal.
Thus firmly established by imperial decree,
Chin Temür named Sharafuddin as his vizier
on account of his long service and experience
and made Baha’uddin Muhammad Juvayni
chief of his divan. Each of the amirs sent a bit-
igchi to the divan on behalf of a prince. The di-
van thus ﬂourished.
Chin Temür was going to send Görgüz back
as an envoy to the Qa’an’s court, but Külbolad
disagreed, saying, “He is an Uyghur. He will
do everything he can to advance his own inter-
ests. It is unwise to send him.” Chin Temür re-
fused to listen. When Görgüz arrived at court
and
was
asked
about
the
affairs
of
the
provinces, he reported as it suited him. The
emperor liked his manner of speech and sent
him back with all his wishes and requests
granted. Chin Temür died around then.
Now that the history of the khaqans, caliphs,
sultans, maliks, atabegs, and Mongol amirs
who were contemporaries of Ögödäi Qa’an
during this six-year period has been written,
we will begin with the history of Ögödäi Qa’an
after this period, God willing. [663]
The History of Ögödäi Qa’an from the
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
319

beginning of Qonin Yil, the Year of the
Sheep that began in Jumada I 632 [January
1235], [472, M115] through Hükär Yil, the
Year of the Ox that began in Sha‘ban 638
[February 1241], a period of seven years.
During this period two great quriltais were
held, and princes and amirs were sent to
Qipchaq and Machin territory and to other
places. In every spot magnificent structures,
cities, palaces, and the like were constructed.
Ögödäi Qa’an died during the last year, the
thirteenth from his accession and the fifteenth
from Genghis Khan’s death.
History of the Qa’an’s convocation of a
quriltai, and the assignment of princes and
amirs to the frontiers of various territories.
When he returned from conquering Cathay in
the Year of the Horse, the Qa’an held a quriltai
in Talan Daban. In this Year of the Sheep he
wanted to assemble once again all the sons,
relatives, and amirs and make them listen again
to the yasa and ordinances. As commanded, all
presented themselves, and he rewarded them
all with various shows of favor. For one full
month he and his relatives banqueted, and, as
was his custom, [664] he gave away everything
in the treasuries.
When they were finished feasting and revel-
ing, they turned to serious matters of state and
the military. Since some outlying areas had not
been
conquered,
and
rebellions
were
in
progress in others, in order to deal with these

himself for the Qipchaq Steppe. However,
Möngkä Qa’an, although he was still a youth,
made an intelligent observation worthy of an
older man on the Qa’an’s motion. “We are all
sons and brothers,” he said, “and we stand
ready to obey any order given and are willing
to give our lives for anything that is command-
ed. Let the Qa’an enjoy himself and not be
obliged to endure the hardships of travel. Oth-
erwise, what is the benefit of having relatives,
officers, and innumerable soldiers?”
All those in attendance applauded these wise
words and adopted them. The Qa’an then de-
cided that the princes Batu, Möngkä Qa’an,
and Güyük Khan would set out to conquer the
territories of Qipchaq, Rus, Bular, Magyar,
Bashghurd, As, Sudaq, and that area with
another group of princes and many troops.
They got busy making preparations.
Also during that year, in the plain of
Asichang, Ögödäi Qa’an assigned his son
Köchü and Jochi Qasar’s [grand]son Prince
Qutuqu to go to Machin, which they call
Nankiyas. They departed and captured the
towns of Sang Yampu [Xiangyangfu] and
Karimpu [Jianglingfu]. Along the way they
plundered the territory of Tibet.
Also during that year Hoqutur was sent with
an army to Kashmir and Hindustan. They cap-
tured and pillaged a portion of those territories.
Also during that year [665] a qubjur was le-
vied on animals at the rate of one head per
hundred. The Qa’an ordered that for every ten
measures of grain, one should be given to be
spent on the poor.
Because there was so much necessary ex-
change of envoys between the princes and the
court on various matters, yams [relay stations]
were established throughout the realm,1 and
they were called tayan yams. For the establish-
ment of the yams, the following emissaries rep-
resenting the princes were appointed: on behalf
of the Qa’an, Bitigchi Qoridai; on behalf of
Chaghatai, Emälägchin Tayichi’utai; on behalf
of Batu, Suqu Mulchatai; on behalf of Tolui
Khan, Alchiqa went by order of Sorqaghtani
Beki. These amirs went and established tayan

The Qa’an sent emissaries to all parts of the
empire to announce that no creature should
molest any other, and the strong should not use
force against or oppress the weak. Thus the
people enjoyed ease, and a reputation for jus-
tice was spread.

The buildings commissioned between the
time the princes went to the Qipchaq Steppe
and the time they returned, and a mention
of the way stations and his summer and
winter quarters.
The Qa’an spent the period of seven years
from the beginning of Qonin Yil, which corre-
sponds to 632 [1235], when he sent the princes
to the Qipchaq Steppe, until Hükär Yil, which
corresponds to 638 [1241], when Güyük Khan
and Möngkä Qa’an returned, in revelry and
celebration. He moved merrily back and forth
between summer pastures and winter quarters,
and he constantly enjoyed all sorts of pleasures
with beautiful ladies and comely companions.
Most of the time he turned his mind to
thoughts of dispensing justice and beneficence,
eradicating injustice and tyranny, making the
towns and provinces ﬂourish, and building var-
ious edifices. He neglected not one iota of the
responsibilities incumbent upon a world ruler. 
1Prior to this, the references to ordus (in the plural)
has been to Genghis Khan’s four Great Ordus. Hence-
forth, reference to a ruler’s, or prince’s, ordus is to the
multiple camp establishments maintained for the various
wives. Carpini comments in this regard: “Cumq; Tar-
tarorum vnus habet vxorum multitudinem, vnaquaeq;
per se suam habet familiam & stationem. Et vna die Tar-
tarus comedit & bibit & dormit cum vna, altera die cum
alia. Vna tamen inter caeteras aior habetur, cum qua
frequentius quã cum alijs commoratur. Et licet, vt dictum
est, sint multae, nunquam tamen de facili contendunt in-
ter se” (p. 79); “Whensoeuer a Tartar hath many wiues,
each one of them hath her family and dwelling place by
her selfe. And sometime the Tartar eateth, drinketh and
lieth with one, and sometime with another. One is ac-
compted chiefe among the rest, with whom hee is often-
er conuersant, then with the other. And notwithstanding
(as it hath bin said) they are many, yet do they seldome
fal out among themselues” (p. 112).
Since he had previous brought masters of
every craft and trade from Cathay, he ordered
them to construct in his yurt in Qaraqorum,
where he was usually in residence, a palace of
a magnificence appropriate for such a high-
minded monarch. It was constructed. Each side
was an arrow shot in length, and in the middle
was raised a pavilion of great height. The
buildings were decorated as elaborately as pos-
sible and ornamented with the skills of painters
and artists. It was named Qarshi.2 He made it
his capital and ordered each of his brothers and
their sons and all the other princes [671] who
were in attendance to build magnificent man-
sions in the vicinity. They all obeyed the order,
and when the construction was completed it
looked like a vast assemblage. Then he ordered
the master goldsmiths to make of gold and sil-
ver for the sharabkhana implements of assem-
bly in the shape and form of animals like ele-
phants, lions, horses, et cetera. They were set
out in place of munquraqs (drinking vessels)
and filled with wine and kumiss. In front of
every one was placed a basin of silver, and
from the openings in the animals wine and ku-
miss poured into the basins. 
“What city on the face of the earth is more
beautiful?” he asked.
“Baghdad,” they said.
Then he ordered a magnificent city built on
the banks of the Orkhon River, and it was
named Qaraqorum. From the provinces of
Cathay to that city they established yams [post
stations]—other than the tayan yams—and
called them narin yams.3 There was a yam
every five leagues, which came to a total of
thirty-seven yams. At every way station a haza-
ra was stationed to provide protection.
2Qarshi, the Mongolian for ‘palace.’

He had commanded that every day five
hundred carts loaded with foodstuffs and drink
should be delivered there from the provinces
and placed in the storehouses, from which they
could be brought out for use. For bägni and
sorma (beer and ale) large carts that took six
oxen to pull were arranged. 
He ordered the Muslim craftsmen to con-
struct a pavilion at a one-day’s distance from
Qaraqorum, in a place that had once belonged
to Afrasiab’s falconers and was called Kähär
Chaghan. [He usually went there] in the spring
for falconing. In the summer he was in Ör-
mügätü, where he had had a tent pitched in
which everyone could fit, and it was never tak-
en down. The outside was ornamented with
gold studs, and the inside was covered in bro-
cades. It was called Shirä Ordu.1 In the autumn
he would be in Kösä’ür Na’ur, a four-day jour-
ney from Qaraqorum, and there he would re-
main for a period of forty days. In the winter
he was in Ong Qin, [672] hunting in the Tulun-
gu and Jalingu mountains. After having passed
the winter he usually spent the spring in the
vicinity of Qaraqorum.
His summer pastures were in the meadows of
Örmügätü; his autumn residence was between
Kösä’ür Na’ur and Usun Qol, a one-day’s dis-
tance from Qaraqorum; and his winter quarters
were at Ong Qin. When he set out for Qaraqo-
rum, he would eat and spent a day in pleasure
in a magnificent pavilion he had built two
leagues from the city and named Tuzghu Baliq,
i.e. Tuzghu City, and the next day all the peo-
ple would don clothing of one color and from
there he would enter Qarshi while slender

youths stood in front. He would engage in rev-

Every evening he would have archers, cross-

At his winter quarters in Ong Qin he had or-
dered a wall built. It was a two-day journey
long and was made of wood and clay, and it
had gates. He called it a chihik. When a hunt
was held, soldiers in all directions would be in-
formed, and they would form a circle and head
for the wall, driving the prey toward it. From a
one-month’s distance away, taking all precau-
tions and keeping the circle intact at all times,
they drove the prey to the chihik, and then the
soldiers would form a circle and stand shoulder
to shoulder. First Ögödäi Qa’an and his elite
would enter the circle, watch for a time, and
then hunt. When he was tired, he would go up
on a rise inside the circle and the princes and
amirs in their turn would enter. Then the com-
moners and soldiers would have their turn to
hunt. Then he would let some of them go for
the uruqlamishi (round-up), and the bökä’üls
would divide all the prey among the princes
and amirs so that no one failed to receive a
share. They all would perform the ceremony of
tägishmishi [presentation of gifts], and after
nine days of banqueting every clan would re-
turn to its home yurt. [673]
The Qa’an falls ill and dies.
The Qa’an was inordinately fond of wine and
drank too much. Day by day he grew so much
thinner that his courtiers and well-wishers tried
to prevent him from drinking, but it was to no
avail. Despite their efforts, he drank even
more.
Chaghatai
assigned
an
amir
as
a
guardian over him to keep him from drinking
more than a certain number of cups a day, and
since he could not disobey his brother’s order

325

he took to drinking from large cups instead of
small ones so that the number would remain
the same. His guardian also gave him wine and
kept him company in order to have himself
made an advisor, so his companionship was of
no use to the Qa’an.
Ibaqa
Beki,
Sorqaghtani
Beki’s
sister
Genghis Khan had given to Kähätäi Noyan,
had a son who was a ba’urchi. Every year
Ibaqa Beki used to come to court from Cathay,
where her yurt was, to consult with Sorqagh-
tani Beki. When she came she always gave a
banquet at which she offered a cup to the
Qa’an. In the thirteenth year of the Qa’an’s
reign, she came as usual and, together with her
son the ba’urchi, offered a cup to Ögödäi
Qa’an. That night the Qa’an died in his sleep
from
overindulgence
in
wine.
The
next
morning the khatuns and amirs accused Ibaqa
and her son of having poisoned the Qa’an with
the cup they offered. Elji’idäi Noyan, who was
a kükäldash and an amir of consequence from
the Jalayir tribe, said, “What nonsense is this?
Ibaqa Beki’s son is a ba’urchi who has always
held the cups. The Qa’an always drank too
much. Why must we badmouth our Qa’an by
saying he was assassinated by others? His time
had come, that’s all. No one should speak of
this nonsense again.” Since he was an intelli-
gent man, he realized that the death had been
caused by drinking too much. [674] He also
knew how serious the end of overindulgence in
wine was.
The Qa’an had acceded to the throne in a
Hükär Yil, and he died the next Hükär Yil,
which corresponded to 638 [1241], the thir-
teenth year of his reign. In the history written
by Khwaja Ala’uddin Sahib-Divan it is said
that he died in the Year of the Tiger corre-
sponding to the 5th of Jumada II 639 [Decem-
ber 11, 1241].1
Ögödäi Qa’an’s bones and his ghoruq are on
an extremely high mountain called Boldaq
Qasar. It is always covered with snow. At
present it is called Yäkä Ündür. From that
mountain ﬂow the Yesün Mörän, the Tärkän,
and the Usun, which ﬂow into the Irtysh River.
From the mountain to the Irtysh is a ten-day
journey. Chapar has his winter quarters in the
vicinity of that river.
The Qa’an had a physician named ___. He
versified a chronogram for his death and sent it
to a friend in Transoxiana. It is as follows.
In KHLT [639] the Qa’an had more plexus than
ever,2 and day and night he gave news of those
who were passed out. This assisted greatly in
the dysfunction of his humors.3
Now that the history of Ögödäi Qa’an has
been written from from the beginning of Qonin
Yil, the Year of the Sheep corresponding to 632
[1235], through Hükär Yil, the Year of the Ox
corresponding to 638 [1241], a period of seven
years, in the last year of which he died, now
we will give an abbreviated history of the
khaqans of Machin, the caliphs, some of the
sultans who were left, the maliks, atabegs of
Iran, and some of the Mongol princes and
amirs who ruled throughout the realm. [675]
1“Khwaja Ala’uddin Sahib-Divan’s history” is the
Tārīkh-i jahāngushāy (History of the World Conqueror)
by Ala’uddín Ata-Malik al-Juwayni.
2The pun is irreproducible in English. The Persian
word for plexus, khilt (ﺧﻠﻂ), itself gives the date, 639.
3The poem is lacking in JTK.

History of the khaqans of Machin, the
caliphs, and the sultans and maliks who
were left.
History of the emperors of Cathay and
Machin during this period.
Shouxu.1 This Shouxu was the last of the em-
perors of Cathay. He was killed in Morin Yil,
[676] the Year of the Horse that began in Juma-
da I 631, as was explained in the section on this
year, and the realm of Cathay came completely
under the control of the Qa’an. 
History of the rulers of Machin who have
been mentioned during this period.
Li Zong,2 [ruled a total of] 41 years, [of
which] 7 years [were before this period and] 7
years [were during this period]. 
History of the caliphs, sultans, maliks, and
atabegs during this period.
History of the caliphs.
This Abbasid caliph was al-Nasir-li-dinillah.
He died in the year 627, and his son, Zahir suc-
ceeded him. He died in the year 628, and al-
Mustansir-bi’llah was elevated to the caliphate.
al-Mustansir-bi’llah was the caliph of the
House of Abbas, and during these years he be-
gan and completed construction of the Mustan-
siriyya Madrasa.
History of the sultans.
In Mosul was Badruddin Lu’lu’.
In Anatolia was Sultan Ala’uddin.
In Kirman was Ruknuddin Qutlugh Sultan,
son of Baraq. His history during this period is
as follows. In 637 [1239–40] [677] his father
Baraq Hajib sent him to the Qa’an’s court.
Along the way he received news of his father’s
death, and when he reached his destination, the
1Shouxu (守緒) = Ai Zong (哀宗) of the Jin, ruled
1224–34. See note to text p. 544 above.
2Li Zong (理宗) of the Southern Song, ruled 1224–64.
Qa’an, as was his imperial custom, received
him with great warmth and favor. Because he
had obeyed the decree that he come to court,
he was given the title of Qutlugh Sultan and
awarded a yarligh (imperial decree) making
him ruler of Kirman. The Qa’an also ordered
that Ruknuddin’s brother Qutbuddin, who had
taken charge of affairs after his father’s death,
should hasten to court and pay homage. When
Ruknuddin arrived in Kirman, he dispatched
his brother via Khabis to the Qa’an’s court.
When he arrived he remained a time in service
to Mahmud Yalavach while Ruknuddin was
occupied with ruling.
History of the maliks and atabegs.
In Fars was Atabeg Abubakr b. Sa‘d.
History of the princes in the Qipchaq
Steppe.
In the autumn of Quluqana Yil, the Year of
the Rat that corresponds to 637 [1240], when
Güyük Khan and Möngkä Qa’an returned, by
order of the Qa’an, [678] from the Qipchaq
Steppe, Prince Batu and his brothers Qada’an,
Büri, and Böchök mounted on an expedition to
the territory of the Rus and the Black Hats.3
They took the great city of the Rus, which was
called Mankärmän,4 in nine days. After that
they went in järgä formation, tümän by tümän,
to all the towns of Vladimir, seizing the
fortresses and territories that lay along the way.
Together they laid siege to the town of Üch-
Oghul Avladimür [Vladimir Volynsky] and
took it in three days.5
3The “Black Hats” (kulāhsiyāhān in Persian for the

lished as their frontier guards on the middle Dnieper.
The Russians called them чорные клобуки. See Mi-
norsky, “Caucasia III,” 230.
4Mankärmän is one
of the many names by which
Kiev was known.
5Minorsky explains the unusual epithet, Üch-oghul

The Kiral, the ruler of those realms, was driven

The news of the Qa’an’s death still had not

After that, in the Year of the Tiger [1242],
many Qipchaqs came to fight Kötän [679] and

They gave Ila’udur an army and dispatched

At the beginning of Taulai Yil, the Year of

History of the amirs of Khurasan.
When Chin Temür died, an emissary was
sent to announce it to the Qa’an. Amir Nosal
was ordered to replace him in Khurasan and
Persia. He was an aged Mongol, more than a
hundred years old. As ordered, the amirs and
