bitigchis of the divan moved from Chin
Temür’s house to Nosal’s and occupied them-
selves with administrative affairs. Sharafuddin
Khwarazmi went to Batu’s service, and Görgüz
came and went as usual.
A conﬂict ﬂared up between Baha’uddin and
Mahmudshah Sabzavari, so [Baha’uddin] went
to the Qa’an to report it. The Qa’an said, “In
the absence of adversaries no judgment can be
rendered. Let them come together so that an in-
quiry can be made.” When Malik Baha’uddin
returned and delivered the order, Nosal and
Külbolad did not agree with Görgüz’s claims,
[680] but Görgüz set out, got the governorship
for himself, and returned. Nosal was content
with the command of the military until he died
in the year 637 [1239–40]. Taking the bitigchis
and the revenue agents, Görgüz administered
fiscal affairs, put the affairs of Khurasan and
Mazanderan in order, and made a census. He
fixed the assessments, made a good foundation
for the workshops, and created the best admin-
istration of justice and equity possible.
Sharafuddin returned from Batu, and since he
and certain others had lost their authority
through Görgüz’s presence, they persuaded
Chin Temür’s eldest son, Edigü Temür, to ask
for his father’s post. He sent Tonquz to the
Qa’an’s court to report the confusion in
Khurasan. A group of those opposed to the
Qa’an’s vizier Chinqai took advantage of an
opportunity to convey Edigü Temür’s report.
An order was given for Amir Arghun Aqa, Qor
Buqa, and Shamsuddin Kamargar to go and
make an investigation. When Görgüz found
out, he set out for the Qa’an’s court. He met
the others in Fanakat and refused to turn back
merely on their say-so. Tonquz set upon him
and broke his teeth. Görgüz sent his blood-
stained nightshirt with Temür to the Qa’an’s
court and was forced to turn back. When he
reached Khurasan, Külbolad and Edigü Temür
assembled
and
drove
the
bitigchis
from
Görgüz’s house to their houses with sticks and
clubs. An
investigation
into
matters
was
launched, and Görgüz kept coming up with ex-
cuses until Temür returned forty-five days lat-
er, bearing a decree to the effect that all the
amirs and maliks should present themselves
and that no investigation should be conducted
there. When the Qa’an had been shown
Görgüz’s bloody shirt, he had ﬂown into a rage
and sent a message to Görgüz saying that he
should present himself at court. Görgüz mount-
ed at once with a group of trusted officials.
[681] Külbolad and Edigü Temür also set out
with a group of informants.
In Bukhara, Sayin Malikshah gave them a
banquet. When Külbolad went out to relieve
himself, a group of fida’is who were trailing
him stabbed and killed him. When they
reached the court they first pitched the tent
Chin Temür had provided. The Qa’an was in-
side enjoying a banquet, but when he went out
to relieve himself a gust of wind arose and col-
lapsed the tent, injuring a concubine. The
Qa’an ordered the tent torn to shreds and car-
ried away as plunder. On account of this, Edigü
Temür lost face.
A week later, the tent Görgüz had brought
was pitched, and revels were held. One of the
gifts was a belt studded with jaundice stones.
As a pleasantry, the Qa’an put it on, and the
slight discomfort he was experiencing from
overeating was dispelled. This was taken as a
good omen, and Görgüz’s prospects began to
look up.
For three months an investigation into their
affairs was held, but no conclusion was
reached. Finally the Qa’an undertook the
examination himself, and Edigü Temür and his
followers were convicted. “Since you are
connected to Batu,” the Qa’an said, “I will
send your case to him. Batu commands you.”
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
329

The Qa’an’s vizier Chinqai said, “Batu’s supe-
rior is the Qa’an. What dog is this that his case
needs a council of padishahs? The Qa’an com-
mands him.” The Qa’an pardoned him, made
peace among them, and sent them all back in
Görgüz’s company. “It is Genghis Khan’s great
Yasa that lying informants be killed,” he told
them. “You should all be killed, but because
you have come such a long way, and your
wives and children are expecting you, I will
pardon you. Henceforth do not do such things.
Say to Görgüz, ‘If you continue to live with
them on the basis of vengefulness, [682] you
too will be at fault.’ ”
It was ordered that Görgüz should command
all the territory from the Oxus River that Chor-
maqan’s army had subdued. Heralds were sent
ahead to Khurasan while he went to visit
Batu’s brother Tangqut. From there he went via
Khwarazm to Khurasan. In Jumada II 637 [Jan-
uary 1240], he dismounted at his own quarters,
summoned the amirs and nobles, and read
them the orders. He sent his son to Persia, Ar-
ran, and Azerbaijan, where, after much debate
with Chormaqan, he took control of those ter-
ritories in accordance with the decree and fixed
the amount of tribute. 
Görgüz chose the city of Tus as his resi-
dence, and there he began construction of
many buildings. He arrested and imprisoned
Sharafuddin Khwarazmi and gave the vizierate
to Asiluddin Rughdi. He sent Temür to the
Qa’an’s court to inform him of Sharafuddin’s
situation, and he himself went on Temür’s
heels. While on his return journey, he encoun-
tered one of Chaghatai’s amirs named Käjävü
on a bridge in Transoxiana. An exchange of
words ensued. The amir said, “You wait and
see if I don’t report you!”
“To whom are you going to report me?”
countered Görgüz.
Chaghatai had died not long before, and the
amir went weeping before Chaghatai’s wife
and told her what Görgüz had said. The khatun
sent a message to the Qa’an, saying, “Just be-
cause Chaghatai is dead, can a commoner like
Görgüz speak so boldly?” The Qa’an ordered
Görgüz arrested and his mouth stuffed with dirt
until he died. In the meantime Görgüz had
come
to
Khurasan.
The
khatun’s
envoys
brought Külbolad’s son the decree that said he
should seize Görgüz and turn him over to
them. Görgüz escaped, however, and went into
the Tus fortress. After three days of battle they
got him out, tied him up in chains, and turned
him over to the envoys, who took him away
and killed him [683] by stuffing dirt into his
mouth. [684]
Part Three of the history of Ögödäi Qa’an.
His good character, his sayings, decrees, and
orders, and events that occurred during his
reign not included in the above two parts
but learned from miscellaneous books and
persons.
The Qa’an was known for his good character,
nobility, and good customs. He constantly re-
warded and honored all classes of mankind,
and friendliness and generosity were so dom-
inant in his nature that not for the batting of an
eyelash was he negligent of propagating justice
and clemency. Sometimes his ministers and
courtiers tried to undo his excesses, but he
would always say, “It is known to all on this
earth that the world is not faithful to any crea-
ture. Wisdom necessitates that a man keep
himself alive through the eternality of a good
name.” 
An eternal memory is reckoned by the wise to
be a second life. Such a treasury is enough for
you, like good works that last forever.
Whenever the manners and customs of past
rulers and kings were mentioned, when it came
to talk of treasures, he would always say,
330
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

“Those who have striven for such things were
deprived of their fair share of wisdom, for no
difference can be imagined between buried
treasure and dust. Both are equally beneficial,
and when one’s appointed time of death arrives
they give no benefit, and it is not possible to
come back from the other world. [685] We
want to place our treasures in the corners of
hearts, and everything that is on hand and
ready, or that will come, we want to give to the
deprived and the needy so that we may store
up a good name.” 
As examples of the overall content of his
deeds and words several anecdotes will now be
given in detail, but they are but one out of a
thousand and only a few of many.
❈
It is the custom of the Mongols that during
the day in spring and summer no one sits in
water, washes his hands in a brook, carries wa-
ter in gold or silver vessels, or spreads washed
clothes in open spaces, for they claim that
these things cause an increase in thunder and
lightning, of which they are deathly afraid.
One day the Qa’an was out hunting with
Chaghatai. Along the way they saw a Muslim
sitting in water making his ablutions.
Chaghatai, who was quite exacting in his ap-
plication of the Yasa, wanted to kill the Mus-
lim, but the Qa’an said, “It is late, and we are
weary. Let them hold him tonight, and tomor-
row he can be tried and executed.” Turning the
man over to Danishmand the chamberlain, the
Qa’an secretly ordered a bar of silver thrown
where the man had been making his ablutions.
Then he sent word for the man to be told that
during the trial he should say, “I am a man of
limited means. I had a little capital that had
fallen into the water. I went in to get it out.”
The next day during the inquisition he pled
his excuse, and when men were sent there, they
found the bar in the water.
“Who would dare to transgress the Great
Yasa?” said the Qa’an, “However, this wretch
has sacrificed himself for the sake of this paltry
thing out of helplessness and poverty.” He par-
doned him and ordered him given ten more
bars from the treasury, and he was made to
pledge that henceforth he would not dare to do
such a thing.
For this reason the valiant of the world made
themselves slaves to his good character, [686]
for the soul is better than abundant treasure.
❈
At the beginning of his reign the Qa’an or-
dered that no sheep or other edible animal
should be slaughtered by having a knife drawn
across its throat but rather, as was customary
among the Mongols, the breast should be slit.
One day a Muslim bought a sheep, took it
home, shut the gates tight, and in the inner part
of the house slaughtered it in the Muslim fash-
ion. By chance, a Qipchaq had seen him in the
market, followed him home, and gone up on
the roof. As soon as the man drew the knife
across the sheep’s throat, he rushed down, tied
the man up, and took him to the Qa’an’s court.
The Qa’an sent deputies out to investigate.
When they reported what had happened, he
said, “This poor man has obeyed our order,
while this Turk has broken it by going up on
his roof.”
He let the Muslim go, and the Qipchaq was
executed.
❈
Players had come from Cathay, and they
were performing amazing plays from behind a
screen. One of them had types representing
every nation. During the play an old man with
white hair and a turban was tied behind a horse
and being dragged along.
“What is this a representation of?” asked the
Qa’an. They told him it was a Muslim rebel
because that was how the soldiers exiled such
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
331

people from cities. The Qa’an ordered the
show stopped and had brought from the
treasury fine textiles and jewel-studded gar-
ments from Baghdad and Bukhara and Arabian
horses and other valuable items like jewels,
gold, silver, etc. that are found in these areas.
Then he had Cathaian wares brought and
placed them opposite to show the inestimable
difference between the two sorts of goods. 
“The
poorest Tajik
Muslim
has
several
Cathaian slaves standing in attendance,” he
said, “but not one of the greatest generals of
Cathay has a Muslim captive. [687] This can
only be due to divine wisdom, for it is aware of
the worth and rank of every nation in the
world, and Genghis Khan’s blessed Yasa is
also in agreement, for the blood money for a
Muslim is forty bars of gold while that of a
Cathaian is one donkey. With such clear proofs
how can the people of Islam be subjected to
ridicule? You should be made to pay for your
act, but this time I will spare your lives. Go
from our court, and henceforth do not perform
such things.”
❈
One of the maliks of Iran sent an ambassador
to the Qa’an to enter into fealty. Among the
gifts he had sent was a polished ruby that had
come to his ancestors by inheritance. It had the
blessed name of the Apostle of God carved
above, and below were the names of the
sender’s ancestors.
The Qa’an ordered the engravers to leave the
name of the Apostle for good luck, to erase the
other names, and to carve the Qa’an’s name
beneath the Apostle’s. Then he sent it back.
❈
A Persian speaker who did not accept the re-
ligion of Islam came to the Qa’an, knelt, and
said, “I dreamed of Genghis Khan, and he said,
‘Tell my son to kill many Muslims, for they are
an evil people.’ ”
The Qa’an reﬂected a moment and then
asked, “Did he speak to you through an inter-
preter, or did he say this to you himself?”
“He spoke directly to me,” he answered.
“Do
you
know
Mongolian?”
asked
the
Qa’an.
“No,” he said.
“Then you are obviously lying,” said the
Qa’an, “for I know for certain that Genghis
Khan knew no language other than Mon-
golian.”
Then he ordered the man to be killed.
❈
There was a poor man who had no way of
earning a living and knew no trade. He sharp-
ened a few pieces of iron into things like awls,
mounted them on sticks, [688] and waited on
the roadside for the Qa’an to pass. The Qa’an
spied him from afar and sent someone to
investigate. 
“I am a poor man with few possessions and a
large family,” he said. “I have brought these
awls to offer.” The officer reported the man’s
condition, but the awls were so miserable and
bad that he didn’t show them.
“Bring me what he has brought,” the Qa’an
said. Then, taking the awls in his hand, he said,
“Even things like these are useful. The herds-
men use them to stitch their kumiss sacks.”
And he rewarded the man with a bar of silver
for each awl, which wasn’t worth a barleycorn.
❈
There was a pathetic old man who came to
the Qa’an and asked him to give him two
hundred bars of gold to trade with on the em-
peror’s behalf. The Qa’an said they should be
given. 
“This man is in his twilight years,” the
courtiers said. “He has no residence, children,
or slaves. No one knows anything about him.”
“He has been hoping and looking for such an
opportunity his whole life,” said the Qa’an.
332
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

“To turn him away from our court in disap-
pointment is not a high-minded thing to do and
unworthy of the emperorship God has granted
us. Give him immediately what he asks for. He
should not meet his death not having attained
his desire.” 
In accordance with the command, the bars
were turned over to him, but before he could
pick them all up he gave up the ghost.
❈
Someone petitioned for five hundred bars of
gold to be given him from the treasury to form
the basis of a commercial enterprise. 
“Give them to him,” said the Qa’an. 
“But this man has no credentials,” said the
courtiers, “no property or money. Furthermore,
he is in debt to this amount.”
“Give him a thousand bars,” said the Qa’an,
“so that he can give half to his creditors and
use the rest as capital.” [689]
❈
A treasure map was found that indicated that
in such-and-such a spot in the vicinity of the
area in which the Qa’an’s yurt was located
there was a treasure placed there by Afrasiab.
In the treasure map it was written that there
had not been enough animals in the area to car-
ry it away.
“We have no need of the treasure of others,”
said the Qa’an. “What we have we give away
to God’s servants and the poor.”
❈
An ortaq came to court and took away from
the treasury a hundred bars of gold to buy
commercial goods with. After a time he re-
turned and offered an absurd excuse, saying
that the bars were all gone. 
“Give him another five hundred bars,” said
the Qa’an. The man took them and returned the
next year, even more bankrupt than the last
time, and offered an excuse.
“Give him another like amount,” said the
Qa’an. 
Back he came with an excuse, but this time
the bitigchis were afraid to relay his words. Fi-
nally they said, “So-and-so squanders and eats
money in the towns.”
“How can he eat bars of gold?” asked the
Qa’an.
“He gives them away to the rabble and
spends them on food and wine,” they said.
“Inasmuch as the bars remain the same,” said
the Qa’an, “and those who take them from him
are our subjects, they remain in our hands.
Give him more as you did before, and tell him
not to squander them.” 
❈
The people of Taianfu, a city in Cathay, peti-
tioned, saying, “We owe eight thousand bars,
and it will break us because our creditors are
demanding payment. If it be commanded that
they go easy on us, we will pay the debt gradu-
ally and not be driven to desperation.”
“To force the creditors to go easy will result
in loss to them,” said the Qa’an, “while to do
nothing will result in distress to the subjects. It
would be better for us to pay it from the
treasury.”
A herald
then
announced
that
creditors
should bring their promissory notes. The credi-
tors came and took cash from the treasury, but
many people showed up claiming to be debtor
and claimant and took bars fraudulently, [690]
and thus many times what they had stated was
taken.
❈
Once on a hunt someone brought the Qa’an
three melons. Since he did not have any gold
or textiles with him at the time, the Qa’an told
Mögä Khatun to give the poor man the pearls
she had in her ears. 
“This poor man doesn’t know what those
pearls are worth,” said the assembly. “Let him
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
333

come to court tomorrow and get the gold and
textiles he can claim.”
“This poor man doesn’t have the patience to
wait,” said the Qa’an. “Anyway, these pearls
will come back to us.” And as ordered, they
handed the pearls to the poor man, who went
away rejoicing and sold them for a pittance.
The buyer thought to himself, “Such valuable
pearls are worthy of kings.” The next day he
took them to the Qa’an, who said, “Didn’t I
say these pearls would return to us? This way
the poor man was not deprived.” And, giving
them back to Mögä Khatun, he gave the man
who had brought them a handsome reward.
❈
A poor man knelt and offered a pair of ar-
rows. When his condition was inquired into, he
said, “My trade is arrow making, and I owe
seventy bars. If it is ordered that this amount
be paid from the treasury, I’ll bring ten thou-
sand arrows a year as payment.”
“This poor fellow must be in a dreadful fix to
accept to make so many arrows for that many
bars,” said the Qa’an. “Give him a hundred
bars in cash so that he can put his affairs in or-
der.” They were immediately turned over to
him, but he was unable to carry them away.
The Qa’an laughed and ordered a pair of oxen
and a cart to be given to him. He loaded them
and departed.
❈
One day, when he had laid the foundations of
Qaraqorum, he went into the treasury and saw
nearly a hundred thousand bars. 
“What benefit do we derive from all these
stores?” he asked. “They have to be constantly
guarded. Have it announced that everybody
who wants a bar should come and take one.”
[691]
The people of the city, high and low, rich and
poor alike, all rushed to the treasury, and
everyone got an abundant share.
❈
Since it was too cold in the vicinity of
Qaraqorum for there to have been much agri-
culture, it was introduced during the Qa’an’s
reign. Somebody planted turnips and raised a
few, which he brought to the Qa’an. The Qa’an
ordered the number of leaves counted. There
were a hundred, so he ordered the man to be
given a hundred bars.
If the heart and hand are sea and mine, they
are the heart and hand of the king.
❈
He had built a pavilion two leagues outside
of Qaraqorum and named it Tuzghu Baligh.
Near it someone planted several willow and al-
mond trees. In that area trees do not usually
grow because it is so cold, but by chance these
ﬂourished. The Qa’an ordered a gold bar given
to that man for every tree.
❈
When his generosity and liberality became
known in every quarter, merchants from all
over ﬂocked to his court. He would order that
all their wares, good and bad, be purchased and
full price paid. Usually he would pay for them
sight unseen, so the merchants would present a
bill for ten items for every one that was actual-
ly there. Once all the merchants realized this,
they would leave their wares unopened and
then come back in two or three days, when the
Qa’an would have given them away. Then they
would come and name any price they wanted.
He had also ordered that they be paid a pre-
mium of ten percent over the total. One day the
courtiers said, “There is no necessity for the
extra ten percent, for the price of their goods is
inﬂated anyway.”
“Merchants deal with the treasury in hopes of
a profit,” the Qa’an said, [692] “and they have
an expense to pay off you bitigchis. It’s the
debt they owe you I’m discharging lest they
334
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

come away having taken a loss in dealing with
us.”
❈
Some people brought two elephant tusks
from India.
“How much are they asking for them?” the
Qa’an asked. 
“Five thousand bars,” he was told. Without
batting an eyelash he ordered it paid. The
grandees of the court objected violently, say-
ing, “How can so much money be given for
such a miserable thing that comes from enemy
territory?”
“No one is an enemy to me,” he replied.
“Give it to them and let them go.”
❈
Someone brought him a hat of the sort worn
in Iran. In a drunken state he ordered a voucher
written for two hundred bars, but they withheld
the red seal, fearing that he might have spoken
simply out of drunkenness. The next day his
gaze fell upon that person. The officials told
him what they had done.
He ordered them to give him three hundred
bars. Once again, and for the same reason, they
held it in abeyance. Every day he increased the
amount until it reached six hundred. Then he
summoned the amirs and scribes and asked
them, “Is there anything in this world that will
last forever?”
“There is not,” they all said unanimously.
Turning to Sahib Yalavach, he said, “They
are wrong, for a good name and a good memo-
ry will last forever.” Then he said to the
scribes, “You are my real enemies, for you
don’t want a good name and repute to be left
behind by me. Thinking that I was giving mon-
ey away in drunkenness, you hold payment in
abeyance and deprive the person to whom it’s
due. There is nothing to be done but to make
an example of one or two of you in retribution
for what you have done.”
❈
Before Shiraz submitted, a person from there
came and knelt, saying, “I am a family man,
and I owe five hundred bars. I have come from
Shiraz,
having
heard
of
your
imperial
generosity.”
The Qa’an ordered him to be given a thou-
sand bars, [693] but the officials delayed pay-
ment and said, “To give more than he asked for
is nothing but squander.”
“Having heard of us, this poor man has
crossed so many mountains and plains and en-
dured so much heat and cold. His request will
not cover his debt and his expenses. If it is not
increased, it will be as though he were sent
back deprived—and that cannot be. Pay him in
full what has been ordered, and let him depart
happy.”
❈
A poor man came to the Qa’an’s court with
ten thongs tied to a stick. After offering prayers
on the Qa’an’s behalf, he said, “I had a little
goat, and I used the money from its ﬂesh to
cover expenses for my family, but I made its
skin into these thongs I have brought for the
men-at-arms.”
The Qa’an accepted the thongs, took them
into his own hands, and said, “This poor man
has brought us the best part of the goat.” And
he signaled for a hundred bars and a thousand
head of sheep to be given to him.
“When this is spent,” he said, “come back
and we’ll give you more.” 
❈
It was the Qa’an’s habit to go hunting for
three months of the year during the winter.
Every day of the other nine months, when he
had finished his meal, he would sit on a chair
outside the court with piles and stacks of all
the various sorts of goods and wares to be
found in the world, which he would give away
to Mongols and Muslims. It often happened
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
335

that he would tell burly men to take as much as
they could carry. 
One day one of them carried off a huge
stack. Along the way a piece of clothing fell,
and the man came back to pick it up.
“Why would anyone take so much trouble
for a piece of clothing?” the Qa’an asked, and
he motioned for the man to take away once
more as much as he could.
If Hatam were alive and could see the gen-
erosity of your palm, there is no doubt that he
would believe in your hand. [694]
❈
Someone brought him two hundred whips
made of red willow wood. In that area they use
that kind of wood for kindling, but he ordered
the man given two hundred bars.
❈
Someone brought him two hundred bone ar-
row heads. He gave him a like number of bars.
❈
Once, when he was riding through Qara-
qorum, he noticed a shop full of jujubes, and
he developed a craving for them. When he dis-
mounted he ordered Danishmand the chamber-
lain to buy a bar’s worth of jujubes from the
shop. He went, got a tray full of jujubes, and
gave a quarter bar, which was many times the
price of the jujubes. 
When he brought them, the Qa’an said, “One
bar was a small price for so many jujubes.”
Danishmand took out the rest of the bar and
said, “What I gave was more than the price.”
The Qa’an rebuked him and said, “When in
his whole life has that man had a customer like
us?” And he ordered the rest of the bar and ten
more given to him.
❈
The Qa’an ordered a hundred bars given to a
poor man.
“The Qa’an thinks a hundred bars is like a
hundred dirhems,” the officials said, and they
spread the amount on the road in front of him.
“What is this?” he asked.
“They are the bars the poor man will be giv-
en,” they replied.
“It certainly looks small and paltry,” said the
Qa’an. “Give him twice as much!”
❈
Someone sold the Qa’an’s amirs and wives
something for a hundred bars.
“Give it to him in cash,” said the Qa’an.
The next day he saw a poor man standing at
the gate of his palace, and he thought it was the
merchant. “Why haven’t you given him his
money
yet?”
he
asked.
Immediately
the
hundred bars were taken to him and he was
told, “This is the price of your wares.” 
“I haven’t sold any wares,” said the poor
man. Back they came and said, “It’s not the
same person.” [695]
“Now that you’ve taken the bars out of the
treasury,” said the Qa’an, “you can’t put them
back. It was slated for this man. Give them all
to him.”
❈
One day he saw an Indian woman carrying a
child on her shoulders. The Qa’an ordered that
she be given five bars. The man charged with
giving the bars withheld one and gave her four.
The woman objected.
“What is she saying?” asked the Qa’an.
“The woman has children and she was pray-
ing for them,” came the reply.
“She has children?” asked the Qa’an.
“Yes,” they said.
The Qa’an went into the treasury and cried
out to the woman, saying, “Take away howev-
er much you can of any fabrics you want.”
She took enough brocades to form the capital
of a wealthy man.
❈
336
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

One day a bird keeper brought a falcon, say-
ing, “It’s sick and needs to be be treated with
chicken meat.” The Qa’an said, “Give him a
bar to buy a chicken with.” The treasurer gave
the bar to the moneychanger to convert into
chits good for several chickens. Then, when
the Qa’an asked the treasurer about the bird
keeper, he told him how clever he had been. 
The Qa’an got angry and said, “I have placed
in your hands all the wealth of the world,
which cannot even be counted. Is that not
enough for you? That bird keeper didn’t want a
chicken. It was just an excuse to ask for some-
thing for himself. Every creature that comes
before us, be they ortaqs who say, ‘We’ll take
bars and make a profit on them,’ or people who
bring wares, or people of every sort who come
to this court, I don’t know whether they are
laying traps or whether they’ll take something,
but I want them to enjoy ease and prosperity
on account of us and have a share in our good
fortune.” Then he ordered several bars given to
the bird keeper.
❈
There was a bow maker who made really bad
bows. He had become so notorious in Qaraqo-
rum that nobody would buy a bow from him.
[696] One day he tied twenty bows on the end
of a stick and stood by the gate to the court.
When the Qa’an came out and saw him, he or-
dered his people to inquire into the man’s
condition. 
“I am a bow maker,” he said, “but nobody
buys my bows, and I have become very poor. I
have brought these twenty bows for His
Majesty.”
The Qa’an ordered the bows taken and twen-
ty bars of gold given to the man. 
❈
The Qa’an had been brought a very valuable,
jewel-studded belt as a rare and precious gift.
He put it on, but there was a loose stud on one
end. It was sent to a goldsmith to tighten the
stud.
The goldsmith sold the belt, and every time it
was demanded of him, he made excuses. Final-
ly he was put under guard and confessed that
he had lost it. He was bound and brought to
court. When the truth was told, the Qa’an said,
“Although he has committed a serious crime,
to have perpetrated such a thing shows that he
was in great poverty and need. Give him a
hundred fifty bars so that he can straighten out
his affairs, and henceforth let him not have the
audacity to do such a thing.”
❈
Someone brought the Qa’an a goblet from
Aleppo. The courtiers took it away while he
was absent and then told him about it.
“The man who brought it must have gone to
a lot of trouble to get such a rare novelty here,”
he said. “Give him two hundred bars.”
The man was sitting at the gate, wondering
whether his words had been conveyed to the
Qa’an or not, when all of a sudden he was giv-
en the good news and the bars were handed to
him.
That same day a mention was made of
Abyssinian servants. The Qa’an asked the man
if he could obtain some.
“That is my métier,” he said. The Qa’an or-
dered another two hundred bars to be given
him. A travel decree was penned, but he never
returned.
❈
There was a man in Qaraqorum who was ex-
tremely poor. [697] He fashioned a cup from a
mountain goat’s horn and sat on the roadside.
When the Qa’an passed by, he jumped up and
offered it.
The Qa’an took it and ordered that he be giv-
en fifty bars. One of the scribes repeated the
number.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
337

“How many times do I have to tell you not to
question my gifts?” said the Qa’an. “Do not
withhold my money from those who ask for it.
Instead, give him a hundred bars.”
❈
A Muslim had borrowed four bars of silver
from an Uyghur amir and was then unable to
repay it. He was arrested, and during the hear-
ing he was given the choice either of renounc-
ing the Muhammedan religion and becoming
an idolator or of being stripped naked in the
marketplace and receiving a hundred lashes.
He asked for a respite of three days.
He went to the Qa’an’s court and told him of
his situation. The Qa’an ordered the man’s
creditors to be summoned, and he convicted
them of coercing the Muslim. The Uyghur’s
wife and home were given to the Muslim, and
the Uyghur was stripped naked in the market-
place and given a hundred lashes. The Muslim
was awarded a hundred bars.
❈
There was an Alid from Chargh in Bukhara
who was known as Alavi Charghi. He had tak-
en bars from the treasury on commercial spec-
ulation. When it came time for repayment, he
said, “I have paid it with interest.” The receipt
was demanded as proof.
“I gave it to the Qa’an,” he said. 
He was brought to court, and the Qa’an said,
“I don’t know you. Where and in whose pres-
ence did you turn it over?”
“You were alone,” he said. 
The Qa’an reﬂected for a moment and then
said, “It is abundantly clear what he is up to.
However, if an investigation is made, people
will say the Qa’an has gone back on his word
and made an investigation.” Then he added,
“Leave him alone, but do not accept any of the
wares he has brought to the treasury to sell.”
That day a large group of merchants had
come, and their wares were being purchased.
[698] The Qa’an gave all of them extra pay-
ment. All of a sudden he said, “Where is that
sayyid?” He was brought in.
“Aren’t you sorry your goods aren’t being
taken?”
he
asked. The Alid
begged
and
pleaded.
“What is the price of your goods?” he asked.
“Thirty bars,” he replied.
The Qa’an ordered them to give him a
hundred.
❈
One day one of the Qa’an’s female relatives
entered and eyed the raiments, pearls, and jew-
els of his wives. He said to Yalavach, “Bring
all the pearls that are on hand.” Twelve trays
full, which had been purchased for eighty thou-
sand dinars, were produced. Then he ordered
all the pearls dumped in her lap.
“Have you had enough pearls?” he asked.
“How long will you gaze upon others?”
❈
Someone brought him a pomegranate as a
gift. He ordered the seeds counted and divided
up among those present. He gave the man one
bar for every seed.
❈
From a place called Qara Tash in the region
of Tangqut a Muslim brought him an edible
walnut and then asked for permission to return
home. He granted permission and gave him a
bar of gold.
❈
On a banquet day when all the day guards
were in a drunken stupor, somebody stole a
golden goblet from the ordu. They searched for
it high and low, but it was not to be found. The
Qa’an ordered it heralded that if whoever had
taken it would return it, his life would be
spared and he would be granted anything he
asked for. 
338
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

The next day the thief brought the goblet.
“For what reason did you commit such an au-
dacious act?” he was asked. 
“To give a warning to the emperor of the
world,” he replied, “so that he wouldn’t trust
the day guards.”
“We spare his life,” said the Qa’an, “and
such a person should not be killed. [699] Oth-
erwise we would have ordered his breast cut
open and we would have seen what kind of a
heart he has.”
He also awarded him five
hundred bars and many horses and garments,
made him an officer over several thousand sol-
diers, and sent him to Cathay.
❈
One year when the wheat had sprouted, a
hailstorm came and wiped it out. In fear of
shortages a maund of ﬂour was not to be had in
Qaraqorum for a dinar. The Qa’an ordered the
following heralded: “Let those who have plant-
ed wheat not allow themselves to fear, for we
will make up from the treasury any loss they
may incur. Let them water their crops once
more. If there is no harvest, they may take full
compensation from the storehouses.” 
Thus they did, and that year there was such a
harvest that it had no end.
❈
The Qa’an loved to watch wrestling. At first
there were Mongol, Qipchaq, and Cathaian
wrestlers. Then he was told about wrestlers
from Khurasan and Persia. He sent an envoy to
Chormaqan to tell him to send wrestlers. The
champion wrestlers Pila and Muhammadshah,
along with thirty others, were given horses and
provisions and dispatched from Hamadan.
When they reached the Qa’an’s court he was
highly pleased by Pila’s build and physique
and the proportion of his limbs. 
Amir Elji’idäi of the Jalayir tribe was present
and said, “What a shame for the expense of
horses and provisions to have been wasted on
them.”
“You bring your wrestlers for a match with
them,” said the Qa’an. “If they win, we’ll give
you five hundred bars. If they lose, you give us
five hundred horses.” 
If was agreed, and that night the Qa’an sum-
moned Pila, gave him a goblet and told him to
make merry. Pila placed his forehead on the
ground and said, “It is hoped through the for-
tune of the lord and master of the world that
this affair will turn out as he wishes.” [700]
Elji’idäi brought a man from his division
called Orghana Bökä, and at dawn the next day
all assembled.
“The rules are that they have to grab each
other’s legs,” said Elji’idäi, and they started
wrestling. Orghana pinned Pila. 
“Hold me with all the strength you have,”
said Pila, “and don’t let go.” Then he made a
movement, spun Orghana around like a top,
and threw him to the ground so hard that the
cracking of his bones could be heard by all.
The Qa’an jumped up like a lion and said to
Pila, “Hold your opponent tight!”
Then to Elji’idäi he said, “Was he worth the
horses and provisions or not?” And Elji’idäi
was forced to concede the five hundred horses.
In addition to honors and other awards, Pila
was given five hundred bars.
Then he said to Muhammadshah, “Will you
wrestle with Pila?”
“I will,” he said.
“You are fellow townsmen and kinfolk,” the
Qa’an said.
After a time he gave Pila a beautiful girl, but,
as he was accustomed in order to preserve his
strength, he did not touch her. She was mysti-
fied and went to the court. As a joke, the Qa’an
asked, “How did you find the Tajik? Have you
had a full share of his pleasuring?” (Among the
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
339

Mongols it is a standing joke that Tajiks have
huge members.) 
“I haven’t had any pleasure from him yet,”
she said, “because we are apart.”
The Qa’an summoned Pila and discussed the
situation with him.
“Since I have acquired a reputation as a
wrestler at the Qa’an’s court,” he replied, “and
no one has beaten me, if I get into that sort of
thing, my strength will be sapped, but I mustn’t
lose my standing at court.”
“It was my intention that you should have
children,” said the Qa’an. “Henceforth I ex-
empt you from having to wrestle.” [701]
❈
In the province of Anatolia was a man in bad
straits who made his living as a jester. When
the Qa’an’s reputation for liberality spread
throughout the world, this man got the idea of
going there. However, he had neither the provi-
sions for a journey nor a mount. His friends
took up a collection and bought him a donkey,
on which he set out.
Three years later he came back and saw one
of his friends in the marketplace. He got off his
mount, greeted him, and took him to his quar-
ters, where he offered him all sorts of food and
drink. There were gold and silver vessels and
plates, Chinese slaves standing in attendance,
and many horses and camels tied in the stable.
He conversed warmly with his friend, but the
friend couldn’t place him. After three days he
asked who he was.
“I am the jester who departed with one don-
key,” he replied. When the man inquired fur-
ther, he said, “I went on that same donkey as a
beggar before the Qa’an. I had a bit of dried
fruit with me. I sat down on a hill by which he
would pass. From afar his gaze fell upon me.
He sent someone to find out who I was. ‘I have
come from Anatolia because of the Qa’an’s re-
putation for generosity and liberality,’ I replied.
‘I started out with nothing but destitution in or-
der for his felicitous glance to fall upon me and
for my lucky star to rise.’ They presented to the
Qa’an the plate of fruit along with my petition.
He put a few pieces of fruit into a bowl. When
he saw the courtiers’ veiled disapproval, he
said to them, ‘He has come a long way. Before
getting here he must have visited many shrines
and sacred sites and seen many holy men. This
is an opportunity to gain some blessing from
such a person. I took the fruit to take to my
children. You can divide up the rest.’ So say-
ing, he rode off. [702]
“When he dismounted in the ordu, he asked
Danishmand
the
chamberlain
where
the
dervish was staying. 
“ ‘I don’t know,’ said Danishmand. 
“ ‘What kind of Muslim are you,’ he asked,
‘that you don’t know anything about a dervish
who has come to our court from a far-away
place? Go yourself and find him, put him in a
nice place, and see to his every need.’ 
“Now I had settled in the Grand Bazaar, and
they were running around looking for me left
and right. Finally one of them found me and
took me to his house. The next day the Qa’an
was out riding and saw several carts loaded
with bars of gold being taken to the treasury.
There were seven hundred bars. To Danish-
mand the chamberlain he said, ‘Summon that
person.’ When I came before him, he gave me
all those bars and promised me even more.
Thus, from the straits of poverty I fell into the
luxury of wealth.”
❈
A man came from Baghdad and sat by the
roadside. When the Qa’an was passing by, he
asked who he was.
“I am a poor old man,” he said. “I have ten
daughters, but I am too poor to get them
married.”
340
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

“Why doesn’t the caliph give you something
to help you get your daughters married?” he
asked.
“Every time I ask the caliph for alms he
gives me ten dinars in gold,” he replied, “but
that doesn’t last a week.”
The Qa’an ordered that he be given a thou-
sand bars of silver.
“How can I carry so many bars?” he asked.
The Qa’an ordered that he be given a horse and
other necessities.
“The road is long, and there are many tribes
and brigands along the way,” said the man.
“How am I to get these bars back home?”
The Qa’an gave him ten Mongols as escorts
to take him and the money safely back to his
homeland, but the man died along the way.
When the Qa’an was informed he said, “Let
them take the bars to Baghdad and deliver
them to the man’s house, and let them say,
‘The Padishah has sent these as alms [703] in
order to get the girls married.’ ” 
❈
A female relative of the Qa’an’s was being
married, and for her dowry he ordered a chest
of pearls it took eight men to carry. It was
brought to him, but he was in the midst of rev-
elry when it arrived. He ordered the chest
opened, and it contained matchless pearls, each
of which weighed from one mithcal to two
dangs. He gave them all away to those present.
“These were brought as a dowry for the girl,
as you ordered,” he was told.
“Then give her another chest exactly like this
one,” he said.
❈
The Atabeg of Fars sent his brother Taham-
tan to the Qa’an’s court with gifts and presents.
Among the gifts were two strings of extremely
fine pearls. When they were presented he real-
ized how valuable pearls were in the eyes of
the giver. He ordered a long chest full of regal
pearls brought, and the emissary and those
present were astonished by the sight. The
Qa’an ordered that at the banquet those pearls
should be dropped into the wine goblets until
they were all distributed to those present.
❈
There was a Mongol named Minghuli Bökä
who had a ﬂock of sheep. One night a wolf got
in amongst the sheep and killed most of them.
The next day the Mongol went to court and re-
ported what had happened to his ﬂock. 
“Where will the wolf go?” asked the Qa’an.
By chance, just then some Muslim wrestlers
were coming. They had muzzled a live wolf
they had captured in the vicinity and brought it
in. The Qa’an bought the wolf from them for a
thousand bars. Then he said to the Mongol,
“You won’t gain anything by killing this wolf.”
And he ordered that he be given a thousand
sheep. Then he said, “We will set this wolf free
so that he can inform his friends of the situa-
tion, [704] and they will leave this area.” 
When the wolf was turned loose, the dogs at
the gate fell upon it and tore it to pieces. The
Qa’an
was
angered
by
this
and
ordered
vengeance extracted from the dogs for the
wolf. Then he went into the ordu, sad and pen-
sive, and, turning to the ministers and elite, he
said, “The reason I turned the wolf loose was
that I had felt a weakness in my constitution. I
thought that if I saved a living creature from
death,
the
eternal
God
might
grant
me
recovery. Just as the wolf did not escape the
dogs’ clutches neither will I make it through
this pass. It is no secret that kings are raised up
by divine assistance and they have inspirations
so that they may know things.”
❈
Now that a few lines have been written about
the Qa’an’s generosity, liberality, clemency,
and forgiving nature, for which the Necessarily
Existent singled him out so all may know that
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOUR: ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN
341

in the world there is no characteristic better
than the acquisition of a good name, for after
many years he is still remembered by the peo-
ple of the world for his beneficence and
justice—
Sa‘di, a soul with a good repute never dies.
Dead is he who is not remembered for good
—let us also now record an anecdote about his
punishment, awesomeness, and might so that
all may be fully informed of both aspects upon
which world rule are based. [705]
A story of his policy.
Once it was rumored among the Oyirat, one
of the Mongol tribes, that their daughters were
going to be given in marriage by imperial com-
mand to a certain group of people. Out of fear
they affianced their daughters amongst them-
selves and delivered several of them to their
husbands. When this was reported to the
Qa’an, he ordered an investigation and it was
found to be as stated. A decree was issued that
all the girls of that tribe above the age of seven
be assembled, and those who had been given to
husbands that year were to be taken back. Four
thousand girls were assembled.
Then he ordered those who were daughters
of amirs to be separated, and a command was
given for all present to have intercourse with
them. Two of the girls died. The rest were put
into two rows. Those who were worthy of
court were sent to the harem; some he gave to
cheetah keepers and falconers; others he gave
to various court retainers; and a few he sent to
brothels and the emissary hostel. Those who
remained he ordered the Mongols and Muslims
present to seize, while their fathers, brothers,
husbands, and relatives stood watching, no one
daring to speak.
❈
The Qa’an awarded the entirety of the realm
of Cathay to Sahib Mahmud Yalavach. From
Beshbaliq and Qara Khocho in Uyghuristan,
Khotan,
Kashghar,
Almalyk,
Qayaliq,
Samarkand, and Bukhara as far as the banks of
the Oxus went to Mas‘ud Beg, Yalavach’s son.
From Khurasan to the frontier of Anatolia and
Diyarbekir he awarded to Amir Görgüz. They
gathered the revenue from all these places and
sent it to the Qa’an’s treasury.
❈
End of anecdotes on Ögödäi Qa’an son of
Genghis Khan. [706]
342
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

❦ SECTION FIVE
THE HISTORY OF JOCHI KHAN, SON OF GENGHIS KHAN, CONSISTING OF
THREE PARTS.
Part One is on Jochi Khan’s family, his
wives, sons, and grandsons who have branched
off down to today; a picture of him, and a ge-
nealogical chart of his sons and grandsons. 
Part Two is the history of his reign, a picture
of his throne and his wives, princes, and offi-
cers at his enthronement; a mention of his sum-
mer pastures and winter quarters; some of the
battles he fought and the victories he achieved;
the length of his reign.
Part Three is on his character, miscellaneous
stories, various pronouncements and good say-
ings of his not included in the previous two
sections, culled from various books and per-
sons. [708]
Part One. The family of Jochi Khan, his
wives, sons, and grandsons who have
branched off down to today; a picture of
him and a genealogical chart of his sons and
grandsons.
With the exception of his elder sister Füjin
Beki, Jochi Khan was the oldest of Genghis
Khan’s children. He was born of Genghis
Khan’s chief wife, Börtä Füjin, the daughter of
Däi Noyan of the Qunqirat who was the moth-
er of four sons and five daughters.
In the beginning, before Genghis Khan had
achieved the status of world conqueror, his
pregnant wife was carried off by a tribe that
was then on terms of truce with Ong Khan of
the Kerayit, although they had been at enmity
prior to that. Because of their status then, they
sent Börtä Füjin to Ong Khan. Inasmuch as he
had been friends with Genghis Khan’s father
and called Genghis Khan “son,” he held her in
honor and respect and gave her status as a
daughter-in-law to preserve her from the gaze
of strangers and non-intimates. Because she
was
extremely
pure
and
competent,
Ong
Khan’s amirs asked one another why Ong
Khan didn’t take Börtä Füjin. “She is like my
own daughter-in-law,” he replied, “and she is
in my safe keeping. To look upon her with
treachery would not be chivalrous.” [709]
When Genghis Khan learned what had hap-
pened, he sent an amir of the Ongqa’ut of the
Jalayir, Säbä by name (the grandfather of the
Sartaq
who
served
as
the
amir-ordu
in
Khurasan and Mazanderan during Arghun
Khan’s childhood by order of Abaqa Khan), to
Ong Khan to ask for the return of Börtä Füjin.
Ong Khan responded by sending her with
Säbä, and along the way home a son was born
unexpectedly, for which reason he was named
Jochi.1 Since the road was dangerous and there
was no opportunity to make a cradle, Säbä
made a bit of dough, wrapped the child in it,
and took it on his lap to protect it from harm
until he delivered them to Genghis Khan.
When he grew up, Jochi was always in his
father’s service and helpful in good times and
bad. There were, however, constant obstinacy,
bickering, and disagreements between him and
his brothers Chaghatai and Ögödäi. On the oth-
er hand, there was always agreement between
him and Tolui Khan and his family, who never
1See note to text p. 299.

taunted him but considered him legitimate.1
During his youth Jochi Khan married Jagam-
bu’s daughter, Begtutmish Füjin, the sister of
both Genghis Khan’s wife Ibaqa Beki and
Sorqaghtani Beki, the wife of Tolui Khan. She
was Jochi Khan’s chief wife, but aside from
her he had many wives and concubines by
whom he had many children.
Reliable sources say that he had nearly forty
sons and innumerable grandsons; however, be-
cause of the vast distances and because no real-
ly informed person could be located, most of
the lines have not been ascertained. [710]
Those of his sons and grandsons who are
known will now be given in detail.
Jochi Khan’s sons and grandsons who have
been born down to the present.
Those of Jochi Khan’s sons whose names are
known number fourteen, as follows: (1) Orda,
(2) Batu, (3) Bärkä, (4) Bärkächär, (5) Shiban,
(6) Tangqut, (7) Bo’al, (8) Chila’uqun, (9)
Shingqor, (10) Chimbai, (11) Muhammad, (12)
Udur, (13) Toqa Temür, and (14) Shinggüm.
Jochi Khan’s first son, Orda.
He was born of a great lady, Sorqan by name,
of the Qunqirat tribe. During his father’s life-
time and after his death he was of great impor-
tance and influence. Although Jochi Khan’s
successor was the second son, Batu, in decrees
written by Möngkä Qa’an, Orda’s name has
precedence. Orda gave his consent to Batu’s
becoming ruler and seated him on his father’s
throne. Orda commanded half of Jochi Khan’s
troops, and Batu commanded the other half.
He, his troops, and four of his brothers, Udur,
Toqa Temür, Shingqor, and Shinggüm, went to
the left wing, and until now they are called the
Princes of the Left Wing. At present their fami-
1This is the only place in the Jami‘u’t-tawarikh where
the imputation of illegitimacy is expressed.
lies are together with Orda’s family. [711] The
yurt that belongs to him and to those brothers
and their troops is toward the left on the fron-
tier, where his sons and ulus live as before.
From the beginning none of Orda’s offspring
who succeeded him ever went before the khans
of Batu’s family because they were so far away
and ruled their ulus in autonomy. However, it
has been their custom that their ruler and king
should recognize Batu’s successors and write
their names at the top of their decrees.
Qonchi’s son Nayan,2 who is the ruler of
Orda’s ulus at present, went to Toqta, the ruler
of the Ulus Batu, for a quriltai because his
cousin Küilük had rebelled against him and he
was frightened into going to the frontier of
Toqta’s territory, as will be described later.
Orda had three main wives, Jükä Khatun of
the Qunqirat; Tobaqana, also of the Qunqirat;
and the third was also of the Qunqirat—her fa-
ther’s name was Ögä Khan, and he married her
after his father’s death. He also had many con-
cubines. By these wives he had seven sons:
Sartaqtai, Quli, Qurumshi, Qongqiran, Chor-
maqai, Qutuqui, and Hülägü. These seven sons
and their sons and grandsons will now be de-
scribed one by one. [712]
(1) Orda’s first son, Sartaghtai, was born of
Jükä Khatun of the Qunqirat. He had four main
wives and several concubines. By a wife
named Hujan, who was the sister of Hülägü
Khan’s wife Qutui Khatun, he had a son named
Qonchi.3 He ruled the Ulus Orda for a very
2In the text, “Bayan.” See note to text p. 712.

which seems to reflect Qoyunchi. It is sometimes

Qonichi (andﻮــﻗ

ــ ــ ــ
ﯽis most likely simply a misdotted

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

long time, and he was friendly to and support-
ive of Arghun Khan and then of the Padishah
of Islam, and they constantly exchanged am-
bassadors to reaffirm their sincere friendship.
[Qonchi] was very fat and rotund, and day by
day he grew fatter. Finally it got so bad that his
guards had to watch him day and night lest he
fall asleep and die from the rolls of fat around
his neck. He was so huge that no horse could
carry him, so he travelled in a cart. Finally he
fell asleep, and the fat from around his neck
came out and he died.
Qonchi had four main wives. The first was
Toqoluqan of the Qunqirat; the second was
Buqulun of the Märkit; the third was Chingtüm
of the Qunqirat; and the fourth was Barqujin of
the Jäjirät, descended from a great amir who
was the chief of Chaghatai’s qorchis.
Qonchi had four sons, Nayan, Bachqirtai,
Chaghan Buqa, and Maqudai. These four sons
and their sons and grandsons are as follows.
(i) Qonchi’s first son, Nayan,1 was born of
Toquluqan Khatun of the Qunqirat. [713] After
his father’s death he married three of his step-
mothers, Barqujin, Chingtüm, and Toqoluqan,
and he had three other wives, (1) Elgän of the
Qunqirat, daughter of Mögä of the line of the
emissary Käläs who came here, (2) Qutulun of
version ofﯽ ــ ـﻧﻴﭽﻮـﻗ); if it is Turkish it should be either Qoy-
chi or Qoyunchi. Marco Polo calls him “Conci” (for
Qonchi): “Jn tramontana quidem est quidam rex nomine
conci qui est tartarus & omnes eius gentes tartare sunt
& manutenet rectam legem tartarorum qua multum bes-
tialis est” (Marco Polo, Description 2:119). Pelliot
(Marco Polo 1:404) thinks that Marco Polo’s “Conci”
may have actually been Conici for the full Mongolian
form, Qonichi; but since the second vowel could easily
have been elided early on, we will standardize the name
throughout as Qonchi.
1Nayan (.-ن) ~ Bayan (/-ن): both spellings occur fre-
quently. Bayan is a much more common name, but
Nayan occurs more frequently in the manuscripts.
the Oghuz, daughter of Buqayan Tügütai, and
(3) Altachu of the Qunqirat, daughter of the
Tödäi Bahadur who was a relative of the great
princess Bulughan Khatun. Nayan had four
sons, (1) Shadi by Elgän daughter of Mögä, (2)
Sati Buqa by Qutulun Khatun, (3) Tägänä by
Altachu Khatun, and (4) Saljiqutai, whose
mother’s name is not known. 
At
present
Nayan
occupies
his
father
Qonchi’s position and commands his father’s
ulus. He is friendly to and supportive of the
Padishah of Islam and constantly sends emis-
saries. Before now Temür Buqa’s son Küilük
claimed that since his father had ruled the ulus,
it should have gone to him by inheritance. He
gathered a force and took troops from Qaidu
and Dua with which he attacked Nayan. Nayan
was defeated and went to the frontier of the
territory occupied by Batu’s successor Toqta.
After spending the winter there he went before
Toqta at a quriltai in the spring and asked him
for assistance. Since Toqta was at war with No-
qai and on bad terms with the Padishah of Is-
lam, he made excuses and gave him no troops;
however, he sent emissaries to Qaidu and Dua
to send him Küilük, and he issued a decree that
Nayan should command the ulus as before.
Until the present Nayan has fought anywhere
eighteen battles with Küilük and Qaidu’s and
Dua’s troops. [714] Six times he has ridden to
battle himself, and no matter how many envoys
Toqta sends to Qaidu’s son Chapar and to Dua
to send Küilük, they do not respond and just
make excuses. They think to themselves, “Let
us assist Küilük so that he may become ruler of
the ulus and then unite with us in our dispute
with Ghazan Khan.”
Last year, which was 702 [1302–3], Nayan
sent ambassadors to the Padishah of Islam
headed by Käläs of the Qunqirat, who was an
amir during Qonchi’s time, and Tuq Temür of
the Besüt. These two, and other liege men too,
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIVE: JOCHI KHAN
345

were received by the Padishah of Islam in
Baghdad around the beginning of Jumada ii
last year [February 1303], and they presented
falcons and a letter, the contents of which were
as follows. “It is begged that you always send
emissaries with good news and wait until the
commanders mount in any direction ordered
and perform valiantly. We this year have
mounted against Chapar, and Toqta is at one
with us, having promised to send troops.” And
[Toqta] did send twenty thousand to join the
Qa’an’s forces at Däräsü inasmuch as at the
frontier of their territory the Qa’an’s territory is
near, indeed formerly they were contiguous. In
the last several years Qaidu, imagining that
they might possibly join the Qa’an’s forces,
sent his second son Yangichar and his son Shah
along with Tödä Temür (the son of Möngkä
Qa’an’s son Shirägi) and Ariq Bökä’s son Ma-
lik Temür to the frontier of Nayan’s territory
and turned that area over to them so that they
might act as a buffer between the Qa’an’s
troops and Nayan’s forces and not allow them
to join. Küilük came to his assistance on
Qaidu’s and Dua’s behalf with the troops that
had deserted Nayan and seized some of
Nayan’s territory and ulus, although Nayan
commands most of Orda’s ulus by succession,
[715] but on account of these constant battles
his forces have become impoverished, some
mounted and some on foot, but they fight
nonetheless with a powerful enemy and ask for
monetary assistance from here. From Tabriz
the Padishah of Islam sent back the emissaries
who came to him in Baghdad and dispatched
with them gold, clothing, and letters for him
and his wives.
(ii) Qonchi’s second son, Bachqirtai, was
born of Buqulun Khatun of the Märkit. He had
a wife named Kökälün of the Kerayit, and he
had by her a son named Yeratai. 
(iii) Qonchi’s third son, Chaghan Buqa, was
born of Chingtüm Khatun, who has been men-
tioned. He had a wife named Sürmish of the
Kerayit, the daughter of Qosh Temür, and by
her he had a son named Täkä.
(iv) Qonchi’s fourth son, Maqudai, was born
of Barqujin Khatun of the Jajirat. He had no
sons.
End of the branch of Orda’s first son,
Sartaghtai, the father of Qonchi. [716] ❧
(2) Orda’s second son, Quli. He is the one
who was sent with troops from Orda’s ulus
when Hülägü Khan came to Iran and a prince
from every direction was ordered to join him
with auxiliary troops. He entered [Iran] from
Khwarazm through Dehistan and Mazanderan.
He
had
several
major
wives:
one
was
Nändikän
of
the
Qunqirat;
another
was
Qadaqan of the ___ tribe; another was Köktäni,
and she came here and died in this realm. He
had five sons: Tümgän, Tümän, Mingqan, Ay-
achi, and Musalman. Each of these and their
branches will now be mentioned. 
(a) Quli’s first son, Tümgän, had three major
wives, Bulaghan of the Tatar, the daughter of
Soghal Noyan, Boralun Khatun, and ___ of the
___ tribe. Öljäi was a concubine. He had three
sons, (i) Charuq, who had a wife named Yau
Qorichaq; by her he had two sons, Noqai and
Satalmish; (ii) Mubarak, born of the Boralun
Khatun mentioned above; he had two sons, El
Buqa and Törä Temür; (iii) Küchük, born of
the concubine Öljäi. [717]
(b) Quli’s second son, Tümän, was born of
Nändikän Khatun. He had several wives and
concubines. His chief wife was named Bo-
ralun. He had seven sons: (i) Aq Köpäk, who
had a son named Boralqi, (ii) Danishmand, (iii)
Qurtaqachi, (iv) Qutlugh Buqa, (v) Qutluq
Temür, (vi) El Temür, and (vii) Yaylaq. The lat-
ter six had no sons. The names of the mothers
346
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

of Aq Köpäk, Danishmand, Qurtqachi, and
Qutluq Temür are unknown. Qutluq Buqa was
born of Boralun, and El Temür was by a
concubine.
(c) Quli’s third son, Mingqan, was born of
___ Khatun, and he had many wives and con-
cubines, but their names are not known. He
had three sons: (i) Khalil, who had no sons, (ii)
Bashmaq, who had one son named Hasan, and
(iii) Olqutuq, who had no sons.
(d) Quli’s fourth son, Ayachi. His wives’
names are not known. He had one son named
Ghazan by the daughter of Görgüz’s son Qut-
lugh Buqa. Ayachi came here as a child, and
during Abaqa Khan’s time he was in Khurasan
with Arghun Khan. After being rewarded he
and [718] his son were sent back with mes-
sages of friendship and advice to his ulus.
(e) Quli’s fifth son, Musalman, was born of
Qadaqan Khatun. He had many wives, one of
whom was Orda Tegin of the Naiman. He had
four sons: Ja’utu, Yaylaq, Khwaja, and Ilyas,
born of Orda Tegin.
End of the branch of Orda’s second son,
Quli. ❧
(3) Orda’s third son, Qurumshi, had no sons,
and his wives’ names are not known. 
(4) Orda’s fourth son, Qongqiran, command-
ed the ulus after Orda’s death. He had no sons.
(5) Orda’s fifth son, Chormaqai, had no sons,
and his wives’ names are unknown.
(6) Orda’s sixth son, Qutuqui. It is not known
whether he had sons or not. [719]
(7) Orda’s seventh son, Hülägü, had two
chief wives, Soluqun Khatun of the ___ tribe
and Qoyarchin of the Qipchaq. By them he had
two sons, Temür Buqa and Olqutu. 
(a) Hülägü’s first son, Temür Buqa, had four
major wives, Kökächin, daughter of Yesün
Noyan of the Qungirat; Arghun Tegin of the
Arghun tribe, daughter of Qori Qochghar;
Qutuchin of the ___ tribe; and Bayalun of the
Qunqirat, sister of Qutui Khatun, Hülägü
Khan’s wife. Aside from these he had many
concubines. By the wives he had six sons,
(i) Küilük by Kökächin, (ii) Toqa Temür by
Arghun Tegin, (iii) Changqut by Qutuchin,
(iv) Buqa Temür by Bayalun, (v) Saisi, also by
Qutuchin, and (vi) Ushanan, also by Kökächin.
(b) Hülägü’s second son, Olqutu, was born of
Qoyarchin. He had four sons: Üch Qurtqa,
Besh Qurtqa, Buqa Temür, and Däräk.
End of the branch of Jochi Khan’s first son,
Orda. [720] ❧
Jochi Khan’s second son, Batu.
He was born of Öki Füjin Khatun, the daugh-
ter of Elchi Noyan of the Qunqirat. He was
called Sayin Khan [the good khan1] and was
highly influential and powerful. He ruled the
ulus and army in Jochi Khan’s stead and lived
a long life. When Genghis Khan’s four sons
were all dead, he was the eldest of all the
grandsons and was highly respected by them.
In quriltais no one could go against his word,
and all the princes obeyed him. Genghis Khan
had earlier ordered Jochi to go with the army,
take and bring under control all the lands to the
north, from Ibir-Sibir, Bolad, the Qipchaq
Steppe, Bashghurd, Rus, and Circassia to the
Caspian Straits, which the Mongols call Temür
Qahalqa, but Jochi had retired. When Ögödäi
Qa’an was enthroned as emperor, he ordered
Batu to take over, and he assigned his nephew
Mänggü Qa’an, his brother Böchök, and his
son Güyük Khan to go with great commanders
like Sübätäi Bahadur, the general from the Uri-
angqat who came to this realm with Jäbä, to
join Batu and complete the conquest of the
north. In Bechin Yil, the Year of the Monkey
that began in Jumada ii 633 [February 1236],

they set out and conquered most of those ter-
ritories. In the spring of Quluqana Yil, the Year
of the Rat corresponding to 637 [1240], Güyük
Khan and Möngkä Qa’an returned to the Qa’an
by his order. For some time after that Batu and
his brothers and generals continued to conquer
those territories, as his offspring still do. [721]
Batu had many wives and concubines, and he
had four sons, Sartaq, Toqoqan, Äbügän, and
Ulaghchi.

(2) Batu’s second son, Toqoqan, had ﬁve

had wives and concubines. The names of his

TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIVE: JOCHI KHAN
351

352
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Part Two of the history of Jochi Khan. The history of his reign, a picture of his throne and
his wives, princes, and officers at his enthronement; a mention of his summer pastures and
winter quarters; some of the battles he fought and the victories he achieved; the length of
his reign.
Genghis Khan, having bestowed upon Jochi
Khan all the territory and peoples in the area of
the Irtysh River and the Altai mountains, along
with the summer and winter pastures of that
area, issued a command that he conquer and
bring into subjugation the Qipchaq Steppe and
the realms in that direction. His yurt was in the
vicinity of the Irtysh, and there was the loca-
tion of his throne.
A summary account of Jochi Khan.
Since Jochi Khan predeceased his father, the
stories that pertain to him separately cannot be
given in a separate section, and therefore a
summary account of his history that was in-
cluded in the section on Genghis Khan will be
written here, and his illness and death will be
reported.
At Genghis Khan’s order, Jochi Khan was
continually mounted on expeditions, [732] and
he conquered many lands and territories. When
Genghis Khan set out on campaign for Tajik
lands and reached the area of Otrar, he as-
signed Jochi Khan to conquer Otrar and sta-
tioned him there. As has been said in the histo-
ry
of
Genghis
Khan,
Jochi
took
Otrar,
destroyed the fortress, and returned, conquer-
ing the territories that lay on his path until he
rejoined his father in the vicinity of Samar-
kand.
Once again Genghis Khan sent him out, this
time with his brothers Chaghatai and Ögödäi,
to conquer Khwarazm. Because of his inability
to agree with Chaghatai, the conquest was not
possible. Genghis Khan ordered Ögödäi to lead
the assault. He cleverly made peace between
his two brothers, and together they took
Khwarazm. Chaghatai and Ögödäi set out to
rejoin their father in the fortress at Taligan, and
Jochi left Khwarazm and headed for the Irtysh,
where his aghruq was, to rejoin his camps. Pri-
or to that, Genghis Khan had ordered Jochi to
conquer the northern territories like Bular,1
Bashghurd,
Rus,
Circassia,
the
Qipchaq
Steppe, and other areas. When he excused him-
self from that labor and returned to his own
tents, Genghis Khan was extremely angry and
said, “I will subject him to the Yasa without
seeing what was in his mind.”
Jochi was afflicted with an illness, and there-
fore, when his father returned from the lands of
the Tajiks and settled in his homeland, he was
unable to attend him. He sent several loads of
prey and apologized. Several times thereafter
Genghis Khan ordered him to present himself,
but he was too ill to come and sent apologies.
[733] After that, someone from the Mangqut
tribe was passing by Jochi’s yurts, among
which Jochi was moving and proceeding, al-
though ill. Coming to a mountain that was his
hunting preserve, Jochi sent his amirs out to
hunt even though he himself was too weak to
participate. When the passer-by saw the assem-
blage hunting, he thought it was Jochi, and
when he came to Genghis Khan and was asked
about Jochi’s illness, he reported, “I know
nothing of his illness, but at such-and-such a
mountain he was busy hunting.” At these
words the ﬂames of Genghis Khan’s wrath
blazed, for he imagined that Jochi had rebelled
and
was
disregarding
his
father’s
orders.
“Jochi has gone mad,” he said, “to do such
things.” He ordered the army to mount and
1In JTRM, “Kilar.”
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIVE: JOCHI KHAN
353

proceed
in
the
direction
of
Jochi,
with
Chaghatai and Ögödäi in the lead while he
himself followed behind. Just at this time news
of Jochi’s death arrived, and Genghis Khan
was sorely grief-stricken. When the matter was
investigated, the report was proven false and it
was established that Jochi had been ill at the
time and not on the hunting field. The man was
summoned to be executed, but he couldn’t be
located.
Trustworthy emissaries who have come at
various times from his ulus have reported that
Jochi’s death occurred between his thirtieth
and fortieth years, and this is in consonance
with analogy, for some say that he died at the
age of twenty, but that is an obvious error. Af-
ter his death and that of Genghis Khan, when
Ögödäi Qa’an mounted the throne, in accor-
dance with Genghis Khan’s order that had pre-
viously been issued concerning Jochi Khan, his
offspring were granted the conquest of the
northern lands, and they, with the help of other
princes, occupied themselves with that. [734]
The accession of Batu as his father’s
successor, and the history of his reign.
When Jochi Khan died, his second son, Batu,
succeeded him on the throne of his ulus, and
his brothers all obeyed him. During Ögödäi
Qa’an’s reign, as has already been mentioned
and explained, he and his brothers were nom-
inated, along with other princes, by prior com-
mand, to conquer the northern territories. They
all gathered around him, mounted together,
and, as has been mentioned, took most of those
areas. 
After the return of the princes Möngkä Qa’an
and Güyük Khan, he and his brothers, as has
also mentioned at the end of the section on
him, occupied themselves with conquering the
remaining territories. In the first part of the
year 637 [1239], when Ögödäi Qa’an died,
Batu was already suffering from flaccidity be-
cause of old age, and when he was summoned
to a quriltai, he excused himself on that ac-
count. Because of his absence, however, he be-
ing the eldest of all, the matter of the Qa’anate
was undecided for nearly three years, during
which time the eldest of Ögödäi Qa’an’s wives,
Törägänä Khatun, ruled. It was during that
time that disturbances and chaos befell both
the periphery and the center of the empire.
The Qa’an had made his grandson Shirämün
his designated heir, but Törägänä Khatun and
some of the amirs withheld their consent, say-
ing that Güyük Khan was older. In order to en-
throne him they summoned Batu once again,
and although he had been insulted several
times by them and was fearful of disastrous
consequences from past actions, he nonetheless
set forth and proceeded slowly. Before he and
the other brethren arrived, however, they went
ahead on their own and enthroned Güyük
Khan. Since Güyük Khan suffered from chron-
ic illnesses, [735] he took his troops and set out
for the Imil-Qojin area, claiming that the cli-
mate in the old yurt his father had given him
agreed with him. When Batu got near there, his
fear increased.
Sorqaghtani Beki, Tolui Khan’s chief wife,
sent him a secret message because of the spe-
cial friendship that had been maintained be-
tween Jochi Khan and Tolui Khan from
Genghis Khan’s time on. In the message she
said, “Güyük Khan’s coming to that area is not
devoid of deceit.” Therefore Batu’s trepidation
increased and he waited for Güyük Khan’s
arrival with guarded precaution. When Güyük
reached the vicinity of Samarqand,1 he died of
1Not the city Samarkand, but another place, the name
of which derives from Qum Sangar, or Sangar Qum. It
was located “somewhere along the upper course of the
Uruungu, probably at the point where it ceases to ﬂow
from North to South and makes a sharp turn to the West”
354
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

his illnesses in a place that is a one-week jour-
ney from Beshbaliq—and that was in the year
64[5] [1248]. Once again the emperor’s throne
remained vacant for a time, and Törägänä
Khatun ruled.
When news of [Batu’s] illness was spread,
Sorqaghtani Beki had sent her son Möngkä
Qa’an to him. Batu was overjoyed by his
arrival, and since he noticed signs of majesty
and cultivation in him, and also since he had
been insulted by Ögödäi Qa’an’s sons, he said,
“Möngkä is Tolui Khan’s eldest son, and Tolui
Khan was Genghis Khan’s youngest son, who
commanded his ancient yurt and home. This
son is exceptionally competent, skilled, and
able to rule. While he lives, how can another
become emperor? Particularly when Ögödäi
Qa’an’s sons went against their father’s order
by refusing to enthrone Shirämün. They also
broke the ancient Yasa and Yosun, for, without
consulting their brethren, they put to death
Genghis Khan’s guiltless daughter, the one he
loved the most of all his children and whose
husband he called Cha’ur Sächän.1 For this
reason the emperorship should not go to them.”
So saying, he himself raised Möngkä to the
emperorship [736] and had all his brothers,
kinsmen, and amirs render him obeisance. He
also sent his brother Bärkä and his son Sartaq,
who was his designated heir, along with three
tümäns of troops to escort Möngkä back to the
Onon-Kerulen region, Genghis Khan’s original
yurt, and seat him upon the throne, where they
would deal with the plots and machinations of
Ögödäi Qa’an’s sons, who had contemplated
treachery.
In short, the transfer of the emperorship to
the House of Tolui Khan and the giving of
right where it was due were on account of
(JTBy, 121, note 95).
1See text p. 302.
Sorqaghtani
Beki’s
cleverness
and
Batu’s
friendly assistance. After that, until the end of
his life—and even after his death, during the
time of Sartaq and Ulaghchi and during most
of Bärkä’s time—there was unanimity and
friendship between Tolui Khan’s and Batu’s
progeny. 
It was during Batu’s lifetime that Möngkä
Qa’an dispatched his third brother, Hülägü
Khan, with troops to Iran, and on the part of
every prince two out of every ten were ap-
pointed to go with Hülägü Khan and help him.
Orda sent his eldest son, Quli, with a tümän of
soldiers via Khwarazm and Dehistan, and Batu
sent Shiban’s son Balaqan and Tutar, the son of
Mingqadur, the son of Jochi Khan’s seventh
son, Bo’al, via the Qipchaq Straits. They came
and assisted Hülägü Khan’s troops and fought
valiantly.
Batu died in 650 [1252–53] in Sarai on the
banks of the Volga at the age of forty-eight.
Möngkä Qa’an welcomed his son Sartaq, set-
tled the throne and realm upon him, and gave
him permission to withdraw. Along the way
home he too died, so Möngkä Qa’an sent emis-
saries to console his wives, sons, and brothers.
He enthroned Batu’s grandson Ulaghchi [737]
and rewarded everyone with shows of favor.
Ulaghchi also died shortly thereafter, leaving
the throne and realm to others. [738]
Bärkä rules the Ulus Jochi, and what
happened during that time.
When Batu passed away and his sons Sartaq
and Ulaghchi who succeeded him also died,
Batu’s younger brother Bärkä succeeded. His
command became effective throughout the
ulus in the year 652 [1254], and he continued
to tread the path of friendship and amity with
Tolui Khan’s progeny. 
In the year 654 [1256] Balaqan, who was in
this land, plotted treachery against Hülägü
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIVE: JOCHI KHAN
355

Khan and practiced sorcery.1 An ayghaq (infor-
mant) came forward, and he was put on trial.
He confessed, and therefore Hülägü Khan, in
order that no insult be engendered, sent him in
the company of Amir Su’unchaq to Bärkä.
When they arrived and his guilt was proven,
Bärkä sent him back to Hülägü with this mes-
sage, “He is guilty. Do with him as you will.”
Hülägü Khan had him executed.
Shortly thereafter Tutar and Quli also died.
An accusation was made that they had been
poisoned, and this caused an estrangement be-
tween Bärkä and Hülägü. Bärkä rebelled
against Hülägü and, as will be mentioned in
the section on Hülägü, they did battle in
Shawwal 660 [August 1262]. The troops that
had come to this land with Quli and Tutar
mostly took flight, some going to Khurasan
and seizing the mountains of Ghazna and Bini-
i-Gav as far as Multan and [739] Lahore, the
frontier of Hindustan. Their main commander
was Negüdär. Ötägü China and some of
Hülägü Khan’s amirs went out in pursuit of
them, while others went home via Derbent.
The feud between Bärkä and Hülägü lasted
throughout their lives. Bärkä’s commander-in-
chief was Noqai, the son of Tatar and grandson
of Prince Boqal. He was exceptionally brave
and heroic in battle. When Hülägü Khan died
in his winter quarters in Jaqatu in 663 [1264]
and his son Abaqa Khan assumed the throne in
his stead, the enmity between Bärkä and him
continued uninterrupted.
In the year 663 [1264] Bärkä returned from
battle with Abaqa Khan in the Shirvan area,
and after passing through Derbent he died near
the Terek River in 664 [1265–66]. [740]
Möngkä Temür, son of Batu’s second son,
1See text p. 1034 (Balaqan ~ Balagha). The account
there is at some variance with the version given here.
Toqoqan, assumes the rule of his ulus.
When Bärkä died, Möngkä Temür was en-
throned. He too was in conflict with Abaqa
Khan for a time, and they fought several bat-
tles in which Abaqa Khan gained the upper
hand. In the end, they were forced to sue for
peace in 66_,2 as will be narrated in the section
on Abaqa Khan. From that time on, he ceased
hostilities until the reign of Arghun Khan,
when in Ramadan of 687 [October 1288] he
came once again with a large army under the
command of Tamma Toqtai.3 Arghun Khan had
set out from his winter quarters in Arran for his
summer pastures, but he turned back when he
heard the news of their arrival and sent his of-
ficers out in the vanguard with troops. Battle
was fought, and many of the leaders of the
armies were killed, while those who remained
took flight. 
From that time until the present, which is the
blessed time of the Padishah of Islam, they
have not engaged in hostilities and have per-
force chosen peaceful co-existence over con-
flict. Outwardly they claim friendship and ami-
ty and constantly sent ambassadors bearing
gifts and news to the Padishah of Islam. [741]
The accession of Tödä Möngkä, Möngkä
Temür’s brother; his dethronement by Tölä
Buqa and Könchäk and their joint rule;
Toqta flees from them and then kills them
by guile with Noqai’s assistance.
After Möngkä Temür had ruled for sixteen
years and died in the year 681 [1282–83], Tödä
Möngkä, Toqoqan’s third son, assumed the
throne that same year and ruled for a time. Af-
ter him, Möngkä Temür’s sons Alghui and
Toghril[cha] and the sons of Toqoqan’s eldest
son Tartu, Tölä Buqa and Könchäk, deposed
2According to the narrative on text p. 1068, the date
should be 667. Möngkä Temür ~ Mänggü Temür.
3See text p. 1163.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

him, claiming he was insane, and ruled jointly
for five years. Möngkä Temür’s son Toqta was
the son of Öljäi Khatun and thus a grandson of
Kälmish Aqa Khatun. When they recognized
signs of bravery and manliness in him, they
conspired to assassinate him. He, however,
learned of it, escaped from them, and took
refuge with Yilqichi, a [grand]son of Bärkä-
chär’s. 
To Noqai, who had been Batu’s and Bärkä’s
commander-in-chief, he sent a message, say-
ing, “My cousins are attempting to kill me.
You are the elder, so I take refuge with you to
keep them from harming me. As long as I am
alive I am subject to my elder brother’s com-
mand and will never do anything to earn your
displeasure.” When Noqai learned of the affair,
his zeal was stirred and he set out from the ter-
ritory of the Rus, the Vlachs,1 and the Poles,
which he had conquered and made his yurt,
[742] feigning illness. He crossed the Uzi
[Dnieper] River, and, placating every hazara
and amir he came across, he said, “Old age has
set in, and I have abandoned conflict, fighting,
and disputes. I have neither intention of con-
tending with anyone nor thought of doing bat-
tle. However, we have been commanded by
Genghis Khan that if anyone in his ulus or
urugh goes astray and upsets the ulus, we must
investigate and make them content to agree.”
The troops and soldiers, listening to his ad-
vice and realizing that he was genuinely con-
cerned on their behalf, all swore allegiance to
him. When he was near the camp of the above-
mentioned princes, he made himself appear ill

by

dissimulation, although in secret he had sent a
