When you are informed, come with what
troops you have on hand.”
Tölä Buqa’s mother, having heard that Noqai
was weak and in ill health and that he was
coughing up blood, charged her sons, saying,
“Go as fast as possible and meet that weak old
man who is about to depart this life for the
hereafter. If you do not, your mother’s milk
will be forbidden to you.” Abandoning all pre-
caution, they acted upon their mother’s words
and went to visit the sick Noqai, who spoke to
them as an advisor, saying, “My sons, I served
your fathers and am due debts of gratitude
from long ago and from more recently. There-
fore you must listen to me, for I have no ulteri-
or motive. Let me turn your hostility into true
agreement. Your best course of action lies in
peace. Hold a quriltai so that I may make
peace among you.” All the while he was
coughing up congealed blood.
While keeping the princes off guard with this
smooth talk, [743] he sent word to Toqta, who
arrived without warning with several hazaras,
seized the princes, and killed them on the spot.
Noqai pulled out at once, crossed the Volga,
and headed for his home yurt. [744]
Toqta assumes the rule of his ulus; hostilities
break out between him and Noqai; they do
battle, and Noqai is killed.
After Toqta had killed the above-mentioned
princes with Noqai’s assistance and consolidat-
ed his position in autonomy on Jochi’s throne,
he sent one emissary after another to Noqai to
summon him with promises of good things to
come. Noqai refused to respond. 
Toqta’s father-in-law, Salji’udai Gürägän of
the Qunqirat, who was married to Kälmish Aqa
Khatun, had requested Noqai’s daughter Qiyan
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIVE: JOCHI KHAN
357

in marriage to his son Yaylaq, who had been
born of that lady.1 Noqai had agreed. Sometime
after the marriage rites were completed, Qiyan
Khatun became a Muslim, and since Yaylaq
was an Uyghur, they could not get along and
constantly fought over religion and beliefs.
When Qiyan was subjected to contempt, she
sent a message to her father, mother, and broth-
ers. Noqai was highly insulted and sent an
emissary to Toqta with a message, saying, “All
the world knows how much trouble I went to,
making myself known for faithlessness and
breach of promise, in order to obtain Sayin
Khan’s throne for you through treachery. Now
Salji’udai Gürägän rules on that throne! If my
son Toqta wishes the father-son relationship to
continue between us, let him send Salji’udai
Gürägän back to his own yurt,” [745] which
was near Khwarazm. Toqta refused to comply,
and once again Noqai sent an emissary asking
that Salji’udai be sent. Toqta said, “He is like a
father to me, a nurturer and an officer. How
can I give him into the hands of an enemy?”
And he refused to turn him over.

of discord and enmity broke out between the
two sides. Toqta assembled his troops, and in

and camped for the summer on the banks of
the Don.
The next year Noqai crossed the Don with
his sons and wives and started his trickery once
again by saying, “I am going for a quriltai in

he had only a few with him, he hastened as fast

ma Toqta, Balagha [Balaqan]’s son who had

he mounted a large army and set out for battle

Noqai’s sons learned of this message and set

padishah’s generosity is such that he will par-

In secret he had dispatched Jögä with a large
force to cross the Tarkar upstream and then at-
tack Toqta and his forces. Toqta’s scouts cap-
tured a spy, who told them what was hap-
pening. When Toqta learned of his perﬁdy, he

with a thousand horsemen in the direction of
the Kilar and Bashghurd. While Noqai was
fleeing with seventeen horsemen, one of Toq-

khan.” The man seized his reins and was
taking him to Toqta, but he gave up the ghost
along the way. Toqta returned to Batu’s Sarai,
which was their capital, and Noqai’s sons wan-
dered around. When they achieved no fortune,
Tügä, his mother Chübäi, and Büri’s mother
Yaylaq said to Jögä, “The best thing for us to
do would be to cease hostilities and go to Toq-
ta.” Jögä was afraid of that plan and killed his
brother and stepmother. Then he wandered
around with a group of followers, finally
taking refuge in a castle, the approach to which
was as narrow as Sirat2 and tight as a miser’s
heart. What happened to him in the end?
Prior to this, Noqai had initiated friendly re-
lations with Abaqa Khan and Arghun Khan. In
the year ___ he sent his wife, Chübäi, with his
son Büri and an amir named ___ to Abaqa
Khan to request a daughter of his in marriage.
He gave his daughter to Büri, and they re-
mained there for a while before being sent
back with honors. When he and Toqta had

fought he had constantly sent ambassadors of
importance to the Padishah of Islam [748] and
asked him for assistance, desirous of becoming
attached to this court. The truth is that it was
an excellent opportunity, but the Padishah of
Islam was too high-minded to comply. Not
wanting to take undue advantage of the situa-
tion, he said, “At this time treachery and
breaking promises are remote from chivalry,
and treachery and deceit are considered blame-
worthy both in Muslim law and in the Yasa.
However friendly we may be to Noqai, we will
not intervene in his enmities and hostilities, for
to take advantage of a situation is a characteris-
tic that is not praiseworthy—particularly for
great rulers.”
Since Toqta was in fear and apprehension,
His Majesty used to send for the emissaries of
both sides to allay their suspicions and say,
“We will not intervene between you two, and
we will not take advantage of the situation. If
you would make peace with each other, it
would be best.” In order to calm their fear and
apprehension, he did not go to his winter quar-
ters in Arran and wintered in Baghdad and Di-
yarbekir instead, just to allay their fears.
Until the present he maintains friendship
with both Toqta and with Noqai’s sons, and
many times he has said, “Let none of my aqas
or inis initiate strife or provoke hostilities with
them. We will never start anything that may
lead to contention lest the blame for harm to
the ulus come back to haunt us.” One would
think the Maker had created his pure essence
and luminous soul of sheer goodness and ab-
solute kindness. He is a padishah who is
known for his good moral character, justice,
and beneficence, and in all corners of the earth
he is renowned as a ruler who encourages reli-
gion, spreads justice, makes armies, treats his
subjects kindly, and is auspicious and good.
May God keep him for many years over the
people of the world and let him enjoy long life,
wealth, kingdom, and rule [749] through the
sanctity of the chosen prophet Muhammad and
his select family.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

❦ SECTION SIX
THE HISTORY OF CHAGHATAI KHAN, SON OF GENGHIS KHAN, IN THREE
PARTS
Part One contains his lineage and a list of his
wives, sons, and grandsons who have branched
off down to the present; a portrait of him and a
genealogical chart of him and his sons and
grandsons. 
Part Two is on the history of his reign, a pic-
ture of his throne and his wives and princes; a
mention of his ulus and some of the battles he
fought and the victories he achieved; the length
of his reign.
Part Three is on his character, miscellaneous
stories, various orders and sayings of his that
are not found in the previous two sections,
having been culled from various books and
persons. [751]
Part One. His lineage and a list of his wives,
sons, and grandsons who have branched off
down to the present; a portrait of him and a
genealogical chart of him and his sons and
grandsons.
Chaghatai was Genghis Khan’s second son.
His mother was Genghis Khan’s chief wife, the
mother of the four sons, Börtä Füjin of the
Qunqirat clan, daughter of Däi Noyan, the
chief of that clan. 
Chaghatai had many wives, but the most im-
portant were two. The ﬁrst was Yesülün
Khatun, the mother of all his children; she was
the daughter of Qata Noyan the son of Daritai,
the brother of the ruler of the Qunqirat. Börtä
Füjin, Genghis Khan’s chief wife, and Yesülün
Khatun’s father were ﬁrst cousins. The second
was Tögän Khatun,1 a sister of the above-men-
tioned Yesülün Khatun. Chaghatai married her
when Yesülün died.
His sons and grandsons who have branched
off down to the present.
Chaghatai had six sons, as follows: (1)
Mö’ätükän, (2) Mochi Yäbä, (3) Bälgäshi, (4)
Sarban, (5) Yesü Möngkä, and (6) Baidar.2
Each of these six will now be described in de-
tail. [752]
Chaghatai’s first son, Mö’ätükän.
He was born of Yesülün Khatun. His father
loved him more than any of his other sons, and
since Genghis Khan also loved him very much,
he was usually with him. When Genghis Khan
had sent Chaghatai with Jochi and Ögödäi to
lay siege to Khwarazm while he was occupied
with the siege of the fortress at Bamian,
Mö’ätükän was shot from the fortress and
killed. Genghis Khan was greatly vexed by
this, and when he took the fortress he de-
stroyed it completely, killed all the inhabitants,
and renamed it Mau Qorghan (“evil fortress”). 
When Chaghatai returned, he arrived just as
the fortress was being razed, and Genghis
Khan ordered that no one tell him what had
happened. For a few days he told him that
Mö’ätükän had gone somewhere else. After
1In JTRM her name is spelledﺮﰷ ــﺗ; other texts haveﻮﰷن ــﺗ
(Tögän).
2Other versions give eight sons, adding Qadatai and

that he got angry with his sons intentionally on
some pretext and said, “You do not listen to
what I tell you, and you have spoiled every-
thing I have told you.” 
Chaghatai knelt and said, “We will do what-
ever Genghis Khan commands. If we fail, let
us die.” 
“Is what you say true?” Genghis Khan asked
again several times. “Will you really do it?”
“If
I
do
not
keep
my
word,”
replied
Chaghatai, “may I die.”
“Mö’ätükän is dead,” said Genghis Khan,
“and you must not cry or bemoan.” Chaghatai
was consumed by an inner ﬁre, but he forbore
as his father had commanded and did not cry.
After a time, on the pretext of some necessity,
he went out and wept in silence in a corner for
a moment. Then, drying his tears, he returned
to his father.
Mö’ätükän had four sons, Baiju, Büri, Yesün-
to’a, and Qara Hülägü. Their branches are as
follows. [753]
(1) Mö’ätükän’s ﬁrst son, Baiju, had one son,
Tödö’än, who had a son named Böjäi, who had
a son named Abdullah.
(2) The second son, Büri, was born as fol-
lows. It used to be the custom for the wives of
the ev-oghlans to gather in the camp for work.
One day Mö’ätükän went into the camp and
saw a lot of women. He took one who was
very beautiful off into a corner and lay with
her. When it occurred to him that she might be
pregnant, he ordered her kept apart from her
husband. As it happened, she had become
pregnant. Büri was born of her, and she was re-
turned to her husband. Büri was extremely
bold and courageous, but when he drank too
much he cursed. It got so bad that once during
Möngkä Qa’an’s reign when he was drinking
he cursed Batu because of a grudge he har-
bored toward him. When Batu heard of it he
summoned him. Mängäsär Noyan took him at
Möngkä Qa’an’s order to Batu, and Batu killed
him.1 Büri had ﬁve sons.
(a) The first was Qadaqai Sächän, who had
four sons, (i) Nalighu, who had three sons,
Temür, Oradai, and Tümän, (ii) Buqu, who had
two sons, Dhu’l-Qarnayn and Ali, (iii) Buqa
Temür, who had two sons, Örüg Temür and
Öljäi, and (iv) Buqa, who had no [sons]. [754]
(b) Ahmad, who had two sons, (i) Baba, who
had three sons, Habil Temür, Qabil Temür, and
Yulduz Temür, and (ii) Sati, of whom no sons
are known. 
1Büri’s execution is described by William of Rubruck
as follows: “…Ban [Büri] dominus eorum fuerat inter-
fectus tali occasione. Ipse non erat in bonis pascuis. Et

cusauit se, quia ebrius erat: (quia solent condonare
ebrijs:) & Baatu respondit: Quomodo audebas me nom-
inare in ebrietate tua? Et fecit ei amputari caput” (p.
177f.); “…their lord & master Ban [Büri] was put to

Am not I of the stocke and kinred of Chingis Can, as
well as Baatu? (for in very deede he was brother or
nephew vnto Baatu.) Why then doe I not passe and

as freely as Baatu himselfe doeth? Which speeches of

And they did so. Then Baatu demanded of him whether
he had spoken any such words? And hee confessed that
he had. Howbeit, (because it is the Tartars maner to par-
don drunken men) he excused himselfe that he was
drunken at the same time. Howe durst thou (quoth

that hee caused his head to be chopt off” (p. 226).

(c) Ajiqi, who had two sons, (i) Örüg, who

Baraq
sent
his
brothers

keep him distracted, but he realized what they
were doing and said, “This is what you intend.
Turn back willingly, or I’ll seize you and take
you with me.” Fearing this threat, they turned
back, and when they saw Jalayirtai they said,
“He has gone too far to be overtaken.” He too
turned back with them.
When Baraq crossed the Oxus River in de-
feat and was deserted by most of his relatives
and soldiers, he sent Yasa’ur to Qaidu with a
message saying, “The aqa-inis and men you
sent were not faithful, and every one has left
on some pretext. This was begun by Qipchaq,
and his actions caused the defeat of the army.”
When Qaidu heard this message he asked
Yasa’ur, “When he sent you with Mu’min and
Negübäi in pursuit of Qipchaq, had he sent any
troops after you or not?” Yasa’ur said no.
Qaidu then realized what had happened and
said, “A disgraceful defeat came about because
your tongue was not straight with your heart.
Wasn’t Jalayirtai coming after you with troops
to seize Qipchaq?” Yasa’ur recoiled in fear,
and Qaidu seized him and threw him into
chains.
Then he took counsel with the amirs and
mounted as reinforcement to Baraq so that
somehow he might repel him. When he was
near the canal news came that those who had
gone after Negübäi Oghul and Ahmad had
killed them. Baraq sent a messenger asking
why his anda Qaidu had taken such trouble and
telling him to turn back since there was no ne-
cessity for reinforcement. [757] [Qaidu] paid
no attention and arrived late at night and
camped in the environs of Baraq’s camp. Baraq
died that very night. The next morning, when
no one came forth, he sent someone to ﬁnd out
what was going on. It was ascertained that
Baraq had died, so Qaidu entered his camp,
conducted the mourning, and sent the body to a
mountain for burial.1
After Baraq, his cousin Buqa Temür, the son
of
Qadaq[ai],
became
ruler
of
the
Ulus
Chaghatai,2 and after him the rule was given to
Baraq’s son Dua, and he is in league with
Qaidu and his sons. Before this, when he grad-
ually gathered Chaghatai’s troops and Nawroz
had rebelled, he went before him and Qaidu,
and he knew the roads and conditions in
Khurasan well. He enticed them into attacking
Khurasan. They raided Israfayin. Because of
Nawroz
much
damage
was
done
to
the
province, and innocent Muslims were killed, as
will be related in the story of the Padishah of
Islam. After that, Qutluq Buqa’s son Uighurtai
ﬂed and went to Dua, and he knew the roads in
Mazanderan well. When Baidu proved treach-
erous to Gaikhatu and the amirs gathered
around him and killed him and he sat on the
throne, Dua, at Uighurtai’s direction when the
army was coming from Khurasan in this direc-
tion, went across the desert to Mazanderan and
took some of the aghruqs of the soldiers of the
Padishah of Islam who were in that area and
turned back. This will be described in the his-
tory of the Padishah of Islam.
Together with Qaidu, Dua did battle several
times with the Qa’an’s forces, and they were
defeated. The last time both were wounded.
[758] Qaidu died of his wound, and Dua was
paralyzed. One of Dua’s sons is the Qutluq
Khwaja to whom was turned over the province
of Ghaznin and the Qara’una troops, who have
long been attached to them. They summer in
the area of Ghor and Gharjistan, and in the
1The episode with Baraq is given in greater detail on
text pp. 1065ff.
2Cf. text p. 773 below, where the Buqa Temür who be-
came ruler of the Ulus Chaghatai is said to be Buqa
Temür son of Qadatai.
364
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

winter they are in the province of Ghaznin and
that area. They must constantly do battle with
the sultan of Delhi, and the Delhi troops have
often struck at them. They come into this realm
at all times as bandits and highway robbers and
cause trouble. Buzma wanted to join the
Qa’an’s service, but Qaidu learned of it and
killed him.
(4) Mö’ätükän’s fourth son, Qara Hülägü,
had a son named Mubarakshah, who had ﬁve
sons, (i) Öljäi Buqa, who had a son named
Qutluqshah, (ii) Boralqi, who had a son named
Qutluq, (iii) Horqadai, (iv) Esän Bolad, and (v)
Qadaq.
Chaghatai made Qara Hülägü his successor
in place of his father, Mö’ätügän. His wife was
Orghina Khatun, who was Mubarakshah’s
mother. When Qara Hülägü died, Baidar’s son
Alghu, his cousin, became the ruler of the Ulus
Chaghatai by Ariq Bökä’s order. He married
Orghina Khatun and died not long thereafter.
Mubarakshah then succeeded to his father’s
position, and Baraq came at Qubilai Qa’an’s
order. [759] When he found Mubarakshah rul-
ing, he said nothing, but gradually he gathered
forces and then usurped the rule of the ulus. He
convicted Mubarakshah of a crime and made
him the chief of his leopard keepers. When
Baraq went to Khurasan to ﬁght Abaqa Khan,
Mubarakshah was with him. He ﬂed and joined
Abaqa Khan. This story will be told in detail in
the proper place, God willing.
Chaghatai’s second son, Mochi Yäbä.
His mother was a servant girl in Yesülün
Khatun’s camp. One night she was laying the
bedclothes while the khatun was outside.
Chaghatai dragged her off and made her preg-
nant. For this reason Chaghatai did not attach
great importance to [Mochi Yäbä], and he was
given fewer troops and less territory. He had
eleven sons, as follows.
(1) Täkshi, who had a son named Tabuduqar,
who had four sons, Toghan, Oqulqu, Qoridai,
and one other whose name is not known.
(2) Negüdär; he had three sons, Umar (who
had two sons), Qutlugh Temür, and Eki Temür. 
(3) Ahmad;
(4) Tämüdär;
(5) Qotan;
(6) Chächä;
(7) Chichäktü, who had two sons, Shadban
and Qushman;
(8) Ishal, who had two sons, Tai Buqa and
Uladai.1 [760]
Chaghatai’s third son, Bälgäshi.
When Mö’ätükän, Chaghatai’s heir, died,
Chaghatai wanted to make this son his heir, but
he too died, aged thirteen and without issue.
After that, he made Mö’ätükän’s son Qara
Hülägü his heir designate.
Chaghatai’s fourth son, Sarban.
He had two sons, Qoshiqai and Negübäi.
Chaghatai’s ﬁfth son, Yesü Möngkä.
He was such an extremely heavy drinker that
they say he was never sober long enough to
hand a falcon over to the falconers. He had a
wife named Naishi who was highly inﬂuential
and domineering, and she ran things because
her husband was constantly drunk. Since she
was in league with Güyük Khan, even though
Chaghatai’s appointed heir was Qara Hülägü,
[Güyük] made [Yesü Möngkä] the ruler of the
Ulus Chaghatai because Yesü Möngkä was op-
posed to Möngkä Qa’an. After that, when
Möngkä Qa’an became emperor, he ordered
Qara Hülägü to take charge of the Ulus
Chaghatai and to kill Yesü Möngkä. Qara
Hülägü died along the way, so his wife Orghi-
na Khatun had [Yesü Möngkä] killed, and she
1Other versions add three more sons to make eleven:
Nomquli, Bük Buqa, and Toghan.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SIX: CHAGHATAI KHAN
365

ruled on her own for ten years. After that, Ariq
Bökä gave the ulus to Baidar’s son Alghu.
When Alghu rebelled against Ariq Bökä,
Orghina Khatun became his wife, as has al-
ready been reported. Yesü Möngkä had no
sons. [761]
Chaghatai’s sixth son, Baidar.
He was a short man, but he was a very good
archer. They say that one day ___ was playing
with him and said, “You are short. Come, let’s
shoot arrows together.” 
He had a son named Alghu, who had three
sons, (a) Qaban, (b) Chübäi, and (c) Tuq
Temür, who had two sons, Esän Bökä and
Aghruqchi.
Chübäi had ﬁfteen sons, whose histories will
come later: Toqta, Yasa’ur, Dögöläs, Ejil Buqa,
Nomquli, Boyuntash, Aq Buqa, Sati, Qoyat-
mish, Daud, Gambu Dorji, Chigin Temür,
Jirghudai, Mingtash, and Könchäk Dorji. [762]
366
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SIX: CHAGHATAI KHAN
367

Part Two of the History of Chaghatai Khan. The history of his reign; a picture of his throne
and his wives, princes, and amirs as he sits on the throne; a mention of his ulus and some of
the battles he fought and the victories he achieved; the length of his reign, and a history of
his offspring down to the present.
Chaghatai was a just, competent, and awe-
some ruler. His father Genghis Khan told his
commanders that any who had a desire to
know the yasa and yosun of the kingdom
should follow Chaghatai; any who liked pos-
sessions and wealth and wanted to follow the
path of chivalry and ease should follow
Ögödäi; and any who desired courtliness, cul-
ture, bravery, and weaponry should join Tolui.
When he was dividing the troops, he gave
Chaghatai four thousand men, as has already
been described in the section on the division of
the military. Of the commanders, Qarachar of
the Barulas clan and Mögä the father of Yesün
Noyan of the Jalayir went to him, and he re-
ceived the territories and yurts from the Altai,
the yurt of the Naiman nation. As commanded,
he rode on campaigns [763] and performed
outstanding feats, conquering territories as has
already been described.
In the autumn of Qonin Yil, the Year of the
Sheep that began in Sha‘ban 607 [January
1211], when Genghis Khan mounted for the
Cathay
campaign,
Chaghatai,
along
with
Ögödäi and Tolui, took ﬁve cities, Yunnei,
Dongsheng, Wuzhou, Shuozhou, and Ning-
zhou.1 Thereafter, after having besieged and
taken the city of Zhuozhou, the three of them
were dispatched in the Year of the Monkey to
the foot of Mount Huailai, and they took all the
cities and fortresses from Fuzhou to Huai [and]
Meng. From there they went down the Yellow
River, turned back, and took and pillaged the
1See above, text p. 443. As before, for the text’sﮏــﻧﻮــﻓ
ﭼﻴﻮ, read ﻧﻮﻧﮓ ﺟﻴﻮ (Nung-jiu) for 寧州 Ningzhou.
cities of Pingyangfu and Taiyuanfu and depen-
dencies.2 The booty from Taiyuanfu went to
Chaghatai.
After that, in the winter of Luy Yil, the Year
of the Dragon that began in Dhu’l-Hijja 616
[February 1220], when Genghis Khan set out
for the realm of the Tajiks and came to Otrar,
he sent Chaghatai and his brothers Ögödäi and
Tolui to lay siege and conquer it. After that
they took Banakat and most of the cities of
Turkistan, rejoining their father after the con-
quest of Samarkand. After that, he sent him,
Jochi Khan, and Ögödäi to besiege Khwarazm.
Since he and Jochi could not get along, their
father ordered Ögödäi to take charge, even
though he was younger, and he cleverly made
peace between his brothers so that together
they could take Khwarazm. Jochi then went to
his aghruq.
In the summer of Morin Yil, the Year of the
Horse that corresponds to 619 [1223], they re-
joined Genghis Khan at Taligan and paid
homage. [764] Having spent that summer in
the vicinity of Taligan, Chaghatai, Ögödäi, and
Tolui went with their father in pursuit of Sultan
Jalaluddin to the banks of the Indus, where
they defeated the sultan’s forces even though
the sultan escaped across the river. That sum-
mer they remained in that area, conquering
various territories. After that they accompanied
their father to their original homeland, and in
Taqiqu Yil, the Year of the Rooster correspond-
ing to 622 [1225], when Genghis Khan mount-
ed for a campaign to Tangqut, which had re-
2See above, text p. 448.
368
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

belled again, he ordered Chaghatai to be in the
wing of the army behind the camps. He did as
ordered until his brothers Ögödäi and Tolui,
who were with their father, returned home,
with Genghis Khan’s coffin brought after
them. Together they conducted the mourning
ceremonies, and then they each went to their
respective yurts and homes.
Since of all the brothers only Chaghatai was
friendly with both Ögödäi and Tolui, he made
great efforts to have Ögödäi enthroned and
kept insisting until they elevated him to the
rule in accordance with their father’s com-
mand. Together with Tolui and the other rela-
tives he bent his knee and made tägishmishi of-
ferings. Despite his being the eldest brother, he
paid Ögödäi all respect and observed all forms
of propriety with him. One instance is as
follows.
One day the two were riding fast horses.
Dead drunk, one said to the other, “Let’s bet on
a race.” They made a wager and raced.
Chaghatai’s horse was a little faster and won
by a head. That night, when Chaghatai was
thinking about it in his tent, he said to himself,
“How could it be right for me to make a bet
with the emperor? How could I have let my
horse pass his? This was an act of great impro-
priety. [765] If this keeps up, we and the others
will become brazen, and it will result in weak-
ening of the kingdom.” Before dawn he sum-
moned the amirs and said, “Yesterday I com-
mitted an affront by committing such an
action. Let us go to Ögödäi, and let him try me
for my affront and apply whatever punishment
is required by the Yasa.” He and the amirs
mounted together in a large group and arrived
at
the
kiriyäs
earlier
than
usual.
When
Ögödäi’s guards reported that Chaghatai had
arrived with a large group, although Ögödäi
had complete trust in Chaghatai, he wondered
what could have caused such a thing. He there-
fore sent men to his brother to make inquiry.
“We aqa-inis have all spoken together at a
quriltai,” he answered, “and we have given
written pledges that Ögödäi is the Qa’an and
sworn to obey him and not disobey him in any-
thing. Yesterday I ran a race with him on a wa-
ger. What right have I to make a wager with
the Qa’an? I am therefore guilty of an offense,
and I admit my guilt. I have come to be judged
by the Yasa. Whether the emperor has me
killed or beaten, he is the ruler.”
Ögödäi was embarrassed by this and held his
brother in even greater love and affection. In
humility he sent back a message saying, “What
words are these? He is my elder brother. What
importance do such triﬂes have?”
[Chaghatai] refused to listen, but in the end
he consented that the Qa’an should spare his
life and he would present nine horses. The bit-
igchis therefore composed documents for all to
know that the emperor had spared Chaghatai’s
life and that Chaghatai had presented gifts in
return for the forgiveness of his offense. After
that, he came into the ordu and reported to all,
with the great eloquence he possessed, what
had happened. On this account the agreement
between the brothers increased, and the other
relatives submitted humbly to the Qa’an’s de-
crees. [766]
During Ögödäi’s reign, the territories that
had
not
been
conquered
during
Genghis
Khan’s time were all subjugated, and the em-
pire grew stronger under the rule of his family
and armies.
Since Chaghatai lived in such harmony with
Ögödäi, Ögödäi placed his own son Güyük
Khan in Chaghatai’s retinue to serve as a
guard, and Chaghatai’s status reached a mag-
niﬁcence that is beyond description. He ruled
over his ulus and the army Genghis Khan had
given him and was ﬁrmly ensconced upon the
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SIX: CHAGHATAI KHAN
369

throne in Beshbaliq. Ögödäi sent emissaries to
consult with him on all matters of importance
and never took action without his approval.
Chaghatai was always in full agreement and
supportive of Ögödäi and kept him informed of
everything that happened to him. Whenever
there was a matter of great concern he went for
a quriltai, and all Ögödäi’s sons and amirs
went out to greet him and escort him into the
emperor’s presence, where he would present
gifts and then go into the inner apartments. For
the thirteen years Ögödäi was on the throne
Chaghatai was in agreement with and support-
ive of him. He died in 638 [1241], seven
months before Ögödäi. [767]
The status of rule over the Ulus Chaghatai
after Chaghatai’s death, and his successors’
accessions until the present.
After the deaths of the Qa’an and of
Chaghatai, although Qara Hülägü (the eldest
son of Mö’ätükän, who had died of an arrow
wound at the fortress of Bamian during
Genghis Khan’s time) was the designated heir,
Güyük Khan sent Chaghatai’s ﬁfth son, Yesü
Möngkä, to rule the Ulus Chaghatai because he
was opposed to Möngkä Qa’an. Then, when
Möngkä Qa’an became emperor, he issued a
decree for Qara Hülägü to kill Yesü Möngkä
and become the ruler of the Ulus Chaghatai as
the heir designate. Before reaching the Ulus
Chaghatai, Qara Hülägü died on the road, and
his wife, Orghina Khatun, the daughter of
Törälchi Gürägän of the Oyirat, had Yesü
Möngkä killed in accordance with the decree
and took the rule upon herself in her husband’s
stead.
When Möngkä Qa’an died, Qubilai Qa’an
sent Abishgha, the eldest son of Mö’ätükän’s
second son Büri, to remove Orghina Khatun
and become ruler of the Ulus Chaghatai in
Qara Hülägü’s place. Since at that time there
was a dispute between Qubilai Qa’an and Ariq
Bökä, Ariq Bökä’s troops seized Abishgha on
the road and took him to Ariq Bökä. Möngkä
Qa’an’s son Asutai was ordered to kill him. Al-
ghu, the son of Chaghatai’s sixth son Baidar,
was with him [Ariq Bökä], and he was issued a
decree to become the ruler of the Ulus
Chaghatai [768] to protect the borders from
Qubilai Qa’an’s troops and from the forces of
the Jochid family and to collect tribute, provi-
sions, and supplies for the army from Turkistan
and send them to [Ariq Bökä] so that he would
have the means to mount a campaign against
Qubilai Qa’an. Alghu delivered the decree and
became powerful as ruler. Orghina Khatun
went to Ariq Bökä with many complaints of
Alghu. She remained there for a long time. Af-
ter a time Ariq Bökä sent envoys there to take
two of every ten animals and to collect money
and weapons for the army. The names of those
envoys are Äbügä[lün],1 Boritai Bitigchi, and
Shadi. They went and delivered the decree to
Alghu, and they began to collect the animals,
weapons, and money in the province. When
only part had been collected, they dispatched
it. In 661 [1263] Alghu arrested them and said,
“When the other liege men arrive with their
tasks completed, you may go together.” Some
time later, when they arrived, they made in-
quiry of the liege men, saying, “Why did you
stop?”
“Alghu prevented us,” they replied. They
then went to the gate of Alghu’s ordu and sent
in a message saying, “We came by decree of
Ariq Bökä to collect taxes. What right have
you to prevent us?”
Since Alghu had set his sights on the tax
money, he ﬂared up in anger at the envoys’
words, had them arrested, and threw them into
1Text here has “Äbügän Kä’ün.” Below (text p. 882) it
is the diminutive Äbügälün.
370
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

chains. Then he took counsel with his amirs
and asked what should be done.
“Council should have been held before they
were arrested,” they said. “Now that we have
made an enemy of Ariq Bökä, we should rebel
against him totally and go over to Qubilai
Qa’an.” He then had the envoys killed and
seized the money and weapons, which enabled
him to be powerful.
Orghina Khatun had returned, and Alghu
married her and sat in absolute power on the
throne of the Ulus Chaghatai. [769] When the
news reached Ariq Bökä, he mounted a cam-
paign against Alghu. Battle was fought, and
Ariq Bökä was defeated twice, but the third
time Alghu
suffered
defeat
and
went
to
Bukhara and Samarkand. There he obtained
money, weapons, and animals from wealthy
men and gave them to his soldiers. Ariq Bökä
raided his aghruqs and, after a year had passed,
he pulled out of the area in order to repel the
Qa’an’s forces. The next year, which was 6[6]2
[1264], Alghu died. Since all the amirs and sol-
diers were under Orghina Khatun’s orders, she
elevated her son Mubarakshah, the son of Qara
Hülägü, to the throne. The army, as it was wont
to do, pillaged and tyrannized the population.
Since Mubarakshah was a Muslim, he did not
allow the peasantry to suffer injustice. When
Ariq Bökä was forced to go to the Qa’an, the
troubles in the province subsided.
To the Ulus Chaghatai the Qa’an sent Baraq,
the son of Mö’ätükän’s third son Yesünto’a
who had been in his retinue for a while, with a
decree making him co-ruler of the ulus along
with Mubarakshah. When Baraq arrived and
found Mubarakshah and Orghina Khatun ﬁrm-
ly in power, he did not show the decree.
Mubarakshah asked him why he had come, and
he replied, “I have been away from my ulus
and home for a long time, and my people have
dispersed without a leader. I asked for permis-
sion and have come to gather my er-akhta
[cavalry] and join you.” Mubarakshah was
pleased by this reply, and Baraq comported
himself competently with him, all the while
gathering soldiers from all nooks and crannies.
Then, without warning, a bitigchi amir of
Mubarakshah’s and some of the army con-
spired with Baraq to depose Mubarakshah, and
Baraq became the absolute ruler. Mubarakshah
was so demoted [770] that he was made chief
of Baraq’s leopard keepers.
Since Qaidu and Ariq Bökä were in league
and both refused to respond to the Qa’an’s
summons, the Qa’an had sent Baraq to deal
with Qaidu. To that end, when Baraq had
gained enough strength, he set out to attack
Qaidu. They fought several battles. The ﬁrst
time Baraq was defeated, and the second time
they began to ﬁght, Qipchaq, the son of Ögödäi
Qa’an’s son Qada’an Oghul who was friendly
with Baraq, made a truce between them and
had them swear oaths to be anda with each oth-
er. Secure from this threat, Baraq mounted the
throne of the Ulus Chaghatai.
After that, he held a quriltai and said to
Qaidu, “Our army has grown large, and this
territory cannot support it. I will cross the
Oxus and and take the province of Khurasan,
and my anda Qaidu must assist me.” Since
Qaidu wanted him out of the territory, and
since he was also at odds with Abaqa Khan, he
agreed to this and assigned Qipchaq Oghul and
Chabat, the son of Güyük Khan’s son Naqu, to
go with reinforcements to assist Baraq.
Baraq led his army across the Oxus and
camped
in
the
vicinity
of
Merv.
When
Tü[b]shin, Abaqa Khan’s brother, gave battle, a
hazara amir named Shächäktü heard that
Qipchaq had come with Baraq. He ﬂed to them
and said, “My cha’ur (company of a hundred)
and I are Qipchaq’s.” So saying, he led out ﬁne
horses to present to his ruler, but Qipchaq said
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SIX: CHAGHATAI KHAN
371

to him, “Take a few horses and present them to
Baraq.” Shächätü did this. The next day in
Baraq’s ordu Jalayirtai said to Qipchaq, “Has
Baraq come with so many thousand soldiers to
wield the sword on your behalf?”
“So what?” said he.
“What
will
be?”
he
replied.
“Although
Shächäktü and his company are attached to
you, why has he not come to you for such a
long time? Today he has come here under
Baraq’s good fortune. You took him to your-
self, and you took the ﬁne horses that were ﬁt
for Baraq and told him to give Baraq the ones
that were ﬁt for you.”
“Who are you,” said Qipchaq, “to interfere
between elder and younger brothers?”
“I am Baraq’s servant,” said Jalayirtai, “not
yours that you should ask me who I am!”
“When has a commoner ever answered a
question from Genghis Khan’s family,” said
Qipchaq, “that a dog like you should give an
impolite response to me?”
“If I am a dog,” he said, “I am Baraq’s dog,
not yours. Have some respect for yourself and
go about your own business.”
With this, Qipchaq’s zeal was ignited, and he
said, “If you dare to answer me, I’ll cut you in
two. Baraq Aqa will say nothing to me on your
account.”
Jalayirtai reached for his dagger and said, “If
you try to kill me, I’ll cut your gut to shreds.”
Even when things reached this point, Baraq
said nothing. Qipchaq realized that he would
support Jalayirtai, so in a pique of wounded
pride he left Baraq’s camp, took counsel with
his
soldiers,
left
his
own
camp
below
Maruchaq,1 and ﬂed with his troops across the
river. When Baraq found out about it, he sent
his brother Negübäi Oghul in pursuit, and on
his heels he dispatched Jalayirtai with three
1The modern Maruchak in western Afghanistan.
thousand horsemen (as was described at the
end of the section on Baraq). After that, Chabat
also took ﬂight with his men and went to
Qaidu.
In short, Baraq was defeated, and most of his
soldiers were killed by Abaqa Khan’s troops,
and the few who escaped scattered. The defeat-
ed Baraq went to Bukhara, where he fell ill of
despair and grief. He set out in a litter to attack
Ahmad Oghul, the son of Chaghatai’s son
Mochi Yäbä, who had refused to help him, and
he sent a message to Yasa’ur and another to
Qaidu, [772] saying, “Your sons’ troops have
failed to assist, and therefore our armies have
been defeated. My illness notwithstanding, I
am setting out in pursuit of them. If my anda
will send reinforcements, I will capture them
and subject them to retribution.” As has been
said previously, Qaidu seized Yasa’ur and put
him in chains. Then he and his troops were go-
ing ostensibly as reinforcements but actually to
deal once and for all with the weakened Baraq.
When his men seized and killed Ahmad Oghul,
[Baraq] regretted having summoned Qaidu and
sent a message saying, “There is no necessity
for my anda Qaidu to go to any trouble. Let
him turn back.”
Paying no attention, Qaidu proceeded and
camped in a circle around Baraq’s camp. As
was said in the section on Baraq, Baraq died
that night, and the next day Qaidu held
mourning and buried him. The amirs and
princes who were in his camp came to Qaidu,
knelt, and said, “Until now Baraq has been our
ruler. Now Qaidu is our aqa and ruler. We will
ﬁght as he commands.” Qaidu rewarded them
and distributed to his own troops Baraq’s pos-
sessions, which he had them carry away as he
withdrew to his own yurt.
After that, Baraq’s eldest son, Beg Temür,
and Alghu’s sons Chübäi and Qaban rebelled
and went to the Qa’an. Ögödäi’s nephew Cha-
372
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

bat and a group of amirs also joined the Qa’an,
after which Qara Hülägü’s son Mubarakshah
went to Abaqa Khan, who received him with
all honors and put him in charge of Negüdär’s
troop in the vicinity of Ghazna.
In the year in which Abaqa Khan went to
Herat to repel the Qara’unas, Mubarakshah’s
sons came to Abaqa Khan’s service with all
their ordus, and they are still here. It was at
that time that Yasa’ur, Baraq’s brother, [773]
submitted.
After Baraq’s death the rule of the ulus was
given to his cousin Negübäi, the son of Sarban,
and he ruled for three years. After that, Qaidu
gave it to Buqa Temür, the son of Chaghatai’s
seventh son Qadaqai, and he ruled for a time.1
He was afflicted with scall, and all his hair and
beard fell out. He died of that disease. 
After him, Qaidu gave the rule of the ulus to
Baraq’s son Dua, who is now the ruler, al-
though he is ill. Last year, when he and Qaidu
did battle with the Qa’an’s troops, they were
both wounded. Qaidu died of his wound, and
Dua is still suffering from his wound, which
has resisted treatment.
Stories of Chaghatai’s deputies, Vazir and
Habash Amid.
Chaghatai had two viziers, Vazir2 and Habash
Amid. Vazir was originally from Cathay and
was a servant of a Cathaian physician in
Chaghatai’s retinue. After the physician’s death
he became a herdsman for Qoshuq Noyan of
the Jalayir nation, one of Chaghatai’s amirs.
One day by chance Chaghatai asked Qoshuq
1Grousset (Empire, 334) calls this Buqa Temür “Tuqa
Timur” and his predecessor “Nikpai Oghul.”
2Although Vazir’s name is coincidentally spelled in
Persian exactly likeﺮــﻳ وزvazīr (‘vizier’), it is actually de-
rived from the Sanskrit v¿ vajra (‘thunderbolt’) via the
Mongolian and/or Uyghur vajir > vazir. See JTBy 154,
note 43.
Noyan, who was old and much experienced
and knew about former times, about Genghis
Khan and which territories he had taken in
which years. Since he did not have a ready an-
swer, he went home and asked everyone in his
service, who told him what they knew. The
Cathaian herdsman heard from outside the tent
and responded to the truth or falsehood of each
statement in such a way that could be clearly
heard by those present, and everyone agreed
with what he said. [774] Qoshuq summoned
him inside and asked how he knew such
things. He produced a notebook in which he
had recorded all the things they were looking
for with their dates day by day. Qoshuq re-
joiced and took him and the notebook to
Chaghatai, and since Chaghatai loved such
wisdom, he was pleased and, requesting the
Cathaian from Qoshuq, made him a member of
his retinue. Within a short time he had become
quite bold in service and attained prominence
and fame. The Qa’an recognized his clever-
ness, and when he saw how conﬁdential he
was with Chaghatai, he named him vizier. He
was short and mean looking, but he was ex-
tremely brave, quick-witted, clever, eloquent,
and had a prodigious appetite for food and
drink. His rank was increased until he sat
above most of the amirs, and he spoke more
boldly than any in Chaghatai’s service. One
day Chaghatai’s wife began to speak during a
report, and he shouted at her, “You are a wife.
You have no right to speak in this regard.” One
of Chaghatai’s daughters-in-law was also ac-
cused of adultery with someone. Without con-
sulting Chaghatai, Vazir killed her. When
Chaghatai learned of it, Vazir said, “How can a
daughter-in-law be allowed to commit a dis-
pleasing act and sully the names of the other
women?” Chaghatai approved of his action.
Since it was customary at that time for every
word the ruler said to be written down day by
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SIX: CHAGHATAI KHAN
373

day, and since most of what they said was in
rhyme and obscure, each of them had one of
his conﬁdants to write down what he said.
Chaghatai’s pronouncements were written by
Vazir. The Qa’an had an Uyghur deputy named
Chinqai. One day the Qa’an asked Chaghatai,
“Is your vizier better than mine?”
“Of course,” he answered, “he is better [than]
Chinqai.”
One day at a banquet both of them issued
statements, and he took them down and then
went outside to write them out. [775] Both
Chaghatai and the Qa’an kept a record so as to
make a test to see if Vazir could write them or
not. Just as Vazir started writing, Möngkä
Qa’an passed by and spoke to him. “Don’t dis-
tract me,” said Vazir, “let me write down what
I have heard.” When he produced his record,
they read it. He had written it down with only a
few words in the wrong order. “Chaghatai is
right. His vizier is better than mine,” the Qa’an
confessed.
As long as Chaghatai was alive, Vazir was
inﬂuential in his service. They say that during
Ögödäi Qa’an’s time Chaghatai wrote a decree
giving to someone else a portion of Transoxi-
ana the Qa’an had put under Yalavach’s con-
trol. Yalavach reported this to the Qa’an, who
repealed the decree and sent a letter to
Chaghatai, ordering him to give an answer. In
answer Chaghatai wrote, “I did it unknowingly
and misguidedly. I have no answer I can write
to you, but since the Qa’an has commanded me
to write, I am emboldened to write this much.”
The Qa’an was pleased by this reply and ac-
cepted his excuse. He also gave the region as
an appanage to Chaghatai. Afterwards, when
Yalavach went to Chaghatai, he called him on
the carpet and cursed him. Yalavach said to
Vazir, “I have something to say to you in pri-
vate.” When they were seated together, he said,
“I am the Qa’an’s deputy. Chaghatai cannot
kill me without consultation. If I complain of
you, the Qa’an will kill you. If you make repa-
ration to me, well and good; if not, I will not
speak on your behalf before the Qa’an. If you
speak of this to Chaghatai, I will deny it no
matter how many times they ask me, and you
have no witness.” [776] Vazir was therefore
compelled to make recompense. There are
many stories about Vazir, of which this is but
one example. Vazir often said to Chaghatai,
“On your account I have left myself no friends.
After you no one will have mercy on me.”
When Chaghatai died, he was executed on
charges of having poisoned Chaghatai.
Habash Amid, Chaghatai’s bitigchi, was a
Muslim, originally from Otrar. ❧
Part Three of the history of Chaghatai: His
conduct, pleasing character, various stories,
and words of wisdom he spoke, including
some things already given in the previous
two sections and things gathered from
miscellaneous sources.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

❦ SECTION SEVEN
THE HISTORY OF GENGHIS KHAN’S SON TOLUI KHAN, IN THREE PARTS
Part One is on his offspring, his wives, and
his sons and grandsons who have branched off
down to the present, aside from those of his
sons who became rulers, to each of whom a
separate section is devoted.
Part Two is his history, aside from what has
already necessarily been said in the course of
the history of his father and brothers; a picture
of his throne, wives, princes, and amirs at his
enthronement; a mention of the battles he
fought and the victories he achieved; the length
of his reign.
Part Three is on his conduct and good moral
character, with miscellaneous stories, anec-
dotes, sayings, and good orders he gave, aside
from what was included in the previous two
sections. These things have been culled from
various books and persons. [778]
Part One: His offspring, his wives, and his
sons and grandsons who have branched off
down to the present, aside from those of his
sons who became rulers, to each of whom a
separate section is devoted.
Tolui Khan was Genghis Khan’s fourth son,
the youngest of the four main sons, who were
called the “four külügs” (stalwarts). His moth-
er was Genghis Khan’s chief wife, Börtä Füjin,
who gave birth to his three elder brothers. His
title was Yäkä Noyan and Ulugh Noyan, [both
of which] mean “great commander,” and those
were the names by which he was known.
Genghis Khan called him nökär (liege man).
He had no peer in bravery, courage, strategy
and tactics. His father arranged a marriage for
him while he was young with the daughter of
Jagambu, the brother of Ong Khan, the ruler of
the Kerayit nation. Her name was Sorqaghtani
Beki, and she was the eldest and most beloved
of Tolui Khan’s wives and the mother of his
four principal sons, who were like Genghis
Khan’s four sons in being the mainstays of his
realm. Aside from Sorqaghtani Beki he had
many other wives and concubines, and he had
ten sons, as follows: (1) Möngkä Qa’an, (2)
Jörikä, (3) Qutuqtu, (4) Qubilai Qa’an, [779]
(5) Hülägü Khan, (6) Ariq Bökä, (7) Böchök,
(8) Mögä, (9) Sögätäi, and (10) Sübügätäi.
Tolui Khan’s ﬁrst son, Möngkä Qa’an.
He was born of Sorqaghtani Beki. Since he
was a ruler, a separate section will be devoted
to him and his offspring.1
Tolui Khan’s second son, Jörikä.
He was born of a wife named Saruq Khatun.
He died young without offspring.
Tolui Khan’s third son, Qutuqtu.2
He was born of Linqum Khatun. He had no
sons, but he had a daughter named Kälmish
Aqa, who was married to Salji’udai Gürägän of
the Qunqirat. He was an amir in service to the
1See text p. 820 below. Möngkä’s name occurs
throughout the Jami‘u’t-tawarikh both in its Mongolian
form, Möngkä (‘eternal’), and in its Turkish form,
Mängü (or Mänggü, with the doubled ‘g’ occasionally so
indicated in Persian). Carpini and William of Rubruck
spell it variously as Mangu and Mengu. In Chinese
dynastic lists he is given the title 憲宗 Xian Zong.
2Variously spelled as Qutuqtu ~ Quduqdu ~ Qutughtu.

ruler of the Ulus Jochi, and he died in 701
[1301–2].
Kälmish Aqa is still alive and living there.
Toqta and the other princes [780] hold her in a
position of great imiportance. Since she is the
offspring of Tolui Khan, she shows constant af-
fection to the Padishah of Islam and continual-
ly sends emissaries to inform him of events
that transpire in that realm. It is due to her that
friendship has been maintained and strife and
enmity avoided between Toqta and Jochi
Khan’s other offspring and Tolui Khan’s house.
When Qubilai Qa’an’s son Nomoghan was sur-
prised and seized by his cousins and sent to
Möngkä Temür, the ruler of Jochi Khan’s ulus,
Kälmish Aqa exerted herself to have him sent
back to his father with honor in the company
of some of the princes and great amirs, as has
already been described in the history of Jochi.
Her husband, Salji’udai Gürägän, was the
cause for the hatred and battles fought between
Toqta, the ruler of the Ulus Jochi, and Tatar’s
son Noqai, who commanded the forces of the
right wing of that ulus and with whose help
Toqta became ruler, as has also been described
in the section on Jochi.1 Things finally got so
bad that Noqai was killed and his sons were
overthrown.
Tolui Khan’s fourth son, Qubilai Qa’an.
He was born of Sorqaghtani Beki. Since he
became emperor, a separate section will be de-
voted to him and his sons.2 [781]
Tolui Khan’s ﬁfth son, Hülägü Khan.
May the sun of his fortune shine; may his
shadow be perpetual, and may he live forever.
His genealogy will be mentioned separately
in the section devoted to him.3
1See above, text pp. 744–48.
2See below, section ten, text pp. 863–69.
3The section on Ghazan Khan begins on text p. 1205.
Tolui Khan’s sixth son, Ariq Bökä.
He was also born of the chief wife. Since he
disputed with Qubilai over the throne and em-
perorship, they fought many battles. His histo-
ry will be subsumed under that of Qubilai, but
his sons will be listed here. He had ﬁve sons:
(1) Yobuqur, who had five sons: Hulachu, Ili
Buqa, Öljä, Öljä-Temür, and Urla; (2) Malik
Temür, who had six sons: Mingqan, Achiqi,
Yesün-Tö’ä, Ba’aritai, Oyiruda, and Mahmud;
(3) Qutuqa, whose sons are unknown; (4) Tam-
machi, who had one son named Bayan; and (5)
Naira’u Buqa, who had five sons: Nachin,
[782] Samishkah, Bayan Äbügän, Ura-Temür,
and Qurtuqa.
Tolui Khan’s seventh son, Böchök.
He was born of ___ Khatun. He had wives
and concubines by whom he had sons. He was
his father’s successor and was called Säbilgär
because he had a hundred sons.4 His sons are at
present with Temür Qa’an, but their names
have not yet been ascertained with certainty.
Those who are known are: (1) Sayin Buqa,
who had two sons, Dashman and Ila’udar; (2)
Ja’utu, who had one son, Törä Temür; (3) Täk-
shi, whose sons are not known; and (4) Tüb-
shin, who had four sons, Bültachar, Sa’ut, Bäk-
täi,5 and Boralqi.
Tolui Khan’s eighth son, Mögä.
He was born of ____ Khatun. He had three
sons, Chingtum,6 Äbügän, and Bolad.

Tolui Khan’s ninth son, Sögätäi.
He was born of ___ Khatun. He had a son
named Tuq Temür who was very brave and an
extremely good archer. In battle [783] he al-
ways used to ride a gray horse. “Do not choose
horses of a jerdä (reddish) or other color be-
cause blood won’t show up on them to make
the foe bolder,” he used to say. “I always
choose a roan because, just as rouge enhances
the beauty of women, the beauty of men is
enhanced by blood that spills from a wounded
rider and horse onto clothing and the horse’s
body to be seen from afar.” Because he was so
dauntless, many seditious thoughts entered his
mind. When Qubilai sent Nomoghan with the
Däräsü troops in the company of the princes to
Qaidu, this Tuq Temür was with them and pro-
voked the others to seize Nomoghan, as will be
described in the history of Qubilai Qa’an.1
Tolui Khan’s tenth son, Sübügätäi.
[text missing]
A picture of Tolui Khan and a genealogical
chart of his sons are as follows.2 [784]

Part Two of the history of Tolui Khan. His history, aside from what has already necessarily
been said in the course of the history of his father and brothers; a picture of his throne,
wives, princes, and amirs at his enthronement; a mention of the battles he fought and the
victories he achieved; the length of his reign; stories of Tolui Khan’s accompaniment of his
father during his lifetime, the battles they fought and the cities they conquered.
Most of the time Tolui Khan accompanied
his father, and Genghis Khan consulted him on
all matters, large and small, and called him
nökär [liege man]. Genghis Khan’s yurt, ordus,
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVEN: TOLUI KHAN
377

goods, treasuries, er-akhta [cavalry corps], of-
ficers, and elite troops all came into his posses-
sion, for it has been the Mongol and Turkic
custom since ancient times for a father during
his lifetime to separate his elder sons’ posses-
sions, flocks and herds, and followers and send
them away. What remains belongs to the
youngest son, who is called the otchigin, i.e.
the son who gains possession of the ﬁre and
hearth, and indicates that the foundation of the
home rests upon him. The Turkish word ot ba-
sically means ﬁre, [785] and tegin means com-
mander, i.e. he is the commander and lord of
the fire. Since the word tegin cannot be pro-
nounced correctly in the Mongolian dialect,
some say otchigin and others say otchi, but the
basic meaning of the word is as has been said.
Genghis Khan entertained the notion of
turning over the office of qa’an and the imper-
ial throne to him and making him his designat-
ed heir, but he said, “By virtue of your position
you will command my yurt, ordu, army, and
treasury. You will be better off and more at
leisure. In the end, since much of the army will
belong to you, your sons will be more power-
ful and more magniﬁcent than the other
princes.” However, since he recognized signs
of greatness in [Tolui Khan’s sons], it occurred
to him that things would turn out such that the
office of qa’an and the emperorship would be
settled upon them, as actually did happen for
all to see.
Inasmuch as the entirety of the armies and
right- and left-wing commanders of ten thou-
sand and one thousand were written in detail at
the end of Genghis Khan’s history, it can be
learned from there what he gave to the other
sons, what he gave to his brothers, and which
they are. All that was not distributed came into
Tolui Khan’s possession, and those troops and
commanders were inherited as they were by
his sons, as can be observed—except only a
few who involuntarily, on account of bulqaqs
[disturbances], have fallen in various directions
to various princes. The rest are in service either
to the Qa’an or to the Padishah of Islam.
Tolui Khan was extremely successful in bat-
tle. No prince achieved such conquests as he
did. What occurred during his father’s lifetime
will be given in summary, and a portion of
what befell after that will also be introduced. 
When Genghis Khan mounted for an expedi-
tion to Cathay [786] and arrived at the city of
Taiyuanfu, which is extremely large, there was
an enormous population with great strength
and power, and no one could get near. Genghis
Khan sent Tolui Khan with Alchu Noyan’s son
Chigü Gürägän of the Qunqirat and an army.
They did battle, got up on the walls, and took
the city. After that, he laid siege to Cho-chou
and took it. Then he dispatched troops with his
elder sons and amirs from the right and left
wings, and he himself and Tolui Khan set out
with the middle group, the center, conquering
and devastating every city and territory along
the way as far as ___.1 The spoils of Zhending-
fu, one of Cathay’s great cities the Mongols
call Chagha’an Balghasun, were Tolui Khan’s.
The spoils that Tolui Khan took from that terri-
tory went by inheritance and division to his
family, and what is in Cathay, the Qipchaq
Steppe, and other territories is well marked. Of
the
possessions
in
Cathay
that
were
the
Qa’an’s and then his wives’, the portion that
was Hülägü Khan’s and his children’s was or-
dered to be well guarded and kept until there
was an opportunity for it to be sent. 
After they returned from the realm of Cathay,
Genghis Khan set out for Tajik territory. When
he reached Otrar, he left Jochi, Chaghatai, and
1Text has hereـﯽـﭘ
ﻮ ــﭼﻴ, but it probably should beﻮ ــﺟﻴﯽـﻣ
(密州Mizhou), to which Muqali was dispatched as
mentioned in the account on text p. 448 above.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Ögödäi to lay siege and conquer Khwarazm,
while Tolui Khan went with his father to take
Bukhara.
From
there
they
proceeded
to
Samarkand, which they subdued along with all
its surrounding territory. From there they went
to Nakhshab and Termez, and then from the
Temür Qahalqa (Iron Gates) in the Badakhshan
vicinity
he
sent
Tolui
Khan
to
conquer
Khurasan. Over the three months of that winter
he took Merv, Maruchuq, Sarakhs, Nishapur,
and all that area, and then in the spring he
turned back from Nishapur [787] at Genghis
Khan’s command. Along the way he took
Quhistan, that entire area, and Herat. He re-
joined Genghis Khan in Taligan just as he had
conquered and was destroying the fortress
there. That same summer he and his brothers
Chaghatai and Ögödäi went with their father in
pursuit of Sultan Jalaluddin as far as the banks
of the Indus. They vanquished the sultan’s sol-
diers, who crossed the river in rout. They
turned back there and launched a campaign
against Tangqut. Chaghatai was left with a
contingent to guard the rear of the ordus, and
Ögödäi and Tolui both remained with their fa-
ther until he fell ill. As was mentioned in the
previous section, Genghis Khan sat privately
with his two sons, advised them, and sent them
back to their own homes and lands. It was on
that campaign that he died.
The history of Tolui Khan after his father’s
death, when he consolidated his position in
the home yurt on his father’s throne, which
went to him by right; his agreement with his
brothers; the battles he fought and the
victories he achieved; and his end.
Genghis Khan died not long after Tolui Khan
returned home at his father’s order from
Tangqut territory with his brother Ögödäi, who
had been designated his father’s heir. After his
coffin was brought to the ordus and mourning
was held, the other brothers and princes [788]
departed for their own yurts, and Tolui Khan
mounted the imperial throne in the home yurt,
where Genghis Khan’s throne and his great or-
dus were.
As for his agreement with his brothers and
his battles and victories after his father’s death,
Tolui Khan so served and respected his broth-
ers and aqa-ini that all were grateful to him.
Most of the time he was in attendance upon
Ögödäi Qa’an, and he played an important role
in his enthronement as qa’an. When Ögödäi
Qa’an set out toward Namging to attack the Al-
tan Khan in Cathay on the banks of the Qara
Mörän (Yellow River), he sent Tolui Khan in a
different direction. He emerged via Tibet and
passed through the Cathaian province the in-
habitants
of
which
are
called
Hula’an
Tägäläns, meaning Red Jackets. Because the
Qa’an’s route was longer, Tolui Khan mean-
dered at a leisurely pace until the next year,
when there were no supplies left. Things got so
bad they had to eat human ﬂesh, carrion, and
dry grass. Having formed a järgä, he proceed-
ed through the plains until he reached a place
called Tungqal Qahalqa,1 and there he came
opposite the Altan Khan’s great army. As has
been explained in the section on the Qa’an,
Tolui Khan played an important role in defeat-
ing through good tactics such a powerful army,
which was many times their own in numbers.
He discovered a crossing over the Yellow Riv-
er, which had never suffered crossing before,
got across, and joined his brother, victorious
and triumphant. The Qa’an was overjoyed at
his arrival and commended his brother, [789]
for whom he hosted banquets and revelries.
As for his end and the cause of his illness
and death, after returning from the battle men-
tioned above, Tolui Khan went to his brother
1Tungqal Qahalqa is the Mongolian for Tongguan (湩
關).
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVEN: TOLUI KHAN
379

Ögödäi. Since he had been on that expedition
for a time, as the Qa’an turned back, he sta-
tioned Toqolqu Chärbi with a large army to
ﬁnish off the Altan Khan. Tolui remained with
the Qa’an. By chance the Qa’an fell ill, and ac-
cording to custom the shamans gathered and
were working their shamanism by chanting
spells over his illness and washing it with wa-
ter. Just then Tolui Khan came in, turned his
face to heaven in supplication, and said, “O
great eternal God, if you are afflicting him be-
cause of sin, my sins are more than his, for I
have killed more men in battle, pillaged more
women and children, and carried off more
mothers and fathers into captivity. If you want
to take your servant to your court because of
physical beauty, attractiveness, power, and
skill, I am more worthy. Take me instead of
Ögödäi and cure him of this illness. Place his
illness upon me.” Having said this with the
greatest of supplication, he took the bowl of
water in which the shamans had been washing
the Qa’an’s illness and drank it. Through di-
vine power, the Qa’an got better, and Tolui
Khan asked for permission to go to his family.
Along the way he fell ill and died in Moghai
Yil, the Year of the Snake corresponding to 630
[1233]. [790]
May God cause the cream of his offspring,
the Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan, the best
ruler in the world, to enjoy long life and let
him enjoy his expansive kingdom for all eter-
nity, through the sanctity of the Prophet and his
pure house. [791]
The history of Tolui Khan’s wife,
Sorqaghtani Beki, and his sons after his
death, and how they attained the office of
emperor through the efforts of their capable
and intelligent mother.
After Tolui Khan’s death, his sons and their
mother were with Ögödäi Qa’an, who held
them in positions of great respect and honor
and granted their requests instantly. One day
Sorqaghtani Beki requested one of the ortaqs
from the Qa’an’s court. The Qa’an refused, and
Sorqaghtani Beki wept and said, “For whom
did that person who was my beloved sacriﬁce
himself? For whose sake did he die?” The man
relayed these words to the Qa’an, who said,
“Sorqaghtani Beki is right.” He apologized and
granted her request.
Sorqaghtani Beki was extremely intelligent
and clever. She outshone all women in the
world, and she possessed chastity and purity to
the fullest degree. She was so competent that
when her sons were orphaned of their father as
children, she exerted herself to raise and edu-
cate them and teach them skills and manners.
She never allowed even an iota of disagree-
ment to come between them, and she made
certain that their wives loved each other too.
With good tactics and skill she maintained and
kept together all the sons, grandsons, great
commanders, and soldiers [792] left to them by
Genghis Khan and Tolui Khan, and since they
realized how highly intelligent and clever she
was, they never disobeyed her command in any
way. It was just as when Genghis Khan was
orphaned of his father when he was a child and
his mother Ö’älün Ekä maintained him and all
the soldiers—even often mounting herself and
riding on campaigns and keeping them in or-
der—until Genghis Khan was grown and ready
for world command. It was through his moth-
er’s efforts that he was able to achieve great
things. So too did Sorqaghtani Beki strive to
educate her sons in that same fashion. Howev-
er, it has been said that in one regard she was
even more patient than Genghis Khan’s moth-
er, for when Genghis Khan understood from
her hints that his mother was inclined to take a
husband, he gave her to Münglig Echigä,
whereas
when
Ögödäi
Qa’an
summoned
Sorqaghtani Beki through an emissary to give
380
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

her to his son Güyük Khan, when the Qa’an’s
yarligh was delivered, she replied, “How can
one change the decree of a yarligh? Nonethe-
less, I had thought I would raise my sons to
manhood and do my best that they be educated
and not part from or detest one another so that,
perhaps, something might come of their unity.”
When she did not give her consent to be mar-
ried to Güyük Khan and rejected the offer with
such an apology, no doubt remained as to
whether or not she had any inclination to get
married. For this reason she has been preferred
to Genghis Khan’s mother, Ö’älün Ekä. [793]
During Ögödäi Qa’an’s reign, and after Tolui
Khan’s death, the Qa’an gave to his son Kötän,
of his own accord and without consultation
with his aqa-ini, two hazaras of Suldus from
the troops that belonged to Tolui Khan and his
sons. When the commanders of ten thousand
and one thousand who were attached to Yäkä
Noyan were apprised of this, they went togeth-
er to Sorqaghtani Beki, Möngkä Qa’an, and
their aqa-ini and said, “The two hazaras of
Suldus troops belong to us by virtue of
Genghis Khan’s yarligh. Now they are being
given to Kötän. How can we allow Genghis
Khan’s order to be changed? We will petition
the Qa’an.”
“What you say is right,” Sorqaghtani Beki
replied, “but with the wealth we have inherited
and acquired, we lack nothing and are not in
need of anything. Both the soldiers and we be-
long to the Qa’an. Whatever he orders is law,
and we will obey.” When Sorqaghtani Beki
said this, the officers fell silent, and everyone
who heard what she had said approved of it.
Without doubt, through the intelligence and
competence she possessed she made her sons’
rank surpass that of their cousins and got them
to the rank of emperor. The principal reason
her sons attained the emperorship was as
follows.
When Ögödäi Qa’an died, Törägänä Khatun
would not let Shirämün become emperor even
though he had been designated the heir. In-
stead, she took it upon herself to rule. When
she enthroned her eldest son, Güyük Khan,
Batu, who was the eldest of them all, did not
attend, excusing himself on account of the
gout. Güyük Khan was offended by this and
started contemplating treachery against Batu.
Then, claiming that the climate in Imil was
good for his illness, Güyük decided to go there.
When Sorqaghtani Beki learned of his plans,
[794] she sent a secret message to apprise
Batu. Soon thereafter Güyük died, and Ögödäi
Qa’an’s sons and people wanted to elevate
Shirämün to the throne. First they summoned
Batu, but he said, “I have the gout. If they
come to me, that will be all right.” Törägänä
Khatun and Ögödäi Qa’an’s family considered
this absurd and said, “Genghis Khan’s capital
is here. Why should we go there?” Batu, how-
ever, was aged and the eldest and greatest of
all the princes, and thus the choice of ruler was
with him. 
To her eldest son, Möngkä, Sorqaghtani Beki
said, “Since the others will not go to Batu, and
he is the eldest of all and ill, you go visit him
in his sickness.” As ordered by his mother, he
went there, and Batu, in gratitude and because
of older obligations too, became a supporter of
his and raised him to the Qa’anate. As has been
mentioned, Sorqaghtani Beki was clever not to
have raised an objection with Kötän over the
matter of the Suldus troops but to remain on
friendly terms with him, for when Ögödäi
Qa’an’s family disputed the Qa’anate with
Möngkä and were plotting against him, Kötän
allied himself with Möngkä and helped him.
When Kötän died, Möngkä Qa’an left the
troops that had been with Kötän in Tangqut as
they were with his sons and always showed
them honor and respect. Even at the present

they remain as they were and now belong to
Öljäitü Qa’an. This will all be explained in the
section on Möngkä Qa’an, God willing. [795]
