❦ SECTION EIGHT
THE HISTORY OF GÜYÜK KHAN, SON OF ÖGÖDÄI QA’AN, SON OF GENGHIS
KHAN, IN THREE PARTS
Part One is on him, his wives, and the
branches of his sons and grandsons down to
the present. Since his genealogical chart was
drawn in the section on his father, it has been
omitted here.
Part Two is on the dates and history of his
reign, a picture of his throne, wives, princes,
and amirs during his enthronement; a mention
of the battles he fought and the victories he
achieved; a preface to his accession.
Part Three is on his conduct and character,
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections and
were culled from various books and persons.
[798]
Part One. On Güyük Khan, his wives, and
the branches of his sons and grandsons
down to the present. (His genealogical chart
was included in the section on his father.)
Güyük Khan was Ögödäi Qa’an’s eldest son,
and he was born of Ögödäi’s chief wife,
Törägänä Khatun. He had many wives and
concubines, but the chief of them all was
Oghul Qaimish.
Güyük Khan had three sons. The eldest was
Khwaja Oghul, and the second was Naqu.
They were both born of Oghul Qaimish. Naqu
had a son named Chabat. When Baraq crossed
the river to ﬁght Abaqa Khan, Qaidu sent this
Chabat with a thousand horsemen attached per-
sonally to him in Baraq’s company as rein-
forcements, but he got angry with Baraq and
turned
back.
When
he
reached
Bukhara,
Baraq’s son Beg Temür tried to seize him. He
escaped with nine horsemen and took the
desert road to Qaidu, where he fell ill of fear
and died.
The third son was named Hoqu, and he was
born of a concubine. He had a son named Tüg-
mä, and this Tügmä had a son also named Tüg-
mä. At present he is in dispute with Qaidu’s
son Chapar over the kingship and does not
obey his orders. 
It is not known whether Khwaja Oghul had
sons or not. Their genealogical chart was given
in the section on Ögödäi Qa’an. [799]
Part Two of the history of Güyük Khan, on
the dates and history of his reign, a picture
of his throne, wives, princes, and amirs
during his enthronement; a mention of the
battles he fought and the victories he
achieved; events leading to his accession.
When Ögödäi Qa’an passed away, his eldest
son, Güyük Khan, had not yet returned from
the Qipchaq campaign. Mögä Khatun also died
shortly afterwards, and Törägänä Khatun, the
mother of the elder sons, through shrewd tricks
and on her own, without consulting the aqa-
inis, seized control of the kingdom and won
over the hearts of her relatives and the com-
manders by giving various gifts and presents
until all were inclined to her side and came un-
der her control. Chinqai and the Qa’an’s other
ministers and advisors remained in their posts
as before, as did the governors of various
provinces. Since she had been offended by cer-
tain persons during the Qa’an’s reign and har-

bored a desire for revenge in her heart, when
she became the absolute ruler she wanted to
pay back each and every one of them. She had
a chamberlain named Fatima who had been
brought from Mashhad in Tus when Khurasan
was conquered. This woman was extremely
shrewd and clever, and she had the khatun’s
fullest trust and was privy to her secrets. [800]
The officials used her as a means to get things
done. On this chamberlain’s advice, officers
and ministers who had served in exalted posts
during the Qa’an’s reign were dismissed, and
in their place were put ignorant men. They
tried to have Chinqai, the Qa’an’s chief vizier,
arrested, but he learned of their plot and ﬂed to
Kötän and sought his protection. Fatima har-
bored an old grudge against Mahmud Yala-
vach, whom the Qa’an had made chief of the
administration, and when she found an oppor-
tunity she nominated a man named Abdul-Rah-
man to take his place and sent Oqal Qorchi as
an envoy to arrest Yalavach and bring him in
along with his liege men. When the envoys
arrived, Yalavach came out cheerfully and
showed them all honor and respect. He kept
them occupied with hospitality for two days,
during which time he kept saying, “Today let’s
drink. We can hear the contents of the decree
tomorrow morning.” All along he was secretly
making preparations for escape, instructing his
liege men what to do when Oqal Qorchi or-
dered them to be seized and bound. “Cry out
against me,” he said, “and say, ‘We are infor-
mants on Yalavach. For what crime are you
arresting us? We have been hoping for just
such a day.’ ” On the third night Yalavach plied
the envoys with wine and got them drunk.
Having put them to bed, he and several horse-
men ﬂed to Kötän, thus escaping the harm that
would have been done to him. 
Having
taken
refuge
with
Kötän,
both
Yalavach and Chinqai were showered with fa-
vors by him. The next day, when Oqal Qorchi
was informed of Yalavach’s escape, he released
Yalavach’s liege men from bondage and set out
after Yalavach. When he came before Kötän,
he delivered Kötän’s mother’s decree that
Yalavach be arrested and brought in, [801] and
on his heels came another envoy for the same
purpose. Kötän replied, “Tell my mother, ‘The
kite that takes refuge in a bramble patch from
the talons of the hawk is safe from his enemy’s
might.’ Since they have sought refuge with us,
to send them back would be unchivalrous. In
the near future a quriltai will be held, and I
will bring them there with me. In the presence
of my relatives and the amirs an investigation
into their crimes can be undertaken, and they
can be punished accordingly.” Envoys were
sent several more times, but each time Kötän
gave the same excuse. When Amir Mas‘ud
Beg, the governor of Turkistan and Transoxi-
ana, saw what was going on, he ﬁgured it was
not in his best interests to remain where he
was, so he hastened to Batu’s court.
Qara [Hülägü] Oghul, some of Chaghatai’s
wives, Orghina Khatun, and some others had
sent Qurtuqai Elchi and Amir Arghun Aqa to
arrest Görgüz in Khurasan. When Amir Arghun
brought Görgüz in for execution, he was ap-
pointed to Khurasan in Görgüz’s stead. 
During this interregnum and bulqaq [distur-
bance], everyone was sending envoys and
emissaries in every direction; rumors were ﬂy-
ing; everyone on every front was using any and
every pretext to gain protection and to keep
what protection they had—save only Sorqagh-
tani Beki and her sons, who remained constant
on the path of the Yasaq and did not swerve
one iota from the great Yosun.
Törägänä Khatun sent envoys east and west
to summon all the princes, Chaghatai’s sons,
commanders of the right and left wings, sul-
tans, maliks, grandees, and sadrs to a quriltai.
384
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

During all this, since the ﬁeld was still empty
and Güyük Khan had not yet arrived, Genghis
Khan’s brother Otchigin Noyan wanted [802]
to seize the throne himself by force. With this
thought in mind, he set out for the Qa’an’s
ordu with a large and well-equipped army.
With this, the whole of the soldiery and the
ulus rose up in alarm. Törägänä Khatun sent an
envoy, saying, “We are your daughter-in-law,
and we rely upon you for help. Why are you
coming with soldiers, weapons, and equip-
ment? The entire ulus and army are upset.” She
sent back Otchigin’s own son, Orutai,1 an at-
tendant at the Qa’an’s court, along with Mängli
Oghul, grandson of ___, with the clans and fol-
lowers they possessed. Otchigin repented of
his plan and offered an apology on the pretext
that there had been a death and he was coming
to offer condolences. Just then news arrived
that Güyük Khan had descended in his ordu on
the banks of the Imil. Otchigin’s regret in-
creased, and he returned to his yurt. 
In short, for nearly three years the emperor’s
throne remained under Törägänä Khatun’s
command, and not only was her word law
throughout the realm but she also managed to
antagonize all the officials, and no quriltai
could be held because the attendance of the
princes could not be gained. When Güyük
Khan came to his mother he made no effort to
attend to affairs of state, and Törägänä Khatun
continued to rule until she had the office of
emperor conﬁrmed upon her son, two or three
months after which she died.
Now an Alid from Samarkand named Shera
who was Qadaq’s cupbearer accused Fatima of
having bewitched Kötän to make him fall ill.
When Kötän’s illness got worse, he sent en-
voys to his brother Güyük Khan to say that Fa-
1JTK hasاو/ﰏ;اوSیin other MSS; Wolutai in the Yüan
Shih. Boyle reads Orutai.
tima had caused him to be ill, and if anything
happened, retribution should be taken on her.
Immediately afterwards news of Kötän’s death
arrived. Chinqai was reinstated, and he remind-
ed the Qa’an of the contents of Kötän’s mes-
sage. When Güyük Khan mounted the throne,
the ﬁrst inquisition held was that of Fatima.
[803] After she was given the bastinado and
tortured, she confessed. Her bodily oriﬁces
sewn closed, she was wrapped in felt and
thrown into the river. Her retainers were also
put to death. 
After Güyük Khan’s death, Ali Khwaja of
Imil made the same accusation of the afore-
mentioned Shera, saying, “He is bewitching
Khwaja Oghul.” Shera was imprisoned, and,
faced with impossible demands, he despaired
of his life. He too was detained until he con-
fessed to a crime he had not committed and
was thrown into the river, and his women and
children were put to the sword. 
After the emperor’s throne was graced by the
auspicious accession of Möngkä Qa’an and
Bürilgitäi was made governor of Beshbaliq,
Khwaja [Oghul] was brought, and he sent a
messenger to summon Ali Khwaja, who had
become one of his elite. He was accused of the
same crime, and Möngkä Qa’an ordered him
beaten left and right until all his limbs were
crushed. He died of this painful torture, and his
wives and children were reduced to the ig-
nominy of slavery.
When you have done evil, sit not secure from
afﬂictions, for retribution is necessary by the
law of nature.
This has been a short account of Törägänä
Khatun and her chamberlain. Now we will be-
gin the history of the reign of Güyük Khan,
God willing. [804]
Güyük Khan accedes to the khan’s throne.
During his lifetime Ögödäi Qa’an had select-
ed his third son, Köchü, a son of Törägänä
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION EIGHT: GÜYÜK KHAN
385

Khatun’s, as his designated heir; however, he
died while the Qa’an was still alive. Since the
Qa’an had loved him the most of all, he com-
manded that his heir and successor should be
Köchü’s eldest son, Shirämün, a very intelli-
gent young man with great prospects who had
been raised at the Qa’an’s court. During the
very year in which he would die, the Qa’an
dispatched messengers to summon Güyük,
who turned back in obedience to the summons.
Before he arrived, however, the Qa’an passed
away, and father and son were not able to see
each other again. When Güyük was informed
of this, he hastened to the Imil, and then he
proceeded to his father’s ordu. With his arrival
the hopes of the greedy were dashed. 
Envoys had been sent out in all directions to
summon the princes, commanders, sultans, ma-
liks, and scribes, and each and every one set
forth in response to the invitation. At the be-
ginning of spring in the Year of the Horse that
began in Rabi‘ II 643,1 the princes and com-
manders of the right and left wings arrived,
[805] each with his followers and retainers,
and they assembled in Kökä Na’ur—all except
Batu, who had been offended by something
and excused himself on the pretext of weak-
ness of constitution and suffering from the
gout.
The ﬁrst to arrive were Sorqaghtani Beki and
her sons, bedecked with the trappings of luxury
and ﬁnery; from the east came Otchigin with
eighty of his offspring; Elji’itäi and the other
uncles and cousins came; from Chaghatai’s
ordu came Qara Hülägü, Yesü Möngkä, Büri,
Baidar, Yesün Toqa, and other sons, grandsons,
and nephews of Chaghatai; from Jochi’s ordu
Batu sent his brothers Orda, Shiban, Bärkä,
Bärkächär, Tangqut, and Toqa Temür; the noy-
1The Year of the Horse is 1246, but that year began in
Ramadan 643, not Rabi‘ II.
ans and great amirs who were attached to every
party
came
escorting
their
princes.
From
Cathay
came
officers
and
officials;
from
Turkistan and Transoxiana came Amir Mas‘ud
Beg accompanied by the dignitaries of that re-
gion; from Khurasan came Amir Arghun ac-
companied by the amirs and important people
of that land and those of Persia, Luristan, Azer-
baijan, and Shirvan; from Anatolia came Sul-
tan Ruknuddin; from Georgia came the two
Davids; from Aleppo came the brother of the
ruler; from Mosul came Sultan Badruddin
Lu’lu’s ambassador; from Baghdad came the
chief cadi Fakhruddin. There were also emis-
saries from the Franks, from Fars, from Kir-
man, from Ala’uddin the lord of Alamut, and
from the governors of Quhistan, Shihabuddin
and Shamsuddin. This assemblage came, all
with baggage and gifts appropriate to such a
court, and for them nearly two thousand tents
had been prepared. There were so many people
in the vicinity of the ordu that there was no
place to stay, and food and drink escalated in
price and became scarce. 
The princes and amirs discussed the emper-
orship, saying, “Since Kötän, whom Genghis
Khan appointed to be emperor after the Qa’an,
has passed away, [806] and the Qa’an’s des-
ignated heir Shirämün has not yet reached his
majority, it would be best for us to install
Güyük Khan, the Qa’an’s eldest son.” Now
Güyük, who was known for his authoritarian-
ism, was favored by Törägänä Khatun, and
most of the commanders were in agreement
with her. After discussion they agreed to en-
throne Güyük.
As was customary, he refused and offered the
job to every prince, using his illness and weak
constitution as an excuse. After the comman-
ders insisted, he said, “I will accept on condi-
tion that henceforth the emperorship remain
among my offspring.” All agreed to this and
386
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

gave möchälgäs [written pledges], saying, “So
long as there remains of your progeny a piece
of ﬂesh a dog wouldn’t take if it were wrapped
in fat and a cow wouldn’t accept if it were
wrapped in grass, we will give the khanate to
no other.” Then a shaman’s pole was erected,
the princes doffed their hats, loosened their
belts, and sat him on the khan’s throne.
In Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that be-
gan in Rabi‘ II 643,1 in accordance with custom
all took goblets and spent a week banqueting.
When they were ﬁnished, he gave much money
to the khatuns, princes, and troop commanders.
After that, he began to administer the kingdom.
First came the trial of Fatima Khatun. Second
they took up the adventure of Otchigin and
made a minute inquiry into that. Since the in-
vestigation was extremely sensitive, no one
was allowed to attend the proceedings, with
only Möngkä Qa’an and Orda making the in-
vestigation, and no one else allowed entry. Af-

ter the inquisition a group of officers put him
to death.
Qara [Hülägü] Oghul was Chaghatai’s suc-
cessor, and Yesü Möngkä, Chaghtai’s own son,
was not allowed a say. Because of Güyük
Khan’s friendship with Yesü Möngkä, he said,
“While the son is alive, how can the grandson
be the heir?” And thus he awarded Chaghatai’s
place to [807] Yesü Möngkä and strengthened
his hand therein.
Since after the Qa’an’s death every one of
the princes had taken unbridled actions, writ-
ing vouchers against the empire and handing
any- and everybody paizas, an investigation of
this was held. Since it was outside the Yosun
and Yasaq, they were humiliated and hung
their heads in shame. Every paiza and yarligh
was taken back and placed before the one who
had issued it: “Read thy book; thine own soul
will be a sufﬁcient accountant against thee, this
day.”2
Sorqaghtani Beki and her sons remained
unashamed and held their heads high in pride,
for they were not charged with any infraction
of the Yasa. Güyük Khan even praised them as
worthy examples, while he ridiculed the others.
He reconﬁrmed all the statutes of his father and
said, “Every yarligh that contains the Qa’an’s
red seal shall be renewed without review.”
After that, he assigned soldiers in all direc-
tions and sent them off. He sent Sübädäi Baha-
dur and Chaghan Noyan with large armies to
Cathay and Manzi. He sent Eljigitäi with an
army to the west and ordered him to take two
out of every ten Tajik soldiers in Iran and, be-
ginning with the Heretics, subdue all areas in
rebellion. Güyük himself was determined to
follow after him. Although he turned all those
soldiers and peoples over to Eljigitäi generally,
in particular he awarded him the administration

of Anatolia, Georgia, Mosul, Aleppo, and Di-
yarbekir without anyone else’s interference and
also with the provision that the governors of
those areas forward the tribute from those ar-
eas to him.
Abdul-Rahman, whom Törägänä Khatun had
sent to Cathay as governor, was executed, and
the realm of Cathay was given to [808] Sahib
Yalavach. Turkistan and Transoxiana were
turned
over
to
Amir
Mas‘ud
Beg,
and
Khurasan, Persia, Azerbaijan, Shirvan, Lur,
Kirman, Georgia, and parts of Hindustan were
entrusted to Amir Arghun Aqa. The amirs and
maliks who were attached to each of these
were all awarded yarlighs and paizas, and ad-
ministrative affairs were entrusted to them. He
gave the sultanate of Anatolia to Sultan
Ruknuddin and deposed his brother. He made
David, the son of Qiz Malik,1 subordinate to
the other David. To Baghdad he sent via an
emissary threats and dire promises to the
caliph on account of a complaint Chormaqan’s
son Shirämün had made against them, and he
also ordered a reply written in the harshest of
terms to a letter the emissaries from Alamut
had brought. He favored Chinqai and gave him
the post of vizier. Then all the officials and
dignitaries of the surrounding realms returned
home.
The end of Güyük Khan’s reign; his
extraordinary generosity; his setting forth
for the Imil; and his passing away in the
vicinity of Samarqand.
Since Qadaq, who belonged to the Christian
nation, had served as atabeg to Güyük Khan
from his childhood on, Güyük’s nature had
been imprinted with that stamp. Afterwards
1“Qiz Malik” means simply ‘girl queen’; the reference
is to Queen Rusudan of Georgia and her son, David Nar-
in. The “other David” is David Lasha. See Grousset,
Empire, 272.
Chinqai had also helped in that regard, so for
these reasons he always favored priests and
Christians. When this became known, priests
from Syria, Anatolia, As, and Rus set out for
his court. With Qadaq and Chinqai in atten-
dance, he was not a little inimical to the reli-
gion of Islam, while the Christians enjoyed
great prosperity under him, and no Muslim
dared raise a voice against them.
Since Güyük Khan wanted his own reputa-
tion for generosity to surpass his father’s, he
was extreme in his liberality. [809] He ordered
that the goods brought by merchants from all
over should be valued as they had been in his
father’s time and their bills paid. Once their
bills amounted to 70,000 bars, for which
vouchers had been written against provinces.
As the wares piled up in mountainous heaps
that couldn’t be carried, the ministers reported
the condition to him. “It’s such a bother to
guard all that stuff,” he said, “and nobody de-
rives any beneﬁt from it. Distribute it to the
soldiers and courtiers.” For days they distrib-
uted things and sent them to all the subject
peoples, and still there was a lot left, so he or-
dered them to let it be plundered.
That year he wintered there, and when the
new year began he said, “The air at the Imil
agrees with my constitution, and the water
there is good for my illness.” So saying, he de-
camped with great pomp and circumstance and
headed west. At every farm he came to and
every time he saw a group of people along the
way he ordered that they be given bars of gold
and fabrics so that they might be rescued from
the shame of poverty.
Sorqaghtani Beki, being extremely intelligent
and clever, realized that his haste on that trip
was not free of trickery, and secretly she sent a
messenger to Batu, saying, “Be prepared, for
Güyük Khan is headed in your direction with a
huge army.” Grateful for this warning, Batu
388
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

made ready for battle with him, and when
Güyük Khan reached the Samarqand (Sängir
Qum) area, a one-week’s journey from Besh-
baliq, his appointed time came, depriving him
of the chance to place his foot one step further.
The length of his reign was one year. (May the
Padishah of Islam live to enjoy long life and
prosperity!) [810]
After Güyük Khan’s death the roads were
closed and an ordinance was issued for every-
one to stop wherever he was, be the spot inhab-
ited or in ruins. By Oghul Qaimish’s order
Güyük Khan’s body was taken to the Imil,
where his ordu was. As was customary,
Sorqaghtani Beki sent Oghul Qaimish condo-
lences, clothing, and a boghtaq [headdress].
Batu also sent condolences and sympathy, say-
ing, “Oghul Qaimish will continue to adminis-
ter the affairs of the realm, as before, in con-
sultation with Chinqai and the ministers, and
let her neglect nothing. On account of illness,
old age, and gout, it is impossible for me to
move. You inis are all there, and you will do
what is necessary.” 
Little was done, however, except dealing
with merchants. Most of the time Oghul
Qaimish sat in private with the shamans, lis-
tening to their blithering and fables. Khwaja
and Naqu set up two courts in opposition to
their mother, so now there were three courts in
one place. On all sides the princes wrote de-
crees and gave orders for whatever they want-
ed. Since there was disagreement among moth-
er, sons, and the others, and because opinions
and ideas conﬂicted, things got out of control.
Amir Chinqai sat dumbfounded by the tasks
with which he was confronted, and no one lis-
tened to his advice or counsel. Their relative
Sorqaghtani Beki sent admonishments and ad-
vice, but the sons were children and acted arbi-
trarily. Encouraged by Yesü Möngkä, they in-
dulged in terrible things—until the khanate
was conﬁrmed upon Möngkä Qa’an and things
were brought back under control. This has
been the history of Güyük Khan. [811]
Part Three of the history of Güyük Khan,
on his conduct and character, the
pronouncements and orders he gave;
incidents that occurred during his reign that
were not included in the previous two
sections and were culled from various books
and persons.
[Güyük Khan was a monarch as grand as
heaven and an emperor as magniﬁcent as the
ocean, possessed of the arrogance of grandeur
and conceit of pride. When the news of his glo-
rious accession spread throughout the world—
and when his harshness, authoritarianism, and
severity
of
punishment
became
similarly
known—before his orders ever reached his
foes, their hearts were ﬁlled with fear and
dread of him, and those who dwelt in neigh-
boring territories, once they heard of his repu-
tation, were too afraid of his wrath and fury to
have any rest by day or repose by night. His
court ministers, even his most elite courtiers,
could not make a move and never dared to ut-
ter a word on any matter before he initiated a
conversation. Those who came from far and
near approached not a span nearer than the
place where the horses were tethered unless
they were sent for. During the days of his reign
amirs, rulers, tax gatherers, and deputies from
east to west and from north to south went to his
ordu, as during the time of the quriltai, when a
thousand white tents were pitched for guests
and there was no room to alight in the vicinity
of his ordu—and still dignitaries and nobles
kept arriving from all directions. Such a throng
of people had never before been witnessed, and
there is no record of such a thing in history
books.
There were so many tents, people, and pavil-
ions that no ﬂat space remained on the plain.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION EIGHT: GÜYÜK KHAN
389

When he was conﬁrmed in the khanate, he
forbade any change in the commands and or-
ders of his father, just as he had allowed no
change in the Yasa of his father, and he ordered
that every yarligh sealed with Ögödäi Qa’an’s
red seal be renewed without being submitted to
him for review.
Güyük Khan was basically of a sickly consti-
tution, and mostly he was not without some ill-
ness. Nonetheless, most of his time was spent,
from dawn to dusk and from dusk to dawn, in
constant drinking and in the embrace of beau-
ties. This caused his illness to get worse, but he
would not give it up. Since Christians had been
in attendance upon him from his childhood on,
like his atabeg Qadaq and his deputy Chin-
qai—and some of his physicians were also of
that community, his nature had been indelibly
stamped, and he favored priests and Christians.
When this became known throughout the
world, priests and monks from all over came to
his court. He was also by nature not devoid of
an aversion to the Muhammedan religion.
During his reign he was melancholy and
cared little for conversation. He turned over all
administrative affairs to Qadaq and Chinqai.
During his time Christians were in the ascen-
dant, and no Muslim dared raise his voice
against them. In liberality he went beyond ex-
cess, wanting his reputation to surpass his fa-
ther’s, but he was not granted the time to do it.]
[812]
A summary history of the emperors of
Cathay and Machin and the amirs, caliphs,
sultans, maliks, atabegs of Iran, Egypt,
Syria, and North Africa who were
contemporary with Törägänä Khatun and
Güyük Khan from the beginning of Bars
Yil, the Year of the Leopard that began in
Sha‘ban 639 [February 1242], through
Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that began
in Ramadan 643 [January 1246], a period of
ﬁve years.
Emperors of Cathay and Machin during
these ﬁve years.
The realm of Cathay during this period was
completely under the control of the Genghisid
house. The last of the emperors, Shou-hsü, was
vanquished at the beginning of Ögödäi Qa’an’s
reign, and the dynasty came to an end.
During this period the emperor of Machin
was Lizong,1 who ruled forty-one years, seven
of which were before this period and twenty-
nine were after this period. [813]
The amirs, caliphs, sultans, maliks, and
atabegs during this period.
Amir Görgüz, the governor of Khurasan, was
arrested and bound by order of Ögödäi Qa’an
because of a quarrel he had on a bridge with a
certain individual attached to the Chagha-
tayids, and by the time he was taken to court
Ögödäi Qa’an had passed away, so he was tak-
en to the ordu at Ulugh Ef. There the amirs
held an inquiry. “If you can make a ﬁnal deci-
sion on my case,” he said, “then I will speak.
Otherwise, it would be better not to say any-
thing.” For that reason his case remained in
abeyance, and he was taken to Törägänä
Khatun’s ordu, from which Chinqai had ﬂed.
Görgüz did not pay much attention to the other
amirs who were in power, and he had no mon-
ey with him to advance his case. He was taken
to Chaghatai’s ordu, and after his guilt was
proven, he was executed. At the end of his life
he became a Muslim. In his stead Amir Arghun
Aqa was sent as governor of Khurasan, and
Sharafuddin Khwarazmi was made his deputy.
History of the caliphs.
At the beginning of this period the Abbasid
caliph was al-Mustansir-bi’llah. The Mongol
1Lizong (理宗) of the Southern Song, ruled 1224–64.
390
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

forces were advancing upon Baghdad in droves
under the command of Baiju Noyan, and they
laid siege to Arbela and took it by force. The
people of the city withdrew into the fortress
and fought hard, [814] but since there was no
water in the fortress so many died that it was
impossible to bury them all and they had to be
burned. The Mongols destroyed the city and
used catapults against the citadel. When the
caliph was apprised, he sent Shamsuddin Ars-
lan Tegin with three thousand cavalrymen to
reinforce them. Learning of his arrival, the
Mongols suddenly decamped and ﬂed. The
caliph asked the jurists to issue a legal opinion
which was better, pilgrimage or holy war. They
unanimously agreed that holy war was better.
The caliph therefore decreed that no one
should go on pilgrimage that year, and so the
learned, jurists, courtiers, and common folk,
both native and non-native, got busy learning
archery and the arts of weaponry. He also or-
dered the moat and walls of Baghdad repaired
and catapults set up on the walls. 
Once again the Mongols returned to attack
Arbela, the inhabitants of which had already
been sorely afflicted. Amir Arslan Tegin and
his troops constantly stood outside the city,
waiting for their arrival. When the Mongols
learned of this, they turned back and headed
for Daquq and the outskirts of Baghdad. They
murdered, looted, and took captives. Sharafud-
din Iqbal Sharabi the khatib exhorted the peo-
ple to holy war until they went out. Jamaluddin
Qosh-Temür commanded the vanguard. The
two sides met at Jabal al-Hamrin.
The Caliph Mustansir came out of Baghdad,
summoned elite and common alike, and ad-
dressed them, saying, “From all directions ene-
mies and foes of our religion are attacking our
territory. To repel them I have nothing but this
sword, but I am determined to go out myself
and ﬁght them.” The maliks and amirs said,
“The caliph must not trouble himself. We are
his slaves, and we will go.” And they all went
with strong hearts and fought. The Mongols
pulled back in rout from Jabal al-Hamrin, and
the caliph’s Turks and military slaves pursued
them, killing many and taking back the cap-
tives from Arbela and Daquq. [815]
On Friday the 10th of Jumada ii 640 [De-
cember 5, 1242] the Commander of the Faith-
ful al-Mustansir-bi’llah passed away, and his
son al-Musta‘sim-bi’llah became caliph in his
stead.
History of the sultans.
In Anatolia, Sultan Izzuddin ruled. His broth-
er Ruknuddin went to the Qa’an’s court, and
after Möngkä Qa’an was enthroned he gave
him the office of sultan and deposed his
brother.
In Mosul was Sultan Badruddin Lu’lu’, who
was at the pinnacle of his power. He sent an
emissary to the Qa’an’s court, and when
Möngkä Qa’an mounted the throne he sent the
emissary back with all honor. He showed favor
to Sultan Badruddin Lu’lu’ and sent him a
yarligh and a paiza. During these years Sultan
Badruddin took Nasibin.
The sultan in Egypt was Malik Salih Naj-
muddin Ayyub, son of al-Kamil, son of al-Adil.
He was afflicted with a chronic illness, and he
was at constant war with the Franks.
In Kirman was Sultan Ruknuddin. He dis-
pensed justice and equity, and no untoward
event occurred. [816]
In Seistan was Malik Shamsuddin Kurt.
History of the maliks and atabegs.
In Diyarbekir and Syria, Sayyid Tajuddin
Muhammad Salaya was appointed governor of
Arbela in 639 [1241–42]. Also in the same
year Baraka Khan, the son of Dawlatshah, one
of Sultan Jalaluddin’s amirs who commanded
the remnants of the defeated Khwarazmian
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION EIGHT: GÜYÜK KHAN
391

troops, proposed marriage to Malik Adil’s
daughter, who was the mother of the lord of
Aleppo. The envoy was humiliated, so Baraka
Khan amassed his troops and set out for that
territory. The army of Aleppo came out, and
battle was fought at Manbij. The Khwarazmi-
ans defeated the Aleppans, massacred, pil-
laged, and took captives. After that, the lord of
Aleppo and the lord of Homs joined to ﬁght
the Khwarazmians, but there was no defeat of
either side. 
Also during this year some Khwarazmians
who had been in Kirman joined the others in
Ana. Baraka Khan’s son Muhammad came to
Baghdad and entered the caliph’s service in the
retinue of Mujahiduddin Aybak the Davatdar.
In 640 [1242–43], once again a battle was
fought between the Khwarazmians and the
Aleppans. The Khwarazmians were defeated
and abandoned their wives, children, horses,
and ﬂocks. [817] The Aleppans took much
plunder.
In 642 [1244–45] once again the Mongol
army went to Diyarbekir and Khabur. They
seized Harran and Ruha (Edessa) and took
Mardin peacefully. Shihabuddin Ghazi ﬂed to
Egypt, where he settled and received support.
In Fars the ruler was Atabeg Abubakr, who
was occupied with organizing his army. [818]

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

❦ SECTION NINE
THE HISTORY OF MÖNGKÄ QA’AN, SON OF TOLUI KHAN, SON OF GENGHIS
KHAN, IN THREE PARTS
Part One is on his progeny, a detailed ac-
count of his wives and his sons’ offspring who
have branched off down to the present; a pic-
ture of him, and a genealogical chart of him
and his sons.
Part Two is the story of his enthronement, a
picture of his throne, wives, princes, and amirs
during his enthronement; the dates of his reign;
the battles he fought and the victories he
achieved.
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections and
were culled from various books and persons.
[820]
Part One. On Möngkä Qa’an’s progeny, a
detailed account of his wives and his sons’
offspring who have branched off down to
the present; a picture of him, and a
genealogical chart of him and his sons.
Möngkä Qa’an was Tolui Khan’s eldest son,
and he was born of the chief wife, Sorqaghtani
Beki daughter of Jagambu, the brother of Ong
Khan, the ruler of the Kerayit.
He had many wives and concubines, but his
chief wife was Qutuqtai Khatun, the daughter
of [H]uludai son of Butu Gürägän of the Ikiräs
“bone.”1 (Butu Gürägän was Genghis Khan’s
son-in-law.) By this lady he had two sons. The
elder
was
Baltu,
and
the
younger
was
Ürüngtash.
1For Huludai, see text p. 161 above. 
Ürüngtash had two sons, Sarban the elder
and Könchäk the younger. They both died
young and had no children. Sarban went on the
Däräsü campaign with Nomoghan; however,
Sarban allied himself with Shirägi, and they
seized Nomoghan and took him to Möngkä
Temür, the ruler of the Ulus Batu. Shirägi was
taken to Qubilai Qa’an, who sent him to the
coast and hot regions, where he died.
Also by that wife [Qutuqtai Khatun], Möng-
kä had a daughter named Bayalun. She was
married to Märik,2 the son of Cha’uqurchin,
who was Huludai’s brother. Huludai was the
father of this girl’s mother.3
He had another great lady wife named Oghul
Qoymish of Oyirat “bone” of the family of
Qutuqa Beki. She was the “sister” of Öljäi
Khatun.4 This lady was extremely domineer-
2The name isﻣـﺮﻳـﮏ(Märik?) in all Persian versions. In

3A graphic representation may help to clarify this

ing. Having been engaged ﬁrst to Tolui Khan,
she called her husband’s brothers Qubilai
Qa’an and [821] Hülägü Khan “son,” and they
were afraid of her. There were no sons by this
wife, but by her he did have two daughters.
The elder was named Shirin and the younger
was Bichqa, who was also called Kö’ünän.1
Shirin was married to Chochimtai, the son of
Taichu
Gürägän.
Taichu
was
married
to
Genghis Khan’s youngest daughter, Altalun,
and was of Olqunu’ut “bone.” When Shirin
died, Taichu Gürägän’s son was given Bichqa.
He had two concubines of importance. One
was Baya’ujin of the Baya’ut clan, and by her
he had one son named Shirägi. He had a son
named Ulus Buqa. The reason Möngkä took
this Baya’ujin is that her father stole a bow

for
execution
along
with
his
daughter
Baya’ujin. He saw her there and took her.
He had another concubine named Küitani of
the “bone” of the Eljigin. By her he had a son
named Asutai, who was in league with Ariq
Bökä against Qubilai Qa’an. This Asutai had
four sons. The eldest was Öljäi, then Hulachu,
Hantum, and Öljäi Buqa. These four sons were
with the Qa’an, but their history is not known
in detail.
The genealogical chart is as follows.2 [822]
was actually the great aunt of Öljäi Khatun, one of
