Part Two. The story of his enthronement, a
picture of his throne, wives, princes, and
amirs during his enthronement; the dates of
his reign; the battles he fought and the
victories he achieved.
The reason the khanate was transferred to
Möngkä Qa’an, and events leading to his
enthronement.
The transfer of the khanate to Möngkä Qa’an
through the intelligent efforts and planning of
his mother, Sorqaghtani Beki.
When Güyük Khan passed away, once again
the empire was thrown into confusion, and
Güyük’s wife Oghul Qaimish administered the
realm in consultation with the ministers. Prior
to that, when Ögödäi Qa’an had launched his
expedition to Cathay and Tolui Khan died, the
Qa’an constantly bemoaned his loss, and when
he was drunk he wept a great deal and said, “I
miss my brother so much. That’s why I choose
to get drunk. Maybe for an instant my inner
burning will be quelled.”
On account of the great sorrow he felt for
Tolui Khan’s sons, he ordered the administra-
tion of the ulus and the management of mili-
tary affairs assigned to Tolui Khan’s chief wife,
Sorqaghtani Beki, who was the most intelligent
woman in the world. Thus both her sons and
the army were at her command. In taking care
of her sons, as well as in arranging their affairs
and those of the army and ulus, Sorqaghtani
Beki laid a foundation that would have been
beyond the capability of any crowned head.
[823] The Qa’an consulted with her on all im-
394
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

portant administrative matters and never disre-
garded her advice or allowed any change in
what she said. Her retainers were distinguished
by the care, concern, and respect she gave
them. In no bulqaq [disturbance] was anything
ever done by her that contravened any long-
standing or recent ordinance. At the enthrone-
ment of every ruler, all the princes were made
to suffer humiliation for their actions—all ex-
cept Sorqaghtani Beki and her sons. This was
exclusively due to her great intelligence, per-
fect competence, and farsightedness, for from
the time of Tolui Khan’s death on, she always
maintained the good will of her kinfolk and
relatives
through
gifts
and
presents,
and
through generosity and favors she kept the
troops and foreigners obedient and on her side.
Therefore, after Güyük Khan most of the peo-
ple were unanimous in declaring that the
khanate should go to her eldest son, Möngkä.
She continued to curry favor with all parties
until God seated the bride of kingship in
Möngkä’s embrace through Sorqaghtani Beki’s
competence and intelligence.
Although she herself was a follower of the
Christian religion, she also strove to promote
the Muhammedan law and gave alms and gifts
to the leaders and shaykhs of Islam. Proof of
this is that she gave a thousand silver bars for a
madrasa to be built in Bukhara of which
Shaykhu’l-Islam Sayfuddin Bakharzi was to be
the superintendent. She also ordered villages
purchased and placed in endowment and teach-
ers and students appointed. She sent alms to all
regions and gave support to poor and needy
Muslims. She continued in this path until
Dhu’l-Hijja 649 [February 1252], when she
passed away. [824]
Events leading to his enthronement.
When Güyük Khan died, Batu was suffering
from the gout, and so he dispatched envoys in
all directions to his aqa-inis summoning the
tribes and relatives, saying, “Let all the princes
come here. We will hold a quriltai, elect one
who is worthy and whom we consider best,
and enthrone him.” This invitation was refused
by the sons of Ögödäi Qa’an, Güyük Khan,
and Chaghatai, who said, “The original yurt
and throne of Genghis Khan is the Onon and
Kerulen. We do not have to set foot upon the
Qipchaq Steppe.” Khwaja and Naqu sent as
their representatives Qonqurtaghai Noyan and
Temür Noyan, the prince of Qaraqorum, to
sign for them to whatever was agreed by the
princes. “Batu is the elder of all the princes,”
they said, “and we are all subject to his com-
mand. We will in no way go against what he
considers proper.” 
After that, Sorqaghtani Beki said to Möngkä
Qa’an, “Inasmuch as the sons have disobeyed
their aqa and not gone to him, you go with
your brothers and visit him in his illness.”
Möngkä Qa’an set out in accordance with his
mother’s wish and went to visit Batu. 
When he arrived, he performed the custom-
ary services. Batu, seeing on his forehead
traces
of
maturity
and
intelligence,
said,
“Among the princes, only Möngkä has the tal-
ent and ability to be khan, for he has seen the
vicissitudes of the world and tasted the bitter
and sweet of every labor. Many times he has
led troops in all directions, and he is more in-
telligent and competent than any of the others.
Ögödäi Qa’an and the other princes and com-
manders thought he possessed a full measure
of gravity and dignity, as he does. The Qa’an
dispatched him and his ‘brothers’ Kölgän and
Güyük with me, Batu, and Orda and Jochi’s
progeny to conquer the Qipchaq territory and
the realms that lay in that direction. He ren-
dered submissive and obedient the tribes of the
Ülirlik, Qipchaqs, Uruqsaqs, and Circassians.
[825] The Qipchaq leader Bachman, the Cir-
cassian chieftain Tuqfas, and the As chief Ajis
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION NINE: MÖNGKÄ QA’AN
395

were captured by Möngkä, as was the city of
[Man]-Kärmän [Kiev]. He massacred, pillaged,
and rendered them submissive. After that, in Ut
Yil corresponding to 638 [1241], the Qa’an
sent a decree for the princes to return. By the
time they arrived, the Qa’an had died, leaving
a command that his grandson Shirämün should
succeed him. Törägänä Khatun ignored his or-
der and elevated Güyük to the khanate. Now
the one who is worthy of ruling is Möngkä.
What other scion is there of Genghis Khan’s
progeny who can manage the empire and the
army with insight and intelligence? Möngkä is
the son of my good uncle Tolui Khan, the
youngest son of Genghis Khan, and he com-
mands his great yurt. According to Mongol law
and custom the father’s place goes to the
youngest son. Therefore, the rule belongs to
Möngkä.”
When Batu had ﬁnished expressing this
thought, he sent envoys to Genghis Khan’s
wives, Ögödäi Qa’an’s wives and sons, Tolui
Khan’s wife Sorqaghtani Beki, and the other
princes and commanders of the right and left
wings, saying “The one prince who has seen
with his own eyes and heard with his own ears
Genghis Khan’s yasaq and yarligh is Möngkä.
The best thing for the ulus, army, subjects, and
us princes to do would be to seat him upon the
throne.” At his command his brothers Orda,
Shiban, and Bärkä, all of Jochi’s offspring, the
princes of the right wing, and Chaghatai’s son
Qara Hülägü gathered and held banquets for
several days. Thereafter they agreed to en-
throne Möngkä, who refused to consent to as-
sume such a magniﬁcent post [826] or even to
contemplate such a thing. The more they insist-
ed, the more he refused. 
Möngkä’s brother Mögä Oghul rose and said,
“At this assembly we have all promised and
given our written pledges that we would not
disobey the command of ‘Sayin Khan.’ How
can Möngkä deviate from what he thinks is
right?”
Batu approved this sentiment highly and
praised him for saying it, and with that
Möngkä gave in. As was the custom of the
Mongols, Batu arose, and he and all the princes
and lords opened their belts, removed their
hats, and bent their knees. Batu held out a gob-
let and offered the khanate to its rightful own-
er. All those present swore allegiance and
promised that they would hold a great quriltai
in the new year. With that thought in mind,
they all departed for their own yurts and camp-
ing grounds, and the good news was spread
throughout the world.
Then Batu ordered his brothers Bärkä and
Toqa Temür to take a large military contingent
to escort Möngkä Qa’an to Genghis Khan’s
throne place in Kerulen and to hold a quriltai
in the presence of all the princes to seat him on
the imperial throne. With this, they departed
from Batu—
Glory and fortune to his right, and victory and
triumph to his left.
—and camped in järgä formation.
Sorqaghtani Beki, in the meantime, was pla-
cating and winning over her relatives and kins-
men with kindness and displays of courtesy,
and she invited them to a quriltai. 
A group of princes from the Qa’an’s and
Güyük Khan’s family, as well as Chaghatai’s
sons Yesü Möngkä and Büri, kept postponing
action and causing division within the ranks,
saying that the khanate should remain in the
Qa’an’s and Güyük Khan’s family, and several
times they sent emissaries to Batu to say, “We
are far from agreeing to this and have no part
in this covenant. The rule should come to us.
How can you give it to another?” [827]
“We have deliberated this action together
with our aqa-inis,” Batu replied, “and the mat-
ter has been settled in such a way that it is not
396
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

possible to abrogate it. Had it not been done in
this way, and had anyone other than Möngkä
Qa’an been nominated, the affairs of the em-
pire would have suffered beyond redemption.
If you, my sons, will contemplate this action
and look with farsightedness, you will realize
that the maintenance of such an empire is be-
yond the Qa’an’s sons and grandsons, for the
administration of such a vast and broad realm
stretching from east to west is not within the
capacity of children.”
While these arguments continued, the year
appointed [for the quriltai] ended, and the next
year was half over. With each passing year the
affairs of the world and the empire grew shaki-
er. Since there were such vast distances sepa-
rating them, it was impossible to assemble for
a council, so Möngkä Qa’an and Sorqaghtani
Beki sent representatives to each one to placate
them and win them over. Since no amount of
reason or advice had any effect on that group,
they resorted to repeated messages containing
promises of kindness and threats. The recipi-
ents kept making excuses, but they countered
their
objections
every
time,
hoping
that
through conciliation they might be restrained
and awake from their slumber of heedlessness
and pride. 
When that year too came to an end, they sent
envoys in every direction to invite all their rel-
atives to assemble in Kerulen. Shilämün Bit-
igchi was sent to Oghul Qaimish and her sons
Khwaja and Naqu. Alamdar Bitigchi was sent
to Yesü Möngkä to say to him, “Most of
Genghis Khan’s offspring have gathered, and
the quriltai awaits your presence. No excuses
or postponement will be accepted. If you have
any thoughts of cooperativeness and unity, you
must come to the quriltai so that together the
bests interests of the empire may be served.”
[828] When they realized that they had no al-
ternative, Naqu Oghul set out. Qadaq Noyan
and a group of commanders from Güyük
Khan’s court and Chaghatai Khan’s grandson
Yesün
Toqa
Oghul
came
with
them
to
Shirämün. All three then gathered in one place,
and after that Khwaja also set forth. They were
still imagining that the quriltai could not pro-
ceed without them.
Bärkä sent a message to Batu, saying, “We
have been wanting to place Möngkä Qa’an on
the throne for two years. Ögödäi Qa’an’s and
Güyük Khan’s sons and Chaghatai’s son Yesü
Möngkä have not come.” 
“Seat him on the throne!” replied Batu. “And
any creature that disobeys the Yasa will lose
his head.”
The following princes and commanders who
were with Möngkä Qa’an assembled: Bärkä,
the great amir [Har]qasun, the princes of the
Left Wing, Jochi Qasar’s sons Yegü and
Yesünggü,
Qachi’un’s
son
Elji’idäi,
Otchi
Noyan’s son Taghachar, and Bälgütäi’s sons,
who were all Genghis Khan’s nephews; of the
princes of the Right Wing, Chaghatai’s son
Qara Hülägü, Ögödäi Qa’an’s son Qada’an,
Ögödäi’s grandson, Kötän’s son Möngätü, and
Möngkä Qa’an’s brothers Hülägü Khan, Qubi-
lai Qa’an, Mögä, and Ariq Bökä.
At the time of his blessed accession they
gave thought how to make a yasaq for the or-
der of precedence. It was unanimously decided
that Bärkä should sit because of his gout, that
Qubilai should also sit, and that everyone
should heed Qubilai’s words. He ordered Mögä
to stand at the door so that he could hold the
princes and amirs back, and he ordered Hülägü
to stand before the ba’urchis and qumuzchis so
that no one would speak or listen to frivolous
words. Thus it was arranged, [829] and the two
of them went back and forth until all arrange-
ments for the quriltai had been made. 
The astrologers chose an auspicious ascen-
dant, and one of the indications of Möngkä’s
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION NINE: MÖNGKÄ QA’AN
397

ever-increasing fortune was as follows. During
those few days the sky in that area was clouded
over and it was constantly raining, so no one
saw the face of the sun. By chance, at the very
hour the astrologers had chosen, just as they
were about to take a sighting, suddenly the sun
came out from behind the clouds and the sky
cleared to reveal the whole body of the sun.
The astronomers were easily able to ascertain
the elevation, and all the assembled princes,
great commanders, tribal chieftains, and innu-
merable soldiers who were there removed their
hats and threw their belts over their shoulders.
In Qaqai Yil, the Year of the Pig that began in
Dhu’l-Hijja 648 [February 1251] they seated
Möngkä Qa’an on the imperial throne in
Genghis Khan’s capital in the vicinity of
Qaraqorum. The amirs and soldiers outside the
ordu accompanied the princes in bending their
knees nine times.
When Möngkä sat auspiciously upon the four
cushions of state, he magnanimously desired
that relief be afforded all sorts and classes. He
commanded that during those regal days no
one should dispute or quarrel with anyone else
and that all should enjoy and relish the specta-
cle to the fullest. Just as all varieties of the
human species were enjoying themselves, do-
mesticated animals, whether brutes for riding
or beasts of burden, should not be subjected to
being ridden, burdened with loads, or bound or
shackled, the blood of those that could lawfully
be eaten should not be spilled, and wild crea-
tures that ﬂy in the air, crawl upon the ground,
or swim in water should not be subjected to
hunter’s arrow or snare but be allowed to roam
in the meadows of security wherever they
wanted. [830] The surface of the earth was not
to be troubled by stake or disturbed by horse-
shoe, and ﬂowing water was not to be sullied
by impurities.
God be praised for having made him the
source of such clemency and a paragon of the
virtues of equity to such an extent that he was
desirous of the comfort of all things animate
and inanimate. How great must his regal con-
cern have been for rectifying the condition of
the weak and for spreading justice and welfare
among the elite and common alike! May God
let his renowned offspring enjoy kingdom and
fortune for many long years and generations
yet to come! 
They spent that day like that, and the next
day a banquet was held in a tent Sahib
Yalavach had arranged—of such brocaded and
gold-spun fabrics of all colors that never be-
fore had its like been erected. In the manner
depicted,1 the emperor of the world sat upon
the throne, the princes assembled on his left
and right like the necklace of the Pleiades, and
his seven exalted brothers standing politely be-
fore him. To his left sat houri-like ladies while
silvery-limbed cupbearers circulated draughts
of kumiss and wine with ewers and goblets. In
the
midst
of
the
lords
was
their
chief,
Mängäsär, standing servilely among the ranks
of the qorchis, and the secretaries, viziers,
chamberlains, and deputies with Bolgha Aqa at
their head stood politely in their place. For a
week the celebration and rejoicing continued in
this manner, and every day the wine house and
kitchen requisitioned two thousand carts of
wine and kumiss, three hundred horses and
oxen, and three thousand sheep. On account of
Bärkä’s presence they slaughtered all in accor-
dance with Islamic law.
In the midst of the banqueting Qada’an
Oghul, [831] his nephew Malik Oghul, and
Hülägü arrived, and they offered their congrat-
1The depiction planned to accompany the text is, of
course, missing.
398
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ulations in the customary manner and then
turned to enjoy the pleasures of the celebration.
Some of the princes from Ögödäi Qa’an’s
house plot against Möngkä Qa’an, but the
plot is discovered by Käsägä Qushchi, who
informs on them, and they are arrested.
While waiting for the arrival of the other
princes, they indulged in excessive revelry, and
no one imagined that Genghis Khan’s ancient
Yasa could be change or altered, and since no
altercation or quarrel of any kind took place
among the family, they neglected to take pre-
cautions during their celebrations.
Ögödäi Qa’an’s grandsons Shirämün and
Naqu and Qarachar’s son Totoq, having band-
ed together, arrived in the vicinity, and with
them were many carts full of weapons, for they
were harboring deceit and treachery in their
hearts. 
By happy coincidence—which is what good
fortune consists of—a falconer named Käsägä1
of the “bone” of the Qanqli who was one of
Möngkä Qa’an’s falcon keepers, lost a camel.
He went out in search of it and fell in among
the horde of Shirämün’s and Naqu’s soldiers.
There he saw a lot of soldiers with innu-
merable carts loaded ostensibly with food and
drink for a congratulatory banquet. Unaware of
what was going on, he inquired after his lost
camel. Along the way he came across a lad sit-
ting in front of a cart. The boy thought he was
one of their own horsemen and asked him to
help him ﬁx the cart. Käsägä got off his horse
to assist him, and his gaze fell upon the arms
and implements of war that were in the cart.
He asked the lad, “What is this load?”
“It’s weapons,” he replied. [832] “The same
as in the other carts.” 
1In the texts,ﮏ ـ ـﮐﺸandﮏ ـ ـﮐﺴ. Readﮐﺴﮕ
ـ ـ ـ
ﻪ(Käsägä), the
Koxiejie of the Yuan shi. See JTBy, p. 207, note 47, and
Cleaves, “Aqa Minu,” 73 and note 65.
Käsägä realized that going with carts ﬁlled
with weapons was not devoid of treachery and
deceit, but he feigned ignorance, and when he
had ﬁnished helping the lad, he went to a tent
that night and stayed as a guest. Gradually
growing bolder and bolder, he inquired about
things. When he was apprised of the situation,
he realized for certain that the band was con-
templating treachery for during the banquet,
when everybody was drunk, they were going to
“step off the path of respect” and carry out the
attack they had plotted together. As the saying
goes, “There is no evil plot that does not re-
bound upon its perpetrator.” 
With this realization Käsägä could no longer
restrain himself. Taking a few camels, he tra-
versed a three-day road in one day, and then he
burst into the court without permission and be-
gan to speak boldly, saying, “You are indulging
in play and sport while your enemies have
risen up to attack you! They are waiting for an
opportunity and have their weapons ready.” He
reported everything just as he had seen it and
urged them to make all haste to repel the
attack.
Since such treachery was not customary
among
the
Mongols—particularly
during
Genghis Khan’s reign and that of his sons—
they could not believe what he said and asked
him to repeat it many times. He repeated it ex-
actly without any variation, but Möngkä Qa’an
refused to listen and paid no attention. Käsägä
insisted, and his distress could be clearly seen,
but Möngkä Qa’an’s calm and reserve were
immutable. The princes and lords who were
present disagreed with such steadfastness as a
precaution against the evil eye, and before the
opportunity would be lost, all the princes want-
ed to set forth to deal with this affair, each
wanting to go himself to investigate. [833] In
the end they agreed unanimously that Amir
Mängäsär Noyan, the chief of the amirs of
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION NINE: MÖNGKÄ QA’AN
399

court, should go in the vanguard and investi-
gate. As ordered, he set out with two or three
thousand horsemen, and by dawn they had
arrived near where the others were camped. He
charged forward with ﬁve hundred warrior rid-
ers until he was near their tents, and then the
soldiers poured in from left and right. Prior to
this, Shirämün had left his contingent and
a’ughruq in Maski and was coming unencum-
bered
with
ﬁve
hundred
horsemen. Amir
Mängäsär, Prince Mögä as head of the army,
and Choqbal Gürägän of Kerayit “bone” had
surrounded Shirämün, Naqu, Totoq, and the
other princes who were with them in Sa’ari
Kähär and sent an envoy to say, “It has been
reported to the emperor that you are approach-
ing with evil in your hearts. If this report is
false, it will be sufficient proof for you to head
to court at once, without stopping to think or
hesitate. Otherwise, we are ordered to arrest
you and take you there. Which of the two
would you prefer?”
When they heard this message and saw them-
selves surrounded like a point in the middle of
a circle, and their supporters and followers far
away, they were perplexed. There was little
they could do but give in to their fate and deny
the report, saying, “We are coming with good
intentions.” When they had undertaken to set
out together for Möngkä Qa’an’s court, the
amirs came before Shirämün and the princes,
offered each other goblets, and then set out for
the emperor’s court, escorted by only a few
horsemen. When they approached most of their
liege men and weapons were seized and held.
It was ordered that the amirs who were with
the princes should stand outside. They were all
restrained, and having performed tägishmishi
in groups of nine, they entered the interior of
the ordu. [834] For three days they were ban-
queted, and not a word was asked of them. 
On the fourth day, when they went to court
and were about to enter, Möngkä Qa’an’s en-
voy came and said, “Stay here today.” Immedi-
ately another envoy arrived to say, “Let every
liege man and soldier who is with them return
to his unit of a thousand, hundred, or ten. Any-
one who remains here will be executed.” As
ordered, all withdrew, and the princes were left
alone with guards stationed to watch them.
Möngkä Qa’an goes to Genghis Khan’s
ordu and conducts the princes’ trial himself.
The
next
day
Möngkä
Qa’an
went
to
Genghis Khan’s ordu and sat on a chair to con-
duct the trial of Shirämün and the princes
himself.
“A report has been ﬁled about you,” he said.
“No matter how untrue and unreasonable it
seems, and regardless of its unacceptability to
the ear of wisdom, it is necessary to investigate
it in an amicable fashion in order for the dust
of doubt and suspicion to be wiped from the
countenance of certainty. If it is defamation
and slander, the lying slanderer will pay for his
action for all the world to see.”
The princes denied the accusation, saying,
“We have no knowledge of any such thing.”
Möngkä Qa’an ordered Shirämün’s atabeg,
Qata Kürin,1 summoned. When he was ques-
tioned, he denied the report. Then he was inter-
rogated with the bastinado. This time he con-
fessed,
saying,
“The
princes
have
no
knowledge of it. We amirs held a council and
conspired together, [835] but Möngkä Qa’an’s
good fortune intervened.” He then stabbed
himself with his own sword and died.
Mängäsär Noyan conducts a trial of the
amirs who plotted treason with the princes.
The next day he ordered arrested the group
of noyans and amirs like the great noyan
1See Juvaini/Boyle 2:580, note 88.
400
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Elji’itäi, Taunal,1 Jangi, Qalkhitai, Sorghan,
Taunal the younger, Toghan, and Yasa’ur, each
of whom considered himself of such a rank
that the celestial spheres could not touch him.
Also arrested was another group of tümän
commanders and leaders it would take too long
to name. Amir Mängäsär the yarghuchi was or-
dered to sit with a group of amirs and begin an
investigation. They questioned them until ﬁnal-
ly an inconsistency in their testimony was
found, and no doubt of their guilt remained.
They all confessed that they had conspired to
commit treason. Möngkä Qa’an wanted, as was
his praiseworthy custom and habit, to pardon
them, but the princes, noyans, and amirs said,
“To neglect to repel an opponent when the op-
portunity is nigh is far from being correct.”
Where you ought to apply a burning brand, it
is useless to apply salve.
When Möngkä Qa’an realized that they spoke
from sincerity [836] and not out of rancor and
selﬁshness, he ordered them all bound and im-
prisoned. Then he thought for a while about
what to do with them. One day when he was
seated on the throne, he ordered the amirs and
ministers to say what they thought about the
criminals. Everyone spoke according to his in-
telligence and knowledge, but nothing said im-
pressed the emperor. At the end of the session
Mahmud Yalavach was standing, and Möngkä
Qa’an said, “Why doesn’t that äbügän say
anything?”
Yalavach was told to step forward and say
something.
“It is better to be an ear in the presence of
kings than to be a tongue,” he said. “However,
I remember a story. If so ordered, I will tell it.”
Möngkä Qa’an ordered him to tell it.
1Deleting Qata Kürin from this list. Since he commit-
ted suicide in the preceding paragraph, he cannot have
been arrested “the next day.”
“Once,” he said, “when Alexander had con-
quered most of the realms of the earth, he was
about to set out for India. His commanders and
ministers then ceased to obey him, and each
one began to speak of independence and
despotism. Alexander was astonished and sent
a messenger to his unrivaled vizier Aristotle in
Greece to inquire why his commanders were
rebellious and to ask what the remedy was.
Aristotle went into a garden with the messen-
ger and ordered the large, well established
trees uprooted and weak little saplings planted
in their places. He did not, however, give the
messenger an answer. Having grown weary,
the messenger returned to Alexander and said,
‘He gave no answer.’ Alexander asked what he
had seen. He said, ‘He went into a garden and
had the large trees uprooted and put little sticks
in their place.’ Alexander said, ‘He did give a
reply. You just didn’t understand it.’ Then he
destroyed the commanders who were so unruly
and appointed their sons in their places.”
Möngkä Qa’an was highly pleased by this
story and realized that [837] he would have to
subject the group to his wrath and appoint oth-
ers in their stead. Therefore he ordered the
commanders who had been imprisoned and
those who had forced the princes to rebel and
led them to the brink of such a crime to be exe-
cuted. There were seventy-seven of them, and
they were all executed. Of them, Eljigitäi’s two
sons’ mouths were stuffed with stones until
they died. Their father was arrested in Badghis
and taken to Batu to join his sons.
Chaghatai’s grandson Yesün Toqa, his wife
Toqashi, and Büri arrive, and what
happened to them in this affair.
Yesün Toqa, his wife Toqashi, and Büri also
arrived. They had stationed all their soldiers on
the road and come themselves with only thirty
horsemen. Büri was sent to Batu under escort
by emissaries so that after his guilt was proven
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION NINE: MÖNGKÄ QA’AN
401

he could be executed. Qara Hülägü conducted
the trial of Toqashi Khatun in Yesün Toqa’s
presence. He ordered her to be kicked to death,
and thus he relieved his breast of an old
grudge.
When Shirämün and Naqu set out, Qadaq re-
alized that he had instigated the plot. Since he
was incapable of making amends, he hung his
head low. Suddenly the wardens of court
arrived like avenging angels and said:
All your friends are gone. Now it’s your turn.
Since he was pretending to be sick, he was
seated on a cart and taken away. When he
reached the court, although his guilt was clear-
er than Satan’s inﬁdelity, a trial was ordered.
[838] After he confessed to his crime, it was
decreed that he be dispatched after his friends
and comrades.
Möngkä Qa’an summons Oghul Qaimish
Khatun and Güyük Khan’s son Khwaja;
Oghul Qaimish is executed, and the Idiqut is
put to death.
Since some of the criminals had not yet
arrived and minds were still troubled by the
enormity of their action, Möngkä Qa’an dis-
patched Büri[l]gitäi Noyan with ten tümäns of
intrepid Turkish soldiers to the vicinity of
Ulugh Taq, the Khangai range,1 and Qum Sän-
gir,2 which is situated between Beshbaligh and
Qaraqorum, so that from there his yärgä could
join Qonquran Oghul,3 who was in the vicinity
of Qayaliq and who had formed a yärgä to the
edge of Otrar. He also dispatched Mügä Noyan
with two tümäns of soldiers to the border of
Qirqiz territory and Kämkämji’üt.
1See Juvaini/Boyle 2:585, note 107.
2See Juvaini/Boyle 2:585, note 108 and note to text p.
735 above.
3Qonquran (~ Qongqiran), the fourth son of Jochi
Khan’s son Orda. See text p. 718 above.
To Oghul Qaimish and Khwaja, who had not
yet arrived, he sent Shilämün Bitigchi as an en-
voy with a message saying, “If you did not par-
ticipate in this conspiracy, your welfare de-
pends upon your coming directly to court.”
When
Shilämün
discharged
his
mission,
Khwaja Oghul wanted to do something terrible
to him, but one of his wives, who was by many
degrees inferior to the others in rank but vastly
superior to them in intelligence, prevented him
for acting upon his wish, saying, “It is incum-
bent upon a messenger to deliver his message,
and in no age have messengers—even of
rebels—been subjected to harm. How can you
do injury to an envoy who has come from
Möngkä Qa’an’s court? By taking one life
what injury can you do to his kingship, espe-
cially when many evils can be imagined
springing therefrom? By committing this act,
an ocean of unrest and strife will billow forth,
and the world, which is now at peace, will be
cast into commotion. A ﬁre of calamity will
blaze up, [839] and then it will be too late to
repent. Möngkä Qa’an is the elder and stands
in the place of a father. You must go to him and
obey his command.”
Khwaja heeded this compassionate advice
and showed Shilämün honor and respect. Then,
together with his wife, he set out for court. By
listening to good advice, he avoided falling
into a bottomless abyss of trouble and stopped
on the shore of security.
Khwaja’s mother, Oghul Qaimish, sent the
envoy back to say, “You princes pledged and
gave möchälgäs that the rule would always re-
main among Ögödäi Qa’an’s offspring and that
you would never rebel against his sons. Now
you have broken your word.”
When this message was relayed, Möngkä
Qa’an became extremely angry and had a de-
cree written to this effect: “The wives of Jochi
Qasar, Otchigin, and Bälgütäi Noyan, the
402
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

brothers of Genghis Khan, have attended the
deliberation of the quriltai, but Oghul Qaimish
has [not]. If the shamans or Qadaq, Chinqai, or
Bala (who were Güyük Khan’s amir-ordus)
call or proclaim anyone padishah or khatun, or
if anyone becomes a padishah or a khatun by
their word, they shall see what they shall see!” 
Immediately he dispatched an envoy to de-
tain her and bring her to court with both hands
stitched in rawhide. When she arrived he sent
her and Shirämün’s mother, Qadaqach Khatun,
to Sorqaghtani Beki’s ordu. Mängäsär Yarghu-
chi stripped her naked and brought her to trial.
“How can anyone else look upon a body that
only an emperor has seen?” she asked. But she
was tried, wrapped in felt, and cast into the
river.
Chinqai also arrived, and he was dealt with
by Danishmand the chamberlain.
In Ramadan 650 [November 1252] in Besh-
baligh, the Idiqut, the leader of the idolators,
conspired with a group of people to rise up on
a Friday, when the Muslims were gathered in
the congregational mosque, and kill them all.
[840] A slave who had become Muslim be-
came aware of this plot and informed on them.
Their guilt was established, and after the Idiqut
was brought in and tried, he confessed to his
crime. It was ordered that he be taken to Besh-
baligh and executed in the presence of all the
people on a Friday after the prayer.
Möngkä Qa’an sends commanders in every
direction to deal with the remnants of the
rebels, and he pardons his relatives’ crimes.
Since several trouble-makers remained in
various corners, and it would have either taken
too long or involved too much trouble to bring
them
in,
the
emperor
dispatched
Bala
Yarghuchi and a group of liege men to Yesü
Möngkä’s armies to inquire about them and put
to death all who had participated in the con-
spiracy. He also sent another commander on
the same matter to Cathay.
When his august mind was relieved of worry
over these evildoers, the emperor’s good dis-
position led him to realize that to maintain
good family relations was obligatory upon
every
individual.
Therefore
he
ordered
Shirämün
to
escort
Qubilai,
Naqu,
and
Chaghan Noyan to Cathay. Khwaja was exem-
pted from participating in the campaign in
gratitude for the pleasing words his wife had
spoken, and he was assigned a yurt in the
vicinity of the Selenga near Qaraqorum.
Generally, from that time on, division ap-
peared among the Mongols. Genghis Khan had
advised his sons to maintain agreement and
unity, saying, “So long as you agree with each
other, fortune and triumph will be your friends,
[841] and no opponent can achieve victory.” It
was through this quality that it was possible for
him and his offspring to conquer most of the
countries of the world. 
It is said that one day, when he was ﬁrst ris-
ing to power, he was giving advice to his sons,
and by way of example he took an arrow from
his quiver and gave it to them, saying, “Break
it!” It broke with only a little force. Then he
gave them two arrows. They too broke easily.
In this manner he kept adding arrows until
there were ten, which even the strongmen and
champions of the army were unable to break.
“You are like these,” he said. “So long as you
support each other, no one can achieve victory
over you, and you will enjoy kingship for a
long time.” Had the rulers of Islam followed
this path, their dynasties would not have been
extinguished.
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION NINE: MÖNGKÄ QA’AN
403

The princes and commanders request
permission to return home from Möngkä
Qa’an’s court, and he sends them off with
honor.
Now that Möngkä Qa’an’s mind had been re-
lieved of urgent matters, the kingdom in tur-
moil had settled down, and the rule had been
turned over to him with the agreement of all
the princes, the princes and commanders re-
quested permission to depart for their homes.
He ordered them to disperse (targhamishi) and
go each to his own home, having showered
them with all displays of honor and affection.
Since Bärkä and Toqa Temür had the farthest
to go and had been away from Batu the
longest, he dismissed them ﬁrst with various
gifts. With them he sent Batu gifts and presents
beﬁtting such a ruler. [842] He awarded the
sons of Kötän’s son Möngädü, Qadaghan
Oghul,1 and Malik Oghul each an ordu from
the ordus and tents of the Qa’an along with his
wives. After that, he dismissed Qara Hülägü
with honor and awarded him his grandfather’s
place that had been seized by his uncle Yesü
Möngkä, and he withdrew happy. However,
when he got to the Altai mountains he died
without reaching his goal. The other princes,
commanders, and lords were rewarded accord-
ing to their rank and dismissed. He made
Käsägä a tarkhan and rewarded him with so
much wealth that he became a rich man of very
exalted position. 
When the princes and commanders had with-
drawn and their business had been completed,
he turned his attention to consolidating the ad-
ministration of the kingdom and caused the
world to ﬂourish through his justice.
Möngkä Qa’an turns his attention to the
administration of the realm; he puts it in
1Qadaghan ~ Qada’an, the sixth son of Ögödäi.
good order and commands mercy for all
classes; he dismisses governors of various
regions.
Since Möngkä Qa’an’s imperial attention
was focused upon patronizing the pious and
punishing the rebellious, and the reins of his
blessed thought were turned toward the welfare
of his subjects and lightening their burdens, in
his perfect intelligence he chose seriousness
over levity and gave up drinking wine. First he
dispatched his soldiers to the farthest reaches
of the orient and occident and the realms of the
Arabs and Persians. The realm of the east he
entrusted to Sahib Mahmud Yalavach, who had
performed past services with great devotion
and joined Möngkä’s service before he was en-
throned. The countries of Turkistan and Tran-
soxiana, [843] the lands of the Uyghur, Fer-
gana, and Khwarazm he gave to Amir Mas‘ud
Beg, who had suffered much fear and trem-
bling because of his devoted and sincere ser-
vice to court, as had his father, and they had
preceded all others in prostrating themselves at
court. As a reward for such service they were
returned [to their former posts], and those who
had come with them were singled out for vari-
ous rewards.
After that, Amir Arghun Aqa, who had
arrived after the quriltai and targhamishi be-
cause of the vast distance but who had already
received distinction at court for his sincere ser-
vice, had all his wishes fulﬁlled and requests
granted, and the realms of Iran—Khurasan,
Mazanderan, Iraq, Fars, Kirman, Azerbaijan,
Georgia, Lur, Arran, Armenia, Anatolia, Di-
yarbekir, Mosul, and Aleppo—were turned
over to him, and the maliks, amirs, deputies,
and secretaries who were in his service were
rewarded as he saw ﬁt. He set out to return on
the 20th of Ramadan 650 [November 24,
1252]. Ali Malik was sent as his liege man, and
Isfahan and Nishapur were awarded to him.
404
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

They were given the following order: “Con-
duct a new census and determine the entire
ulus and army and the amounts of tribute due,
and when that is ﬁnished, return to court.” To
each of them he said, “Make an inquiry into
the amounts of previous taxes, for we are con-
cerned for the welfare of the subjects, not for
the proliferation of treasury revenue.” He is-
sued a decree reducing the subjects’ tax
burdens.
Inasmuch as after Güyük Khan many of the
ladies and princes had given innumerable
yarlighs and paizas to their people, dispatched
envoys to all parts of the empire, and taken
high and low alike under their protection as or-
taqs and in other capacities, [844] an imperial
decree was issued to the aforementioned group
to conduct investigations in their territories and
recall all the yarlighs and paizas that people
had received from them and other princes dur-
ing Genghis Khan’s, Ögödäi Qa’an’s, and
Güyük Khan’s reigns. Henceforth, the princes
would not issue instructions concerning any
matter connected to the administration of the
provinces without consulting the representa-
tives of court. Great emissaries would not have
the use of more than fourteen post horses, and
they were to proceed from relay station to relay
station and not requisition people’s animals.
During the Qa’an’s reign it had been custom-
ary for merchants coming to Mongolia [to have
the use of post horses]. This he denounced,
saying, “Merchants travel in order to make a
proﬁt. Why should they ride post horses?” He
ordered that they should come and go on their
own animals.
He also ordered that emissaries should not
enter any city or village in which they had no
business, and they should not take more than
the established amount of provisions. 
Since oppression and aggression had in-
creased, and the peasants in particular were
hard pressed by the large amount of exactions,
levies, and taxes—so much so that their entire
crops would not have covered half the de-
mands—he ordered that noble and commoner
alike, ortaqs and ﬁnancial and administrative
agents, should act leniently and compassion-
ately with their underlings, and every person
should pay what he owed, without delay or ex-
cuse, in accordance with his ability, except for
those who were exempt from levies and im-
posts by imperial order of Genghis Khan or the
Qa’an. In this category were Muslims like
great sayyids, important shaykhs, and imams,
Christians like ärkä’üns, priests, monks, and
scholars, idolators like the toyins,1 and of all
classes those of advanced age who were no
longer able to make their living. 
In order that every administrative agent
might not have to make a different assessment
every day, he instituted an annual rate whereby
in Cathay a very wealthy man [845] paid up to
ten dinars and so on in a graduated manner
down to a base person, who paid one dinar. In
Transoxiana it was the same. In Khurasan and
Persia a wealthy man paid seven dinars and a
poor man one. The tax collectors and scribes
were not to show partiality, try to second-
guess, or accept bribes and pay-offs. The tax
on animals called qubchur was assessed as fol-
lows: everyone who possessed a hundred head
of one kind of animal would pay one, while
those who owned less than a hundred would
pay nothing. Taxes in arrears, no matter where
or by whom they were owed, were not to be
taken from the peasants. 
1Ärkä’ün (priest) here refers to Nestorian priests. By
“idolators,” here and almost everywhere, is meant Bud-
dhists. Toyin (from the Chinese 道人daoren) means
Buddhist priest. See Doerfer, TMEN 1:123–25 §15
(ärkä’ün) and 2:648 §993 (toyin).
TOME ONE, PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION NINE: MÖNGKÄ QA’AN
405

Of all nations and groups, he showed the
people of Islam the most favor and honor, and
he ordered alms given. An example is during
the Fitr holiday in the year 650 [December 5,
1252], when Qazi Jalaluddin Mahmud Khujan-
di and a group of Muslims came to the gate of
his ordu. The qazi delivered the sermon and
led the prayer, including the caliph’s titles in
the khutba and offering prayers for Möngkä
Qa’an’s well-being. The Qa’an ordered that
they be given as a holiday gift carts laden with
gold and silver bars and precious textiles, of
which most of the people received a share.
He ordered the unconditional release of all
prisoners throughout the empire, and to effect
it he dispatched envoys in all directions.
Were we to begin to give a detailed account
of the ever-increasing justice and equity insti-
tuted by His Majesty, it would ﬁll volumes and
still not end. “A little is indicative of the
much.” 
When his reputation for justice and equity
had spread throughout the world, Turk and
Tajik came from far and near willingly to take
refuge as his subjects, and the kings of coun-
tries that had not yet submitted sent gifts and
presents. Since a bit about his ﬁne moral char-
acter has already been introduced in a summa-
ry fashion, [846] a story will be given that
shows much of his character so that everyone
may realize that this narration is free of
embellishment.
Merchants from all over used to frequent
Güyük Khan’s court and have enormous deal-
ings with his representatives, for which they
received drafts against the provinces. Upon his
death these drafts fell into abeyance and were
not honored. Nonetheless, his servants, sons,
and nephews continued to deal in this manner,
issuing drafts against the provinces, and mer-
chants arrived in droves to make deals and re-
ceive drafts. When Möngkä Qa’an assumed the
throne and was informed of what these people
were up to, some of the merchants had not re-
ceive a tenth of the payment for their wares,
others had not yet reached the places against
which their drafts were drawn, others had not
received their drafts, others had not delivered
their goods, and a few had not even ﬁxed their
prices. Wondering what to do, they went to
court as a test in hopes of receiving his justice
and generosity and reported their situation to
Möngkä Qa’an. Although the ministers tried to
prevent him by saying that it was not necessary
for the prices of such transactions to be paid
from the imperial treasury and that no one
could raise an objection, in his perfect clemen-
cy he spread the wings of his favor over the
entire group and ordered that all the bills be
discharged from his demesne. It amounted to
more than ﬁve hundred thousand bars of gold
and silver, and had he withheld it, no one could
have raised an objection. With such largesse he
put the most generous kings to shame. In what
history has it ever been read or from what nar-
rator has it ever been heard that a king paid
another king’s debt? 
This is a sample of his good qualities and re-
gal character, [847] and from it one can deduce
the rest.
He ordered that whenever there was to be an
investigation into the affairs of people, Amir
Mängäsär Noyan and a group of expert amirs
should conduct it on the basis of justice. Bol-
ghai Aqa, who held a special place on account
of his past services, he ordered to be the chief
scribe, and he would write and copy his letters
and decrees. He ordered the Muslim bitigchis
Amir Imadulmulk, who had held the same post
under Ögödäi Qa’an and Güyük Khan, and
Amir Fakhrulmulk, who had been one of the
court elite, [not] to give paizas to merchants so
that there would be a distinction between them
and administrative officials. For goods brought
406
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

for sale to the treasury, one group was to evalu-
ate jewels, another textiles, another furs, and
another coins. Similarly he appointed experts
for issuing yarlighs, stamping paizas, main-
taining the arsenal, arranging birds and animals
for the hunt, and taking care of the business of
persons of every nation and group, and a de-
cree was issued that these people should be
free from any taint of hypocrisy and avoid ex-
cessive cupidity. They were not to detain any-
one, and they should communicate everyone’s
petition to the emperor as soon as possible.
Scribes were in attendance from every group—
Persians, Uyghurs, Cathaians, Tibetans, and
Tangqutans—so that whenever anyone had to
write a decree for a place it could be issued in
the language and script of that people. Even
during the reigns of ancient kings and sultans
of times past, when there was perfect order,
had they been alive then they would have fol-
lowed his example. [848]
Möngkä Qa’an sends his brothers Qubilai
and Hülägü with armies to the east and
west, and he goes on campaign himself to
conquer the realms of Cathay that were still
not in submission.
When Möngkä Qa’an mounted the throne
and brought victory to his friends and defeat to
his enemies, he spent the entire winter in Ong
Qin near Qaraqorum.
As the second year began, after a large quril-
tai was held, and now that he was ﬁrmly estab-
lished upon the throne and free of worry from
foes, he turned his august attention to conquer-
ing the remotest territories of the east and west.
First, a group of litigants from the lands of
the Heretics had presented themselves before
his imperial gaze. To deal with them he as-
signed his younger brother Hülägü, on whose
forehead could be read signs of world conquest
and rule and imperial glory. In the Year of the
Ox [1253] he sent him off to Tajik lands. 
In the Year of the Tiger [1254] he assigned
his middle brother, Qubilai, to defend and con-
quer the lands of the east. He was sent off in
the company of Muqali Guyang of the Jalayir.
The histories of these two will be given in sep-
arate sections since they both became au-
tonomous rulers. 
When Qubilai set out, he sent a messenger
back to say, “No provisions can be found along
the way and the going is extremely difficult. If
it is so ordered, I will go to the province of
Qarajang.” Permission was granted, and Qubi-
lai attacked and raided that land, which is
known here as Qandahar,1 and then returned to
Möngkä Qa’an. After that, Möngkä Qa’an held
a quriltai for everyone in Qorqonoq Jubur,2
which is situated in the middle of Mongolia—
it was at this place that Qutula Khan [849]
danced with his liege men so much beneath a
tree when he had achieved a victory that the
earth sank into a ditch.3 When the quriltai was
concluded and the people had been given
targhamishi [an order to break camp] in
droves, each of the amirs and princes spoke a
bilig [word of wisdom]. During this, Därgäi
Gürägän of the Ikiräs, Genghis Khan’s son-in-
law, said, “The kingdom of Nankiyas is so
near, and it is also in rebellion against us. What
are we waiting for?”
Möngkä Qa’an liked this speech and said,
“Our fathers and elder brothers who were past
monarchs each did something valiant and took
a realm to make their names known among the

2Qorqonagh Jubur on the Onon is mentioned several

3“As for the rejoicing of the Mongghol, they were

their ribs;’ until there was ‘Dust up to their knees’ ” (Se-
cret History §57).

people. I myself will also go on campaign to
Nankiyas.”
The princes all said of one accord, “How can
someone who is emperor of the face of the
earth and has seven brothers mount and go out
himself to do battle with an enemy?”
But he said, “Now that the issue is settled, it
would be unwise to contravene it.”
Thus, in Taulai Yil, which began in Muhar-
ram 653 [February 1255], the sixth year of his
reign, he set out to do battle with “Jaugan,”1
the emperor of Cathay, and he appointed his
youngest brother, Ariq Bökä, as the head of the
ordus and Mongol soldiers who remained be-

All of the tribes of the Mongol army mount-

had the armies of the Left Wing move off with
Prince Taghachar on a different route. They
were thirty tümäns altogether, and their leader
was Taghachar. In that council Bälgütäi Noyan
said, “Qubilai has ridden on one campaign and
performed his task. Now he is suffering from
the gout. If so ordered, let him go home.”
Möngkä Qa’an approved of this. Bälgütäi Noy-
an was a hundred ten years old, and he died
that year.
They set out in the Luy Yil that began in
Muharram [851] 654 [January 1256]. On the
right was Möngkä Qa’an and Sübätäi’s son
Kökchü
with
ten
tümäns.
That
summer
Möngkä Qa’an arrived in the vicinity of
Tangqut and Nankiyas territory and spent the
entire summer in a place called Liupan shan.1
(That was the place where Genghis Khan fell
ill and died when he was setting forth against
Cathay.) In the autumn he headed for Yesün
Qahalqa, which is on the frontier of Nankiyas
territory. He took twenty fortresses in that area.
That province is called Khan Sina. He camped
encircling the great fortress called Tuolecheng
and laid siege.2 He had sent Taghachar Noyan
with a hundred thousand horsemen along the
great river Qa’an Gang (the Yangtse) to lay
siege to the great cities of Xiangyangfu and
Fang Cheng3 and bring them into submission.
When he arrived there he besieged them with
his army for a week, but since victory was not

possible, they pulled back and settled in their
own tents. Möngkä Qa’an was furious over this
and reproached them (qaqimishi), sending a
message saying, “On the way back I will chas-
tise you appropriately.” Yesünggä’s brother
Qoriqchi sent a message to Taghachar, saying,
“Qubilai took many cities and fortresses, while
you have returned with stolen battles”—by
which he meant that they had been too busy
drinking and eating.
Qubilai is ordered to head for Nankiyas and
lay siege to the city of Yauju, and he returns
and crosses the River Gang.
After that, Möngkä Qa’an said, “Qubilai, de-
spite the great pain he was in, has gone out
once again on campaign. This time let him turn
the expedition over to Taghachar, [852] who
will ride in his stead.” When the order arrived,
Qubilai sent a message in which he said, “My
feet are better. How can it be proper for my el-
der brother to mount on an expedition while I
sit at home?” Immediately he mounted and set
out for Nankiyas. Since the road was extremely
long and difficult, the entire country was ﬁlled
with rebels, and the air was putrid, to save
themselves they fought only two or three bat-
tles a day as he proceeded until he reached the
city of Yauju,4 to which he laid siege until no
more than two of ten tümäns remained. Then
Qubilai withdrew from the expedition and left
Uriangqadai and Bahadur Noyan, the son of
Muqali Guyang’s son Chila’un Guyang, there
with ﬁve tümäns of soldiers. He had a bridge
of boats constructed across the Gang Mörän
(Yangtse River). From the direction of Nanki-
yas innumerable soldiers arrived, and the Mon-
gol contingent wanted to cross the bridge but
couldn’t. Many of them fell into the river or

were killed by the Nankiyas. Some got stuck in
that territory, but when the Nankiyas were
ﬁnally conquered those who were still alive
came home. Qubilai came out of there and
reached the ordu in the vicinity of the city of
Jungdu [Peking], where he camped. During
this time Möngkä Qa’an was busy besieging
the fortress mentioned above.
Möngkä Qa’an is stricken and dies; his
coffin is taken to his ordus, where mourning
is held.
Möngkä Qa’an laid siege to the fortress men-
tioned above, and when summer began the
weather turned very hot. Due to the climate
there an epidemic of dysentery broke out,
cholera spread among the Mongol soldiers, and
many of them died. [853] The monarch of the
world drank wine to ward off the cholera, and
he continued so to do. Suddenly he developed
an indisposition, and his illness came to a
crisis.
In the Moghai Yil that began in Muharram
655,1 he passed away at the foot of the unlucky
fortress. He was ﬁfty-two years old, and this
was the seventh year of his reign. After his
death, Asutai Oghul put Qundaqai Noyan in
charge of the army and took his father’s coffin
back to his ordus, and mourning was held in
the four ordus, the ﬁrst day in Qutuqtai
Khatun’s ordu, the second day in Qutluq
Khatun’s ordu, the third day in the ordu of
Chabui Khatun, who had been with him on this
expedition, and the fourth day in Küi Yäbä
Khatun’s ordu. Each day in a different ordu,
they placed the coffin upon a throne and wept
and wailed bitterly. After that he was buried in
Bolqan Qaldun, which is called Yäkä Qoruq
1Muharram 655 began in January 1257, but this can-
not be correct. August 11, 1259 is the date usually given
for Möngkä’s death (Grousset, Empire, 284), and Qubi-
lai succeeded him to the throne in May 1260.
[great sanctuary], next to Genghis Khan and
Tolui Khan. May God grant the Padishah of Is-
lam many years and long life, and may he en-
joy kingship, fortune, and rule.
The rest of the history of Qubilai on that
expedition, and the arrival of the news of
Möngkä Qa’an’s death.
When Qubilai set out and reached the great
river of the Nankiyas territory, which they
called Khui Kho [Huai He2], there he heard the
bad news about Möngkä Qa’an. He took coun-
sel with Muqali Guyang’s grandson Bahadur
Noyan and said, “Let us pay no attention to
these fables.” He sent Buluqan Qalja’s son
Ärkä Noyan of the Barulas to the vanguard,3
[854] and he followed along behind. They cap-
tured the scouts of the Nankiyas army and
killed them so as not to allow the news to get
out. Crossing the two-league-wide Yangtse
River by boat, he came to the city of O-chou,4
laid siege, and took it. A division that had been
ﬁghting Möngkä Qa’an turned back and came
to the aid of the city. Their commanders’
names were Gia Dao and Ulus Taifu.5 When
they arrived, Qubilai had already taken the
city.
Immediately
emissaries
arrived
from
Chabui Khatun and the amirs of her ordu,
Tayichi’utai Noyan and Yegü Noyan. The mes-
sengers’ names were Toqan and Äbügän. When
they had informed him of Möngkä Qa’an’s
death, Qubilai realized that it was true, left the
army, and held mourning. He was alone in

Nankiyas territory: Hülägü had gone to the
west and Tajik lands, and there was a great dis-
tance between them and the capital. No sooner
had Ariq Bökä heard the news of his brother’s
death than his eyes fell upon the imperial
throne, and his amirs and retainers also urged
him to rebel against Qubilai. The entire history
of Ariq Bökä, Möngkä Qa’an’s sons Asutai and
Ürüngtash, and the other sons and grandsons
will be included in the section on Qubilai
Qa’an, God willing.
Now that the history of Möngkä Qa’an and
his reign has come to an end, let us commence
a summary history of the emperors of Cathay
and Machin and the amirs, caliphs, sultans,
maliks, and atabegs of Iran, Syria, Egypt, and
the Maghreb who were contemporary with him
from the beginning of Qaqai Yil, the Year of
the Pig that corresponds to 648 [1251], through
the Moghai Yil that began in Muharram 655
[January 1257]. [855]
A summary history of the amirs, caliphs, atabegs, sultans, maliks, and atabegs of Iran,
Syrian, Anatolia, Egypt, and North Africa who were contemporary with Möngkä Qa’an
from the beginning of Qaqa[i] Yil, the Year of the Pig corresponding to 648 [A.D. 1250]
through Mogha[i] Yil, the Year of the Serpent corresponding to 655 [A.D. 1257], and
extraordinary events that took place during this period.
History of the emperors of Cathay and
Machin who were during this period.
Lizong1 [ruled] forty-one years, of which
seven years were after and five were before
this period. During Ögödäi Qa’an’s and Güyük
Khan’s reigns was an interregnum of which
eight years…and the rest was seventeen years.
History of the amirs.
Amir Arghun Aqa, the governor of most of
Iran, set out for Möngkä Qa’an’s court in Ju-
mada II 649 [August 1251] to attend the quril-
tai. [856] When he arrived, the quriltai had al-
ready been concluded, the princes and amirs
had been dismissed, and Möngkä Qa’an was
busy dealing with administrative affairs. The
day after his arrival, the ﬁrst of Muharram 650
[March 14, 1252], Amir Arghun performed
tägishmishi, reported on the unsettled state of
Iran, and was received favorably. After the
qalan [tax] on the inhabitants of this area had
1Lizong (理宗) of the Southern Sung, ruled 1224–64.
been ﬁxed at an annual rate of seven dinars for
a wealthy man and one dinar for a poor person,
the Qa’an said that no further demands should
be made. He gave Arghun Aqa a decree, reas-
signed him to the post he held, and dismissed
him. He obtained the post of sahib-divan for
Baha’uddin Muhammad Juwayni and Sirajud-
din, who had been a bitigchi on behalf of
Negübäi, and he got patents and paizas for
them. In 651 [1253–54] they set out to return
home.
When Amir Arghun reached Khurasan, he
read out the orders and delivered the or-
dinances to the great delight of the people. He
ordered that no one act contrary to these orders
or oppress the subjects, and thus he put the af-
fairs of Iran in order. As ordered, he went via
the Qipchaq Gates to Batu’s court accompa-
nied by Najmuddin Gilabadi, a census of Iran
was conducted, and tax rates were set. Thus he
continued to administer the realm until Hülägü
Khan arrived.

History of the caliphs in Baghdad.
In Baghdad was the Caliph al-Musta‘sim-
bi’llah, a pious and ascetic man who never
touched intoxicants or women other than his
wives. 
During these years Husamuddin Khalil Badr
b. Khwarshed al-Salyuji, a grandee among the
Kurds, [857] rebelled against the caliph and
took refuge with the Mongols. Prior to that he
had worn the habit of dervishes and considered
himself to be a disciple of Sidi Ahmad. At that
time he plotted with a group of Mongols and
went to Khulanjan in the vicinity of Najaf and
attacked a group of Sulaymanshah’s followers,
killing and plundering. From there he set out
for the fortress of Wahar, which belonged to
Sulaymanshah, and laid siege to it. Sulayman-
shah found out about it and requested permis-
sion from the caliph to go drive him away.
When he reached Hulwan an innumerable
army gathered around him. A group of Mus-
lims and Mongols had also gathered around
Khalil. They clashed at a place called Sihr. Su-
laymanshah had laid an ambush, and when the
battle grew heated he turned to run away with
Husamuddin in pursuit. As he passed the am-
bush place, he turned around and his soldiers
sprang from ambush, surrounding them and
killing many. Khalil was taken prisoner and
then killed. His brother took refuge in a moun-
tain, and from there he requested amnesty and
then came down. Sulaymanshah took two
fortresses from their territory. One was Shikan,
a very strong fortiﬁcation, and the other was
Dizbaz in the middle of the town of Shapur-
khwast.1
Also during these years a group of Mongols,
nearly ﬁfteen thousand horsemen, went from
1Shapurkhwast
is
the
modern
Khurramabad
in
Luristan.
Hamadan to attack the environs of Baghdad.
Another contingent attacked Khanaqin. They
fell upon a troop of Sulaymanshah’s supporters
and
came
away. Another
group
went
to
Shahrazur.2
The caliph ordered Sharafuddin Iqbal Shara-
bi, Mujahiduddin Aybak the lesser davatdar,
and Ala’uddin Altun Bars the greater davatdar
to lead a large contingent of his slaves and
Arabs. They placed catapults on the walls of
Baghdad. News arrived that the Mongols had
reached the fortress of ___. Sulaymanshah and
this group of liege men arranged the battle.
The Mongols [858] came as far as the environs
of Ja‘fariyya, but during the night they lit ﬁres
and withdrew. Suddenly the news arrived that
the Mongols had pillaged Dujayl, so Sharabi
took a contingent to drive them away.
History of the sultans in Anatolia.
In Anatolia was Sultan Izzuddin Kay-Ka’us.3
His brother Ala’uddin rebelled and went to An-
guriya,4 whence he was brought and impris-
oned for seven years in the Hushyar fortress.
In Mosul was Sultan Badruddin Lu’lu’. Dur-
ing these years he was outﬁtting an army and
asked for assistance from Tajuddin Muhammad
ibn Salaya, the ruler of Arbela. He sent a thou-
sand men. Badruddin headed for Mardin. The
sultan of Mardin also mustered an army and
asked for help from Aleppo. When the two
armies came together, the Mardin left wing
was broken, [B345] and the Mosul army went
out in pursuit, taking booty. Qaymari’s son, the
leader of the Aleppo army, attacked and broke
the center of the Mosul army. Sultan Badrud-
din took ﬂight and went to Mosul with ten
2Shahrazur was in the vicinity of Halabja of recent
infamy.
3Izzuddin Kay-Ka’us II of the Seljuqs of Rum, r.
1246–1248.
4The modern Ankara in Turkey.

men. His treasury was plundered, and his sol-
diers took ﬂight and straggled in after him.
In Egypt the sultan was Malik Salih Najmud-
din Ayyub b. al-Kamil.1 When he died the
amirs and people of Egypt summoned his son
Malik Mu‘azzam Turanshah, the governor of
Hisn Kefa.2 When he reached the city of Dam-
ascus [859] he took it over and then proceeded
to Egypt. In 648 [1250] he was conﬁrmed as
the ruler of Egypt.3 He did battle with the
Franks who had taken over Damietta and parts
of Egypt and defeated them. Nearly thirty
thousand Franks were killed. One of their
kings, Afridis,4 was taken captive along with
an inestimable number, and Damietta was tak-
en. After that, the Bahri Turks conspired to kill
the sultan, and Aybak the Turcoman, the chief
of the amirs, went before the sultan while he
was at table. While he was talking the sultan
said something to him. Aybak got up, drew his
sword, and struck the sultan. The sultan ward-
ed off the blow with his arm, but he received a
serious wound and ﬂed into a wooden house.
The Turks said to Aybak, “Finish what you
started!” They brought naphtha-throwers and
hurled a vial of naphtha into the house. It
caught ﬁre, and the sultan went up on the roof.
Aybak shot an arrow at him, but the sultan
dove into the river and got out on the bank.
They went in pursuit, kicked him to death, and
threw his body into the river.
When the captive Franks learned of this, they
broke the chains from their legs and started

They
completely

brother, son, and a group of relatives as

to turn over the money.5
In the year 652 [1254–55] Aybak the Tur-
coman took over Egypt.6 [860] None of Malik
Kamil’s sons was left. Aybak put Amir Aqtai
the Jamadar to death in the citadel without
warning and ordered the khutba and coinage to

In Kirman was Sultan Ruknuddin.7 In 650
[1252] Qutbuddin came from the court, and
immediately Ruknuddin ﬂed, trying to take
refuge in Baghdad, but they were too afraid of
the Mongols to let him in. From there he head-
ed for the court with Qutbuddin following be-
hind. He was brought to trial. After proving his
guilt, Ruknuddin was turned over to Qutbuddin
for execution, and the sultanate of Kirman was
awarded to Qutbuddin, who mounted the
throne.8 [861]

pronouncements and orders he gave,

413

were not included in the previous two
sections and were culled from various books
and persons.
A summary indication of Möngkä Qa’an’s
character and good qualities has been reported
in previous sections, and as a detailed account
this little bit will have to suffice. By way of
corroboration, one story that sums up his jus-
tice and generosity will now be recorded so
that the people of the world may know for cer-
tain that this report is free of any taint of exag-
geration. It is as follows.
Merchants from all over the world had gone
to Güyük Khan and transacted huge deals, but
since Güyük Khan did not reign long, most of
[what the merchants were owed] was held in
abeyance and was not paid to them. Nonethe-
less, even after his death, deals with his wives,
sons, and nephews continued on a grander
scale than during his reign, and drafts against
the provinces continued to be written. When
the situation of this group changed and they
lost authority, some of the merchants received
not even a tenth of the value of the drafts that
had been written, and others had not yet
reached the places against which their drafts
were written. Some still had not delivered their
wares or had the prices determined, and yet
others had not received drafts. When Möngkä
Qa’an assumed the throne, the merchants went
to him as a test, partially hoping to see his jus-
tice and partially in despair of receiving pay-
ment for their transactions. They explained the
situation to him, and although all the courtiers
and ministers advised that it was not necessary
for the amounts to be paid from the emperor’s
treasury [862] and that no one could raise an
objection, the emperor spread the wings of
generosity over them all and ordered a decree
for the settlement of all their claims from the
income of his realm. It amounted to more than
ﬁve hundred thousand bars of silver even
though, had he withheld it, no one would have
been able to raise an objection.
This is just an example of his imperial cus-
tom, from which his character in other matters
can be deduced. [863]

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

❦ SECTION TEN
THE HISTORY OF QUBILAI QA’AN, SON OF TOLUI KHAN, SON OF GENGHIS
KHAN, IN THREE PARTS
When Ariq Bökä took it into his head to be-
come emperor, he rebelled against his elder
brother Qubilai Qa’an and assisted Möngkä
Qa’an’s sons Asutai and Ürüngtash and their
sons and kinsmen. In the end, the attempt
failed, and they submitted to Qubilai Qa’an.
For this reason their history will be given in
this section, which consists of three parts.
Part One is on his progeny, a detailed ac-
count of his wives and his sons’ offspring who
have branched off down to the present; a pic-
ture of him, and a genealogical chart of him
and his sons.
Part Two includes events leading to his en-
thronement, a picture of him and his wives,
princes, and amirs during his enthronement;
stories of his reign; the history of Ariq Bökä
and the princes who conspired with him; the
battles the emperor fought and the victories he
achieved.
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections and
were culled from various books and persons.
[864]
Part One, on his progeny, a detailed account of his wives and his sons’ offspring who have
branched off down to the present; a picture of him, and a genealogical chart of him and his
sons.
His magnificent lineage.
Qubilai1 Qa’an was the fourth son of Tolui
Khan and was born of Sorqaghtani Beki. His
1Qubilai’s name is obviously derived in some way
from the Mongolian qubi (lot, portion), but the manner
of derivation is far from certain. It is not a normal Mon-
golian form (see Pelliot, Marco Polo 1:565). The vari-
ous guises in which “Qubilai” occurs are legion; among
them are the Chinese transcription (忽必烈Hubilie),
Qublai, Khubilai, Kublai, Qubla, and, of course, Co-
leridge’s “In Xanadu did Kubla Khan / A stately
pleasure-dome
decree.”
Marco
Polo
tends
to
use
“Cublai.” Qubilai was born on September 23, 1215, as-
cended the throne on May 5, 1260, and died on February
18, 1294 (ibid. 1:566). His dynastic title (temple name)
in Chinese sources is 世祖 Shizu.
nurse was Mögä’s mother, a concubine from
the Naiman nation. It so happened that two
months prior to Mögä’s birth, Qubilai Qa’an
was born, and when Genghis Khan’s gaze fell
upon him he said, “Our sons are all of a ruddy
complexion, but this boy is swarthy, just like
his maternal uncles. Tell Sorqaghtani Beki to
give him to a good nurse to be brought up by.”
He was given to Mögä’s mother, Saruq by
name. Two months later, when Mögä was born,
his mother gave him to a nurse from the
Tangqut people to be reared while she reared
Qubilai until he was grown. She considered
him her own son, and she cared for him and
protected in all respects. The Qa’an held her in
great honor, and when she died he constantly

remembered her and gave alms for the repose
of her soul. [865]
His wives and children
Qubilai Qa’an had many wives and concu-
bines. The greatest of them all was Chabui
Khatun,1 the daughter of Elchi Noyan of the
ruling clans of the Qunqirat. She was extreme-
ly comely, possessed of beauty, and beloved by
[Qubilai Qa’an]. She died before Qubilai
Qa’an in Bechin Yil, the Year of the Monkey
corresponding to 682 [1284].
Qubilai Qa’an had twelve sons of note. Just
as Genghis Khan’s four sons who were born of
his chief wife, Börtä Füjin, were of more im-
portance, the four of Qubilai Qa’an’s twelve
sons whose mother was Chabui Khatun were
more important. The names of the twelve sons
are as follows. 
(1) Torji,2 born of Chabui Khatun. He did not
marry and had no children. He was a year older
than Abaqa Khan. He was always feeble and
sickly and died of that chronic condition.
(2) Jimgim. When he was born he was
Gimjim.3 He was born of the great lady named
Taikhu who was of the “bone” of the Qunqirat.
“Taikhu” means the mother of a qa’an.4
Jimgim died young, leaving three fine sons.
[The first was] Kammala, who had three sons,
Yesün Temür, Jungshai, and Dälgär Buqa.
[866] The second son was Tarmabala, who fa-
thered three sons, Khaishang, Amuga, and
1Chabui was Qubilai’s consort who was promoted to
empress (皇后huanghou) in 1260. In Chinese her name
is transcribed as 察必Chabi; she died in 1281, not 1284
as given in the text here. See Pelliot, Marco Polo 1:568.
2Torji ~ Dorji, from the Tibetan rDo-rje (‘diamond’).
3The name is Chinese, 真金Zhenjin (‘true gold,’ but
reflecting the older pronunciation of 金as gim). Marco
Polo calls him Cinchim (Pelliot, Marco Polo 1:278).
4“Taikhu” is the Chinese 太后taihou ‘mother of an
emperor.’
Ajurpariyabatra.5 The third son was Temür
Qa’an, who is now the qa’an of the age. He is
called Öljäitü Qa’an and has two sons, Tishi
Taishi and Maqabalin.
(3) Mangqala,6 also born of Chabui Khatun.
He had a great wife named Putri, which means
“born of a lord” in the Indian language. She
was the granddaughter of Elchi Noyan of the
Qunqirat tribe, and she had three sons. The
first was Arslan Buqa, the second was Altun
Buqa, and the third was Ananda. The reason
for this name is that when he was born they
were near an enemy people, the name of whose
commander was Ananda, so they named him
the same. He is a Muslim. The Qa’an awarded
him the territory of Tangqut. He has one son,
Örüg Temür, and a daughter whose name is not
known.
(4) Nomoghan.7 He was also born of Chabui
Khatun. There are many stories about him, and
each will come in its proper place. He had two
daughters whose names are not known.
(5) Qoridai. He was born of Qoruqchin
Khatun of Märkit “bone,” whom Qubilai
Qa’an married before any of his other wives.
She was also older than the others. In the end
she lost status. [867] She was the daughter of
Qutuqu, the brother of Toqto’a Beki, the ruler
of the Märkit who was an enemy during
Genghis Khan’s time and with whom he often
did battle. In the end he was forced to
surrender.
5Tarmabala is the Sanskrit Dharmabala; Ajurpariyaba-
tra is the Sanskrit Ayurparibhadra. Such Buddhist names
are generally filtered through Mongolian into Persian.
6This name is variously spelled, Mangqala ~ Ming-
qalan ~ Mangala ~ Manggala. Hambis (Yuan che, 114)
prefers Manggala; we will opt for the most common Per-
sian spelling, Mangqala.
7Nomoghan, Mongolian for “peaceful.” Marco Polo
transcribes his name as Nomogan.
416

(6) Hügächi.1 He was born of Dörbäjin
Khatun of the Dörbän tribe. The Qa’an award-
ed him the territory of Qarajang. One day he
took a duck in a village by force, and when the
Qa’an heard about it he ordered him to receive
seventy lashes, and his delicate flesh was torn
to shreds. When he died he left a son named
Esän Temür, whom the Qa’an appointed in his
father’s place in the territory of Qarajang. In
the Indian language they call it Kandar,
meaning large province.
(7) Oqruqchi. He was born of Dörbäjin
Khatun. The Qa’an awarded him the territory
of Tibet. He had two sons. The first was Temür
Buqa, who had a son named Shasgaba. When
Hügächi died the province of Tibet was given
to this Temür Buqa. The second son was Ejil
Buqa.
(8) Ayachi. His mother was Hushijin, the
daughter of Boroqul Noyan of the Hushin clan.
This son married, and they were together for a
time but had no children. [868]
(9) Kököchü. This son was also born of Ay-
achi’s mother, Hushijin of the Hushin clan.
Now ___, and before now he has been on ex-
peditions with Nomoghan. He came to Däräsü

ciation of “Hügächi.” See Pelliot, Marco Polo 1:394.
to fight Qaidu. He and Nomoghan were cap-
tured, but after a while they were sent back to
the Qa’an.
(10) Qutluq Temür. His mother’s name is not
known. He was born the year Ariq Bökä re-

twenty years old. He had married but had no
children. 
(11) Toghan. He was born of Baya’ujin
Khatun, the daughter of Boraqchin Khatun of
the Baya’ut tribe. He has one son named Lao-
jang. In the province of Manzi, which is called
Machin, there is a magnificent city called Jing-
ju [Yangzhou], a nearly ten-tümän province.
The Qa’an awarded it to him.2

Khatun,4 Nachin Gürägän’s daughter the Qa’an
married after Chabui Khatun died. A year later
he brought her into the yurt and ordu inasmuch
as

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
417

Part Two, events leading to his enthronement, a picture of him and his wives, princes, and
amirs during his enthronement; stories of his reign; the history of Ariq Bökä and the
princes who conspired with him; the battles the emperor fought and the victories he
achieved; the commanders he stationed on every frontier, the princes who were with him,
and the names of his commanders.
Prior to his ascending the throne.
When the just monarch Möngkä Qa’an as-
cended the throne in his capital near Qaraqo-
rum in the Onon-Kerulen region, after arrang-
ing administrative affairs he assigned his
brother Qubilai to the lands of the east and the
realm of Cathay and sent his younger brother
Hülägü to the west and the lands of the Tajiks.
As has already been mentioned in the section
on him, he ordered eighty tümäns of soldiers
consisting entirely of Mongols and Ja’uquts to
go with Qubilai to Cathay and take up resi-
dence there in order to conquer the province of
Nankiyas, which borders Cathay. Qubilai set
forth and scouted out the roads of Nankiyas,
[870] and because the rulers of that land had
removed all sources of provisions from vil-
lages that lay along the way, the going was ex-
tremely rough. A messenger was sent to
Möngkä Qa’an to report the situation and ask
permission for them to go first and conquer the
country of Qarajang and Chaghanjang1 so that
the army might acquire provisions, and then go
to Nankiyas.
These two realms are called Dai Liu in the
Cathaian language, meaning “great realm.”2 In
1“The Mo-so region of Likiang in northwest Yün-nan”
(JTBy, p. 246, note 21).
2Pelliot (Marco Polo 1:177) suggests that “Dai Liu” is
for 大理國Daliguo, the Kingdom of Dali, the name of
418
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

the Indian language it is called Qandar and, in
the language of this area, Qandahar. It borders
on Tibet and Tangqut, part of the realm and
mountains of Hindustan, and the realm of
Cathay and the “Gold-Tooth” people.1
In short, Möngkä Qa’an approved of this
suggestion and gave his permission. Qubilai
massacred and pillaged the province in the Luy
Yil that began in Muharram 654 [January
1256]. He captured the ruler, who was called
Maharao, which means great emperor, took
him with him, and left the army. 
After that, when Möngkä Qa’an set out to
conquer Nankiyas, he ordered that since Qubi-
lai had the gout, and since he had already been
on campaign and reduced a rebellious province
to submission, this time he could rest at home.
As ordered, he rested in his ordus, which were
in Qara’un Jidun in Mongolia.
A year later, when Taghachar Noyan and the
princes of the Left Wing who had gone to
Nankiyas
returned
empty-handed,
Möngkä
Qa’an chastised them severely, and an edict
was issued as follows: “Qubilai has sent a mes-
sage saying, ‘My gout is much better. How can
it be fitting for Möngkä Qa’an to ride on cam-
paign while I sit at home?’ Let him therefore
take the soldiers who were commanded by
Taghachar Noyan and head for the land of the
Nankiyas.” As ordered, [871] he took control
of one tümän of elite soldiers and several
tümäns of Ja’uquts that had been Taghachar
Noyan’s and set forth. When he reached the
frontier of Nankiyas, he conquered many of the
towns and provinces.
During that time Möngkä Qa’an was besieg-
ing the fortress of Tuolecheng, but the air was
so foul that a cholera epidemic spread, and
Möngkä Qa’an was stricken and died. The
the kingdom that became Yunnan.
1For the “Gold-Tooth” people, see text p. 442 above.
news of his death was received by Qubilai on
the banks of the Quiqa Mörän (River Huai),
but he consulted with Bahadur Noyan, the
grandson of Muqali Guyang and father of Han-
tum Noyan of Jalayir “bone,” saying, “We
have arrived here with soldiers like ants and lo-
custs. Why should we turn back without hav-
ing done anything just because of some
rumors?” Proceeding to the Nankiyas, he at-
tacked their army without warning, seized their
scouts, crossed the Yangtse River,2 which is
like a sea two leagues wide, by means of a tal-
isman made from a toz (birch) tree he had set
up, and laid siege to Ozhou, a magnificent
city.3
Prior to that, Möngkä Qa’an had dispatched a
contingent from one side of Nankiyas led by
Sübädäi Noyan’s son Uriangqadai and consist-
ing of three tümäns. Along with him he sent
Chaghatai’s grandson Abishqa and fifty princes
of the Left Wing. Since the roads were difficult
and the villages and fortresses were well forti-
fied, they fought many battles. Their ways in
and out were then blocked, and because of the
foul air so many of the soldiers fell ill and died
that no more than fifty thousand remained. Re-
ceiving news of Qubilai’s arrival, he set out to
join him, and after twenty days they met in the
vicinity of that city, [Ozhou]. Reduced to dire
straits, the inhabitants sent out emissaries and
surrendered. Then, without warning, the army
that had been dispatched to deal with Möngkä
Qa’an returned rejoicing over his death, [872]
and the inhabitants of the city were heartened
by their arrival.
During all this, messengers from Chabui
Khatun and the commanders of her ordu,
Tayichi’utai and Yegü, arrived to deliver this
2The text’s gang is simply the Chinese jiang 江‘river’
and refers to the Yangtse (倀江 Changjiang).
3This “Ozhou“ is Wuchang, the modern Wuhan in
