PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
419

message: “The great commanders Dorji and
Alamdar have come on behalf of Ariq Bökä
and are taking away Mongol and Ja’uqut
turqaqs, but the reason is not known. Should
we give them the soldiers or not?” They also
brought a riddle, saying, “The heads of the big
fish and the little fish have been cut off. Aside
from you and Ariq Bökä, who is left? Is it pos-
sible for you to return or not?”
Two days later Ariq Bökä’s messengers also
came to Qubilai, saying, “We have been sent to
obtain news of your well-being and your safe
arrival.”
“In what direction are you sending the
turqaqs and expeditionary force you are rais-
ing?” he asked.
“We servants do not know,” they replied.
“It’s a lie anyway.”
Since they were keeping the truth hidden,
Qubilai became suspicious and thought, “If he
wanted a troop to send somewhere, why would
he conceal it? There must be some deceit and
trickery afoot.” In secret he consulted with Ba-
hadur Noyan and Uriangqadai, saying, “This is
how things are, and it is not known what Ariq
Bökä has in mind for us. You two stay here
with some troops until I return to the Qara
Mörän (Yellow River) in Cathay, make an in-
vestigation, and send word back to you.” On
that understanding he turned back.
The princes Taghachar, [Narin] Qada’an, and
Yesünggä were sent out with the rest of the
army, and they captured countryside and vil-
lages and wrought destruction. 
When Qubilai reached the city of Nan-ching
on the banks of the Yellow River, he found out
that Dorji and Alamdar had come in search of
soldiers and put much pressure on the Mongols
and Ja’uquts. [873] He sent a messenger to
Ariq Bökä, saying, “Nothing is going to be
gained by the turqaqs and troops that are being
taking away from Mongol households and
Ja’uqut country. Give back the property and
animals you have taken from the provinces,
and give us the troops that were with me,
Taghachar, Yesünggä, Narin Qada’an and the
troops of the Left Wing. Also restore the troops
of the Right Wing that went with Möngkä
Qa’an and are now with Mögä, Qada’an, Asu-
tai, and Ja’utu, the commanders of the Right
Wing, so that we may provide ourselves with
mounts, provisions, and weapons and fight the
Nankiyas.” This is the message he sent.
At that time Alamdar had gone from there,
and Dorji had remained in the city of Jungdu,
which is now called Khanbaligh. Qubilai sent a
message to him saying, “You too send a liege
man with these envoys.” But he secretly sent
word through his liege man to Ariq Bökä, say-
ing, “It seems that Qubilai is aware of what
you are thinking. The best thing to do now
would be for you to send with these envoys a
noyan from among the great commanders bear-
ing falcons and hawks so that Qubilai may feel
safe and grow careless.” Ariq Bökä approved
of this plan and sent a noyan with five falcons
as a gift in the company of the envoys, saying,
“The noyan is coming to bring back news of
your safety.” He charged the noyan and Dorji
Noyan to speak nicely to Qubilai so that he
would feel secure enough to turn back soon.
Accordingly, they spoke pleasantly and, to-
gether with Ariq Bökä’s envoys, reported to
Qubilai that the rumor concerning the requisi-
tioning of turqaqs and auxiliary forces was
false.
“Now that you have explained that upsetting
rumor, minds are at rest,” said Qubilai as he
sent them back without a care. Then he sent
envoys to Bahadur Noyan and Uriangqadai,
saying, “Abandon the siege of Oju and return,
[874] for our situation has taken another turn,
like the revolving of the celestial sphere.” By
the
time
the
envoys
arrived,
Taghachar,
420

Yesünggä, and Narin Qada’an had already
started back, and Bahadur and Uriangqadai had
come away with their troops and returned to
Qubilai. 
When Dorji and Toqan went before Ariq
Bökä and informed him of the situation, he
said, “Since Qubilai is sufficiently aware of
our treachery and deceit, it would be best for
us to summon the princes and commanders
who are presently living in their yurts and set-
tle the khanate, which is currently vacant, upon
ourself.” After
holding
council,
they
dis-
patched messengers in all directions. Tagha-
char’s son Naimadai and Jibi[k] Temür’s
younger brother Yesü1 both came to him, but
the other princes all stayed away on some pre-
text or other. Since there was not a quorum,
Ariq Bökä took counsel with the amirs once
again, saying, “It would be best for us to send
Qubilai more messengers who can fool him
into thinking he is safe.” Dorji and two others
from among the amirs and bitigchis were sent
with a message saying, “It would be appropri-
ate to hold mourning for Möngkä Qa’an. It is
necessary for Qubilai and all the princes to
come.” They had planned to seize them all
when they arrived; however, when the messen-
gers
came
before
Qubilai,
the
princes
Taghachar, Yesünggä, Narin Qada’an, and oth-
ers, as well as the noyans, had already come to
Qubilai in Jungdu. The envoys delivered the
message, whereupon all said of one accord,
“This proposal is perfectly correct. It behooves
us all to go. However, we have just come from

campaign. First let us go home, and then we
can gather.” [875]
“Let my liege men take this word back,” said
Dorji. “In the meantime I will stay here so that
I can escort you.” With that agreed to, he sent
his liege men off, and afterwards Qubilai sent a
messenger to the army that had gone into
Nankiyas territory with Möngkä Qa’an, and he
also sent a message to Asutai telling him to
come
quickly.
(Mögä
had
died
on
the
expedition.) 
When Dorji’s envoys delivered the message
to Ariq Bökä, the princes who were there asked
unanimously, “How long can we wait for
them?” So saying, they agreed to elevate Ariq
Bökä to the throne in the summer residence in
the Altai mountains. The group consisted of
Qara Hülägü’s wife Princess Orghina, Möngkä
Qa’an’s
sons
Asutai
and
Ürüngtash,
Chaghatai’s grandson Alghu, Taghachar’s son
Naimatai, Ching Temür’s “younger brother”
Yesü, Qada’an’s son Dorji, Orda’s son Qu-
rumshi, Qarachar, and a son of Bälgütäi Noy-
an’s. 
When Asutai was brought from the army,
Alamdar was sent as commander and shahna
over the army to guard them and keep them
happy so they wouldn’t disperse.
After that, envoys and missives were sent to
Ögödäi Qa’an’s ordu, to Kötän’s and Ching
Temür’s sons, to the realm of the Mongols, to
Tangqut and Ja’uqut to spread the following
message [from Ariq Bökä]: “Hülägü, Bärkä,
and the princes have agreed to elevate me to
the khanate. You must not pay any attention to
Qubilai, Taghachar, Yesünggä, Yäkä Qada’an,
or Narin Qada’an or obey their orders.”
Such documents they fabricated and sent off,
but Ching Temür and the commanders of
Cathay seized the envoys and sent them and
their letters to Qubilai. Then he realized for
certain that Ariq Bökä had created a bulqaq.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
421

After that, the following gathered and held
deliberations:
Taghachar,
Yesünggä,
Yäkä
Qada’an, Narin Qada’an, [876] Ching Temür,
Ja’utu, and other princes; the amirs, Muqali
Guyang’s son Qurumshi, Nachin Gürägän,
Därgäi Gürägän; amirs of the Left Wing, Bor-
cha’s son Sodon Noyan, Qorchi’s son Ejil, both
of whom were tarkhans; all the amirs of the
Right Wing. “Hülägü has gone to Tajik territo-
ry,” they said, “and Chaghatai Khan’s and
Jochi Khan’s progeny are too far away. Those
who are in league with Ariq Bökä are acting
ignorantly. Princess Orghina has been persuad-
ed by the amirs to join Ariq Bökä’s camp on
behalf of the Chaghatai before Hülägü and
Bärkä could get here. If we do not appoint
someone as qa’an now, how can we survive?”
Having agreed to this, they were unanimous
in elevating Qubilai Qa’an to the throne in the
middle of summer of the Bechin Yil that corre-
sponded to 658 [1260] in the city of Kaipingfu.
He was then forty-six years old. As was
customary, all the princes and commanders
gave möchälgäs (written pledges) and bent
their knees.
After enthroning Qubilai Qa’an the princes
send emissaries to Ariq Bökä, who does
battle several times with the qa’an but is
defeated in the end.
After that, a hundred envoys on behalf of the
princes were assigned and dispatched to Ariq
Bökä with the following message: “We princes
and commanders have held council together
and have agreed to seat Qubilai as qa’an.” That
day was spent in banqueting, and when night
fell Dorji escaped. [877] When his flight was
discovered, an envoy was sent out after him.
The yamchis seized him and brought him in.
He was questioned with threats and confessed
to the bulqaq and plots that had been made
from beginning to end. He was then impris-
oned. After that, Abishgha, the son of Büri, son
of Chaghatai’s son Mö’ätügän, was assigned to
head his grandfather’s ulus and dismissed, and
in his company they sent his “younger brother”
Narin Qada’an. Ariq Bökä’s envoys and a large
troop of soldiers came across them on the fron-
tier of Tangqut territory, seized them, and took
them to Ariq Bökä, who arrested them and held
them under guard, although he sent Qubilai’s
envoys back. 
That summer many envoys were sent back
and forth, but no agreement could be reached.
After that, it was announced that Hülägü Khan,
Bärkä, and other princes had arrived and were
supporting Ariq Bökä. Many such rumors were
started. When autumn came, Ariq Bökä gave a
troop to Hülägü’s eldest son Jumghur, Udur’s
son Qarachar, and some other princes and sent
them out to battle Qubilai, whose vanguard
was
commanded
by Yesünggä
and Yäkä
Qada’an. When the two sides reached each
other, they did battle in Baski. Ariq Bökä’s
troops were defeated. Jumghur and Qarachar
managed to get out of the fray with a few men.
Terrified, Ariq Bökä and his soldiers fled in
rout and dispersed. Before that, however, they
killed the two princes who had been impris-
oned and the hundred envoys and entered
Qirqiz territory.
It was customary for food and drink to be
brought to Qaraqorum from Cathay by cart.
Qubilai cut off the supply, and this resulted in
shortages and severe inflation. Ariq Bökä was
helpless. [878] “It would be best,” he said, “for
Alghu, the son of Chaghatai’s son Baidar, who
has long served the throne and knows the ways
and customs of everything, to go and take
command of his grandfather’s throne and ulus
and send us supplies and arms. He can also
guard the frontier along the Oxus lest Hülägü
and Bärkä’s soldiers come to assist Qubilai.”
With this thought in mind, he curried favor
with Alghu and sent him off.
422
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Alghu departed like an arrow shot from a
bow and made his way to Kashgar, where
around a hundred fifty thousand warrior horse-
men gathered around him and he initiated a re-
bellion. Since the Qa’an had mounted for the
campaign, he proceeded as fast as possible to
Qanqi Daban, where he heard that Ariq Bökä
had killed Abishgha, the two other princes who
were with him, and the hundred envoys. He
flew into a rage and killed Dorji Noyan, whom
he was holding under arrest. Before mounting
on the campaign he had dispatched the princes
Yäkä Qada’an, Jochi Qasar’s son Qaralchu,1
several other princes, and Büri with a huge
army to Tangqut territory because it had been
reported that Ariq Bökä had sent Alamdar and
Qundaqai as commanders and shahnas at the
head of the army that had gone with Möngkä
Qa’an to Nankiyas and which was later com-
manded by Asutai, who came to him unencum-
bered. These were on the frontiers of Tangqut.
When Yäkä Qada’an and Qaralchu reached
them they gave battle. Alamdar was killed dur-
ing the fighting, and some of the soldiers were
killed and others scattered. Those who re-
mained took flight to Ariq Bökä in Qirqiz
country.
When Qubilai Qa’an reached the borders of
Qaraqorum he overtook the four ordus of
Genghis Khan and the ordus of Kölgän and
sent them back. He wintered on the Ongqin
Mörän river.2 [879]
Ariq Bökä, distraught and distracted, was on
the river Yus3 with emaciated and hungry
troops on the Kämkämji’üt frontier. Fearing
the arrival of the Qa’an, he sent envoys and
1Reading Qaralchu (see text p. 277) for theﻮ ــ ـﺑﻴﭽﺎـﻗof the
text.
2The modern Ongin Gol.
3Yus, a tributary of the Yenisei (Hambis, “Notes sur
Käm,” 300, note 69). It may also be another tributary of
the Yenisei, the Us (see JTBy 254f., note 47).
begged pardon, saying, “We younger brothers
have committed a crime and done wrong out of
ignorance. You are my elder brother. The rule
is yours. Wherever you say, I will come, and I
will not disobey my elder brother’s command.
Let me fatten my flocks and horses and then
come to you. Bärkä, Hülägü, and Alghu are
also coming, and I am expecting their arrival.”
This is the message he sent. 
When the envoys came before the Qa’an and
delivered the message, he said, “These boys
went astray. Now they have sobered up and
come to their senses by admitting their crime.”
As a reply he sent this message: “When
Hülägü, Bärkä, and Alghu arrive there, let
them send envoys, and when their envoys
arrive we shall determine where we should
gather. You must keep your word before then,
and if you come before they arrive, so much
the better.” With this, he sent the envoys back
and returned himself to his ordus at Qara’un
Jidun, giving the expeditionary force leave to
disband and go to their yurts. He also let
Genghis Khan’s and Kölgän’s ordus go to their
yurts, telling them to stay there. The Qa’an sta-
tioned his cousin Yesünggä with ten tümäns of
soldiers on the frontier of the ulus and told
them to stay there until Ariq Bökä came, at
which time they should accompany him.
At that time Hülägü and Alghu were in favor
of the Qa’an, and they were constantly sending
envoys to each other. Hülägü sent envoys to re-
proach Ariq Bökä and keep him from action.
He also sent envoys to the Qa’an, as did Alghu.
When he realized that Qaidu and Qutuqu were
siding with Ariq Bökä, [880] he attacked them
several times and put them to flight. 
At that time the Qa’an sent a message to
Hülägü and Alghu, saying, “The provinces are
in revolt. You, Hülägü, must take over and
guard well the lands of the Tajiks from the
banks of the Oxus to the river of Egypt against
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
423

all who have disputed the Mongol army and
the good name of our ancestors. Let Alghu
command and keep the el and ulus from the
Altai to the far side of the Oxus. I will guard
this side from the Altai to the shores of the
ocean.”
Bärkä kept sending messages to both sides
and trying to keep both happy. 
When Ariq Bökä had fattened his horses
throughout the summer and autumn and had
failed to keep his word, he mounted again to
wage war on the Qa’an. When he arrived near
Yesünggä, who was positioned on the frontier,
he sent an envoy to say, “I am coming to sur-
render.” He thus took Yesünggä unaware and
turned back Genghis Khan’s and Kölgän’s or-
dus as well as his own. Crossing the desert,
Yesünggä set out for the Qa’an to inform him
that the rebel was approaching. The Qa’an sent
a messenger to Taghachar and got together a
force. He himself was in the forefront with
Taghachar,
Elji’itäi’s
son
Hulaqur,
Yäkä
Qada’an, and the soldiers they had. Hulaqur,
Nachin Gürägän, Därgäi Gürägän of the Ikiräs,
Oradai, and Qada’an all performed outstand-
ingly and fought well in the vanguard. Yesüng-
gä did not participate in that battle because his
men were scattered. During this expedition the
Qa’an and the aforementioned forces encoun-
tered Ariq Bökä on the edge of the desert, and
they did battle at a place called Abji’a Kötägär1
in front of a hill known as Khucha Boldaq and
a na’ur (lake) called Shimu’ultai. They defeat-
ed Ariq Bökä [881] and killed many of the Oy-
irat tribes. 
When Ariq Bökä and his troops were broken
and routed, the Qa’an said, “Do not go in
pursuit of them, for they are ignorant children.
They must realize and feel sorry for what they
1Mentioned in the Secret History as Abji’a Ködeger
(§187) and Abjigha Köteger (§191).
have done.” (A picture of this battle is as
shown.)
Ten days later Möngkä Qa’an’s son Asutai,
who was Ariq Bökä’s gäjigä (rear guard),
caught up with Ariq Bökä and heard that
Taghachar’s army and the Qa’an’s other troops
had turned back. Ariq Bökä and Asutai took
counsel, turned back themselves, and gave bat-
tle in the afternoon on the edge of the sandy
desert called Älät at Shirgän Naghur and
Shilügälig hill. The Qa’an’s army broke Ariq
Bökä’s right wing, but his center and left wing
kept fighting until evening and forced the
Qa’an to retire farther back during the night.
Both armies retreated to their camps, but most
of the soldiers perished on account of the long
road and having to go on foot. During the win-
ter both sides retired to their homes, where
they spent the spring and summer. 
After Ariq Bökä had asked Alghu several
times to assist him with arms and provisions
and received no answer, he mustered his army
and set out against him.
Alghu has a falling-out with Ariq Bökä and
does battle with his army; Alghu is defeated
but re-equips himself as Ariq Bökä loses
strength.
When Ariq Bökä nominated Alghu, the son
of Chaghatai’s son Baidar, as head of the Ulus
Chaghatai, Alghu set out on his way. When he
reached Turkistan nearly a hundred fifty thou-
sand horsemen [882] gathered around him.
Orghina Khatun, then the ruler of the Ulus
Chaghatai, went to Ariq Bökä’s court. Alghu
dispatched Negübäi2 Oghul with five thousand
horsemen
and
one
of
his
amirs
named
Uchachar, Habash Amid’s son the bitigchi Su-
layman Beg, and a yarghuchi named Abishgha
to Samarkand, Bukhara, and the provinces of
2Negübäi, son of Chaghatai’s son Sarban; see text p.

Transoxiana in order to guard the frontiers of
those areas and carry out Alghu’s orders.
When they arrived there, they put all Bärkä’s
dependents and liege men to death, even mar-
tyring on that pretext the shaykhzada of Islam,
Burhanuddin, the son of the great Shaykh Say-
fuddin Bakharzi. They seized all those people’s
property, animate and inanimate, some of the
more valuable things were sent to Negübäi
Oghul, and Uchachar went to Khwarazm. 
During all this, Ariq Bökä’s envoys headed
by Boritai Bitigchi, Yoshmut’s son Shadi, [and]
Äbügälün1 delivered the decree that flocks,
horses, and arms be taken away, and in a short
time they had accumulated a great deal of
property. Covetous of so much wealth, Alghu
sought a pretext to arrest them until one day
Alghu was told that they had said, “We have
gathered these things at Ariq Bökä’s order.
What does Alghu have to do with them?” He
took offense at this and in anger ordered them
arrested and the property confiscated. His
amirs said, “Now, as a consequence of your
having taken such an action, Ariq Bökä’s sup-
port will be lost, especially since Orghina
Khatun has gone to complain and we do not
have the ability to withstand her wrath. It
would be best, now that we have revolted
against Ariq Bökä, for us to fight on behalf of
the Qa’an.” Fully agreed upon this, they killed
the envoys and divided the property among the
soldiers. When Ariq Bökä heard this, [883] he
flared up in anger and headed out against Al-
ghu, saying, “Let the people of Qaraqorum ac-
company us.” But the imams, bakhshis, and
Christians said, “This order is harsh. What can
we do?”
“What ranks are these three groups going to

break?” he asked. “And what good will they be

No sooner had he departed than the Qa’an
arrived in Qaraqorum with a large force and
surrounded the city. He treated the people
kindly,
maintaining
Ögödäi
Qa’an’s
and
Möngkä Qa’an’s order that they be tarkhan,
and then set out in pursuit of Ariq Bökä. En-

confusion in Cathay due to the Qa’an’s ab-

of Cathay. 
Qara Buqa, commander of Ariq Bökä’s van-
guard, did battle with Alghu in the vicinity of
Bolad in a place called Süt Köl (Lake Say-
ram).2 Alghu was victorious, and Qara Buqa
was killed. Puffed up with pride in having de-
feated Ariq Bökä’s vanguard and having killed
Qara Buqa, Alghu retired unguardedly to the Ili
River, where he camped in his own ordus and
disbanded his forces. Asutai, who had been
Ariq
Bökä’s
gäjigä
(rear
guard),
arrived,
crossed the mountains called Temür Qahalqa
(Iron Gates), selected troops (ilghamishi), cap-
tured the Ili River and Almalyk area, and
seized Alghu’s ulus. Since Alghu’s troops had
been disbanded, he picked up his wife and the
soldiers of the right wing that Asutai had not
yet reached and fled to Khotan and Kashgar.
On his heels came Ariq Bökä, [884] who
stayed at the Ili and Almalyk that winter, con-
stantly engaged in revelry and in killing and
plundering Alghu’s people. One month later
the soldiers who had fled reached Alghu, and
he and his aghruq decamped and headed for
Samarkand. Hülägü Khan’s son Jumghur was
suffering from a slight illness and asked Ariq
Bökä for permission to go to Samarkand for
2For Bolad, see text p. 40 above.

425

treatment. 
In Quluqana Yil, the Year of the Rat that
started in Rabi‘ I 662 [1264], he parted from
him, and since Ariq Bökä was shamelessly
killing Alghu’s innocent people and causing
hardships, his commanders also left him, each
one using some pretext or other, saying, “He
ruthlessly
kills
the
Mongol
soldiers
that
Genghis Khan put together. Why should we
not revolt and turn against him?” 
That winter they went no further forward,
and when spring came there was such scarcity
and famine in Almalyk that the soldiers had to
feed their horses wheat instead of barley. Not
having green grass to eat, the horses all per-
ished, and many of the inhabitants of Almalyk
died of starvation. Those who were left alive
took refuge with God from the oppression of
the soldiers and stretched out their hands in
supplication.
One day Ariq Bökä was busy reveling and
carousing when suddenly a fierce wind came
and tore out the stakes and broke the poles of
his court tent, resulting in the injury of several
people. The court ministers and commanders
took this as an omen of his demise and totally
abandoned him. Ariq Bökä and Asutai were
left there with only a few soldiers, realizing for
certain that their distress was a result of the
curses of the poor people who had died during
the famine—and what doubt is there that many
a palace has been destroyed by the cries of the
oppressed!? [885]
The sigh of an oppressed person at dawn is
surely worse than arrows and spears.
At that time Möngkä Qa’an’s son Ürüngtash
was in Mongolia, in front of the Altai sands at
the river called Jabqan Mörän.1 When the com-
manders of a thousand arrived there they sent
1The modern Mongolian river Dzavhan Gol, which
empties into Ayrag Nuur and thence into Hyargas Nuur.
him a message saying, “We and our soldiers
are going to consult with the Qa’an. What say
you?” Ürüngtash approved of this and agreed
with them, sending an envoy to Ariq Bökä and
demanding his father’s great jade seal, which
was with him. He sent it to him, and he, the
regimental commanders, and soldiers went to
the Qa’an.
When Alghu was apprised of Ariq Bökä’s
weakened condition, he attacked him. Having
learned of his advance and realizing how close
he was, Ariq Bökä gave Orghina Khatun leave
to depart in the company of Mas‘ud Beg and
sent her to Alghu to calm him down. Alghu
married her and, in order to placate her, treated
Mas‘ud Beg kindly by making him divan chief
of his realm and sending him to administer
Samarkand and Bukhara. He went there, con-
stantly took tribute from the subjects, and sent
it to Alghu. Thereby Alghu recovered and re-
assembled his dispersed troops. Once he did
battle with Bärkä’s army and defeated it, and
he pillaged Otrar. He died a year later. Togeth-
er with the amirs and viziers, Orghina Khatun
elevated her son Mubarakshah to Alghu’s
place, as was said in the section on Chaghatai.2
[886]
Ariq Bökä goes in helplessness to the qa’an
and confesses to his crime; his end.
When Ariq Bökä was abandoned by his sol-
diers and commanders, and the princes each
went off on his own, he was left dumbfounded.
With little or no alternative, he set out for the
Qa’an’s court. Arriving there in Quluqana Yil,
the Year of the Rat corresponding to 662
[1264], it was ordered that many troops be sta-
tioned, and it was commanded that Ariq Bökä
perform tägishmishi. It is the custom in such
cases that during tägishmishi a tent flap is
thrown over the shoulders of the criminal.
2See text p. 769. above.
426
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Covered in that fashion, he performed tägish-
mishi. After a time he was given permission to
enter. He entered and stood in the place of the
bitigchis. The Qa’an looked at him for a while,
and his fraternal compassion was stirred. Ariq
Bökä burst into tears, and the Qa’an too wiped
away tears from his eyes and asked, “My dear
brother, during this strife and contention, were
we right or were you?”
“We were then,” he replied, “but you are
today.”
An envoy from Hülägü Khan named Ching-
qun had come and was present. When he re-
turned he reported the situation to Hülägü, who
sent a message to the Qa’an, saying, “How can
it be appropriate to the Yasaq to allow a mem-
ber of our family to do tägishmishi in this fash-
ion or that our aqa-ini should suffer such
humiliation?”
The Qa’an heard and approved of these
words and sent back the following reply:
“Hülägü is right. I acted out of ignorance.”
After that, he did not allow Ariq Bökä into
his presence for a year.
During that time Ajiqi, the brother of the
Abishgha who had been killed by Asutai, said
to Asutai, “You killed my brother.”
“Yes,” he replied, “I killed him by order of
the ruler of the time, Ariq Bökä. [887] I did not
want a member of our family to be killed by a
commoner. Today the ruler of the face of the
earth is Qubilai Qa’an. And if he so com-
mands, I will kill you too.”
The Qa’an said to Ajiqi, “This is not the time
for such talk. Their wrath is severe.”
In the midst of this exchange Taghachar
Noyan arose and said, “It is the Qa’an’s com-
mand that we should not investigate past af-
fairs today but should be indulging in banquets
and revelry.” The Qa’an approved of this, so
they quaffed goblets that day.
“Ariq Bökä is standing,” said Taghachar.
“Let the Qa’an appoint him a place to sit.”
Qubilai indicated that he could sit with his
sons. That day was spent in banqueting and
revelry.
The next day at dawn the princes and great
commanders,
Otchi
Noyan’s
[grand]son
Taghachar, Jochi Qasar’s son Yesünggä, Hu-
laqur,
Yäkä
Qada’an,

son
Ching

“I am the author of this crime, which has

This was unacceptable, and the Qa’an said,

string a bow in his face, and there was only a
slight difference of opinion. However, all the

world knows how they were punished for the
little rebelliousness they harbored in their
hearts. You who have stirred up all this con-
tentiousness and cast such strife and unrest
among everyone that it has resulted in the loss

Then Tümän Noyan, [888] who was the se-
nior among them and of great “bone,” said,
“Officers, why do you not answer? Why have
your eloquent tongues turned mute? On the
day we seated Ariq Bökä on the throne we
swore to each other that we would die before
his throne. Today that day of death has come.
Let us keep our word.”
“Well done,” said the Qa’an. “You have kept
your word.” 
Then he asked Ariq Bökä, “Who incited you
to sedition and rebellion?”
“Bolgha and Alamdar said to me, ‘Qubilai
Qa’an and Hülägü are both on expeditions, and
the Qa’an has turned the great ulus over to you.
What do you think? Will you let them cut our
throats like sheep?’ I said, ‘Have you consulted
Dorji?’ ‘Not yet,’ they said. I said, ‘Consult
Tümän, Toquz, Alichar, and Khucha,’ and they
all agreed in council. Since Dorji was not there
because of illness, I said, ‘Summon him so we
can finish this talk.’ He too came and agreed in
council. That group undertook this thing to-
gether, and of them only Tümän did not fail to
disobey my orders, and he carried out whatever
I ordered. It was Ching Temür who caused
harm, that is, he spoke words about the Qa’an
that were beyond the competence of one like
him.”
The amirs all said unanimously, “It was just
as Ariq Bökä says. He is speaking the absolute
truth.”
“But Ariq Bökä himself instructed me,” cried
Ching Temür. “How is he now attributing it all
to me? Bulgha Aqa is a witness to this and
knows it all.”
Then the Qa’an ordered Ching Temür to con-
front (tapishmishi) Ariq Bökä. Ching Temür re-
peated the same words to Ariq Bökä’s face.
This was difficult for Ariq Bökä to take, and he
said, “If this is how it is, then you will live and
I will die.” 
When this was reported, the Qa’an realized
that Ching Temür’s words were true, [889] and
he let him go.
Then he consulted with all the elder and
younger princes and said, “Bulgha Bitigchi has
heard the words of Ögödäi Qa’an and Möngkä
Qa’an. We will let him live. He can also be a
witness in this case to Hülägü and the other
princes.” Upon the advice of all the princes he
let him go. When Asutai learned of his release
he said, “How can it be right for Bulgha to re-
main alive? I will confront him and expose his
heinous crimes.”
“You have quoted a Mongol proverb,” Asutai
said to Bulgha, “the meaning of which is that
we have done something upon which we
should [not] turn our backs or be negligent.
This is your crime for which you should die.”
Bulgha Noyan not only did not deny it but
even acknowledged it.
When his words were reported, the Qa’an
said, “Since it is so, let him be executed.”
Elji’itäi’s crime was greater that those of the
others because he had made false accusations
against Qada’an’s son Qurumshi that resulted
in his death. Therefore he was turned over to
Qada’an to be executed.
Doquz’s crime was also great, for he had a
hand in killing many of the Qa’an’s people. All
the aforementioned officers were executed.
Güyük Khan’s son Hoqu, Naqu’s son Chabat,
and
Qarachar’s
son
Totoq
were
sent
to
Turkistan along with several other princes.
After that, the Qa’an wanted to try Ariq
Bökä, and he would have waited for the arrival
428
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

of Hülägü Khan, Bärkä, and Alghu, but since
they were very far away and it would have tak-
en too long, the princes who were in the area,
Taghachar, Yesünggä, Yäkä Qada’an, Hulaqur,
Ching Temür, Ja’utu, and other princes and
commanders of Mongolia and Cathay assem-
bled to put Ariq Bökä and Asutai on trial. [890]
The princes and officers of Mongolia and
Cathay try Ariq Bökä.
When ten of Ariq Bökä’s officers had been
killed and Ariq Bökä’s own trial was begun,
the monarch issued a decree to all parts of the
realm. All the commanders took counsel and
said, “How shall we look upon Ariq Bökä’s
and Asutai’s crime? For the Qa’an’s sake, let
us spare their lives.” They sent envoys to
Hülägü, Bärkä, and Alghu, saying, “Since it is
not possible for you to attend because you are
too far away and too occupied with matters,
and since there was a possibility, had we wait-
ed longer, for breaches to have been made in
the fabric of the empire that could not have
been repaired, we have therefore executed their
officers, tried them, and are consulting with
you. We brothers are all agreed that Ariq
Bökä’s blood should be spared and Asutai
should be released. What say you?”
The envoys came first to Alghu and delivered
the message. He replied, “I sat in Chaghatai’s
place without consulting the Qa’an or Hülägü
Aqa. When all the aqa-inis assemble and con-
firm whether I was right or wrong, if they ex-
onerate me, and if I then have anything good or
bad to say, I will say it.”
After that, the envoys went to Hülägü Khan,
who said, “Provided all the aqa-inis assemble,
take counsel, and make a decision, then let it
be so. When Bärkä sets out for a quriltai, we
too will ride quickly.” And he sent his own en-
voys along with the others to Bärkä to decide
when they should go before the Qa’an for a
quriltai. When they arrived before Bärkä and
reported the situation, [891] he said, “Anything
the Qa’an, Hülägü Khan, and all the aqa-inis
decide is all right. We too will set out in Hükär
Yil, we will traverse the distance during Bars
Yil, and we will accompany Hülägü Khan to a
quriltai in Taulai Yil.”
When the envoys returned and reported to
the Qa’an, Ariq Bökä and Asutai were permit-
ted to give an oath of allegiance (huljamishi)
and were brought into the ordu. 
During the autumn of that year, which was
the Year of the Leopard corresponding to 664
[1266], Ariq Bökä fell ill and died. A dispute
and battle broke out between Hülägü and
Bärkä that will be mentioned in the relevant
sections. They both died soon after that. (May
God extend the kingdom of the Padishah of Is-
lam Ghazan Khan for many years and innu-
merable generations, and may he enjoy long
life and prosperity!) When their deaths were
reported to the Qa’an, he appointed Hülägü’s
eldest son Abaqa to his father’s place as head
of the Mongols and Tajiks of Iran, and he gave
the Ulus Jochi to Möngkä Temür.
Alghu also came down with a long illness
during that time, and he was unable to attend
the quriltai. He also died, and Orghina Khatun,
with the agreement of her amirs, sat her son
Mubarakshah in Alghu’s place. Baraq, the son
of Yesünto’a, son of Chaghatai’s son Mö’ätü-
kän, asked the Qa’an, “Why does Mubarak-
shah sit in my uncle Alghu’s place? If it be so
ordered, let me take over my uncle’s position.
My loins are girded in service and obedience.”
The Qa’an gave Baraq a decree making him
the commander of the ulus until Mubarakshah
was grown. Baraq went and took Mubarak-
shah’s place. Alghu’s sons Chübäi and Qaban
and their aqa-inis left Baraq and took their sol-
diers to the Qa’an’s court. [892]
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
429

The Qa’an sends his sons Nomoghan and
Kököchü with other princes to wage war on
Qaidu; the princes plot treachery against
them both.
When the Qa’an’s mind was at ease with re-
gard to Ariq Bökä’s sedition and revolt, the
princes girded their loins in obedience to
him—all except Qaidu, the son of Ögödäi
Qa’an’s son Qashin, and some of Chaghatai’s
sons. Qubilai Qa’an sent them an emissary to
win them over and say, “All the other princes
are here. For what reason have you not come?
It is our wish that we be happy in seeing one
another. After we consult on various matters,
you will be shown all sorts of favor and al-
lowed to return home.”
Qaidu, who had no intention of submitting,
excused himself saying, “Our animals are lean.
When they are fattened up, we will obey your
command.”
Three years passed with him making such
excuses. After that, he and Qonchi Noyan to-
gether drove away the ___1 who were attached
to Möngkä Qa’an’s son Ürüngtash and who
were near them, killing and plundering them.
By this means they initiated sedition and strife,
and
therefore
the
Qa’an
sent
his
son
Nomoghan with the following princes of the
Right and Left Wings to deal with Qaidu’s in-
surrection: Möngkä Qa’an’s son Shirägi, Ariq
Bökä’s sons Yobuqur and Malik Temür, the
Qa’an’s nephews Sögätäi’s son Tuq Temür and
Uruqutai,2 and the Qa’an’s cousin Otchigin
Charaqu, along with innumerable officers and
soldiers under the command of Hantun Noyan.
Having summered along a river bank, the

Qa’an hunted for a few days and then parted
from the others. During the hunt Tuq Temür

ing, “Let us together seize Nomoghan and

“The rule will come to you, for the Qa’an has

his brother Kököchü were sent to Möngkä

“We are much under obligation to you,” Tuq
Temür and Shirägi said to Qaidu, “and we
haven’t forgotten. We are sending you Qubilai
Qa’an’s sons and officers who were out to at-
tack you. We must not harbor suspicions of
each other but work together to repel the foe.” 
The envoys returned with the following mes-
sage from Qaidu: “We are obliged to you, and
we expect that you will remain in that area,
where there is abundant water and grass.”
Tuq Temür mounted and attacked Ögödäi’s
and Chaghatai’s ordus, seizing the princes who
were in charge, Sarban and Minqa Temür’s
brother, and letting it be known that the sons of
Batu and Qaidu and the princes would be arriv-

arrived and it became clear to the ordus that

was false. Tuq Temür and Sarban had joined
Shirägi and were fighting together against the
Qa’an’s soldiers, and Tuq Temür, Shirägi, and
Sarban took flight, headed for the Ba’arin tribe
on the banks of the Irtysh River, where they
began to equip themselves. Tuq Temür mount-
ed from there to attack Qirqiz territory, but the
Qa’an’s
army
arrived
and
plundered
his
a’ughruq. He turned back looking for it and

spond. Tuq Temür took umbrage and turned

back. Chancing upon Sarban on the road, he

At that time the distance between them and

“There is no audacity or boldness in Shirä-

When Shirägi saw that he had no alternative,

“Why should we ask you for the rule and

When Shirägi realized that he could not op-

Shirägi
informed
Yobuqur, but he refused and would not go be-
fore Sarban. Tuq Temür led his army out
against him, and when they were near, he sent
a messenger to say, “We have decided thus in
council. If you agree, well and good. If not, get
ready for battle!”
Yobuqur sent the following reply, “I do not
want to fight. I want a respite of five days to
prepare myself for a tägishmishi.” So saying,
he got busy arranging his soldiers, and on the
fifth day he came out with his army [895] and
drew up ranks for battle. Tuq Temür made a
charge, but his entire army turned around at
once and went over to Yobuqur. [Tuq Temür]
managed to flee with twelve liege men. Three
days later he arrived at some Mongols’ tents
wearing black felt and asking for water. They
did not recognize him and brought some yo-
gurt. Immediately thereafter a posse arrived
looking for him, and when they got wind of
him, they set out after him. Coming suddenly
across a brook full of water and mud, he said
to his liege men, “It would be better for us to
fight and die with a good name.”
“You, a member of the family, will not suffer
loss,” they said, “but it will be bad for us.”
Having lost hope in his liege men, he threw
down his weapons and was taken captive by
the foe. They took him before Yobuqur. Shirägi
asked Yobuqur for Tuq Temür, but Yobuqur
said, “If you protect him you will be a great
enemy to me.”
“If he has done one bad thing,” he replied,
“he has done ten good things.” It was to no
avail. Tuq Temür was put to death.
Sarban came to Shirägi and said, “Tuq Temür
made me do it.” Shirägi took his soldiers from
him so that he was left to wander about with
only two or three liege men. After a time [the
men Shirägi had taken] fled in droves to the
Qa’an. Shirägi wanted to go after them and
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
431

bring them back, but he was afraid Sarban
would stir up strife. So he sent him with fifty
liege men to Jochi’s [great-]grandson Qonchi.
As it happened, their way lay through Sarban’s
khaylkhana in Jand and Özkand. Sarban’s men
assembled, seized the fifty liege men, and
freed Sarban, who then mounted again with an
army, waylaid Shirägi’s a’ughruq, and told
them to go to the Qa’an. In advance he sent a
messenger to inform of his situation. Shirägi
was apprised and came to stage an encounter
with Sarban, but his army at once went over to
Sarban, and he was left alone. [896] Sarban or-
dered five hundred horsemen to keep watch
over him. When Yobuqur heard of this, he led
his army out to encounter Sarban. His soldiers
too went over to Sarban, and he too was cap-
tured and turned over to five hundred horse-
men to be taken to the Qa’an. Feigning illness,
Yobuqur requested a few days’ respite, but in
secret he sent a great deal of cash and jewels to
Genghis Khan’s nephew Otchigin, whose yurt
was in that area, and asked him for help. With-
out warning Otchigin attacked and waylaid the
soldiers. Sarban managed to escape with only
his wife. When one of Otchigin’s warriors saw
that his wife was fleeing, he set out to capture
her, but she shouted out and Sarban turned
back and felled the man with one arrow. He
and his wife then went to the Qa’an. Shirägi
had already arrived when Sarban got there, but
the Qa’an did not allow him entry. It was or-
dered that he dwell on an island with extremely
foul air, and that is where he spent the rest of
his life.
The Qa’an rewarded Sarban with lands and
troops, but he too died after a time. Yobuqur
took Shirägi’s and Sarban’s ordus and entered
Qonchi’s horde. Malik Temür and Qurbaqa
joined Qaidu. Shirägi’s son Ulus Buqa joined
Qonchi’s horde, where he remained for a
while. Yobuqur tired of serving Qaidu and fled
to the Qa’an, as did Ulus Buqa and his mother
and ordus. When Jochi’s grandson Möngkä
Temür died, Tödä Möngkä was elevated to his
position,
and
Noqai,
Tödä
Möngkä,
and
Qonchi consulted together and sent Nomoghan
to the Qa’an, saying, “We are all in submis-
sion. We will come to a quriltai.” Qaidu also
sent Hantun Noyan back, but he did not go to
the quriltai. [897] With this, [Noqai, Tödä
Möngkä, and Qonchi] changed their minds.
Nomoghan died a year later.
The Qa’an sends troops to Nankiyas and
subdues that realm.
When the Qa’an had let the Mongol troops
rest from campaigning for several years, he
said, “Since the realm of Cathay is completely
subjugated, we should also take Nankiyas.” 
During Möngkä Qa’an’s time, the ruler of
that country maintained a firm friendship with
Möngkä, and emissaries were always coming
and going between them because the monarchs
of Nankiyas were noble and of puissance, and
in olden days they had held the kingdom of
Cathay also. The Altan Khan of Cathay was of
the race of Jurchids, who had revolted and
seized the kingdom. Since the ancient emper-
ors of Nankiyas, as will be explained in their
history, which forms an appendix to this book,
were enemies of the emperors of Cathay, they
assisted Genghis Khan when he was conquer-
ing the realm of Cathay. More especially dur-
ing Ögödäi Qa’an’s reign they sent massive
troops to render assistance in totally over-
whelming the emperor of Cathay, as has al-
ready been said.
In the beginning Möngkä Qa’an intended to
conquer Nankiyas, and Qubilai Qa’an even set
out to do it, particularly since his capital was
Cathay and near the Nankiyas. However, every
time he sent an expedition to their borders it
failed. This continued until the year ___. Then
a man named Bayan—a son of Kököchü, a
432
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

great amir of Ba’arin “bone” whose grandfa-
ther Alaq Noyan had been executed on charges
of a great crime1—[898] fell by lot as a slave
to Qubilai Qa’an, and since he was in Abaqa
Khan’s service in Iran, Qubilai Qa’an sent
Sodon Noyan’s son Sartaq Noyan along with
Abdul-Rahman on a mission to summon him.
(Abdul-Rahman remained behind here in order
to settle the accounts of these provinces.)
When Bayan arrived, the Qa’an outfitted thirty
tümäns of Cathay soldiers and appointed to
head the army of Cathay Sämäkä Bahadur, a
Cathaian officer from the city of Chaghan Bal-
ghasun who had surrendered during Möngkä
Qa’an’s time and performed valiantly and sin-
cerely. As head of the Mongol army he as-
signed the aforementioned Bayan and Amir
Achu,2 a grandson of Sübädäi Bahadur of the
Uriangqat clan. He ordered that Sämäkä Baha-
dur be the leader of the joint army because his
ordinance was severe and he had always per-
formed
well. Thus
he
sent
them
off
to
Nankiyas. Sämäkä had to return because of ill-
ness along the way, and Bayan and Achu be-
came the commanders of both armies.
Since the expanse of the Nankiyas realm was
extremely vast and their soldiers were innu-
merable, it was difficult to conquer and could
only be accomplished over a long period of
time. For nearly four years they made every ef-
fort and managed to conquer parts of it. After
that, they sent messengers to the Qa’an, saying,
“The army is insufficient.” Since the Qa’an
could not raise an army on short notice, he sent
out a decree that all prisoners in Cathay should
be brought forth—there were nearly twenty
thousand men. 
“You are all going to die or be killed,” he
said. “For my own sake I set you free. I will
1See text p. 198 above.
2The Achuqan of text p. 156 above.
give you horses, arms, and clothing and send
you to the army. If you perform well, you may
become officers and men of standing.” [899]
He outfitted them, made the talented among
them officers of units of a thousand, a hundred,
and ten, and sent them off to join the great
army. After that he sent an envoy to summon
Bayan and Achu by post horse. They arrived
with seven changes of relay, and he instructed
them how to fight in battle. Then they returned.
In the seventh year from the time they went
to that country they did battle on the banks of
the Gang Mörän River [Yangtse], beating sev-
en tümäns of Nankiyas soldiers and capturing
the country. They killed the emperor, Shaozhu
by name,3 and conquered the countries of Kan-
dar,
Iki-Buzih,
Maquman,
Kalang,
Kyay,
Kafjih-Guh,4 and others.
The kingdom of Solanggha (Korea), which
had submitted during Möngkä Qa’an’s reign
but then reverted to rebelliousness, sent repre-
sentatives to court when Qubilai Qa’an sat on
the throne and submitted again.
He sent an army from the realm of Hindustan
to Java, and they took it in battle. By boat he
sent ambassadors to most of the realms of In-
dia for them to submit, and they were com-
pelled to comply. Until now emissaries have
been coming and going back and forth discus-
sing the terms of submission.
He divided the realms of Nankiyas among

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
433

the princes and stationed a contingent of sol-
diers in each part of that realm. Amir Bolad
Chengxiang, who is very familiar with the situ-
ation of that realm, reports that although it was
the Nankiyas custom for only the nobles who
led the people and had followings to be count-
ed, the census there came to 990,000. There is
no kingdom of greater extent, for it is written
in books that five climes begin in that realm.
This notwithstanding, it is uninterruptedly in-
habited, and until the present those Mongol
and Ja’uqut soldiers are resident there and have
never left. Every tümän commander resides to-
gether with an army in a given realm, and the
governorship of that area is entrusted to him
along with four bitigchis representing the di-
van. [900] When the taxes of a province are
due, the Qa’an’s yarligh decree is sent to that
officer, and he collects them from all the cities
attached to that area in accordance with the or-
der and remits them. None of them has any
connection with any other labor. The members
of the prisoner corps have all become officers
of note and acquired summer and winter resi-
dences for themselves.
Now that the history of Qubilai Qa’an from
his birth until the time he mounted the throne
and completely conquered Cathay and Machin
has been given, we will record several other
stories pertaining to his realms, the regulations
and rules he introduced, and the troops he sta-
tioned in every area and frontier of those
provinces, God willing. 
The buildings the Qa’an made in Cathay,
and the rules, customs, and regulations
practiced in that realm.
The province of Cathay is an extremely vast
and broad realm, and it is as thickly inhabited
as possible. Trustworthy sources report that in
the entire inhabited quarter of the globe the
habitation and population that are there are to
be found nowhere else. 
There is a gulf, not very large, that extends
inland from the ocean from the southeast along
the borders and coast that separate Manzi and
Gauli.1 It comes into Cathay to within [twen-
ty]-four leagues of Khanbaligh, and one can go
that far by boat. Because of the nearness of the
sea it rains a lot. Part of the country has a
warm climate, and part has a cold climate. 
In his time Genghis Khan conquered most of
this realm, and then during Ögödäi Qa’an’s
reign the rest was taken. [901] Genghis Khan
and his sons had no capital in Cathay, as has
been mentioned in every history; however,
since Möngkä Qa’an gave that realm to Qubi-
lai Qa’an, who, with his farsighted view, could
see what an extremely flourishing land it was
and what important countries and realms
neighbored it, he chose it as his capital. He
designated as his winter residence the city of
Khanbaligh, which is called Zhongdu in Catha-
ian and had been an imperial capital. It had
been chosen as a site in ancient times by as-
trologers and philosophers under a highly fa-
vorable ascendant, and it was always consid-
ered to be very auspicious and lucky. Since
Genghis Khan had destroyed it, Qubilai Qa’an
wanted to rebuild it, so for his own fame and
reputation he built another city next to it. That
city was named Dai Du.2 The two are contigu-
ous, and the latter’s ramparts contain seventeen
towers with a distance of one league between
every two towers. It is so flourishing that innu-
merable buildings have been built outside of
every tower. All sorts of fruit-bearing trees
have been imported from every country and
planted in the gardens and orchards, and most
have done well.
1The gulf is the Bo Hai. “Gauli,” Marco Polo’s
“Cauli,” is for the Chinese 高麗Gaoli, Korea. See be-
low, note to text p. 909.
2Marco Polo calls it Taidu, from the Chinese 大都
Da(i) Du ‘great capital.’
434
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Inside the city he built a truly magnificent
palace for his ordu. It is called Qarshi,1 and its
pillars and paving are all of marble. It is quite
beautiful and very nice. Surrounding it are four
[concentric] walls with a distance of an arrow
shot between one wall and the next. The outer
wall serves as a kiriyäs,2 and the next inner
wall is for the amirs to sit who congregate
every day at dawn. The third wall is for the
gäzigtäns (bodyguards), and the fourth is for
the elite. In the winter the Qa’an resides in this
palace. Artists have often illustrated it in histo-
ry books, and its shape is as drawn.3 [902]
Khanbaligh and Daidu have a huge river that
comes from the north, where summer pastures
are located, from Chamchal.4 There are other
rivers too, and outside the city a very large
na’ur (lake) has been constructed that is like a
small sea. A dam has been made on it so that
boats can be launched in it for pleasure cruises.
The water of this river used to flow through
another place and empty into the gulf that juts
inland from the sea near Khanbaligh. Because
the gulf in that vicinity was narrow and boats
could not get through, cargos were mounted on
animals and brought to Khanbaligh. The archi-
tects and wise men of Cathay determined and
reported that it was possible for boats to come
to Khanbaligh from most provinces of Cathay
as well as from the capital of Machin, the city
of Hangzhou, Zayton, and other places. The
Qa’an ordered a large canal cut, and the water
of the aforementioned river, as well as that of
another river that flows ulam-ulam (uninter-
ruptedly) from the Qara Mörän (Yellow River)
1Qarshi (gA-rsI харш) is the Mongolian word for
palace.
2For the various senses of kiriyäs, see the glossary.
3Illustration lacking, regrettably.
4Chamchal, for Chabchiyal, the Mongolian name of
the Juyong (居庸) Pass northwest of Peking. See Doer-
fer, TMEN 1:310 §183, and text p. 446f. above.
and others into the cities and provinces, was
diverted into that canal. From Khanbaligh to
Khingsai and Zayton, which is the port to Hin-
dustan and the capital of Machin, is a forty-day
journey by boat. Many dams have been built
on this river to provide water to the provinces.
When a boat reaches those dams, it and its car-
go, no matter how large, are lifted by wench
and crane and replaced in the water on the oth-
er side of the dam. The canal is more than thir-
ty yards wide. Qubilai Qa’an ordered the walls
of the canal sheathed in stone so that earth
would not fall into it. Next to the canal is a
large highway that goes to Machin, a forty-day
journey. [903] The entire length of the road is
paved in stone so that when it rains a lot, ani-
mals will not get mired in mud. On the side to-
ward the road, willow and other sorts of trees
have been planted so that the entire length of
the road is shaded, and no person, military or
other, may break a branch from those trees or
give leaves to his horses. On both sides are vil-
lages, shops, and temples so that the whole
forty-day route is inhabited.
The walls of Daidu are made of earth, for it
is the custom in that country to set up two
boards and then pour damp earth into the area
between them and tamp it down with a big
stick until it is firm. Then they take the boards
away, and it is a wall. Because there is so much
rain there and the earth is not strong, even such
strong walls get damp, so at the end of his life
the Qa’an ordered stone brought, for he intend-
ed to face the wall with stone, but he died. God
willing, Temür Qa’an will be able to finish it.
The Qa’an wanted to build another such
palace in his summer residence in the city of
Kaipingfu,5 which is fifty leagues from Daidu.
5The text’sﻮـﻓﲔـﻤـ ـ ـﮐﻴis for 開平府Kaipingfu, Qubilai’s
summer residence Marco Polo calls “Chemeinfu,” the

There are three roads from the winter residence
to that place. One is the road that has been
made a ghoruq [preserve] for hunting; only of-
ficial envoys may travel that road. The second
goes to [Fuzhou1] along the banks of the Sang-
gan river,2 where there are many grapes and
fruits. There is another town near the city, and
it is called Simali.3 Most of the people there
are from Samarkand, and they have built many
gardens after the manner of Samarkand. The
other road is via a low hill called Singling.
Once past the hill, it is all open plain and
grassy meadow as far as the city of Kaipingfu.
Previously the summer residence was in the
aforementioned city of Fuzhou,4 but then Kaip-
ingfu was chosen. [904] To the east of it he
built himself a palace called Liang Dian.5 One
night he had a dream and abandoned it. He
consulted with the wise men and architects
over where another palace could be built. They
agreed that the place with the best qualities
was the na’ur [lake] in a meadow next to Kaip-
ingfu. They wanted to drain the lake. In that
country is a stone used in place of kindling.6

They gathered a lot of the stone and much
charcoal and filled in the na’ur and its source
with pebbles and small pieces of pottery. Then
they melted tin and lead over it to seal it tight.
They raised it above the surface of the earth to
a man’s height and built a plinth on top of that.
Since the water had been trapped inside the
earth, over time it seeped out in other direc-
tions into more distant meadows, and springs
began to flow. On top of the plinth they built a
qarshi (palace) in the Cathaian style. All
around the meadow a wall of marble was
made, and from the wall to the qarshi they
placed a wooden barricade so that no one could
enter the meadow. All sorts of game animals
were gathered in the meadow, and they have
multiplied.
In the midst of the city they built a smaller
palace and qarshi, and they made a lane from
the outer qarshi as a private passageway into
the qarshi. For a kiriyäs, a wall was built
around the qarshi at a distance of one bow
shot. Most of the time the emperor resides in
the qarshi outside the city.
There are many magnificent cities in that
realm, and each one has been given a name
that contains a special derivational signifi-
cance. The ranks of governors can be known
from the titles of the cities so that there is ab-
solutely no necessity for anything to be written
in edicts or for there to be any discussion as to
which governor of which city has precedence.
In assemblies they have no dispute over seat-
ing, [905] for it is clear from every rank which
governor must rise to greet another or bend the
knee. The titles and ranks are as follows: first
rank, jing; second rank, du; third rank, fu;
well, I tell you that they keep fire all night so well that
one finds some in the morning. These stones make no
ﬂame except a little at ﬁrst when they are lighted, as
charcoals do, and staying thus glowing they give great
heat” (Marco Polo, Description 1:249).

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

fourth rank, zhou; fifth rank, chi; sixth rank,
gun; seventh rank, xian; eighth rank, zhen;
ninth rank, cun.1 The first is used of a vast
realm, such as Anatolia, Fars, or Baghdad; the
second is used of a country that is a monarch’s
capital; and so on down to the seventh, which
is used for small cities; the eighth is for towns;
and the ninth for villages and plantations, al-
though muzim is also used for plantations and
villages.2 Ports and harbors are called matou.3
Such rules and organization do not occur in
other countries. Most of the administrative af-
fairs of the realm are organized along these
lines. [906]
The officers, viziers, and bitigchis of Cathay,
details of their ranks, the rules and
regulations that pertain to them, and the
technical terms of that group.
Great officers who hold the office of deputy
or vizier are called chengxiang, army comman-
ders are called taifu, a commander of ten thou-
sand is wanshuai, and officers, viziers, and
deputies of the divan who are Tajik, Cathaian,
and
Uyghur
are
called
pingzhang.4

customary for there to be four chengxiangs

The officers’ and governors’ posts are ac-
cording to rank, and their ranks are as follows.
Of the first rank are chengxiangs; they hold the
posts of vizier or deputy. The second rank is
taifu, which is an army commander. Regardless
of how great a taifu may be, he defers to a
chengxiang. The third rank is pingzhang,
which is a divan deputy or vizier from various
peoples. The fourth rank is youcheng, the fifth
is zuocheng, [907] the sixth is canzheng, the
seventh is canyi, the eighth is langzhong,5 and
the ninth is not known, but all scribes are under
him.
In Qubilai Qa’an’s time the following offi-
cers
were
chengxiang:
Hantun
Noyan,
Uchachar, Öljäi, Tarkhan, and Dashman. At the
present time Hantun Noyan is no longer alive,
but the rest are still in office and serve together
as Temür Qa’an’s chengxiangs. The rank of
pingzhang was formerly given only to natives
of Cathay, but at present it is also given to
Mongols, Tajiks, and Uyghurs. The chief
pingzhang is called shu pingzhang, meaning
the cream of the pingzhangs. At the present
time, which is the reign of Temür Qa’an,6 the
head of all is Bayan Pingzhang, the son of
Sayyid Nasiruddin and grandson of Sayyid
Ajall. He, i.e. Bayan Pingzhang, is also called
Sayyid Ajall. The second is Umar Pingzhang, a
Mongol. The third is Täkä Pingzhang, an
5For the terms see Doerfer, TMEN: youcheng (右丞),
1:554f. §407; zuocheng (左丞), 3:215f. §1201; canzheng
(參政), 1:342 §215; canyi (參儀), 1:342 §216;
langzhong (郎中), 1:492f. §358.
6Note that at this point the narrative switches to “the
present,” i.e. Temür Qa’an’s reign.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
437

Uyghur. Formerly there was Lachin Ping-
zhang, a nephew of Amir Su’unchaq; and at
present there is his son, Karmana by name. The
fourth is Yighmish Pingzhang, who has taken
Temür Pingzhang’s place. He too is an Uyghur.
Since the Qa’an resides most of the time in
Daidu, which they call sheng,1 a place has been
made in which they hold the great divan. It is
customary for a deputy to be present who has
charge of the gates. Bularghus (ownerless
properties) that are taken are carried before
that deputy,2 and he investigates. The name of
that divan is lisha.3 When they make an inves-
tigation they write down the minutes and send
them along with the bularghu to the lusha di-
van,4 which is higher in rank. From there it is
sent to the third divan, which is called shumi
yuan.5 From there it is sent to the fourth divan,
which is called tongzheng yuan; affairs dealing
with post stations and couriers pertain to it.6
[908] The last mentioned three divans are all
under the supervision of the [first] divan. Then
it is taken to the fifth divan, called yushi tai,
which deals with military affairs.7 Thence it
1Rashiduddin’s shing, Marco Polo’s scieng, is the Chi-
nese 省sheng ‘secretariat.’ The secretariat in Peking
was the 中書省Zhongshusheng, the ‘Grand Secretariat’;
see Doerfer, TMEN 1:370f. §247; Pelliot, Marco Polo
2:827–29.
2For bularghu, see Doerfer, TMEN 1:213–15 §93.
3The text’s lisha may represent either 吏司li si, a bu-
reau that dealt with civil functionaries, or 禮司li si, the
bureau of ceremonies. See Doerfer, TMEN 4:19 §1734.
4The text’s lusha may represent 路司lu si, the bureau
that dealt with roads and communications. See Doerfer,
TMEN 4:17f. §1732.
5The chubiyuwan in the text represents 樞密院shumi
yuan, the Bureau of Military Affairs (Farquhar, “Institu-
tions,” 30; Doerfer, TMEN 3:45f. §1060).
6Tunjunyuwan in the text; it represents 通政院
tongzheng yuan, the Bureau for Transmission Services,
which operated the state postal system (Farquhar, “Insti-
tutions,” 30; Doerfer, TMEN 2:642f. §985).
7Zhushitai in the text; it represents 御史臺yushi tai,
goes to the sixth divan, which is called xuan-
wei si.8 That is where all envoys, merchants,
and comers and goers report. It also deals with
yarlighs and paizas. At present it is under the
exclusive supervision of Amir Dashman. When
a matter has been taken through all six divans,
it is then taken for inquiry to the Great Divan,
which is called sheng.
“Fingerlines” of persons interrogated are tak-
en. The meaning of the word “fingerline” is as
follows.9 It has been ascertained by experience
that the finger joints of people are different.
Whenever a deposition is taken from anyone,
the paper is placed between his fingers, and on
the back of the deposition they draw a line
around the place of his finger joints so that, if
he ever denies it, they can compare it with the
marks of his fingers. If they match, he cannot
deny it.
When a matter has been carefully passed
through all the divans in this fashion, it is re-
ported to the throne, and whatever action is or-
dered is carried out.
It is customary for the aforementioned offi-
cers to go to the sheng every day to investigate
persons and administer the affairs of the realm.
The four chengxiangs also sit in, and the other
office-holders and bitigchis sit according to
rank. In front of each one is placed a shirä,
which is something like a stool, on which is
placed an ink stand. Normally that is where
the Censorate, which investigated official conduct (Far-
quhar, “Institutions,” 30; Doerfer, TMEN 3:216 §1202).
8In the text sanwisha, which represents 宣慰司xuan-
wei si, the Pacification Office (Farquhar, “Institutions,”
34; Doerfer, TMEN 3:281 §1277). 
9It is clear from his definition that Rashiduddin had
only the vaguest idea what a fingerprint was. He thinks
it has to do with the joints (band-i angushthā) and calls
it khaṭṭ-i angusht ‘finger line.’ I hesitate to translate the
Persian term as ‘fingerprint’ because khaṭṭ-i angusht is
obviously a phrase Rashiduddin has made up to describe
a phenomenon he does not really understand.

they are. Each officer has a mark and a seal.
Several bitigchis are employed whose duty is
to record the name of each individual who

salaries can be docked if they do not come for

divan without a good excuse, he is discharged
from office.
The four chengxiangs report directly to the
Qa’an. [909]
The Khanbaligh sheng is huge, and several
thousand years worth of records are kept there.
They are well kept, and they maintain good
records. There are nearly two thousand em-
ployees in that sheng. 
There is not a sheng in every city, only in

The governor there was once Zhen, the brother

Since these provinces are distant from one
another, there is a prince or officer of conse-
quence resident in each one, along with troops.
It is to him that the inhabitants of the province
and administrative affairs are referred, and he
keeps order and guards the province. The
sheng of each province is in the largest city of
the area, and every sheng is as large as a vil-
lage, since they have been constructed with

many houses and chambers, outbuildings, and
dependencies. To it are attached many working
slaves and servants, and the rules and regula-
tions of the divans are extremely tight and ex-
cellent. It is the custom for some criminals and
lawbreakers to be killed and for others to be
stripped of their families and possessions and
sent, without a single family member, to dig
clay, pull wagons, or carry stones so that when
people see officers and important people in
such a state they may learn a lesson. Their reg-
ulations and organization are of many sorts.
There are many stories of all sorts concerning
that realm, but since the history of that area
will be given separately in an appendix, this
much must suffice here.
The lands that border the Qa’an’s realm; a
mention of the princes and officers who are
stationed with troops to guard the frontiers.
To the southeast the Qa’an has no enemies,
for all the countries that lie on that side as far
as the ocean are inside his empire—save only a
large island in the sea near the coast of Jürcha
(Manchuria) and Kauli (Korea). It is called
Jimingu.1 It is nearly four hundred leagues in
circumference and has many cities and vil-
lages. [912] It has a separate ruler, and he is, as
he was before, unsubdued. The inhabitants are
short of stature and have short necks and large
bellies. There are many mines there. 
Directly to the east to the shores of the ocean
and the borders of Qirqiz territory there is no
enemy. To the southwest of Manzi, between
the provinces of Kongi (Canton) and Zayton,
there is an immensely large forest along the
coast. One of the sons of the ruler of Manzi es-
caped into it, and although he has no power or
strength, he lives by robbery and banditry.
To the south is a province called Kafjih-Guh
1The “Jimingu” of the text is for the Chinese 日本國
Ribenguo, i.e. Japan, which Marco Polo calls “Çipingu.”
[Tonking]. It has thick forests, and it borders
the province of Qarajang, part of Hindustan,
and the shore. There are two cities there,
Lochak and Khainam.2 It has a separate ruler
who is inimical to the Qa’an. The Qa’an’s son
Toghan, who resides in Lukin Fu in Manzi
with troops, guards the province of Manzi and
keeps watch against that foe. Once he went
with his soldiers against the cities on the coast,
took them, and stayed on the throne one week.
Then, without warning, their army sprang an
ambush from the sea, forests, and mountains
and attacked Toghan’s soldiers, who were busy
collecting booty. Toghan got out safely and is
still resident in Lukin Fu.
To the northwest, which is the border of Ti-
bet and the “Gold-Tooth” people,3 there is no
foe except in the one direction that adjoins
Qutluq Khwaja’s army. However, there are for-
midable mountains in between and the enemy
cannot enter. Nonetheless, some soldiers have
been stationed to guard that direction. 
The northeast adjoins laterally Qaidu’s and
Dua’s territory,4 and from their border to the
border of the Qa’an’s realm is a forty-day jour-
ney through the wilderness. Soldiers and
scouts are stationed along the borders on both
sides to keep watch. [913] Occasionally battles
erupt. This border of the Qa’an’s realm is a
one-month journey in extent, stretching east-
wards. Soldiers and scouts are necessary in
2“Apparently the Leichow Peninsula and Hainan Is-

1:242–44.
3For the meaning of Tibet, see note to text p. 120. For

4Qaidu’s and Dua’s territory (the Imil River and

way it is couched means that the northeast corner of
Cathay abuts Qaidu’s and Dua’s territory laterally from
the east.

The history of Sayyid Ajall Bukhari’s son,
who was the Qa’an’s vizier, and of his
grandson, Bayan Pingzhang.
Sayyid Ajall Bukhari was Qubilai Qa’an’s
vizier after Yalavach,4 and the Qa’an entrusted
the province of Qarajang to him. When Qubilai
Qa’an went to that province at Möngkä
Qa’an’s order and his army was hungry and

that Qubilai Qa’an undertook to serve as his

rewarded him greatly. When it was Qubilai
Qa’an’s turn to rule, he rewarded him with the

jang. He served as vizier for twenty-five years,

death,
which
is
a
truly
rare

Nasiruddin remained as governor in Qarajang
and came to make a presentation to the Qa’an.
He died sometime within the last five years
and was buried in his garden in Khanbaligh.
Prior to that, Nasiruddin[’s son] Abubakr, who
is now known as Bayan Pingzhang, was sent to
Zayton as governor.
When
Sayyid Ajall
died, Amir Ahmad
Fanakati became the Qa’an’s vizier with dis-
cretionary powers. During the time that Chabui
Khatun was still in her father’s house Amir Ah-
mad was on intimate terms with them, and
when she became the Qa’an’s wife he became
an attendant in her ordu, acquired influence,
and became the chief of all the amirs with
power over the entire realm. The officers of
Cathay grew jealous of him. Jimgim in particu-
