he hit him on the head with a bow and cut his
face. When he came before the Qa’an, the
Qa’an asked, “What has happened to you?”
“A horse kicked me,” he replied.
Jimgim was present. He was offended and
said, “Are you too ashamed to say that Jimgim
struck you?” And in the very presence of the
Qa’an he struck him many times with his fist.
Ahmad was constantly in fear of him.
During the summer of that year, when the
Qa’an was about to go from Daidu to his sum-
mer residence, he stationed Ahmad and an offi-
cer named Tärkän of the Qipchaq tribe as
heads of the divan and treasuries to guard the
qarshi. The amirs of Cathay who were present
and
in
attendance
conspired,
bearing
old
grudges and hatreds, to assassinate him. [916]
The history of Amir Ahmad Fanakati, who
was the Qa’an’s vizier, and how he is killed
by Gau Pingzhang; Manzi is conquered by
Gau Pingzhang.
During Qubilai Qa’an’s time Amir Ahmad
Fanakati Pingzhang was the Qa’an’s vizier. A
Cathaian named Gau Pingzhang was also viz-
ier. Since Amir Ahmad had total authority, they
called him shu pingzhang, meaning “awake
vizier.” Shu is a title for great pingzhangs. Gau
Pingzhang had many followers, and he was
jealous of Amir Ahmad.
During the summer mentioned above, when
the Qa’an stationed him over the qarshi and di-
van of Khanbaligh and Daidu, Gau Pingzhang
hatched a plot with a group of Cathaians to as-
sassinate him. However, a slave, one of Amir
Ahmad’s retinue, got wind of it and informed
him. By night Amir Ahmad took forty select
horses from among the Qa’an’s personal geld-
ings that had been tied in the barley fields and
set out. The Cathaians learned of it and, when
it was day, got to a village five leagues away
called Shandai (the Tajiks call it Deh-i-Khula
and Sayyid Ajall’s yam). The Cathaians, hav-
ing traversed the way previously, did not allow
him to cross the bridge. Then he tried to get
across the river, but the Cathaians blocked his
way. During all this, Gau Pingzhang caught up
with them, grabbed Amir Ahmad’s halter, and
said, “The Qa’an has stationed us here to tend
to the affairs of the divan. Why are you going
without having consulted us?”
“The Qa’an has summoned me,” he replied,
“and I am going.”
Gau Pingzhang would not allow him to pro-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
443

ceed, and during this discussion four envoys
arrived from the Qa’an, headed for Khanba-
ligh. When Amir Ahmad saw them, he cried
out, “I’m going to the Qa’an, but they won’t let
me.”
“The Qa’an has sent us to summon Amir Ah-
mad,” the envoys said. [917]
“He has stationed us to deal with divan mat-
ters,” said Gau Pingzhang, “and we have busi-
ness with this man.”
The envoys insisted and obtained his release.
He proceeded and joined the Qa’an at his sum-
mer residence. He got a black platter, scattered
pearls on it, laid a knife on top, covered it with
red silk, and took it to the Qa’an.
“What is this?” asked the Qa’an. “And what
does it mean?”
“Before now, when I came to court,” he
replied, “my beard was black like this platter. It
became white like these pearls in service. Gau
Pingzhang wants to make my beard as red as
this silk with a knife.” In this manner he re-
ported the situation as it happened, and the en-
voys who had witnessed it confirmed what he
said.
The Qa’an ordered them to go arrest Gau
Pingzhang, but since he had realized that the
situation had been reported, he took flight to
Xiangyangfu, which is on the border of Manzi
on the banks of the Qara Mörän (Yellow Riv-
er), half on one side and half on the other.1 In
olden times half the taxes were paid to the em-
perors of Cathay, and the other half were paid
to the emperors of Manzi, for such was the
truce between them. When Cathay came under
Mongol control, the emperor of Manzi took
control of the whole of the city. On this side of
the town is a strong fortress, strong walls, and
a deep moat, and no matter how often the
1Xiangyangfu (襄陽府) is the modern Xiangfan in
Hubei on the Han, not the Huang (Yellow), River.
Mongols went against it, it couldn’t be con-
quered. When Gau Pingzhang went there, he
was an officer of influence and renown, and
the people were encouraged by his arrival and
relied on him. He became an amir of influence
there too.
The Qa’an ordered Bayan to go in pursuit of
him with a troop. Before that there had not
been any large Frankish catapults in Cathay,
but Talib, a catapult-maker from this land, had
gone to Baalbek and Damascus, and his sons
Abubakr, [918] Ibrahim, and Muhammad, and
his employees made seven large catapults and
set out to conquer the city. Gau Pingzhang sent
a spy to the commanders of the army to say, “I
have committed no crime. There was bad
blood between me and Amir Ahmad, and we
tried to have each other assassinated. Now I
have fled here in fear. If the Qa’an spares my
life, I will turn the city over to him. This city is
the key to Manzi, and when it is taken, all the
rest of the kingdom will fall.”
Gau Pingzhang’s messenger was sent to the
Qa’an to report the situation. The Qa’an re-
warded him and sent a writ of safe conduct and
a sword. He was encouraged by this. The army
then trained their catapults on the fortress and
destroyed the towers. Gau Pingzhang made a
hole from inside and got out. 
When the emperor of Manzi was apprised of
the destruction of the towers and Gau Ping-
zhang’s treachery, he abandoned the fortress
and went with many people to the other side of
the river. As Bayan took this side of the
fortress and was killing and plundering, [the
emperor] and the army escaped from the other
side, but he was unable to make a stand any-
where against the Qa’an’s army, and so all the
realm of Manzi capitulated and was conquered.
Gau Pingzhang joined the Qa’an’s army, and
when he came to the Qa’an’s court he was sin-
gled out for all sorts of rewards and was rein-
444
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

stated in his post of pingzhang as before. He
became a partner to Amir Ahmad.
Amir Ahmad held the post of vizier honor-
ably for nearly twenty-five years. After the
Gau Pingzhang episode, he served jointly with
him for nine more years, hating and despising
him as before. After nine more years Gau
Pingzhang tried once again to assassinate Amir
Ahmad. This came about as follows.
A certain Cathaian claimed holiness and
sanctity and made himself known in the ordus
for his asceticism and piety. One day he pre-
tended to be ill and sent several of his disciples
to the officers, saying, [919] “I shall die and
come back to life in forty days.” They came
and spoke [to the officers, who] sent a group to
investigate, and they found him lying in his
house as though dead, his sons weeping and
wailing. They imagined that he was really
dead. After forty days he came out and gave
out the news that he was alive. The Cathaians
gathered around him, and he was thriving
mightily.
Gau Pingzhang and the lords of Daidu came
to consult with him on how to deal with Amir
Ahmad. Since Amir Ahmad was highly cau-
tious and watchful and always had guards with
him, and it was not known where he slept, they
decided they would send two thousand men to
the valley four leagues out of Daidu known as
Chamchal, which they would hold. One thou-
sand men would spread the word that Jimgim
was coming. Amir Ahmad would go out to
greet him, and they would kill him. Gau Ping-
zhang sat in a palanquin. (It is the custom of
rulers there sometimes to sit in palanquins, and
at night they usually travel in them.) From the
valley heralds and messengers were sent con-
tinuously to say that Jimgim (of whom Ahmad
was afraid) was coming. All those he sent
ahead were killed. By night they proceeded
with torches and candles, as was the custom of
rulers, and when they were near the qarshi,
Amir Ahmad went out to offer a cup. They
took him down and killed him. Amir Tärkän,
his liege man, had exercised precaution and
sensed that something was amiss. Standing
afar with his liege men, he reached for an ar-
row and shot Gau Pingzhang dead in the palan-
quin. With this the Cathaians fled. Tärkän sat
in the qarshi. That night much killing and great
disturbance occurred. The Cathaians fled into
nooks and crannies. When it was reported to
the Qa’an, he ordered Amir Bolad Aqa and
Hantun Noyan to take troops and kill all the
Cathaians who had stirred up the trouble. [920]
He also ordered four thousand bars given for
the expenses of Amir Ahmad’s funeral, and he
sent grandees and officers to bury him in state.
Forty days later the Qa’an was looking for a
large stone to have mounted on his crown, but
it couldn’t be found. There were two mer-
chants there, and they came and said, “We
brought a large stone for the Qa’an and gave it
to Amir Ahmad.”
“He didn’t bring it to me,” the Qa’an said.
Then he sent out for a search to be made of
Amir Ahmad’s house, and it was found in the
possession of his wife, Enchü Khatun. She was
brought before the Qa’an, who was highly of-
fended by this action and asked the merchants,
“If a slave did such a treacherous thing, what
would his punishment be?”
“If he was still alive,” they replied, “he
would have to be killed. If he was dead, he
would have to be taken out of his grave and
dishonored so others would learn a lesson.”
The Cathaians had also said to Jimgim, “He
was your enemy. That’s why we killed him.”
Thus they had planted a hatred for him in the
Qa’an’s heart. He therefore ordered him taken
out of his grave, a rope bound to his feet, his
body hanged in the crossroads in the market-
place, and wagons driven over his head. Enchü
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
445

Khatun was also killed. The forty other wives
and four hundred concubines he had were par-
doned, but his property was forfeited to the
treasury. His sons Amir Hasan and Amir
Husayn were taken away and skinned alive.
His other children were spared.
After his death the vizierate was given to an
Uyghur named Sanga, who held sway over the
realm for five or six years. His story will be
given next. [921]
The story of Sanga the Uyghur, who was the
Qa’an’s vizier after Amir Ahmad, and how
he met his end.
During Sanga’s vizierate a group of Muslim
merchants came from Qori, Barqu, and Qirqiz
territory to the Qa’an’s court and presented as a
gift a white-legged falcon with a red beak and
a white eagle. The Qa’an rewarded them and
gave them food from his own table, but they
did not eat it. “Why don’t you eat?” he asked.
“Because this food is carrion to us,” they
replied. Offended, the Qa’an ordered that Mus-
lims and People of the Book should no longer
slaughter sheep [in their own fashion] but
should slit the breast and side as in the Mongol
manner. Anyone who did slaughter a sheep [in
the Muslim fashion] would be killed, and his
wife,
children,
and
property
would
be
confiscated.
Isa Tarsa Kalimachi, Ibn Ma‘ali, and Bun-
duq, who were the prime evil trouble-makers
of their time, used this edict as a means to ob-
tain a decree stating that they could execute
anyone who killed a sheep even in his own
house. With this pretext they seized much
property from people, and they duped slaves of
Muslims by saying, “If you inform on your
master, we will set you free.” In order to obtain
their own release they informed on their mas-
ters and accused them of the crime. Isa Kali-
machi and his accursed followers went so far
that for four years Muslims could not even
have their sons circumcised.
Our lord Burhanuddin Bukhari was a student
of the late Shaykhu’l-Islam Sayfuddin Bakhar-
zi, and he was a preacher in Khanbaligh. He
was falsely accused and sent to Manzi, where
he died. Conditions became so bad that most of
the
Muslim
grandees
[left
the
country].
Baha’uddin Qunduzi, Shadi Zhuchang, [922]
Umar Qirqizi, Nasiruddin Malik Kashghari,
Hindu Zhuchang, and other men of conse-
quence banded together and accepted to pay a
large sum to Sanga the vizier so that he would
report to the Qa’an as follows: “All the Muslim
merchants have departed, and no one is coming
from Muslim territories. The tamgha (customs)
is
bankrupt,
and
tansuqs
are
not
being
brought—all because for the last seven years
no one has been able to kill a sheep. If so com-
manded, let them slaughter them so that the
merchants will come and customs taxes may
be collected.” An edict was so promulgated. 
Again, since the Christians practiced great
fanaticism against the Muslims during the
Qa’an’s time, they hatched a plot and said,
“There is a verse in the Koran that says ‘Kill
all the polytheists.’ ” They reported this in such
a way that the Qa’an was offended and said,
“How do you know this?”
“A letter in this regard came from Abaqa
Khan,” they said. The Qa’an asked for the let-
ter and summoned the scholars. He asked the
chief of them, Baha’uddin Baha’i, “Is there
such a verse in your Koran or not?”
“There is,” he replied.
“Do you think the Koran is God’s word?” the
Qa’an asked.
“Yes,” he said.
“Since God has ordered you to kill the infi-
dels,” he said, “why don’t you do it?”
“The time has not yet come,” he answered,
“and we do not have the power.”
The Qa’an flared up in anger and said, “I at
446
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

least do have the power!” And he ordered him
executed.
Amir
Ahmad
the
vizier,
Qazi
Baha’uddin, who also held the rank of vizier,
and Amir Dashman managed to forestall the
order on the pretext that they would ask others.
They summoned Mawlana Hamiduddin Sabiq
Samarqandi, who was a cadi, and the Qa’an
asked him the same question.
“This verse exists,” he said.
“Why don’t you kill them?” asked the Qa’an.
“God has said, ‘Kill the polytheists.’ If the
Qa’an orders me to say who the polytheists
are, I will tell him.”
“Speak!” said the Qa’an.
“Since you write the name of the great god
on your edicts, you are not a polytheist. [923]
A polytheist is someone who does not recog-
nize God, ascribes a partner to Him, or denies
His existence.”
The Qa’an was highly pleased, and the
mawlana’s words took root in his heart. He
honored Mawlana Hamiduddin, and the others
obtained release through his words. 
In short, Sanga served as vizier for seven
years. One day by chance the Qa’an asked him
for a few pearls.
“I don’t have any,” he said.
There was at the Qa’an’s court a man from
Damghan named Mubarakshah, and he was in-
timate with the Qa’an, who believed every-
thing he said. He was just waiting for a chance
to attack Sanga. Immediately he said, “Sanga
has a load of pearls and jewels in his house.
I’ve seen them. Let the Qa’an keep him occu-
pied while I go bring them from his house.”
The Qa’an kept Sanga occupied near him,
and Mubarakshah brought a pair of chests from
Sanga’s house. When they were opened, they
were found to contain fine pearls and match-
less gems. The Qa’an showed them to Sanga
and said, “How is it that since you have such
pearls, you didn’t give me any when I asked
for a few?”
Ashamed, Sanga said, “The Tajik lords gave
them to me”—and this was the group of whom
each one had been appointed as governor of a
province.
“Why didn’t they bring me pearls and gems
too?” the Qa’an asked. “You bring me ugly
raw fabrics and take matchless jewels for
yourself.”
“They gave them,” said Sanga. “If the Qa’an
so orders, I’ll give them back.”
Since he had spoken so boldly and impolite-
ly, the Qa’an ordered him arrested. Filth was
stuffed in his mouth, and he was executed
along with Hindu and some of the Tajik offi-
cers who were there. Word was sent to have
the others, who were in Manzi, arrested. When
Baha’uddin
Qunduzi,
Malik
Nasiruddin
Kashghari, Umar Qirqizi, and Shadi Zhuchang
were brought, he ordered [924] that they be
killed too. “I asked Baha’uddin Qunduzi’s fa-
ther for him,” he said. He shouted at him,
struck him several times on the face, and had
him pinioned with a doshakha and thrown into
a dungeon. Of Nasiruddin he said, “I sum-
moned him from Kashgar. Give him back his
property.” When he was rewarded, since he
was a generous man with many admirers, no
sooner had he mounted than many people also
mounted to ride with him. Along the way he
came across Amir Gäräi Ba’urchi, who was so
old he had to travel in a palanquin. Malik
Nasiruddin did not see him because of the
great crowd and thus did not notice his greet-
ing. Amir Gäräi was offended, and Pahlavan
Malik of Badakhshan, who once came here,
said to him, “This is the Malik Nasiruddin they
were going to kill. No sooner was he released
than he got carried away by pride and conceit.
Now he has so many horsemen riding with him
and every year he sends more than a thousand
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
447

tangas to Qaidu’s army.”1 Gäräi was offended,
and when he reached the Qa’an’s court he ac-
cused him falsely. An edict was issued for him
to be brought back and executed.
Prince Ajiqi interceded on Umar Qirqizi’s
and Shadi Zhuchang’s behalf and got them par-
doned. The Qa’an also released Baha’uddin
and appointed Öljäi Chengxiang in Sanga’s
place.
The Qa’an’s great officers; the names of
their chief men and the function of each.
One of the Qa’an’s great officers was Bayan
Noyan of the Ba’arin tribe who was taken from
here and died eight months after the Qa’an. He
had sons and daughters.
Another is Hantun Chengxiang, [925] who
was seized along with Nomoghan and died one
year before the Qa’an.2
Another is Uchachar Noyan, who is still in
power at present and holds his post with Temür
Qa’an, as does Öljäi Chengxiang. Dashman is
also still influential and is in charge of
yarlighs, paizas, ortaqs, and persons who
come and go.
Tarkhan Chengxiang is more influential now
than he was before and serves in the divan.
Naliqu, Jirqalan, and Chirtaqu are three
brothers in charge of the qushchis (falconers)
and the bureaux of totqavuls (highway patrols)
and gätüsüns (state police).3 With all they com-
1The tanga was the main unit of Mongolian currency
and continued to be issued throughout the post-Mongol
period. It was taken to India with the Timurids and was
one of the main units of weight and currency in the
Mughal Empire. The word tanga has ultimately given
the modern Russian word for money, деньги. It has also
been resurrected recently as the unit of currency in
Kazakhstan, the тэнгэ, and in Uzbekistan as the танга.
See Doerfer, TMEN 2:587–92 §946.
2For the story of the seizure of Hantun and Nomo-
ghan, see text pp. 892ff. above.
3For totqavul see Doerfer, TMEN 1:251f. §124. For
mand they need only speak for someone to be
arrested. Naliqu died two years after the Qa’an.
Badam Noyan was the grand qushchi (fal-
coner) and brother of Su’unchaq Aqa. When he
died his son Lachin Pingzhang became the
chief officer of the bitigchis. He too died, and
at present his son Yäkä Pingzhang occupies his
position and is in charge of the bureau of yams
[post stations].
Gäräi Ba’urchi died after the Qa’an.
One of the great officers of the army was
Ambai, who was the commander-in-chief. He
still occupies that post at present. Muqbal
Pingzhang was the bökä’ül of the army, and he
still is. Hoqotai was the commander of four
gäzigs and still is. 
The commanders of the sükürchis (parasol
bearers) are Ismail, Muhammadshah, Akhtachi,
Mubarak, Turmish and his brother Yighmish.
Yighmish was brought up by Temür Qa’an,
and he records the Qa’an’s words, as is their
custom.
The Qa’an does battle with Nayan Noyan of
Taghachar Noyan’s offspring and the
princes who conspired with him; Jimgim is
made heir designate.
It is related that in Qaqai Yil corresponding
to 68[6],4 Nayan Noyan of Taghachar Noyan’s
offspring, a descendant of Otchi Noyan, [926]
rebelled along with some of the sons of
Yesünggä Aqa and other princes, who became
alienated from the Qa’an and set out to join
Qaidu and Dua. The Qa’an’s army went out in
pursuit and did battle, but they overwhelmed
the army. When the news was brought to court,
although
the
Qa’an
was
suffering
from
rheumatism and was old and weak, he set out
gätüsün see ibid. 1:488f. §353.
4The Year of the Pig was 1287, which was 686 of the
Hegira. The missing sitta wa- should be restored to the
text.
448
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

in a palanquin on the back of an elephant. The
Qa’an’s army was almost defeated, but the ele-
phant with the palanquin was driven up a hill
and the battle drums were sounded. Nayan
Noyan and the princes fled with their troops,
and the Qa’an’s army went out in pursuit. They
were taken captive by their very own soldiers
and brought before the Qa’an for execution.
Their troops were divided and dispersed. After
that, the Qa’an could not move very much be-
cause of the gout, and the troops resided on
Dua’s and Qaidu’s borders.
In previous years, before Nomoghan was
seized by Qaidu’s troops, there had been talk
of Nomoghan’s becoming the heir designate,
and that is what the Qa’an had in mind. After
that, when he saw how intelligent and compe-
tent Jimgim was, he loved him exceedingly,
and when Tödä Möngkä sent Nomoghan back,
the Qa’an said that Jimgim should be elevated
as emperor. This was hard for Nomoghan to
take, and he said, “When he becomes qa’an,
what will they call you?” The Qa’an, offended,
reprimanded him, drove him away, and said,
“Let
him
not
come
before
me
again.”
Nomoghan died not long thereafter. The Qa’an
elevated Jimgim to the rule, and he was emper-
or for three years. He too died, and they sealed
his throne. His wife, Kökächin by name, was
extremely intelligent, and the Qa’an was on
very good terms with her. She had the ultimate
say-so.
Toward the end of the Qa’an’s reign there
was a rebellion in a Manzi province called
Lung-hsing on the coast below the province of
Sayan Fu. [927] To deal with it he sent [the
Mongol commanders Yighmish and Tarkhan,
the Cathaian commander Suching], and the
Tajiks Ghulam Samjing and Sayyid Ajall’s
brother Umar Yuching with troops. They
crushed them and plundered. 
On the front with Qaidu and Dua, the qar-
avuls (scouts) were constantly skirmishing, but
there was no major battle. At the end of the
Qa’an’s reign Dua mounted an expedition and
came to the border and shibä,1 where Chübäi
was watching the frontier with twelve thousand
men. Dua wanted to make a surprise attack on
him, but he got wind of it and attacked Dua’s
vanguard by night, killing three or four thou-
sand men. Informed during the night, Dua had
all his troops mount, and they clashed at dawn.
Many were killed on both sides. Chübäi had
mounted in great haste without informing Ajiqi
or Ananda, and consequently he was unable to
offer a resistance and had to flee. When Ajiqi
was informed, he sent word to Ananda to
mount. By the time they had gathered their
troops and mounted, however, Dua had already
withdrawn and so the troops were unable to
catch him. This situation was one reason for
Dua’s boldness against the Qa’an’s troops.
When the Qa’an was apprised, he blamed Ajiqi
1This word is read by Boyle as sübä, a Mongolian
word meaning eye of a needle or narrow passage. Doer-
fer (TMEN 1:349–51 §227) sees the word as sibä,
which, in all its variants (sibä ~ shibä ~ sübä) and mis-
spellings (legion), means wall, barricade, palisade, and
the like. It is without doubt the same as the shibä that
occurs on text p. 954 below, where, as here, it seems to
mean barrier in the sense of a frontier border. Blochet
(JTBl 536, note l) defines the word correctly without of-
fering a reading: “il signifie une portion de la frontière
de l’empire chinois gardée par un cordon de troupes ré-
parties tout le long de cette ligne.” There is also a dis-
tinct possibility that it is what is meant by the obscure
phrase manglai SWYH found some two hundred fifty years
later in Mirza Haydar Dughlat’s Tarikh-i-Rashidi (text p.
9, trs. p. 7) when he speaks of the area Chaghatai gave to
Ortu Börä, i.e. manglai sübä ‘front barrier,’ or some
such. True, this does not accord with the definition he
gives (āftābrō, ‘facing the sun’), but the original sense
may have been lost by his time. The area of which he
speaks is exactly the territory between Qara Khocho
(near Turfan) in Uyghuristan and Tibet where Chübäi
and Ajiqi were stationed (see text p. 913 above).
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
449

and had him beaten nine blows. Later, however
he restored him to favor and sent him back at
the head of the troops, where he remains in
command of the border until today. Qaban,
Chübäi’s elder brother, had died some time be-
fore this battle.
It is well known that the realm of Turkistan
was first devastated by Alghu, then by Qaban,
Chübäi, Baraq, and Qonchi’s son Nayan, who
were princes of the Right Wing who were ini-
tially with Qaidu but later submitted to the
Qa’an. [928]
The history of Sayyid Ajall, the Qa’an’s
vizier who was entitled Bayan Pingzhang.
One of the grandsons of the late Sayyid Ajall
was named Abubakr. The Qa’an entitled him
Bayan Pingzhang, made him a liege man to
Öljäi, and assigned him as pingzhang, i.e. di-
van chief. He was vizier for two years in Qubi-
lai Qa’an’s time, and during that period ayqaqs
(informants)
against
him
arose
from
the
Qa’an’s divans and reported that he had lost
6,000,000 bars. The Qa’an questioned him, and
he replied, “I left this money with the subjects
because there had been three disastrous years.
There was no crop, and the subjects were
impoverished. Now, if the Qa’an so orders, I
will sell their wives and children and transfer
the money to the treasury. However, the realm
will be destroyed.”
The Qa’an was pleased by his compassion
for the subjects and said, “All the high-ranking
officers worry about themselves, but Bayan
Pingzhang worries about the kingdom and the
subjects.” He rewarded him highly and garbed
him in jewel-studded robe with a belt, and then
he turned over all administrative affairs to him.
Around the same time Kökächin Khatun,
Temür
Qa’an’s
mother,
summoned
Bayan
Pingzhang and said, “Now that you have been
rewarded so well, and the Qa’an has turned
over the administration to you, go ask him
what he intends to do about Jimgim’s throne,
which has been sealed for nine years now.” (At
that time Temür Qa’an had gone on an expedi-
tion against Qaidu and Dua.) Bayan Pingzhang
repeated the question, and the Qa’an was so
overjoyed that he got up from his sick bed,
summoned the officers, and said, “You have
been saying this sarta’ul (Persian) is a bad
man. It was he who was compassionate enough
to report the subjects’ plight, and now he
speaks of the emperor’s throne and is con-
cerned for my children lest quarrel and [929]
dispute break out after me.” 
Once again he rewarded Bayan Pingzhang
and gave him his grandfather’s grand title of
Sayyid Ajall. He honored him and his seven
brothers who were present with yarlighs and
paizas and said, “Mount this very instant and
bring back my grandson Temür, who is riding
with the army against Qaidu, and seat him on
his father’s throne as qa’an. Hold banquets for
three days and make him monarch. After that,
let him mount and ride with the army.”
Sayyid Ajall went as ordered, turned Temür
Qa’an back, and sat him on Jimgim’s throne in
K‘ai-p‘ing fu. Three days later he set off with
the army, and Sayyid Ajall returned to court.
Temür Qa’an loved wine inordinately—so
much so that the Qa’an often advised him
against it and tried to stop him, but it did no
good. Things got so bad that he had him beaten
three times and set guards over him to keep
watch so he wouldn’t drink. He had an atten-
dant scholar named Razi from Bukhara, who
claimed to have a knowledge of alchemy and
talismans. Through trickery and sleight-of-
hand he had wormed his way into Temür’s
heart, and he often used to drink wine in secret
with Temür. The Qa’an was very angry with
him for this, and no matter how hard they tried
to keep him away from Temür, it couldn’t be
done because he was a sociable man and a
450
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

good conversationalist. Since the guards and
watchmen stood in the way of Temür’s drink-
ing, on Razi’s instruction they would go into
the bath and tell the attendant secretly to pour
wine instead of water into the channel so that it
would go through a pipe into the pool and they
could drink it. The guards found out about it
and reported it to the Qa’an, who ordered Razi
kept away by force. Then he sent him on some
pretext to Shingi, and he was killed in secret
along the way. [930]
Now that Temür has become qa’an he has
voluntarily given up wine and drinks little and
rarely. God removed the love of wine from his
heart when he attained great fortune, for other-
wise Qubilai Qa’an was never able to stop it
either by insistence or by force.
Although he is young, only twenty-five years
old, he suffers constant pain from the gout. He
used to ride in a palanquin atop an elephant,
but at present he rarely does it on account of
the superstitiousness of the people.
The bakhshis who were and are in
attendance upon the Qa’an, and a mention
of their influence.
At the end of Qubilai Qa’an’s reign there
were two Tibetan bakhshis, one named Tanba
and the other Kanpa.1 Tanba Bakhshi’s two
front teeth were so long that he could not put
his lips together. They resided in the Qa’an’s
private temple, which the Nankiyas call Dai
Miau, and they were related to each other.
They had great influence over the Qa’an and
were grand bakhshis. Their lineage went back
1Tanba Bakhshi is the Tibetan grand lama whose name
the Chinese transcribe as Danba. See JTBl 543, note r.
The text’s “Kanpa” is probably the Tibetan m-khan-po
‘master, lama’; see JTBl 544, note b.
to the kings of Tibet. Although there were and
are many Cathaian and Indian bakhshis, the Ti-
betans have more influence.
There is another bakhshi, a Kashmiri called
Qarantas Bakhshi. He is also of importance.
Temür Qa’an still believes in them, and the
two Tibetan bakhshis are dominant and in con-
trol. They have made their servants who know
medicine attendants upon the Qa’an, and they
keep Temür Qa’an from eating and drinking
too much. When there is an occasion to make
him stop, they beat two sticks against them-
selves so that the sound of the sticks can be
heard, and Temür Qa’an is thus warned and de-
creases the amount he drinks. He attaches great
importance to what they say. One story of Tan-
ba Bakhshi’s influence will come in the next
section on Temür Qa’an, [931] God willing.
The death of Qubilai Qa’an.
In Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse that cor-
responds to 693 [1294], after ruling for thirty-
five years Qubilai Qa’an died at the age of
eighty-three,2 bequeathing the transitory world
to his grandson, the Qa’an of the age, the
renowned monarch, Temür Qa’an. May God
cause his urugh to enjoy many years of success
and fortune, especially the Shahanshah of Is-
lam, the most magnificent sultan, “master of
the necks of nations,” Ghiyasu’d-dunya wa’d-
din Öljäitü Sultan Muhammad—may God ex-
tend his reign forever. [932]
2Qubilai was born on September 23, 1215 (27 Jumada
I 612), ascended the throne on May 5, 1260 (22 Jumada
I 658), and died on February 18, 1294 (20 Rabi‘ I 693).
He would have been eighty years old by our calculation
but eighty-three calculating by the lunar years of the He-
gira. For the Western dates see Pelliot, Marco Polo
1:566.
A summary and short history of the emperors of Machin and the sultans, maliks, and

451

atabegs of Iran, Syria, Egypt, North Africa, &c. who were contemporaries of Qubilai Qa’an
from the beginning of Bechin Yil, the Year of the Monkey corresponding to 658 [1260],
through Morin Yil, the Year of the Horse corresponding to 693 [1294], as well as the
unusual events that occurred during this period.
History of the emperors of Machin.
Lizong [ruled for] forty-one years, twenty-
six [of which were] before, and fifteen [of
which were] after this period.1
Duzong [ruled for] ten years.2
After Duzong, “Shaozhu” became emperor
of that realm.3 When two years of his reign
had passed, Qubilai Qa’an’s troops took the
realm and pacified it entirely. [933]
History of the sultans.
In Anatolia was Sultan Izzuddin Kayka’us,
the son of the Sultan Ghiyasuddin Kaykhus-
raw. He was defeated by the Mongol army un-
der the command of Baiju Noyan at Kösä
Dagh. He ruled jointly with his brother, Sultan
Ruknuddin. Mu‘inuddin Parvana not only was
Ruknuddin’s administrator but raised him too.
A dispute arose between the [two brothers],
and Sultan Izzuddin ceded the rule to his
brother and went to the land of Nicaea. From
there he went before the Byzantine emperor in
Istanbul. When Bärkä’s troops arrived in Is-
tanbul, they took him before Bärkä, and he
was given the rule of the city of Crimea,
where he died. His brother Ruknuddin was
killed by the infidels in 664 [1265–66], and
his [brother Qilich Arslan’s] son Ghiyasuddin
Kaykhusraw succeeded to the rule. He was
killed in Erzinjan, and after him the sultanate
went to Kayka’us’ son Ghiyasuddin Mas‘ud,
who is presently sultan.4

2Duzong (度宗) of the Southern Song, r. 1265–1275.
3The Chinese shaozhu (少主) ‘young ruler’ represents
Gongdi (恭帝), r. 1275–1276.

and

was

Badruddin Lu’lu’.
In Egypt and Syria was Aybak the Tur-
coman. He gained dominion over Egypt. He
had several disputes with the lord of Aleppo
and Damascus, but in the end they made
peace. Quduz [934] rebelled against the Tur-
coman and killed him, and he gained control
over Egypt and Syria. After Hülägü Khan took
Aleppo and Damascus and withdrew, Quduz,
together with the commanders of Syria and
Egypt and the khans of Khwarazm who were
the remnants of Sultan Jalaluddin’s army, did
battle with Ket Buqa Noyan.5 Malik Nasir
Salahuddin Yusuf was the lord of Syria. When
he went to see Hülägü Khan he was executed
on the Mush plain, and when Quduz retired
from the battle with Ket Buqa Noyan, Bun-
duqdar killed him and usurped the kingship.
When Bunduqdar returned from Anatolia and
the battle with Toqu and Tödä’än, he died, and
Alfi became ruler. After Alfi, his son Ashraf
succeeded.6
In Kirman was Sultan Qutbuddin. When he
zuddin Kayka’us II, r. 1246–1248. Kayka’us II and
Ruknuddīn Qilich Arslan IV ruled jointly 1248–49.
Ghiyāsuddīn
Kaykhusraw
III
ruled
1265–82,
and
Ghiyāsuddīn Mas‘ūd II ruled 1282–84 and again 1284–

5At the Battle of ‘Ayn Jālūt, September 3, 1260.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

died he left two sons, Muzaffaruddin Hajjaj
and Jalaluddin Soyurghatmish. The title of
sultan went to Sultan Hajjaj, but the absolute
rule was in the hands of Tärkän Khatun. Since
Tärkän Khatun’s daughter Padishah Khatun
was married to Abaqa Khan, she used to come
to court every two or three years and return
laden with honors. Once she came here, and
when she was returning home, Sultan Hajjaj
went out to welcome her. Before they met he
grew anxious and went back to Kirman and
then set out for Hindustan, where he sought
refuge with Sultan Shamsuddin of Delhi. He
was there for nearly fifteen years, and then he
died. Tärkän Khatun was extremely just, and
administrative affairs in Kirman went smooth-
ly because of her fairness and equity. During
Sultan Ahmad’s reign she had came to the
ordu and died in the vicinity of Tabriz. Her
body was taken back to Kirman, [935] and the
rule was settled upon Jalaluddin Soyurghat-
mish. In truth, she was an extremely intelli-
gent and competent ruler. During Gaikhatu
Khan’s reign his wife Padishah Khatun went
to Kirman, arrested her brother Soyurghat-
mish, and imprisoned him in the fortress. He
escaped and came in disguise to Gaikhatu
Khan’s court to seek asylum. Gaikhatu sent
him to Padishah Khatun, and she kept him un-
der guard for a few days and then killed him.
When Baidu rebelled, Shah-i-Alam, Soyur-
ghatmish’s daughter and Baidu’s wife, sent an
envoy. Kürdü[n]chin, Prince Mänggü Temür’s
daughter who had been Soyurghatmish’s wife,
seized Padishah Khatun and was bringing her
to the ordu when she was killed in revenge
somewhere between Shiraz and Isfahan.1
1The Qarakhitai rulers of Kirman are as follows: Qut-
buddin ruled 1252–1258. Qutlugh Tärkän Khatun ruled
as regent 1258–1282. Sultan Ḥajjāj died in Delhi in
1272. Soyurghatmish ruled 1282–92 and was executed
in 1294. See Khwandamir, Habibu’s-siyar 3:269.
History of the maliks and atabegs.
In Fars was Atabeg Muzaffaruddin Abubakr.
He died in the year 658 [1260]. His son
Atabeg Sa‘d had gone to the Qa’an’s court and
was returning ill. He received the news of his
father’s death in Torqu, a dependency of Para-
han, but he died twelve days later. When the
news of his death was taken to Shiraz, his
twelve-year-old son Atabeg Muhammad [936]
was seated on the throne and called Sultan
Azududdin. His mother, Tärkän Khatun, the
daughter of Atabeg Qutbuddin Mahmudshah,
served as regent. The boy too died soon there-
after, and his mother became ruler. Muham-
madshah, Atabeg Abubakr’s nephew, had mar-
ried her daughter Salghum. He began a quarrel
with his mother-in-law, but in the end he was
killed. Tärkän Khatun married her youngest
daughter, Abish Khatun, to Prince Mänggü
Temür. In short, Tärkän Khatun became the
wife of Saljuqshah, but after a time he killed
her and imprisoned both her daughters in the
Saped fortress. This situation was reported to
the court, and Amir Altachu was sent with
troops to go with Tärkän Khatun’s brother
Ruknuddin Atabeg Ala’uddawla of Yazd and
the maliks of Shabankara and the Tajik troops
of the area to seize Saljuqshah. When the
troops reached Abarquh, six thousand Shirazi
horsemen came forth. Atabeg Ala’uddawla at-
tacked them with five hundred horsemen and
drove them back to Shiraz. Saljuqshah took
refuge in Kazarun. The army went there and
fought, taking the city and massacring and pil-
laging. Saljuqshah was taken out and killed,
and his head was sent to Shiraz. Atabeg
Ala’uddawla was wounded there, and he died
several days later. The girls were taken out of
the fortress, and their grandmother, Yaqut
Tärkän, the daughter of Qutluq Sultan Baraq
Hajib of Kirman, took them to the emperor’s
court. Abish Khatun was married to Prince
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
453

Mänggü Temür. The post of atabeg of Shiraz
was nominally hers. The other sister, Bibi Sal-
ghum, was married to Atabeg Yusufshah of
Yazd, who was her cousin on her mother’s
side.
Abish
Khatun
died
during
Arghun
Khan’s reign, and her body was taken to Shi-
raz [937] and buried in the Azudiyya Madrasa,
which her mother had built and named for the
above-mentioned Atabeg Azududdin Muham-
mad. Princess Kürdü[n]chin was her heir, and
although for several years now the function of
the malik of Shiraz has been performed by or-
taqs and merchants, the nawbat is still per-
formed at the atabegs’ palace and the great di-
van is held there.
In Seistan, Malik Shamsuddin Muhammad
Kurt had, in accordance with a decree from
Möngkä Qa’an, put to death Malik Shamsud-
din of Seistan and become the ruler. After that,
Malik Nusratuddin, the nephew of the slain
malik, took an envoy from Hülägü Khan’s
court, recovered Seistan from Shamsuddin
Kurt, and took over the country. He is still
governor and malik there.
Unusual events that occurred during the
period.
In the year 659 [1261] Badruddin Lu’lu’
died in Mosul.
On the 17th of Rajab 664 [April 24, 1266]
Mu’ayyiduddawla Urzi, who was unique in
the mathematical sciences and a wise philoso-
pher, died.
At dawn on the 19th of Safar 669 [October
7, 1270] there was an earthquake in Nishapur
of
such
proportions
that
it
was
thought
unimaginable that any stone could remain atop
any other in the mountains or that there could
be a clod of earth on the plain not shattered to
smithereens. It lasted fifteen days and nights,
and the earth trembled every hour.
In the heart of winter in 661 [1262–63]
[938] a great earthquake occurred in Tabriz.
The earth moved from time to time for four
months.
On Monday the 17th of Dhu’l-Hijja 672
[June 24, 1274] Khwaja Nasîr[uddin Tusi]
died at sundown in Baghdad. The khwaja had
left instructions for his burial in the Musa-
Jawad shrine.1 At the foot of Musa’s tomb an
empty spot had been found—a grave had been
made and lined with tiles, and when it was in-
vestigated it was discovered that the Caliph al-
Nasir-li-dini’llah had had it excavated for his
own tomb, but his son Zahir had gone against
his father’s wishes and had buried him among
his ancestors in Rusafa. It is one of the
strangest coincidences that the very day the
subterranean chamber was finished was the
day of Khwaja Nasir’s birth, i.e. Saturday the
11th of Jumada i 597 [February 17, 1201]. He
lived seventy-five years, seven months, and
seven days.
On the 25th of Dhu’l-Hijja 673 [June 21,
1275] Arghun Aqa died in the Radkan mead-
ow in Tus. [939]
1The Kāẓimayn Shrine in the Kāẓimiyya section of
Baghdad, where the Seventh Imam, Mūsā Kāẓim, and
the Ninth Imam, Muḩammad Jawād, are buried.

On the wives and children of Ariq Bökä,
after whose death the Qa’an divided his
ordus among his sons.
After the fires of sedition died down, when
Ariq Bökä went to his brother Qubilai Qa’an
and apologized, he took all the wives he had
and stationed his four sons, Yobuqur, Malik
Temür, Naira’u Buqa, and Tammachi, in his
yurt. His summer pasture was in Ilyastu [the
Altai], and his winter quarters were in Uri-
angqat and Qirqiz [territory], a three-day jour-
ney in between. Sorqaghtani Beki was there. 
Ariq Bökä was with the Qa’an for one
month and six days, and after that he died.
They took his body to Buda Ündür, where the
great sanctuary of Genghis Khan was, near the
Selenga River. Sorqaghtani Beki and the other
princes are also buried there, with the excep-
tion of Qubilai Qa’an. [940]
One of Ariq Bökä’s wives was Elchiqmish
of the Oyirat tribe. The second was Qutuqta
Khatun of the Güchügür clan of the Naiman;
by her he had two daughters. The elder was
Chaluqan Aqa, who was married to Nayanqa
Gürägän of the Baya’ut. Chaluqan’s daughter
is married to Malik Temür. Her name is
Negüdär,1 and she resides in Sorqaghtani
Beki’s
yurt
and
dwelling
place. Another
daughter by her is named Qamtai, and she has
not been married yet. The other daughter [by
Qutuqta] was Nomoghan. She was married to
Chupan Gürägän of the Oyirat.
The third wife was Qutlu Khatun of the
Qunqirat. She also resides in Sorqaghtani
Beki’s yurt and has no children.

He had a concubine named Iraghui of the
Barulas clan, the sister of the Qada’an who

He had another concubine who is still alive.
Her name is Eshitäi of the Qunqirat tribe.2 She
was in Qutuqta Khatun’s ordu. By her he had

When Ariq Bökä died, his wives went to
their yurt. Three years later the Qa’an ordered
Ariq Bökä’s sons to come see him. When they

Chalun Khatun of the Qaranut, which is a

Khan. [941]
There was also one of Tolui Khan’s wives

there of Hülägü Khan’s, they said, “Why

Malik Temür has another wife named Törä,

jasa’ul. By her he has two sons, [942] Oyi-

The
other

Malik
Temür’s
sons
are
four:
Mangqan, Ajiqi, Yesün To’a, and Baritai, all

Qubilai Qa’an gave the ordu of Elchiqmish
Khatun of the Oyirat, Ariq Bökä’s senior wife,
to Ariq Bökä’s son Naira’u Buqa. She tried to

Afterward, when he went to the Qa’an, the
yurt was left in Malik Temür’s hands, and now

Tammachi was given Qutuqta Khatun’s yurt,
but before they could come together Qutuqta
died. In her place he married Er Tegin, the
daughter of Sorqadu Ba’urchi of the Naiman,
the nephew of the Sartaq and Burunduq who
live here. When he took that wife to the
Qa’an’s court, the yurt remained vacant.
Nairaqu
Buqa
has
five
sons:
Qurbaqa,
Bachin, Samskar, Bayan Äbügän, and Ara
Temür. Ara Temür’s mother is Öchin Egächi
of the Olqunu’ut tribe. The other four sons’
mother is Ashightai Khatun of the Qunqirat,
the niece of Chabui Khatun, Qubilai Qa’an’s
chief wife.
Tammachi has two sons, Bayan and Dörbän.

Malik Temür’s officers.

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TEN: QUBILAI QA’AN
457

❦ SECTION ELEVEN
THE HISTORY OF TEMÜR QA’AN, SON OF JIMGIM, SON OF QUBILAI QA’AN, SON
OF TOLUI KHAN, SON OF GENGHIS KHAN, IN THREE PARTS
Part One is on his blessed lineage and a de-
tailed account of his wives and the branches of
his sons down to the present; a picture of him,
and a genealogical chart of his sons.
Part Two includes events leading to his en-
thronement, a picture of him and his wives,
princes, and amirs during his enthronement;
stories of his events that have occurred from
the beginning of his imperial reign down to the
present; some of his battles and conquests that
are known.
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections and
were culled from various books and persons.
[946]
Part One, on his blessed lineage and a
detailed account of his wives and the
branches of his sons down to the present; a
picture of him, and a genealogical chart of
his sons.
Temür Qa’an,1 who is also called Öljäitü
Qa’an—may the shadow of his justice and eq-
uity lie forever over the heads of all peoples—
is the son of Jimgim, the son of Qubilai Qa’an,
the son of Tolui Khan, the son of Genghis
Khan. He was born of Jimgim’s chief wife,
Kökächin Khatun, in Hükär Yil, the Year of the
Ox corresponding to 663 [1265]. There are
many wives and concubines in his ordus, but
1Temür is known as 鐵木耳Tiemuer in Chinese
sources. ␀His dynastic title is 成宗 Cheng Zong.
because of the distance and closure of the
roads not all their names have been ascer-
tained. His chief wife is called Buluqan
Khatun, of Baya’ut “bone.” By her he has one
son named Tishi Taishi.2 By another wife he
has another son named Maqabalin. A genealog-
ical chart of his sons and grandsons is as fol-
lows. [947]
Part Two, events leading to his
enthronement, a picture of him and his
wives, princes, and amirs during his
enthronement; stories of his events that
have occurred from the beginning of his
imperial reign down to the present; some of
his battles and conquests that are known.
Prior to his accession to the throne.
The very day Qubilai Qa’an died in Morin
Yil, the Year of the Horse corresponding to 693
[1294], his son Jimgim’s chief wife, the mother
of Temür Qa’an, sent, with the agreement of
the officers, Bayan after Temür to inform him
of the Qa’an’s death and bring him back to sit
on the imperial throne. During the year it took
Temür Qa’an to get there, Kökächin Khatun
administered the affairs of the realm.
2Readingﯽ ــ ـﺗﻴﺸ(Tishi) for JTK’s]ﳽ. See Hambis, Yuan
che, p. 136.

When he finally arrived under good auspices,
a great quriltai was held. Present were the fol-
lowing: his uncles Kököchü and Toghan; his
brother Kammala and [his son] Yesün Temür;
his cousin Ananda Oghul son of Mangqala;
[his uncle] Oghruqchi’s sons Temür Buqa and
Ejil Buqa; great amirs like Bayan Chengxiang,
Uchachar Noyan, Toqtaq, Ölüg, Öljäi Cheng-
xiang,
Altun
Chengxiang,
Dashman
Aqa,
Jirqalan, Nalighu, Ambai of Tangqut, Babusha
of Yesünggä’s urugh,1 Qutuqu Chengxiang of
the Tatar nation, and Arqasun Tarkhan [948]
Chengxiang of Badai’s urugh; and princesses
like Nambui Khatun and her daughter Begchin
Khatun, Manzitai, Kökächin Khatun, Buluqan
Khatun,
and
other
princes,
officers,
and
princesses it would take too long to mention.
There was a dispute for the throne between
Temür and his brother Kammala, who was old-
er, and words were exchanged. Kökächin
Khatun, who is extremely intelligent, said to
them, “Chechän Qa’an (i.e. Qubilai Qa’an)
said that whoever knows the biligs [maxims]
of Genghis Khan better should occupy the
throne. Each of you now pronounce his biligs
so that the elders who are present may see
which of you knows it better.”
Since Temür Qa’an is very eloquent and
masterful, he pronounced the biligs well with a
nice ayalghu [intonation]. Kammala, on the
other hand, has a slight stutter and is not so
perfectly endowed in this regard, so he did less
well. All unanimously shouted, “Temür Qa’an
knows the biligs better and pronounces them
better. He is worthy of the crown and throne.”
In the city of Kaipingfu in the [Qonin] Yil that
corresponds to 694 [1295], he was seated upon
the imperial throne under good auspices as
1This “Babusha” is mentioned in the Yüan shih as Ba-

they performed the rites and rituals that are

The Qa’an’s arrangements for the
administration of the empire.
When they were finished banqueting and cel-
ebrating, and when the rites of congratulation
were over, the Qa’an turned his attention to the
administration of the army and realm, appoint-
ing princes and officers to the provinces and
assigning viziers and divan chiefs.
He gave his elder brother Kammala a large
share of the wealth inherited from their father
and sent him to Qaraqorum, where Genghis
Khan’s yurts and ordus are still, and put the
troops in that area under his command. He
guards and protects the areas of Qaraqorum,
Chinas, Shina’uchi, the Onon, the Kerulen, the
Kämkämji’üt, the Selenga, and Qayaliq as far
as Qirqiz territory and Genghis Khan’s great
ghoruq. The four great ordus and another five,
making nine in all, are there. Not everyone is
allowed access since it is the great ghoruq.
They have made images of them and constant-
ly burn incense and aromatics. Kammala has
also made a temple for himself there.
He sent Prince Ananda at the head of his
army and ulus to Tangqut territory.
Prince Kököchü and Görgüz, the Qa’an’s
son-in-law, were sent to Qaidu’s and Dua’s
frontier.
Toghan and an army were dispatched to
Manzi to protect that area.
Amir Ajiqi was sent with an army to Qara
Khocho. 
He kept Bayan Pingzhang as divan chief.
The title Sayyid Ajall carries great weight with
the Tajiks, and when the Mongols also saw that
the chief vizier was called by that title, [950] it
became the loftiest title for them. The Qa’an
thus gave Bayan Pingzhang the title of Sayyid
2Illustration lacking.

459

Ajall as an acknowledgement of his impor-
tance and power. At present he is an extremely
grand and powerful vizier. The functions of the
great divan are carried out in collaboration
with Öljäi Tarkhan, Yäkä Pingzhangg, Toba,
Abdullah Pingzhang, Amir Khwaja Sami, Qut-
buddin Samjing, and Mas‘ud Lanjun, and they
administer the realm.
The history of Prince Ananda (son of
Mangqala, son of Qubilai Qa’an), who is
ruler in the province of Tangqut and has
become a Muslim; a mention of some of the
features of that province, and a report on
his realm.
Prince Ananda is the son of Mangqala, Qubi-
lai Qa’an’s third son, and elder brother to
Nomoghan, whom the princes who were ac-
companying him on an expedition to deal with
Qaidu rebelled against, seized, and sent to the
Ulus Jochi. Then, when Tödä Möngkä became
ruler of that ulus, he apologized and sent him
back to Qubilai Qa’an. He died not long there-
after. Temür Qa’an awarded to Ananda the
troops Qubilai Qa’an had given to Mangqala
and the province of Tangqut, which had also
belonged to [Mangqala]
Tangqut is a large country in length and
breadth. In the Cathaian language it is called
Hexi, meaning large river of the west.1 It has
been so named by them because it lies on the
western side of Cathay. The large cities there
that are the capitals of their rulers are as fol-
lows: Jingzhaofu, Ganzhou, Eriqai, Khalajan,
[951] and Aqbaligh.2 In that country are twen-
1The Chinese 河西Hexi, ‘river of the west,’ for Tanq-
gut is well attested. From Hexi is derived the Mongolian
Qashi(n). See Pelliot, Marco Polo 1:315.
2The Persian “Kenjānfū,” Marco Polo’s “Quengianfu,”
is Jingzhaofu (京兆府), the modern Sian (Xi’an) in
Shaanxi. Ganzhou (甘州) is the modern Zhangye in
Gansu. Eriqai is the city of Erighaya (寧夏Ningxia),
Marco Polo’s “Egrigaia”; see text p. 135 above. The
ty-four large cities. Most of the people there
are Muslims, but the cultivators and peasants
are idolators, and they resemble Cathaians in
form. Previously they used to pay tribute to the
rulers of Cathay and gave their cities Cathaian
names. Their manners, customs, ordinances,
and habits are similar to each other’s.
Since Nomoghan left no son, Ananda was
turned over to a Muslim from Turkistan named
Mihtar Hasan Aqtachi to be brought up. That
man’s wife was named Zulaykha, and she
nursed him. That is why Muslimism took firm
root in his heart. He learned the Koran and
writes the Tajik script very well. His time is
spent mostly in acts of devotion. He has con-
verted to Islam nearly a hundred fifty thousand
Mongol soldiers who are attached to him. Sar-
taq, one of his amirs who was opposed to Is-
lam, went to the Qa’an’s court and complained
that Ananda was always in the mosque, pray-
ing, fasting, and reciting the Koran, and that he
had circumcised most of the Mongol boys and
converted most of the military to Islam. The
Qa’an was highly offended by this and sent
Jirghalang and Chirtaqu, two brothers who
were in charge of the falconers, to forbid him
to worship, to prevent the Muslims who were
with him from having access to him, and to en-
courage him to bow down before idols and
burn incense in the temples. Rejecting their
message, Ananda refused to listen and said,
“Idols are made by humans. How can I bow
down to such a thing? The sun, which is a cre-
ation of the great God, the soul of the corporeal
world and the sustainer of life and animal and
plant growth—even to that I do not consider it
“Khalajān” of Persian texts is Marco Polo’s “Calacian,”
i.e. Zhongxingfu, which later became Ningxia. This
Aqbaligh is Marco Polo’s “Acbalec Mangi,” i.e. the
Aqbaligh of Manzi, which is Hanzhong (漢中), to be
distinguished from the Aqbaligh of Cathay, which is
Zhendingfu (眞定府) (Pelliot, Marco Polo 1:7).
460
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

licit to bow down. How could I bow before a
graven image made by a human? I bow down
to the one who created me and the Qa’an.”
[952]
The Qa’an was highly enraged by this speech
and ordered Ananda imprisoned, but he contin-
ued firm in his faith and belief and kept saying,
“Our fathers were monotheists. They consid-
ered God to be one and worshipped Him. It
was due to that good belief that the eternal God
rewarded them with the entire face of the earth
and made them leaders and rulers of human be-
ings that became exalted and noble. They nev-
er bowed before an idol.”
The Qa’an summoned him and asked, “If
you had a dream or an inspiration or were
shown something or someone led you to be a
Muslim, tell me so that he can guide me too.”
“The great God guided me to knowledge of
Him,” said Ananda.
“That way was shown to you by a demon,”
said the Qa’an.
“If a demon guided me,” he said, “who guid-
ed Ghazan Khan, my elder brother?”
The Qa’an fell silent and thought for a mo-
ment. Kökächin Khatun advised him, saying,
“You have been on the throne for two years,
and your kingdom has not yet been consolidat-
ed. Ananda has many troops, and all those sol-
diers and people of the province of Tangqut are
Muslims and opposed to this state of affairs.
They are also close to enemy territory. Let
them not be alienated. It is not wise to make
him recant. He knows best about his religion
and community.”
The Qa’an realized that her advice was given
in compassion. He released Ananda, gave him
much consolation, won him over, and showed
him honor, and then he sent him back to head
the army and rule Tangqut and awarded him
the kingdom of Tangqut.
Although Ananda had believed in and prac-
ticed Islam from childhood, he went to great
extremes when he heard that the Padishah of
Islam—may God extend his kingship forev-
er—had truly become a Muslim, a monotheist,
and a man of pure religion, that he had con-
verted all the Mongols in this land to Islam,
and smashed all the idols and destroyed all the
temples. Like him, Ananda too strove to propa-
gate the religion of Islam. From the situation of
Ananda and his soldiers one can estimate [953]
how Islamism in those provinces will soon
reach perfection and—as God says, Thou shalt
see the people enter into the religion of God by
troops1—they will enter in droves and become
believers, monotheists, Muslims, and of pure
religion. 
The sons and grandsons of the Mihtar Hasan
mentioned above, Hindu, Dawlatshah, Hamid,
Jamal Aqa, and Muhammad Aqtachi, are all
greatly influential and powerful. Some of them
are in the confidence of Temür Qa’an’s mother,
and they strive to propagate the religion of
Islam. 
Sometime during the last several years Anan-
da went to the Qa’an’s court for a quriltai. The
Qa’an honored him greatly, and he made a
great show of being a Muslim. When the
Qa’an heard of the Padishah of Islam’s conver-
sion—may God extend his kingship forever—
he approved and said, “Ananda has become a
follower of Ghazan in being a Muslim. Let him
practice his religion however he wants, for I
have thought about it and see that Islam is a
good way and religion.” On that account Anan-
da made great efforts to spread Islam. Once
again he returned to the head of Tangqut
province and his troops, and he commands
them overall. Despite the fact that the Qa’an’s
deputies
and
bitigchis
officiate
over
the
tamghas [customs imposts], most of the rev-
1Kor. 110:2.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION ELEVEN: TEMÜR QA’AN
461

enue raised there is spent on his troops and lit-
tle gets to the divan. At present Sartaq, who
was so opposed to Islam and informed on
Ananda, has also become a Muslim.
One of his great commanders is ___. Another
is Mängli, who is also a Muslim.
Ananda is thirty years old at present. His
complexion is wheaten, and he has a black
beard. He is tall and full-bodied. He has a son
named Örüg Temür, and he sits in power and
might on the ruling throne over his ulus. He
has built houses of worship and mosques in his
ordus and yurts and is constantly engaged in
reciting the Koran and acts of devotion.
Four years after Temür Qa’an’s auspicious
enthronement, Baraq’s son Dua set out to at-
tack [954] the princes and officers mentioned
above who were manning Temür Qa’an’s fron-
tier. As is the custom of the military, there is a
qaravul resident on every shibä.1 From Ajiqi’s
and Chübäi’s shibä, which is in the extreme
west, to Muqali’s shibä, which is in the east,
yams [post stations] have been established and
heralds are available. At that time they sent
word to each other that an army had been spot-
ted. By chance, Princes Kököchü, Jungqur, and
Nankiyadai2 had assembled for a banquet and
were enjoying conviviality and wine. Word
arrived by night, and they were too dead drunk
to mount. Temür Qa’an’s son-in-law Görgüz
Gürägän did get to horse with his troop, and
the enemy arrived immediately. Since they had
not assessed the situation, and some of the
troops of the Right and Left Wings were un-
aware and far away, they were unable to join.
Baraq’s son Dua and his troops fell upon
Görgüz, who had no more than six thousand
men and could not offer resistance to Dua. He
was routed and headed for a mountain, with
1See note to text p. 927 above.
2See above, text p. 913.
the foe hot on his trail. They caught him and
were about to kill him when he said, “I am
Görgüz, the Qa’an’s son-in-law.” Dua’s com-
mander-in-chief ordered that he not be killed
but held. The routed troops went before the
Qa’an. Kököchü, the Qa’an’s uncle, was afraid
because he had not reached the troops through
negligence, and so he stopped and hid in an
out-of-the-way place. He was summoned sev-
eral times, but he didn’t appear. Finally the
Qa’an sent Prince Ajiqi to mollify him and
bring him to court. When the routed troops
reached the Qa’an’s court he was offended by
the officers’ actions and had Jungqur and
Nankiyadai
seized
and
imprisoned.
“How
could you be so negligent and allow such a
waste of time?” he asked them.
The princes Yobuqur and Ulus Buqa and
[955] Amir Dordaqa had fled and gone over to
Qaidu during Qubilai Qa’an’s reign, and Qaidu
had sent them to Dua. At this time they con-
spired to desert Dua and go over to Temür
Qa’an’s side with twelve thousand soldiers.
When the Qa’an heard that they were coming,
he put no trust in them because Dordaqa had
already
come
back
once
during
Qubilai
Qa’an’s time and taken the above-mentioned
princes away. Therefore he sent Chirtaqu,
Mubarakshah Damghani, and Satuq with Ajiqi
to bring them. Yobuqur and Dordaqa both
arrived, having left Ulus Buqa with their fami-
lies in Qaraqorum with the understanding that
he would follow along behind at a slower pace.
He had pillaged Qaraqorum and plundered the
market and storehouses. When he came before
the Qa’an he was accused of the crime and
asked, “How could you take such a hostile ac-
tion
against
the
resting-place
of
Genghis
Khan?” He was thrown into chains and impris-
oned. As a justification he said, “I came there
as a refugee, and Dua’s troops were on my
heels. They mingled in with us, and they did
462
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

the pillaging.” His excuse was not accepted. 
Tarmabala’s wife Taiki, with whose son
Khaishang the Qa’an was on extremely good
terms, interceded on behalf of Ulus Buqa, who
was Tarmabala’s cousin, and got him released,
but the Qa’an no longer trusted him and did
not send him on the campaign. “Let him be in
attendance upon the throne,” he said.
He treated Yobuqur well and said, “He com-
mitted no crime.”
He was, however, very angry with Amir Dor-
daqa and said, “Let him be executed, for he has
fled twice.”
Weeping, Amir Dordaqa said, “I fled in fear
of Qubilai Qa’an. The whole time I was there I
never fought with or attacked the Qa’an’s
troops. Since Temür has become qa’an, and
now that an opportunity has presented itself, I
have come on these princes’ advice, bringing
back more troops than I took with me, and in-
tending to fight on your behalf. If I am par-
doned, [956] I will take the soldiers I have
brought and others I also command, and go af-
ter Dua to make up for what I have done. Per-
haps I can get Görgüz back.” The amirs report-
ed these words and interceded on his behalf.
The Qa’an pardoned him and said to let him
go. He even sent a regular troop with him. 
However, he ordered Yobuqur [not] to go.
[Amir Dordaqa] interceded on his behalf, say-
ing, “We have come in order to fight. Let all
our retainers remain here, but let us go because
we know that land and the military. We are
obliged
to
make
amends
to
the
Qa’an.”
Yobuqur was also given honors and consola-
tion and set off with him.
Dua, complaisant after having attacked the
troop, was proceeding at a leisurely and slow
pace, intending to head for his own ordus and
to dispatch troops to the sübäs and frontiers of
Ananda, Ajiqi, and Chübäi, who were on the
frontier at Qara Khocho, to attack them, give
them a whipping, and send them packing. At
this point, when the soldiers were about to dis-
perse, on the banks of a large river they were
about to cross, Yobuqur, Ulus Buqa, and Dor-
daqa appeared from nowhere and attacked Dua
and his men. Many were killed, and many were
drowned. No matter how hard they tried, how-
ever, they could not get hold of Görgüz, but
they did seize Dua’s son-in-law named ___ and
returned victorious and triumphant to be re-
warded by the Qa’an. 
After that, the officers had an idea to release
Dua’s son-in-law in order that he might send
back the Qa’an’s son-in-law. Within a few days
envoys came from Dua and delivered a mes-
sage, saying, “We have perpetrated an act for
which we have been requited. Now we have
Görgüz, and you have our son-in-law.” Görgüz
also sent one of his servants with them with a
message, saying, “I am well, but I have no ser-
vants and am destitute. [957] Send me two or
three servants and some wherewithal.” Four of
his officers were sent with abundant money
and food along with Dua’s son-in-law. By the
time they got there, however, Görgüz had been
put to death. As an excuse, they said, “We sent
him to Qaidu, but he died en route.” 
The Qa’an’s troops do battle twice with
Qaidu’s and Dua’s army; Qaidu is wounded
during the fighting and dies of that wound.
After that, Qonchi’s son Nayan, who is of
Orda’s offspring and is presently ruler of that
ulus, reported that one of his cousins, Küilük,
had rebelled and taken refuge with Qaidu and
Dua. Several times battles had been fought be-
tween them. As was related in the section on
Jochi Khan, Nayan sent an envoy to the Qa’an,
saying, “Let your troops mount at once from
there, and let the Army of Badakhshan, which
is constantly being harassed by them, march
from the east. From the west the army of the
Padishah of Islam will of course assist, and
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION ELEVEN: TEMÜR QA’AN
463

from all sides we can trap Dua and Qaidu in
the middle and be done with them once and for
all.”
When this was discussed in private, Kökä-
chin Khatun, the Qa’an’s mother, said, “In the
realms of Cathay and Nankiyas, our ulus is nu-
merous, and Qaidu’s and Dua’s realm is dis-
tant. If you mount an expedition it will take a
year or two before it is accomplished. Be care-
ful that in the meantime no damage occur that
cannot be repaired in the long run. For now, it
is necessary to be patient and send a message
saying, ‘We agree; wait for further instruc-
tions.’ ”
They therefore delayed, and two or three
years later, in the year ___, the Qa’an’s army
[958] equipped itself for an expedition against
Qaidu and Dua and set forth in the direction
that was nearer to Qaidu. They armies clashed,
and a fierce battle was fought. Qaidu was
wounded, and his army was routed. Since Dua
was farther away, he arrived several days later,
and another fierce battle was fought. Dua was
also wounded. Qaidu died of the wound he had
suffered.
The fraud perpetrated by the Qa’an’s
officers and viziers over jewels and gem-
studded ornaments they purchased from
merchants; Tanba Bakhshi intercedes by
means of a stratagem, and they obtain
release.
Tanba the Tibetan bakhshi who was men-
tioned in the section on Qubilai Qa’an had
enormous influence with Temür Qa’an. One of
the stories of his influence is as follows.
Some merchants had brought a lot of gem-
studded ornaments and jewels they sold to the
Qa’an. Officers, viziers, and brokers were
present. The amount of sale was determined to
be 600,000 bars, and that amount was taken
from the treasury. Nearly 150,000 of that
amount was paid by the merchants to the offi-
cers and viziers.
Now there was an officer called Muqbal
Pingzhang, who had previously been dismissed
from office because of a report made by those
other officers. The Qa’an had made him a
totqavul [highway patrol], which is called ling
qish in Cathaian.1 There were also two brokers
the other brokers did not allow to participate.
These two said to the officer, “Those gems are
not worth more than 300,000.” Muqbal report-
ed this to the emperor, and an order was given
for a re-evaluation. Shihabuddin Qunduzi, who
had been the chengxiang of the city of Hang-
zhou [959] but was then out of office, was
summoned, and he evaluated them at 300,000.
The Qa’an ordered the merchants and brokers
arrested. They confessed how much they had
given to every officer, and therefore the offi-
cers and viziers were also arrested. They were
twelve in all: Dashman Chengxiang, Toba, Sar-
ban, Yighmish, Yäkä Pingzhang, Isa Kali-
machi, Bayanchar, Bayan Pingzhang’s brother,
Shamsuddin Qunduzi, and three other ping-
zhangs. They were imprisoned in the divan-
khana in the sheng, and it was decreed that
they would all be put to death.
Their
wives
and
dependents
went
to
Kökächin Khatun for intercession. She did her
best to get them released but failed. After that,
they besought Tanba Bakhshi. By chance, that
very day a comet had appeared, and therefore
Tanba Bakhshi sent a message to Temür Qa’an
telling him to make yalbarmishi (prayer) for
the comet. Temür Qa’an went there. The
bakhshi said, “Forty prisoners must be re-
leased.” Then he said, “A hundred prisoners
must be pardoned.” By this means they ob-
1The Persian ling qīsh is thought to be a transcription
of a putative Chinese 領客使lingkeshi. The 令史ling-
shi ‘secretary of commands’ is known as the title of offi-
cers of the 客省使kexingshi, a body that received am-
bassadors. See Doerfer §1730.

tained release. After that he told the emperor
that he should send a decree through the realm.
The Qa’an did yalbarmishi for seven days in a
temple and then came out. All the members of
the group were reinstated to their posts, and
their followers and adherents rejoiced. Howev-
er, 300,000 bars, the amount overcharged on
the jewels, were taken back. [960]

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION ELEVEN: TEMÜR QA’AN
465

❦ SECTION TWELVE
THE HISTORY OF HÜLÄGÜ KHAN, IN THREE PARTS.
Part One is on his offspring, his wives, and
his sons and grandsons who have branched off,
and the names of his sons-in-law; a portrait of
him and a genealogical table of his sons’
branches.
Part Two is on events leading to his en-
thronement, a picture of him and his wives,
sons, grandsons, and commanders at his en-
thronement; stories of events that occurred dur-
ing his imperial reign; some of the battles he
fought and the conquests he achieved.
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections and
were culled from various books and persons.
[962]
Part One, on his offspring, his wives, and his
sons and grandsons who have branched off,
and the names of his sons-in-law; a portrait
of him and a genealogical table of his sons’
branches.
Hülägü Khan was the fourth son of Tolui
Khan, Genghis Khan’s fourth son. Hülägü
Khan’s mother was Sorqaghtani Beki, the
daughter of Jagambu, the brother of Ong Khan,
the ruler of the Kerayit tribes. Jagambu’s name
was Kerayidai, but when he fell into Tangqut
territory and attained status there, the rulers of
Tangqut gave him the title Jagambu, which
means magniﬁcent and great commander of a
realm. Since Genghis Khan and Ong Khan
were friendly and had a father-son relationship,
he proposed marriage between his sons and
Ong Khan’s brother’s daughters, Begtutmish
for Jochi Khan and Sorqaghtani Beki for Tolui
Khan. Tolui Khan had ﬁve sons and one
daughter by Sorqaghtani Beki, as has already
been
mentioned
in
the
section
on
him.1
Genghis Khan took for himself another of
Jagambu’s daughters, Ibaqa Beki by name.
One night he had a dream, and that very night
he gave her to Kähätäi Noyan.2 [963]
A detailed account of his wives.
Hülägü Khan had many wives and concu-
bines. The names of those who are known,
both those he inherited by custom from his fa-
ther and those he married of his own accord,
are as follows.
His chief wife was Doquz3 Khatun of the
great “bone” of the Kerayit, the daughter of
Ong Khan’s son [Abaqu].4 Since she had been
his father’s wife, she was greater than the other
wives, even though he had married some of
them before her. He married her after crossing
the Oxus River. Tolui Khan had not yet
touched her. She had inﬂuence and was ex-
tremely domineering. Since the Kerayit tribes
were originally Christian, she constantly fa-
vored Christians, and during her time that
group became strong. For her sake Hülägü
Khan also favored them and held them in hon-
or, so much so that they built churches
1See text p. 778.
2See text pp. 118, 196 and 361 above.
3Doquz Khatun’s name varies throughout as Doquz ~
Toquz. We will opt for Doquz.
4Readingﻮ ــ ــﺑﻘ ا(Abaqu, as on text p. 119 above) for the
text’s اﯾﻘﻮ, which Arends (p. 16) reads as Уйку.

throughout the realm. A church was always
made at the gate to Doquz Khatun’s ordu, and
the naqus was sounded.1 Her death occurred
after Hülägü Khan’s, four months and eleven
days before Abaqa Khan’s enthronement. The
date will be mentioned in the proper place.
Abaqa Khan awarded her ordu to her brother’s
daughter Tuqitani Khatun,2 who had been
Hülägü Khan’s concubine and was attached to
that ordu. She maintained the same customs, as
will be told in the section on Abaqa Khan. She
died on Thursday the 2nd of Ikindi Ay in Luy
Yil corresponding to the last day of Safar 691
[February 21, 1292], and the ordu was given to
Kökächi Khatun, who had been brought from
the qa’an’s court on account of the kinship she
had with the senior Bulughan Khatun, the
Padishah of Islam’s wife. She died in Sha‘ban
695 [June 1296], [964] and the ordu was given
to Kärämün Khatun, daughter of Abatai Noy-
an’s son Qutlugh Temür Noyan and the junior
Bulughan Khatun’s cousin.3 She too died quite
suddenly in the summer pastures at Hula’an
Mörän in the vicinity of Joma Saray on Tues-
day the 12th of Jumada II 703 [January 21,
1304], and now the Sultan of Islam has mar-
ried, in her stead, Qutlughshah Khatun, the
daughter of Sarucha’s son Irinjin, the nephew
of Doquz Khatun, and installed her there. At
present the ordu is still maintained.
Another wife was Güyük Khatun of the
“bone” of the rulers of the Oyirat tribes. She

Another wife was Qutui Khatun, daughter of
___ of the “bone” of the rulers of the Qunqirat

[Güyük Khatun’s] ordu to her.
Another wife was Öljäi Khatun, daughter of

Another wife was Yesünjin Khatun of the

She was from Güyük Khatun’s ordu. She and

His sons and grandsons.
Hülägü Khan had fourteen sons and seven
daughters. Following are their names and a
summary account of them and their offspring. 
(1) Abaqa Khan.
Hülägü Khan’s ﬁrst son was Abaqa Khan by
Yesünjin Khatun. He was born in Mongolia.
He and his father came to Iran together. He
was the eldest and best of the brothers and, as
his father’s designated heir and successor, he
inherited the throne and rule of the ulus and the
army. An account of his wives and children
will come in the section on him.4
(2) Jumghur.
Hülägü Khan’s second son was Jumghur,5
who was born of Güyük Khatun in Mongolia
one month after Abaqa. When Hülägü Khan set
out for Iran, he left him and his ordus with
4See text pp. 1055–57 below.
5The spelling varies, Jumghur ~ Jumqur.

Mänggü Qa’an. The other aghruqs he took
with him he left in the vicinity of Almalyk in
Turkistan. At the time of Ariq Bökä’s dispute
with Qubilai Qa’an, since Jumghur was in
Mänggü Qa’an’s ordus and Ariq Bökä was
there and Qubilai was far away, Jumghur was
forced to take Ariq Bökä’s part, and that is the
reason he fought on Ariq Bökä’s behalf against
Qubilai’s soldiers. After Ariq Bökä did battle

him a message to stand down. From there he
joined Qutui and set out to join his father, but
he died en route, an account of which will be

She was married to Su’unchaq’s son Shadai
Gürägän. By her he had children, a son named
Habash and two daughters,3 Gunjishkäb, who
is the Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan’s ﬁrst

7The boqtaq (boghtaq) was the Mongolian lady’s

worn by Saray Malik Khanïm: “The rest of her head-
dress was very like the crest of a helmet, such as we men
wear in jousting in the tilt yard: but this crest of hers was
of red stuff and its border hung down in part over her
shoulders. In the back part this crest was very lofty and
it was ornamented with many great round pearls all of
good orient, also with precious stones such as balas ru-
bies and turquoises, the same very finely set. The hem of
this head covering showed gold thread embroidery, and
set round it she wore a very beautiful garland of pure
gold ornamented with great pearls and gems. Further the
summit of this crest just described was erected upon a
framework which displayed three large balas rubies each
about two finger breadths across, and these were clear in
colour and glittered in the light, while over all rose a
long white plume to the height of an ell, the feathers
thereof hanging down so that some almost hid the face
coming to below the eyes. This plume was braced to-
gether by gold wire, while at the summit appeared a
white knot of feathers garnished with pearls and pre-
cious stones. As she came forward this mighty head-gear
waved backwards and forwards, and the Princess was
wearing her hair all loose, hanging down over her shoul-
ders…. To keep this crest and the other adornments
steady on her head the Princess was attended by many
dames who walked beside her” (González de Clavijo,
Narrative, 258).

(3) Yoshmut.
Hülägü Khan’s third son was Yoshmut. His

“bone.”

Hülägü Khan’s fourth son was Täkshin, born

Hülägü Khan’s ﬁfth son was Taraghai, born

along with his father. He had two other sons.

Khan’s
thirteenth

Shi-

(14) Taghai Temür.
Hülägü Khan’s fourteenth son was Taghai
Temür. His mother was a concubine from Qu-
tui Khatun’s ordu from the “bone” of the ___.

Now that the names and lineages of Hülägü
Khan’s sons and grandsons have been given,
insofar as they are known, we will begin the
section on his daughters and sons-in-law.
Hülägü Khan’s daughters and sons-in-law.
Hülägü Khan had seven daughters as fol-
lows.
The ﬁrst was Buluqan Aqa, born of Güyük
Khatun. [971] She was married to Joma
Gürägän, son of Jochi of the Tatar nation, who
was the brother of Nuqdan Khatun,1 the mother
of Gaikhatu Khan and chief wife of Abaqa
Khan. Jochi had come here with Hülägü, and
he too was a gürägän, for he was married to
Genghis Khan’s brother Otchi Noyan’s daugh-
ter Chechägän, and she was Joma Gürägän’s
mother.
The second daughter was Jamai (?), born of
Öljäi Khatun. After her sister Buluqan Aqa
died she was given to Joma Gürägän in her
stead.
The third daughter was Mänggügän, born of
Öljäi Khatun. She was married to Buqa
Temür’s son Jaqir Gürägän of the Oyirat na-
tion. This Buqa Temür had come with Hülägü,
and he was Öljäi Khatun’s brother [born] of
Güyük
Khatun’s
mother,
Chächäyigän,
[Genghis Khan’s] daughter. Jaqir Gürägän’s
son was Taraqai Gürägän, and he was Mänggü
Temür’s son-in-law who ﬂed to Syria.2
1For Joma Gürägän and Nuqdan Khatun, see text p. 88
above.
2The son-in-law who fled was Taraqai (see text p. 102
above). He was first married to Mänggü Temür’s daugh-
ter Qutlugh and, after her death, to this Mänggügän.
The fourth daughter was Tödögäch. Her
mother was a concubine from Doquz Khatun’s
ordu named ___. She was married to the Täng-
giz Gürägän of the Oyirat tribe who had for-
merly been married to Güyük Khan’s daughter,
___ by name, but she died.3 [When] Tänggiz
Gürägän died, his son Sülämish married her,
and at present Tänggiz’s grandson Chechäk has
married her.
The ﬁfth daughter was Taraqai, born of Irqan
Egächi. She was married to Musa Gürägän of
the Qunqirat tribe, Genghis Khan’s grandson,
the son of ___.4 His name was Taghai Temür,
but a learned man who was his tutor named
him Musa. He was the brother of Martai
Khatun.5
The sixth daughter was Qutluqqan, born of
Mängligäch Egächi. She was married to Yesü
Buqa Gürägän, the son of Urughtu Noyan of
the Dörbän tribe. When he died his son Tükäl
took her. [972]
The seventh daughter was Baba, born of
Öljäi Khatun. She was given to Lagzi Gürägän,
son of Amir Arghun Aqa of the Oyirat tribe.
Arghun Aqa came here in the capacity of a bit-
igchi with Hülägü Khan by order of Mänggü
Qa’an.
The histories of some of these wives, sons,
daughters, and sons-in-law who have been
mentioned may have to be given again in cer-
tain other sections in more detail; however, in
general they are as has been reported.
The genealogical chart of the sons, other than
those who became rulers, who will be treated
separately, is as follows: [973]
