‘whose beard is long, his comprehension is short’ (Sa‘id
al-Khuri al-Shartuni, Aqrab al-Mawarid 2:1135).
Kalwadha Gate were also martyred, and no
Abbasid who could be found was left alive,
save only a few who did not count and
Mubarak Shah, the caliph’s youngest son, who
was given to Öljäi Khatun, who sent him to
Khwaja Nasíruddin in Maragha. He was mar-
ried to a Mongol woman who bore him two
sons.
On Friday the 16th of Safar [February 22]
the caliph’s middle son was dispatched after
his father and brother, and the reign of the
House of Abbas, which had mounted the
throne after the Umayyads, came to an end.
Their caliphate lasted ﬁve hundred twenty-ﬁve
years, and there were thirty-seven of them, as
follows: (1) Saffah, (2) Mansur, (3) Mahdi, (4)
Hadi, (5) Rashid, (6) Amin, (7) Ma’mun, (8)
Mu‘tasim, (9) Wathiq, (10) Mutawakkil, (11)
Muntasir, (12) Musta‘in, (13) Mu‘tazz, (14)
Muhtadi, (15) Mu‘tamid, (16) Mu‘tadid, (17)
Muktaﬁ, (18) Muqtadir, (19) Qahir, (20) Radi,
(21) Muttaqi, (22) Mustakﬁ, (23) Muti‘, (24)
Tayi‘, [1019] (25) Qadir, (26) Qayim, (27)
Muqtadi, (28) Mustazhir, (29) Mustarshid, (30)
Rashid, (31) Muqtaﬁ, (32) Mustanjid, (33)
Mustadi, (34) Nasir, (35) Zahir, (36) Mustansir,
and (37) Musta‘sim, who reigned for seventeen
years.
The very day the caliph was martyred, his
vizier,
Mu’ayyiduddin
Ibn
Alqami,
and
Fakhruddin Damghani were sent into the city
as vizier and chief of administration respec-
tively. Ali Bahadur was made shahna and head
of the corps of ortaqs [merchants] and uzes [ar-
tisans]. Imaduddin Umar Qazwini was appoint-
ed as Amir Qaraqai’s deputy, and he restored
the caliph’s mosque and the Musa-Jawad
shrine. Najmuddin Abu-Ja‘far Ahmad Imran,
who was called Malik Rastdil,2 was appointed
2Rastdil ~ Dilrast. See text p. 1017 above. He is
known as Ibn Imran. See Khwandamir, Habibu’s-siyar
494
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

to the districts of East Baghdad, viz. the
Khurasan Road, Khalis, and Bandinjin. Niza-
muddin Abdul-Mu’min Bandinjin [was made]
chief cadi. Elgäi Noyan and Qara Buqa were
sent into Baghdad with three thousand Mongol
cavalry to undertake reconstruction. Everyone
buried his dead, the dead animals were cleared
from the roads, and the markets were restored.
On Thursday the 29th of Safar [March 7] the
vizier’s son Sharafuddin and the Sahib-Divan
came to court to inquire after certain matters
and then returned. 
On Friday the 23rd [March 1] Hülägü Khan
left and camped at Shaykh Makarim’s Dome.
From there he proceeded stage by stage to his
ordus at Khanaqin.
When
Baghdad
was
besieged,
several
learned Alids had come from Hilla to request a
shahna. Hülägü Khan sent Tükäl and Amir
Nahli Nakhjiwani there, and on their heels he
dispatched Öljäi Khatun’s brother Buqa Temür
to test the people of Hilla, Kufa, and Wasit.
The inhabitants of Hilla came out to greet the
army, made bridges over the Euphrates, and re-
joiced at the army’s arrival. [1020] Buqa
Temür saw that they were committed [in their
support]. On the 10th of Safar [February 16,
1258] he decamped and set out for Wasit,
arriving on the 17th [February 23]. The people
did not surrender, so he camped and took the
city, massacring and plundering. Nearly forty
thousand people were put to death.
From there he went to Khuzistan, taking
Sharafuddin Ibn al-Jawzi with him to get the
city of Shushtar to surrender. Some of the
caliph’s soldiers and Turks ﬂed and others
were killed. Basra and that area also surren-
dered. Amir Sayfuddin Bitigchi pleaded with
the court to send a hundred Mongols to Najaf
3:96f.
to guard the shrine of the Commander of the
Faithful Ali and the inhabitants there.
On the 12th of Rabi‘ I [March 19] Buqa
Temür arrived at the camp, and on the 19th
[March 26] the emissaries from Aleppo who
had come to Baghdad were sent home carrying
a letter Khwaja Nasíruddin Tusi had written in
Arabic at Hülägü Khan’s order. A copy of that
letter follows: “We stopped in Baghdad in the
year 656, and ‘an evil morning it was unto
those who were warned in vain.’1 ‘We called
upon its lord, but he refused, so he suffered
what the text says: We chastised him with a
heavy chastisement.’2 Now we call upon you
to obey us. If you come, well and good; if you
refuse, woe betide you. Do not be like one who
digs his own grave or bloodies his own nose
lest you be one of those whose works are vain,
‘whose endeavor in the present life hath been
wrongly directed, and who think they do the
work which is right.’3 ‘Neither will this be dif-
ficult with God.’4 And peace be with him who
follows the right path.” 
On Wednesday the 11th of Rabi‘ II [April 17]
Hülägü Khan reached his aghruq in the vicini-
ty of Hamadan and Siyah Koh and dismounted
from the expedition. He had been unwell, but
he recovered.
On the 16th of Rabi‘ II [April 22] Kökä Bit-
igchi died. On Wednesday the 20th of Rabi‘ II
[April 26] Elgäi Noyan and some commanders
arrived at court. On Thursday the 2nd of Juma-
da
II [June 6] Mu’ayyiduddin the vizier of
Baghdad died, [1021] and his son Sharafuddin
was appointed in his stead.

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWELVE: HÜLÄGÜ KHAN
495

The city of Arbela is conquered by Uruqtu
Noyan, and he lays siege to the citadel there.
When Hülägü Khan set out to conquer Bagh-
dad, he assigned the Arbela fortress to Uruqtu
Noyan. It is a bastion set ﬁrmly upon a glacis
and has no like in the inhabited quarter of the
globe. When Uruqtu Noyan laid siege, the
Kurds began to ﬁght from the citadel, and
Tajuddin Ibn Salaya, the lord of Arbela, came
to surrender and performed good services.
Uruqtu said, “The sign of your true surrender
will be the turning over of the citadel.” Tajud-
din went to the citadel gate, but the Kurdish
soldiers would not let him in. After much insis-
tence he gave up and came away, returning to
Uruqtu, who sent him to Hülägü Khan. He was
found guilty at a trial and executed.
Uruqtu besieged the citadel for a time, but
the defenders refused to give in. Then he re-
quested reinforcements from Sultan Badruddin
Lu’lu’. He sent a few soldiers. One night the
defenders of the citadel came down and
launched a surprise attack on the Mongols,
killing all they could ﬁnd, setting their cata-
pults ablaze, and retreating into the citadel.
Uruqtu was stunned and summoned Badruddin
Lu’lu’ for consultation. Badruddin Lu’lu’ said,
“The best plan is to postpone this until sum-
mer, when the Kurds will ﬂee from the heat
and go into the mountains, for now the weather
is nice and they have plenty of supplies. [1022]
The citadel is highly impregnable and impossi-
ble to take except by stealth.” Uruqtu stationed
Sultan Badruddin there and went to his sum-
mer pastures in Tabriz. When the weather
turned hot, the Kurds came down, turned the
citadel over to Sultan Badruddin, and went to
Syria. Sultan Badruddin destroyed the ram-
parts, and thus the citadel was also conquered.
The riches of Baghdad and the Heretics’
fortresses are taken to Azerbaijan and
deposited in the mountain stronghold by
Lake Salmas; Badruddin Lu’lu’ and the
sultan of Anatolia come to the padishah’s
court.
Hülägü Khan sent the abundant treasuries he
had obtained in Baghdad to Azerbaijan with
Amir Nasiruddin Ala’uddin, the lord of Rayy.
The riches he had garnered in the Heretics’
fortresses, Anatolia, Georgia, Armenia, Luris-
tan, and Kurdistan were likewise sent. He or-
dered Malik Majduddin of Tabriz to construct a
lofty building of great strength on the moun-
tain called Tala on the shore of Salmas and Ur-
mia Lake. All the cash was melted down and
turned into bars and deposited there. Some of
the rare objects he sent to Mänggü Qa’an to
announce his victory and triumph. He also in-
formed him of his conquest of Iran and his in-
tention to go to Egypt and Syria. On this mis-
sion went Amir Hulachu. The qa’an was
jubilant over the news.
That same year Sultan Badruddin Lu’lu’ set
out in haste for court by order of the qa’an,
arriving at Maragha on the 29th of Rajab 656
[August 1, 1258]. [1023] He was more than
ninety years old. Hülägü Khan showed him
great honor and sent him home on the 6th of
Sha‘ban [August 8].
On the 7th of Sha‘ban [August 9] Atabeg
Sa‘d, the son of Atabeg Abubakr of Fars, came
to court to offer congratulations on the con-
quest of Baghdad. He was rewarded and al-
lowed to depart.
On the 4th of Sha‘ban [August 6] Sultan Iz-
zuddin of Anatolia arrived at court in Mu…q in
the environs of Tabriz. On Wednesday the 8th
of the month [August 10] Sultan Ruknuddin
arrived on his heels. Hülägü Khan had been of-
fended by Sultan Izzuddin’s inattention to Bai-
ju Noyan and his having done battle with him,
and after the conquest of Baghdad Sultan Iz-
zuddin became very apprehensive and tried to
496
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

save himself by ruse from the brink of the dis-
aster occasioned by his offense. He ordered a
pair of very ﬁne, regal boots made, and on the
soles he had his portrait painted. During his
tägishmishi he gave them to the padishah, and
when his gaze fell upon the portrait, the sultan
kissed the ground and said, “Your slave hopes
the padishah will elevate this slave’s head with
his royal foot.” Hülägü Khan had mercy on
him. Doquz Khatun undertook to patronize
him and asked that he be pardoned. Hülägü
Khan forgave him.
Just then Khwaja Nasíruddin Tusi reported
that when Sultan Jalaluddin Khwarazmshah
had been defeated by a superior Mongol force
and arrived in Tabriz, his soldiers were aggres-
sive toward the peasantry. The khwaja’s opin-
ion was asked. “We are at present conquerors,
not potentates,” he said. “In times of conquest
maintenance of the peasantry is not obligatory.
When we become potentates we will dispense
justice to those who ask for it.”
“We, thank God, are both conquerors and po-
tentates,” said Hülägü. “With foes we are con-
querors, and with our subjects we are poten-
tates. We are not afﬂicted with weakness and
inability like Jalaluddin.” [1024]
Mawlana Nasíruddin builds an observatory
in Maragha at Hülägü Khan’s order.
On the above-mentioned date an order was
given for Khwaja Nasíruddin Tusi to construct
an observatory in any place he considered ap-
propriate. He chose the city of Maragha and
had a very ﬁne observatory built there. The
reason for this is as follows. Mänggü Qa’an
was distinguished among Mongol rulers for his
intelligence, perspicacity, sharp wit and mind,
and he even solved some problems left by Eu-
clid. In his regal highmindedness he had
thought that a star catalogue should be made
during his reign and that it should be undertak-
en
by
Jamaluddin
Muhammad
Tahir
b.
Muhammad al-Zaydi of Bukhara, but some of
his observations were faulty. Since Khwaja
Nasíruddin’s reputation for excellence had
spread throughout the world, when Mänggü
Qa’an was bidding his brother farewell, he
said, “When the Heretics’ fortresses are con-
quered, send Khwaja Nasíruddin here.” How-
ever, since he was occupied with the conquest
of Manzi at the time and was far from his cap-
ital, Hülägü Khan ordered the khwaja to con-
struct an observatory here [1025] since he was
aware of his good character and wanted him in
attendance. Seven years after Hülägü Khan
mounted the khan’s throne the Ilkhanid cata-
logue was completed with the collaboration of
four scholars, Mu’ayyiduddin Urzi, Fakhrud-
din Maraghi, Fakhruddin of Akhlat, and Naj-
muddin Dabiran Qazwini.1
Hülägü Khan goes to Syria and conquers
Aleppo and the realm of Damascus.
The sultan of Aleppo had sent his vizier,
Sahib Zaynuddin Haﬁzi with regal gifts and
presents to the qa’an’s court, and he had ac-
quired a great reputation there and was award-
ed a yarligh and paiza. When Hülägü arrived
in Iran, he secretly pledged his allegiance to
him, and he was accused of this before the sul-
tan of Syria and an attempt was made on his
life. He ﬂed and took refuge with Hülägü
Khan, and no sooner had he arrived than the
padishah’s desire for an expedition to Aleppo
increased. In advance he sent emissaries to
Badruddin Lu’lu’, saying, “Since you are over
ninety years old, I exempt you from participat-
ing militarily, but you must send your son Ma-
lik Salih to ride with the imperial banners to
conquer Syria and Egypt.” In accordance with
this command he sent his son, and when he

arrived at Hülägü Khan’s court he was given
one
of
Sultan
Jalaluddin’s
daughters
in
marriage.
In the vanguard was dispatched Ket Buqa
Noyan with a large army. In the right wing was
Shiktür and Baiju, [1026] and in the left wing
were
Su’unchaq
and

commanders.
Hülägü himself set out for Syria in the qol
[center] on Friday the 22nd of Ramadan 657
[September 12, 1259] with Scorpio in the
ascendant. 
When he reached Bala Tagh, he liked the
meadow there and named it Labna Saghut.
Then he entered Akhlat and the mountains of
Hakkari, which were nests of outlaw Kurds,
and they killed all they found.
When he reached Diyarbekir, ﬁrst he con-
quered Jazira1 and assigned his son Yoshmut in
the company of Sönitäi Noyan to lay siege to
the fortress at Mayyafariqin. He sent Malik
Salih with a contingent to conquer Amid, and
he himself set out for Ruha,2 which he con-
quered. From there he went to Dunaysir, Nasi-
bin, and Harran, all of which he took in battle
and then massacred and plundered. Crossing
the Euphrates, he surrounded Aleppo without
warning. The inhabitants, trusting in the im-
pregnability of their citadel, refused to surren-
der and continued to do battle.
At the Jews’ Gate was Uruqtu Noyan, at the
Anatolia Gate was Ket Buqa Noyan, at the
Damascus Gate was Su’unchaq, and Hülägü
Khan camped at the Antioch Gate. A chapar
[stockade] was assembled around the city, and
catapults were installed. For a full week the
battle was fought hard by both sides, but in the
end, in Dhu’l-Hijja 657 [November 19–De-
cember 17, 1259], it was taken from the Iraq
1Jazira, the modern Cizre in Turkey.
2Ruha (~ Urhay) is Edessa, the modern Urfa (Şanlıur-
fa) in Turkey.
Gate and a full week of massacre and pillage
ensued, during which many people were killed.
For forty days and nights they battled against
the defenders in the citadel, and catapult stones
and arrows rained from both sides. Amir Qor-
chan, Achu Sükürchi, and Sadun Gurji were
wounded several times in the face, for which
the padishah gave them large rewards, saying,
“Just as rouge is an adornment to women’s
faces, red blood is a cosmetic adornment to the
faces and beards of men.”
In the end the citadel was also conquered.
[1027] Many artisans were made prisoner, and
untold olja (booty) was taken. For a long time
they were occupied with a siege of the Harim
Fortress,3 but in the end the defenders asked
for
quarter. When
Fakhruddin,
known
as
“Saqi,” swore an oath, they came down under
amnesty, but Hülägü Khan was extremely an-
gry with them and ordered them killed at once
along with their wives and children. Only an
Armenian goldsmith was spared. 
When the Aleppo citadel was taken, Hülägü
Khan turned it over to Fakhruddin Saqi and in-
stalled Tükäl Bakhshi as shahna. 
After he departed from Aleppo, the people
complained of Fakhruddin and an order was
given for him to be executed, and the gov-
ernance of Aleppo was transferred to Zaynud-
din Haﬁzi.
The people of Damascus were apprehensive
of attack by the Mongol army, and since they
knew that everything surrounding Syria was
entirely under Hülägü Khan’s control, the dig-
nitaries and grandees came to court bearing all
sorts of gifts and the keys to the city gates as a
show of surrender. Hülägü Khan ordered Ket
Buqa Noyan to go to Damascus and test them.
The inhabitants turned out to greet him and

asked for amnesty. Ket Buqa sent the nobles
and dignitaries to Hülägü Khan, who had mer-
cy on them and granted their requests. The
Mongols entered the city without having to lay
siege or do battle. A Mongol shahna and three
Tajik liege men were assigned. Ala’uddin
Hashi, Jamaluddin Qaraqai Qazwini, and Qazi
Shamsuddin Qummi were appointed to consol-
idate Damascus. In brief, in a short time Bagh-
dad, Diyarbekir, Diyar Rabi‘a,1 and Syria were
completely conquered and brought under the
control of Hülägü Khan’s deputies.
He also took over the realms of Anatolia, and
while he was engaged there emissaries arrived
from the east [1028] with Shiktür Noyan at
their head. He had set out from here in all haste
to announce Mänggü Qa’an’s death. Hülägü
Khan was sorely grieved, but he did not show
it. Stationing Ket Buqa Noyan to protect Syria,
he withdrew from Aleppo and arrived in
Akhlat on Sunday the 24th of Jumada II 658
[June 6, 1260].
When Hülägü Khan had arrived in Aleppo,
Malik Nasir, the sultan of Aleppo and Syria,
had ﬂed to the fortress at Karak. Ket Buqa
wanted to lay siege, but he asked for quarter
and came down. Ket Buqa sent him to court,
and the padishah promised that when he took
Egypt he would give him the governorship of
Syria.
In the Bechin Yil that corresponds to 658
[1260] a number of great commanders passed
away. Among them were Torji Gürägän, Buqa
Temür, Qubai Noyan, …l…na Noyan, Borong-
tai Noyan, and Salji’udai Noyan.
Hülägü Khan was distressed by Mänggü
Qa’an’s death and Ariq Bökä’s rebellion. 
1Diyar Rabi‘a, the upper Tigris region.
Ket Buqa Noyan goes to Egypt, does battle
with the Egyptian army, and is killed.
When Hülägü Khan departed from Syria, he
sent a Mongol emissary with forty liege men
on a mission to Egypt, saying, “God the great
has elevated Genghis Khan and his progeny
and given us the realms of the face of the earth
altogether. Everyone who has been recalcitrant
in obeying us has been annihilated along with
his women, children, kith and kin, towns, and
servants, as has surely reached the hearing of
all. [1029] The reputation of our innumerable
army is as well known as the stories of Rustam
and Isfandiar. If you are in submission to our
court, send tribute, come yourself, and request
a shahna; otherwise be prepared for battle.”
At that time there was no one left of Kamilite
lineage worthy of ruling, and a Turcoman had
become ruler. When he died he left an infant
child named Muhammad, who was elevated to
his father’s position with Quduz as his atabeg.
Muhammad died suddenly, and Quduz became
ruler. He curried favor with the people through
largesse. Most of the soldiers of Syria and
Egypt were the defeated troops of Sultan
Jalaluddin who had ﬂed from the gates of
Akhlat and gone to Syria. Their leaders and
commanders were Barakat Khan and Malik
Ikhtiyaruddin Khan son of …,2 and Malik Say-
fuddin Sadiq Khan son of Mingbuqa, Malik
Nasiruddin Güshlü3 Khan son of Beg Arslan,
Atlas Khan, and Nasiruddin Muhammad Qay-
mari. When Hülägü Khan set out for Syria,
they went into hiding in the surrounding areas,
and after he pulled out, they reassembled and
headed for Cairo in Egypt, where they told
their sad story to Quduz. He showed them fa-
vor, sympathized with them, and gave them

much money. They all became wholehearted
supporters of Quduz’ rule.
When the emissaries arrived, Quduz sum-
moned them and consulted with them on what
to do, saying, “Hülägü Khan has proceeded
from Turan with a huge army into Iran, and no
one, caliph, sultan, or malik, has the ability to
withstand his onslaught. Having conquered all
lands, he has come to Damascus, and were it
not for the news of his brother’s death he
would have added Egypt to his conquests too.
In addition, he has stationed in this area Ket
Buqa Noyan, who is like a raging lion and ﬁre-
breathing dragon lying in ambush. If he attacks
Egypt, no one will be able to contend with
him. [1030] Before we lose all power of self-
determination, we must come up with a
strategy.”
“In addition to being Genghis Khan’s grand-
son, Tolui Khan’s son, and Mänggü Qa’an’s
brother,” said Nasiruddin Qaymari, “Hülägü
Khan has power and might beyond description.
At present he holds from the gates of Egypt to
the borders of China in his mighty grasp, and
he has been singled out for heavenly assis-
tance. If we go before him under amnesty, it
will not be blameworthy. However, willingly
to drink poison and to go out to greet one’s
own death are far from the path of wisdom. A
human being is not a grape vine that doesn’t
mind having its head cut off. He does not keep
his word, for with no warning he killed Khwar-
shah, Musta‘sim, Husamuddin Akka, and the
lord of Arbela after having made promises to
them. If we go to him he will do the same to
us.” 
“At the present time,” said Quduz, “every-
where in Diyarbekir, Diyar Rabi‘a, and Greater
Syria is ﬁlled with lamentation. The land from
Baghdad to Anatolia lies in ruins, devoid of
farmers and seed. If we don’t make a pre-emp-
tive strike and try to repulse them, soon Egypt
will be destroyed like the others. Given the
multitudes with which he is proceeding in our
direction, one of three things must be done: we
must make a truce, offer resistance, or go into
exile. Exile is impossible, for there is nowhere
we can go other than North Africa, and a
bloodthirsty desert and vast distances lie be-
tween us and there.”
“A truce is also imprudent,” said Nasiruddin
Qaymari, “for their word is not to be trusted.”
The other commanders said, “We do not have
the power to resist either. You must say what
you think the best plan is.”
“My opinion,” said Quduz, “is that we go out
to battle together. If we win, ﬁne; otherwise,
we will not suffer blame from the people.”
[1031]
After that, the amirs agreed, and Quduz con-
sulted with Bunduqdar, his chief amir, in pri-
vate. “My opinion,” said Bunduqdar, “is that
we should kill the emissaries and ride as one to
attack Ket Buqa. Win or die, in either case we
will not be blamed, and we will have people’s
gratitude.”
Quduz approved this plan, and by night he
had the emissaries cruciﬁed. The next morning
they perforce committed themselves to battle
and mounted. Amir Baidar, who was the leader
of the Mongol yäzäk [advance troop], sent a
man named Aghlabak to Ket Buqa Noyan to
inform him of the movement of the Egyptian
troops. Ket Buqa sent in reply, “Stay where
you are and wait for me.” 
Before Ket Buqa arrived, Quduz attacked
Baidar and drove him to the banks of the
Orontes. Ket Buqa Noyan, his zeal stirred,
ﬂared up like ﬁre with all conﬁdence in his
own strength and might. Quduz stationed his
troops in ambush and, himself mounted with a
few others, stood waiting. He clashed with Ket
Buqa and his several thousand cavalry, all ex-
perienced warriors, at Ayn Jalut. The Mongols
500
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

attacked, raining down arrows, and Quduz
pulled a feint and started to withdraw. Embold-
ened, the Mongols lit out after him, killing
many of the Egyptians, but when they came to
the ambush spot, the trap was sprung from
three sides. A bloody battled ensued, lasting
from dawn till midday. The Mongols were
powerless to resist, and in the end they were
put to ﬂight.
Ket Buqa Noyan kept attacking left and right
with all zeal. Some encouraged him to ﬂee, but
he refused to listen and said, “Death is
inevitable. It is better to die with a good name
than to ﬂee in disgrace. In the end, someone
from this army, old or young, [1032] will reach
the court and report that Ket Buqa, not wanting
to return in shame, gave his life in battle. The
padishah should not grieve over lost Mongol
soldiers. Let him imagine that his soldiers’
wives have not been pregnant for a year and
the mares of their herds have not folded. May
felicity be upon the padishah. When his noble
being is well, every loss is compensated. The
life or death of servants like us is irrelevant.”
Although the soldiers left him, he continued to
struggle in battle like a thousand men. In the
end his horse faltered, and he was captured. 
Near the battleﬁeld was a reed bed in which a
troop of Mongol cavalrymen was hiding.
Quduz ordered ﬁre thrown into it, and they
were all burned alive. After that, Ket Buqa was
taken before Quduz with his hands bound.
“Despicable man,” said Quduz, “you have
shed so much blood wrongfully, ended the
lives of champions and dignitaries with false
assurances, and overthrown ancient dynasties
with broken promises. Now you have ﬁnally
fallen into a snare yourself.”
When the one whose hands were bound heard
these words, he reared up like a mad elephant /
And replied, saying, “O proud one, do not
pride yourself on this day of victory.”
“If I am killed by your hand,” said Ket Buqa,
“I consider it to be God’s act, not yours. Be not
deceived by this event for one moment, for
when the news of my death reaches Hülägü
Khan, the ocean of his wrath will boil over,
and from Azerbaijan to the gates of Egypt will
quake with the hooves of Mongol horses. They
will take the sands of Egypt from there in their
horses’ nose bags. Hülägü Khan has three
hundred thousand renowned horsemen like Ket
Buqa. [1033] You may take one of them
away.”
Quduz said, “Speak not so proudly of the
horsemen of Turan, for they perform deeds
with trickery and artiﬁce, not with manliness
like Rustam.”
“As long as I have lived,” replied Ket Buqa,
“I have been the padishah’s servant, not a mut-
ineer and regicide like you!
Let the malevolent retain neither head nor
body, for he deprives his prince of life.
Finish me off as quickly as possible.” Quduz
ordered his head severed from his body.
They then attacked throughout Syria as far as
the banks of the Euphrates, overthrowing
everyone they found, plundering Ket Buqa’s
camp, taking captive his wife, child, and re-
tainers, and killing the tax collectors and shah-
nas of the provinces. Those who were warned
escaped, and when the news of Ket Buqa Noy-
an’s death and his last words reached Hülägü
Khan, he displayed his grief over his death and
the ﬁre of his zeal ﬂared up. “Where will I ﬁnd
another servant who will show such devotion
and allegiance in the face of death?” he said as
he showered those left behind by Ket Buqa
with favor.
One day prior to that, he had rewarded Malik
Nasir of Aleppo. Then he gave him the gover-
norship of Damascus and sent him off with
three hundred Syrian cavalrymen. After the
news of Ket Buqa arrived, a Syrian said, “Ma-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWELVE: HÜLÄGÜ KHAN
501

lik Nasir of Aleppo is not with you wholeheart-
edly. He wanted to ﬂee to Syria and assist
Quduz, and it was his plan to attack Ket
Buqa.”
Hülägü Khan dispatched three hundred Mon-
gol horsemen after him. The lead men caught
up with him and got him to dismount by say-
ing, “We are ordered to give you a banquet so
that you may receive a full reward.” [1034] As
was the Mongol custom, they got him dead
drunk. Suddenly the rest of the three hundred
horsemen arrived, and they killed Malik Nasir
and his three hundred Syrians. Of the entire
troop only Muhyiddin Maghribi was left alive,
and he escaped by claiming to be an astrologer.
Hülägü Khan sent Elgäi Noyan to Syria with
a large army. When they arrived the soldiers
began to plunder. Bunduqdar, who had become
the ruler of Egypt in the meantime, learned of
it and went out to repulse them. When Elgäi
Noyan learned of his approach, he left for Ana-
tolia with the Mongols who remained in Syria.
In Damascus the khutba and coinage were put
in Bunduqdar’s name.
Hülägü Khan wanted to lead his army back
to Egypt and Syria in revenge for Ket Buqa,
but on account of Mänggü Qa’an’s death and
the dispute that had sprung up between him
and his relatives, time and circumstances
would not allow it. Therefore he put it off.
At the same time Shiban’s son and Jochi’s
grandson Prince Balagha died suddenly during
a banquet, and after him Tutar Oghul was ac-
cused of sorcery and alienation. After proving
his guilt, Hülägü Khan sent him escorted by
Su’unchaq to Bärkä. When his crime was re-
ported, Bärkä sent him back to Hülägü Khan,
in accordance with Genghis Khan’s Yasa, and
he was executed on the 17th of Safar 658 [Feb-
ruary 2, 1260]. Sadruddin Sawaji was also
martyred on a charge of having written a
charm for him. After that, Quli also died.
After the princes mentioned above died, their
trains dispersed in ﬂight to Qipchaq territory
via Derbent and the Caspian Sea. [1035]
Prince Yoshmut and the commanders Elgäi
Noyan and Sönitäi go to Diyarbekir, where
they conquer Mayyafariqin and kill Malik
Kamil.
Prince Yoshmut and the great commanders
Elgäi Noyan and Sönitäi Noyan had set out at
Hülägü Khan’s command, and when they
reached the vicinity of Mayyafariqin they sent
an envoy to Malik Kamil calling upon him to
submit and surrender. Malik Kamil replied,
“The prince should not ‘beat cold iron’ and ex-
pect something that is not possible, for there is
no reliance on your word, and neither am I go-
ing to be taken in by your sweet talk nor am I
worried by the Mongol army. As long as I am
alive I will wield the sword, for you are the son
of that father who made promises and pacts
with
Khwarshah,
the
caliph,
Husamuddin
Akka, and Tajuddin of Arbela. In particular,
Malik Nasir came under your promise of
amnesty, but in the end he got what he got. I
too will of course suffer what they did.”
When the envoys delivered this message, the
prince and commanders committed themselves
to battle. Malik Kamil encouraged the people
of the city, saying, “I will not withhold from
you any of the silver, gold, or grain in the
treasury and storehouses, and I will give it all
away to those who need it. Thank God, I am
not a slave to dirhems and dinars like Mus-
ta‘sim, who lost his head and the kingdom of
Baghdad through his stinginess and miserli-
ness.” The citizens all allied themselves with
him, and the next day Malik Kamil went out
with his retinue of horsemen, skirmishes were
held, and a few on both sides were killed.
There were two brave riders with Malik Kamil.
One was Sayfuddin Lukili, and the other was
Ambar Habashi. They both killed several men
502
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

and fought hard. After a time they went into
the city and began to ﬁght from the battle-
ments. [1036]
On the second day the same two riders came
out and killed nearly ten brave horsemen. On
the third and fourth days they performed like-
wise. From this side a Georgian aznavur
[knight] went opposite them, attacked a unit by
himself, fought for a moment, and was killed.
When he was killed,
The mounted Turks rose up, clapping their
hands in vengeance.
They went back into the city. There was some-
one there manning a catapult who was ex-
tremely accurate and had killed many with his
projectiles. The commanders were helpless to
do anything about him. Badruddin Lu’lu’ also
had an extremely good catapult engineer he
summoned. He set up a catapult directly oppo-
site the catapult in the city, and the two shot
stones from the pan at the same time. The
stones collided in midair and shattered. The
people on both sides were astonished by the
mastery of the two catapult engineers. In the
end, the catapult outside was burned.
The defenders of the city fought hard. When
Hülägü Khan was apprised of the situation, he
sent Uruqtu and a troop to reinforce Elgäi Noy-
an and a message saying, “Stay where you are
until the city runs out of money.” Uruqtu
arrived to deliver the message, and while he
was speaking the same two riders came out and
threw the Mongol troops into disarray. Uruqtu,
who was drunk at the time, turned to do battle
with them. They clashed, and suddenly Elgäi
was set upon and unhorsed. Mongol horsemen
rushed in from all directions and got Elgäi sad-
dled again. Once again the riders broke some
ranks and pulled back.
The Turks were amazed by the champions,
every warrior biting his lip in vengeance.
[1037]
Thereafter, the two riders came out every day,
killing some and wounding others, and this
continued for two years. There was neither
food nor fodder left in the city, and the animals
were dead. They began to eat carrion. They
even ate dogs, cats, and mice. Then they start-
ed being cannibals, devouring each other like
ﬁsh. Since the two riders had no straw or bar-
ley, they killed their horses and ate them. Then
they wanted to go out on foot and ﬁght until
they were killed, but Malik Kamil did not al-
low it. The few who were left sent a letter to
the prince in which they said, “There is no one
left in the city with any strength. There are
only a few, and they are alive in spirit but dead
in body. Sons are eating their fathers, and
mothers their children. If the army comes now,
there is not a single creature to resist.”
The prince sent Uruqtu, and when he went
into the city he found everyone lying dead on
top of each other. He discovered only seventy
persons hidden in the houses, and they were
half dead. Malik Kamil and his brother were
taken captive and brought before Yoshmut.
When the soldiers began to plunder, the two
brave riders went up on the roof of a house and
shot every Turk that passed. Uruqtu came and
ordered a few brave Turks to kill them. They
came down from the roof, put their shields in
front of their faces, and fought hard until they
were ﬁnally killed.
Malik Kamil was taken to Hülägü Khan’s
court at Tall Bashir on the other side of the Eu-
phrates. He had previously gone to the qa’an’s
court, where he was favorably received, and
come back with a yarligh and paiza. After that,
at the time of Hülägü Khan’s expedition to
Baghdad, he went to Malik Nasir of Syria and
said, “It would be best for us to assist the
caliph with a large army,” [1038] but Malik
Nasir pretended not to understand and failed to
heed. After the conquest of Baghdad, Kamil
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWELVE: HÜLÄGÜ KHAN
503

grew afraid and was in rebellion for two years,
as has already been mentioned. This time,
when he was captured and taken to court,
Hülägü Khan counted off his offenses and said,
“Didn’t my brother show you favor and kind-
ness along with your whole family and peo-
ples? Is that kindness to be repaid with
rebellion?” 
After that he ordered his ﬂesh cut off and
stuffed in his mouth until he died in the year
657 [1259]. He was an ascetic and religiously
observant man, and he made his living by
tailoring.
Prince Yoshmut goes to Mardin and takes
the fortress there.
When Prince Yoshmut and the commanders
were ﬁnished with Mayyafariqin, Hülägü Khan
ordered
them
to
go
together
to
conquer
Mardin. When they arrived there and laid
siege, they were bafﬂed by the height and im-
pregnability of the fortress. Uruqtu Noyan sent
an envoy to Malik Sa‘id, the lord of the
fortress of Mardin, with a message saying,
“Come down from your stronghold and gird
your loins in service to the lord of the world so
that you may retain your head and your wife
and children. ‘Be your castle strong and high,
do not pride yourself on your battlements or
the loftiness of your bastion,’ for although its
head may scrape the sky, it will be reduced to
dust by the Mongol forces. Even if fortune
smiles upon you, heed my advice. [1039] If
you do not, and if you act contrary, God the
eternal knows what will happen.”
Malik Sa‘id replied, “I entertained the notion
of surrendering and appearing at the padishah’s
court, but I cannot trust you since you made
pacts with others, and when they came out un-
der your guarantee, you killed them. Thank
God, our fortress is replete with supplies and
provisions and full of Turkish warriors and
Kurdish ﬁghters.”
Uruqtu ordered catapults placed, and battle
ensued with arrows and stones. For eight
months the ﬁght was hard fought by both sides,
and Malik Sa‘id relied on the strength of his
fortress. Since the Mongols were unable to
reduce the fortress, they plundered the city of
Mardin and the nearby Dunaysir and Arzan.1 In
the end shortages, famine, and pestilence ap-
peared inside the fortress, and every day peo-
ple were dying in droves. Malik Sa‘id also fell
ill. He had two sons. The elder was Muzaf-
faruddin, who was an intelligent young man.
He said to his father, “It would be best to go
down from the fortress since resistance to this
army is impossible.” The father refused to hear
of it. The son then gave his father medicine of
which he died, and he sent a message to Uruq-
tu, saying, “The one who opposed you is dead.
If it be ordered that the soldiers stand down
from ﬁghting, I will come down and turn over
the fortress.” Uruqtu ordered the ﬁghting to
cease, and Muzaffaruddin and his brother and
people came down.
The padishah took him to task for his father’s
murder, saying, “Has anyone ever legally taken
his father’s life?”
“I did it,” he replied, “because no matter how
much I begged and pleaded with him to surren-
der the fortress and not to spill the people’s
blood, he refused. I undertook this individual
action for the public good. I knew that eventu-
ally the fortress would be taken through the
padishah’s good fortune and a hundred [1040]
thousand innocent men would be put to death.
In any case, the sacriﬁce of one life is better
than a hundred thousand, particularly since he
was a tyrant who had killed his own son and
the people were discontent with him. I admit
my guilt. If the padishah pardons me and
1Arzan, also known as Arzan al-Rūm, is the modern
Erzurum in Turkey.
504
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

awards me my father’s place, it is his to com-
mand.” Hülägü Khan pardoned him and gave
him the realm of Mardin. 
Muzaffaruddin ruled there until 695 [1295–
96] and never rebelled against his Mongol
overlords. When he died his son Shamsuddin
Daud took his place. When he died, Muzaf-
faruddin’s other son, Sultan Najmuddin, who
was known as Malik Mansur, took his place.
He was a highly intelligent ruler with great
perspicacity, and he conducted himself with
the padishah so well that he was awarded a
parasol and a regal crown and made a peer. He
was also awarded some of the realms of Di-
yarbekir and Diyar Rabi‘a.
The death of Sultan Badruddin Lu’lu’; the
history of his son Malik Salih, who was
favorably received and then rebelled; the
destruction of Mosul.
Sultan Badruddin Lu’lu’ ruled for ﬁfty years
in great prosperity. He died in Mosul in the
year 659 [1261], when he had returned from
Hülägü Khan. He was ninety-six years old.
Hülägü Khan awarded the rule of Mosul to his
son, Malik Salih. After a time he left Mosul
and went to Syria and Egypt, where he fell
from the height of power to the depths of servi-
tude. [1041] Ruknuddin Bunduqdar patronized
him and sent him back with a thousand Kur-
dish horsemen to gather his treasuries and
buried hoards and bring them to Egypt. When
his wife, Tärkän Khatun, the daughter of Sul-
tan Jalaluddin Khwarazmshah, was apprised of
his going to Egypt and Syria, she sent a mes-
sage to Hülägü Khan’s court, and an order was
issued for the army that was in Diyarbekir to
block his path.
In the year 659 [1261] Sandaghu Noyan was
assigned to take a division of Mongol soldiers
to take Mosul and deal with Salih. On his heels
was sent Malik Sadruddin of Tabriz with a ex-
peditionary force of Tajiks. When Salih arrived
in Mosul, the Mongols blocked all roads
against him. He camped in Jusaq and started
indulging in revelry. When he was dead drunk
he heard the sound of battle drums and trum-
pets. The people of Mosul were ﬁlled with in-
describable terror, and Salih went into the city
and shut the gates. His forces consisted of
Kurds, Turcomans, and Shuls. He paid them to
encourage them to ﬁght, saying, “When Bun-
duqdar learns of this, he will send us reinforce-
ments from Egypt.”
The Mongol troops arrived and camped in
the environs of the city, throwing up a chapar
[stockade]. On both sides catapults were con-
structed, and battle began. The citizens started
ﬁghting at Salih’s word, and from both side
catapult stones and arrows rained down. A
troop of Kurds fought bravely, and for nearly a
month the furnace of war blazed hot. One day
eighty Mongol champions got up on the walls,
but the Mosulis killed them all and, embold-
ened by this victory, threw their heads from the
ramparts into the midst of the Mongol army.
During the battle Malik Sadruddin took his
helmet off, and an crossbow arrow grazed the
top of his head, causing blood to flow. [1041]
For this reason he obtained permission from
Sandaghu Noyan to go to Tabriz. He reached
Hülägü Khan’s court at Ala Tagh, where he re-
ported the struggles of the citizens of Mosul.
Another army was sent to reinforce Sandaghu.
When Bunduqdar learned of what Salih had
done, he sent Aghush Arbuzlur with troops to
assist him. When he got to Sinjar he wrote a
letter announcing his arrival, tied it to a currier
pigeon, and sent it off. The pigeon came but,
by chance, landed on the Mongols’ catapult.
The catapult engineer caught it and sent the let-
ter to Sandaghu. When he read it, he realized
that it was a sign of his good fortune and im-
mediately dispatched a division of soldiers at
the gallop to deal with him. Near Sinjar they
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWELVE: HÜLÄGÜ KHAN
505

divided into three units, laid an ambush, and
attacked the Syrians. The Syrians stood their
ground and resisted the Mongols. Suddenly a
strong wind arose and blew sand and grit into
the Syrians’ eyes, and they had to stop ﬁghting.
The Mongols attacked and killed most of them,
the rest taking ﬂight. The Mongols also put
many of the Sinjaris to death and took their
women and children captive. Then they put on
Syrian garments, let their hair down Kurdish
style, and set out for Mosul. Sandaghu was in-
formed
that
they
would
arrive
the
next
morning with the booty they had taken in their
victory. 
The next day, when they were near, the peo-
ple of the city, thinking they were Syrians
coming to help them, went out to greet them
rejoicing. The Mongol army surrounded them
on all sides and left not a single one alive.
After the battle had gone on for six months,
and the sun had entered Cancer and the weath-
er turned very hot, both sides wearied of war.
When the sun entered Leo, famine and pesti-
lence hit the city, and the people went out into
the ﬁelds from hunger, where they became
morsels for Mongol swords. [1042] Malik Sal-
ih sent a message to Sandaghu Noyan saying,
“I regret what I have done. I will come out in
order to make reparations for what has passed.
However, this is on two conditions. One is that
you not take me to task for my past offenses.
The other is that you send me to Hülägü Khan
and request that my life be spared.” Sandaghu
gave him a guarantee of safety, and he came
out bearing tuzghu and tribute. Sandaghu did
not partake of the food and did not even allow
him to come before him but put him under
guard by several Mongols.
In Ramadan 660 [July–August 1262] the city
of Mosul was taken, and those citizens who re-
mained were put to the sword. Some artisans
were taken captive, and not a soul remained in
Mosul. When the Mongols left, nearly a thou-
sand persons crept out of the mountains and
caves and assembled.
When
Sandaghu
Noyan
came
to
court,
Hülägü Khan was extremely angry with Salih
and ordered that he be covered with sheep fat,
trussed with felt and rope, and left in the sum-
mer sun. After a week, the fat got maggoty, and
they started devouring the poor man. He died
of that torture within a month. He had a three-
year-old son who was sent to Mosul, where he
was cut in two on the banks of the Tigris and
hung as an example on two sides of the city
until his remains rotted away to nothing.
Rotted and disintegrated—isn’t this enough for
you? You nurtured that lovely one with kind-
ness and then turned him over to the teeth of
maggots. [1043]
A dispute breaks out between Hülägü Khan
and Bärkä; Noqai comes hither in Bärkä’s
vanguard to do battle; he is defeated at
Derbent.
When Hülägü Khan had taken most of the
territory of the realm of Iran and taken care of
foes and opponents in every quarter, he turned
his attention to administration and matters of
state. 
He was sick and tired of Bärkä’s overbearing
demeanor. Batu had sent [Bärkä] in the compa-
ny of Mänggü Qa’an to the capital at Qaraqo-
rum to seat Mänggü on the throne among his
aqa-ini, and for a while he had been in atten-
dance upon Mänggü Qa’an’s throne. Relying
on this position, he was constantly sending
emissaries to Hülägü Khan and barking orders
on every front. Because Bärkä was an elder
relative, Hülägü Khan tolerated him, but when
his relatives Tutar, Balagha, and Quli died, his
enmity and nastiness surfaced and grew day by
day. In the end Hülägü Khan said, “Even if he
is an elder, since he knows nothing of shame or
modesty and addresses me with threats and vi-
506
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

olence, I will no longer treat him with forbear-
ance.”
When Bärkä was apprised of Hülägü’s anger,
he said, “He has destroyed all Muslim cities
and overthrown the dynasties of all the rulers
of Islam. He makes no distinction between
friend and foe. He annihilated the caliph with-
out consulting the aqa-ini. If God the eternal
assists me, I will requite of him the innocent
blood he has shed.” With this, he dispatched
Noqai, his general and a relative of Tutar’s,1
with thirty thousand horsemen in his vanguard.
Passing Derbent, they camped outside Shirvan.
[1045] When Hülägü Khan learned of their ap-
proach, he ordered troops to proceed from all
corners of Iran, and in Säkisinch Ay, corre-
sponding to the 2nd of Shawwal 660 [August
20, 1262], he ordered a march from Ala Tagh
with
Shirämün
Noyan
in
the
manqlai
[vanguard]. 
Samaghar Noyan and Abatai Noyan arrived
in Shemakha in Dhu’l-Hijja [mid-October].
Bärkä’s army attacked Shirämün and massa-
cred them. Sultanchuq they killed in the river.
On Wednesday the last day of Dhu’l-Hijja [No-
vember 15], Abatai Noyan arrived and attacked
Bärkä’s troops one league from Shabaran,
killing many of them. Noqai ﬂed. When
Hülägü Khan was apprised of the ﬂight of the
enemy, he mounted on Tuesday the 6th of
Muharram 661 [November 20] in the vicinity
of Shemakha to do battle with Bärkä. At that
stage a group of ayqaqs attacked Sayfuddin
Bitigchi, the personal vizier, Khwaja Aziz, who
was a governor of Georgia, and Khwaja Maj-
duddin of Tabriz, captured them, and took
them to Shabaran. After a trial all three were
executed.
1Noqai s/ Tatar was a first cousin to Tutar s/ Mingqa-
dur. See text p. 726 above.
On the eve of Thursday the 8th of Muharram
[November 22], Husamuddin the astrologer
was tried, and after his guilt was proven, and
on account of the möchälgä he had given in
Baghdad,2 he too was executed. Malik Sadrud-
din of Tabriz and Ali Malik, who was the gov-
ernor of Persia and part of Khurasan, both es-
caped with only a few lashes. 
On Friday the 23rd of Muharram 661 [De-
cember 7, 1262] a call for arms was given.
They arrived in Derbent on the Caspian at
sunup. There was an enemy troop on the walls
of Derbent, but they were driven away by ar-
rows from this side. The walls were taken from
the foe, and Derbent was conquered. On the
other side of Derbent they kept on ﬁghting, but
defeat ﬁnally befell the enemy. The killing
continued until the end of Saturday.
On the ﬁrst of Safar [December 15] Noqai
and his army went to crushing defeat, and
Hülägü Khan’s army was triumphant. [1046]
Abaqa Khan had been sent with a large troop
to
reinforce
them.
After
Noqai’s
defeat
Shirämün and Abatai said to him, “Let the
prince return to his father. We will go in all
haste on the heels of the foe.” In his zeal and
chivalry he gave no reply.
A command was issued on behalf of Hülägü
Khan for Elgäi Noyan, Tödä’ün Bahadur,
Salji’udai, Chaghan, Balarghu, and Doghuz to
go in pursuit of the enemy. They captured
Bärkä’s soldiers’ tents and crossed the Terek
River as ordered, where the tents of all Bärkä’s
commanders and soldiers glittered like stars in
the night. The Qipchaq Steppe was ﬁlled from
one end to the other with tents and pavilions,
horses, camels, oxen, and sheep, and not one of
the soldiers was in his tent. All had taken
ﬂight, abandoning their wives and children,
and our soldiers settled into their tents, where
2See text p. 1007 above.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWELVE: HÜLÄGÜ KHAN
507

they spent three days reveling and carousing
with lovely girls.
When Bärkä and his soldiers learned of the
fate of their tents, families, possessions, and
ﬂocks, they banded together as one and poured
from the plain like ants and locusts down on
the heads of the commanders and soldiers. On
the ﬁrst of Rabi‘ I of that year [January 13,
1263] a ﬁerce battle raged on the banks of the
Terek from dawn until the end of the day.
Since the enemy’s reinforcements kept coming
in, our soldiers turned in ﬂight. The Terek was
frozen, and they were crossing when suddenly
the ice broke and many soldiers were drowned.
Abaqa Khan reached Shabaran in safety. Bärkä
and his army withdrew to Derbent.
On the 11th of Jumada II [April 22, 1263]
Hülägü Khan reached Tabriz, crushed by this
humiliating defeat, and began to make plans
for revenge. [1047] He ordered all realms to
send weapons, and once again troops were
armed and arrayed. The next year news arrived
that Noqai was approaching, having emerged
from Derbent. Hülägü Khan sent Shaykh
Sharif Tabrizi as a spy to the mountains of
Lagzistan, but he ran into Noqai’s forces and
was captured and taken before Noqai, who
questioned him on all fronts. “What news do
you have of Hülägü?” he was asked. “Is he still
killing in his rage and wrath our nobles, digni-
taries, ascetics, religious men, and merchants
or not?” 
“Before now the padishah was enraged by
his brothers’ opposition and was ‘burning wet
and dry,’ but now ‘he is so just that ﬁre does
not burn silk and fawns drink lion’s milk. /
From his equity the people are at ease, and all
tyrants are miserably downtrodden.’ ”
Around then emissaries arrived from Cathay
to announce that Qubilai Qa’an was on the
throne and that Ariq Bökä was in obedience to
him. Alghu was dead, and Hülägü was com-
manded to rule from the Oxus to the farthest
reaches of Syria and Egypt. Thirty thousand
Mongol horsemen had been sent to reinforce
him. Noqai took fright at these words and
turned pale. Tucking his tail between his legs,
he said nothing more. Shaykh Sharif came to
Hülägü Khan’s court and reported, and Hülägü
Khan rewarded him and ﬁlled the world with
justice and equity. [1048]
The history of the end of Hülägü Khan’s
reign; Abaqa Khan is sent to Khurasan; the
provinces are transferred to the
commanders and governors; Hülägü’s
illness and death.
Hülägü Khan loved to build, and many of the
ediﬁces he had constructed still remain. He
built a palace in Ala Tagh and a temple in
Khoy. In that year he occupied himself with
construction projects and civil and military ad-
ministration. When autumn came he set out for
his winter quarters at the Zarina, which the
Mongols call both Jaghatu and Naghatu.1 He
went to Maragha, where he was insistent that
the observatory be completed. A great lover of
wisdom, he encouraged the learned to debate
the basic sciences and rewarded them all with
stipends and salaries. His court was adorned by
the presence of philosophers and scientists. He
was exceptionally fond of the science of alche-
my, and its practitioners received extraordinary
patronage from him. According to their own
delusions and fancies they lit ﬁres, burned in-
numerable potions, and spouted a lot of useless
hot air to young and old alike about making
“pots of the clay of wisdom,” but the beneﬁt of
it reached nothing but their nostrils and palates.
In transmutation they had no luck, [1049] but
1The text’sﻮــﺗﺎ ــ ــﺗﻐ(Naghatu) should probably beﻮــﺗﺎ ــ ــﯾﻐ
(Yaghatu), a normal variant of Jaghatu, although an ini-
tial j ~ n variation in Mongolian is not unknown (cf.
järgä ~ närgä).
508
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

they were miracles of cheating and fraud,
squandering and wasting the stores of the
workshops of lordly power. In supplying them,
meeting
their
demands,
and
paying
their
salaries, more was spent than Qarun made by
alchemy in his whole life.1
The entire realm of Persia, Khurasan, and
Mazanderan as far as the Oxus he turned over
to Abaqa, his eldest and best son. Arran and
Azerbaijan to the limits of the sibä2 he entrust-
ed to Yoshmut, and Diyar Rabi‘a to the banks
of the Euphrates he gave to Amir Tödä’ün.
Anatolia was given to Mu‘inuddin Parvana;
Tabriz went to Malik Sadruddin; Kirman to
Tärkän Khatun; and Fars to Amir Vangianu.
When Sayfuddin Bitigchi was martyred, Sahib
Shamsuddin Muhammad Juwayni was elevated
and promoted to the office of chief of adminis-
tration with full discretionary powers. Baghdad
he gave to Sahib Shamsuddin Muhammad’s
brother Sahib Ala’uddin Ata-Malik.
[Hülägü] reorganized the bureaucracy, de-
plored the rapacity of his greedy relatives, and
occupied himself with arranging matters to
make up for what had passed. He reorganized
the army. Jalaluddin, the son of the “Little”
Dawatdar, was elevated to a grand position and
made himself appear as the most compassion-
ate person in the whole nation in the padishah’s
eyes. He said to the padishah, “Inasmuch as an
expedition to the Qipchaq Steppe has been de-
cided, there are still in the caliph’s territory
several thousand Qipchaq Turks who know the
roads in Qipchaqbashi well. If it is so ordered,
I’ll go assemble them to be an advance front
for the war with Bärkä.”
Hülägü Khan approved this and gave him a
paiza and a decree saying, [1050] “Let the
1Qarun, whose name is derived from the Biblical Ko-
rah (Num. 26:10, e.g.), is the Islamic equivalent of Croe-
sus, whose touch turned everything to gold.
2For sibä ~ süba, see note to text p. 927.
governors of Baghdad give Jalaluddin whatev-
er gold, arms, and implements he wants, and
let no one interfere with him so that he can ex-
ecute the mission with which he is charged.”
In 662 [1264] he went to Baghdad as ordered
and got everyone he saw and liked of the offi-
cer corps. Occasionally he made hints and allu-
sions, saying, “The padishah will take you to
make you a shield against the onslaught of the
foe, and you will either die there or make a
name for yourselves. If you are not killed in
that battle, you will suffer that fate in another.
You all know what my lineage and worth are. I
am of the same race as you, and no matter how
much Hülägü Khan favors me, I will not allow
you to be ‘sword fodder.’ I am thinking of
abandoning the fortune and state of the Mon-
gols and extricating myself and you from the
Mongol yoke. You must be at one with me.”
That group was seduced by his words, and af-
ter he assembled the dispersed soldiers he
mounted with drums and banners, crossed the
Tigris at Baghdad, and attacked the Khafaja
Arabs,3 plundering a few oxen and camels. He
took from the Baghdad treasury the horses,
weapons, and money the soldiers needed and
ordered his men to decamp with their women,
children, followers, goods, and possessions.
Crossing by bridge, he said, “Let us take our
families and dependents along in order to visit
the shrines, for henceforth we will be living in
Derbent, Shirvan, and Shemakha. We soldiers
will go and get provisions for the road from the
Khafaja Arabs, who are enemies.” Then, once
he was across the Euphrates he told his sol-
diers, “I am going to Syria and Egypt. Anyone
who wants to may come with me; otherwise let
the rest turn back here.” In fear of their heads

the

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION TWELVE: HÜLÄGÜ KHAN
509

they could say nothing, and so they accompa-
nied him via Ana and Haditha [1051] heading
for Syria and Egypt. When this news reached
the padishah’s hearing, he was extremely an-
gry, for in the meantime he had been making
delicate plans for dealing with his enemies, and
now this was added to his list of worries.
When the Year of the Ox began in Rabi‘ II
663 [February 1264], Hülägü Khan spent sev-
eral days in banquets and hunting. Without
warning, after a bath, he was afﬂicted with an
illness with which he felt a heaviness in him-
self and took to bed. On the eve of Saturday
the 7th of Rabi‘ II [February 7, 1264] he took a
laxative prescribed by Cathaian physicians,
and as a result he lost consciousness and had a
heart attack. Skilled physicians tried their best
by giving him purgatives, but since the span of
his life had reached the point of death, nothing
could be done and no medicine had any effect.
Just then a comet shaped like a cone appeared.
It reappeared every night, and when it disap-
peared in [Ikindi] Ay corresponding to Sunday
eve the 19th of Rabi‘ II [February 19, 1264], he
gave up the ghost. He was forty-eight full solar
years old. His ﬁnal journey to the next world
was begun next to the Jaghatu, and Khwaja
Nasíruddin Tusi composed the following elegy
on him:
When Hülägü went from Maragha to his win-
tering place, destiny brought his life to an end.
/ The year was six hundred sixty and three, the
eve of Sunday, which was the eve of the nine-
teenth of Rabi‘ II.
His great ghoruq was made on Shahu moun-
tain, which is opposite the village of Khwara-
kan. Mourning was held in his ordus, and his
coffin was buried in the ghoruq.
On the ﬁrst day of Ikindi Ay, corresponding
to the 8th of Rabi‘ II [February 8], Arighan
Khatun, the mother of Ajai, died. [1052]
Around the same time, Amir Alghu Bitigchi
also died. On the 2nd of Shün Ay of Hükär Yil,
i. e. the ﬁrst of Ramadan 663 [June 27, 1264]
Doquz Khatun died. She had been inherited by
Hülägü Khan from Tolui Khan. Her death oc-
curred four months and eleven days after
Hülägü’s, three days before Abaqa Khan’s
accession.
May God grant many years of life and count-
less generations of prosperity to the Padishah
of Islam, Ghazan Khan. [1053]

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

❦ SECTION THIRTEEN
THE HISTORY OF HÜLÄGÜ KHAN’S SON ABAQA KHAN, IN THREE PARTS.
Part One is on his progeny with details of his
wives, sons, daughters and grandsons who
have branched off down to the present, the
names of his sons-in-law, and a genealogical
table of his sons’ branches.
Part Two is on events leading to his en-
thronement, a picture of him and his wives,
sons, grandsons, and commanders at his en-
thronement; stories of events that occurred dur-
ing his reign; battles he constantly fought and
the victories [1054] he achieved; a mention of
the rebellions and events that occurred.
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections and
were culled from various books and persons.
[1055]
Part One, on his progeny with details of his
wives, sons, daughters and grandsons who
have branched off down to the present, the
names of his sons-in-law, and a genealogical
table of his sons’ branches.
Abaqa1 Khan was the eldest and best of
Hülägü Khan’s sons. He was born of Yesünjin
Khatun of the Suldus. He had many wives and
concubines.
After his father’s death he took Öljäi Khatun.
He took Tuqtani2 Khatun as well, who had
been his father’s concubine, and installed her
in Doquz Khatun’s place. He placed a boghtaq
on her head, and she became a khatun.
1The spelling of Abaqa’s name varies, ا#ﻏﺎ ~ ا#ﻗﺎ. 
2See text p. 119 above.
The first wife he married was Dorji Khatun.
When she died he took Nuqdan Khatun of the
Tatar and installed her in [Dorji Khatun’s]
place. When she passed away, he married
Eltüzmish Khatun, daughter of Qutlugh Temür
Gürägän and sister of Taraqai Gürägän of the
Qunqirat, and installed her in her place.
After that he married Padishah Khatun,
daughter of Sultan Qutbuddin Muhammad
Khan of Kirman, and installed her in the place
of his mother, Yesünjin Khatun. [1056]
After that, he married Martai Khatun of the
Qunqirat; she was the sister of Musa Gürägän,
the son of Genghis Khan’s daughter. Musa’s
mother was also the mother of Qutui Khatun,
and they were cousins. Martai Khatun died
during Arghun Khan’s reign. Arghun Khan
placed a boghtaq on Tödäi Khatun, also of the
Qunqirat, and installed her in her place.
After that he married the senior Bulughan
Khatun, a relative of Noqai Yarghuchi’s. Since
he loved her very much, he seated her above
Martai and Täspinä. When Abaqa Khan passed
away, Arghun Khan took her, and when she
died he installed in her place the Bulughan
Khatun who is alive now.
Another wife was Täspinä Khatun, daughter
of the king of Trebzon who is called βασιλεύς.3
One of his concubines was Qaitmish Egächi.
Another was Kawkabi, the mother of Toghan-
chuq, who was the wife of Nawroz. Another
was Bulughanchin Egächi. Another was Bulu-
3Täspinä Khatun is Maria Despina, illegitimate daugh-
ter of the Byzantine Michael VIII Palaeologus.

jin Egächi. Another was Shirin Egächi, who
later became the wife of Amir Pulad. Another
was Altai Egächi. There were many others
whose names are not known. 
His sons, daughters, and sons-in-law.
Abaqa Khan had two sons, both of whom be-
came monarchs. One was Arghun Khan, whose
mother was Qaitmish Khatun. He became khan
of the age after his father’s brother. The other
was Gaikhatu Khan, who became padishah af-
ter Arghun. His mother was Nuqdan Khatun.
Their sons and grandsons will be detailed in
separate sections.
Abaqa Khan’s daughters were seven, as
follows.
The first was Yol Qutlugh. Her mother was
Tödäi Khatun. She was married to Eljitäi
Qushchi [1057] and after him to Elbasmish.
She died at Gavbari [in Arran].
The second was Taghai. Her mother was also
Tödäi. [She was married to Ahmad brother of
Qunchuqbal. After him] she was married to
Doladai Idächi. She died ___.
The third was Malika. Her mother was Bu-
lughan Khatun. She was married to Noqai
Yarghuchi’s son Toghan Buqa of the Baya’ut
tribe. She also died ___.
The fourth was Toghanchuq. Her mother was
Kawkabi Khatun. She was married to Arghun
Aqa’s son Amir Nawroz of the Oyirat tribe.
She died in 690 [1291]. 
Fifth was El Qutlugh. Her mother was Bulu-
jin Egächi, and she was married to Ghurbatai
Gürägän of the Hushin tribe.
Sixth was Öljätäi, whose mother was also
Bulujin. She was married to the son of David,
king of Georgia.
Seventh was Nujin, whose mother was Mar-
tai Khatun. [1058]
Part Two is on events leading to his
enthronement, a picture of him and his
wives, sons, grandsons, and commanders at
his enthronement; stories of events that
occurred during his reign; a mention of the
rebellions and events that occurred.
When Hülägü Khan died, the roads were
closed, as has been mentioned previously, and
a decree was issued that no one was to budge.
An emissary was immediately sent to Abaqa
Khan in Khurasan, for he was the eldest son
and the heir presumptive. Arghun Aqa, who
held the vizierate and was in attendance upon
Abaqa, was also summoned. At that time
Abaqa was in his winter quarters in Mazander-
an. Yoshmut reached Derbent and Arran, which
belonged to him, on the eighth day after his fa-
512
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ther’s death. After having taken the comman-
ders’ pulse and assessed the situation, since he
knew that he was not going to be able to effect
anything, he turned back after staying there
two days. [1059]
Abaqa arrived at the ordu on the Jaghatu in
Hükär Yil, on the 19th of Jumada I 663 [March
9, 1265], and all his relatives and the amirs
came out to greet him. Since Elgäi Noyan was
the commander of the ordus and had long been
a loyal supporter of the Ilkhan, he gave Abaqa
food and drink and then reported his father’s
death to him in private.
After the rites of mourning were held, all the
ladies, princes, sons-in-law, and amirs gathered
and discussed his accession to the throne. At
that time there were still many grand old com-
manders left like Elgäi Noyan, Su’unchaq
Noyan, Sönitäi Noyan, Samaghar Noyan, Shik-
tür Noyan, Arghun Aqa, and others it would
take too long to list. Among them, Shiktür
Noyan, to whom the Ilkhan had given his last
testament and entrusted his biligs (pronounce-
ments), and Su’unchaq Aqa gave testimony be-
fore anyone else to Abaqa’s being the heir des-
ignate and his father’s successor. He refused
and suggested his brothers. The brothers knelt
and said, “We are servants, and we consider
you our father’s successor.”
“Qubilai Qa’an is our aqa,” said Abaqa.
“How can there be a coronation without his
command?”
The princes and amirs said, “You are here,
you are the eldest of all the sons, you know
well the customs and ancient yosun and yasa,
and Hülägü Khan made you the heir designate
during his lifetime. How can anyone else ac-
cede to the throne?”
They agreed unanimously, and on Friday the
5th of Shün Ay of Hükär Yil, the Year of the
Ox, corresponding to the 3rd of Ramadan 663
[June 19, 1265], at an auspicious hour selected
by Khwaja Nasîruddin Tusi with Virgo in the
ascendant, they enthroned Abaqa Khan in
Chaghan Na’ur in the vicinity of Barahan and
observed all the customary rites and rituals.
[1060]
Abaqa Khan’s organization of the
bureaucracy and appointments in the realm.
After mounting the khan’s throne, Abaqa
Khan gave away such untold amounts of mon-
ey, jewels, and precious textiles to the ladies,
princes, and commanders that the benefits
made their way to the ordinary soldiers.
After holding congratulatory banquets, he
turned his attention to organizing the civil and
military bureaucracies. Although he possessed
the crown and throne, he sat on a chair to dis-
pense orders until emissaries arrived from
Qubilai Qa’an with a decree in his name. First
he commanded that the ordinances Hülägü
Khan had given and the decrees that had been
issued in any regard were all to be maintained
in force, immune to change or alteration. The
powerful were not to use force or coercion
with the weak, and all groups were to retain the
customs
and
habits
of
their
fathers
and
forefathers.
A week later the shah sent a decree through-
out the realm announcing his accession, and he
sent back with their hearts’ desires fulfilled the
sultans, maliks, amirs, governors, and the
needy who had come. 
First he sent his brother Yoshmut with a large
army to Derbent, Shirvan, and Mughan as far
as the Alan border to guard the area from the
enemy. Another brother, Tübshin, he sent with
a large army to Khurasan and Mazanderan as
far as the Oxus. Elgäi Noyan’s son Tughu Bit-
igchi and Su’unchaq Noyan’s brother Tödä’ün
[1061] (the grandfather of Amir Chupan and
father of Malik) he sent to Anatolia. When they
died, he sent Samaghar and Kähürgäi in their
places. He assigned Dorbai Noyan to Di-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
513

yarbekir and Diyar Rabi‘a, the border of Syria.
Georgia was assigned to Chormaqan’s son
Shirämün. The enchüs (crown lands) were
turned over to Altachu Aqa, and Baghdad and
Fars were given to Su’unchaq Aqa. Arghun
Aqa, the muqati‘-i-mamalik (assigner of fiefs),
was retained at his post. Sahib-Sa‘id Shamsud-
din Muhammad Juwayni retained the office of
vizier as before.
He made Tabriz the capital and selected Ala
Tagh1 and Siyah Koh as his summer quarters
and Arran and Baghdad as his winter quarters,
and sometimes Jaghatu. He assigned Sahib
Ala’uddin Ata-Malik in Baghdad as Amir
Su’unchaq Aqa’s deputy, and the vizierate of
Khurasan was given to Khwaja Izzuddin Tahir,
and after him to his son Khwaja Wajihuddin.
The governance of Fars was kept in the name
of Atabeg Abubakr’s sons, and the muqati‘ was
Shamsuddin Tazigu. He entrusted Kirman to
Tärkän Khatun, Tabriz to Malik Sadruddin, Di-
yarbekir to Jalaluddin Tarir and Malik Raziud-
din Baba, Isfahan and most of the province of
Persian Iraq to Khwaja Baha’uddin Muham-
mad son of Sahib-Divan Shamsuddin, Qazwin
and some of Persia to Malik Iftikharuddin
Qazwini, Diyar Rabi‘a to Malik Muzaffar
Fakhruddin Qara Arslan, Nimroz to Malik
Shamsuddin Kurt, and Georgia to David and
his son Sadun. Nearly a hundred learned men
who were students of Khwaja Nasîruddin Tusi
and in attendance at court received stipends.
That year he spent the winter in Mazanderan,
and in the spring of 663 he returned to the cap-
ital at Tabriz.2 [1062]
Abaqa Khan’s army does battle with Noqai
1The Ala Tagh meadows are northeast of Lake Van.
2Text has clearly spelled out in Arabic 663, but it must
be a mistake for 664. The spring of 663 (October 24,
1264–October 12, 1265) had already passed before he
assumed the throne.
and Bärkä and defeats them.
At the beginning of Abaqa Khan’s reign a
group of malcontents and jealous people at-
tacked this country, as Noqai set out once
again with a large army from Derbent in re-
venge for Tutar’s death. Scouts reported his
movement, and on the 4th of Altinch Ay of
Hükär Yil, corresponding to the 3rd of Shaww-
al 663 [July 19, 1265], Prince Yoshmut mount-
ed to repulse Noqai. He crossed the Kura Riv-
er, and the two armies met near Chaghan
Mürän, which is called Aq Su.3 Battle lines
were drawn, and fighting began. Many were
killed on both sides. Taghachar Aqa’s father
Qutu Buqa performed feats of bravery in that
battle until he was killed. Noqai also suffered
an arrow wound in the eye. His forces were de-
feated and withdrew to Shirvan. Abaqa Khan
crossed the Kura, while from the other side
Bärkä arrived with three hundred thousand
cavalry. Abaqa Khan recrossed the river back
to this side and camped while the bridges were
cut. On both sides of the Kura närgäs4 were
drawn and arrows were shot back and forth.
Bärkä stayed on the river’s edge for fourteen
days, but since it was impossible for him to
cross he set out for Tiflis in order to cross
there. He fell ill along the way and died. His
coffin was taken to Saray Batu and buried, and
his soldiers dispersed. 
In 664 [1265–66] Abaqa Khan ordered a sibä
[wall] built on the other side [1063] of the
Kura River from Dalan Na’ur to the Kurdaman
Steppe, which adjoins the Kura, and a deep
3The two names are synonymous: Chaghan Müran is
Mongolian and Aq Su is Turkish for “White River.” The
rivers should be the one on which is located the modern
Akhsu in Azerbaijan, just north of the Shirvan Steppe
and west of Shemakha.
4The närgä of the text is a dialect form of yärgä (~
järgä), battle or hunting circle. See Juvaini/Boyle 1:28
and Doerfer, TMEN 1:291 §161.
514
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

trench dug, and there he stationed a division of
Mongols and Muslims to keep guard. Caravans
from both sides, however, passed to and fro.
When Abaqa Khan’s mind was at ease con-
cerning Derbent, he left Prince Mänggü Temür
there with Samaghar Noyan and Öljäi Khatun,
and in the winter of 665 [1266–67] he set out
for Khurasan, wintering in Mazanderan and
Garrakan. 
Mas‘ud Beg comes to Abaqa Khan’s court;
Qutui Khatun arrives with Hülägü Khan’s
aghruq, which had been left there.
During the winter of the year mentioned
above, Mas‘ud Beg the vizier, the son of Mah-
mud Yalavach, came on an embassy from
Qaidu and Baraq to settle the accounts related
to their enchüs. When he arrived at Abaqa
Khan’s court, he donned the clothing of
Genghis Khan’s regular day guard1 and sat
above all the commanders except Elgäi Noyan.
An order was given for Khwaja Sa‘id Sham-
suddin Alakani to complete the account within
a week and turn it over. Since he had not come
with good intentions, he was anxious to return.
After a week he was favored with permission
to withdraw and set out. A day later news came
that the enemy’s army had appeared on the
banks of the Oxus. [1064] Abaqa Khan real-
ized that Mas‘ud Beg had played a trick on
him and had come as Baraq’s spy. Immediately
he dispatched envoys after Mas‘ud Beg to
bring him back, but he had taken precaution
and had arranged for post horses at every way
station. The envoys went as far as the Oxus,
1Reading, for JTAZ’sﺎق ـﻗﺮـﻳ
#وﱃ, at Doerfer’s suggestion
(TMEN 1:383 §261), either asﺎوﱃ ـﻗﺎق ـﻗﺮـﺗ, turqaq-i qavulī,
which he translates as “da saß er, weil er die Kleidung
der regelmäßigen Tagwache trug, über allen (anderen)
Emiren,” or asﺎق ــــﻗﺮ ــــﺗ
#وﱃ, turqaq ba’oli, a type of court
robe. In either case, Mas‘ud Beg was wearing some par-
ticularly significant piece of court clothing.
but they arrived just as he crossed, so they
turned back.
Abaqa Khan then set out for Khurasan and
went as far as Sarakhs,2 wintering in Mazan-
deran and that area. News of the arrival of
Hülägü Khan’s aghruq arrived, and he went
out in greeting. In the vicinity of Kabudjama,
Qutui Khatun arrived with her two sons Täk-
shin and Tägüdär, Jumghur’s sons Jüshkäb and
Kingshü, Taraghai’s son Baidu, and Abaqa
Khan’s mother Yesünjin Khatun. Their story is
as follows.
When Hülägü Khan set out for Iran he left
his aghruq with Mänggü Qa’an. Then, during
Ariq Bökä’s “disturbance,” Jumghur was with
him. When Ariq Bökä was defeated in battle
by Alghu and went to the Qa’an’s court,
Jumghur stayed behind on the pretext of being
ill and receiving treatment and took up resi-
dence there. When the news reached Hülägü
Khan in 662, he sent Abatai Noyan to summon
Jumghur and the aghruq. When Jumghur, who
was ill, died en route, Abatai Noyan left the
aghruq in the vicinity of Samarkand and re-
turned to Hülägü Khan’s court to report the sit-
uation. He was convicted of an offense and
given seventy lashes and told that he had not
guarded his charges well on the road and had
been too busy eating, drinking, and carousing
with the ladies. In short, an Indian guided
them, found a good way for them to get out,
got them across the Oxus, and delivered them
to the Kabudjama area on the 19th of Jumada I
666 [February 5, 1268]. The guide was reward-
ed and made a tarkhan. In the vicinity of
Badakhshan, Qutui Khatun was told of Hülägü
Khan’s death, and she cried her eyes out.
Abaqa Khan rejoiced over their arrival and en-
riched them with money and goods. A concu-
2The modern Sarakhs/Serakhs on the Iran–Turk-
menistan border.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
515

bine named Arighan [1065] had come to
Hülägü Khan’s service from Qutui Khatun’s
ordu, and Qutui Khatun’s share of booty and
plunder had been turned over to her. She had
accumulated vast amounts of valuable items
and property, so when Qutui Khatun arrived in
the ordu she found it well stocked with all sorts
of things. 
Abaqa Khan assigned her a tonluq (stipend)
from Diyarbekir, Mayyafariqin, and several
other
places,
which
amounted
to
nearly
100,000 gold dinars every year, and from time
to time he gave her grand entertainments as a
show of concern.
That spring he returned from Khurasan and
spent the next winter at the Jaghatu. That sum-
mer he went to Ala Tagh and Siyah Koh. The
next winter he was in Arran, and during the
summer of 668 [1270] he mounted an expedi-
tion against Baraq.
Baraq comes from Transoxiana to
Khurasan and does battle with Abaqa
Khan’s army; he is defeated and withdraws
in rout.
When Baraq overthrew Mubarakshah and
took control of the Ulus Chaghatai, he adopted
an aggressive and expansionist attitude. Qaidu
tried to keep him from acting in that manner,
but they had a falling-out for that reason.
While a man named Mogholtai was shahna of
Turkistan on the Qa’an’s behalf, Baraq sent
Amir Begmish to take his place. Mogholtai
went to the Qa’an to report the situation. The
Qa’an sent a great commander, Qoyunchi by
name, with six thousand horsemen to wipe out
Begmish and retake the office of shahna.
Baraq sent out an amir [1066] with thirty thou-
sand men to repel the attack. When Qoyunchi
realized that he could not offer resistance, he
went back to Cathay. Baraq’s army raided
Khotan. 
When Baraq was completely in control, he
set out to attack Qaidu and Mänggü Temür.
Mas‘ud Beg reported his aggression to them
and urged them to go to battle with him. In the
end the armies met on the banks of the
Jaxartes. Baraq had laid an ambush and defeat-
ed Qaidu’s and Qipchaq’s army by a ruse,
killing and taking captive many of them and
taking much plunder. He then became overly
bold, and his pride and conceit increased.
When the news of Qaidu’s and Qipchaq’s de-
feat reached Mänggü Temür, he grew angry
and sent his uncle Bärkächär with fifty thou-
sand horsemen to reinforce Qaidu. He assem-
bled his dispersed soldiers and did battle with
Baraq, defeating him and putting him and his
men to rout. Many of his army were killed and
wounded.
Totally undone, Baraq went to Transoxiana,
where he reassembled his dispersed army and
took counsel with the amirs. “With this group
around who are out to attack us,” he said, “my
kingship will not be stable. The best thing for
us to do now is to destroy these rich provinces
through pillage and plunder, beginning with
Samarkand.” The amirs were delighted by
these words.
When
Qaidu,
Qipchaq,
and
Bärkächär
learned of the situation, they discussed the ad-
visability of going after him and chasing him
from the territory. “When he becomes aware of
this,” said Qaidu, “he will plunder even more.
If we send an envoy to advise him and ask for
a truce, it would be better.”
“The bonds of friendship between him and
me are firm,” said Qipchaq. “If permitted, let
me go and win him over with sweet words.”
Knowing how persuasive and eloquent Qip-
chaq could be, they sent him to Samarkand
with two hundred select horsemen. [1067] He
516
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

camped in Sughd1 and sent a cavalryman to
Baraq to announce his arrival and start peace
talks.
When the message reached Baraq, he con-
templated it for a while and then said to his
amirs, “It is not obvious what hostility is con-
cealed beneath this ‘peace.’ ” Then, to the en-
voy he said, “Tell Qipchaq I asked about him,
and tell him to come as soon as possible, for I
will be delighted to see him again.” Then he
ordered the court tent decorated and armed sol-
diers lined up at the gate, and he mounted the
throne as potentates do. When Qipchaq came
in, Baraq got down from the throne and greet-
ed him warmly and with honor. They embraced
each other, and Baraq took Qipchaq by the
hand and led him onto the throne, where they
offered each other goblets. Baraq conversed
with him warmly and said, “What could be
better than to meet friends and relatives with
whom one is united?”
Qipchaq began to speak of peace, friendship,
and kinship. 
“Well you say,” said Baraq. “From time to
time I think of the necessity of maintaining
these ties and am ashamed of my actions, for
we are all cousins. Our dear departed fathers
seized the world by dint of the sword and be-
queathed it to us. Why don’t we now enjoy the
world in friendship? Why should there be sedi-
tion and strife among us? Our other princely
relatives possess great cities and happy grazing
grounds. I have nothing but this miserable little
ulus, and yet for the sake of this realm Qaidu
and Mänggü Temür have risen up to attack me
and make me run around the world in distress.”
“Bravo,” said Qipchaq. “You have spoken
well, [1068] but it would be better for us not to
dwell on the past. Let’s hold a quriltai together
and cleanse our breasts of old hatreds. Let us
1Sughd, an agricultural suburb of Samarkand.
get past petulance and obstinance and make a
pact with each other that we will be united and
never oppose each other under any circum-
stances.”
Since Baraq had been worn down by so
much running around he assented to a truce,
and one week later Qipchaq withdrew with
permission. Qaidu and Bärkächär also agreed
to the truce with Baraq and praised Qipchaq. 
In the spring of 667 [1269] the princes as-
sembled in the meadow of Talas and Kanjak,
and on the eighth day, after a week of ban-
quets, they held a council and quriltai. First
Qaidu said, “Our dear departed grandfather
Genghis Khan seized the world through his
strategy and tactics by sword and arrow, and he
put it in order, made it ready, and left it to his
progeny. If now we consider our fathers’ sides,
we are all kin, and there are the other princes,
our aqa-inis, among whom there is no conﬂict.
Why should there be among us?”
“That is exactly how it is,” said Baraq, “but I
too am a fruit of this tree. I too should have an
assigned yurt and livelihood. Chaghatai and
Ögödäi were Genghis Khan’s sons. Qaidu is
descended from Ögödäi Qa’an; I am descended
from Chaghatai. Bärkächär and Mänggü Temür
are descended from Jochi, who was the eldest
brother. Qubilai Qa’an is descended from
Tolui, who was the youngest brother, and he
now holds the east and the realms of Cathay
and Machin, the length and breadth of which
