only God knows. The west from the banks of
the Oxus to the farthest reaches of Syria and
Egypt are held by Abaqa and his brothers as
enchü from their father. Between these two
uluses [1069] lies the territory of Turkistan and
Qipchaqbashi, which is under your control.
With all this, you attack me. As far as I can
tell, I don’t think I have committed any
offense.”
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
517

“You are right,” they said. “Henceforth we
will not remember the past. We will divide the
summer and winter yurts equitably and dwell
in the mountains and plains, for this territory is
devastated and uncultivated.” With that, they
decided that two thirds of Transoxiana would
be Baraq’s and one third Qaidu’s and Mänggü
Temür’s. They put this to Mänggü Temür, and
he agreed to the settlement.
The seal to their agreement was to be that in
the spring Baraq would cross the Oxus and
lead his army to Iran to take some of Abaqa
Khan’s territory in order to expand his grazing
grounds and land for his army. “If you consent
to this,” said Baraq, “let us take an oath and
make a binding pact.” As was their custom
they swore an oath on gold and stipulated that
henceforth they would dwell in the mountains
and plains and not hang around cities, or graze
their animals in cultivated areas, or make ex-
orbitant demands on the peasants. Breaking
camp, each one went off to his own yurt.
For a time Baraq kept his promise and stuck
to the terms of the treaty. At the princes’ sug-
gestion, he sent Mas‘ud Beg to the provinces
to win over the peasantry and restore the towns
and villages to habitation and agriculture.
Mas‘ud Beg reassembled the peasants who had
run way, and, with his expertise, he put the ad-
ministration of Transoxiana back on the good
footing it had been on before.
Once again Baraq began to engage in aggres-
sive expansion by making exactions and de-
mands on the people, rustling all the ﬂocks and
herds of Transoxiana, and tyrannically seizing
people’s
property
and
possessions.
[1070]
When he decided to go to Iran, Mas‘ud Beg
said, “It would be unwise to undertake this ac-
tion, for if that territory is not conquered, it
will be impossible to return to this land.”
Baraq abandoned that idea.
In 666 [1267–68] Abaqa Khan was occupied
with dispensing justice and equity in Iran.
Prince Negüdär Oghul, the son of Chaghatai’s
son Mochi Yäbä, was in attendance with a di-
vision of soldiers, and Abaqa Khan held him in
great honor and esteem. Baraq sent a group of
envoys to Abaqa Khan, and with them he also
sent beläg [gifts] for Negüdär Oghul. Among
the gifts was an arrow of the type the Mongols
call toghana. When they gave it to him they
made an extremely discreet motion to indicate
that there was something in the arrow. He split
it open in private, and in the middle of the ar-
row he found a letter containing the following
message: “Let Negüdär Aqa know that I have
assembled a huge army and am going to attack
Abaqa’s territory. It is expected that when he
mounts to repel us, you will not go with him.
Make it so that he will not be able to face us
and so that we can get hold of his land any way
possible.” 
When Negüdär was apprised of the contents
of this letter, he asked for permission to go
home to Georgia. He received permission and
left. There he placed this secret proposition be-
fore his amirs. 
Day after day envoys arrived from Khurasan
giving information on Baraq. Abaqa Khan, oc-
cupied with important affairs connected to the
military and the ulus, summoned Negüdär
Oghul for consultation and sent several envoys
to ask him to come. Each time he used some
excuse not to come. “I am resolved,” he told
his amirs, “to go via Derbent and join Baraq.”
So saying, he set out immediately in that direc-
tion. Shirämün Noyan, who was in that area,
set out with his army on his heels and sent Ali-
naq in the vanguard. [1071] After them he sent
Abatai Noyan with another division. The two
armies chanced to meet atop a hill. Negüdär
ﬂed without a fight and headed for Derbent.
When the others took to the road he was forced
518
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

to turn his reins toward the mountains of Geor-
gia, where he went into a forest and got lost.
The Georgian amirs surrounded the forest, and
King David sent him a message saying, “There
is no way out of this forest. Turn back and
don’t distress yourself.” At his advice he came
out of the forest. Shirämün and his army came
upon him and killed many of his soldiers and
took others captive. In the end, in Ramadan
668 [April–May 1270] they forced Negüdär [to
surrender], and in Rabi‘ I of that year [Octo-
ber–November
1270]
he
came
to
Abaqa
Khan’s court with his wife and children. In his
infinite mercy the padishah spared his life, but
he had the six amirs who had shared his secrets
executed. His army was divided into units of
hundreds and tens, and fifty Mongols were set
as guards over him. He was imprisoned at the
river called Kabudan, but a year later, when
Baraq was defeated, he was freed. He used to
come and go to the ordu until he died.
In his boldness and conceit, Baraq sent a
message to Tübshin Oghul saying, “On both
sides the path of kinship is trod. The meadows
of Badghis as far as the gates of Ghaznin and
the banks of the Indus River were our fathers’
and forefathers’ grazing grounds. You must va-
cate Badghis so that our retinue may encamp
there.”
Tübshin replied, saying, “These territories
belong to my elder brother Abaqa Khan, who
is the khan of the land of Iran. He has awarded
them to me. Baraq Aqa must not speak such
nonsense, and he should mind his station.” He
sent a messenger to Abaqa Khan informing
him of the situation. In reply Abaqa Khan said,
“This land came to us by inheritance from our
dear departed father [1072] and is our enchü.
Today we hold it by the sword. If Baraq attacks
us, we also stand ready to repel him. If he takes
the path of agreement and truce, we will also
tread the path of unity and kinship.”
When Baraq heard this message, he ﬂared up
in anger, ordered the army assembled, and set
out for Khurasan in all preparedness. When he
was about to cross the Oxus he sent an envoy
to Qaidu requesting reinforcements in accor-
dance with their prior agreement. After con-
sulting
with
his
amirs
Qaidu
dispatched
Qipchaq Oghul, the son of Ögödäi’s son
Qada’an, and Chabat Oghul, the son of Güyük
Khan’s son Hoqu, with their personal troops,
saying to them, “When Baraq crosses the
Oxus, Tübshin Oghul will of course hasten to
do battle with him. When that happens, you
find some excuse to turn back, for Abaqa Khan
will soon come to repulse Baraq with an army
no mountain would be able to resist.” 
When they came before Baraq they consulted
in private. Malik Shamsuddin Kurt joined
them, and he reinforced ten times over what
they had been thinking about. Baraq ordered
all the animals rustled from the provinces that
belonged to Qubilai Qa’an and Abaqa Khan,
and they did not leave even plow oxen. They
built bridges over the Oxus. In his own place
he stationed his son Beg Temür with ten thou-
sand horsemen in Kish and Nakhshab,1 and he
crossed
the
river.
When
he
arrived
in
Maruchuq2 in the year 668 [1270], Prince Tüb-
shin was waiting for him. He and his amirs, to-
gether with Arghun Aqa, went out to battle
Baraq. There was a commander of a thousand
named Sächäktü of a (h)uja’ur [tribal branch]
that was attached to Qipchaq. When he heard
that Qipchaq had come, he turned back and
joined Baraq, saying, “My huja’ur belongs to
Qipchaq.” [1073] He was taken before him,
and he presented as tägishmishi the fine Arabi-
an horses.
1Kish and Nakhshab, both former names of the mod-
ern Shahrisabz and Karshi respectively in Uzbekistan.
2Maruchuq is the modern Maruchak in Afghanistan.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
519

In short, Tübshin Oghul went to Mazanderan
and sent messengers to Abaqa Khan’s court to
inform him of Baraq’s arrival. Arghun Aqa got
busy arranging the army, and they waited for
the arrival of Abaqa Khan’s banners.
On the other side, Qipchaq ordered Sächäktü
to present several horses to Baraq. The next
day in Baraq’s camp Amir Jalayirtai said to
Qipchaq, “Has Baraq come with several thou-
sand soldiers to wield the sword on your
behalf?”
“Speak politely,” replied Qipchaq. “What has
happened?”
“If Sächäktü is attached to you,” he said,
“why has he not come to you for so long? To-
day he has come in support of Baraq and you
have taken the fine horses that were worthy of
Baraq, and you have ordered those that were
suitable for you given to Baraq.” 
Qipchaq said, “Who are you to interfere be-
tween aqa and ini?”
“I am not your slave,” said Jalayirtai, “that
you can ask me who I am. I am the slave of
Shah Baraq.”
“Since when does a commoner dare to bandy
words with Genghis Khan’s offspring?” said
Qipchaq. “Since when does a dog like you an-
swer me impolitely?”
“If I am a dog,” he replied, “I am Baraq’s
dog, not yours. Have some respect for yourself
and mind your own business.”
Qipchaq’s zeal was stirred, and he said, “You
dare to answer me impudently! I’ll cut you in
two, and what will Baraq Aqa say to me on
your account?”
Jalayirtai put his hand to his dagger and said,
“If you strike me with your sword, I’ll slit your
belly open with my knife.”
Qipchaq was highly offended, but Baraq said
nothing. Realizing that Baraq was taking
Jalayirtai’s part, Qipchaq left in high dudgeon,
crossing under the bridge at Maruchuq, where
Baraq’s camp was, and went home to his yurt,
which was about three leagues away. When he
related the incident to his amirs, they all got
angry. That night he and group of his intimates
[1074] mounted, ostensibly to go hunting.
Worried that Baraq would attack his aghruq
when he went, he left his tent where it was and
set out with two thousand horsemen. His wife,
Bai, also sent a man to Baraq that night to say,
“Qipchaq has left with his soldiers because of
the offense Jalayirtai has given. It is not known
in what direction he is heading.”
Baraq became anxious over this news, and
the people of his camp worried that a surprise
attack might be made. Baraq ordered his sol-
diers assembled, and in the morning he ordered
his brothers Mu’min and Yasa’ur and Abachi1
Bitigchi to go in all haste after Qipchaq. When
they found him, if he listened to reason and
turned back, well and good; otherwise, they
were to capture him on any pretext and hold
him until Jalayirtai and his three thousand cav-
alry got there to bring him back by force. The
three set out, and Jalayirtai followed them with
three thousand horsemen at a distance of less
than a league.
Qipchaq rode ten leagues that night, and the
next morning he dismounted and left his horses
to graze. When he had eaten he remounted, but
he was worried by Baraq’s troops and said, “If
we go fast, the horses will tire. We’ll have to
travel slowly.” 
The second day they were approaching Merv
when a messenger came to say, “We come
from Baraq Aqa. Stop for a moment so that we
can deliver his message. Afterwards you can
do as you like.” 
1The name may be Ayachi. Both Abachi and Ayachi
are Mongolian names, and both occur as variants of this
person’s name through this section.
520
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

“I have no quarrel with Baraq Aqa or with
you,” Qipchaq said in reply. “I could not toler-
ate the words of a commoner. As I have come I
will return with my soldiers and go before
Qaidu Aqa. You need not trouble yourself. You
turn back, for I am certainly leaving.”
Just then Mu’min, Yasa’ur, and Abachi
arrived. They all embraced, [1075] wept, and
said, “Baraq Aqa sent us [to say to you,]
‘Qaidu sent you and Chabat to help me. With-
out having heard anything from me that would
cause anyone distress, you had words with
Jalayirtai and then left in anger without having
heard a reply from me. I was going to chastise
him the next day, but then I heard you had got-
ten angry and left. You must return, and I will
requite Jalayirtai however you want.”
Qipchaq replied, “I’m not a child you can de-
ceive with sweet talk. I came at Qaidu’s order.
Since you don’t want me, I’m going home, but
I’m leaving my camp and followers here for
you to send in safety after me. If you don’t, I’ll
take your followers captive in their stead.” 
When they realized that he would not go
back with them, they said, “Since you are go-
ing, we have bit of wine. Let’s have a cup, and
then we’ll turn back.”
“Wine is drunk in times of happiness,” he
said. “The army is coming right now on your
heels. You just want to distract me with wine
until they get here. It would be better for you
to turn back; otherwise I’ll take you with me,
and even if all Baraq’s soldiers come after me,
they won’t be able to turn me back.” When he
began to be rough with them, they started wor-
rying that the army would appear and he would
take them prisoner. Therefore they stopped
talking and turned back.
Qipchaq rode in all haste until he entered the
Amuya
desert.
Jalayirtai
caught
up
with
Mu’min and Yasa’ur in the evening, and they
reported what had happened. Jalayirtai wanted
to go after Qipchaq, but they said, “Qipchaq
will have entered the desert. Even if you catch
up with him, you won’t be able to do any-
thing.”
Therefore,
to
preserve
his
honor
Jalayirtai turned back, accompanied by them.
[1076] When they reached the edge of the
desert, Qipchaq had already gone ahead, and
since their soldiers were not prepared, they all
turned back together and went to report to
Baraq. 
Baraq sent Qipchaq’s followers off in safety,
and when Qipchaq heard this, he did nothing to
their people. However, he seized Mas‘ud Beg’s
sons and subjected them to harassment. Then
he sent a message to Abaqa Khan informing
him of his return. 
After that, friendship existed between Abaqa
Khan and Qaidu, and they called each other or-
taq [partner]. When Qipchaq reached the bor-
ders of Bukhara, Baraq’s son Beg Temür
Oghul sent him a message from Kish and
Nakhshab saying, “I would be delighted to see
you.” Qipchaq paid no attention and passed on.
When he came before Qaidu, he rejoiced and
showed him favor.
After Qipchaq left, Baraq kept Chabat, who
waited for an opportunity until Baraq went to
Herat, and then he and his soldiers ﬂed. Two
days later Baraq learned of it and took council
with his amirs, who said, “We have come to
Khurasan to wage war, and we still haven’t en-
gaged the enemy. Whether we go after him or
whether we send soldiers, he won’t turn back
and will certainly stand in battle. Soldiers on
both sides will be killed, and we’ll have a bone
to pick with Qaidu. Qipchaq and Chabat left of
their own accord. Let’s send a messenger to
Qaidu saying, ‘You sent them to us to help us
in time of battle with the enemy, but before
they ever saw the foe they altered your decree
and pulled back of their own accord. Let Qaidu
take them to task.’ ” Thus they sent envoys off.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
521

When
Chabat
reached
the
borders
of
Bukhara, he stopped for a few days on the
banks of the Haramkan canal. The amirs of
Bukhara went with Tazik Aqa [1077] to Beg
Temür Oghul to inform him of Chabat’s
arrival. Beg Temür said to Tazik Aqa, “You and
five hundred renowned horsemen were not
able to repulse him?”
“Chabat is urugh.” said Tazik. “How could a
commoner like me do battle with him?”
Beg Temür mounted and made a surprise at-
tack on Chabat, who ﬂed with ten men. He de-
stroyed the Haramkan bridge, but the rest of
his soldiers were killed. Beg Temür’s army
went in pursuit for thirty leagues but couldn’t
catch up with him. Baraq took Qipchaq’s and
Chabat’s ﬂight as a good omen. He divided the
meadows among the soldiers and ordered them
not to ride their horses but to let them rest until
they got fat, and he ordered the soldiers to oc-
cupy themselves with banquets and revelry to
regain their strength. [In the meantime they
can] travel by oxen and donkey. To Yasa’ur he
gave Badghis in Herat as a grazing ground, and
he had Margha’ul, who was the mainstay of
that army, ride with a troop to Nishapur and
Tus, for he was a warrior who knew the roads
and would be the vanguard in the expedition to
Persia. Baraq himself stayed in Taligan.
On Monday the 26th of Ramadan 668 [May
19, 1270] Baraq’s army fell upon Nishapur,
killing and pillaging. The next day they left.
Baraq assigned an amir to stage massacre
and pillage in Herat, but Qutlugh Temür said,
“This is far from the right thing to do, for Ma-
lik Shamsuddin Kurt, the governor there, will
rebel, and his complaint will cause the great
ones of Iran to hate us. Let me go first and
bring him.” Baraq approved and sent him with
five hundred horsemen to bring him. When he
reached Herat, Malik Shamsuddin came out in
greeting laden with gifts and offered food and
tribute. Qutlugh Temür went before Malik
Shamsuddin Kurt in the Khaysar fortress and
delivered Baraq’s message, “We have come
and taken Khurasan. We intend to take Persia,
[1078] Azerbaijan, and Baghdad too. If you
undertake to render service, you will receive
our favor, and we will reward you with all the
realms of Khurasan.”
“We hear and obey,” said the malik. Two
days later he set out in the company of Qutlugh
Temür and went to Baraq, where he saw an
army whose “breasts were filled with ven-
geance” and whose every word was of audaci-
ty and bravery and the killing and plunder they
would wreak on Tabriz and Baghdad. He was
struck dumb by their awesomeness. Baraq sin-
gled him out for much favor and said, “I award
you the realm of Khurasan, and I will turn over
to you whatever I conquer henceforth.” Imme-
diately he asked him which the richest men in
Khurasan were so that he could have their
names recorded. Malik Shamsuddin Kurt was
an extremely intelligent and clever man, and he
knew that this would mean Baraq’s downfall. 
In short, Baraq made a group of Mongols
liege men to Malik Shamsuddin and ordered
him to take tribute, arms, and animals from the
wealthy of Herat. The malik was given permis-
sion to withdraw. 
The people of the city came out to greet him
upon his return, and he reported what Baraq
had ordered. At that point everyone abandoned
hope of life and property.
Meanwhile, news arrived from Persia that
Abaqa Khan was coming with a huge army.
The malik went into the citadel and waited
confidently for the arrival of Abaqa Khan’s
army. 
From this side Abaqa Khan marched with all
his brothers except Tübshin and with his com-
manders, ministers, and innumerable soldiers
for Persia and Khurasan, setting forth from
522
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Azerbaijan on Sunday the 4th of Ramadan 668
[April 27, 1270] in Yunt Yil. At that time the
crops had sprouted, but in his perfect justice he
decreed that no creature was to damage a sin-
gle stalk. When he reached Sharuyaz, which is
now called Qonqur Öläng,1 an envoy, [1079]
Täkächäk by name, arrived. This Täkächäk had
been seized and held under arrest by Baraq as
he was coming from Qubilai Qa’an’s court to
Abaqa Khan, but he had found an opportunity
to escape and join the court, where he reported
on Baraq exactly as the situation was, i.e. he
described Baraq’s men as perpetually drunk
and engaged in frivolity. Their horses had got-
ten qadaq (useless), and Baraq was unaware of
the incident with Negüdär Oghul. Abaqa Khan
speeded up the pace, and when he passed by
Rayy, Prince Tübshin and Arghun Aqa came
out to greet him, joining him in Qumis. Sultan
Hajjaj of Kirman also accompanied them.
Abaqa Khan rewarded them all and singled
them out for favor. Prince Arghun also kissed
the royal hand there and was rewarded. From
there they proceeded to the meadows of Rad-
kan, and there he gave the soldiers much mon-
ey, and he honored the commanders and won
them over with promises.
From there they went to Bakharz. Quburtu
Bahadur was sent out to reconnoiter, but he
could not get near and had to return. The next
time Topchaq Bahadur and Negübäi Bahadur
were sent from the station at Faryab with a
hundred horsemen. They showed themselves
[to the enemy,] who lit out after them to keep
them from returning, but they attacked them,
killed many, and managed to return safely to
report what they had learned. 
Abaqa Khan was occupied with administra-
tive matters having to do with the soldiers that
1Originally called Sharūyāz and renamed Qonqur (~
Qonghur) Öläng, this place later became Sulṭāniyya.
were his in his aqa-inis’ charge. He sent Yosh-
mut Oghul to the left wing; he stationed Abatai
Noyan in the center; he dispatched Prince Tüb-
shin to the bridge at Chaghcharan, which was
Margha’ul’s yurt. When he got there he at-
tacked Margha’ul’s scouts and killed some. He
also plundered his baggage. Margha’ul went to
Baraq to report the arrival of the army. Baraq
said, “If Tübshin and Arghun Aqa have come
back to battle, they are the very ones I’ve had
experience with before. [1080] If it’s Abaqa,
that’s a different story. You go and block their
way until we array the army.” 
Abaqa Khan headed for the saints’ shrines
and asked the Creator for assistance. When he
got to Badghis he sent a clever and eloquent
emissary to Baraq to say, “We have come to
Khurasan from Persia to save you the trouble
and bother of traveling. Know for certain that
the kingdom of this world cannot be gained
through tyranny and oppression, only through
placating and maintaining the peasantry and
observing the strictures of divine command-
ments. An intelligent man will consider it nec-
essary to avoid and shun anything the end of
which is grave, while you ‘cast fire and burned
cities: from whom did you learn to hold the
world?’ Nonetheless, if you do not want there
to be contention and struggle between us, then
choose one of three things. First, truce: I will
give you from Ghaznin and Karman …niyan to
the banks of the River Indus. Second, return in
felicity to your country and region, and do not
allow yourself to think of the impossible.
Third, get ready for battle. ‘Either the shining
sword that is defiled by blood, or the fire of
good fortune that rises.’ ” 
Baraq thought about it for a while. Then he
said to his commanders, “ ‘Three roads has he
threateningly placed before me. See what ad-
vice this vengeful one gives.’ Which of these
three would you choose?”
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
523

Yasa’ur, who was the best of the comman-
ders in strategy and tactics, [1081] said, “The
best thing to do would be to make a truce, for
Qipchaq and Chabat have turned back. Our
horses are useless while theirs are ready. Let us
go to Ghaznin and spend a year or two there.
We will suffer no disgrace by abandoning war,
for Abaqa Khan is a mighty monarch, and a
truce with him would be a source of pride for
us. Many other things can be requested from
him, and he will grant them all.”
Margha’ul got angry at those words and said,
“One should not be pessimistic in the presence
of kings or allow oneself to fear. Where is
Abaqa Khan? He has taken his army to Egypt
and Syria. Tübshin Oghul and Arghun Aqa
have fabricated all this and let out a rumor that
he is on his way here.”
Jalayirtai said, “We’ve come to do battle. If
you wanted to make peace, it would have been
better to do it in Transoxiana.”
Baraq agreed with Margha’ul and Jalayirtai,
and they agreed to do battle. An astrologer
named Jalal was with him, and he asked him to
cast a horoscope to choose a good hour.
“If you stop for a month it will be better for
you,” he reported.
It did not suit Baraq to stop, and Jalayirtai
ﬂew into a rage, saying, “What importance do
good and evil portents in the stars have—par-
ticularly when a powerful enemy is near?”
Margha’ul expressed the same sentiment,
and then they concluded that they would fight.
Spies were sent out to find out whether Abaqa
Khan was really coming or not.
Back on our side, the grazing grounds in
Badghis in Herat were becoming too small for
the animals, and Abaqa Khan said to his com-
manders, “Baraq came hot to conquer Persia,
but in the face of opposition and resistance he
quickly cooled down. He has neither an inten-
tion to make peace nor the heart for battle.”
Abaqa Khan had ordered Herat plundered,
[1082] but he had mercy on the people and re-
scinded his order, for which the Heratis lifted
their hands in supplication and asked God to
give him victory.
He assigned Amir Toghuz to select a good
site for battle. Toghuz chose an expansive plain
on the skirt of the mountains, in front of which
was a river the Mongols call Qara Su. There he
found three spies he seized and took to Abaqa
Khan. He ordered them tied to tent poles and
questioned with threats of violence. One said,
“I will tell you anything you want to know.
Baraq has no idea that Abaqa Khan has come.
The commanders have doubts. Some say Tüb-
shin and Arghun Aqa have assembled an army
and put forth a rumor that Abaqa Khan has
come. He sent us to find out and take word
back to him.” 
When Abaqa Khan learned of their situation,
he thought for a while and came up with an in-
genious plan. He went out of the pavilion and
summoned a very competent and eloquent
Mongol and hatched a plot with him that he
would run into the court like a courier and re-
peat the words Abaqa taught him. After a while
Abaqa went back in and sat on his throne as
usual, enjoying himself with his commanders.
When two hours of the night had passed and
the padishah and commanders were talking
about Baraq, the Mongol with whom he had
conspired came in wearing his arms, kissed the
ground, and said, “Three months ago the
padishah left his camps. Since then enemies
and rebels have risen up all over the country,
and soldiers have poured in from the Qipchaq
Gates like ants and locusts, looting the com-
manders’ camps and tents. They have killed
and pillaged so much in that area that nothing
is left, and everywhere from Derbent to Arme-
nia and Diyarbekir is covered with foreign
armies. [1083] If you don’t hasten to return,
524
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

you won’t find your camps or people.” When
the commanders heard this, they went to pieces
worrying over their homes and children.
“We have done a good piece of work,” said
Abaqa Khan. “We have saved Herat from one
foe, but we have left our own territory, sub-
jects, and camps at the mercy of another. We
should turn back tonight to find our wives and
children, and when we have finished that, we
can come back here to deal with Baraq.” Im-
mediately the drums were sounded and they
decamped in the direction of Mazanderan to
reach Tabriz in ten days. The whole plain was
full of tents and pavilions, which they left just
as they were. In front of the assembled crowd
Abaqa Khan ordered an amir to kill the three
spies, but in secret he told him to kill only two
of them and to let the third one escape, and that
order was carried out. 
They decamped from there, and the next day
they stopped in the Jina plain, which had been
chosen for battle. Abaqa Khan sent a messen-
ger to the city of Herat to Qazi Shamsuddin
Babari, saying, “The imperial order is that you
not go out tomorrow to greet Baraq, and do not
open
the
gates. Thus
we
will test
your
allegiance.”
The spy who had been allowed to escape got
hold of a horse and ﬂed, so happy he could
scarcely contain himself. He strutted into
Baraq’s court and informed him of Abaqa
Khan’s situation. In a comical manner he re-
counted how he had escaped, taken a horse,
and come, and then he added, “At present there
is nothing in the plain but tents, pavilions,
robes, hats, and belts.” Baraq rejoiced and
laughed, saying to himself, [1084] “ ‘Is what I
see real, O Lord, or is it a dream?’ ” Then he
asked the spy about the commanders’ and sol-
diers’ bravery and might.
“They have many weapons and animals,” he
said, “but there is not much bravery among the
commanders.” Baraq was heartened by this.
Margha’ul and Jalayirtai hastened to offer him
felicitations, and king and army congratulated
each other on their upcoming victory.
The next morning they all mounted together
in a show of magnificence that caused moun-
tain and plain to tremble. When they were near
Herat, Amir Mas‘ud Beg and several others
rode forward and found the gates closed. He
called for the governor of Herat, Qazi Sham-
suddin Babari, who appeared and bowed low
to the amir from the wall.
“What’s the reason for closing the gates?”
asked the amir.
“When Abaqa Khan departed,” the cadi said,
“he turned the city over and said we were not
to open the gates to the enemy. He made us
swear not to do it. You know, my lord, that to
break an oath is a vile thing to do, and a traitor
is punishable in both this world and the next.”
“It’s in your best interests to open the city
gate,” the amir said. “Come out and offer what
you have to the soldiers and tell them how
weak and pitiful you are. Otherwise I fear what
the outcome of this audacity may be. I would
not like to see you wounded by these vengeful
warriors, for then it will be too late for
regrets.”
They refused, and Mas‘ud Beg returned to
inform Baraq of the rebellion on the part of the
citizens of Herat. Baraq ﬂew into a rage, but he
was so happy that Abaqa Khan’s army had tak-
en ﬂight that attached little importance to it.
When they crossed the Herat River, they
found the whole plain full of [1085] tents and
pavilions and rejoiced, pillaged everything,
and then camped south of Herat. They spent
that day in revelry. The next morning at dawn
they mounted, and when they had gone two
leagues they found an endless plain, like a
shoreless sea churning with soldiers. Baraq’s
joy turned to dismay, and he made camp next
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
525

to the Herat River on the banks of the Qara Su
near the bridge.
After Baraq camped, Abaqa Khan summoned
his commanders and said, “I have trapped
Baraq with cunning and ruse. Now you must
go into the battlefield united and as one for the
sake of your lives and those of your wives and
children, and for the sake of your good name
and reputation and in gratitude for the good
things our fathers and forefathers have done.
Get all doubts and hesitation out of your
minds, and strive mightily, for to die in battle
with a good name is better than to suffer the
taunts and reproaches of the enemy. I trust in
God that when we go together to battle Baraq,
we will vanquish him and return triumphant
and victorious.” 
When the padishah had finished speaking, of
one accord a cry arose, “ ‘You are the prince,
and we are slaves. We are proud to do your
bidding.’ ” And all mounted in unison and co-
operation and headed out to the battlefield.
Abaqa Khan entrusted the right wing to Tüb-
shin Oghul along with Samaghar and Hindu
Noyan. The left wing was given to Yoshmut,
Sönitäi, Arghun Aqa, Shiktür Noyan, Boroltai,
and Abdullah Aqa. The armies of Kirman and
Yazd were with Sultan Hajjaj, and Atabeg
Yusufshah was with Arghun Aqa’s division.
[1086] In the center, which they call the qol,
were Abatai Noyan and a group of com-
manders. 
When Baraq saw this, he had a sinking feel-
ing and said, “Our plan was wrong.” As his
commanders
tried
to
encourage
him,
Margha’ul said, “I’ll tear this army to pieces
with one charge.” Jalayirtai said, “I’ll pulverize
this army with one unit, and I’ll break the cen-
ter and wings apart.
Today I’ll doubtlessly perform a deed that will
put to shame the renowned warriors of this
age.
Qaidu’s and Mänggü Temür’s armies ﬂed in
the face of your good fortune. This army is not
more powerful than they were, but it is unfor-
tunate that their horses are ready while ours are
useless and we have no access to water.”
“I’ll go forward and open a way to water,”
said Margha’ul.
The armies were arrayed on both sides, and
battle lines were drawn. Margha’ul galloped
left and right and made parries and feints. Sud-
denly an arrow of misfortune struck him in the
breast.
When the shaft kissed his finger, it passed
through his spine. The celestial sphere said,
“Mercy upon that hand, and two hundred
‘bravos’ for such a shot.”
Baraq and his soldiers were stunned and dis-
heartened when Margha’ul was killed. Jalayir-
tai bowed and said, “I’ll hurl myself against
this army and put them to ﬂight.” So saying, he
and his horsemen charged the left wing at a
gallop and struck Arghun Aqa, Shiktür Noyan,
Yusuf[shah, Boro]ltai, and [1087] Abdullah
Aqa, killing and unhorsing many of their sol-
diers. The rest were routed. Jalayirtai went af-
ter them for nearly four leagues, as far as
Pushang of Herat, but when he wanted to re-
turn he could not get his soldiers in order be-
cause
the
units
and
divisions
had
been
dispersed.
On this side, Abatai Noyan was holding his
ground in the center, and the right wing was
also intact. When the left wing was lost, Abaqa
Khan ordered Yoshmut to go to the left wing,
and once again the soldiers were arranged and
put in order. Jalayirtai took fright and ﬂed.
Baraq lost hope. Abaqa Khan sent Bola Temür
in pursuit of Jalayirtai, and he killed everyone
he found.
Then a cry was given to the army, “It is a day
of glory and renown!” And they made a con-
certed attack, wielding blade and spear, attack-
526
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ing from left and right, and overthrowing their
opponents. 
Sönitäi Noyan, who was ninety years old, got
off his horse and sat on a stool between the two
armies, saying to the commanders and soldiers,
“We have enjoyed the fruit of Abaqa Khan’s
patronage for just such a day. Everyone has to
die eventually. If they kill Sönitäi, they will
only have killed a ninety-year-old man. If you
abandon me, where will your wives and chil-
dren be safe from Abaqa Khan and Genghis
Khan’s urugh? Fight like men and trust in God
so that He will give us victory.”
They attacked and fought hard. In the third
attack Baraq was broken and left unhorsed. He
was crying out for his liege men, but not one of
his soldiers paid any attention to him. In the
end a man named Sali from among his body-
guards recognized him, dismounted, and put
Baraq on his horse. He asked Baraq for some
arrows. He pulled several from his quiver,
tossed them to him, and rode off. [1088]
The next day Baraq reached his army, and
those who were left alive gathered around him,
naked and on foot. His aqa-inis who had man-
aged to escape had crossed the river but had
not camped. Abaqa Khan’s soldiers charged
left and right and killed or captured all they
found. Elgäi Noyan’s nephew Hulqun and two
thousand horsemen came to submit.
Had it not been for Jalayirtai’s audacity and
courage, not one of Baraq’s men would have
escaped alive, for he assembled those in rout
and drove them into the sands of Amuya.
When the army approached he stood in battle
and held his ground until the routed men got
away. Only then did he proceed on his way.
With such valor he saved a group from the
sword.
Along the way was a ruined kiosk in which a
group of riders took refuge. A detachment of
our soldiers rained down arrows on them, but it
had no effect. Suddenly Abaqa Khan’s banner
appeared, and he ordered them to place a lot of
kindling around the kiosk and set fire to it. The
men were all burned alive. 
After that, Abaqa Khan returned victorious
and triumphant. He entrusted the realms of
Khurasan and Mazanderan as far as the banks
of the Oxus to his brother Tübshin Oghul. He
also rewarded the people of Herat, and he pun-
ished the commanders who had ﬂed. Alinaq in
particular had made valiant showings during
the battle, for which he acquired inﬂuence and
renown.
The battle took place on the first of Dhu’l-
Hijja 668 [July 22, 1270]. [1089]
Baraq’s history after he crosses the river in
defeat and his forces are dispersed and
scattered.
When Baraq crossed the river in rout, he
stood perplexed and dumbfounded. He then
took to reproaching a group of his aqa-inis and
thinking and planning how he could chastise
them. Around then he was stricken with paraly-
sis and could not ride. The aqa-inis and com-
manders, who feared him, each and every one
separated themselves from him on some pre-
text and went home. Of them, Ahmad Oghul,
the son of Chaghatai’s [grand]son Büri, re-
belled and took his troop to Beshbaliq. Offend-
ed, Baraq said, “What ill did I do to these peo-
ple, who basked in the sun of my patronage for
so long and accumulated such vast wealth? I
took counsel with my aqa-inis and comman-
ders, and we crossed the river, and all along
they were saying they would do thus and so.
On the day of battle they went back on their
word and ﬂed, leaving me on foot in the midst
of the enemy. Now that I am stricken with ill-
ness they turn their backs on me. If I recover,
where do they think they can go?”
When Baraq’s wife Nögä Khatun heard this,
she said, “Since you are ill, let me mount with
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
527

the army, seize Ahmad, and bring him back.”
Such words struck at Baraq’s honor, so he
summoned his commanders, and after consul-
tation he ordered Na’uldar, one of his com-
manders of a thousand, to go in the vanguard
in pursuit of Ahmad. On his heels he set out
himself in a litter, proceeding slowly with
many soldiers. 
After two stations he heard that Negübäi, the
son of Chaghatai’s son Sarban, had gone to
Khujand, so he dispatched Nalighu [1090] (the
son of Qadaqai, son of Büri, son of Mö’ätükän,
son of Chaghatai) with a large troop in pursuit
of Negübäi. 
When he reached the vicinity of Chach,1 he
sent his brother Yasa’ur Oghul to Qaidu to say,
“When I set forth for Khurasan and Persia
upon the advice of Qaidu Aqa, we fought a big
battle with Tübshin on the banks of the
Chaghcharan,
where
we
were
victorious.
Qipchaq got offended by a slight exchange of
words he had with Jalayirtai while drinking
wine, and, before I could investigate the mat-
ter, he abandoned his camp and tent and turned
back. I sent Mu’min, Yasa’ur, and Abachi after
him to placate him. No matter how much ad-
vice they gave him, and no matter how they
stressed that he had come as an anda at
Qaidu’s order and that it was inappropriate for
him to turn back when we were near the ene-
my, he refused to listen and departed. This left
our troops dispirited. When we set out for Her-
at, Chabat also turned back for no reason. I did
not send anyone in pursuit of him, for I knew
that he would not listen to reason and that it
would only result in a fight. For these reasons
our plans were dealt severe blows, but I took
my army to Herat. From the other direction
came Abaqa with many troops, and although
our army had been disheartened by the depar-
1Chach, also Shash, the early name of Old Tashkent.
ture of Qipchaq and Chabat, it was of course
necessary to do battle. When we faced each
other, Jalayirtai attacked their left wing and put
it to rout. During the battle an arrow struck and
killed Margha’ul, and the army fell into utter
rout. I fell from my horse, and the entire army
passed by me. Of the commanders and body-
guards I recognized and called out to, saying,
‘I am Baraq, your king. Give me a horse,’ not
one paid the slightest attention to me in such
an
emergency
but
kept
going.
Finally
a
Qara’una named Sali recognized me, [1091]
got down off his horse, and put me on it. He
asked me for arrows, and I gave him a few.
With the greatest of difficulty I extricated my-
self from the midst of the foe and made it the
next day, on foot and wounded, to some of my
soldiers. They all gathered around me, and I
sent one of them to take the good news that I
was alive and well to Nögä Khatun and to tell
her that we were coming with our wounded
foot soldiers and she shouldn’t break camp and
ﬂee. When we got there, every one of our aqa-
inis who had arrived and waited for our arrival,
as well as those who were in the aghruq, re-
joiced. Having remained there, she had the
pages bring me all the weapons, food, and
clothing she had. Aside from Jalayirtai and the
commanders of thousands who had gone
ahead, not a soul came out to greet me. Of my
aqa-inis, every one of them who arrived there
had already crossed the river without waiting.
When I came to Nögä Khatun and heard what
my aqa-inis and soldiers had done, I said in
anger, ‘When I catch up with them, I know
how to get even with them!’ After crossing the
river I joined my aghruq, and some of the aqa-
inis started coming in droves. Neither they nor
the commanders have yet all reassembled, but
now I am stricken by paralysis. With me in this
condition, Ahmad Oghul has rebelled and gone
to Beshbaliq. With no reliance any longer on
528
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

anyone, I have sent Na’uldar with a thousand
horsemen in pursuit of him. I myself am in a
litter and am proceeding slowly to catch him
and bring him back. Just now news has arrived
that Negübäi Oghul has set out with his aghruq
and troop for Khujand, and I have sent Nalighu
Oghul with a detachment in pursuit of him. 
“When I reached the borders of Chach, I sent
my brother Yasa’ur to inform you, my anda, of
the situation, hoping that you would assist me
with forces to catch these people who had re-
belled against me and bring their troops back.”
[1092]
When Yasa’ur went before Qaidu and deliv-
ered his message, Qaidu said, “When Qipchaq
turned back because he was offended, it is
clear that when Baraq sent you with Mu’min
and Abachi after him to persuade him to go
back, he also sent a troop after you so that if he
didn’t return, they could seize him and take
him back. Is that so or not?”
“There was no troop,” replied Yasa’ur. 
Since Qaidu had ascertained from Baraq’s
envoys and from Qipchaq’s aghruq that Baraq
had sent Jalayirtai on their heels, he said to
Yasa’ur, “The aqa and ini and the troop turned
back on account of your crooked heart. Now
that he has sent you and asked me for assis-
tance, I have asked you, and you give me an
untrue answer. How can anyone be straight
with you?”
Yasa’ur became extremely ashamed and
worried. 
Then Qaidu said, “Baraq Anda got carried
away by his own machismo and said, ‘I will
face Tübshin Oghul and break him! No matter
why Qipchaq got offended and left, let him be
seized and brought back. I will take the realm
of Khurasan so that it may be known that
Baraq and his soldiers have seized Khurasan
through manliness.’ Because you were evil and
crooked inside, God the eternal gave Abaqa
good fortune and helped him to defeat you and
chase you miserably out of Khurasan. When
you got to this realm you incited strife among
your own aqa-inis. Finally he had to lie in a lit-
ter in pain and say, ‘I’m going on campaign.’
Doesn’t he realize what could be done to him
when his arms and legs were sound and his
army in good order? Now that he suffers ill
health and has no soldiers, what can he do?
Does Baraq Anda, who lies sick in a litter,
want to conquer realms? Do you want to un-
tangle the twisted fabric of his lies?”
With this he ordered Yasa’ur held under
guard [1093] and summoned his commanders
and ministers for council.
“For several years now Baraq has been eat-
ing up our territory,” he said. “When he came
to make war on us, he was defeated. Qipchaq
tricked us into making a truce, and pacts were
made and oaths sworn that we would neither
cross each other again nor think of treachery
and deception. We swore an oath on gold that
he would command his territory and we ours.
We sent envoys to bring tribute from our terri-
tory, and again and again we sent envoys ask-
ing for the tribute. Not only did they not give
it, but they beat the envoys. Since a pact was in
effect, I forbore with patience. Then he set out
for Khurasan and asked me for assistance. In
good faith I sent Qipchaq and Chabat with
troops. Qipchaq was not received honorably,
and, having been insulted by Jalayirtai, a com-
moner, he turned around and ﬂed. He sent
troops after him to seize him. It didn’t work.
Chabat also turned back in offense. His son
came here in fear. Now he is leading his troops
again, this time from a litter, and has begun to
create strife and contention among the aqa-
inis. He sends his brother Yasa’ur to engage in
trickery and asks for assistance. If we help him
with troops, our territory will be ruined be-
neath the hooves of horses. If we do not send
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
529

assistance, he will withdraw from us and get
himself with the few troops he has to Besh-
baliq. There he will unite himself with the
Qa’an and create strife again to attack us. The
best path I can see is to hold his brother
Yasa’ur here. I myself will mount with two
tümäns of soldiers and send a message that I
am coming to assist Baraq Anda. If he has al-
ready done battle by the time we get there, he
will surely have been defeated and fallen by
the wayside. If Baraq has been defeated, let’s
side with his enemy and, at one and the same
time, be done with him and make them obedi-
ent to us and not let them get out of this realm.
[1094] If he has defeated them, then surely
their soldiers will have come over to his side.
When we get there we’ll turn Baraq back and
fix it so that we can remove him in the best
fashion possible, put another in his place, make
his soldiers obedient to us, and put down this
strife and rebellion.”
The commanders and ministers said, “This is
the correct way to proceed.” 
After that, Qaidu mounted with two tümäns
and sent a message saying, “We are sending
several thousand soldiers as reinforcements.”
However, he kept his own coming secret until
he got to Baraq.
Na’uldar had gone to Ahmad Oghul, and he
sent messengers to say, “You are a prince, and
I am a commoner. Baraq has sent me to per-
suade you to come back. If you don’t, it means
war. It would be best for you to return.” 
Ahmad was extremely drunk, and his com-
panions
kept
saying,
“Many
troops
have
arrived. You have to turn back so that he will
turn his army around. By that time you’ll have
sobered up and we can hold council.” No mat-
ter how much they insisted, he paid no atten-
tion and refused to listen. He attacked Na’ul-
dar, but Na’uldar turned his back and said, “He
is urugh. How can I fight with him?” When
Na’uldar put himself to ﬂight, Ahmad turned
back, and Na’uldar went after him with his
troops. Ahmad looked and saw that Na’uldar
was near again. In his drunken stupor he imag-
ined that his liege men were going to seize him
and turn him over to Na’uldar. He chose a few
fine horses, stole away from the camp with
some of his intimates, and ﬂed into the by-
ways.
Na’uldar
became
aware
of
it
and
galloped off after him, shooting arrows. Sud-
denly one hit Ahmad in the back and went
straight through his chest. He died on the spot.
When the soldiers realized what had happened,
they all surrendered. Na’uldar sent a messen-
ger to Baraq to inform him of the situation.
On the other side, Nalighu Oghul, [1095]
who had gone in pursuit of Negübäi Oghul,
sent him a messenger to say, “Stop until we
reach you, and we can proceed together.”
Negübäi Oghul thought he was speaking hon-
estly and stopped. The next morning Nalighu
attacked him and rained arrows down on his
troop. Negübäi was hit and died, his camp was
looted, and his soldiers were turned away.
News arrived that Ahmad Oghul had been
killed by Na’uldar. Since he was a relative of
Ahmad’s, Nalighu took ﬂight and went to
Beshbaliq.
By the time all this news reached Baraq and
Negübäi’s and Ahmad’s soldiers joined him,
Qaidu had arrived nearby and sent him a mes-
sage saying, “I have come with many soldiers.
Where should we go?”
Baraq sent a reply, saying, “Why has Qaidu
Anda taken the trouble to come such a dis-
tance? The affair with Ahmad and Negübäi is
over and I’m turning back because I’m sick.
Let Qaidu Anda also turn back. When I have
recovered, we can see each other.”
When Qaidu heard this, he said to his com-
manders, “Baraq is near death, but he still
won’t cease his tricks. He wants to get us out
530
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

of here by a ruse without seeing us.” That very
night he had all his soldiers ride and dismount
surrounding Baraq’s camp. He intended to
meet with him in the morning to plan what
would be most expedient; however, the news
reached Baraq, and he died of fright that very
night.
In the morning Qaidu sent envoys to ask for
örgäjüt [supplementary gifts], but from Baraq’s
camp they heard the sound of wailing and
mourning and saw the bodyguards with their
hair down. Realizing that Baraq had died, they
turned around and informed Qaidu. By the
time they arrived, Mubarakshah, Chübäi, and
Qaban had been informed of Baraq’s death and
Qaidu’s arrival. They came and offered tägish-
mishi. They arrived while they were eating and
delivered the news. Qaidu cried out and wept,
and all the aqa-inis wept along with him.
[1096] Qaidu sent several of his intimates to
Nögä Khatun to console her and say, “We too
are mourning here.” 
After that, Qaidu ordered Baraq buried on a
high mountain. The next day Mubarakshah,
Chübäi, and Qaban came with all the comman-
ders of units of thousands and ten thousands.
They knelt before Qaidu and said, “After to-
day, Qaidu Aqa is our aqa. We will obey any-
thing he commands. While he was alive Baraq
was tyrannical to us and all his aqa-inis and
appropriated our inherited and acquired wealth.
If Qaidu Aqa is kind enough to allow us to re-
main alive, we will perform valiantly for him.
If not, it is his to command, but we will will be
bewildered and distressed. 
Qaidu said, “Let the identifiable property he
seized be returned. Since you want me, I will
give you what consolation I can and restore
your property and territory to you.”
After that, as they were breaking camp,
Mubarakshah took all the cash and goods he
could
find
in
Baraq’s
treasury.
He
even
snatched with his own hands two valuable
pearls from Nögä Khatun’s ears. They divided
all the animals and property among them-
selves, and not a thing remained.
Abaqa Khan returns from battle with Baraq
triumphant and victorious; envoys arrive
from the Qa’an’s court bearing diplomatic
honors and a writ of khanship; Abaqa Khan
is enthroned a second time.
When Abaqa Khan defeated Baraq and
cleansed the realm of Khurasan [1097] from
the sedition and strife of Baraq’s henchmen, he
returned to Persia and Azerbaijan, his former
capital. Along the way, despite the vast num-
bers of soldiers and retinue, not a creature suf-
fered the slightest harassment. On the first of
Rabi‘ I 669 [October 18, 1270] he dismounted
in Maragha. On Thursday the 20th of that
month [November 6] he rejoined his wives’ or-
dus at the Jaghatu. Also on that date envoys
from the Qa’an’s court arrived bearing a writ,
crown, and honors for Abaqa Khan and naming
him khan of Iran in his late father’s place, to
rule after the manner of his fathers and
forefathers.
On Wednesday the 2nd of Rabi‘ II 669 [No-
vember 18, 1270] of Morin Yil, in Jaghatu, by
command of the Qa’an he mounted the throne
a second time, and as was customary congratu-
lations and rejoicing were in order.
Also around that time envoys arrived from
Mänggü Temür with gifts and presents of fal-
cons, hawks, etc. to congratulate him on his
victory over Baraq. Abaqa Khan ordered the
envoys shown all honor, and with them he sent
regal belägs [gifts]. 
On the 2nd and 3rd of Safar 669 [September
20–21] he hunted in the vicinity of Jaghatu. By
chance his royal hand was wounded by a
mountain ox’s horn. A vein was severed that
would not stop bleeding. Qorchan Aqa, the fa-
ther of Tuq Temür Idächi, picked up a bow, un-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
531

strung it, and wrapped the string around the
wound so that it swelled and stopped the ﬂow
of blood. Abaqa Khan rewarded him. He also
rewarded Täkächäk, who had borne his arms
for him during those two or three days and per-
formed good service, and he became grand and
inﬂuential. Since the place that had been
wounded turned tumorous and became like a
sack, he was in pain, but the great physicians
were unable to open it. [1098] He could not
bear it any longer. Khwaja Nasîruddin Tusi as-
sured him that opening it would not cause him
any injury, so he ordered Abu’l-Izz the surgeon
to open it and clean it out. Immediately the
pain diminished, and within a week he had no
further pain. The people rejoiced.
On Saturday the 8th of Dhu’l-Hijja [July 18,
1271] Prince Yoshmut died. On the 4th of Sa-
far 670 [September 11, 1271] Täkshin Oghul
passed away.
On the last of Rabi‘ II of that year [December
5, 1271] the people of Girdkoh surrendered
their stronghold.
In Jumada
II of that year [January 1272]
Yesünjin Khatun, the mother of Abaqa Khan,
died. Her ordu was given to Padishah Khatun.
Thereafter the people of Iran dwelt secure in
the shadow of Abaqa Khan’s justice and equity
for a long time, and they prayed for his contin-
ued good fortune.
Aq Beg comes to Abaqa Khan’s court and
takes the army to devastate Bukhara; the
end of that episode; an earthquake occurs in
Tabriz.
A man named Aq Beg had long been warden
of the Amuya fortress and guarded the banks of
the river on Baraq’s behalf, and he had also ha-
rassed the people greatly. In the year 671
[1272–73], he came to Abaqa Khan’s court at
K…tü and reported, “Foreign troops on the
other side of the river are being reinforced
from Bukhara and getting ready to invade
these regions. It would be best to destroy that
place.” [1099]
Abaqa Khan assigned Yesüdär Oghul, who
had become the governor of Khurasan after
Tübshin Oghul, to Bukhara and said, “If the
people there accept to leave their homeland
and come to Khurasan, do not harm them. Oth-
erwise, plunder Bukhara.” So saying, he sent
Negübäi Bahadur, Chardu, Aladu, and a divi-
sion of soldiers with him. When they got there
they attacked Kish and Nakhshab several
times. After that they set out for Bukhara and
camped in the vicinity of the city. Amir
Mas‘ud Beg was in Qaidu’s ordu. In his ab-
sence Sadr-i-Jahan was in charge of affairs. Aq
Beg had a servant there named Zerak son of
Lachin, a very nosey and seditious person. He
sent him with a Mongol liege man of his on a
mission into the city to deliver a message say-
ing, “It is Abaqa Khan’s command that you
leave the city along with your wives, children,
property, and animals and go to Khurasan.”
The rabble and lower classes paid no attention
to Sadr-i-Jahan’s words and killed Zerak. The
Mongol liege man returned and informed Aq
Beg of the murder of Zerak son of Lachin. At
once he mounted and set out for the city. The
people of Bukhara shut the gates and fought
for a whole day. By night Sadr-i-Jahan sum-
moned the dignitaries of the city, who decided
that they should make a truce. Aq Beg was the
son of an Indian woman and grandson of
Tajuddin Zerak, and one of the city gates was
his responsibility. At dawn he opened it and let
the soldiers into Bukhara.
In Aram Ay of Daqiqu Yil, corresponding to
the first of Rajab 671 [January 22, 1273], they
began to massacre, pillage and plunder, and
take captives as rivers of blood ﬂowed in the
city. Mas‘ud Beg’s madrasa, the largest and
greatest of the madrasas there, was set afire
and burned along with its precious books. The
532
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

killing and looting continued for a week.
[1100] On the last night they were about to set
the city on fire when suddenly several Mongol
riders arrived bringing the news that Chübäi
and Qaban, the sons of Alghu (the son of
Chaghatai’s son Baidar), were approaching
with ten thousand horsemen. Aq Beg and
Negübäi decamped and crossed the Haramkan
Canal carrying many items, animals, slaves,
and captives.
Early the next morning Qaban, Buqu, and
Naqu arrived on the other side of the canal and
cried out, saying, “Why have you done such a
thing?”
“By command of your aqa Abaqa Khan,”
they answered. “Here is his decree.”
Qaban did not think it wise to cross over and
attack them since he had no more than five
thousand horsemen, but he demanded sawqat
from Aq Beg and Negübäi. They sent him a
share of the plunder and loot, and he turned
around and killed what remained of the fight-
ing men. Nearly fifty thousand persons were
killed.
On both sides Aq Beg, Qaban, and Chübäi
continued killing and looting for three years
until such a magnificent city and its country-
side was totally devastated. There was not a
living soul in the vicinity for seven years.
When Aq Beg had been sufficiently enriched
by the loot, he wanted to take ﬂight and go to
Qaidu. One of his brothers came to Prince
Arghun and told him of his brother’s plan. The
prince sent an envoy to bring him in chains,
and he was sent to Abaqa Khan, where he was
tried. He refused to confess, but when he was
beaten he confessed and was executed at
Kökchä Tängiz [Lake Sevan].
Also in the year 671 [1272–73] a violent
earthquake occurred during the winter in
Tabriz. The tops of minarets fell, and many
houses were destroyed.
In Dhu’l-Hijja of that year [June–July 1273]
Malik Sadruddin of Rayy [1101] was killed.
Jangla’un Bakhshi, who was highly regarded
by the Mongol monarchs and particularly ven-
erated by Hülägü Khan and Abaqa Khan, died
on the 19th of Dhu’l-Hijja of that year [July 7,
1273].
In Dhu’l-Hijja of 673 [July 1275] Arghun
Aqa passed away in the Radkan meadows of
Tus and was buried there.
Bunduqdar comes to Anatolia, and Abaqa
Khan heads there and vents his wrath on
the people of Anatolia; some of the amirs of
Anatolia and Parvana are martyred; the
Sahib-Divan Shamsuddin goes there.
In the year 674 [1275–76] Ziya’uddin and
the son of Khatir and the son of Parvana went
from Anatolia into Syria to Ruknuddin Bun-
duqdar, whom they encouraged to invade Ana-
tolia. In 675 [1276–77] he set out with a huge
army for Anatolia, emerging via Abulistan [El-
bistan] from Mount Abulistan. On the borders
there were stationed the Mongol amirs Elgäi
Noyan’s son Tuqu, his brother Uruqtu, and
Sodon’s son Tödä’ün of the Suldus, the brother
of Su’unchaq Noyan, each with a division of
soldiers. The armies met on Friday the 10th of
Dhu’l-Qa‘da of that year [April 15, 1277], cor-
responding to the 12th of Ütünch Ay of Hükär
Yil, and battle ensued. It was terribly cold.
Tuqu and Tödä’ün dismounted with their sol-
diers and fought hard. After noon the Mongol
army was defeated, and only a few escaped.
Bunduqdar went to Qaysariyya [Kayseri] and
spent a week there, putting the coinage and
khutba in his name. Then provisions grew
scarce.
Mu‘inuddin
Parvana
[1102]
was
in
the
fortress at Toqat [Tokat]. Bunduqdar sent a
messenger summoning him, but he refused to
comply. Bunduqdar killed some Christians and
Armenians and pulled back. Along the way
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
533

their horses were afflicted by a pestilence, and
many of the soldiers had to go on foot. One of
Tödä’ün’s liege men named Bökädäi came and
reported the situation. Abaqa Khan grew ex-
tremely angry and set out that very day from
Tabriz. In Safar 676 [July 1277], which was in
the spring, he set out for Anatolia, and when he
reached Elbistan and Aqcha, Sultan Ghiyasud-
din came to court with Sahib Fakhruddin Isfa-
hani. When he saw the bodies piled one on top
of another in Elbistan, he wept and grieved for
Tuqu and Tödä’ün. In his anger he ordered a
group of Turcomans who had stirred up trouble
and several dignitaries of Anatolia executed
and he commanded that some of the Anatolian
countryside be subjected to massacre and pil-
lage. Sahib Shamsuddin Juwayni ransomed
several cities, but half of Sivas was looted.
Sahib Shamsuddin reminded him that just
kings do not inﬂict general punishment for an
individual’s crime, and his advice was accept-
ed and they were spared. Nuruddin Jarangi and
Zahiruddin ibn Hud were martyred.
Abaqa Khan wanted to go to Syria. However,
it was the middle of summer, and since the
commanders said the end of autumn or winter
would be more appropriate, a halt was called
and he sent a messenger to Bunduqdar with
threats, saying, “You attack our scouts and pa-
trols without warning like bandits and kill
some. When word reaches us and we mount to
deal with you, you run away like thieves. If
you intend to fight, come out into the field like
men and stand firm. [1103]
Come see my spear and test my reins. / If you
are a mountain, I’ll bring you down; if you are
a stone, you won’t remain where you are. /
Where have you ever seen men of battle? You
haven’t even heard the cry of the fox.
Even if you don’t come forth, our troops intend
to do battle with you at the beginning of win-
ter, and when the fire of our wrath reaches Syr-
ia it will burn everything of yours. God the
eternal has given the kingdoms of the world to
Genghis Khan and his urugh and made warrior
chiefs subservient to us. Anyone who opposes
the lords of fortune will be branded with
misfortune.”
Before Bunduqdar reached Damascus he
dreamed that the Apostle handed him a sword.
That very week he mounted the throne, and
then he dreamed that the Apostle said, “Give
back what we entrusted to you,” and took back
the sword and gave it to Malik Mansur Sultan
Sayfuddin Qala’un, known as Alfi. When he
awoke he realized that it was the end of his life
and that fortune would smile upon Alfi. He
summoned him and said, “Since you are going
to be sultan, take good care of my children.”
He died in Damascus in Dhu’l-Hijja 676 [May
1278] and was buried in the madrasa he had
built there.
Abaqa
Khan
gave
Anatolia
to
Prince
Qongqurtai Oghul so that he could guard it
from the enemy and so that he could destroy
the fortress at Toqat and the bastion at
Kughaniya, which was Mu‘inuddin Parvana’s
home. [1104]
In Hükär Yil corresponding to 676 [1277] he
returned to Ala Tagh. Parvana came trembling
to the ordu. The amirs said he was charged
with three crimes: one, ﬂeeing from the foe;
two, not reporting Bunduqdar’s arrival imme-
diately; and three, not coming soon enough to
court. He was ordered put under watch. When
the envoys returned from Bunduqdar, they re-
ported that he had said, “I came at Parvana’s
invitation because he had promised that if I
came he would give me the kingdom of Anato-
lia. After I got here he took ﬂight.” When this
was reported to Abaqa Khan he ordered Par-
vana executed. He was put to death by Küchik
Tughchi on the first of Rabi‘ I 676 [August 2,
1277] in the summer quarters at Ala Tagh.
534
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

On the 17th of Rabi‘ II of that year [Septem-
ber 17, 1277] he dispatched Sahib Shamsuddin
to placate the peasantry, overpower foes, and
regulate affairs in Anatolia. He went and re-
stored the ruined cities to habitation. He also
imposed the tamgha tax in Anatolia, although it
had not been customary. 
In the vicinity of Uruch [?] on the outskirts
of Anatolia a man named Qahraman lurked in
the forests, making the roads unsafe. The
Sahib-Divan mounted together with Kähürgäi
Noyan and Arqasun Noyan and burned him up
together with the forests..
In Safar of 676 [July 1277] Izzuddin Aybak
the Syrian, who had ﬂed with ten men and
come here, was rewarded and made governor
of Malatya. For his and his men’s provisions
an annual stipend of five thousand dinars was
appropriated. When he got to Malatya, he took
three hundred thousand dirhems from the peo-
ple under blows and lashes and took off again
to Syria.
When
Sahib-Divan
Shamsuddin
returned
from Anatolia, he went via Derbent to the Cau-
casus and Lagzistan and arranged it so that
those tribes, which had never surrendered to
anyone at any time, submitted. [1105]
Khwaja Nasîruddin Tusi died at Baghdad in
Dar Susiyan at sunset on Monday the 17th of
Dhu’l-Hijja 672 [June 24, 1274].1 
Erudition and the sciences died with him, so
peace be with erudition and the sciences.
Malik Shamsuddin Kurt comes hither; he is
imprisoned and dies.
Malik Shamsuddin Kurt was one of the ma-
liks of Ghor, and he was an extremely compe-
1What the text’s “Dār Sūsiyān” is supposed to repre-
sent is unknown—perhaps a quarter or village. It is
known, however, that he was buried in the Musa-Jawad
Shrine in Kazimayn in Baghdad. See text p. 938 above
and Khwandamir, Habibu’s-siyar 3:106.
tent and brave man. When Hülägü Khan
arrived in Transoxiana he went to court and
was favorably received and appointed to the
post of malik of Herat, Sabzavar, Ghor, and
Gharcha. When Baraq came he conspired with
him to open the gates of Herat to the foe. Tüb-
shin Oghul summoned him several times, but
he refused to comply and did not go to court.
For that reason Abaqa Khan was offended and,
in 674 [1275–76], he was about to send forces
to capture him. The commanders and the
Sahib-Divan said, “Khurasan is in ruins and
cannot bear the comings and goings of an
army. It would be better to have him persuaded
to come in.” An order was issued for the Sahib-
Divan to go. 
“If it is so commanded,” he said, “let my son
Baha’uddin Muhammad, who is in Persia, un-
dertake this mission.”
An order was so given, and after consultation
with Qazi Fakhruddin of Herat and Nizamud-
din Awbihi, Baha’uddin wrote to Malik Sham-
suddin, [1106] saying, “I wanted to come my-
self, but because of many obstacles I was
unable to attain that happiness. At present there
remains no favor or good will. It is necessary
to come.” Sahib-Sa‘id Shamsuddin Sahib-Di-
van also sent the following occasional poem:
Splendor of the realm, Malik Shamsuddin
Muhammad Kurt, it is you who, like an angel,
are spirit from end to end. / The torment my
soul has suffered from separation from you
cannot be imagined by human or djinn. / In my
eyes, which have no regard for this world or
the next, the dust of your steed is like collyri-
um. / What torments will come upon a weak,
grieving heart if you do not trouble yourself to
come hither? / My constitution will diverge
from health if, God forbid, you change your di-
rection. / For your clear-sighted mind, truly it
is fitting that you read a letter of longing like
this one. / With the wind of your travel you fan

535

the ﬂames of your determination; with the wa-
ter of your kindness you make settle down dust
that does not exist.
The grandees mentioned above also wrote
letters saying, “If Khwaja Baha’uddin goes to
Herat with the maliks, sadrs, and grandees of
Persia, he will not render the malik suitable
service, ancient honor will be lost, and he will
covet the kingdom of Herat. It would be better
for you to proceed hither without worry.”
With the envoys Malik Shamsuddin sent
back his chamberlain Baha’uddin and Jamal
Harun with a message saying, [1107] “Let the
khwaja not worry, for I will come to him
soon.” 
Baha’uddin treated them well and sent a robe
of honor back for the malik. Jamaluddin went
and encouraged him to come. He set out for Is-
fahan. Baha’uddin showed him all honor and
made arrangements himself for all the items
necessary for presentation to the padishah,
such as animals, clothing, etc. After a time he
escorted him to court, and he was allowed the
felicity of making tägishmishi in Tabriz. Since
Abaqa Khan had been really offended, he paid
no attention to him. Sahib Shamsuddin wanted
to trick him into showing favor, but it didn’t
work and the malik was imprisoned in the
fortress at Tabriz. He complained of the Sahib
and his son, but since he knew he would be as-
sassinated and his troop plundered, his atten-
dants said he had beneath the stone in his ring
poison he took with noodles. He died in 676
[1278] in that prison. *One of his friends com-
posed the following on his death: “In the year
six hundred and seventy and six, in the month
of Shawwal, destiny took an augury from the
book of the ages / in the name of the leader of
the Iranians, Muhammad Kurt, and the follow-
ing verse emerged: al-shamsu kuwwirat [the
sun was folded up].”*1
When his death was reported, since he had
been such a sly man and might have faked his
death in order to escape, it was ordered that
Hulqutu, the amir of …, should go and nail his
coffin shut and place it in the grave, as a
precaution. 
In the same year informants rose up against
Malik Iftikharuddin Qazwini and reported that
he had embezzled much money. He paid
500,000 to prevent an audit. He was in destitu-
tion in the ordu for nearly two years, and then
he died in 678 [1279–80]. [1108]
Abaqa Khan hunts at Shahrod, and those
people initiate a revolt.
In the Tongquz Yil corresponding to 674
[1275] he wintered in Arran. One day he rode
out to go hunting, and when he passed five
leagues from Shahrod and was hunting a
mountain ox in a forest, a group with faces like
men but acting like beasts attacked the royal
servants with blades and spears. The horsemen
charged them, and a battle was fought. In the
end they ﬂed. It was ordered that the provincial
militia be brought in to remove them. When
the army assembled, the ruler of the tribe took
fright and came to court with a sword and
shroud. He was embraced by regal clemency,
and their lives were spared.
The Negüdäris’ army comes and pillages
Fars and Kirman.
In the winter of 677, corresponding to Bars
Yil [1278], nearly two thousand Negüdäri
horsemen attacked Fars. Balaghan the shahna,
Muhammad
Beg
a
relative
of
Mahmud
Yalavach’s, Tuinaq, Shamsuddin Tazigo, and
the amirs of Fars went out with an army. The
Negüdäris laid an ambush in the vicinity of

Kalbar, and in front was a large irrigation
canal. Najmuddin Shul said, “It is not wise to

and said, “Coward, why are you frightening

[1109]
but
the
others

The
Negüdäris sprang their ambush and killed most
of the soldiers. Shamsuddin Tazigo and Bal-
aghan managed, with great difficulty, to es-
cape. Tuinaq and Muhammad Beg were killed
along with the soldiers. The Negüdäris went to
the gates of Shiraz, rustled horses from the
Pirozi Garden, and attacked and pillaged on the
outskirts of the city.
Until
698
[1298–99]
the
leader
of
the
Negüdäris was Mochi’s son Abdullah,1 a great-
grandson of Chaghatai. After that, Baraq’s son
Dua summoned him, put him under arrest, and
sent his own son Qutlugh Khwaja in his place.
He too sent his soldiers to plunder Fars in 700
[1300–1]. The reason he was so audacious is
that the Padishah of Islam’s imperial banners
were headed for Syria and that front had been
left empty.
Abaqa Khan’s banners proceed to
Khurasan; the Qara’una amirs come into
submission; Prince Arghun Khan goes to
Seistan.
On the first of Muharram 677 [May 25,
1278] corresponding to Tavushqan Yil, Abaqa
Khan departed from Tabriz and set out for
Khurasan. 
On the 3rd of Rabi‘ I 678 [July 14, 1279] he
dispatched Prince Arghun with a division to
deal with the Negüdäris. He went to Seistan,

laid siege, and returned, bringing Mubarak-
shah’s eldest son, Öljäi Buqa, and other mem-
bers of his family. 
On the 14th of Rabi‘ I of that year [July 25,
1279] Abaqa Khan went to Herat. On the last
day of the month [August 10], the Qara’una
amirs came into submission, [1110] and on the
2nd of Rabi‘ II [August 12] they made ul-
jamishi. He rewarded them.
Then he returned to his capital in Tabriz and
said, “Inasmuch as our dear father conquered a
realm of such length and breadth, it behooves
us to give a share to his wives and sons.” He
gave a portion of Mayyafariqin to Qutui
Khatun, part of Diyarbekir and the province of
Jazira to Öljäi Khatun, Salmas to Jumghur’s
wife Tolun Khatun and his sons Jüshkäb and
Kin[g]shü. He also gave some territory to the
other sons by concubines. 
Amir Buqa, the son of Högöläi Qorchi of the
Jalayir, was a child when his father died.
Abaqa Khan took him under his patronage and
raised him until he became a highly inﬂuential
inaq [advisor], entrusted with the narin [royal]
treasuries and the red [seal]. He became one of
the great commanders. 
In Luy Yil, Abatai Noyan passed away in Sa-
far 679 [June 1280]. 
Majdulmulk Yazdi becomes an informant
for Abaqa Khan, and Sahib Shamsuddin
and his brother Ala’uddin suffer a reversal
of fortune.
In 677 [1278–79] informants arose in all
quarters against the Sahib-Divan Shamsuddin.
One of them was the Majdulmulk Yazdi whose
father was called Safiulmulk and had served
the atabegs of Yazd. Majdulmulk was an atten-
dant on Khwaja Shamsuddin Sahib-Divan’s
son Khwaja Baha’uddin in Isfahan for a time,
and from that position he got himself into
Khwaja Shamsuddin’s service. [1111] The
khwaja patronized him and assigned him two

or three tasks, one of which was a census of

at sea he was attacked by pirates who stole his money,
took him captive, and carried him to India, where they

a position in the vizierate would mind his own business

installation, and all the grandees were present. It was

fore the atabeg, set on a golden cloth, and placed before
the vizier so that he could put his seal on documents.
That day, a bowl bearer of the atabeg’s, who was ex-
tremely bold and also served as a chamberlain, came in
as usual and requested in his impudent fashion that he
take the inkpot and cloth out and place them before the
vizier. The atabeg, unaware of the prior arrangements,
granted his request. When the appointed hour drew near,
the bowl bearer came in, placed the cloth and inkpot be-
fore Majdulmulk, and gave him a document to seal. Ma-
jdulmulk ﬂew into a rage, threw the document away, got
up, and left angrily. At once he set out for Isfahan, say-
sense in him qualities that inspired trust, he
was less than enthusiastic in his reception and
patronage of him. When Majdulmulk realized
that, he got permission to go to Yazd, where he
resided at home for a while. Then he rejoined
Khwaja Baha’uddin’s service. Through that
connection Khwaja Shamsuddin Sahib-Divan
sent him on a mission to Anatolia, where he re-
mained for a time. When he returned he served
Khwaja Ala’uddin as usual. 
One day Majduddin [Ibn al-]Athir, Sahib-
Sa‘id Khwaja Ala’uddin’s deputy, happened to
be with him, and during the tales he related he
spoke of the might and magnificence of the
army of Egypt and of their great numbers and
invincibility. Majdulmulk took this as a pretext
to go to Yesü Buqa Gürägän to report that the
Sahib-Divan’s
brother’s
deputy,
with
the
connivance of the two brothers, had united
with the Egyptian enemy. They therefore knew
all about [the Egyptians’ plans] and were sim-
ply waiting for an army to come to this land in
order to turn over Baghdad.
Yesü Buqa Gürägän reported this to Abaqa
Khan, who ordered Majduddin Ibn al-Athir
arrested and questioned concerning this report.
During the yarghu [inquisition] he received a
hundred lashes, but still no case was proven
against him. He was turned over to the Sahib-
ing, ‘How can one keep control of the affairs of a ruler
who, despite all conditions and promises, in the very
first act, lets a bowl bearer act like a chamberlain?’ No
matter how much they pleaded, he refused to listen and
left. In Isfahan he joined Khwaja Baha’uddin’s service
and was one of his intimates for a while. Once he real-
ized how irritable and quick-tempered Baha’uddin was,
he managed to insinuate himself into Sahib-Sa‘id Sham-
suddin’s service. The sahib sent him to conduct a census
of Georgia, and in a short time he had completed that
task to everyone’s astonishment. The next time he sent
him to Mosul and Diyarbekir to collect taxes and tribute
and pacify the provinces. He accomplished that task too
satisfactorily and returned.”

Divan, and the Sahib-Divan pardoned Majdul-
mulk [1112] and issued him a writ of gov-
ernance of Sivas. When he learned of his
impoverished condition, he gave him a bar of
gold, a ruby, and a draft in the amount of ten
thousand dinars drawn against the ruler of
Anatolia.
Having done what he had done, Majdulmulk
had become wary and therefore joined Yesü
Buqa Gürägän’s service, constantly making
every attempt to undermine the two Sahib-Di-
vans in every way possible. He bided his time
until around the beginning of Dhu’l-Qa‘da 678
[March 1280], when Abaqa Khan set out for
Khurasan.
When Abaqa reached Qazwin and Prince
Arghun came out to greet him, Majdulmulk
went before the prince through the offices of
one of his confidants, a man named Ayachi. “I
have been wanting to say a few words for more
than a year,” he said, “but I have not been able
to have my words conveyed by amirs or
courtiers because every time I made an initia-
tive, the Sahib-Divan learned of it and paid out
huge bribes to them from the padishah’s
treasury to make them keep it quiet. Recently it
occurred to me that although the amirs are
willing to sell the padishah’s interests for fa-
vors and bribes, the prince would not sell his
interests. I have therefore come to report that
most of what comes into the padishah’s
treasuries from the realm is income from the
Sahib-Divan’s holdings, which are derived
from the padishah’s own property. Indeed, the
Sahib-Divan’s ingratitude has reached such
proportions that he is at one with the sultans of
Egypt, the Parvana of Anatolia is united with
Bunduqdar on his advice, and Tuqu, Tödä’ün
Bahadur, and Uruqtu were killed through his
vile machinations. His brother Ala’uddin has
grabbed the realm of Baghdad, has made for
himself a jeweled crown worthy of kings, and
has stashed away innumerable treasures and
uncountable buried hoards. If the padishah fa-
vors me, [1113] I will prove that the Sahib-Di-
van has purchased in his own name nearly
forty million dinar’s worth of the padishah’s
property and that he has another twenty million
in cash, ﬂocks, and herds. If in all the
padishah’s treasuries there is ten million in
gold, aside from what has been brought from
the Heretics’ fortresses, I am mistaken and
should pay with my life. Because I know all
about this, he has given me a writ of gov-
ernance of Sivas, a bar of gold, a ruby, and a
draft worth ten thousand dinars as ‘hush
money.’ ”
When he had divulged all this to Prince
Arghun, the prince reported it to Abaqa Khan,
who said, “Speak of this to no one until it can
be taken care of quietly.”
When Abaqa Khan went to Tabriz, he spent
the winter in Arran. That winter Malik Raziud-
din
Baba
Qazwini
and
Jalaluddin
Khatti
[Khutani] were martyred.1 
That spring, when he went to Sharuyaz, he
was in the bath in Ribat-i-Muslim one day.
Majdulmulk went into the disrobing room of
the
bath
under
the
patronage
of
Amir
Taghachar and reported everything he had told
Prince Arghun and more. Abaqa Khan grew
angry at the Sahib-Divan and sent envoys into
all parts of the kingdom to have his deputies
arrested and brought to him along with their
account books for an investigation at court.
The Sahib-Divan sought the aid of Öljäi
Khatun and penned a document declaring that
all the properties he had purchased belonged to
