the padishah. On the top of the document the
khatun wrote a petition for him that induced
Abaqa Khan to restore him to favor. Thus she
rescued the Sahib-Divan from the brink of dis-
aster. Decrees were issued recalling the en-
voys, and the Sahib-Divan’s deputies were not
molested. 
In desperation Majdulmulk wrote a petition
saying, [1114] “Now that the Padishah has re-
stored the Sahib-Divan to favor, he will not al-
low me a moment of safety. I hope the
Padishah will either entrust me to an amir who
can protect me from him or command me to
leave the kingdom.”
In reply Abaqa Khan said, “Although I have
restored the Sahib-Divan to favor, I do not con-
sider Majdulmulk to be at fault. He will contin-
ue to serve the ordu and accompany Taghachar,
Joshi, and Ordu Qaya.” Majdulmulk was paci-
fied and continued in service according to the
order that had been issued, biding his time
along with Sadruddin Zanjani, until the spring
of 679, when a decree was issued for Majdul-
mulk Yazdi to be the overseer of the entire ter-
ritory from the banks of the Oxus to the gates
of Egypt jointly with the Sahib-Divan. One day
when Abaqa Khan was in the temple in
Maragha with all the ladies, princes, amirs,
ministers, and grandees of court, he ordered
the decree to be read. All said of one accord,
“Never have Mongol rulers given such a de-
cree to a Tajik!”
Abaqa Khan said to Majdulmulk, “Be very
careful of the affairs of state, treasury, and mil-
itary, be aware of everything that happens, and
supervise everything your deputies do. Watch
yourself closely, and do not, for any reason, lag
behind the ordu. If anyone attempts to kill you,
he will answer to me.” When he attained such
favor everyone deferred to him and honored
him. Therefore the Sahib-Divan Shamsuddin’s
fortunes suffered a reversal, and there was
nothing he could do about it. Majdulmulk sent
the following quatrain to Sahib Shamsuddin:
[1115] “I shall sink into an ocean of grief for
you: I will either drown or bring forth a pearl. /
To attack you is dangerous, but I will do it: I
will either win or lose my head.” 
In answer he sent the following: “Since it is
inappropriate to make a complaint to the king,
one must grieve over the age. / In this contest
in which you are engaged you will both win
and lose your head.”
When Majdulmulk saw that his plots were
not going to have any effect on the Sahib-Di-
van, he turned on his brother Ala’uddin and
initiated attacks on him from all quarters. An
order was given for his arrest, and his deputy
Majduddin Ibn al-Athir sat opposite him and
inquired how much he had obtained from such-
and-such a source and how much he had from
such-and-such a person.
When Sahib Shamsuddin realized how black
the situation was, he sent a message to his
brother, saying, “Don’t deny anything at all
until you are forced to, for it has been said, lā
bāraka ’llāhu ba‘da ’l-‘arḍfi’l-māl.1 Ala’ud-
din accepted to pay a fine of three million in
gold. After paying it, as will be explained,
more was demanded of him. It got so bad that
he was put in chains and held over the Bagh-
dad Bridge, beaten and given all manner of tor-
ture until he gave everything he had. After that
he had to sell even his sons, and he lost every-
thing as Majdulmulk’s fortunes rose. [1116]
Abaqa Khan goes to Syria; Prince Mänggü
Temür does battle with the Egyptians; the
Padishah returns to Baghdad.
Because the Syrians were attacking the bor-
ders of Anatolia and Diyarbekir, wreaking hav-

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

oc on Muslim territory, devouring grain and
stirring up strife, Abaqa Khan was angry with
them and decided to launch an expedition
against that land. Ostensibly hunting, he went
as far as the Khabur and Rahabat al-Sham.1 He
did not cross the Euphrates, but he dispatched
his brother Mänggü Temür in the vanguard.
When he reached Homs he camped, and Abaqa
Khan stopped on this side of the river opposite
Dayr Bir. The inhabitants of Dayr ﬂed. An or-
der was given for the place to be pillaged, and
the fortress of Zalibiya was burned. Battle was
fought with the people of Rahabat.
On the 29th of Jumada II 680 [October 15,
1281] he pulled back to Sinjar. On the 15th of
Rajab [October 30] he rejoined his ordus in
Muhallabiyya, a dependency of Mosul. On
Thursday the 14th of Rajab, corresponding to
the 17th of Toqsunch Ay of Moghai Yil [Octo-
ber 29] the two sides clashed in the vicinity of
Homs, and the battle lines extended for nearly
four leagues. Mazuq Aqa and Hinduqur’s army
were in the right wing; Alinaq, Taichu Baha-
dur, and Princes Hulachu and Qara Buqa
rained down arrows on the Turks’ left wing,
wounding some of the Egyptians and Syrians.
In one charge Alinaq broke their right wing
and chased them to the gates of Homs. They
were put to fear by that attack, and all at once
they charged the center. Prince Mänggü Temür
was still a child and had not participated in
heated battles. The great amirs Tägänä and
Doladai Yarghuchi were the planners, [1117]
and they were somewhat worried and pulled
back. The soldiers broke ranks, and many of
the Mongol army were destroyed. When this
news reached Abaqa Khan, he was extremely
angry with the amirs and said, “Next summer
1al-Raḥaba, or Raḥabat al-Shām, a town on the Eu-
phrates between Ar Raqqah and Anah (Abu’l-Fida,
Taqwim, 280).
during a quriltai an investigation of those are
fault will be held. Next year I will go there my-
self and make up for this fiasco.”
On Sunday the 17th of Rajab [November 1]
he crossed the Euphrates and camped in
Kashshaf. From there he headed to Baghdad.
On Sunday the 2nd of Sha‘ban [November 16]
he camped in the vicinity of Muhawwal.
Majdulmulk had come to Baghdad to collect
the three million Khwaja Ala’uddin had ac-
cepted to pay. He gave over at once everything
he had, and he even sold his children. After
that he gave a möchälgä that if thereafter so
much as a dirhem was proven against him he
would submit to conviction. Abaqa Khan had
mercy on him, and on the 4th of Ramadan 680
[December 17, 1281] he was released from pri-
son. Majdulmulk attacked him again. An order
was given for him to go to Baghdad with Amir
Taghachar and Ordu Qaya to audit Khwaja
Ala’uddin’s accounts and collect the 1,300,000
in gold he still owed. If he didn’t pay it upon
request, it was to be taken through beating and
torture. When nothing was gotten, they began
torturing him, parading him around the city,
and beating him. 
Abaqa Khan dies in Hamadan after
returning from Baghdad.
Abaqa Khan set out from Baghdad for
Hamadan on the 3rd of Dhu’l-Qa‘da 680 [Feb-
ruary 13, 1282]. [1118]
On Wednesday the 6th of Dhu’l-Hijja [March
18, 1282] he arrived in Hamadan and stopped
at the palace of Malik Fakhruddin Minuchihr,
where
he
was
continually
occupied
with
jirghamishi (celebration) and enjoying various
pleasures. 
On the eve of Wednesday the 20th of Dhu’l-
Hijja 680 [April 1, 1282], corresponding to the
21st of Ikindi Ay of ___ Yil, after drinking too
much, he came out after midnight to relieve
himself. The Angel of Death showed himself
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION THIRTEEN: ABAQA KHAN
541

as a black bird perched on the branch of a tree.
“What is that black bird?” he cried out. Then
he told his qorchi to shoot an arrow at it.
Search as they might, they could find no bird.
Suddenly he closed his eyes and gave up the
ghost on his golden throne. 
On Monday the 16th of Muharram 681
[April 26, 1282] Mänggü Temür also passed
away in the outskirts of Mosul.
Mourning was held in Abaqa Khan’s ordus,
and his coffin was taken to Shahu Tala and
buried next to the Great Ilkhan. His renowned
urugh became his heirs. *Someone has versi-
fied a chronogram of his death as follows:
“Tyranny became apparent and justice went
into obscurity with the death of Abaqa king of
the world. / During the months of six hundred
and eighty, on the twentieth of Dhu’l-Hijja be-
fell this tragedy.”*1 [1119]
1Omitted from JTAZ and JTRM; taken from JTK.
Part Three, on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave;
incidents that occurred during his reign that
were not included in the previous two
sections and were culled from various books
and persons.
*In the year 6__ in the city of Nishapur and
some of the villages an earthquake occurred
during the night. It was such that in the whole
city no enough of the walls remained for a bird
to take shade in. Half of the minaret of the con-
gregational mosque was found an arrow shot
away. Nearly ten thousand persons of conse-
quence were counted, aside from poor persons
in the villages no one knew. An order was giv-
en for a new city to be built next to the ruins of
the old one, and the Nishapur that exists now is
that one, but it has no rampart walls. It has
been heard that this was the third Nishapur to
be destroyed by earthquake.*2 [1120] 
2Omitted from JTAZ and JTRM; taken from JTK.
542
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

❦ SECTION FOURTEEN
THE HISTORY OF HÜLÄGÜ KHAN’S SON TÄGÜDÄR, WHO BECAME PADISHAH
AND WAS CALLED SULTAN AHMAD—IN THREE PARTS.
Part One is on his progeny with details of his
wives, sons, daughters and grandsons who
have branched off down to the present, the
names of his sons-in-law, and a genealogical
table of his sons’ branches.
Part Two is on events leading to his en-
thronement, a picture of him and his wives,
sons, grandsons, and commanders at his en-
thronement; stories of events that occurred dur-
ing his reign; a mention of the rebellions and
events that occurred.
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections and
were culled from various books and persons.
[1122]
Part One, on his progeny with details of his
wives, sons, daughters and grandsons who
have branched off down to the present, the
names of his sons-in-law, and a genealogical
table of his sons’ branches.
Ahmad Tägüdär was Hülägü Khan’s seventh
son, born of Qutui Khatun. He had many wives
and concubines. The chief of his wives was
Töküz Khatun of the Qunqirat. After her he
married Armini Khatun, also of the Qunqirat.
After her he married Baytegin, daughter of
Husayn Agha. After her he married Tödägü
Khatun, daughter of Musa Gürägän. After her
he married El Qutlugh, daughter of Kin[g]shü
and mother of Toghachaq, who was cast into
the waters of the Kura River on charges of sor-
cery.1 He married her during his reign and gave
her a boghtaq. Finally he married Tödäi
Khatun.
His sons were three, Qaplanchi by Armini
Khatun, Arslanchi also by Armini Khatun, and
Noqachi by a concubine named Qurquchin.
He had six daughters as follows. The eldest
was named Küchük, born of Töküz Khatun.
She was married to Alinaq. [1123]
The second was Könchäk, whose mother was
Armini Khatun. At present she is the chief wife
of Sarucha Agha’s son Amir Irinjin. 
The third was Chechäk, also born of Armini
Khatun. She was married to Borachu son of
Durabai, the amir of Diyarbekir.
The fourth was Mainu, also by Armini
Khatun. She was given to Jandan son of Gäräi
Ba’urchi.
The fifth was Sailun by Tödägü Khatun, and
she was given to Qaracha, an ev-oghlan of
Örüg Khatun’s ordu.
The sixth was Kältürmish by a concubine
named Qonqurchin; she was given to Bughu’s
son Shadai, a commander of ten thousand. At
present she is married to Shadai’s son, Toghan.
[1124]
1For this episode see text p. 1180 below.

Part Two, on events leading to his
enthronement, a picture of him and his
wives, sons, grandsons, and commanders at
his enthronement; stories of events that
occurred during his reign; a mention of the
rebellions and events that occurred.
When Abaqa Khan passed away, the ladies,
princes, and amirs held mourning in Jaghatu,
and Ahmad came from Kurdistan. Before
Abaqa Khan’s death, Nardu Akhtachi, the
shahna of Tabriz, had gone to summon Prince
Arghun on some item of business. He had gone
there unencumbered. At that time Shiktür Noy-
an was also sent out to summon him. At the
fourth way station he reached the prince, and
the prince and a few of his companions re-
joined the ladies and princes in Maragha. They
offered him a goblet in condolence for his fa-
ther. Buqa joined his service and ordered the
sükürchis, aqtachis, qorchis, and other atten-
dants who had been in Abaqa Khan’s personal
service to continue as before in service to the
prince. The grand amirs Buqa, Shishi Bakhshi,
Doladai Idächi, [1125] Joshi, and Ordu Qaya
were attending.
After the rites of condolences were held they
went
to
Yaghatu.1
Before
Prince Arghun
arrived, the princes who were there, Tägüdär,
Ajai, Qonqurtai, Hulachu, Tagha[i] Temür,
Jüshkäb, Kin[g]shü, and Baidu, consulted with
the ladies and amirs concerning the succession.
It occurred to them that since the throne was
vacant, [something must be done] lest damage
be done to the kingdom before the other
princes arrived. 
In that council Qonqurtai, Hulachu, Jüshkäb,
and Kin[g]shü and the amirs Shiktür Noyan,
Su’unchaq Aqa, Arab, Asiq, and Qara Buqa
agreed with the other group that Ahmad should
be padishah. Öljäi Khatun and the amirs who
were with her wanted Mänggü Temür. Buqa
and his brother Aruq, as well as Aq Buqa and
others of Abaqa Khan’s intimates, said, “Prince
Arghun is superior to all in terms of intelli-
gence, farsightedness, and policy-making. He
is worthy of ruling.” Just then news arrived
that Prince Mänggü Temür had died, so they
were relieved of having to consider him. Qutui
Khatun was also inclined to Prince Arghun,
1Yaghatu ~ Jaghatu. 
544
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

and she exerted herself on his behalf. In short,
disagreement prevailed among them.
Shishi Bakhshi was an extremely intelligent
and clever amir. When he saw that most of the
amirs were inclined to Ahmad, he said to
Prince Arghun, “It would be best for you and
for us if you consent to Ahmad’s being ruler so
that we can get out of this midst alive.” Since
the prince had no soldiers along, he necessarily
consented.
On the 7th of Üchünch Ay of Qonin Yil, cor-
responding to the 26th of Muharram 681 [May
6, 1282], all came to an agreement and con-
firmed the rule upon Ahmad. Prince Arghun
withdrew from Ala Tagh three days later
[1126] and went to Siyah Koh, where he took
over his father’s treasury. Taghachar was on his
way from Fars and joined him there. Qutui
Khatun and the princes who were in league
with her also went to Ala Tagh. Shamsuddin
the Sahib-Divan was also in Prince Arghun’s
service, but when the rule was settled upon Ah-
mad, Asiq, who was Qutui Khatun’s amir-
ordu, sent word for him to be brought to Ah-
mad’s ordu.
On Sunday the 13th of Rabi‘ I 681 [June 21,
1282] möchälgäs (written pledges) were given
as was customary. Qonqurtai raised Ahmad’s
right arm, Shiktür Noyan held his left arm, and
together they sat him on the throne. As was the
Mongols’ custom the rites and rituals of cele-
bration and congratulation were held. Since he
claimed to be Muslim they called him Sultan
Ahmad.
Prince Arghun comes before Ahmad after his
enthronement; the cause of Prince Qonqurtai’s
death; Khwaja Ala’uddin Ata-Malik is patron-
ized, and Majdulmulk is executed.
After celebrations were staged, he ordered
the treasuries that were in Shahu Tala brought
and distributed among the ladies, princes,
amirs, courtiers, and the needy. He gave every
individual in the army 120 dinars. Without
warning Prince Arghun appeared with two or
three thousand horsemen and began to chastise
him, saying, “Why didn’t you wait for my
arrival so that I could seat you on the throne?”
Ahmad welcomed him and showed him honor,
giving him with his own hand twenty bars of
gold he was keeping for him. [1127] He also
gave two to Prince Baidu.
That day a firm friendship was formed be-
tween Arghun and Qonqurtai in the ordu of
Toqiyatai Khatun, who had mediated the
friendship, and they swore that henceforth en-
voys would be exchanged. This was the reason
Qonqurtai was killed, as will be explained
later.
Prince Arghun withdrew from Ala Tagh with
Ahmad’s permission and camped at Siyah Koh
on the 26th of Rabi‘ I [July 4, 1282]. Envoys
were sent to Hamadan to bring Sahib Ala’ud-
din Ata-Malik, who was imprisoned, and Maj-
dulmulk. Majdulmulk, whose patron with Ah-
mad was Altachu Aqa’s son Yesü Buqa, started
up the same old fight again with Khwaja
Shamsuddin, and he was very nearly given
overall supervision of the administration, but
Sahib Shamsuddin took refuge with Armini
Khatun, under whose patronage he ﬂourished
as before. He did, however, stir up a number of
people to calumniate Majdulmulk. Reports
were made on him, both true and false, and
during that time Majdulmulk sent a message to
Prince Arghun saying, “I am your enchü. The
Sahib-Divan poisoned your father. Since he
knows that I am aware of it, he is going to try
to kill me. If anything happens, the prince
should be aware.”
Majdulmulk’s nephew Sa‘duddin was in-
formed of the situation, and around that time,
because Majdulmulk had expelled him from
his position as treasurer over a quarrel, he had
been hovering around nursing a grudge against
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOURTEEN: TÄGÜDÄR KHAN
545

him. Some of the Sahib’s friends seduced him
and took him before the Sahib, who promised
to make him auditor general of Persia and cur-
ried such favor with him that he went and re-
ported that Majdulmulk was in cahoots with
[1128] Prince Arghun and had sent an envoy to
him. A decree was issued for all Khwaja
Ala’uddin Ata-Malik’s possessions and belong-
ings that had been confiscated to be returned,
and he was reinstated to favor and awarded
textiles
and
commercial
goods. Ala’uddin
brought them all and said, “Everything we
brothers have acquired has been due to the
great generosity of the Ilkhan. I hereby at this
quriltai do offer them as a gift.” So saying, he
motioned for everything to be given over to
pillage. 
An order was given for the great amirs
Su’unchaq Aqa and Uru’ut to make an investi-
gation of Majdulmulk. Among his belongings
was discovered a piece of lion skin on which
was written in an illegible script something in
yellow and red. Since the Mongols have a hor-
ror of sorcery, they were afraid of the writing
and submitted it as evidence to the investiga-
tion, where it was much discussed. The
bakhshis and shamans said it was a talisman
that should be dipped in water and he should
be made to drink it so that the magic would re-
bound upon him. They tried to make Majdul-
mulk do it, but he refused because the talisman
had been made by Shaykh Abdul-Rahman and
hidden among his effects, and he knew that it
was not devoid of trickery and deceit. After he
was indicted, Su’unchaq Aqa refused to con-
sent to shedding his blood. The more they in-
sisted, the more he refused. Finally he got the
gout and Shaykh Abdul-Rahman went to visit
him and kept insisting until he gave in and ac-
quiesced to his execution. Ahmad’s decree was
issued for him to be turned over to his adver-
saries to be put to death. When the news of his
committal was published, a large group of peo-
ple gathered. Sahib Shamsuddin would not
give his consent to his death and asked that he
be pardoned. Khwaja Ala’uddin and Khwaja
Harun [1129] were most insistent *and he was
turned over at night to a crowd that tore him
limb from limb. He was killed on the eve of
Wednesday the 8th of Jumada I 681 [August
14, 1282] at Ala Tagh,*1 and his body parts
were sent in all directions. 
Ahmad favored Khwaja Ala’uddin and gave
him Baghdad. Since he had not been in office
for a time, he did not go himself but rather sent
his deputies to act on his behalf. 
The beginning of the dispute between
Ahmad and Prince Arghun; Arghun comes
from Khurasan to Baghdad and then
returns to Khurasan.
Several times Ahmad sent envoys to Arghun
to summon Buqa, but every time he came up
with an excuse. In the end he gave him permis-
sion, and Buqa set out in tears. When he came
before Ahmad, Qutui Khatun showed him
great favor and honor and garbed him in a coat
that had been the Great Ilkhan’s own. He re-
mained there, but he did not initiate anything. 
1Instead of the portion marked *…*, JTK has the fol-
lowing: “and took him to Khwaja Ala’uddin’s tent,
where he questioned him from afternoon until evening
about jeweled utensils, property deeds, paizas, and
yarlighs. He gave him encouragement and took back
from him what he had found, for, aside from real estate,
3,000,000 had come to him from the revenues of Bagh-
dad, and real estate in excess of that. He wanted to re-
port it, but they kept him from it lest he be pardoned. On
the eve of Wednesday the 8th of Jumada I 681 at Ala
Tagh he was killed in Ajighi’s tent behind Ahmad’s
ordu. As his head was being stuffed with straw to be sent
to Baghdad, the writer of this document, Rashid Khwafi,
spoke these words: ‘We saw that head, in which was so
much ambition and craving for the vizierate, / full of
straw, as his enemies would wish, and every tender limb
of his body was in someone else’s hands.’ ”
546
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Prince Arghun set out from Soghurluq for
Khurasan. On the 4th of Rabi‘ II 681 [July 12,
1282] Ahmad rewarded Qonqurtai, gave him
Toqiyatai Khatun, and sent him off to guard
Anatolia. On the 19th of Rabi‘ II [July 27] he
sent Amir Aq Buqa after him. 
[Ahmad] held Shaykh Abdul-Rahman in
such reverence that he called him “father,” and
he called Ishan Mängli, a disciple of Babi
Ya‘qub who resided in Arran, his qarindash
[brother]. He used to go often to his house,
[1130] which was near the back gate of the
ordu, and participate in sama‘, paying little at-
tention to matters of finance and state. His
mother, Qutui Khatun, who was extremely in-
telligent and clever, took care of fiscal affairs
together with Asiq. Although he had become
ruler through Shiktür Noyan’s and Su’unchaq
Aqa’s efforts, and he had given Shiktür a para-
sol and rewarded him well, he paid them little
attention. In short, with Shaykh Abdul-Rah-
man’s and Sahib Shamsuddin’s approval he
sent Mawlana Qutbuddin Shirazi, the most
learned man in the world, on an embassy to
Egypt on the 19th of Jumada I 681 [August 25,
1282].
On the first of Muharram 681 [April 11,
1282] Amir Ali Chäkibän, who was Khwaja
Ala’uddin’s protector, and Qutlughshah, a son
of his slave, came to Prince Arghun and report-
ed that the Sahib-Divan had sent someone to
Khwaja Wajihuddin to poison the prince. An
order was given for Khwaja Wajih to be appre-
hended in Quchan and his quarters plundered.
With Bulughan Khatun’s intercession he was
pardoned and set free on the 23rd of Jumada II
[September 28]. Amir Ali was ordered to at-
tend court until the matter could be investi-
gated.
Arghun set out to winter in Baghdad. In
Rayy he rewarded Malik Fakhruddin by rein-
stating him as governor of that area as before.
When Ahmad heard that, he sent an envoy to
apprehend the malik and take him to Shirvan,
where he was tormented with all sorts of impo-
sitions. Prince Arghun learned of it and sent a
message to the amirs and the Sahib-Divan, say-
ing, “My father gave the malik to me, and I as-
signed him to a delicate position. What is the
meaning of these impositions and torment? If
he is harmed I will take revenge. Does the
Sahib-Divan think I will ignore what he has
done?” [1131]
When the prince arrived in Baghdad, Naj-
muddin Asfar, Khwaja Ala’uddin’s deputy, had
died. He said, “I demand the balance of what
Ala’uddin owed from my father’s time.” And
he seized his deputies and those attached to
him and subjected them to confiscation and
impositions. Najmuddin Asfar was disinterred
and thrown into the street. 
When this news reached Khwaja Ala’uddin,
he was dreadfully hurt and saddened. Over-
come by a headache, he died of that affliction
in Arran on the 4th of Dhu’l-Hijja 681 [March
5, 1283]. Khwaja Shamsuddin’s son Harun was
sent as governor of Baghdad in his stead.
That winter Prince Arghun was in Baghdad,
attended by a division of Qara’una soldiers
who wintered in Baghdad and summered in
Siyah Koh and who had belonged personally to
Abaqa Khan. Their leaders, Princes Gaikhatu
and Baidu, and the amirs Taghachar, Cha’uqur,
Hanqutur, Doladai Idächi, [El]chi Totqavul,
Joshi, Qunchuqbal, and other gäzigtäns and at-
tendants of Abaqa Khan’s were all devoted to
Prince Arghun. Worried by their unity, Ahmad
assigned a troop led by Jüshkäb, Uruq, and Qu-
rumshi to winter in Diyarbekir so that it would
be impossible for the others to get from Anato-
lia to Baghdad and he would be safe. When
spring came Prince Arghun returned from
Baghdad to Khurasan. Prince Arghun stationed
Jüshkäb with the amirs mentioned above with
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOURTEEN: TÄGÜDÄR KHAN
547

his ordus and took Ordu Qaya and Buqdai Aq-
tachi with himself. 
When he reached Rayy he had the shahna
Ahmad had stationed there severely beaten, put
a dushakha on him, mounted him on an ass,
and sent him off to Ahmad. After that, he sent a
stream of envoys to summon the Sahib-Divan
on the matter of his having poisoned Arghun’s
father. [1132] He summoned the members of
his personal retinue Ahmad had taken back.
Thus the fire of sedition ﬂared up between the
two.
When he reached Mazanderan, Emgächin
Noyan came out with a division of soldiers to
greet him. He summoned Hindu Noyan, who
had two divisions guarding the banks of the
Oxus, and said, “While my father was still
alive he summoned me. As ordered, I set forth
without soldiers. When I arrived there he had
already died, and things were in turmoil. Since
I had no soldiers there was nothing I could do
but consent. Now, if you amirs help me, I will
get my father’s crown and throne out of the
usurper’s hands. Your efforts will be rewarded,
and our good name will be preserved.”
Hindu Noyan replied, “Although the situa-
tion is as the prince says, Ahmad is the aqa,
and if he has become khan in that land, you,
thank God, are commander and padishah in
this region. Listen to the words of this old man,
and do not quarrel with him. If he attacks you,
we servants will give our lives to requite it.”
He was most eloquent in such advice, but the
prince refused to listen, so Hindu Noyan turned
away and took Ahmad’s part because by uja’ur
[clan] he was from Qutui Khatun’s ordu. The
prince continued to reﬂect in that regard.
Pacem. [1133]
The case of Prince Qonqurtai and his death;
Ahmad goes to Khurasan; Prince Arghun
gains a victory after being in a weakened
state.
From this direction Ahmad went to his sum-
mer quarters in Ala Tagh. 
He sent Shaykh Abdul-Rahman on an em-
bassy to Egypt, but in Damascus he was
thrown into prison for life, where he remained
until he died.
Ahmad summoned Qonqurtai for a quriltai.
As ordered, he appeared and attached himself
to court. He sent one of his intimates, Chärig
by name, with tansuqs from Anatolia to
Arghun Khan as an apology. Arghun rewarded
Chärig handsomely and sent two leopards back
with him for Qonqurtai. When Ahmad learned
of this, he lost all trust in Qonqurtai, and things
got so bad between them that those who were
there were able to notice the change in attitude
of both. It began to be said that Qonqurtai was
plotting with Arghun to seize Ahmad on the
day of künyanglamishi [new year’s celebra-
tion], and that Küchük Unuqchi and Shadai
Aqtachi were in league with him. A number of
soldiers were sick of [Ahmad’s] overbearing
ways, so they joined Qonqurtai to seize him
and appointed a certain night to execute the
deed. Ahmad learned of the conspiracy, and
one day before the künyanglamishi he went to
his son-in-law Alinaq’s quarters and got him to
agree to attack Qonqurtai at dawn the next day,
seize him, and bring him before Ahmad. On
the 26th of Shawwal 682 [January 17, 1284] he
said, “The sultan need not worry. I will bring
Arghun to court with his hands bound.” Ahmad
rewarded Alinaq [1134] with promotion and
gave him soldiers.
At dawn the next day, künyanglamishi, the
first day of Bechin Yil, they took care of Qon-
qurtai in Qara Bagh in Arran. The ordu was
cordoned off, and for six days trials were held.
548
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Küchük Unuqchi and Shadai Aqtachi were
executed. 
When that affair was over, an order was giv-
en for Jüshkäb, Uruq, and the group of amirs
Arghun had stationed over his ordus in Bagh-
dad to be arrested—like Taghachar, Cha’uqur,
Hanqutur, Doladai, [El]chi Totqavul, Joshi, and
Qunchuqbal. They were imprisoned in Tabriz
(but when Arghun Khan arrived they were set
free1). Gaikhatu submitted and was sent to Ah-
mad. Along the way he escaped from his
guards and went to Arghun Khan in Sawa. Ah-
mad assigned Alinaq a troop to do battle with
Arghun, and when that news reached Qazwin,
Qazi Raziuddin informed the basqaq of Rayy,
and he set out by post horse to report to
Arghun, saying, “Qonqurtai has been removed,
his amirs and intimates have been executed,
and the grand amirs are held in chains. Ahmad
has given Alinaq one of his daughters and sent
him with a large contingent as an advance
force to attack you. He will follow behind.”
On Thursday the 18th of Muharram 683
[April 6, 1284] he married Tödäi Khatun.
Ahmad dispatched more than a hundred
thousand select Mongol, Muslim, Armenian,
and Georgian horsemen amply supplied and
armed with Tubut, Alinaq, Yasar Oghul, Achu
Shükürchi, Ghazan Aqa, Eshik Tughli, and
Su’unchaq’s son Shadai in the vanguard with
fifteen thousand horsemen [1135] on the 9th of
Dhu’l-Qa‘da 682 [January 29, 1284]. Three
days later much snow fell, and on account of
the difficulty, it caused Tubut and Yasar, who
were in front, to get stuck. Then Alinaq set out
from Qazwin with Yasar Oghul and Taghai,
Ahmad’s kükältash, in the vanguard. They
galloped as far as Varamin, seized and plun-
dered three hundred households of artisans
1I.e. later, when Arghun had arrived back. See text p.
1147 below.
who belonged to Arghun Khan, and returned to
the camp.
When Arghun was apprised of this event he
sent envoys to the treasury at Garrakan to bring
everything that was available. He also sent to
the workshops at Nishapur, Tus, and Isfarayin
to have cloth brought. Within twenty days
quantities of gold, jewels, and textiles were de-
livered to Adiliyya in Jurjan, and he distributed
it
among
the
amirs
and
soldiers.
Malik
Fakhruddin of Rayy inventoried it and had
written “an inventory of items distributed to
the victorious soldiers” when Arghun entered
the treasury and snatched the pages from his
hand. Although he had no familiarity with the
Persian script, he picked up a pen and fortu-
itously wrote the word “victorious” quite nice-
ly. Qawamuddin the vizier of Fars was present
and was astonished to see such a thing. “Since
the word ‘victorious’ was written by the
Padishah’s blessed pen,” he said, “it was an in-
dication that God would give him victory.”
The next day an envoy arrived from Rayy
saying that Alinaq and his liege men and sol-
diers had reached the vicinity of Qazwin.
Arghun sent Ulai Temür as a vanguard, and on
his heels he dispatched Emgächin Noyan while
he himself set out via Tamisha, having sta-
tioned Shishi Bakhshi over his aghruqs.
On the 8th of Safar 683 [April 26, 1284] Ah-
mad set out from Pilsuvar in Mughan with
80,000 soldiers. On the 13th of the same month
an envoy arrived saying that Arghun’s army
[1136] had appeared in the vicinity of Taliqan.
Ahmad sent Alinaq’s son Qurumshi from the
Ardabil area to his father to say, “If you are
more numerous, do battle; if not, wait patiently
until we arrive.” Having stationed Äbügän
over his aghruq, he set out from Ardabil on the
18th of Safar2 and went two marches.
2This date cannot be correct in view of the date of the
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOURTEEN: TÄGÜDÄR KHAN
549

Arghun sent an envoy to Nawroz for a
Qara’una division under his command to come
from the rear. He also summoned Hindu Noyan
with his division. Arghun himself charged with
six thousand horsemen, and the forward scouts
met in the vicinity of Khayl-i-Buzurg. One of
Arghun’s scouts was captured and taken to Ali-
naq, who got him drunk, questioned him, and
learned all about his deployment. Tubut, Yasar
Oghul, and Shadai Gürägän had mustered and
mounted fifteen thousand cavalry, over and
above Arqasun’s division.
On Thursday the 16th of Safar 683 [May 4,
1284], the two armies clashed in the vicinity of
Aq Khwaja near Qazwin. Prince Arghun at-
tacked like an enraged lion and killed many.
The battle lasted from noon until evening, and
in the end Tubut and Alinaq were defeated and
forced to retreat from the gates of Jamalabad to
the vicinity of Abhar, a distance of nearly ten
leagues. On the other side Achu Shükürchi,
Ghazan Bahadur, and Eshik Tughli of the
Jalayir attacked Arghun’s baggage train and
carried off Najib Khadim along with some of
the baggage. Arghun was so outraged he could
not be calmed. He wanted to pursue those in
retreat, but the amirs advised against it.
Alinaq had an Arabian mare that ran after
him in battle, and when his steed failed him he
would mount the mare. It was wandering
around the battlefield, unable to find Alinaq.
Arghun recognized the mare and ordered it
surrounded. Amir Nawroz lassoed it, [1137]
and Arghun gave it to him. Then he sent a mes-
sage to Alinaq, saying, “I never thought, with
the reputation you have for bravery and
courage, that you would turn your back on this
little army and take ﬂight. I have caught your
following battle (16 Safar). However, no other ordinal
number resembles hijdahum (18th) closely enough to be
commonly confused with it.
famous mare like a wild ass, while you have
ﬂed like a mountain sheep before the cry of an
attacking lion.” 
After sending such a message he pulled back
at his amirs’ advice. When he reached Tihran
in Rayy, Emgächin Bahadur and other amirs
agreed, saying, “When we reach our camp and
aghruq and the Qara’una join us from that
side, if Ahmad’s army comes after us we can
do battle with them in the vicinity of Kalpush
above Jajarm. This will be better because we
will have our backs against our homes and our
horses will be rested.” With this thought in
mind he pulled back, but when he reached
Damghan he found no trace of the Qara’unas,
for they had heard along the way that Arghun’s
army had been defeated and therefore turned
back, attacking and plundering as they went. 
When Arghun reached Bistam he visited the
shrine of Bayazid and sought his intercession
for God to give him victory. Ahmad had taken
refuge with Shaykh Babi and his followers and
asked them for help. In the end the effective-
ness of the two at God’s court became
apparent.
Doubtless he will be ruined who takes refuge
with a dead Babi, / But he will ﬂourish who
seeks assistance from Bayazid.
On Monday the 20th of Safar [May 8]
Tubut’s envoy came before Ahmad to relay this
message: “We have done battle with Arghun,
and he has fled. We have taken many of his
soldiers captive [1138] and will bring them, but
the gäjigä [rear] force has not reached us.”
That day they celebrated.
On the 23rd of Safar [May 11] Ahmad joined
Tubut in Sharuyaz, and Tükäl Bakhshi’s son
Chärig Temür was executed on a charge of
having supported Arghun. The next day Hu-
lachu Oghul and a division of soldiers were
dispatched to Rayy, and all the amirs were or-
dered to give written pledges that they would
550
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

not disobey Buqa. They all acquiesced except
Alinaq.
On the 28th of Safar [May 16] he decamped
from Qonqur Öläng, leaving Armini Khatun
and the ordus there. He made Su’unchaq Aqa
his attendant. From the vicinity of Qazwin the
soldiers,
especially
the
Georgians,
began
killing and pillaging again. They harassed the
people with all sorts of torments and carried
off everything they found until they reached
Khurasan.
When Arghun learned of this advance he
wanted to gather his dispersed soldiers. He sent
Lagzi and Ordu Buqa as ambassadors to Ah-
mad, and they reached him in Aq Khwaja in
Qazwin. They entreated him for a truce, and
the next day promises and pacts were made
and they withdrew. Arghun’s message was as
follows: “How can I draw a sword in my aqa’s
face? It was never in my mind to rebel against
him, but when Alinaq came and plundered and
took my artisans captive, I had to repel him in
order to free my people. He had the audacity to
lead an army against me, and it was necessary
for me to do battle.”
The amirs said unanimously, “Arghun is your
son, and the two armies are one. The weather
is hot, and many animals have been lost. The
best things to do would be to withdraw, partic-
ularly since Arghun regrets what he has done.”
Ahmad refused to listen. The next day the late
Khwaja Nasîruddin Tusi’s sons Sadruddin and
Asiluddin [1139] reported that according to
heavenly portents leading an army was not ad-
visable. Ahmad was highly incensed and had
them punished. 
On Wednesday the 14th of Rabi‘ I 683 [May
31, 1284], Prince Arghun and Tägüdär Oghul’s
son Umar Oghul met in the village of Surkha
in Simnan. Noqai Yarghuchi was with them,
and Shishi Bakhshi and Arghun’s envoys pro-
posed a truce. On the third day, [Ahmad] sent
back the princes Tagha[i] Temür and Sögä and
the amirs Buqa and Doladai Yarghuchi from
Ribat-i-Akhari to reply to the embassy and say,
“If Arghun is in submission, let him either
come himself or send Gaikhatu.” 
“Since we are going under truce,” Buqa said
to him, “you must not move ahead.”
“I will stop in the meadows at Kharraqan
until you come,” he replied.
Ahmad decamped from there on the 17th of
Rabi‘ I [June 3], and the next day he arrived in
Damghan, where the people were pillaged and
subjected to all sorts of torment. On the 20th of
the month [June 6] he reached Kharraqan, and
from there Prince Ghazan and his companions
turned back. During those few days Jirqudai
Amir-Hazar and his brother Yesüdär, Bulughan
the shahna of Shiraz, and a group of qushchis
submitted. He sent Alinaq with a troop in the
vanguard. On Wednesday the 28th [June 14] he
dismounted in Kalpush.
On Friday the last day of Rabi‘ I [June 16]
Prince Gaikhatu and the princes Taghai Temür
and Sögä and the amirs Buqa, Nawroz, and
Boralghi arrived. When Buqa saw that Ahmad
had not kept his word to wait, he was insulted
and attributed it to Arghun’s good fortune. The
next day, the first of Rabi‘ II [June 17], he sent
Nawroz and Boralghi back. On Monday the
3rd [June 19] he decamped from Kalpush. Dur-
ing those few days Yulai Temür and Sönitäi
Noyan’s son Emgächin [1140] submitted. Ah-
mad chastised Buqa and the other amirs for
stopping.
“Was my plan better or yours?” he asked
Buqa.
“The Padishah’s words are correct,” Buqa
replied. “Where would the plans of qarachu
(commoners) like us get us?” 
“When we reach Qutui Khatun,” said Ah-
mad, “we will repeat these words there.” Since
he was speaking in threats and had belittled
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOURTEEN: TÄGÜDÄR KHAN
551

Buqa and aggrandized Aq Buqa in his place,
Buqa became more tempted to support Arghun.
On Sunday the 9th of Rabi‘ II [June 25] Ah-
mad reached Quchan, where he heard that
Arghun had fortified himself in Kalat Koh.
Arghun had gone from Quchan to Kalat Koh
by
night
with
Boralghi,
Nawroz,
Buqdai
Akhtachi, and Tarabai, and by morning not
more than a few individuals of [Ahmad’s] elite
remained with him. Arghun went into the Kalat
fortress with Bulughan Khatun, and when
Nawroz heard that Alinaq was arriving, he
knelt before Arghun and said, “The best plan
would be for us to mount right away, cross the
Oxus, and go to Qonchi. From there, with his
help, we can go repel the enemy.” Arghun paid
no attention to these words.
Lagzi, his wife, and Arghun Aqa’s wife sur-
rendered to Ahmad, and Lagzi said, “If so or-
dered, let me go bring Arghun.” Ahmad gave
him permission. Lagzi went with a troop and
attacked Qutlugh Khatun’s ordu and pillaged
her baggage. Nawroz went to him and asked
for her back, but he refused. Lagzi came for-
ward gravely, grabbed Nawroz’s reins, and
said, “I will not let you go back. You must
come to Ahmad and pay homage.” 
Nawroz put his hand on his sword and said,
“So long as I am alive I will not turn my back
on Arghun. I only live to serve him. It is for-
tunate for him that the world does not remain
in one condition.” [1141]
By the time you turn your ring around, this
world will have changed a hundred times.
When Lagzi realized that he was not going to
get anywhere with him, he let Nawroz go and
went to Ahmad with vast treasures, a large
share of which Ahmad gave him.
Arghun was consulting with his amirs in the
fortress when Alinaq arrived. Arghun went
down from the fortress alone, and when he was
near the soldiers and Alinaq he cried out. 
Alinaq came out on foot in front of the lines
and kissed the ground, saying, “Prince of the
World, your uncle is anxious to see you.” 
Altai said, “Arghun is going to see Ahmad.” 
Immediately
he
set
out
with
Bulughan
Khatun for Ahmad’s camp, and on Thursday
the 13th of Rabi‘ II [June 29, 1284] he came
before Ahmad, who embraced him and kissed
his face. Then he turned him over to Alinaq
and said, “Keep him well until we get to Qutui
Khatun to try him.”
“Since the foe has fallen into our hands, it
would be better to deal with him this very
night,” said Alinaq.
“He has no soldiers or money,” said Ahmad.
“What can he do?” Then he ordered Shishi
Bakhshi, Qada’an, Ur Temür Qushchi, and Bo-
ralghi seized.
On Friday the 14th of Rabi‘ II [June 30] he
decamped. On Saturday the 15th [July 1] Bu-
lughan Khatun’s banquet took place, as did the
executions of Ur Temür Qushchi, Negübäi
Qushchi, and the brother of Qajar Akhtachi for
supporting Arghun.
Since Ahmad desired Tödäi Khatun, he sent
Alinaq to guard [Arghun] and stationed the
princes at the head of the army. He set out with
his intimates on Sunday the 16th of Rabi‘ II
[July 2] for the aghruq. 
Buqa said, “Since Qipchaq Oghul of Jochi
Qasar’s family has come to obtain permission
to marry my daughter, and there is friendship
and unity between us, I want to accompany
him and offer a toast.” [1142]
“Let it be,” said Ahmad. On this pretext
Buqa stopped.
Arghun was sad and downcast in the hands
of his guards, but Bulughan Khatun encour-
aged him by saying, “The night is pregnant.”
Amir Buqa wanted to discharge his obliga-
tions to Abaqa Khan by doing something to
make Arghun king, so he won over Yesü Buqa
552
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Gürägän, Aruq, and Qurumshi, who were rela-
tives of his. After that, he made a proposition
to Tägänä, and after him to Arqasun Noyan the
son of Kökä Elgä, and to each and every one of
the amirs he said in the absence of the others,
“Ahmad has agreed with his intimates Sögä,
Tubut, Alinaq, and Äbügän to kill all the amirs
in the vicinity of Isfarayin when he had fin-
ished with Arghun. This being so, if we do not
look to our own devices today, while there is
still an opportunity, what will happen?”
Aruq, an attendant of Jüshkäb’s, said, “What
he says is true, for Hinduqur’s son Qurumshi
came and reported that on the day of Bulughan
Khatun’s banquet he was saying this very thing
to Alinaq and his liege men.” Buqa and Aruq
reported this to Jüshkäb, and Tägänä told Hu-
lachu, Buqa, and the amirs that in advancing
this deed Hulachu should be the leader on be-
half of the princes. They replied, “Buqa is the
elder from among the amirs,” and they all
agreed not to disobey his command. Arqasun
Noyan also joined with his division. 
Since Alinaq had won his victory he had
been pridefully indulging in revelry night and
day, heedless of the convolutions of fate. 
Amir Buqa summoned Emchäk, one of
Arghun’s guards, and made him swear an oath
in Mongolian that he would not divulge the se-
cret he was about to be told. Then he said,
“Tell Arghun to be especially nice to Alinaq
tonight and to give him and his liege men lots
of wine. But tell him to stay sober himself.”
After that, he sent Amir Boralghu, Arghun’s
kükäldash, to him on this same mission, [1143]
and he plotted with Aruq and Qurumshi to get
Qara Noqai and Taitaq dead drunk. Together
they threw a party and invited Alinaq. “I’m on
duty to guard Arghun tonight,” he said. “I can’t
come drinking.” Jüshkäb promised to watch
[Arghun], and Alinaq was coaxed into drink-
ing. By the time of the evening prayer he had
fallen over in a dead drunk. 
That night Buqa and three horsemen went
into the yärgä as though to patrol. He sent one
of the men to sneak into the tent and wake
Arghun up. “Buqa is here in fidelity to you,”
he said. “He has gotten the princes, amirs, and
soldiers on your side and has come to get you
out.”
Thinking this was a trick, Arghun was some-
what afraid, but the man swore he was telling
the truth and there was no reason to fear.
Arghun went out of the tent, saw Buqa, and
asked, “What sedition is this?”
He said, “ ‘Fortune has smiled upon you. The
enemy’s lot has been overturned.’ ” Then he
got Arghun on a horse.
When they reached the third picket, a Mon-
gol said, “There were four of you when you
went in, and now there are five of you coming
out. How’s that?”
“We were five,” said Buqa. “Your eyes must
have been affected by sleep and confused two
of us. You’ve made a mistake, that’s all.” 
“That’s how it must have been,” said the
Mongol. 
They passed through in safety and went to
Buqa’s quarters. Arghun put on his weapons
and mounted an Arabian horse, and then they
went to attack Alinaq, whom they killed in his
tent. Amir Ali the tamghachi of Tabriz, one of
Buqa’s attendants, lifted the skirt of the tent,
severed his head from his body, [1144] and
threw it outside. This took place on Tuesday
eve the 18th of Rabi‘ II 683 [July 4, 1284].
That same night they sent Arqasun as an en-
voy to Hulachu and Tägänä at Sher Koh to say,
“We have killed Alinaq and Taitaq. You must
kill Yasar Oghul and Äbügän.” Hulachu hated
Yasar, so he strangled him with a bowstring,
but he kept Äbügän. That night they seized Al-
tachu Bitigchi’s son Qara Buqa, Taitaq, Tubut,
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOURTEEN: TÄGÜDÄR KHAN
553

and some others, and the next day they killed
some of them and let others go.
Arghun, who had been a prisoner when night
fell, woke up in the morning as the emperor of
the face of the earth. When this occurred, Ah-
mad had not yet reached Jurbad1 or joined his
ordus and Tödäi Khatun. Prince Kin[g]shü was
accompanying him, as were the amirs Emgä-
chin, Aq Buqa, and Lagzi. At noon one of
Taitaq’s hazaras joined him and reported. Ah-
mad took counsel with his amirs and turned
back to do battle. Suddenly someone arrived
from Mazuq Qushchi to tell him, “All those at-
tached to you have been killed, and they are
coming together to attack you. It’s too late to
do anything about it. If you have the stamina
and the opportunity, ﬂee!”
Ahmad turned back in defeat. When he
reached Kalpush he had a moment in private
with Tödäi Khatun.
On the 19th of Rabi‘ II 683 [July 5] he set out
in ﬂight from the vicinity of Isfarayin. Along
the way he came across Yulai Temür and his
followers who were coming from Mazanderan.
He killed them and turned in the direction of
Qumis and Persia.
When the princes and amirs killed Alinaq,
they sent Börä the shahna of Isfahan to tell the
Qara’una division, which was in the Siyah Koh
area, to mount and seize Ahmad. A Mongol
named Chärig, [1145] who had been Qonqur-
tai’s amir-ordu, was sent with four hundred
horsemen to track down Ahmad, and on his
heels Doladai Yarghuchi was dispatched with
another four hundred horsemen. They pursued
him so relentlessly that just as he decamped
1Jūrbad, Arabicized as Jarbādhqān. There were two of
them: one (the modern Golpayegan) between Isfahan
and Hamadan and the other, doubtless the one meant
here, between Astarabad (modern Gorgan) and Jurjan
(modern Gonbad-e-Kavus). See Abu’l-Fida, Taqwim, p.
419.
from a place they would alight. When Börä
met the Qara’una, they too mounted at once
and set out to find Ahmad. 
Hulachu and Kingshü arrived at Arghun’s
court on Monday the 24th of Rabi‘ II [July 10]
in Kharraqan. They seized Amir Aq Buqa, who
had become Ahmad’s advisor and against
whom Buqa held a grudge.
The princes and amirs held council regarding
the rule. Buqa was inclined to Arghun, Aruq to
Jüshkäb, and Tägänä to Hulachu. 
“Hulachu is the son of Hülägü Khan,” said
Tägänä. “So long as a son is around, the rule
cannot go to grandsons.” 
“The great yurt is commanded by Jüshkäb,”
said Aruq and Qurumshi. “He is the eldest in
age. He is worthy.”
Buqa said, “The Qa’an who was the emperor
of the inhabited quarter of the globe and the
aqa of all the urugh of Genghis Khan awarded
the rule of the realms of Iran, after his brother
Hülägü Khan, to his eldest son Abaqa Khan,
who was the most intelligent and most perfect.
After him, it should go by inheritance to his
true son Arghun. If busybodies had not med-
dled in the affair, he would have left the crown
and throne to his sons, and all this strife would
not have occurred. God only knows where all
this sedition will end.”
Tägänä began to speak roughly and sharply.
Buqa drew his sword and said, “As long as this
sword is in my hand, no one other than Arghun
is going to sit on the throne!”
The amirs asked Tänggiz Gürägän, “What
was Abaqa Khan’s will?”
“Shiktür Aqa and I heard him say, ‘After me
Mänggü Temür should be ruler, and after him
Arghun should be ruler,’ ” he replied. [1146]
Tägänä shouted at him, saying, “Where did
you hear that? You’re making it up!”
554
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Arghun said, “Leave me alone. I don’t want
to be ruler. I am content with the Khurasan my
father awarded me.”
“Prince,” said Buqa, “before, you unknow-
ingly accepted Ahmad as ruler. Now you disin-
genuously give your consent for sedition to in-
crease. Anyhow, when we haven’t yet captured
the enemy, why are we fighting and quarrel-
ing? What we should do is to go in several
groups around the kingdom and get hold of
Ahmad. Then, when we reach Öljäi Khatun
and the other ladies, we can hold council with
all in attendance and settle the rule on one of
the princes. Since [Ahmad] came to assassinate
Arghun, let [Arghun] set out in pursuit of [Ah-
mad] in the vanguard.” With this he concluded
his speech.
On Tuesday the 25th of Rabi‘ II [July 11]
Arghun and Buqa set forth in the vanguard in
pursuit of Ahmad. After them went Aruq and
Jüshkäb, and after that Hulachu, Kingshü, and
Tägänä took charge of all the aghruqs and set
forth. 
On Thursday the 27th [July 13] Ahmad
alighted in Qonqur Öläng, where he pillaged
Buqa’s quarters. He wanted to molest Buqa’s
wife and child, but Su’unchaq prevented it.
The next day he rode from Sharuyaz, and on
Monday the 2nd of Jumada I 683 [July 17] he
reached his own ordus. To his mother he said,
“I have put the Arghun affair aside and have
come first to see you.” Then he got busy
making preparations to take ﬂight. He went out
toward Derbent, but Shiktür Agha got wind of
it and sent a message to Qutui Khatun, saying,
“We are servants of the throne. Just now en-
voys have arrived to say that all the princes
have commanded that Ahmad be seized. What
fault is it of us servants? The prudent thing to
do is for us to seat Ahmad alone [1147] in a
tent until the aqas and inis arrive and confront
whatever accusations there are to be made.” 
Qutui Khatun gave permission, and Shiktür
Noyan set three hundred men as guards over
Ahmad. 
All of a sudden the Qara’una army arrived
and plundered those ordus so thoroughly that,
aside from ashes in the fireplaces, not a trace
remained. They left Qutui Khatun, Tödäi
Khatun, and Armini Khatun naked, and two
thousand of them took up guard over Ahmad.
On Wednesday the 11th of Jumada I [July 26]
Arghun crossed the Tamur (?) River and dis-
mounted in the ladies’ camp. He sent Nüregäi
Yarghuchi to be Ahmad’s guard. On Sunday he
camped at Abshor near Yüz Aghach, and that
day the amirs Taghachar, Qunchuqbal, and
Doladai, who had been in prison in Tabriz,
were released and came to him. The ladies and
amirs agreed that Arghun should be ruler and
gave their hands in fealty. Ahmad was sum-
moned
and
tried
by
Tägänä,
Nüregäi
Yarghuchi, and Qonqurtai’s liege men, who
asked, “For what reason did you kill Qonqurtai
and Küchük, who had performed valiantly for
Abaqa Khan and who had helped to make you
king? When Arghun accepted you as king, al-
though his father’s place should have gone to
him, and was content with only Khurasan, why
did you send Alinaq to raid his artisans and
people and take them captive?”
“I did wrong,” he said. “I won’t do it again.”
Arghun and the amirs wanted to placate his
mother, Qutui Khatun, who held such an exalt-
ed position, by overlooking his crime, but
Qonqurtai’s mother and his sons and people
shouted out. Just then Yesü Buqa Gürägän
arrived and said, “What is this talk of pardon
[1148] when Princes Hulachu and Jüshkäb
have gathered a large contingent in the vicinity
of Hamadan and are thinking of rebelling?” An
edict was therefore issued for Ahmad to be ex-
ecuted in retaliation for Qonqurtai’s blood.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FOURTEEN: TÄGÜDÄR KHAN
555

On the eve of Thursday the 26th of Jumada I
683 [August 10, 1284], corresponding to the
28th of Altinch Ay of Daqiqu Yil, they put him
to death in the same manner in which he had
killed Qonqurtai. “As you judge so shall you
be judged.” Pacem. [1149]
Part Three, on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave;
incidents that occurred during his reign that
were not included in the previous two
sections and were culled from various books
and persons.
*The writer of this blessed book says, “Dur-
ing the reign of Abaqa Khan, when calamity
befell the mighty sahibs Khwaja Ala’uddin and
Khwaja Shamsuddin, I was in my youth and
was serving them. I had purchased a ten-year-
old slave boy, adopted him as a son, and was in
Baghdad. One day Eljidäi Qushchi saw him in
a lane, grabbed him and seated him by force
behind him on his horse, and carried him off. I
ran around in search of him for a long time, but
it was to no avail. When Ahmad mounted the
throne I thought to myself, ‘Since he is a Mus-
lim ruler, and I have clearly been subjected to
such tyranny, he will issue a decree for them to
return my slave.’ 
“I attended court for long periods of time and
was in the ordus at Ala Tagh until one day I got
a chance to kneel [before the emperor] in Ishan
Mängli’s quarters and present my petition.
When he heard it, all I could hear him say was,
‘It must have been his deed.’ And he said
something to Ishan Mängli—I don’t know
what. The next day he sent a dervish to me
[inviting me] to Amir Eljidäi’s quarters, but he
was not at home. [The dervish] whispered
something into the amir’s wife’s ear and then
we departed. All he said to me was, ‘Eljidäi is
not at home today. We’ll come another time.’ 
“Two or three days later it happened that one
of Eljidäi’s people who had witnessed the
event, a Muslim, saw me and said, ‘I have been
looking for you for two days. Eljidäi has said
to his men, “If he ever comes here again, seize
him. Otherwise, wherever you find the master
of this slave, kill him.” And thus he charged
his men.’
“This is the sort of the conduct and character
I saw of him and of his shaykh, Ishan Mängli!
As God is my witness, that is how it was.”*1
[1150]

556
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

❦ SECTION FIFTEEN
THE HISTORY OF HÜLÄGÜ KHAN’S SON ARGHUN, IN THREE PARTS.
His blessed birth occurred in the vicinity of
Baylaqan on Saturday the 25th of Aram Ay in
Daqiqu Yil, corresponding to 660 [1261] of the
Hegira, during the first hour of the day when
the sun had risen five degrees, and the ascen-
dant at the time was the constellation Pisces.
He ascended the throne on Friday the 27th of
Jumada I 683 [August 11, 1284], the 29th of
Altinch Ay of Daqiqu Yil.1 He died on Satur-
day the 7th of Rabi‘ I 690 [March 10, 1291],
corresponding to the 8th of Ikindi Ay of ___
Yil.2 His life span was thirty-three years,3 and
he reigned for seven years.
Part One is on his progeny with details of his
wives, sons, daughters, and grandsons who
have branched off down to the present, the
names of his sons-in-law, and a genealogical
chart of his sons’ branches.
Part Two is on events leading to his en-
thronement, a picture of him and his wives,
sons, grandsons, and commanders at his en-
thronement; [1151] battles he fought and victo-
ries he achieved. 
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections but
learned from various persons. [1152]
Part One, on his progeny with details of his
11284 was a Year of the Monkey (Bechin Yil), not
Rooster (Daqiqu) as in the text.
21291 was a Year of the Hare, Taulai Yil.
3Needless to say, by no reckoning do the years of his
life add up to thirty-three.
wives, sons, daughters, and grandsons who
have branched off down to the present, the
names of his sons-in-law, and a genealogical
chart of his sons’ branches.
Arghun was Abaqa Khan’s eldest son. He
was born of Qaitmish Egächi.
He had many wives and concubines. The
first he married was Qutlugh Khatun, daughter
of Tänggiz Gürägän. When she died he mar-
ried her niece Öljätäi, Sülämish’s daughter
whose mother was Tödögäch. Since she was
only a child, he did not touch her. After that, he
married Örüg Khatun, daughter of Sarucha and
sister of Amir Irinjin of the Kerayit. (Sarucha
was the brother of Toquz Khatun.) After her, he
married Saljuq Khatun, daughter of Sultan
Ruknuddin of Anatolia. After her he took the
senior Bulughan Khatun, who had been Abaqa
Khan’s wife. When she died he married in her
place Bulughan Khatun,4 the daughter of
Abatai Noyan’s son Otman, and she is still
alive. After her he married Tödäi Khatun, one
of his father’s concubines, and installed her in
Märtäi Khatun’s place. He also took Qultaq
Egächi and another named Qutai, daughter of
Qutlugh Buqa son of Husayn Aqa. Another
was Ärgänä Egächi, who had formerly been a
concubine [1153] of Abaqa Khan’s.
His sons were four. First was Ghazan Khan,
whose mother was Qultaq Egächi.
Second was Yesü Temür, whose mother was
Örüg Khatun.
4The junior Bulughan Khatun of the Qunqirat, see text
p. 160 and note to p. 964,.

Third was Öljäitü Sultan, whose mother was
also Örüg Khatun.
Fourth was Khitai Oghul, whose mother was
Qutlugh Khatun. He was called Sängirgäs.1
He also had four daughters. First was Öljätäi,
whose mother was Örüg Khatun. Öljätäi was
affianced to Qunchuqbal,2 and after him she

was given to Aq Buqa. At present she is kept
