Part Two, on events leading to his
enthronement, a picture of him and his
wives, sons, grandsons, and commanders at
his enthronement; battles he fought and
victories he achieved.
As has already been explained in the section
on Ahmad, after Ahmad’s death all the ladies
and amirs gathered at Abshor in the vicinity of
Yüz Aghach and agreed to make Arghun
padishah. 
Decamping from there, he dismounted at
Sögätü’s yurt, and the princes Hulachu and
Gaikhatu arrived and agreed with the others.
On Friday the 27th of Jumada I 683 [August
11, 1284], corresponding to the 29th of Altinch
Ay of Daqiqu Yil, after the astrologers had
chosen a felicitous ascendant in the constella-
tion Sagittarius, Hulachu took Arghun’s right
arm and Anbarchi his left, and together they
seated him on the throne. All of one accord put
their belts around their necks, as was custom-
ary, knelt, and began drinking, banqueting, and
celebrating. [1155]
558
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Orders for general and fiscal matters
Arghun Khan gave after his enthronement.
After the banqueting and celebrations were
concluded, the shah first sent a decree to all
parts of the kingdom concerning winning the
good will of the peasantry so that the world in
turmoil would regain peace. Then he rewarded
the princes and won them over with promises
of good things to come. 
On the last day of Jumada I [August 14,
1284] Prince Kingshü arrived. Although he and
Jüshkäb had not earlier consented [to Arghun’s
enthronement] and were planning to rebel, on
that day they submitted möchälgäs along with
everyone else. 
After that, Äbügän, the son of Chormaqan’s
son Shirämün Noyan, was tried. Since he had
been
one
of Ahmad’s
intimates,
he
was
executed.
After that, a decree was issued that no crea-
ture was to harm or molest Ahmad’s people,
and it was heralded that everyone should main-
tain the ways of his fathers and forefathers,
they should not use force or compulsion on
each other, and the peasants should occupy
themselves with improvements to land and
agriculture with peace of mind.
Princes Jüshkäb and Baidu and Amir Aruq
were assigned to the governorship and emirate
of Baghdad and Diyarbekir. He sent Princes
Hulachu and Gaikhatu to Anatolia. Georgia he
gave to his uncle Ajai. Khurasan, Mazanderan,
Qumis, and Rayy he turned over to his son
Ghazan, and Prince Kingshü was assigned to
assist him. Nawroz was awarded the emirate of
Khurasan. 
Then an order was given to break camp, and
he departed for Sughurluq. An edict for the
vizierate of the realm was issued in Buqa’s
name. On the 3rd of Rajab 683 [September 15,
1284] he ordered so much gold poured over his
head that he almost disappeared under it.
[1156] Among the Mongols he was an ex-
tremely competent and clever man, possessed
of vision and administrative ability. Fiscal af-
fairs of the kingdom, both in general and in de-
tail, were entrusted to him, and his word be-
came law.
What happened to Sahib-Sa‘id Shamsuddin
Sahib-Divan after Ahmad’s death; he stops
in Persia and then goes to Arghun Khan’s
court, where he is shown favor and then
martyred.
When Alinaq was killed in Khurasan and Ah-
mad was put to ﬂight, Sahib Shamsuddin
mounted a camel in the Jajarm vicinity and ﬂed
with two or three servants, taking the desert
road to Isfahan. When the people of Isfahan
learned of the revolution fate had brought
about, they wanted to arrest him along with the
atabeg of Yazd, whom the shahna of Isfahan,
Tabanai by name, had seized and imprisoned
because he had been a supporter of Arghun
Khan and had never gone before Ahmad. They
held council in this regard, but since the out-
come of things was still not known for certain,
the shahna delayed acting. The Sahib learned
of the planned attack and left the city, ostensi-
bly to visit a shrine. Mounted on a ﬂeet steed,
he headed for Qum. When he arrived there, he
stopped in the shrine outside the city and took
up residence there. His attendants all had dif-
ferent ideas on what he should do, but finally
they agreed that the best thing would be for the
khwaja to get himself to Hormuz, where he
could make up his losses.
“To leave one’s sons captive in the hands of
the Mongols and to turn one’s back is not the
proper course,” he said. “The best thing would
be for me to go to court. [1157] If Arghun
Khan can be placated through the offices of
Amir Buqa, who is an old friend, well and
good. Otherwise, I will submit to my fate.”
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIFTEEN: ARGHUN KHAN
559

With this thought in mind he stopped for a few
days.
Suddenly Malik Imamuddin Qazwini arrived
from court in search of the Sahib’s where-
abouts. Then Atabeg Yusufshah of Lur and
Qumäri arrived in rapid succession and gave
him the good news that Arghun Khan had said,
“Since God the Eternal has shown me favor
and awarded me my late father’s crown and
throne, I hereby pardon all criminals’ crimes. If
the Sahib-Divan comes to court, I will receive
him with honor.” 
Qumäri met with the Sahib in Sawa, and two
or three days later they set out, arriving in Qur-
ban Shirä on Friday the 10th of Rajab 683
[September 22, 1284], where he stopped with
Buqa. Since they were old friends they were
happy to see each other. The next day Buqa
took him to Arghun Khan’s court to perform
the ritual of uljamishi. Arghun Khan did not
pay much attention to him, but he did not
exhibit any anger. 
When he returned to the house, needy people
ﬂocked to him. “Henceforth,” the Sahib said,
“I will accept no employment, unless it be the
office of deputy to Amir Buqa—and that only
as long as he is here.”
Amir Ali Tamghachi had gone to Tabriz,
arrested and imprisoned the Sahib’s son Yahya,
and confiscated his property and possessions.
He, Fakhruddin Mustawfi, and Husamuddin
Hajib, all of whom had been elevated by Sahib
Shamsuddin’s patronage, were so greedy for
status that they plotted his downfall and said to
Buqa, “So long as the Sahib is alive you will
not ﬂourish. Once he gets power he will do to
you what he did to Arghun Aqa and other
amirs.” They convinced Buqa to attack him at
Arghun Khan’s court, [1158] and Buqdai
Idächi was set as guard over the Sahib, al-
though nominally he was made his attendant to
keep creditors away. 
When the court set out for winter quarters in
Arran, an edict was issued in Ujan for
20,000,000 in gold to be taken from the Sahib.
“I have no money,” he said in a message to
Buqa. “I have not stashed gold away under the
earth like some fools. What I got I invested in
real estate. Now I have so many holdings that I
have an income of 1,000 dinars a day.” He sent
a message to Buqa, saying, “Amir Buqa, don’t
do it. Don’t teach the padishah to kill viziers,
for they may kill me today, but the time may
not be far off when they will kill you too. So
know for certain that it will not profit you.”
Doladai Yarghuchi and Qada’an were sent to
try him. He confessed to no cash and only re-
peated the same words. Just then he asked for
an inkstand and paper. He wrote a will, a copy
of which, as written by his own hand, follows:
Sahib Shamsuddin’s will
“When I took an augury from the Koran, the
following verse emerged: As for those who
say, Our Lord is God, and who behave upright-
ly; the angels shall descend unto them, and
shall say, Fear not, neither be ye grieved; but
rejoice in the hopes of paradise, which ye have
been promised.1 Since the Creator has kept His
slave well in this transitory life and withheld
nothing from him, He has willed that even in
the ephemeral world he be given glad tidings
of the eternal world. This being so, it seemed
incumbent
to
convey
this
good
news
to
Mawlana Muhyiddin [1159] and Mawlana
Fakhruddin, my brothers in religion, Mawlana
Afzaluddin, Mawlana Shamsuddin, Mawlana
Humamuddin, and the great shaykhs, mention
of whom would take too long, so that they
might know that we have severed our relations
and set out. May they also assist us with
prayers for our well-being, and may they enjoy
eternal felicity. May all my sons—may God
1Kor. 41:30.
560
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

preserve them—pray for me. They have been
left in God’s care, and God does not lose what
is given in trust to Him. It was in my mind that
there would be a meeting and my last testa-
ment could be made, but since there was no
such day, it has fallen to the next world. Let
them commit no shortcoming in keeping my
children. Let them encourage them to study
and in no way allow them to take up imperial
service. Let them get along with what God has
given. If my son Atabeg and his mother,
Khoshak Khatun, want to go to their land, let it
be permitted. Let Nawroz and Mas‘ud, togeth-
er with their mother, be attached to Bulughan
Khatun. Let them reside at the tomb of us two
brothers. If they can add to the buildings at
Shaykh Fakhruddin’s khanaqah, let them help
in any way they can. Let them also go there.
Next, Fulani has never had rest from us: if she
wants to, let her get married. Let Faraj and his
mother be with Atabeg. I have given Zakariya,
along with the real estate in the tümän of Sha-
hanshah Ani and other places, to amraq (dear)
Amir Buqa. Let that be given to him. Let the
other properties be probated, and if anything is
left over, well and good. Otherwise let them be
content. May the Exalted Creator bless us and
you. At this time my mind is with God. Let
them not forget our dear portion. Whatever
happens may there be eternal happiness. If
anything is graciously allowed from the prop-
erties let them take it and be satisfied with it.
Where can my chief wife go from Tabriz? Let
her stay there. ‘And peace be with him who
follows the right path.’ ” [1160]
He tossed this document to the guards. When
they read it and saw that there was no money,
Tuqluq Qara’una of the Jalayir beat him sev-
erely, but it did no good. An order was given
for him to be taken to execution. On Monday
the 4th of Sha‘ban 683 [October 16, 1284], af-
ter the second prayer, he was martyred at the
Ahar city gate on the banks of the river. May
God have great mercy upon him. At that time
Mawlana
Nuruddin
Rasadi
composed
this
chronogram: “Regulator of the scope of the
horizons, the Sahib-Divan Muhammad son of
Muhammad, the unique pearl of the age, / In
the year six hundred eighty-three on the fourth
of Sha‘ban, on Monday afternoon at the river
at Ahar, / with the hand of resignation and free
will, was forced to taste the portion of poison
from the brimful goblet of the blade.”
Buqa sent Amir Ali to Tabriz to take control
of his property and holdings. After a time his
son Yahya was also martyred on the playing-
field in Tabriz. The fates of his remaining sons
will be given in the proper places.1 [1161]
Bolad Chingsang and other envoys arrive
from Qubilai Qa’an; ordu Qaya comes from
there bringing an edict of Arghun Khan’s
khanship; he is enthroned a second time.
When Arghun Khan reached Saray Man-
suriyya in Arran, Amir Bolad Chingsang, Isa
Kalimachi, and other envoys arrived from the
Qa’an’s court. That winter Lagzi was tried and
given a hundred lashes.
In the spring he set out for summer quarters,
and between Saraw and Ardabil, in the village
of Sayin, a great quriltai was held.
On the 11th of Rajab 684 [September 12,
1285] Aruq was sent to Baghdad after the sum-
mer had been spent in Sughurluq. On the 20th
of Rajab 684 [September 21] [Arghun] went to
Tabriz and from there to winter in Arran. When
he reached Arran, the trial of Atabeg Abish
Khatun was held, whose retainers had killed
Amir Imad Alavi, who had gone to be gover-
nor of Fars by order of Arghun Khan. After
guilt was proven, Malik Khan, Abish Khatun’s
relative, was executed and the governors of
Fars were beaten. 
1See text p. 1175 below.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIFTEEN: ARGHUN KHAN
561

On the 27th of Dhu’l-Hijja 684 [February 23,
1286] ordu Qaya came from the Qa’an’s court,
bearing an edict investing Arghun as khan in
his father’s place [1162] and awarding Buqa
the title of Chingsang.
On the 10th of Safar 685 [April 7, 1286]
once again Arghun Khan sat on the khan’s
throne, and the rites and rituals were observed.
The army goes to deal with the Kurds of
Mount Hakkar; Bulughan Khatun dies; the
Khwaja Harun affair.
On the 20th of Safar 685 [April 17, 1286] an
order was issued for the amirs Mazuq Qushchi,
Nurin Aqa, and Eshik Tughli’s brother Ghazan
of the Jalayir to take sixteen thousand cavalry
to the mountains of Hakkar in Kurdistan.1 They
killed some of the Kurds who were committing
highway robbery and causing trouble.
On Friday the 23rd of Safar 685 [April 20,
1286] Bulughan Khatun died on the banks of
the Kura River. Her coffin was taken to Mount
Sujas.
In the spring Arghun Khan came to Tabriz.
Buqa Chingsang gave him a banquet and of-
fered suitable gifts.
On Friday the 12th of Rabi‘ II [June 7, 1286]
he decamped from there and set out via
Maragha for Sughurluq. That summer Amir
Aruq and a group of bitigchis from Baghdad
arrived at court with Sahib Shamsuddin’s son
Harun in attendance. In all audacity, and rely-
ing on his brother Buqa’s exalted position,2
Aruq
had
killed
Majduddin
Ibn
al-Athir,
Fakhruddin Mustawfi’s brother Sa‘duddin, and
Ali Chäkibän without the padishah’s leave.
Since
Majduddin
Ibn
al-Athir
had
been
Gaikhatu’s enchü, Gaikhatu was so angry at
1Hakkar is the mountainous region around the modern
Hakkâri in extreme southeastern Turkey.
2Amir Aruq and Buqa were the sons of Ögöläi Qorchi
of the Oyat clan of the Jalayir. See text p. 70 above.
Aruq that he was going to make an attempt on
his life. Yesü Buqa Gürägän was also involved
in the plot. [1163] 
Since Buqa had great inﬂuence, he undertook
to protect his brother. Some people said to
Gaikhatu, “Aruq took these actions at Harun’s
word.” He was going to Anatolia and taking
Harun with him, [but when he got] as far as
Ala Tagh, he killed him. Around that time Yesü
Buqa Gürägän died, and the affair blew over.
Arghun Khan went to Tabriz in the autumn.
On Friday the 6th of Sha‘ban 685 [September
27, 1286] he descended there, and on Thursday
the 28th of Ramadan [November 17, 1286] he
set out for Arran. One day he was combing his
hair, and a lot of hair came out in the comb.
“This is evidence of poison that Wajih the son
of Izzuddin Tahir has given me,” he said. En-
raged by this, he ordered him executed. On the
20th of Dhu’l-Qa‘da 685 [January 7, 1287] and
on the 5th of Dhu’l-Hijja of that year [February
6, 1287] Arghun Khan took Tödäi Khatun to
himself and installed her in Märtäi Khatun’s
place. 
On the 19th of Safar 686 [April 5, 1287] he
went to Bilasawar. On the 24th of Rabi‘ II of
that year [June 8, 1287] he went to Tabriz. For
the summer he went to Ala Tagh, and from
there he returned. On the 2nd of Ramadan 686
[October 11, 1287] he set out for winter quar-
ters in Arran. On the 15th of Muharram 687
[February 20, 1288] envoys from Khurasan
arrived with news from Kingshü and Nawroz
that thirty thousand horsemen from Qaidu’s
army under the leadership of Yisa’ur Noyan
had crossed the Panj River3 and, having pil-
laged the frontier of Balkh and Merv and the
3The river Panj (Пяндж), the upper Oxus that forms
the modern border between Afghanistan and Tajikistan
north of Qonduz.
562
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

vicinity of Sheberghan, had reached as far as
Khwaf and Sangan.
On the 7th of Safar of that year [March 13,
1288] Qutlugh Khatun, daughter of Tänggiz
Gürägän of the Oyirat and Prince Khitai
Oghul’s mother, died. 
On the 7th of Rabi‘ I [April 11, 1288] envoys
came from Noqai’s ulus, and on the banks of
the New Canal they presented a sharil (relic).
Among idolators it is believed that when
Shakyamuni [1164] Burkhan (the Buddha) was
cremated, a translucent bone like a bead from
in front of his heart remained unburned. They
call it a sharil and claim that when anyone who
has reached an exalted degree like Shakyamuni
Burkhan is cremated, his sharil does not burn.
In any case, when they brought it, Arghun
Khan went out to meet them, scattered gold
over it, and rejoiced. Several days were given
over to banqueting and revelry.
On the last day of Rabi‘ I [May 4, 1288],
when Arghun Khan was camped in the vicinity
of Bilasawar, news arrived that Tamma Toqtai
Märtäd had crossed with five thousand cavalry
from Derbent and plundered all the ortaqs and
merchants. On Saturday the first of Rabi‘ II 687
[May 5, 1288] he set out to repel them. Cross-
ing the Kura River, he reached Shemakha on
the 5th of the month and stopped atop a hill,
whence he sent Buqa, Qunchuqbal, and some
princes as a vanguard. Four or five days later
they returned with the good news that the foe
had pulled back past Derbent.
The beginning of the fame Sa‘duddawla
acquired by collecting taxes from Baghdad.
In the year 683 [1284–85], Tonska was sent
to be shahna of Baghdad. When he arrived, he
appointed as his deputy and chamberlain
Sa‘duddawla (son of Hibatullah son of Mu-
hazzibuddawla Abhari), a wealthy and intelli-
gent man who knew all about the fiscal situa-
tion of Baghdad. Although he had nothing else
to recommend him, because of his competence
and knowledge of the situation [1165] he be-
came the absolute ruler. At that time the gover-
norship of Baghdad belonged to Qutlughshah,
a son of one of Ala’uddin Sahib-Divan’s
slaves, and his liege man Majduddin [ibn
al-]Kibti
and
others.
With
[Sa‘duddawla]
around, however, they could not exercise much
power. 
In the year 686 [1287] [Qutlughshah and the
others] went to the court summer quarters at
Sughurluq to complain to the amirs and viziers
of [Sa‘duddawla]. “Sa‘duddawla is a physician
without equal,” they said to Joshi, Quchan, and
the sükürchis, “and it would be appropriate for
him to be attached to court.” This was con-
veyed, and an edict was issued for him to re-
main at court and not go to Baghdad. That au-
tumn and winter, seeing how inﬂuential ordu
Qaya was, [Sa‘duddawla] laid the foundations
of a friendship with him and represented to
him that there was much to be gained in the
revenues of Baghdad. “If you can get the gov-
ernorship,” he said, “I will be at your disposal.
Not only will I remit treasury taxes better than
the others, but there will also be surpluses for
the amir’s personal account. There are also un-
told back taxes due from the Baghdad collec-
tors, and I will settle those accounts too.” ordu
Qaya conveyed this to Arghun Khan.
“How much are the back taxes of Baghdad?”
he asked.
“Five million,” replied Sa‘duddawla.
The padishah was well pleased by Sa‘dud-
dawla’s cleverness and his manner of report-
ing, so he favored them and sent them off with
a yarligh and paiza enabling them to settle the
taxes in arrears and to collect the taxes due to
the Baghdad treasury. There they went, and by
means of beatings and torture they collected a
huge amount, returning to court at Qonqur
Öläng, where they turned over the treasury.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIFTEEN: ARGHUN KHAN
563

The padishah was highly pleased. On the 4th
of Jumada I 687 [June 6, 1288] the office of
amir of Baghdad was given to Amir ordu
Qaya, and since Tonska had died, Baidu
Sükürchi was appointed to the office of shah-
na. Sharafuddin Simnani was made malik, and
Sa‘duddawla went with them as mustawfi (au-
ditor general) to Baghdad, [1166] where they
took up their offices. 
Around that time Amir Qunchuqbal was also
favored
and
appointed
to
his
grandfather
Abatai Noyan’s position, i.e. as commander of
the center of the army.
Buqa’s situation; the attack on him by
envious amirs, who are victorious; Buqa is
killed.
When Sahib-Sa‘id Shamsuddin was martyred
and Buqa was enjoying authority, it was not
long before he had accumulated a great deal of
wealth. Proud and conceited of his status and
riches, he overstepped himself and began to
look deprecatingly at Arghun’s elite amirs
Taghachar, Qunchuqbal, Doladai Idächi, Sultan
Idächi, Toghan, Joshi, and ordu Qaya, who
were intimates at court. They were highly in-
sulted and turned against him. In particular
Sultan Idächi and Toghan often discussed his
overbearing pride and relayed their thoughts to
the person of the emperor, who did not pay
much attention in view of his endebtedness to
Buqa. Because Toghan had twice been caned at
Buqa’s order for infractions of the Yasa and
had been cursed by him, he hated him extreme-
ly and was inﬂamed enough to attack him. At
every opportunity the group mentioned above
couched tales about Buqa to Arghun Khan in
the worst possible light.
Meanwhile, in Baghdad, Aruq was comport-
ing himself not in the manner of an amir but
more like a king. Neither did he pay attention
to Arghun’s envoys nor did he forward tax
monies to the treasury. ordu Qaya and Sa‘dud-
dawla once gathered five million in taxes
[1167] from every conceivable source and
brought it back, and when Arghun Khan was
told that Aruq had carried off that much every
year, he did not react visibly, but he did send
ordu Qaya, Malik Sharafuddin, and Sa‘dud-
dawla there to be amir, malik, and overseer re-
spectively, and Aruq was dismissed from of-
fice.
On
Taghachar’s
behalf,
Sadruddin
Zanjani, Taghachar’s deputy, rose up to attack
Buqa because Buqa had demanded from him
the back taxes of Fars. “Buqa has created an
empire for himself,” he told Taghachar, “for he
does whatever he wants without the emperor’s
order or consultation with the amirs, he dis-
burses the tax monies however he wishes, and
Arghun Khan is considered less an emperor
than Buqa is. Things have gone so far that
when envoys go to Tabriz with yarlighs and
paizas, unless Buqa’s red seal is on them, they
are not given any consideration whatsoever by
Amir Ali the governor and return empty-
handed.”
When such reports had been conveyed to
Arghun Khan’s hearing, he grew so vexed with
Buqa that he became sick and tired of his pres-
ence. Around that time Buqa fell ill, and the
above-mentioned amirs concentrated their ef-
forts on bringing about his downfall. When he
regained his health, Arghun Khan reinstated
him to favor as before and sent him back to
work. However, the enchü estates that he had
previously administered were given to Amir
Taghachar, and the command of the center of
the army was assigned to Amir Qunchuqbal.
Buqa was insulted and went less often to the
ordu. Since everyone who frequented Buqa
was
accused
of
supporting
him,
people
shunned and avoided his society. Then some
Mongol amirs were offended again, and since
Buqa no longer enjoyed the esteem in the peo-
ple’s eyes he once had, he ceased going to
564
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

court on the pretext of being ill. It was reported
to Arghun Khan that Buqa was only pretending
to be ill, and a decree was issued to the effect
that
the
divan
and
accounting
office
be
removed from Buqa’s quarters and his agents
and deputies [1168] be dismissed from office.
First Amir Ali Tamghachi, the governor of
Tabriz, was dismissed, and this was a great
blow not only to Buqa’s prestige but also to his
financial situation. Following that, ayqaqs (in-
formants) from Fars arrived and proved a
shortfall of 1,500,000 against Husamuddin
Qazwini, who had gone there as Buqa’s
deputy. From Diyarbekir and that area reports
of complaints against Aruq poured in cease-
lessly. Buqa completely fell out of favor with
Arghun. When he saw things slipping from his
grasp, he despaired totally. He spent untold
amounts of money in bribing a group of amirs
into plotting an attack on Arghun Khan. They
were the likes of his brother Aruq, Hindu Noy-
an’s son Qurumshi, who was an amir-tümän,
Amir Ujan, who was one of the amirs of
weapons, Qada’an Elchi, Naya’a Noyan’s son
Zangi, who was Öljäi Khatun’s amir-ordu,
Maichu the commander of a division of a thou-
sand, and others of his retainers like Ghazan
Bahadur, his brother Eshik Tughli, a comman-
der of four divisions of a thousand, and Tugh-
luq Qara’una, a commander of a thousand—all
of whom were Jalayir—plus Bayan, Alghu Bit-
igchi’s son Mäkritäi, Chärig Bitigchi, and oth-
ers of his retainers and supporters, to mention
all of whom would take too long. 
It is reported that Buqa knew that an attack
on Arghun Khan could be carried out only by a
prince. Prince Jüshkäb was on the banks of the
Euphrates.
He
sent
a
messenger
to
say,
“Arghun Khan is angry with me on account of
reports by Taghachar, Sultan Idächi, Toghan,
and others envious of me. He has forgotten
what he owes me. It is known to you and all
the princes—indeed to the entire ulus—that he
acquired his father’s throne through my patron-
age. Now he has elevated others over me and
made them privy to his secrets. You, thank
God, out of all Hülägü Khan’s family possess
imperial splendor. Without your support it will
not be possible to undertake this action. [1169]
If you accept my proposal and undertake this
task, I will gird my loins in service to you and
render crown and throne yours, for many of the
amirs
and
soldiers
are
with
me
in
this
endeavor.” 
When this message reached Jüshkäb, he was
astonished and said, “Good God! This man has
lost his senses and gone mad to elect another
over Arghun Khan, the emperor of this land.
What more rank does he want than what he
has? Does he have designs on the throne too?
Does he think he can dupe me into imagining I
am an emperor? This is the same game he
played and charm he worked on Ahmad. Does
he think I too will break my oath of loyalty?”
Then to the messenger he said, “Return, con-
vey my greetings to Buqa, and say, ‘The plan
you had for me is extremely fine, but my heart
cannot trust your word. If it is true, let those in-
volved in this thing write their names and send
möchälgäs
so
that
I
may
be
absolutely
certain.’ ”
Buqa and the amirs involved in the conspira-
cy wrote pledges and sent them. When Jüshkäb
saw the paper, he feared for himself and sent a
message back saying, “If courage doesn’t fail,
one must act. I will get my army together, and
on such-and-such a night I will arrive. Wait for
me.” He meant to inform Arghun Khan of the
situation as fast as possible lest the evil touch
him, and with that thought in mind he set out. 
On the night of the rendezvous Buqa armed a
group of soldiers, had them mount, and stood
waiting for Jüshkäb’s arrival, but he did not
come that night. The next morning Sultan
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIFTEEN: ARGHUN KHAN
565

Idächi informed Arghun Khan that the night
before a group of riders with arms had been
spotted. Just then Jüshkäb arrived and rushed
into court. Arghun Khan received him warmly
and rejoiced at his arrival. [1170] When the
amirs had dispersed, Jüshkäb reported Buqa’s
plans. Arghun Khan said, “I have too much re-
liance on him to be made mistrustful of him by
the mere passage of time or the words of just
anybody. What proof have you of his actions?”
Jüshkäb pulled out Buqa’s and the amirs’
pledges of conspiracy and showed them. When
Arghun Khan saw the papers, he ﬂew into a
rage and said, “Did I elevate Buqa over all the
amirs, place the administration of the realm un-
der his control, and put the peasants and sol-
diers in his hands for him to plot treachery
against me?” That very night he ordered the
soldiers to mount and go out to arrest Buqa.
They encircled his quarters on the banks of
the Kura, and the next morning Sultan Idächi,
Doladai, and Toghan charged into his tent, but
they did not find him, for he had learned of the
attack, taken a boat across the Kura, and
sought refuge in Öljäi Khatun’s tent. She did
not receive him, and when he turned away,
Naya’a’s son Amir Zangi, Öljäi Khatun’s amir-
ordu, hid him in his tent. When Doladai and
Toghan heard that he had crossed the river dur-
ing the night, they attacked Öljäi Khatun’s
quarters. Amir Zangi came out trembling in
fear, and they asked him about Buqa’s where-
abouts. “He’s sitting in this tent,” he said. Im-
mediately they arrested him and took him be-
fore Arghun Khan. 
“What is this turmoil and strife you have
stirred up?” Amir Shiktür asked him. “Do you
want to enthrone a new emperor every day?”
“I have nothing to do with the emperor,”
Buqa replied. “I have risen up only against
Sultan Idächi and Toghan of Quhistan, who are
my adversaries.” 
Jüshkäb produced the papers signed by him
and his liege men, and with this Buqa started
trembling and fell silent. At once Arghun indi-
cated that he was to be done in. He was
dragged out, [1171] and Jüshkäb requested that
he be allowed to dispatch him. When he came
to the place of execution, Toghan kicked him
in the chest and said, “You coveted the throne
and emperorship. This is your reward.” With
one blow Jüshkäb decapitated him. After he
had removed the hide from his back and
stuffed his head with straw, he was hung under
the Chaghan bridge over the marketplace to
serve as an example on Saturday the 21st of
Dhu’l-Hijja 687 [January 16, 1289].
The next day trials were begun, and some of
the amirs who had conspired with him, who
have been mentioned, were executed. Since
Qada’an was the Qa’an’s envoy, he escaped.
Because Bayan Bitigchi gave a true account,
he was also set free. Mäkritäi was pardoned
through the amirs’ intercession. The Tajiks
Amir Ali Tamghachi, Husamuddin Qazwini,
Imaduddin Munajjim, Shim‘un known as Rum
Qal‘a, and Baha’uddawla Abu’l-Karam Nas-
rani were all executed. The same day Buqa
was seized, Baytmish Qushchi, Tamudai, and
Buqa’s son Shadai were dispatched to Di-
yarbekir with five hundred horsemen to arrest
Aruq and his followers. From Arran they made
it to Arbela in six days, and there they killed
Buqa’s eldest son Ghazan, who was an atten-
dant of Aruq’s. Aruq was taken in the Kushaf
fortress. When he reached the Chaghan bridge
and saw Buqa’s head hung there, he said,
“Where is the head of Ujan Amir-Salih, who
was his servant?” On the 29th of Muharram
688 [February 22, 1289] Aruq and Ujan were
killed.
When it came Amir Zangi’s turn, Arghun
Khan ordered that, since Öljäi Khatun was re-
sponsible for him, he be sent to her. Öljäi
566
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Khatun ordered him beheaded, saying, [1172]
“Were it my own son Anbarchi in Zangi’s
place, the order would have been the same.”
After his father’s death, Buqa’s son Ayachi
became attached to Toghan, who took him un-
der his protection and wanted to obtain a re-
lease for him. Acting in haste, one day he said,
“Let Ayachi come and perform huljamishi.”
Since the emperor was still angry, he ordered
the entire family extinguished. Ayachi and his
brothers Malik, Tarkhan Temür, and Qutlugh
Temür were all killed. 
Jüshkäb is killed; the princes who were
accused of conspiring with Nawroz are
imprisoned.
After Buqa and Aruq were killed and the tri-
als were completed toward the end of Safar
688 [March 1289], Arghun Khan rewarded
Jüshkäb and sent him back. After that he
learned that Jüshkäb’s heart was not “right”
with him and sent a group of amirs to bring
him back. Jüshkäb had already started for Di-
yarbekir,
and
Arqasun
Noyan,
Baytmish
Qushchi, Ghurbatai Gürägän, Durbai’s son
Borchu, and Bughdai met up with him on the
banks of the Qaraman River between Arzan
and Mayyafariqin. There he did battle and took
ﬂight. Three days later they caught him and
took him before Arghun Khan on the 19th of
Jumada I 688 [June 10, 1289]. He too was
executed.
Because Arghun Aqa’s son Nawroz had re-
volted in Khurasan, and the princes Hulachu
and Yoshmut’s son Qara Noqai were accused
of conspiring with him, they were arrested on
the 8th of Jumada I of the above-mentioned
year [May 30, 1289] on the report of ordu
Qaya’s brother Muqbal, who was attached to
Qara Noqai and had reported his rebellion.
They were sent to Girdkoh, where they were
executed on the 20th of Ramadan [October 7,
1289] in Damghan. [1173]
On the 28th of that month [October 15]
Toghan was sent with troops to Khurasan to as-
sist Prince Ghazan in repelling Nawroz. 
Malik Jalaluddin Simnani is martyred, and
by that means Sa‘duddawla’s fortunes wax.
In this year, when Arghun Khan returned
from wintering in Arran, he camped in the
summer pastures of Qonqur Öläng. ordu Qaya
and
Sa‘duddawla
returned
from
Baghdad,
bringing a full treasury once again. Arghun
Khan was highly pleased, and Sa‘duddawla
said, “If obstreperous bitigchis had not pre-
vented it, the taxes would have been many
times more than this.” An order was given for
the bitigchis to be executed. Rabib Avchi and
Qutlughshah were killed, and their heads were
sent to Baghdad. Majduddin ibn al-Kibti and
Khwaja Ala’uddin’s son Mansur were brought
from Hilla and martyred at the gates of Dar
Shatina. Malik Jalaluddin Simnani had also
been accused of conspiring with Buqa because
of his attack on Toghan, but he was left alive
through the intercession of Baranda Bakhshi,
although for a very long time he was unable to
gain access to the emperor.
Around the beginning of Jumada II 688 [late
June 1289], in the summer quarters at Sug-
hurluq, Arghun Khan appointed Sa‘duddawla
as vizier.
Malik
Jalaluddin’s
brother
Sharafuddin
Simnani had been imprisoned on account of
unpaid taxes from Baghdad. One morning
[Malik Jalaluddin] set out to see him, and
along the way he came across Amir Bolad Aqa,
who inquired warmly after the malik and asked
about his dismissal and the reasons for it.
[1174] The malik said, “I am not at fault. The
emperor has elevated a Jew over me and favors
him.” These words were immediately reported
to the emperor. Bolad Aqa was asked about it,
and he related the incident exactly as it had
happened. “It is my fault,” the emperor said,
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIFTEEN: ARGHUN KHAN
567

“for leaving him alive.” He then ordered
Täkächäk, who was in the gazig (bodyguard),
to go and execute the malik, and it took place
on the 17th of Rajab 688 [August 6, 1289] at
Saray Muzaffariyya in Siyah Koh. 
After [Malik Jalaluddin] was killed, Sa‘dud-
dawla’s fortunes waxed, and he became ex-
tremely powerful. Day by day his power and
grandeur grew. Khwaja Baha’uddin Muham-
mad Sahib-Divan’s sons Mahmud and Ali re-
ported their destitution, and a decree was is-
sued for some of the Sahib’s properties in
Persia to be given to them. Ali and his mother,
the daughter of Izzuddin Tahir, went to Isfahan
for that reason. Majduddin Mu’minan Qazwi-
ni, the comptroller of enchüs in Persia, came
and said, “Because control of every enchü that
is ﬂourishing has been taken by the Sahib’s
sons, the income from the enchüs of Persia has
been slashed.” Arghun was angered and or-
dered all of Sahib-Divan Shamsuddin’s sons to
be executed. On the 3rd of Rajab [July 23,
1289] Mas‘ud and Farajullah were martyred in
Tabriz. Pandid Bakhshi and Nardu the shahna
took Mahmud under their protection, claiming
that in the edict only the Sahib’s sons had been
specifically mentioned and Mahmud was a
grandson. (Out of fear he was afflicted with
palpitation of the heart and died toward the end
of Gaikhatu’s reign.) Yesüdär had been or-
dered, when he was being sent to arrest Atabeg
in Yazd, to execute Ali in Isfahan. He sent a
servant from Kashan [1175] to seize and kill
Ali. The place where he was killed and buried
later became a major shrine. Yesüdär was also
killed in Yazd sixteen days later, and none of
Atabeg Sahib’s children were left alive. Za-
kariya was in Abkhaz and thus escaped harm.
All the rest were killed.
With that, Sa‘duddawla’s fortunes really
rose. In Baghdad the nawbat was removed
from the gate of the caliph’s palace to the gate
of his quarters. On the 7th of Sha‘ban 688 [Au-
gust 26, 1289] he dispatched his brother
Fakhruddawla,
Muhazzibuddawla,
and
Ja-
maluddin Dastajirdani to govern Baghdad. He
gave the realm of Fars to Muntajibuddawla
Munajjim’s son Shamsuddawla, he turned Di-
yarbekir over to another brother, Aminud-
dawla. The office of overseer of Tabriz he gave
to his cousin Muhazzibuddawla Abu-Mansur
Tabib. Constantly fearful and on his guard
against
the
grand
amirs
Shiktür
Noyan,
Taghachar, Samaghar, Qunchuqbal, and others,
he requested an assistant who could guard his
person. “I cannot tend to all the affairs of state
by myself,” he said to Arghun Khan. “I need
several competent servants who are not greedy
to report every night the day’s surpluses and
shortfalls and tell us what is going on.” He
took ordu Qaya as his personal assistant. The
office of amir of Shiraz he gave to Joshi and
that of Tabriz to Quchan. All three became his
liege men and assistants, and he made it such
that no amir other than these three who were
his liege men had access to him.
During that year Amir Joshi and Su’unchaq
Aqa’s son Sarban went to be the amir and tax
collector of Fars. The next year they returned.
Jalaluddin Sarvistani gave a written pledge that
he would give a million as the income from
Shiraz. The bölük amirs and bitigchis there
gave written pledges that they would give five
million
tümäns
[1176]
on
condition
that
Jalaluddin be enchained and given to them. He
was thrown into chains and sent to them. The
amirs Joshi and Sarban returned for that pur-
pose, and when they went there and made
much effort without collecting anything, since
the bölük chiefs and the bitigchis were not able
to fulfill their promise, an edict was issued that
they be executed. Jalaluddin was set free;
Shamsuddin Husayn Alakani and his son Niza-
muddin Abubakr the vizier, Sayfuddin Yusuf,
568
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Majduddin Rumi, and Fakhruddin Mubarak-
shah
were
martyred
in
Koshk-i-Zar
near
Shiraz. 
Sa‘duddawla was a man who possessed ex-
pertise in administrative and financial affairs,
and he left no effort in that regard undone.
Arghun Khan goes to winter in Arran;
enemies arrive from Derbent, but they are
routed.
On the 4th of Ramadan 688 [September 21,
1289] Arghun Khan dismounted in Maragha
and went to see the observatory. It was there
that he began to take the black medicine, men-
tion of which will come later. Then he set out
for winter quarters in Arran.
On Wednesday the 9th of Rabi‘ I 689 [March
22, 1290], corresponding to the 2nd of Ikindi
Ay of Bars Yil, he married Bulughan Khatun,
the daughter of Abatai Noyan’s son Otman,
and he installed her in [the senior] Bulughan
Khatun’s ordu. 
On the 13th of Rabi‘ I [March 26] envoys
arrived bringing news from Derbent of the
arrival of the enemy army. [1177] An order
was given for Tükäl, Shiktür Noyan, and
Qunchuqbal to mount on an expedition. On the
15th [March 28] Taghachar and the other amirs
set out on their heels. News of the enemy’s
depredations poured in constantly. On the first
of Rabi‘ II [April 13] the emperor moved out
from Bilasawar and went as far as Nuntaq hill
on the other side of Shabaran. On the 15th
[April 27] he arrived in Shabaran before the
aghruq, and on the 17th of the month [April
29] he met the the vanguard of the army on the
banks of the Qara Su on the other side of Der-
bent. On the other side were Ayachi, Mänggü
Temür’s son Mängli Buqa, Yäkächä,1 and Toq-
tai Märtäd with one division. On this side were
1This name is far from certain. Arends (trs. p. 127)
transcribes it as Екече.
Taghachar,
Qunchuqbal,
Toghrilcha,
and
Buqu’s
son
Taichu
the
commander
of
Qunchuqbal’s hazara. Toghrilcha and Taichu
charged into the water to get across, and with
that audacious action the foe’s soldiers turned
in rout. Nearly three hundred of their horsemen
were killed, and several were taken captive.
Among the slain were Boroltai and Qadai, both
of whom were commanders of thousands, and
Yäkächä’s brother. Among the captives were
Chärigtäi, one of Toqta’s great amirs. After this
they returned from the other side.
On the 20th of Rabi‘ II [May 2, 1290] he
went to Bilasawar and dismounted in the or-
dus, where several days were spent in banquet-
ing, revelry, and celebration. Sa‘duddawla dis-
patched news of the victory with heralds in all
directions. 
Taghachar goes to assist the army of
Khurasan; the building of the city of
Arghunia in Shamm-i-Tabriz.
Around the end of Rabi‘ II [early May 1290]
news of the enemy’s despoilings and move-
ments arrived from Khurasan. Taghachar set
out to repel the foe, [1178] and that very week
Khwaja Najibuddawla was sent to Khurasan as
a liege man to Toghan in order to divide
monies among the army. 
On the 7th of Jumada I [May 18, 1290] the
news of Prince Yesü Temür’s death was given
to his father Arghun Khan. Prior to that Su’un-
chaq Aqa and his son Shadai had both died in
Maragha.
Toward the end of Rajab [early August 1290]
the imperial banners arrived in Tabriz.
On the 2nd of Sha‘ban [August 10, 1290]
Majduddin Mu’minan Qazwini was executed
in Tabriz, and the imperial banners set forth for
summer quarters in Ala Tagh, where they
arrived on the 13th [August 21]. From there a
return was made via Van and Vustan. At that
station Mawlana Qutbuddin Shirazi came to
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIFTEEN: ARGHUN KHAN
569

court and presented a map of the western sea
and its gulfs and shores, which included many
territories of the west and north. The emperor
was highly pleased by his conversation since
he explained the territories of Anatolia. During
this discussion the emperor’s gaze fell upon
Amoria, which is inner Anatolia, and asked the
mawlana to explain it. He gave a very nice ex-
position containing praise and extolment of the
emperor, who was greatly pleased. 
Then he set out to go hunting, saying to the
mawlana, “When I return, come so that we
may converse, for you speak very nicely.” He
indicated to Sa‘duddawla that all three—i.e.
Amir Shah, Fakhruddin Mustawfi, and Hajji
Lili’s son—should be summoned, for all three
had been arrested and brought from Anatolia.
Mawlana Qutbuddin chastised Sa‘duddawla
over Amir Shah. He ran after the emperor and
got him released. Hajji Lili’s son was killed.
Fakhruddin was put under guard and killed a
week later.
On the 23rd of Ramadan 689 [September 29,
1290] Aq Buqa, Doladai, Elchi, and Qaban
arrived from Anatolia. On the 5th of Shawwal
[October 11, 1290] Aq Buqa returned there.
When Arghun Khan arrived in Tabriz, the
Ramadan festival was approaching, [1179] so
he ordered four pulpits erected in Tabriz and
all cadis, imams, and the generality of the pop-
ulation to attend. The festival prayer was con-
ducted with great pomp, and he honored the
cadis and preacher and dismissed them. 
Since Arghun Khan was very fond of build-
ing, he had a magnificent city constructed in
the village of Sham-i-Tabriz, and there lofty
chambers were erected. He commanded that
anyone who wanted to could build a house
there, and he had a canal built. He named [the
city] Arghunia. He also built a large city in
Sharuyaz; vast amounts were spent on it, but it
was not completed. 
He had a special inclination for the craft of
alchemy, in which certain people encouraged
him.
Arghun Khan takes sulphur and quicksilver
as medicine on the bakhshis’ advice; he goes
on a forty-day retreat after their fashion;
the beginning of his illness.
Arghun Khan was highly devoted to the
bakhshis and followed their path. He constant-
ly patronized and favored them. One bakhshi
came from India and claimed to have lived a
long
time.
Arghun
asked
him
how
the
bakhshis’ lives were so prolonged there. He
replied that it was due to a special medicine.
“Can that medicine be found here?” Arghun
Khan asked.
“It can,” he answered, and Arghun ordered
him to make some. The bakhshi made a con-
coction in which were sulphur and quicksilver,
and for nearly eight months Arghun took it. Fi-
nally he made a forty-day retreat in the fortress
at Tabriz, and during that time, other than ordu
Qaya, Quchan, and Sa‘duddawla, no one was
allowed near him—save of course the bakhshis
who attended him day and night to discuss
[1180] their beliefs. When he emerged from his
solitude he set out for winter quarters in Arran.
There he developed symptoms, and Khwaja
Aminuddawla the physician undertook to treat
him. Together with other physicians he made
every effort, and after a time he regained his
health thanks to their treatment. Suddenly one
day a bakhshi came in and gave Arghun Khan
three goblets of wine. When it had penetrated
his body he had a relapse, and the illness
turned chronic. The physicians were incapable
of treating him. After he had suffered for two
months, the amirs gathered to deliberate and
make inquiry into the reason for his illness.
Some said that it was caused by the evil eye,
and alms should be given. Others reported that
the shamans had seen that the reason for the
570
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

illness was sorcery, and the accusation fell
upon Toghachaq Khatun. She was beaten and
tortured during the inquisition, and in the end
she and a number of other women were cast
into the river. That took place on the 16th of
Muharram 690 [January 19, 1291]. 
Arghun Khan is beset by illness; the amirs
revolt; some amirs and Sa‘duddawla are
killed.
On the 24th of Muharram 690 [January 27,
1291] Arghun Khan crossed the Kura River
and dismounted in the Baghcha yurt in Arran.
He was so wracked with illness that the amirs
despaired of his life. Taghachar and the other
amirs had all offended each other, and they
were all on bad terms with Sa‘duddawla, from
whose conceitedness and arrogance they had
all suffered. On the 4th of Safar [February 6]
they agreed amongst themselves, Taghachar
and Qunchuqbal, [1181] together with Tükäl
and Toghan. On the 14th of Safar [February
16] they swore oaths of conspiracy and began
to attack their enemies. First complaint of Sul-
tan Idächi was opened for discussion, and they
said, “A shaman has said that he had a vision
of Hulachu’s and Qara Noqai’s infant children
coming before Arghun Khan and saying to
him, ‘For what crime did you order us killed?’
He replied, ‘I know nothing of it. Sultan Idächi
killed you without my leave.’ ”
On Friday the 28th of Safar [March 2] Sultan
Idächi was arrested together with a group of
amirs and put on trial. “Why did you kill the
princes’ children and Toghachaq Khatun?” he
was asked. 
“By imperial command,” he said.
The amirs sent Ordu Qaya into the ordu to
ask. He returned and said, “The emperor says
he knows nothing about it.”
“The emperor is so sick that he hasn’t been
able to speak for some time,” said Sultan. “It
would be amazing if he has actually spoken.” 
“Since he cannot speak,” said the amirs in
unison, “you must have killed them of your
own accord. Your tyranny and injustice are the
cause of the emperor’s illness. Why should you
commit a crime and he suffer the conse-
quences?” Therefore he was executed on the
first day of Rabi‘ I [April 2, 1291]. That same
day Prince Khitai Oghul’s birthday was being
celebrated, and Joshi and Ordu Qaya were
arrested. Toghan was sent to arrest Quchan and
Sa‘duddawla, and that night Joshi and Quchan
were killed.
The next day Ordu Qaya and Sa‘duddawla
were tried in Taghachar’s quarters, and both
were executed. Tükäl and Toghan went to
Sa‘duddawla’s estates, and the soldiers began
to pillage. The homes of both Muslims and
Jews there were completely ransacked, and the
ﬂoors of tents were dug up in search of buried
treasure. At dawn the soldiers moved out and
created chaos, [1182] carrying away every-
thing they found and leaving the people
enmeshed in turmoil and strife.
Arghun Khan’s illness ends with his death
in Baghcha in Arran.
From the first of Shawwal until early Rabi‘ I
[early March 1291] Arghun Khan was ill, and
because of that the kingdom fell into such dis-
array that no one was safe from the conse-
quences. In the end, he passed away on Satur-
day the 7th of Rabi‘ I 690 [March 10, 1291],
corresponding to [the 8th of] Ikindi Ay of
[Taulai] Yil, at mid-morning in the village of
Baghcha in Arran, bequeathing the ephemeral
world to the renowned members of his family.
Mourning was held in his ordus, and on Mon-
day the 9th of Rabi‘ I [March 12] his coffin
was carried to Sujas. (May God endow the
Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan with many
years and countless generations of life and
make him to enjoy good fortune.) 
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIFTEEN: ARGHUN KHAN
571

The amirs differ after Arghun Khan’s
death, and an account of them during that
time.
On Thursday the 12th of Rabi‘ I [March 15,
1291], corresponding to the 13th of Ikindi Ay,
Qaban Aqtachi was sent to summon Prince
Ghazan. The next day Qubai Noyan’s son
Taitaq, Abaqa Khan’s kükältash and [1183]
Ahmad’s amir-ordu, was sent to Baghdad to
summon Prince Baidu. Lagzi was sent to Ana-
tolia to summon Prince Gaikhatu.
The amirs broke into so many factions that
when they got ready to decamp drums were
sounded in twenty different places. 
Baidu was a modest and reserved prince who
did not enjoy absolute command over the
army. Taghachar, Qunchuqbal, Toghan, Tükäl,
and some others who were stirring up trouble
feared only Ghazan’s might and power, and
therefore they wanted Baidu. The amirs Shik-
tür, Samaghar Noyan, Doladai Idächi, Tägänä,
Eljidäi Qushchi, Bughdai, and the amirs of the
left hand agreed with them, but Baidu had not
yet arrived. On the 11th of Rabi‘ I [March 14]
they held council in that regard, and on the
16th [March 19] they made their decision and
reported it to the ladies.
On Monday the 16th of Rabi‘
I, Samaghar
Noyan was sent to Anatolia. The next day
Baliya Zad was dispatched to have Lagzi re-
turn. On Saturday the 21st of Rabi‘ I [March
24] they killed Izzuddin Jalal, Sa‘duddawla’s
deputy who was always ailing. By the begin-
ning of Rabi‘ II envoys had twice arrived from
Khurasan with news of disturbances.
On Friday the 26th of Rabi‘ II [April 28,
1291] the amirs gathered together in the ordu
and sent back the envoys who had come on be-
half of the princes. On the 8th of Jumada I
[May 9] Amir Aladu arrived from Khurasan
and Persia bringing news that the Lurs had re-
belled, taken Isfahan, and killed Baidu the
shahna of Isfahan and some others. They had
also attacked Mongol troops who were sta-
tioned in the vicinity and dispersed them, and
reports of their depredations were constantly
coming in. That same day Buqu’s son Shadai
and Chingqor’s son Boralghi were sent to sum-
mon Prince Baidu. Doladai Idächi was sent to
deal with the Lurs’ invasion. [1184]
On Wednesday the 22nd of Jumada I [May
23, 1291] Prince Sögä and the amirs Chuban
and Alinaq’s son Qurumshi had the ladies’ or-
dus decamp toward Prince Gaikhatu at Ala
Tagh. This was done on Tükäl’s advice. Bu-
larghu Qayatai, the commander of four haza-
ras, was sent out after them, and therefore
Baidu’s chances came to naught. This was
Örüg Khatun’s plan. The next day the amirs
went to Prince Baidu in the village of Kuy-i-
Buldaq in the vicinity of Sughurluq. On the
eve of the 25th, Sati, Quban, and Tödächü took
ﬂight and headed for Anatolia to join Prince
Gaikhatu. The next night the ev-oghlans of the
ordus also departed. The next night Eljidäi
Qushchi and Temür Buqa departed, and the
next night Qunchuqbal went. All headed for
Gaikhatu, and thus Baidu’s chances of en-
thronement as emperor were dashed. The deci-
sion was made in favor of Gaikhatu. “God
knows best, and untimately to him all things
return.” [1185]
Part Three, on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave;
incidents that occurred during his reign that
were not included in the previous two
sections but learned from various persons.
*Arghun Khan was an intelligent ruler who
possessed a refined nature. Anyone who spoke
intelligently to him and gave a rational exposi-
tion was shown favor. The people rested in the
shadow of his clemency. He was extremely
fond of building and was an avid builder like
his father and grandfather. On the western side
572
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

of Tabriz, in the vicinity of Shamb, which the
common people call Sham, he built two mag-
nificent palaces and a city between the two.
There he constructed two lofty porticos that
were as grand as the arch at Ctesiphon. They
had stalactited ceilings and bowed arches. He
commissioned beautifully painted buildings.
He named it Arghunia, as has already been
mentioned. During his reign Tabriz was so
populous that it became an Egypt with Arghu-
nia as the capital like Cairo. He also built a city
in the meadows of Qonqur Öläng next to
Sharuyaz, and there he caused springs and
canals to ﬂow. He spent a lot of money on it,
but he did not live long enough to see it fin-
ished. Öljäitü Sultan completed it during his
reign and called it Sultania. He also built a
pavilion in the summer pastures of Lar at the
foot of Mount Damavand, and at present it is
known as Arghun’s Kiosk. He also built mag-
nificent palaces in many places. He was also
enthralled by alchemy, and alchemists came to
his court from far and wide to encourage him
in this art. Untold amounts of money were
spent on it, but he never chided them for it and
even cheerfully authorized more expenditures.
One day an extremely subtle point was dis-
cussed in the presence of Mawlana Qutbuddin
Shirazi. When the alchemists had left, Arghun
said to the mawlana, “Since I am only a Turk
and you are a wise man, do you think these
people are taking me for a ride? I have often
wanted to put them to death, but since it is cer-
tain that this science exists and there must be
someone who knows about it, if I withdraw my
patronage from these ignorant men and put
them to the sword, that one learned person will
not trust me.” 
In short, during Arghun Khan’s reign the al-
chemists spent untold amounts on their various
experiments, but after much experimentation
and tests, the veil of doubt was lifted from
everyone’s
eyes,
and
nothing
had
been
achieved other than financial loss and ruin.*1
[1186]

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION FIFTEEN: ARGHUN KHAN
573

❦ SECTION SIXTEEN
THE HISTORY OF ABAQA KHAN’S SON GAIKHATU KHAN, IN THREE PARTS
His blessed birth occurred on the eve of
Thursday the 5th of the ancient month of Bah-
man in the year 638 of the Yazdagird era,1 cor-
responding to 64_ of the Hegira, in ___, with
Virgo in the ascendant. On Sunday the 24th of
Rajab 690 [July 23, 1291], corresponding to
the 25th of Altinch Ay of Taulai Yil he was ele-
vated as padishah. He died on Thursday the 6th
of Jumada I 694 [March 24, 1295]. He lived for
___ years, and the length of his reign was three
years and ten months.
Part One is on his progeny with details of his
wives, sons, daughters and grandsons who
have branched off down to the present, the
names of his sons-in-law, and a genealogical
chart of his sons’ branches.
Part Two is on events leading to his en-
thronement, a picture of him and his wives,
sons, grandsons, and commanders at his en-
thronement; a history of his reign and events
that transpired therein. [1188]
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
the pronouncements and orders he gave; inci-
dents that occurred during his reign that were
not included in the previous two sections.
[1189]
1The 5th of Bahman would nominally be the fifth day
of Aquarius (ca. January 25), but the months of the Per-
sian calendar had “slipped back” over time because of
the lack of a corrective for the precession of the
equinoxes. In the early seventeenth century Bahman
usually began around January 10th. In the late thirteenth
century the first of Bahman was probably around Janu-
ary 15th.
Part One, on his progeny with details of his
wives, sons, daughters and grandsons who
have branched off down to the present, the
names of his sons-in-law, and a genealogical
chart of his sons’ branches.
Gaikhatu was Abaqa Khan’s second son. He
was born of Nuqdan Khatun of the Tatar na-
tion. The bakhshis named him Irinjin Dorji.2
He had many wives and concubines.
The first he married was Ayisha Khatun,
daughter of Toghu son of Elgäi Noyan. After
her he married Dondi Khatun, daughter of Aq
Buqa son of Elgäi Noyan of the Jalayir. After
her he married Eltüzmish Khatun, daughter of
Qutlugh Temür Gürägän of the Qunqirat. After
her he married Padishah Khatun, daughter of
Qutbuddin Sultan of Kirman. After her he mar-
ried Örüg Khatun, daughter of Saricha of the
Kerayit.
After
her
he
married
Bulughan
Khatun. He had a concubine named Nani
2From the Tibetan Buddhist name Rin-ch’en rDo-rje,
“Jewel Diamond.” See Blochet, Introduction, p. 225.
See also a farman surviving from the period, dated late
Jumada II 692/early June 1293 (Soudavar, Art of the Per-
sian Courts, p. 34f.) that bears the superscription [Irin-
ji]n [Do]rji yarlıghındın | Shiktür, Aq Buqa, Taghachar
sözindin | Ahmad Sahib-Divan sözindin (“by decree of
Irinjin Dorji, by word of Shiktür, Aq Buqa, and
Taghachar, by word of Ahmad Sahib-Divan”). As in the
Timurid period, the yarlıgh superscription indicates the
ultimate reigning (Genghisid) authority; the söz sub-
scription indicates the actual issuing authorities, in this
case the triumvirate of amirs Shiktür, Aq Buqa, and
Taghachar and the chief of the bureaucracy, the Sahib-
Divan Sadruddin Ahmad Zanjani.

whom Alafrang took after Gaikhatu’s death.
There was another named Esän, daughter of
Beglämish, brother of Ujan of the Orulat.
He had three sons. The eldest was Alafrang,
whose mother was Dondi Khatun. The second
was Iranshah, also by her. The third was Ching
Pulad by Bulughan Khatun.
He had four daughters. One was Ula Qut-
lugh. She was married to Ghurbatai. The sec-
ond was El Qutlugh; she was married to Amir
Qutlughshah.1 Another was Ara Qutlugh. All
three were born of Ayisha Khatun. He also had
daughters by Dondi.2  [1190]
Part Two, events leading to his
enthronement; a picture of him and his
wives, sons, grandsons, and commanders at
his enthronement; a history of his reign and
events that transpired therein.
In the beginning most of the amirs—and es-
pecially the group that had stirred up re-
bellion—were of the opinion that they would
enthrone Baidu. When Amir Chupan, Qu-
rumshi, and others set out for Gaikhatu, the
rest wavered in their support of Baidu, who
also refused to accept the office. Toghan, who
had been the most eloquent in support of him,
took fright and ﬂed to Gilan with soldiers on
his heels. They seized him and brought him
back to the amirs. Baidu undertook to protect
1See text p. 1300.
2Thus in the text. JTAZ’s MS S adds a fourth daughter’s
name, Qutlugh Malik.
him and had him put under guard until
Gaikhatu should arrive. When Gaikhatu real-
ized that the amirs were waiting for him, he set
out from Anatolia for Iran. At Ala Tagh he
joined the ladies, amirs, and princes, and they
all enthroned him in the vicinity of Akhlat on
Sunday the 24th of Rajab 690 [July 23, 1291].
[1191]
The amirs who had stirred up rebellion are
arrested and put on trial.
When the banquets and celebrations were
over, in early Sha‘ban [early August 1291] all
the amirs were arrested and trials were begun,
for Gaikhatu wanted to have an investigation
made of his brother Arghun Khan’s death and
the murders of the amirs and viziers. In the be-
ginning he sat in on the trials himself. He
asked Shiktür Noyan, who was the chief of the
amirs, “What actually happened?”
“The amirs are present,” he replied. “Let the
emperor inquire of them so that my guilt and
theirs may be clear.”
The amirs said unanimously, “The rebellion
was initiated by Taghachar and Qunchuqbal.
Then they told Samaghar and Tägänä. In the
end they all conspired together and divulged
their plot to Shiktür. He said, ‘I am also in with
you on whatever you have decided.’ ”
When their confession reached this point,
Shiktür Noyan said, “So many dominant amirs
had made such wicked plans. I am a weak old
man, and my brothers on whom I might have
relied were with the emperor in Anatolia. Had I
spoken in opposition to their plan, not only
would I not have been given free rein, but the
same thing that happened to Joshi and Ordu
Qaya would have happened to me.” 
Gaikhatu pardoned and released him. After
the trial was completed he showed all the amirs
favor. Since they all had hopes of pardon after
Shiktür Noyan was forgiven, they quickly con-
fessed their crimes. [1192] Toghan was impris-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SIXTEEN: GAIKHATU KHAN
575

oned, and Joshi’s and Ordu Qaya’s wives and
sons wanted to take retribution on him for their
fathers’ blood. Aq Buqa was on bad terms with
Toghan, and so was Örüg Khatun. Gaikhatu
hesitated, however, to allow him to be killed.
Örüg Khatun said, “If, with all the rebellion
and strife Toghan has caused, you do not kill
him and take retribution for the amirs he mur-
dered, no one will serve you wholeheartedly
from this day forth.”
“Certainly that is what someone who does
what he has done deserves,” replied Gaikhatu.
No sooner had Aq Buqa heard the emperor
speak these words than he went out and sent
Ordu Qaya’s children to put an end to Toghan. 
On the 9th of Shawwal [October 5, 1291]
Gaikhatu encamped at Ala Tagh. The next day
the amirs Taghachar, Qunchuqbal, and others,
having been absolved of their crimes, per-
formed tägishmishi.
On Friday the 4th of Ramadan [August 31]
Gaikhatu set out to return to Anatolia. 
Gaikhatu goes to Anatolia; Shiktür Noyan is
appointed as his deputy with absolute
power.
When Gaikhatu set out from Ala Tagh for
Anatolia, he appointed Shiktür Noyan as his
absolute deputy in the realms of Iran. From
there he went to Tabriz, and together with the
amirs he went to Arran to spend the winter. He
camped at Qara Chali on the banks of the
Kura, his old yurt, and there he turned his at-
tention to matters of state and finance, dis-
patching envoys and the red seal to all parts of
the kingdom.
Toward the end of that winter, on Sunday the
28th of Muharram 691 [December 31, 1291],
Yoshmut’s son Prince Zambu [1193] died at
Jaghatu.1
1For Prince Zambu, see text p. 966 above.
Gaikhatu had sent Prince Anbarchi with a di-
vision of soldiers to Khurasan, and he had
stopped for the winter in the vicinity of Rayy.
Taghachar being a liege man of Shiktür Noy-
an’s, he asked him for permission to see his
children and set out for home. Sadruddin Zan-
jani was [Taghachar’s] deputy, and he was sent
to Qazwin with a Qazwini named Baba.
[Sadruddin’s] brother Qutbuddin sent a mes-
sage saying, “The Turcomans of Anatolia and
the Qaramanids have been victorious over
Gaikhatu and killed him, and all the amirs are
unanimously for Prince Anbarchi as emperor.
It is necessary that my brother hasten to him
and report what has happened so that he may
cancel his expedition to Khurasan and return to
Arran.” Qutbuddin told this to Shaykh Jamal
Shirazi, an attendant of the prince’s, and he
told the prince. Being extremely clever and in-
telligent, [Prince Anbarchi] realized the neces-
sity of maintaining cautiousness, so he sent one
of his liege men, Mulayid by name, as an en-
voy to Shiktür to find out what was happening.
Along the way Mulayid came across Tagha-
char, and Sadruddin said to him, “It is not wise
for you to go to Shiktür. Return and go in haste
so that the prince may come as quickly as pos-
sible and mount the throne.” Mulayid, who
was also clever and quick, said, “It would be
appropriate for me to do that, but since our
tents are near, I will go see my people and then
return.” When he passed by them he headed
for Qara Chali, where he came before Shiktür.
Along the way he saw envoys coming from
Anatolia with yarlighs, for Gaikhatu had dis-
patched gifts and presents for the ladies,
princes, and amirs. Among them he found a
friend of his he trusted, and he asked him about
Gaikhatu. [1194] He reported that Gaikhatu
was hale and hearty. Mulayid realized that
Sadruddin had tried to trick him, and if the
truth came out Anbarchi and his amirs would
576
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

not be safe. Immediately he went to Shiktür
and discharged his mission as messenger for
Prince Anbarchi in public. After that he asked
for a private audience, at which he reported
everything from beginning to end. Shiktür
Noyan, having already suspected what had
happened, replied pleasantly and sent him back
to Anbarchi with gifts and presents.
Shiktür himself mounted with two thousand
horsemen, and the next morning they attacked
Taghachar’s quarters and seized him. He also
took Sadruddin to his house and kept him im-
prisoned there until the springtime, when the
news of Gaikhatu’s arrival came and he sent
them with five hundred sturdy horsemen to
greet him. They came upon Gaikhatu in the
vicinity of Arzan al-Rum.1 He then passed
through hazara after hazara until he dismount-
ed in the summer pastures at Ala Tagh.
On Sunday the 12th of Rajab 691 [June 29,
1292], corresponding to the 14th of Altinch Ay
of Luy Yil, the princes and amirs together gave
written pledges and sat Gaikhatu on the throne
again, as was customary, in Ala Tagh, after
which revels and celebrations were held.
The office of vizier is transferred to
Sadruddin Zanjani, and the office of chief
justice is given to his brother Qutbuddin.
That summer Gaikhatu was in Ala Tagh.
Ghazan set out from Khurasan to see him,
[1195] but when he got to Tabriz he was sent
back without having seen him.
Sadruddin Zanjani presented some of the
vast wealth he had realized from those who
had been killed. Taking refuge with Boraqchin
Egächi, Gaikhatu’s extremely inﬂuential nurse,
Sadruddin requested the office of vizier. Sham-
suddin Ahmad Lakushi was also seeking the
same office with the support of a group of
amirs. Through the good offices of Sharafud-
1The modern Erzurum in Turkey.
din Simnani, Sadruddin curried favor with
Amir Aq Buqa and made him his patron, and
he also promised to provide all [those who sup-
ported him] with estates.
Around that time news arrived from Anatolia
that an enemy army had come from Syria and
Malik Ashraf had laid siege to Qal‘at al-Rum.
In the month of Rajab, Mänggü Temür’s son
Taichu Oghul, Taghachar, Buqdai Aqtachi, and
Tammachi Inaq headed in that direction with a
large army to repel the foe. In Sha‘ban, Prince
Sögä, Amir Temür Buqa, and Qaracha set out
for Qal‘at al-Rum via Akhlat and Erjish. In late
Rajab, Malik Ashraf took Qal‘at al-Rum,
killing some of the inhabitants and taking oth-
ers captive, and turned the fortress over to his
castellans before withdrawing. As Gaikhatu
was returning from Ala Tagh, he married Bu-
lughan Khatun in the vicinity of Albaq in the
month of Sha‘ban 691 [July–August 1292].
On Tuesday the 18th of Ramadan of that year
[September 2, 1292], at the Tasu station in the
Tabriz area, Gaikhatu became indisposed, and
it turned into a dreadful illness. The physicians
Rubaybuddawla and Safiuddawla Nasrani were
in attendance, and they treated him vigorously.
Within forty days he had completely regained
his health. 
On the 6th of Dhu’l-Hijja 691 [November
18, 1292], in the Arran winter quarters, the of-
fice of chief administrative officer was given
to Sadruddin, and he requested of Gaikhatu
that he be entitled Sadr-i-Jahan and his brother
be called [1196] Qutb-i-Jahan. He got the title
Qawamulmulk for his cousin and the office of
chief justice for his brother. The governorship
of Tabriz was also given to him, and that of
Persia was given to Qawamulmulk. 
On the 3rd of Jumada I 692 [April 11, 1293],
Tägänä Totqavul died at Saray Mansuriyya in
Arran, and his body was taken to Maragha.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SIXTEEN: GAIKHATU KHAN
577

On the 13th of Jumada II [May 21, 1293]
Gaikhatu went to Tabriz. On the 12th of Rajab
[June 18] he left Maragha for Siyah Koh.
On the 7th of Sha‘ban [July 13] envoys from
Qonchi Oghul arrived to express good will and
ask for an alliance.1
On the 9th of the month [July 15] Qut-
lughshah Noyan and Örüg Temür Oghul’s en-
voys, as well as those of Nawroz, arrived from
Khurasan. That day also coincided with the
arrival of Ayisha Khatun from Anatolia, and
Baytmish came from Diyarbekir.2
On the 17th of Sha‘ban [July 23] Mänggü
Temür’s son Gäräi Oghul, Qunchuqbal, and
Doladai Idächi, all of whom who had gone on
an expedition to Khurasan, returned.
Toward the end of Sha‘ban camp was made
in Ashkamar (?). Sadun of Georgia’s son Qut-
lugh Buqa was executed there.
On the 12th of Ramadan [August 16] [the
emperor] went to Ujan. On the 19th he went to
Hashtrod, and from there he went out toward
Maragha to Arran, where he wintered.
On the 28th of Rabi‘ II [March 28, 1294]
emissaries came from Toqta under the leader-
ship of Prince Qalintai and Bolad, arriving at
court at Dalan Na’ur to propose a truce and
treaty, and they also made all sorts of requests.
On the 3rd of Jumada I [April 1, 1294] they
were sent back with all honor.
On the 10th of Jumada I [April 8], a large
city was founded on the banks of the Kura, and
it was called Qutlugh Baligh. [The emperor]
returned from winter quarters. In Bilasawar a
review of the military was held.
1For the Jochid Qonchi, who ruled the Ulus Orda, see
text p. 712 above.
2Baytmish Aqa is the amir named in the farman cited
above.
In early Jumada II 693 [early May 1294] a
council was held concerning chao (paper
money).
On the 7th of Rajab [June 3] Mänggü
Temür’s son Gäräi Oghul died. [1197]
On the 16th of Rajab [June 12] Prince Baidu
came to court at Ala Tagh, and Gaikhatu chas-
tised him. On the 15th of Sha‘ban [July 11] he
was given permission to withdraw through the
intercession of Boraqchin Egächi. 
On the 7th of Ramadan [August 1] they
reached Ala Tagh, where a quriltai was held. It
was finished on Thursday the 21st of the
month [August 15].
The history of the unlucky chao, and the
havoc it wrought in the kingdom.
Occasionally Sadruddin and some of the
amirs discussed the chao, which was current in
Cathay, and they made plans to introduce it
here. This was proposed to the emperor, and
Gaikhatu asked Bolad Chingsang about it. He
reported that the chao was a piece of paper on
which was the ruler’s seal, and it was used
throughout Cathay instead of minted coins.
The unit of currency there is the balish (bar),
which goes into the imperial treasury. Since
Gaikhatu was an extremely generous ruler and
carried his liberality to such excess that the
wealth of the entire world would not have been
enough for him, he approved of this sugges-
tion. Sadruddin wanted to implement an impo-
sition in the kingdom that no one else had ever
done. Therefore he made great efforts in that
regard. Shiktür Noyan, the most intelligent of
the amirs, said that the chao would cause ru-
ination in the kingdom, defamation of the em-
peror, and dispersal of the peasantry and sol-
diers. Sadruddin countered that Shiktür Noyan
was only trying to discourage the implementa-
tion of chao because he loved gold so much.
A decree was issued for it to be achieved
soon. [1198] On Friday the 27th of Sha‘ban
578
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

[July 23, 1294] Aq Buqa, Taghachar, Sadrud-
din, and Tammachi Inaq set out for Tabriz to
implement the chao. They arrived there on the
19th of Ramadan [August 13] and delivered
the decree. Many chaos were prepared, and on
Saturday the 19th of Shawwal 693 [September
12, 1294] the chaos were brought out in Tabriz
and put into circulation. A command was is-
sued that anyone who did not accept them
would be immediately executed. For one week
they were accepted out of fear of the sword,
but in return for them very little was given to
anyone, and most of the people of Tabriz chose
to leave town. Goods and victuals were with-
drawn from the market, and finally there was
nothing to be found. In order to eat fruit the
people had to resort to the orchards, and such a
bustling city was totally emptied of inhabitants
as ruffians and rabble stripped everyone they
found in the streets, and caravans ceased com-
ing. By night ruffians lay in ambush at the
heads of streets leading to the orchards, and if
an unfortunate happened to have acquired a
load of grain or a basket of fruit by some ruse
and was carrying it home, they would take it
from him. If he resisted they would say, “Sell it
and take the price in ‘lucky’ chaos so that you
can show where you bought it.” In short,
everyone was caught in such a predicament.
The poor raised their hands in supplication.
By chance one day Gaikhatu was strolling in
the marketplace and saw how empty the shops
were. When he asked what the reason was,
Sadruddin said, “Sharafuddin Lakushi, who
was the head man here, has died, and it is a
custom of the people of Tabriz to leave the
market during mourning for their leaders.”
One Friday in the congregational mosque
Qutbuddin was mobbed until the crowd was
dispersed. In the lanes food was sold for gold,
and still people were killed on that pretext.
Commercial transactions and tax revenues
completely fell away. [1199] One day a poor
man grabbed Sadruddin’s reins at the head of
the market and said, “ ‘The odor of scorched
passions fill the world. If you don’t notice, it’s
some nose you have!’ ” Moved by this,
Sadruddin and his liege men obtained a decree
for food to be sold for gold, and thereby the
people grew bold enough to carry out transac-
tions openly in gold. Therefore the chao came
to naught and was abandoned, and the people
were relieved of the nuisance.1

and silver he rejected them. And he promulgated a royal

And he made slips of paper from papyrus which could

and so on up to ten dînârs. And he called them ‘Shâw’
[chao]. And the heralds proclaimed throughout the city,

fices of the Government to be stamped therein with [the
word] Shâw, and giveth it up and taketh [in exchange]
Shâw shall die the death.’ And thus men remained in a
state of great tribulation and indescribable difficulty for
a space of two months.
And TÂBRÎZ, which was the royal city of the mon-

and dispersed themselves about the country, and only a

are not able to describe the famine, and scarcity, and
hardship which arose therein. For men would not con-
sent to use the contemptible slips of paper, and they
clung to the use of money. And the people cried out
against the SÂHIB DÎWÂN until at length they hurled
