Baidu rebels; the amirs disagree, and some
rebel against Gaikhatu; Gaikhatu’s end.
When Prince Baidu obtained release through
Boraqchin Egächi’s intercession and went back
to his old camping ground, because of his hurt
feelings he complained of Gaikhatu to his
amirs both openly and by allusion. When the
amirs Tödächü Yarghuchi, Chechäk Gürägän,
Arghun Aqa’s son Lagzi, and Hinduqur Noy-
an’s son El Temür went to Baghdad, he won
insults and abuse at him when they were face to face
with him. And they made him to hear jeers and scoffs,
and they would not submit to be convinced and to hear
his word. And he remained stupefied and astonished; to
go back on his word (or, to withdraw it) would bring ig-
nominy upon him, and to carry out his will he was un-
able. And there was not a single maker of verses who
did not gibe at this act, and not a single singing man
who did not string together poems and ditties and ad-
mirable verses [about it]. And being urged by those in-
side [the city] and those outside [it], the SÂHIB
DÎWÂN issued another royal command, saying, ‘Every
man according to his wish and according to his inclina-
tion. If he wisheth for the Shâw let him use it, and if he
wisheth silver [let him use it]. There is no compulsion
for any man.’And the King of Kings also said, ‘We wish
you to have a comfortable existence, and a quiet life,
and an abundance of good things, and moreover, we do
not wish that everything which a man hath to give
should be taken from him. But let every man use, ac-
cording to what [his] need is for goods (i.e. ﬂocks and
herds) and equipment (or, furniture). In the twinkling of
an eye let the slips of paper by thousands and by tens of
thousands be sunk in the sea and done away. And now
let every man who is not pleased [with them] know that
we do put pressure on any man.’And there was great joy
in every country and city, and the roads were opened
[again], for during these two months the merchants
could not trade, and the roads were cut, and the khâns
(i.e. inns) were closed, and buying and selling ceased.”
them over and united them with himself to
rebel against Gaikhatu. Jamaluddin Dastjir-
dani, one of the Baghdad secretaries and tax
collectors, [1200] conspired with them and
made arrangements for his, the amirs’ and the
soldiers’ necessities, weapons, mounts, money,
provisions, etc. Baidu sent envoys to Baghdad
to kill Muhammad Sükürchi, the shahna of
Baghdad by Gaikhatu’s command. Thus they
openly announced their rebellion and began to
create
disorder.
When
Ghurbatai
Gürägän
learned of this, he sent a messenger to inform
Gaikhatu of Baidu’s rebellion and the amirs’
conspiracy with him. He also advised Gaikhatu
to guard himself from the treachery of the
amirs Doladai Idächi, Qunchuqbal, Tükäl,
Eljidäi, and Bughdai, all of whom were in at-
tendance upon him and were in on the conspir-
acy. Gaikhatu consulted with Amir Aq Buqa,
had the amirs arrested and thrown into chains,
and sent them to Tabriz for imprisonment—
aside from Tükäl, who was in Georgia. Then
from winter quarters in Arran he sent envoys to
Bay Buqa in Diyarbekir for Baidu to be seized
and sent, but when the envoys reached the
vicinity of Arbela on the banks of the Zab Riv-
er they found Bay Buqa arrested and in the
hands of Baidu’s envoys. They turned back and
came in all haste to report what had happened
to Bay Buqa. 
On Thursday the 28th of Rabi‘ II 694 [March
17, 1295], corresponding to the end of Ikindi
Ay of ___ Yil, the amirs Aq Buqa and
Taghachar were sent on a campaign against
Baidu. Taghachar had sent a secret message to
Baidu encouraging him to rebel. When they
reached the banks of the Jaghatu river, Aq
Buqa said to Taghachar, “You are a clever and
tricky man. Do you realize what you are up
to?” (Of course, he knew nothing of the mes-
sage to Baidu.) When Taghachar heard this, he
imagined that Aq Buqa knew his secret and
580
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

was speaking about that. Frightened, he con-
spired with the hazara amirs in the middle of
the night [1201] and set out for Baidu’s side.
When Amir Aq Buqa saw this, he turned back
and went to Gaikhatu’s court in the Ahar re-
gion with three hundred of his elite horsemen.
Gaikhatu was perplexed and wanted to go to
Anatolia. Some of his unwise attendants said,
“It is not prudent to hand over crown and
throne to a rebel and take ﬂight. Our soldiers
are stationed throughout the region. Let us as-
semble and go out to fight the enemy.”
From there he returned to Arran, and the next
day he went to Bilasawar. Buqu’s son Amir
Hasan, who had been his attendant from the
cradle, ﬂed with his companions in the middle
of the night and headed for Baidu. When the
news reached Qunchuqbal and Doladai in
Tabriz, they got out of prison and ﬂed. Amir Ir-
injin, Baichaq, and some others conspired and
got Baidu’s son Qipchaq Oghul out of prison
and took him to his father.
On Thursday the 6th of Jumada I [March 24,
1295] Taitaq and Toghrilcha did battle in the
vicinity of Hamadan with Bashmaq Oghul and
Qaracha, Sultan Ahmad’s son-in-law. Victory
was Taitaq’s. Tükäl, coming with a troop from
Georgia, sent a messenger to Tabriz to the
amirs who were imprisoned, saying, “I am
heading for Arran with a large troop to help
Prince Ildär attack Gaikhatu. You must join me
as soon as possible.” They departed at once
and joined Tükäl on the banks of the Kura. To-
gether they set out in search of him. The
Ba’arin hazara,1 which was in Bilasawar,
found out where Gaikhatu was. They went
there and seized him and then turned him over
to the rebel amirs for execution on Thursday
1Reading #رﻳﻦ (Ba’arin) with the variant in JTAZ.
the 6th of Jumada I 694 [March 24, 1295], cor-
responding to the 7th of Üchünch Ay of ___
Yil. Tammachi Inaq, It-Oghli, and It-Tuqli,
who were his intimates, were killed along with
him. It-Tuqli, who had been in charge of the
session where Baidu was investigated and pun-
ished,2 [1202] was arrested and sent for Baidu
to execute however he saw fit. When he got
there Baidu said, “He carried out the action at
the command of the padishah. He is not to
blame.” He therefore spared his life.
Aq Buqa and Taichu were arrested, and when
Ghazan was battling Baidu they were taken
near Hashtrod and killed.
On Wednesday the 19th of Jumada I 694
[April 6, 1295] at the junction of the Kökrä and
Jaghatu rivers the amirs sent Amir Ramazan to
Prince Ghazan to announce Gaikhatu’s death.
Emissaries were also dispatched to Baidu for
him to come in all haste and mount the throne.
When Baidu heard this, he rejoiced and killed
a number of amirs with whom he was on bad
terms. Then he set out for this region. His his-
tory will be contained in the section of Ghazan
Khan, God willing. [1203]

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SIXTEEN: GAIKHATU KHAN
581

❦ SECTION SEVENTEEN
THE HISTORY OF ABAQA KHAN’S SON GHAZAN KHAN, IN THREE PARTS.
His lineage is as follows: Shah Ghazan Khan,
son of Arghun Khan, son of Abaqa Khan, son
of Hülägü Khan, son of Tolui Khan, son of
Genghis Khan. He was among Genghis Khan’s
noble offspring in the fifth generation, and he
was the sixth khan. His life span was thirty-
two years, five months and twelve days. Of
that period he was on the throne of the khanate
for nine years.1
Part One is on his lineage and his history
from the moment of his blessed birth until the
time of Arghun Khan’s accession; a mention of
his wives and children, and a genealogical
1Section missing in JTAZ and JTRM; taken from JTK.
chart of his noble branch.
Part Two is on events leading to his en-
thronement, a picture of him and his wives,
sons, grandsons, and commanders at his en-
thronement; a history of his reign and the bat-
tles he fought and the victories he achieved. 
Part Three is on his conduct and character;
monuments of his justice and beneficence,
charity, and piety; the pronouncements and or-
ders he gave for the benefit of all people; and
rare stories and unusual events not included in
the two previous sections: these are divided
into two divisions, one further subdivided into
forty stories, and the other on various and mis-
cellaneous events and incidents. [1206]
Part One, on his lineage and his history from the moment of his blessed birth until the time
of Arghun Khan’s accession; a mention of his wives and children, and a genealogical chart
of his noble branch.
Ghazan Khan was the eldest son of Arghun
Khan. Arghun Khan requested Ghazan’s moth-
er, Qultaq, the daughter of Kihtar Bitigchi of
the Dörbän tribe, at the age of twelve from
Küräk Temür, the brother of Uruqtu and Mulai.
Her elder sister Ashlun was married to Prince
Tübshin. Qultaq was extremely beautiful, and
Arghun Khan loved her exceedingly, so much
so that on the day she was being brought to the
ordu for the wedding he wanted to go out to
greet her, but the amirs Sartaq and Jochighan
forbade it. He was so infatuated that he went to
a pole in the court tent, sat down on a stake,
and watched her from afar. In short, after the
wedding ceremonies the noble components of
Ghazan Khan’s being were mingled, and the
“oyster shell” of that “chaste moon” became
pregnant with an imperial pearl. After nine
months, at the most felicitous hour of dawn on
Friday the 29th of Rabi‘ I 670 [November 4,
1271], corresponding to the first of Birye-
girminch Ay of Qoyin Yil, at Abuskun in
Mazanderan,1 under the auspicious ascendant
of the constellation Scorpio with the vector of
fortune and the vector of the unseen rising,
1Ābuskūn was the port of Jurjān (see Abu’l-Fida,
Taqwim, 438) and is more or less the modern Bandar
Turkman on the Caspian.

[1207] the regal Ghazan Khan stepped from
nonexistence into the world. All the expert as-
trologers who were in attendance took celestial
readings and cast horoscopes with all care.
Finding his natal extremely auspicious, they all
said of one accord, “ ‘I have looked into your
ascendant and have seen that your estates will
be a hundred thousand souls.’ ” All agreed that
he would be an extremely magnificent and
awe-inspiring ruler, and unanimously they
cried, “ ‘Lofty are his ascendant and his luck;
his throne will be raised to the shining sun.’ ”
He was given to a wet nurse of good charac-
ter named Moghalchin, the wife of a Cathaian
named Eshing who had come with Qultaq
Khatun. She was a pure woman of good con-
duct who was suitable for nursing princes. Her
own son Hindu is still alive. In short, this kind
nurse raised him in the lap of compassion.
While he was still in the cradle, in accor-
dance with the line of poetry that says “In the
cradle he speaks out of the felicity of his
grandfather, and traces of nobility shine as
proof,” he loosened his tongue with eloquent
words and phrases to the astonishment of all.
It is the Mongol custom for the husbands of
princes’ nurses not to be allowed to approach
their wives, but Eshing the Cathaian lay with
his wife during that time, and she became
pregnant. [1208] Her milk caused diarrhea in
the prince, and so he was taken away from
Moghalchin.
At the age of three he was seated on a horse.
He was given to the mother of Hasan, the amir
of the tuqchis, of the Suldus tribe. (Hasan’s fa-
ther’s name was Ashtu, and his mother’s name
was Ashtai. Ashtu’s son is the Tolai who serves
as an idächi and ba’urchi.)
When the prince was three years old, Arghun
Khan sent Amir Qutlughshah from the winter
quarters in Mazanderan to Abaqa Khan’s court
on several matters of business, and he joined
the court at Mughan. Abaqa Khan inquired af-
ter Prince Ghazan and was told that he was
three years old and was already riding horses.
Abaqa Khan developed a craving to see him,
and when Qutlughshah was setting out to re-
turn he said, “I have grown old, and from time
to time thoughts of the afterlife cross my mind.
My son Arghun loves his son Ghazan, and
since he is his only son, he will not want to
part with him, but I desire that he be sent to me
to learn to shoot sparrow hawks and turumtai
[merlin] and to hunt alaghu [killer?] lions.”
When Amir Qutlughshah delivered this mes-
sage to Arghun, he said, “I have only this one
son. How can I send him away? However, my
father’s command is law, so it would be best
for me to go to court and take him there with
me.” At the beginning of the spring that fell in
the year 673 [1275], he set out from Mazander-
an for his father’s court with the prince at his
side, joining the court at Qonqur Öläng. When
Abaqa Khan heard that they were arriving, he
was so anxious to see the prince that he went
out to greet them, and when he saw him he lift-
ed him from his horse and sat him in front of
his own saddle, rejoicing at the sight. [1209]
Since he could discern traces of regality in his
features, he said, “This boy is worthy of being
with me, and I will raise him.” Even though he
already loved Arghun very much, his love for
him increased on account of the affection he
bore for Ghazan, and all the while he was en-
camped Abaqa Khan was constantly engaged
in banquets and revelry and spreading largesse
for the safe arrival of the child.
When it came time to send [Arghun] back,
Abaqa Khan said, “Let your son Ghazan re-
main here for me to raise.” 
Since the senior Bulughan Khatun had no
male child, Arghun said, “If so ordered, I will
give him to Bulughan Khatun as a servant and
page.” Abaqa Khan approved.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
583

Bulughan Khatun had already set out for
Sughurluq, and Arghun went out a stage after
her, offered her a goblet, and turned Ghazan
over to her before returning to Khurasan. Bu-
lughan Khatun was extremely happy and said,
“This is a gift from God. He will be like a child
of my own.” Arghun left ten of his liege men
with her—[among them were] Hasan, Kökä,
Majar, Adram, Buqa, Qardaghmish, Quljai,
and Altun Buqa Aqtachi of the Ongqut. Abaqa
Khan said, “Let Ghazan be in this ordu, and let
the ordu be in his name. After me, let this ordu
belong to him, and let him be my successor.”
In short, Prince Ghazan lived in Bulughan
Khatun’s ordu, and he attended Abaqa Khan’s
court. Since he was a child, [and] Abaqa Khan
loved him more than his own young son
Gaikhatu, if Gaikhatu hurt Ghazan during play,
he punished him for it.
Since Abaqa Khan was annoyed by the press
of crowds, when he married Tödäi Khatun,
whom he loved very much, [1210] he took her
nearly half a league away from the ordus, and
none of his brothers or sons was allowed there.
However, he loved Ghazan so much that he
had him camp nearby, and in drunkenness and
sobriety, in hunting grounds, during travel and
at home, at any and all times, he kept Ghazan
with him and could not bear to be away from
him for a moment. He always used to say,
“Great good fortune shows on the boy’s head.”
Ghazan was very precocious. In his early
youth he gathered children and youths and
taught them the Yosun and Yasaq and methods
of hand-to-hand combat. He assigned them to
ranks of aqa, ini, anda, and quda, and if any of
them trespassed his bounds, he requited him
after the manner of the Yasa and chastised him.
He did not engage in sport and play as other
children do, but when he played he had images
of men and horses made of felt and cloth, put
arms on them, set them opposite each other
like two opposing armies, and then ordered
them to fight. 
When he was five years old, Abaqa Khan
turned him over to Yaruq Bakhshi for his edu-
cation, and he taught him Mongolian and
Uyghur writing and their sciences and cus-
toms. Over a period of five years he learned
these things to perfection. Thereafter he began
to learn to ride and shoot.
Still from his mouth came the odor of milk, but
his thoughts were on swords and arrows.
He constantly practiced falconry and rode
horses in a manner that astonished all. 
In the year 678 [1279–80], when Abaqa
Khan [1211] went to Khurasan to repel the
Qara’una army that had ravaged Fars, he took
Bulughan
Khatun
and
Ghazan
with
him.
Arghun came out in greeting and joined the
court at Simnan. Thus father and son saw each
other again. When they moved out of Simnan,
they went hunting at Akhri Koh,1 which is be-
tween Simnan and Damghan. Prince Ghazan
was eight years old. There he brought down
prey, and since it was his first hunt, they
stopped in Damghan for three days to perform
yaghlamishi on his hand and celebrate.2 Qorchi
Buqa, who was a märgän, i.e. a good hunter,
performed yaghlamishi on the prince. When he
set out from Damghan, since it was early
spring and the grass had not yet come up fully,
he ordered Bulughan Khatun and Ghazan to go
via Mazanderan while he took the Bistam road.
They went via Shahrak-i-Naw and joined
Abaqa Khan in the meadows of Radkan.
When Abaqa Khan set out for Kitu in Jam
and Herat he sent Arghun Khan toward Ghor
and Gharcha to repel the Qara’una. “If so com-
1This should be the fairly low (8000-foot) spur of the
Alborz Mountains that eventually becomes the Kuh-i
Daristan considerably east of the Simnan–Damghan line.
2For the Mongolian custom of yaghlamishi, see text p.
536 above.
584
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

manded, let me go and offer my father a gob-
let,” said Ghazan. Abaqa Khan assented, gave
him a bottle of special wine, and told him to go
after Arghun. He offered him a goblet in
Husayn’s
garden
below
Tus,
bade
him
farewell, and returned.
When Abaqa Khan was sending Saljuq
Khatun to Damavand, he sent Ghazan back
with her. He summoned Maichu Bakhshi, Amir
Taramdaz’s father, and his mother Tükältäni
and said, “I have complete trust in you, and so
I am turning Ghazan over to you as a son.
Yaruq Bakhshi of Cathay will also be with you.
Go with Saljuq Khatun to summer pastures in
Damavand so that Ghazan may have a good
time.” [1212] That summer they were in
Damavand, and when autumn came and Abaqa
Khan
returned,
Ghazan
rejoined
him
at
Varamin in Rayy.
Abaqa Khan loved him so much that early in
the morning he used to put an old hat on his
head and go into Ghazan’s quarters in disguise,
get into bed and play with him, stripping him
naked. He used to tell Ashi’tai Egächi not to
put a pillow for him, and she did not. Although
it is the custom of princes for a pillow to be
bound to their saddles, he used to order that he
be mounted on a bare saddle so that he would
get toughened up.
Toqiyatai Khatun often used to say, “Since I
have no child, if the padishah gives me Ghazan
as a son, it is his to command.” But since
Abaqa Khan loved Bulughan Khatun very
much and wanted her ordu to be Ghazan
Khan’s, he used to reply, saying, “His father
Arghun gave him to Bulughan Khatun as a
son. How can he be taken away from her?” He
also used to say, “The signs of fortune and
good luck on this child’s forehead are obvi-
ous.” He also used to quote a Mongolian
proverb that says “He is like a tooth in the mid-
dle of a belly”—i.e. a soft belly in which a
tooth has grown—and playfully he used to call
him that.
When Abaqa Khan was returning from Bagh-
dad and died in Hamadan on the 20th of Dhu’l-
Hijja 680 [April 1, 1282], Ghazan was ten
years old. He wept so much over the death that
all the ladies and amirs were greatly moved by
his grief. 
Arghun Khan came from Khurasan and
reached the ordus at Maragha, but he returned
after
Ahmad’s
enthronement.
Ghazan
re-
mained, as before, with Bulughan Khatun. 
In the year 681 [1282–83], when Bulughan
Khatun was spending the winter in Baghdad,
the princes Gaikhatu and Ghazan were with
her. Ahmad was in Arran, [1213] and Arghun
went from Khurasan to Baghdad, where he
stayed that winter. When spring came Bu-
lughan Khatun set out for Khurasan, and
Arghun requested her and married her. Ghazan
remained in her ordu as before. When Ahmad
set out for Khurasan, Arghun requested that he
be allowed to return, as has already been stated
in the section on Arghun.1 She sent Ghazan to
him, and he joined him in the vicinity of
Simnan. Ahmad saw regal glory in him,
showed him favor, and consoled him. At Bis-
tam he gave him permission to withdraw.
When Arghun came before Ahmad, Ildär was
with Ahmad and spoke stupidly about Arghun.
Ghazan was so eloquent on his behalf that all
were astonished by his repartee. 
After God gave Arghun victory and he set
out for Azerbaijan in pursuit of Ahmad, Bu-
lughan Khatun also set out in that direction.
Ghazan was left in Khurasan as Arghun’s rep-
resentative, and most of the aghruqs and ev-
oghlans, Esän Buqa, who was the officer of the
ordu, and all the treasuries remained there for
Ghazan.
1See text p. 1131 above.

Some
time
after
[the
senior]
Bulughan
Khatun died, Arghun married the [junior] Bu-
lughan Khatun who is now alive and settled in

few items of clothing and gold and silver uten-

stores, yurt, and ordu belong to Ghazan by or-
der of Abaqa Khan. They are to be sealed.”
Those who had seen the storehouse reported
that no one had ever possessed its like, for
there were more jewels, utensils, and precious
pearls therein than could be described. The rea-
son for this is that, because Abaqa Khan loved
Bulughan Khatun excessively, [1214] every
time he went into the treasury he picked up a
precious jewel and gave it to her in secret.
When the treasurers pilfered things after Bu-
lughan Khatun’s death, Ghazan found out
about it and was constantly asking for an in-
vestigation, but the treasury remained sealed. 
When Arghun Khan died, Gaikhatu married
[the junior] Bulughan Khatun against her will
and refused to let Ghazan go to her. As has al-
ready been said in the section on [Gaikhatu,1

from Khurasan and mounted the throne, he left
Ghazan there in his place. After that they never

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Part Two, events leading to his enthronement, a picture of him and his wives, sons,
grandsons, and commanders at his enthronement; a history of his reign and the battles he
fought and the victories he achieved.
Events leading to his enthronement, from
the time Arghun Khan stationed him as his
viceroy in Khurasan until the time of
Baidu’s conquest.
His history in Khurasan during his father’s
time.
When Arghun Khan escaped, with the Cre-
ator’s assistance, from Ahmad’s clutches and
went in pursuit of him to Azerbaijan, where he
mounted the throne, he had left Prince Ghazan
in his stead in Khurasan. He gave him that
realm along with large troops and entrusted the
border, which is one of the greatest frontier ar-
eas, to him. In accordance with his father’s
command he dwelt there and tended to the af-
fairs of the region. [1217] Envoys were con-
stantly coming and going for any and every
item of business. Amir Nawroz was in atten-
dance, and he performed valiantly in military
affairs.
In Dhu’l-Hijja 687 [January 1289], when
Prince Ghazan returned from wintering in
Merv, and Nawroz, who was with him, grew
apprehensive over the rumor that Buqa and his
liege men had been killed, he said, “Since
rumors of the foe are coming, I want to go
home and inspect my hazara. If need be, I will
mount on expedition.” On this pretext he got
permission and departed, leaving at court his
wife Princess Toghan1 with his mother, Sür-
mish, his brothers Yaratai Ghazan, Hajji, and
Narin Hajji, and his nephews.
1Variant: Toghanchaq ~ Toghanchuq, the Princess
Toghanchuq of text p. 1056 above, daughter of Abaqa
Khan.
Arghun Khan sent Amir Tägänä as leader of
the amirs and as governor to Khurasan, and he
and Buqa were in attendance. Ghazan, howev-
er, did not find Tägänä’s conduct pleasing, and
since he did not suit his nature he could not do
what he wanted. 
Amir Qutlughshah Noyan had returned from
Azerbaijan and taken up residence in the
Khuchan2 vicinity on account of an indisposi-
tion from which he was suffering. Nawroz
went to Dara-i-Jaz,3 which was their wintering
place, and that winter Prince Kingshü spent the
winter in Herat by imperial command. When
spring came, Prince Ghazan decamped from
Merv to Sarakhs and spent a few days there.
After that, he went to Qara Tapa in Sarakhs
and indulged in banquets and hunting while his
animals were being fattened. 
Because of the fear he harbored of Arghun
on account of the accusation of Buqa, Nawroz
kept sending messages with excuses saying
that the gout prevented his coming to court.
Summoning his troop commanders and his re-
tainers, he said, “I have heard that a decree
from Arghun Khan has reached Prince Ghazan,
[1218] and it says, ‘Because Nawroz and his
henchmen conspired with Buqa they should all
be arrested and executed.’ ” Because Prince
Kingshü had married Nawroz’s sister, Nawroz
2Khūchān, an attested variant spelling of Qūchān; the
variants in MSS L, I, & PB in JTAZ have Khabūshān, the
area along the Atrak River west of Quchan.
3Dara-i-Jaz is the modern Daragaz directly north of
Rādkān and very near the Iranian border with Turk-
menistan. There is another place of the same name near
Gurzuwan in modern Afghanistan.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
587

also sent him a message with similar contents
that frightened him into joining him.
Around then Sadaq Tarkhan and Beglämish,
whom Ghazan had sent to Arghun Khan’s
court, arrived. Ghazan stayed in Qara Tapa for
a month. Rumors of Nawroz’s insurrection and
rebellion were rife, and during that time Amir
Qutlughshah also arrived. Nawroz’s mother
Sürmish, Princess Toghan, and his brothers and
nephews who were there asked for permission
to leave on the pretext that Nawroz had given a
daughter to Negübäi’s son Sarban and every-
one was waiting for them to go to hold the
marriage. Promising to return after the ban-
quet, they left and joined Nawroz.
In early Rabi‘ I 688 [late March–early April
1289] Ghazan decamped from Qara Tapa and
went to Tus and Radkan. He sent Sadaq as an
envoy to Nawroz to say, “We have decamped
and will arrive there. You must come out to the
Murghana River, which is the Kashafrod.”1
When Sadaq came before Nawroz, Nawroz
seized him, tied him up tight, and beat him,
asking, “You were at Arghun Khan’s court. Tell
me what he said about me!”
“It was all good,” he replied. Then [Nawroz]
threatened to kill him, and in fear of his life
Sadaq mumbled a few meaningless words.
[Nawroz’s] mother, Sürmish, and Princess
Toghan prevented Nawroz from killing him,
but he was thrown into chains and put in pri-
son. Then Nawroz sent word out and began to
rebel. 
Ghazan had camped at the Mu‘in Bridge on
the Kashafrod. On Thursday the 27th of Rabi‘ I
688 [April 20, 1289] Nawroz and the soldiers
[1219] he had attacked the royal camp. By
chance, Buqa, Tägänä, Küräk, and other amirs
had gone into the river, and such a huge throng
1The Kashafrod flows southeast from Rādkān into the
Harírúd south of Sarakhs.
had gathered that the camp had to be moved
away from the river next to a hill. Since divine
favor was with Ghazan, [when] Nawroz at-
tacked he thought [the crowd] was the camp,
so he encircled them, as was the Mongol cus-
tom. The alarm was given and shouts were
raised. Through divine favor Ghazan had risen
early and was washing his face with his inti-
mates
there,
and Amir
Qutlughshah
was
mounted. When the attack came and the shouts
grew loud, Ghazan mounted and set out with
Amir Qutlughshah via Nishapur for the Sang-
bast Ribat.2 By divine grace he escaped from
that unforeseen sedition.
Nawroz seized Amir Buqa, Tägänä, and
Küräk and ordered the ordu and tents to de-
camp and sent them to Bazaw…gan.3 Every-
thing was plundered. He killed Buqa and kept
Tägänä and the other amirs imprisoned with
himself. 
When Ghazan reached Nishapur, the amirs
Satilmish4 and Mulai were there and joined
him. Then he set out for Mazanderan. His per-
sonal chain mail, to which he was quite at-
tached and which was extremely fine, had been
accidentally thrown away by the akhtachis.
They looked for it for a long time, but it was
never found. The reason for going to Mazan-
deran was that Prince Hulachu was there, and
2Nishapur is the conventional Anglicized spelling. Ac-
cording to legend it was named Nay Shapur because it

though Abu’l-Fida (Taqwim, 450) says that in his day
(ca. 1330) it was known as Nisāvur and the name
Naysābūr had been forgotten. Sangbast, still there, is
roughly forty kilometers south of Mashhad, about half

3This probably represents Buzangān, which lies half
way between Mashhad and Sarakhs. The Arabicized

4Satilmish ~ Satalmish.

rumors were being spread that he was in league
with Nawroz, for Nawroz had written letters to
the surrounding regions with the superscription
Hulachu yarlıghındın, Kin[g]shü buyruqındın
(“by decree of Hulachu, by command of
Kingshü”).1
Ghazan, wanting to seize Hulachu before he
could reach Nawroz, galloped as fast as he
could and reached the outskirts of Shahrak-i-
Naw on the fifth day after mounting in Nisha-
pur.2 Amir Kür Temür remained separate, and
the amirs of the Mazanderan division joined
the prince. Hulachu [1220] was outside Jurjan
near Kur Daghi. On Friday the 7th of Rabi‘ II
[April 30, 1289] they charged down on Hu-
lachu. When they reached his tents the alarm
was given. Hulachu had the gout. Without
putting his boots on, he came out with his ar-
rows and started to flee. When the soldiers
reached his tent and didn’t find him, the amirs
Mulai and Bayanchar went out in pursuit of
him. They seized him near Sang-i-Sawad,
brought him back, and pillaged his tents. When
they brought him before the prince and asked
him about Nawroz, he denied everything, say-
ing, “I have no knowledge of him. I was not
allied with him. I have never had such a
thought.”
That day Ghazan camped in the vicinity of
Jurjan. The next day he sent Hulachu to
Arghun Khan escorted by Bai Temür. Remain-
ing there one day, he held a review of troops
and then set out for Khabushan, Tus, and Rad-
kan to repel Nawroz. On the seventh day he
camped in Sultan Maydan in Kilidar,3 a dis-
1For the sense of the superscription, see note at text p.
1189 above.
2The location of Shahrak-i-Naw (“Newburg”) is not
known, but according to the preceding citation (text p.
1211) it should have been between Damghan and

3Kilīdar is still there, some forty kilometers west of
tance of nearly eighty leagues. At day’s end in-
formation arrived from the scouts that the ene-
my’s army had been spotted. An order was
given for all the soldiers to arm themselves.
When the enemy soldiers saw the victorious
army from afar, they went to Radkan. That
night the regal banners were in Sultan Maydan,
and such a heavy rain came that most of the
breastplates and armor were ruined. The next
morning, the 15th of Rabi‘ II [May 8, 1289],
the regal banners set out for Radkan in search
of Nawroz.
At midmorning, in a place called Inchkä Su,4
they came across Nawroz, and both sides drew
up battle lines. The victorious army charged
bravely and fought fiercely, particularly Amir
Qutlughshah. On the other side Kingshü,
Nawroz, and Tägänä stood firm, and eventual-
ly a chink was made in the army of this side
and they fled, [1221] many regal banners left
where they had stood. [Ghazan] ordered the
amirs Qutlughshah, Satilmish, and Sö’ätäi to
reassemble their troops, but no matter how
hard they tried they couldn’t do it. Then the re-
gal banner moved out via Arghian to Juwayn.5
On the heels of the amirs, Uighurtai Ghazan’s
and others’ troops arrived, but from the entire
region of Juwayn not a soul came to court ex-
cept Mihtar Najibuddin Farrash, who came out
and made obeisance as soon as they arrived in
the village of Zerabad. He presented extremely
fine horses and provided all manner of good
service. (Of course, when the padishah became
firmly seated on the throne he ordered that he
be suitably rewarded. He made him an intimate
Radkan and forty-five kilometers south of Qūchān; and
Sultān Maydān is about five kilometers west of Kilīdar.
4Inchkä Su is Turkish for ‘narrow river,’ which could
be any of the many rivulets in the area.
5Juwayn is the district in Nishapur along the Juwayn
River, which flows from the mountains north of Nisha-
pur to south of Jājarm.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
589

at court, gave him the village of Zerabad,
which was enchü, gave him a decree making
him tarkhan, and appointed him as treasurer. In
the village of Buzinjird, a dependency of
Hamadan, the emperor built a khanaqah that is
an extremely fine building and possesses many
endowments in villages and real estate. The su-
perintendence of the endowments was given to
him and his offspring. In short, he received im-
perial favor, and everyone knows that anyone
who performs good service for kings will be
rewarded and gain respect in the eyes of all.
Until the present, which is the reign of Öljäitü
Sultan—may God make his reign eternal—he
continues in that post and is highly respected.
In truth he is an honorable man of good con-
duct and possessed of virtue who was worthy
of the patronage of kings, and he constantly
does charitable acts, and many pious, learned,
and other people of all classes have benefited
from his existence.) [1222]
In short, when the regal banners came near
Jajarm, a council was held. “Would it be best
for us to go to Arghun Khan’s court,” they
asked, “or should we halt at Kalpush?”
“Since we have dispatched the envoys Yigh-
mish and Irmini Bala,” Ghazan said, “we
should wait patiently to see what order is giv-
en.” He therefore stopped at Kalpush. Since
that place was Uighurtai Ghazan’s yurt, and
since he also commanded Mazanderan, he per-
formed good services. Scouts were stationed as
far as Samanqan and Jarmaqan.1
During those days Nizamuddin Yahya came
from Bayhaq,2 bringing supplies for the ordu,
fine horses, gold and silver utensils, tents and
pavilions, carpets, vessels, pack animals, and
1Jarmaqān (Arabicized as Sharmaqān) was a small
town near Isfarayin. See Abu’l-Fida, Taqwim, 458.
2Bayhaq was the district west of Nishapur. Its seat was
Khusrawjird (modern Khusrawgird just west of Sabza-
vār). See Abu’l-Fida, Taqwim, 442.
camels. He performed good services for the
amirs and then returned to Bayhaq as ordered
to arrange for tribute and provisions for the
army. 
Two days prior to the battle with Nawroz,
Amir Aladu and other Qara’una amirs had at-
tacked Nawroz’s tent and plundered every-
thing. When Nawroz learned of this, he set out
after them. Kingshü and the others camped in
Radkan. As was the custom of the Qara’unas,
after plundering they broke into two or three
bands, deserting Amir Aladu, and some of
them joined Nawroz while others went home,
where they fomented strife and trouble. When
Aladu saw how unruly and uncontrollable they
were, he moved his tents to a protected valley
in the vicinity of Badghis and went himself to
court. Ghazan had clemency on him and
showed him much favor. 
For forty days camp was maintained in Kal-
push. When the reinforcements arrived from
Arghun Khan, their leader Prince Baidu and
Nurin Aqa and his son joined the court [1223]
and spent several days in banquets. From there
they decamped for Samanqan under a favor-
able ascendant. 
When Nawroz learned of the approach of the
soldiers from Persia and realized that they
were going to attack him, he sent his tents and
retainers to Herat while he himself went to Jar-
maqan. When he saw that he did not have the
force to offer resistance, he turned back, and
the victorious army went in pursuit of him as
far as the Jam area. In the village of …khar
Saray, which is above Jam, Öljäitü and a band
of Qara’unas surrendered along with Yäkä
Yandun’s son Tammachi, both Nawroz’s liege
men. When they reached Kharjird in Jam,3
3Kharjird (modern Khargird) is a few kilometers south
of Khwāf (now Rād) on the road leading southeast from
Turbat-i-Haydariyya.
590
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Nawroz had rounded up every quadruped he
could find in Khurasan—both those belonging
to him and his soldiers and those belonging to
the Arabs, Turcomans, and others. When the
victorious army arrived on their heels, they
found all the mountains and wilderness from
the gates of Jam to the gates of Herat full of
the animals he had rounded up. In several
places some of them had sickened, died, and
putrefied so badly that it was impossible to
pass. The Mongols seized those animals and
took them away: in the villages a sheep was
sold for a pittance. Since it had been ordered
that no attention be paid to olja [booty], they
couldn’t take more. Nawroz picked up the cash
and goods that were light enough to carry and
set out through the waterless wilderness for
Farah and Sabzawar1 with Princess Toghan, his
brothers’ households, and a few others. 
Since it was the hot season, Ghazan did not
think it prudent to send his soldiers out after
him, so he camped at the gates of Herat next to
the Malan Bridge and sent the amirs out in
search of Kingshü and the great ordu in
Badghis. When Kingshü learned of this, he and
his wife, children, and retainers left for the
mountains of Ghor and Gharjistan. He had the
amirs of the great ordu, [1224] Tägänä, and the
Qara’una troops that were with him all decamp
and go to Herat. It was a measure of Kingshü’s
steadfastness that during that entire period he
had not spent one dinar from the personal
treasuries or from the belongings and flocks
and herds of the amirs’ houses that were
there—indeed, he had rendered good service.
Several days later they decamped from Herat
and went to Radkan. From there Uighurtai
Ghazan was sent with Tägänä to Arghun
1Farāh is the region, now in southwestern Afghanistan,
northeast of Seistan. Sabzawar (now Shīndand) is north
of the town of Farah.
Khan’s court to report on the situation in
Khurasan. Despite the turmoil and rebellion
that held sway in Khurasan, Ghazan did not
neglect one iota of justice and equity and exert-
ed himself to the utmost in taking care of the
peasantry. He issued a decree that no soldier or
anyone else put an animal in anyone’s sown
field or orchard. Absolutely they were not to
graze their animals in grain fields, and they
were not to cause damage to the land or use
force on the peasants.
The Qara’una band that had been stationed in
the vicinity of Jam was moved from Radkan to
Shutur Koh for the summer, and there they
spent their time indulging in revelry and wine
with Prince Baidu, Amir Nurin, and other
amirs, whom Ghazan received very well.
During that time reports came in from scouts
that the enemy had been spotted, so the regal
banners set out for Radkan. It turned out to be
a false report. [Ghazan] was drinking so much
wine that he developed an indisposition. From
there they went to Khabushan, and his illness
lingered for nearly forty days before he re-
gained his health completely. During that time
Amir Shiktür Aqa and Toghan arrived from
Arghun Khan’s court, and that summer and au-
tumn they were in the vicinity of Khabushan,
Radkan, and Shutur Koh. When the weather
turned cold they decided to spend the winter in
Nishapur. Ghazan spent the winter in Mawedi.
[1225] Prince Baidu wintered in Shamagan be-
tween Bayhaq and Nishapur. That winter the
cold was extreme and so much snow fell that
most of the horses died and the men were left
to go on foot. 
When the spring of 689 [1290] came, they
moved
to
summer
pastures
in
Radkan,
Khabushan, and Shutur Koh. That year there
was security on all fronts, and the strongboxes
were brought from Arghun Khan’s court and
distributed among the soldiers. Toghan went to
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
591

the Badghis vicinity and came back. In early
summer, because provisions were not to be
found in Khurasan, an order was given that
Prince Baidu and the soldiers who had gone
from Persia and Azerbaijan should return, and
that Nurin Aqa should be in attendance. Ghaz-
an went out as far as Bam and Arghian to bid
farewell to Baidu, and then he returned. 
During that summer a group of Qara’unas re-
volted and entered the district of Juwayn. Their
leader was Danishmand Bahadur, and they
wrought havoc. Amir Mulai was assigned to
repel them. That summer and autumn Ghazan
hunted in the vicinity of Khabushan and Rad-
kan while the amirs saw to the affairs of the
military and civil administration, collected tax-
es, and made arrangements for provisions. 
Ghazan then ordered that the winter would
be spent on the Tedzhen in Bavard, and he or-
dered a dam built on the river called Kal
Tedzhen. He also founded several villages.
That autumn Khwarazmi Tarkhan came from
Arghun’s court to review the fiscal operations
in Khurasan. Ghazan ordered whatever had
been commanded to be done. By command
Toghan’s agents in Quhistan were seized and
brought to court, and all the scribes and tax
collectors of Khurasan were imprisoned or put
under guard.
Toward the end of the winter a group of
Qara’unas revolted in Sarakhs and went to
Merv. The regal banner set out for [1226]
Dara-i-Murgha, and Aladu Noyan was sent to
deal with them and bring them back into sub-
mission. For a time [Ghazan] was in Arjah and
Shugan. From there he went to Sarakhs and
camped at Qara Tapa, which is called Sher
Sayl.
Amir Nawroz’s rebellion.
In 690 [1291] a rumor was heard that
Nawroz was coming with Sarban, Äbügän
Oghul, Örüg Temür, Yisa’ur’s amirs, and a
large army to attack Khurasan. The reason for
this was as follows. 
Previously, when Nawroz withdrew in rout
from Herat and fled, he went to Qaidu. After
performing many services for him, he request-
ed an army. As he requested, Qaidu sent him
off with an army, and on his heels he dis-
patched his son Sarban with troops. 
*Amir Nawroz goes to Qaidu Khan in
Turkistan.
Nawroz and a ragtag group crossed the Oxus
and set out for Badakhshan to see Prince
Qaidu, the son of Ögödäi Qa’an’s son Qashin,
saying, “A pawn won’t become a queen unless
it moves.” When he came before Prince Qaidu
he made a great display of his devotion and al-
legiance, but Qaidu interrogated him on the
reason for his leaving his homeland. In answer
he said, “It was this devoted slave’s fervent
wish to see this regal court, for reports of the
honors to be attained here and the renown of
the prince of this mighty court have spread
throughout the world.” Without mentioning his
fright and fear, he related his history and fin-
ished his speech with these words: “He who
knows and sees all is aware that I am more in-
nocent than Joseph’s wolf of the crime and
treachery of which I have been accused.”
Never has it crossed my tongue or mind, and
never has it occurred to me.
“Then what was the cause of your rout and
flight?” Qaidu asked.
“It is exactly like the story of the fox running
in haste. A jackal asked why it was running
away. ‘The king is seizing donkeys,’ the fox
answered. ‘Since you aren’t a donkey,’ the
jackal said, ‘why are you running away?’ ‘My
friend,’ the fox replied, ‘before it can be
proven that I am not a donkey, I would suffer
many injuries from pitiless nobodies.’ ”
592
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Qaidu was highly pleased by this story,
showed him great favor, and housed him near
himself, undertaking to give him much more.
For three years Nawroz wandered through
Turkistan like a donkey in mud or a chameleon
in water, making up for his unfortunate period.
Since he was by nature stubborn and proud,
even in exile and want he conducted himself
with Qaidu’s amirs and advisors not like a
stranger or a guest, for Nawroz had lived for
thirty years in the center of the realm of Iran
and Khurasan in luxury, wealth, and splendor
under the Mongol khans, and in the Third and
Fourth Climes his father Arghun Aqa’s word
was law and he possessed untold lands, proper-
ty, cash, herds, and flocks. Among a foreign
people, although he had lost his nobility and
lands and abandoned home and family, he
could not tolerate Qaidu’s amirs’ overbearing
demeanor, and they did not show him respect
or conduct themselves in a friendly manner.
This notwithstanding, he did not give in and
kept on as haughty as before until he grew
homesick and asked for permission to return
home. After showing him much favor, Qaidu
gave him thirty thousand horsemen with the
princes Äbügän and Örüg Temür and the amirs
Yisa’ur, Köpäk, and others as reinforcements
and sent them to attack Khurasan and wipe out
Nawroz’s enemies. The soldiers they had sta-
tioned in the vicinity of Amuya were also put
under their command as well as the soldiers
that wintered and summered with [Qaidu’s]
son Sarban on the banks of the Oxus, Badghis,
and Sheberghan. Nawroz set out in the van-
guard.
In the year 690 [1291] reports came in that
Nawroz was headed for Khurasan with the
armies of Transoxiana and Turkistan.*1 Ghazan
1This section is lacking in the text; it is given in JTAZ
in приложение 4 (p. 477f.).
sent Qabartu out with a body of warriors to re-
connoiter. They went as far as the Murghab
and returned, saying, “The foe is really com-
ing, and there are many soldiers.” Since the
soldiers were not assembled at the time, they
decamped from Qara Tapa and set out for the
place known as the Murghana, or Kashafrod,
and waited for Amir Qutlughshah and his sol-
diers, who were wintering in Herat, to arrive.
Amir Könchäk was sent to summon the sol-
diers of Mazanderan.
When they reached the Mu‘in Bridge, Amir
Mulai asked for permission to go to Quhistan
in order to bring the soldiers who were there.
Since reports of the enemy’s approach were
pouring in, they decamped from there and
camped above Imam Riza’s shrine,2 waiting for
Amir Qutlughshah. 
One day Qaban Akhtachi came from Azer-
baijan, reporting that the amirs who had
fomented rebellion there had killed Joshi, Ordu
Qaya, and Sa‘duddawla and sent him [Qaban]
together with several trouble-makers to stir up
trouble in Khurasan. He had come and reported
that the armies of Azerbaijan and Persia were
coming from Arghun Khan. [Ghazan] was per-
ceptive and clever enough to realize that what
Qaban was saying was a lie, [1227] but since
reports on the foe were constantly coming in,
he did not bother to investigate the matter.
The next day Amir Qutlughshah arrived and
reported that the enemy army had reached the
Sangbast Ribat. Ghazan rewarded him, gave
him a royal tunic, and sent him back by night
to bring the soldiers to him the next morning
below the shrine so that they could do battle. 
At midnight a report came in from the scouts
that the enemy army had crossed the Mu‘in
Bridge. The prince realized that the imperial
2I.e. the shrine that has since become the city of
Mashhad.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
593

ordu and the ladies would have to be sent to Is-
farayin that night. The next morning, which
was the first of Rabi‘ II 690 [April 3, 1291], he
mounted.
The
amirs
Nurin
Aqa,
Aladu,
Uighurtai Ghazan, and others were in atten-
dance. Having moved to below Imam Riza’s
shrine, he stopped there for a moment and ar-
rayed the army while waiting for Amir Qut-
lughshah’s arrival in order to do battle. At noon
Chamcha came from Amir Qutlughshah and
said, “When we reached the Sangbast Ribat, all
the soldiers had set out in the direction of
Nishapur for Janak and Ishaqabad.” On his
heels came Amir Qutlughshah. After a while
the army came into view. Since they were
many, and there were only a few on this side,
the amirs held council to decide whether to
fight or not.
“It would not be wise for us to fight them,”
said Aladu
as
he
quoted
the
Mongolian
proverb: “ ‘It is easy to tangle with a foe but
hard to break loose.’ You have answered to
Arghun Khan for many battle days,” he contin-
ued. “This day I will be answerable.”
The prince decided they would pull back to a
place where all the soldiers could gather, and
from there he had them go to Radkan, with the
enemy on their heels. At the end of the day
they fell upon the enemy army near Tus and
did battle. [1228] The next day they decamped,
stopping in several places to do battle. It hap-
pened that he stopped for the night in Sultan
Maydan, and the next morning he decamped.
Aladu said, “Since battle is not possible now,
and my tents and those of most of the soldiers
have gone toward Juwayn, if so commanded,
let me go in search of them.” Having been giv-
en permission, he left. Ura Temür, the father of
Shirin Egächi, also said, “My tents and soldiers
have gone to Nishapur. Let me go bring them.”
He too departed. 
Uighurtai Ghazan loved Prince Mubarak-
shah’s daughter Tüzmish Khatun, and he had
sent her with his tents to Kabudjama. He had in
mind to get her and go to Nawroz. He too left
on the pretext that he was going in search of
his tents and to organize the Mazanderan sol-
diers and guard that region. Having received
permission, he left too. 
The amirs Nurin Aqa, Qutlughshah, and
Sö’ätäi were in attendance. [Ghazan] had them
move along the Arghian road. News of the foe
was constantly coming in. In Isfarayin he
stopped for a moment, passed on from there,
and camped in the village of Kisirgh,1 a depen-
dency of Isfarayin. At midnight Nurin, Qut-
lughshah, and Sö’ätäi learned that a band of
Qara’unas which they had brought into the
ordu for ___,2 were intending to rebel and had
conspired to revolt and withdraw. They report-
ed this situation, and they thought it wise to
move off and let Amir Qutlughshah stop and
tend to the situation while the regal banners
proceeded toward Jurbadh, arriving the next
morning. The band pulled back from there and
fell upon the tents of Könchäk, Qutlugh Khwa-
ja, and other sükürchis, plundered everything
they could find, and joined the enemy. [1229]
The enemy army kept on coming in pursuit
as far as Jurbadh. When the padishah arrived
there he ordered the tents of Sartaq’s son
Qachir, Suqar, Sö’ätü, and other Qara’unas
who had camped there to go to Jajarm and Bis-
tam, and he stayed there until the end of the
day. When Amir Qutlughshah arrived and re-
ported the approach of the enemy, he de-
camped and went to Jajarm, where he stayed
the night. The enemy pulled back from Jur-
badh.
1Kisirgh ~ Kisirq: the name is verified by Ala’uddawla
Simnani, “Fi dhikr asami mashayikhih,” Opera Minora,
p. 5.
2Unknown word, #"ی.
594
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

More killing, pillage, and destruction were
wrought that year in Khurasan than can be de-
scribed. The city of Nishapur was besieged,
but God kept the people safe, through Ghaz-
an’s fortune, from falling into the evil hands of
the infidels. However, the villages were raided
and many captives were carried away. In
Barubaqi in the Nishapur vicinity, where the
people are courageous warriors, the enemy at-
tacked, but it is a well fortified place, and
many people took refuge there with their be-
longings and animals. The enemy went into a
valley, and the local people poured down on
them from the slopes, killing nearly a thousand
of the enemy’s horsemen. Pulling back from
there, they went to the Mashhad shrine in Tus
and plundered it. They even carried off four
silver globes that had been placed on top of the
tomb. In Khurasan so many soldiers were
killed that when they reached Badghis and had
a review, nearly five thousand horsemen were
missing. For this Nawroz was indicted and
beaten.
The next day the royal banners moved out of
Jajarm and went to Bistam and Damghan. All
the amirs knew of Arghun Khan’s death, but
they kept it from Ghazan. When he reached
Bistam he stopped there for a day because the
ladies were there. From there he went to
Damghan. Prior to that he had sent Aladu’s
brother Abishqa on a mission to Arghun Khan.
When he heard of Arghun Khan’s death he
stopped in Damghan, [1230] all the inhabitants
of which had gone away. Some had gone with
Shah Ildüz to Gird Koh, and others had holed
up in the village of Mayan,1 a well fortified
place. Therefore Abishqa turned back from
Damghan and rejoined the court at Bistam to
report on the situation of the people of
Damghan. 
1Māyān, still there, a few kilometers east of Dāmghān.
When the royal banners stopped in Dam-
ghan, not a soul came out, and no gifts, provi-
sions, or fodder had been arranged. Ghazan
Khan grew angry and ordered the notables of
the town, who were holed up in Mayan, to
come out, but they refused. He therefore or-
dered the place besieged, and after three days
and nights of battle, they asked for amnesty
and submitted, presenting a large quantity of
cash, goods, provisions, cattle, and sheep for
the soldiers. Ghazan Khan was so clement and
kind that he pardoned these offenders, but he
ordered the fortress destroyed. (After his en-
thronement he had the place rebuilt.) From
there he proceeded to Simnan.
In the midst of all this, Mu‘inuddin Mustaw-
fi, the divan chief, and a group of bitigchis
who were going to Nishapur were seized and
brought to court. He paid them no attention
and ordered their patents and al tamghas [red
seals] given back to them. They were given
permission to depart.
When Ghazan Khan reached Simnan, the
amirs held council and informed him of
Arghun
Khan’s
death.
The
prince
held
mourning
there
and
ordered
the
feathers
removed from hats according to Mongol cus-
tom. Amir Mulai came across the desert to
Simnan from Quhistan and joined the court,
where he was very well received. An order was
given that Amir Satilmish’s sister should be
given to him. 
When Uighurtai Ghazan left Sultan Maydan
and went to Kabudjama and Jurjan, he still had
the
same
dastardly
notion.
Picking
up
Tüzmish, he went to Sultan Duvin and [1231]
Astarabad,
where
he
announced
that
the
province belonged to Qaidu. He also harassed
the Mongol soldiers who were in the area and
stirred up trouble. Since the great amirs were
not present, Saighan Ayachi, Mamlaq, and oth-
ers conspired to make a surprise attack on him
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
595

and drive him away. They pursued him until
they chased him out of Jurjan and Kabudjama.
He and a few others became wanderers. Prior
to that he had harassed the sayyids, citizens,
and peasants in Mashhad of Tus. 
Ghazan Khan’s situation after Arghun
Khan’s death until he sets out for
Azerbaijan during Gaikhatu’s reign and
then returns from Tabriz to Khurasan.
After that, the royal banners stopped for a
few days in Simnan before moving out for
Firozkoh via Damavand near Mishan, where
they camped for a few days. Bulughan Khatun
Khurasani gave birth to a son there, but the
child died.
When they came to Firozkoh news arrived
that Gaikhatu was coming from Anatolia. The
amirs who had stirred up trouble in the ordu
dispersed, some joining Gaikhatu and others
uniting with Baidu. Toghan fled to Khurasan.
Therefore Ghazan ordered that Mulai be arrest-
ed and imprisoned. When the news arrived that
Toghan had been seized, Mulai was set free
through the amirs’ intercession. 
When the news of Gaikhatu’s election as
padishah was confirmed, Amir Qutlughshah
[1232] was sent as emissary to Gaikhatu to re-
port on the devastation of Khurasan and the
army there. A group of amirs like Horqudaq,
Cha’urchi’s son Qara, Qutlugh Temür, and oth-
ers was sent to Khurasan.
In the summer of 690 [1291], [Ghazan]
camped in the village of Asiran, which is be-
tween Firozkoh and Simnan and is also called
Nägätü Yaylaq, and there he constantly held
banquets and hunted while the administrators
gathered provisions for the soldiers and col-
lected the taxes of the province.
Amir Qutlughshah reached Gaikhatu’s court
in Arran
and
reported
the
situation,
but
Gaikhatu was too busy with revelry and sport
to pay much attention. Amir Qutlughshah re-
turned to Ghazan Khan.
In the autumn the royal banners proceeded to
Damghan and Bistam and from there to Kal-
push. Qutlugh Khwaja and Lala were sent to
Bayhaq to summon Nizamuddin Yahya be-
cause he had committed outrages in Khurasan
like killing a group of notables even though
they were attached to him and taking too much
from the people. Fearful, he declined to come.
The royal banners went via the fortress of
Janashik to Jurjan. That winter was spent in
Sultan Duvin in Astarabad.
Gaikhatu sent Prince Anbarchi and the amirs
Doladai, Qunchuqbal, and El Temür to Ghazan
to reinforce the army of Khurasan, and they
paid homage to him in Sultan Duvin and were
ordered to winter in the Qara Toghan area. 
Toward the end of winter reports had it that
Nawroz had come to the Nishapur area and
was headed for Juwayn to get Nizamuddin
Yahya out of the Andimad fortress. Since the
weather was still cold and the animals were
lean, the royal banners went to Kalpush and
spent a few days there. Heralds were dis-
patched in all directions. [1233] Nawroz and a
few men made a raid as far as Juwayn and then
pulled back. 
The royal banners returned to Jurjan to fatten
up the animals. 
In the early spring of 691 [1292] he sent
Prince Anbarchi and the forces that had come
with him to Dehistan, Yazir, Nasa, and Abi-
vard. Horqudaq was sent with them to arrange
for provisions and necessities lest they harass
the countryside and wreak devastation. The
royal banners also set out.
That year, there was such scarcity on account
of the disturbances in Khurasan that a hundred
maunds of grain could not be purchased for a
hundred dinars. Khwaja Sa‘duddin was ap-
pointed over all the divan chiefs to arrange for
596
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

the soldiers’ provisions and to collect the taxes
of Khurasan, Mazanderan, Qumis, and Rayy.
During that expedition most of the soldiers de-
rived sustenance by hunting.
The royal banners camped along the banks
of the Herat River, which is the Chuqchuran.1
They were greatly hindered in crossing by the
flooding of the river. Prince Anbarchi and the
amirs of Persia arrived.
News came from a scout that the enemy
army had been spotted. The royal banners
moved to Badghis and camped in Yoldaq in
Badghis. Heralds were sent in all directions,
but no sign or news of the foe was found any-
where. Since the soldiers’ provisions were ex-
hausted, and supplies were not to be had, the
soldiers stole each other’s horses and ate them.
They were sorely vexed by lack of food. The
amirs reported the situation. “The barley in
Herat is nearly ripe,” they said. “It would be
best to go there.” So saying, they set out and
camped beside the Malan Bridge. The nobles
and grandees of Herat were not in the city be-
cause of the strife and turmoil. Malik Sham-
suddin Kurt was residing in the Khaysar
Citadel, and he had imprisoned his eldest son,
Fakhruddin, on account of an offense he had
received. [1234] His younger son, Ala’uddin,
he had sent to be in attendance at court. 
Since the province of Herat had been devas-
tated by the passage of troops and had not been
restored, Ghazan had clemency on the inhabi-
tants and ordered that they not be harassed.
The people of Fushanj,2 however, had gone
into the fortress, and when the armies of Persia
arrived and had requested provisions, they had
not given anything and fought. Ghazan Khan
was angered by their action and ordered that
1I.e. the modern Chaghcharan in Afghanistan.
2Fushanj (~ Pushang ~ Bushanj) is a well-known vil-
lage seven leagues from Herat (Abu’l-Fida, Taqwim,
454).
place besieged. It was taken with much diffi-
culty, and many horses, cattle, sheep, and pro-
visions were taken from there, and most of the
people were taken captive. 
When the royal banners pulled back from
Herat they went to Fushanj. The people there
reported their plight, and [Ghazan] had mercy
on them, ordering their women and children
who had been taken captive all to be returned.
Thus having won them over, he mounted under
favorable auspices and set out for Radkan.
Since Gaikhatu was not sending money for
the troops of Khurasan, and many soldiers had
assembled there, [Ghazan] decided to go to
Gaikhatu and orally report the situation exactly
as it was. Later, however, he canceled his trip
and went to Shutur Koh. Since there was no re-
port of the foe, and since provisions could not
be found, he gave Prince Anbarchi and the
armies of Persia and Azerbaijan permission to
leave. 
[Ghazan] spent the summer at Shutur Koh
and built the Murad Pavilion. Never before had
rulers built anything in that area.
Around that time news arrived that rabble
had gathered in the town of Jizhad in the dis-
trict of Khwaf, put to death the sons of the ma-
lik of Zuzan and a group of notables of the
area, and taken a fortress. An order was given
for the amirs Sö’ätäi and Mulai to mount an
expedition to deal with them. [1235] When
they approached, Shah Ali, the son of the malik
of Seistan, had come from Quhistan greedy for
Khwaf and laid siege to the fortress. The amirs
attacked him and drove him away, seizing his
soldiers, putting most of them to death, and
plundering their possessions and animals. Shah
Ali managed to get out of the fray by stealth
and took flight.
After that, the amirs rendered the fortress
submissive,
killing
the
troublemakers
and
fomenters of strife. They placated the peas-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
597

antry and sent them back to their labor before
withdrawing.
In Sha‘ban of 691 [July–August 1292], an
order was given for Imaduddin the khatib of
Nishapur, a grand man who had overstepped
his boundaries on account of rumors about
Nawroz, to be arrested and brought from
Nishapur for execution. 
That summer nothing much happened. When
winter came [Ghazan] wintered in Sultan Du-
vin in Astarabad. He sent Amir Nurin to
Samanqan and Shaqan. 
In early spring a rumor of the foe was heard,
and the royal banners set out toward Jurjan,
Shahrak-i-Naw, and Murchabad. There Amir
Nurin came to court. In early 692,1 he de-
camped from there and spent a few days in
Samalqan. Reconnoiterers were sent out in all
directions, and the rumor proved to be false, so
once again he thought of going to Azerbaijan.
[1236]
Ghazan goes to Ala Tagh to see Gaikhatu,
but he turns back from Tabriz; Nawroz is
routed; the victory at Nishapur.
Having consulted with the amirs, he decided
to go to Azerbaijan. Stationing the great amir
Qutlughshah
Noyan
and
others
to
guard
Khurasan, he turned back at Samanqan with
the amirs Nurin, Satilmish, and Sö’ätäi in at-
tendance. Proceeding via Shahrak-i-Naw, they
entered Mazanderan. Amir Qutlughshah also
came to be in attendance as far as Tamisha.
Then, having wed Jirghutai’s daughter, he
turned back. The royal banners proceeded from
Tamisha to Shuzil in the province of Mazan-
deran,2 where the great ordu was. Nearly thir-
1The year 692 began on December 12, 1292.
2Neither “Tamisha” nor “Shuzil” has been identified;
Arends reads them similarly, из Тамишэ…до Шузиля
(p. 156). Tamisha occurs on text p. 1135 and again on
text p. 1267; “Shuzil” does not occur again.
ty-one leagues were traversed in one night.
One of the muqaddams [chieftains] of Mazan-
deran took fright and did not come to court, for
which he was branded a rebel. Ghazan, howev-
er, did not pay much attention and continued
on toward Persia and Azerbaijan via Shahdiz
into Firozkoh. 
Halting for several days at Damavand, he as-
signed Amir Satilmish and Khwaja Sa‘duddin
to assess and collect the taxes of Khurasan,
Mazanderan, Qumis, and Rayy and to see to
troop provisions, and then he set out for Tabriz,
accompanied by Nurin Aqa. He sent Yighmish
ahead to announce his arrival, but he returned
to him in the vicinity of Abhar and said, [1237]
“Gaikhatu says, ‘What need had Ghazan of
coming here? He should return to Khurasan.
Let him send others to conduct his business,
and his requests will be granted.’ ” 
Ghazan said, “Since we’ve come this far,
how can we turn back without having seen
each other?” He sent Amir Aladu and Mulai
ahead by post horse to conduct his business
while he continued on toward Tabriz. At Pul-i-
Zirih, Arghun Khan’s elite khwajas Najib, Am-
bar, and Rayhan came.
When he reached Tabriz under good auspices
he stayed there several days, but Gaikhatu’s
emissaries arrived one after another to say,
“Let Ghazan turn back.” In the end Kämjü and
Nardu arrived and said, “He said for you to
turn back this very day. He has also sent a little
something.”
Ghazan paid no attention and replied, saying,
“Since he doesn’t want to see us, we don’t
want to see him a hundred times over.” So say-
ing, he withdrew from Tabriz under favorable
auspices and camped in Yüz Aghach. He re-
quested Amir Tugh Temür’s daughter Eshil
Khatun, and the marriage was held there.
Amir Muhammad Idächi, who had been
named as amir of Isfahan, arrived and present-
598
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ed suitable gifts. He was warmly received and
became a member of the court.
A month later the royal banner set out toward
Khurasan. At Abhar, the khwaja and other
emissaries Arghun Khan had sent to the Qa’an
to bring back one of the senior Bulughan
Khatun’s relatives to be put in her place arrived
with Kökächin Khatun and Chinese and Catha-
ian rarities suitable for kings. Ghazan Khan
camped there and married Kökächin Khatun.
After the marriage was concluded, he sent a
tiger and several of the other gifts to Gaikhatu.
[1238] Then he set out for Damavand. 
When he reached the vicinity of Firozkoh,
emissaries from Amir Qutlughshah arrived to
give him the good news that they had done bat-
tle with Nawroz and defeated him, and that he
had withdrawn in rout and on foot to the
mountains of Nishapur. All of his possessions,
herds, and horses had been captured. 
The royal banners set forth for Damghan and
Bistam. At Bistam, Amir Qutlughshah and the
amirs arrived to present the booty they had tak-
en, and they were shown all sorts of favor. 
From there they entered Jurjan via the Khur-
ramaba Rod and camped in Sultan Duvin in
Astarabad, where they banqueted and hunted.
Amir Qutlughshah fell critically ill from hav-
ing drunk too much, and the physicians were
ordered to attend him until he regained his
health. From that time on, he swore off drink,
and until the present he has not had a drop.
Kia Salahuddin, who avoided presenting
himself when they reached his territory on
their way to Azerbaijan, came forth upon the
return from Tabriz and presented himself at
court in Rayy. Through Amir Nurin’s and other
amirs’ intercession Ghazan Khan pardoned his
offense. However, no sooner had he returned to
his own territory than he rebelled again. Ghaz-
an Khan ordered Amir Sö’ätäi to deal with
him. That winter he was polished off, and
much wealth and many animals were brought
from there to be divided among the soldiers.1
1Beginning here JTK has two versions of the text print-
ed in two columns, extending to p. 878. The left-hand
column agrees with the text of JTAZ and is translated
above. The right-hand column contains the following
wordier and somewhat fuller account:
When the spring of 693 [1294] began, the prince set
out toward Damghan in the direction of Damavand,
emerging via Sultan Maydan at Firozkoh. He summered
at Damavand, engaging every day in celebrations, ban-
quets, hunts, and falconry. Amirs Mulai and Horqudaq
reported that the people of Nishapur were about to rebel.
The prince sent envoys and edicts containing promises
and threats, but it did no good. At the beginning of au-
tumn he set out to hunt, and in Dhu’l-Qa‘da 693 [Sep-
tember 23–October 22, 1294] he arrived at Nishapur and
stopped in Mawedi. In the lead Sahib Sa‘duddin Sawaji
was sent into the city as an emissary to advise the people
to make peace and surrender. Qazi Sadruddin, Pahlavan
Umar, and the people of Nishapur hastened out to him,
and he gave them promises and threats. In reply they
said, “We are servants, but we fear for our heads and our
lives. If we receive assurances of our lives, we will
make haste to come out.” 
Sa‘duddin undertook to report this to the court in such
a way that no harm would come to them or to their pos-
sessions. Immediately Qazi Sadruddin, Pahlavan Umar,
and a huge crowd came out of the city and went to the
great amirs.
From Mawedi the prince decamped to the outskirts of
Nishapur. He granted the miscreants surety of their lives
and said, “How can we let the kingdom and subjects be
ruined or driven to desperation by the seditiousness of a
group of ignorant busybodies? You are commanded to
turn over the group who have been causing sedition,
Fakhruddin Ra’is, Husamuddin Aybak Khita’i, Abubakr
Ayisha, Usman Mishkani, and Muhammad Abdul-Malik,
and to pay the tribute so that we may withdraw from
here in safety.” The Nishapuris made excuses to keep
from surrendering them. An order was given for the
Nishapuris to be besieged. The people of the city took
refuge in the congregational mosque. The soldiers plun-
dered the city quarters and then headed for the mosque.
Within one hour they had made holes in the mosque
walls in several places, and cries and pleas for amnesty
arose from the women and men. Out of his great
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
599

clemency the prince forgave the wretches despite the
enormity of their transgressions and forbade the soldiers
to kill or pillage. However, because the soldiers had
poured down all at once into battle, it was not possible
to keep them from it, so the prince himself mounted and
went into the city, where he executed several soldiers
and commanded that their limbs be hung on the gates.
With this, the soldiers ceased killing and pillaging. The
troublemakers were found and put to death. Not a single
human being was allowed to be taken prisoner, and not a
single animal was taken out of the city. 
Then, after the citizens were placated, they were set to
restoring and planting. An order was given for Qazi
Sadruddin and Pahlavan Umar to come to the prince,
and the imperial banners headed toward Mazanderan,
where the winter was spent in Sultan Duvin.
The story of Nawroz’s regret and repentance and his
subsequent surrender and obedience.
Although Amir
Nawroz
had
been
renowned
in
Khurasan for his courageousness, valor, and bravery, he
was blamed by all for his rebellion against his benefac-
tor. For a long time, free of all encumbrance, he stum-
bled around like a blind camel, spending every night in a
different place like the moon, [873] never staying in the
same place two nights in a row. When he struck in all di-
rections, he and his mighty soldiers charged right and
left. He concentrated solely upon discharging tasks of
utmost danger and taking on difficult expeditions. He
stirred up trouble and unrest, his mind was plagued by
demonic temptations and selfish thoughts, and he tor-
mented himself with imaginings. What his end would be
was hidden from him. Toghan Khatun, his sympathetic
wife and confidant, was a princess of great intelligence,
and between them was total agreement and affection.
When she saw her husband sorrowful, regretful, and
saddened, she loosed her tongue in good advice, saying,
“Friend of my bosom and kind confidant, know that
there is a cause for every thing. Every cause has a moti-
vation, and every motivation has a manifestation. The
affairs of the world are based upon happiness as well as
upon misery. Since, as a matter of course, throne and
fortune do not always favor a person, and felicity seeks
to turn away from favoring a person, the more you think
something is beautiful, the uglier it appears. A wise man,
however, should remain firm and stable in the face of
the mutability of affairs. [874] Even though things may
deviate from the center of your desire, in the end they
will come back to the initial point, like the circumfer-
ence of a circle, and return to the beginning. To place
one’s foot on a bramble or to put one’s hand on a snake’s
tail is better than withdrawing the foot of resignation
into the skirt of inattention. It often happens that fate
veils the countenance of what is right from a wise and
clever man, and destiny hides the right course of action
from him. In the face of fate manliness and competence
are not enough, and bravery and courage do little good
against chance. There has never been a rose without
thorns or wine without a hangover. In the end, these im-
possible knots are solved, and old wounds heal. You
have been given such mighty things to do and been
handed such a difficult fate, and yet you have learned
nothing from them. It is not hidden from the wise that
one cannot box with a banner or strike a blow to a wave
in the sea. Now, if you want rest and repose, and you re-
gret and repent what has passed, go to the Prince of the
World, gird your loins with the belt of obedience, stand
before him on one foot like a candle, keep yourself sole-
ly among the ranks of his favored servants, for your wel-
fare and safety lie in submitting and surrendering to him
and in abandoning disputatiousness, quarrelsomeness,
and contentiousness. [875] Relative to the prince’s gen-
erosity and valor, your offense is like a dust mote next to
a mountain or like a mosquito next to a raging storm. By
humility and entreaty wash away the dust of contention
from the page of his mind with the water of apology and
amends, for a sincere apology has a great effect in clear-
ing away difficulties. Clear the air of your offense by
showing the innocence of your intentions and the truth
of your speech. Live the rest of your life in the shade of
his daily-increasing imperial fortune.”
For a moment Nawroz remained transfixed, as silent
as a fish. Finally he smiled like a rose blossoming and
said, “I am worrying about the final outcome and think-
ing of my head. A head is not a leek that will grow back
when it is cut.
Beware! Keep a lookout for the right moment, for you
are not a leek that will grow back when it is cut.
Nonetheless, no matter how many the causes for con-
tention may have been, the right action for us lies in
truce, and success lies in accepting this advice. If the
prince agrees and fortune is favorable, therein lies the
best course for us.”
When this notion had taken root in their minds, [876]
she sent Eygü Temür Khatun, a relative and co-religion-
600
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ist of hers, to the prince’s court to convey Nawroz’s re-
gret and repentance. “He is sorry for what he has done,”
she said, “and hopes for pardon through your clemency.
At present he is not in rebellion against the court. If,
through the machinations of fate and destiny, he was
emboldened to undertake unwarranted actions, it was
out of fear for his life. If the prince grants him pardon,
deigns to overlook his offenses, and accepts to gaze
upon him with favor and reckon him among his ser-
vants, he will have ennobled him and elevated his head
to the skies. Henceforth, so long as there is life in his
body, he will serve single-mindedly.”
When Ghazan heard this good news he was greatly re-
lieved, for he considered Nawroz’s support to be a major
part of his fortune, but he did not pay much attention to
the woman’s words.
Around the first of Muharram 694 [November 21,
1294] Nawroz sent his good liege men Satilmish and
Esän Buqa with a few others to the prince’s court to say,
“Even though your old but guilty servant Nawroz has
committed too many offenses to hope for pardon, he has
not despaired of the innate generosity and valor of his
master and son of his master. He conveys his submis-
sion, servitude, weakness, and humility and says that de-
spite his thousands of sins he is still a servant and ser-
vant’s son to this dynasty. Having been duped into
disloyalty and bewitched by self-interested persons, who
succeeded in creating a rift between the sun and its shad-
ow, he says, ‘I am miserable in being deprived of court
and the sight of the imperial countenance. Like a grist-
mill, I revolve around myself and remain where I was in
the beginning. If no crimes were committed by servants,
kings’ ability to pardon would never have appeared. If
the prince will wash away this slave’s sin with the water
of pardon and penance, henceforth, as long as there is
life in my body, I will act and strive in servitude. I am
ready to apologize for my shortcomings and to make ex-
piation for what has passed for the remainder of my life
provided that the prince not remember my past offenses
and not remind me of my past faults and slips. “We will
make up and take the path of fidelity anew provided that
no one remember what has passed.” ’ ” 
The prince, moved by the great clemency in his innate
nature, accepted this sincere repentance and apology and
forgave him his faults and offenses. 
If you still intend to make peace, come back, for you will
be more acceptable than you were.
Then the prince said, “Kindness and forgiveness should
never be denied to offenders. If Nawroz’s heart is at one
with his tongue and he keeps his word, we will overlook
all his crimes and offenses.”
On both sides a solemn pact and covenant was writ-
ten. When the pact was completed, Nawroz’s people
said, “If a troop comes as reinforcements to Maruchuq
so that Nawroz can join them when he severs his
connections with the enemy, it would be good, for if the
enemy learns of it and comes after us, together we can
repel the foe.”
In reply the prince said, “Since it is the dead of winter,
and the borders and frontiers are secure, we will move
out to that region as though to go hunting.” Then he
showed kindness to Satilmish and Nawroz’s other amirs
and sent them off with an edict restoring Nawroz to fa-
vor. Nawroz was as overjoyed at this news as a lover is
with the arrival of his beloved. He made a pact with
Örüg Temür Gürägän to clear all traces of the enemy
from the Amuya vicinity. When this news spread abroad,
Örüg Temür was chided and blamed. Frightened,
Nawroz pulled back and took his troops to strike Yisa’ur
and kill some people. Thus his connection to the amirs
of Transoxiana was completely severed. Nawroz took
the road to Khurasan. 
When Prince Ghazan saw that the words [of Nawroz’s
envoys] were free of digression and ornament, he judged
the inner contents by the title on the cover, but he sub-
mitted the test of this coin to the opinion of the amirs.
Each one spoke in accordance with his station and abili-
ty. The great amirs Nurin and Qutlughshah said support-
ively, “Nawroz is a man of cunning, and it is not known
whether at base he is fair or foul. To make peace with
one’s enemies is like having a serpent as a companion. It
would be best to draw him here by the magnet of entice-
ments and the amber of promises. If he accepts the mes-
sage and comes willingly and without displaying signs
of rebellion and disobedience, then his heart must be in
conformity with his tongue. This is what occurs to your
majesty’s servants: your majesty may add to it whatever
seems appropriate to him.”
Since fortune was favoring the Prince of the World, he
paid no attention to them and said, “Based on the pact
and covenant that have been made, there is firm friend-
ship and trust on both sides.”
The prince decided to go there. While hunting with
the amirs Nurin and Qutlughshah and many soldiers, he
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
601

proceeded toward Yazir, Nasa, and Abivard. When he
reached Kushk and Bir Husayn in the Yazir region,
Nawroz’s brother Hajji and Chardu Bahadur’s son Injil
[Ejil?] came again as emissaries and repeated what they
had said before. The prince showed them favor.
From
there
he
went
to
Dasht-i-Khawaran
near
Sarakhs. Now this was in the dead of winter, and there
was bitter cold, and it was raining and snowing. In the
middle of Safar [January 4, 1295] they decamped and
stopped in Dalan Quduq, from which they went to She-
berghan. When they emerged from the mountains and
hills, between Merv and Sheberghan they saw a vast
plain filled with many tents and animals grazing. Out of
suspicion they stopped where they were, thinking, “If,
God forbid, he had had any thought of mutiny or treach-
ery, much damage could have been wrought by his
might.”
Prince Ghazan ordered Ba’udai, the chief officer of
the qorchis (meaning that the saqa and the gäjigä [rear
guard] were in his charge), to investigate that army. He
went in haste and quickly came back to Nawroz’s liege
man Satilmish and said, “This army is Nawroz’s horde.”
The prince sat atop a hill, thinking and looking down on
the valley in amazement. Nawroz had might, power, and
strength. 
When Nawroz learned of the prince’s arrival, he and
Princess Toghan came out of their tent in the midst of all
