that cold and snow, mounted, and went out to greet him.
Near the town of Baghshor, which the Mongols call
Möre Shupurghan, he was honored to perform tägish-
mishi. Presenting nine fine horses, he said, “ ‘To place a
locust’s leg before Solomon is insulting, but it is a dis-
play of skill for an ant.’ ” 
In accordance with the might and felicity of the time
and place several banquets and celebrations were held at
that river. Since civilization, people, and settled places
were distant, and no wine was to be had, an order was
given for the amirs to do yarashmishi [reconciliation]
with water. At that place he ordered a stele erected,
which the Mongols call oba. 
Nawroz kissed the ground humbly and said, “If I have
done anything amiss or failed in my duties to the emper-
or, it is hoped that the prince in his perfect clemency will
pardon my mistakes, for no creature is free of imperfec-
tion and flaw.”
If no mistakes were ever made, pardon by rulers would
not be necessary.
Ghazan said, “When suspicion emerges from the dust
of doubt, and the veil of misgiving is lifted, if some
trace of former alienation remains it should be erased
from the tablet of the mind, for new agreement annihi-
lates all old quarrels. Now my trust in your love and af-
fection is more than can be expressed.” With such affec-
tionate expressions he allayed Nawroz’s fears and
soothed his troubled mind. 
With such special favor the shah honored him and dis-
regarded his guilt.
Ghazan ordered that henceforth he should be at ease.
In truth I intended to chastise you greatly, but when you
entered you apologized for the past.
“As long as you continue on the right path and your
words and actions are correct, you will continue to be
promoted and your wishes will be granted. God is wit-
ness to this promise, and I will never even contemplate
breaking this pact.
You are safe and secure from me, and the God of the
world is my witness.
However, regardless of the fact that I have total and
complete trust in your word, my mind cannot rest at ease
unless you swear an oath and make a covenant that you
will not break or seek to subvert so long as you are in
power,” said Ghazan. 
Therefore they swore the most binding of oaths to
confirm the pact that had been made in their absence by
their emissaries, and they made a covenant that they
would not hurt each other. Nawroz sealed his covenant
with an oath that he would serve the khanate in complete
servitude as long as he was in power.
When the oath had been sworn, Ghazan Khan said,
“What is past is past. Henceforth and in the future, in re-
pelling enemies and dealing with rebels we will act as
one hand.” 
After that, Ghazan Khan took the road to Panj Deh
and Maruchuq, and there the officers of the Qara’una
troop received the honor of performing tägishmishi.
Then he went via the Andkhud road. The sons of Umar
Oghul, Eygü and his brothers, joined the court. While
marching from there to Faryab, the scouts came across
the foe, and during a skirmish several were killed. Then
he took the road to Sheberghan across a large, waterless
wasteland. 
From there Nawroz turned back with the Qara’una
troop and turned his reins toward his own yurt. The foe,
following in the rear like an unforeseen calamity in fear
602
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

of the Qara’unas, struck the mothers of children. That
night they camped in Inchkä Su in the vicinity of She-
berghan, and a command was given, saying, “Let no one
was light a fire or cook lest by the light of the fire the
enemy become aware of our presence. In the morning,
while the foe is still fast asleep, we will make a surprise
attack.” The enemy, however, having learned of the
arrival of the imperial banners, left the road and went to
San-u-Charyak. When, at the Sheberghan river, the
prince heard of the enemy’s retreat, he sent Amir Qut-
lughshah with a group of officers in pursuit of the foe
while he himself camped in the vicinity of Juzjanan.
In the month of Rabi‘ I 694 [January 1295], the offi-
cers came upon the enemy and pounced on them like
leopards. They rejoined the prince at Juzjanan, and all
proceeded together under good auspices. When they
reached Faramarzan, Nawroz’s wife, Toghanchuq, and
his tents were there. After banqueting and reveling, he
set out in the direction of Sarakhs and stopped at Qara
Tapa in Sarakhs. At that stage Bughdai Idächi came
from the center of Azerbaijan and His Highness
Gaikhatu Khan to report the rebellion by Baidu and his
officers. Since Nawroz’s tents had gone in the direction
of Badghis in Herat, Nawroz obtained permission here
to depart. The prince proceeded along the road to Arjah
and Shugan. Baidu’s emissaries arrived with a man
named Qutlughshah at their head and reported that all
the aqa-ini, amirs, and noyans were in agreement that
the prince should proceed to the center of the state and
take up the crown and throne that were his by inheri-
tance and merit. After showing the emissaries great fa-
vor and rewarding them, the prince sent them back, and
he also dispatched a messenger to summon Nawroz. He
stayed a while in Radkan at the Gulasp spring, and from
there he proceeded via Khabushan to Dubar. Since the
ordus, tents, and amirs’ soldiers were in Mazanderan,
and Qara Buqa’s son Prince Sögä had reached Mazan-
deran by Gaikhatu’s command, the prince determined to
hasten forward. He entered Shahrak-i-Naw in Jurjan and
stopped in Sultan Duvin in Astarabad, which was his
birthplace, where he reveled for a while. He took coun-
sel with the great amirs concerning Baidu and sent Ura
Temür Idächi to Baidu with a message saying, “We are
determined to go to the capital and will arrive shortly.
What needs to be said will be said in the presence of the
aqa-ini.” After that, Ghazan realized how much he owed
Nawroz for his good services and singled him out for re-
That winter was spent in Mazanderan, and
there was no report from any direction. When
spring came they set out for Damavand,
emerging on the Chahar Deh road and spend-
ing a month in Damghan. From there they set
out via Sultan Maydan1 for Firozkoh and spent
the summer in Damavand. From there he sent
the amirs of the army Mulai and Horqudaq to
Khurasan, and they sent word back that the
people of Nishapur [1239] were acting up and
not giving their all. Ghazan Khan paid no at-
tention, and indeed out of his native clemency
he often dispatched envoys to warn and threat-
en them. It did no good. In the autumn he set
out in that direction, arriving in Dhu’l-Qa‘da
693 [September–October 1294]. He camped in
Mawedi and sent Khwaja Sa‘duddin into the
city to warn them and advise them to submit,
for it was not fitting for old servants to be
killed on account of the actions of a few cor-
rupt trouble-makers.
When Khwaja Sa‘duddin went into the city,
Qazi Sadruddin, Pahlavan Umar, and the no-
bles of Nishapur came forward and said, “We
are concerned for our lives. If the khwaja ac-
cepts to give us amnesty, we will come out and
pay homage.” Khwaja Sa‘duddin made a
pledge, saying, “I will present your petition,
and I will see to it that you will not be
harmed.” Qazi Sadruddin and Pahlavan Umar
came out of the city along with a group of peo-
ward and favor, putting him in charge of all fiscal affairs
of the empire and elevating him in status above all his
peers. An imperial edict was promulgated, saying, “All
territory from the banks of the Oxus to the frontier of
Persia held by us, for all of which Arghun Aqa was
deputy on behalf of our good fathers, we do hereby en-
trust to Nawroz and put into his capable hands.” And
thus the seal of rule and power fell into Nawroz’s hands.
1Thus in the text, but a route from Damghan to
Firozkoh via the Sultan Maydan in Khurasan is absurd.
It must be a different Sultan Maydan.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
603

ple and went to the great amirs, who sent them
to court. 
Ghazan Khan decamped from Mawedi and
then stopped in the vicinity of Nishapur and
said, “We are not going to destroy our own
land and subjects on account of a few busybod-
ies. Let them turn over the trouble-makers
Fakhruddin Ra’is, Husamuddin Aybak Khata’i,
Abubakr Ali Ayisha, Usman Mishkani, and
Muhammad Abdul-Malik, and let them pay
their taxes correctly so that we can withdraw
from here in safety.” 
They, however, delayed in turning over the
persons named above, so a command was giv-
en for Nishapur to be besieged. The inhabitants
took refuge in a strong mosque as the amirs en-
tered the city, each from a different direction.
When the soldiers had them surrounded, they
ceased what they were doing in fear and fright.
The soldiers plundered the city quarters [1240]
and lanes as they headed for the mosque. Then,
having driven several mines, they gained the
walls and dragged the poor people out yelling
and screaming. The people requested amnesty,
and Ghazan Khan was so clement that he
granted it to the wretches despite their many
offenses. Although several people had been
killed, he ordered that the soldiers be prevented
from pillaging and killing, but since the sol-
diers had begun moving all at once, it was im-
possible to control them. Ghazan Khan himself
mounted and went into the city, where he had
one or two of the gazigtäns executed and or-
dered their limbs hung from the city gates. The
soldiers were cowed by this and stopping their
killing and plunder. The trouble-makers men-
tioned above were caught and executed, but
[Ghazan Khan] would not allow a single ani-
mal to be taken from the district. Having thus
won over the population, he put them to work
restoring and rebuilding the agriculture. It was
ordered that Qazi Sadruddin and Pahlavan
Umar should set forth with the court and the
royal banners moved toward Jurjan. That win-
ter was spent at Sultan Duvin in Astarabad. 
Nawroz submits and comes back to Ghazan
Khan’s court, where he gives a banquet and
offers gifts.
In early Muharram 694 [November 1294],
Nawroz’s liege man Satilmish arrived on
Nawroz’s behalf and said, “Nawroz says, ‘I am
your ancient servant and offspring of your ser-
vants, but on account of bad people’s slander I
exiled myself from your court. If the prince
will have mercy on me, [1241] pardon my of-
fenses, and not remind me of my crimes, I will
come to court, and serve valiantly from this
time forward.’ ” Inasmuch as the padishah was
perfectly
clement
and
just,
he
pardoned
Nawroz’s offenses and regally accepted his
apology. At the end of his mission Satilmish
said [on Nawroz’s behalf], “ ‘If the padishah
shows mercy, let him send an auxiliary troop to
Maruchuq, for when I turn away from this
group I will join them, and if anyone comes in
pursuit of me, they can assist me in repelling
them so that I may reach the court through the
padishah’s good luck.’ ”
To this the padishah replied, “Since it is win-
ter and there are no reports on any side, I will
move out myself in that direction, ostensibly to
go hunting.”
Satilmish was shown much favor and with-
drew to deliver a message saying that Nawroz
was expected to keep his word. The padishah
meanwhile set out accompanied by the great
amirs Nurin and Qutlughshah. 
When he reached the territory of Yazir,
Nawroz’s brother Hajji and Chardu Bahadur’s
son Ejil arrived on Nawroz’s behalf at Kushk
and Bir Husayn, bearing the same message that
Satilmish had delivered. The prince rewarded
them and left there for Sarakhs, where he cele-
604
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

brated the new year and then decamped for
Dalan Quduq.1 
When they emerged from the mountains and
hills they found the Merv and Sheberghan
plain filled with tents and animals. An order
was given for Ba’udai, the chief of the qorchis,
to investigate. After a time he returned with
Satilmish, Nawroz’s liege man, who said, “It is
Nawroz camped there, waiting for the arrival
of the royal banners.” The padishah stood atop
a hill, and immediately Nawroz and [1242]
Princess Toghan rode down and performed
tägishmishi. The padishah remained in that vil-
lage for three days, and banquets were held.
Since the nearest town was far away and there
was but little wine, he ordered the amirs to mix
it with water and to set up a stele, which the
Mongols call oba.2 He pardoned Nawroz and
showed him much favor.
Then he returned to Maruchuq, setting off
down the Shakh road. Nurin Aqa was beset by
a severe attack of the gout, and he suffered
greatly during that trip. The commanders of the
Qara’una division, Toghai and others, joined
the court. Then he decamped to Andkhui. The
sons of Umar Oghul Eygü and others joined
the retinue. He set off for Faryab. A scouting
party came across an enemy scouting party and
killed many of them. Some were taken prisoner
and brought to court. They were interrogated
1Dalan Quduq ~ Dalan Qudugh, Mongolian for Seven-
ty Wells.
2Several such memorial stones still exist—not this
one, of course. An example is the one set up by Amir
Temür when he was in pursuit of Toqtamish Khan in
1391. It was discovered in the Altyn Chuk mountains
near the Karasakpay river in Kazakhstan and is now in
the Hermitage in St. Petersburg. See N. N. Poppe,
“Карасакпайская
Надпись
Тимура,”
in
Государ-
ственный Эрмитаж: Труды Отдела Востока 2
(1940): 185–87. See also Thackston, Century of Princes,
68, note 6.
and said, “The enemy army is in Faryab and
Juzjana[n].” 
When Ghazan camped in Faryab he stationed
there his treasury, baggage, and soldiers whose
horses had gone lame. Then he set out for She-
berghan, but the road was all waterless desert.
He camped by night near Sheberghan in
Inchkä Su and ordered that no one light a fire
lest the enemy discover them. Thus they would
be able to surprise them the next morning. The
enemy, however, had already learned that the
royal banners had reached Faryab, so they had
withdrawn and taken the San-u-Charyak road
out.3 The victorious army camped along the
Sheberghan river, and an order was given for
the great amir Qutlughshah and others to go in
pursuit of the enemy while the royal banners
made camp in that area. The Qara’una troops,
which had taken refuge in places of difficult
access in fear of the enemy, all came to court,
and they were ordered to proceed to Sarakhs.
The amirs who had gone out in pursuit of the
enemy [1243] caught up with them in the
vicinity of the San-u-Charyak mountains, and
in early Rabi‘ I 694 [mid-January 1295] they
fought a fierce battle. The enemy was defeated,
and many of them were killed. The amirs came
back to court with many captives and countless
articles of booty. 
They remained there for twenty days, and all
the soldiers who were in attendance took grain
from the storehouses, ate it, and gave it to their
horses. There was such an abundance that no
diminution was felt. 
During those days Nawroz also joined the
court, and after that, Ghazan Khan decamped
from there. When they reached Faramarzan,
Princess Toghan and Nawroz’s tents were
3Sān-u-Ch(ah)āryak is the modern Sangcharak in
Afghanistan.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
605

there. They gave banquets for several days and
presented as many gifts as they could. 
From there he moved out toward Sarakhs.
When
they
reached
Qara
Tapa,
Bughdai
Akhtachi came from Gaikhatu to report the op-
position of Baidu and the amirs. He paid no
attention. 
Nawroz requested leave to take his tents back
to Badghis, and the royal banners remained
there for a few days before setting out down
the Arjah and Shugan road. When he reached
Dara-i-Jaz, he set out for Radkan in order to
hunt stork. An emissary named Qutlughshah
and a group of envoys came from Baidu to re-
port Baidu’s opposition to Gaikhatu. “The aqa-
ini and the ladies and amirs are in agreement,”
they said, “that the Prince of the World should
move in that direction and sit on the throne of
emperorship, which belongs to him by inheri-
tance and by merit.” The prince paid no atten-
tion and sent the envoys back. He held council
with his great amirs and sent a messenger to
summon Nawroz. After staying several days in
Radkan and at the Gulasp spring, they came to
Khabushan, [1244] and several days later they
set forth. When they camped at Duvin, Nawroz
came. Since the aghruqs, most of the soldiers,
and
Prince
Sögä,
who
had
come
from
Gaikhatu, were in Mazanderan, the prince de-
cided to go to Sultan Duvin in Astarabad and
thence to Persia and Azerbaijan. Entering Jur-
jan via Shahrak-i-Naw, he camped in Sultan
Duvin in Astarabad, where a few days were
spent in banquets and revelry. He sent Ura
Temür Idächi to Baidu to say that he would be
following close behind.
Ghazan Khan leaves Khurasan for Persia;
he does battle with Baidu in the vicinity of
Hashtrod and Qurban Shirä.
After dispatching Ura Temür Idächi, Ghazan
Khan moved out from Sultan Duvin under fa-
vorable auspices and headed for Persia and
Azerbaijan. Taking the Chahar Deh road, he
entered Damghan. He wanted to have a look at
the Gird Koh fortress, but the amirs said,
“Since such an important task lies ahead, it
would not be auspicious to go into a fortress.”
An order was then given for Tajuddin Eldüz’s
sons, who were the wardens of the fortress, to
come out with their wives and children. They
turned over the keys to Khwaja Sa‘duddin
Habash and surrendered the fortress.
When Simnan was reached, Ordu Buqa came
from Gaikhatu with several loads of chaos and
white and vermilion paper. Ghazan Khan said,
“In Mazanderan and this area it is so damp that
iron implements and weapons do not last. How
can paper last?” So saying, he ordered it all
burned.
From there he took the Firozkoh road to
Tihran. [1245] Boralghi and the amirs of Persia
paid homage there. When they arrived in
Khayl-i-Buzurg, Ura Temür Idächi came back
from Baidu and said, “He has gone back on his
word and is entertaining notions of being the
ruler.
The
amirs
Taghachar,
Qunchuqbal,
Doladai, and others who were stirring up trou-
ble and killed Ordu Qaya, Joshi, and others,
since they were afraid of Ghazan, have all
agreed to support Baidu and are planning mis-
chief.” 
Since
Ghazan
Khan
had
not
imagined
Baidu’s opposition, he had not brought many
soldiers, and his companions had not brought
their weapons of war. They had even left the
royal tugh and regal drum there. Therefore he
took council with the amirs and in all regal au-
dacity paid no attention. He sent Mulai and
Yighmish on an embassy to Baidu to say, “We
are coming ourselves. Where shall we meet?”
And he requested örüglük [safe passage].
When he reached Aq Khwaja in Qazwin,
Shadai Gürägän, who had been sent by Baidu
and his amirs, came to court and spoke the
606
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

very sort of words masters of deception and
dissimulation use. The gist was as follows: “I
had no notion or desire to be padishah, but be-
cause of the distance of Prince Ghazan, sedi-
tion and bulghaq [disruption] have erupted in
the ulus. Therefore, aqa-ini and amirs are
agreed to elevate me to the rule. Now, anything
the prince desires will be granted, and there
will be no stinting, but he must turn back from
the place to which he has come.” 
Ghazan paid no attention and continued on.
When he reached Qonqur Öläng, Mulai and
Yighmish arrived and repeated the same care-
fully crafted words. That very day Na’uldar
came as a herald from Baidu and was allowed
to perform tägishmishi, for which he was am-
ply rewarded. [1246] Decamping from there,
he took the Muslim Ribat road and camped.
Shadai Gürägän and Baidu’s envoys were sum-
moned and had them so interrogated that
Shadai Gürägän despaired of his life. Harsh
messages were sent concerning Baidu’s rule.
During the time that Mulai and Yighmish had
gone there, Ildär had said in drunkenness, “We
aqa-ini have agreed to elevate Baidu to the
rule. If Prince Ghazan does not agree, there
will be disagreement amongst us.” In short, he
dismissed the envoys and ordered the amirs
Nurin and Qutlughshah to array the army. Esän
Buqa Bitigchi was dispatched on a mission to
say, “We are coming.” Taking the Tükätü road,
he crossed the Safedrod, and the next day,
Tuesday the first of Rajab 694 [May 17, 1295],
corresponding to the 2nd of Shün Ay, the news
of Prince Ghazan’s imminent arrival reached
Baidu, who sent Prince Ildär and the amirs
Elji’idäi and Chechäk out as an advance force.
On this side Amir Qutlughshah and Nurin Aqa
manned the left wing, while Prince Sögä, Bo-
ralghi, Nawroz, and other commanders stood
in the center with Ghazan Khan. When they
were near Baidu, he sent Bughdai Akhtachi
forward, and he spoke in every way possible of
peace, friendship, and kinship. Ghazan did not
deign to pay attention. 
The armies clashed. Amir Qutlughshah in the
vanguard stood as firm as a mountain. Since
Prince Ildär had boasted so much, it was re-
quired by Ghazan’s fortune that he be the first
to suffer chastisement. No sooner had the
drums of the center been sounded and the sol-
diers of the center begun to move than Amir
Qutlughshah charged them. He swept the divi-
sion aside with one attack, so by the time the
news reached the center, they had been routed.
[1247] Nearly eight hundred men were killed,
and the rest had fled. Ildär’s lieutenant Taghai
was killed, and Arslan Oghul was brought to
court on foot. The army of Khurasan wanted to
attack in unison, sweep them away, and annihi-
late them, but Ghazan Khan was innately so
merciful that he forbade it. “All these soldiers
are servants of our fathers and forefathers,” he
said. “How can we kill them simply on account
of the mischief of a few trouble-makers who
elevated Baidu to the rule?” Nawroz and the
other amirs insisted that he should take advan-
tage of the situation, but he yelled at them to
be quiet.
When the captive Arslan Oghul was brought
in, his own cousin Boroltai said, “Since he has
drawn a sword in the face of the servants of the
crown, if the padishah gives permission, I will
kill him.” The padishah paid no attention and
ordered robes, hats, belts, and boots brought
from his personal treasury and put on him, and
he ordered one of his own equerries to give
him a mount. Then he ordered those who had
been wounded in battle brought in, and he put
balm on their wounds with his own blessed
hand and gave them medicine dissolved in
wine. (Of course, as a reward for such clemen-
cy and mercy, God placed the whole of the
kingdom in his royal hand.)
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
607

When Baidu and his amirs saw that Ildär and
Tükäl, their greatest champions, had been rout-
ed, they realized that they did not have the
power to resist. They therefore took the path of
accommodation and intercession, and in the
midst of the battlefield, on top of a hill, Baidu
and his amirs Taghachar, Doladai, and Qun-
chuqbal came, and the Padishah of Islam, even
though he had defeated and crushed them,
processed out to them, surrounded by his ret-
inue. With him were Nawroz, Nurin, Qut-
lughshah, and Sö’ätäi. The members of the two
delegations met and exchanged pleasantries.
“A covenant and pact must be made [1248]
that we will not harm each other,” he said. 
The amirs on this side shouted, “First the is-
sue of the rule must be settled! Then the matter
of pacts and promises.” In short, wine was
brought and drunk with gold dissolved in the
goblets. Those who were Muslims took each
other by the hand and swore oaths that they
would harbor no evil. The matter of the rule
was to be settled the following day. When day
was done everyone withdrew to his own place.
In that midst, the ev-oghlans of the great lady
Bulughan the elder, Horqasun, and others de-
serted Baidu and joined the court. 
Since the armies of Baghdad and Mughan
were near, Baidu kept sending envoys to get
them to come while the talks were going on.
From moment to moment commanders were
arriving with their troops, and by the end of the
day they constituted an impressive number.
The next day the two armies proceeded togeth-
er to Qurban Shirä. The padishah’s army en-
tered a narrow valley a league long. There was
only one road. Kökätü Bahadur and two thou-
sand horsemen charged and took the head of
the valley. Qunchuqbal was coming behind
him to assist. When Baidu was informed and
realized that it would result in battle, he dis-
patched an envoy to have them open the road
and not prevent passage. He was angry over
their action.
That night they camped opposite one another
but so near that they could all drink from one
spring. All the soldiers spent that night holding
their horses and armed, and no one rested. 
The next morning, which was Monday the
7th of Rajab [May 23, 1295], a group came out
to arrange a truce. Amirs like Tugh Temür and
Sö’ätäi agreed that a court tent would be
pitched in the middle and Tödäi Khatun, whose
yurt was the nearest, would come and swear
both sides to a truce. 
Just then Qunchuqbal came and said, “If
Ghazan gains the victory, [1249] Amir Aq
Buqa will attack us amirs.” Therefore he was
executed that very day.
After much discussion it was decided that the
amirs would gather in the midst of the battle-
field and, with each other’s approval, put an
end to it. From this side went the amirs
Nawroz, Nurin, Qutlughshah, and Tugh Temür;
from Baidu’s side went Taghachar, Qunchuq-
bal, and Doladai. Deliberations continued until
noon, Baidu’s forces increasing moment by
moment. When the amirs saw that this was the
case, they decided to send to Prince Ghazan
the ordus of Arghun Khan, the great lady Bu-
lughan, Örüg Khatun, and Prince Kharbanda
along with the other princes and to turn over
his possessions and treasury. Furthermore,
from
that
side
of
the
Sapedrod,
Persia,
Khurasan, Qumis, and Mazanderan would be
Ghazan’s, along with half of the realm of Fars
and the entirety of the enchüs there.
When this was told to Ghazan, he said, “Let
them turn over Taghachar too along with the
one Qara’una division that was Arghun Khan’s
personal enchü so that this can be definitely
decided and we can withdraw.”
Baidu replied to the amirs, saying, “Prince
Ghazan knows that Arghun Khan considered
608
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

me too like his own son, and he assigned every
son winter quarters in some area, to be accom-
panied by an amir. Taghachar and the Qara’una
troop were my constant companions in Bagh-
dad. If he decides according to what Arghun
Khan commanded, it is his to rule.”
The padishah and the amirs settled upon that
and said, “Let him turn over what has already
been fixed so that we may withdraw.”
Baidu sent Doladai to court with food and
wine to perform tägishmishi and offer a goblet.
The padishah indicated that they would pull
out on the Siyah Koh road. Baidu and his amirs
did not agree to this because the Qara’una
troop was there and they were afraid [1250]
that if Ghazan Khan went that way, those sol-
diers would join him and once again trouble
would be stirred up. Bolad Chingsang was sent
to court to tell Ghazan to return the same way
he had come.
The next day Baidu sent his son Qipchaq
with a group of amirs to perform tägishmishi,
offer toasts, and say, “Baidu says, ‘Since the
prince has come here auspiciously, and peace
and agreement now prevail between us, if we
part without seeing each other for a moment,
everyone will imagine that we are still on bad
terms. It would be better for us to sit for a
while and renew our pledge to meet again.
Then he can depart auspiciously.’ ” The amirs
Sö’ätäi and Tugh Temür went back and forth
several times to arrange this request, and final-
ly it was decided that a tent would be pitched
between the camps and that the two, accompa-
nied by several of their elite, would come and
see each other for a time. 
That day the padishah showed Qipchaq much
favor, clad him in robes of honor, sat him on a
horse, and sent him back. Then, in consulta-
tion, Nawroz, Nurin, and Qutlughshah dis-
agreed with the plan, as did the astrologers,
who reported that it was an inauspicious day.
Sö’ätäi and Tugh Temür were sent to Baidu to
say, “Not only is the day not auspicious but
evening is also nigh. We can meet in the
morning.”
[Ghazan] then told Nawroz [1251] and Tugh
Temür to stay and go to Baidu the next
morning to arrange diplomatic matters and get
the ordus moving. Then, by night, after fires
had been lit in all the tents, [Ghazan] slipped
out and rode so fast that by morning he had
crossed the Sapedrod. The amirs who were
there joined him. Proceeding via Deh-i-Manar,
he spent the night in Zanjan.
The next day, he sent Kür Temür from Mus-
lim [Ribat] to Baidu to say, “We have set out
for Damavand. We have left the amirs Nawroz
and Tugh Temür there. You must keep your
word to allow the ordus and the ladies to leave
and
to
stick
to
the
terms
of
our
oral
agreement.” 
From there he passed by Qonqur Öläng and
went to Kararod, which the Mongols call
Türgän Mürän.1 There Kashhar Bakhshi came
to deliver a message from Baidu: “It was ex-
pected that we would meet again and have a
chance to converse for a while. Since the
prince moved off, doubtless he considered it
best. Now each of us must keep his word.” 
The padishah sent back Ibrahim Sükürchi
with the bakhshi, and he delivered a message
to Baidu, saying, “It is imperative that you let
Nawroz, Tugh Temür, and Kür Temür finish
their work and send them back as soon as
possible.”
From there he set out for Damavand, where
he spent that summer. When the amirs Nawroz,
Tugh Temür, and Kür Temür returned, Baidu
produced unreasonable excuses for not arrang-
ing fiscal and diplomatic matters and for not
sending the ladies and ordus. That he did not
1Türgän Mürän, Mongolian for “swift river.”
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
609

keep his promise angered the padishah, who
ordered all the amirs and their troops to go to
pasture and fatten up their animals.
What had happened to Nawroz and the others
is as follows. When they went before Baidu
and requested that a decree be issued con-
cerning the rule and that he allow the ordus
and ladies to depart, Baidu grew apprehensive
over the padishah’s departure and held the
amirs under arrest. He dispatched Qunchuqbal,
Doladai, and Elji’idäi as an advance troop in
pursuit, he himself setting out the next day. On
Wednesday the 9th of Rajab [May 25, 1295],
they crossed the Sapedrod, and on Friday the
11th of Rajab [May 27] Kür Temür came on
his mission. The amirs’ troops spread out as far
as Sharuyaz and then turned back and joined
Baidu in the vicinity of Sujas.
On Monday the 14th [May 30, 1295] they
marched to the hill at Sharuyaz and then re-
turned. [1252] Baidu asked the amirs in coun-
cil, “What’s to be done with Nawroz and Tugh
Temür?”
“They cannot be harmed,” they said in agree-
ment. Tükäl, who was trying to get Nawroz
killed, said, “Ghazan’s mainstay is Nawroz. He
must be killed.” Taghachar and the other amirs
refused to allow this because of kinship and
friendship. Taking offense, Tükäl left to go to
Georgia, where his home was, and did not re-
turn until after Baidu’s death.
Taghachar had grown to hate the idea of
Baidu’s rule because of Tödächü’s opposition
to him. Sadruddin also encouraged him in this
because the vizierate had not been given to
him. Uniting himself with Nawroz in order to
strengthen
Ghazan’s
cause,
he
persuaded
Nawroz to make a show of agreeing with
Baidu and making a pact with him. After that,
Baidu patronized Nawroz and reported that he
had made a pact and covenant with him to send
Ghazan bound. Therefore he received permis-
sion to withdraw and was singled out for par-
ticular favor. The emirate of Yazd on Baidu’s
behalf was settled on his son Sultanshah, and
ten thousand dinars’ worth of billets against
Yazd were issued to him.
On Tuesday the 15th of Rajab 694 [May 31,
1295] Nawroz, Tugh Temür, and the other en-
voys were sent back, and the next day Elji’idäi,
who had gone out in pursuit of Ghazan, came
back. Baidu turned his reins in the direction of
Sughurluq, arriving at the great yurt there on
Saturday the 19th of Rajab [June 4, 1295].
[1253]
*Events that transpired between Baidu and
Nawroz.
After Prince Ghazan departed, Amir Nawroz
and Tuq Temür were kept under guard and tor-
tured for a week, threatened with being killed,
beaten, and cursed. Nawroz never gave in un-
der questioning but bravely and magnificently
gave adamant responses. Unable to do any-
thing with him, the amirs made his brother
Lagzi, one of Baidu’s pillars of state, a go-be-
tween to create a truce between Baidu and
Nawroz since they knew that the stability of
the realm and the ulus lay in obtaining
Nawroz’s agreement, for “only lead works on
diamonds.” Lagzi encouraged Nawroz with all
sorts of promises to become friendly toward
Baidu and tried to get him to break his pact
with the prince. “My brother,” Nawroz replied,
“after the old rebellion and disobedience, it has
been three months since I swore a solemn oath
to Ghazan in Sheberghan that so long as there
was life in my body I would neither oppose
him on any account nor offer any sort of resis-
tance. I swore I would be a friend to his friends
and an enemy to his enemies. Under what dis-
pensation can I break my pact with him? You
want me to be reprehensible in this world and
castigated and chastised in the next life? My
love and support for Ghazan Khan are such
610
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

that so long as his reign continues, they cannot
change until my life ends, for today he is the
khan by right and the emperor absolutely.
Whatever he commands, I consider obedience
a necessity. He is truly Nawroz’s king and
khan. I have nothing to do with anyone else.”
“Brother,” said Lagzi, “So long as you per-
sist in your belief in this, you will never escape
from these people with your life.”
“We are resigned to what God has ordained,”
said Nawroz. “What has fate ever drawn that
has not been scratched out, and who has ever
been born who has not died? If God has or-
dained that I should die here in this manner,
who can change it? If he has not so ordained, I
have no worry about even a hundred thousand
undefeatable enemies. 
Baidu’s amirs came in straight-away and en-
tered the discussion, trying to mollify Nawroz
and win him over, but in any discussion
Nawroz was too clever to be toppled by an op-
ponent. He dropped the reins of discussion
fearlessly, taking no consideration of his oppo-
nents and accounting them as no more than
“wind in a warehouse” or “a basket in the wa-
ter.” The amirs despaired of him and said to
each other, “ ‘The cavalier of the world, Das-
tan son of Sam, cannot be tricked into putting
his head into a snare.’ ”1
Since Nawroz knew exactly what his oppo-
nents were thinking, and seeing that it was in
his best interests to be crafty and dissimulating
and to placate and be agreeable, he made a se-
cret pact with Taghachar that they would help
each other bring Baidu down. In order to pla-
cate Taghachar, the amirs agreed to try to get
Nawroz set free—all save Qunchuqbal, who
refused to agree to anything except the total
destruction of Nawroz. To Baidu he said,
1A quotation from Firdawsi, Shāhnāma (Moscow,
1967) 6:251, line 553.
“Your enemy has been caught. Kill him! Don’t
let the opportunity slip away.”
Since Nawroz knew that his only chance for
escape lay in trickery, deceit, dissimulation,
and humility, he began to curry favor by com-
plimenting the amirs and working his deceit by
saying, “I will obey whatever Baidu Khan
commands.” Baidu Khan summoned him in
private and praised him greatly for his manli-
ness and valor, saying, “I have found your de-
meanor to be better than what I was led to be-
lieve, and what I have seen is better than what
I had heard. Your manliness, stout-heartedness,
courage, and bravery are known. Your stead-
fastness, valor, and courage are the same. 
A king is worthy of kingship who patronizes
such servants. / He who has one like you be-
hind him need have no worry of difficult days.
Now that you are seeking deliverance from me,
if you will renew your pledge and promise that
you will seize Ghazan and turn him over to me,
swear a solemn oath that you will not break
your promise.”
In accordance with the dictum “Necessity
cancels discretion,” Nawroz swore without he-
sitation that he would turn Ghazan over bound
up. Poor Baidu was taken in. He showed him
favor, gave him a billet payable in Yazd for a
thousand dinars, and assigned the emirate of
Yazd to Nawroz’s son Sultanshah, his son by
Sultannasab
Khatun,
the
daughter
of
the
Atabeg
Ala’uddin,
the
son
of
Atabeg
Mahmudshah. 
On Tuesday the 15th of Rajab 694 [May 31,
1295] Nawroz and Tuq Temür were given
leave to depart. Nawroz raced off with the
speed of the wind, like an arrow shot from a
bow or a streak of lightning. In four days he
went from the vicinity of Maragha to Firozkoh
in Damavand. On the 27th of Rajab [June 12]
he arrived at Prince Ghazan’s court, where he
attained the honor of tägishmishi and reported
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
611

what had happened. “There was nothing to be
done with them but to plead and entreat until,
through the lord of the world’s good fortune, I
managed to escape from the claws of the roar-
ing lion,” he said.
“Which of Baidu’s amirs did you find the
most intelligent?” the prince asked.
“Qunchuqbal,” he replied, “who was the
most adamantly determined to spill my blood.
The affair was like the story of the owls and
the ravens in Kalila and Dimna.”1
In order to fulfill his promise, Nawroz
wrapped up a brass kettle (ghazan) and sent it
to Baidu. Baidu and his amirs were amazed by
this subtle word play2 and rare joke, but there
was nothing they could do about it. To Baidu
the amirs said, “ ‘The lion you caught in a trap
you let go, and you were made ridiculous.’ ”
He regretted having let Nawroz go, but there
was nothing to be done—as has been said, any-
one who overcomes his foe but allows the ad-
vantage to slip away will never again have
power over him, and regret and remorse profit
nothing.*3
1The story to which reference is made is that of the
owls and the ravens, on how best to deal with an im-
placable enemy (Nasrullah, Kalila u Dimna, 191–201).
In Husayn Va‘iz Kashifi’s late fifteenth-century setting
of these fables, it is the lead story in the chapter on “ob-
serving the situation of one’s enemies and never being
safe from their plots and deceitful tricks” (Anvar-i
Suhayli, 265–73). 
2Reading with Vassaf (Tarikh, 320), who quotes this
passage verbatim, اﳞﺎم for JTK’s ﭼﺮﻳﮏ.
3The text between asterisks (after text p. 1253 to here)
is omitted from JTAZ and JTRM.
The blessed breast of the Padishah of Islam
Ghazan Khan is expanded by the light of
faith as he and his amirs profess Islam in
the presence of Shaykhzada Sadruddin
Hamoë Juwayni—may his blessedness
endure forever.
When God has willed from all eternity to
make one of his servants felicitous and to sin-
gle him out for various favors, once the ele-
ments of that person’s being are intermingled,
a receptivity to felicity is kneaded and mixed
in his innate nature. The truth of this assertion
is confirmed by the prophetic dictum “Felici-
tous is he who is felicitous in his mother’s
womb.” After that, the nurturer of divine grace
raises him in the cradle with the hand of favor
and elevates him gradually through the stages
of perfection. With the passage of months he is
guided to look upon the actuality of things so
that he may contemplate forms and intrinsic
meanings and be informed of the truth and
falsehood of every thing. By means of this
power of discrimination and contemplation the
signs of felicity move from potentiality to actu-
ality, as does that which is required by divine
wisdom at the time of willing such felicity, in
accordance with the text of the Koran, “for the
command of God is a determinate decree.”4
By virtue of the foregoing, when divine favor
and will necessitated that the lassitude that had
invaded the Islamic nation with the vicissitudes
of months and years and the succession of days
and nights should be rectified by one of his
particular servants who would take over the
rule of towns and cities, it made Ghazan Khan
the happy recipient of the lights of right guid-
ance and divine inspiration. When he was with
his grandfather Arghun Khan in his early
youth, he was turned over to one or two
bakhshis, [1254] to whose path and beliefs he
4Kor. 33:38.
612
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

was amenable, and Arghun Khan ordered that
they should exert themselves to the utmost to
teach him and encourage him in acquiring their
customs. They were constantly in attendance
upon him and always encouraged him in their
beliefs. He was so intelligent and clever that in
a short time he had learned to perfection the
most obscure points of their teachings. Indeed,
he acquired such perfect mastery that he be-
came highly expert in the art of the bakhshi.
However, by virtue of divine influence, he
gazed into the mysteries of idolatry and con-
templated the truth of various religions and
communities with his piercing mind and un-
failing insight. Through the effulgence of in-
spiration, the rays of the light of the Muham-
madan religion shone upon his enlightened
mind, and inwardly he was inclined to the Na-
tion of the Truth, but he continued firmly and
steadfastly in his former path. In order to show
his fervor, he built lofty idol temples at
Khabushan in Khurasan, and he performed his
duties in such a way that all the bakhshis and
monks were astonished by his degree of asceti-
cism and rigor. Nonetheless, he was very seri-
ous in searching out God’s mysteries and as-
certaining the right way. 
When he came together with Baidu, and the
amirs were present for the pact and covenant,
the Muslims swore on the Koran, while the
Mongols swore on gold. In this regard Nawroz
said, “How would it be if the padishah of the
world were to strengthen the religion of Islam
with his own faith?” 
“This thought has been on my mind for a
long time,” he answered.
All of a sudden Nawroz took out a one-of-a-
kind polished ruby, bent his knee, and said,
“Although it is improper for a qarachu [com-
moner] to be so bold as to offer a beläg [gift]
to princes, will the kind padishah deign to keep
this beläg until your servant arrives back at
court?”
After that, when Nawroz and the other amirs
returned from Baidu unsuccessful, [1255] the
padishah grew angry and voiced a notion about
chastising him. Nawroz once again brought up
the topic, and the great Shaykhzada Sadruddin
Ibrahim, the son of Qutb al-awliya Shaykh
Sa‘duddin Hamoë,1 was present. He was usual-
ly in attendance upon the padishah, who con-
stantly asked him about the religion of Islam
and posed questions about fine points to him.
In accordance with the dictum “God expands
to embrace Islam the breast of him whom He
wishes to lead,” the descent of the sakina2 into
his blessed breast strengthened the light of
faith in his mind, a right guidance took control
of him. He said, “It is true that Islam is a very
strong and obvious religion. [A297] It em-
braces all religious and secular foundations.
The miracles of the Prophet are attractive, and
the traces of their soundness are obvious and
without suspicion on the pages of time. Conti-
nuity and close observance of its obligations,
supererogations, and strictures lead one to
God, while the worship of idols is sheer insuf-
ficiency and alien to reason and knowledge.
For a rational person to place his head down
before an inanimate object is utter ignorance
and stupidity, and to one who possesses spirit
and intelligence it appears horrible. It certainly
follows that no complete human being could
acquiesce in having others place their heads on
1Shaykh Sa‘duddin Hamoë (~ Hamawayh ~ Hamúya),
a well-known religious figure who died in 650/1253 and
was buried in Bahrabad. He was intimately associated
with Najmuddin Kubra, the eponymous founder of the
Kubrawiyya Order. See Jami, Nafahat, 428–30.
2The wordﺳﮑﻴﻨ
ـ ـــ
ﻪsakīna (a cognate to the post-Biblical
Hebrewשכינה) occurs several times in the Koran (2:248;
9:26, 40; 48:4, 18, 26). It is usually taken to mean a di-
vine aura of tranquility.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
613

the ground before him. In truth, the form of an
idol is worthy of being placed at the threshold
of a gate so that all who pass through may
tread on it. Also, the agreement of all people in
being Muslim and the rejection of idolatry are
not metaphorical.”
In short, Ghazan Khan, at the beginning of
Sha‘ban 694 [June 1295], together with all the
amirs, pronounced the profession of monothe-
ism in the presence of the great Shaykhzada
Sadruddin Ibrahim Hamoë, and they all be-
came Muslim. That month they gave banquets
and occupied themselves with religious acts.
[Ghazan Khan] rewarded all the sayyids,
imams, and shaykhs, giving them purses and
alms, [1256] and he issued strict orders for the
building of mosques, madrasas, khanaqahs,
and charitable institutions. When the month of
Ramadan came, he occupied himself with acts
of devotion in the company of imams and
shaykhs. 
It is obvious to all who have any intelligence
that the Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan’s con-
version to Islam was true, sincere, and free of
any taint of hypocrisy, for with all his might,
majesty, and dominion, compulsion was out of
the question, and given his lack of need and
necessity, hypocrisy was not a possible factor.
The Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan’s
imperial banners proceed toward Baidu a
second time, and his amirs surrender.
After Ghazan Khan pronounced the word of
monotheism and all the amirs followed him in
becoming Muslim, Baidu’s emissaries—one
Qutlughshah by name and the other Shaykhu’l-
Mashayikh Mahmud—arrived. They used all
their powers of eloquence, and Shaykh Mah-
mud took the opportunity to convey to Ghazan
messages from the amirs who were with Baidu
that they were supportive of Ghazan. Having
delivered this message and received gold seals
in reply, they were given leave to depart on the
third day. When Shaykh Mahmud returned and
delivered the gold seals to that group, they all
put their hopes in the Padishah of Islam’s vic-
tory and were unanimous in their support of
him. Since Sadruddin Zanjani had no expecta-
tions of Baidu’s being emperor because the
vizierate had been given to Jamaluddin Dastjir-
dani, and he was encouraging Taghachar to
rebel, [1257] they were wary of his machina-
tions. Having been amply rewarded, he was
given a patent and badge, and sent as governor
to Anatolia. When he set out and reached the
vicinity of Hashtrod, he sent his household and
retainers with Amir Yaghlaqu, who was accom-
panying him, to Tabriz while he himself pro-
ceeded unencumbered to Saraw on the pretext
of collecting on a loan. By that road he went to
Gilan. When he set out from Sughurluq headed
in the direction of Anatolia, he sent Mängli, his
old slave and confidant, to Qazwin to inform
his brother Qutbuddin of his plans. He too got
out of town on some pretext and headed for
Gilan, where he joined his brother, and the two
of them proceeded together to the court of
Ghazan Khan at Firozkoh. In the presence of
Amir Nawroz, who had recently come from
Khurasan, they delivered pleasing words pur-
portedly from the tongue of Taghachar. Since
Nawroz had mustered the army, a command
was given for all the soldiers to gather. This
took place in Shawwal.
Since Baidu was fearful and wary, he sent
Qutlughshah
back
with
insincere
words.
[A299] The Padishah of Islam was too clever
not to know that this was not free of treachery
and deceit. He ordered Qutlughshah stripped
naked and questioned while being beaten with
sticks and clubs. He revealed everything about
Baidu, his officers, his army, and his plans for
attack. “They sent me,” he said, “to find out
whether you were headed in that direction or
not.” Then an order was given for him to be
614
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

chained and imprisoned in the fortress of Us-
tunaband at Habalrod.
On Friday the 15th of Shawwal [August 28,
1295] the imperial banners proceeded to Rayy,
with the amirs Nawroz and Qutlughshah in the
vanguard. As was his custom, Nawroz started a
rumor [1258] of there being a plethora of sol-
diers. When the Padishah of Islam reached Ha-
balrod, Amir Chupan and Alinaq’s son Qu-
rumshi Gürägän were received at court, having
fled from Baidu. The Padishah of Islam was
delighted by their arrival and took it as a good
omen. He rewarded them amply and gave them
robes, hats, and jewel-studded belts.
From there they moved and camped at the
Qoha River, where they remained for a few
days. The amirs Chupan and Qurumshi said,
“If the Padishah of Islam rewards us, will will
serve valiantly and act in concert in the van-
guard with the great amirs Nawroz and Qut-
lughshah.” The emperor gave them permission,
and they joined the amirs. After that, the
Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan left Bulughan
Khatun there and set out after the amirs. When
he reached Aq Khwaja in Qazwin, Argha Bit-
igchi, the brother of Bughdai Akhtachi, came
from Nawroz and represented that the amirs
Taghachar and Bughdai had parted from Baidu
and were coming to the Padishah of Islam.
They joined Nawroz. The emperor set out from
there to Sujas, and from there Prince Kharban-
da and Prince Ildär arrived. When he came to
Bihistan on the banks of the Sapedrod, the
amirs Doladai Idächi and Hinduqur’s son El
Temür came to court with a group. From there
they marched and camped in Yüz Aghach in
Maragha, waiting for the amirs Nawroz and
Qutlughshah, who had gone out in pursuit of
Baidu
and
Tükäl
in
the
direction
of
Nakhichevan and the Araxes. After that he pro-
ceeded to Ujan. Amir Bayanchar came from
Nawroz and Qutlughshah, saying, “Baidu has
been seized and taken from the vicinity of
Nakhichevan to Tabriz. He says he has some
things to say to the emperor. What is com-
manded?” The emperor knew full well that he
had nothing of any consequence to say [1259]
and was only seeking a pretext. An order was
given that he not be brought to court; an end
could be put to him where he was. Baidu had
been taken out of Tabriz to the garden at
Naykash. On Wednesday the 23rd of Dhu’l-
Qa‘da 694 [October 4, 1295] he was put to
death there. 
An edict was given that all the bakhshis’
temples and houses of worship, as well as
Christian churches and Jewish synagogues,
were to be destroyed in Tabriz, Baghdad, and
other Islamic places, and for that victory most
of the people of Islam rendered thanks since
God had not seen fit to grant this wish to past
generations. 
After that, the Padishah of Islam set out for
Tabriz. Sadruddin Zanjani, who had gone to
the city to make arrangements, came out as far
as Kandraw to greet him. Since he wanted to
show off his position to the people, he made so
bold as to speak [to the emperor] while still
mounted on his horse. Amir Mulai, who was
the bodyguard of the day, told him twice that
such was not his privilege and that he should
not make so bold. Sadruddin paid no attention,
so Mulai struck him several times with his
whip and drove him away. For this and several
other reasons Sadruddin suffered a set-back.
On Wednesday the 23rd of Dhu’l-Qa‘da [Oc-
tober 4, 1295], the Padishah of Islam arrived in
the outskirts of Tabriz and settled with all mag-
nificence in the palace at Shamm. Elji’idäi
Qushchi, in accordance with imperial com-
mand, was executed without a trial. All he had
was given to Bulughan Khurasani. After that,
Nawruz and Qutlughshah arrived, and Bu-
lughan Khatun and the other ladies came from
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
615

Sughurluq and held banquets in the Adiliyya
kiosk. Qunchuqbal and Chechäk were put on
trial. Qunchuqbal was executed in expiation
for Aq Buqa’s blood. From there they proceed-
ed to Qara Tapa. Chechäk was beaten, and
Tödächü was set free. Amir Nurin was sent
with a troop to Khurasan [1260] and Mazan-
deran, and the emperor returned to Tabriz,
where a proclamation was made that everyone
should mind his own business and no one
should apply force to any other, they should
not stir up sedition and strife, and not a fraction
of a coin was to be given to anyone without au-
thorization by the gold seal. All the people re-
posed in the glory of the Padishah of Islam’s
justice, and all raised their voices in prayer for
his ever-increasing fortune. Untold alms were
given in thanks for “the world had languished
long without king or leader: now a worthy em-
peror has come to be its head.” From Tabriz,
Amir Mulai was sent to be governor of Di-
yarbekir and Diyar Rabi‘a. Amir Nawroz was
amply rewarded, and an edict was promulgated
that the vizierate of the entire ulus was to be
given to him. For the time being he was to re-
main in Tabriz, but when he had tended to the
affairs of the people, he should follow the em-
peror to Arran. On Monday the 6th of Dhu’l-
Hijja 694 [October 17, 1295] the emperor left
Tabriz to winter in Arran. While still in the
Tabriz vicinity he married Bulughan Khan. Al-
though his father Arghun Khan had known her
carnally, since they had joined under a differ-
ence of religion (the lady was a Muslim), this
marriage was legal. The marriage was celebrat-
ed under favorable auspices, and the customary
banquets were held. After that they proceeded
via Ahar
and
Peshkin
to
Mughan. They
camped in the vicinity of Abubakrabad in the
village of Pul-i-Khusraw. Two weeks later
Nawroz arrived, and all the ladies, princes,
amirs, ministers, and notables gathered at
Qarabagh in Arran [1261] and agreed unani-
mously that the Padishah of Islam should be
emperor. All gave möchälgäs [written pledges]
to that effect, and Sunday the 23rd of Dhu’l-
Hijja 694 [November 3, 1295], corresponding
to the 23rd of Toqsunch Ay of Qoyin Yil, was
chosen for his enthronement. Under a favor-
able ascendant the Padishah of Islam was seat-
ed on the throne, and all the ladies, princes,
and amirs knelt in their proper places, held
forth goblets, and pronounced congratulations
upon his blessed accession.
The Padishah of Islam begins to arrange
military and civil affairs after his glorious
accession.
After the celebrations and rejoicing, he
turned his attention to organizing and arrang-
ing affairs of state. On Wednesday the 30th of
Dhu’l-Hijja 694 [November 10, 1295] he sent
Amir Taghachar as commander and guardian
of Anatolia because he was a man who was
mercurial and it was best to have him as far
from court as possible. 
On Friday the 31st of Muharram 695 [De-
cember 9, 1295] envoys came from Khurasan
to report that the princes Dua and Qaidu’s son
Sarban had entered Khurasan and Mazanderan
on account of the absence of imperial troops
and begun to pillage. The Padishah of Islam
consulted with his commanders, and it was de-
cided that Prince Sögä [1262] and Amir
Nawroz would go there to repel them. Sögä
went to his tents, and no matter how many
times he was summoned to appear, he came up
with excuses for staying where he was. The
Padishah of Islam sent Horqudaq to bring him.
Sögä spoke seditiously in a drunken state and it
was reported to the imperial hearing, but the
emperor was too grave and noble to pay atten-
tion. When Sögä did finally appear at court, he
was received very warmly and assigned to
Khurasan. With him in the vanguard were sent
616
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

the tümän commanders Barula son of Khwaja
son of Yisa’ur Noyan of the Olqunu’ut tribe
and Arslan Oghul, who was a descendant of
Jochi Qasar. Nawroz and Horqudaq were sent
in the service of Prince Taichu Oghul. Hajji
Narin, Nawroz’s brother, and Satilmish, an old
liege man of his, were appointed as deputies.
They departed from the ordu on Friday the
21st of Safar [December 30, 1295]. On Mon-
day the 24th they set forth in the direction of
Persia. Suddenly news was received that Toqai
Gürägän, the commander of the Oyirat who
was in Diyarbekir and that region, had set out
for Syria with the amirs Yesütäi son of Tash
Mänggü Qushchi and Köktäi Bahadur, along
with their households and Oyirat hazaras.
Amir Mulai had mounted to repel them, but
they had defeated him and proceeded.
On the last day of Rabi‘ I [February 6, 1296]
news was received that Ildär had fled with
three hundred horsemen. Buqur’s son Shadi
and Eshik Tughli’s brother Inabeg had come
upon him with three thousand men and fought
a battle in which he was victorious. He tarried
for a time in the vicinity of Erzurum, but in the
end he was seized in a village. He was put to
death by Iqbal, son of Uruqtu, son of Elgäi
Noyan.
On Thursday the 20th of Rajab [May 24,
1296] Yesütäi, son of Tash Mänggü Qushchi,
who had stirred up trouble in Diyarbekir, was
put to death. 
On the 6th of Rabi‘ II [February 12, 1296]
Boralghi Qi[ya]tai Sükürchi, who had allied
himself with rebellious amirs at the end of
Arghun Khan’s reign [1263] and who had
meddled in seditious affairs ever since, was
executed. 
Sögä and Barula contemplate opposition;
the army sets out to deal with them; the
final outcome of that affair.
When Sögä and Barula set out from Arran,
they held council with many soldiers along the
way, saying, “They are sending us to Khurasan
in order to divide up our women and children
here and give them to the army of Khurasan.”
After consultation they agreed first to repel
Nawroz and then to attack the ordus and ele-
vate Sögä to the throne. This happened at
Kararod,
which
they
call
Türgän
Mürän.
Nawroz learned of this decision and attacked
Sögä in the morning. A pitched battle was
fought, during which Barula was killed. Sögä
took flight in the direction of Kharraqan and
Sawa. Horqudaq and a retinue of riders went
out in pursuit, caught him in the vicinity of
Kharraqan, and brought him to Markoy in
Rayy. Horqudaq said to Laodai’s son Sati,1
who was in agreement with him, “You kill
Sögä.” He went into a tent to kill him in the ac-
customed manner for princes, but Sögä pulled
a knife, stabbed Sati in the stomach, and killed
him. A liege man of Horqudaq’s named Bai
Temür ran in, grabbed the knife, and killed
Sögä. 
At that time the Padishah of Islam had left
Abubakrabad to hunt in Aq Baq. On the 8th of
Rabi‘ II [February 14, 1296] Satilmish Kälchi
came from Nawroz to report Sögä’s insurrec-
tion. [1264] The Padishah of Islam turned back
immediately and camped next to Mänggü
Temür’s bridge with the amirs Qutlughshah,
Satilmish, and Sö’ätäi in attendance. The next
morning he dispatched men to arrest Qonqur-
tai’s son Esän Temür and Barula’s brother Qu-
rumshi for having taken part in Sögä’s in-
surrection. After a trial Esän Temür, who was
the vanguard of the Mongol expeditionary
1Arends reads these names as Сати сыну Лаодая.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
617

force and his amir-ordu, and Qurumshi were
executed. The amirs Qutlughshah, Chupan,
Satilmish, Sö’ätäi, and Elbasmish gathered the
soldiers, and during the yasamishi [muster]
Amir Mulai arrived from Khurasan with news
that Nawroz had killed Sögä and Barula, that
Amir Nurin had seized Chechäk and Doladai
in Khurasan, and that everything was all right.
Most of the enemies had been vanquished, and
those who remained had made Arslan Oghul
their chief and come to Bilasawar, whence they
had gone to Saray Mansuriyya and Deh Baqi
and camped. The Padishah of Islam immedi-
ately ordered the amirs Chupan, Sülämish, Qu-
rumshi, Toghrilcha, Taitaq, and Elbasmish to
mount and repel them. They clashed in the
vicinity of Baylaqan, and a fierce battle was
fought. The amirs who were with Arslan
Oghul—Tüläk, the cousin of Ujan the amir-
silah, and Eshik Tughli’s son Inabeg from the
Jalayir, Taichu Bahadur’s son Ghazan, Musa
Tarkhan, and Narin Ahmad’s son Sergis—held
sway that day. From among our soldiers
Toghrilcha was so severely wounded that he
almost fell. Alinaq’s son Qurumshi saved him,
and Horqudaq and Barim, with two thousand
men, went to help our soldiers.
The next day they made a concerted stand,
and [the enemy’s] soldiers submitted without a
fight, and their officers retreated. Horqudaq re-
turned, captured Sergis, and took him to the
ordu. [1265] The others amirs went after those
who had fled. They captured Tüläk and
brought him in. He was executed together with
Sergis. 
On Wednesday the 23rd of Jumada I 695
[March 29, 1296] Arslan Oghul was captured,
brought in, and killed. Taichu Bahadur’s son
Ghazan was executed after him. During those
days Sadruddin Zanjani was seized, and the
taxes that Jamaluddin Dastjirdani had assessed
him were demanded. Bulughan Khatun pro-
tected him, and through her intercession he
was saved and transferred to her baggage train.
On Thursday the 7th of Jumada II [April 12,
1296] the Padishah of Islam mounted to visit
Pir Ibrahim, and two days later he dismounted
at his ordus. He sent Amir Horqudaq to be
chief officer of Fars to supervise fiscal affairs
and collect taxes.
That year there had been war between Toqta,
the padishah of the Ulus Qipchaq, and Noqai,
the son of Tatar. Noqai had been killed, and his
people had scattered. Noqai’s wife Chabui
Khatun and his youngest son Büri came to the
Padishah of Islam to seek his support in re-
venge for Noqai’s blood. In his supreme com-
passion, the Padishah of Islam gave them con-
dolences and assuaged their wrath. 
On the eve of Wednesday the 26th of Rajab
[May 30, 1296], the Padishah of Islam gave his
sister Öljäi Temür, who had previously been
Tükäl’s wife, to Amir Qutlughshah. 
Since Taghachar had been the cause of much
unrest and strife, and since the Padishah of Is-
lam wanted to eliminate completely all causes
for sedition, he sent Amir Kharmanchi to Ana-
tolia that winter so that, together with Baltu,
Arab, and the amirs of the Anatolian army, he
could placate Taghachar and then, when an op-
portunity was at hand, execute him in private.
Although the Padishah of Islam was loathe to
have him killed, he issued the order in the best
interests of the state. In this regard he said to
his close associates, [1266] “In olden times
there were two kings at war with each other in
Cathay. One of them was beaten and his army
was scattered. The victorious army went out in
pursuit of the defeated for several days. An of-
ficer who discovered the defeated king had
compassion on him and wanted to save him be-
cause he was so helpless and miserable. He
came across a well in that region and said,
“Get into this well so that our soldiers won’t
618
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

see you.’ When the troop arrived, because it
was a sandy desert and the wind was blowing
and effacing all tracks, they couldn’t find their
way. ‘His tracks are gone,’ the amir said, ‘and
there is no telling which way he has gone. No
matter how hard we search, we won’t be able
to find him. It would be better for us to turn
back.’ When they had gone, the king came out
of the well and went to his own land, where lit-
tle by little he gathered an army and then came
out again to fight. This time, he defeated and
killed the king who had been victorious the
time before and took over his kingdom. He
covered the officer to whom he owed his life
with special favors and took him into his
closest confidence, assigning him to the high-
est office and making him his absolute deputy.
One day, one of the officers said to the king,
‘This person did not recognize his obligations
to his king. Not only was he unfaithful to him
but he also caused his death and brought about
your rule. How can he be left alive? It will not
be long before he contemplates the same
treachery with you.’ The king, being extremely
clever, listened to this person’s words and mo-
tioned for the officer’s execution. The officer
cried out, ‘You owe me your life!’ The king
wept and said, ‘You are right, and I am in no
way pleased to put you to death. However, in
the best interests of the state and throne there is
no alternative: it is imperative that you be
killed.’ The king did have him killed, but he
wept. 
“Such things are necessary for keeping regal
affairs under control, and no matter how diffi-
cult it is for me to have someone killed, [1267]
in the interests of maintaining affairs both
great and small, if executions are not carried
out it is impossible to rule.”
At the beginning of spring the Padishah of
Islam set out from Bilasawar for the capital
Tabriz, where he dismounted under favorable
auspices at the palace in Shamm.
On the 27th of Rajab [May 31, 1296] Inabeg
was seized and brought to Tabriz. On Saturday
the 29th he was executed in the public square. 
On Wednesday the 10th of Sha‘ban [June 13,
1296] Amir Aladu arrived from Khurasan and
reported on affairs there. The Padishah of Is-
lam left Tabriz for the meadow at Sayin, which
was between Saraw and Ardabil. On Wednes-
day the 17th of Sha‘ban [June 20, 1296] a
quriltai was begun at that yurt, and it ended on
the 19th. 
The affairs of Nurin Aqa; Nawroz’s plot
against him, and the beginning of Nawroz’s
downfall.
Nurin Aqa, who was from the Qiyat tribes,
held a high position of trust and confidence
with the Padishah of Islam, and he was power-
ful
in
Khurasan
and
Mazanderan.
Amir
Nawroz’s brother Oyiratai was a liege man to
him, but because of his own exalted lineage
Nurin did not treat Oyiratai with much respect.
Oyiratai complained of this treatment to his
brother. This resulted in a quarrel. After that,
when Nawroz arrived in Khurasan, he blamed
Nurin for the dominance of the enemy, and he
spoke harshly of him both in his hearing and
behind his back. When they met in Jurjan, they
thoroughly despised each other. Prince Taichu
arrived from Tamisha. Out of wrath Nawroz
boldly said, “I was ordered to ask Nurin [1268]
how he managed to allow the enemy to enter
this territory so easily. Now, in the presence of
Prince Taichu, I ask him.” All were offended
by his conduct and chastised him. This was the
first crack in Nawroz’s power, and it was on
account of his stubbornness and obstinacy. 
From there they proceeded to Khabushan,
where a review of troops was held. A messen-
ger arrived from the scouting party saying that
the enemy had been spotted in the meadows of
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
619

Radkan. Nawroz mounted, but when it was in-
vestigated, the news was found to be false.
Then he consulted with the officers in Mash-
had at Tus, saying, “I intend to raid as far as
the borders of Herat with four thousand horse-
men in order to inform myself of the enemy’s
situation. On the 17th of Rajab [May 21, 1296]
he set out on this campaign. He dispatched
Prince Taichu and Amir Nurin to Radkan. On
the 25th of Rajab [May 29] Amir Nawroz came
back to Prince Taichu’s ordu without having
accomplished anything. “I heard,” he said,
“that my wife was ill. I will go to the Padishah
of Islam. You see to ordering the army until I
arrive.” And immediately he set out for Azer-
baijan, neglecting the affairs of Khurasan and
the army. The miscreants the padishah had sent
with him to be the vanguard of the army in bat-
tle all set out after Nawroz. When Nawroz left,
the soldiers of Khurasan concocted rumors
every day and dispersed until they were all
gone. A hazara amir named Olsum1 fled with
four hundred men and went to his home yurt in
the vicinity of Ardabil. When Amir Nawroz
heard of his flight while in Sharuyaz, he
mounted in the vicinity of Saraw without in-
forming the Padishah of Islam, went to [the
amir’s] tents, and harassed them. The Padishah
of Islam was angered by his return and sent a
messenger to tell him to go back. Nawroz said,
“My wife, Princess Toghan, is ill. How can I
go back without having seen her?” This refusal
also caused anger. [1269]
On the 21st of Sha‘ban 695 [June 24, 1296]
he reached the Padishah of Islam at Sayin, and
he was received warmly and favorably. The
Padishah of Islam then went to Ujan, and on
Monday the 29th of Sha‘ban [July 2] he mar-
ried Eshil Khatun. When Qutlughshah and the

other amirs perceived that the padishah was
angry with Nawroz, they said that sending him
to Khurasan had not been a good move and
that he should be investigated since “one can
deduce from his countenance features of sedi-
tion and corruption.” However, since the ex-
panse of the Padishah of Islam’s heart was as
endless as the ocean and his clemency was too
great to be described, he said, “Although your
words are true, I nonetheless cannot allow my-
self to break my word or go counter to an
oath.”
On Wednesday the first of Ramadan [July 3,
1296] Nawroz was ordered back to Khurasan,
accompanied by Nizamuddin Yahya as his
deputy. When he reached Khurasan, the sons of
Toqtai Yarghuchi made a secret assassination
attempt on Amir Nawroz in retaliation for their
father’s blood. Nawroz became afraid of them,
and just at that time his wife, Toghan, passed
away, and Nawroz’s affairs began to decline.
However, he kept up a brave front and contin-
ued to strive.
On the 8th of Ramadan [July 10] the
Padishah of Islam stopped on the banks of
Na’ur Dul on the Tabriz Road, and there he
laid the foundation of an imperial garden and
pavilion. During that time the sultan of Mardin
arrived, presenting abundant tribute in cash
and jewels. He withdrew having been show-
ered in favor.
On the 13th of Shawwal [August 14, 1296]
Husamuddin Lur was killed in Hashtrod. 
On the 26th [August 27] the anniversary of
the death of Dondi, Alafrang’s mother, was
observed.
On the 8th of Dhu’l-Qa‘da [September 7,
1296] Baighut, the son of Chormaghun’s son
Shirämün Noyan, was executed at Se Gumbad.
The Padishah of Islam arrived in Maragha
and went to the observatory, where the sci-
entists gave a banquet. That same day a letter
620
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

written by Qonqurtai’s son Ildär to Baltu
[1270] urging him to rebel was shown to the
padishah. He immediately ordered a decamp-
ing, returned to the ordus, and arrested Ildär.
After his crime was proven he was killed.
The imperial banners head for Baghdad;
Afrasiab the Lur, Jamaluddin Dastjirdani,
and Mawlana Izzuddin Muzaffar Shirazi
are executed; the birth of Princess Öljäi
Qutlugh.
On Tuesday the 18th of Dhu’l-Qa‘da 695
[September 17, 1296] the imperial banners de-
parted Maragha for winter quarters in Baghdad
via Hamadan.
On the 24th of the month [September 23]
Nurin
Aqa
arrived
from
Khurasan.
The
Padishah of Islam received him warmly and
showed him favor. 
Taishi’s1 son Baltu had been in Anatolia since
Abaqa Khan’s reign, and there he had gained
great power. Samaghar Noyan had died, and
his son Arab was still a child, and therefore
Baltu’s strength and power had increased. No
matter how often the Padishah of Islam sum-
moned him, he made excuses not to come. Af-
ter Taghachar was executed, his power and ar-
rogance went beyond all bounds, and the name
of rebel was attached to him. His opposition
was reported in the year 696, and accordingly
Amir Qutlughshah and three divisions of sol-
diers set out for Anatolia to repel him. Baltu
took flight and sat in ambush behind a moun-
tain. Amir Qutlughshah went in pursuit with
Sülämish, Arab, Boroltai Oghul, and Abishqa,
with Abishqa in the vanguard. When he
reached the mountain, Baltu sprang from am-
bush, and there were wounded on both sides.
[1271] Then Amir Qutlughshah arrived in the

Mala[t]ya plain, and with one charge Baltu was

for

reached

On the 8th of Dhu’l-[Hijja2] 695 [October 7,
1296] a one-month halt was observed, and the
maliks of Persian came to court, performed
their business, and withdrew.
Horqudaq returned from tax-gathering in
Fars, and he brought back with him Atabeg
Afrasiab the Lur, who had received favor and
was returning home. When he arrived at court,
the padishah inquired after the state of Fars.
“First,” he said, “I will report on this Tajik.
When I was going to Fars I passed through Lur
territory, but he did not show his face. From
Shiraz I sent an agent to collect the tribute
from Koh Giluya, but his people made trouble
for him and said, ‘We took this land by the
sword, and its taxes have fallen at [our] feet.
We do not speak of the sedition of time, the
killing of Baidu the shahna of Isfahan, the
leading of the army to Isfahan, the seizing of
Firozan, or other such actions of ours.” The
Padishah of Islam flew into a rage and ordered
that Afrasiab be executed.
When they reached the vicinity of Deh Sa-
pandan,3 Shaykh Mahmud and Sadruddin Zan-
jani enticed a group to inform on Jamaluddin
Dastjirdani, and on he 28th of Dhu’l-Hijja 695
[October 27, 1296] a trial was held and he was
put to death. 
From there the Prince of the World made
Kharbanda his locum tenens and sent him to

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
