Khurasan. Also around that time Izzuddin
Muzaffar, a nephew of the Amid of Fars, in-
formed on the governor of Fars, Shaykh Jamal
Ibrahim Sawamili, [1272] with Sadruddin Zan-
jani assisting him. Even though no act of
treachery could be proven against him, he was
executed.
From there he moved out, and on Wednesday
the 14th of Safar 696 [December 12, 1296] he
arrived safely in Baghdad, stopping in the out-
er pavilion called Muthanna. Several days later
he went out hunting in the direction of Nayl,
Nu‘maniyya, and Sib Wahla as far as the
blessed shrine of Sidi Abu’l-Wafa. After twen-
ty-four
days
he
returned
and
stopped
at
Marzubaniyya.
On the 9th of Rabi‘ II [February 4, 1297] he
mounted for a hunt in the direction of Hit and
Anbar, stopping after eight days in Muhawwal,
where he visited the holy Kazimiyya shrine
and the grave of the great Imam Abu-Hanifa
Kufi. On Friday he attended the congregational
prayer in the mosque at Suq al-Sultan. On
Thursday the 4th of Jumada I [February 28] he
set out for the return. 
On Thursday the 18th of Jumada
I 696
[March 14, 1297] Princess Öljäi Qutlugh was
born in Shahraban. 
The story of Qaysar, Amir Nawroz’s slave;
Nawroz’s sons and brothers are executed
and his fortunes are completely reversed;
Nawroz is killed at Herat.
On Wednesday the 17th of Jumada I 696
[March 13, 1297] Alamuddin Qaysar, Naw-
roz’s messenger, was arrested in Baghdad.
Shaykh Mahmud sent his brother Sulayman to
inform the court of this incident, which came
about as follows. 
During Baidu’s time Nawroz wanted [1273]
to overthrow him and get the throne of the
khanate for the Padishah of Islam Ghazan
Khan so that by means of this good service his
offenses might be totally forgotten. Since it
could not be brought about merely by money
and numbers of troops, he sent the above-men-
tioned Qaysar, who had been a slave to Bagh-
dad merchants and had traveled to Syria and
Egypt, on a mission to the padishah of Egypt to
say, “Baidu is an infidel and we are Muslims.
Together we must remove him.” By the time
Qaysar brought back the answer, Baidu had al-
ready been vanquished, the kingship had de-
volved upon the Padishah of Islam, and
Nawroz had attained the pinnacle of success,
and therefore he did not consider it politic to
report the situation to the emperor. He ordered
Jamaluddin Dastjirdani, who was [the emper-
or’s] deputy, to write a letter appropriate to the
time, and a fair copy was made in an unknown
hand and submitted to the court. As ordered, he
encouraged Qaysar and sent him back. At the
time of Jamal Dastjirdani’s trial this affair was
reckoned
among
his
offenses.
Fakhruddin
Rumi, who was an attendant of Amir Na’uldar,
the shahna of Baghdad, knew this Qaysar and
was aware of the letter. He spoke of it to Amir
Na’uldar, who reported it. It was ordered that
Fakhruddin Rumi go to Baghdad and make an
inquiry into Qaysar’s affairs. When Nawroz
was leaving for Khurasan, since he knew that
he was out of favor with the Padishah of Islam,
he sent Sadruddin, the son of the Shaykhu’l-Is-
lam of Herat, whom he trusted, to court to be
in attendance to look after his interests during
his absence. This Sadruddin also knew of the
sending of Qaysar, and he let slip a word or
two concerning Nawroz’s friendship with the
sultan of Egypt to one of his acquaintances.
That person carried the story to the Shaykhu’l-
Mashayikh Mahmud, [1274] and together they
reported it to court. The padishah encouraged
the Shaykhzada Sadruddin and, promising him
many good things to put his mind at ease, sent
him to Baghdad to undertake an investigation
622
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

of Qaysar and find out whether he had come
from Khurasan or not. 
Sadruddin went from Hashtrod to Baghdad
by post horse and came back to the Padishah of
Islam at Chamchamal to report that Qaysar had
not come yet. An order was given for Sadrud-
din to go back to Baghdad and get hold of
Qaysar. When he went there, Qaysar had
arrived with three liege men and was going to
set out within the week. He and two of his
liege men came to Sadruddin’s house in friend-
ship, and Sadruddin informed the counselor.
He laced two plates of halva with knock-out
potions and sent them to the shaykhzada to
give to his guests. Qaysar and his liege men ate
it all and fell unconscious on the spot. That
friend had been waiting with a group of his
liege men for this opportunity: they attacked
the house, captured Qaysar and his liege men,
and tied them up.
Sadruddin Zanjani, who had only recently
become vizier, was constantly on the look-out
for an opportunity to undermine Nawroz.The
reason for this was that in the beginning, when
he was expecting to be made vizier, Nawroz
had named Jamal Dastjirdani as his own
deputy, and from that time on there was hostili-
ty and enmity because he was out of a job. In
this affair he and his brother Qutbuddin found
the opportunity they were looking for: miracu-
lously they wrote six letters, purportedly from
Nawroz, to the amirs of Egypt and Syria. The
contents of the letters were as follows: “The
padishah, thank God, is a Muslim, but when I
want to propagate the religion of Islam, the
amirs prevent it. It is hoped that together we
may undertake to repel them in a manner that
would be pleasing to the religious law and to
reason. I myself have written to my brothers
Lagzi and Hajji telling them that if they can
gather troops before we unite, they should do
it. Otherwise we will do it ourselves. [1275] I
will occupy the territory of Iran and turn it
over to you. I have sent several suits of cloth-
ing by the hand of Qaysar, the bearer.” These
forged letters they stashed, along with seven-
teen suits of clothing, in Qaysar’s baggage.
Then
Sadruddin
wrote
a
letter
in
Amir
Nawroz’s name to Hajji Narin, to whom he
went and offered a toast. While [Hajji Narin]
was unaware, he placed the letter in his qab-
turqai [satchel] and left. Shaykh Mahmud then
sent his brother Sulayman to court to report the
situation. 
The Padishah of Islam turned back from the
field in the vicinity of Kirmanshahan and rode
to Shahraban in one day, a distance of thirty
leagues. On Sunday the 21st of Jumada
I
[March
17,
1297]
Shaykh
Mahmud
and
Sadruddin Zanjani’s brother Qutbuddin escort-
ed Qaysar into Shahraban and reported his
condition. The Padishah of Islam said, “Report
it correctly.” Qaysar reported in such a way
that no fault was reflected upon Nawroz. Then
they asked for his bags, and the clothing and
letters were taken out. All together gave testi-
mony that the writing was that of Hajji Ra-
mazan, Nawroz’s secretary. The Padishah of
Islam ordered Qaysar and the liege man to be
beaten to death with cudgels. Shaykhzada
Sadruddin undertook to produce the other two
liege men, and for that purpose he went to
Baghdad, but it was impossible for him to
seize them. When he was unable to produce
them, he too was killed. This provoked the
Padishah of Islam’s rage to burst out in tongues
of flame that scorched everything as he said,
“When information is gained on his secrets,
before the appearance of traces of treachery
and subterfuge, all precaution must be taken.”
An edict was issued for Amir Nurin and
Bayanchar to arrest and execute the entirety of
Nawroz’s people, sons, servants, and follow-
ers. 
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
623

From there the imperial banners decamped to
Haruniyya. Hajji was about to mount when
Bayanchar [1276] arrived and arrested him and
drove his khaylkhana in another direction. Pri-
or to this Satilmish, Nawroz’s deputy, his son
Qutlugh Temür, and Nawroz’s son Ordu Buqa
were executed. Hajji Narin was brought to the
meadow at Khanaqin, and Amir Nurin put him
on trial. After establishing his guilt by produc-
ing Sadruddin’s letter from his satchel, he was
stripped naked, paraded around the tents, and
executed, and his tents and flocks were plun-
dered. His twelve-year-old son Taghai fled and
took refuge in the tent of Amir Injil, who was
the amir-ordu of the great lady Bulughan
Khurasani. There he was protected for a time
until the padishah’s wrath should subside.
Thereafter he petitioned and was pardoned,
and at present he is an attendant upon the
flocks and herds of Amir Husayn Gürägän. His
people
were
given
to
Bulughan
Khatun
Khurasani. Kamal Küchik, his deputy, was
killed. Lagzi was put to death on the 7th of Ju-
mada II [April 2, 1297] in the square in May-
dasht. Nawroz’s nephew Güshlüg and his
brother Yol Qutlugh were handed over for
blood retaliation. Because of this victory the
great square was named Qutlugh Maydan.
Edicts were dispatched to all territories for all
his relatives and followers to be executed. Hin-
duqur’s sons Shidun1 and El Buqa were killed
in the vicinity of Qasr-i-Shirin. 
On Tuesday the 20th of Rajab [May 14,
1297] Prince Kharbanda arrived at court in Be-
sutun. On the 5th of Sha‘ban [May 29, 1297]
Amir
Qutlughshah
arrived
in
Asadabad,
Hamadan from Mughan. After that Amir Chu-
pan and Pulad Qaya arrived from Rayy. An or-
der was given for Pulad Qaya to go to

Khurasan to arrest Nawroz and join Horqudaq
and Amir Sö’ätäi. Two days later Amir Qut-
lughshah was also dispatched. Qutlugh Qaya
was also sent on their heels. [1277]
Around the beginning of Sha‘ban, Sülämish
and Arab seized Taishi’s son Baltu, who had
rebelled, in Anatolia and brought him to
Tabriz. The Padishah of Islam moved from
Asadabad to summer pastures in Ala Tagh, and
in the vicinity of Kararod the Prince of the
World Kharbanda was dispatched to guard the
territory of Khurasan. When he reached Naw-
shahr, messengers brought the good news from
Qutlughshah that Nawroz had done battle and
been defeated, and Borolcha Kükältash had
brought Toghanchuq. The story is as follows. 
When Amir Qutlughshah reached the vicinity
of Damghan, Horqudaq and Sö’ätäi had killed
Nawroz’s shahnas who were in Rayy, Varamin,
Simnan, Damghan, and Bistam. When they
reached Isfarayin, Buqa Temür’s and Alghu’s
sons joined them seeking vengeance for their
father’s blood from Nawroz. During those days
one of Nawroz’s amir-hazaras named Danish-
mand submitted. Amir Qutlughshah sent him
forth as his vanguard, and Iratai Qazan went to
Nishapur to inform Nawroz of the approach of
the army. Nawroz decamped from there and
met face to face with Danishmand Bahadur’s
forces at the post station. Battle ensued, and al-
though Danishmand’s soldiers were few in
number, Nawroz was defeated and fled with a
few men. The next morning his baggage and
treasury
fell
into
his
opponents’
hands.
Horqudaq, ___2 Yarghuchi’s sons, and a divi-
sion of soldiers proceeded in all haste in his
tracks. That night Nawroz reached his herds in
Jam, and he dismounted among his herds, or-
dering his liege men to lie in ambush behind

the walls. At midnight the army arrived. They
wanted to rustle the horses, but Nawroz and his
liege men sprang from ambush shooting ar-
rows. Many were killed and disabled. Nawroz
retreated, and the soldiers of this side emerged
as Nawroz fled in rout. When he reached the
gates of Herat, [1278] Shamsuddin Kurt’s son
Fakhruddin invited him into the city. As
Nawroz was contemplating this, his amirs
Babakr, Sarban, and Sadum said, “Amir, we do
not trust this man. It would be better to pass on
in safety from this walled trap and not have to
rely on his word.”
“I have missed three days of prayers,”
Nawroz replied. “I want to make them up.”
The amirs left to save themselves. Nawroz and
four hundred horsemen entered the city and
went into the citadel. 
When
Amir
Qutlughshah,
who
was
in
pursuit, reached Mashhad in Tus, he visited the
shrine, where he performed two cycles of
prayer, prostrated himself, and said, “O God, I
do not know whether I am right or wrong in
this. Both we opponents are Muslims. You
alone know all secrets. If you know that
Nawroz is at fault and has foolishly rebelled
against Ghazan Khan, make him fall prisoner
into my hands.” Then he mounted, and when
he reached Herat his solders surrounded the
city and battle broke out. The amirs Turghai1
and Chamchai fought hard. The next day Amir
Qutlughshah ordered ladders placed against the
ramparts and fire hurled into the city, but this
led to nothing. Nawroz came out onto the ram-
parts and watched as his soldiers were fighting.
The weather was extremely hot, and many
said, “It would be better for us to pull back
since the Herat ramparts are very strong, and it
will not be easy for Nawroz’s opponent to pre-
vail.” Amir Qutlughshah was highly offended
1According to Arends, Нурагай.
and said, “Our opponent has become weak and
mean, and the walls are left without guard.
How can we pull back? What excuse could we
offer the emperor? Let us be brave and strive
so that, with divine assistance, we may have an
unexpected victory.”
He ordered the Shaykhu’l-Islam of Jam, who
was an attendant of the amir and whose son-in-
law Malik Fakhruddin was, to write a letter to
the malik saying, “You must do something to
remedy this situation; otherwise, Herat and the
whole realm of Khurasan will be lost over this
affair.” [1279] When it was signed by the amir,
it was smuggled into the city by a spy. Once
the amir had read it, he took it to Nawroz, who
said confidentially to his trusted elite, “By this
act it is clear that the malik is true to me.” 
Hajji Ramazan said privately to Nawroz, “It
would be best for us to seize Malik Fakhruddin
and put him in chains. When everything is
over, if we win, we can set him free with hon-
or; if not, they can take charge of him. We at
least will have taken every precautionary
measure.”
Nawroz did not accept this suggestion. An
officer from Seistan was eavesdropping, and
he immediately conveyed the news to the ma-
lik. The malik took fright, held council with the
leaders and nobles of the city, and said, “In the
end Ghazan Khan’s soldiers will storm the city
and take our women and children prisoner, and
thus a house of so many years will fall.
Nawroz swore an oath to Ghazan that he would
never rebel against him, but he has. It would be
best for us to defend ourselves and seize him
by stratagem and trickery. Let us make a show
of submitting and get a writ of amnesty from
Amir Qutlughshah, and then we can turn him
over.” 
The people of the city said, “Let whatever
the malik thinks best be done.”
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
625

After putting this plan into action, the malik
went to Nawroz and said, “The soldiers of Her-
at and Ghor are not performing well in battle.
To remedy this, set two of your own soldiers
over every ten of them in order to encourage
them in battle and not let them flag.” In com-
pliance with this suggestion Nawroz distrib-
uted his men among the others, remaining
alone in the citadel himself. The malik then or-
dered his soldiers to seize all of Nawroz’s men
and hold them in chains while he and several
brave Ghoris went into the citadel, [1280]
seized Nawroz, and bound him tightly. “It has
been ordered,” he said, “that we turn you over
to Amir Qutlughshah.”
It is one of the amazing quirks of fate that
during the reign of his father, Malik Shamsud-
din Kurt, this same Malik Fakhruddin was so
undutiful, headstrong, and rebellious that Ma-
lik Shamsuddin imprisoned him in Khaysar
fortress. After he had been held for seven
years, Nawroz came and entreated the father
for his release. Shamsuddin had said, “I know
what kind of person he is. He is faithless and
treacherous. After failing to keep faith with his
father, he will not keep faith with you.” Naw-
roz, however, continued to intercede on his be-
half and insisted. The malik said, “I will re-
lease him on one condition, that you give me a
written statement taking responsibility for any-
thing he does henceforth.” Nawroz wrote such
an undertaking and had him released. 
Now, as he was being taken, he said, “I did
not do ill by you that you should thirst after my
blood. If there is absolutely no other way, give
me my gray horse and my sword so that I can
ride bareback into the fray and be killed in bat-
tle. Then I will be both a warrior and a martyr.”
“Henceforth,” the malik replied, “you will
see horse and sword under the thighs and in the
grasp of others.”
When he had seized him, he beheaded Hajji
Ramazan and sent the head with a messenger
to Amir Qutlughshah
informing
him
that
Nawroz, his brothers, and his liege men had
been captured. Then he requested a writ of
amnesty and a solemn promise that the amir
would intercede with Ghazan Khan on his and
the Heratis’ behalf and not seek retaliation. 
The messenger threw the head before Amir
Qutlughshah and said, “The malik submits and
says that by the amir’s great good fortune vic-
tory has been achieved. Nawroz and his liege
men are taken prisoner and are being held in
chains.” When the amir saw Hajji Ramazan’s
head, [1281] he realized that the words were
true, and he ordered Khwaja Ala’uddin Khata’i
to write a writ of amnesty as the Heratis had
requested. On the top of it he wrote an oath
and sent Amir Pulad Qaya, Khwaja Ala’uddin,
and the Shaykhu’l-Islam of Jam to convey it to
the city. The malik met them with all honor and
then sent them back, saying, “By night I will
send Nawroz, hands bound, to the amir.” They
returned and reported. That night the malik
sent Nawroz with a troop of Ghori officers.
Qutlughshah rejoiced greatly over this victory
and asked him, “Why did you do it?”
“Ghazan can put me on trial,” he replied,
“but not you.” After that, no matter what they
asked him, he gave no answer because he
knew he had committed no crime. 
Amir Qutlughshah ordered him pulled down
and cut in two. His head was sent to court with
Pulad Qaya, and from there it was sent to
Baghdad, where for several years it was on a
pole at the Nubi Gate. His brothers Arghun
Hajji and Bolduq were also killed there. This
took place on the 23rd of Shawwal 696 [Au-
gust 14, 1297].
Sadruddin Zanjani’s station is elevated
through the killing of Amir Nawroz; the
imperial banners come from Ala Tagh to
626

Tabriz; a magnificent palace is constructed
in Shamm-i-Tabriz.
After Nawroz was killed, Amir Qutlughshah
decamped from the gates of Herat and went to
the meadow at Shuran. Nawroz’s amirs Buran-
char, Alanchaq, Tükäl Qara, [1282] and some
others were killed, but Qarasun escaped to
Amir Qutlughshah. The Padishah of Islam de-
camped from Ala Tagh and reached Tabriz on
Friday the 24th of Dhu’l-Qa‘da1 [September
13, 1297]. The next day Baltu and his son were
executed in the public square in Tabriz.
With the killing of Nawroz, Sadruddin’s for-
tunes rose: he was shown favor by the padi-
shah and entrusted with the al tamgha. 
On the first of Dhu’l-Hijja [September 20] he
went from Shamm into Tabriz and was present
at the Friday prayer in the congregational
mosque. He gave untold amounts to the poor
and unfortunate, and he did the same the fol-
lowing Friday. 
On Saturday the 16th of Dhu’l-Hijja 696
[October 5] he laid the foundation for a lofty
dome in Shamm in the midst of the Adiliyya
Garden. He took a great interest in the project,
and constantly visited the master builders and
workmen. When the structure of the sardab
had been raised above ground level, the archi-
tects asked him in how many places they
should place skylights for lighting. “What
for?” he asked. “For illuminating the below-
ground level,” they said. He answered, “The il-
lumination of there should be brought from
here; otherwise, the accidental brightness of
the sun in that place does no one any good.”2

should be Dhu’l-Qa‘da.

On Monday the 18th of Dhu’l-Hijja [October
7, 1297] Qutlughshah Noyan arrived from
Khurasan.
In the middle of Muharram 697 [November
2, 1297] the emperor bound a turban with all
the amirs, and the next day they gave a ban-
quet.
On Friday the 20th of Muharram [November
7], after performing the prayer, he set out from
Tabriz for winter quarters in Arran. There was
news of disturbances in Georgia. Amir Qut-
lughshah was dispatched there to subdue the
province, and he quickly returned, bringing
Malik Daud’s brother with him. He was shown
favor and allowed to return. 
The imperial banners set out in the direction
of Baku, and several days later they camped.
[1283]
On Friday the 9th of Rabi‘ II 697 [January
24, 1298] Prince Khitai Oghul died in Dalan
Na’ur.
On the 9th of Jumada I 697 [February 22,
1298] Prince Alchu was born in Dalan Na’ur,
and many days were spent in celebration and
banqueting. 
Sadruddin Zanjani falls from grace and is
executed.
On Friday the 13th of Jumada II 697 [March
28,
1298]
Sayyid
Qutbuddin
Shirazi
and
Mu‘inuddin Khurasani knelt before the emper-
or and reported Sadruddin Zanjani’s embezzle-
ment of state funds. Now, most of the time
there had been friendship between the author
of this book, Rashid the physician, and Sadrud-
din, but a group of divan chiefs had tried to
create a rift between us by conveying all sorts
of stories, but [the emperor] paid no attention
to them. When they despaired of me, they went
to Sadruddin and angered him with their nasti-
ness. When little attention was paid to that,
Sadruddin knelt before the emperor on the 15th
of Jumada II [March 30] to denounce me, and I
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
627

began to answer him. The padishah, however,
shouted at him and said, “He has never report-
ed your words to me.” Then I began to speak,
but the padishah said, “Do not sully your
tongue by answering him. Maintain your digni-
ty.” Sadruddin realized my innocence and be-
came very angry with the group who had slan-
dered me.
On Sunday the last of Jumada II [April 14],
Taichu Oghul and his comrades were seized on
the banks of the Qara Küdäri on account of
sedition, and the shaykh who was in attendance
upon him and who had promised him the king-
ship suddenly [1284] reported the situation to
the padishah’s hearing. On the 2nd of Rajab
[April 15] Taichu Oghul and four of his com-
rades were executed on the banks of the canal
that had been newly dug in the vicinity of
Dalan Na’ur. The padishah crossed the water
and camped in the ordus at the new canal.
While the padishah was in Dalan Na’ur,
Amir Qutlughshah returned from Georgia and
rebuked Sadruddin over the tribute from there.
Sadruddin became afraid of him and reported
that Qutlughshah’s men had ruined Georgia,
and for that reason the padishah rebuked Qut-
lughshah both in drunkenness and in sobriety.
The amir asked Sadruddin if he knew who had
complained of him to the emperor. Sadruddin
replied, “It was Rashid the physician, on
Nawroz.” Amir Qutlughshah left the emperor’s
presence, and we chanced to meet. “We have
been together in one käshik, and nothing has
ever come between us to cause anger. Why
have you attacked me before the padishah?”
“I have received no injury from you that
would cause me to attack you,” I replied. “You
must tell me who has conveyed these words to
the emperor. Otherwise, I will report it my-
self.” When he refused to tell me, I reported it
during a hunt.
The padishah summoned the amir and said,
“My son, tell me the truth. Who told you this?”
“Sadruddin,” he said.
The Padishah of Islam was greatly vexed and
said, “Although I have desired this man to give
up his tricks and seditious ways, there seems to
be no remedy, for his very nature is molded in
this fashion.” 
On Wednesday the 17th of Rajab [April 30]
Sadruddin was put on trial. He fearlessly gave
unanswerable responses and made no attempt
to curry favor with the inquisitors. If they had
given him an opportunity to speak, he would
have been able to save himself from certain
disaster, but the padishah ordered Qutlughshah
to put an end to Sadruddin. At midmorning on
Sunday the 21st of Rajab 697 [May 4, 1298] at
the Jandar canal, Amir Sö’ätäi took one of his
arms, Pahlavan Malik Ghori took the other,
and Amir Qutlughshah cut him in two. God
only knows how much effort he had put into
aggrandizing himself and how much discontent
and strife he had stirred up. In the end, when
he got what he wanted, he derived no enjoy-
ment from it. 
From there the imperial banners proceeded to
Bilasawar and then stage by stage until they
arrived in Tabriz on Saturday the 12th of
Sha‘ban [May 25].
On Monday the 21st of Sha‘ban [June 3]
Qazi Qutbuddin and his nephew Qawamul-
mulk were executed at the Varjuna Gate in
Tabriz. Their relative Qazi Zaynuddin escaped
from the Tabriz prison by night and made his
way to Gilan. He came back two or three years
later, but he fled again. This time he was cap-
tured and killed.
On Sunday the 10th of Shawwal 697 [July
21, 1298] the common people of Tabriz rose up
and destroyed all the remaining churches and
synagogues. The Padishah of Islam was angry
and had some of the instigators executed. 
628
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

On Monday the 9th of Dhu’l-Qa‘da [August
18, 1298] Su’unchaq Noyan’s son Sarban died
in Tabriz. 
On the 25th of Dhu’l-Qa‘da [September 3,
1298] Boroltai Oghul of Jochi Qasar’s progeny
died. [1285]
The imperial banners proceed from the
capital Tabriz to winter quarters in
Baghdad; the office of the vizierate is
conferred upon Khwaja Sa‘duddin; news is
received of Sülämish’s rebellion, and troops
are dispatched to deal with him.
On Thursday the 3rd of Dhu’l-Hijja 697
[September 11, 1298] the imperial entourage
set out from Tabriz via Ujan for winter quarters
in Baghdad. The office of the vizierate was
conferred upon Khwaja Sa‘duddin, whose loy-
alty had been shown by his constant atten-
dance. Amir Nurin was dispatched to Arran to
guard Derbent.
On Friday the 2nd of Muharram 698 [Octo-
ber 10, 1298] the emperor dismounted in
Marghzarak in the Hamadan vicinity. In the re-
gion of Burujird, Abubakr Dadqabadi, the gov-
ernor of Hamadan, was executed after his guilt
was proven. 
Traveling through the Kurdish mountains,
the emperor stopped in the Juqin meadow in
the vicinity of Wasit on Saturday the 22nd of
Safar [November 29]. Passing through Bata’ih
Sib, he entered Wasit. During that time news of
Sülämish’s revolt was constantly being re-
ceived from Anatolia. The background is as
follows.
When
Baltu
was
executed,
the
Padishah of Islam assigned the emirate of Ana-
tolia to the amirs Bayanchar, Buchqur, Qur-
temürdad, and Sülämish, himself the chief offi-
cer of the army of Anatolia. They deposed Sul-
tan Mahmud on a charge of having collaborat-
ed with Baltu and gave the sultanate to his
nephew Ala’uddin Kayqubad, son of Faramarz,
and he went to Anatolia with the aforemen-
tioned officers. [1287]
That winter the cold was extreme, and huge
amounts of snow fell, blocking the roads and
cutting off routes of communication. A rumor
was started that the ordu was in turmoil. For
these reasons Sülämish joined with Iqbal,
Tashtemür, and a group of officers. Without
warning he seized Bayanchar and Buchqur,
killed them, and began his rebellion. He invit-
ed soldiers from all parts of Syria and the fron-
tiers, and he brought into submission the sol-
diers that were stationed in Danishmand’s
territory in the Qazawa plain. He also gathered
innumerable rabble and gave away the tax
money and property of the territory to the army
until he had assembled nearly fifty thousand
horsemen. The Syrians contracted to supply
twenty thousand. He gave the title of amir to
some and awarded them sanjaqs [banners] and
naqara [the privilege of drums]. Since the
roads were blocked and emissaries and mes-
sengers could not get through from this side,
his conceit increased. When the news reached
the imperial hearing of the Padishah of Islam,
Ghazan Khan, on Sunday the 12th of Jumada I
698 [February 15, 1299] Amir Chupan went
forward in the vanguard, and after Amir Qut-
lughshah was dispatched Amir Sö’ätäi with an
army. In the spring the two armies met in the
Aqshahr plain in Erzinjan. On the 24th of Ra-
jab [April 27], after a battle, Sülämish was de-
feated and fled toward Syria. The amirs cap-
tured him and brought him in. 
The Padishah of Islam decamped from Juqin,
headed for Baghdad, and on Saturday the 21st
of Jumada I [February 24] he set out from
Shahr-i-Nil for the shrine of the Commander of
the Faithful Ali, which he visited and the in-
habitants of which he rewarded with bounteous
gifts. [1288]
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN

On Wednesday the 29th of Jumada I [March
4] a group of Syrian and Egyptian officers,
Sayfuddin Qipchaq, Sayfuddin Begtemür, El-
begi, and Azar, who had fallen out with the
ruler of Egypt, Lachin, arrived with three
hundred horsemen. At Ra’s al-‘Ayn they had
heard the news of Lachin’s death and repented
of their action, but since there was nothing to
be done they came on. They gave reports of all
sorts and every description.
On the 3rd of Jumada II [March 8, 1299] the
Padishah of Islam dismounted in Baghdad. On
Thursday the 15th of the month [March 20] he
mounted and left Baghdad, headed for May-
dan. One of the Egyptians who had submitted,
Bolar, fled with a troop, and soldiers were sent
in pursuit. Most of the Syrians were killed, and
seven were taken prisoner. Only Bolar escaped
by himself and got away.
Around the beginning of Sha‘ban 698 [May
4, 1299] a hazara of Qara’unas led by a man
named Buqa, which had been stationed in the
Tarum vicinity, took flight to Persia, passing
through Yazd and Kirman, plundering as they
went. At Bini-i-Gav they joined the Negüdäris.
On Saturday the 14th of Sha‘ban [May 17]
Yaghlaqu Sükürchi arrived from Anatolia with
the
good
news
that
Amir
Chupan
and
Bashghurd had defeated Sülämish, who had
taken flight with a few men. All the troops he
had
commanded
had
surrendered.
Alghu,
Elji’idäi Qushchi’s brother who had gone with
him, had been killed. Iqbal, the son of Elgäi
Noyan’s son Uruqtu Noyan, and Tashtemür
Khita’i had been captured and brought in. The
Padishah of Islam had camped at Quchin-i-
Buzurg in the vicinity of Sughurluq. At Qurban
Shirä, Nurin Aqa had returned from Arran.
On the 25th of Sha‘ban [May 28, 1299] the
imperial banners stopped in Ujan, and the
Prince of the World Kharbanda arrived from
Khurasan. The brothers were glad to see each
other again, and a quriltai and banquets were
commenced. [1289] When the quriltai was
over, Iqbal was executed on the 28th of
Sha‘ban [May 31]. On Wednesday the 24th of
Ramadan [June 25] the Anatolian officers
Kärzä, Charkas, and Esän, who had joined
Sülämish, were executed.
On Thursday the 16th of Shawwal 698 [July
17, 1299] the Padishah of Islam married
Kärämün Khatun, the daughter of Abatai Noy-
an’s son Qutlugh Temür, and a wedding ban-
quet was held with six hundred thousand __1 as
dowry. He installed her in the great ordu in
Doquz Khatun’s place. 
Around the beginning of Dhu’l-Hijja the em-
peror ordered that Prince Kharbanda should re-
turn to Khurasan to keep that province from
falling into turmoil. 
On Friday the 14th of Dhu’l-Hijja [Septem-
ber 12] the imperial banners arrived in Tabriz.
The captured Sülämish was brought from Ana-
tolia. On Tuesday the 29th of Dhu’l-Hijja [Sep-
tember 27] he was killed in a hideous fashion
in the public square in Tabriz. His body was
burned and his ashes scattered to the wind.
The padishah was slightly discomfited by
symptoms of ophthalmia. In order to ward off
the evil eye, the people burned wild rue and
prayed.
The Padishah of Islam goes out in the
direction of Syria and Egypt to do battle
with the Egyptians; they are defeated, and
the province of Syria is conquered.
Not long after the Padishah of Islam had
arrived under good auspices in Tabriz, emis-
saries arrived one after the other from Anatolia
and Diyarbekir with news that the Syrians had
come out to the frontier of their land and were
making raids, practicing banditry, burning
crops, and harassing the people. They had sur-

630
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

rounded Mardin and taken many Muslims pris-
oner. [1290] During the month of Ramadan
they had engaged in abominations with the
daughters of Muslims in mosques, and some
had even drunk wine. The very citadel of
Mardin was not safe from their evil. They had
pillaged all the rest of the cities of the area, and
from there they were approaching in this direc-
tion, repeating their despicable deeds. At Ra’s
al-‘Ayn they had wanted to continue what they
were doing, but the people there were coura-
geous soldiers. [The Syrians] had fought with
them in the narrow lanes and were unable to
achieve a victory, but everything they found
outside the city, animals and everything else,
they carried away. Those they had taken pris-
oner were sold for high prices in Aleppo as an
act of gratitude. When this news reached the
emperor’s hearing, out of zealousness for the
religion of Islam he flared up in anger and
swore to repel the evil of these rebels. After
obtaining a fatwa from the ulema that it was a
necessary act to repel them from the Muslim
lands held by the Padishah of Islam, he com-
manded that his soldiers be assembled, and he
dispatched his officers, as he thought best, to
the right and left. 
The imperial banners moved from Tabriz for
Syria on Friday the 19th of Muharram 699
[October 16, 1299], and the next day they set
out from the outskirts of the city in the direc-
tion of Maragha. From Dehkhwaraqan, Nurin
Aqa was sent back to Arran. On the 10th of Sa-
far [November 6] the Zab River was crossed,
and camp was made opposite the Kushaf
fortress. On Tuesday the 14th of Safar [No-
vember 10] the emperor mounted under good
auspices under the sign of Pisces, and the
ladies who had escorted him out bade him
farewell at Mosul and turned back. 
On Monday the 27th [November 23, 1299]
he dispatched Qutlughshah Noyan in the van-
guard, and on Tuesday the 12th of Rabi‘ I [De-
cember 7] he crossed the Euphrates under fa-
vorable auspices opposite the fortress of Ja‘bar
and [1291] Siffin.1 Good news of the rebels
arrived—that they had fallen out amongst
themselves. On Sunday the 17th of Rabi‘ I
[December 12] the imperial banners arrived in
Aleppo. From there they moved out along the
road until they came to a field. The soldiers re-
joiced, saying, “We will have grain to feed the
horses.” But the padishah turned his reins away
and passed beside the field, saying, “Anyone
who lets his horse feed on this or any other
grain will be executed, for it is not lawful to
give people’s food to animals.” 
On Tuesday the 19th of Safar [November 15,
1299] they arrived in the vicinity of Sarmin.
Moghultai Idächi and his Qipchaq liege men
took flight. On Monday the 25th of Rabi‘ I
[December 20, 1299] he passed by the city of
Hama
and
camped
opposite
the
city
of
Salamiyya. There a band of rebels appeared,
but the Padishah of Islam saw that his troops
were unprepared for battle. He mounted him-
self with a group of champions to inspect the
battlefield and learn of the enemy. Then he or-
dered it announced in the camp that the enemy
had arrived. All the soldiers starting to work
getting their arms ready for battle. After that,
Amir Chupan turned around and said, “It is not
the enemy. The reason for the announcement
was so that when we approach the enemy you
will be awake and aware.” When they were
ready for battle and standing prepared, he re-
connoitered and realized that [the enemy] had
assumed exactly the same array they had dur-
ing Mänggü Temür’s time and taken up a good
1The fortress of Ja‘bar, formerly known as Qal‘at
Dawshar, lay five leagues from the town of Balis, which
was on the Euphrates, and five leagues from al-Raqqa.
Opposite Ja‘bar was the “land of Siffin” (Abu’l-Fida,

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN

position to put this side at a disadvantage.
Then, wondering how he could spoil their
arrangement, he saw that it would be best not
to make a head-on attack. Therefore he ordered
a shift to his left, which [would be opposite]
their right.
On Wednesday the 27th of Rabi‘ I [Decem-
ber 22, 1299] he ordered encampment made
beside a small river three leagues from Homs.
[1292] Then he ordered three days’ worth of
water drawn and entered the desert in order to
take them from the rear. They would be forced
to go in that direction, and thus the array they
had taken up would be ruined. As his men got
busy drawing water, the Egyptians thought the
Mongol army was moving aside before with-
drawing. Although the battle had been set for
Thursday,
they,
imagining
a
withdrawal,
mounted on Wednesday and came opposite.
When the Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan was
apprised of the approach of the enemy, he
prayed two cycles of prayer with the army,
mounted, and faced the foe with as many sol-
ders as he had. In command of the first section
of the right wing was Amir Mulai, and behind
him was Amirzada Satalmish; behind him was
Amir Qutlughshah; behind him were Yaman
and Märtäd,1 each with his own division; and
in the center was the Padishah of Islam, stand-
ing like a mountain of glory in the forefront of
the center, with the Amirs Chupan and Sultan
Chupan to the right and Sultan to the left,
while in the right of the center was Toghrilcha
son of Achu Sükürchi; behind the great center
was Eyü Oghlanan. Behind him was Elbasmish
with his division; behind him was Chechäk;
behind him was Alinaq’s son Qurumshi. Last
1There are massive variants of the first name. The vo-
calization of the second is highly uncertain. Arends
reads them as Яман и Муртад.
of all was Kör Buqa Bahadur commanding the
flank. 
Before the armies were completely mounted
and arrayed for battle, the Syrians were relying
so heavily on their superior numbers that they
didn’t realize they had “put their foot on a
snake’s tail and their hand on a thorn.” Qut-
lughshah Noyan ordered the battle drums to be
beaten. The Egyptians, thinking the padishah
was in that rank, launched an attack in that di-
rection. Thousands upon thousand poured in,
broke the rank, and unhorsed champions. A
large number of the amir’s men were wounded
or killed. Amir Qutlughshah and a troop of
horsemen joined the emperor, and the Egyp-
tians,
exactly
in
the
manner
of
Mänggü
Temür’s time, [1293] had put Isa Muhanna in
an ambush with five thousand Arab horsemen
to one side. The Padishah of Islam realized this
and ordered Kör Buqa to hold the rear of the
army with five thousand Mongol horsemen.
Then, during battle, the Arab army sprang their
ambush: Kör Buqa rushed at them and scat-
tered them all. The Padishah of Islam cried out
“from the right side of the valley,”2 “Fear not!
Thou hast escaped from unjust people.”3 With
that, untold strength was generated in his
blessed being, and, roaring like an enraged
lion, he broke the army’s lines and overthrew
their champions with blows of his lance. Then
he cried out to the army to come down, and
they, firing arrows, remounted and charged.
Battle raged from midmorning till evening, and
in the end the Egyptians were vanquished and
fled in rout. 
After the battle Abishqa arrived from Anato-
lia, accompanied by the Tekvur of Sis4 with

five thousand men. The Padishah of Islam
went after the Egyptians slowly until he
stopped above Homs, one league from the
town. The people of the city of Homs surren-
dered.
On Sunday the 2nd of Rabi‘ II [December 27,
1299] the treasury of the sultan of Egypt was
carried off and distributed among the officers,
and most of them were garbed in the sultan’s
fine garments. 
The next day he decamped for Damascus,
and messengers were dispatched to Tabriz and
all corners of the empire with the good news of
victory. On Thursday the 6th of Rabi‘ II [De-
cember 31] the nobles and grandees of Damas-
cus came out to greet him, to offer their surren-
der, and to request a shahna. Qutlugh Qaya
was appointed to the office of shahna.
On the 9th of Rabi‘ II [January 3, 1300] he
camped in the Rahit meadow below Damascus,
and all the people of the city came to take
refuge in the shade of his graciousness. The
Padishah of Islam asked them, “Who am I?”
[1294]
“You are Shah Ghazan, son of Arghun Khan,
son of Abaqa Khan, son of Hülägü Khan, son
of Tolui Khan, son of Genghis Khan,” they
said. 
After that he asked, “Who was Nasir’s
father?”
“Alfi,” they replied.
“And who was Alfi’s father?” he asked.
All fell silent as they realized that those peo-
ple had gained the sultanate by accident, not by
merit, and they were all slaves of the renowned
urugh of the Padishah of Islam’s ancestor. 
“There is nothing good among those of you
who are alive,” said the Padishah of Islam,
ﺲ ــﺳﻴﻮر ـ ـﺗﮑ(probably correct). Sīs is the modern Osmaniye,
directly west of Adana and north of Iskenderun in

“but among your dead there is much good. I
forgive the crimes of you ignorant people for
the sake of your dead.” With this the people of
Damascus rejoiced and took heart as they
prayed for his success. 
On the 12th of Rabi‘ II [January 6] he went
on a tour of the fields, and when he found the
earth to be extremely fertile, he knew that it
should be protected. He stationed a troop of
guards at Bab Tuma to keep the soldiers from
harassing the citizens, and he ordered the other
seven city gates kept shut and the soldiers not
to enter the orchards or to wreak havoc. The
emirate of Damascus he gave to Qipchaq, who
had previously been amir there and then sub-
mitted. The office of shahna went to Qutlugh
Qaya, while authority in fiscal affairs and the
guardianship went, as before, to Fakhruddin
Ibn al-Shirji and Sayyid Zaynuddin, and he or-
dered that they conduct themselves according
to custom. If they had any business to conduct,
they should consult the viziers of court. The
sultan’s functionaries who were there, like the
scribes of the treasury and the scribes of the
army, etc., were all rewarded and maintained in
their offices. 
The amirs said, “So long as the defenders of
the citadel do not surrender, the citizens will
not trust us. It would be best for us to plunder
the city.” All the amirs were unanimous on this
point, and therefore all the people of the city
became
greatly
distressed.
[1295]
The
Padishah of Islam had mercy, however, and did
not approve the suggestion, ordering instead
that no one was to harass or bother any of the
citizens. He also commanded that absolutely
no amir or soldier who wanted to enter the city
was to be allowed in without having obtained a
specific written pass from the divan. 
On Tuesday the 18th of the month [January
12, 1300], because they had been ordered to
scour the orchards for limbs that could be used
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
633

in catapults for taking the citadel, a group of
kötälchis
[grooms]—Armenians,
Georgians,
and apostates1—invaded Jabal al-Salihiyya,
where they killed, pillaged, and took captives.
The Padishah of Islam was enraged and imme-
diately ordered Araghi the son of Ket Buqa’s
son Qonchi to go there to protect the people
and to execute those who had plundered. When
he got there the soldiers had already wrought
their devastation and dispersed. Thereafter the
houses of the Georgians and Armenians were
searched, and those they had taken captive
were released.
On Saturday the 29th of Rabi‘ II [January 23,
1300] Amir Mulai, who had pursued the routed
enemy as far as Gaza, returned. Since the
weather was turning hot, the padishah paid no
attention to the people of the citadel, who were
being disobedient to Egypt. On Saturday the
13th of Jumada I [February 5] he withdrew
from Damascus, stationing Amir Qutlughshah
and Amir Chupan there to protect the city until
spring came, at which time they would come.
Amir Mulai was ordered to remain there over
the summer with a large contingent of soldiers.
Nasiruddin Yahya was assigned as a liege man
to Qipchaq. Begtemür and Elbegi, who had
come to court, were both appointed to suitable
posts. In the end, however, they and Qipchaq
forgot their obligations to the Padishah of Is-
lam and put forth various rumors that caused
Amir Mulai and his men to pull back. 
In short, on Wednesday the 24th of Jumada I
[February 16, 1300], the Padishah of Islam
crossed the Euphrates [1296] opposite the
fortress of Ja‘bar on an island of his own de-
vising consisting of kalaks [rafts] made of tree
bark tied together with rope. That same day he

rejoined his urugh. Sultan Yesavul, who had
gone to Gaza, arrived. He joined the ladies in
the vicinity of Sinjar. Envoys arrived from Kir-
man to report the rebellion of Mahmudshah
and his henchmen, the killing of Mawlana
Fakhruddin the cadi of Herat and his sons, and
the trouble they had stirred up. 
On Tuesday the 15th of Jumada II [March 8,
1300] he reached Mosul. On Sunday the 5th of
Rajab [March 27] Qutlughshah arrived from
Syria to report the rebellion of Qipchaq and his
liege men. On the first of Sha‘ban [April 22]
the Padishah of Islam crossed the Tigris. On
the 17th of Sha‘ban [May 8] Amir Mulai
arrived from Damascus. On the [2]9th of
Sha‘ban [May 20] Amir Nurin, Chechäk, and
Toghan, who had returned from Arran, joined
the court in the vicinity of Darband-i-Zangi.
On Saturday the 15th of Ramadan [June 4] the
imperial banners stopped in Maragha, and the
emperor inspected the entire place at a leisure-
ly pace and inquired about everything. The dif-
ficulties notwithstanding, he understood most
of the minutiae and ordered an observatory
constructed next to the lofty dome and the
charitable institutions. It was to serve several
purposes, and he explained the purposes in de-
tail in such a way that the scientists present
marveled at his power of deduction, for no
such undertaking had ever been made. The sci-
entists said, “To build such a thing would be
virtually impossible.” However, he taught them
and guided them in such a way that they tried
out the theory and brought it to completion in
accordance with his instructions. They and all
the expert architects were in agreement that no
one had ever built or dreamt of such a thing.
From there he decamped and went to Ujan.
[1297] On Tuesday the 24th of Shawwal [July
13] a quriltai was commenced. Upon its con-
clusion, on Saturday the 3rd of Dhu’l-Hijja 699
[August 20, 1300], Prince Alchu died in Ujan.
634
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

His coffin was taken to the Lofty Dome in
Tabriz.
On the 6th of Dhu’l-Hijja [August 23] Prince
Kharbanda was given permission to withdraw
to Khurasan, and the emperor himself set out
auspiciously for the capital, Tabriz. Every day
he went up on the lofty-domed edifice. 
The Padishah of Islam goes to Syria a
second time.
When autumn came, the Padishah of Islam
set out once again for Syria. On Monday the
first of Muharram 700 [September 16, 1300]
Amir Qutlughshah and a numerous army
moved forth in the vanguard, and the imperial
banners set forth from Tabriz on the 15th [Sep-
tember 30]. On the 3rd of Safar [October 18]
Nurin Aqa was sent back from Jaghatu to Ar-
ran. On the 4th of Rabi‘ I [November 17] the
emperor reached Mosul under favorable aus-
pices, and there jirghamishi [revelry] was held
for several days. In the vicinity of Abu-Miri he
mounted from the ordu and dispatched the
amirs Chupan and Mulai in the vanguard. 
Toghanshah
Khatun,
the
daughter
of
Mubarakshah, died in the vicinity of Sinjar on
the 6th of Rabi‘ II [December 19, 1300], and
the ladies who had come out to bid farewell
turned back in the vicinity of Ra’s al-‘Ayn. 
On the 12th of Rabi‘ II [December 25] Shin-
qa arrived from the army to say, “Our yäzäk
[commanded by] Qabartu clashed with a few
horsemen under Güshlüg, their vanguard, and
one of their officers was killed.”
On the 7th of Safar [October 22, 1300] the
Padishah of Islam crossed the Euphrates oppo-
site Ja‘bar and Siffin. On Tuesday the 21st of
Safar [November 5] he dismounted above Hab-
ul near Aleppo. Qabartu Bahadur arrived, hav-
ing brought several captured Syrian soldiers.
[1298] On the 27th an alarm was given that the
enemy had arrived. An order was given for the
soldiers to mount at once, but it was later as-
certained that the news was false, and all
dismounted. 
On the 5th of Jumada I [January 16, 1301]
they passed by Aleppo and camped at Ribat
Wasihi next to the Quwayq River, the river on
which the city of Aleppo is situated. 
On the 7th of the month [January 18] they
camped opposite Qinnisrin. Since there was no
news of the enemy, and the sultan of Egypt had
been too afraid to come out, the Padishah of Is-
lam had mercy on the territory of Muslims and
went forward. He ordered Qutlughshah to stop
with his soldiers in Sarmin. That winter much
rain fell, and by coincidence Amir Sö’ätäi and
some of the army of Amir Shiba’uchi, who had
come from Anatolia, camped in a bad spot.
Without warning a heavy rain came, and it
turned very cold. So much mud was produced
that the two amirs could not join each other,
and many of their animals perished in the mud
and cold. The padishah dispatched Amir Mulai
with a division of the army to get them and
their animals out. When he arrived there he
was able to extract himself only with much
difficulty.
The padishah turned back on the 22nd of Ju-
mada I [February 2, 1301], passed opposite the
city of Raqqa over a bridge that had been con-
structed, and visited the shrine of Ammar b.
Yasir and the martyrs of Siffin.1
On Saturday the 15th of Jumada II [February
25, 1301] he joined the ladies and ordus at
Chahar Taq below Sinjar. 
Amirzada Satalmish, son of Boralghi and rel-
ative of Altachu Aqa, had died in the vicinity
of Kushaf on the last day of Rabi‘ II [January
12, 1301]. The padishah was greatly saddened
by the news of his death. 
1‘Ammār ibn Yāsir, a companion of the Prophet and
partisan of Ali ibn Abi-Talib who was killed at the Battle
of Siffin, A.H. 37/A.D. 657. See The Encyclopaedia of Is-
lam (1960) 1:448.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
635

On Thursday the 11th of Rajab [March 22,
1301] Sultan Yesavul arrived from Syria. On
the 15th of Rajab [March 26] Amir Qut-
lughshah also came back. Several days were
spent in revelry, celebration, and hunting. One
day the Padishah of Islam was chasing an ante-
lope and shot an arrow. [1299] It appeared that
the arrow had missed, but suddenly the ante-
lope fell. All those in attendance inspected it
closely. There were nine wounds on the ante-
lope from the arrow, and when everyone had
looked at it, they realized how the nine wounds
had come about. The arrow was one the Mon-
gols call tona: the shaft has three feathers, and
it is extremely sharp. When the antelope was in
the air and all four of its legs were together, the
arrow had pierced all four legs and wounded
them. From there it had passed into the chest,
belly, and under the armpits, every feather
making a lengthwise wound. Then it went into
the neck and throat, producing two more
wounds. In this way it made nine wounds in
all. This affair recalled the story of Bahram
Gor, who had stitched an antelope’s leg to its
ear with an arrow. People had marveled at that
feat and recorded it on walls and in inscriptions
for fifteen hundred years, but it was completely
forgotten. More than two thousand people wit-
nessed this feat.
On Wednesday the 23rd of Sha‘ban [May 3,
1301] emissaries arrived from Toqtai, the
padishah of the Ulus Jochi. They were admit-
ted to court, but they soon withdrew.
On Wednesday the last of Sha‘ban [May 10,
1301] the Tigris was crossed. Along the way
Kurds who had committed various atrocities
were ordered seized, and many of them were
killed. 
On the 24th of Ramadan [June 2, 1301] the
emperor reached the City of Islam, Ujan.1
1The epithet of Ujan, the “City of Islam” (shahr-i is-
Khwaja Sa‘duddin Sahib-Divan receives
favor, and his rivals are executed.
When the Padishah of Islam returned auspi-
ciously from his expedition to Syria, he
stopped in the City of Islam Ujan. On the 27th
of Dhu’l-Qa‘da 700 [August 3, 1301] [1300]
he granted Khwaja Sa‘duddin great favor, en-
trusted the red seal to him, and turned over the
office of divan chief to him. 
On the first of Dhu’l-Hijja [August 7, 1301]
the marriage of Qutlughshah Noyan to El Qut-
lugh, Gaikhatu’s daughter, was held. 
At
those
summer
quarters
a
group
of
courtiers and divan chiefs like Sayin Qazi,
Shaykh Mahmud, Sayyid Qutbuddin Injü Shi-
razi, and others had held council on eliminat-
ing the khwajas, and they were lying in wait
for an opportunity. During one session at
which the padishah was drinking wine and
talking about the amirs, Sayyid Qutbuddin Shi-
razi was present and said, “Basmish is a man
of good conduct.” The padishah said, “You
think well of him because you went to Shiraz
together, and he was the means whereby you
prospered and made a great fortune.” Then he
added, “You are constantly in search of sedi-
tion and evil.”
Qutbuddin replied in drunkenness, “The
padishah is too kind. One would think he was
present at our council.”
The padishah had guessed what they were up
to and ordered Shaykh Mahmud put under
guard that very night. The next morning Sayin
Qazi, Sayyid Qutbuddin, Mu‘inuddin Khura-
sani, Aminuddin Idächi, and Sa‘duddin Habash
were seized and put on trial. After seven days
Aminuddin was let go, and after ten days
Sa‘duddin Habash was released since those
two were innocent. On Monday the 23rd of
Dhu’l-Hijja [August 29, 1301] Qazi Sayin,
lām) as the seat of the “Padishah of Islam.”

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Sayyid Qutbuddin, and Mu‘inuddin were exe-
cuted at Dul. On Wednesday the middle of
Muharram 701 [September 20, 1301] Shaykh
Mahmud
was
released
through
Bulughan
Khatun’s intercession. The Padishah of Islam
was extremely clement and did not desire to
harm any creature. If a fly fell into his food he
would carefully pick it out with his own hand
[1301] so that its wings would not be damaged.
Then he would hold it until it regained its
strength and let it fly away. He used to say, “It
is more difficult for me to kill an innocent fly
than a guilty man, for to leave a seditious per-
son alive leads to great harm, particularly in
matters of state.” 
The Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan goes to
Ala Tagh, and from there he proceeds via
Nakhichevan to winter quarters in Arran;
the emissaries who had gone to Egypt
arrive.
On Wednesday the middle of Muharram 701
[September 20, 1301] the imperial banners set
forth for Ala Tagh. On the 21st of the month
[September 26] Qutlughshah Noyan set forth
with an army in the direction of Maragha,
headed for Diyarbekir. 
On Thursday the 2nd of Safar [October 7]
the Padishah of Islam dismounted at the palace
in Ala Tagh. On Sunday the 2nd of Rabi‘ I
[November 5] he set out from Ala Tagh for Ar-
ran via Nakhichevan. An order was given for
Amir Qutlughshah to return from Diyarbekir.
On Monday the 16th of Rabi‘ II [December
19] Qazi Kamaluddin Mawsili and Ali Khwaja,
who had gone on an embassy to Egypt, arrived.
Since the ordus had camped in the yurt at
Qarabagh in Arran, the Padishah of Islam did
not stay there long and mounted to go hunting
for several days in the mountains of Shirvan
and Lagzistan. From there he headed off to
hunt swans in the direction of Gavbari, where
he remained for a while catching birds and
fish. From there he went to a gulf1 the padishah
named Qush Qoyun. The whole sea shore
there, as far as ___,2 is where cranes and other
waterfowl go for the summer after returning
from the winter. [1302] When the imperial
banners reached that area, which is near Der-
bent, Toqta, the padishah of the Ulus Jochi,
pulled back, and his princes and amirs who
were near here, suspecting that the world-con-
quering banners were headed in that direction,
withdrew and crossed the great rivers. After a
while, however, they stopped when the reality
turned out to be other than what they had sus-
pected, and once again merchants began to
come and go. 
At that time all the amirs of Lagzistan, who
had long been rebellious and hiding in the
forbidding mountains, came and surrendered
voluntarily. Some thieving rabble that had
come from Azerbaijan and taken refuge in
those mountains, from where they committed
highway robbery, were caught and killed. 
Returning from that area, the emperor re-
joined the ordus at Bilasawar and went out
hunting in Talishan and Ispahbad. He ordered
two walls constructed of tree trunks and
branches for a one-day’s distance between the
mountains in such a way that the two walls
would extend a one-day’s distance in the shape
of a cone and gradually come within fifty yards
of each other. At the mouth something like a
corral was made of wood. After that, the sol-
diers created a hunting circle, and the animals
were driven between the walls so that all
would be gathered in the corral—wild oxen,
jür [deer], antelopes, wild asses, jackals, foxes,
wolves, bears, and other wild animals and

PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
637

beasts. When they were between the walls with
no exit, they all necessarily went into the cor-
ral, and the Padishah of Islam and Bulughan
Khatun sat in a pavilion constructed of wood in
the midst and watched the animals. [1303]
Some were shot and others were released. 
Decamping from there, the emperor proceed-
ed from station to station, sightseeing, until he
reached Tabriz. All the inhabitants, men and
women, young and old alike, lifted their hands
in voluntary prayer and loosened their tongues
in praise of the ruler. The people of Tabriz,
along with the ulema of Islam, came out to per-
form
the
rituals
of
welcoming,
and
the
Padishah of Islam showed them great favor
and beneficence by exempting them from un-
warranted taxes and impositions.
The Padishah of Islam hosts a general
banquet in the Golden Ordu in the garden
at Ujan; a recitation of the Koran is made,
and he makes general charity.
The Padishah of Islam had previously given
an order to the master craftsmen to construct a
golden tent and a golden throne with appropri-
ate appurtenances. For three years many peo-
ple had worked on it. When the emperor
arrived in Tabriz this time, it had been com-
pleted, and toward the end of Dhu’l-Qa‘da 701
[July 1302] he moved from Tabriz to Ujan,
where a wall had been constructed for the royal
descent in the midst of an extremely pleasant
green meadow with brooks and springs. Large
ponds and pools had been made, and all sorts
of birds and beasts had taken refuge there. It
was a square divided into equal portions.
Along two sides were planted rows of willow
and poplar trees to serve as avenues for people,
but no one was allowed inside the meadow,
and every group was assigned a particular way
to enter and exit. [1304] Inside the square were
constructed kiosks, towers, a bathhouse, and a
magnificent complex so that the golden tent
might be pitched in the middle of the garden
along with special courtyards and canopies. All
the farrashes and builders gathered, and within
one month they were able to arrange every-
thing and install the extremely huge throne set
with gems and precious stones.
Before
the
banquet
was
held,
sayyids,
imams, cadis, and shaykhs were admitted in
deference to Islam, and after them other groups
of people were let in. The emperor faced the
assembled crowd and spoke eloquently, giving
the various groups good advice and rendering
thanks for God’s great blessings. 
“I, a humble servant of God,” he said, “admit
and confess my weaknesses, shortcomings, and
many sins, and I am not worthy of the magnifi-
cence of such gifts, but God’s mercy and
beneficence toward his slaves are without
bounds. His gifts are too numerous to be enu-
merated by a human being or any other crea-
ture. I am not unaware that I must be grateful
and thankful that God has placed all the peo-
ples of Iran, who are my responsibility from
the divine court, around my neck as a test of
my subservience. I am not deceived by pride in
kingship, which lasts but a short time and has
been taken back from so many thousands of
people. One of the many blessings God has be-
stowed upon me is that he has given me what
he has not given to other kings and he has
granted me what those who preceded me only
wished for, namely that his servants have
found rest from burdens imposed by me and
are happy and content with my rule. Therefore,
I had no desire to enter this tent and court with
pomp and pride, but rather it is necessary now
for ruler and ruled, that is you and me, [1305]
to express our gratitude for this great gift to-
gether without hypocrisy and to enter this tent
with humility, pleading for forgiveness of our
sins. Let us begin with a recitation of the glori-
638
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ous Koran and by performing an act of wor-
ship; then we may indulge in sport and play.” 
Having expressed these pure sentiments, he
pronounced the name of God and his apostle,
placed his blessed foot into the tent, and re-
clined on the throne of success. He ordered
countless gold and textiles brought, and after
the people were fed with all sorts of victuals he
gave all the gold and textiles away in alms
with his own hand so that all received a por-
tion. For three days and nights the Koran was
recited, and every group performed its reli-
gious duties after its own fashion. On the ban-
quet day he placed on his head a jeweled
crown, the likes of which had never before
been seen, bound himself with an appropriate
belt, and clad himself in expensive gold-bro-
caded garments. The ladies and princes, amirs
and courtiers were commanded to bedeck
themselves with their finery, and all mounted
matchless horses and paraded around. 
After all this, he turned his attention to mat-
ters of state and finance and to the welfare of
the subjects. In consultation with the amirs of
state and the grandees of court, he ordered
Prince Kharbanda to spend the winter in Maza-
nderan and to go to Tus, Abivard, Merv,
Sarakhs, and the Badghis area in the summer.
Amir Nurin, as before, would spend the winter
in Arran with his troops and remain there.
Amir Qutlughshah would go to Georgia with
his troops. Some of the Georgian troops would
go to Diyarbekir and join Amir Mulai’s divi-
sion and prepare for an expedition to Syria.
Hulachu’s division [1306] would go to Fars
and Kirman so that if need be they could join
Amir Sadaq and the sultan of Kirman. Having
stationed troops in this manner, he dismissed
them all.
The imperial banners head from Ujan to
Baghdad; what transpired along the way;
the arrival at Wasit and Hilla; the decision
to go to Syria.
On the first of Muharram 702 [August 26,
1302] the Padishah of Islam set out from Ujan
for Hamadan in preparation for an expedition
to Syria. During that time it was decided that
Amir Nurin would spend the winter in Arran in
order to guard that area. Before he requested
permission
to
withdraw,
he
proceeded
to
Hashtrod with the emperor. 
The sons of Sharafuddin Abdul-Rahman,
who had been governor of Tabriz for a time
and then went to Anatolia as mustawfi-i-mama-
lik [auditor general], clad themselves in black
and sought justice at the court because their fa-
ther had been ordered killed by Khwaja Wa-
jih’s son Nizamuddin Yahya. When the imper-
ial banners reached Hashtrod, Amir Nurin held
a goblet and turned back, headed for Arran. On
Ashura,1 Khwaja Wajih’s son Nizamuddin
Yahya and Abubakr Dadqabadi’s son Dawlat-
shah were executed in the vicinity of Yüz
Aghach and Hashtrod. The next day Arabshah,
the grandson of Sultan Hajjaj of Kirman, was
also executed. 
Proceeding from there toward Hamadan, the
emperor stopped at the blessed shrine he had
ordered constructed and endowed with innu-
merable grants in Buzinjird village.2 It is an ex-
tremely fine and exalted complex. [1307] From
there he went to Chaghan Na’ur in Farahan,
and there he stayed a few days. Then he took
the road to Nihavand and Chamch[am]al. In
the vicinity of Besutun three Syrian amirs led
by Ali-Sher surrendered. The Padishah of Is-
lam rewarded them and showed them favor. 
During Nawroz’s rebellion, when his broth-
ers and people were caught in the vicinity of
Kirmanshahan, one night [the emperor] and a
1Ashura, the tenth of Muharram, fell on the fourth of
September that year.
2See text p. 1221 above.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
639

group of courtiers had been left in a field with-
out a tent, and they slept under a cliff opposite
which a shady tree had grown. Before Lagzi
was caught, and before the outcome of the
Nawroz affair was known, the imperial mind
was upset, and he had contemplated in that
very spot. A revelation had come to him from
the unseen realm and given him relief. This
time, when he reached that spot, the affair hav-
ing resolved itself satisfactorily, he remem-
bered the spot and the tree, and he set out to
visit it with all the ladies and amirs. He wept
when he remembered the supplication he had
made there before and rendered gratitude for
the victory and triumph he had attained, pray-
ing two rak‘ats of prayer and placing his head
on the ground in humility before God to ask
for divine assistance in all conditions. Then he
lifted his head and spoke advice to all present,
saying, “Ask for God’s help morning and
evening, and never despair of his mercy. Be
not proud or conceited of anything, and know
for certain that he is not absent from you for
even the twinkling of an eye. Do not be de-
ceived by your own power and strength, but
fear divine zeal.” So saying, he asked God for
what he desired and made charitable intentions
of every sort, in particular that he be more just
and equitable. All those present tied tokens to
the tree, and it became like a shrine. [1308]
Thereafter entertainers played something,
and the amirs danced. Amir Bolad Chingsang
was present, and he reported that Qutula
Qa’an, the Padishah of Islam’s forefather’s un-
cle, was the ruler of several tribes in his time,
and he was so heroic and manly that he had be-
come proverbial for heroics and much poetry
had been composed about him. His voice had
been so loud and terrifying that it could be
heard across seven hills. One day it happened
that he had mounted to do battle with the
Märkit. While on the road he came across a
tree, dismounted, and spoke to God, asking
him for victory and swearing that, if he tri-
umphed over his enemy, he would make that
tree a shrine for himself and decorate it with
pieces of colored cloth. God did give him vic-
tory over his enemy, and afterwards he re-
turned to the tree, which he decorated as he
had sworn, in gratitude to the creator. He and
his soldiers danced beneath that tree, and they
stomped so hard that the area around the tree
sank a yard into the earth. 
The Padishah of Islam was highly pleased by
this narration and said, “Were it not for our an-
cestors’ sincerity and devotion, God would not
have made them rulers of the kings of the
world and would not have elevated their proge-
ny to high status.” 
He spent a time under that tree dancing with
pleasure before he set off after the ordus. Sud-
denly
messengers
came
from Amir
Qut-
lughshah, bringing the Syrian amirs who had
fled from Syria and surrendered. They were led
by Ala’uddin. The padishah rewarded them
and won them over with promises of good
things. 
In that same area, emissaries of the vasileus
[βασιλέυς], the ruler of Istanbul, arrived with
gifts and a message saying, “The vasileus
wants to bask in the shade of the Padishah of
Islam, and he is sending his daughter as a con-
cubine.” The padishah showed them favor.
From
there
he
proceeded
to
Bandinjin,
[1309] and three days later he sent the ladies
and aghruqs to Baghdad. 
On Wednesday the 14th of Rabi‘ II [Decem-
ber 6, 1302] he mounted at Bandinjin to go
hunting in Juqin. He hunted for several days in
the vicinity of Sib,1 Wasit, and the shrine of

tioned above on text p. 936 or the Sib Wahla mentioned
on p. 926. They are all in the same general vicinity.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Sidi Abu’l-Wafa. He visited the shrine and re-
warded the residents with alms and gifts. He
also ordered improvements made along the
canal that had been cut from the Euphrates into
that waterless wilderness, and thanks to which
the shrine had become like a city. From there
he went to Hilla and dismounted in the ordus. 
Mawlana Qazi Nasiruddin Tabrizi and Qazi
Kamaluddin Mawsili, who had been sent from
Arran to Egypt, returned accompanied by
emissaries from Egypt, and they joined the
court at Hilla. They delivered replies to the
messages they had taken, but the replies were
not pleasing.
Toqtai’s1 emissaries also came with three
hundred horsemen. On Sunday the first of Ju-
mada II [January 21, 1303], which correspond-
ed to new year’s day in the Turkish calendar, a
banquet was held, and the ambassadors from
Egypt and Toqtai performed tägishmishi. Toq-
tai’s men were shown much favor, and the
Egyptians were sent to Tabriz to surround the
city.
On Monday the 9th of Jumada II [January 29]
the emperor crossed the bridge at Hilla, headed
for Syria. On Monday the 16th [February 5] he
visited the shrine of the Commander of the
Faithful Husayn. The massive curtains he had
ordered for the shrine were hung, and he gave
untold amounts in alms to the residents of the
shrine and those in attendance. He earmarked
from the income of the Ghazan Canal, which
had been constructed there and which at
present goes to the shrine, a daily allotment of
three thousand maunds of bread for the sayyids
in residence there. 
That day Irmini Bala arrived from Khurasan,
bringing the news that three or four thousand
enemy horsemen had come; the imperial army
had attacked them and wounded or annihilated
1Read ﺗﻮﻗﺘﺎء (Toqtai) for the text’s ﺑﻮﻗﺘﺎء.
them all. [1310] The padishah was highly
pleased, and his love and compassion for his
brother increased. 
On Friday the 4th of Rajab 702 [February 22,
1303] a messenger arrived with news that Amir
Nurin Aqa had died in winter quarters in Arran
around the first of Jumada ii. The Padishah of
Islam was greatly saddened by this tragic
event.
He proceeded along the banks of the Eu-
phrates, and when he reached Haditha, he or-
dered most of the ladies and all the aghruqs to
cross the Euphrates and go stay in Sinjar. He
himself went with the army to Ana. Bulughan
Khatun and some of the other ladies accompa-
nied him to say good-bye, and on Saturday the
12th of Rajab [March 2, 1303] he dismounted
in Ana. Truly there is no place in the world
more pleasant. The city is on an island in the
middle of the Euphrates, with gardens and or-
chards full of trees, flowers, and herbs for a
distance of a league on both sides. The trees
are so thick that the sun does not shine on the
ground. There are kiosks, magnificent build-
ings of carved marble that rise from founda-
tions set on the river bottom.2 On the sides are
terraces3 overlooking the Euphrates and the
paradisiacal gardens. Indeed, the beauty and at-
tractiveness of the gardens and orchards are
beyond description. For a distance of ninety
leagues there are such flourishing places be-
longing to the Euphrates districts, beginning in
Sikr Faluja in the vicinity of Anbar and stretch-
ing to Saruj and Harran. For the entire length

(“foundations set on [or, brought up] from the bottom”)
