PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
641

and at a width of a league or more on both
banks of the Euphrates there are so many con-
tiguous flourishing places that the shade of the
trees is uninterrupted. There are continuous
dykes with mills on both sides, turning day and
night with water, kiosks and lofty edifices one
after the other.
On the eighth day Bulughan Khatun bade
farewell and crossed the river, heading for Sin-
jar. The imperial banners and the victorious
soldiers proceeded toward Rahabat al-Sham,
[1311] but before they reached there a rumor
was heard that the enemy had been spotted in
Syrian territory. Although the rumor was false,
the padishah ordered the soldiers arrayed and
weapons and armor made ready. On the 28th of
Rajab [March 18, 1303] they drove to the out-
skirts of Rahabat. The people there had made
ready carts and other things, but [the emperor]
paid no attention and set off by night from his
tent in the camp to near the citadel. Amir Ala-
muddin Ghanami and the people of Rahabat
had holed up in the citadel. 
On the last of Rajab [March 20] the emperor
ordered the amirs Sö’ätäi and Sultan, along
with the author of this book, Rashid the physi-
cian, and Khwaja Sa‘duddin the Sahib-Divan,
to go to the citadel and invite them to surren-
der. As ordered they went to the base of the
citadel and had a document written in Arabic
as follows: “The reason for this expedition is
the misguided actions of the Egyptians, who
have been undertaking such things for a long
time. Many times emissaries bearing threats
and advice have been sent, but their advice has
gone unheeded and discourteous replies have
been sent. Attributing this to ignorance and
lack of experience in matters of diplomacy, I
have borne it, but now that it has gone beyond
all bounds, the victorious army has of necessity
moved to take revenge and has no alternative
but to pass across this territory. Otherwise we
have no ill intent toward you Syrians. You
should contemplate this matter and recognize
that it is in your interests to preserve your lives
and property by coming forth in submission
and surrender. Since you know that God is
with us, you should not be stubborn or expose
yourselves to danger.” 
Such an edict was penned, sealed, and sent
into the citadel, but the envoys who delivered
it were sent back with a message saying,
“Since the expression of the document is ex-
tremely eloquent, we desire an extension of
time for this night [1312] so that we may fath-
om the meaning, and tomorrow we will give
our answer.”
The next day, Thursday the first of Sha‘ban
[March 21, 1303], Jamaluddin Iskandari and
Shaykh Sharafuddin, a disciple of Sidi Ahmad
Kabir, were sent out with a reply to the edict.
“We are in obedience to the command of the
Padishah of Islam,” they said. They were re-
warded and sent back. The next day Husamud-
din Lachin, the deputy of Alamuddin Ghanami,
the castellan of the citadel, came down and
surrendered. He too was shown favor and sent
back. 
The next day he and Mihtar Ghanami’s son
Sayfuddin Qilich, Qazi Najmuddin, and a
group of notables of Rahabat came down and
completed the terms of surrender. They were
honored to be admitted to the imperial court,
and solemn documents pertaining to taxes,
tribute, princes, deputies, judges, bureaucrats
and to amnesty for the people of the city,
citadel, and province were written in Arabic,
sealed with the imperial seal, and turned over
to them.
On Tuesday the 6th of Sha‘ban [March 26,
1303] the emperor marched from the Rahabat
citadel. Good news came from Khurasan that
Qaidu’s soldiers had been routed, Qaidu was
dead, and Dua was wounded. 
642
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

During this time Amir Qutlughshah, Chupan,
and Mulai had crossed the Euphrates with their
soldiers near Raqqa and arrived near Aleppo.
The Padishah of Islam camped above Dayr
Basir on the banks of the Euphrates, and there
he remained for three days. All the amirs and
their troops were sent out to join Amir Qut-
lughshah and the others.
Since spring had come, the waters had risen,
and the weather was warm, all set out for Sin-
jar and crossed the Euphrates on the 13th of
Sha‘ban [April 2, 1303]. The Khabur was
crossed at the city of Maksin. The envoys from
Khurasan, Saighan and Qonchi Aqtachi, were
shown favor and given permission to return.
[The imperial retinue] proceeded through that
wilderness filled with tulips and camomile,
sightseeing and hunting. 
On Sunday the 25th of Sha‘ban [April 14,
1303] he rejoined the ladies who had come out
to greet him at Chahar Taq [1313] below Sin-
jar. After staying there two or three days, he
dismounted in the ordus at Tall A‘far on the
first of Ramadan [April 19]. He turned over the
rule of the entire area of Diyarbekir and Diyar
Rabi‘a to Sultan Najmuddin of Mardin and
gave him the title al-Malik al-Mansur. Then,
crossing the Tigris, he stopped in the meadow
at Kushaf. 
The people of Mosul had raised to the heav-
ens their cries for help from the tyranny and
aggression of Fakhr Isa Nasrani. A command
was given that when Sultan Najmuddin went to
Mosul he should eliminate him. Having de-
ceived him with promises of making him his
deputy, the sultan did away with him after a
few days. 
Qutlughshah Noyan comes face to face with
the army of Egypt and retreats; the imperial
banners return to Ujan.
The Padishah of Islam waited at Kushaf for
the arrival of the troops that had gone to Syria.
When they arrived at Homs they began to pil-
lage and stage massacres. When they were near
Damascus and heard that the enemy was near-
by, at dawn on Saturday the first of Ramadan
[April 19, 1303] they mounted and rode out
nearly five leagues. Having crossed much wa-
ter and mud, they came across the enemy at
Marj al-Suffar.1 They next day, the 2nd of Ra-
madan [April 20] they gave battle. Our left
wing struck their right wing, and thirteen of
their major officers, including Husamuddin
Ustadu’l-Dar and many others, were killed or
wounded. As they fled, a group of our
champions went in pursuit of them for several
leagues. Qutlughshah Noyan left the center for
the left, intending to assist, but the right wing,
having been separated and left alone, [1314]
was struck by the Egyptians’ left wing. Be-
cause they were few, they pulled back, and by
the time Amir Qutlughshah reached the left
wing they had finished fighting and night was
falling. The amir went atop a hill and stood
there. Our soldiers headed in that direction and
spent the night on horseback, both men and an-
imals suffering from thirst. By night the Egyp-
tians encircled the hill, and when day broke
Amir Pulad Qaya’s troop and those of Täkä
Temür, son of Amir Injil,2 and Nasiruddin
Yahya were left opposite them. They did battle,
and Amir Qutlughshah said to Taitaq and
Tarsa, “Yesterday you did not do battle. Today
you will go to help them.” Both together went
out and joined the battle. The Syrians and
Egyptians abandoned their encirclement of the
hill and charged them in one concerted attack.
Since most of the soldiers’ lines had fallen
apart and the troops were scattered, it was im-
possible to make a proper battle array. They
1Marj al-Ṣuffar, south of Damascus.
2The reading of this name is uncertain. In the text it is
اﳒﻴﻞ; it may be the name اﳚﻴﻞ (Ejil).
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
643

stood until around noon, but after that they re-
treated. In their way was a lot of water and
mud, and many of the horses got stuck and the
soldiers were scattered. Taitaq and Tarsa could
not be seen.
Amir Qutlughshah and Täkä Temür arrived
before the emperor in the Kushaf plain on the
19th of Ramadan [May 7, 1303], and the next
day the imperial banners went on the march,
stopping in a garden outside Arbela. From
there they decamped and took the road to Dar-
band-i-Zangi through the mountains of Kurdis-
tan. Id al-Fitr [May 19] was celebrated in the
vicinity of Darband-i-Zangi. On Saturday the
17th of Shawwal [June 4] Amir Chupan, who
had stopped to take care of the soldiers that
had been left on foot and was proceeding slow-
ly via Baghdad, reached the emperor, by whom
he was shown great favor. When they arrived
at Pul-i-Surkh in Maragha, [1315] the emperor
sent the ladies and aghruqs via Se Gumbad and
Yüz Aghach to Ujan while he himself went un-
encumbered to Mount Sahand to hunt. After
hunting there for a week, on Thursday the 10th
of Dhu’l-Qa‘da 702 [June 26, 1303] he dis-
mounted in the City of Islam Ujan. 
The amirs and soldiers who return from
Syria are tried; a quriltai is held in Ujan,
and they perform tägishmishi.
The day after the imperial banners reached
Ujan, which was the 12th of Dhu’l-Qa‘da
[June 28, 1303], a trial was begun. The minuti-
ae were examined, and when the transcript was
submitted to the emperor, he objected to sever-
al points and had the trial done over from the
beginning so that those points might be re-
solved. In the end, on the first of Dhu’l-Hijja
[July
17],
the
trial
was
over,
and
___1
Tarkhan’s son Aghutai Tarkhan and Toghan
1Texts all have the incompletely dotted nameﮏ ـ ـ ـﺣﯩﯩ: it
could be either ﭼﻴﻨﮓ (Ching) or ﺟﻴﺒﮏ (Jibik).
Temür of the Mangqut clan were executed, and
all that was required by the great Yasa was put
into practice. 
Then, on Thursday the 2nd of Dhu’l-Hijja
[July 18], a banquet and quriltai were com-
menced, and the amirs were honored to per-
form tägishmishi. [1316]
The Padishah of Islam is stricken by
ophthalmia; the princes arrive from
Khurasan; the imperial banners, heading
for Baghdad, camp at Hula’an Mürän.
The emperor arrived in the capital Tabriz on
Thursday the 25th of Muharram 703 [Septem-
ber 8, 1303] and dismounted at the citadel, or-
dering troops and arms made ready. Several
days later symptoms of ophthalmia became
rampant, and the doctors and physicians began
to treat him with medicines. The symptoms
persisted for a long time, however, and the
time to leave for winter quarters was growing
short. 
On Monday the 4th of Safar [September 17]
the great lady Eltüzmish Khatun arrived from
Khurasan with the princes Bistam and Abu-
Yazid. The Padishah of Islam, overjoyed at
their arrival, affianced his daughter Öljäi Qut-
lugh to Prince Bistam. He kept them with him
constantly and showed them great kindness. 
Toward the end of his stay in Tabriz, in ac-
cordance with the treatment of the Cathaian
physicians, his regal body was cauterized in
two places on Sunday the 7th of Rabi‘ I [Octo-
ber 19]. On Friday the 19th of Rabi‘ I [October
31] he left Tabriz. Since some elephants had
been brought to court from India, he ordered a
platform placed on an elephant’s back, and he
left the city riding on an elephant as far as
Maydan. From midmorning until midafternoon
he occupied himself with riding and driving
elephants. The people of the city turned out in
droves, men and women, to watch and pray for
his health. That night he stopped in Baghistan
644
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

in Tabriz, and the next day he proceeded on the
road to Ujan. [1317] He was, however, unable
to hold the reins of his horse because of the
pain in his stomach from the burning and gen-
eral weakness, and so most of the time he rode
in a litter. Each day a small portion of the route
was covered.
At the end of Rabi‘ I [October 13–November
11, 1303] Amir Qutlughshah returned from
Yüz Aghach to winter in Arran and guard that
frontier. On Monday the 14th of Rabi‘ II [No-
vember 25, 1303] Gürägän arrived in the vicin-
ity of Joma Saray. In Sughurluq and the
Hamadan region much snow had fallen and the
cold was very intense, for which reason it was
impossible to take the Baghdad road in that di-
rection. Therefore the trip to Baghdad was can-
celled, and camp was made on the banks of the
Hula’an Mürän, also a major wintering site and
actually a very pleasant one, from all around
which good foodstuffs could be had and there
was abundant kindling. All the men settled in
their own yurts and began to tend to their busi-
ness at leisure.
One day the Padishah of Islam, in expiation
for a small sin, was going to feed and clothe
ten poor people. Since he wanted to do this
with his own hand, he ordered ten poor people
brought in. Najibuddin Farrash, one of his inti-
mates and confidants, brought ten poor people
to court, and he fed them with his own hand.
Then he ordered ten suits of clothing brought
from the treasury. He looked at them for a
while, gave eight of the poor people a suit, and
then gave the other two back to Mihtar Na-
jibuddin and said, “Go bring two other poor
men for me to give these to. These two are
Christians.”
“Didn’t you say you were Muslims?” Na-
jibuddin asked.
“Yes,” they said, “we told you so because we
were greedy, but we cannot lie to the Padishah
of Islam. He is right. We are both Christians.”
(This story is a clear indication that the emper-
or was one of God’s saints.) [1318]
The Padishah of Islam withdraws into
solitude in his winter quarters at Hula’an
Mürän; Alafrang’s plot to rebel is
uncovered, and the conspirators are
executed.
While at these winter quarters the Padishah
of Islam desired to withdraw into solitude as a
type of retreat. A tent was pitched for him out-
side the court, and he retired there by himself
and did not allow any eunuchs or bodyguards
to come to him. Every day he contented him-
self with just a little food.
While this was going on, a very strange thing
happened. A group of men who looked like
shaykhs but who were really meddlesome, led
by Pir Ya‘qub Baghbani in Tabriz, had won
over Prince Alafrang on account of his love of
status and money, and they wanted to display
saintly miracles, the power for which they did
not possess. During those days they sent a dis-
ciple named Mahmud into the ordu in order to
win over a group of courtiers. This man, out of
ignorance, divulged the secret and said, “A
person forty yards tall and five yards wide is
coming to Shaykh Ya‘qub from the Marand
and Iqan mountains. He will instruct him and
reveal secrets to him. He has now given the
kingship to Prince Alafrang, and like it or not
the kingship is his, and the dervishes have giv-
en it to him.” These words reached the hearing
of Khwaja Sa‘duddin the Sahib-Divan. He had
the man seized and put into prison. Then he re-
ported the affair to the Padishah of Islam, and
he sent Jäbäi1 Akhtachi to Tabriz to bring the
malfeasants. Ten days later he came back and
brought Pir Ya‘qub, Nasiruddin the Qa’an’s
emissary, Shaykh Habib the khalifa of Rashid
1Reading, with JTAZ, ﺟﺎﰉ (Jäbäi) for JTK’s ﺧﺎﱏ.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
645

Bulghari, and Sayyid Kamaluddin Tamamat.
Shaykh
Rashid
was
Sadruddin
Zanjani’s
shaykh, [1319] and Sayyid Kamaluddin was
also one of his attendants. What is amazing is
that when the Padishah of Islam saw them, he
said, “I seem to remember that these seditious
men were attached to Sadruddin Zanjani.”
When it was investigated it turned out to be
true. He said, “Even from the grave he’s still
stirring up trouble.” After that he sat by him-
self, and in the presence of the amirs and
courtiers he investigated the report. The group
of ignorant men spoke incredible nonsense,
and when he got to the bottom of it, it was ob-
vious that the basis of their beliefs was Maz-
dak’s creed and that they wanted to re-establish
that creed among the people. When their crime
was proven, Ya‘qub said, “Our lords will pro-
tect us.”
The Padishah of Islam replied, “My lords are
God, the Prophet, and Murtaza [Ali b. Abi-Tal-
ib]. Let us see whether their power is greater or
yours.” He ordered [Ya‘qub] thrown off the top
of the mountain they were on, and his hench-
men were executed. 
He forgave Prince Alafrang’s crime. “Now
that the padishah has shown me favor,” the
prince said, “let me confess the truth of the
matter. Two or three times in Tabriz they took
me to Shaykh Ya‘qub on a pretext of going
hunting. While having a sama‘ and that sort of
thing, he and his disciples claimed to have the
power of miracles, and they duped me with
promises to make me king. I was too afraid to
reveal this and kept it hidden.”
Yetmish, Taitaq’s deputy, was also tried, and
when he confessed his guilt he too was execut-
ed. Although Taitaq’s son Aq Buqa had partic-
ipated in the discussions and was a prime
mover in the affair—Alafrang said that the
entire guilt was his—nonetheless since he was
a young child and his father had displayed
kichämishi [valor] in the Syrian war and been
taken captive by the enemy, the Padishah of Is-
lam forgave him and merely had him impris-
oned. [1320]
A banquet is held in Eltüzmish Khatun’s
ordu for Prince Abu-Yazid’s birthday, and
the padishah comes out of retirement.
On Sunday the first of Jumada II [January 10,
1304]
a
banquet
was
held
in
Eltüzmish
Khatun’s ordu for Prince Abu-Yazid’s birthday,
as was customary. The Padishah of Islam and
all the ladies, princes, and amirs were present
for the rituals of congratulation and celebra-
tion, and much revelry was held. The Padishah
of Islam rewarded the princes, ladies, and their
followers and showed them much favor. 
After that, the Padishah of Islam came out of
his retreat and turned his attention to matters of
state. He had regained his health and spent his
time happily. All the ministers and officials
were glad and relieved that the shaykh’s and
his henchmen’s plot had been discovered. 
The Padishah of Islam favors Khwaja
Sa‘duddin the Sahib-Divan on account of
the loyalty he had shown during the
Alafrang affair.
Khwaja Sa‘duddin the Sahib-Divan immedi-
ately arrested Pir Ya‘qub’s emissary who had
come into the ordu to win converts by making
promises to everyone, and sent word to the
court. [1321] Because of this the emperor be-
gan to trust him inordinately and realized that
he could rely upon him totally in all respects.
This was highly appropriate, for his honesty
and sincerity in his devotion and loyalty are
such that if he is rewarded a hundred ways
every day, it is no more than he deserves. For
this reason the emperor wanted to favor him in
some way that his rank and station would be
increased and his magnificence would be even
greater. Since the reins of the fiscal affairs and
646
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

administrtion of the empire had already been
put into his capable hands—and it was impos-
sible to imagine anything greater than that—
the emperor rewarded him by putting him in
command of a hazara of Mongol soldiers and
giving him a tugh and kähvärgä [drums]. He
also ordered all the amirs to go and congratu-
late him. The truth is that his angelic self, the
repository of all humane qualities and well-
spring of all human perfections, is worthy of a
thousandfold such rewards every instant, for he
is the cause for the repose of high and low
alike and the adornment of state and empire, of
faith and Islam. May God cause him to enjoy
high station and great magnificence. 
The death of Kärämün Khatun, whose body
is taken to Tabriz; the few wise words the
Padishah of Islam spoke about life.
At twilight on the evening of Saturday the
12th of Jumada
II 703 [January 21, 1304],
Kärämün Khatun, Abatai Noyan’s son Qutlugh
Temür’s daughter and the Padishah of Islam’s
wife, died suddenly in winter quarters in the
vicinity of Saray Jorma. [1322] Her body was
taken with all pomp to Tabriz. Since she had
been in the bloom of youth and had scarcely
enjoyed the world, her death greatly affected
the Padishah of Islam, who was severely
pained. After her death he went into her ordu
and wept much. He ordered that whatever
arrangements
and
ceremony
she
deserved
should be carried out. After her coffin was tak-
en away, tears welled up in his imperial eyes
every time he thought of her. 
One day when the pillars of state were
present, he asked, “What is there in the world
than which nothing is more difficult or hard?”
“To be taken prisoner by an enemy or to be
brought low by a foe,” some of the amirs
replied. Others said, “Poverty.” Some said,
“Death.” 
“No,” he said, “the most difficult thing is to
be born, to come into the world, because all tri-
als and tribulations, all suffering and torment,
are due to life. If there were no existence, there
would be no difficulty. There is no greater re-
pose for a human being in the world than
death, and my reasoning is as follows. There
are two people on the road: one is running and
the other is walking slowly. Which of the two
is more rested?”
“The one who is walking,” they replied.
“If one is walking and the other is sitting,
which one is more rested?”
“The one who is sitting,” they said.
“If one is sitting and the other is asleep,
which is more rested?”
“The one who is asleep,” they answered.
“Therefore, on this basis and by correct anal-
ogy, a dead man is more rested than one who is
asleep, and the redemption and complete bene-
fit of souls lie in escaping from the strictures of
nature. No bond, prison, hell, or torment is
harder than ignorance and love of the world.
Even though this world is hell for men of God
and the next life is heaven for them, as is con-
firmed by the words of the Prophet, ‘The world
is a prison for the believer and paradise for the
infidel,’ an ignorant man absolutely does not
want to escape from the prison of nature. In his
total ignorance he thinks the soul is dead and
the body is alive; [1323] he does not realize
that in reality it is just the opposite. He takes
pride in all sorts of ignorance and stupidity,
and he does not know that death is a pleasant
condition and pure justice, for if fathers did not
die, how could imperial possessions and great-
ness come to their sons? Although the death of
a father is hard and difficult, nonetheless be-
cause it gives another a chance, it is pleasing.
There is not much benefit in a long life unless
one is headed toward perfection and his soul
advances day by day. It is best to content one-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
647

self with what God has allotted, for if people
lived more than eighty years, their organs
would cease to function, their senses would be-
come sluggish and useless, they would become
mean and low in the eyes of others, and both
their relatives and strangers would despise
them. Inasmuch as the benefit of life lies in
perfection, after acquiring perfection every-
thing else is a deficiency. Long life, therefore,
is not a benefit.”
In this way he spoke precise words, all of
which were pure wisdom.
At the end of Sha‘ban 703 [March 9, 1304–
April 6, 1304], the emperor decamped from his
yurt at Hula’an Mürän, which he had named
Öljäitü Buynuq. Having stationed the ladies
and aghruqs in the vicinity of the fortress at
Juq, one stage away from Saray Jorma, he pro-
ceeded unencumbered with the pillars of state
and the grandees of court to Maraq. He spent a
few days hunting in the vicinity of the moun-
tains in Kharraqan and Mazdaqan and then
went to the city of Sawa. The Sahib Khwaja
Sa‘duddin gave a general banquet and present-
ed goblets to the Sultan of Islam and all the
ladies, princes, and amirs as he performed
tägishmishi. He was rewarded by the sultan
with all sorts of shows of favor. Likewise, the
grand sadr, Khwaja Shihabuddin Mubarak-
shah, the chief scribe of the empire and head of
all the pillars of the mighty state. Since his an-
cient house was in Sawa, and his father, Khwa-
ja Sharafuddin Sa‘dan, [1324] a scion of the
grandees of Iran, was resident and governor
there, he gave a general banquet and presented
suitable gifts to the sultan, the ladies, and the
princes. He also made noble presentations to
all the lords and gave abundant textiles, dinars,
and dirhems to servants and members of the
retinue. 
Three days later the imperial banners depart-
ed from there and headed for Rayy. From the
time he had left winter quarters, the imperial
constitution
had
completely
regained
its
strength, and he was able to ride a horse across
long and distant stages and to partake of all
sorts of food. Now, however, after leaving
Sawa, he had a relapse: symptoms of the ill-
ness reappeared, and he lost his appetite.
Nonetheless, he exerted himself and continued
to ride as usual. 
Camp was made in the vicinity of Rayy for a
few days. When symptoms of illness overtook
him at Khayl-i-Buzurg, a dependency of Rayy,
a messenger was sent to the aghruqs to sum-
mon the great lady Bulughan Khatun with all
speed. When she arrived, they had already de-
camped from Khayl-i-Buzurg and, having pro-
ceeded a short distance every day, come to
Peshkala in the Qazwin vicinity. When the
khatun arrived at the end of Ramadan, they
were still camped there. As the khatun entered
and found the emperor in such a state, they
both wept and shed tears. 
After that, the emperor summoned all the
amirs, elite courtiers, and pillars of state and
court and gave each of them advice as befitted
his station. He also reconfirmed his will most
precisely that his elder brother be designated as
his successor, as he had done five years previ-
ously and often repeated in various gatherings.
[1325] He urged everyone most strenuously to
observe and preserve the terms of that will.
Most of the time he chose to be alone, and al-
though there was weakness of constitution, he
possessed his full faculties. His senses were al-
ways sharp, and he was eloquent of speech.
Since, however, his divinely destined days had
come to their end, in accordance with the [Ko-
ranic dictum,] “When their end has come, they
can neither put it off or hasten it so much as an
hour,”1 in the late afternoon on Sunday the
1Kor. 7:34.
648
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

11th of Shawwal 703 [May 17, 1304] his pure
spirit was translated from the mortal world to
the abode of eternal bliss. With this event, such
a great calamity to the world, the celestial
spheres clad themselves in indigo blue, and
rivers flowed from the eyes of the people of
the inhabited quarter of the globe.
After the rites of washing and shrouding
were performed, his noble coffin was placed
on his own special horse, and the ladies and
amirs followed behind to Tabriz. From the
towns and villages men and women came out,
head and feet uncovered and clad in sackcloth,
and poured dust on their heads as they wept.
Over that just and pious king’s coffin wept time
and space. / Everyone said alas and alack, for
the sun of the world had gone behind a cloud.
In all the towns of Iran minarets were
covered in sackcloth. The population poured
out into the markets, streets, and squares, and
old and young alike, men and women, tore
their clothing, put on sackcloth, and mourned
for seven days. When the imperial coffin
reached one stage outside of the capital Tabriz,
the people of the city rushed out distraught,
men and women, old and young, wearing
mourning clothing. [1326]
All headed into the countryside, beating their
breasts with stones in distress.
Soldiers, members of the retinue, and servants
gathered around the imperial coffin, weeping,
and proceeded to Shamm, where the emperor
was buried in the lofty dome he had construct-
ed. “Everything is going to perish save His
face: His is the command, and unto Him will
you be returned.”1
May God drown that happy sultan in a shore-
less ocean of mercy. May he give the Emperor
of Islam Öljäitü Sultan, his heir, his heart’s de-
sire. “He is the lord of response.” May God be
content
with
Muhammad
and
his
family.
[1327]
1Kor. 28:88.
Part Three of the story of the Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan, on his conduct and
character; monuments of his justice and beneficence, charity, and piety; the
pronouncements and orders he gave for the benefit of all people; and rare stories and
unusual events not included in the two previous sections: these are divided into two parts,
one further subdivided into forty stories, and the other on various and miscellaneous events
and incidents.
The part subdivided into forty stories con-
tains the following: (1) the Padishah of Islam’s
various accomplishments and knowledge and
his learning of different crafts; (2) the Padishah
of Islam’s being free of all vile traits; [1328]
(3) his eloquence, his fine repartee with all
peoples; (4) his patience, steadfastness, and
trustworthiness; (5) on the fact that mostly
what he said came true; (6) his praiseworthy
generosity and kindness; (7) his elimination of
idolatry and total destruction of idol temples;
(8) his love for the family of the Prophet and
his respect for great sayyids; (9) his bravery,
his tactical deployment of the army during en-
gagements, and his persistence in battle; (10)
his advising cadis, shaykhs, ascetics, and peo-
ple of learning and piety; (11) his forbidding
all soldiers and others to make heathenish
statements; [1329] (12) his love for building
and his encouragement of others in that regard;
(13) his charitable institutions in Tabriz and
Hamadan, and the vows he made in the
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
649

provinces; (14) his elimination of forgeries and
false claims, and his elimination of the treach-
ery of the dishonest; (15) he eliminates the
practice of forging documents and annuls out-
dated deeds; (16) he outlaws the division of
plunder and various types of confiscation; (17)
he protects and maintains the peasantry and
eliminates their subjection to injustice and ha-
rassment; (18) he repeals the ulagh and does
away with a superﬂuity of envoys in the realm;
(19) he eliminates thieves and highway robbers
and protects the roads of the realm from their
predation; (20) he reforms the gold and silver
standard better than it had ever been; (21) he
corrects monetary and scale weights and fixes
the yard, standard grain measure, the qafiz, and
the taghar; (22) he regularizes the giving of
patents and badges of office to people; (23) he
takes back duplicate patents and badges of of-
fice held by people; [1330] (24) he enfeoffs
villages in every province to the Mongol army;
(25) how he organized a separate troop for the
person of the emperor; (26) he forbids giving
money for lucre and abominable monetary
transactions; (27) he forbids unlimited prenup-
tial agreements and fixes the rate at nineteen
and a half dinars; (28) he builds baths and
mosques in villages throughout the realm; (29)
people are forbidden to drink wine and other
sinful intoxicants; (30) he regularizes stipends
for the imperial table and wine for the Great
Ordu; (31) he arranges provisions for the ladies
and ordus; (32) he regulates factories and
arranges their funding; (33) he organizes the
armories; (34) his reorganization of imperial
ﬂocks and herds; [1331] (35) his reorganiza-
tion of the corps of falconers and cheetah keep-
ers; (36) his reorganization of tax collection
throughout the realm; (37) his planning for the
improvement of fallow lands; (38) the building
of envoy hostels throughout the realm and the
forbidding of envoys to lodge in people’s hous-
es; (39) he forbids muleteers, camel drivers,
and messengers to impose upon people; (40)
he forbids the practice of forcing young
women to enter brothels.
Story One: The Padishah of Islam’s various
accomplishments and knowledge; his
learning of different crafts and discovery of
their secrets.
Let it not remain concealed from the people of
the world that when the Padishah of Islam was
in his infancy, his grandfather Abaqa Khan
kept him near and reared him. Over him as at-
tendants and teachers he set the idolatrous
bakhshis, [1332] and by that means that prac-
tice became firmly rooted in his soul, particu-
larly since his fathers had believed in that sect
and practiced that way. The practice of idola-
try, which had been completely eliminated
throughout the region from the beginning of Is-
lam, reappeared during their time, and that
group had become powerful. All sorts of
bakhshis were brought with all honor and re-
spect from India, Kashmir, Cathay, and Uyghur
lands. Temples were built in every place, and
vast sums were spent on them. This sect had
risen to the apex of power, as was apparent to
all. The Padishah of Islam was constantly in
the company of the bakhshis in the temple ob-
serving their rites. Day by day his inclination
to that sect increased, and his belief became
firmer. When Abaqa Khan passed away and
[Ghazan’s] father Arghun Khan sent him to
Khurasan as governor and commander of the
army,
he
built
major
idol
temples
in
Khabushan, and he spent most of his time con-
versing, eating, and drinking with the bakhshis
in those temples. The belief he had for that sect
and the worship he performed of the idols were
beyond description. When [Ghazan} began to
retake territory Baidu had seized, inasmuch as
God had foreordained him for happiness and
destined that the rule be his, that through di-
650
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

vine assistance he should make manifest traces
of justice and equity in the world, rectify
things that had gone amiss, and restore lands
that had been devastated, and that the propaga-
tion of the religion of Islam and the divine law
should be brought about by him, while both he
and the world were unaware of it, suddenly,
when the time was ripe, through the effulgence
of divine loving kindness, the light of guidance
descended into his pure breast. With that, he
set his blessed foot into the circle of Islam,
caught hold of the strong rope of faith, and is-
sued a statement condemning the doctrines of
false religions. [1333] Most of the people sus-
pected that the reason for his conversion was
the encouragement and insistence of some of
the amirs and shaykhs, but after it was investi-
gated it became apparent that such a suspicion
was wrong. 
Once in private he said to this humble ser-
vant, the writer of this book, “There are some
sins that God will not forgive. The greatest of
those is for someone to place his head on the
ground before an idol—for that there will ab-
solutely be no forgiveness. The poor people are
caught up in ignorance in placing their heads
on the ground before idols, and I too was like
that. However, God gave me illumination and
comprehension, and I was delivered and puri-
fied by God of that sin. The gist of these words
is that there is nothing that will take a person to
hell as easily as ignorance; rather, ignorance is
a hell one cannot get out of. How can the mind
accept that a person should place his head on
the ground before an inanimate object? Such a
motion is a sign of sheer ignorance. 
“Originally idolaters said, ‘There was a per-
fect individual, but he passed away. We have
made an image of him, and we set it up as a re-
minder. We recollect him in order to seek help
from his psychic power, and we take refuge in
him, worship him, and prostrate ourselves be-
fore him.’ All the while they were ignorant of
the fact that when that person was alive, when
that which is the germ of humanity was still to-
gether with his body, he never desired any such
thing and never allowed anyone to place his
head on the ground in front of him lest conceit
and self-aggrandizement be born in himself.
Therefore, when they worship him and pros-
trate themselves to seek help from his psychic
power, how can his soul possibly be content to
have those people place their heads on the
ground before an image of his body. Even if
they have good intentions for his psychic pow-
er—and let us imagine that there is some trace
of that power—assuredly it would be a bad and
unhappy psyche, not a good and happy one. 
“Furthermore, one should know as a given
truth that the body has no importance, and
thereby one may forget to love one’s own
body. [1334] One should also know that what
will depart from this body is one’s essence.
One should therefore contemplate just what it
is that will depart, where it will go, and how it
will remain. If one thinks of that thing, that
place, and that state, as a consequence one may
come to know them. When one believes in a
form made in the shape of a body and bows
down before it, one cannot think about or seek
the essence that is paradise itself. Quite the op-
posite, one inclines to that which is the lowest
depth of sheer hell. The more one thinks about
it, the more one realizes that the only use an
idol has is to be turned into a threshold so that
people will step on it coming and going in or-
der that the spirit of which this thing is sup-
posed to be the body will be content with them
because it will be thinking, ‘While I was in the
world I attained perfect humility; after my de-
parture the form of the body is also in that
state.’ It will also be thinking, ‘My soul had
such perfection. Its body has turned to dust and
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
651

is worthy of being a threshold to be stepped
on.’ 
For us who have no such perfection, how
will our bodies be? One should detach one’s
heart from the body’s condition altogether and
think about the next world, pure stages, and the
conditions of holy spirits. Let one constantly
think about those states so that perhaps one
may attain something of that which is reality,
so that there may be some benefit to one’s hav-
ing come into the world, so that one may attain
some perfection, since the goal of creation is
for one to go from the world of darkness into
the world of light.”
As he expressed himself so well and in such
precise ways, his inner light, veracity, and puri-
ty are well established. After that, he constant-
ly gave speeches of this sort and spoke words
of mysticism deeper than have ever been heard
from any philosopher or mystic. 
After he had been on the throne for two or
three years, [1335] his efforts to propagate Is-
lam increased daily, and he strove truly and
sincerely to observe the religion as much as
possible. It was clear and obvious to everyone
that the reason for his conversion to Islam was
not the urging of any of the amirs or shaykhs
but rather divine guidance, for it is known
from experience that if a king or governor
forces the least man convert to Islam, that per-
son’s inclination to his own religion will re-
main as it was, and when he has an opportuni-
ty, either in his own country or in another, he
will return to his own religion. What need then
could such a puissant emperor possibly have
had to pay the slightest attention to the words
of anyone in such an important regard? Why
should he have changed his religion or chosen
another religion by force—particularly since
his fathers, during the age of their disbelief,
had conquered all the countries of the world?
For all the foregoing reasons it was clear that
his reward in this regard was like the reward of
Abraham: when first he perceived the error of
idolaters through the light of guidance, he
broke his own idol and came thereby to recog-
nize God through conscientious faith. The
Padishah of Islam’s conversion to Islam was of
this sort, for he came to the religion of Islam
from idolatry despite his regal pride and power.
He broke all the idols in the realm of Iran,
totally destroyed idol temples and all illegal
houses of worship, and brought the totality of
idolaters, infidels, and Mongols, who were
more numerous than the sands of the desert,
under the aegis of Islam so that it was not nec-
essary to have a single person put to death. Of
course, his reward will be great. 
The things that have been mentioned are
clear proofs of his perfect knowledge and wis-
dom. Another is as follows. When young men
engage in entertainment, pleasure, and wine
drinking, they desire sport, jokes, and various
games. By contrast, when the Padishah of Is-
lam relaxes, most of the time he delves into the
words of wise men [1336] and undertakes in-
depth research into stories and discussions far
beyond the comprehension of any philosopher
or wise man. He loves to hold discussions with
wise and rational men of discrimination. If he
sees a proponent of wisdom who possesses a
good mind, discrimination, and polish and who
is unadulterated by falsehood, he approves of
him.1 He immediately assesses the worth of
any of this type who comes to him, and no
trickster or false person ever has an opportuni-
ty to speak words laced with falsehood with
him. And if he does, he isn’t able to speak
long, for the emperor recognizes him for what
he is and never allows him access again. If he
sees a wise man, [even if] he speaks a lot of
