ﲢﻴﻞ # آن gر ﻧﺒﺎﺷﺪ اورا ﺑﭙﺴـﻨﺪد.
652
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

foolishness, he immediately recognizes his de-
pth. As an example of this, let us tell the fol-
lowing story.
In Khurasan was a person named Hibatullah
who had come from Turkistan. He was a man
of good character and presence who know
something of every branch of learning. He
knew the Syriac and Turkish languages, and he
had committed many proverbs to memory. He
spoke in the manner of shaykhs, and the em-
peror and the amirs believed what he said. For
a time he was in attendance on the emperor,
and when he came to the throne he sent a mes-
senger to summon Hibatullah. He showed him
honor, made him an intimate at court, and re-
warded him with gold, textiles, and a large
monthly allowance. He entrusted him to this
well-wisher of the state and commanded me to
look after him, which I did. He was constantly
at court, where he spoke deep things about
wisdom and mysticism. Although he was a
learned man, there was a vast difference be-
tween what he said and what the emperor said.
“It is unlikely that the emperor doesn’t realize
the difference between this man’s knowledge
and his own,” I thought in amazement, “and if
he does realize it, why is he so greatly devoted
to him?” It would have been inexcusable to
question anyone he held in such high regard,
for it would have amounted to an insult. I re-
mained perplexed by this for a time until, one
day, he was speaking deep words and said,
“This is something to which not everyone has
access. [1337] Most people are superficial and
know only the external aspect: they never get
to the core meaning. Not everyone has access
to a king’s treasury: the elite go into the
treasury while others can only go around the
outside. It’s like Shaykh Hibatullah, whose
way is to sit outside the treasury and know
what is on the outside. However, he does not
have the manner of one who goes inside the
treasury and knows the details of the goods
there.”
After that I said, “I have wanted to ask about
this for a long time, but there was no opportu-
nity. Now I know for certain that the emperor
knows everyone’s worth even when he honors
all.”
“It doesn’t surprise me,” he said, “that he or
another does not know the likes of these mys-
teries, but I like what they do know and there-
fore I do them honor. By conversing with them
I try to remember what God has given me.
Even though a whetstone is softer than steel, it
sharpens steel, and this is because the essence
of steel increases through the stone. Sharpness
is inherent in the essence of steel, but it be-
comes sharp through the softness of the stone.”
In gatherings and groups, when all sorts of
people were present, the learned men and
philosophers were amazed by the questions he
asked. Although he spoke in the idiom of the
Mongols and not everyone immediately under-
stood, nonetheless when what he said was re-
peated and interpreted, some understood and
many did not comprehend. His manner of wis-
dom and knowing God was as has been
reported.
He also knew so much about the conditions
of various religions and the beliefs of every
single group that when he debated with the
leaders of each religion they would be unable
to respond to one of every ten questions he
posed, while he knew the answers to them all. 
Of various languages, Mongolian was his
own, but he also knew something of Arabic,
Persian, Hindi, Kashmiri, Tibetan, Cathaian,
Frankish, and all other languages. [1338]
Of the manners, customs, and administra-
tions of past sultans and kings he knew in de-
tail what the customs of each one were in bat-
tle and banquet, in health and sickness, what
they ate and wore, and what they rode. He also
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
653

knew what their other conditions were and are
now. He would explain all this in detail to each
group, and they would be amazed.
As for his knowledge of the dates and history
of Mongols that are of great importance to
them, the names of their forefathers, ancestors,
and relatives, both male and female, and those
of Mongol officers, both ancient and modern,
who were and are in the kingdom, he knew the
branches of descent of each one in more detail
and better than anyone of all the Mongolian
tribes—excepting only Bolad Aqa—and every-
one learned from him. This history of the Mon-
gols that has been written has been possible
mostly by benefiting from him. There are
many secrets and stories of the Mongols he
knew that were not included in this history. He
also knew most of the histories of the kings of
the Persians and Turks and of India, Kashmir,
Cathay, and other nations. These he would tell
to each group, and they would be amazed. 
As for his bravery and knowledge of customs
and deployment in battle, he knew these to per-
fection, and a separate chapter will be devoted
to it.
As for various crafts, there was no craft he
could not execute with his own hands better
than
any
master
craftsman—be
it
gold-
smithing, blacksmithing, carpentry, painting,
metal casting, lathing, or any other. He worked
so well that he could guide the masters. The
emperor could guide and teach any master
builder who wanted an arcane instrument un-
known to his trade. 
He was enamored of the art of alchemy, the
most difficult of all the crafts, and he mastered
it in a short time, but since he knew for certain
that not just anybody could succeed in the
operation, [1339] he summoned those who
claimed to be able to do it. However, instead of
spending large amounts of money on their rec-
ommendation, as was usual, he did not allow
them to make any expenditures. What he or-
dered them to do was to perform the operations
they knew and of which they were capable,
like making enamel, dissolving talc, melting
crystal, making red lead, sublimations, and
making something like gold and silver. These
and other operations they performed in his
presence so that he learned how to do them. “I
am not learning these things in order to make
gold and silver,” he said, “because I know it is
impossible, but I wanted to learn the meticu-
lous arts involved therein and do them, for ac-
complishment lies in learning, not being satis-
fied with just that, and in advancing from
operation to operation.”
As for his knowledge of medicine, he was
perfectly aware of the general practice among
the Tajiks, Cathaians, and Mongolians, as well
as in India and Kashmir. He also knew the
methods prescribed by each group and was fa-
miliar with all medicines. Most physicians are
familiar with these only in pharmacists’ shops,
but he could identify all types of medicines in
the field. At present he can recognize from a
leaf a plant whose root is medicinal, and when
they pick it, it turns out to be that very thing.
Many medicines that used to be attributed to
the regions of Turkistan, Cathay, and India
were brought by merchants and sold for enor-
mous prices, but he discovered them in this
land. Others he made known himself by exper-
imentation. He summoned several renowned
Persian
and
Turkish
herbalists
from
the
provinces and took them with him to the
mountains and fields during hunts and other
travels in order to do research until he had
learned their method. At present no one among
the herbalists or physicians knows these things
as he does. [1340] To Faruq’s antidote he
added twenty-four non-compound medicines
that had been tested and were known to all for
being antidotes, each of which was by itself an
654
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

absolute antidote. He tested that antidote and
found it extremely beneficial, and it became
known as the Ghazanid antidote. 
As for his knowledge of minerals, through
much questioning of those who knew about it
he could say of any place he saw in the moun-
tains or plains what sort of mineral that place
contained, and when it was investigated he
would be right. He knew the method of extrac-
tion of every sort of mineral and how to smelt
it with the help of various implements and
operations, for he had done it all and per-
formed experiments himself. 
As for spells, he knew what was recited for
every sort of calamity. He knew in detail the
particulars of the shapes of men and beasts and
what they indicated in accordance with what
had been recorded in books. 
As for astronomy and uranology, since he of-
ten went to the observatory in Maragha where
he asked for an explanation of the instruments
and investigated how it was done, he learned it
and was aware of the generalities of that sci-
ence. Latterly, from his own nature, he ordered
them to construct what pertains to the site and
building of an observatory. In order to measure
the circular path of the sun he had a dome built
according to his own taste and discussed it
with the astronomers. They all said, “Even
though we have never seen such an instrument,
it is reasonable.” At the observatory next to the
Abwabu’l-birr in Tabriz,1 a dome was con-
structed that contains those things, as can read-
ily be seen.
He knew something of every science one can
imagine, and God withheld no accomplishment
1The complex of charitable institutions founded by
Ghazan Khan in Shamb, Tabriz. The name Abwābu’l-
birr (‘gates of piety’) is both a generic term for such in-
stitutions and, apparently here, the specific name given
to the complex. For the terms of endowment, see text
pp. 1377ff. below.
from him but rather adorned him with good
moral qualities, [1341] as will be described in
other chapters. He never allowed himself to
fall prey to pride on this account, and he used
to say, “The queen of the sciences is theology.
The object in learning other sciences and crafts
is to pronounce the name of perfection over
theology. Not knowing is an imperfection.
Therefore, one must know something about
everything in order not to be imperfect; other-
wise, why would I go to all this trouble?” He is
even now engaged in teaching and learning.
A line or two has now been mentioned of the
Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan’s knowledge,
and the people of this era are aware of it and
bear witness that this is how it is, lest readers
in later times accuse us of exaggeration. May
God grant him a new accomplishment every
day!
Story Two: The Padishah of Islam’s chastity
and sinlessness.
Persons who were intimates at court report that
the Padishah of Islam never committed any
forbidden act. If he chanced to have regard for
anyone, he never allowed it to go beyond mere
regard lest he commit lust. When he was away
from home on expeditions for long periods of
time with the military making conquests, the
officers used to choose beautiful girls taken in
plunder they considered suitable and bring
them to him. Although it is the Mongols’ cus-
tom to keep such girls in concubinage in order
to enjoy themselves in times of war and con-
quest, the Padishah of Islam was never so in-
clined and used to say, “How can I pollute my
body with them? How can I become acquaint-
ed with them in such an inappropriate fash-
ion?” He never paid any attention or accepted
them. During all this time, as has been wit-
nessed, no action ever issued from him that
would be considered adultery, [1342] sodomy,
or an abomination in law. He never gazed upon
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
655

other men’s wives with lust. In all the times he
went to conquer Syria, he paid no attention to
the Mongol girls in Damascus or others who
were there, no matter how many were present-
ed to him. No matter how long he was away
from home he was able to control himself
patiently. 
His noble mind never allowed anyone else to
indulge in sodomy or abominations, and he
constantly issued strong-worded edicts forbid-
ding such things. He had several persons exe-
cuted for that sin in accordance with Islamic
law and the Yasaq. The chastity of his noble
mind is as unadulterated as pure gold. May
God protect and preserve that peerless being
from the calamities of time and guard him
from the evil eye, through the Prophet and his
family.
Story Three: The Padishah of Islam’s
eloquence and fine repartee with all peoples.
Previously most imperial administration was
conducted by officers and ministers, and it was
they who tended to fiscal affairs. Emperors
were free of such matters and spent most of
their time hunting and enjoying themselves.
Now, one can easily imagine what administra-
tion by disagreeing officers and ministers was
like. Furthermore, when envoys arrived from
rulers near and far, the emperor’s reply was
conveyed by officers. 
With his correct ideas the Padishah of Islam
reformed and put into order all fiscal affairs,
which had been left to suffer for years and the
bases of which had been destroyed. Insisting
upon his own orders, [1343] he neither enter-
tained the ideas or words of any officer or min-
ister nor allowed anyone else to give weight or
importance to his own opinion. All became
subject to his order and command, and no one
had a chance to question the least affair. Con-
versely, everyone waited with bated breath for
the emperor to give an order. Finally, everyone,
young and old, learned and ignorant, carried
out his orders. This was not difficult for any-
one to do, for they saw that his mind was better
and sharper in all respects. His action and inac-
tion are so well regulated that by contrast they
have seen themselves as nothing, no matter
how competent they may be. Despite his
youthful years he knows so many choice
proverbs, dates, and subtle stories that when he
tells them his listeners are astounded. Whenev-
er an envoy arrives from anywhere, without re-
course to or consultation with ministers of state
he gives correct replies. Naturally great rulers
send extremely clever ambassadors to other
lands, but wise, eloquent, and experienced am-
bassadors who have come until now—as well
as great philosophers and physicians who have
arrived—have all been impressed with his elo-
quence and conversational abilities and with
his good moral qualities. He usually tells them
stories and events from their own countries,
and he can relate in detail the beliefs of any na-
tion that comes to him and recount the manners
and customs of any country or people, be they
ancient or modern. Consequently his fame has
spread to all countries, Chin and Machin, Hin-
dustan,
Turkistan,
Kashmir,
the
Qipchaq
Steppe, Rus, Frank, Egypt, and Syria, [1344]
and everyone takes account of and praises him
for his awesomeness, punishment, competence,
and perspicacity. May God make this Padishah
of Islam, this divinely chosen one, who is the
most intelligent and most perfect son of the
age, rule over the people of the world forever.
Story Four: The Padishah of Islam’s
patience, steadfastness, and trustworthiness.
Let me quote several examples of the patience,
forbearance, steadfastness, and trustworthiness
that are part of his character, for to give a full
report would take too long. 
Nawroz mutinied against him in Khurasan,
and although he was a servant of the court, he
656
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

attacked and surrounded the ordus, as has been
reported in the history. He also attacked several
other times, and damage in Khurasan and dis-
tress in the ordus were due to him. Never had
what he did been done by anyone. After that,
he joined forces with Baidu, and for a long
time he wrought destruction. When he was
reduced to helplessness he came to the court to
appeal for amnesty and a pact. Despite all his
evil actions, which no one should have borne,
the emperor pardoned him and rewarded him
with the rule of the entire kingdom. Since
Nawroz had a strange personality and signs of
rebelliousness showed clearly in him, and
since he did not speak straightforwardly either,
the officers often said, “He has undertaken so
many displeasing actions, and various crimes
have been committed on his account. He ought
to be eliminated.” The Padishah of Islam re-
fused to agree and said, “You are right, and it
is very clear and obvious. [1345] Yet I cannot
break my oath.” No matter how many evil ac-
tions and horrid deed were committed by him,
the emperor bore them patiently until Nawroz
went to Khurasan and began to stir up trouble
and rebellion. He actually wanted to seize all
the territory from there to Shiraz and Kirman,
and the realm was almost destroyed once again
by him. When this became clear, an order was
given to muster the troops. The officers said,
“We have said many times that he was harbor-
ing such things in his heart.” “I also knew it,”
said the emperor, “but I wanted him to be the
initiator, not me.”
Another time he had some officers executed
but spared the lives of others. (There is no ne-
cessity for giving all their names, for it is irrel-
evant.) During their trial the emperor said to
the officers, “I have known of their misconduct
for five years. I know all about it, but I have
been patient. Some have often suggested to me
improper things, each one of which would
have destroyed the realm. Had I had regard for
or listened to the various tricks of which they
spoke, more trouble than could be imagined
would have arisen. Some I do not want even to
give voice to. I spoke with them several times
in private. Although the first time they spoke to
me I realized that it was sheer chicanery and
would destroy the world, they shamelessly de-
nied it. For five years they repeated it and
spoke in another manner. It is strange that they
saw I did not approve and did not do it, but out
of ignorance they kept on repeating it. Ignorant
and stupid they were for wanting to catch me
in ignorance and draw me into their net. When
this went beyond all bounds and their sedi-
tiousness became apparent, they confessed.
Now I have revealed it.” From the state of af-
fairs it was clear to everyone [1346] that he
spoke thus. 
It had been a long time since they had spoken
those words, and all were astonished how he
could have borne it with patience, and when he
expressed it, they were even more astonished. 
It was also experienced that he immediately
recognized and got on bad terms with anyone
at his court who attacked people or engaged in
prevarication and mendacity, but through pa-
tience he was not hasty in revealing his wrath:
the ignorant man did not know that the emper-
or knew and was being patient. If the person
persisted in his ways, the emperor would have
him killed in the end. This group was large.
One of them was the cadi of Simnan who was
called Qazi Sayin. He was the worst of God’s
creation, truly more evil than Satan. The em-
peror understood what Sahib Isfahani and sev-
eral others whose names do not need to be
mentioned were doing. After waiting patiently
for a long time, he had some of them executed
through an informant and detractor, and others
he banished from court.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
657

Those who knew his nature, who avoided
speaking evil and stirring up strife, and who
constantly spoke beneficially and reasonably
as is demanded by their souls—such persons
he weighed in the scales of his perfect mind,
approved of, and considered reliable. Since his
illuminated mind was aware of them, if others
spoke derogatorily of them in envy and enmity,
or if they attacked them, he did not listen. In-
stead, he was patient and strengthened their
hands in the labors with which they were
charged so that affairs would run smoothly and
without interruption. He has often said, “There
is nothing in the world more noble or tangsuq
[precious] than a reliable and honest man.”
Consequently reliable, honest men are held in
the highest esteem by him, and he has killed
any who is corrupt, a thief, or a criminal. If
those who know swear the most solemn of
oaths [1347] that the Padishah of Islam has
never killed anyone except persons who are the
worst of creatures and whom it is proper and
necessary to kill since their existence is detri-
mental to all, their oath is correct and unde-
serving of retribution. Truly the result is that he
will order executed any other corrupter that
comes to his court, for the characteristic of his
noble soul with regard to corrupt people is like
that of emeralds with respect to vipers.1 Such
corrupters who remain are simply those he has
not seen or known, for otherwise his noble soul
is like a jeweler who knows crystal from ru-
bies: he knows those persons immediately.
This notwithstanding, he does not rush into
anything except charitable acts. 
Many, many times he advised his officers,
judges, and ministers, saying, “When a group
comes to complain of a governor or adminis-
trator, do not accept what they say right away,
1It was a common belief that emeralds were effective
amulets against vipers.
for it is possible that they have not paid their
taxes previously, or placed their burden on oth-
ers, and the governor has forced them to pay.
Such people, of course, will complain. If others
also come to support what they say, it is quite
possible that they previously held employment
and want to get their jobs taken away from the
present holders and given back to them. It is
also possible some people will come who are
old enemies of the governor or administrator,
or they may come on behalf of a friend, to vili-
fy the governor. Examine all these possibilities
carefully, and find out from the generality of
the tax-paying population whether the gover-
nor is tyrannical or not and whether they like
him or not so that the truth of his situation may
be ascertained. The words of the people carry
great weight when they are not self-interested;
the words of the self-interested and certain oth-
ers do not carry so much weight. Those with
whom the subjects are content and whose na-
tures are inclined to justice are hard to find.
[1348] A governor who has one or two ﬂaws
and many virtues—particularly unambitious-
ness, strictness, and honesty—should not be
dismissed from office.”
Because he constantly keeps it in mind to ex-
ercise caution, guides his officers and minis-
ters, and never swerves so much as an iota
from perspicacity and farsightedness, may God
cause the Padishah of Islam to enjoy many
years of life and rule.
Story Five: On the fact that most of the time
everything he says comes true.
Courtiers who have been in attendance from
the time of the Padishah of Islam’s youth re-
port that every time a matter or story crossed
his lips it came true. In recent years experience
has shown that every time he spoke in serious-
ness or in sport it happened likewise. He would
predict that a certain thing would happen to
someone, or that an envoy of a certain descrip-
658
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

tion would come from someplace, or that a
prisoner of a certain look would be brought, or
a piece of good or bad news would come. Al-
though such things are not unexpected from
rulers who are born under felicitous conjunc-
tions and to whom God has granted fortune
and happiness, to this extent it has never been
told or witnessed from any ruler.
Since he was passionate for all branches of
learning, he pursued and learned geomancy
and horses’ collar bones and teeth and other
signs by which good and bad fortunes have
been tested and recorded in books, and various
fortune-telling devices practiced by every na-
tion and country. [1349]
He is so familiar with most of the stars and
planets known to astronomers, and he is so
aware of the rising and setting points and the
particulars of each one that those who have
heard him speak of them are astonished. 
He knows the characteristics of all animals,
wild and domestic, in all their varieties and
shapes, their manners and movements, where
they live in summer and winter. 
All this is impossible except through great
intelligence.
Story Six: The Padishah of Islam’s
praiseworthy generosity and kindness.
When the Padishah of Islam mounted the
throne, his forefathers’ treasuries were empty,
the provinces lay in ruins and were uncon-
trolled, administrative properties were open to
loss, collection of taxes was impossible, and
the mismanagement of former ministers and
governors had allowed administrators to em-
bezzle property. It would take a long time to
put the affairs of the kingdom in order before
taxes could reach the treasury.
First, the treasures Hülägü Khan had brought
from Baghdad, the Infidels’ territories, and oth-
er places and put in the fortress of Tala-u-Sha-
ha had been stolen by the guards over time,
and bars of gold and jewels were being sold to
merchants. Because they all saw what each
other were doing and knew what was in each
other’s hearts, no one said anything. By
chance, one of the fortress towers, which was
on the river, collapsed, and on the pretext that
ingots and jewels had fallen into the river they
stole vast amounts. What remained Ahmad
gave to the soldiers because he wanted to curry
favor with the military, get the rule for himself,
[1350] and do battle with Arghun Khan. Very
little else remained. It was reported that it
amounted to no more than a million five
hundred thousand. Arghun Khan had gathered
treasures of all descriptions in Sughurluq, but
that too had been stolen by some and lost by
others. After that, when the amirs rebelled and
some amirs and courtiers killed Arghun Khan,
some of the treasury Arghun Khan had ac-
quired during his reign was distributed among
the conspirators, while others suggested giving
it to the soldiers. Thus it was lost. Gaikhatu ac-
quired nothing, and if any of Arghun Khan’s
treasury remained, he gave it to his men. 
For these reasons, nothing remained of past
treasuries at the time of the accession. Just
when
his
soldiers
came
with
him
from
Khurasan, rebels went to Khurasan and carried
off their homes, herds, and ﬂocks. No matter
how much the Padishah of Islam wanted to
give them something, there was nothing in the
treasury to give, and nothing was coming in
from the provinces. Nawroz managed fiscal af-
fairs and taxes for a while, but since he contin-
ued in the old fashion nothing was acquired.
After him, Malik Sharafuddin Simnani and
Sadruddin managed the administration, but
nothing was acquired then either. Expeditions
needed money, and if an ambassador came
from near or far and they wanted to honor him
or give him a gift befitting his station, there
was nothing in the treasury. People did not be-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
659

lieve that the treasury could be so empty and
attributed it to the emperor’s negligence and
carelessness. Things got so bad that complaints
began to come in from everyone, and when
they reached the imperial hearing, many times
he spoke to the amirs and his confidants and
said, “You think there is anything in the chests
loaded on those few camels and pack horses
[1351] we call a treasury? Since I love crafts
and always occupy myself by carving things in
wood and making implements, what they carry
is mostly pieces of wood and the tools of every
craft. There are also a few weapons. It is not
hidden from you, and the treasurers also know.
How can I give away what I don’t have? No
treasures were left to me by my fathers, and
taxes don’t come from the provinces. I have
been set over a ruined country. You go collect
taxes from the provinces and bring them in.
Then, if I don’t give you anything, the fault
will be mine.” From these words it was clear to
all that he was right.
Two years later, when the job of restoring or-
der to the fiscal administration was done and
the borders and marches were secure, rebels
and those who were stirring up strife and trou-
ble had been eliminated or punished, he turned
his attention to regularizing the affairs of the
provinces, reorganizing the fiscal administra-
tion, and collecting taxes and imposts. He sat
every day from dawn to dusk, correcting with
his own pen the rough drafts of things that had
to be written. He developed forms for fiscal
matters, laid down rules, and ordered how
everything was to be done. Provincial territo-
ries given in fief were to be given to reliable
people and not taken from them for three
years. No attention was to be paid to informa-
tion supplied by every beggar and nobody. He
also stipulated how taxes were to be gathered
and how much was to be collected from each
province. He also defined established expendi-
tures allowed to most places and regularized
them in a way that will be mentioned in other
chapters. 
Day by day taxes poured into the treasury
from all over, and year by year amounts in-
creased. [1352] Textiles from the royal factory,
which previously did not arrive any more than
taxes did, did not amount to a third of what
they should have, but now orders arrive in full.
Once money had been acquired, he began to be
generous. “There is nothing in the world more
difficult than giving money away,” he said to
the amirs and ministers of state. “Genghis
Khan said that there is nothing worse than
giving money or not giving money. Those who
don’t give are obviously stingy, and what is
worse than stinginess? To give, however, [is
also difficult] since if one person is given too
little and another is given more, or if one per-
son is given something and another is not giv-
en anything, or if someone is given later what
he should have been given earlier—all this is
harder for people than death, and they will be-
come inimical. Rare is the person who can ob-
serve all these minutiae, who will think of all
this. It is not possible for everyone to do all
this. Now, insofar as we are able, we will
maintain this rule.”
The few treasuries that came to him at the
beginning consisted of two or three million,
and he turned them over to his officers and
deputies, saying, “I have no attachment to what
they have brought. I will not put it in the
treasury. Let them put aside things that are
brought from the provinces so that they can be
given to the officers.” After that he told them
to which people it should be given and how
much should be given to each group, and the
officers gave it away accordingly. 
In recent years he said, “Once upon a time
the officers gave everything. I too have a de-
sire to give something myself.” During a quril-
660
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

tai in Ujan he ordered the great court tent
pitched and all the treasures that had been
brought from around the empire assembled. He
and several important officers sat and designat-
ed greater reward for persons who held larger
commands and who had done good service and
performed valiantly. He expressed the reason
for rewarding them more as follows, “I am
giving these people more, and the reason is so
that henceforth others [1353] may also strive to
perform valiant deeds and render pleasing ser-
vice.” After that he had those who had paternal
or filial relationships come forward. Then he
gave to the commanders of divisions of the left
and right as was customary. He ordered textiles
placed according to various sorts and bags
filled with gold and silver separated according
to weight; on each bag was written how much
it contained and which tribe it was for. Accord-
ing to their deserts he called out to each and
every group and ordered them to take their
share in his presence. Thus he gave money
away for ten or eleven days, and it amounted to
three million of cash in gold, twenty thousand
items of textiles, fifty jewel-studded belts,
three hundred golden belts, and a hundred bars
of gold. Thereafter he constantly gave cash and
textiles from the treasury, and never did he as-
sign so much as a fraction of a coin or a single
piece of fabric he gave away to be paid by a
province. No matter how much the amirs and
viziers told him to do so, he did not assign any-
thing and only gave and gives cash; however,
he keeps in mind the size of the deed and the
worth of the individual and doesn’t give too lit-
tle to those who should be given much or too
much to those who should be given little. His
treasury is never empty, and as much as he
gave away, God blessed him through his jus-
tice and good administration, and the treasury
did not decrease. A day never passes that from
ten to twenty thousand dinars and one, two, or
three hundred pieces of textile are not dis-
persed from the treasury. Such generosity and
gift giving are necessary.
One day, in the presence of the amirs and
grandees of state he said, “The best thing a
human being can do is to take on the qualities
of God. This is particularly true for kings.
[1354] Generosity and liberality are God’s
qualities, but that is a generosity such that no
matter how much is given away it never de-
creases or ceases. What a human can do is but
a drop in the sea compared to God; nonethe-
less, it is incumbent to try as hard as one can.
Rulers and all people should spend as much
money as they are able. If one gives without
restraint for a few days and then is unable to
spend anything or even to eat, what benefit is
this to anyone? To give everything away to a
few people and completely deprive others is
[not] God’s way. A ruler should be like the sun,
whose rays reach everyone, and let his treasury
be shared by all, especially the deserving, the
needy, and those who have done good deeds—
among them the soldiers. How can it be proper
to give to only a few people and then sit emp-
ty-handed and neither give to anyone nor be
able to give? What benefit do they enjoy from
such a person? What is the good of having im-
perial power in that case? 
“The
generosity
and
liberality
of
kings
should be like the water of a well or spring: no
matter how much is taken out, more comes,
and the amount never decreases. This is not
possible without good administration of the
kingdom, improvement of the land, fairness,
and implementation of criminal retribution.
Those who maintain an equilibrium in all
things will receive compensation in proportion
to the amount they give away. Otherwise,
‘when you take away from a mountain and put
nothing in its place, in the end the mountain
will be leveled.’ 
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
661

“If we and you are inclined to wealth, gen-
erosity, and gift giving, we must practice jus-
tice and truth, for it is a characteristic of justice
that to the extent that we know where the mon-
ey comes from that fills the treasury, no matter
how much we give away, the treasury will not
be emptied. It is good for us to be always capa-
ble of giving; otherwise, [1355] what use is a
king who is capable one day and incapable the
next, or rich for a time and poor for a time?
Such is not a characteristic of a king. If it were,
he would have to spend his days in grief and
worry, and the people would be deprived of his
gifts and learn to do without him as king. 
“We must observe this rule and make it such
that we give away however much comes in,
neither piling everything up nor bankrupting
ourselves all at once. There should always be a
certain amount of capital, for it is the property
of money that when there is a small amount of
capital, more quickly comes in. It is like a
hunter who has no bird to place in his snare for
other birds of its feather to ﬂock to: he can’t
catch anything. When he has one bird as his
capital, with it he can catch many thousands of
birds a year.”
The amirs and ministers of state praised these
words of the Padishah of Islam, and all were
happy. From that date until this, gold and tex-
tiles have been ﬂowing from the Padishah of
Islam’s treasury like water from a spring. Nev-
er at any time has any past king given away so
much cash and textiles as he has. Of course,
people take this to be an exaggeration and say,
“Who has ever seen past kings or knows what
their treasuries were like? How can anyone
make such a comparison?” However, the
touchstone of this statement lies in the registers
of inventory and expenditures of past genera-
tions, all of which are placed in the house of
registers. They are extant at present. What bet-
ter witness could there be than a register,
which has no vested interests? When they are
examined, the absolute veracity or falsity of
this statement can be obtained. May God cause
this generosity and liberality to last forever!
[1356]
Story Seven: The elimination of idolatry,
destruction of temples, and smashing of all
idols.
When, through divine guidance, the Padishah
of Islam Ghazan entered the Muslim faith, as
has been mentioned previously, he commanded
that all idols be smashed and all temples and
other places of worship disallowed by law in
the lands of Islam be destroyed. Most of the
idol-worshipping bakhshis were converted to
Islam, but since God had not slated them for
success, the faith they held was not correct:
outwardly they appeared to be Muslims, but
from their foreheads showed traces of infideli-
ty and error. 
After a while the Padishah of Islam compre-
hended their hypocrisy and said, “Let any of
you who so desires go to India, Kashmir, Tibet,
or his native country. Those who remain here
will not practice hypocrisy: let all act upon
what is in their hearts and minds and not sully
the pure religion of Islam with their hypocrisy.
If, however, I learn that anyone has built a fire
temple or idol temple, I will put him to the
sword without mercy.” Some continued to
practice hypocrisy as before while others occu-
pied themselves with their disgusting ideas. 
“My father was an idolater,” the emperor
said, “and in that belief he died. He built for
himself an idol temple and endowed it in the
name of the idolaters. I destroyed that temple,
but you may go reside there and enjoy the
income.” 
The ladies and amirs said, “Your father built
a temple and put his own image on the walls.
Now that it is in ruins, snow and rain fall on
the images of your father, who was an idolater.
662
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

If that place were restored, your father’s soul
would rest in peace, and his good name would
be assured.” The emperor did not consent or
approve of this. Then they suggested turning it
into a palace. Still he did not consent and said,
“Even if I intended it to be a palace and they
put pictures therein, since it has been an idol-
aters’ temple, it would be inappropriate. If a
palace must be built, let it be built elsewhere.”
There are many such stories and cases, but it
would take too much time to tell them all. 
In short, he said to the bakhshis, “It is known
to me that you have no knowledge, but to
maintain group cohesion it is incumbent upon
kings to have all sorts of people in their ﬂocks.
For that reason they protect and maintain them
all. Even beasts, which have no understanding
or intelligence, are kept and maintained by
kings, people of Islam, and people in general
for their own purposes and needs. You too are
of this sort, but you must not exhibit an iota of
idolatry, fanaticism, or incorrect behavior; if
you do, I will make you fodder for the sword.”
At present the few of them that remain do not
even think of having an opportunity to show
that they have a creed or religion. In this they
are like the Magian peoples or the heretics,
who have been in these lands from long ago
but keep their beliefs hidden. 
May God cause this Padishah of Islam to last
forever! [1358]
Story Eight: The Padishah of Islam’s love
for the family of the Prophet.
The Padishah of Islam twice saw the beauty of
the lord of creation in a dream, the Prophet
gave him good promises, and they conversed
long. With the Prophet were the Commander of
the Faithful Ali, Hasan, and Husayn, and he in-
troduced them and said, “You should be broth-
ers.” He told the Padishah of Islam to embrace
them, and brotherhood was accepted on both
sides. From that time on, the Padishah of Islam
achieved many victories and successes, the
greatest of which was that he spread charity,
order, and a system of justice and punishment
throughout the world. He thus attained a good
name and stored up for himself a treasure of
prayers from the people for his well-being.
What felicity or gift can be greater than that? 
From that date forward, his love for the
house of the Prophet has increased, and he
constantly gives assistance to aid pilgrims and
visits shrines to that family. He makes vows
and sends [to shrines the money he vows]. He
honors and holds sayyids in great respect and
gives them alms and stipends. When he was
having khanaqahs, schools, mosques, and oth-
er charitable institutions built all over and was
endowing them and considering the duties and
salaries of every group, he said, “How is it that
there are [such institutions] for the poor and for
Sufis and other groups but not for sayyids? The
Alids should also have them.” Therefore he or-
dered “sayyid houses” (daru’s-siyada) built in
Tabriz
and
other
great
provinces
[1359]
throughout the realm like Isfahan, Shiraz, and
Baghdad, for sayyids to stay in. He stipulated
amounts to cover their provisions as he saw fit,
as the deeds of endowment bear witness, in or-
der that they too should have a share of his
charity. He constantly says, “I deny no one. I
recognize the greatness of the Companions, but
since I saw the Apostle in a dream, and he cre-
ated a brotherhood and friendship between his
offspring and me, I am more friendly to the
members of his house. This is not to say that I
reject the Companions, God forbid!”
He commanded a canal constructed to the
shrine of Husayn, as will be described. He al-
ways praises the Prophet’s family without fa-
naticism, for, thank God, he is wise and per-
fect. May God keep this just emperor for the
people of the world for long years!
Story Nine: The Padishah of Islam’s
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
663

bravery, his tactical deployment of the army
during engagements, and his persistence in
battle.
From his childhood the Padishah of Islam was
in Khurasan, the most difficult frontier, the di-
rection from which foreign forces have come
from ancient times until now. Not a year passes
in which one or two expeditions do not have to
be mounted. He has therefore often fought
foes, engaged in fierce battles, and endured
many hardships and difficulties. He is perfectly
aware of and extremely expert in the minutiae
of the field. He has become so stout of heart
that he has no trepidation whatsoever, even in
the mightiest cases, [1360] and hesitation finds
no way into his mind. Even when he knows
that things are going to be difficult and the foe
is strong, he is patient and valiant and does not
allow any trace of worry to appear. “No profit
is derived from fear,” he says. “It only results
in the failure of one’s strategy and helping the
enemy.” Such things have been witnessed
many times by his attendants in Khurasan. It
would take too long to describe them all, but
one thing that happened in this region is the
case of him and Baidu. 
He charged out of Khurasan like lightning,
struck [Baidu and his men] with only a few
soldiers, and persisted patiently. After that, it
was decided that they would see each other in
private with only a few liege men. When they
met, in jest he slapped [Baidu] so hard on the
back that he was pained and realized that
[Ghazan] had no respect for him and there was
no fear in his mind. After that he mustered his
troops, attacked him with a few soldiers when
he had the opportunity, and captured [Baidu]
so that the kingdom and the military suffered
neither harm nor trouble.
He got his hands on the amirs who had
stirred up trouble during his father’s and his
uncle’s times, and although they had powerful
protectors, he acted out of stoutness of heart
and rightness of thought, paying no attention to
anyone’s attempts to intercede, got rid of them
all, and put the kingdom in order. 
Another time, when Sögäi rebelled and Ar-
slan turned around with a troop arrayed and at-
tacked him,1 [Ghazan] kept receiving news and
realizing that when he got there he would not
be able to offer resistance because there were
no troops available, but he absolutely did not
give in. Every day he occupied himself as usu-
al, and when Arslan got near he sent out a
troop that was there as though to go hunting,
but he himself did not make a move although
not everyone was informed of this. He stayed
where he was, laughing, playing, [1361] and
telling stories of all sorts. He summoned the
physicians and astrologers and said, “I want to
make a laxative. Go get the ingredients and se-
lect a day.” He apparently paid absolutely no
attention to the rebel, and his mind was not dis-
turbed in the slightest that anyone could tell.
Because of that courage and patience no dis-
ruptions occurred, no rumors were spread, and
the people remained as they had been. If so
much as an iota of change had been detected in
him, everything would have been lost, particu-
larly since it was still early in his career, and
the kingdom and army had not been consoli-
dated. The soldiers, who had created distur-
bances before, were still avid for plunder, and
he looked like a puppet to them. This affair
turned out well thanks to the assistance of the
Creator and through the patience and courage
of the Padishah of Islam, and nothing was
struck by the evil eye. 
Another instance is the following. During the
war with Egypt and Syria people thought that
he would take up a position in a corner of the
array, as was the custom of kings, where no
1See text p. 1264. for this episode.
664
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

one would know where he was. Contrary to
this, he came forward boldly, positioned the
entire army himself, and stood in the forefront.
He charged repeatedly like an enraged lion,
and if they hadn’t taken his reins, he would not
have stopped fighting. Although those near
him forbade it, he went into the midst of the
enemy several times and charged, putting them
to ﬂight and killing several before he returned.
Suddenly a troop nearby was routed. On the
sides, some were not aware of the battle and
others had not yet arrived in the field. To the
left and right of the Padishah of Islam was
empty. He himself stood his ground before the
foe with only a few men and Sultan. Because
the first strike had been against the center, the
soldiers went far away and stood, not making a
move and thinking that when the enemy at-
tacked
there
would
be
no
reinforcement.
[1362] The foe was making concerted and re-
peated hard strikes. Like a roaring lion, the
padishah persisted from noon until late after-
noon, repelling the charges by himself, resist-
ing such a numerous force by his good tactics
and strategy, and keeping on fighting. What
lion-hearted
champion
would
have
such
courage and fortitude? In the end, when the
troops of the left hand, who had been standing
afar waiting to turn back, saw what was going
on, they turned to face the foe, and some of
those who were farther back on the right came
in. The foe, having been exhausted by the
Padishah of Islam’s persistence, pulled back in
defeat. 
There have been many such instances, but
we will content ourselves with this much as an
example.
He constantly instructs, guides, and advises
the victorious troops and says, “Everyone has a
moment of death. Wherever it may be—at
home, on the road, in battle, during a hunt—
everyone has to die. Why then should one fear
and be afraid of an enemy standing opposite?
Since death is inevitable, it is better for a man
to see his own blood, for unseen blood just pu-
trefies in the body and results in nothing but a
stench. Just as rouge is an ornament to women,
blood is an ornament to men. The good names
of such men remain in this world, and in the
next world they go to paradise. When anyone
dies at home, his wife and children have to
bear the wearisome chore of tending to him,
and in their view and that of other loved ones
he becomes an object of pity. If he dies in bat-
tle, he is freed from such concerns, and his
loved ones grieve for him, but the monarch of
the age honors and consoles them and takes his
sons under his patronage so that they are well
taken care of.”
He also said, “When the army goes on an ex-
pedition, if it is a strike, one must insure that
news not get out, [1363] and the horses must
be kept fit. One should proceed day and night
in such a manner that one arrive suddenly lest
the enemy have a chance to group and retreat.
If you go every year, you should strive to go at
different times; otherwise, when the appointed
season arrives, the enemy will have prepared
himself beforehand. You must also strive to go
by a different route every time so the enemy
will not learn of your approach. Scouts must be
reliable and know the roads. If a large contin-
gent goes, the greater the noise of their ap-
proach, the better. In battle one should go
slowly, for a large army cannot proceed with
haste. When the enemy has already learned of
your approach, made his preparations, and is
waiting for you to come, you must not rely on
the numbers, small or large, of the army so
long as it moves quickly, for victory cannot be
predicted. When you act with deliberation and
broadcast news of your arrival, it is possible
that the enemy may take fright at the rumor,
chaos and disagreement may erupt, another en-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
665

emy may attack from another direction, there
may be a rumor of some event, or they may
suffer from lack of fodder and provisions.
When such an expedition is launched, before
the news is broadcast, you should already have
taken all precautions for water, fodder, and
game. When you stop in such places, one must
not consume the provisions that have been pre-
pared for difficult places. Spies have to be sent
forward to learn of the enemy. After they have
reconnoitered, their information should be the
basis of action because fighting without fore-
knowledge is like throwing punches in the
darkness. After taking all precautions, you
must insure that the choice whether to do battle
or not is yours, not the enemy’s, for if you are
left with no alternative and act in haste without
stopping and come across the enemy suddenly,
your position may be bad and you may have no
alternative but to do battle, while the enemy
may have a good position. The most important
thing is discipline among the troops. Do not al-
low a single soldier to go anywhere without
permission, for experience has shown that
thereby the foe gains time and is helped. Even
more importantly, absolutely do not allow any-
one to go on his own into villages and take
anything, for once they learn how to do it, a
large army can never be kept from it and dis-
cipline will be impossible. In the same way,
during battle they will occupy themselves with
booty and plunder, and there is no way to pre-
vent it. Every evil that has happened to any
army has happened mostly because of taking
booty. When the battle is over you can see to
where booty and plunder are to go. As for dis-
cipline, one must not look into people’s hearts
and restrain oneself from killing, for if two or
three persons are not executed, ten or twenty
thousand may perish instead, and the whole
kingdom may be lost on that account.”
“From the time of riding away from home
on,
one
should
constantly
entertain
good
thoughts, think of God, keep oneself pure, and
not commit evil deeds. Be kind to one’s people
and kingdom, and do not apply force to anyone
so that the people will send good thoughts and
offer prayers for success that will be answered.
For an army, there is no advance force better
than a prayer for success and a good thought.”
“One should not boast or allow pride and
conceit to enter one’s mind. Do not underesti-
mate your enemy, but fear him. Know that you
are weak and God is great. Fear God so that
your plans may succeed and the battle may be
won. Know for certain that anyone who boasts
or has vain thoughts will stir up God’s zeal:
greatness is appropriate to God alone, and such
a person is vying with God. If anyone vies with
God, [1365] God will take the other side and
help them to teach him a lesson. Such a thing
is easily within God’s power, and he will
exhibit his wrath in a way that will never have
occurred to the mind of any champion, no mat-
ter how intelligent he may be.”
He constantly gave and still gives the officers
and soldiers advice of this sort. He has spoken
many words even pithier than these, which I do
not remember, and anyway, if I were to begin
to expand on them, it would take too long.
Since I only intended to include an example,
this much will suffice, and everyone knows the
rest. May God keep this protector of the world
and maintainer of the subjects and army for-
ever!
Story Ten: His advice to cadis, shaykhs,
ascetics, and people of learning and piety.
Every time these groups of people came to
court he would give them various pieces of ad-
vice, but once in an assembly for which the
great and important of these classes came to
court for a quriltai he said, “You have put on
the garb of advocacy, and this is a mighty af-
666
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

fair. You do not make this claim with the peo-
ple, however; you make it with God. It is pos-
sible that the people will accept your claim for
a few days while they are not aware of what
you really are, but God is well informed of
what is in your minds, and hypocrisy and dissi-
mulation do not work with him: they only stir
up his zeal, and he will requite you and punish
you for it in both this world and the next. If
anyone garbs himself in the clothing of a char-
latan, God will disgrace him among the people,
[1366] and his garb and name will be nothing.
He will be shamed before the people, and in
their eyes he will be low and mean, an object
of ridicule for commoner and elite alike. Those
who have not put on the garb of advocacy are
straightforward: they do not distinguish them-
selves from others or have notions of power,
leadership, asceticism, or occultation. No one
has any objection to them. They expect them to
live as befits their clothing. What we have said,
that you have put on the clothing of advocacy,
means that you are like other men, but on ac-
count of your clothing you have acquired a
great name that has several special meanings
not found among others. You have accepted
this name and its meaning for yourselves and
you have undertaken to give people their due.
You say, ‘We are thus and so,’ or ‘We will do
thus and so.’ Now, consider well whether you
are able to discharge the obligations involved
in this pact and covenant and the claim that is
part and parcel of this clothing and whether
you can keep your word, for your position is
very fine and pleasing before God and the peo-
ple, and it is higher and better than that of oth-
ers. If not, it will result in shame before God
and the people. 
“You have chosen to take upon yourselves
troubles and responsibilities. Know for certain
that God made me king and set me over the
people so that I would regulate their affairs and
maintain justice and equity among them. He
has made it incumbent upon me to speak the
truth, to act judiciously, and to punish crimi-
nals in accordance with their offenses. God’s
eternal decree necessitates that the requital of
the elite be greater, and that is why the beasts
are not answerable for crimes. Kings must like-
wise make the great and those who are in the
forefront of their nations more answerable and,
having made this a rule, so put their kingdoms
in order. For this reason I investigate your of-
fenses and call you on the carpet first. [1367] I
do not look into your hearts, and don’t think I
look at your garb, for I look at your deeds and
actions. Your must follow the path and custom
of the Apostle and perform your duties. Show
others the right way, and eschew corruption
and meddlesomeness. Do not allow through es-
oteric interpretation what is not stipulated in
the letter of the law. Be honest and truthful and
have good thoughts so that the whole world
and we too may be protected through the bless-
ing of that. Be not fanatic with one another,
and do not practice fanaticism with other na-
tions where God and the Apostle have not so
commanded, for to be more fanatical than nec-
essary and to be stricter or more lenient on the
people than God and the Apostle for the sake
of a good name is ignominious and iniquitous. 
“If I do something contrary to the law or rea-
son, warn me and apprise me of it. Know for
certain that your words will have an immediate
effect on me and will be listened to so long as
your inner beings and your advocacy are in
harmony with each other, for then you will be
speaking with truth, honesty, and self-confi-
dence. Of course it will be effective. To follow
the truth on account of what you say will result
in praise and reward both for me and for you
and in rest and repose for the people of the
world. If they are otherwise, your words will
have no effect on me, and the fire of my wrath
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
667

will be kindled against you, and this will result
in loss for me, for you, and for the people in
general.
“There are many such stories and fine points
I wanted to say, but for now this much I have
said; if it is pleasing to you and you accept it, it
will benefit me and you. My words will be ac-
ceptable to you, and love for me will take firm
root in your hearts; otherwise, my words are
hard for you to take, and enmity toward me
will take root in your hearts. My inside is
aware of your hearts, and you too will be hate-
ful to me. [1368] By this, damage will be done
to the world and religion. Let us cut this short
here for today. Henceforth, if success is grant-
ed, we will tell you fine points.”
In this manner he gave advice to the
grandees and important cadis, shaykhs, and
ulema who came before him. They were all
amazed by it and prayed for the court. At other
times, in various sessions he gave similar ad-
vice, but it would take too long to recount it.
May God cause the shadow of the Padishah of
Islam’s justice, which is adorned with various
perfections, to extend over the heads of all
classes of people forever! 
Story Eleven: The Padishah of Islam forbids
all soldiers and others to make heathenish
statements.
The Padishah of Islam heard that when some
of the soldiers and others went off to battle and
gained a victory, they boasted, saying, “We did
this,” or, “Because of our tactics, deeds of
great valor were performed,” or, “So-and-so
performed great heroics,” or, “Through So-
and-so’s efforts the enemy was broken.” In this
manner they attributed heroics to their own
competence
or
manliness.
They
spoke
grandiosely and were conceited. If occasional-
ly they returned unsuccessful, they would say,
“It must have been God’s will, for we did our
best and fought with all our strength.” Such
words had gained great currency among the
people, and the Mongols and Tajiks spoke like
this even of trivial affairs. 
Reports of this speech often reached the im-
perial hearing, and he did not like it. Angered,
he said, [1369] “These words are really hea-
thenish. Most labors of ours, soldiers and com-
mon people alike, fail because of the inauspi-
ciousness of such statements. They should
realize that every good thing that happens to
us, to soldiers, or to other people comes from
God’s mercy and compassion, and every bad
and untoward thing that happens is a result of
their own sinfulness and evil. They should not
say anything that shows conceit or pride.”
He therefore ordered an edict written in this
regard and sent to the Mongols and Tajiks in
all parts of the realm: “Henceforth anyone who
believes in or makes statements as our forefa-
thers did will be considered an offender, and
his place will be in hell in the next world. You
should recognize that good things come from
God’s grace and bad things stem from your
own displeasing actions. Any person who
comes to the door of your houses should be
given to eat of what you have. Adopt the way
of virtue, and live with all people in humility.
By virtue of this edict we have commanded,
persons who come to people’s houses should
not demand anything; and let them not think
that it is incumbent or necessary for anyone to
give them anything except insofar as that act
issues from virtue.” In this manner he issued
an edict and ordered it heralded throughout the
realm. The blessedness of the edict took effect
generally during his imperial time with God’s
help, and it continues to increase. 
Story Twelve: His love for building and his
encouragement of others in that regard.
Previously the Mongol emperors and some of
the Padishah of Islam’s ancestors and forebears
liked to build. They began buildings, [1370]
668
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

but they seldom completed them, as has been
seen. Everywhere they laid a foundation enor-
mous amounts were spent. Tapqur funds, ani-
mals, tools, and hired workers were brought
from the provinces, and the people suffered a
lot of trouble, but mostly it all went to waste.
Those who were in charge made money disap-
pear overnight, and not much building was ac-
complished. Those that were built were not on
sound foundations, so within a short time they
went to wrack and ruin. 
The Padishah of Islam has made arrange-
ments for construction, nothing better than
which could be possible. Wherever he found a
reliable and honest khwaja, he has chosen him
and put him in charge of a building, and funds
are turned over to him. He has assigned impor-
tant khwajas, honest scribes, architects and en-
gineers. He has also stipulated the maximum
price to be paid for all tools and the wages to
be paid for that many tools so that if there is
any shortcoming in management, they will be
responsible for the loss. The overseers and
contractors keep a constant count of the tools
used, and in this manner they keep the foreman
of every gang accountable. Things are so or-
derly that if a hundred years hence anyone
wants to audit the accounts he will be able to
compare the clerks’ registers with the tools
used. Now the difference between right and
wrong is clear, and there is absolutely no lati-
tude. No one can come forth to denounce what
those khwajas and builders do. There are
trustees appointed to every job, and they do not
allow bad tools to be used or too little plaster
or cement to be employed or mixed with dirt.
The
maintenance
of
these
rules
is
their
responsibility. 
Also, all wooden and iron tools have been
contracted at fixed prices so that all types are
stipulated. He has ordered projects in every
province, [1371] and canals and underground
water channels are under construction. The
greatest of these, and the one that will do the
most good, is an enormous canal in the
province of Hilla. Its name is the Upper Ghaz-
anid Canal, and it carries water to the shrine of
the Commander of the Faithful Husayn and has
made the sweet waters of the Euphrates ﬂow
through the entire Kerbela plain, which was
waterless wasteland and had no drinking water
for the shrine. Now all the environs of the
shrine are under cultivation, and gardens and
orchards have been established. Boats that ply
the shores of the Tigris and Euphrates from
Baghdad and other cities can go to the shrine.
Produce amounts to nearly a hundred thousand
taghars, and grains and vegetables grow better
there than in any of the dependencies of Bagh-
dad. The sayyids resident at the shrine have be-
come very well-off, and since they were a poor
people and very numerous, he has ordered for
them all stipends that are paid yearly.
In the vicinity of the Abu’l-Wafa shrine,
which is in a waterless desert, there used to be
no sweet water for drinking. One year the em-
peror went hunting in that desert. No water
could be found for the animals, and the on-
agers and deer were very skinny and emaciated
due to the lack of water and vegetation. He or-
dered a canal cut from the Euphrates to there
so that there would be water and agriculture at
the shrine, so that the desert animals might
have relief, and so that when people went into
that desert they wouldn’t find the animals suf-
fering from lack of water, and so that they
would have barley and straw for fodder. Within
a short time a magnificent canal was cut, and it
was called the Lower Ghazanid Canal. After
that, another canal was cut to that desert from
the west, and it was called the Ghazanid Canal.
He put several feddans from the water and land
in endowment to the shrine, [1372] and he pur-
chased with his own money the rest of the vil-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
669

lages that were constructed and endowed them
all to the Abwabu’l-birr in Tabriz.
Recently he has had gardens and orchards
constructed at the Sidi Abu’l-Wafa Shrine, and
now sweet water and all sort of vegetables
have appeared, which they never had before.
Since that shrine is far from habitation and the
residents were being harassed by rebellious
Arabs, he ordered a rampart wall made as
around a city, and inside they built a bath and
new buildings. It will soon become a city.
He has had and continues to have innu-
merable construction projects made in most of
the provinces, and he constructs canals and
subterranean water channels. If we were to go
into detail, it would take too long. There is no
end to what he has ordered reclaimed and im-
proved
by
decree
and
contract
with
the
deputies
of
the
Department
of
Royal
Demesnes. During his blessed reign, through
his all-encompassing justice, thousands of men
are employed by them on projects; and what
people do on their own amounts to many times
that. Houses and gardens that were formerly
worth a hundred dinars are now worth a thou-
sand. Previously they destroyed things to the
extent that they now make improvements. The
projects that are now on-going in the realm
have never been undertaken during the reign of
any monarch after the reign of the Chosroës. It
would be amazing if so many people were en-
gaged in building even during the reign of the
Chosroës because, although the realm ﬂour-
ished greatly at that time, it was accomplished
over many long years, and at that time there
had not been such devastation.
The city of Tabriz, which is now the capital,
had smallish ramparts, and they were worn
down, and there were many houses and build-
ings outside the city. “How can a city with so
many thousands of people living in it—and
which is the capital—not have ramparts?”
[1373] he said. He ordered a survey made to
determine where and how walls could be built.
Since there were gardens and orchards adjacent
to the built-up part of the city, it would have
been necessary to build the walls through peo-
ple’s property. It was also suggested that since
there were innumerable foreigners and resi-
dents in Tabriz, most of whom were wealthy,
they should divide the walls and let each group
construct a portion with their own funds over a
period of two to three years. 
With his high-mindedness, perfect compas-
sion, and mercy, the Padishah of Islam said,
“How can it be right for land people have built
up to be substantially destroyed through an act
of charity on our part? Why should they suffer
loss? When they were laying the foundations
for the city of Tabriz, how could they have sus-
pected that now it would have reached a point
that so many thousands of houses would be
built outside the walls? How could they have
known that within such a short time, as has ac-
tually been witnessed, the population would in-
crease so dramatically and so many buildings
would be built outside? If it continues to in-
crease like this, it is hoped that the people of
this city will become extremely numerous. One
must think grandly, and the walls must be con-
structed such that all the people’s gardens,
along with their houses, be inside the perime-
ter. Gardens should not be destroyed, and their
value should increase, for thereby we will be
rewarded. It is also possible, if God grants suc-
cess, that over time there will be such popula-
tion and crowding that the entire encompass-
ment will be built with houses next to each
other and there won’t be any room left for peo-
ple. It has been learned from experience that in
some cities God favors with fortune to ﬂourish,
there are so many people that they run out of
room and have to build houses of two and
three stories. The lanes become narrow, the
670
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

walls become high, and the air becomes putrid,
and for that reason contagion appears, all sorts
of sufferings are engendered, and the city falls
back into ruins—like the city of Khwarazm.”
[1374] 
Therefore he ordered the walls built outside
the gardens. As for the suggestion that the peo-
ple resident in the city give money, he said,
“Although they will benefit from the building
of this wall, peasants and common folk are
short-sighted and cannot comprehend long-
range consequences. It would be hard for them
to give money. This is a charitable act, and we
will give the money from our demesnes so that
the heavenly reward will accrue to our good
name and the subjects and people will be left
in peace. For this reason let no one make any
demands on them.” To this effect he issued a
decree, and this year, two years from the be-
ginning of construction, God willing, it will be
completed. 
He also ordered another city larger than the
encompassment of Old Tabriz built in Shamb
(also called Shamm), where the Abwabu’l-birr
was constructed, in such a way that it encom-
passed the Abwabu’l-birr and most of its gar-
dens. He called it Ghazania, and he ordered
that merchants coming from Anatolia and Eu-
rope unload there, but the customs official for
there and the city of Tabriz is the same lest
there be dispute. 
He ordered a large caravansary, a crossroads
market, and a bath, with workshops and places
for animals, to be built just inside the city next
to every gate of New Tabriz. Merchants who
come from all directions enter by the gate in
the direction from which they come and stop at
that caravansary. The customs official stamps
their goods, they enter the baths, and then go
into the city. When they have found their par-
ticular places they can move if they want.
Likewise, when merchants go from Tabriz to
all parts they stop there for the customs official
to inspect their goods, and then they can set
forth. 
He has ordered many improvements in all
parts of the realm. He has also ordered saplings
and cuttings of all types of fruit trees, herbs,
and grains from all parts of the realm, which
were unknown in Tabriz and which no one had
ever seen, grafted and planted. [1375] This was
carried out, and now they are all found in
Tabriz, and daily they ripen. The people have
benefited more than can be described and pray
for the success of the state. He has sent envoys
to all distant lands, India, Cathay, and others,
to bring seeds of things peculiar to those
places. May God cause him to enjoy long life
and prosperity! 
Story Thirteen: The charitable institutions
he founded and constructed in Tabriz and
Hamadan, their endowments and
mausoleums, and the charities he vowed in
the provinces.
Until now it has been the custom of the Mon-
gol emperors of Genghis Khan’s urugh to be
buried in unmarked places far from habitation
in such a way that no one would know where
they were. They made the environs ghoruq and
stationed trusted men who would not allow
anyone to get near. When the emperor became
Muslim and elevated the customs of religion to
the skies, he said, “Although such was the cus-
tom of our fathers—and if a Muslim does not
desire his burial site to be marked there is no
religious objection—there is no benefit in it.
Now that we have become Muslim we should
conform to Islamic rites, particularly since Is-
lamic customs are so much better.”
Early in his career he visited the holy shrine
at Tus in Khurasan and went to the mau-
soleums of Sultan Bayazid, Abu’l-Hasan Khar-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
671

raqani, Shaykh Abu-Sa‘id Abi’l-Khayr,1 and
others, [1376] where he witnessed the arrange-
ments for those holy sites and how the inhabi-
tants were. After that, when he became Mus-
lim, he visited the blessed shrine of the
Commander of the Faithful Ali and other
saints’ shrines in Baghdad. One day he said,
“How can one consider a person who has died
in this manner and has a shrine or visitation
site like this to be among the dead? Dying like
this is better than other people’s living. Even
though we do not possess the rank of pious
people, nonetheless in imitation of them we
can build a charitable institution to spend eter-
nity in, and in that manner there will be charity
and alms, the blessings of which will attract
God’s mercy, and there will be an eternal re-
ward stored up. It will be very good. Let us be-
gin now, while God has given us the strength,
so that it may be completed successfully.”
Since he was in the capital Tabriz, he chose it
as the site and laid the foundation himself out-
side the city to the west in the place called
Shamb. They have been working on it for sev-
eral years now, and it is planned to be much
more magnificent than the dome of Sultan San-
jar the Seljuq in Merv, which is the most mag-
nificent building in the world and which he
saw. The plan for the royal foundation is as fol-
lows: [1377]

FOR THE DESERVING
Every year two thousand sheepskin coats will be
bought and given away.
Education
of children who are thrown into the streets. They
will be picked up, nurses will be hired, and their
needs will be tended to until they reach the age of
discrimination.
Preparation
of the bodies of strangers who die in Tabriz and

Seed
for all varieties of birds during the six months of

one who attempts to harm them will suffer God’s
curse and wrath and will be prevented and chas-
tised by the superintendent and residents of the in-
stitution; if they do not do this, they will be guilty.
Poor widows
will be given cotton annually as capital. Each of
five hundred widows will be given four maunds of
carded cotton.
To replace
jars and jugs broken by servant boys and girls. The

In order to
clear the roads of rocks and to build bridges over

Wages
for deputies and employees of the bureau of en-

Fund
for repairing the Lofty Dome and the charitable

Fund for repairs

Since the emperor intended for most classes
of people to benefit from the charities and in-
stitutions, he stipulated as given above and en-
dowed
the
institutions
with
everything
throughout the realm he owned absolutely and
outright by law in such a way that no one could
raise an objection. He had all the muftis, unim-
peachable learned men, and cadis of Islam is-
sue certificates of authenticity, and he ordered
seven copies of the deed of endowment made
and registered. One was to be held by the su-
perintendent, one was to go to the Kaaba, one
was to be placed in the seat of the judiciary in
Tabriz, one was to be placed in the seat of the
judiciary in the City of Peace Baghdad, one
___, one ___, and one ___. Every so often the
cadis of Baghdad and Tabriz should renew the
authentications, and every cadi who took up
the judgeship should register it immediately
upon taking office. He also commanded that
those who were the most learned and most ex-
cellent of the age should reside in the Ab-
wabu’l-birr. 
In the province of Hamadan, in the vicinity
of Safed Koh, in the village of Buzinjird, he
built a major khanaqah [1385] and endowed it
with much property. Travelers find rest and re-
pose there, as all can witness.
674
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Furthermore, in every province he went to
and every time he beseeched God’s court for
something and made a vow of alms, he ful-
filled his vow. When he defeated the army of
Egypt and sat on the throne in Damascus, he
fulfilled several vows he had made when he set
out, some in this realm and some in that realm.
One was for golden lamps, carpets, and rugs
for the shrine of Sayfullah Khalid ibn al-Walid,
in the vicinity of which the battle took place.
This one was fulfilled right there. 
Another was a vow he made to endow sever-
al villages in the district of Damascus to
Jerusalem and Abraham’s shrine. 
He also made a vow, saying, “The rulers of
Egypt and Syria long provided administrative
and military expenses for Mecca and Medina
and the pilgrimage route, and they used an es-
oteric interpretation to give themselves this
privilege even though it was not really right.
Now that God has given me this land, they
spend all the proceeds from the endowments
on themselves and do not spend anything at all
for the military or administration.” Then he
added, “This territory is now under our juris-
diction, and when we pull back, we shall sta-
tion a large army to protect it. The charitable
intention we have made must be carried out.”
In this Abwabu’l-birr he issued an edict and
made a vow in this realm that two hundred
thousand [dinars] taxes from royal enchüs be
given as stipends, endowments, and alms to
amirs, commoner and noble, rich and poor, and
soldiers who gather every year for a quriltai.
When he pulled back he fulfilled the vow, and
he awarded every class, [1386] group by group
according to their ranks, with jewel-studded
belts, plain belts, and various articles of cloth-
ing. The two hundred thousand dinars he had
vowed for stipends and alms is now fixed in
every province and is awarded year by year.
Aside from this he ordered that of all money
brought to the treasury, one of every ten dinars,
one of every ten pieces of cloth, and a tenth of
other articles be separated and entrusted to a
eunuch, who would serve as custodian and
give it to the poor and deserving. He was not to
give anything to the undeserving but let it go to
the treasury. Every year curtains, candlesticks,
and lamps are sent to all the holy shrines.
He is always in supplicative converse with
God, and he knows for certain that his needs
will be granted without question at that court
on account of his charities, alms, and vows, for
these things do not go unrewarded. There is no
doubt that in no age has anyone seen such
charitable acts, stipends, and alms awarded by
any ruler. May God reward this emperor for his
generosity. 
Story Fourteen: His elimination of forgeries
and false claims, and his elimination of the
treachery of the dishonest.
In his perfect justice the Padishah of Islam
eliminated all sorts of forgeries and false
claims and forbade cadis and khatibs who were
not learned in the law to issue legal receipts
and documents. [1387] He ordered all cadis to
write documents in one fashion so that all fine
points of the law were observed in order to
close the gates of contention among the people.
Since the details are fully covered in the edicts,
copies of the edicts will be given to avoid repe-
tition. The edicts and decrees are as follows: an
edict given to judges on the delegation of judi-
cial authority, an edict ordering that thirty-
year-old claims not be heard, an edict con-
cerning proving a seller’s ownership prior to
sale, and edict reaffirming prior orders and
governing the form of documents, to which all
the religious authorities of the age agreed.
Copies of these edicts are as follows.1 
1Sylistically the texts of the following edicts contain a
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
