Text of an edict on the delegation of judicial
authority.
In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merci-
ful, and by the might of God and the auspiciousness
of the Mohammedan nation.
Decree of Sultan Mahmud Ghazan.
Be it known to basqaqs, maliks, and persons who
govern on our behalf in N.___ that we have ap-
pointed N.___ to the office of judge of that place
and its dependencies in order that any case, affair,
or business pertaining to the law in that province
may be referred to him for final judgment. He will
guard well the property of orphans and absent per-
sons, and other than him no one, be he who he may,
will interfere in his affairs. No one will release
from prison anyone he has legally imprisoned.
[1388] Those whose jobs are involved with the law
will not contradict him. Inasmuch as it was
Genghis Khan’s great edict that judges, scholars,
and Alids not pay qalan or qubchur tax, we have
commanded that they will accordingly be exempt.
Taxes and qubchur will not be taken from them.
Ulagh and süsün will not be taken from them ei-
ther. No one will stop in their houses, and envoys
will not be quartered there. Stipends will be paid
them annually and without stint according to the
registers. If anyone speaks harshly in the presence
of a judge, answers harshly, or shows disrespect,
we have ordered the shahna to punish him. No one
will summon a judge into his presence. Since a
judge administers the law, he will take nothing
from anyone on any excuse or pretext, in accor-
dance with the document and möchälgä (written
pledge) he has given. When he writes a new docu-
ment, old documents will be brought to the court
basin, thrown in, and washed clean, in accordance
with a separate edict we have issued. Claims not
made for thirty years and old documents bearing a
date of more than thirty years will not be heard, in
accordance with an edict we have issued separately.
curious mixture of highly Arabicized legalese and “chat-
ty,” rambling prose. If passages in the translation sound
somewhat inharmonious or out of place in what was, af-
ter all, an imperial document, it is due to the varied tones
of the original. 
When such old documents are presented, they are
not to be given to litigants or claimants but washed
off in the court basin. Cases based on fraud are not
to be heard, and persons who have done such will
have their beards shaved, be mounted on oxen, be
paraded around town, and be publicly disgraced.
After that they will not be allowed to witness docu-
ments; and if they do, it will not be considered. 
When two claimants come before the judge, if
anyone comes to protect them, or if they bring a
group of hoodlums to court to help them, the judge
must not hear the case until they leave the court.
[1389] Absolutely he must not question them on le-
gal matters so long as their protectors are present.
If a case is between two Mongols or between a
Mongol and a Muslim, or if there are other cases
that are difficult to decide, we order the shahnas,
maliks, bitigchis, cadis, and learned Alids to meet
twice a month in the congregational mosque to in-
vestigate. Let them hear the cases together, get to
the bottom of them, make decisions in accordance
with the law, write and record their decisions, and
give their signatures in witness thereto so that after-
ward no one can raise any objection or invalidate
the decision. 
If a piece of property is in dispute, let none of the
following classes become involved in or purchase
same:
royal
mothers,
tärkäns,
khatuns,
sons,
daughters, sons-in-law, commanders of ten thou-
sand, one thousand, a hundred, or ten, Mongols,
bitigchis of the Supreme Divan, cadis, Alids, schol-
ars, shaykhs, or chieftains. In accordance with the
decree we have given, the judge N.___ will exer-
cise all precaution not to write a document in the
name of any of these aforementioned people for
any piece of property or transaction that is in dis-
pute. If he sees that anyone else has so written, he
must invalidate it. 
When prenuptial agreements are paid, they are to
be nineteen and a half dinars and no more, in ac-
cordance
with
a
decree
we

In territories dependent upon the province of

ing a judge appointed, a trustworthy magistrate

should be appointed, and in accordance with the

documents or make legal decisions. They should
send him a report every month. They should not
hear claims and cases, render decisions, or record
real estate transactions in the vicinity of villages
where a judge has been appointed. Other than recit-
ing the khutba and writing documents of loans and
marriage settlements they should not write any
piece of paper. If a case is difficult or a claim is im-
portant, let them come to town and present the case
to the city judge for him to render a final decision. 
A trustworthy and religiously observant person
should be appointed to record the dates of docu-
ments and keep a day book. He should be careful
that it be clear if anyone has sold or mortgaged a
piece of property and then wants to resell it or put
it up as collateral. Anyone who does such a thing
will have his beard shaved and be paraded around
town. If the recorder of dates has any awareness of
such dealings or hides anything, he will be guilty
and liable to execution.
Text of edict ordering that thirty-year-old claims
not be heard, under the conditions listed.
In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merci-
ful, and by the might of God and the auspiciousness
of the Mohammedan nation.
Decree of Sultan Mahmud Ghazan.
Be it known to judges of the realm that our entire
mind is concentrated upon the elimination of injus-
tice, aggression, and false claims from the people
so that the world and those in it may spend their
days with peace of mind and at ease, and so that the
effects of our justice may reach common and elite,
far and near, [1391] and encompass them all, that
causes for difference and dispute may be eradicated
among all peoples, that right may prevail, and that
the gates of falsification, imposture, and artifice
may be closed forever. To this end, we have repeat-
edly sent decrees to all judges and ulema who deal
with legal and religious matters telling them to de-
cide cases and settle disputes among all people in a
way that satisfies the principles of the religious law
and the codes of justice. They must be free of
doubts, falsification, imposture, fraud, and partiali-
ty. The most important matter of all is that they
examine closely forged documents and falsified
deeds and registers. They must get to the truth of
the matter and neglect not one iota in their investi-
gation of the antiquity purported by the outward
appearance of the documents and in good-faith
maintenance of the customs of former judges and
governors.
As for documents that have not been presented
for claim within thirty years, any forger or cheat
may have fabricated them and, under the protection
of ruffians, trampled upon the rights of private
property and subjected the people to harassment.
Judges have not been able to right this wrong as
they should have. Prior to now, during the days of
former rulers, it has been mentioned in all decrees
and edicts that thirty-year-old claims are not to be
heard, and until now no one has gotten to the bot-
tom of this affair as they should have, and redress
has not been totally achieved. Recently we have
commanded judges of Islam to investigate and re-
port to us. Since we wanted to do right in these
matters both on the part of claimants and on the
part of judges so that neither party would be able to
insist upon a wrong and thirty-year-old invalid doc-
uments would not be used as evidence, we ordered
that a pledge that would conform to the law and
truth be taken from judges of Islam to the effect
that they would neither look into people’s hearts
[1392] nor allow any group of ruffians to insist
upon asking irrelevant and illegal questions or to
bring force to bear upon judges and magistrates.
We ordered the late Qazi Fakhruddin of Herat to
compose a draft of the pledge, and it was written
on the reverse of the decree so that such a pledge,
with no additions or subtractions, would be taken
from them and housed in the treasury. The decree
and the pledge written on the back would be before
them so that elite and common would fear and ruf-
fians would not be able to insist, and thus false
claims would be abandoned. Let them consider
nothing beyond the scope of this order and pledge
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
677

on the reverse. If they contravene this order, they
will be dismissed from the judgeship and be la-
beled as criminal. Let them know for certain that I
will listen to no excuse from them, and if a power-
ful person tries to exercise inﬂuence on them and
insists, or if they do not pay attention to what is
written on the back of the pledge and do not render
decisions accordingly, the names of such persons
will be written and sent to our presence so that we
may brand them as criminals and punish them in
such a manner that all will learn a lesson. 
Written on the third of Rajab in the year six
hundred ninety and nine [March 25, 1300] in
Kushaf.
Text of the pledge written on the back of the
aforementioned edict.
Whereas the emperor of the world and all in it, the
king of kings of Islam and Islamic peoples, he who
is distinguished by God’s mercy, Ghazan Khan—
may his fortune remain and increase forever—has
concentrated his lofty attention from the beginning
of his reign on allowing his subjects to pass their
time with peace of mind and ease [1393] during the
days of his rule, on encompassing elite and com-
mon, far and near, Turk and Tajik, with his perfect
justice, compassion, and mercy, on eliminating
matters of contention and strife in all transactions
from among the population, on giving right where
it is due, and on closing completely the gates of fal-
sification, imposture, and chicanery, 
Therefore, in the contents of all imperial edicts
and decrees—may they remain in effect from east
to west forever—all judges and learned men en-
gaged in legal affairs and in charge of religious
matters have been admonished to decide cases and
settle litigation among members of the population
at large in a manner that preserves the principles of
the religious law and is in accordance with the
codes of justice and equity. They must be free of
falsification, forgery, partiality, and imposture. In
particular they must examine and investigate falsi-
fied documents and forged deeds and registers, and
get to the bottom of the matter insofar as they are
able. [They must judge whether] the outward ap-
pearance of the document indicates antiquity, and
in good faith they should maintain the customs and
manners of past judges and governors and neglect
not an iota in their investigation and search. Let
them not lay the burden on another, for it often
happens that a person has a property that he has ini-
tiated, created, or received from another. He has
documents and deeds drawn up proving his owner-
ship, they are verified by judges and officers of the
law and recorded. [1394] After a time the property
is transferred by legal conveyance to a second par-
ty, and from him to a third, and so on. The docu-
ments remain in the home of the first owner, pass
through the hands of several heirs, and then after a
long time an ambitious distant heir produces the
documents, claiming, “On such-and-such a date it
was my ancestor’s property, and today it has come
to me through inheritance.” People testify to the
veracity of his claim of inheritance, and disputes
drag on. In some provinces, some judges who do
not possess a firm footing in religiosity, piety, or
knowledge of jurisprudence may render a judgment
without getting to the bottom of the affair and with-
out being able to distinguish truth from falsehood,
and that results in the denial of right to its owner. 
Therefore, inasmuch as past rulers, in order to
avoid such possibilities, have ordered that claims
on real estate and material goods presented after a
period of thirty years, which is considered a gener-
ation in common law, will not be heard or granted
validity. They have also ordered that no decision be
made on falsified and forged documents and deeds
before exercising all precaution and making an in-
spection. After them, the edict of the Great Ilkhan
Arghun Khan was added to those rules. When ref-
erence was made to the statements of religious au-
thorities and the interpretation of the learned, it was
apparent that a majority of latter-day authorities
and the learned were in agreement that if two per-
sons are in one place and one usurps property be-
longing to the other, and if a just governor and a
competent judge are both present in that place, and
if there is no other party to the suit and no proof of
apparent rightfulness, and if a period of a full thirty
years passes and the first party does not make a
claim against the other who is the usurper, he will
678
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

not thereafter be entitled to bring suit, and the
judge will not accept to hear the case. [1395]
Now, I, who am N.___, judge and competent to
render a judgment in the province of N.___, give
my signature and undertake that from this date I
will execute all that is written in this document. I
will not transgress or deviate from what is exacted
by the Mohammedan law in hearing cases, render-
ing judgments, or settling disputes. To the best of
my ability I will endeavor to report and examine
cases and investigate deeds and documents to the
utmost degree. I will not hear, pay any attention to,
or entertain any claim made after thirty years with
the provisions made hitherto. If I act contrary to
any of the above, I will be worthy of chastisement
and liable to beating and dismissal.
Thereto I swear before a group of competent wit-
nesses on the date ___.
Text of edict on proving a seller’s ownership
prior to sale.
In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merci-
ful, and by the might of God and the auspiciousness
of the Mohammedan nation.
Decree of Sultan Mahmud Ghazan.
Be it known to all basqaqs, maliks, judges, bit-
igchis, deputies, authorities, nobles, elders, and all
subjects of the province that, in accordance with
the Koranic text, “O David, we have made thee a
vicegerent on the earth, so judge thou among the
people with righteousness,” and in accordance with
the Prophet’s command, “An hour of justice is bet-
ter than forty years of worship,” the totality of our
regal mind is concentrated upon the welfare of the
population at large, and we are desirous that our
justice and equity spread throughout the world, that
no powerful person exercise force or restraint upon
a weak person, [1396] that no one’s rights be sacri-
ficed through chicanery or any form of falsification
or machination, and that all forms of dispute be er-
adicated from among the people. Having contem-
plated the yasamishi, the ordering, and the basis of
every thing, we realize that one of the greatest
causes for dispute and contention among the inhab-
itants of the world is false claim through old docu-
ments, deeds, and duplicate titles of ownership that
have remained in the hands of individuals. This
comes about as follows. A person owns a property,
and in his own interests he makes two copies of a
document of ownership, or, if he owns many prop-
erties, he obtains a clear title and makes two
copies. Thereafter, the property may be divided
among that person’s heirs, sold, or transferred to
others by various conveyances. After much time
has passed, some of all those deeds, titles, and doc-
uments may remain in the seller’s hands or with his
heirs. After a time the seller may make a false
claim, and assuredly he will have thought long and
hard about how to do this and how to get witnesses
to verify his claim. Having become expert in such
techniques, he will use a thousand tricks and
sleights-of-hand. He may even put witnesses under
oath and catch them off guard, or he may get un-
trustworthy and unreliable people to testify. If the
seller himself does not bring suit, his heirs may
find the documents in his house. They may not
know for sure whether the property has been alien-
ated, or they may bring suit even though they do
know [that the property has been sold]. Of course,
when deeds recorded and authenticated by a living
witness are brought before a judge and they are de-
termined to be sound, the judge must decide in fa-
vor of their validity, for how can he know whether
property has been transferred by legal conveyance
to another party? It is well known that a judge is
helpless before two witnesses. If several well-
known
and
respected
judges
have
previously
recorded a deed, [1397] if competent live witnesses
are produced even though they are unaware of the
later sale and transfer of the property, and if the ti-
tles, whether duplicated or not, remain in the hands
of the seller and are not turned over to the buyer, of
course they can bear witness. The judge will record
the deed and find for its validity. The claimant will
go and either take possession with the help of ruffi-
ans and by force of the deed that has recently been
judged valid and recorded or sell it to those same
ruffians. The buyer suffers loss thereby, and the
dispute and contention between them goes on for a
long time. 
Now, since deeds and titles are considered suffi-
cient evidence, and legal possession has the great-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
679

est weight in the eyes of the law, if duplicate or in-
valid deeds proliferate in everyone’s hands, to base
a claim on such things becomes suspect and doubt-
ful. Since certain evil persons are inclined to prac-
tice fraud, the best thing to do is for seller and buy-
er both to go before a judge at the time of sale and
produce evidence through whatever titles there are.
The seller must prove his ownership through unim-
peachable witnesses who testify that the property
belongs to the seller, is in his possession, and, inso-
far as they know, no one else has legal claim to it.
Those titles must be washed in water. If they do not
have titles, and witnesses can testify in accordance
with the foregoing, and it can be proven that the
property has been in the seller’s possession either
for a long time or recently, and if the seller swears
that he does not possess titles—or, if they are
found, they will be invalid—then his ownership
can be recorded, witnesses’ testimony can be writ-
ten, and the judge can record the sale and find for
its validity. After that, a document of sale should be
recorded beneath the proof of ownership. If an at-
testation is made and a legal conveyance is effect-
ed, even if later some of the titles, deeds, or affi-
davits of the property are found in the hands of the
seller, [1398] his children or relatives, or any other
person, be he who he may, no Islamic judge will
give them any consideration. If he does see them,
he will insist on taking them or take them by force
and wash them off. If he has ruffians or the protec-
tion of powerful patrons, and they do not listen to
the judge, let him tell the shahna of the city to take
them by force and wash them off in the courthouse.
If they fail in their duty, they will be reprimanded. 
Those who write titles and deeds of sale should
be clerks of the court. No one else should write
them. Of course, it is necessary that when a judge
sits in judgment in court he should have on a stool
a basin full of water, which we have named the
Basin of Justice. The titles for every claim and case
that is decided should be demanded and washed in
the water. If a seller sells a portion of his personal
property and retains possession of the rest, the
amount that is sold should be recorded on the back
of the document in the presence of judges and com-
petent witnesses [in words such as] “of the property
mentioned within this document, ___ amount has
been sold to N.___ on the date ___.” The document
will remain, as before, in the hands of the seller. In
the buyer’s document it should be written that the
seller had X amount of property, of which he sold
X amount to this individual and retains X amount
in his possession. In this case an unwashed deed
will remain in the hands of the seller.
Item. If a person certifies orally or in writing to a
sale or mortgage, [1399] and that same person later
brings suit against either the buyer or mortgagee,
the case will not be heard, and that person will
have his beard shaved, be mounted on a donkey,
and paraded around town. If anyone sells to anoth-
er a piece of property he has previously mortgaged,
pledged to another, or sold, this will constitute
fraud, and the case will not be heard. The plaintiff
will have his beard shaved, be mounted on a don-
key, and paraded around town. If anyone has sold
property to another or mortgaged it and then sells
or mortgages it to someone else and it is found out,
those persons will be executed. 
Item. We have commanded that judges should
neither expect nor take a cent for recording or hear-
ing cases. They should be content with the salaries
we have ordered. A scribe who writes a document
may take one dirhem per document worth a
hundred dinars. For those worth more than a
hundred dinars they may take one dinar and no
more. A bailiff who produces witnesses may take a
half a dinar for every document duly witnessed. No
matter how many times a case is reheard, he should
content himself with that same rate. Any advocate
who takes something from both parties to a suit
will be admonished, his beard will be shaved, and
he will be discharged from the advocacy.
Item. We have written a separate edict con-
cerning thirty-year-old claims and made stipula-
tions therein. Let these remain in force. Any judge
who acts contrary to the orders we have written
will be punished and dismissed from the judiciary.
We have ordered that the basqaqs and maliks of
every city throughout the realm should summon the
judges of that place and take from them and send a
pledge to this effect according to the draft we have
sent. Now, N.___ and N.___ must summon the
680
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

judges of that place, take a pledge from them in ac-
cordance with the draft that has been sent, and send
it in the company of these messengers. Written in
the city of ___ in the year ___. [1400]
Text of edict reaffirming prior orders.
In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merci-
ful, and by the might of God and the auspiciousness
of the Mohammedan nation.
Decree of Sultan Mahmud Ghazan.
Be it known to the judges of the realm that, inas-
much as we realize that the smooth functioning of
the world and those in it depends upon the regula-
tion of legal affairs, prior to now we sent an edict
to all parts of the realm from the Oxus to the bor-
ders of Egypt concerning redress of breaches in the
fabric of the judiciary. Therein we commanded
judges to investigate legal decisions with all delib-
eration and care, admonished them to maintain all
conditions necessary to the investigation of notary
documents, deeds, titles, and affidavits, and warned
them about implementing decisions in which there
is doubt of falsification, fraud, imposture, misrep-
resentation, or any other form of chicanery. We
have given them to understand the necessity of not
paying attention to the mere antiquity of documents
or to prior judges’ decisions, which may not have
been devoid of negligence or partiality. We have
made them adhere to customary rules and details
that insure soundness of religion, salvation in the
next world, and preservation of honor. We have
commanded that this be read out to court officials
once every month throughout the realm so that it
may be ingrained in their minds by repetition, so
that false claimants will be tormented within them-
selves and adopt the correct path, and so that pow-
erful persons will not be tempted to force judges to
render a decision outside the path of correctness,
particularly since we have emphasized this com-
mand by ordering that written pledges be taken
from all judges, to wit that henceforth they will not
look into people’s hearts, [1401] that they will not
be partial to any side other than God’s, and that
they will strive to their utmost in examining claims,
deeds, and documents in order to be delivered from
the sedition of falsification and fraud. No claim not
brought forward for more than thirty years despite
the existence of the claimant’s ability to bring suit
and the absence of extenuating circumstances will
be heard if suit is brought after the expiration of
that term, and no decision will be given, for the
corruption of such cases is obvious and to hear
them is improper. The Seljuq sultans prior to now
researched such cases, and with the help of the de-
cisions of the authorities of the age they forbade
them to be heard. After that, the authorities, judges,
and learned men of Islam came forward in this case
to write letters and reaffirm that decision, copies of
which are published abroad. An edict of our fathers
was also issued in this regard. 
This edict will be carried out for two purposes.
[1402] First, the reaffirmation of the former order
so that all may realize how strongly we are com-
mitted to the smooth functioning of religious af-
fairs, so that the mischief of negligence in matters
of the law may be eradicated from minds and the
excellence of steadfastness and surefootedness may
take its place, and so that all may know as a cer-
tainty that anyone who deviates from this will suf-
fer the reprimand that the cadi of Ardebil suffered,
who, when he did not avoid executing fraudulent
cases, was put to the sword in the most horrible and
terrifying manner.
Second, since our mind is always concentrated
upon the right functioning of the affairs of the peo-
ple of the world and upon the acquisition and per-
fection of the same, we have desired to add to for-
mer orders several necessary provisions that are
acquired by instinct of sound mind and following
the path of the provisions of the religious law and
to make judges of the realm understand the necessi-
ty of following them meticulously and without
stint. First is the reaffirmation of precaution in
hearing testimony, around which most cases re-
volve. It is obvious that judges are negligent in that
regard and do not strive to verify and render judg-
ments without having inner certainty or assurance
of testimony and without having a preponderance
of conviction of the soundness and truth thereof.
Instead, they cling to the legal principle that “a
judge is helpless before two witnesses” and do not
fear the enormity of such negligence. It happens
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
681

that a case may be critical in and of itself, and if a
decision is rendered without the truth of the situa-
tion having been reached and without precaution
having been taken, some wealthy people may be
wiped out by these means, for even though two
witnesses constitute legal proof, the outcome
should still depend upon justice. Justice is a mighty
thing that is only rarely found in individuals. Self-
interest reigns supreme in most people, and a judge
must always wonder if A’s or B’s testimony is not
devoid of self-interest, selfish imagination, or par-
tiality. Merely because testimony appears in and of
itself to describe good men, or if it so seems exter-
nally, or if the speech is adorned with artifice, one
must not be deceived. In ascertaining the truth and
extracting the inner meaning of a subtle case, con-
templation and clarity of mind must be exercised so
that the manner of the case may be clear, and ob-
fuscation and obscurity may be eliminated. Since it
was part of the Maker’s wisdom in creation that
traces of falsehood, however much it is hidden in
the interior, will appear in a speaker’s utterances—
as the Commander of the Faithful Ali said, “What-
ever a person has in his heart will be apparent to
people in the slips of his tongue”—therefore, any-
one who concentrates with a sound mind upon as-
certaining the inner aspect of a person can compre-
hend it from his speech. [1403]
Based on the foregoing, we have commanded
that in hearing any testimony about the acceptance
of which the mind has the slightest doubt, great
caution should be exercised. Each and every wit-
ness should be questioned in order to ascertain any
difference among their testimonies, for the touch-
stone of verification lies in finding a difference in
the words of witnesses. Each one should also be
questioned repeatedly in different sessions, and sit-
uations should be investigated obliquely. One
should rely on questioning points such as times,
places, quantities, and qualities of the case as well
as subtle inquiries that have a bearing upon ascer-
taining the truth. Through such effort one of two
things will become apparent: either soundness,
upon which a judgment one may trust can be given,
or a doubt that annuls the case and saves one from
the brink of rendering an incorrect judgment. Since
most of the breaches of justice that occur in cases
happen because property is declared licit as alms
by people who are not pure in and of themselves,
precaution should be taken more in this regard, and
the necessity of following the separate section on
the allowance property as alms should be realized.
Item.
Deliberate
slowness
and
deliberation
should be exercised in deciding on letters they seal,
for in this regard great doubt arises. In most cases
that will be implemented in their own villages and
districts, owners go before judges in other jurisdic-
tions for authentication. The reason for this is that
in that other district no one is aware of the particu-
lars of the case, and the truth or falseness remains
hidden from the judges. Without verifying, they
send a document sealed to other judges to be
opened, and they judge it proven, and thus false-
ness gains currency in the guise of truth. Deliver-
ance from this brink of disaster lies in the follow-
ing. Judges must not write approval or [1404] put
their seals upon a document until they are aware of
the situation of a case exactly as it is and the neces-
sity of referring it to a different venue; so let them
open sealed documents. Until they know the neces-
sity of proving it before the judge who sealed it, let
them not imagine that he was in the right, and let
them not hasten to open and render a decision. 
Item. Great precaution should be exercised in
cases pertaining to the writing of deeds, docu-
ments, various letters, and all kinds of written deci-
sions and records, for few situations in which writ-
ing is involved are devoid of breaches of justice,
and it often happens that the end result of the
breach is upholding falsehood and deprivation of
rights. These breaches of justice stem from the
writers’ ignorance of the conditions of writing,
looking into people’s hearts, or partiality. Since
total redress is necessary in this regard, we ordered
some judges, authorities, and learned men known
for their acumen to delineate how many types of
documents were generally written in court, and
they composed for each type a model containing all
possible provisions and fine points that could not
be objected to or challenged, and to it was added an
appropriate exhortation containing many beneficial
points. They gathered the models in one volume,
682
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

and outstanding learned men gave their signatures
to certify the soundness thereof. When the desider-
atum was presented, copies were made and sent to
all parts of the realm so that every type that needed
to be written could be copied from the model.
Judges of the realm should first consider it with
caution, and when they find that it agrees with what
is desired and is in conformity with the law, they
too should add their signatures and compel clerks
henceforth not to go beyond the model for any rea-
son but copy it letter for letter. The point has been
stressed previously [1405] that they should write
only when a judge’s order to write has been given;
they should not do it frivolously. 
Item. It has been learned that the negligence,
misappropriation of authority, and venality of some
judges has reached the point that they have placed
in the hands of two litigants in one case two written
documents at variance with each other—and both
have been recorded. Thinking it would never be
discovered, they had no compunction in doing so.
We have commanded that henceforth they will not
commit this action for any reason or under any ex-
tenuating circumstances. Furthermore, they will do
all they can to rectify past abuses. In the court of
any judge before whom any two such documents
are presented, all effort will be made to ascertain
the truth of the case. If referral to authorities is
needed, let a gathering be held and let the truth be
ascertained based on correct principles. Let them
uphold whichever side is clearly in the right and
wash the other document in the Basin of Justice. If
such action cannot be taken immediately, let them
turn over both documents in trust to the bailiff to be
held—and under no circumstances given to the liti-
gants—until the case can be decided. To place such
evidence in the hands of litigants will result in
nothing but corruption, sedition, and breach of jus-
tice. In that there is no doubt, for each litigant, or
his heirs, will find an opportunity for obfuscation at
some time or other to present the document and file
suit. The judge at that time may not possess the ev-
idence and testimony that nullified the case and
may then render an incorrect decision. If both doc-
uments are held and it is made clear to the litigants
that they will not be returned to them, they will
reappear when court is held, and thus, when the in-
vestigation has been completed, right can be
established. 
Item. With the agreement and approval [1406] of
the authorities of the age, Sultan Malikshah gave
an order and had it codified in the interests of the
people of the world that if anyone makes a con-
cealed trust or writes an encumbrance on property
in secret and keeps it hidden, and if later he or any
of his heirs brings forth the property that is in the
deed of endowment or encumbrance and tries to
sell it, judges of the realm will not hear such a case
and will nullify the deed of endowment or encum-
brance. They will also give the perpetrator the nec-
essary chastisement and admonition and allow the
property to the purchaser. A group of renowned au-
thorities met sometime thereafter in Qazwin and
reaffirmed on their own initiative matters of reform
upon which the best interests of the people depend-
ed, writing that it is incumbent upon judges to act
in accordance therewith. One of their points was
that no property legally in the hands of a possessor
can be taken away from him simply because of the
appearance of a document at variance with that per-
son’s ownership. It must be left in his possession.
We too have ordered judges of the realm to act in
accordance thereto and not to infringe upon that de-
cision, which was reached unanimously and which
aimed at establishing rights. 
Item. It has been heard that some short-sighted
people who are entrusted with the trusteeship of an
endowment are enticed by greedy people either to
sell or transfer their trusteeship, and thereby dam-
age is done to the endower. We have commanded
that if anyone has in his possession an endowed
property suspected of having been conveyed, the
intentions of the endower will be investigated. If
permission to convey was included therein, no ob-
jection will be made; if not, the conveyance will be
nullified and the deed of conveyance will be
washed in the Basin of Justice. Henceforth no one
will allow any conveyance, permission for which
was not so stipulated by an endower. If anyone acts
contrary to this, [1407] the conveyer, recipient, and
writer will all be fined and admonished. 
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
683

Item. Inasmuch as it is obvious to all that in these
orders that are being executed we have no view
other than to maintain the side of God, to strength-
en the Mohammedan law, and to spread justice and
welfare among our subjects; in warning judges to
follow the path of truth and justice and in the ad-
monition and exhortation that are repeated our pur-
pose is only to force them, not to break them, to el-
evate their worth, not to belittle them, and to honor
them, not to imprecate them. Let them hear these
things obediently, learn their lessons, and know for
certain that anyone who acts accordingly, who
takes God’s side and holds the sacred law above
the stain of falsification, and who exercises all due
precaution in judging cases will be covered with fa-
vor in addition to receiving abundant reward and a
good name. If there is anyone on whom such
strongly-worded decrees, emphasis, and reaffirma-
tion has no effect, we will not henceforth issue
another decree on these matters, and the dictum
“the sword is a more efficacious informant than let-
ters” will be applied. So let them know this for cer-
tain, and therein is sufficiency for him who can
learn a lesson. 
Amir N.___ and governors must entrust to judges
this decree or a ministerial copy thereof that will
arrive, and take a receipt that they have received
same. Let them together make a copy of the decree
and the draft models, let them certify that they have
been compared to insure accuracy, and let them be
sent to all appointees, persons of authority, and
judges of the provinces in order that they may be
aware. Let them take a pledge against misdeeds
that henceforth they will act in accordance and see
to it that these matters are made clear to all. [1408]
Story Fifteen: He eliminates the practice of
forging documents and annuls outdated
deeds.
Prior to this, in the time of the caliphs and sul-
tans, every possible effort was made to propa-
gate the work of the judiciary and the good re-
pute of the law, great caution was exercised,
and religious and wise people of importance
were chosen to occupy the judiciary. They too
appointed religious men of honor from among
well-known learned people to the bench. As a
consequence, legal matters and religious cases
were run in accordance with the commands of
God and his Apostle, the people were given
their due, and the gates of injustice and tyranny
were completely shut. Parsimonious, dishon-
est, rapacious, officious, fraudulent, and slan-
derous persons had no opportunity to burden
these momentous matters with any sort of
chicanery, fraud, or subterfuge; on the con-
trary, such persons were not allowed entrance
to parties or gatherings, and no one paid them
any
attention.
Such
regulation
and
order
notwithstanding, during the reign of Sultan
Sa‘id Malikshah, because there were so many
old deeds and duplicate titles in people’s
hands, as there are in this time, they took them
to judges and, by employing tricks that forced
the judges to hear their cases, had them vali-
dated. (When confidence men have the chance,
they will always disguise falsehood as the
truth.) This resulted in harassment of the peo-
ple. Later it was ascertained that their claims
were false and their deeds and titles were du-
plicates, the properties having been conveyed
to others. 
These disputes and contentions were often
brought
before
the
hearing
of
Malikshah
[1409] and his vizier Nizamulmulk. They real-
ized that the main tools of these confidence
men’s trade were the old deeds and duplicate
titles that had remained in the hands of the for-
mer owner or his heirs after the transfer of the
property. With the passage of time no one re-
membered the situation, until suddenly one of
the offspring of the former owner produced the
deed and brought suit. It was possible that the
purchaser of the property or his heirs had never
seen those deeds, or they may have been lost or
pillaged during times of unrest. They may even
have been stolen from their ancestors and giv-
en to the seller, who, knowing that they did not
684
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

have a record of transfer, brought suit based on
his old deed and had it validated. There were
many such instances. 
In short, when Malikshah and Nizamulmulk
became aware of the situation, they wrote an
edict in a legally appropriate form, ordering
that no claims be made or cases heard based on
documents that had not been contested for
more than thirty years. They sent this order to
all the muftis of Khurasan, Persia, and Bagh-
dad so that decisions would be rendered in ac-
cordance with the law. Afterward it was sent to
the seat of the caliphate for signature. This let-
ter is still extant, and copies of it are spread
abroad. 
Judges and court officials at that time being
as has been mentioned, even such religious and
respected judges, sultan, and vizier were so
helpless at the hands of miscreants that they
had to issue such a decree. 
During the days of the Mongols it happened
that the people gradually became aware that
the
Mongols
could
recognize
judges
and
learned men merely by their turbans and tu-
nics; they had absolutely no awareness of or
way to judge their learning. Therefore, igno-
rant and vile men put on the turban and tunic
of impudence and joined the Mongols’ ret-
inues, ingratiating themselves with all sort of
ﬂattery and bribes, so that they obtained judi-
cial posts and received patents of office. [1410]
This had not gone on for long before great
learned men who were religious and honorable
gradually began to withdraw from those posts
and jobs. Why should decent men choose to
expose themselves to such people? One group
of the great and respectable, however, who
were extremely well known, i.e. Tajik viziers
and governors, did not leave the miscreants
alone but constantly worked to expose them,
and they were in a position to defend their rep-
utations against anyone’s imprecations. Thanks
to this, a few great judges remained in their
posts, even if most did as has been mentioned.
Since there were many ignorant and vile men
in the guise of the learned in the realm, and
they saw that people like them could obtain
great posts, they rose up in contentiousness
against each other, and there were so many dis-
putes and conﬂicting claims that not only did
the Mongols realize how avaricious and impu-
dent they were, but they also imagined that all
learned men were like that. The good repute of
and respect for the great—indeed of the nation
of Islam—were lost on account of these igno-
rant men, and all were disgraced and looked
upon as vile and mean. Every commander and
noble took one of them under his patronage,
and no sooner was one appointed judge than
another was dismissed from office. Things got
so bad that judgeships were auctioned off.
Now a judge should render decisions with im-
partiality and firmness and he should not take
anything from anyone. When a judgeship is
auctioned or awarded as a fief, one can realize
how bad things are. 
During Gaikhatu’s reign, the vizier was
Sadruddin, who styled himself Sadr-i-Jahan.
His brother was the chief judge, and he styled
himself Qutb-i-Jahan. Shaykh Mahmud was
the chief shaykh, and he was in charge of some
religious matters. In their time things had got-
ten completely out of hand, and judicial posts
were awarded as fiefs. In past years it got to
the point that because the road to false claims
had been reopened, [1411] merely owning
property was worse than having a hundred ene-
mies since hungry malefactors and confidence
men intimidated and discredited great lords
and respectable officials over old deeds, forged
documents, and all forms of chicanery, without
limit. Since the judiciary was auctioned and
given in fief, such things suited the judges and
court officials, and they instigated claimants,
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
685

encouraged them with promises, and then ne-
glected the cases or left them in abeyance for
months or even years. In the interim they made
off with everything available and got annually
from the contending parties as much as they
wanted while the case was pending. Many
properties were tied up in suit for years, and
every year more was spent in court than the
case was worth. A hopeful litigant would say,
“My case is still pending. Let me give some-
thing more so that it may be found in my favor
through someone’s inﬂuence.”
Beggars obtained positions and acquired
fame. People like them saw that they had ac-
cess to the great with their false claims, and the
great would give them something to preserve
their honor and not have to go to court, and
those who did go would settle out of court and
pay them blackmail. When they saw this, they
too thought, “Since with all our tricks and in-
timidation we cannot earn a dirhem a day,
there cannot be anything better to take up this
trade.” So they too took up the trade. Some had
old deeds of their own, some became involved
with others through [threat of] impudence and
calumny, and some got people who could forge
all sorts of handwriting to write registered
deeds, and these people all helped each other.
There was another group who wrote things like
past rulers’ edicts and old documents in scripts
[1412] that were not detectable and backdated
them by a hundred fifty years. Although a doc-
ument without authentication is not valid,
every one of these people came under the pa-
tronage of a Mongol or a powerful person
when they got into suits with others. Although
those who enjoyed judicial fiefs did not render
judgments, to protect their own interests they
remained silent in the disputes and did not
speak the truth. Through their underlings they
would intimate to litigants in secret, saying,
“These people are powerful, and we cannot
give an absolute response.” In this manner they
passed their days, taking something in the in-
terim. The case was like gristmill: the more it
turns, the faster it turns. 
It got to the point that more invalid claims
were made in the realm than could be counted.
Since the false claimant was under a powerful
person’s protection, the poor defendant, who
was the rightful owner, in fear of losing his
property and honor, would be forced to seek
the protection of another. This resulted in con-
tention between the two powerful men.
It has long been the natural course of things
to wield the sword for property, and as a sad
corollary most of the powerful men took up
disputes and feuds with each other that were
about to end in wielding swords, particularly
when they were mostly cases of a false
claimant’s having sold to a hoodlum for any-
where from thirty to a hundred dinars a village
worth ten thousand dinars in the hands of its
rightful owner. [The buyer] would then think,
“This village used to belong to him; now it be-
longs to me.” Some village khatibs and others,
out of ignorance and dishonesty, would indoc-
trinate him by saying, “This sale is correct. The
village is your inalienable property.” When the
Mongols, contrary to former times, developed
a craving for property, [1413] their efforts in-
creased, and it got to a point that the property
was about to be lost altogether in such cases.
The general population became insecure of
their property, honor, and lives. Judges, help-
less in the face of these fraudulent malefactors
and unable to afford redress, beseeched God to
deliver them from this quandary. 
When the emperor’s regal reign began and he
saw this pernicious practice, he contemplated
how to reform it by giving an order and ap-
pointing trustworthy messengers to announce
in every territory where there was a fraud
whose imposture was obvious that others not
686
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

be allowed to hide or protect him. Those
whose situations were obvious were sum-
moned at once and executed when their guilt
was proven. By this means many frauds and
false documents were uncovered. The falsifiers
were executed by the Padishah of Islam Ghaz-
an Khan’s justice.
In accordance with the decision Sultan Ma-
likshah had written, that thirty-year-old claims
were not to be heard, an edict was issued dur-
ing the reign of Hülägü Khan as suggested by
the Tajik viziers; after that, during the time of
Abaqa Khan and Gaikhatu Khan it was recon-
firmed, but no trace of its implementation re-
mained for two reasons. One was that several
very important provisions of law, reason, and
common practice were missing in those de-
crees; and since an absolute order that no case
be heard involving thirty-year-old documents
did not appear legal, it was left in abeyance.
The second reason was that governors and
leaders have to implement the provisions of a
decree, but since most of them wanted to buy
as much property as possible with as little
money as possible—and that could only be
done through such schemes—how were they
going to implement the forbidding of such a
thing? Naturally, although they were they very
ones who suggested it, they neglected it.
[1414]
When the Padishah of Islam wanted to im-
plement his decree, he ordered that a draft of
the edict be completed in agreement and con-
sultation with the great judges of the world.
The late Fakhruddin, the judge of Herat who
was one of the great scholars of the age and a
man of great learning, and the chief judge of
the age were unequaled in composition. They
wrote the text of the edict and included the
stipulations and conditions that were necessary.
Therefore the order was implemented, and it
was decreed that the salaries of persons who
dealt with the judiciary throughout the realm
and who were competent by agreement of all
were to be fixed, and they were to content
themselves with that much and not to take any-
thing from anyone under any circumstances. A
decree was issued giving various precautions
to be taken in every regard, and the guidelines,
upon the correctness of which authorities were
agreed, were sent. Since the texts of all these
and of the decree mentioned above have been
given in past sections, there is no need for
repetition.
Story Sixteen: He abolishes extraordinary
tax appraisals, muqasamas, and other types
of mulcts.
We have already alluded brieﬂy to how taxes
and divan imposts were collected in every
province and to how many there were. Thanks
to the mismanagement of the viziers and the
various tyrannies they had adopted for any and
every reason, they were ruining the provinces
and impoverishing the peasants to the point
that they were scattering. We are not exagger-
ating in this regard. Although readers at this
time know that the tyranny [1415] was many
times what can be reported, when in later times
the people enjoy welfare and ease by virtue of
the Padishah of Islam’s justice and equity, they
will forget those harassments; and children and
those who will be born later, not having seen
that injustice and aggression, will naturally
imagine that these things have been exaggerat-
ed. Therefore, let us give a short report. 
The emperor of the world reformed the situa-
tion in Persia, Azerbaijan, and provinces where
the divan imposts were qubchur and tamgha.
How these places had suffered breaches of jus-
tice, and what they were like later was as fol-
lows. These provinces were assigned in fief to
governors, to each governor a fixed total was
given, and customary expenses were allowed.
A governor would levy qubchur on the peas-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
687

ants ten times a year, though in some places
qubchur was levied twenty or thirty times. It
was the practice of governors to make a
subtotal of the amount of qubchur that had
been charged to him, and whenever envoys
came to the province on business or to demand
money or provisions, the governor would use
them as a pretext to impose a qubchur. No
matter how many envoys arrived—and their
expenses and demands were without limit—the
governor would rejoice at their arrival, for he
would impose a levy once in the name of taxes,
once in the name of provisions and expenses,
and once in the name of contracts and de-
mands. Some of it he would spend on supplies,
and some he would take himself; some he
would give to the shahna and bitigchis so that
they would support him and corroborate his
falsification. Out of so much produce taken
from the peasants, not a load was ever sent to
the treasury, and the taxes of the provinces
were consumed by allowed expenses and bil-
lets. In Khurasan eight of ten billets were still
owing, and when envoys and holders of billets
and drafts came to the divan, [1416] the re-
sponse would be, “The money is still owing
against the province. How is it they haven’t
paid it?” They would write a renewal of the or-
der, emphasizing that they should send the
funds soon. Back they would go, and once
again expenses were incurred. On that pretext
the governor made impositions and told the
peasants, “You see how many envoys are stay-
ing here. If it weren’t for their expenses,
redress would be possible.” No one was able to
say to him, “You ought to give them money
because at the very first of the year you took
many times the assessment and squandered it.”
Two
thirds
of
this
impost
were
divided
amongst themselves, and one third was spent
on the envoys’ expenses. In the end [the en-
voys] would return without having collected
any money, and there was so much coming and
going in this manner that the billets grew old in
their hands and they ceased to count on them
as they languished for years in their satchels.
Although it is common practice for it to be
known in the divan how much the base tax for
each province is and against what place a billet
is written for collection, never was anyone
aware of this, and draft after draft was written
on demand against various places. Since the
deputies and viziers knew that the money was
not coming, they acted coquettishly to stall for
time and put people under obligation by say-
ing, “As a favor to you we are writing these
billets.” By playing this game they sent them
off happy, but the net result was the ruination
of the provinces. 
In addition, a deputy or vizier would say to
the emperor, “There are a lot of tax collectors
in the provinces. They ought to be bringing
something to the treasury.” Immediately an
edict would be written stopping payment to tax
collectors and billet holders, or else saying that
such and such amounts should have been paid,
and they ought to have covered expenses and
gifts for the vizier and deputy and promissory
notes, [1417] and the governors were demand-
ed to pay. Letters were written saying, “Since
we have stopped payment to the tax collectors,
they should soon send the royal funds from the
province.” With such chicanery they took cash
for the promissory notes. The vizier would also
conspire with provincial governors and not re-
lease funds until they had seen it in a billet or
letter. The envoys and tax collectors would
come back perplexed, and new obligations
would be placed on them and the amirs by re-
newal of letters. In this manner the interests of
the vizier would be served, and he would gain
his object. Because of the conspiracy between
the provincial governors and the vizier, and be-
cause they always took the vizier’s part, the
688
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

governors grew bold and audacious enough to
commit all sorts of injustice and outrage. Every
year two or three qubchur and tamgha taxes le-
vied on cities to pay for envoys’ expenses and
contracts were squandered, and the people
wondered why the governor didn’t keep the
tamgha cash to be spent on such nonsense.
They were unaware that the governor had
adopted that course for the purposes of fraud
so that on that pretext he could get many times
the amount of the tax, take it, and then, at the
time of accounting, get two or three times that
much for the envoys’ expenses and use that as
a pretext not to remit the divan’s share. In truth
not a cent ever reached the treasury from those
provinces, and not two out of ten dinars of the
allowable expenses that were to be charged
against the base tax were ever paid. No one
ever saw a customs official in the customs of-
fice, for they had all run away; and if they
were caught by the tax collectors, they would
get a beating. Insofar as they were able they
would appoint people in secret to collect the
tamgha tax like plunderers stealing into houses
at night. Of necessity they were content to let
the tamgha tax go to money lenders for half, or
else they would give the customs official a
bribe, and thereby only a fraction of the cus-
toms was collected. What was collected went
to pay for envoys’ provisions, [1418] and their
servants sat around threateningly until they
collected. Since there wasn’t enough for every-
one, they would fight with each other, and
those who were stronger would win. Not a cent
of stipends, salaries and workers’ wages, or the
fixed expenses upon which the development of
the province depended and without which fis-
cal operations could not be carried out, was
every paid to anyone since pay-offs were sub-
tracted from the tax base before anything
else—and with the connivance of the gover-
nors. At the beginning of the year they would
claim that the treasury money had priority, and
after that they would say, “We’ll give it at har-
vest time.” When the many envoys and tax col-
lectors, whose jobs were never done, would
come, the governor would use them as a pre-
text to say, “So many troops of envoys are sit-
ting on top of me. They’ll have to be taken
care of first.” People with stipends and salaries
and those dependent upon alms were put off
from the beginning of the year to the end and
left naked and hungry. Those who were bold
enough to apply to the governors’ deputies,
could, with much pleading, sell off their rights
for half their worth, and in return they were
sold goods at double the price: with a thousand
tricks they might get a quarter. Anyone who
managed to get that much counted himself
lucky, and they were envied by the rest, who
were totally deprived. If from time to time,
with great effort and difficulty, one of the de-
prived got into the ordu to present his petition,
a letter would come from the Supreme Divan
saying, “We released these funds prior to all.
Why have they not been paid?” The governor
would bring forward an excuse, saying, “The
taxes are still owing in the province. That’s
why we didn’t pay it. I will write a billet so
that this man can get his money.” There was
nothing the poor man could do but take a billet
against money owed. Since the governor had
already overtaxed by so much, [1419] as has
been described, how was he going to get what
was owed? On account of amounts still owed
from excess taxes levied, some peasants, inca-
pable of giving over and over again, had aban-
doned their villages and homes and ﬂed. The
governor would curry favor with powerful or
highly-placed persons who could withstand ex-
cess levies by saying, “We won’t demand this
last levy from you. We’ll discount it by half”—
although the full amount of the levies would
have been recorded in the auditor’s register.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
689

Given that one qubchur did not produce a lot
of money, and taking into consideration that
some gave, some gave less, and some did not
give anything at all, something was always
owed from the last levy. It was called “remain-
der.” Since the auditors and clerks shared in
the duplicate levies and theft, they would write
that “a certain amount is remaindered against
X village,” thus leaving an obscure record. If
deputies or viziers asked if the remainder was
part of the base tax or a surtax, even when it
was clear that they knew full well what was
going on, since they got bribes on the surtaxes
from the governors, their lips were sealed. 
The acts described were perpetrated by all
previous viziers, but it was the particular craft
of Sadruddin Chawi, and he was a master of it.
He elevated corruption and venality to a fine
art and ruined the fiscal administration of the
realm and provinces. During his term of office
no one ever got paid for a billet against a
province, and no one with a stipend or salary
ever got his due, for all his billets and drafts
were nothing but sheer chicanery. When any of
the poor, deserving, or elderly came to him to
plead, he would write that person a billet for
five hundred dinars—of which he had never
seen a hundred aqchas. He would call this gen-
erosity, and the poor person would be happy;
[1420] but when he went to ask for the money,
it was a different story. “I have five hundred
dinars,” he would think. “Let me borrow a
hundred dinars to pay for a mount, supplies,
and provisions for the road. After I repay the
loan, four hundred dinars will be left.” While
entertaining this hope he would be given such
a run-around trying to collect his money that
his decrepitude would be forgotten and he
would learn how to act like a beg or a tax col-
lector and his thugs. But it did no good. In the
end, he would ﬂee the realm in debt.
Because of such mismanagement and waste,
most of the peasants in the provinces aban-
doned their homes and settled in foreign parts.
Towns and villages were empty. Every so often
an envoy who went to gather runaways would
harass them a lot and take many times the
amount of the qubchur from them. They were
never inclined to go to their homelands, for
they had developed an antipathy to that great
realm. Despite the many envoys who went in
all directions to gather runaways at various
times, they never succeeded in returning a sin-
gle peasant to his home. 
Of those who were left in towns, most had
walled up the doors of their houses and came
and went across the roofs. They would ﬂee
from tax collectors, and when the collectors
came into the city quarters they would find a
scoundrel who knew the houses. With his guid-
ance they would drag people out from nooks
and crannies, cellars, gardens, and ruins. If
they couldn’t get hold of the men, they would
take their wives and drive them like a ﬂock of
sheep from quarter to quarter to the presence of
the tax collectors. They would hang them from
their feet by a rope and beat them as the
women’s cries rose to heaven. It often hap-
pened—and we have witnessed it—that a tax
collector went up on a roof, [1421] found a
peasant, and chased him. The poor peasant
would be running away so hard that he was
about to throw himself off the roof when the
tax collect would go grab him by the shirt and
say with a show of compassion, “Don’t throw
yourself off the roof! You’ll be killed.” The
poor fellow, helpless, would fall and break his
leg. 
Of all the provinces, Yazd had degenerated to
the point that anyone could wander through all
the villages and not see a soul he could speak
to or ask the way. The few who remained had
stationed lookouts, and when they saw anyone
690
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

approaching from afar, they would spread the
word, and everyone would hide in the subter-
ranean water channels or in the sands. When
any lord who had property in Yazd went to in-
spect his property, he never saw a single
farmer of whom he might inquire after his or-
chards. In most towns, in fear of having envoys
quartered in their homes, people had made the
entrances to their houses under the ground with
narrow passageways in hopes that the envoys
would not want to stay there, for all envoys
that were quartered in people’s houses, in addi-
tion to wearing out rugs, bedding, and house-
hold implements, picked up anything they
wanted and took it, or else their grooms stole
things. If anyone had garnered a bit of provi-
sions or kindling, they took it all. They also
burned doors for firewood and wrought other
devastation. 
One instance has been heard of a great man
of Yazd who had a house in town. In the year
695 [1296], Nawroz’s son Sultanshah and his
mother stayed there while Nawroz was in pow-
er. They remained for four months, and, after
leaving no moveable property in the house,
when they departed [1422] and the city consta-
bles went to inspect, they found that the house,
which had been worth nearly fifty thousand di-
nars, was not worth two thousand. They had
burned extremely fine ornate doors and done
other damage. If the house of a religious fig-
ure, the mufti of the city, could be used like
this, what of the ordinary people and peasants?
There was nothing harder for lords and peas-
antry to bear than this. 
The chärbis [quartermasters] had learned that
they could “sell off” a hundred houses on the
pretext of envoys and then quarter them there.
Every year they carried off many thousands of
the people’s rugs, bedding, kettles, tools, and
implements. They put their animals in people’s
gardens, and a garden that had taken more than
ten years of hard work to improve would be ru-
ined in a day. If there happened to be a subter-
ranean water channel there and an animal fell
in, the owner would be seized, and many times
what the animal was worth would be taken
from him. If there was a breach in a wall and
an animal got out, the same thing happened.
Envoys’
assistants,
captains,
and
grooms
would pull down garden walls; and in the win-
ter they would cut down trees for firewood. If
there was a tree in a garden, the governors and
powerful would have it cut down or requisition
it, claiming it would be used as a soldier’s
spear. In some provinces there were so many
of their tax collectors, servants, and captains
that there were actually two of them for every
citizen. 
It has been related that in the year 691 [a.d.
1292], when Umarshah Samarqandi’s son Ali
Khwaja was governor of Yazd, a landlord went
to a village called Firozabad—one of the
largest villages in the area—in order to collect
something from the harvest on his land. [1423]
No matter how hard he tried, he could not lo-
cate a single villager for three days and nights.
He found only seventeen billet-holding tax col-
lectors sitting in the middle of the village.
They had seized a field guard and two peasants
from the fields, brought them to the village,
tied them up, and were beating them in order to
get hold of the others to obtain something to
eat. Even so they failed. 
All these tax collectors and their followers
had to have provisions, fodder, wine, and en-
tertainment. One can imagine what other types
of injustice there were. And how were such
bad customs to be reformed in a short time
when they had taken root over time in evil
men? Even though special edicts had been re-
peatedly issued in every reign and sent every-
where to gain the favor of the subjects and to
defend them from these injustices, it had never
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
691

worked,
and
the
general
population
had
despaired. 
In this age, which is the imperial reign of the
Padishah of Islam Ghazan Khan—may God
make his rule last forever and extend his jus-
tice and beneficence—the emperor’s mind is
totally concentrated upon pure good and justice
and he thinks of nothing but redressing the
abuses that have crept into the fabric of the ad-
ministration, abolishing totally innovations and
corruption, and striving so that all people in the
world may be at peace. “These things are the
main benefits of a human being’s life,” he said.
Then he added, “In this regard all effort must
be made to reform abuses like the qubchur in
the provinces.”
“When the Yasaq and criminal justice are
suspended and great breaches occur,” he said,
“in order to rectify the situation one must begin
first with small matters so that the people of
the world may know that when arrests are
made, trials are held, and executions are car-
ried out for trivial matters, they will certainly
be many times that in large matters. Of neces-
sity they will cease doing these things.” [1424]
He also said, “If overall principles are main-
tained, all the details will be subsumed therein.
If we go after details one by one, by the time
one is fixed and we turn our attention to anoth-
er, the one that was fixed will have gone wrong
again and it will be impossible to rectify.”
He also said, “When a nation has long be-
come inured to something, and it has become
second nature to them, it is extremely difficult
to forbid them to do that thing or to get the
habit out of their nature—like these thugs and
governors who have become habituated over
all these years to use force on the peasants and
extract taxes from them repeatedly while
giving nothing to the divan. Every year they go
to court, give bribes, and survive by telling a
few stories. If a few of them are killed, the oth-
ers will imagine that it was only chance. They
won’t learn a lesson. ‘So-and-So was out of fa-
vor,’ they will say, ‘for otherwise, if it had been
on account of taxes and administration, many
others ought to have been chastised.’ Even if
we execute half these people, it will still be im-
possible for the others to abandon their habits
and cease their tyranny and aggression. The
peasants will still be tormented, and no taxes
will reach the treasury or the military. The best
course of action is for us to think up a way to
tie provincial governors’ hands completely in
their authority over taxation so that they will
have absolutely no way to be aggressive on
any pretext. This is like the story of the fox
who said, ‘It’s only with a thousand tricks that
I manage to escape from the dog. It would be
best for me not to see him and for him not to
see me.’ In this case too it would be better for
provincial administrators not to be able to
write a draft for even a cent against the peas-
ants.” To this end he said, “A competent clerk
should go to every province, make a detailed
census, village by village, [1425] and then fix
the qubchur equally in accordance with the
numbers without trying to create an excess. He
should make it so that the peasants are well off
and happy.”
He also ordered that an investigation be
made of all enchü properties, endowments, and
lords’ estates that had been held without dis-
pute for the past thirty years. They should be
recorded with the names of the owners and en-
tered into the registry of deeds so that if any-
one lost a title or someone else wanted to usurp
the property, they could refer to the registry
and proceed in accordance with what had been
registered. In this way no one will have an op-
portunity to falsify or usurp. As ordered, the
clerks went to the provinces. Despite the fact
that honest and trustworthy men are few and
far between, they strove their utmost to record
692
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

the tax rolls of the provinces and bring them
back. 
After that he ordered that no malik, basqaq,
or bitigchi ever place pen to paper to write a
billet or draft. If any billet was written, the
governor who had allowed it would be execut-
ed and the clerk who wrote it would have his
hand cut off so that other clerks would see him
and learn a lesson. One clerk for every
province was appointed to be in attendance in
the Supreme Divan here, and at the beginning
of the year that clerk would write tax bills by
name and in detail in accordance with the tax
rolls, village by village. The deputies of the
Supreme Divan would add their attestations,
and the bills would be authenticated by being
stamped with the gold seal and sent to the
provinces for the peasants to remit to the agent
appointed in every province in two install-
ments plus a five per cent commission for the
treasury.1 The agent would pay out part in cash
to holders of billets authenticated by the gold
seal and send the rest to the imperial treasury,
where it, together with the treasury commis-
sion, would be submitted to the treasurers. If
exceptionally
a
tax
collector
or
headman
brought an amount to the agent, [1426] a cash
treasury commission of five and a half per cent
would be paid.2 Otherwise tax collectors would
bring cash amounts and turn them over, along
with the treasury commission, to the treasurers.
He ordered that since they would take cash in
the provinces, under no circumstances would it
be permitted that so much as one dinar’s worth
of goods be brought, and if anyone brought
goods, he would have to take them to the mar-
1Reading, with JTAZ’s MSS PB,
#ﻧ دﻩ
ــــــــ
ﲓ(‘plus five per
cent’) for JTAZ’s and JTK’s 
# دﻩ و ﻧﲓ. 
2The formula given isـ ـﯾﻨ دﺪـﺻ وﲓـﻧﮓـﻧدا و دﻩ
ﺎر ـ ـﯾﻨ دﲓـﻧﺎررا,
which should be a rate of ½ on 10⅙, or an insignificant
fraction short of 5%, plus half a dinar on a hundred di-
nars, or 0.5%.
ket, sell them, and remit in cash. Amounts of
stipends, salaries, and fixed expenses allowed
in every place would all be paid in cash in
full—not a cent less—so that all people would
increase their prayers for the well-being of the
empire. With detailed tax bills endorsed with
the gold seal and taken to the provinces from
here, all peasants in villages would know how
much their taxes were and they would not have
to give a cent more than that. They would also
have the written record of the tax rolls stating
how much and in what manner their obliga-
tions were.
When the edict was promulgated that provin-
cial governors could not write billets, the malik
of Rodrawar, a dependency of Hamadan,
thought it was just like past edicts and allowed
a clerk to write several billets on the province.
An order was given for him to be executed and
for the clerk’s hand to be cut off. When he re-
ceived news that an emissary was coming for
that purpose, he ﬂed. Three years later he died
in the place to which he had taken ﬂight. The
clerk was caught after a time in Nihawand, and
his hand was cut off. 
In Hamadan a greengrocer gave his partner a
draft against villagers to settle a balance due in
the amount of two maunds of sumac. He was
arrested and ordered executed. After much in-
tercession he was given a hundred twenty lash-
es and fined a thousand dinars. 
Recently some elephants were brought from
India. [1427] When they got to Hamadan it
was winter and no fodder could be found. The
governors said, “We’ll have to requisition
some from the gardens.” When this reached the
imperial hearing he said, “We have budgeted
for provisions and fodder for the elephants.
How can they take it from people’s gardens? If
it’s available, let them buy it; if not, why do
they think they can requisition it? This time we
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
693

will overlook it, but if they do any such thing
again, we will have them executed.”
In short, in recent years, no one throughout
the realm has been or is able now to give a
draft for so much as a maund of straw or a
grain of gold. Billet writing has been complete-
ly eliminated.
Last year it was learned that since governors
can no longer put surcharges on the fixed taxes
of villages, headmen and village elders were
levying surcharges among themselves any way
they wanted. An order was implemented by
which village headmen would record the estab-
lished amount that had been registered in the
tax rolls along with the names of the peasants
and sent a copy to the divan so that henceforth
they would not be able to levy surcharges.
When every one of the peasants would know
his amount exactly, he would not give anything
extra. They would also not be able to make de-
mands on strangers or other persons whose
names were not in the rolls. For this reason all
peasants are busy [praying for] the fortune of
the Sultan of Islam. Runaways came home
without anyone’s going in search of them, and
now they won’t sell for a thousand dinars
houses that used to be worth a hundred.
Provincial funds have more cash than the mint,
and they are brought to the treasury two or
three times a year without excuse or complaint,
as is witnessed by all. 
In recent years not a fraction of gold, a
measure of provisions, a load of straw, a sheep,
a maund of wine, or a chicken has been
charged to any province in the name of sur-
charges, nemäri [supplementary tax], yam
[post tax], [1428] savuri [donation tax], tuzghu
[provisions tax], alafa [supplies tax], alufa
[fodder tax], or anything else. God has so
blessed the taxes that, no matter how much the
emperor has disbursed to the military in recent
years or ordered given for requests, gifts, or
expenses of whomever—and all in cash from
the treasury—at no time has it happened that
the treasury has been devoid of gold or fabric. 
It is clear from ancient and modern registers
that in no era or time has so much cash and
fabric as the Padishah of Islam spends or gives
away in a year ever been spent by others over a
period of five years, and still the treasury is full
of gold and fabric. 
Even though previously administrators never
gave anyone anything from provincial funds,
when they made their reckoning of billets and
drafts at the end of the year they were
swamped by them, not to mention the addition-
al expenses the administrator had to deal with.
Now, thanks to the emperor’s kindness and
good tactics, the realm has been made to ﬂour-
ish, administrators in the provinces have extra
money from the harvests, and much of the pre-
vious year’s grain remains in the storehouses
so that it is not necessary to dole it out to the
people. Every year when the grain ripens it
does not have to be sold in haste. Whereas pre-
viously grain was used up in prepayments be-
fore it ripened, at the present time the divan al-
ways has a one-year harvest in the storehouse
and funds in the treasury. 
“Now that I have ordered these measures, I
have tied governors’ hands in the matter of
writing billets, and I have made the peasants’
taxes known in detail,” the Padishah of Islam
said. “Now that these rules have become fixed
and habitual, it has become quite simple to pay
what they owe, and they pay it willingly. Now
one should think how to make these rules firm,
stable, and continuous so that, despite unto-
ward events that happen in the world, [1429]
no breach of them occur. Under no circum-
stances should anyone have an opportunity to
issue so many billets from the Supreme Divan
that provincial funds get eaten up by demands,
and deputies and viziers of the age should not
694
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

be negligent in their overseership by allowing
governors to issue billets. Never again should
assistants do as they want and unleash tyranny
against the peasants. The peasants should not
suffer and have no opportunity for questions
and answers. All the praiseworthy benefit that
has accrued from taking so much trouble
should not be lost again. The world should not
be devastated once more, and treasury funds
and soldiers’ wages should not be consumed.
Since fortune has smiled upon us and God has
entrusted the running of the realm to us and
given us the strength to do so, we must strive
mightily and not to allow negligence or over-
sight, and we must place these guidelines and
rules on such a firm basis that it will be impos-
sible to change or alter them.” Therefore he is-
sued to the entire realm a single decree, copies
of which were to be recorded in the registers
and rule books of every province, and it was to
be done so that the order was clear to all. The
text is as follows. [1430]
Text of the edict proclaiming that provincial
taxes be determined in detail by the Supreme
Divan and forwarded and that maliks and
governors of provinces never write billets.
In the name of God, the Compassionate, the
Merciful.
Decree of Sultan Mahmud Ghazan.
Be it known to basqaqs, maliks, deputies, adminis-
trators, judges, sayyids, imams, comptrollers, lords,
grandees, headmen, elders, and all subjects and
peoples of cities and provinces from the River
Oxus to the borders of Syria and Franks’ territory
that our entire attention and thought during these
few days of the imperial era has been concentrat-
ed—in accordance with the Koranic text, “God
commandeth justice and the doing of good,”1 and
in accordance with the command to “judge there-
fore between men with truth”2—upon the elimina-
