1Kor. 16:90.
2Kor. 38:26.
tion of all types of injustice, aggression, force, and
cruelty to which tyrants have become habituated by
claiming, “We found our fathers practising a reli-
gion; and we are guided in their footsteps.”3 They
have turned the blood and property of Muslims into
their own livelihood and morsels. We said, “We
shall promulgate an edict so that henceforth no per-
son will repeat his avarice and dishonesty and so
that the kingdom and fiscal affairs will be so regu-
lated and ordered that the benefit will accrue both
now and later to the generality of God’s people and
it will result in their welfare and ease.” In accor-
dance with the saying, “He who establishes a good
custom receives not only a reward for that but also
the reward of anyone who follows it,” we will re-
ceive a good name both in this world and in the
next, for we know surely that since “an hour of jus-
tice is better than seventy years of worship,” no
better benefit can be imagined, [1431] and nothing
can provide better provisions for the afterlife than
this.
Now the people of the world know that, with
God’s help, we have made our motto the Prophet’s
dictum that “the most beloved and nearest of all
people to God is a just ruler, and the most despica-
ble is a cruel ruler.” To the extent we have been
able, we have redressed some of the injustice and
aggression. A detailed account of that has been ad-
dressed separately, but one provision is the fixing
and establishment of taxes of the realm and the
abolition of extraordinary appraisals, imposts, all
varieties of administrative fees, and the abrogation
of the ulagh and alufa for tax collectors and envoys
sent into every province to collect taxes, as well as
all sorts of intimidation, ruination, and waste of
money. 
To that end, clerks have been dispatched through-
out the realm to record in detail every province, re-
gion, and village and to fix the tax and amounts
due so that all people may thereby find rest and be
thankful and content. Hitherto ruffians and tyrants
used to extract many times the amount of taxes in
the name of expenses, fees, and many other pre-
texts too numerous to mention in detail, and mostly
3Kor. 43:22.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
695

they themselves and their evil agents and captains
carried it off so that not only did the divan and
treasury benefit nothing, but it also caused damage,
ruination of the land, and the loss of money. The
goal of those who undertook to collect divan funds
by fief and auction was only to gain control, to do
as they wanted, and to take many times the amount
of taxation entrusted to them; they performed none
of their responsibilities, and therefore when there
was a need for the work of the military, the protec-
tion of the frontiers, or the necessities of the land,
there were no funds in the treasury. Of necessity
there was recourse to confiscation, nemäri [supple-
mentary tax], and extraordinary impositions on the
generality of the people, and thereby the land,
[1432] province, and subjects were shaken and suf-
fered hardship, and the military was left destitute
and weakened. 
Now, with God’s help, it has been possible to
make a detailed record of all villages in the empire
and a tax roll, village by village. This has never
been done in any era, and never before have regis-
ters or copies thereof been assembled. The taxes of
those villages have been fixed and established. Al-
though no one can ever insure absolute equality as
it ought to be—sometimes on account of lack of
knowledge, and sometimes because of self-interest
and greed, and few are those in whom these evil
traits are not found—nonetheless, insofar as possi-
ble tax rolls have been made. When they were
brought to our presence, if an enormous difference
was found or a grievous error against anyone had
been made, it was reported and the deputies of the
Supreme Divan redressed it. Most divan villages
were given to agents who were judges, farmers, or
landlords, and stipulations to be in effect in perpe-
tuity were confirmed by the divan device, em-
bossed with our gold seal, and given so that they
might administer and remit what is due to the divan
annually. When all the various sorts of injustice,
aggression, imposts, and divan fees that used to
pertain were eliminated, if prior to now there was a
slight difference or error in equality, it was so in-
significant in relation to the former injustices and
excesses that no one fought over it. Now all people
are thankful and content, and they give praise in
comfort. They have been delivered from extraordi-
nary exactions and impositions and divan fees and
charges, the number of which was great. 
In order to put a stop to the practice of persons
who were not God-fearing, who were irreligious
and could not see the consequences of their actions,
i.e.
using
drafts,
billets,
unwarranted
control,
blameworthy thoughts, and all sorts of chicanery to
get hold of the people’s money and blood, we have
commanded that provincial governors and officials
not write drafts or billets against the detailed and
fixed taxes established for every village in the tax
rolls. [1433] Thereby a stop will be put to their
many thugs and captains, who outnumber by far
the tax-paying peasants, and whose livelihood has
come from the helpless peasants’ blood and proper-
ty. “If the fly snatch anything from them, they can-
not recover the same.”1 They will be deprived of
that illicit livelihood, and of necessity they will
have to find a licit means of making a living, like
trade, farming, raising ﬂowers, or other sorts of
beneficial work, and instead of evil habits they will
take up good trades and a licit means of earning
their daily bread. Two or three years after they have
exchanged their bad habits for good, they will for-
get their former bad habits and customs, and the
world will acquire a new guise. In accordance with
the dictum “to wean from what one is used to is
difficult,” the more it was contemplated, the more
it was realized that redress, which could not be ac-
complished by the sword, blows, torture, and pri-
son, could be accomplished only by this means. 
Provincial administrators and their thugs have
grown accustomed to reporting to the Supreme Di-
van many times the actual assessment of any vil-
lage the ruler gives as a stipend, allowance, fief,
alms, or charity to anyone, or puts in endowment,
or any place that is under the protection of any of
the khatuns, princes, or amirs if the divan taxes are
not paid or if, by chance, the village becomes ru-
ined. They enter this in their balance sheets and
then abscond with the funds. Since the deputies of
the divan do not know what the base tax of the as-
sessments of any village is in detail, how can they
1Kor. 22:73.
696
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

know how much it is? Naturally they listen to the
words of the administrator and persons who have
vested interests. They accept the administrator’s
false testimony and abscond with the proceeds. By
this means they have made off with huge amounts
of cash. From now on, since the established rates of
every place have been registered in the tax rolls of
the Supreme Divan, no one will be able to commit
such fraud. [1434] Also, it will be simple and easy
for rulers of the time and their deputies to effect
these things, and no one in their time will be able to
tyrannize others. Inasmuch as the extent of the ben-
efits of detailed tax rolls and the fixing of taxes is
clear and obvious to the intelligent and wise, it is
not necessary to explain them at length. Now that
success has been achieved and we have had some
experience, the tax roll of every locale has become
a reality, and by that means detailed tax bills with
the gold seal have been written by the Supreme Di-
van, the fruits are obvious: the subjects are at rest,
and the provinces ﬂourish. The sense of the text has
been achieved: “Thou seest the earth sometimes
dried up and barren: but when we send down rain
thereon, it is put in motion, and swelleth, and
produceth every kind of luxuriant vegetables.”1
Thugs are no longer able to commandeer a cent of
money or a maund of goods. The peasants of every
village and locale are aware of how much their
fixed taxes are, and anyone who takes more than
that from them does so contrary to imperial decree
and without the permission of the divan. The sub-
jects do not obey the orders of tyrants, and they re-
mit only the amount that has been established ac-
cording to the bills with the gold seal. The total in
cash is paid to the storehouse, the military, or the
treasury.
At this time we have thought that, since the goal
in these arrangements is not only the welfare of the
people but also to store up heavenly reward, the
harder we strive to lay firm foundations and the
stronger they are, the more the reward will be. 
We have appointed a clerk in the Supreme Divan
to write tax bills for each province. Once written,
the bills will be stamped with the divan’s devices
1Kor. 22:5.
and sealed with our gold seal. [1435] To make the
devices and affix the seal much time and leisure are
required, however; and it is possible that with the
vicissitudes of time and the unavoidable affairs of
kingdom, frontiers, disturbances, and troubles of
which the world of generation and corruption can
never be devoid, the writing of so many detailed
bills, stamping them with devices, and affixing the
seal may not be possible. Since delay and negli-
gence will certainly take place, it necessarily fol-
lows that blanket bills will be written against
provinces, and once again thugs will find a way to
issue billets and stretch forth their hands shame-
lessly. In the same old way the world will be devas-
tated, and treasury funds will be trampled under-
foot as before. Payment of allowable expenses of
the provinces too, like improvements, salaries,
stipends, allowances, alms, etc., will be delayed on
the pretext that treasury funds are never delivered,
and there will be other excuses and fabricated sto-
ries exactly as before. They will continue like this
year after year, and everyone will be deprived. Our
rule, which was put into effect after so much effort
over such a long time, and which gave so much re-
lief to the people of the world, will fall into
abeyance. The helpless subjects will be dominated
by men emboldened to lust for injustice, and once
again things will be beyond reform as funds are de-
pleted and consumed and honesty disappears, as it
was before. Such a situation will not suit the rulers
of the time, the army, or the subjects. 
To prevent this situation, it has occurred to us to
have a detailed tax roll made village by village and
locale by locale. All the provincial books will be
gathered in the library attached to the dome,
khanaqah, and charitable institution we have built
in Tabriz. There they will be entrusted to custodi-
ans, to whom we have given salaries so that they
may protect and preserve them, and we have en-
dowed it as mentioned in the deed of endowment.
We have also written a document of anathema
[1436] so that no one will render it null. Any prob-
lem that occurs henceforth can be referred there,
and if anyone’s contract or deed is lost, they can is-
sue a copy from there. 
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
697

We have placed one copy of the tax rolls in the
Supreme Divan and one in every province and put
copies of contracts into the hands of judges, lords,
and subjects and commanded that they write the
provisions of the tax rolls in every village and lo-
cale. They can inscribe them on a stone or a bronze
plaque, whichever they want, or, if they desire,
they can incise it in plaster. This they shall place at
the village gate, mosque, or minaret, whichever
they want. In Christian and Jewish villages it
should be at the door of the place of worship or at
the village gate, as they desire. Nomads should
erect a stele in whatever place they think best. 
As for provinces, let them make copies of the es-
tablished tax roll with our gold seal, without addi-
tion or subtraction, in the presence of judges,
sayyids, imams, and city grandees; and let no sub-
ject of any village or locale liable to taxes and im-
posts in those provinces fail to remit within twenty
days, in complete accordance with the tax roll as
mentioned. Let the copy be set up firmly with plas-
ter and spikes in various locales so that it will re-
main for many years and no one will change or al-
ter it.
Villages that have been designated as cash-pay-
ing will remit in cash; those that have been des-
ignated as kind-paying will remit in kind. Each of
these types will necessarily be paid by the due date
established. 
Likewise, customs imposts are being fixed. Let
them be inscribed on a plaque in accordance with
the rates as written on the back of this edict in or-
der that it may be known in what manner every rate
of the various taxes that have been registered and
fixed in various provinces should be written,
[1437] what the due date of every one is, and in
what manner the collection of each will be. Every
rate must be written on the plaque exactly as in the
text so that the cash amount may be collected on
the seasonal due date by the headmen and peasants
of every village and brought to the town square. It
is established that the tax collector will pitch a tent
in the town square, and from the beginning of the
due date until the date given as grace period cash
amounts should be brought five times a day either
in full or in part to the treasurer we have appointed
in every province and turned over to him. Under no
circumstances will the tax collector take from any
village anything else in the name of provisions, ser-
vice fees, or anything else. Under no circumstances
will any billet or tax gatherer be sent to any village
or province by the divan. 
If headmen and peasants are negligent and do not
remit by the due date established, the tax collector
will seize them and take a fine in the amount of one
dinar for every hundred dinars of the base tax; and
any person who has failed will receive seventy
lashes so that this rule and regulation will remain
firm, and its benefit will encompass common and
elite alike, and so that the people of the world will
no longer be subjected, on account of the negli-
gence and ignorance of a few persons, to the cruel-
ty of irreligious thugs who do not fear God.
Now, the due dates of cash taxes and harvests
that have been fixed and established in accordance
with the tax rolls in perpetuity, as has been de-
scribed, are as follows.
Due dates for cash taxes of every province whose
rates are various: let the rate of the type that has
been registered be written on a plaque in every vil-
lage; let them remit accordingly. [1438]
Qubchur and imposts of village-dwelling peas-
ants who customarily remit twice a year:
• Of the annual imposts of every village, half is
to be paid within the first twenty days after new
year’s day. 
• The other half is to be paid within twenty days
from the time the sun enters Libra. 
Qubchur
and
assessments
of
nomads,
who
customarily remit once at the beginning of the year:
• The poll tax and other taxes that were estab-
lished long ago as cash taxes are to be paid once
within twenty days from new year’s day. 
• Poll tax and cash taxes in some places have
been so established that they will be paid at the
time of summer harvest—like Baghdad, etc.
• Customs fees have been recorded on the back in
a manner suitable to every province individually.
Let them be written on a plaque and placed at the
gate of every place subject to customs so that they
can be paid by installment. Let no one create any
innovation, and let assignors of fiefs not take more
698
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

than the fees on a pretext that the customs have
been increased, and let them not establish any new
custom. [1439]
Due dates and manner of collection and remit-
tance for all types of harvest levies, in both cold
and warm climates, for both winter and summer
crops, and from some locales that have no summer
crop, are as follows: 
Provinces with warm climates and with both
winter and summer crops: 
• Winter crops of wheat, barley, &c.—that which
is established for the village, except for special
agreement, will be transported at the beginning of
the month of ___ on own animals to the storehouse
assigned to the area and turned over to the re-
ceiving agent; maximum grace period twenty days. 
• Summer crops of produce outside of special
agreement will be transported in accordance with
the register in the month of ___ on own animals to
the storehouse assigned to the area and submitted
to the receiving agent; maximum grace period forty
days. 
Places in provinces with cold climates with sum-
mer crops and those without summer crops: 
• Winter crops—in accordance with the register,
after special considerations, the established amount
in full will be transported in the month of ___ by
own animals to the storehouse assigned to the area;
maximum grace period, twenty days. [1440]
• Summer crops—in accordance with the register,
after special considerations, amount in full to be
transported to the storehouse assigned to the area;
maximum grace period twenty days.
Likewise, in every province that has been given
to khatuns, princes, and amirs or entrusted in fief to
soldiers, or which we have given to fund letters of
credit, salaries, allowances, accounts, rewards,
stipends, alms, and endowments under the control
of anyone, in the same manner in accordance with
the tax rolls a plaque will be placed in every village
so that the aforementioned administrators may not
take at their whim more than the tax obligations to
the divan, and so that the people of that place may
not suffer, for it is necessary that the emperor’s jus-
tice should reach everyone in every place, like the
light of the sun.
Like the sun in the belly of the sky, whose light
covers the earth from east to west.
Since the main purpose in this imperial age is the
welfare of the people, organization of the army,
preservation of the borders, increasing treasury rev-
enues, and eliminating workers of corruption,
thieves,
and
ruffians,
these
goals
have
been
achieved so that many times the revenue that used
to come to our fathers’ treasuries is raised, and
there is no necessity for confiscation. Assuredly the
points that have been mentioned are appropriate to
all just rulers and suitable for the consideration of
all honest, compassionate, and competent officers,
ministers of state, viziers, and deputies of any age
or era, as God has said, [1441] “Therein is an in-
structive example unto those who are endued with
understanding. It is not a new invented fiction: but
a confirmation of that which was before it, and a
direction and mercy unto people who believe,”1 and
“if they transgress, it will necessitate their disgrace
and punishment. And whoever coveteth any be-
yond these, they are transgressors,”2 for this was
done for the general good. The people generally
have relief thereby, and taxes were fixed. If any un-
just person allows any change or alteration, let him
fear the outcries and condemnation of the people,
for no hell more painful than that can be imagined.
“They who act unjustly shall know hereafter with
what treatment they shall be treated.”3 Let them not
commit this. “Clothe not the truth with vanity, nei-
ther conceal the truth against your own knowl-
edge.”4 Consequently, anyone who changes or al-
ters will suffer the curse of the creator and creation.
“He who shall change it after he hath heard it, sure-
ly the sin thereof shall be on those who change it,
for God is he who heareth and knoweth.”5 
To this effect we have sent an edict to all the
realm. This edict we have sent to the province of
___ in order that every rate of tax and transaction
in that province may be written on a plaque in ac-
1Kor. 12:111.
2Kor. 23:7.
3Kor. 26:227.
4Kor. 2:42.
5Kor. 2:181.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
699

cord with what has been fixed and recorded on the
back of this edict. Let this be done soon, and any-
one who fails will be indicted. 
Written during the middle ten days of Rajab in
the year three and seven hundred [February 17–26,
1304] in Öljäitü Buynuq at Hula’an Mürän; and
praise be to God, Lord of the Universe, and prayers
and salutations upon the best of his creation,
Muhammad and his family.
As for provinces whose taxes and divan im-
posts consisted of harvests and cash taxes,
[1442] most of the taxes were raised by extra-
ordinary assessments and levies. They were
subjected to the whims of governors, tax
agents, and fiscal administrators who had made
innovative customs and rules in every age and
appointed many workers under various guises.
Most years they demanded taxes in advance,
and when prices were established it was very
difficult for the peasants and farmers to make
up the difference. The various sorts of tyran-
nies were more than could be counted. 
When the abuse had reached epic proportions
in Baghdad and Shiraz, two of the largest
provinces, [the emperor] ordered redress and
reform and set the taxes according to the tax
rolls. He gave villages in perpetuity to tenants
and fief-holders in such a way that the taxes,
which formerly had not arrived at all, now
come in many times over what is stipulated; all
landlords, owners, and peasants are at ease and
thankful; governors have completely ceased to
demand unwarranted exactions; and the tyran-
ny of villains has been totally eliminated. The
sorts of breaches that were in the administra-
tion and the methods of redress have each and
every one been addressed in detail in the edict
that was written for the provinces. Since it is
clear, obvious, and well known to all, one may
be brief. 
May God cause this ruler who promotes jus-
tice to enjoy life and fortune for ever and ever,
and may the rewards for these good acts reach
his regal days, which would cause Dara, Arda-
van, Ardashir, and Anoshirvan to be jealous. 
Story Seventeen: He protects and shepherds
the peasantry and eliminates their
subjection to injustice and harassment.
Since the various forms of injustice and ag-
gression to which the subjects were exposed
have been mentioned in previous sections, and
the harassments of every sort to which they
were subjected have been explained, [1443] we
need not repeat. One can realize by analogy
that mud clods and street sweepings had more
worth in the eyes of governors and others than
did the subjects, and dust in the street was not
subjected to the humiliation the peasants were
subjected to.
In his perfect justice the Padishah of Islam
Ghazan Khan got to the bottom of the affair
and ordered redress. Thanks to his equity, all
obtained repose, as has been mentioned. That
to which this chapter pertains is that every time
he witnessed or heard a report of any of the
courtiers or soldiers intimidating or annoying a
peasant or taking anything, he immediately or-
dered the perpetrator to be forced, by beating
with sticks and cudgels, to return it. In this way
it would serve as an example to all the people
in the world.
Every time he mounts to go hunting and
comes to the outskirts of a village, he com-
mands that sheep, chickens, and supplies need-
ed for personal consumption be purchased at
full price. He likewise orders that anything
from Mongol ﬂocks and herds worth one dinar
be bought for two or three dinars. His purpose
in this is so that when others see it, they may
realize their own limits and restrain themselves
from practicing violence and excess by follow-
ing his excellent example.
Every time his exalted mind imagines that
one of the amirs or soldiers has used force or
700
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

excess in a province, he has minor amirs in-
dicted and beaten and grand amirs put on trial
and admonished. One day he said, “I am not
partial to the Tajiks. If it were in my interests
to pillage them all, no one would be more able
to do it than I, and we would pillage together;
but if henceforth you expect to requisition sup-
plies and meals, I will reprimand you severely.
Just think—if you use violence on the peasants
and take their cattle and grain or let your hors-
es graze in their fields, what you will do next?
When you beat or hurt their wives and chil-
dren, [1444] just think how dear our own
wives and children are to us. Their children are
just like that to them; they too are human be-
ings like us. Since God has entrusted them to
us, and we will be made to answer for them,
what reply will we make when we mistreat
them? We are all satiated, and we lack nothing:
why should such treatment be necessary? What
greatness or valor does one acquire by mis-
treating one’s own subject? None. But one will
answer for the shame, and there will be no suc-
cess in anything one attempts. The difference
between an obedient subject and a rebellious
one should be obvious: obedient subjects
should have no cause to fear us, and rebels
should fear us. Why shouldn’t we let our obe-
dient subjects rest in peace? Why should they
be in torment from us? Of course, their curses
and imprecations will be answered, and one
should consider that well. I constantly give you
this advice, but you will not be warned.” 
Because of these pieces of advice the harass-
ment that used to be inﬂicted has decreased a
thousand fold, and the subjects of the realm
have increased their prayers for the state. May
those prayers be answered. 
Story Eighteen: He repeals the ulagh and
does away with a superﬂuity of envoys in
the realm.
Although the dispatching of messengers and
envoys in all directions is necessary for rulers,
and matters of state depend upon them, it has
become a habit to send them to inform of well
being, to deliver gifts and presents, and to tend
to frontier business and state secrets. Obvious-
ly there is a need to dispatch envoys several
times a year on such matters, [1445] but previ-
ously it had gradually reached a point that all
the khatuns, princes, officers of the ordu, com-
manders
of
ten
thousand,
thousand,
and
hundred, shahnas of provinces, falconers, leop-
ard keepers, equerries, arms bearers, provision-
ers, and other classes assigned to any function
whatsoever would send an envoy into the
provinces on any business great or small and to
the Mongol khaylkhanas on any matter. It had
become customary for people of the provinces
to give their sons as enchüs or as ortaqs to
khatuns, princes, and amirs, and in return for
them they would receive a little something.
Such people had vast property and possessions
as well as numerous lawsuits, for each of
which they took an envoy to conduct their bus-
iness, fairly or unfairly. Their adversaries were
driven to desperation by so much harassment
and expense that they had no choice but to get
protection from others. They would hire an en-
voy to take retaliation on the others, who
would bring still more envoys. On account of
those people, envoys were constantly coming
and going, and the protectors would also send
envoys one after another out of zeal and fanati-
cism and in all seriousness. 
There was another group. When someone
died and his heirs did not get along with each
other, each of the heirs, in hopes of getting
more of the inheritance, would get a patron to
send envoys to attack the other heirs. Since
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
701

such envoys had lifelong employment, other
people took after them until it became a career
for the generality of the population. 
Another group consisted of village headmen.
Each of them would acquire a different patron,
and on account of disputes over the office of
headman envoys would be brought into the
provinces. 
Another group sent envoys on the pretext of
obtaining tansuqs in a certain province, but
their expenses were many times what they
would bring back. Idächis sent so many envoys
into the provinces to collect funds for supplies,
[1446] provisions, tribute, etc. that the divans
were filled with them. Officers of armaments,
horse, hawks, etc. likewise. It got to the point
that envoys used force on caravans and travel-
ers. Even if there had been five thousand hors-
es at every post station they wouldn’t have suf-
ficed for their transport. They would have
taken all the Mongol herds at summer and win-
ter pastures. Caravans and travelers coming
from Cathay, Hindustan, and other places near
and distant, as well as amirs, basqaqs, maliks,
bitigchis, judges, sayyids, imams, and petition-
ers who went back and forth to the ordu—all
these they would force to dismount, take their
horses, and leave them stranded on the road—
and sometimes in dreadful places. It had gotten
so bad that thieves and robbers disguised them-
selves as envoys. Coming onto the road, they
would say they were envoys and commandeer
travelers’ horses, and then they would seize
them, tie them up, and plunder their baggage.
Often envoys commandeered horses from oth-
er envoys, claiming that their business was
more important. It got to the point that whoev-
er had more swords and power would com-
mandeer the other’s mounts. When thieves
learned of this, they rarely told envoys much
about themselves, but they would commandeer
their mounts by force and plunder them, taking
their patents and badges too. Thus most thieves
practiced highway robbery, armed with badges,
patents, and bands of grooms. Falsely claiming
to be envoys, they would strike caravans and
real envoys and take their animals and bag-
gage. [1447]
Envoys were not content with their al-
lowances for mounts and supplies: anyone they
came across they would strip clean and press
until they had taken large amounts of money.
Their grooms took any of the people’s clothing
and turbans they saw. They intentionally took
too many pack animals and then sold them off.
Anything they saw in villages they would com-
mandeer by force. If they passed by ten vil-
lages and khaylkhanas a day, they would take
from them all many times the provisions al-
lowed by custom and the law. Since it was
more than they could consume, they sold the
surplus. As they were constantly engaged in
transactions to sell provisions, the result was
that merchants ceased to come from Cathay
and India.
From the description given it is possible to
realize how many thousands of envoys came
and went every year, how many mounts and
how much provisions they took, and how many
people they robbed, attacked, and mistreated.
Since the peasants were in their clutches satis-
fying their demands for provisions and other
requests, and by night they had to guard their
horses and baggage, it is a wonder they ever
managed to farm for the people’s sustenance—
it can only be attributed to God’s blessing that
his creatures were not deprived of their daily
bread altogether.
When most of those so-called envoys who
wandered aimlessly came to a place, they
would say they were sons or brothers of great
lords traveling on some urgent mission. Those
who manned the post stations, governors, and
village headmen knew full well that it was a
702
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

bald-faced lie. If a real envoy happened to
travel on important business, he had very little
standing in the people’s eyes because they as-
sumed he was like the others. Thus envoys had
lost all respect and become the worst creatures
in everyone’s opinion. [1448] Since by mistake
even real envoys had no standing, they did not
receive mounts at the post stations, or the
mounts they were given were emaciated. Since
travelers and nomads had grown fearful, they
avoided traveled paths and made their homes
in the hills. 
For all these reasons, when an envoy went on
state business, no matter how sensitive it was,
it took him two or three times as long as it
should have. Naturally this led to breakdowns,
and the keepers of relay stations had to be con-
stantly investigated because the post horses
were so skinny. Even though five hundred
horses were maintained at every station, there
were never two horses fat enough for an ex-
press courier to mount. Aside from this, in
cities where huge sums of money were re-
leased for the post and envoys’ expenses,
provincial governors took other taxes on that
pretext from the peasants, some of which they
spent and some of which they embezzled. In
all provinces the customs tax, which is the one
tax paid most in cash throughout the realm,
had been earmarked for envoys’ expenses, but
it did not suffice even for their transport. Gov-
ernors would charge provisions to the customs
tax and then abscond. Since there wasn’t
enough, the customs official would also disap-
pear. The envoys were left to squabble among
themselves, and the one who finally came out
on top would take the funds. This usually be-
ing determined by the preponderance of one’s
followers, they all tried to gather as many liege
men as they could and recruited them from
among their friends and relatives. It got to the
point that an envoy the emperor or great amirs
wouldn’t have recognized would take two or
three hundred horsemen with him on the most
triﬂing business. Those who were more well
known
would
take
anywhere
from
five
hundred to a thousand. Sometimes nearly two
hundred seats [1449] would be placed in a city
divan for envoys. Governors would say, “Let
me take care of the one whose business is the
most urgent.” The envoys would fight among
themselves, and when one of them won, the
governors would be saved from the rest by be-
ing under the winner’s patronage. They would
put him off, occasionally paying him some lit-
tle service, and thus spend their time until, at
the end of the year, all the envoys would return
without having accomplished their tasks but
having piled up huge expenses. The varieties
of abuses committed because of the envoys
were too many to describe.
The Padishah of Islam realized in his perfect
justice that these things had to be reformed, so
he promulgated an order, saying that such a
large-scale affair, to which the population in
general had become habituated, could not be
eliminated at once but would have to be dealt
with gradually and with deliberation. Reform
was begun, and the first year he said, “We must
establish a separate post system for express
couriers to use on important state matters and
border business. No one else may ride those
horses so that those envoys may be distin-
guished from the others and so that they may
quickly reach their destinations.” An edict was
issued for post stations to be established on
major highways at three-league intervals, and
three fattened horses were to be kept there. In
some locales that were not so urgent, there
could be fewer horses. He also ordered that
those post horses not be given to anyone unless
there was a letter in the emperor’s handwriting
and with the emperor’s own gold seal. 
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
703

Every post station was entrusted to a great
amir, and to defray their expenses designated
territories were put under their control in such
a way that there was more than enough rev-
enue to meet their expenses, and thus they
would have no excuses [for abuse]. He said, “I
am giving you excess funds so that there will
be no shortcoming. You will spend the surplus
on your own needs, for every day an informant
rises up to claim that your expenditures are
more than your expenses, which makes your
job irksome, or else you have to give the mon-
ey to someone else, and the post is left in the
lurch. [1450] Since you are great amirs, excess
funds are not being withheld, but you must
perform your jobs in an orderly fashion.”
Since it was necessary for officers of the bor-
derlands to send envoys via the post to report
on conditions, the emperor gave each of them
several letters with his own customary device
and tamgha seal for them to give to envoys.
Some were valid for two horses, and some
were valid for three or four horses. The keep-
ers of relay stations were ordered not to give
mounts without authorization. 
Then he said, “The point of an express couri-
er is for him to get where he is going fast. Even
if a courier is the son of a lord, he will mount
at most four horses.”
He also said, “If the matter is extremely ur-
gent, let a letter be written and stamped with
the seal to be sent by post riders. Let it be writ-
ten at the top of the letter, ‘From X place to Y
place.’ ” He gave every officer along the bor-
der a horseman seal to stamp on such letters.
Since the keepers of relay stations know the
roads, and since there is a relay station every
three leagues, when various ulaghchis ride fast,
they can cover sixty leagues in a day and night.
Urgent news can travel from Khurasan to
Tabriz in three or four days, whereas if an en-
voy goes it takes him more than six days. 
He also arranged for there to be two messen-
gers at every post station so that if there was
interprovincial business a messenger seal could
be stamped at the top of a letter with the super-
scription “sent from X place.” After testing it
was learned that by changing mounts messen-
gers could cover thirty leagues in a day and
night. Thus any news there was could arrive in
a short time. 
Later he said, “Bodyguards and attendants at
our court who attend us day and night in the
heat and cold on hunts and in battle provide
their own mounts and provisions. Why should
persons who go on business have to travel at
state expense, requisition provisions, and claim
expenses from surtaxes when they arrive in the
provinces?” [1451] Since this was reasonable,
an imperial decree was issued to this effect.
After it had been applied for a period of time,
the post stations of the tümäns fell into
abeyance, and the money that had been spent
on them came to the treasury. When the envoys
the emperor dispatched had no right to ulagh,
how could others claim it? 
He also ordered that, other than servants of
the court, no one should dispatch envoys.
Therefore others’ envoys ceased to exist.
An order was given that if anyone hired an
envoy on personal business in a province or
any other place, he was not to be given sup-
plies, and the governors of that place were to
arrest him and imprison him. This being so,
persons who used to requisition envoys for
personal business abandoned the practice. 
Then he said, “We will give envoys who go
to the provinces a provisions allowance from
the treasury sufficient for their round-trip so
that they will not have to requisition supplies
in any locale. When they arrive at their des-
tination they will be fed from a special surtax.”
Thus any envoy who was assigned to a
province was given cash from the treasury to
704
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

cover his provisions on the way. This became
known in all provinces and locales, and when
envoys dispatched by the emperor did not have
the right to requisition supplies, why should
people give them to others? Therefore, during
the last two years throughout the realm sup-
plies of mounts and fodder for envoys have
been
eliminated
in
cities,
villages,
and
khaylkhanas. Indeed, no one in the realm sees
an envoy, for those who travel on the pony ex-
press are traversing vast distances day and
night and do not dare even to stop for a small
meal. From the provinces thirty envoys, more
or less, are dispatched, but since they have no
right to requisition provisions along the way,
no one distinguishes them from other travelers.
Because of such all-pervasive justice, the gen-
erality of the people rest in peace. [1452]
Mongols and nomads relax in their yurts,
merchants and travelers ply the roads in safety,
the inhabitants of cities and villages engage in
improving the land and agriculture in comfort,
and everyone, along with their wives and chil-
dren, pray for the emperor’s fortune from the
bottom of their hearts. May their prayers be
answered!
He also ordered that if occasionally it was
necessary to sell horses or donkeys for certain
people to reach a province, they should pay the
full price, and the animals would then be
theirs. Under no circumstances was the word
ulagh to be uttered.
Prior to this, falconers and leopard keepers
brought their falcons and leopards from the
provinces via the ulagh. The emperor ordered
that [they should pay for transport, and any]
animals that remained after arrival would be
theirs.
By means of these arrangements the land
ﬂourished and acquired a new splendor. The
funds that had been earmarked for post stations
and envoys’ expenses and the money that had
been taken by force now comes into the
treasury, and what used to be taken from the
subjects and squandered now remains with its
owners. May God cause the blessings of this
justice to reach the emperor’s time.
Story Nineteen: He eliminates thieves and
highway robbers and protects the roads of
the realm from their predation.
It is well known to all how great the lawless
ascendancy of highway robbers and thieves
was previously. In addition to their ranks’ be-
ing swollen with Mongols, Tajiks, Märtäds,
Kurds, Lur, Shul, and Syrians, run-away slaves
also joined them, and urban rabble went to
them. Some villagers and country folk also act-
ed in concert with them, serving as guides.
[1453] They had spies in all cities to inform
them when various people set forth. Those who
had
long
practiced
highway
robbery
had
gained a reputation for their trade, and if they
were occasionally caught, they would be pro-
tected by certain groups, who would say, “How
can such a champion be killed? He should be
patronized.” This caused other thieves to grow
even bolder and more audacious. Although the
ancient Yasaq required that when a robber at-
tacked, all caravan people, envoys, and travel-
ers should join together to repel the foe, during
that period, those people did not help each oth-
er when robbers showed up. Mostly the thieves
knew every detail of the people they were at-
tacking and would say, “We have nothing to do
with those who don’t have anything or with
those who have only a little.” Such people
would stand aside while the thieves robbed and
killed the others. If they robbed in the vicinity
of a post station, village, or town, where it
should have been possible to defend against
them, not only would the inhabitants refuse to
help but it also got so bad that robbers had
friends and accomplices among every group of
nomads and villagers. Many people knew
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
705

about it, but they would not reveal it; and even
if it was occasionally discovered, it would not
be reported to the emperor. Thanks to the
connivance of village headmen and certain vil-
lage elders who were acquainted with and
friendly to the robbers, their needs were taken
care of in all seasons of the year. Many of them
went to those people’s houses as guests, and
when there was fear they would ﬂee to them.
They also had acquaintances in cities who
fenced their goods, and often they would pass
a convivial month or two with them, spending
their ill-gotten gains on each other. The rob-
bers’ domination had reached a point that an
amir’s house would be attacked at night and
pillaged. 
Patrolmen and highway guards did nothing
more than take whatever they wanted from
wayfarers. [1454] They would stop caravans
and hold them, claiming, “There are thieves
and stolen property in your midst,” until the
robbers could be informed and set out. They
never went after thieves themselves, and way-
farers never had so much trepidation of thieves
as they had for patrolmen and guards, for loss
to thieves happened only occasionally, but they
fell into patrolmen’s clutches twice at every lo-
cale. Woe betide the caravan that chose distant
and difficult roads to escape the exactions of
patrolmen and road guards!
Realizing that it was necessary to redress this
situation, the Padishah of Islam first ordered
that anyone who was separated from his com-
panions when robbers attacked and did not par-
ticipate with the others in defending them-
selves would be considered a criminal and held
liable for the blood and property of his
comrades.
Next he ordered that in any locale, be it
khaylkhana or village, in the vicinity of which
an act of robbery took place, the responsibility
for pursuing and apprehending the thieves
would fall upon the inhabitants, more especial-
ly since they were probably the ones who had
informed
the
robbers
in
the
first
place.
Whether night or day, they would have to pur-
sue the thieves on horseback or on foot until
they found them.
Next he ordered that if it was discovered that
anyone—Mongol
or
Muslim—in
a
khaylkhana, village, or city had colluded with
thieves, that person would be executed without
remorse. To this task was assigned Amir Inqul,
a confidant at court who was renowned for not
looking at faces or hearts and having absolute-
ly no pity. He captured many of the robbers
and executed most of them, although some
were brought in under restraint. The informant
who guided Amir Inqul and knew those people
was made a tarkhan. An edict was issued for
him to continue his investigations, [1455] and
since the emperor was pleased that Amir Inqul
had executed those people, he awarded him all
their property and animals and said, “Anyone
who steals so much as a chilbu’ur [halter] will
be executed.” Therefore there was such fear of
execution in the realm that after that no one
dared to be an accomplice to thieves. When the
thieves realized that no one was going to help
them or give them supplies or shelter, they
robbed less, and a certain amount of security
reigned. 
After that, he ordered that patrolmen should
be stationed on roads that were unsafe in any
locale throughout the realm. As a toll they
might take half an aqcha for every four don-
keys carrying loads in caravans and half an
aqcha for every two camels; under no circum-
stances might they take more. For animals that
were not loaded and for those that carried
foodstuffs and grain they should take nothing.
If a robbery occurred, the patrolman nearest to
the location would have to capture the thief;
otherwise he would be responsible for the
706
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

amount stolen. Written pledges to this effect
were taken from all the patrolmen, and they
were put under the jurisdiction of Amir Boral-
ghi, the son of the Amir Junqur who had been
chief officer of the highway patrol during
Arghun Khan’s reign. The emperor ordered
him to turn every highway over to a trustwor-
thy person in order to insure that the patrolmen
did not stay in places that were safe and easy
while neglecting unsafe locales. They should
also not sit around more than necessary. He
also ordered that they should take all precau-
tions, and in necessary places they should erect
steles of stone and plaster and plaques on
which should be inscribed the number of pa-
trolmen for that locale and the pertinent stipu-
lations of the law. This was so that they would
not sit outside of those places and so that no
more than the assigned number would be there
and no more than the fixed amount of tolls
would be taken. Such plaques were called
Plaques of Justice. Prior to this, anyone from
the khaylkhanas who so desired could sit on
the roads and take tolls, claiming to be high-
way guards. [1456] Now, however, since it is
written on the plaques that anyone who sits
outside of stipulated locales will be considered
a robber, no one, Mongol or Tajik, can sit any-
where else. During the two years this law has
been effect fewer robberies have been commit-
ted in the realm, and when robberies do happen
from time to time, the thieves are apprehended
with their loot and executed. For this reason
most of those people have abandoned their
trade, and safety on the roads has been
achieved.
He also ordered that any caravan or wayfarer
intending to take a highway near a village or
khaylkhana should first ask the headmen
whether there are any thieves about or not. If
they say there are, travelers should stop in the
khaylkhana or village, and they should not be
prevented from doing so. If they say there are
no thieves, and travelers who stop in the
wilderness are attacked, the responsibility will
fall upon the headmen. This decree was not put
in effect in the vicinity of cities, for in those lo-
cales they are released from responsibility. 
When the roads were organized according to
the foregoing, and detail lists of the names of
patrolmen and their officers were given to
Amir Boralghi, there were nearly ten thousand
men—which would form a full military divi-
sion—engaged in this task. It has been ordered
that they do no other work but only protect the
lives and property of travelers so that all may
come and go at leisure and pray with all sin-
cerity for the emperor’s continued fortune.
May their prayers be answered. [1457]
Story Twenty: He reforms the gold and
silver standard better than it has ever been.
It is well known that, from ancient times until
the present, in no reign has there been coinage
throughout the realm in the name of the ruler
who held all the territory, especially in eras
during which this realm was in the hands of
several rulers or sultans. The gold and silver
standard has always varied from locale to lo-
cale. In several lands where they tried to
standardize coinage, no matter how many or-
ders were given, things never proceeded ac-
cording to command and they were never able
to regulate it. There is no doubt that one of the
prerogatives of rulers is to have the khutba and
coinage in their names, as up until now in Ana-
tolia, Fars, Kirman, Georgia, and Mardin
coinage has been struck in the names of the
kings and sultans of those places, but the coins
were of different standards. 
In several places during the reigns of Arghun
Khan and Gaikhatu it was decreed that silver
coins should be struck at a standard of 9:10 sil-
ver. That was the nominal standard, but [it was
actually] never more than 7:10 or 8:10. The
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
707

aqchas of Anatolia, which were relatively bet-
ter than those of other places, degenerated to
the point that not more than two out of ten di-
nars had the standard amount of silver—all the
rest were copper. 
Often Mongol envoys or Tajik bitigchis were
ordered into the provinces to investigate the
adulteration of coins, and they piled up great
expenses, took bribes, and never brought a sin-
gle criminal to trial. They had absolutely no
shame in striking and putting into circulation
such aqchas, which looked altogether like cop-
per and had no more than a trace of silver.
Since they were used by number, it was com-
mon practice to clip the edges of aqchas. And
since the standards in the provinces were dif-
ferent, merchants perforce [ceased to] deal in
goods,
[1458] and wherever they went they
would purchase gold and silver coins that had a
better standard than that of their destination,
for they made more profit thereby, and for that
reason commercial goods were in short supply
in most places. 
It got to the point that coins were taken for
less than their nominal worth; otherwise they
would not be accepted. Now, if one has to bear
a loss of more than ten dinars—and sometimes
even twenty dinars—to buy something in a
province for a hundred dinars, there is nothing
more difficult than such a confiscation. If peo-
ple who are not merchants have to lose two or
three dinars on every ten or twelve dinars of
the money they have to purchase what they
need—and if they have to suffer a great deal of
harassment in addition before the coins will be
accepted, especially in villages and nomads’
khaylkhanas, where they don’t know anything
about the standard, they will hesitate to accept
them because they will wonder which one is
better.
Gold and silver are beneficial to the extent
that they enable people to buy what they need
and to acquire quickly something they want.
When gold and silver coinage degenerates to
the point that it is a cause for argument and
trouble, and no one will accept it when it is
used for payment, it is contrary to the natural
state of the world. 
To redress this situation the Padishah of Is-
lam had the following idea. First, he ordered
that coins should be made in a fashion of his
own design, and a device that would be impos-
sible to forge should be put on them. He also
ordered that throughout the realm gold and sil-
ver coins should be struck in every place with
the names of God and the Apostle, and his own
name should also be on them. Even in Georgia,
where coins had never had God’s and the
Apostle’s names, they would necessarily be so
struck, for there was to be no other legal cur-
rency. Even until now they strike coins like
that despite the fact that they are in rebellion,
for otherwise their coins would not be accepted
anywhere. 
In accordance with the foregoing, throughout
the realm the minting of gold and silver in one
type of coin has been established. [1459] With
regard to the standard, he said, “If we permit
the slightest deviation from the official gold
and silver standard, as is the case with the
Caliphal, Egyptian, and North African coinage,
they will use that permission to lessen it by a
lot and they will use all sorts of tricks and
chicanery to make the adulteration look like
something else. Our inspectors do not have the
necessary knowledge to detect it, or else they
will take bribes to overlook it. The best course
of action is for them to beat the official gold
standard until it can be wrought into sheets and
for the official silver standard to be repeatedly
refined until it can be dissolved in quicksilver.
Thereby, if an iota of adulteration is present it
will show up in the color and softness. If it is
heated in a ﬂame it will immediately be obvi-
708
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ous, and anybody will be able to judge its
worth. 
Since he wanted the entire realm to have a
standard of this sort, and since places varied
greatly in their standards, he said, “If this order
is carried out all at once, the generality of the
people will suffer loss and cry out. It would be
better, since previously every dirhem was
struck as four dangs,1 and without there being
any good reason for doing so, they made half-
and-half-dangs,2 now let them strike true half-
mithcals, and the adulterated halves and half-
dangs will be worth half-mithcals of the offi-
cial silver standard.3 When the purchasing
power of gold and silver is according to its
standard, anyone who has adulterated half-and-
half-dangs he spends as one-dirhems will let
them be unadulterated and turned into half-
mithcals so he can spend them as one-dirhems.
When all necessary steps were taken and
things turned out nearly as desired, and since
there was not much loss involved, people will-
ingly exchanged the three and a half mithcals
of [adulterated] silver they had for three mith-
cals of officially minted silver coinage. 
He ordered an investigation made to deter-
mine the worth of the official gold standard
and ordered it struck and evaluated so that
there be no difference. He also ordered the
Hormuz gold piece, which no one could distin-
guish from miscellaneous other gold coins of
1Four dāngs is the Persian expression for two thirds.
Apparently, the former practice was to strike dirhems as
two thirds of a mithcal. At the time, most fractions could
not be expressed with a numerator other than one.
2“Half-and-half-dang” = 1/2 + 0.5/6 = 7/12, or 1/12 short of
2/3 (four dangs).
3I.e., after the restoration of the currency, 1 silver di-
nar of 3 mithcals (13.6 grams) of silver = 6 dirhems of
½-mithcal of silver each. See I. P. Petrushevsky, “The
Socio-Economic Condition of Iran under the Il-Khans,”
The Cambridge History of Iran 5:495.
lesser standard, [1460] evaluated a bit higher.
His goal in this was that when moneychangers
realized that there was profit to be made in
melting them down, they would buy them and
turn them into gold. Since they did realize the
benefit, within a year no one saw a less-than-
standard gold mithcal anywhere in the realm.
Prior to this, red gold was rare in the mar-
kets, and if anyone brought any into the market
there would be hundreds of buyers. It is well
known that during the days of the Mongols
many fabrics of thread and weave in which
gold was wasted were kept. Such things were
also commercial goods for India, where they
were taken. For these reasons gold became
scarce. At the present so much gold circulates
in the hands of villagers in the markets that
there is no end to it. All transactions are done
in it, and throughout the realm there is no gold
or silver left that has not been minted into
coins.
An order was promulgated that anyone in
whose hands adulterated gold or silver was
seen would be considered a criminal and, un-
like olden times, he would not be told, “Point
out the person who gave you these.” In those
times there were many types of adulterated
coins, but now it has been ordered that no one
conclude a transaction in anything other than
standard gold and silver. Anyone who doesn’t
know how should show his coins to someone
else to test. This being the case, no forger
makes counterfeit coins because he knows that
no one will accept them, for everyone takes
precautions.
During the period such a great thing has been
enacted in the realm, it has not been necessary
to kill anyone. The law has been enforced
throughout the realm so that there is nothing
but standard coins.
The emperor also ordered that minted coins
be spent by weight, three mithcals to the dinar,
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
709

so that no one would clip them. When coinage
was standardized throughout the realm, the
people rested in peace, and merchants, who
had turned their goods into cash, now transport
all sorts of goods into every province. They
profit thereby, and all the people share in the
benefits. [1461] The name of the Padishah of
Islam has spread for goodness, and the khutba
and coinage of the realm are in his blessed
name. 
He
ordered
that
hundred-mithcal
gold
medallions be struck, and he had his name
struck on coins in the scripts of all provinces
so that when they were read in all places they
would realize that it was his minting. Koranic
verses and the names of the Twelve Imams are
also engraved on that coin, and it is such an ex-
tremely beautiful coin that no one who gets
one ever wants to part with it.
“When we order a reward for someone’s val-
or,” he said, “let us give him one of those
medallions.”
Such mighty deeds, which no caliph or past
sultan has ever achieved, have been done by
the Padishah of Islam, and they have insured
the repose of the people. May God reward him
eternally! 
"Story Twenty-One: He corrects monetary
and scale weights and fixes the yard, the
standard grain measure, the qafiz, and the
taghar.
Previously the weights of gold, the load, the
yard, grain measures, the qafiz, and the taghar
varied in the realm. Even now there are differ-
ences among various regions within a single
province. For that reason there was much
abuse in prices, and merchants purchased few-
er commodities because when they took the
currency of one place to another they made a
profit merely because of the difference of
weight. There was a slump in commodities in
some provinces while in others they were not
to be found. In every village there were two or
three different qafiz measures:
[1462] the
smaller was used in transactions with strangers
and the larger was used in transactions among
the natives. A stranger, whether he knew what
was happening or not, had no choice but to ac-
quiesce. Villagers would bear false witness for
each other that the qafiz was true, and the
taghars they gave to the army and as savuri,
which should have been one hundred maunds
on the scale, were actually only seventy, sixty,
or even less. The powerful got the extra
amount through beatings, and on that account
the people were constantly in quarrels and
disputes. 
The Padishah of Islam said, “The entire
realm is under our command. What is the ne-
cessity for this variance? Let us order it regu-
lated so that it will be equal in all places. Let
us make it such that there will be no different
weights in the markets, provinces, and villages
so that they will not be able to rob each other.”
After consideration, he issued an edict contain-
ing provisions for reform, and it is as follows.
Text of the edict the emperor decreed on the
gold and silver standard in the best way.
In the name of God, the Compassionate, the
Merciful.
Decree of Sultan Mahmud Ghazan.
Be it known to shahnas, maliks, bitigchis, deputies,
judges, sayyids, imams, sadrs, grandees, those in
authority, the eminent, residents in general, travel-
ers, and merchants of the realm that our regal mind
is entirely focused upon the welfare of our subjects,
justice and honesty among them,
[1463] and the
fundamentals of charity. We desire to eliminate the
tyranny, injustice, innovations, and dishonesty that
have spread among the people over long periods of
time and thereby to do away with the complaints,
quarrels, useless suits, fights, and contention that
are rife among the general population. We desire to
unburden them of all sorts of fraud and injustice so
that they may be freed in this world from sedition
710
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

and strife and in the next world from torment and
hell fire.
Lately, when we have been investigating fiscal
affairs and the interests of the people and creating
guidelines for every job, it has become apparent
that in the markets of the ordu and cities everyone
makes weights of stone, mud, iron, &c. in his own
best interests, increasing or decreasing the weights
at any time however they wish, and they buy and
sell using those weights, deceiving the poor and
causing them loss. This situation does not suit our
world-adorning mind and is highly displeasing to
us. Therefore we have commanded that throughout
the realm, from the River Oxus to Egypt, weights
of gold and silver, standard loads, grain measures,
and the yard be corrected. Let them all be made of
iron and authenticated with our seal and device,
which we have established ourselves. Let them be
followed throughout the realm, and let no one
transgress. The details are as follows.
First, the weight of gold and silver must be equal
and standardized in all part of the realm against the
standard weight of Tabriz so that no one will add to
or subtract from it or practice injustice on the peo-
ple. Coins will not be transported from province to
province because of a difference in weight, and the
official standard of gold and silver will be equal
throughout the territory.
Weights too will be standardized, and to this end
we
have
appointed
masters
Fakhruddin
and
Baha’uddin Khurasani to make gold and silver
stones of octagonal shape. They will assign two
trusted men on their behalf in every province,
[1464] and one trustworthy individual will be dis-
patched by the cadi of that province to the presence
of the muhtasib. The arrangements for standardiza-
tion are as follows. Anyone in any province who
needs a weight stone will have one made from iron
in the shape of the gold stones in accordance with
the octagonal models made and stamped by
Fakhruddin and Baha’uddin Khurasani, and then he
will go before the four trustworthy individuals just
named, who will have been appointed in every
province, for them to insure that the standard is
correct, stamp it with a seal, and turn it over to him.
No one else, be he who he may, may make that seal
or put it on a stone. Anyone who does make such a
seal and puts it on a weight will be a criminal and
liable to execution.
Next, the names of all to whom sealed weights
are given must be recorded in registers to keep oth-
ers from being able to forge at will. Every month
all weights in general use are to be inspected and
compared. If anyone adds to or subtracts from
weights, or if anyone places a seal of his own voli-
tion, or if anyone buys or sells using a weight that
does not have the seal and stamp, or if anyone
forges a weight, he will be arrested and taken be-
fore the shahna to be executed according to the
command of the edict.
Next, weights of loads will be arranged similarly,
but it is established that in every locale in which
weights are less than the Tabriz standard, weights
will be adjusted to the Tabriz standard.1 Those that
have hitherto been more than the Tabriz standard
will be likewise adjusted. However, all weights
must be made of iron in an octagonal shape in ac-
cordance with the model, inspected, and sealed;
and let all those responsible carry out these
arrangements. Load weights from ten maunds to
one dirhem are to be made in the following eleven
sizes: ten-maund, [1465] five-maund, two-maund,
one-maund, half-maund, quarter-maund, eighth-
maund, ten-dirhem, five-dirhem, two-dirhem, and
one-dirhem.
For
heavy
loads
of
one
piece,
tamghachis of cities must make reliable scales on
which they can weigh them so that there be neither
extra nor shortfall in weight.
Next, because in every province the grain
measure, the qafiz, the jarib, and the wheat and
barley taghar conventionally vary, and because the
grain measure is added to and subtracted from, and
because every person makes grain measures how-
ever he wants and these are difficult to reconcile,
and not every person understands this—it is partic-
ularly a cause for debate with peasants when Mon-
1The Tabriz standard to which weights were made to
conform is the “little maund,” also known as the “canon-
ical maund” (man-i shar‘í). It is equivalent to 833
grams. The dirhem weight is 3.2 grams. See Hinz, Is-
lamische Masse, 18.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
711

gol garrisons, merchants, and strangers go to
provinces to collect and purchase divan supplies,
and they give more to anyone who is dominant or
powerful, which causes loss and trouble and creates
argument among the people of the world—for these
reasons, we have decreed that in all parts of the
realm the grain measure will be made equal to the
standard Tabriz ten-maund, each maund of which
consists of two hundred sixty dirhems.1 Ten such
measures will equal one taghar.2 Other than the
grain measure and taghar mentioned, no other
measure or convention will be in use among the
people. This is to insure that transactions and reck-
onings be correct and there be no defrauding of
each other. When a taghar is given it will be deliv-
ered by that measure so that there be no extra or
shortfall. Since grains like wheat, barley, rice,
chickpeas, beans, sesame, millet, etc. are lighter or
heavier in comparison with each other, a separate
measure to equal ten maunds is to be made for each
of these grains. Let it be written on all four sides of
the measure what grain it is for. This task will be
entrusted by the judicial authority to the same agent
assigned to inspect weights for gold, silver, [1466]
and loads, and let him and the muhtasib inspect the
grain measure and place their own seals on the
sides so that there be no fraud or difference. Let
them carry out an inspection in every city and
province once a month. Anyone found in posses-
sion of a measure fabricated without a seal will be
arrested and turned over to the shahna to be pro-
claimed a criminal, to have his hand cut off, and to
be fined. 
Henceforth, for no reason or cause whatsoever
will there be any grain measure, qafiz, or jarib oth-
er than the ten-maund grain measure and the
hundred-maund taghar in any part of the empire,
from the River Oxus to Egypt. Any that exist will
not be valid. Let no other measures be made. If it is
desired to make half measures of five maunds,
there is no objection, provided that twenty half-
measures equal one taghar. 
11 grain measure (kíla) = 10 Tabrizi maunds = 8.33 kg.
See Hinz, Islamische Masse, 42.
21 taghar = 10 kīlas = 100 Tabrizi maunds = 83.3 kg.
Next, measures of syrup, vinegar, and oil must be
designated separately, every measure equivalent to
ten Tabriz maunds. If so desired, half measures
may be made provided they be equal to five Tabriz
maunds. Syrup casks brought for meals in the ordu
and as donations will be five measures, or fifty
maunds. Those brought for banquets will be four
measures, or forty maunds. 
Next, all yard measures by which fabric is
measured must be adjusted to the Tabriz standard—
except for the yard of Anatolia, which differs great-
ly.3 Let the seal that masters Fakhruddin and
Baha’uddin Khurasani have made, a model of
which has been given, be placed on both ends of
yard measures, and let the above-mentioned au-
thorities in all cities record them as described. Any-
one who changes or alters them will be a criminal
and liable to execution. 
May God cause the blessings of such justice
and equity to reach the emperor’s time.  [1467]
Story Twenty-Two: He regularizes the
giving of edicts and badges of office to
people.
Concerning edicts, he ordered that anything
that has to be said should be said at the right
moment and in times of sobriety. Even when
he has been drinking wine, although no one
can obtain permission to speak improprieties
by way of chicanery, and it is not possible for
him to utter any inexcusable word or to do
anything in haste, he ordered that when he was
in that condition nothing be said in such re-
gards. He also ordered that after a request was
made, a draft edict would be made by amirs
who had the best interests of the state in mind.
They should not write edicts at anyone’s re-
quest for anything unwarranted. There are
many matters on which reference must be
made
to
registers
for
place
names
and
3It is difficult to know which linear measure is meant
here. The gaz is both the yard (equivalent to around 95
cm) and the ell (equivalent to the canonical ell of 49.875
cm).
712
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

amounts: precaution should be taken before
preparing drafts for such things. Then, together
with the Mongol bitigchis they should read
them out word for word and then present them
to the emperor so that if a correction is neces-
sary it can be made by the imperial pen or the
imperial word. After that, a fair copy may be
made and shown to the emperor. Thereafter
they can stamp it with the read seal and say, “It
is X edict for X person, presented to the em-
peror on X day, and read on X day for approval
for the seal.”
Formerly the keys to the great seals were
kept by bitigchis, but now they are in the impe-
rial satchel. When needed they are given so
that the bitigchis together may use the seals
and return them. There are also four amirs ap-
pointed from four gäzigs; each one has been
given a separate black seal so that when an
edict is sealed they can place their seals on the
reverse in order that no one deny his knowl-
edge of it.
Once again the edict is shown to the viziers
and divan chiefs [1468] so that they can insure
that no mistake has been made. They also
place divan seals on the back and turn it over
to the individual. A bitigchi has been appointed
to record word for word in a register the text of
every edict sealed in red. He also makes note
of the day it was sealed, who wrote it, and
when it was presented to the emperor. At the
end of every year a new register is begun so
that there will be a register for each year. This
is to prevent confusion and to keep anyone
from denying that an edict was presented, writ-
ten, or sealed. Furthermore, if an decree has
been given to someone and someone else finds
it and wants to obtain an order contrary to it,
reference can be made to the register to ascer-
tain the original situation and so prevent a con-
tradictory application from being made. If
complaint is made of a patent-holder, it can be
ascertained from the register whether or not he
has overstepped his bounds, and either he or
his detractors can be reprimanded. Thus all af-
fairs will always be in order, and unwarranted
complaints will be prevented. 
He also ordered that the sealers take nothing
from anyone for stamping the seal—and the
truth is that relative to the greed that was prac-
ticed previously, they have taken very little.
For every important affair a separate seal has
been designated. For awarding governorship to
important sultans, amirs, and maliks and for
important fiscal affairs of state there is the
great jade seal; for judges, imams, and shaykhs
there is another, also of jade but slightly small-
er; for affairs of middling importance there is a
large seal of gold; down from that is one of
jade; and for ordering mounting and dismount-
ing of troops there is a special seal of gold with
the regular inscription and design but around it
is a picture of a bow, a cudgel, and a sword. It
is ordered that immediately upon seeing that
seal, a soldier will neither mount nor dismount
at the order of an amir or any other person—
except for scouts who tend to border affairs,
[1469] and except for a common soldier who
mounts or dismounts at an officer’s order to re-
connoiter the way. A small gold seal has been
made for sealing treasury and provincial bills
and receipts, commercial papers, and state cor-
respondence dealing with transactions, water,
and land. After the divan bitigchis have written
them with approval and devices are affixed, a
summary in Mongolian script will be written
on the back so that they can be sealed. 
At the present time whenever many bills and
letters have piled up, they are presented, the
keys are taken, and the viziers and deputies of
the divan stamp them with the seal in the em-
peror’s presence, while others record them in
the registers that are also kept in the same box.
This is so that it may be clear at what time and
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
713

by what person they were sealed. With such
elaborate arrangements how can there be any
opportunity left for anyone to write a voucher
for a fraction of a coin without imperial
approval?
After these rules and regulations were put
into effect, the emperor said, “There are too
many affairs of state and requests from the
people for all drafts to be read aloud. We must
think up some other method to insure that the
people’s business not be delayed and those in
need not suffer. When they make a separate
draft for every piece of business, of course the
bitigchis cannot remember everything as they
should. The next time, a mistake is made in the
wording, and a difference appears in decrees
written for the same sort of thing.” 
To rectify this, he ordered all various types of
business and requests the people might make
to be recorded, and a comprehensive draft for
each type made that would contain all the stip-
ulations and fine points of that type. When
they were all written he summoned the amirs
and said, “Decrees that are issued are com-
manded by me and approved by you. Since no
one should be able to [misinterpret them] on
account of inconstancy or vacillation, [1470]
we will read the drafts together. We will all
think about them deeply and say what we
think. Then we will correct them so that no
fine point of precaution will have been neglect-
ed. They will then conform to our mind and
yours. We will make them models, and hence-
forth we will decide all cases and issue all
commands accordingly so that all affairs may
run along one path and one yosun [custom],
and there will be no disparity in what we say.
We must consult and correct them with all cau-
tion so that you all agree. After that, they will
be read once again in your presence, and if any
minor point strikes you, we will consult and
correct it. Only then will it be finally decided.”
According to his command, after correction
all the drafts were written in a register, and it
was named the Roll of Orders. Then he said,
“Henceforth orders will be copied from these
drafts without addition or subtraction. If oc-
casionally a case comes up that is not men-
tioned, a draft should be made and presented.
If occasionally something extra has to be
added for a person, place, or exigency of situa-
tion or time, let the additional words be written
separately and submitted.”
Since there had never been such a rule in any
era, he said, “The gates are closed to the argu-
ment and contention that used to arise over dif-
ferences in wording. The perplexity people
with petitions used to experience in finding the
right moment for presentation has been elim-
inated. The people rest at ease. Everyone has
confidence in the matter of edicts. Respect for
edicts resides in hearts. The demands and harsh
words of corrupt and officious people who
used to get decrees saying whatever they want-
ed are over. The limits of elite and common,
governor and governed, tyrant and tyrannized
are recognized.” The benefits of this rule is
more than can be described.  [1471]
As for the matter of handing out badges, he
ordered that a large round badge with a lion’s
head be made for sultans, shahnas, and maliks.
The name of the individual should also be writ-
ten on it and recorded in a register. It could be
retained as long as the person served at his
post, but after leaving office it would have to
be turned in, for a badge was to be for a partic-
ular province and used for many years. Under
no circumstances was it to be given to anyone
for another territory. Previously, if twenty gov-
ernors were sent to a province over twenty
years, the custom was to give each one a
badge, and after leaving office each one would
consider the badge his own and use it to dis-
patch people anywhere on personal business. 
714
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

For shahnas and maliks of middle rank a
smaller badge was designated with a special
device and the name of the individual con-
cerned written on it. The former practice of
giving letters for badges to be struck in the
provinces was outlawed. A special goldsmith
was assigned to be in attendance in the ordu to
make badges. When a badge was awarded, a
stamp made of steel with a design no one could
easily fabricate was used to imprint the device
permanently on the badge, using a mallet in the
emperor’s presence. This was so that forged
badges could be discovered by means of the
design. The same round badge was designated
for use by envoys traveling on state mounts.
On it was written “Treasury Badge,” and the
envoy’s name was recorded in a register. Upon
return it would be turned in. Envoys who trav-
eled by express post had a long badge with a
moon-shaped device at the top; they were giv-
en and turned in similarly. Since it was neces-
sary for officers on the frontiers to dispatch en-
voys via the express post, their commanders
were issued five badges made of copper and
similarly stamped. Officers of middle rank
were issued three badges to give to express en-
voys. Previously every prince, khatun, and
amir had a variety of badges [1472] they used
to dispatch people to the provinces on any bus-
iness they wanted. 
It is obvious to all what the effects of this
arrangement have been and what ease the peo-
ple have acquired. May God cause the bless-
ings of this justice and equity to reach every-
one during the regal days of the padishah!
Story Twenty-Three: He takes back
duplicate patents and badges of office held
by people.
It is natural in the world that in the reign of
every emperor a group of people who suit his
manners and customs be promoted to the fore
and the fiscal administration of the realm and
provinces be assigned to them. Following the
manner of that emperor, they execute his or-
ders by justice or by force and give his decrees
and edicts to the people. When the rule goes to
another, he will naturally want to transfer those
jobs to people who follow his manners and
customs and to give orders in a manner that
suits the nature of his reign, for every era is
different. 
Prior to now, during the era of the Padishah
of Islam’s fathers and forefathers, it was seen
that every time an emperor wanted to collect
