old edicts and badges that were held by people,
whether properly or improperly, he would dis-
patch to all parts of the empire great envoys
armed with harshly-worded edicts command-
ing that anyone who hid or retained one in se-
cret would be criminal. Those envoys piled up
such expenses on the road and in the provinces
that they were beyond reckoning, and they
arrested, beat, and abused everybody, whether
they had edicts or not. An owner of an edict
would spend huge amounts to get his edict giv-
en back to him, even though it was of no use to
him, [1473] in order to preserve his honor and
not appear disgraced before the people, for
such edicts represented honor and respect.
Badges were the same. Envoys constantly
roamed about the world using them as pretexts
to get money; and they didn’t bring back one
out of a hundred patents. Furthermore, during
those years people would bring in an old edict
and get the bitigchis to give them another
strengthening and expanding their powers. Al-
though invalid patents were taken back, many
differing and conﬂicting patents were given to
everyone, for at that time edicts were given in
the following manner. Ordinary people would
become protégés of an amir and get an edict
saying anything they wanted. Due to the differ-
ing interests of disputants and the obsession of
their protectors, so many conﬂicting edicts
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
715

were constantly being issued that it is beyond
description. Thus they spent their days, and
when the original litigants and their amirs
passed away, their sons occupied themselves in
the same fashion, each one with fifty conﬂict-
ing edicts in hand so that if they had ever gone
to court, ten days would not have sufficed to
explain the situation or to figure out the edicts
year by year. If the situation had finally been
understood, it would have turned out that all
the edicts were baseless and invalid, having
been written out of obsession or obtained by
bribery or issued without the emperor’s order
or approval. 
It also often happened that the great amirs
would agree and present a certain edict for ap-
proval for someone. The draft would be written
with yasamishi [according to rule], but that
person would find a few words that would
change totally the import of the decree the
amirs had agreed upon when it came out. By
trickery he would manage to get the change in-
corporated into the draft, or else he would give
something nice to the scribe to write it that
way. [1474] Then he would use the decree as a
means to confound the affair. 
It also sometimes happened that the minor
clerks would lie in wait for a chance to give
people whatever edicts they wanted without
the great amirs’ approval. If they gave one per-
son an edict by order of the emperor, when
another person showed up of the same descrip-
tion and trade, they would use it as a excuse to
give the second person an edict like the first.
Therein lay the cause for the thousand conﬂict-
ing cases over which a hundred thousand argu-
ments and disputes had arisen among the peo-
ple. Since every litigant had a decree, no
matter how badly judges wanted to render a fi-
nal decision on a case, it was so involved and
complicated and there were so many edicts and
badges in everyone’s hands that they absolute-
ly could not reach a verdict. It got to the point
that every year many people killed each other
over lawsuits. Aside from the fact that it was
impossible to collect all the duplicate edicts
and badges, every year huge sums of money
were given to people by the terms of edicts. 
Now that the Padishah of Islam has contem-
plated how to redress these abuses, he has
commanded that edicts be sent to all parts of
the empire, all with one wording as follows:
Let basqaqs, maliks, and provincial governors have
all old and new edicts and badges that are in the
hands of people brought in, and let them under no
circumstances consider them valid, for we have
rendered them all null and void. As for edicts we
ourselves have given and those that were issued
during the first three years when we were still
making arrangements for the army and eliminating
the devastation and unrest that had occurred, we
could not then deal with particular matters, and it
was necessary to extend the validity of former de-
crees to placate the people so that matters would
run smoothly. For those reasons Nawroz, Sadrud-
din, and other deputies issued decrees to people ac-
cording to their own whim and desire. [1475] All
such decrees are null and void. Now that we our-
selves are occupied with regularizing and putting
into order the affairs of the realm, we have ordered
that edicts must be presented and drafts read to us
before they can be given to people. Anything is-
sued after this date will be considered valid.
Furthermore, our own edicts and those of our
predecessors will not be valid until they are all
brought to court, and those that are worthwhile will
be validated. Doubtless, many edicts of former
rulers are good and worthwhile for us to validate so
that families may retain their power, dignity, and
honor. How can we allow ourselves to revoke
them? When the designated seal has been stamped
on the back, we will return them for their owners to
keep, and they will be reconfirmed. 
Henceforth we shall strike badges in a different
shape. Anyone who possesses a badge must bring it
in within six month so that we can give a new
badge to any who merits one. After six months any-
716
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

one caught possessing an old badge will be arrested
and convicted, and his badge will be taken from
him.
When he ordered thus, everyone realized that
they had to bring in their edicts and have them
renewed. Those that merited were validated,
and those that did not were taken back. In this
manner truth was distinguished from false-
hood, and men of honor were saved from the
shame of association with the vile. 
Since old edicts, particularly the duplicate
ones, had no validity, even if people still kept
them, they could not show them, for not only
would they not have been taken into considera-
tion, but the owner would have been convicted.
The same applied to badges.
When this order was promulgated, all edicts
and badges disappeared. Some got renewed
ones instead, and others could not show them
any more. Now that this has become generally
known, no one will ever consider them valid at
any time, for people realize that if they had any
validity, they would be shown during the age
of such a just ruler.
[1476] This procedure
should be that of all rulers, amirs, and gover-
nors at any time.
If gold or silver badges remain in people’s
possession, and they know that if they show
them they will not be given a new one in ex-
change, all who are far-sighted will either turn
them in or melt them down and spend the
proceeds.
Certainly it will soon reach a point that not
one of all the badges that were illegitimately
received for any and all pretexts and reasons
over the last seventy years will be left. The
Padishah of Islam thus effected such a great
thing through a small tactic he implemented in
his perspicacity. May God make his shadow of
justice extend forever!
Story Twenty-Four: He enfeoffs villages in
every province to the Mongol army.
Prior to now the generality of Mongol soldiers
did not have wages, clothing allowances,1 fiefs,
or provisions. Some great officers received an
amount for provisions, but most did not. For-
merly, when [the Mongols’] customs were still
in effect, for the entire army an annual qubchur
of horses, sheep, cattle, felt, skins, etc. was re-
served for the ordus and soldiers that had been
impoverished. After that, in the reign of the
padishah, troops that were nearer were given a
small amount of provisions. The Padishah of
Islam increased the amount gradually, but
since the provisions were charged to the
provinces and the administrators were too wily
to give it, the Mongols attacked them and ter-
rorized the provinces over their demands for
provisions and piled up expenses involved in
collecting for mounts, supplies, and fodder.
Aside from the harassment of governors and
administrators, the peasants, upon whom the
provisioning fell, were at their wits’ end.
[1477] Even so, the increase in provisions did
not reach the soldiers—some on account of the
mispayments of the administrators, some on
account of the fact that the bökä’üls took
bribes and neglected their jobs, some on ac-
count of the fact that the provisions clerks did
not pay on time—the soldiers were incapable
of collecting, so the idächis bought things for
themselves at half price. The soldiers always
had vouchers in their hands and were in dis-
putes and quarrels with the idächis. 
The situation was constantly reported to the
great annoyance of the emperor. Finally most
of them were broke and took up old claims—
many still had billets they had received. 
1The allowance is called jāmagī, which suggests that,
at least originally, it had something to do with clothing
(jāma).
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
717

After witnessing this situation for four or five
years, the emperor ordered that in every
province, storehouses from winter and summer
pastures should be filled at the time of the har-
vest, turned over to the provincial shahna, and
paid in cash from the stores upon demand. He
also ordered the bökä’üls not to take bribes or
ask for provisions and fodder. By this means
payments were made and some were given
cash money from the treasury, so in the last
three or four years no one could say that even
one maund of provisions was owing to the
divan.” 
Thereafter, around the beginning of the year
703, it occurred to the emperor that, despite all
the provisions assigned to the army, not more
than two out of ten individuals received any-
thing. “I want our bounty to be for all,” he
thought.
“Furthermore,
when
the
soldiers
mount on expedition, they cause trouble for the
provinces, and every one of them, rightly or
wrongly, says, ‘I have nothing, and I am owed
back wages. Because of cold, disease, and oth-
er catastrophes our animals are dead.’ Every
moment it is necessary to collect money and
give it to them, for the world is never free of
untoward events. Sometimes it is impossible to
collect money in haste, and one always has to
be scheming and thinking up ways to provide
the soldiers’ wages and supplies. [1478] The
best course of action would be for us to give
them in fief all those parts of the realm the
army crosses, where their summer and winter
pastures are, and those territories in which they
are constantly causing trouble by usurping vil-
lages and capturing peasants. We will appor-
tion them by units of thousands for them to
control and consider their own. Their eyes and
hearts will be satiated, and since in this era
most of the soldiers have a desire to own land
and farm, when they get land in fief, they will
have what they want. It will no longer be nec-
essary for the treasury to expend for their sup-
plies because every one will get his own sup-
plies and livelihood from his own land. They
can also make improvements with their own
slaves, grooms, oxen, and seed. When they
have straw and barley in order, even if there is
a yut,1 every one will be able to tether two or
three horses and keep them fattened so that
when it is necessary they can mount more
quickly. Most of the failure of our army is
attributable to the death of animals that are not
watered or fed. When we give territory in fief
to the soldiers, and when we also put territory
in fief for the necessary post system, for the
ash of the princes and ladies, and for other nec-
essary outlays, we will have fewer expenses
and
there
will
be
fewer
petitioners
and
applicants. 
“The few provinces remaining, across which
the army does not tread or in which they do not
dwell, will be for our personal expenses. They
can be maintained without difficulty, and the
taxes realized from them will suffice. In this
manner the important tasks of the army and
others will be well regulated, and henceforth
they will remain organized on this principle.
The benefits will encompass all rulers, amirs,
viziers, soldiers, and peasants.”
Having contemplated this plan, he gave an
order, and from the River Oxus to the borders
of Egypt fiefs were assigned to the generality
of the army within two or three months. An
edict was promulgated,
[1479] the text of
which will be included in this section so that
readers may be informed of the points that
were included.
1The yut is a catastrophic livestock blight. It occurs
when snow melts and then refreezes, or when frost
freezes hard, effectively rendering the underlying pas-
turage unavailable to grazing animals. The phenomenon
is called жут in Kazakh and Kyrgyz.
718
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Text of the edict giving fiefs to the Mongol army.
In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merci-
ful, and through the power of God and the auspices
of the Mohammedan nation.
Decree of Sultan Mahmud Ghazan.
Be it known to mothers, grandsons, khatuns, sons,
daughters, sons-in-law, commanders of tümäns,
hazaras, sadas, and dahas, sultans, maliks, bit-
igchis, and the generality of the population of all
provinces from the River Oxus to the borders of
Egypt that through the might of God our great an-
cestor Genghis Khan was singled out at creation for
divine assistance and inspiration. He never deviat-
ed a hair’s breadth from his Yasaq, and no human
creature ever dared to twist his neck at his order or
step outside the path of honesty. Consequently by
this means he conquered and liberated the face of
the earth from east to west with his Mongol sol-
diers and inscribed the pages of time with his eter-
nally glorious name. In expanding the scope and
breadth of his kingdom he endured every sort of
hardship and ordeal, and he bequeathed his ulus
and realms directly to his sons and urugh. Our
good fathers and forefathers entrusted that kingdom
under the same arrangement and rule to their sons,
and thereafter a good name was left on the register
of time by each of their sons who kept the Yasaq
and custom of the kingdom in order and did
chidamishi [mastered] well the discharging of the
labor of keeping the world. [1480] Those who did
not preserve the ulus and practiced tyranny and ag-
gression left behind a bad name.
What they have left behind is indicative of them.
Gaze after them therefore upon the traces they have
left.
The truth of this assertion is abundantly clear to us,
and we realize that eternal and everlasting life in
this world is impossible. The only benefit imagin-
able from this world is to store up a good name. We
think, therefore, that during these few days in
which it is our turn to rule we should strive to store
up a good name and provide the totality of the ulus
entrusted to us with ease and comfort so that we
may inscribe on the pages of the world a good
mention and reward, for that is what constitutes
eternal and everlasting life, and so that our renown
for justice may remain eternally on the face of
time. May God grant us success through his kind-
ness and succor us with his help.
Now it is obvious to all that prior to this, in the
time of our good fathers, the Mongol ulus was
called upon to endure every sort of demand and
hardship, like qubchur on livestock, keeping large
post stations, carrying the burden of the strict
Yasaq, and qalans, all of which we have eliminated
totally in this age. Most of them were deprived of
provisions and supplies, but despite those burdens
they fought valiantly and served wholeheartedly,
content to endure the hardship of long treks. Even
until now—and of this there is no doubt—the Mon-
gol army has not obtained much wealth or posses-
sions. During this age, when God has granted us
the ulus and realm our fathers ruled and awarded us
their throne of world rule, our whole regal mind is
concentrated upon regulating and putting into order
all the affairs and interests of the ulus [1481] so
that the Mongol chärig henceforth, so long as they
multiply and reproduce, will in no way suffer
yadamishi [impoverishment] and will pass their
days in comfort and ease. After us, when it is some-
one else’s turn, let us turn the kingdom and the
army over in a way that they have no cause for
complaint, and let them rest on a foundation that
will insure stability in the realm and ulus, an eter-
nal good name, and an increase of prayers for well-
being.
It is known to all that of the entire Mongol chärig
from the River Oxus to the borders of Egypt, some
used to be given provisions, and some were given
bonuses on rare occasion, but mostly they were de-
prived and had no share. Now we have commanded
that the whole Mongol army be included in imper-
ial kindness and gifts so that none be deprived of
good things and so that when they perform valiant-
ly and mount on expeditions they will have power,
strength, and ability to preserve the realm, for the
stability and order of affairs of the state depend
upon them. Therefore, we have ordered that vil-
lages with water and land in the kingdom, places
that are near to and suitable for them, enchü [royal
demesnes] and dalai [state property], farms both
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
719

ﬂourishing and in ruins as recorded in the registers
and tax rolls be selected (ilghamishi) and assigned
as fief and turned over to every hazara and put un-
der their control. 
Now ___ has been assigned to ___ hazara as will
be detailed. The conditions and stipulations of the
fiefs relating to each division will be as follows.
First, places that belong to enchü or the divan: all
peasants who have been subjects of such places and
tilled the soil as of old will continue so to till. They
will give a portion correctly to the chärig [1482]
and remit taxes, qubchur, and divan assessments as
advised according to the details that have been
mentioned—no more, no less. Furthermore, troop-
ers will not form a connection to or interfere in the
share of the property or lands of landowners, lords,
or endowments. Taxes, qubchur, and divan assess-
ments of those places will be remitted correctly in
accordance with the registers of the tax rolls and
the details that have been mentioned. 
Next, let them not plow1 the pasture lands of di-
van villages, farms, and locales that are in ruins
and included in their yurts. Let them plant other
lands with their own bondsmen, slaves, oxen, and
seed, and let them harvest their crops. If the owner
of a ruined place appears and stakes a claim of
ownership or endowment administration, and if it
has been under his control for a long time and his
right can be proven in accordance with the law, and
if the troopers have farmed there with their own
bondsmen and slaves, they will remit to the owner
one tenth of the total and take the rest in partner-
ship with their farmers. 
Next, peasants of both ﬂourishing and ruined vil-
lages given to them who have been classed as run-
aways for thirty years or more and who have not
been included in the census and tax rolls of other
provinces, no matter with whom they are, will be
returned. If they are harboring peasants of other
provinces, let them return them too. Under no
circumstances will they harbor peasants of other
1Reading, with JTK’s and JTAZ’s variant in LI,ﺪ ــــﻓﻨﲀ ــ ــﻧﺸ
for JTAZ’sﺪــﻓﻨﲀ ـ ـﺑﺸ. The following stipulation to plant other
lands seems to mean that pasture lands, even those of ru-
ined villages, should not be plowed.
provinces and locales, and let them not form a
connection with ___2 claiming that they are peas-
ants of distant provinces. Under no circumstances
may they collect them or protect them. Let them
not allow them in their villages. Let the men of the
chärig not take peasants of villages that have been
given to them from the village of their huja’ur [ori-
gin] to other villages by saying,
[1483] “Both
farms and villages are our fiefs, and they are our
peasants.” Let peasants of every village till the soil
in their own locales. Let them not say, “The peas-
ants of these locales have been given in fief to us:
they are our bondsmen.” Soldiers have no more au-
thority over peasants than to keep them farming
their own villages and to take from them correctly
the share of taxes and divan assessments. They may
not force a peasant to do any labor other than
farming in his own place. A peasant who cannot or
will not till the soil cannot be forced to farm if he
has remitted the tax established in the register. Let
them not apply force, and let them treat them like
their own sons (asaramishi). 
Next, let the men of the chärig neither form a
connection to nor till the soil in villages in the
vicinity of their villages. Let them not qorimishi
[deny] the water and land on account of its being
yurt, and let them not deprive anyone of a suffi-
cient amount of pasture to graze his oxen, sheep,
and donkeys. 
Next, inasmuch as we have awarded them the lo-
cales mentioned as fiefs, intending thereby to in-
sure the welfare of the generality of the people, to
acquire a good name, and to maintain the Yasaq
and justice, and inasmuch as they are happy and
glad of this favor and gift, and inasmuch as the
commanders of units of thousand, hundred, and ten
and chärig have given many pledges that they will
strive to the best of their ability to implement jus-
tice and honesty and not engage henceforth in mal-
treatment and aggression or bring force to bear, and
that they will not undertake any of the sorts of in-
justice previously practiced, it is therefore incum-

ants, but none helps. JTRM omits the word.

JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

bent that they keep their word and not demand
anything in the name of tuzghu, alufa, taghar, &c. 
Next, it is established that under no circum-
stances will billets be written from the divan
against fiefs, [1484] and they will not be subjected
to any sort of remittances. As established, each in-
dividual of the chärig will remit to the royal store-
house fifty Tabrizi maunds; aside from that, noth-
ing
will
be
demanded
of
them
under
any
circumstances. 
Next, we have ordered that at the present time,
when these fiefs consisting of water and land, both
ﬂourishing and in ruins, as detailed, are being dis-
tributed among the hazaras, a group of experts
from the province will appear before the bitigchi
N.___, who has been assigned. They will divided
the territory into ten sections by casting lots. There-
after they will be divided among the sadas and da-
has by casting lots. This bitigchi, to whom we have
awarded the title assessor, will record the portion of
each sada and daha by name in a register and stip-
ulate whether it is improved or unimproved. He
will keep the register, one copy of which will be
sent to the Supreme Divan, one copy of which will
be entrusted to the commander of the hazara, and
he will give registers of the sadas to the officers.
Thereafter the assessor bitigchi will conduct an in-
spection every year and record the name of every
person who shown industry in farming and of every
person who has exhibited shortcoming, and he will
record the improvements or lack thereof of each
portion and present it to us so that we may single
out for reward those who have shown industry and
indict those who have exhibited shortcomings or
wrought devastation. The fiefs we have bestowed
may not be sold or given away. They may not be
given to anda [blood brother], quda [ally], aqa [el-
der brother], ini [younger brother], or relatives, or
as prenuptial agreement or qaling [bridal gift].
Anyone who commits such an act will be pro-
claimed criminal, and he will die. In accordance
with the Prophet’s dictum and in accordance with a
separate edict proclaimed previously, prenuptial
agreements have been fixed at nineteen and a half
dinars. 
Next, let all know that these fiefs are given to the
men of a chärig that are included in qalan and who
serve with valor. When anyone of them dies, one of
his sons or brothers will be designated as his suc-
cessor, [1485] and the deceased’s fiefs will be giv-
en to him and so recorded. If he has no family, let it
be given to his oldest slave. If he has no slave, let it
be given to the individual in the sada who is con-
sidered worthy. If anyone in the sada or daha vio-
lates the Yasaq, let the officers of the hazara or
sada indict him and give his fief to another who
can serve with valor, and let it be recorded under
his name. Let the register be presented annually.
We have commanded that if the men of a chärig
demand any taxes, qubchur, &c. more than what is
recorded in the tax rolls, the assessor will disallow
it. If they take anything by force, the assessor will
not keep it hidden but will write the name of the
perpetrator and present it to us.
Next, when this chärig is reviewed for expedi-
tion, in accordance with the edict, the bitigchi
N.___ will record participants by name a register.
First it will be shown to the commander of the
sada, then to the commander of the hazara, then to
the
commander
of
the
division. After
being
checked and presented, it will be shown to the
commander of the chärig of the qol. It is estab-
lished that since hazara commanders’ fiefs are
fixed and established, they will not interfere in the
fiefs of the chärig. So also have we given the as-
sessor an assignage in a different province; there-
fore let him not write billets against the chärig’s
fiefs.
Inasmuch we have thus commanded and awarded
chärigs fiefs as mentioned above, if the men of the
chärig take anything more from the peasants than
what is recorded in detail in the registers of the tax
rolls, or if they protect a peasant we have not given
to the chärig or peasants of other provinces and al-
low them in, or if they transgress upon places of
water and land that are in the vicinity of their vil-
lages, or if they qorimishi [fence off] agricultural
lands or pasture lands for oxen, sheep, or donkeys,
or if they do not remit their number or tribute every
year and fall into arrears, or make excuses, or send

another to the chärig instead of themselves, they

N.___, who has been assigned as bitigchi of this

This edict we have given in the ___ hazara so

Story Twenty-Five: How he organized a
separate royal troop.
Previously the Mongol army was smaller than
it is now. The Padishah of Islam increased the
number of Mongol and Tajik soldiers through
his strategy and competence and said, “The
frontiers and borders of our realm, Khurasan,
Fars, Kirman, Baghdad, Diyarbekir, Anatolia,
and Derbent, are extremely far from each oth-
er. Despite the fact that separate troops have
been stationed in all those places as sübä,2
when need arises, if they go from one end to
another, it takes them a long time to get there
because of the vast distances. Due to the fact
that they are hungry and naked, and their ani-
mals get emaciated and die, they are of ab-
solutely no use.
Therefore the emperor ordered that in every
family in which there were two sons, brothers,
or kötälchis, one or two would be designated
as extra. Of all these he created a separate
1Kor. 2:181.
2Readingﺳـﻮﺑـﻪ(sübä) for JTAZ’sﺳـﻮﺳـﻪand MS L’s variant
ﺳﻮﯾﺒﻪ. For sübä (~ sibä), see note to text p. 927.
troop and dispatched them in all directions as
auxiliaries to attend others.
[1487] To main-
tain passes and difficult places on the frontier
where one could go on foot he assigned Tajik
troops; and he gave them all allowances and
fiefs. Prior to this the Tajik troops used to be
assigned allowances, but there was no order,
and their commanders used to take their al-
lowances on various pretexts and so there were
never any soldiers. Now the emperor has or-
dered them to be assigned to units of a thou-
sand and hundred, and their names and de-
scriptions are written in registers. There is a
review every three months, and their weapons
and supplies are inspected [to insure that] both
horsemen and foot soldiers are in accordance
with the rules and regulations that were imple-
mented in the edict.
He organized the Mongol troops in a similar
fashion, and edicts granting them fiefs were
written. There is no necessary for repetition. 
Enough soldiers were assigned to every bor-
der to suffice for that place. Of the soldiers
who have yurts and homes in the provinces,
those who were nearer to a frontier were or-
dered to form a gäjigä [rear guard] when need
arose. He also saw to it that no soldier on one
side of the empire would have to go help the
other side. Over and above custom he orga-
nized another troop to be in attendance like the
gäzigtäns [bodyguards]. He also won over the
amirs by ordering that one or two of every
amir’s brothers or sons who were not in the
military rolls would be appointed so that every
hazara was increased by one or two hundred
individuals. Within one year they were all
present and accounted for. The Padishah of Is-
lam gave them bonuses, allowances, and fiefs.
They, and the hazara of the qol, which gradu-
ally came to number two or three thousand,
and the gäzigtäns are in attendance. 
722
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

For the past many years there has been con-
tention and strife among the urughs of Jochi,
Chaghatai, and Ögödäi, i.e. the cousins of the
Padishah. Their troops have constantly plun-
dered each other’s aghruqs [1488] and carried
off each other’s sons as bondsmen and sold
them to merchants. Many of them have also
been compelled by poverty to sell their chil-
dren. This got the Padishah’s zeal up, and he
said, “Most of the Mongol tribes stem from the
great commanders who fought with valor in
Genghis Khan’s time. Now the offspring of
those commanders enjoy honor with the Qa’an
and other rulers. How can they sell their rela-
tives in bondage to Tajiks? How can they fall
into poverty? To maintain their rights and to
protect their honor something must be done to
remedy this situation. If things continue like
this, the awe of the Mongol army, which
reached the apex, will be broken, and they will
sink low in the eyes of Tajiks. Mostly too they
are taken by enemies into other territories.”
He therefore ordered that however many
boys were brought from the Mongols were to
be purchased for the court. They were to be
bought at full price in cash to acquire a good
name and heavenly reward. A royal troop of
käbtä’üls [night watchmen] of them was to be
in attendance. Over the last two years he has
purchased many of them and assigned them a
living allowance and provisions. To fund them
he has set aside the territories of Maragha. He
awarded Bolad Chingsang the command of
that troop and assigned commanders of units of
thousand and hundred from among the court
elite. Nearly a division was assembled. By
rule, as many as are brought in are purchased
to complete a division and more. All having
been made royal käbtä’üls and enchü, they are
in attendance.
In no era has there been such a finely orga-
nized and regulated army as there is now. All
have been assigned fiefs, and every frontier is
guarded and protected by a separate troop that
needs no one else’s assistance. Fiscal affairs
are in order, and the people enjoy comfort and
ease that increases day by day.
[1489] May
God cause the shadow of the Padishah of Is-
lam’s justice to last for ever and ever!
Story Twenty-Six: He forbids giving money
for lucre and abominable monetary
transactions.
When the Padishah of Islam spread the shadow
of his justice and contemplated the best inter-
ests of common folk and elite alike, he realized
that paying usury and various illegal transac-
tions were injurious to the commonweal, par-
ticularly in those days, when so many had
stepped off the highway of equity and indulged
in illegal transactions.
“To remedy this is an obligation,” he said,
“lest the onus of injurious illegality become
epidemic.” To this effect he issued an edict that
no one was to undertake any such blamewor-
thy, illegal action. Since the vast benefits that
accrue from this wisdom are apparent to all the
sons of this age, if they come in this book all
will know that they are absolutely true, and
those of generations yet to come will become
aware that the Padishah of Islam’s wisdom in-
cluded the elimination of several major abuses.
Therefore, certain of these abuses will be
recorded so that everyone in the world may
know what corruption and dishonesty are en-
gendered by the commission of only one ille-
gal deed.
First, in the time of Abaqa Khan, who, as
everyone knows, was a just emperor during
whose reign the people rested secure and the
administration of the Yasaq and criminal jus-
tice system of his father Hülägü Khan, who
was truly the star-blessed monarch of the age,
was maintained, and there were the amirs, min-
isters, and viziers of his father as well as some
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
723

who came to power during his reign. At that
time some ortaqs [merchants] invested their
capital in a few sets of armor—breastplates,
horse armor, weaponry, and the like [1490]—
and some thoroughbred horses and brought
them to Abaqa Khan’s court. Through the in-
ﬂuence of the officers of the armories and sta-
bles they received a price that assured them a
profit. When others saw how much profit they
had made, they too followed in their footsteps.
Finally things got so bad that people who had
no capital borrowed money on interest and
spent it, thinking they would repay the loan
with the profit and build up capital for them-
selves. The custom became that they would
take to the divan receipts from the armory offi-
cers and stable masters for the goods they sold.
There they would receive vouchers, and then
they would go to demand payment. Many low-
ly people and persons who had not a thing in
God’s world acquired great riches, repaid their
loans, and joined the ranks of the wealthy. Sud-
denly they rode Arabian horses, wore kingly
garments, possessed beautiful slave boys, and
were surrounded by many bodyguards. They
traveled with fully loaded camels and horses as
they passed through the streets, cities, and mar-
kets. The people, amazed by them, asked,
“How did they manage to get all this in such a
short time?” When they learned how they got
so rich, other beggars and bankrupts developed
an irresistible urge to emulate them in that type
of trade. Several thousand bankrupts, Muslims
and Jews alike, hucksters and chärchis [ped-
dlers]—that is, people who used to sell cumin,
coriander, and gewgaws from sacks slung over
their shoulders—weavers, and those who had
never possessed two pennies to rub together—
indeed who had never had enough to eat—took
up the trade by borrowing money. What they
borrowed they spent not on weapons and hors-
es, but on their own clothing and finery or on
bribing officers and getting receipts, for exam-
ple, for “a thousand items of perfect weaponry
[1491]
and
several
horses.”
They
would
present the receipt to the clerks, who would
take as much “hush money” as they thought
they could get away with and write out requisi-
tions and billets against cash money in taxes
from the provinces. 
When some of these people succeeded in be-
coming wealthy, they lent money to others on
interest, and many others took up the trade and,
greedy for success, gave the lenders every
dirhem and dinar, all their tools and clothing,
and every animate and inanimate possession
they owned. Things got so bad that, whereas
formerly these beggars had been satisfied with
ten tümäns, which is equivalent to a hundred
thousand dinars, they were no longer satisfied
with a hundred tümäns. The swindlers, who
styled themselves bazargans [merchants] and
mesäschis [arms dealers], employed any crea-
ture who knew the least bit of Mongolian script
and had them write receipts however they
wanted and forge the device of any officer they
desired. These they would take to the clerks, to
whom they would of course give a few dinars
on every tümän, and the clerks would write
requisitions and billets. Indeed, the tümän be-
came so ludicrous in their view that they called
it a “chickpea.”
After that, they took their claims to the divan
and presented them to Abaqa Khan’s court.
They had so many vouchers and receipts that if
all the gold and silver in the kingdoms of the
world had been amassed and everything hidden
in mines had been added to it, it wouldn’t have
sufficed. 
The amazing thing is that if we imagine a
thousand men stacking their full arms some-
where, it would make a pile as high as a moun-
tain and wouldn’t fit in a hundred storehouses.
Ten thousand horses can scarcely fit in a field;
724
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

how then could two or three hundred thousand
men with arms and several hundred thousand
horses? Their claims amounted to many times
that much,
[1492] and they had requisitions
and vouchers in their hands! 
Abaqa Khan was far too regally lofty-minded
and magnificent to worry where all these hors-
es and weapons were, to what soldiers they had
been distributed, in what storehouse they had
been deposited, or in what meadow they were
tethered. The officers and ministers who knew
the truth had been content with a little hush
money and were too corrupt to want to do any-
thing about it. Each of the swindlers had also
attached himself to an officer or lady, to whom
they gave some paltry bribes and with whom
they curried favor by giving them a sheep or a
ﬂask of wine.
When things had gone beyond all bounds,
the Sahib-Sa‘id Khwaja Shamsuddin Sahib-Di-
van demanded a reckoning. He assembled the
swindlers and said, “The amount of money you
demand does not exist in the whole world. I
know that you have had no expenses other than
a few bribes. Now I will be a partner to you: I
will get from the emperor two hundred dinars
on the thousand, and it will be divided equally
between us.” Since they had not spent half a
dinar for every thousand they demanded, that
satisfied them. He also obtained the officers’
consent and said, “Of every ten tümäns the em-
peror releases I will save eight and write
vouchers for two against the provinces for the
merchants to collect.” This was approved.
Then he took their requisitions and wrote a
voucher for two of every ten tümäns against
expected tax revenues. Since half belonged to
him, he gave their half share in goods that were
not worth a quarter and got cash in return. 
As for those who had lent the swindlers mon-
ey for interest, no matter how hard the
swindlers requested more loans and promised
to repay them in full when what they were
owed was released, they had long refused to
give them anything because they had despaired
of both their interest and their capital. When
the transaction with the Sahib-Divan was com-
pleted
[1493] and it became known that the
arms-dealing money had been paid, the agents
rejoiced and gave them all the cash and goods
they had for interest. The swindlers were so
avaricious and bold that once again they sat in
their houses and wrote out receipts they pre-
sented to the Mongol clerks or forged requisi-
tions and vouchers. When the Sahib-Divan
learned of this, he was dumbfounded. 
One of that group was a Jew, a huckster who
had taken refuge in the ordus during Hülägü
Khan’s time. He gathered a group of Mongols,
took them to threaten the Sahib-Divan, and de-
manded payment for his deals.
“How much are you owed?” he was asked.
He showed five million dinars’ worth of requi-
sitions and vouchers. Astonished, the Sahib-
Divan asked, “Do you have a house in Tabriz?”
“I do,” he replied.
“Is it large or small?”
“Small,” he said.
“If they take five million dinars of gold and
dump it on the roof of your house, will it fit or
not?” he asked.
He admitted that it would not. Such was the
iniquity of these people. Even the Sahib-Divan
was helpless in the face of such cases and un-
able to effect reform. 
Day by day people spent everything they had
on this thing, and if they did not have anything
they borrowed to the point of impoverishment
and spent their days in hopes of getting the
tens of thousands stipulated in their vouchers.
After a time, when the money did not reach the
merchants, the lenders lost hope and stopped
helping them with loans and money to cover
their expenses. 
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
725

“We keep nothing hidden from you,” the
swindlers told the lenders. “Since we owe you
for various favors, we won’t withhold money
from you. We have requisitions and vouchers
that have been validated for much money as-
signed against the tax collection of the empire.
We’ll own them jointly, [1494] and we’ll each
hire an envoy from a lady and a prince so that
we can get our money and give you your
share.” When the lenders saw the requisitions
and vouchers offered them in joint ownership,
which spoke so eloquently of amounts many
times the amounts of the loans, they fell prey
to their own avarice and made arrangements to
supply what those people needed. When more
was needed, they borrowed and sold their
property. Most of them went with them to the
provinces, where they took up the trade. In the
end they got nothing and were left bankrupt
and in debt, having lost their homes. 
After the reign of the padishah [Abaqa
Khan], during the reigns of Ahmad, Arghun
Khan, and Gaikhatu, these people were still af-
ter their money, and every one got an envoy
from the ladies, princes, and amirs; having ac-
cepted triﬂing emoluments, they went to the
provinces, where the cash of the realm was
consumed in covering their provisions and ex-
penses. Provincial governors also, hoping that
they would give in cash to the treasury thirty or
forty dinars for goods that were not worth ten,
gave them jewel- and pearl-studded belts and
other goods at high prices. This suited them
very well, for if they got nothing more than
rocks and pottery in return for this transaction,
they got it free. They therefore sold the gems
for low prices or pawned them for paltry sums.
As a result, the value of gems plummeted and
the gem market crashed. With this, they could
not realize enough to cover the expenses and
promises to the envoys. In the end, the
swindler merchants and their backers were left
hungry and naked, and they were unable to
transact enough business to derive their daily
sustenance. The money of the treasuries was
being lost, and no one could do anything to
stop it. 
When it came the Padishah of Islam Ghazan
Khan’s turn to rule [1495] and he ordered that
money was not to be given on interest, these
people’s trade was halted and there was noth-
ing they could do about it. In recent years all
those people with all those requisitions and
vouchers have disappeared. They have stopped
engaging in those transactions, which never
had any real basis, and no one remembers it
any longer. Those who caused the bubble have
all returned to their former trades, and the dis-
tinction between a wealthy man and a beggar
and between an ignoble and a noble was re-
stored. All classes are content and pray for the
success of the Padishah of Islam. 
What has been described is only one example
of the damage done by giving usury. Another is
the following.
Most of the people who gave money for in-
terest during those times were Mongols and
Uyghurs. Of course, how can people who are
slated for ill fortune prosper when they give
money for interest? In the end they were un-
able to pay, and their wives and children suf-
fered humiliation when they were put in
bondage. Thanks to the justice of the Padishah
of Islam that humiliation was lifted from the
people of Islam.
Another instance is as follows. The really
great damage was that during those times the
maliks and administrators of the provinces who
were upright and honorable people were un-
able to remit the amount of provincial taxes
due, and so they avoided taking that job. When
swindling beggars saw that they could ex-
change ten years of poverty-stricken life for
ten days of kingly luxury, they borrowed mon-
726
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ey on interest, paid it in bribes, and got the
governorships of provinces, thereby attaining
the ranks of maliks and sultans. [Such a per-
son] would get a province by taking a heavy
muqata‘a [assignage] upon himself, and since
they had to have cash for expenditures for the
ordu, to pay for slave boys, animals, fine cloth-
ing, and luxuries, naturally they borrowed on
interest. Lenders, knowing that they were
putting their money at great risk, wouldn’t give
anything unless they thought they could make
a large profit. Hence [the borrowers] could
only get one dinar for three or four dinars,
[1496] and when they went to the provinces,
the income of the local treasury would never
suffice to repay their loans. It became neces-
sary then to take many times the amount due
from the peasants, and so many thousands of
God-fearing, tax-paying men were intimidated
and tortured. Even when the divan chiefs knew
of a governor’s mischief, they could do noth-
ing to prevent it because money was needed,
the governor was squandering everything, and
he had compromised them with bribes. He was
just one person in bankruptcy, but there were
many poor subjects who allowed this to hap-
pen and pretended not to notice. As soon as he
got any money, he had to give bribes to the
shahna and bitigchis of the province so that
they wouldn’t stand in his way. If they hadn’t
taken [bribes], it would not have been possible
to stave them off. With all this, no cash ever
reached the treasury. If occasionally some
goods were brought in, they did not cover a
quarter of the worth. For that reason the sol-
diers suffered from destitution, and year by
year so did the province as they continued to
take. The great lords at court chose never to ac-
cept employment because it would have in-
volved their being underlings to those no-count
bankrupts. The wise have said that the seeds
for the destruction of a nation are sown when
men who are worthy of jobs are dismissed and
the unworthy are put to work. This is how
things were for a long time. 
When Sadr Chawi became vizier, the situa-
tion of borrowing on interest had become so
bad that it would be impossible to describe.
(However, now that it has been mentioned, a
short report is necessary. Since the generality
of the people of the day saw it, it cannot be
called a fabrication, and therefore let future
readers
not
think
it
far-fetched.)
During
Sadruddin’s time the muqati‘s [assignors of
fiefs] of the provinces were the stingiest men
of the age. Since they knew it was his habit to
“sell a cow for a calf,”1 [1497] a muqati‘ bor-
rowed large amounts of cash on interest and
gave it in bribes. A muqati‘ would buy for
twenty dinars something worth ten dinars and
then sell to Sadruddin for thirty, and he would
accept. After that he would say, “The divan
needs cash.” The muqati‘, of course, would
say, “Here they give money for interest, and
the amount that I gave in bribes I raised only
through a thousand tricks.”
“You won’t lose anything,” he would say.
“Sell to us for however much you buy for.”
When that person would hand in his bill, the
base price plus the markup would be calculated
into the total. A dealer would purchase some-
thing for thirty dinars and then sell it to
[Sadruddin] for forty, immediately making a
profit of ten dinars. Since Sadruddin was al-
ways strapped for cash, his deputies would say,
“It is worth ten dinars, but nobody will buy it
for more than six.” [After selling the item for
its real worth,] they would pocket the four di-
nars difference. In sum, of the original forty di-
1The expression used here, gāvē bi gosē (=gosāla)
firokhtan, ‘to sell a cow for a calf,’ apparently means to
pad expenses, to represent a purchase as costing more
than it actually did—a practice not unknown to modern
bureaucracies.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
727

nars, he got not more than six, and it was the
divan’s money he was wasting.
One of these dealers bought several thousand
sheep for [Sadruddin’s] personal property from
a merchant at the rate of five dinars a head
with a grace period of two months. When pay-
ment time came there was no money, and most
of the sheep had become lean. He ordered all
the sheep sold at a low price to pay the two
months’ interest, and the principle was extend-
ed for another two months. Naturally, with
such transactions the tax money of the realm
was lost and nothing was brought into the
treasury. Not a cent of any grant Gaikhatu
made to a noble ever reached anyone, and
fixed provisions, salaries, and expense ac-
counts were the same. It was for this very rea-
son that the military turned against Gaikhatu,
and this is why Sadruddin was constantly
bankrupt. After he died the people were left
with thousands upon thousands of grievances.
How many houses full of wealth and luxury
were emptied by him!? Generally sultans and
maliks who governed provinces
[1498] and
who came to the ordu fell into debt in this
manner, borrowing from thousands of Muslims
and Mongols whose property was lost. Some
of those people died with law suits around their
necks, and others lost everything they had by
engaging in this scheme, as everyone saw and
heard, so everyone knows that it is no exagger-
ation. Actually, the example given is only a
drop in the bucket.
It would be difficult for any monarch, no
matter how just, harsh, or mighty he was, to
rectify such a situation, which, with the pas-
sage of time, had firmly established itself in
the minds of commoner and elite since, for the
reasons mentioned, all the princes, ladies,
amirs, viziers, clerks, grandees, and retainers
were either beholden to the swindlers, having
accepted bribes from them, or in partnership
with them. However, the Padishah of Islam,
with his wisdom, competence, and intelligence,
contemplated the situation and realized that the
underlying cause for all this corruption was
commerce in money for lucre. If he forbade it,
both the prophetic law would be strengthened
and the people would be led from the brink of
error to the highway of right guidance, and
with the banning of usury many great abuses
would be eliminated.
After having that thought, he issued an impe-
rial decree in Sha‘ban 698 [May 1299] that no
one in the realm was to buy or sell on usury.
Most of the people, who were addicted to it,
decried the ban, and some of the nobles who
had the opportunity said, “It will put a stop to
all commercial transactions.”
“We are ordering it in order to put a stop to
all
despicable
transactions,”
the
emperor
replied.
Some self-interested ignorant men said, “The
treasury always needs cash. If loans are not
made to the governors of provinces, they will
be unable to remit taxes.” 
The emperor and
[1499] his viziers said,
“Here we do not need money from any gover-
nor or administrator.” And he gave a strict
command, saying, “We will not allow anyone
who lends money at interest to a divan agent to
get back any of the principle or the interest.”
He also repeatedly told the ladies, princes,
and amirs not to lend money to those people on
any account. He also had the following an-
nounced, “If any of you lends money to those
people, we will not allow you to make any
claim against them in life or their estates in
death, for we do not demand money from you
in advance, and if you squander the divan’s
money, your own properties will be forfeited to
pay for it.”
Another time it was reported to him that
some needy people had urgent requests for
728
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

loans to transact business. “Why does someone
who does not have the money to cover his trav-
el expenses come here?” he asked. “What use
is he to us, and what use are we to him? He
should stay at home instead of coming here.”
When reports of various sorts were made to
him, he said, “Do God and the Apostle know
what is best for the world, or do we? Of
course, one must say they do. God and his
Apostle have commanded thus, and we will not
listen to any contrary talk.”
From that time on, no one who wanted mon-
ey on interest was given any, and if a cheat
tried to bring force he was stopped by the
edict. At present, thank God, because no one
lends money at interest, the abuses that had oc-
curred
have
been
eliminated,
commercial
transactions have been regularized, and equity
prevails among the people. Most taxes reach
the treasury in cash, and it is not permitted to
remit in kind. The value of jewels and gems
has been restabilized, and no one who has any
money gives it to a swindler who will trick him
out of it. The people earn their livelihoods ac-
cording to the law, and blessing prevails. Most
of the people occupy themselves with agricul-
ture, trade, and beneficial crafts.
[1500] By
this means the world ﬂourishes anew. This sit-
uation is appreciated by the people of this age,
who witnessed the abuses of the past. How will
those who will come into existence in the fu-
ture and will not have witnessed those abuses
be able to imagine the beneficial effect of this
order? 
During the time this edict has been in effect,
some of those in whose hearts the love of
usury remained have lent certain goods at ex-
orbitant prices, falsely claiming that it was a
commercial transaction and sale and not usury.
In the end the debtors came to the divan to re-
port how the goods had been given and to say
that money was being demanded. The emperor
ﬂew into a rage and said, “If they do not give
up these tricks and misrepresentations, I will
command that no matter what anyone borrows,
under no circumstances will he pay back either
the principle or the interest. If people have
money, why should they lend it? They should
buy property to develop and plant or engage in
trade.” The people took fright, and usury and
inequitable transactions diminished. Very soon
the result will be that they will disappear
altogether. 
May God grant this emperor success in eradi-
cating all despicable customs and in laying the
foundations of the religious law.
Story Twenty-Seven: He forbids unlimited
prenuptial agreements.
The Padishah of Islam said, “The divine wis-
dom in legislating marriage is so that human
beings may reproduce and multiply. Therefore
the law says that if a person divorces, whether
in seriousness or in jest, whether willingly or
in anger,
[1501] it takes effect immediately,
for if there is no accord between a wife and a
husband, it is better for them to be apart. Oth-
erwise disagreement leads to anger and wrath,
and to live together in anger is the habit of
beasts. In any case, it leads to hatred, and when
there is hatred it is impossible to beget chil-
dren. For these reasons the way for divorce is
open without any restraints. When a woman
has been married under a large prenuptial
agreement, no one can divorce her for fear of
having to pay so much, and no matter how
much husband and wife are in irreconcilable
disagreement, they are forced to live together,
and this is contrary both to the divine law and
to reason, for, as has been previously stated, di-
vine wisdom necessitates that if a person is he-
sitant in his love for or ability to get along with
a woman, he should be able to separate himself
from her without any debate or constraint. 
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
729

“People also have children, and child support
is incumbent upon fathers. They also have to
pay taxes, and some of them have to go into
the military. When a father’s property is ex-
hausted by a woman’s prenuptial agreement,
where is the child support and tax money to
come from?
“For the foregoing reasons, and because the
Prophet recommended a modest prenuptial
agreement, they should be very modest. It has
been carefully calculated, so that no alms
would be necessary, that all prenuptial agree-
ments should be fixed at nineteen and a half di-
nars, for there is no sin in having a small
prenuptial agreement. On the one hand, a per-
son who loves his wife cannot be separated
from her by any amount of force, while on the
other it would be better for those who cannot
agree to separate as quickly as possible and be
rid of each other. This is in the interests of
both, for it is known from experience that there
are some women whose husbands do not love
them, but when they get divorced, others marry
them and love them. Therefore this carries ben-
efit to both parties.”  [1502]
Therefore he issued an edict to this effect.
Story Twenty-Eight: He builds baths and
mosques in all the villages of the realm.
There is no dispute over the fact that people
need baths and mosques. In some provinces of
the realm neither had been built in the villages.
Prior to this Muslim rulers had not made
arrangements, and of course in a place where
people do not perform their prayers in congre-
gation and do not make ablutions or keep
themselves clean as they ought, their standing
as Muslims will be reduced. The emperor com-
manded and issued an edict to the effect that
throughout the realm mosques and baths be
constructed in villages, and those who did not
build them would be considered criminals. Af-
ter nearly two years they had built them every-
where in the empire there had not been any. 
At present a large profit is realized from the
baths, and he ordered that the profits be spent
on
necessities
and
provisions
for
the
mosques—repairs, furnishings, servants’ ex-
penditures. As soon as he ordered this good
arrangement, such charity became current in
many places in the empire, the motto of Islam
appeared, and the people gained rest and re-
pose. May God grant him a reward for such a
blessing. 
Story Twenty-Nine: People are forbidden to
drink wine.
Most people in the empire were drinking wine
and partaking of intoxicants, and people were
getting into fights and quarrels in the market-
places and public places on account of drunk-
enness. [1503] Some of these resulted in death
and others in injury, and it was necessary to
hold trials. In all religions and nations intoxi-
cants are disapproved and forbidden. It is not
necessary to recount the damage that results
from this vileness; it is enough that wine has
been called the “mother of abominations.”1
To rectify the situation the Padishah of Islam
said, “Even though the Legislator—peace be
with him!—and all the other prophets have de-
clared it forbidden, and the texts are eloquent
on this point, people will not be constrained
and will not give it up. Even if we forbid it ab-
solutely, it will not go away. Now, I will order
this much: anyone who comes into cities and
marketplaces drunk will be arrested, stripped
naked, and tied to a tree in the middle of the
market so that people can pass by and revile
him. Thereby he will be warned and con-
strained.” According an edict was heralded
(tungqamishi) to all parts of the empire, and at
1Ummu’l-khabā’ith, ‘the mother of abominations,’ the
common Islamic appellation of wine and intoxicants. 
730
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

present no one dares to come into the street
drunk, much less engage in drunken quarrels.
The public spectacle of drinking and the fight-
ing and quarreling of drunks have been elim-
inated in markets and public places.
He also ordered that no one should go for
searches in people’s houses lest their minions
misbehave and people be harassed.
May God grant success to this religion-pro-
tecting monarch in continually issuing such or-
ders.  [1504]
Story Thirty: He regularizes stipends for the
imperial table and wine for the Great Ordu.
Everybody knows that previously there was
constant debate over arranging funds for provi-
sions. The provisioner clerks were constantly
denouncing on each other, and most of the
amirs’ time had to be spent in investigating
them. Certain people had made it a practice to
pad the accounts of what was spent, and to the
expenses connected to provisions they added
things like tips and salaries, food for hawks
and cheetahs, provisions and comestibles for
envoys, emoluments for some of the princes
and ladies, qaratu [household] necessities, im-
plements for the kitchen, and the like. This
resulted in an enormous sum, and to it they
added provisions for banquets that never took
place. They put the highest price to all the
goods and assigned payment to the provinces.
Since divan revenues were disorganized and in
shambles at the same time, and the governors
and administrators had no thought of giving
anything to the divan, as has already been re-
counted, the fiscal situation of the provinces
was in a great mess, and funds for provisions
did not arrive on time. The bitigchis who went
to collect for it took a lot of bribes to look the
other way and left the affair in abeyance. The
next time, when payment fell on another
province, the envoys did the same thing. Over
the course of a year so many envoys went to
the provinces for provisions money that their
expenses and provisions amounted to more
than the amount they went to collect, so still no
money was obtained. Although the expendi-
tures for provisions were fixed, i.e. for each
person who did a certain task, he and so many
others would receive a daily allowance, when
[the funds] did not arrive,
[1505] the provi-
sions officers borrowed at exorbitant interest.
Sometimes they bought a hundred maunds of
wine worth ten dinars for anywhere from twen-
ty to forty dinars, whereas if they had planned
well they could have gotten it for five. At that
rate, even when funds arrived and there was a
surplus, it wasn’t enough—what then of the
times when they had two-year-old vouchers in
their hands? The greatest abuse lay in the fact
that when envoys came to collect for provi-
sions, provincial governors, thinking that pro-
visioning was more sensitive and it should be
dealt with first, neglected the business of other
envoys. Of course, they didn’t get that accom-
plished either, but other funds were neglected
and fell short. By delaying the envoys, huge
expenses were incurred uselessly. If the gover-
nor was dismissed from office at the end of the
year, he would make excuses, claiming that the
money was still due from the province or had
been lost. If he was not dismissed from office,
the divan chiefs would spend a long time
making accounts, debating, and auditing in or-
der to get their share and collect bribes.
The responsibility for all this mismanage-
ment fell on the provisions officers, who were
in constant quarrels with the divan, and the two
sides put the blame on each other and de-
nounced each other. Organized victuals were
never provided ten days in succession. If one
goes and checks the registers, amounts of mon-
ey beyond description will be found to have
been squandered. One can only imagine what
provisioning was like under such an arrange-
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
731

ment. Food and wine were transported with
loathing, and there were even disputes about
that too. When things did reach the ordu and
there was an unexpected decampment, they
were left on the ground. When the court set out
for summer or winter quarters,
[1506] more
savuris [gifts] than provisions were loaded,
and in the midst the provisions money got lost
or carried off. At all times the provisions offi-
cers borrowed wine from wine sellers and
sheep from butchers. It often happened that
they didn’t pay for them, and so those people
chased after them, yelling and screaming, or
went and knelt before the amirs, but that didn’t
do any good either. Many wine sellers and
butchers were ruined. The instances of such
mismanagement are beyond description: this is
enough. 
To redress this wrong the Padishah of Islam
said, “The money for necessary daily provi-
sions will be given in advance every six
months from the treasury so that the goods
needed can be purchased and what is produced
in the provinces can be transported. If they can
be bought more cheaply, let the difference re-
main in the treasury. Let no one have any ex-
pectations of pocketing the difference if he
saves on the price of wine, sheep, or goods.
These must be purchased more cheaply than
the prices fixed in the registers. As for unnec-
essary expenses they used to collect for and the
many banquets, let them not be spent, and let
the surplus of the daily allotment, which will
be much less, go to the treasury.” 
With these savings on provisions, within two
years so much money had been amassed that
they were able to buy five hundred camels and
five hundred pack horses. They were turned
over to caring camel drivers and stable masters
to be always ready to transport wine and provi-
sions. Of the amount that used to be spent
every year to hire transportation, some went
for fodder and other expenses for those ani-
mals. Wine, a hundred maunds of which used
to be bought for thirty to forty dinars is pur-
chased for less than five dinars. Wine, sheep,
and other necessities are always ready. Even if
they request many times the allotted amount, it
is there and needs no debate. Formerly, be-
cause the provisions officers purchased wine
from wine sellers, the rate was extremely high,
[1507] but now the market is low. No envoy or
tax collector goes to the provinces to demand
sums for provisions, and hence neither do they
incur expenses nor is the money used up. Cash
comes into the treasury, and provisions and
victuals are well arranged. Transportation is
also better organized than it was during the
reign of any monarch. Absolutely not more
than a quarter of what used to be wasted is
spent. If the expenses the envoys used to incur
are
taken
into
consideration,
it
wouldn’t
amount to a tenth. This reorganization is due to
the efforts of the vizier of the realm, Khwaja
Sa‘duddin, and he does not allow a cent of this
money to be wasted. 
May God cause the shadow of this monarch
of perfect intelligence to extend forever.
Story Thirty-One: He arranges funding for
the board of the ladies and ordus.
During he time of Hülägü Khan and Abaqa
Khan, funds for meals in the ordus and for the
ladies was in accordance with Mongol custom,
and not too much expenditure was involved
here. When booty was brought from enemy
territory, a part of it was given to them. Each
[of the ladies] also had an ortaq, and they
brought in something in the name of asigh
[profit], or someone would present a gift. They
also had some herds, and there were the profits
from their increase. Funds for their meals and
necessities came from those sources, and they
were satisfied with that. 
732
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

Toward the end of Abaqa Khan’s time a
small ash tax was instituted, and after that, dur-
ing Arghun Khan’s time, funds were ear-
marked for every ordu, with payment assigned
to the provinces. When the ladies’ envoys and
pages went to collect, however, the governors
would use the pretexts explained elsewhere
[1508] to avoid paying. They would keep the
agents occupied with collecting provisions al-
lowances and taking promissories and bribes.
Even if a bit was set aside for payment, it got
squandered, and the administrators usually
made off with the funds. When funding for
board in the ordus reaches this point, one can
realize what the arrangement was like. 
During Gaikhatu’s time it was the same.
Great sums of money were lost between the
provinces and the pages. 
During the Padishah of Islam’s regal reign a
dispute broke out between the pages of the or-
dus. They informed on each other, and trials
were held. Some of the money was still owing
in the provinces, and some had been embez-
zled by the pages, for which crime some were
chastised and others were dismissed from
office. 
After that, the emperor said, “It is not proper
for taxes to be wasted or for provincial gover-
nors to embezzle them. Neither is board in the
ordus insured nor do any funds reach the
treasury or the army.” Therefore he command-
ed that for every ordu certain locales of the
provincial royal demesnes be designated, de-
tached from the divan, and put under their su-
pervision. The taxes would be determined by
the divan and billed according to the tax rolls,
and funds for the ladies’ board, provisions, and
necessities of wardrobe and mounts would be
assured, as would be funds for supplies for the
departments of potables and stables, for camels
and pack horses, and for wages for maids, eu-
nuchs, custodians, kitchen help, caravan dri-
vers, muleteers, and other servants and retinue
as necessary. Expenses would be paid from the
total revenues, and any surplus would be put in
that lady’s treasury and kept there under the
seal of the two amirs who were assigned to
every ordu. It could not be spent except by or-
der of the emperor’s decree, so that each of the
ladies would always have a treasury for use in
an emergency.  [1509]
He also said, “Those enchü properties will
henceforth be the enchü and property of the
sons of that lady.” He endowed them to their
male offspring, not the females. If a lady did
not have a son, it became the property of the
sons of the other ladies. 
At present all the provinces and properties
are in the hands of the ladies’ deputies under
the supervision of the divan. They have been
improved, and much more income than before
is realized. Funds for board in the ordus and
necessary supplies are all insured, assured, and
arrive on time. Funds for the ladies’ treasuries
are also designated. Recently, when there was
a need for more funds for army supplies, he or-
dered them to give a thousand thousand dinars
to the army from their treasuries. In this way it
was paid, and the army was greatly helped.
Never in any era has there been such an
arrangement. God willing, it will last for ever.
Story Thirty-Two: He regulates the treasury
and arranges its business and supplies.
Prior to now it was not customary for anyone
to maintain written accounts of the Mongol
emperors’ treasuries or to keep track of addi-
tions and outlays. They used to appoint a few
khizanachis [treasurers] to receive whatever
was brought in. Together they placed things in
the treasury and gave out what was expended.
When nothing was left, they would say so. A
few custodians also maintained the treasury,
and they did the loading and unloading. The
whole thing was so disorganized that there was
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
733

not even a tent: they simply piled things in the
open and covered them with felt. From this one
can deduce what the situation was like.
When a treasure was brought in, it was also
customary for the amirs and the treasurers’
friends to go to the treasurers and request
something as bariqu [gift], and the treasurers
would give each one something, according to
his rank. The ba’urchis, sharabdars, farrashes,
and akhtachis also took edibles and potables,
etc., and when they made requests the treasur-
ers would consult together and give them
something. Since the farrashes took care of the
maintenance, all their requests were granted.
The treasurers also gave each other bariqu and,
[1510] after consultation, each one would take
something home. In this manner four fifths of
the treasury was squandered every year, and
only one fifth was spent as the emperor or-
dered. When provincial governors, having real-
ized that this was the case, occasionally paid
funds into the treasury, they would give a “ser-
vice fee” and get receipts for twice the amount
they gave. When very little money was brought
to the treasury, and what was brought was kept
in this manner, it is obvious what the emperor
was able to disburse from it. It was always like
this.
The highway patrols had been ordered to
keep a look-out and arrest anyone who had tak-
en clothing or anything else out of the treasury,
but they only arrested one person every few
years, and that only because of some other rea-
son for which they had been lying in wait to
get an indictment for that person. This did not
happen more than two or three times during all
the reigns but because of it they abandon gem-
studded items and red gold.1 It would take too
long to explain the situation in full.
1Arends translates: И из-за этого отказываются от
драгоценностей и золотых денег!
At this time the Padishah of Islam has regu-
lated affairs to such an extent that various
treasuries are kept separately. Anything that is
jewel-studded is placed by his own imperial
hand in a chest so that if any disbursement is
made it will be obvious immediately. Every jot
and tittle is recorded in a register by the vizier.
The emperor himself closes the lock and seals
it with his own seal, and one of the treasurers
and a eunuch so appointed guard it, and it is
their responsibility.
[1511] No other person,
neither treasurer nor custodian, has anything to
do with it.
As for red gold and fabrics manufactured in
the royal workshops or brought from distant
territories as tangsuq [rare objets], they are
recorded in detail by the vizier and given to the
care of the same two individuals mentioned
above. Unless the emperor gives unequivocal
permission, they do not disburse anything at
all. 
For white gold and various fabrics that are
constantly being disbursed, he assigned a dif-
ferent treasurer and eunuch, and they are re-
sponsible for them. The vizier totals them and
records them in a register. He ordered that
when anything is disbursed, the vizier must
write a permission slip and present it for the
emperor to sign his approval. The vizier’s
deputy records it in the register and gives it
out. Without that approval, nothing is given to
anyone. The first treasury is called narin, and
the second is called bidün. 
In order to avoid having to show permissions
slips at all times, every month the vizier writes
out a detailed list of what has been disbursed
by command, and when there is time he sits in
private with the emperor and presents them
one by one for approval. Every six months or
once a year the vizier conducts an inspection to
see whether what has been deposited in the
treasury is still there or not—as a precaution-
734
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ary measure lest, for any one of many reasons,
treasury funds be depleted. 
Prior to this, some nobles and friends re-
quested loans from the treasury. Now an impe-
rial decree has been issued that nothing be
touched without imperial approval, and so such
requests have ceased. He also ordered a special
seal to be made with which every item of
clothing brought into the treasury should be
stamped immediately so that substitutions can-
not be made. He also ordered that the many
custodians who used to meddle in treasury af-
fairs stick solely to being custodians and have
nothing to do with the treasury, which is the re-
sponsibility of the four persons [named above],
[1512] for whom it is also necessary to have an
audit to square their accounts with approval
slips. He also ordered that under no circum-
stances would there be weight stones in this
treasury, but items would be sealed with the
Stones of Justice when they were received or
disbursed. No one was to be allowed to give so
much as a yard of karbás in place of money to
a voucher holder, and they were not to cause a
moment’s delay in payment but to give cash
money or clothing, whichever was assigned, at
once. Goods should be turned over with the
treasury seal. 
[Treasury officials] were not to expect any-
thing from anyone. For every one hundred di-
nars of funds brought in from the provinces,
two dinars are stipulated as treasury fee. More
than that they do not take. 
He also established another treasury and ap-
pointed a eunuch for it. Of every ten dinars
cash and of every ten articles of clothing
brought into the treasury one dinar and one ar-
ticle is put aside and turned over to the eunuch
to be placed in this treasury. [When the emper-
or] assigns payment of alms, they are brought
from this treasury so that he can give them
away with his own hand—or given away in his
presence—to the deserving. Organization of
this treasury is similar to what has been ex-
plained for the others. The armory treasury is
similarly organized. 
Never have the possessions of any landlord,
moneychanger,
or
large-scale
merchant
renowned for the safekeeping of money been
so well guarded or protected, much less the
treasuries of kings. It is absolutely unimagin-
able that so much as a fraction of a coin could
be embezzled.
At the time of going to summer or winter
quarters, [the emperor] tends to the treasury
himself for several days, and what he wants
transported is put aside. Heavy loads are metic-
ulously recorded by the vizier and placed in
Tabriz under lock and seal. Whenever the em-
peror wants to know the situation of the
treasury with regards to the quantity and quali-
ty of the base or expenditures, he asks the viz-
ier, who has only to refer to his registers to be
able to report immediately. 
Since the Padishah of Islam is divinely as-
sisted, and it also happens that [1513] not only
is his vizier perfectly competent, perspica-
cious, knowledgeable, and skilled but also no
one is more trustworthy than he, not a fraction
of a coin or a yard of material can be lost, and
no one can embezzle anything. 
Thanks to the blessing of the order and
correctness
the
Padishah
of
Islam
has
achieved, and thanks to such honesty and reli-
giosity, so much cash ﬂows out of the treasury
that if it were a sea it would be exhausted. In
no ancient or modern register that has been
read has there been a mention of so much mon-
ey and fabric as is given from there, and never
has anyone been given so much from a king’s
treasury. May God cause these blessings to ex-
tend throughout his imperial days.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
735

Story Thirty-Three: He organizes the arms
workshops and armories.
Prior to now there were many uzes [craftsmen]
appointed in every city and province of the
realm—bow makers, arrow makers, bowcase
makers, sword makers, et al. There were also
Mongol craftsmen. Each one presented one or
two implements of his own manufacture, for
which he would receive a salary and wages.
They had been contracted to supply many
weapons every year, and in return they would
receive vouchers against the provinces. In
some cities there were weapons-makers’ work-
shops, and amounts of funding were stipulated.
The weapons officers’ deputies were in charge,
but for every amount they released in payment
not a twentieth of the goods was ever received.
Some of this was due to the fact that several
hundred
troops
of
envoys
went
to
the
provinces to collect on the vouchers, and they
cost as much or more as they collected in pro-
visions, expenses, and transport, while the
vouchers remained unpaid by the provincial
administrators because of the various sorts of
chicanery that has been mentioned previously.
[1514] Some of the shortfall was also due to
the greed and misappropriations of the deputies
and weapons clerks. Some was on account of
the plethora of officers who were in charge,
each one of whom dipped into the funds in
some way. When the craftsmen saw that this
was the case, they failed to produce what they
were supposed to, and whereas their days
should have been spent working, they were in-
undated with disputes with each other, with
bullies, and with denouncers. Their quarrels
reached a point that the officers were dragged
in and fell upon one another, and there were
endless trials of craftsmen and lawsuits. This
resulted in breaches in the running of fiscal
operations, and when audits were made it was
discovered that nothing was there. Every year
three or four hundred thousand dinars had been
charged against unpaid accounts, but it was not
apparent what a cent had been paid for. In the
end deputies and weapons clerks were execut-
ed on that account, and their families were ru-
ined. Most of those who had indulged in this
work went bankrupt, wound up in jeopardy,
and lost their good names. 
To redress this situation the Padishah of Is-
lam ordered that the people of each and every
craft in every city would indemnify each other.
