He also ordered that they be given nothing by
way of provisions or salaries. He stipulated
how many sets of every type of weapon should
be delivered to the royal stores and how much
was to be spent on each. “Although they are
our
craftsmen
and
bondsmen,”
he
said,
“whereas others sell in the market using their
own capital, these people reckon using the cap-
ital of demons.” He appointed a guardian at the
head of every group to serve as guarantor.
Every year he would receive a certain amount,
insure that weapons were delivered according
to contract, and obtain a receipt. To fund all
weapons acquisition a separate province was
assigned so that it would not be necessary to
send envoys into all provinces to collect, while
all they really did was pile up expenses. In this
manner ten thousand full sets of weapons were
contracted to be delivered finished every year.
[1515] (Previously no one had ever seen as
many as two thousand sets.) For imperial use
fifty sets of the finest manufacture were as-
signed. Over and above that, many thousands
of bows, arrows, and sets of chain mail were
arranged to be kept in the treasury for use in
time of need. 
When a comparison was made, it was found
that now not more than a half of what used to
be spent on provisions and salaries for crafts-
men was earmarked for arms. Thus the expen-
736
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

ditures that used to be made in the provinces
ceased completely. 
Whereas previously there had never been any
sign of arms, by means of this good arrange-
ment every year they delivered what was con-
tracted and obtained receipts. The fighting,
quarrels, and trials of craftsmen ceased, and
bitigchis who used to be executed on this ac-
count are now respected and have peace of
mind. The officers who quarreled with each
other on their account are all in agreement and
friendly to each other. 
When in recent years things had been so well
regulated, the arms officers said, “Most of the
types of implements the craftsmen make are
available in the market and can be purchased
more appropriately from there. Prior to this
there were no craftsmen who knew how to
make Mongol weapons, but now most of the
craftsmen in the markets have learned. The
craftsmen, who used to spend their whole days
in arguments, fights, and lawsuits, receiving
money for provisions and supplies and giving
nothing in return, have now been relieved of
that burden and necessarily practice their
trades. They make implements and weapons
using their own capital and sell them in the
markets. Therefore they make better types of
weapons than they used to, and they are avail-
able in the markets. Wouldn’t it be better for
funding for weapons to be brought in cash?
[1516] Instead of our having weapons made
and giving them to the soldiers, we can distrib-
ute cash to them so that they can purchase
cheaply weapons that suit them, and nothing
will be wasted.”
The Padishah of Islam approved of this pro-
posal and commanded that several special
types of weapons that were less available in the
markets should be made on contract. The rest
are purchased in cash. These measures have
prevented the abuses mentioned above that
were prevalent among craftsmen who made
saddles, bridles, and paraphernalia for the royal
stable. They were also prevalent among the
craftsmen who made certain implements for
the use of shükürchis [parasol bearers] and
idächis [provisions officers], but they too have
been redressed. At present all these things have
been corrected and put in order.
Previously it was customary, if some small
implement or thing valued at anywhere from
fifty to around a hundred dinars was needed for
the emperor’s use, an envoy would go off on
that insignificant errand, and his transport, pro-
visions, expenses, and promissories would
amount to five thousand dinars. Now a rule has
been made that a treasurer will either purchase
and obtain anything that is needed or give
someone else cash to purchase the item. In this
manner five hundred troops of envoys and tax
collectors a year have been eliminated from the
provinces, and instead of the five hundred
thousand dinars that used to be spent on
them—with a hundred thousand instances of
trouble, distress, and ruination in the process—
now not more than five thousand dinars is
spent on the supplies themselves. The former
custom has been completely and totally elim-
inated. Rules that have been approved and put
into practice continue in effect. May the bene-
fits of this reform continue for many long
years, God willing.  [1517]
Story Thirty-Four: His reorganization of
imperial ﬂocks and herds.
Formerly the camels and sheep of the qan [im-
perial herd/ﬂock] in the realm were turned over
to qanchis [imperial herdsmen and shepherds],
but there was no accounting or regulation.
When an investigation was made of all that had
been entrusted to them in past times—which
ought to have increased more than a hundred
fold given the fine pasture lands and the many
guards and shepherds who were exempt from
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
737

taxes—not one was to be found. They made
excuses, saying they had died in the cold or
been lost.
“Let them see whether they have any camels
and sheep of their own or not,” the Padishah of
Islam said. The matter was investigated, and it
was reported that they had many.
“The animals of the qan were many times
their own. How is it theirs didn’t perish in the
cold or in a yut, while those of the qan all per-
ished?” It was obvious they were lying and had
stolen them all and sold them. 
An
imperial
decree
was
issued
for
a
tölämishi [reparation] to be made, but it was
not possible and they left it alone. 
After that, the emperor ordered an experi-
ment made. “Let them entrust camels and
sheep to trustworthy people. Since they have
good pasture lands and the qanchis are imper-
ial slaves and musallam and exempt, what ex-
cuse can they make? Let it be established with
them that these principles will stand. Let them
give [payment] several times every year for the
increase in such a way that even after losses
the qanchis will realize a profit and gain. In or-
der that those who do not have pasture lands
and are not imperial slaves will accept this for
the others, let them give at a lesser rate so that
they will not be able to make any excuses.” It
was so established, and pledges were taken
from them. Year by year the increase grows
greater and they deliver more.
He assigned load-bearing camels separately
for transporting the treasury, baggage, and sup-
plies for the ordus. [1518] They were entrust-
ed separately to trustworthy men. Similar
arrangements were made for the sharabkhana
and the hawayijkhana. The regulation of this
affair has, thank God, reached a degree of or-
der that has never been achieved during the
reign of any monarch, Mongol or Muslim.
Never have there been so many camels for
transporting the various departments. Since
there are more than are needed, many are left
in the herds and do not carry loads. They in-
crease day by day. Arrangements for palans
[pack saddles] and paraphernalia are extremely
fine and good. 
God willing, divine assistance of this state
will continue forever.
Story Thirty-Five: His reorganization of the
corps of falconers and leopard keepers.
Formerly falconers and leopard keepers1 used
to catch birds and animals in the provinces. It
was stipulated every year where and in what
places they could catch them, and when they
caught them they would bring them here and
turn them over to the falconer and leopard offi-
cers. They had allowances for provisions, sup-
plies, and wages fixed in every province, but
when they went to collect every year they took
much more than that by beating people with
sticks, and they also incurred expenses in ex-
cess of their allowances, while they brought in
only a paltry few birds and animals via the
post-horse system. In every city, post station,
khaylkhana, and village they came to along the
way they requisitioned many mounts, some of
which they rode, some of which they used to
carry their personal baggage, and some of
which they gave to their companions. Many of
the birds and animals they brought they gave to
their friends and acquaintances or to just about
anybody. For the sake of two or three falcons
1“Falconer” is the Turkish qushchi; the birds are called
jānavar. Both terms are ambiguous: qush and jānavar
(which means simply ‘animal’ in modern Persian) both
essentially mean raptor, including all varieties of hawks
and falcons. The word used in the text for “leopard
keeper” is the Turkish barschi, and the animals are re-
ferred to by the Persian word yūz. Both terms are highly
ambiguous: both bars and yūz can refer to a variety of
large hunting felines such as leopards, panthers, and
cheetahs. 
738
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

or leopards they would take two or three times
what was allotted for their pay and supplies in
the provinces,
[1519] and they piled up ex-
penses along the way for the animals’ food.
There was no limit to what they took by ex-
traction and coercion from villages and way-
farers. They received payment for the number
of animals according to their own calculations,
and there was no stipulation as to manner, how
many, or what. That being the case, they did
not bring in many birds or animals. There was
also no record kept of how many falcons were
maintained. In any province where some wan-
derer caught a falcon in a field or bought one,
he would want to use that as a pretext for ob-
taining an imperial decree making him a
“gamekeeper” or tarkhan. They would use that
distinction to mistreat the people and return
with fixed allowances for provisions and sup-
plies. Now what person would not choose such
a job? Year after year the situation got worse.
For every hundred peasants those people took
under
their
protection,
they
mistreated
a
thousand. 
Falconers and their officers who were in at-
tendance at court kept falcons, and some of
them ﬂew their falcons for the emperor. There
were so many officers, so many tribes, so
many troops, and such a crowd of grooms,
donkey drivers, caravan leaders, and village
rustics who were attached to them—and every
one of them stuck a few feathers in his belt and
hung an iron cudgel (küräbäs) from his waist.
Every person they met would receive a few
cudgel blows on the head as a taste of what
was to come; then there would be words, and
then they would snatch their turbans and hats.
Some of them said, “It is not legal for just any-
one to sew owl feathers on his hat”—on which
pretext they would take the hat. Others did
whatever they wanted without any pretext at
all. 
If anyone passed by the gamekeepers’ tents
or houses, woe betide him. [1520] If caravans,
merchants, or others happened to pass near a
village where there was an aviary or falconers,
they would receive a ﬂeecing that was no less
than plunder. Every village they came to they
would take food for themselves and for their
animals—in addition to sheep and chickens.
For their mounts they would take straw and
barley. When they went to summer or winter
pastures they would not be satisfied with that
much but took from the village headmen along
the way, over and above the provisions and
supplies that were assigned, sheep, ﬂour, bar-
ley, and whatever they needed. They would
send all these things to the pastures using the
people’s requisitioned pack animals. By requi-
sitioning so many pack animals and then sell-
ing them, they got enormous amounts of mon-
ey. They were particularly greedy for fine
donkeys, which they never gave back. Along
the way they plundered everybody they saw. In
order to increase their repute and make the
people fear them, they shaved the beards of
provincial headmen and elders on the slightest
excuse, and everywhere there was a mischief-
maker he went under their protection, doing
anything he wanted to further their interests,
rightly or wrongly, including beating gover-
nors, lords, and peasants. If occasionally one of
their grooms was arrested by a basqaq or a
governor, they would break a falcon’s wing
and then report that the basqaq or governor
had created a ruckus and wounded the falcon.
They would bear witness for each other. Of
course, when monarchs hear that someone has
created a ruckus and broken a falcon’s wing,
they get angry. 
They would also make up stories, saying,
“We had made a certain place a game preserve,
but they went hunting there, or passed through,
and scattered the birds.” If anyone passed by
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
739

the vicinity of that preserve, they would take
his horse and clothing or large amounts of
money as “service fees,” and only with the
greatest difficulty would he escape from their
clutches. There are so many stories of their ex-
cesses that it would take much too long to tell
them.  [1521]
To redress this situation, the Padishah of Is-
lam first had the idea that it was sufficient to
have a thousand falcons and three hundred
leopards brought from the provinces, so he told
the falconer and leopard-keeper officers to
stipulate
the
territories
and
persons
they
thought suitable and to write the names in de-
tail. Aside from them there would be no other
falconers in the provinces. Their wages were
fixed at the number of falcons, trained or un-
trained, that they brought in, and they were to
include supplies and food for home and travel,
and transportation. Everything was fixed in de-
tail so that no room for any pretext was left.
Everyone was given a fixed amount in propor-
tion to the portion of the thousand falcons and
three hundred leopards that was his responsi-
bility. An edict with the gold seal was given,
and in it was stipulated that they were not to
requisition pack animals, supplies, or provi-
sions along the way. It was sent to be heralded
in all parts of the realm. 
When the amount was calculated for falcons
and leopards, provisions and supplies for the
gamekeepers, food, transport, and necessities,
it came to only half of what had been spent be-
fore, when they didn’t bring in a third the num-
ber of birds and animals and expenses for tran-
sport, provisions, and food were two or three
times as much. Whereas the mistreatment of
peasants that had been practiced could scarcely
have been reckoned, now a thousand falcons
and three hundred leopards are brought in
every year with no trouble.
Once it was known in the provinces that they
were not allowed to requisition transport, pro-
visions, or food, even if they tried to take any
secretly or by force, they were not given any.
How then could anyone who did not have the
permission they had for taking supplies request
more? Even if someone did request, they cer-
tainly wouldn’t give him anything. It was nec-
essary for them to turn over the number stipu-
lated every year; otherwise, the balance would
be charged against them and taken back.
Excess falconers and hunters disappeared of
their own accord, and from the date of this de-
cree on, [1522] no one was subjected to mis-
treatment by falconers or hunters, who were
unable to make demands since they had all
been included in the order. Those who had
been under their protection were included in
the qalan, and if anyone was determined to re-
main [in their service], that person’s tax obliga-
tions were charged against theirs. There is ab-
solutely no force or coercion, and those people
have forgotten those methods and turned into
reasonable, equitable human beings. 
As for redress of the falconers attendant at
court, the emperor ordered that their wages and
food for the birds in their care be recorded in
detail. Funding for them in cash would be giv-
en to their chief annually in full, and so they
would not have recourse to any pretext. When-
ever they would be dispersed and sent out for
qushlamishi [bird catching] the number of fal-
coners and falcons would be fixed, and the em-
peror would order royal horses given to them
to carry their baggage in order to run and exer-
cise the horses so they wouldn’t remain jaded
or “raw.” With estimation of the time it would
take for them to go and come in autumn and
winter, vouchers for provisions with the gold
seal would be issued against the tax remit-
tances of those places. Since, aside from feed,
there would be need for doves and chickens
740
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

when the falcons were bavli [in training] or in-
jured, provisions for chickens and doves for
royal falcons would also be made in the vouch-
ers as needed. They would be kept in cages,
and for those that were to be taken somewhere
vouchers would be likewise written in fixed
number. Like this, there would be no excuse
for mistreatment or misbehavior. 
Once these orders were published in the
realm and it became known that funds had
been provided and established for their needs
and that either cash would be given from the
treasury or else vouchers with the gold seal
would be issued, [the falconers and hunters]
could no longer requisition anything extra from
villages. Even if they did demand anything,
since the people were aware [of the provisions
of the imperial order],
they wouldn’t give
them anything. 
Initially it happened once or twice that when
some falconer officers were going to the
provinces, [1523] although fodder and provi-
sions for their horses had been assigned by
voucher with the gold seal and pledges had
been taken that they would not take anything
by force, news was received that they had tak-
en too much. A high-ranking envoy was dis-
patched to indict them for their crime right
there in the midst of the province and give
each of them seventy-seven lashes. They all
learned their lesson and ceased acting like that.
At present rarely does a falconer or leopard
keeper misbehave. Although no wolf is going
to become a lamb, their great injustices have
been curbed, and there is such total confidence
in this justice that very soon the generality of
the population will completely forget the
meaning of the words injustice and aggression,
God willing.
Story Thirty-Six: He commands certain
measures throughout the realm.
Formerly administrators of provinces always
reported that most provinces were in ruins, the
peasants were poor, without means to cultivate
with their own oxen and seed, irrigation and
much land were neglected, and no one paid
any attention to them or made a move to re-
form
conditions.
Furthermore,
the
various
stores of seed that had been assigned and given
from the divan in former times had been sold
during periods of high grain prices to the detri-
ment of both divan and peasants. 
To redress the situation, the Padishah of Is-
lam ordered that from every governor and fief-
assignor a designated amount for the price of
agents, seed, and agricultural necessities be
subtracted from the governor’s or fief-assign-
or’s designated total, and a pledge would be
taken from them that they would keep agents
in the provinces at their tasks to increase agri-
culture. “It is indisputable,” the emperor said,
“that the benefit and profit to farms will be one
in two or one in three, [1524] especially when
there is a governor or administrator to have the
better locales planted and to have more access
to the means of agriculture and improvement.
In order to encourage the people and so that
the governor will have a surplus to spend, we
will establish a rate of one to three so that they
may remit a third or a fourth, and whatever ex-
tra is derived will be theirs. They will work as
hard as possible at improvement in order to de-
rive the maximum profit. When planting will
have been done for two or three years and
things go well, profit will come into the
treasury according to the crop.” It was regis-
tered in the tax rolls accordingly, and cash
amounts were remitted. 
Some left-over administrators who had be-
come addicted to the things that have been
mentioned in several places previously gave no
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
741

thought whatsoever to the necessity of giving
the divan’s money back and considered it ab-
solutely their own. The first year they squan-
dered those funds, and at the end of the year,
when demands were made for the base and
profit, there was nothing anywhere. Their
thought was, “What necessity is there? When
they put the names of ‘oxen’ and ‘seed’ to it,
why should there be anything in the account?”
They produced all sorts of excuses, claiming
loss and heavenly and earthly catastrophes. No
attention was paid to most of these excuses.
Those who had property and possessions had
them taken away in compensation, and some
were held under arrest. Others still observed
the measures and kept seed, and they raised an
income and profit both for the divan and for
themselves. It stands at present, and many peo-
ple both peasants and others, are at ease on its
account as they occupy themselves with im-
provement and planting. 
As for locales in which the giving of seed
was customary, and administrators had squan-
dered or sold it either by chicanery or by mis-
management, and in which previously no one
had redressed the situation, the emperor or-
dered that they all be given seed anew. By that
means in Baghdad and Shiraz [1525] the taxes
increased over the tax rolls by more than five
hundred thousand dinars. The [stores of] seed
one again were functioning, and the manifold
benefits accrued to the peasants. Villages ﬂour-
ished once more, and prices became cheap.
When the emperor assigned fiefs to the mili-
tary, many of the locales they had improved by
these measures were allocated to them. Had it
not been for these measures he would have had
to give them many territories and valuable
land. Still, much remains under the control of
the divan, and the income comes in. In no era
we have seen or heard of has anyone ever im-
plemented such a good arrangement or thought
of such means for improvement and common
good.
As for the beasts and birds he ordered en-
trusted to various persons, it was also estab-
lished that the increase of ﬂocks and herds
would be one to three so that they too would
benefit and build up a stock of capital. The
beasts and birds of the general population are
also safe from incursion from royal beasts and
birds, and no one can ever aggress upon them
or deprive anyone of pasture land. With all of
this, the divan still benefits. Even when the im-
perial banners arrive in an area and some ani-
mals are needed for falconers and others, it is
not necessary to take them from the peasants. 
If a dove or a chicken is needed for a falcon
or the kitchen, it is provided by the privy funds
of the divan. This case is like the elimination
of donkey requisitioning. Previously anyone
who wanted took without compunction. Now if
there is an emergency, compensation is taken
from the divan through the agents. It is impos-
sible to calculate how many donkeys used to
be requisitioned from peasants, merchants, et
al., and how many peasants got their heads,
arms, and legs broken. The peasants were con-
stantly going around looking for their animals,
and some requisitioned mounts were taken
away altogether and never given back. Some
fell on the road and died, [1526] and the peas-
ants were kept from farming and planting.
Now that the Padishah of Islam has forbidden
falconers to take people’s doves and chickens,
they are provided from the funds for the royal
birds.
“The force of the Yasaq must be initiated in
small things,” he said, “and large things will
necessarily follow. If we cannot forbid the
taking of a dove, we certainly cannot forbid the
taking of a sheep, and forbidding the taking of
a cow would be even more impossible, and so
on.” An imperial decree was issued that every-
742
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

where there was a dovecote, hunters absolutely
must not set traps in the area.
With the likes of these grand measures and
the great compassion he shows for the people,
and with the concern he has to eliminate the
evil of tyrants and evildoers, the wisdom, per-
fect conduct, justice, and equity of this justice-
nurturing emperor—may his reign last for ever
and ever—are obvious. In later times the peo-
ple of the world will marvel at these measures.
May the prayers the entire population offers
day and night for his prosperity be answered. 
Story Thirty-Seven: His planning for the
improvement of fallow lands.
It should be readily apparent from history and
intelligent analogy that there has never been a
realm more devastated than this one was re-
cently, particularly places visited by the Mon-
gol army. From the appearance of the human
race no ruler has ever held as much territory as
Genghis Khan and his urugh conquered and
brought under their control, nor has anyone
ever killed as many people as they did. [1527]
As for the vast territories it is claimed that
Alexander conquered, he took lands and con-
tinued on without stopping anywhere, and
everywhere his reputation reached, the people
quickly surrendered because of his awesome-
ness and might. He lived thirty-six years, and
in his twenty-fourth year he took the realm of
Iran and killed Dara. For twelve years after
that he ruled the world, and during his return
home he died in Babylon. During those twelve
years he took many realms, but since he was
always on the move and never stopped, the
people rebelled again after he left. Since he
had no sons or progeny, the kingship did not
descend in his family but went to petty kings,
as can be found explained in history books.
Genghis Khan was just the opposite, for he
conquered with deliberation, all remained obe-
dient, and his family not only maintained what
they had but also took over and added many
other realms they conquered, as is known.
When provinces and great cities were being
subjugated
they
killed
so
many
people
throughout the length and breadth of the
provinces that few were left, like Balkh, She-
berghan,
Taliqan,
Merv,
Sarakhs,
Herat,
Turkestan, Rayy, Hamadan, Qum, Isfahan,
Maragha, Ardebil, Barda, Ganja, Baghdad,
Mosul, Arbela, and most provinces attached to
these places. In some provinces that were on
frontiers crossed by the armies, the people ei-
ther were killed totally or ﬂed, leaving the land
fallow, like the provinces of Uyghuristan and
others that formed the frontier between the
Qa’an and Baidu, some areas between Derbent
and Shirvan, some of the tribal areas of Di-
yarbekir like Harran, Urha, Saruj, Raqqa, and
many cities on both sides of the Euphrates, all
of which are fallow and unproductive. [1528]
Places that have been devastated in other ter-
ritories by killing, like the fallow lands of
Baghdad, Azerbaijan, Turkistan, Iran, and Ana-
tolia, and the ruined towns and villages that
people can see are too many to be counted. If
we make an estimate, not one tenth of the
realm is productive—the rest is totally devas-
tated. Until recently no one thought of making
improvements. If rarely improvement of a
place was initiated—like Hülägü Khan, Abaqa
Khan, Arghun Khan, and Gaikhatu, who want-
ed to build palaces, make improvements, build
a market or city, or make water channels in Ala
Tagh, Urmia, Sughurluq, Sujas, Khuchan, Zan-
jan, and Saray-i-Mansuriyya in Arran—many
territories became even more devastated there-
by and untold amounts of money were spent,
many peasants from other areas were encour-
aged to migrate, and not one of those places
was actually made to ﬂourish, as we can see. It
is clear what the rate of devastation of the
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
743

provinces would be if those projects had been
completed.
God willed that Ghazan Khan revivify the
land and propagate the religion of Islam, for
God had entrusted such great charity, such a
huge labor, to him from all eternity. Thank
God, the propagation of Islam succeeded as
has been detailed, and projects of improvement
and royal charities have also been described
separately. The regularization of fiscal affairs
in the realm, maintenance of the subjects, and
the spread of justice and equity—as have also
been reported—these things are the main rea-
sons for the ﬂourishing of the provinces, as we
can witness and examine. In cities that were
devastated not five of ten houses were inhabit-
ed, and they were destroyed even though they
were habitable. 
Now, thanks to his all-encompassing justice,
in every city more than a thousand houses are
being built, [1529] and a house that was worth
a hundred dinars is now worth a thousand or
more. All this has been recorded before. 
As for fallow lands, no one was inclined to
improve them, and it was not possible for one
person out of a thousand to make improve-
ments with his own money. With his unfailing
intellect and good strategy the Padishah of Is-
lam ordered a reform by summoning the amirs,
viziers, and ministers and saying, “These dev-
astated
territories
and
abandoned
villages,
which belonged to our fathers, are now ours,
and they are classified as state property, royal
demesne,
or
someone’s
freehold
property.
From the reign of Hülägü Khan until now, it is
possible that neither a load or a fraction of a
coin has ever reached anybody from these
places. If anyone wants to make improve-
ments, he doesn’t even begin for fear that it is
state property or somebody’s property or that it
will be taken it back if improvements are made
without permission, even after much hardship
and great expenses have been endured. If we
make it so that those fallow lands can be im-
proved, and one portion goes to the owner if it
is private property and another portion goes to
the divan and the people who make the im-
provements, we can give it to them in such a
way that they may have eternal security and
keep it for their children and grandchildren,
and since they will derive great profit, they
will look after it better. When they realize what
great benefit it has, they will eschew trade, the
hardships of travel, and other transactions and
be inclined at once to the improvement of land
and agriculture, for all people are in search of
profit. This being so, in a short time most of
the devastation will be repaired, and the im-
provement of such ruined places will take
place through the strength, money, and agree-
ment of all people in the world. There is no
other way. [1530] When fallow lands are made
to ﬂourish, grain will be cheap; and when ex-
peditions are mounted for obligatory actions on
the frontiers and borders, provisions will be
readily available. Money will also ﬂow into the
treasury and increase. Lords and property own-
ers will gain a new prestige and confidence,
the peasants will enjoy peace of mind and ease,
and we will have a heavenly reward and enjoy
an eternal good name.”
All those present were amazed by such a
clever idea and subtle words, and after praising
him they said, “No one in the world has ever
had a better or more beneficial idea. Your fore-
fathers laid waste, but you cause to ﬂourish.
There is a palpable difference intellectually, by
common law, and by religious law between the
one and the other. Others brought death, while
you bring life. It is enough to say this; why
should we say more?”
After that, he had contracts and edicts written
with the following stipulations. State properties
that were long untended and villages and farms
744
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

that were not cultivated at the time of his ac-
cession would all be classified as fallow. He
had contracts written and sealed with the gold
seal saying that anyone who was desirous of
making improvements could take such places
in one of three categories. 
In the first category were those that had wa-
ter and irrigation canals and did not entail great
expense or outlay of labor to be cultivated and
irrigated, i.e. they did not need subterranean
water channels, canals, or dams. Once im-
provement projects were begun, the first year
they were cultivated nothing would go to the
divan; in the second year one third of the divan
rate would be given, and two thirds would go
as a commission to the improver to repay his
efforts; in the third year three quarters of the
rate customary in each province would be paid
to the divan, and one quarter would go to the
improver as a commission. Over and above
that, any money realized by the cultivator was
his.  [1531]
In the second category were lands that need-
ed moderate improvement, where irrigation
canals had to be repaired or dug. The stipula-
tions were similar to what has been mentioned,
except that in the third year two thirds of the
rate would be paid to the divan, and one third
would belong to the improver.
In the third category were those on which
improvements were difficult—dams had to be
made for irrigation, and the underground water
channels were ruined and had to be repaired.
The terms were as has been mentioned, but
only half the rate would go to the divan, the
other half going to the improver as a commis-
sion. He stipulated that the rates would be la-
beled as kharaj [land tax], and everyone who
made improvements would own the land, and
it would belong to him and his children in per-
petuity. If he so wished, he could sell it to
another. Sale was permitted, and the divan
would take the established amount of land tax
from the purchaser.
He also stipulated that any fallow land water
for which came from an improved village’s
canal, so long as the owner of the improved
village wanted, they would not give it to anoth-
er lest dispute erupt. 
After that he said, “Since we have abolished
hazr1 and muqasama [payment of tax in crop
shares] in the realm, the divani portion of fal-
low lands should also be fixed and set as deter-
mined by overseers in every province to be re-
mitted as kharaj so that ruffians and tyrants not
use hazr, muqasama, or takthīr [multiple as-
sessment?] as a pretext against the peasants,
and so that those harassments may be com-
pletely eradicated.”
Since the emperor’s realm was extremely
broad and expansive, he expressed the idea that
if every person desirous [of making improve-
ments] were to come to the ordu to get a con-
tract, some would choose not to come because
of the long distances and expenses involved
while others would not have the strength for
the road, so he ordered that one or two reliable
great men in each province be appointed. The
original of the contract decree was given to
them with a letter form, and they were empow-
ered to give such a document to any volunteer
with a copy of the contract decree written on
the back so that it would be reckoned as an
eternal decree to which no one could object,
and thus the job could be easily accomplished
in every province. [1532] When this manner
was adopted, this rule became firm and the job
was done. That divan was named the Bureau of
Royal Demesnes, and until this time the
deputies of that bureau have given many con-
1Arends translates this term as “[податная] отценка
[урожая].” Hazr means literally ‘estimation,’ and it was
presumably an estimated tax on produce.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
745

tracts to people, and vast improvements have
been made and continue to increase day by
day. 
As for private property, he ordered that prop-
erties that had recently been inhabited could be
improved by anyone who so wished. They
should consult with their lords before making
improvements. As for those that had long been
fallow, anyone who wanted could make im-
provements without consultation. If an owner
who could legally prove his ownership showed
up, it remained established upon the improver;
however, the amount to be remitted would be
as has been mentioned in the divan section, but
half would go to the owner and half to the di-
van. This rule was to be observed in a province
in which formerly and now one tenth hazr is
given to the divan. As for a province that was
originally hazr and against which there was no
mál or hazr, the whole of that portion would be
given to the owner, who could not object, for it
had the effect of a divani improver eternally
and forever.
As for devastated places in Mongols’ yurts
that were improved, the same conditions ap-
plied as in the two categories of private and
state property, but he ordered that since the
Mongols were hoodlums, under no circum-
stances were improvements to be made using
peasants of provinces, regardless of whether
they were counted as belonging to another
place or not, they were not to allow any peas-
ant access to their lands, and they were to
make improvements using their own bondsmen
or slaves. Tajiks were likewise not to make im-
provements using peasants who were reckoned
as belonging to other places. If they gathered
peasants who were not reckoned as belonging
to any village, that was acceptable. [1533]
In this manner he made binding contracts and
took all possible precautions in the terms there-
of. Most of those have not been included in
this history, as they are recorded in the con-
tracts. At present they are engaged in making
improvements throughout the realm, and day
by day it is on the increase. The people are bol-
stered by this, and the income of the Bureau of
Royal Demesnes increases every year. Soon
there will be few ruined places.
He also ordered that the fallow lands of
every province should be recorded and brought
to the divan so that when the fallow lands were
given to people, an inspection could be made
every two years to determine whether all im-
provements had been carried out or only part.
If any imperial deputies cheated and hid some
fallow land for themselves or went into part-
nership with anyone, and his tax apportion dis-
appeared from the registers, it could be found
out.
May God cause the blessing of such charita-
ble works to ﬂourish during the emperor’s re-
gal time.
Story Thirty-Eight: The building of envoy
hostels throughout the realm and the
forbidding of envoys to lodge in people’s
houses.
Prior to now there were always more than one
hundred twenty envoys in every city quartered
in the houses of citizens and lords. Many oth-
ers too, over and above the envoys, were
lodged in people’s houses by the shahnas and
maliks as a favor. The job of the chärbis was to
go before an envoy when he arrived in town
and lead him to the house in which he was to
stay, for which they would receive something.
On such a day they would “sell off” two
hundred houses, more or less.1 [1534] In the
1آن در

ﺪ ـــﺧﺘﻨ: Arends trans-
lates literally: “в токой день продавали домов двести”
(p. 324). The not so obvious meaning of the sentence
must be that on a day an elchi arrived in town (with his
retinue), the chärbi would assign some two hundred
746
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

end, they would quarter them in the houses of
persons against whom they had a grudge to put
fear into them. They would take rugs, bedding,
ghazghans [kettles], and other things from peo-
ple’s houses for the envoys. Usually either the
envoys would expropriate those things or the
chärbis would not give them back, claiming
that the envoys had taken them. Even if oc-
casionally something was returned, after hav-
ing been used by an envoy, what was it worth? 
Every basqaq who went to a province would
commandeer at least a hundred of the people’s
houses, and all these people stayed in the hous-
es of lords and citizens. The writer of this book
is aware that when Yesüdär’s son Taghai was
dismissed as shahna of Yazd and his people
left, an inspection was made, and his retainers
had been staying in seven-hundred-odd houses.
Naturally, the envoys and shahnas always
stayed in the best houses. It got to the point
that no one could build a house, and those that
were built were made to look like tombs and
were called caravansaries or schools, but that
did not do much good. Many people closed off
the doors of their houses and made under-
ground entrances that were difficult to maneu-
ver, hoping that they wouldn’t be chosen: they
just cut through the walls and came in. The en-
voys would turn their horses over to the
chärbis, and they would send people to tear
down the walls of people’s gardens and put the
horses there. The day one envoy left another
would arrive because they came continuously.
In the quarter in which an envoy was quartered
the people would be subjected to torment and
intimidation, for the slaves and liege men
would go over the roofs and into the neighbors’
houses and take anything they saw. They
would shoot their pigeons and chickens with
arrows, and it often happened that the people’s
houses and collect his tip for each.
children were struck by arrows. [1535] Any
food, drink, or animal fodder they found they
would snatch from anybody, no matter who he
was. The people suffered such harassment, and
no matter how much they complained, no amir,
vizier, or governor came to their rescue. 
One day an old man, a respectable elder,
came to the divan and said, “Amirs, viziers,
and governors, I am an old man with a young
wife. My sons are away, and they have left
their young wives in my house. I also have
daughters. The envoys have been quartered in
my house, and they are all good-looking, slen-
der young men. They have been in my house
for some time now. The women see them and
cannot content themselves with me and my ab-
sent sons. We are in one house together with
the envoys, but I cannot watch them day and
night. This has happened to many people, as I
see. If things continue like this, in a few years
there will not be a single legitimate child in
this city: all will be half Turk and igdish [half-
breeds].” In this regard he told the following
story:
“In the time of the Seljuq sultans the Nisha-
pur vicinity was where the sultan resided. The
amirs and Turks were quartered in the people’s
houses, and not in the manner they are now.
One day a Turk stopped in a house where the
owner’s wife was a pure young woman. The
Turk craved her and wanted to send the man
away on some excuse. The man knew what
was going on and refused to leave. The Turk
beat the man and said, ‘Take my horse and
give it water.’ The man wouldn’t leave his
wife, but there was no alternative. To his wife
he said, ‘I will stay in the house. You take the
horse and give it water.’ She took the horse and
led it the edge of the river. As was the custom
of young women, she was dressed in her finery
and had adorned herself. [1536] By chance the
sultan was passing, and his gaze fell upon her.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
747

He summoned her and asked, ‘How is it that
you, a young woman, are leading a horse to
water?’ She replied, ‘Because of your injus-
tice.’ The sultan was amazed and asked about
the situation. She recounted what had hap-
pened in detail. Her story affected the sultan,
and his zeal was stirred. He said, ‘Henceforth
no one of the retinue will be quartered in
Nishapur. Let all the amirs and Turks build
houses for themselves in the vicinity.’ That is
why Shadyakh in Nishapur, which is now a
city, was built.” The old man wept as he told
the story, but it had no effect on the amirs and
viziers.
When the Padishah of Islam was organizing
the realm, the first arrangement he made for
envoys was that not one of the one hundred
twenty envoys and their useless henchmen who
used to go to the provinces for no reason was
to go now unless they were sent on urgent state
business. The envoys were to go by yaraltu
[express courier] and fast post horses so they
wouldn’t see villages or cities. They were to
stop only long enough to eat a hasty meal,
change horses, or have an ara-qati [rest stop].
If rarely envoys go to collect taxes, an edict
was promulgated that envoy hostels were to be
built in cities, and furnishings, bedding, and
supplies were to be arranged for their accom-
modations. A fixed amount was stipulated to be
spent in building the envoy hostels. He also or-
dered basqaqs and their retainers to build or
rent houses for themselves. 
Thank God, those abuses have been eliminat-
ed, and the people rest in peace. [1537] The
tallow fees have been forgotten, and no chärbi
dares to demand a loaf of bread or maund of
straw from anyone. The name chärbi has even
disappeared. The people build nice houses with
peace of mind. They raise porticos, occupy
themselves with building, and create fine gar-
dens. Absolutely no one dares put an animal in
the people’s gardens. Houses that previously
sold for a hundred dinars now sell for a thou-
sand. All the absentees who had abandoned
their homes and wandered from city to city for
the last fifty years or more have voluntarily
chosen to return to their former places. They
pray for the Padishah of Islam’s success with
all sincerity: may their prayers be answered.
Story Thirty-Nine: He forbids muleteers,
camel drivers, and messengers to impose
upon people.
Previously, any great lord and grandee who
went into the market to transact business or to
take a bath would be surrounded by several
muleteers who would say, “We need X amount
of money to pay for beauties, wine, entertain-
ers, bread, meat, and our other daily needs.
You’ll have to give it.” If he didn’t give it or
made excuses, they would curse him, and in
the end, they either got the money or beat him
up. It often happened that if someone didn’t
have any money, he would have to borrow and
then, having lost his money, honor, and dignity,
couldn’t leave the market. 
These people stood around in gangs on street
corners, and anyone who escaped the clutches
of one gang would be snared by another, and
the same thing would happen all over again.
When he came across a gang of camel drivers,
the same thing happened. If he ran into a gang
of couriers or messengers, [1538] it was even
worse. It sometimes happened that during the
course of a day one person would get mixed up
with all these gangs because they had made it
their profession and sat at the heads of all the
streets and marketplaces, waiting to snare their
prey. They all had connections to the ladies,
princes, and amirs, and even if someone had
the power to resist them, he never thought it
worthwhile to argue with them because [their
patrons] would be offended, and they thought
748
JAMI‘U’T-TAWARIKH: COMPENDIUM OF CHRONICLES

it was their privilege to have their muleteers,
camel drivers, and couriers act like this. 
On holidays like Nawroz and Künyangla-
mishi they decorated their animals and went
around in gangs to the houses of the great. If
the lord of the house showed his face, they got
what they wanted by insisting, and then they
reviled him and cursed him until they got
more. Naturally, they both disgraced him and
got something. If the lord of the house was not
at home or didn’t show his face out of fear,
they carried off everything they could find and
pawned it for gold with brothel keepers and
wine sellers. When the owner went to redeem
it, he would suffer thousands of curses and in-
sults and then have to pay two or three times
what had been given to get his stuff back. It of-
ten happened that they picked up items of
clothing and either put them on themselves or
clad whores in them and absolutely refused to
give them back. Every year, for five or six days
before and after the holidays, nobody dared
walk the streets lest he fall prey to them and
have done to him what they practiced. They
also hung around shop doors, and because of
their lawlessness the markets fell idle, sales
taxes plummeted, and no one could do any-
thing about it. [1539] The lords and grandees
loved having their muleteers and camel drivers
decorate their animals and put clothes on them
so that they could get something from people.
“Who gave you something and who didn’t?”
they would ask. This gave them the courage to
be even bolder. 
Indeed, the largest nuisance people suffered
and the biggest tax they paid was this. When
the people saw that they could take money and
clothing from others by force, by intimidation,
and by opportuning, which is worse than by
force, most of the people took up the practice
of the muleteers, camel drivers, and couriers
and went into cahoots with them. Around every
muleteer gathered ten idlers and rapscallions.
Things got so bad that it became quite proble-
matic to stop the practice. 
When the Padishah of Islam began to orga-
nize the country, he ordered that any muleteer,
camel driver, or courier who asked anybody
for anything would be executed. On holidays
and new year’s days, any time he heard the
sound of camel bells, he would order the
guards to beat them with cudgels. He also or-
dered it heralded that no one should give any-
thing to muleteers, camel drivers, or couriers
and that the people should beat them if they
drove their animals around. 
Thanks to his justice and punishment, that
torturous nuisance was totally lifted from the
people, and now none of them dares to ask
anyone for even a morsel of bread. The people
are free of such “trade,” the memory of it has
been erased from their minds, and the world is
safe from their evil. May God cause the shad-
ow of the world emperor’s justice and equity to
shade the heads of all people forever. [1540]
Story Forty: He forbids the practice of
forcing young women to enter brothels.
In large cities prostitutes were constantly sta-
tioned next to mosques, khanaqahs, and peo-
ple’s houses. Because brothel owners could
purchase girls who were brought in from vari-
ous parts for better prices than others, most
dealers were inclined to trade in people of that
sort. Some of the girls who had stamina and re-
solve did not want to be sold to brothels, but
they were sold forcibly and unwillingly and
made to participate in vice. 
The Padishah of Islam said, “Making broth-
els and harboring prostitutes is a really low and
mean thing to do. To eliminate it is an obliga-
tion, but since from time immemorial certain
interests have allowed neglect to run rampant
in that area and it has become a general rule, it
will not be possible to forbid it all at once.
PART TWO, CHAPTER TWO, SECTION SEVENTEEN: GHAZAN KHAN
749

Gradual effort must be made so that it may be
slowly eliminated. Now, women who are not
inclined to that sort of activity and have been
forced to do it should be rescued from the
brink of disaster, for much effort is necessary
to turn a deficient thing into a perfect one. It is
clearly an injustice, very evil, and inappropri-
ate to force into vice a woman who has no in-
clination in that direction.” 
Therefore he issued an edict saying that no
girl who was not inclined to the brothels
should be sold to such people. Any who were
already in brothels and who so desired could
come out without restraint, and they would be
paid for at any price that was stipulated, taken
from the brothels, and given to husbands of
their own choosing.

subjects, dependents, the “nation” (i.e. the people, not the geographical area) subject to

ündür (foindo*)
heights (179).
ündür (foindo*)
kumiss sack (115).
urugh (foro))
family, seed, progeny; the offspring of an individual: Genghis Khan’s urugh, a con-
stantly recurring phrase, refers to his lineal descendants (74, D§468).
usun (foso%)
water (99).
utu (fodO)
center of a hunting ground (331).
uz
artisan (1019).
wànshuài (萬帥)
commander of ten thousand (451n).
yadamishi
impoverishment (< iedeeeO) (1481).
yaghlamishi
“thumb-greasing,” a rite observed after a boy’s first successful hunt (< yaghlamaq ‘to
grease’) (536, 1211, D§1800).
yalbarmishi
prayer (959, D§1808).
yam (ie^)
courier relay (< Chinese 站 zhàm) (665).
yamchi (iemcI)
official in charge of a relay station (877).
yaraltu
express courier (1536, D§404).
yärgä
= järgä.
yarghuchi (iergocI)
judge, presiding judge at an inquisition (70).
yarashmishi
reconciliation (1238n, D§1782).
yarligh (ierli))
an imperial decree (677).
yasa ~ yasaq (iese))
ordinance, decree; the Genghisid legal code based on Genghis Khan’s ordinances
(288).
yasal (iese&)
ordinance (207, D§1791).
yasamishi
ordering, organization, particularly military (< ieseeeO) (207, D§1794).

yasaq
= yasa.

sergeant (90, D§1863).
yasun (iesoa)
bone; family; descent (155n).

the wife of an elder brother, equivalent to the Mongolian bärigän (236).

yurt
grazing territory; an appanage assigned to a prince (65).
yurtchi
official in charge of a yurt (98).
yut
livestock blight; the starvation of free-range livestock that occurs when snow melts and
then refreezes, or when frost freezes hard, coating grazing land with ice; the phenom-
enon is known as жут in Kazakh and Kyrgyz (1478, D§1911).
